# Book II. Chapter IV. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

<column-break/>

...inside <note>referring to the fruit described at the end of the previous page</note> lies an oblong seed, much like the true clove, but significantly larger and marked with a curved line, divisible into two segments.

When these cloves are dried, they do not take on a brown or dark red color like the true ones, but instead acquire a dingy, pale yellow color and become wrinkled. They possess no aromatic strength or spice-like quality; rather, their taste is unpleasant, wild, and astringent.

The wood of this tree is hard, dense, heavy, and grayer than the cultivated variety, mixed with a certain brownish hue. While it is not particularly beautiful, it is nonetheless useful for various mechanical purposes. However, it must not touch the ground, otherwise it rots very easily. The fruits flower and ripen at nearly the same time as the cultivated cloves, or a little later—namely in December or January. This tree grows spontaneously in the wild mountains and propagates itself there by its fallen mother-cloves <note>original: "Anthophyllis"; these are cloves left on the tree to over-ripen into seeds for planting</note>.

**Names.** In Latin, *Caryophyllum Silvestre* <note>Wild Clove</note>; in Malay, *Tsjenke utan*. In the Amboinese language, *Babu Lawan Abbal* and *Bubula Wabbal*. By the people of Hitoe, it is called *Ohulawan Aycou*, because this tree, as has been said, has a great affinity with the *Cajoe Mera* <note>Malay: "Red Wood"</note> or *Aycou*, of which more will be said in Book 4.

**Location.** It is found in all the Molucca Islands, even in places where true cloves have never been observed. A certain man from Hitoe told me that he had planted a true clove tree there which, over time, degenerated into a wild one. I experienced the same thing myself with another tree, which I was certain had been placed there during a general planting of true cloves.

**Use.** Since there is no aromatic strength in this fruit, it is neither collected nor used for trade, but is left as food for the birds. It also rarely happens that certain cunning inhabitants deceive new merchants by mixing these wild cloves with the true ones during sale to increase the weight. This is easy for them to do since they ripen at roughly the same time, but if they are caught, they are punished. Anyone who pays close attention can easily distinguish the wild ones, as they are much larger than true cloves, as well as pale and dingy in color. As we mentioned, those that fall naturally from the true trees and are dried in the sun without being smoked look similar; however, the wild cloves are still significantly larger and entirely tasteless.

The wood of this tree, as mentioned, is used in house building for both posts and beams. It is not as suitable for posts because it rots easily in the earth; otherwise, it becomes as hard as iron—so hard that a nail can hardly be driven into it—especially in the houses of the Amboinese, which are usually filled with smoke. Although the wood becomes so hard and durable, square beams can hardly be fashioned from it because the trunk is rarely round, but rather angular and misshapen.

Among the wild cloves, another smaller tree is also counted, which mostly grows only to the size of a shrub. However, it differs too much from the nature of cloves, and we shall describe it later among the wild trees under the name *Caryophyllaster Silvestre* <note>Wild Clove-like plant</note> in Book 5.

If one wishes to use the wild clove wood for fence posts, as is often done, it must first be exposed to smoke, as it then lasts longer. It is also used for the handles of axes and for rice pestles. However, the polished wood should not be exposed to the sun, as it cracks easily. In short, the fresh wood is never used for works where cracking would be a problem, but always the dried wood.

# CHAPTER FIVE.
## Nutmeg. *Pala*. Nutmegs.

Just as it pleased the Supreme Creator, in order to keep men occupied in continuous labor and exercise, to hide glittering gems, yellow metal, and other treasures in the very bowels of the earth, in a similar way He planted two precious spices—namely Cloves and Nutmeg—in a few small islands, and hid them together as if in the furthest corner of the Eastern Ocean.

How Cloves were previously found only in the Molucca Islands and today only in the territory of Amboina has been mentioned above. Now, therefore, we shall pass to the description of the other aromatic tree, namely the Nutmeg tree <note>original: *Nux Myristica*</note>, which is as follows.

The tree of the true Nutmeg—also called the female <note>original: *femina*; the cultivated, fertile variety</note>—bears the form and size of a common pear tree, though some are even taller. Its crown is rounder than that of the Clove tree, yet it nonetheless forms a well-ordered pyramid, though more spread out than the former. It usually rises with a straight trunk, sometimes even double or triple. The branches extend mostly to the sides and do not rise as high as those of the Clove. Among these, however, a few rare branches rise up as straight as if they were poles, and these sometimes form small crowns at the top like a young tree. The bark of the tree is smooth, a dark ash-gray mixed with green, and is reddish and juicy on the inside. The tree bears few thick branches, but these are luxuriant, divided into thin, long twigs which hang down entangled and are pulled downward by the weight of the fruit.

The leaves are like those of a pear tree, but a little sharper, longer, entire, and pointed; they are dark green on top and slightly ashen underneath, which is a characteristic of all Nutmeg species—namely, that the underside of the leaf is more gray or pale than its upper side. Otherwise, they are smooth like Clove leaves, but much thinner and more even, shining a little on top but not at all underneath, and they bear a few side ribs. They are mostly placed in two rows on the branches, but alternating. When chewed in the mouth, they provide a distinctly aromatic flavor. If the tree is cut or its branch broken off, a lightly reddish and sticky juice drips out, almost like thin blood, which soon hardens and dries into a deep red; this drains the tree and stains cloth in such a way that the spots can never be washed out. The young leaves, however, are not red like Clove leaves, but are ashen and a bright green.

The first beginnings of the fruit are small whitish or yellow buds, which unfold into white little flowers like chalices with narrow mouths, divided at the top into three pointed segments, very closely resembling Lily of the Valley <note>original: *Lilium Convallium*</note>, which contain in the center a small, oblong, russet pistil that grows into the fruit. The little flowers give off no scent; they hang from curved stalks mostly bent downwards, two or three together sometimes, and these in turn arise from another stalk that takes its origin from the leaf axils. On the twigs, however, usually only a single fruit grows out, and the other little flowers fall off. One also rarely sees two or three fruits joined together, for the tree would otherwise not be able to bear them all. The growing pistil within breaks open the flowers after it has previously turned a chestnut-brown color. In the ninth month after flowering, the fruit ripens; nevertheless, it is harvested three times a year, as will be indicated later. This happens because the tree flowers and the fruits ripen successively.

The fruits hang from long stalks and by their weight bend all the twigs downward; they have the size and shape of a peach, but the fruit is pointed at the bottom like a pear, and from the stalk itself it is divided into two by a groove around its entire circumference, just as a peach is indented on one side, adorned with a soft point at the top.

<column-break/>

Just as it pleased the Almighty Creator, to keep men constantly busy in labor and effort, to hide the glittering stones, the red metal, and other jewels in the deep entrails of the earth, in the same manner He also planted the two costly spices, namely Cloves and Nutmegs <note>original: *Noote-Musschaten*</note>, in or upon a few small islands, and hid the same together in the very furthest corner of the Eastern Ocean.

How the Cloves were previously found only in the Molucca Islands, and nowadays only in the Amboinese territory, has been said above. Now we shall proceed and step to the description of the second spice-tree, namely of the Nutmegs, which is as follows.

The tree of the true Nutmegs, which people also call females <note>original: *Wyfkens*</note>, has the shape and size of a pear tree, and some are also indeed taller. Its top is rounder than that of the Clove tree, and nonetheless it forms a well-arranged pyramidal crown, yet somewhat more spread out than the Clove tree. It shoots up for the most part with a straight trunk, and sometimes also with two and three; the branches spread themselves mostly to the sides, and do not go as straight up as those of the Clove tree. Yet from these same branches one sees now and then a few shooting up as straight as if they were poles, and which sometimes also get little crowns like a young tree. The bark of the tree is smooth and dark gray, mixed with green, red and juicy inside. The tree has few thick branches, yet these are luxuriant, divided into thin long twigs, which hang somewhat tangled through one another, and are pulled downwards by the weight of the fruit.

The leaves are like those of the pear tree, yet somewhat pointier, longer, and without notches on the edges, with a long point in front, high green on top, and somewhat grayish underneath, which is a mark of all Nutmeg species, namely that the underside must be grayer or paler than the upper side; otherwise they are also smooth, like the Clove leaves, yet much softer and more even, shining a little on top, but not at all underneath, and have also only a few little ribs on the sides. They stand mostly in two rows on the twigs, but not directly opposite one another. Chewed in the mouth, they give a clearly spice-like taste. When one cuts into the tree, or breaks a branch off it, a light red and sticky sap runs out, almost like thin blood, which immediately dries to a deep red, greatly exhausting the tree, and makes such stains in white linen that one can never wash them out. The young leaves are not red like those of the Clove trees, but whitish and light green.

The first beginnings of the fruit are small white or light yellow buds, from which come white little flowers like chalices, with a narrow mouth, divided at the top into three points, very much resembling the *Lilium Convallium*, in German "May-flowers" <note>original: *Mey-bloemen*</note>, or Lilies of the Valley; inside one sees a small oblong russet bud, from which the fruit grows. The little flowers have no smell; they hang on curved stalks mostly bent downwards, two and three together, and those hang again from another stalk which comes forth from the origin of the leaves on the twigs; yet mostly only one fruit comes from it, and the other little flowers fall off. One also rarely sees 2 or 3 fruits together, for the tree would otherwise not be able to bear all of them. The inner bud becoming larger causes the flower to burst, after it has first become chestnut-brown. In the ninth month after blooming the fruit becomes ripe; nevertheless it is plucked three times in a year, as will be said hereafter, which happens because the fruits bloom and ripen one after another.

The fruit hangs on long stalks, and pulls with its weight all the twigs downward; it grows to the size and shape of a peach <note>original: *Persick*</note>, yet somewhat pointed at the back like a pear, divided into two by a cleft in its length all around from the stalk, just as peaches have on one side, with a soft point in the front.

The author frames the discovery of Nutmeg and Cloves as a divine act of hiding precious treasures in remote corners of the world.</summary>

## Book II. Chapter V. AMBOINA HERBAL.

Its outer skin is smooth, at first a bright green, and when the fruit matures, it turns yellowish like a ripe *peach* <note>original: *Persicus*</note>; then the middle groove opens itself and reveals the kernel, with the elegant crimson color of the mace appearing in between. If the fruit hangs from the tree for two or three days, the kernel falls out, and if it lies upon the ground, it easily attracts worms and rots due to the excessive oiliness of the nut, which usually happens during rainy weather. Indeed, even while still on the tree, the outer skin generates short, thick worms that eat the mace <note>original: *macis*</note>. The outer husk has the same thickness as a peach, but is of a harder substance, whitish on the inside and filled with a thin, watery sap, with a sour and astringent taste, making it inedible. Within this husk is contained the kernel or true nut, where the crimson mace first appears, surrounding the black shell of the nut like a net, yet in such a way that the shell can be seen here and there. The nut is wider at the stem, where it remains white for the longest time, but ends in a small point at the top where the divisions of the mace are thickest and most tangled. The mace clings so firmly to the black shell that it forms a groove within it. This black shell is as thick as that of a hazelnut, but by no means as hard, for it can be easily broken and crushed into pieces. Finally, within this is contained the true fruit or kernel called the *Nutmeg* <note>original: *Nux Myristica*</note>, which does not adhere to the shell at all but is loose on all sides; in dried fruits, the nut shrinks slightly so that it makes a rattling sound if the fruit is shaken.

The nut itself is well enough known, being flat on one side (which is its bottom part) and slightly wrinkled all over. It has two forms: one is oblong and the other round. Both are equally good, though the round ones are usually harder. If the nut is pierced with a needle or split, it yields oil; if this does not appear, it is a sign that the nut is dried out and too old. There is only one true aromatic nut, but as mentioned, it has two forms: one tree bears oblong nuts and the other round ones. This difference also appears in the leaves of the tree, for one has longer leaves and the other shorter and rounder ones. However, both are equally aromatic and have the same virtues. The round nuts are called the "females" <note>the fertile, cultivated variety</note> of this tree. There is another kind called the "male," which has a shorter trunk and leaves and a rounder crown, otherwise similar to the former, but it must be distinguished from the other wild tree whose fruits are properly called "males."

The first male tree, called *Pala Boy*, bears many flowers but few and somewhat larger fruits, appearing as twins, which are usually marked on the front with a cross, as is the following *Pala-Bacambar*. They occur rarely and always isolated from other trees in places well-exposed to the sun; it seems this species is a degeneration of the true *Nutmeg*. Besides these two kinds, the aromatic nut has other varieties and "miscarriages" which do not constitute a different species, such as the *Pala-Bacambar* or twin nuts (called *Palakende-kende* in Banda). The fruit has a double groove on the outside running crosswise over it; otherwise, it is like the common one or a little larger. Inside is the *Pala-Bacambar*, bearing two kernels joined together, each included in its own shell and wrapped in its own mace. On the sides where they are joined, they are flat, with a thicker layer of mace placed between them; consequently, the inner nuts are only semi-round.

They have no special properties and are mixed with common nuts or kept as curiosities. It is a fiction and a superstition that if they are used in food, women will give birth to twins because of them.

Another variety is the *Pala Pentsjoeri*, that is, the "thief’s nut" <note>Latin: *furum nux*</note>. These either have no bony shell or only a part of one, and the mace lies against the bare nut. It is neither round nor oblong like the common sort, but slanted and of an irregular, lumpy shape. It is a harmful "miscarriage," for if it is mixed with other nuts or mace, it causes all those it lies near to rot and perish.

<column-break/>

The outer shell is smooth, at first light-green, and when they are ripe, tending toward a pale color, like a ripe *peach* <note>original: *Persick*</note>; then the middle groove opens up and reveals the kernel, with a beautiful *crimson red* color peeking out from between, so that if the fruit remains hanging on the tree for another two or three days, the kernel falls out by itself. If it remains lying on the earth, it very easily gets worms and spoils because of the great oiliness in the nut, which usually happens in rainy weather. Even while still hanging on the tree, the outer shell gets short, thick worms that eat up the mace <note>original: *foelie*</note>. The outer shell or husk has the same thickness as a *peach*, but is somewhat harder in substance, and whitish on the inside, full of thin, watery sap, with a harsh, astringent taste, and therefore not edible. In this shell lies the kernel or true nut, upon which one first sees the *crimson red mace*, surrounding the black shell like a net and as if with small straps, yet in such a way that one can see the aforementioned shell in between here and there. It is somewhat wider at the top by the stem, where it also stays white the longest, and toward the front it runs to a slight point where the straps are thickest and woven together. The mace lies so firmly and tightly upon the black shell that it makes a groove therein. The black shell itself is quite as thick as that of a hazelnut, yet by no means so hard, for it can be easily broken and pushed into pieces. Inside this now lies the true fruit or kernel, which one calls *Nutmegs* <note>original: *Noote-muschaaten*</note>, which in no way clings to the aforementioned shell but is loose all around. The dried ones are a bit shrunken so that they rattle inside when one shakes the nut.

The nut itself is sufficiently known, being somewhat flat at one end (which is its back part) and somewhat wrinkled all over, of two kinds of shape: for one is oblong and the other round, both equally good, though the round ones turn out quite hard. If one sticks a needle into it or bites it open, an oil comes out; if this does not happen, it is a sign that the nut is no good or has grown old. The true spice-nut is but of one kind, yet, as said, has two shapes, namely one tree bears oblong and the other round nuts, which distinction one also sees in the leaves of the tree, one having them somewhat more oblong and the other somewhat shorter and rounder. Yet they are both equally spicy and of equal strength, and these latter or round ones are held to be the "female" <note>the fertile, cultivated variety</note> of the true Nutmeg tree. For it has another special gender which one calls the "male," being much shorter of trunk and leaves, rounder of crown, and otherwise like the common one, yet to be distinguished from another wild tree which one properly calls "male-nuts."

The first male tree then, named *Pala boy*, bears mostly flowers, but very few and somewhat larger fruits like twins, which are usually marked with a cross in front, just like the following *Pala-Bacambar*. They are found rarely, and then always separated from others, also standing well in the sun, and it seems that this sort is a degeneration of the common Nutmeg trees. Besides these two genders, the spicy nut has some other variations and "misfortunes," but which make no special kind, such as first the *Pala-Bacambar*, or twin nuts, named *Palakende-kende* in Banda, whose fruits have a double groove or split on the outside, running crosswise over each other, being otherwise like the common ones or a bit larger. Inside one finds the *Pala-bacambar*, having two kernels joined against each other, each in its own shell and also wrapped with its own mace. On the side where they lie against each other, they are flat, having between the two another thick mace, and consequently the inner nuts are also only half round.

They have no special property and are also mixed among the common nuts or kept as a rarity. It is a fiction or superstition that if used in food, they would cause women to give birth to twins.

Secondly, the *Pala Pentsjoeri*, that is "thief's nuts." These have no wooden shell, or only a piece of one, and the mace lies on the bare nut, it being not truly round nor oval like the common ones, but crooked and lumpy. It is also a harmful "misgrowth," for being mixed among other nuts or mace, it causes all those it lies near to rot and pass away.

<summary>This page provides a detailed anatomical description of the nutmeg fruit, its husk, the reddish mace (aril), and the inner nut. It also distinguishes between the cultivated "female" nutmeg and several "male" or "thief" varieties, debunking local superstitions regarding twin fruits.</summary>

### AMBOINA HERBAL Book II. Chap. V. ###

...since it spoils first and then stains the others as well, it must be carefully selected so it is not mixed with others. Some keep it for medicine, saying it is effective for breaking up bladder stones <note>original: *calculum vesicae*</note>, though I have heard of no such experiment.

The third is the *Pala Radja* <note>King Nutmeg</note> or mace-bearing nuts; these bear fruit similar to the others, but in place of the inner kernel, they bear a small nut wrapped in very thick mace. Indeed, this little nut is often no larger than a grain of pepper, but the mass formed of mace is hard, heavy, and durable; others used to mix it with mace as a whole without removing the nut. Since this mace is much more beautiful and durable than the common kind, some curious enthusiasts keep a portion of it, not so much for curiosity's sake as for medical use. Sometimes they grow on a specific tree, and sometimes mixed with other nuts on one and the same tree.

The fourth variety is *Pala Hollanda* <note>Holland Nutmeg</note>, or *Pala Puti* <note>White Nutmeg</note>, which also does not differ from the common kind, except that it bears a hoary mace, which nevertheless turns yellow when dried; it is nonetheless aromatic. However, because it gives an unpleasant color to other mace, it is selected out and sold separately. There also occur certain trees whose mace is variegated with yellow and red; these are called *Pala Kackerlack* <note>Cockroach Nutmeg, likely named for its mottled appearance</note>.

The fifth and final variety is *Pala Domine* <note>Lord’s or Clergy’s Nutmeg</note>, which bear nuts wrapped in mace on only one side, and therefore covered as if by a pastor's skullcap <note>original: *semi-pileolo*</note>. These are not much sought after by the nut cleaners, as the mace cannot be removed whole but is much broken, and they yield only a small quantity of mace.

Common and vulgar names. This fruit was also unknown to the ancient writers, at least as far as I have been able to discover; indeed, it seems to have become known to the Western people long after Cloves. For mention of it is made only by the most recent Greek writers, and it especially occurs in the work of the Arab *Avicenna*, who lived around the year of Christ 1160; however, it seems likely that it was known long before then, but described by no one. In Arabic, it is called *Giauz-bant*, which others write as *Fauzial-bant*, also *Gjeu-zottibi*, that is, aromatic nuts. It is also called *Gjauz-Bawa*, or as others write in a corrupt tongue, *Gjauz-bawe* and *Bague*, which is of Persian origin, denoting a pleasantly smelling nut. In Latin today it is called *Nux Myristica odorata*, *aromatica*, and commonly *Moschata*, *Muscata*, *Moschocaryon*, and *Moschocaridion* from *Moscho*, that is, *Civet* <note>original: *Zibeto*; refers to the musky scent of the civet cat</note>, not because it has its odor, but according to the custom of the common people, who in former times gave the surname of Musk to many pleasantly smelling fruits, just as grapes and pears are called *Muscatel*. For the same reason, the modern Greeks called this same Myristica nut "Unguentary" <note>original: *Unguentariam*</note>, not because ointments are composed from it, but because they carry the scent of fragrant ointments. In the Deccan or ancient India they are called *Japatri*, by the Portuguese *Noz d'Especia*, by the Dutch *Noote Muschaten*, or simply *Noote*. In Banda, and among all the Malay peoples, *Pela*, in Ternate *Gofora*. In the Chinese language *Lanbau*. The red netting that lies against the woody shell is called by the new Latin word *Macis* <note>Mace</note>, which must be well distinguished from the *Macer* of the Greeks, which is a far different tree, well known in ancient India by the name *Macre* and *Macrure*, called by the Portuguese *Arbore de las cameras* <note>Tree of the Chambers; "chambers" was a common term for dysentery or diarrhea</note>, that is, the red honey-tree, and *Arbore Sancto* <note>Holy Tree</note>. The name *Macis*, however, seems to have taken its origin from the Javanese word *Massa*, by which name it is also called by the Portuguese. Today this netting is called in Malay *Bonga Pala*, and by the Chinese *Lanbau-Hoe*. In Dutch *Foeli*, and *Muscaten bloemen* <note>Nutmeg flowers</note>. By the Arabs indeed *Besbaze*, and by corrupt names *Besbaze*, *Bisbeli*, *Besbaca*, etc. In the Deccan *Jaifol*, which denotes Javanese flowers, since the deceitful Javanese persuaded people that these were fruits growing in their own country; but the Malays understand by *Bonga Pala* the small blossoms, or true flowers of the Nutmeg tree, which they preserve dried for medical uses, and they can be collected in sufficient abundance from the species called *Pala-Boy*, which is considered the male of the domestic Nutmeg tree; on the other hand, the mace is called by them *Sarony* or *Boncus Pala*, that is, the sheath or sack of the nut, and certainly with better right, for what resemblance does mace have to a flower?

Some nonetheless preserve them for medicine, saying that they are powerful for crushing the stone in a person's body, though I have heard of no experience of this.

Thirdly, *Pala Radja*, or *Mace-nuts*; and these are like the others in fruit, but in place of the inner kernel they have a small nut, surrounded by a very thick *mace*. Yes, sometimes one finds the nut therein no larger than a peppercorn, this lump of *mace* being nevertheless hard, heavy, and durable, and they used to deliver them whole (without taking the little nut out) among other mace; but because this mace is much more beautiful and durable than the common kind, some enthusiasts save a little of it, not so much as a rarity as for medicine. They sometimes grow on a particular tree, and sometimes also mixed with other nuts on a single tree.

Fourthly, *Pala Hollanda*, or *Pala Puti*; this also does not differ from the common kind, except that it has a whitish mace, which nevertheless dries yellow, and is no less spice-like. But because it makes the other mace look bad, it is culled out and weighed separately. One also finds some trees whose mace is sprinkled with pale yellow and red, and is therefore named *Pala Kackerlack*.

Fifthly and lastly, *Pala Domine*, being nuts which are only half covered with mace, and therefore wear it like a skullcap <note>original: *Kalotje*</note>, or a minister's cap. But these are not much esteemed by the plantation owners <note>original: *Perkeniers*; refers to the Dutch Nutmeg planters in the Banda Islands</note>, because the mace cannot be taken off without crumbling, and because there is also little mace on it.

In Deccan or old India they are named *Japatri*, by the Portuguese *Noz d'Especia*, in Low Dutch *Noote-muschaten*, or simply *Nuts*. ### BOOK II. CHAPTER V. AMBOINA HERBAL. ###

Volume III C
<meta>Catchwords: EXPLI- UIT-</meta>

**Location.** The tree bearing the **Nutmeg** <note>Latin: *Nucem Myristicam*</note> extends its range more widely than the **Clove** tree, for it occurs throughout almost the entire domain of the Moluccas. However, its true and fixed home is **Banda**, which consists of six smaller islands: namely **Neyra**, **Lontoira**, **Gunung Api** <note>original: *Goenenga-Apia*, meaning "Fire Mountain" or volcano</note>, **Pulo Ay**, **Run** <note>original: *Pælorona*</note>, and **Rozengain** <note>original: *Rossingenia*</note>. Of these, only three—Neyra, Lontoira (also called the "higher land"), and Pulo Ay—produce the aforementioned trees. Some are also found in **Amboina** and the adjacent **Lease Islands** <note>original: *Uliaffensibus*</note>, but they are not cultivated there. Their few fruits are used by the inhabitants and citizens only for the medical arts, and occasionally for food. It seems that in more ancient times, a mutual harmony was cultivated between the inhabitants of Banda and this Province: specifically, that those of Banda would cultivate no Cloves, and those of Amboina would cultivate no Nutmegs. They say, not without reason, that Almighty God has granted to each island its own peculiar gifts, with which men ought to be content.

In **Kelang**, **Seram**, and the islands situated to the Southeast—**Nila**, **Damar**, **Serua**, **Teun** <note>original: *Kouwera*</note>, and **Manuk** <note>original: *Kuffuwoeya*</note>—these trees also formerly grew, but they have been extirpated there, partly by the law of war and partly by voluntary treaties established with the inhabitants.

In the forests of **Little Seram**, some trees were discovered a few years ago which produced very beautiful and large fruits. However, the flavor of these was different from those of Banda, as the Seram nuts as well as the mace were of a much wilder flavor. Thus, it is believed that these trees will gradually degenerate entirely into wild ones, which is also clearly apparent from their leaves; these are much larger than the leaves of the domestic tree. The further this tree is from the territory of Banda, the more "wild" it becomes, and the worse its nuts are; for these are much smaller and never reach perfection, whence it should be considered a wild species rather than a true Nutmeg-bearing tree.

The nuts from **Neyra** are the best and largest, but the most beautiful forests of these trees are found on **Pulo Ay**, an island not much longer than two thousand paces, but flat and mostly planted with very tall nutmeg trees. Here and there, other fruit-bearing trees are found, which offer a pleasant sight and a most delightful walk. This provides such an elegant prospect that almost the entire island appears as one continuous garden. Along the sea shore, certain small hills are visible here and there, overgrown with wild herbs; these must be preserved there so that the sharp sea wind is kept away from the groves. This island is mostly destitute of fresh or rain water; nevertheless, many citizens and masters <note>term: *perkeniers* or plantation owners</note> inhabit it, who supply their lack of water from cisterns, so that Pulo Ay can provide a third of the quantity of Nutmegs consumed in the world.

In **Lontoira**, there are excellent plots <note>term: *perken*, the traditional walled nutmeg parks of Banda</note> for these trees. However, because this island presents a difficult ascent with its very high and steep mountains, it is dangerous to climb these trees. The harvest is always quite difficult, as the trees often grow on the slopes of the mountains, and level ground is rarely found there. Furthermore, the trees located on the tops of the mountains bear few fruits because of the intense cold there.

->This is added in the supplement of Rumphius.<-

One might think, along with certain learned men, that the **Nutmeg**, or at least the **Mace** <note>Latin: *Macis*</note>, was known in the time of **Plautus**, since in his play *Pseudolus* (Act 3), he distinctly calls something *Macidem*—or rather, he might have prophesied that after a span of several thousand years, a certain spice would be known by that same name. But if that passage is examined accurately, we will find that these are the words of a boastful and lying cook who, to show off his skill, uses many invented names—such as *Cicilendrum*, *Polindrum*, *Macidem*, and *Sancaptidem* for fish, and for meat *Cicimandrum*, *Hapalopsidem*, and *Cataractriam*. No one has ever been able to understand these names, which is why the cook's employer bursts out with these words: *“But may Jupiter and all the gods destroy you with your seasonings, and with all those lies of yours!”*

<column-break/>

**Location.** The **Nutmeg tree** is found more widely dispersed than the **Clove tree**, namely through almost the entire Moluccan territory. Its rightful seat, however, is the Province of **Banda**, consisting of six small islands: namely **Neyra**, **Lontor**, **Gunung Api**, **Pulo Ay**, **Run**, and **Rozengain**. Yet of these, only three—Neyra, Lontor (otherwise called the "high land"), and Pulo Ay—bear the mentioned trees. One also has some in **Ambon** and the neighboring **Lease Islands**, though they are not cultivated there; the few fruits are used by the inhabitants and citizens only for medicine, and also sometimes in cooking. It seems that in olden times there was already a mutual agreement between the inhabitants of Banda and the mentioned Province: namely, that those of Banda would not trouble themselves with Cloves, and those of Amboina with Nutmegs. This was not without great reason, saying that God has given each island its particular gifts, with which they should be satisfied.

On **Kelang-Ceram**, and the South-Eastern islands, **Nila**, **Damar**, **Serua**, **Teun**, and **Manuk**, they previously stood as well, but they have been rooted out there, partly through the right of war, and partly through voluntary contracts entered into with the inhabitants.

In the forests of **Little Seram**, trees were found some years ago that bore very large, beautiful fruits, but one could taste a noticeable difference between them and those of Banda; the Seram ones, both the Nutmegs and the **Mace** <note>Dutch: *Foely*</note>, were much wilder in taste. Thus it is to be believed that these trees would in time become entirely wild, which can be clearly perceived from their leaves, being much larger than the tame ones. The further this tree grows from the Banda territory, the wilder it is, and the poorer the nuts turn out, for they remain small and come to no perfection, being held more as a wild race than as a true Nutmeg tree.

The **Neyra** nuts are indeed the best and largest, but the most beautiful nutmeg-forests are found on **Pulo Ay**, an island not much more than 2000 paces long, yet flat and generally planted with tall Nutmeg trees, where here and there various other fruit trees run among them. It is very delightful to look upon and pleasant to walk through, giving such a beautiful sight that the entire island seems to be a continuous garden. It is surrounded only on the seaside with small hills and wild thickets, which must be maintained so as to ward off the feverish sea wind <note>original: *febraale Zee-wint*, reflecting the historical belief that certain winds carried diseases like malaria</note> from the Nutmeg forest. And though this island has a great lack of fresh water, many citizens and **park-owners** <note>term: *Perk-bezitters*</note> nevertheless live there, who can get their necessities from cisterns; so Pulo Ay can deliver a third part of what is ordinarily consumed in the world.

On **Lontor** are indeed the most "parks" <note>plantations</note>, but because this is a very high and mountainous island, the trees there are somewhat dangerous to climb, and the nuts difficult to collect, since the trees stand on the slopes of steep mountains and there are few level areas on them. Also, the trees that stand on the highest mountains bear very little fruit because of the great cold that is there.

->This was added in the supplement of Rumphius.<-

One would think, with some learned men, that they must have had Nutmegs, or at least the Mace called *Macis*, already in the time of **Plautus**, because in his *Pseudolus* (Act 3), he clearly names *Macidem*, or else he must have prophesied that some thousands of years later a spice with the same name would yet come into the world. But when one looks at that passage rightly, one shall find that they are the words of a braggart and a lying cook <note>original: *leugenachtigen bok*, literally "lying buck"</note>, who, to show his art, uses a multitude of invented names, like *Cicilendrum*, *Polindrum*, *Macidem*, and *Sancaptidem* for the fish, and *Cicimandrum*, *Hapalopsidem*, and *Cataractriam* for the meat; names which no one has ever been able to understand. Wherefore also the hirer of the cook burst out in these words: *"May all the devils take you with your spices and with your lies."*

This Nut-bearing tree was first named by Caspar Bauhin in his *Pinax*, where it is called the *Round-fruited Nutmeg*; it is shown under this name by Plukenet in *Almagestum page 265* and *Phytographia Plate 209 Figure 1*, as well as by Breynius in the second edition of his *Prodromus page 88*. # CHAPTER SIX
## The Harvest and Cultivation of the Nutmeg.

**T**he tree bearing the Nutmeg is laden with fruit throughout the entire year, whether they be newly budding, half-grown, or fully mature. However, this is not true of every individual tree. Properly speaking, three seasons are observed in any given year during which the mature fruits are harvested. The greatest Harvest occurs in the middle of the rainy months, specifically toward the end of July or in August; at that time, the trees are most heavily laden with fruit, though the mace is thinner than in the smaller crops, such as the one in November, which is called the *Mette-kay-aroe* crop and serves as a supplement to the first. 
The third Harvest time, or collection of fruit, occurs in the month of March or the beginning of April, called the **Oele-Monsoon** <note>original: *Mousson-Oele*</note>. It is named after certain green worms of Amboina called **Wau** and **Mulatte** <note>likely Palolo worms, which swarm in the sea according to lunar cycles</note>, which are seen floating in the sea around the reefs and from which a good **Atchar** <note>original: *Aatjar*, a type of savory pickle or condiment</note> is prepared. This season of the year yields the best Nuts and the thickest mace, because the trees are not so overcrowded with fruit at that time, nor does so much rain fall. By contrast, in the months of July and August, there are often massive downpours mixed with wind, which frequently causes many fruits to be knocked from the tree or to fall while immature. These are nonetheless diligently gathered—an act the Dutch call *raapen* <note>meaning "to scavenge" or "pick up"</note>. Their mace is indeed sold, though it is of lower quality than the rest; the nuts are smaller, lumpy, distorted, and wrinkled, which is why they are called *rompen* <note>literally "shrivels" or "carcasses"</note>. The proper collection of the nuts is done as follows: once the nuts are ripe—the sign of which is when the outer husk takes on the light reddish color of a ripe peach and begins to split here and there while hanging from the tree—the inhabitants climb the trees. They use long hooks to pull the nuts down with a quick tug. This is done with less damage to the tree and less danger than the harvest of the **Clove** tree in Amboina, for this Nut-bearing tree has thicker branches.

# CHAPTER VI.
## Harvest, and Cultivation of the Nutmegs.

**T**he Nut-tree is not without fruit throughout the whole year, whether with those just coming out, half-grown, or complete, although this does not happen to all trees. However, it properly has three Seasons in each year in which one plucks the ripe fruits: the largest harvest happens in the middle of the rainy Monsoon, namely at the end of July or August, and then the trees hang full of fruits, but the Mace is somewhat thinner than in the small crops, namely in November, which one calls the *Mette-kay-aroe* Monsoon, and is only a tail-end of the preceding harvest.
The third Monsoon, or in-gathering, falls in the month of March, or in the beginning of April, named **Oele-Monsoon**, after certain green worms called *Wau* and *Mulatte* by the Ambonese, which one finds floating in the Sea near the reefs at that time, and from which one makes good **Atchar**. And this Monsoon yields surely the best Nuts and the thickest Mace, because the trees do not hang so full of fruit then, and also not as much rain falls. On the contrary, in July and August, very strong rain showers and hard winds fall, through which it happens that many fruits are knocked off the trees, or fall off too early, which are nevertheless diligently gathered, and which one calls *raapen*, for the Mace is accepted, but is nonetheless poorer than the others, and the Nuts are somewhat smaller, lumpy, crooked, and wrinkled, and are therefore named *rompen*. The proper in-gathering happens thus: when the Nuts are ripe (the sign of which is when the outermost shell shows the light-reddish color of a ripe Peach, and one sees the same bursting here and there on the tree), then the inhabitants climb into the trees and fetch the Nuts from the branches with long hooks and short tugs, which happens with less danger than from the Clove trees in Amboina. ## Book II. Chapter VI. AMBONESE HERBAL.
### Vol. II. C 2

The tree produces thicker and flatter branches, upon which one can stand more easily, and it is blessed with an abundance of long twigs that can be easily pulled toward oneself. The nuts that have been plucked or have fallen are left under the tree among the grasses, as the ground there is not kept as clean as it is beneath the **Clove** trees <note>original: *Caryophyllorum*. Rumphius notes that nutmeg groves were often less manicured than the prized clove plantations.</note>. Indeed, a circle of grass is often constructed under one side of the tree where it leans toward steep and rugged mountains, so that the nuts do not fall too far away. These gathered nuts are soon opened by servants with a knife, and the outer husk is removed and left in heaps in the woods to rot. However, a novice <note>original: *novitianus* / *Nieuwweling*</note>, who does not know how to well distinguish ripe nuts from unripe ones, can easily injure himself if he wishes to open them, driving the knife through an unripe nut—which he mistake for a ripe one—and into his own hand.

The cleaned nuts are carried home, and the **mace** <note>original: *macis* / *Foely*. This is the lacy, reddish-orange covering of the nutmeg seed.</note> is immediately scraped off with a small knife, being kept as whole as possible. The servants are so skilled at this task that it is completed very quickly. This blood-red mace is dried in the sun for several days upon certain square platforms built like large, broad altars. There, the crimson or blood-red color transitions into a dark red, and finally, in sacks or vessels, it takes on a saffron or orange color, which is how it is transported to us. 

The nuts themselves, which are covered in a black shell or skin, used to be dried in the sun for a week on lath floorings made of split **Bamboo**—which they call **Parre Parren**—but this was later found to be unfavorable. Because of the heat of the sun, they crack or develop fissures after long drying, and at night the dew <note>original: *pruina* (frost) in Latin, *dauw* (dew) in Dutch. In the tropical climate of Ambon, "pruina" likely refers to heavy moisture/condensation.</note> penetrates the cracks, causing them to spoil very easily. Therefore, others manage it better: as soon as the mace is removed, they do not leave the nuts in the sun for more than three days, bringing them into their houses every evening at dusk, or placing them immediately on the **Parre Parren** <note>drying racks or stages</note> located inside the houses or under covered roofs. Beneath these, they build a smoky fire so that the smoke penetrates the nuts themselves. If they have been exposed to the smoke for four weeks in this manner, they are removed from the **Parre Parren** and threshed with thick sticks, or a heavy stone is rolled over them until the bony shells are broken. The decayed or corrupt nuts are also broken apart by this threshing or rolling, allowing them to be easily distinguished from the good nuts. At this time, those shriveled nuts called **rompen** <note>original: *cadavera* (Latin for 'corpses') / *rompen* (Dutch for 'shriveled or shrunken ones'). These are nuts that withered inside the shell.</note> reveal themselves, which could not be identified before.

These cleaned nuts are selected by hand and gathered into three heaps, a process called **Garbuleeren** <note>original: *Garbuleeren* or garbling; a technical term for the sorting and grading of spices to remove impurities.</note>. In the first heap are the largest and best nuts, which are transported to Europe. The second heap consists of a middle grade mostly consumed here in the East Indies. In the third heap, those shriveled **rompen** are placed; though they are unpleasant in appearance and wrinkled, they are nonetheless hard, oily, and durable. The inhabitants use these mostly for pressing oil, but they are rarely or never exported to other regions. 

The cleaned nuts must soon be brought to the scales, and the merchant who buys them must take care that they are not left in the warehouses for more than eight days without being coated in **lime** <note>original: *calce* / *kalk*</note>; otherwise, they spoil easily, especially if placed in a damp or dark spot, or if thrown onto the bare ground. The liming is done in the following way: from thinly sifted lime, a thick lime-water is made (such as we use for whitewashing walls), and this is poured into a vat or tub. The nuts are placed in small baskets and dipped two or three times into this, shaking them so the lime-water touches all parts of the nuts, and then they are poured into a heap in the warehouses. The clinging lime preserves the nuts from rot and brings no harm to them, for this lime is burned from soft, white **coral stones** <note>original: *corallii lapidibus*</note> taken from the sea, which have little bitterness. This is the same lime that is used daily for chewing with **Pinang** <note>original: *Pinangae*. This refers to the Betel nut quid, a common stimulant in Southeast Asia composed of areca nut, betel leaf, and lime.</note>. 

It often happens that these limed nuts, when placed upon one another in a closed or cramped space, generate their own heat; if a spark of fire falls upon them, they quickly begin to smoke. Therefore, in the ships in which they are transported, the hatches are not entirely closed so that they remain exposed to the air. However, that danger is not of such great importance on ships because, when

## AMBONESE HERBAL Book II. chapter VI.
### Vol. II. C 2

...placed into the ship, much lime <note>original: *calx*. Lime was used as a preservative/insecticide for the nutmegs.</note> falls off, which causes a bothersome dust, extremely harmful to the eyes; those who handle and receive these in the narrower holds of the ships undergo the danger of suffocation.

Once dried, the **Mace** <note>original: *Macis* / *Foely*</note> likewise must not be left sitting for long, but once weighed, it is placed into large straw sacks interwoven with **Rattan**, called **Sockels** <note>original: *Sockels*. These were standard spice transport sacks.</note>, which are five feet long and one and a half feet wide. The interior part is made from certain long and broad leaves called **Cocoja**, which grows abundantly in the mountains of Banda—though only with the help of men, who, if they pluck the leaves of this plant, tread down the remaining stalk into the ground with their feet so that by touching the earth it may sprout new plants; this will be discussed further in Book 6.

Before the Mace is packed into these sacks, it must first be sprinkled with sea water; two half-pints <note>original: *heminæ*</note> are sufficient for each sack, which prevents the mace from crumbling and preserves its oils. The Mace is packed down as firmly as possible by treading with the feet, and finally, the sack is sewn shut with a small wooden tablet upon which the weight of the sack is inscribed. Each such sack weighs twenty-eight **Banda Catties** <note>original: *Bandenfes Catjes*. A catty is a traditional unit of weight used in East Asia.</note>, which is one hundred and sixty-one Dutch pounds; each Banda Catty is reckoned at 5 ¾ Dutch pounds. In such sacks, the Mace is transported to Europe.

The nutmeg groves are not possessed by the ancient inhabitants today, since they were driven out on account of many murders committed against the Dutch nation, especially in May of the year 1609 against Admiral **Pieter Willemsz. Verhoeven**. The entire region was conquered by arms in the year 1621 by the Governor-General **Jan Pieterszoon Coen** and reduced to a Province of the United Netherlands. At that time, the lands <note>original: *areæ* / *Perken*. Often called "parks," these were the nutmeg plantations.</note> were divided among Dutch citizens and **Mestizos** <note>original: *Misticis*. People of mixed European and local descent.</note>, who must maintain a large number of slaves—usually forty or fifty, and for the largest plots, as many as eighty or one hundred. Those who possessed none of these plots were formerly permitted to send their slaves into the woods to gather fallen nuts; such nuts that fall due to ripeness are the finest and largest, and they have the best surrounding Mace. By strong winds and heavy rains, many nuts are also knocked down, but these are "corpses" <note>original: *cadavera* / *rompen*. Nutmegs that are shriveled or underdeveloped.</note>, though their mace is still good and can be sold; it was for the sake of these that the collection in the woods was permitted. Today, however, this is forbidden, as the plantation owners complained that the gatherers—or rather, thieves—exceeded their bounds and plucked them from the trees, so that now everyone manages their own plot with their own slaves.

It was previously believed that nutmegs could not easily be propagated by human skill, and that it happened only through a certain species of blue pigeon, called **Falor** by the Bandanese, **Burong Pala** by the Malays, and by our people **Nut-eaters** <note>original: *Noote-eeters*</note>. These birds pluck the nuts from the outer husks with their beaks and swallow them whole; they digest only the mace and cast out the whole nut with its bony shell through their droppings. When these fall to the ground among the tall grass, they sprout new saplings. Conversely, it was thought that if men took ripe nuts and committed them to the grass or planted them in the rich soil of their gardens, none would sprout. The cause of this is that if a nut lies on the ground for some time, it easily becomes worm-eaten and rots. Later, however, around the year 1662, they began to use semi-ripe nuts, called **Matta Puti** <note>original: *Matta Puti*. Literally "White Eye" in Malay, referring to the stage where the mace is not yet fully red.</note>, in which the mace was not yet red. These they committed to the ground among the plants, and it succeeded well: for they produced excellent saplings which could be transplanted as desired. These saplings produced fruit in the fifth, sixth, or seventh year, but they must always be placed among grasses or in shade, as they do not bear the sun well; if the ground around them is cleared too much, they very easily perish. Indeed, even adult trees love to be placed among other trees; they especially desire wild trees toward the sea coast, and also that trees be placed around them on the tops of mountains, so that they may be protected from the sea air and the biting winds, which are most harmful to them. For this reason, it is not permitted in Banda to uproot wild trees unless they overly crowd the nutmeg trees and cover them. In that case, some may be cut down so that the nutmeg tree has freer air. Indeed, the nutmeg trees themselves should not be placed so closely that they touch, as they then produce little fruit and grow tall like a Fir tree...

<column-break/>

...in the cramped holds where they are handled, people run the risk of suffocating.

The dried **Mace** <note>original: *Foely*</note> must likewise not lie for long, but being weighed, is filled into large sacks made of straw and interwoven with **Rattan** (called **Sockels**), which are five feet long and 1 ½ wide; the interior is made of certain long and broad leaves called **Cocoja**, which grow abundantly on the mountains of Banda, though not without the assistance of men, who, when they have chopped off the leaves, tread down the crown of this plant with their feet so that they may touch the earth and thereby more easily bring forth new plants, of which more will be said in Book 6.

Before the Mace is filled into the aforementioned sacks, it must be sprinkled a little with salt water, taking two cans for each **Sockol**, which prevents the Mace from crushing and maintains its oiliness. The Mace is trodden in tightly, and packed together as hard as one can, after which the **Sockol** is sewn shut at the top with a small board on top where the weight of the **Sockol** is recorded, each **Sockol** weighing 28 **Banda Catties** net, being 161 Dutch pounds, each **Banda Catty** reckoned for 5 ¾ Dutch pounds, and with which **Sockels** it is transported to Europe.

The **Nutmeg forests** are nowadays no longer possessed by the old inhabitants, as they—due to their numerous murders of the **Dutch Nation**, particularly in May 1609 committed against **Admiral Pieter Willemsz. Verhoeven**—were driven out, and the entire land in 1621 was taken by arms by General **Jan Pietersen Coen** and made into a **Province** of the **United Netherlands**, at which time the **Parks** <note>original: *Perken*</note> were also divided among the **Dutch** and **Mestizo** citizens, who must keep a large number of **Slaves** there, commonly 40 and 50 pieces: but to the large **Parks** belong as many as 80 and 100 pieces. Those who possessed none of these **Parks** were formerly allowed to send their **Slaves** to the woods to pick up the fallen nuts, as such nuts that fall through ripeness are the most beautiful and largest, and also have the best **Mace**. By the hard winds and strong rain many are also knocked off, but those become "shriveled nuts," of which the **Mace** is nevertheless deliverable, and for whose sake this gathering was permitted. But nowadays it is forbidden, as the **Park-owners** have complained that the gatherers reached out a bit too far, and now everyone must tend his **Park** with his own **Slaves**.

It was formerly believed that Nutmegs could not well be propagated by human hands, and that such only happened through a sort of blue wild pigeon, called by the **Bandanese Falor**, by the **Malays Burong Pala**, and by our nation **Nut-eaters**, which peck these nuts out of the outer husks and swallow them whole, of which they digest only the **Mace**, and give the whole nuts with the hard shell back again through their droppings, which then falling into the brush, bring forth new plants; and that on the contrary, if humans took the ripe nuts and sowed them in the brush, or in their gardens, or even set them in a rich soil, nothing came of it; the cause of which was that the nut, when it lies whole and for a long time on the earth, very easily becomes worm-eaten and spoils. But thereafter, around the year 1662, they began to take half-ripe nuts, called **Matta Puti**, that is, those on which the **Mace** is not yet thoroughly red, and sowed them in the brush, and that succeeded well: for good little trees came up from them which one could transplant as desired. These little trees bear fruit in the fifth, sixth and seventh year, but they must constantly stand in the brush or under the shadow of trees, for they do not want much sun, so that if one cleans the place all around them and makes it too bare, they very easily die out; even the old trees like to stand among other trees, and especially they want some wild trees toward the sea-side and also on top of the mountains around them, so that they may remain protected from the sea-air and harsh winds, which are very harmful to them. And for this reason one may not chop down wild trees in **Banda**, unless they stand too thick and cover the Nutmeg tree too much, in which case one may chop down some, so that the **Nutmeg tree** gets a moderate amount of air...

## CHAPTER SEVEN.
## The Powers and Uses of the Nutmeg.

The same holds true here as was said of Cloves: namely, that these nuts provide more use and benefit to European peoples, especially those of the North and the Dutch <note>original: *Belgis* / *Duitsche Natie*. In the 17th century, "German" and "Belgic" were often used broadly to include the people of the Low Countries (the Netherlands).</note>, than to the inhabitants of India. Therefore, we shall not say much regarding their specific powers and properties, but noting them in general, we shall recount their most well-known uses. Some authors have claimed that the "male" nuts possess more power than the "female" ones and are more sought after by the Javanese; however, this is a misunderstanding. If by "males" they mean those large, oblong aromatic nuts, it could be accepted as true; but since we noted above that all aromatic nuts are considered "female," they must necessarily have understood this to refer to the wild nuts, though they were deceived in this matter. For although the Javanese and Malays might have requested two handfuls of "male" nuts from the Bandanese, they did not do so because they were better or more powerful, but because they knew how to prepare medicines from them for which the common nuts were unsuitable.

The true Nutmeg, if consumed, soothes all pain and stinging caused by cold, as well as flatulence of the stomach, intestines, and womb. It strengthens the "crop" <note>The upper part of the stomach.</note> of a cold stomach and thus causes better digestion; it stops vomiting and hiccups. When crushed and mixed with Laurel berries and drunk in wine, it drives out urine, cures difficulty in urinating <term>Dysuria</term>, and provides a good scent to the breath. It is also suitable for colicky pains of the intestines and opens a blocked liver or spleen if used in the aforementioned manner.

When roasted at the fire, the nut is also used mixed with a certain liquid against Diarrhea and Dysentery <note>original: *roode melizoen*. An old Dutch term for the "bloody flux" or dysentery.</note>. Arabic physicians mix a little Opium in such cases; and we have learned from a certain friend, who said he learned this as a great secret from the Persian Moors, against the "blood-flux": namely, a roasted Nutmeg with a little Opium about the size of a <term>Kadjang</term> <note>A Malay term for various pulses or beans, used here as a measurement of volume.</note>, taken with a draught of red wine; or if red wine is lacking, this can be done with a soft egg yolk. However, since our nation is not accustomed to the use of Opium, we have learned another cure: namely, if the nut is hollowed out and a piece of **Benzoin** <note>original: *Benzöes*. A balsamic resin from trees of the genus *Styrax*, used in incense and medicine.</note> is inserted, and this is roasted under hot ashes and taken with a little meat broth, it is particularly good for the womb, abdominal pains, kidneys, and bladder. Some also say it is effective for driving out "the gravel" <note>Kidney stones or sediment.</note> if it is first soaked in almond oil.

Conversely, those who are constipated or troubled by hemorrhoids, and who have thick, coarse, or "burnt" blood, should beware of using these spices; however, if a portion of Ginger is added, it is corrected and has a more penetrating virtue. Daily use of the nuts, due to their oiliness, coats the stomach with mucus and fills the head with heavy vapors, from which a "sleeping sickness" <term>Lethargy</term> easily arises. It is also told that a pregnant woman once went mad from eating ten or twelve nuts at a certain time; to confirm this, we shall bring forward two or three stories that happened in our own time.

In the year 1655, some Germans ate a "cold bowl" <note>original: *koude schaal*. A type of chilled bread-soup or punch made with beer or wine.</note> prepared from common beer and wine, in which, according to their account, they had mixed nothing else but sugar and seven or eight grated Nutmegs. The following day, they all suffered such oppression of the chest and tightness of the throat as if they were suffocating; their mouths became very dry, their lips swelled and stuck together as if coated with glue, and they breathed with difficulty.

<column-break/>

even so: indeed, the Nutmeg trees must not stand so close together that they touch one another, for otherwise they bear little fruit and shoot up as tall as Firs, as is seen in the Lontoir plots. This chopping and felling is left to the judgment of the Forest Warden, without whose permission one may not chop down a single tree.

## CHAPTER VII.
## Powers and Use of the Nutmegs.

What was spoken of Cloves applies here as well; namely, that they provide more notable and greater utility to the inhabitants of Europe and other cold lands, especially to the German nation, than to those of the Indies. Therefore, we shall not write extensively of their powers and properties, but speaking only briefly in general, we shall cite only the most well-known benefits. Some authors have claimed that the "Male" nuts are more powerful and more sought after by the Javanese than the "Females"; but that is a misunderstanding. But if by "males" they mean those large, long spice-nuts, then this saying might pass; but since we have said above that all spice-nuts are held to be "females," they must necessarily have understood this to refer to the wild nuts, though they were nonetheless deceived therein. For even if the Javanese and Malays previously requested a few handfuls of "male" nuts from the Bandanese, they by no means did so because they were better or more powerful, but because they knew how to make medicine from them for which the common ones were unfit.

The true spice-nut, when consumed, soothes all pain and stinging caused by cold and windiness in the stomach, bowels, and womb; it strengthens the crop of a chilled stomach and thus helps it to a better "cooking" <note>An archaic term for digestion.</note>; it stops vomiting and the "hic" <note>hiccups</note>. When crushed and mixed with Laurel berries and drunk in wine, it drives the urine, heals the "cold piss" <note>difficulty or pain during urination</note>, and makes for a good breath. It is also good for colic and pain of the bowels, and opens the obstructed liver and spleen, when used in the manner described above.

The nut is also roasted by the fire, toasted, and taken with some drink to stop the "belly-run" <note>diarrhea</note> and the "red flux" <note>bloody dysentery</note>. The Arabic masters mix a little opium therewith in this case; and we have understood from a certain friend, who said he had learned this as a great secret from the Persian Moors against the bloody flux: namely, a roasted nut with a little opium about the size of a <term>Kadjang</term>, taken with a drink of red wine; and if one has no red wine, one may do the same with a soft egg. But since our nation is not used to the use of opium, we have learned a better cure: namely, if one hollows out the nuts a bit, sticks a piece of **Benzoin** therein, roasts it in the hot ashes, and takes it thus with some broth, this nut is especially good for the "mother" <note>the womb/hysteria</note>, bellyache, kidneys, and bladder. Some say it also serves to drive off "the gravel," soaking it beforehand in almond oil.

But on the other hand, those who are "hard-bodied" <note>constipated</note> or plagued with "the piles" <note>hemorrhoids</note>, and have a thick, coarse, burnt blood, must guard themselves against much use of this spice; though some ginger added thereto improves it and makes it more penetrating. The daily use of the nuts makes the stomach slimy because of their fattiness, and fills the head with heavy vapors, from which a sleeping-sickness also proceeds. It is also recounted that at one time a pregnant woman had gone mad from eating 10 to 12 nuts, and to strengthen this, we shall bring here two or three histories that happened in our times.

In the year 1655, some Germans ate a "cold bowl" made of bad beer and wine, in which they said they had put nothing else but sugar and 7 or 8 grated nuts. These men the next day got such a tightness on the chest and in the throat as if they wanted to suffocate; their mouths became very dry, the lips swollen and sticking to each other, they drew breath with difficulty, and in the head they felt such heaviness and dizziness...

### THE AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chap. VII.

...and they felt such a great heaviness and dizziness of the head that they seemed to be deprived of their memory; their abdomens were hardened and constipated, so that they were finally cured only with great effort and after drinking many Juleps <note>A sweet, liquid medicine, often used as a base for other drugs.</note>, in addition to prescribed bloodletting and purges. At another time, two soldiers slept through the night under a single Nutmeg tree in *Manipa* <note>An island in the Maluku archipelago.</note>, and the next day they were so dizzy that they appeared drunk or half-mad. Similar examples were also observed in Banda; for in the year 1650 there were two soldiers there who ate five or six nuts from their hands, which likewise made them foolish and delirious. Then, in the year 1657, another man was found dead in his bed, and before his bed a basket was found filled with nuts; from this it was concluded that he had eaten such a great quantity of Nutmegs that they had caused him to fall into this fatal and final sleep.

We have mentioned above what harm and inconvenience is suffered by those who inhabit houses, or travel in ships, where limed nuts are stored; from this it is clear that Nutmegs in India bring more harm than benefit, and that the wise Creator fashioned them for the Boreal <note>Northern</note> part of the world, where their fattiness is concentrated by the cold, and is so changed and corrected that they become not only more durable, but also healthier and better-smelling, just as was also said of Cloves.

Green nuts are also preserved in sugar, and are transported not only throughout all of India but even to Europe; this is done in the following way. When the nuts are nearly ripe, but before they have split open, they are gently plucked from the tree so they are not damaged by falling. These are boiled in water and pierced with styli <note>Small pointed tools or needles.</note>, then soaked in fresh water for eight or ten days, which is poured out and renewed daily until their bitterness is removed. Then a Julep is prepared from an equal <note>original: *anatica*, a medical term meaning "of each alike."</note> quantity of water and sugar, in which they are cooked for a longer or shorter time as desired. If hard nuts are required, a certain quantity of lime is added; however, this sugar-water must be poured off every day, heated, and poured over the nuts again, which is done for eight continuous days. Finally, the nuts are boiled again in a thicker syrup made of sugar and preserved in well-sealed stone jars; in this way, they can be transported to Europe without spoiling. By this cooking, the Nutmeg shell acquires a dark red color and is semi-transparent and so tender that there is no need to remove the outer skin, but these nuts are eaten cut into five or six pieces. They are usually placed on the table with other sweetmeats at the end of a meal, and especially offered to guests while drinking tea. If nuts that are too old are preserved in sugar, the outer skin must be peeled off before they are eaten, because it is too hard. The inner kernel with the mace is not eaten, though some gnaw the mace and throw the nut away. If this preserve is used daily, the head and brain are affected by thick vapors, which generates the aforementioned Lethargy <note>A state of profound drowsiness or "sleeping sickness."</note>, or men become forgetful and very prone to dreams; it also upsets the stomach and appetite. Since much sugar is required for this operation, which is not abundant in Banda and the Molucca Islands, they used to pickle whole nuts in brine in vessels or jars and send them to Batavia <note>Present-day Jakarta.</note>, where sugar is more plentiful.

The Chinese in Batavia employ another method of preserving nuts in sugar, which is not so laborious or expensive: they take the nuts preserved in brine and soak them in fresh water until the saltiness disappears, and boil them only once with syrup, which is often made not from white sugar but only from black sugar. These serve for daily use, but they cannot be kept for long. Nuts preserved in brine can also be transported as far as Europe. From the Nutmeg shell, prepared and crushed in the said manner, a Marmalade <note>A thick fruit paste or preserve.</note> is made, which is poured into square boxes and used equally as a sweetmeat and as a medicine. The green and fresh shells of the nuts are first boiled with water in Banda, and then rubbed with wine and sugar, which provides a pleasant food of acidic flavor, like fried Jamboes <note>original: *Jambosarum* / *Jamboezen*. A tropical fruit often called a rose apple.</note> or Quinces. These same shells, slightly bruised (though others crush them finely) and steeped in brine, serve as a condiment, an Achar <note>original: *Atjar*. A type of South Asian or Southeast Asian pickle.</note>

<column-break/>

...that they seemed to have lost their memory; the belly was hard and constipated, so that with much trouble, and with Juleps, one could only then restore those people to health: using bloodletting and purges besides. At another time, two soldiers slept under a Nutmeg tree on Manipa the whole night through, who the next day were so heavy-headed that they seemed drunk and half-mad. Similar examples have also been seen in Banda; for in the year 1650 there were two soldiers there who ate 5 or 6 nuts from their hand, from which they likewise became crazy and half-senseless. After that, in the year 1657, another person was found lying dead on his bunk, and before it stood a small basket full of nuts, from which it was firmly established that he had eaten so many that he had fallen into a deadly sleep because of them.

*What harm and discomfort those suffer who live in houses, or sail on ships, in which limed nuts are kept, we have mentioned above, and from which it appears that the nuts in the Indies do more harm than good, and that the wise Creator made them for the Northern world, where their fattiness, through the contracting cold, is changed and improved in such a way that they become not only more durable, but also healthier and more fragrant, as has also been said of Cloves.*

The green nuts are also candied, and transported not only through all of India, but also into Europe, which happens thus: when the nuts are nearly ripe, yet so that they do not burst, one takes them gently from the trees, so that they are not bruised by falling; these are boiled once in water, and then pierced with awls, soaked for 8 to 10 days in fresh water, renewing the same daily, until they lose their bitterness; after that one makes a Julep of half water, half sugar, and boils them therein long or short, according to how one wants to have them, and if one desires them hard, then one puts a little lime therein; this sugar-water must be poured off every day, made warm, and poured on again, for another eight days long, and finally boiled once more, and a thick syrup made of sugar, and kept in stone pots well-stopped; in this way one can bring them unspoiled to Europe. Through this boiling, the Nutmeg shell gets a dark-red color, becomes half-transparent, and so tender that one does not need to take off the outer skin, but one cuts them into 5 or 6 parts, and eats them so: they are commonly served with other banquets, at the dessert-tables, and especially when drinking tea-water. If one takes nuts that are too old for candying, then the outer skin is too hard, and one must peel it off before eating. The inner kernel with the mace is not eaten, though some chew the mace and throw the rest away; if one uses this preserve daily, the head and brain are filled with thick vapors, and it generates the aforementioned sleep-sickness, through which people dream and become forgetful: it also fouls the stomach and spoils the appetite. Because this work now costs much sugar, with which one is not well provided in Banda and the Moluccan Islands, one used to pickle the whole nuts in small barrels or pots, and so send them to Batavia, where sugar is more abundantly obtained.

The Chinese at Batavia use a shorter and less expensive method, namely, they take the pickled nuts and soak them in fresh water until they lose the saltiness, and then boil them but once with syrup, which they often make not from white, but from black tree-sugar: and these are indeed good for daily use, but cannot be kept long. The pickled nuts can also be carried as far as Europe; one makes from the shell, prepared in the previous manner and rubbed small, also a Marmalade, which is poured into square boxes, and used as well for banquets as for Medicine. The green shells were first boiled with water in Banda, then stewed with wine and sugar, which is then a pleasant food, tart of taste, like stewed Jamboes or Quinces. The same green shell slightly bruised (some rub them small) and put in brine, serves also as an Achar for poor people (to use as a side-dish, and to [increase] appetite...

### II Book. VII Chapter. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...as already mentioned, it serves the common people, being used as a condiment or to stimulate the appetite, just as it is also served with Tea. On the Nutmeg shells that lie rotting in the woods, a certain species of Mushroom grows, called in Latin *Boletus Moschocarianus* <note>The "Musky Nut" Mushroom.</note> and in Malay *Culat Pala*, which in Banda is considered a great delicacy; this will be discussed further in its place in Book 10, Chapter 79.

Since the cheaper husks, as has been said, are in no way suitable for trade and are otherwise useless, they are mostly used for pressing oil. First, the Nutmegs are roasted in a pan, then crushed and heated again. They are placed in bags made of *Runut* <note>A hairy fibrous tissue found at the top of Coconut trees (*Calappi*) between the branches</note> and set between two thick planks, which are pressed tightly together with wedges and mallets. This compression causes a thick oil to flow from the nuts like melted butter; it is collected in square molds where it immediately solidifies into a consistency like suet. It has the color of fresh May-butter, or sometimes a bit whiter. These cakes are about a hand-span long, five fingers wide, and an inch thick, and are transported for medicinal use throughout the Indies as well as to Europe. Formerly they were highly valued, but nowadays they are not held in such high esteem due to their abundance, although no private individual is permitted to prepare them, and all manufactured cakes must be sold to the Company <note>The Dutch East India Company, or VOC, which held a monopoly on the spice trade.</note>.

In almost the same manner, oil is pressed from crushed and heated Mace; it is blood-red in color and remains soft; if dripped onto the hand, it looks like yellow blood. It has a fatty and somewhat bitter taste like Mace, without notable heat. However, much Mace is consumed in the preparation of this oil. It is calculated that at least three Bandanese *Catjes* <note>A local unit of weight; three catjes equal about 17.25 lbs.</note>—that is, seventeen and a quarter Dutch pounds—of Mace are required for one *haemina* <note>A "kan" or roughly a liter.</note> of oil. A clear oil is also distilled from Mace in the same manner and with the same instruments used to make Arack <note>A distilled spirit common in Southeast Asia.</note>. The first part that comes over in the distillation after the water is clear and transparent like water; the next is somewhat more yellow, like old Rhenish wine; and finally, if driven by a stronger fire, it turns reddish. Since this oil is difficult to distinguish from the water or phlegm because of its clarity, and consequently hard to skim off, some people used to put a little crushed Mace into the receiver, which makes it appear like red wine, so that the oil can be more easily distinguished from the water during separation. Both of these oils have the same virtues, being very subtle and penetrating, so that if the vials they are kept in are not well sealed, a large quantity will evaporate. In distillation, ten Bandanese *Catjes* of Mace are required for one *haemina* of oil. If this oil were distilled through tin-lined alembics, it would be precious and useful for internal use, whereas otherwise, when drawn through copper stills, it becomes somewhat rancid and makes the head heavy. Therefore, the expressed oil is considered much healthier and more pleasant for internal use. The expressed oil of the nut, which is also called balsam and named *Geuzi-semen* <note>original: "Geuzi-semen", likely from the Arabic "Jawz al-tib", meaning Nutmeg.</note> by the Arabs, is believed to have the power to cure all diseases of the kidneys and joints arising from a "cold" cause. It also aids in clearing the chest and lungs, making the voice clear. When taken with food or drink, it promotes conception, increases the male seed, and makes people fatter. Applied to the stomach and abdomen, it cures all cold ailments and cramps, drives away spots from the face, and prevents painful urination <note>Dysuria.</note>. The expressed Mace oil is used for the same ailments, and the distilled version is taken internally, though those who use this oil must be free from headaches, as it otherwise increases them. The dregs of the pressed nuts are usually sent to the Hospital to rub the limbs of those suffering from Beri-beri <note>A disease caused by Vitamin B1 deficiency, which Rumphius identifies here as "Indian Paralysis".</note>.

*Pala Pentsjuri* <note>original: "Pala Pentsjuri", or "Thieves' Nutmeg", a wild variety of nutmeg.</note>, or "Thieves' Nuts", taken internally, are highly praised against kidney stones; and the whey-like liquor or milk flowing from the green fruit, mixed with water, or its shell crushed with water, cures thrush if the mouth and throat are rinsed and gargled with it.
