AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chapter VIII.

# CHAPTER EIGHT.
## Male Nutmeg: *Pala Lacki-Lacki.*

Among the wild species, of which six are primarily known, we shall describe the first in this chapter, commonly called the Male Nutmeg <note>original: "Nux Myristica mas"</note>. This tree does not bear much outward resemblance to the true Nutmeg tree. It has a tall trunk and a narrow crown with few branches, and does not offer a pleasing appearance. The leaves are also much larger, some a span <note>About 9 inches</note>, others a foot and a half long, similar in shape to the leaves of the *Canarium* <note>The Java Almond or Kenari nut tree</note>, yet broader and rounder at the top, ending in a short point and woven with many parallel ribs. They are dark green above and dull yellowish-gray beneath, without any shine, where the green ribs protrude. They grow in opposite pairs, and when chewed, they have a notable wild taste, mimicking the true Nutmeg.

The fruits do not hang from the tips of the small branches as in the true Nutmeg, but lower down on the branches, emerging from the leaf axils, two or three together on short, thick stalks. They are round in shape and as large as a true Nutmeg, though some are slightly oblong, others perfectly round, or a little compressed. The outer husk is reddish and fuzzy to the touch, thicker at the sides than at the top or bottom, and tougher and firmer than in true Nutmegs. The kernel or stone also has two forms, both of which are larger than the true or domestic nutmeg. One is globe-shaped and somewhat long, compressed at the sides; the other is round, but both are wrinkled. It is contained within a bony shell thicker than that of common nutmegs, which is blackish or dark gray. On the outside, it is wrapped in a golden-yellow mace <note>The lacy covering of the nutmeg seed</note>, through which the shell can be seen. The shell is marked with small dots and is as rough as a grater. When dried, this mace becomes entirely pale yellow and has an unpleasant taste without any spice. The inner kernel has the same substance as the true nutmeg but is whiter and not as oily, woven with thin, blackish veins. It is hardly aromatic and has an unpleasant, somewhat lime-like taste. If mixed with other nuts, it infects and spoils them, which is why it is forbidden to mix this wild nut with the commercial ones. However, if it is dried in smoke with its shell, like common nutmegs, it is more durable, harder, and heavier than the true aromatic nutmeg, even if it is not coated in lime <note>Nutmegs were often dipped in lime to prevent insect infestation and germination during transport</note>. The leaves on the trees are rarely whole, as they are mostly eaten by worms. If the immature fruit is cut, a kind of milk drips out, which dries like lime. This tree is not tolerated among the domestic ones, for it is believed to make them "thin" or less productive; thus, it occupies and chooses solitary places at the edges of forests and on mountains, where it is left undisturbed to its own nature. Its fruit is given to foreigners as a rarity rather than for any practical utility.

**Names.** In Latin *Nux Myristica mas*, and *montana* <note>Mountain Nutmeg</note>, which were considered two different fruits by Carolus Clusius <note>A famous 16th-century Flemish botanist</note> in his first book of *Exotica*, though they are one and the same fruit. In Banda it is called *Pala Fuker*, that is, Mountain Nutmeg; in Malay *Pala Lacki-Lacki*, that is, Male Nutmeg. In Amboina it is called *Pala Utan* <note>Wild Nutmeg</note>, as well as *Palala*, a word composed of *Pala* and *Ala*, as if to say the "nut of the annual bird," since these birds, called *Ala* in the Amboinese tongue, greedily devour these nuts.

**Location.** It was previously believed that this tree was only found in the Province of Banda, in remote places and mountains where the true nutmegs refused to grow, but I have found it everywhere in the Amboinese islands, though not in great abundance, nor is it much sought after or esteemed by the inhabitants.

**Use.** Among the inhabitants, as has been said, it is not in use, except that its wood is sometimes used for house posts, and they give the fruits to foreigners, as not only the Javanese but also Europeans seek them out.

The Javanese and Malays use them in medicine for headaches and other diseases, but mostly for strengthening male vigor <note>Used as an aphrodisiac</note>, a remedy to which the Moors <note>Muslim traders and inhabitants</note> apply all diligence. Europe-

# CHAPTER VIII.
## Male Nutmegs: *Pala Lacki-Lacki.*

Among the wild Nutmegs, of which six sorts are best known, we shall touch upon the first kind in this chapter, which is commonly called MALE NUTMEGS. This tree has little outward resemblance to the true Nutmeg tree: it has a high trunk and a narrow crown with few branches, and is not beautiful to behold. The leaves are also much larger, some a span, some a foot and a half long, shaped like *Canarium* leaves, but broader and rounder toward the front, ending in a short point, and streaked with many parallel ribs. They are black-green on top, quite pale on the underside, and without shine, where the green ribs stick out. Growing two by two opposite each other, and when chewed, they have a noticeable wild taste like Nutmegs.

The fruits do not hang at the ends of the twigs, like the true Nutmegs, but somewhat further back on the branches, from the origin of the leaves, two and three together on short and thick stalks. They are round in shape and as large as a true Nutmeg, though some are somewhat oblong, and others perfectly round, or a little flattened. On the outside, the husk is reddish and woolly to the touch, thicker at the sides than at the top or bottom, also tougher and harder than the true Nutmegs. The kernel is of two types of shape, and both are larger than the true or domestic Nutmegs: one is ball-shaped and somewhat oblong, but somewhat flat at the end; the other round, but both are wrinkled. It also lies in a bony shell somewhat thicker than those of the common Nutmegs, being blackish or dark gray, and on the outside likewise surrounded by a gold-yellow Mace, through which one sees the shell; being covered there with small pimples, and as rough as a grater. The Mace, when dried, becomes quite pale and is also unpleasant in taste, without any spiciness. The inner kernel has the same substance as the true Nutmegs, but is somewhat whiter and not so oily, being streaked with fine and blackish veins, little like spice, and almost unpleasant in taste. It easily becomes worm-eaten, and if it gets among other Nutmegs, it spoils them as well, which is why it is forbidden to mix it among them. Nevertheless, if it is dried in smoke with its shell, like the common Nutmegs, it becomes more durable, harder, and heavier than the common spice-nut, even if it is not limed. The leaves on the tree are very seldom found whole, being mostly eaten through by worms, and if one cuts into the unripe fruit, a milk comes out which dries up like lime. This tree is not suffered among the domestic ones, for it is believed that it makes them thin; therefore it chooses a lonely place on the edges of the forests and on mountains, where it is left standing undisturbed, more to give the fruits as a rarity to foreigners than for any usefulness.

**Names:** In Latin *Nux Myristica mas*, and *Montana*, regarded by Carolus Clusius in *Exotica, Book 1*, as two fruits, though it is nevertheless only one. In Banda *Pala fuker*, that is, Mountain-nutmegs; in Malay *Pala Lacki-Lacki*, that is, Male-nutmeg. In Amboina it is called *Pala Utan* and *Palala*, with a word joined together from *Pala* and *Ala*, as if one were to say *Annual-birds-Nutmegs*, because those birds, called *Ala* in Amboinese, gladly eat these fruits.

**Places.** It was formerly believed that this tree was only to be found in the Province of Banda, in remote places and mountains where the true Nutmegs would not grow, but I have found them everywhere in the Amboinese Islands, though not many, and they are not much esteemed by the locals.

**Use.** It has, as said, no use among the locals, except that they sometimes take the wood for house posts, and they present the fruits to foreigners, for not only the Javanese but also the Europeans seek them.

The Javanese and Malays use them as medicine for headaches and some other illnesses, but mostly to strengthen the masculine powers, for which remedy the Moors use all diligence. The Europe-

# Book II. Chapter VIII. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

They use them even more superstitiously when they prepare love potions from them, with which they believe they can achieve great things; however, it is not worth the effort to write more about such ridiculous trifles. Some wear them around the neck to be freed from boils. Some Indians <note>In this context, "Indians" refers to the native inhabitants of the East Indies, specifically the Moluccas.</note> have also found that these male nuts are effective against dysentery if they are eaten with half-ripe and roasted bananas <note>original: "Musae fructibus"; Dutch: "Pissang"</note>, especially if a small grain of opium <note>original: "Opii"; Dutch: "Amphioen"</note> is added. The women of Banda also use them for fainting and convulsions in infants, for which purpose they are now beginning to preserve them.

In the year 1683, a remarkable property of these nuts was discovered in a certain Pastor, whose wife gave him three roasted male nuts (which she mistakenly thought were true aromatic nutmegs) to stop tenesmus <note>A distressing sensation of needing to pass stool even when the bowels are empty.</note> and diarrhea. A few hours later, this reverend gentleman fell into a severe dizziness of the head and a delirium <note>original: "mentis alienationem"</note>, such that he performed strange actions; for he shouted out incoherent words in a loud voice, and could not be brought to sleep or tranquility by any force until he had drunk several cups of tea and had a vein opened <note>The practice of bloodletting, common in 17th-century medicine.</note>. Afterward, he fell into a heavy sweat along with a deep sleep; upon waking, he felt no further discomfort, and at the same time, the diarrhea was cured. If he had taken as many true nutmegs <note>Myristica fragrans</note>, he would undoubtedly have been subject to more severe evils, as we indicated above; we only wish to warn here that one should not consume so many spices at once.

In the *Garden of Malabar* <note>original: "Hortus Malabaricus", a famous 12-volume treatise on the medicinal plants of the Malabar Coast.</note> Part 4, Figure 5, a tree is described called *Panam Palka* by the Malabaris and *Wild Male-Nuts* <note>original: "wilde Mannekens-Nooten"</note> by the Dutch, which almost agrees with our tree, except that the leaves on the Amboinese variety are much larger; there is likewise a small difference in the fruit, and in the Malabar variety, no aromatic power or any use is observed, which I believe should be attributed to the different soil and climate.

*In Rumphius’s Appendix <note>original: "Auctuario"</note> these things are added:*

The lower part of the trunk in the Male Nutmeg sends out innumerable roots everywhere above the ground like the Mangrove <note>original: "Mangi Mangi"</note> tree, though not thicker than a finger, and of a reddish-ash color on the outside. The lower ones creep under the earth, while the upper ones are extended like bows; rarely are they curved upward, but gradually bend downward. The subsequent species, however, do not send out such roots.

This tree is called *Spurious Nutmeg, or Panem-Palka* in the *Garden of Malabar Part 4, Table 5*; by *Plukenet in his Almagest p. 265*; and *Oblong Indian Nut internally similar to the Nutmeg* by *J. Bauhin, Volume 1, p. 399*; and *Oblong type of Indian Hazelnut* by *Clusius in Garcia p. 189*; and *Parkinson in his Theater 1643*; and *Ray in his History of Plants p. 1524*. Regarding this, see further *Valentijn’s Reformed History of Simples, Letter XXV, p. 460*, and *Valentijn’s Description of Ambon, p. 202, etc.*

<column-break/>

Europeans use them even more superstitiously, wanting to make love-potions from them, with which they think they can achieve great things; however, of which ridiculous trifles it is not worth the effort to write more. Others wear them on the neck to be freed from boils. Some Indians have experienced that the Male-nuts are also good for the bloody-flux <note>Dysentery.</note>, when one eats the same with half-ripe and roasted bananas, and especially when one adds a grain of opium thereto. The Bandanese women also use them for fainting and convulsions of children, for which end they are now also beginning to preserve them.

In the year 1683, a droll property of the Male-nuts was experienced by a certain Preacher, whose housewife gave him three roasted Male-nuts (*which she mistakenly took for spice-nuts*) to stop the straining and diarrhea. But this Reverend Gentleman fell a few hours later into a heavy spinning of the head and confusion of senses, so that he began to act strangely and to utter reckless propositions with a loud voice; and one could not get him to rest or be silent by any force until he had enjoyed some cups of tea-water and a vein being opened, after which he fell into a violent sweat and a deep sleep, retaining no injury after waking therefrom, and at once the diarrhea was stopped. Had he taken as many real spice-nuts, he would without doubt have been subject to heavier fits, as we have recounted above; and this serves only as a warning that one must not use or take much of such spices at once.

In the *Garden of Malabar Part 4, Fig. 5*, a tree is described named *Panam Palka* in Malabar, and in Dutch called *Wild Male-Nuts*, almost corresponding with ours, except that the leaves on the Amboinese are much larger, also there is a small difference in the fruit, and on the Malabar one there is no spiciness or use at all, which one must attribute to the difference of the lands.

*In the Appendix of Rumphius the following is added.*

The lower trunk of the Male Nutmeg-Tree shoots out innumerable roots all around above the earth, like the Mangrove-Tree, yet not above a finger thick, from the outside greyish-red. Of these, the lowest creep along the earth, the others stand stretched like bows: few are bent upwards, but bend themselves downwards in time: The following species do not have similar roots.

# AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chap. IX.

## CHAPTER NINE.
### The Second Palala. Bird Palala.

Besides the wild or "male" nutmeg <note>original Latin: "nucem Myristicam marem"</note> described in the preceding chapter, five more wild species are found in the Amboinese islands; of these, we shall describe only the largest in this chapter, which we call the *Palala secunda* <note>The Second Palala</note>. This tree rises with a single, straight trunk, though it is not as thick as the preceding true Nutmeg tree. Its bark is smooth, variegated with green and black, and swollen with a red sap—as in the other species—which stains linen with spots that cannot be washed out.

Its branches take the form of thin, long twigs, which do not divide into smaller ones; from these erupt large leaves, placed alternately in two rows, numbering about thirty-two or forty pairs. These leaves are very long and, in proportion to their length, quite narrow: one and a half feet or two spans long, and only four fingers wide, interwoven transversely with many close, parallel ribs. The upper part is dark green and smooth, while the lower part is not dull-yellow like the previous species, but a mixture of reddish-brown and green without any luster; the veins there are covered with a reddish fuzz, as are the tips of the small branches. The fruits grow on the lower part of these twigs, joined three or four together, hanging from a long stalk. They have the shape of a true Nutmeg, but are a little sharper and smaller; on the outside they are smooth without any fuzz, yellowish mixed with a red color, like *Jambos* <note>Rose apples; a tropical fruit often used for comparison due to its waxy, colorful skin.</note>. Beneath the outer husk lies a blood-red mace <term>macis</term> <note>The lacy, red outer covering of the nutmeg seed.</note>, which wraps around the entire kernel, but it is tasteless. Beneath this is found a whitish membrane, soft and about the thickness of a knife’s edge; under this occurs another woody shell, as thick as an eggshell, buff-colored, and brittle. Inside this is contained the true kernel, flat-round and slightly compressed, the size of a small nut, but a bit rounder and smoother, its substance rivaling the true nutmeg, or like an old *Pinang* <note>The Areca nut or Betel nut.</note>. If it is still covered by its shell, it has the shape of a large kernel of <term>Tsjampadaba</term> or <term>Soccum</term> <note>Varieties of breadfruit or jackfruit (Artocarpus species).</note>, oblong and slightly pointed at the top. There is no aromatic virtue in the whole tree, neither in its leaves nor its fruit; rather, everything has a bland and wild taste, which is why none of it is harvested.

The wood of the tree consists of longitudinal fibers and is more solid than the previous kind; the exterior turns reddish once it has been debarked.

**Name.** In Latin *Palala secunda*, in Malay *Palala Burong*, and by the common name *Pala Utan* <note>Literally "Forest Nutmeg".</note>. In Amboinese *Palala Ala Manay* or simply *Ala Manay*, which means "food of the *Ala* bird" <note>The *Ala* or *Jaarvogel* refers to the Hornbill, which feeds on these wild fruits.</note>, which greedily devours these fruits, as was also said of the immediately preceding *Palala*.

**Location.** These trees are frequent in the Amboinese forests, except for those growing in flat places and valleys; they usually grow very straight with a thin and slender trunk.

**Use.** The fruits of this tree are of no use here, but the straight trunks—having the thickness of a thigh—are used for small beams and poles for houses. When green they are very heavy, but they dry out easily; the wood is not durable unless used in places exposed to smoke.

This species also grows abundantly on Buru around *Kagebi*, where it is called *Cottreman*, and in Ternate it is called *Au-au*. Its leaves are also arranged twenty in a row, and beneath them the fruits grow twelve or sixteen in succession, but joined two or three together, hanging from a short, thick stalk. These are not much different from the Amboinese variety, for they are slightly pointed at the top like an egg or a heart, the size of walnuts; on the outside they are furrowed lengthwise, along which they burst open.

The outer husk of the nut has the same thickness as the common Nutmeg; it is juicy and acidic in taste, like a half-ripe Mango <term>Manga</term>.

The nut itself, consisting of a buff-colored and thin woody shell, is oblong-round, and at the end slightly poin...

## CHAPTER IX.
### Second wild Nutmeg tree.

Besides the wild, or "Male" nuts described in the previous chapter, one also finds in the Amboinese Islands the following five wild sorts, of which we shall describe only the largest, being *Palala secunda*, in this chapter. This tree shoots up with a single straight trunk, but not as thick as the upright Nutmeg tree. The bark is smooth, mixed from black and green, and full of light-red sap, like all other Nutmeg families, which greatly ruins linen.

The branches have the appearance of thin, long twigs, which do not divide into others; on them stand or hang large leaves, in two rows opposite each other numbering about 32 to 40 pairs. The leaves are very long, and narrow in proportion to the length, namely one and a half feet or two spans long, and only four fingers wide, drawn through with dense parallel ribs crosswise. The upper side is dark-green and smooth, the underside not buff-colored like the previous nuts, but mixed from reddish and green, without any shine; the veins there are covered with a reddish woolliness. They stand on short thick stalks, also woolly, as is the forward part of the twigs. The fruits grow on the back part of these twigs or branches, three and four together, hanging from a long stalk, in the shape of the true Nutmegs, though somewhat sharper and smaller. From the outside they are smooth without any woolliness, of a light-yellow mixed with red, like the *Jamboesen* <note>Rose apples</note>. Under the outermost husk lies a blood-red mace, which covers the entire kernel, but without taste; under it is a white skin, soft and about a knife-thick; and under that one finds another thin and woody shell, the thickness of an eggshell, buff in color, and weak or brittle. Inside lies the true kernel, somewhat flattened from its roundness, the size of a small Nut, though somewhat rounder and smoother of substance than the true Nutmeg, or like old *Pinang*. When it is still surrounded or enclosed by its shell, it has the shape of a large kernel of the *Tsjampadaba* or *Soccum*, somewhat oblong, and at the belly with a short point. Neither in the whole tree nor the fruits and leaves is there anything spicy, but everything is of a bland and wild taste, therefore one gathers nothing from it.

The wood is longer-grained and firmer than the previous one, and turns reddish on the outside when it is peeled.

**Names:** In Latin *Palala secunda*, in Malay *Palala Burong*, and by a common name *Pala Utan*; Amboinese *Palala ala manay*, or simply *Ala Manay*, that is, food of the bird *Ala*, or *Jaarvogel* <note>Hornbill</note>, which greedily eats these fruits, as was also said of the next preceding *Palala*.

**Place:** These trees grow wild in the Amboinese forests, except those that stand on flat places and in valleys, usually shooting up very straight, with a thin and slender trunk.

**Use:** The fruits of this tree are in no use, but only the straight trunks, in the thickness of a thigh, were used for light timber work, such as small beams and rafters of the houses; being green it is heavy, but dries easily, and is not durable, unless it were used in places that are smoked.

And this sort also grows much on Buru near *Kegeli*, and is named there *Cottreman*, on Ternate *Au-au*. The leaves also stand 20 in a row, and behind them the fruits grow 12 and 16 one after another, though 2 and 3 together, on a short thick stalk, otherwise not much different from the Amboinese, for they are somewhat sharp at the front, like an egg or heart, in the size of walnuts; on the outside they have a seam, going round in the length, along which they burst open.

The outer husk is of the thickness of the common one, being juicy and tart of taste, like half-ripe *Mangas* <note>Mangoes</note>.

The nut itself, consisting of a buff woody and thin shell, is oblong-round, and at the ends somewhat...

# CHAPTER TEN.

## The Remaining Smaller Wild Nutmegs, Palala Kitsjil.

**T**he remaining four wild species all bear much smaller fruits and differ little from one another, so that we shall therefore include them all together in one chapter; the *third Palala* has the smallest leaves of all, also placed in rows opposite one another, though with few pairs. The flowers are small, dull white heads, like grains of Wheat or Barley, opening slightly at the front. The fruits are the size of acorns, but somewhat narrower and more pointed at both ends, green on the outside like apples or like true Nutmegs; the inner part is small and oblong, scarcely a finger-joint long, consisting of a hard black shell, and, as in the true Nutmegs, is surrounded by a very red mace. The inner kernel is like an Olive stone, but more blunt at both ends, and in substance like true Nutmegs, or a little whiter; both the kernel and mace are without any spiciness.

*Name.* Third Palala, and Dyeing Palala <note>Latin: *Palala tingens*</note>. In Malay, *Palala Dauer Kitsjil*, that is, "small-leaved"; and likewise in Amboinese it is called *Palala laun Maun*.

*Location.* It grows mostly on Amboina, in the Hitu region, in the high forests.

*Use.* The straight trunks of the tree serve as poles and thin posts in Amboinese houses. The red mace, when rubbed between the fingers, becomes slimy and stains them a fiery red; but if a little lime and a leaf of the small *Waringin* <note>a species of Ficus or Banyan tree</note> are added, it becomes a red pigment with which the inhabitants dye their teeth to make them red, which they consider an ornament. It is used all the more because it gives off a slight aromatic scent when rubbed, especially when mixed with something acidic. In the same way, they dye their nails with the herb called *Alcanna* <note>Henna</note>, a custom frequent throughout all the Indies that is very ancient and universal. The people of Makassar, however, and some other Indians, prefer shining black teeth, and dye them as such with certain herbs.

*The fourth Palala* has somewhat smaller and narrower leaves than those of the second Palala, also standing in rows on both sides, but fewer in number; they are also smoother and on the underside not pale or gray, but of an ordinary greenness. The flowers sprout from the leaf axils, being many golden-yellow heads joined together in a cluster, shaped like the blossoms of the true Nutmeg, but much smaller and more pointed, slightly open at the front, and showing in the middle a small green knob <note>the pistil</note>, from which the fruit comes. This has the shape of a half-grown *CANARI* <note>the Canarium nut</note>, or slightly narrower, of a deep bluish-green color, with a small groove running all around its length. The kernel and mace inside are like the preceding species, without taste or smell, and have no use, but are left for the wild birds.

The people of Boero <note>Buru</note> cook the husk of the fruit with their fish; for it has a pleasant and tart flavor.

The wild pigeons, Cockatoos, and annual birds eat the entire fruits, but they mostly bite the husk into pieces, and swallow the whole kernel.

# CHAPTER X.

## The Remaining Small Wild Nutmeg Trees.

**T**he remaining four wild species all bear much smaller fruits, and differ little from one another, so that we shall therefore include them together in one Chapter; *Palala tertia* has the smallest leaves of all, also standing in rows opposite each other, but with few pairs: The flowers are small dirty white buds, like Barley grains, opening a little at the front; the fruits are the size of Acorns, but somewhat narrower, and sharper at both ends, apple-green on the outside, or like the true Nuts; the inside is small and elongated, barely a joint of a finger long, consisting of a hard black shell, and as in the true Nuts, surrounded by a very red mace. The innermost kernel is like an Olive-stone, but somewhat blunter at both ends, and in substance like the true Nuts, or somewhat whiter, and both the kernel and mace are without any spiciness.

*Name.* Palala tertia, and Palala tingens: in Malay *Palala Dauer Kitsjil*, that is small-leaved: and likewise in Amboinese *Palala laun Maun*.

*Place.* It was mostly on Ambon, in the Hitu Country, in the high forests.

*Use.* The straight trunks serve for rafters and thin posts in the Amboinese houses; the red mace, rubbed between the fingers, becomes slimy, and dyes them fire-red, but if some lime with a leaf of small Waringin is added to it, it becomes a red with which the inhabitants dye their teeth, to make them red, which is held by them as an ornament, and also used the more because it gives off a small aromatic scent in the rubbing, when it is mixed with some acidity: in the same way as they dye their nails with the herb *Alcanna*, being a custom throughout all the Indies, which is very old and general. But the Macassars, and some other Indians, favor black glistening teeth more, and also dye them so with some herbs.

*Palala quarta* has somewhat smaller and narrower leaves than those of Palala secunda, also standing in rows on both sides, but fewer in number, they are also smoother and on the underside not pale or gray, but of ordinary greenness. The small flowers come forth from the lap of the leaves, being gold-yellow buds, many standing together in a cluster, and shaped like the blossom of the true Nutmegs, but much smaller and sharper, a little opened at the front, and showing in the middle a green bud, from which the fruit comes forth, having the shape of a half-grown CANARI, or somewhat narrower, of a color deep blue-green, with a small cleft going all around the length. The kernel and mace is inside like the preceding, without taste and smell, having also no use, but is left for the wild Birds.

<meta>This page continues the classification of wild nutmeg species from Chapter Ten, specifically detailing the fourth, fifth, and sixth varieties of "Palala" (wild nutmeg), along with the descriptions for the accompanying botanical illustrations in Plates 7 and 8.</meta>

AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. chap. X.

*Name.* In Latin *Fourth Palala*, and *Canary-shaped* <note>original: "Canari-formis," referring to the Canarium nut</note>, in Malay *Palali-Canari*.

The *Fifth Palala* or *Globe-like Palala* <note>original: "Globularia"</note> bears leaves not much larger than those of the true Nutmeg tree, but a little narrower and smoother, being four or five inches long and two fingers wide, with few slanted ribs; they grow solitary and without order, hanging from the small branches. The fruits sprout behind the new shoots from the thicker branches, sitting on thick and woody stems where the flowers were first supported, consisting of similar yellow heads as in the previous species.

The fruits resemble short clusters of grapes, consisting of many individual berries joined together, and they have the size of semi-ripe grapes, but are more oblong, wrinkled on the outside, and somewhat sandy, of a reddish color. Their outer husk is thin but quite hard, gaping into two parts along a thin groove; beneath this is located a blood-red mace <note>original: "macis," the lacy covering of the nutmeg seed</note> surrounding most of the nut, with a slightly sour taste. This small nut is wrapped in a thin and pale-yellow shell, which has on one side a barely noticeable and short point like a little thorn, similar to the *Second Palala*. This shell is filled with a tasteless pith that somewhat resembles the Nutmeg and gradually hardens. The tree is low but quite thick, and it grows in the smaller forests at the base of the mountains.

*Name.* In Latin *Fifth Palala* or *Globe-like Palala*. Among the Amboinese, it has not obtained a specific name, but is called by the common name shared with the previous one, *Palala Kitsjil* <note>original: "Palala Kitsjil"; *Kitsjil* or *kecil* is Malay for "small"</note>.

The *Sixth Palala* does not differ much from the preceding one, but it has a medium-sized trunk covered with smooth and blackish bark, which drips a light-reddish sap if it is cut. Its branches are long, curved, and knotty, and the leaves match the previous species, but four or five are positioned opposite one another at the tips of the small branches. Some of these leaves are eleven inches long, others only seven or eight, with a width of two or two and a half inches, having many transverse ribs; they are grayish-green on the underside. The flowers are like the prior species, and the fruits hang solitary, resembling short Olives, but are a little thicker at the top; the external color is reddish and wrinkled, as if they were sprinkled with sand. Inside is located an oblong small nut, hardly the size of a hazelnut kernel, entirely covered by a thick, red, and slimy mace that is tasteless and resembles pulp more than true mace. Inside this is hidden a small, oblong kernel, a little smaller than an Olive stone, and also tasteless.

*Name.* In Latin *Sixth Palala*, nor does it have a specific name among the Amboinese.

*Place.* The tree grows in the smaller forests in the mountains. The fruits serve as food for birds, and the wood is suitable only for building things that do not need to last long.

## Plate Eight,

Showing a branch of the *Wild Nutmeg*, with simple, oblong leaves and striped clustered fruits. Which is called *Toothed Palala* <note>original: "Palala dentaria"</note> and *Canary-shaped* <note>original: "Canari-formis"</note> by RUMPHIUS.

<meta>catchword: EXPLANATION</meta>

<column-break/>

*Name.* In Latin *Fourth Palala*, and *Canary-shaped*, in Malay *Palali-Canari*.

The leaves of the *Fifth Palala*, or *Globe-like Palala*, are not much larger than those of the true *Nutmeg tree*, yet somewhat narrower and smoother, namely 4 and 5 inches long, and two fingers wide, with few slanted ribs, hanging singly and without order on their short twigs. The fruits come forth behind the shoots on the thicker twigs, and on thick and woody stems, where first the blossom comes forth, consisting of similar yellow buds like the previous ones.

The fruits truly resemble short grape-clusters, consisting of many berries together, and also having the size of half-ripe grapes, yet are somewhat more oblong, rough and sandy on the outside, and of a reddish-tan color. The outermost husk is not thick, but reasonably hard, bursting in two along a dark seam, and beneath it lies a bright red mace, mostly surrounding the little nut, and somewhat sourish in taste. The little nut is covered with a thin and pale shell, having on one side a short and barely recognizable little thorn like the *Second Palala*, and this shell is entirely filled with a tasteless pith, which looks somewhat like the *Nutmeg*, and becomes hard in time. It remains a low but reasonably thick tree, and grows in the light forests on the front of the mountains.

*Name:* In Latin *Fifth Palala*, or *Globe-like Palala*: Among the Amboinese it has no special name, but a common one with the previous *Small Palala* <note>original: "Palala Kitsjil"</note>.

The *Sixth Palala* differs not much from the preceding, but this one grows to a medium trunk, with a black and smooth bark, which also gives out a light-red sap when one cuts into it. The branches are long, crooked, and knotty, and the leaves also resemble the preceding, standing four or five at the ends of the twigs opposite each other: some eleven inches long, and others 7 and 8, as well as two and two-and-a-half inches wide, with many cross-ribs, and blue-green on the underside. The flowers are mostly like the previous ones, and the fruits hang only singly, resembling short Olives, though they are somewhat thicker at the front, orange-yellow or reddish-tan on the outside, and somewhat rough, as if they were strewn with sand. Inside lies an oblong little nut, hardly as large as the kernel of a hazelnut, entirely covered or surrounded with a thick red slimy mace, yet without taste, and resembling a flesh better than a mace; inside that lies a small oblong kernel, somewhat smaller than an olive stone, and also without taste.

*Name.* In Latin *Sixth Palala*: Having also no special name among the Amboinese.

The tree grows in light forests on the mountains. The fruits are for the birds, and the wood is only fit for short-lived timber work.

## CHAPTER ELEVEN.
->Aloeswood and Paradise Wood.<- <note>original: "Agallochum. Calambac." and "Aloës- en Paradys-Hout."</note>

Our intention here is by no means to provide a perfect description of Aloeswood <term>Agallochum: also known as agarwood or oud, a fragrant, resinous heartwood produced by trees in the Aquilaria genus when infected by mold</term>, since the tree that produces this precious wood is thus far unknown to Europeans, as far as I know. It grows in places or regions very far removed from the sea, and indeed among barbarous peoples with whom our nation has almost no conversation, or if they do exercise trade with them, they do not dare to venture deep into their lands. I could not, however, omit noting down those things which I have learned of this wood from the reports or hearsay of others, or have been taught by my own experience. I took this opportunity from the familiarity I maintained with certain Chinese people <note>original: "Sinensibus"</note> who have traveled through those lands and, as I believe, knew it well; especially since I have observed that among us Europeans, a very obscure and uncertain knowledge is found, and various woods are sold as true *Agallochum*, which has nevertheless been held in great esteem and value throughout the entire East since ancient times, and is still so held. The true Aloeswood tree, therefore (as far as I could learn from the reports of the Chinese), has only two primary species, although both come from one and the same tree. The best and most precious species of this is called *Calambac* <term>Calambac: the highest quality of agarwood, often so saturated with resin it sinks in water</term> by the inhabitants, in Latin *Primary Agallochum*; the other or secondary species is called *Garo* <note>commonly known today as gaharu</note>, or *Secondary Agallochum*.

Concerning both these species, the Chinese told me the following. The tree that produces the true *Calambac* or *Agallochum* grows in the Provinces of *Tsjampaa* <note>Champa, in modern-day Vietnam</note>, *Cocinam* or *Quinam* <note>Quinhon</note>, and *Cochin China*, which regions are also called *Tsjampaa, Coinam*, and *Koutsche* by the Chinese merchants. In *Tsjampaa* itself, the best occurs, and since this Province is under the rule of the King of *Coinam* or *Quinam*, all the best *Calambac* is delivered to him alone, so that he alone may trade in it.
These same Chinese told me that the tree is of the genus called by me *Mycrophylli* <note>Latin: small-leafed</note>, described below in *Book 5*, and enjoying the same leaves or perhaps a little larger, called by them *Tsjen-Tsjeny*. However, they do not agree whether it is also a milk-producing <note>latex-bearing</note> tree or not. I myself doubt whether this should not rather be understood of the tree that provides the common *Garo*, since the tree yielding the true *Calambac* grows too far inland and among very wild nations. For then it would also be a vast and wild tree, consisting of many tangled branches, twisted through itself and other trees, living a very long time, and extending itself over a very wide area.

This precious wood is not always produced by this tree, nor does every tree that bears it have it in all its parts, but only in its old age, and then only in certain branches

## XI. CHAPTER.
->Aloeswood and Paradise Wood.<-

Our intention is in no way to give a complete description of *Agallochum* at this place, since the tree that produces that precious wood is until now unknown to Europeans (as far as I am aware); as it grows in places or lands lying very far from the seaside, and then also among certain Barbarous Nations with whom our people have no, or little, interaction, or if they are admitted to that trade, they do not dare to come far inland. I have, however, not been able to pass by without noting down as much as I have learned of the same through hearsay and experience: having been given occasion for this by a familiar interaction I held with certain Chinese, who have traveled through those lands and, by guess, had good knowledge of that wood; also because I have perceived that among us Europeans there is still a very dark and uncertain knowledge of it, and many kinds of wood are sold for the upright Agallochum, which nevertheless has been in such great respect and esteem throughout the entire Eastern World from many or ancient times, and still is. The true Agallochum then (as far as I have been able to learn from the account of the aforementioned Chinese) has only two main sorts, although both come from the same kind of tree, and of which the noblest and very best is called *Calambac*, in Latin *Agallochum Primarium*: and the second or next sort in value *Garo*, or *Agallochum Secundarium*:

And concerning both these sorts, the Chinese have given me the following report: The tree that bears the true *Calambac* grows in the Provinces of *Tsjampaa, Coinam*, or *Quinam*, and *Cochin China*: which lands are also named *Tsjampaa, Coinam*, and *Koutsche* by the Chinese Merchants. But in *Tsjampaa* the best is found, and because this Province stands under the King of *Coinam* or *Quinam*, all the best *Calambac* must be delivered to him, and he then alone deals in it.
The same Chinese also related to me that it is a tree of the genus of Ferns <note>This likely refers to a leaf shape or classification rather than true ferns</note>, named by us in *Book 5* as *Mycrophyllos*, and also with the same leaves, or perhaps somewhat larger, named by them *Tsjen-tsjeny*, but they do not agree on whether it is also milk-giving or not. However, I doubt whether this should not much more be understood of the tree from which the common *Garo* comes, since the tree of the true *Calambac* is found too far inland and among very wild Nations. For then it would also have to be a large and wild tree with many tangled branches, slung through itself and other trees, living very long, and spreading itself far out:
This precious wood it does not always bear, nor does every tree that produces it have it in all its parts, but only in its old age, and that only on certain branches

<header>AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chapter XI.</header>

...great old age <note>original: "ma senectute"</note>, and only in certain branches or parts of the trunk. Since the tree is so vast and wild, growing in high and remote forests, great labor is required to detect the signs by which it can be known if it is mature and "pregnant" with this wood. Most Chinese say that these signs are visible to no one; however, the lord of that place or region, while walking near the tree, sometimes perceives a most pleasant scent. He must follow and investigate this with his nose—one of his five senses—until he perceives the scent is strongest near this or that trunk or branch, from which he judges that *Calambac* <note>high-quality agarwood</note> is contained within.

Others say that a shining and almost fiery splendor can be observed during the night where the mature *Calambac* is hidden. The lord of the place indicates these signs to the King, who then grants him permission to cut around the tree. Without the King's consent, it is forbidden for a private person to uproot such a tree under penalty of death. Then, the owner first performs certain sacrifices to this tree to appease the *Djing* <note>original: "Djing seu genius"; a spirit or local deity</note> who, in their opinion, guards the tree, while simultaneously praying that it will grant him a bountiful supply of wood. This sacrifice begins with cows, pigs, or goats; then he takes a bowl full of cooked *Oryza* <term>rice</term>, making the top so smooth that not a single grain could be removed without it being noticed immediately. To this, he adds a small salted fish, which he places with the rice under the tree, and he lies down there to sleep for the night. He does this with the imagination that if the tree is sufficiently mature and bears perfect *Kila* <note>another term for high-grade resinous wood</note>, he will perceive it in his sleep. Very early in the morning, he inspects the rice closely; if he finds that only three or four grains have been taken, he declares the tree mature and old enough. If, however, a larger amount has been taken, or a large pit appears in the rice, he believes the tree is not yet perfect or mature enough, saying that it is still "too hungry."

The mature tree is immediately cut around and divided into pieces; indeed, it is even dug up to the roots. The two lower segments of the trunk contain the best *Kila*, being dark brown in color and so soft and fatty that it can be indented with a fingernail. These two pieces must be saved for the King, who is said to possess such pieces as large as a medium-sized table. The remaining *Kila*, which is cut from the branches and roots, is also good and soft but of a lower sort and price; it is divided among the nobles and lords of the region. As soon as it is cut, the *Kila* is good and does not need to be buried again. However, some cutters hide certain fragments under the earth, leaving them there until the guard, who was stationed around the tree during the cutting, has departed. The King then records in which year and month such a tree was cut, so that further cutting may be deferred for several years, lest the world acquire too much of this wood and its price and reputation be diminished. For they carry on a precious trade with this wood, which in our time has been much rarer and more costly than in ancient times.

If only wood that can be indented with the nails is worthy of the name *Calambac* or *Kila*, then there are truly few people who have seen it, since the common pieces sold and shown as *Calambac* can hardly pass that test. Nevertheless, they give off a most noble and penetrating scent when placed on hot coals; for no *Calambac* has such a strong scent on its own unless it is rubbed and chafed in the hands for a long time until it grows warm. Others, on the contrary—especially those Chinese whose homeland is *Coinama* <term>Cochinchina, in modern-day Vietnam</term>—relate that no one knows the true tree, but that there are trees of various kinds which sometimes give off this scent. Therefore, they say all *Calambac* pieces come from unknown trees that overflowing rivers leave in the mud or marshes. These are found by chance; once the outer wood has rotted away, the inner, fatty pieces remain, which are left as irregular and disordered as they were found, merely being cleaned of adhering earth. However, this seems to contradict the report that the King of Cochinchina can acquire such huge pieces whenever he desires.

<column-break/>

...branches or parts of the stem: and because it is such a wild tree, growing in high and wild forests, one must take much trouble to know the signs by which one can tell if it is ripe and "pregnant" with that wood. Yet most Chinese say that no one can know this sign, but that the owner of the land, walking thereabouts, sometimes becomes aware of a very lovely smell, which he must then follow with his nose—one of his five senses—until he notices at which stem or branch the smell is strongest. From this, he judges that *Calambac* must be stuck inside.

Others also say that by night one could see a fiery glow or light where the ripe *Calambac* is hidden. These and similar signs are then made known to the King by the owner, and he then gives permission to chop that tree; for without his consent, it is forbidden for a private person to fell such a tree upon penalty of death. Thereupon the owner must first make some offerings to that tree to reconcile the *Djing* <note>original: "Djing, of geest"; spirit</note> who, according to their belief, guards the tree, and to pray that he will richly share this wood with them. This is done with cows, pigs, or goats; after that, he also takes a bowl full of cooked rice, smoothing it so that one cannot take even a grain of it without it being noticed. To this, he adds a salted little fish, which he sets under the tree along with the rice, and goes to lie there to sleep at night with the notion that if the tree now has real old and full-grown *Kilam*, he will see or become aware of it in a dream. Going then in the morning to look closely at the rice, if he finds only 3 or 4 grains have been taken from it, he says that the tree is full-grown and old enough; but if more is taken out and a large hole is in the rice, then he says or believes that the tree is still too young, as having still too much craving and appetite to eat.

The full-grown tree is now immediately felled and chopped into pieces, yes, even dug out to the roots, and the two lowest sections of the stem have the best *Kilam*, being of a dark brown color, also so soft and fatty that one can push into it with a fingernail. And these two pieces one must save only for the King, who is said to have pieces of it as large as a medium table. The other *Kilam* that one chops from the branches and roots is also good and soft, but somewhat lesser, and that is divided among the Great ones and owners of the land. As soon as it is chopped it is good *Kilam*, and it does not need to be buried again; though some of the cutters do hide some pieces under the earth, letting them lie there until the guard, who stands around the tree during the chopping, has departed. And it is recorded by the King in what year and month this tree was chopped down, to the end that one might rest for some years, and the world might not obtain too much of this wood, so that its great esteem would not be lost. For they drive a dear merchant trade with it, being in our time much rarer and more precious than it has been in olden times.

And if only that wood may bear the name of *Calambac* or *Kilam* into which one can push with the nail, then there are in fact few people who have seen it, since the common pieces that one shows and sells for *Calambac* can hardly stand that test, although they nonetheless have a very noble and powerful smell, namely when one lays it on coals; for otherwise no *Calambac* smells so strong of itself, unless one rubs it in the hands so long until it becomes warm. Others, on the contrary, and among them some Chinese who were born in *Coinama* <note>Cochinchina</note>, relate that no one knows the right tree, but that it is many kinds of trees mixed together which sometimes give off the aforementioned air, and therefore that the *Calambac* are pieces of unknown trees which the overflowing rivers leave sitting in the mud or marsh, which one then finds by chance, and on which all the outermost wood is rotted, and the innermost firm pieces remain, which one then leaves as lumpy or uneven as one finds them, merely cleaning them of the adhering earth. However, this seems to conflict with the above story of those large pieces which the King of Cochinchina can get if he wants.

# Book II. Chapter XI. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

True and common <term>Calambac</term> <note>high-quality agarwood or aloeswood</note> or <term>Agallochum</term> is of two colors: the first is a dark brown mixed with ash-gray, and is streaked with long blackish veins; or, if it was gathered from around the knots <note>the gnarled joints of the tree</note>, it is variegated with similar small veins. If this wood is fresh and gathered from true, ancient trees, it has certain sections so fatty and soft that they can be pressed inward; however, if it has been kept for many years, it hardens and becomes heavy.

The other type is more of an ash-gray than brown, consisting of thicker veins, streaked along its length with blackish veins or short lines, and marked with various pits or hollowed out with holes, in which some part of the earth is often still found. It is also lighter than the preceding type, and perhaps this is the kind gathered from the true trunk or branches that has rotted in the swamps. For that which was around the knots is much blacker, consists of shorter fibers, and is harder than the rest. Moreover, everything that tends toward a yellow or pale color and bears black spots, as if it were sweating a black resin, is to be considered a species of <term>Gari</term> <note>a lower grade of eaglewood</note>. The scent of all species of <term>Agallochum</term> is of the same kind, and when the wood is placed upon coals, it is easily recognized and distinguished from all other woods; for it has a peculiar, pleasant scent, and is refreshing and as if strengthening to the heart—which can be better felt than described—and the scent tends toward the smell of dried citron peels; the taste is also somewhat similar to them. The best wood, if chewed, is tough like hard wax, mixed with a small but pleasant and sharp bitterness, filling the whole mouth with a grateful scent. However, all those woods that have an exceeding bitterness are to be considered neither <term>Agallochum</term> nor <term>Gari</term>, but rather as certain bastards of these two species.

Names: In Latin <term>Agallochum Primarium</term> <note>Primary Agallochum</note> and <term>Xylaloë</term> <note>Wood-aloes</note>; in the pharmacies <term>Lignum aloës</term> <note>Aloeswood</note>, and from this in Dutch, <term>Aloës-hout</term> and <term>Paradys-hout</term> <note>Paradise-wood</note>. By the Arabs it is called <term>Agalugin</term> and <term>Aud</term>, and from this among those of Gujarat <term>Ud</term>. In Malay <term>Calambac</term>. In Chinese <term>Kilam</term> and <term>Hokilam</term>, from which perhaps that Malay name is derived, as if you were to say the knots or the pith of <term>Kilam</term>; for the Chinese call "Bac" not only gems <note>or eyes</note>, but also knots, and especially the fattest parts of the tree in which the veins are mixed together and present the form of an eye. This is also the same wood which among the Hebrews is called <term>Ahalim</term> and <term>Ahaloth</term> in the plural number: just as all pleasantly smelling and precious woods that are for sale and sold in small pieces or segments are indicated by them with this word. However, these two denominations are explained in various ways by the translators; for Saint Jerome in the Vulgate <note>the 4th-century Latin Bible</note> at Numbers 24, verse 6, translates it as "tents" <note>original: "tentoria"</note>. In Psalm 45, verse 9, as "Gutta" <note>a fragrant gum</note> and in Proverbs 7 as "Aloë". Modern translators, however, in Numbers 24 translate it as "Sandalwoods" <note>original: "Santalos"</note>; and in other places "Aloes," and the commentators mention nothing else to us except that it is a pleasantly smelling wood, used for precious incense. It is certain that the Hebrew <term>Ahalim</term> or <term>Ahaloth</term> was nothing other than the <term>Agallochum</term> or <term>Xylaloë</term> of the Greeks and Latins, which from ancient times was used for the perfuming of garments, a use which it serves even today. On the contrary, <term>Sandalwood</term> was unknown to the ancients, nor is it used for incense on a fire. But a small difficulty remains: namely, that Balaam, in the aforementioned place, compares the Israelite people to the <term>Ahalim</term> trees, which God planted by the rivers. To which someone might suggest or object: how could Balaam have had knowledge of <term>Calambac</term> trees, since these grow in the farthest parts of India, and their appearance and form are so obscure and uncertain even to this day? To which I answer, the ancients, and especially those who inhabited Mesopotamia and Babylonia under the flourishing Monarchy, had a much better knowledge of many Indian plants than we do today, since at that time those regions could be better traveled through, and the Babylonian majesty exercised greater power and social interaction in the Indian regions. From this, Balaam could without doubt have known that the <term>Ahalim</term> were huge and vast trees, growing in the flat forests and wildernesses near the river Ganges and other rivers there, extending themselves very widely and luxuriously with their branches, and reaching extreme old age, from which this scented wood (which was without doubt sufficiently used and known among the kings of Assyria) came. Therefore, Balaam wished to pronounce that the Israelite people were so blessed by God,
<meta>catchword: tot-</meta>

<column-break/>

*The true and the common* Calambac *is now of two kinds of color, the first being dark brown mixed with gray, and streaked with long black veins, or, if it stood near the knots, marbled with similar small veins. And when this is fresh, and moreover comes from truly old trees, then it has some parts that are so fatty and soft that one can press into them; but when it has been kept for many years, it becomes hard and heavy.*

*The other kind is somewhat grayer than the brown, coarse-grained, streaked lengthwise with black veins or short lines, and hollowed out with various little pits or holes, in which one sometimes still finds some earth stuck. It is also lighter than the preceding, and perhaps is that which comes from the true trunk or the branches, and has lain rotting in the swamps; for that which stood near the knots is considerably blacker, shorter-grained, and harder than the other. All that wood which mostly tends toward yellow or pale, and has black spots as if it sweated some black resin, one must count among the kind* Garo. *The scent of all kinds of* Calambac *is mostly the same, and being laid on coals, it is very recognizable and easy to distinguish from all other woods, for it is of a special loveliness, very refreshing and heart-strengthening, which one can better feel than describe; and the scent must tend somewhat toward that of dried citron peels. The taste must also almost correspond to that; and the best feels somewhat tough in the chewing, like hard wax, mixed with a small, yet pleasant sharp bitterness, and filling the mouth with its pleasant scent. However, one must not take all such woods that have an exceptional bitterness for* Calambac *nor for* Garo, *but rather for bastards of one of those two.*

Names: In Latin Agallochum Primarium, and Xylaloë; in the pharmacies Lignum Aloes, and so in Dutch Aloës-hout and Paradys-hout. Arabic: Agalugin, and Aud, and from those both the Gujaratis use Ud. Malays: Calambac. Chinese: Kilam, and Hokilam, from which perhaps the aforementioned Malay name comes, as if one said knots or the heart of Kilam; for the Chinese call "Bac" not only an eye, but also the knots and the fattest parts of a tree where the veins run through each other and make the shape of an eye. And this is the same wood which by the Hebrews is called Ahalim and Ahaloth in the plural number, just as all sweet-smelling and dear woods that are brought for sale in small pieces or slices were so named by those people. However, the two aforementioned words were explained differently by the translators, for Saint Jerome in the Vulgate, Numbers 24, verse 6, translates it as Tents; Psalm 45, verse 9, Gutta; and Proverbs 7, Aloe. The modern translators translate it in Numbers 24 as Sandalwoods, and in other places Aloe, and the interpreters know nothing else to tell us of it but that it is a sweet-smelling wood, used for costly perfumes. It is certain that the Hebrews' Ahalim or Ahaloth was nothing other than what the Greeks and Latins call Agallochum or Xylaloe, which has been used since ancient times for the perfuming of clothes, as it still is. In contrast, Sandalwood was unknown to the ancients, and is by no means used for perfume on the fire. A small difficulty remains: namely, that Balaam, in the above-mentioned place, compares the people of Israel to the Ahalim trees, which God planted by the water streams. Upon which one might bring in or ask, how Balaam could have had knowledge of Calambax trees, since those grow in the furthest part of the Indies, and whose form is until now so obscurely or dimly known. To which I answer, that the ancients, especially those who lived in Mesopotamia and Babylonia under that flourishing Monarchy, had much better knowledge of many Indian plants than we do today, because then the lands could be more easily traveled through, and the Babylonian Power held more respect and interaction in the lands of the Indies; from which, without doubt, Balaam could have known that Ahalim were large trees, growing in the level forests and wildernesses along the River Ganges and other rivers thereabouts, and spreading themselves very far and luxuriantly with their branches, and coming to a great age, and from which that sweet-smelling wood (which among the Assyrian Kings was without doubt enough...

# BOOK II. CHAPTER XI. OF THE AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...and endowed with so many benefits, that it was as firmly established as the living *Ahalim* <note>original Latin: "Ahalim arbores"; a reference to the Hebrew word for aloeswood used in the Bible</note> trees, and their glory and splendor would likewise be spread throughout the whole world like a gratefully breathing and pleasant scent.

Thus it must also be judged that *Cassia* and *Cinnamon*, although they grow very far away in the Indies, were better known to the *Assyrian* and *Israelite* kings at that time than in the subsequent interval of two thousand years, until these spices were again discovered through the voyages of the *Portuguese* and the *Dutch*.

Why the *Agallochum* wood was called *Paradys-hout* <note>Dutch for "Paradise-wood"</note> or *Paradisal wood* by the Dutch can be more easily and better investigated, since from ancient times it was sought only from those regions situated around the *Ganges*, which river is thought to take its origin from the earthly Paradise itself. It was called Aloes-wood not so much because of its bitterness (which, as has been said, is keenly felt in the true kind), but rather from the harmony of the words *Ahalim* and *Agaluchin*, in which the Greeks observed some similarity to their own *Aloë*, and hence they called it *Xylaloë*, that is, "Wood-Aloe," while also adding a distinction so that it might be taken for a wood and not for the herbaceous Aloe plant.

**Locations.** True Aloes-wood, as far as is known today, grows (as has been said) in *Tsjampaa* <note>Champa, in modern-day Vietnam</note>, called *Champaa* by the Portuguese and *Tsjamfiäa* by the Chinese. This is a tributary province under the great King of *Coinam* or *Quinam*, which region is also called *Cochin-China*, and *Kautfchi* by the Chinese—which denotes someone who has a curved big toe, as the inhabitants and natives of this region have been known by this mark since ancient times. It also grows in *Cambodia* and *Siam*, which regions are neighboring and adjacent to those lands, and without doubt in many other lands very close to them, through which the great river *Ganges* and many others flowing out of the great lake *Kiamhay* annually inundate the surrounding flat lands and forests, filling them with mud, just as the *Nile* does to *Egypt*. By this inundation, many such trees are undoubtedly uprooted and covered in mud; later, pieces of Aloes-wood are found there, specifically after the outer part of the wood has rotted away, leaving the inner and most resinous parts, which are able to resist rot.

**The King of Champa.** He must not only provide the best pieces as tribute to the King of *Coinam*, but must sell all the remaining *Kilam* <note>a high grade of agarwood</note> to him, which he alone holds in trade, and sends most of it to *Japan*. The common people are forbidden under penalty of death from engaging in trade with this wood, so that everything must be bought from the King's hands. Since he is a great enemy of the Dutch, our nation cannot gather much from him, which is why it is so little known to our people. Others, however, believe that the King of *Champa* by no means sends the largest pieces to the King of *Coinam*, being well aware that if he once granted such large pieces, the King would always demand them; thus, the best and largest pieces are undoubtedly found in *Champa*. The current price of this wood in *Champa* is thirty-two *Teyl* <note>taels</note> of silver, that is, forty imperial rix-dollars, for one chest called a *Catti* <note>a unit of weight, roughly 1.25 lbs</note>, or one and a quarter pounds. If it is sent to Japan, one *Catti* is worth a hundred such *Teylen*; however, our people buy it there even more dearly, even at the weight or value of gold. It is not, or very rarely, brought to Europe, since the Japanese, Chinese, and other Indians buy it at the highest price and desire it much more than we Europeans do.

**Usage.** It is used for all precious incense; however, because it is so expensive, it is mostly kept by the Kings and Great Men of India. They mix it with other aromatic barks and gums that have been coarsely crushed, and from these they form small pellets the size of a musket ball, called *Dupa* <note>incense pellets</note> by them. They scent their clothes with the smoke of these, and the Kings reserve this incense for themselves alone; so much so that if a private person were found with his clothes scented by this incense, he would run the risk of falling out of favor if it were noticed.

This common *Agallochum* truly has powers that refresh the heart and brain with its scent, whether it is used in that *Dupa* or placed alone upon coals. For this purpose, with a piece of broken porcelain or glass, one [shaves] from the wood...

*...was known as follows: He wished to say that the people of Israel were so blessed by God, and so firmly grounded, as the living Ahalim-trees, and that their luster, like a precious scent, would travel through the whole world.*

*And so one must also judge that Cassia and Cinnamon (though they also grow far away in the Indies) were much better known to the Assyrian and Israelite Kings back then than in the following two thousand years, until those spices were rediscovered through the voyages of the Portuguese and the Dutch.*

*But why this wood is called* Paradise-Wood *by the Germans is easier to guess: namely, because from of old it was brought only from the lands and harbors that lay around the Ganges, which river was believed to have its origin in the Earthly Paradise. It is called Aloes-wood not so much because of its bitterness (which, as said, must be slight in the genuine kind), but much more after the similarity of the words Ahalim and Agaluchin, in which the Greeks saw some likeness to their Aloe, and therefore called the same* Xylaloë*, that is* Aloes-Wood*, and at the same time as a warning that one should regard it as a wood and not as a herbaceous plant, the Aloe.*

Places: *The genuine Aloes-wood, as far as it is known today, grows (as said) in Champa, called Champaa by the Portuguese and Tsjamfiaä by the Chinese, a province standing under the great King of Koinam or Quinam, which land is also called Cochin-China, and Kautfchi by the Chinese, which means someone who has a crooked toe, as the inhabitants of this land have had of old. It also grows in Cambodia and Siam, which lands border one another with the aforementioned, and without doubt in more other lands bordering them, through which the great river Ganges and more others flow out of the great inland lake Kiamhay, which annually overflow the surrounding flat lands and forests and fill them with mud, just as the Nile does to Egypt, and by which then, without doubt, many such trees are uprooted and buried in the mud, from which one afterwards finds the pieces of Aloes-wood, namely after the outer wood has perished, leaving the innermost and fattest parts, which can withstand the rot.*

*The King of Champa must not only bring the best pieces as tribute to the King of Coinam, but also sell all other Kilam to him, in which he then trades alone, and indeed sends the greatest part to Japan. The common man is forbidden on pain of death to trade in this wood, so that one must get everything from the King's hands, and since he is a great enemy of the Dutch, our nation cannot get much of it, and it is therefore also so little known among our people. And others believe that the Champa ruler nonetheless by no means sends him the largest pieces, as he well knows that if he once accustomed the Coinammer to them, he would always want such pieces from him. So that without doubt the most beautiful and largest pieces are to be found in Champa. The current price of this wood in Champa is 32 Teyl of silver, that is 40 Rix-dollars for a Catti, or 1 1/4 pounds, and being brought to Japan it is worth indeed a hundred Teylen the Catti. However, our people must pay for it there more dearly, even against the weight of Gold. But to Europe it is not or very rarely transported, because the Japanese, Chinese, and other Indians give very much for it, and make significantly more of it than we Europeans have done until now.*

Usage: *It is also used for all kinds of precious incense; but because it is so dear, it remains mostly among the Kings and Great of India, who know how to mix it with other spice-like barks and gums, all coarsely pounded or chopped, and to make small balls from them in the shape and size of a pistol bullet, called Dupa by them, with which they scent thin clothes. And the Kings keep this incense so specifically for their own persons that a commoner would run a risk if it were perceived or noticed on his clothes.*

*The aforementioned Calambac indeed has a scent that strengthens the heart and brain, whether in the prescribed Dupa or smoked alone on coals, for which purpose one [shaves] some from the piece with a bit of broken porcelain or glass...*

The Malays, however, prefer the wood to be chopped into smaller pieces and then coarsely pounded; for they say that scraping makes the incense too fine, and when placed on coals, it vanishes too quickly and does not spread as pleasant a scent as when it has been coarsely pounded. If the Chinese burn it alone as incense, they add a little coarsely pounded *Scented Nail* <note>original Latin: *Unguis odoratus*; likely "Onycha," a fragrant seashell used in incense</note>, called *Hyolo* by them. However, if they can obtain two nodes of this wood, they carve them with many angles and pits until the earthy skin has been scraped away.

They use these shavings for incense, and they hang the cleaned nodes (which sometimes take on the appearance of certain small animals) from their fans, which they continually rub with their hands and sniff. A piece of the finest *Kila* <note>a high-quality grade of Aloeswood</note> or *Agallochum*, which can be pressed deeply with a fingernail, is carried in belts around the body to keep the bowels constricted and to prevent the release of wind <note>flatulence</note> when they appear before the eyes of Great Lords or sit before them for a long time; this is of great use to that nation, which is grave and fond of practicing solemnities. Furthermore, it is used in every medicine composed to strengthen the heart and inhibit its palpitations, as well as against fainting, oppression of the chest, and constriction of the throat caused by heat in the stomach, which is why it also works against *Cardialgia* <note>heartburn or stomach pain</note>. Some Chinese also use it internally against Dysentery, though the reason for this is unknown to me. For it has no astringent power, but rather a drying one—at least as far as I could perceive in the mouth—for I could observe nothing else except a slight bitterness, like Citron peel, and if swallowed, it leaves a small burning sensation in the throat.

Someone might now object to me: if Aloes-wood was known in the time of Moses and believed to be so necessary for all precious and perfect incense, how is it that it was not used for the holy perfume described in the thirtieth chapter of Exodus, where the sharply scented *Galbanum* was included? I answer that this holy perfume did not serve so much to refresh the nose as to foreshadow holy and hidden things, as the learned Jew *Aben-Ezra* <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a 12th-century scholar</note> teaches us. Moreover, it could be that God, the maker of all things, did not wish to tolerate or admit this wood into His Temple, since it is begged for, as if from the hands of the devil, by such idolatrous ceremonies. The Chinese also give this wood, crushed and mixed with weak *Arack* <note>a distilled spirit</note>, to drink against abdominal cramps and pains arising from a cold cause.

Truly, *Agallochum* or *Kila* is detected by this test: when rubbed strongly upon a polished stone, its shavings curl up like small worms or mouse-dung pellets.

## OBSERVATION.

Most authors have distinguished between *CALAMBAC* and *ALOES WOOD*, or *AGALLOCHUM*, and held them to be different woods, as is clear from *Ray's History of Plants, page 1808*, and *Samuel Dale's Pharmacologia in quarto, page 380*, where you should see the descriptions throughout, as well as *Parkinson's Theater, page 1564*, and the *General History of Lyon, book 18, chapter 17, page 1769*, and also its illustration in *Pomet’s General History of Drugs, Book III, Chapter I*, where *WOOD OF ALOES* is depicted and described. See also *Linschoten’s Itinerary, chapter 76*, concerning *Calambac* or *Aloes wood*, and *Valentyn’s Description of Amboina, page 204, chapter IV*, and *Valentyn’s Simplified Reformed History, page 179, chapter VI, and page 591 and following*, where an elegant dissertation occurs concerning *Agallochum*, which is described in the subsequent chapter; see further *Rumphius in the Miscellany of the Academy of Natural Curiosities, decade 2, year 3, observation 22, page 79*, and *Bonetus’ Northern Medicine, part 2, book 8, page 4, section 3*, as well as *Paul Hermann’s Materia Medica, page 107*, and *Jonston’s Natural History, book IX, page 460 and following*, and *Worm’s Museum, chapter 16, page 166*, as well as *Samuel Dale’s Pharmacologia, page 379*, and also *Kaempfer’s Exotic Amenities, page 903*, and *Ray, volume 3, appendix, page 87*.

But the Malays prefer it more if one first chops it into small pieces and then pounds it coarsely, for they say that scraping makes the incense too fine, and when it comes onto coals, it vanishes too quickly, nor does it smell half as lovely as when it is coarsely pounded. Now someone might object to me: if the Aloes-wood was known in the time of Moses and considered so necessary for all perfect perfumes, why then was it not also permitted in the holy perfume described in Exodus Chapter 30, where nevertheless the strong-smelling *Galbanum* found a place? I answer that the same holy perfume did not serve so much to delight the Nose as to represent a holy and hidden matter, as the learned Rabbi *Aben-Ezra* teaches us. Besides this, it may also be that God did not want this wood brought into His Temple because it was begged for with such Idolatrous Ceremonies, as if out of the hands of the Devils. The Chinese use this wood rubbed and drunk with weak *Arack* against cramps in the belly pain arising from cold.

The upright *Kilam* must pass this test: that when rubbed somewhat hard over a smooth stone, its shavings must roll together like small Worms or mouse-droppings.

# CHAPTER TWELVE.
## Secondary Agallochum. Garo.

This secondary or common Agallochum is next in rank to the previously described rare and precious Calambac, and it is this variety that is most frequently exported to our home countries <note>Europe and the Netherlands</note>. The accounts of the Chinese agree on this point: that this wood comes from one and the same tree as the preceding variety. The innermost, fattiest, and oldest pieces provide the true Calambac, while the wood found in the branches or around the knots is the spurious Agallochum, or *Garo*. This most common and least valuable wood is then found in the outer parts of the trunk. However, because I have observed a great difference in scent and color among the woods sold as *Garo*, I have learned through further inquiry from the Chinese that while the best *Garo* is found in the same tree as Calambac, there are also other trees, not much different from the first, which also bear a specific kind of *Garo*. That which comes from Malacca and grows on the islands of Johor and Belitung is also considered genuine *Garo*, though it differs from the variety from Quinam <note>Central Vietnam</note>. We shall therefore divide true *Garo* into two species: namely, the Coinamese <note>from Quinam/Vietnam</note> and the Malay.

*The first or Coinamese variety, called **Thim** and **Thimbio**, is the wood of a certain tree of the small-leafed genus <note>original Latin: Mycrophylli</note>; however, the leaves of the Garo are a little longer. On these trees one often observes very long "whips" or tendrils which hang from the branches like threads, as is also found in the small-leafed species. They also grow in the aforementioned regions of Champa and Quinam. Any owner may cut these down at his pleasure, provided he is well aware that the trees are old enough; they have certain signs for this, and there is no need to purify them with sacrifices as was required for the previous tree. This species consists mostly of knotty pieces which, if they are of good quality, must sink to the bottom in water. The price for a **Catty** <note>a unit of weight, roughly 1.3 lbs</note> of this wood is fixed by the King at three silver **Taels** <note>a Chinese weight and currency unit</note>.*

*This wood is much harder, knottier, and not as dark as Calambac, but tends more toward a yellow color. It is variegated with short black or brown veins; sometimes it is entirely ash-colored with black veins, closely mimicking Calambac, but it is always harder and heavier. In large pieces, black spots appear here and there on the sides as if they were smeared with pitch; these indicate the oiliness of the wood. These spots appear most prominently in the yellow pieces that were cut from around the knots. These pieces resist flame and glowing coals for some time and do not catch fire as easily as Calambac. Even if they do ignite, they do not hold the fire long because the wood is more solid and harder. Nevertheless, when burned, it also yields a small quantity of oil. From this, it is clear that most of the Agallochum found in Europe is of this species, for all writers testify that it resists fire for a time.*

*When placed on coals, this wood differs greatly in scent from Calambac. It has the same general character and quality of scent, but it turns from aromatic toward acidic, and sometimes the scent resembles Benzoin <note>a balsamic resin</note>. Such wood is also whiter or yellower, and its smoke stings the eyes more vehemently; for this reason, such pieces are not much used for incense. If this wood is scraped, the shavings are much finer and smoother than Calambac, and the scrapings do not curl up as much.*

**Name.** *In Latin, it is called **Agallochum secundarium Coinamense**, and in Malay, **Garo Cominjan**, because its smoke smells like **Cominjan**, that is, Benzoin. The Chinese call it **Thim** and **Thimbio**. The Dutch call it **Agel-hout**, from the Portuguese **Pao de Aquila**, which is undoubtedly derived from the Arabic **Agallugin** or the Latin **Agallochum**. Some people, not understanding this, have ridiculously called it **Lignum Aquilæ** <note>original: "Wood of the Eagle"</note> in Latin, and **Arents-bout** <note>original: "Eagle-stick"</note> in Dutch.*

**Locations.** *The best wood grows, like Calambac, in Champa, but it is brought to market in Quinam, where it also grows, though it is of less value than that from Champa.*
