# CHAPTER XII.
## Eagle-wood.

*Next in rank to the aforementioned rare and expensive Calambac is the **Agallochum secundarium**, or the common Eagle-wood <note>Dutch: Agel-hout</note>, which is mostly transported to our lands. The accounts of the Chinese mostly agree that this comes from the same tree as the former, in which the innermost, fattiest, and oldest pieces are the upright Calambac, but that which sits in the branches or around the knots is **Garo** or Eagle-wood, and the very poorest sits on the outside of the trunk. But because I found a notable difference in the smell and color among the timbers sold for **Garo**, I learned by further questioning the Chinese that indeed the best **Garo** occurs in one and the same tree as the Calambac, but that there are also other trees, not much different from the former, which also bear a particular **Garo**. It is also held for a genuine **Garo** that which comes from Malacca, and grows in the islands of Johor and on Belitung; though it differs somewhat from the Coinamese variety. We shall therefore divide the genuine **Garo** into two sorts: namely, the Coinamese and the Malay.*

*The First or proper Coinamese, named **Thim** and **Thimbio**, also occurs on a tree from the family of the small-leafed ferns <note>Note: Rumphius uses "ferns" (Varingen) here loosely for plants with specific leaf patterns</note>, but the Garo leaves are a bit longer, and one also finds on this tree such long threads, hanging like yarn from the branches, just like on the small-leafed plants, growing also in the above-named provinces of Champa and Quinam. Any owner may chop these at his pleasure, as long as he knows the trees are old enough, of which they also have their signs; and they do not need to make any offerings to them, as they did for the former. This sort consists mostly of knots or chunks, and if they are truly good, they must sink in water; the **Catty** of which is set by the King at three silver **Taels**.*

*This wood is much harder, knottier, and not as brown as the Calambac, but pulling somewhat toward the yellow, and speckled with short, black, or brown veins; sometimes entirely gray, with black veins, coming closest to the Calambac, but always harder and heavier. On the large pieces, one sees here and there on the ends some black spots, as if they were smeared with pitch, which is the oiliness of this wood; however, these spots are mostly seen on the yellow pieces, and those that stood around the knots. These pieces withstand the flame or glowing coal for a long time, and do not catch the fire as easily as the Calambac, and even if they have caught it, they do not hold it firmly, because they have a harder and firmer wood. Nevertheless, in burning they also give off a little oil from themselves, from which it appears that most of the Agallochum shown in Europe is of this sort, for all the writers testify that it resists the fire for a time.*

*The smell of this wood, being laid on coals, differs notably from the Calambac; for it has indeed the same property and nature, but pulls from the aromatic somewhat toward the sour, and sometimes a little toward the Benzoin; and the more white or yellow wood is on it, as well as the fewer veins one finds on it, the more it bites in the eyes, which is why one does not easily use such pieces for incense. In scraping, this wood falls much finer and smoother than the Calambac, and the shavings do not curl together so much.*

**Name.** *In Latin **Agallochum Secundarium Coinamense**, and in Malay **Garo Cominjan**, because in smoking it smells like **Cominjan**, that is, Benzoin. Chinese: **Thim** and **Thimbio**. In Dutch: **Agel-hout**, from the Portuguese **Pao de Aquila**, which is clearly descended from the Arabic **Agallugin**, or Latin **Agallochum**, which some not understanding, have ridiculously named **Lignum Aquilæ** in Latin, and in Dutch **Arents-bout** <note>Eagle-stick</note>.*

**Locations.** *The best grows like the Calambac in Champa, but is brought to market in Quinam, where it also grows, but poorer than the Champan variety.*

# BOOK II. CHAPTER XII.
## AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...and usually gives off a sour or musty smell. From these same regions, an even lesser grade of wood is brought, but one that floats on water; it is called *Ittbion* by the Chinese, which means "simple Agallochum," and a <term>Catti<gloss>A weight unit equal to about 600 grams</gloss></term> or chest of it costs one <term>tayl<gloss>A unit of silver currency</gloss></term>. This wood is mostly white, streaked here and there with brown veins, and is so light that it might be mistaken for decayed wood. However, where the oily veins run, it smells most pleasant, whether placed on coals or held in the mouth. Therefore, I conclude entirely that these are the outer and thinnest parts of the tree that yields the true <term>Calambac<gloss>The highest, most resinous grade of agarwood</gloss></term>. For this reason, it is also called *Calambac Poeti* and *Garo Timbol* by the Malays, meaning white and floating Aloes-wood; conversely, I believe the previously mentioned *Thim* comes from a specific and different tree, as was just mentioned.

**Usage.** These two species are used by the Chinese not so much for incense as for medicine, specifically for the same ailments for which we said *Calambac* is useful. In particular, a fine powder is prepared from *Thim*, which they say contains three species of this wood; a certain sweetness is also noted, as if licorice had been mixed into it.

They call this powder *Thimbion Saan*, as if one were to say in English <note>original: Latin "Trium Agallochorum Pulvis"</note> "Powder of the Three Agallochums." They use it extensively in all such diseases where the heart needs strengthening. In fevers, it is taken with pure water and has a pleasant taste. The floating *Garo timbol* is also used alone in medicine, namely against heart palpitations and great anxiety from a burning sensation in the stomach, ground with water and drunk; some also rub the body externally with it against heat.

In the region of Champa near the capital Puri, a tree is said to grow not far from the seashore which yields the true *Thim*. This is a very vast tree which in ancient times was once cut down, but its trunk was left to a height of four cubits <note>approx. 1.8 meters</note> and had sprouted many new branches. The lower part of its trunk was three cubits thick.

Its leaves are entirely similar to the smaller <term>Microphyllum<gloss>Likely referring to a type of small-leaved plant or fern</gloss></term>, but not much longer than a finger joint. It bears no fruit, just like the *Microphyllum* species, and from the branches also hang thick brown threads or "whips" like those of the *Microphyllum*. When the leaves are broken or the bark is wounded, they also exude milk, as does the *Microphyllum*.

This tree often spreads a pleasant *Calambac* scent from itself, but no one dares to cut a piece of it or break off a branch, for whoever does so is mox vexed by abdominal pain and his nose bleeds. The inhabitants believe this is brought about by a specific spirit <note>original: Latin "genio," Dutch "geest"</note> who is the guardian of this tree, and so it stands unharmed for all to see.

Among these species of Coinamese <note>from Quinam, in modern Vietnam</note> Aloes-wood, a third kind must also be included, which is the most common *Agallochum*. The tree for this wood is common throughout Quinam and Champa. These are tall trees that bear small round leaves, smaller than a <term>stuiver<gloss>A small Dutch coin</gloss></term>, many of which sit together on small stems. These trees, along with their branches, are cut down and chopped into smaller pieces, which are left in the forests to rot. Finally, the fragrant inner heartwood is found. This wood consists mostly of hard knots and is so similar to the aforementioned *Thim* that it might be taken for one and the same wood. However, this latter type does not have such black, resinous spots as *Thim*, though it otherwise almost matches it in scent, or is generally somewhat drier. The Chinese call this wood *Sock*, a name they use generally for common Aloes-wood, just as our people consider it the same as the preceding. A <term>Pickol<gloss>A weight of about 60 kilograms</gloss></term>, which is 100 *Catties* or 125 Dutch pounds, costs twenty-five *tayls* in Champa. This *Sock* mostly floats on the water.

The second species is the Malay Agallochum, by which we denote everything that grows in the Malay islands, such as around Malacca, on the islands of Johor, Bintang, etc., and especially on the island of Belitung, all situated between Sumatra and Borneo. This wood does not differ much from the Coinamese, and pieces are found among it that might be taken for true *Calambac*, as they are brown mixed with gray and have thick veins. It is quite light, and if chewed, it yields to the teeth like wax...

<column-break/>

...usually having a sour or musty smell. From these same regions, an even lesser grade is brought, which mostly floats on the water, called *Itthion* by the Chinese, which is simple Aloes-wood, of which a *Catti* costs a *tayl*. *This wood is mostly white, streaked here and there with brown veins, and is so light that one would take it for decayed wood; but where the fatty veins are, it smells very lovely, both when placed on coals and in the mouth. Therefore, I entirely believe that these are the outermost and thinnest parts of the tree that yields the upright Calambac, and that is why the Malays call it Calambac Poeti and Garo Timbol, which is white and floating Aloes-wood. On the other hand, I judge the aforementioned Thim to come from a specific tree, as was just said.*

**Usage:** These both species were used by the Chinese not so much for incense as for medicine, namely for the same defects as the upright *Calambac*. In particular, a fine white powder is prepared from the *Thim*, where they say three kinds of this wood are included, and one also senses a sweetness like that of licorice therein.

This powder they call *Thimhion Saan*, as if one said in Latin *Trium Agallochorum Pulvis* ("Powder of the Three Agallochums"), which they use much in all illnesses where the heart must be strengthened. In fevers, it is taken with clear water, and it is lovely of taste. The floating *Garo-timbol* is also used alone as medicine, namely against heart palpitations and great anxiety from burning in the stomach, rubbed with water and drunk; some also rub it externally on the body against the burning.

In the region of Champa by the capital Puri, it is said a tree stands not far from the shore that bears the upright *Thim*, and that it would be a very large tree which in old times was once chopped off, but the trunk was still kept well four fathoms <note>approx. 7 meters</note> high, and many new branches had sprouted out. The trunk at the bottom was well three fathoms in circumference.

The leaves are entirely like those of the small ferns <note>original: "Varingen"</note>, yet not much longer than a joint of a finger; but it bears no fruits, like the ferns, and from the branches also hang such large brown threads as from the mentioned ferns. The leaves being broken off, or the bark being wounded, likewise give milk, as all ferns do.

This tree spreads from itself a pleasant *Calambac* smell, but yet no one dares to venture to chop a piece from it, or to break off a twig, because he immediately gets belly-ache and his nose bleeds, he who ventures such a thing. Which the inhabitants believe comes from a specific spirit who guards this tree, and it therefore remains thus undamaged to stand as a spectacle.

Among the aforementioned kinds of Quinam Aloes-wood one must also count the third kind, being the common Aloes-wood: and this tree is common throughout Quinam <note>original: "Cautfchi"</note> and Champa. They are high trees, having small round leaves, even smaller than a *stuiver*, which stand many against each other on small twigs. These trees are chopped down and the branches further chopped into pieces, which one then lets lie in the forest to rot, and then one finds the innermost fragrant heart. This wood consists mostly of hard knots, and is so like the above-standing *Thim* that one looks upon it as one and the same; but this latter has no such black resinous spots as the *Thim*, being otherwise in smell almost the same, or generally somewhat drier. And this wood is called *Sock* by the Chinese, with which they name all common Aloes-wood, just as it is also held by our people as the same kind of wood as the preceding. The *Pickol*, that is 100 *Catties* or 125 Dutch pounds in Champa, costs 25 *Tayl*, and this *Sock* mostly floats on top of the water.

The second kind is the Malay Aloes-wood, and so we name all that which falls in the Malay Islands, such as around Malacca, in the islands of Johor, Bintang, etc., and especially on the island of Belitung, all situated between Sumatra and Borneo. This wood does not differ much from the Quinam variety, and one finds pieces among it that one would take for upright *Calambac*, namely brown with gray and coarse veins: reasonably light, yielding to the teeth in chewing as if it were hard wax, and the smell...

# AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II, Chap. XII.

...hard, and the scent is likewise similar to *Calambac* <note>The most precious, resin-saturated heartwood of the Aquilaria tree.</note>, but it differs by one degree of pleasantness and is much smaller and of less value. The best and most numerous of these trees grow on the island of *Belitton* <note>Modern-day Belitung, Indonesia.</note>, which is situated seven or eight miles to the eastern part of the northern coast of *Bancka* <note>Bangka Island.</note>, as well as on other islands situated around *Jabor* <note>Johor, on the Malay Peninsula.</note>.

It is a tall tree, standing back from the seashore, bearing leaves like the *Microphyllus* <note>original Latin: "Microphylli"; Dutch: "Varinga". This likely refers to a species of Ficus or Banyan with small leaves.</note>, but smaller than those of the *Tsjampacca* <note>The Magnolia champaca, known for its fragrant flowers.</note>, or as they were shown to me, in shape and size like those of the *Caju-Lacca*, which belong to the family of the *Lingoo*-leaved plants <note>Referring to the Pterocarpus indicus or Narra tree.</note>, but both the leaves and the trunk lack the milky sap <note>Latex, which helps distinguish it from many Ficus species.</note>.

Its fruit is round like the *Klitji* <note>Likely the fruit of the Soapberry tree (Sapindus).</note> and is of no use. These trees have their owners, just like other fruit-bearing trees, and each man cuts his own during the Western monsoon months when they are mature enough, and leaves them lying there until the Eastern monsoon months. Then, the fattest <note>Resinous</note> parts are selected and sorted into three heaps.

The largest, fattest, and darkest pieces are called *Garo-Capalla* <note>Malay: "Head-Garo", the premium grade.</note>; these must sink to the bottom in water, which is why they are also called *Garo Tingelam* <note>Malay: "Sunken-Garo".</note>. These segments often take the shape of fish, birds, rats, or even caimans. The second species yields smaller pieces, which are indeed fatty and dark and of all sorts of shapes, but they do not sink to the bottom; nevertheless, they are of good quality. This species is called *Garo-ramas*, or *Garo-Tenga-Tenga*, which means the "middle species." The third species is the cheapest, called *Garo-Eckor* <note>Malay: "Tail-Garo".</note>, whose wood is mixed with a white color and floats on water. Thus, these three species come from a single tree. For the first grade in *Belitton*, one must pay at least one <term>Imperial<gloss>A silver Reichsthaler or dollar</gloss></term> for one <term>Catti<gloss>About 600 grams</gloss></term>; in *Java*, three or four. For the other two mixed together, sixteen to twenty Imperials are paid in *Belitton* for one <term>Picool<gloss>A large weight unit, approximately 125-140 lbs</gloss></term>, but in *Java*, twenty-five to thirty. Europeans, however, being ignorant of the difference, pay as high a price for these as for the *Garo-Capalla*, just as in *Belitton* these species are commonly sold mixed together.

From my own experience, I have learned that the *Agallochum* <note>Aloes-wood or Agarwood.</note> from Malacca is much better than that from *Belitton*. The tree there also has the form of the *Microphyllus*, but lacks the milky sap and the hanging roots; it consists of many twisted trunks, entangled in a wonderful way and folded into one another. Some of these are even found on the shore around the coast of *Tanjong-tua* and the little hill of *Bukit-Sina*, but these yield no *Agallochum* wood. On the contrary, this best wood is found in the central region of the *Bunoang* forest-people, some pieces of which might even rival the *Quinam* variety <note>The highly prized Vietnamese Agarwood.</note>. Around *Malacca*, however, a very poor species occurs called *Garo-Masang*, which means the "Wild-Cat Aloes-wood" <note>original Dutch: "wilde katten Agel-hout".</note>, called *Batsjaa* by the Chinese. In appearance, it matches the good *Agallochum* or *Calambac*, and is therefore often mixed in and sold to our nation as good *Calambac*. However, it differs greatly in quality and strength; for though it seems fatty, hard, and angular, it is in truth light and full of splinters. When placed on coals, it gives off a sharp, stinging odor that pricks the eyes. Those forest-dwellers, however, are very skilled at detecting the *Agallochum* wood in old and fallen trees by striking it with their knuckles; by the sound, they can distinguish and know whether the *Agallochum* lies hidden within or not.

**Names.** This species of *Agallochum* is properly called *Garo-Ramas* by the Malays, except for the three thinner species, which they call *Garo-Eckor*. The Chinese, however, call the fattest and best pieces *Thimbio*, and all the others *Sock* and *Söo*.

**Usage.** This entire species is mostly mixed into *Dupa* <note>Incense.</note> for fragrance, of which these woods are the primary ingredients. The cheaper species are sent throughout almost all of India to be used for the cremation of dead bodies. The most experienced Chinese will not give the name *Thimbio* to every kind of *Agallochum* or *Garo*, but consider as true *Thimbio* only a solid, black or dark brown, and hard wood—in some places entirely black—which, when exposed to fire, exudes much oil but does not easily burn. It smells somewhat like *Garo-Cominjan* <note>Agarwood mixed with Benjamin/Benzoin resin.</note>, but not as pleasant or common. it is very rarely found in *Cambodia* and *Champa*. The Chinese trade silver for it, not so much for its pleasant scent, which is not outstanding, but for its medicinal virtues. For they prepare it as a medicine with water...

## BOOK II. CHAPTER XII. AMBOINESE HERBAL.
E 3

...with water or Arrack <note>A distilled spirit made from palm or rice</note>, as a remedy against such great anxiety of the stomach, as if one were being suffocated.

The people of Malacca use their *Agallochum* <note>Aloeswood or Agarwood</note> for all cold illnesses, flatulence, and griping pains in the limbs or other parts. They grind it with Arrack or spirit of wine and drink it; they also mix it with a little *Nutmeg* and apply it externally as an ointment.

Certain Chinese call the best *Garo* <note>Agarwood</note>, which is closest to the fine *Calambac* <note>The most resinous heartwood of the Aquilaria tree</note>, *Susehion*. The lighter *Garo* mentioned above as *Ithion*, they call *Pasoc*. To them, the word *Soc* means hard, because it is always harder than *Kilam*. This last species is used to make the small candles that they place before their Idols, which they call *Hio Soa* <note>Joss sticks or incense sticks</note>. They shave the wood into a fine powder, mixing it with powder of *White Sandalwood* and other less expensive fragrances, using the mucilage <note>sticky sap</note> dripping from the bark of the *Salampoë* tree as a binder. From this mass, they form small, thin candles about the thickness of a straw; they light the upper end and place them before their household gods, where they spread smoke and fragrance day and night.

So it is also read in the book of the *Chinese Embassy* written by *Joan Nieuhof* <note>A Dutch traveler and author (1618–1672)</note>, that the so-called *Eaglewood* <note>original Latin: "Aventshout"; Dutch: "Aarent-hout", likely a typo for "Arendshout"</note> grows in certain southern provinces of China, especially in *Quantung* <note>Guangdong</note>. However, since he says on page 33 that it must be of a purple color, called *Lacca* by the Spaniards, and used throughout China for dyeing silk, I doubt whether the true *Eaglewood* <note>the Aquilaria tree</note> was known to him. I suspect he rather meant the true *Caju Lacca* <note>Lakawood, which produces a red dye</note>, which we shall describe in the seventh book.

Through the instruction and help of the Reverend Mr. *Theodorus Zas*, Minister of the Word of God in Batavia <note>Modern Jakarta</note>, I received in the year 1690 from Malacca some pieces of wood with leaves and roots; according to the reports of those who sent it, this was the true *Malaccan Agallochum*. I have had the accompanying figure drawn from it, which appeared as follows:

The branches were divided into straight, thin, and very fine twigs, upon which the leaves had stood singly and somewhat sparsely, though all had fallen off. The leaves closely matched those of the *Small-leaved Varinga* <note>original: "Varinga Microphylla"; a type of Ficus or Banyan</note>, namely of a common shape with an oblong tip and short stalks; most were 3, some 4 inches long, and 1½ to 2 inches wide, smooth and thin.

Along the sides run many transverse ribs that curve forward, and close along the edge runs a border where they terminate. When handled only slightly, the dried leaves tear along these ribs like *Banana leaves* <note>original Dutch: "Pissang-bladeren"</note>, so that a whole leaf could hardly be found. Attached to these was a piece of a straight branch, two fingers thick, made of a light and spongy wood, just as the dry *Eaglewood* is whitish and porous inside. It was covered with a gray, smooth, and thin bark. Included with it were the barks of a straight trunk, not thick, but very tough and difficult to break crosswise, being able to be pulled into tough fibers <note>original Dutch: "bairtjes"</note>, in which they also resemble the aforementioned *Varinga*; they were grayish with black spots. The roots were thin and long, divided into many fine fibers. Of the wood, it was written that it was very light and brittle, and not at all suitable for transplanting. It was not noted whether the bark of the trunk yielded milk <note>latex</note> like the *Varinga*, nor whether it bore fruit, or where the true pieces of *Agallochum* are found. The taste of the trunk bark was insipid, but in the roots, it was bitter. Furthermore, neither on coals nor in the mouth did they provide any spicy scent or taste.

Afterward, in 1693, through the instruction of the Honorable Mr. *Nicolaas Schagen*, our current Governor, I again obtained branches of the *Malaccan Agallochum*, namely only the twigs with leaves. These matched the previous ones, except they were a little broader and thicker. To my memory, they best matched those I had received some years before from *Bantam* <note>Banten, Java</note>, taken from two large *Varinga* trees that then stood before the King’s Palace. The Chinese assured me that *Calambac* lay hidden within them, as evidenced by the good scent sometimes noticed around them; however, the King did not want them cut down, even though the Chinese had offered him money for them.

medicinal powers: for they use it as medicine, ground with *water or Arrack*, against such oppression in the pit of the stomach as if one were about to suffocate.

Those of *Malacca* use their *Aloeswood* <note>original: "Agel-hout"</note> against all kinds of cold ailments, winds, and pain in the limbs, or wherever it may be, rubbing or taking it with *Arrack or Brandy*; also, ground with a little *Nutmeg*, they smear it on the outside.

Some Chinese call the best *Garo*, which comes next to *Calambac*, *Susehion*, and the light *Garo* named above *Ithion*, *Pasoc*. *Soc* is said by them to mean hard, because it is always harder than *Kilam*. This last variety is used to make the small candles which they place before their Idols and call *Hio-soa*. They shave it to a fine powder, putting under it powder of *white sandalwood* and some other perfumes of small price, with the mucilage dripping from the bark of the tree *Salampoë*, from which they make a mass, out of which they form small and thin black candles the thickness of a straw-stalk, which they light at the top end and place before their Household Gods, where they smoke day and night.

One also finds in the book of the *Chinese Embassy* described by *Joan Nieuhof*, that the so-called *Eaglewood* <note>original: "Arents-hout"</note> grows in some southern Provinces of *China*, especially in *Quantung*; but because he says on page 33 that it must be purple-colored, called *Lacca* by the Spaniards, and used throughout *China* to dye silk, I doubt if he knew the upright *Eaglewood*, and whether he did not much more mean by that the actual *Caju Lacca*, which we shall describe in the seventh book.

Through the instruction and help of the Reverend Mr. *Theodorus Zas*, Minister of the Divine Word at *Batavia*, I obtained in 1690 from *Malacca* some pieces of wood, leaves, and roots, according to their writing of the *Malaccan Aloeswood*. From which I have had the neighboring figure made, and they were thus:

The twigs were divided into straight, thin, and very fine shoots, on which the leaves had stood singly and somewhat sparsely, though they had all fallen off. The leaves came closest to those of the *Small-leaved Varinga* <note>original: "Varinga Microphyllos"</note>, to wit, of a common shape with an oblong point and short stems, most 3, some 4 inches long, from 1½ and 2 inches wide, smooth and thin.

To the sides run many transverse ribs, which curve forward, and close along the edge runs a seam <note>a marginal vein</note> in which they end. The dried leaves, even slightly handled, tear along these ribs like *Banana leaves* <note>original: "Pissang-bladeren"</note>, so that a whole leaf was hardly to be found; with this was joined a piece of a straight branch, two fingers thick, of a light and spongy wood, just as the dry *Eaglewood* is white and porous inside, covered with a gray, smooth, and thin bark; with it were the barks of a straight trunk, not thick, but very tough, and difficult to break across, letting themselves be pulled into tough fibers, in which they also agree with the aforementioned *Varinga*, grayish with black spots. The roots were thin and long, divided into many thin fibers. Of the wood, it was written that it was very light and brittle, by no means to be transplanted; it was not added whether the bark of the trunk was milky, like the *Varinga*, nor whether it bore fruit, and where one finds the true pieces of *Aloeswood*. The taste in the bark of the trunk was insipid, but in the roots bitter. Furthermore, all together, neither on the coals nor in the mouth did they have any spicy scent or taste.

Afterward in 1693, by the instruction of the Noble Mr. *Nicolaas Schagen*, our present Lord Governor, I once more obtained the branches of the *Malaccan Aloeswood*, to wit, only the twigs with leaves, which mostly agreed with the previous ones, except that they were somewhat broader and thicker, and to my memory best agreed with those which I had received some years before from *Bantam*, being taken from two large *Varinga trees*, which at that time stood before the King's Palace, and of which the Chinese assured me that *Calambac* was hidden in them, evidenced by the good scent which was sometimes perceived thereabouts, but the King did not want to let them be chopped down, although the Chinese had offered him money for them.

With these last branches brought from Malacca, certain fruits were joined, though they were not adhering to the twigs; these were about the size of a small plum, rounded at the bottom and pointed at the top, pear-shaped, and all had fallen apart into two separate segments. They had a woody outer shell, thick and very bitter in taste, light and spongy. Inside each segment appeared two oblong cavities or cells, in which pits were located, smaller than Laurel berries; in some, two were found, in others four. Externally they were soft and woolly, slightly pointed on both ends; beneath this woolly coating they were black, but their interior part was mostly dried out. From this I learned that they differ greatly from all fruits of the *Varinga* <note>original: "Varinga"; refers to species of Ficus or Banyan trees</note>.

However, his description is very obscure and therefore uncertain, especially since true *Aloeswood* is brought only from the East Indies.

## CHAPTER THIRTEEN.

### *That Agallochum was known to the Ancients; and how it is adulterated in India.*

**W**e have already suggested above that *Agallochum* <note>term: Agallochum; the fragrant, resinous heartwood of Aquilaria trees, also known as Agarwood or Aloeswood</note> was known and used since ancient times, and we said that the *Ahalim* <note>original: "Ahalim" (Hebrew)</note> mentioned in the Holy Bible could have been nothing other than today’s *Agallochum*. This is chiefly concluded from the forty-fifth Psalm and the seventh chapter of Proverbs, where it is distinctly said that *Ahalim* was used for perfuming precious garments and beds. However, someone might object and ask: by what means could Solomon have acquired and cultivated the *Ahaloth-trees* <note>original: "Ahalotbi-arbores"</note> which are described in the *Song of Solomon 4, verse 14*, in his own garden? To which I reply, it is not necessarily required that all those aromatic trees with which the bride is compared in that passage were actually located in Solomon’s garden, although that could also easily be granted. For what would have hindered that powerful King, famous throughout the whole world—to whom the rarest and most precious things were brought from the heart of the land of the Ethiopians—from being able to fetch for himself with his fleets from *Ophir* <note>A legendary biblical region of wealth; Rumphius suggests it is near the Ganges</note>, where the Ganges flows, some seedlings of the *Ahalim-trees*? Just as he obtained *Calamus* and *Cinnamon* from Ceylon, as well as *Myrrh* and *Frankincense* from *Arabia Felix* <note>original: "Arabia felice"; literally "Happy Arabia," the fertile southern part of the Arabian Peninsula</note>, all of which are celebrated and commemorated in that same garden. Among later writers, both Greek and Latin, no mention of this wood is made from that time until the era of *Dioscorides* <note>A Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD)</note>, who lived under *Augustus Caesar*. No doubt because it was so rare and expensive, it was not known or used for medical purposes by the common people or private individuals. From *Dioscorides*, however, in Book I, chapter 21, certain difficulties arise as to whether the true *Agallochum* was already known to him: first, because he says his *Agallochum* is *spotted*, or rather *punctated* <note>original: "maculosum, vel potius punctatum"</note> or speckled, which subsequent and more recent writers do not mention; wherefore *Matthiolus* <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a famous Italian herbalist</note> in his Com-

<column-break/>

By the last-mentioned branches from *Malacca*, some fruits were joined, though not attached to the twigs. These were the size of a small plum, round in front and somewhat pointed at the back, pear-shaped, and all of them had fallen into two parts from each other. From the outside they had a thick woody shell, very bitter in taste, light and hollow. Inside, in each part, one saw two oblong cavities, and therein the seed-kernels, smaller than a Bayberry <note>original: "Bakelaar"; Dutch term for Laurel/Bay berry</note>; in some two, in some four, on the outside somewhat soft like wool, pointed at the front and back. Under the woolliness they were black, but inside mostly dried out. From which I remarked that they differ much from all *Varingas*-fruits.

## XIII. CHAPTER.

### *That the Agallochum was known to the Ancients, and how it is falsified in the Indies.*

**T**hat the Agallochum has been known from ancient times and was in use, we have cited above, and said that the *Ahalim* mentioned in the *Bible* can have been nothing else than the modern-day *Agallochum*. This follows principally from the *45th Psalm* and *Proverbs 7*, where it is clearly said that the *Ahalim* was used for the smoking <note>Meaning perfuming with incense</note> of costly clothes and beds. But one might object here and ask how *Solomon* could have had the *Ahaloth-trees*, which are described in *Canticles 4 verse 14*, in his pleasure garden? To which I answer, it does not necessarily follow that all those spice-trees with which the Bride is compared in that place must have actually stood in Solomon's garden, although one can easily admit such a thing: for what would have been lacking for that mighty King, so famous through the world, to whom the very rarest treasures were brought from the interior of the land of the Moors, that he would not also have had brought over with his fleet from *Ophir*, where the *Ganges* flows down, some small plants of *Ahalim-trees*? Just as well as *Calamus* and *Cinnamon* from *Ceylon*, *Myrrh* and *Frankincense* from *Arabia Felix*, which were also praised and expressed in the same garden. Among the following writers, both among the Greeks and Romans, one finds no mention made of this wood from that time until *Dioscorides’* time, who lived under the Emperor *Augustus*: no doubt because, due to its rarity and costliness, it was little known among the common man in medicine. # BOOK II. CHAPTER XIII. AMBOINESE HERBARIUM
<note>original Dutch: "AMBOINSCHE KRUYDBOEK"</note>

<column-break/>

Commentators have wished to change that word into another, but in my judgment, it can stand as it is; for I believe that **Dioscorides** <note>a Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note> by no means saw the true **Agallochum** <note>original: "Agallochum"; the resinous wood of the Aquilaria tree, also known as Agarwood or Aloeswood</note>, called **Calambac**, but only the common **Garo**, or spurious Agallochum, which indeed has short little points rather than the veins or lines that are more frequent and compact in one part of the wood than another, where they represent and display certain spots. Furthermore, it is also true that he ascribes a thin skin and not a bark to Agallochum; for it is well known to everyone that the old and knobby nodes of Agallochum, brought out from the mud and rivers, are covered with a kind of earthy skin, which is often left on so that if the pieces are sold, they show a heavier weight. This, however, is often scraped off and cleaned so that it appears like fresh wood, as those do who wish to keep it for themselves. And without doubt, **Nicolaus Myrepsus** <note>a 13th-century Byzantine physician</note> understood this cleaned Agallochum when he prescribed "raw Agallochum" in his compositions. Furthermore, when Dioscorides says his Agallochum is produced from **Arabia**, it must be understood that it was transported from **India** into the capital cities of Arabia situated on the Red Sea. Finally, I cannot guess what Dioscorides means by the "roots" of Agallochum, since today pieces of the tree and the root cannot easily be distinguished; nor do I understand his meaning when he says Agallochum is used in place of **Frankincense**, unless he meant that Agallochum is applied in the same manner as Frankincense, namely for fumigation <term>suffumigium|the burning of aromatic substances to produce medicinal or ritual smoke</term>. Otherwise, I find that the **Chinese** to this day call these woods into use for the same diseases for which Dioscorides writes his Agallochum was customary in his time.

In **Pliny's** <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman author of Natural History</note> Book 12, Chapter 20, a certain wood occurs which he calls **Tarum**, which I entirely think is the modern **Garo**, and perhaps it was formerly written as *Farum*. He says it was brought by the **Nabataean Troglodytes** <note>literally "cave-dwellers"; Rumphius interprets this as a reference to the people of Ceylon</note>, by whom he undoubtedly means the **Sinhalese**, for he says it grows where the **Cassia Cinnamon** originates. Thus, by this should be understood the cheaper species of Garo or Agallochum, which **Serapion** <note>likely Serapion the Younger, a medieval Arabic medical writer</note> calls *Alcumericum*, and the **Portuguese** today call *Aquila Brava* <note>Wild Eagle-wood</note>. Furthermore, it is difficult to say which four species of Agallochum Serapion meant to describe in his book on simple medicines, chapter 197, which he names: 1st. **Indum**, which is the best and heaviest, growing on the island of **Fiuma** or **Fimua**. 2nd. **Mondunum**, so called from **Mondel**, a city in India. 3rd. **Seificum**. 4th. **Alcumericum**, which is the cheapest, although he says that *Seifi* is no more than three days' journey distant from *Alcumeri*. Unless one agrees with **Garcia de Orta** <note>a Portuguese Renaissance physician and pioneer of tropical medicine</note> in his first book on Aromatics, chapter 16, and understands *Seifi* to be **Ceylon**, and *Alcumeri* to be **Cape Comorin**, where he says "Wild Agallochum" or *Aquila Brava* grows. By *Mondel*, however, I understand the **Coromandel** coast. It is true that **Clusius** <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a famous 16th-century botanist</note> corrected these three names to *Mondelinum*, *Seneficum*, and *Alcumericum* in his final notes, trusting the opinion of the **Nubian Geographer** <note>the 12th-century scholar Al-Idrisi</note>, who writes in Part 9 of the first climate, and says that the island of **Tenuma** is five days' journey from the island of **Cumar** or **Camar**; from this island the wood was called *Alcumeri*, which is famous there and also very good, except that the wood of *Essenesi* is better. **Sandalwood** also grows on this island. Near this island of *Cumar*, situated toward the shore, is the island of **Senef** at a distance of three days, and on this island is found the *Senefic* wood. What these regions are, if they are not understood as those three mentioned, is uncertain to define.

Furthermore, regarding what Serapion writes in the said place—that the best Agallochum must be hard, heavy, or seeking the bottom of the water, and resisting the flame for a long time—it is an indication that the true **Calambac** was not known to him, but only the common **Garo** or Agallochum. For *Calambac* is indeed heavy and in a way seeks the bottom, but it is so soft and fatty that, as was said, it yields to a fingernail and to the teeth when chewed, and it catches fire very easily due to its oily and fatty matter; whereas *Garo* is always harder, more solid, and resists flames two or three times longer and more strongly than *Calambac*.

<meta>catchword: Since</meta>

<column-break/>

following **writers** do not testify, and why **Matthiolus** <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, 16th-century Italian physician</note> also in his **Commentaries** wished to have that same word changed into another. But in my opinion, it may remain the same: for I hold it to be that **Dioscorides** by no means saw the true **Calambac**, but only the common **Garo** or **Aloeswood** <note>original Dutch: "Agel-hout"</note>, which indeed has many more short spikes than veins or lines, which standing much closer together in one place of the wood than in others, thereby seem to show some spots. That he further ascribes a skin and no bark to his Agallochum is also true, for the ancient or bulbous knots of the Aloeswood, as they come out of the mud and rivers, are covered with an earthy shagginess like a skin. And people also sometimes leave it on, to weigh heavier in the selling, and also sometimes scrape it off, and make it as clean as if it were fresh wood, as those do who wish to keep it for themselves. And this cleaned Aloeswood must without doubt have been what **Nicolaus Myrepsus** meant or understood when he wanted **Raw Agallochum** taken for his compositions. That furthermore Dioscorides brings forth his Agallochum from **Arabia** must be understood such that it was brought from **India** into the great cities of Arabia, situated on the Red Sea. And what further Dioscorides means or wants to say by the "root" of Agallochum, I cannot well guess, as today one cannot distinguish the pieces of the tree and the roots; nor do I understand his saying that one uses Agallochum in place of **Incense**, unless his meaning was that Agallochum was used in the same way as Incense, namely as perfume <term>reukwerk|scented material for burning</term>. Otherwise, I find that the **Chinese** even to this time mostly use those woods for the same ailments for which Dioscorides writes that his Agallochum was useful and beneficial.

Now one finds in **Pliny**, in the 12th book, chapter 20, a certain wood which he calls **Tarum**, which I fully hold for the modern **Garo**, and was perhaps formerly written as *Farum*, which he says was brought by the **Nabataean Troglodytes**, by whom he without doubt understands the **Sinhalese**, for he says that it grows where the **Cassia Cinnamon** occurs, so that thereby must be understood the poor sort of **Garo** or **Aloeswood**, which **Serapion** calls *Alcumericum*, and the **Portuguese** nowadays call *Aquila Brava*. Furthermore, it is dark to guess what four kinds of Agallochum Serapion in his *Book of Simples*, chapter 197, wants to describe, naming them: 1. **Indum**, the heaviest and best, growing on the island of **Fiuma** or **Fimua**. 2. **Mondunum**, so named from **Mondel**, a city in India. 3. **Seificum**. 4. **Alcumericum**, being the poor sort, although he says that *Seifi* was not more than three days' journey distant from *Alcumeri*. Or one must, with **Garcia de Orta**, Book 1, *Aromatics*, chapter 16, understand by *Seifi* **Ceylon**, and by *Alcumeri* the **Cape Comorin**, where he says "Wild Agallochum" or *Aquila Brava* grows; and by *Mondel* understand the coast of **Coromandel**. It is true that **Clusius**, in his last **Annotations**, has had the three names changed into *Mondelinum*, *Seneficum*, and *Alcumericum*, leaning on what the **Nubian Geographer** writes, Part 9, Climate 1, where he speaks of the island of **Cumar** or **Camar**. From this island the wood *Alcumeri* is named, which is famous there, and it is very good, except that the wood of *Essenesi* is better. But on this island **Sandalwood** also occurs. By this island *Cumar*, on the side of the shore, lies the island of **Senef**, at the distance of three days' journey, and in the same island one finds the wood *Senefi*. But what those landscapes are again, if one does not understand it as the three aforementioned, is again not easy to guess.

Furthermore, that which Serapion writes in the mentioned place, that the best Agallochum must be hard, heavy, and sink in the water, and also resist the flames strongly, proves again that the true **Calambac** was not known to those people, but only the common **Garo** or **Aloeswood**. For the *Calambac* is indeed heavy and sinks somewhat in the water, but it is so soft that one can press into the fat, as said, with a fingernail, and in chewing it gives way to the teeth; it also catches the flame very easily because of its fattiness, but **Garo** is always harder, denser, and resists the flame fully two or three times harder or longer than the *Calambac*.

# HERBARIUM AMBOINENSE Book II. Chapter XIV
<note>original Latin: "HERBARII AMBOINENSIS"; Rumphius’s massive botanical work on the plants of the East Indies.</note>

Since Calambac <note>the highest, most resinous grade of Aloeswood</note> is so expensive and rare, the Chinese—a nation thirsty for gold—use many arts to forge true Calambac, for which the following method of adulteration is practiced. They know how to prepare the best pieces of Garo Ramas <note>a mid-grade variety of Aloeswood</note> so that they resemble true Calambac. Namely, they shave the pieces over their entire surface and expose them to smoke from a small amount of shavings of true Calambac; this is done in a pot so that none of the smoke is lost, which they plug up for this purpose. They repeat this two or three times and keep the pieces enclosed in that pot for a whole month, whereby the parts of the Aloeswood soften slightly and breathe out a pleasant odor like that of Calambac from Champa <note>a region in modern-day Vietnam famous for high-quality wood</note>; otherwise, it is a little more ash-colored and lighter than this prepared Garo. However, this fake scent disappears again within a span of two or three months, during which time that crafty Chinese trader has set sail and sought other lands. With this deceptive art, they not only deceive the leaders of these regions but even the more prudent Japanese.

---

### CHAPTER FOURTEEN.

### Spurious Agallochum, or Garo Champacca.

Since the two primary species of true *Agallochum* <note>Aloeswood</note> were described in the preceding two chapters, it remains for us to list other woods besides these which are sold for it equally in India and Europe. Since the entire nation of the Orient, or India, continually desires perfumes, and true *Agallochum* cannot be obtained in sufficient quantity, other woods must succeed and be substituted in its place, according to what each region produces that bears some similarity to Agallochum. It is not my purpose or intention to list all those woods, but to cite only three of them, with the condition that I knowingly pass over the first wood, called *Wild Agallochum* by Garcia <note>referring to Garcia de Orta, a 16th-century Portuguese physician</note> in Book 1, Chapter 16, and called *Aquila brava* <note>literally "Wild Eaglewood" in Portuguese</note> by the Portuguese, leaving it to others to describe further, since it is so far unknown to me. The second species, which I call *Spurious Agallochum*, I shall describe in this chapter according to my ability, and the third indeed in the following chapter, since it differs too much from the preceding ones and even from this Agallochum.

Large pieces of *Spurious Agallochum*, or *Garo Champacca*, are indeed found, which are sometimes also of an irregular form like true Aloeswood, some being half-eaten away and covered with an earthy crust. The wood itself is saffron-yellow, marked with dark spots, but not woven with true veins; on the outside, if it is dry, it takes on a dark brown and blackish color. If it is chewed, it is soft and gives way to the teeth; the taste agrees with Chamomile, but in the end, it becomes more bitter. The oldest pieces are harder than the rest and break into small pieces; since they are very fatty, they exude a copious oil when placed on glowing coals. The scent differs greatly from all other species of Aloeswood, for it has nothing in common with Citrus peels, but approaches more the scent of Chamomile. And in these lands, it is said to agree with the flowers of the famous *Champacca* <note>a fragrant flowering tree, Magnolia champaca</note>, from which this wood also received its name, and perhaps it is a species of it. For the tree is tall and has leaves similar to Champacca leaves, but they are larger and wider, compared by some with Canarium leaves, and by others with the upper half of the leaf of the Orange called Pomelo <note>original: "Pomelmoes"</note>. It likewise bears many flowers resembling Champacca. The trunk has a thick bark, but the tree itself is not cut down; it is left until, being old, it rots away of its own accord, at which time the outer wood rots away. At other times, even very old trees are cut into pieces, which are hidden for half a year or a little longer in swampy places until the outer wood has rotted and the fattest pieces remain.

However, some inhabitants, out of greed, cut down the trees before they are sufficiently old and mature, and bury the pieces in the said manner; these pieces are indeed large and solid enough, very fatty, and, if chewed, soft, yet by no means so excellent in scent...

<column-break/>

Since Calambac is very dear <note>expensive</note>, and also difficult to find, the Chinese, being a money-greedy nation, employ various tricks to imitate genuine Calambac, among which the following is perhaps the most tolerable: They know how to prepare the best pieces of Garo Ramas in such a way that it resembles genuine Calambac. Namely, they scrape the pieces over the whole body and smoke them with a little scraping of genuine Calambac—specifically in a pot, so that none of the smoke goes to waste—stopping it up tightly, doing this once or twice, and letting it stand for an entire month in the same closed pot. Through this, the pieces of Aloeswood become a little soft and fragrant like Calambac from Champa, which otherwise is somewhat grayer and lighter than the mentioned Garo. But this manufactured scent vanishes again within 2 to 3 months, in which time the Chinese trader figures he can pack himself off again with his vessel. With this art, they deceive not only the Great Men of these lands but even the clever Japanese.

---

### CHAPTER XIV.

### Bastard Aloeswood.

Having described the two main types of the true *Agallochum* in the preceding chapters, there now remain some woods that are sold for it, both here in India and in Europe. For, as the entire Orient or the East Indian nation is constantly inclined toward perfumes, and one cannot obtain genuine Aloeswood in sufficient quantity, other woods must come forward to fill its place, according to what each landscape has at hand that has any resemblance to the Agallochum. It is not my meaning or intention to bring up all the same sorts, but only to touch upon three of them, yet with the condition that I pass by the first sort here, being the *Wild Agallochum* mentioned by *Garcia* in the first Book, Chapter 16, and called *Aguila Brava* by the Portuguese, leaving the same for others to describe more closely, as it is still unknown to me. The second sort, which I call *Agallochum Spurium*, or Bastard Aloeswood, I shall describe in this chapter, and the third sort in the following chapter, as it differs too much from these Aloeswoods, according to my ability.

Of *Agallochum Spurium*, or *Garo Champacca*, one finds quite large pieces and sometimes also of a rare shape, like the Aloeswood, some being half-eaten through and covered with an earthy skin. The wood is high-yellow with dark spots and no proper veins; from the outside, it turns dark brown and blackish. In chewing, it also feels soft and yields to the teeth; the taste draws strongly toward Chamomile, yet is markedly bitter at the end. The oldest pieces turn out harder than the others and break off short; being very fatty in all parts, so that when laid on glowing coals, an abundant oil sweats out. The scent also differs markedly from all other Aloeswoods, for it has nothing in common with that of lemon peels, but draws more toward Chamomile. And here in this country, it is said that it also somewhat corresponds with that of the flower Champacca, from which the wood also takes its name, and perhaps is also a sort of it. For it is a high tree, and the leaves resemble somewhat those of the Champacca, though they are larger and broader, compared by some with those of the Canarium, and again by others with the front part of a Pomelo leaf. It also bears many flowers, also resembling those of the Champacca somewhat; the trunk has a thick bark. One does not chop it down, but lets it grow old and fall over of itself, where then the outermost wood rots off of its own accord. Or one chops such old trees into pieces and buries them for half a year, or a bit longer, in some swampy places, until the outer wood rots away and the fattest pieces are left over.

Nevertheless, some locals, out of greed, chop the trees down before they are properly ripe and bury the pieces as before, and from this come large and massive pieces, very fatty and soft in chewing, but in scent by no means as good as the old, which...

<summary>This page describes the deceptive trade practices used to forge high-quality Calambac and introduces "Spurious Agallochum" (Garo Champacca), detailing its physical characteristics and the process of harvesting it from rotted or buried trees.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Aloeswood varieties. While the previous page focused on the high-value true Calambac and Chinese forgeries, this page transitions into "spurious" or bastard varieties and introduces Muskwood (Lignum Moschatum).</meta>

# BOOK II. CHAPTER XIV. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...as well as old ones, which are found in short knots, and which appear much more yellow and withered to the eye.
**Name.** In Latin, *Agallochum spurium*, which is *Bastard Aloeswood* <note>Dutch: Bastaert Agel-hout</note>. In Malay, it is called *Garo-Tsjampacca*, because it emulates the scent of that flower <note>the Champaca or magnolia flower</note>; in Banggai, it is called *Angaro*.
**Location.** This wood is found on Borneo, in the regions of Sambas and Sukadana; likewise in Palembang, which is situated on the eastern coast of Sumatra. A few of these trees are also found on the island of Banggai, located off the eastern coast of Celebes <note>modern-day Sulawesi</note>, though not throughout the whole island, but only in its smallest part called Gape, around the villages of Bancalang and Labo. The trees themselves are mostly unknown to the inhabitants, as they only find the decayed wood in the forests. The people of Kelang say that they also grow on their island, where they are called *Bakewe*, and are considered a species of wild *Champacca*. These trees were also found on Sula Besi and in Ternate, everywhere bearing leaves similar to those of the *Champacca*.
**Use.** It is a wood of very little value; in Java, a *Picul* <note>a weight of about 132 lbs or 60 kg</note> is sold for one *Real of Eight* <note>a Spanish silver dollar</note>, and it is used there for no other purpose than the fumigation of houses. Some also mix it with common *Dupa* <note>incense</note>, not to make the scent more pleasant, but to increase the bulk; however, it is not worth much for this composition, as it spoils other scents.
In passing, we must also mention another rare species called *Calambac puti*, or *White Aloeswood*. By this, we do not mean the aforementioned light wood *Itthion* or *Simple Agallochum*, but another very rare species, of which only a single tree is found today in Coinama <note>Cochinchina, modern Vietnam</note>. Its wood is so expensive that it cannot be obtained, even if one were willing to pay a hundred *Taels* <note>Chinese currency/weight</note> for one *Catty* <note>approx. 600 grams</note> or chest. The King will not allow this tree to be cut, as no more can be found. It is said that if two or three of its leaves fall into the water and someone drinks it, they will be seized by a burning fever which does not subside unless the King performs a sacrifice to this tree. Many, however, call the following *Muskwood* "White Calambac" as well, but that is a distinct tree.
A third species of *Spurious Aloeswood* is frequent in these Eastern islands and comes from the tree called *Excæcans* <note>The "Blinding Tree," Excoecaria agallocha, known for its toxic sap</note>, which will be described in its proper place in Book 3, Chapter 37. It is classified under the *Calambac* species; indeed, that which is found in the old trunks of *Ligularia Lactea* <note>a milk-sap plant, likely a Euphorbia</note> is considered genuine *Calambac*, about which more will be said in Book 6, Chapter 46.

N. B. Illustrations of *True and Spurious Aloeswood* are shown in the *German Ephemerides* <note>Miscellanea Curiosa, an early scientific journal</note>, decade 2, year 1, at page 55.

## CHAPTER FIFTEEN.
## Muskwood, Caju Casturi.

From Champa, Coinama, and Pegu <note>modern-day Vietnam and Myanmar</note>, a certain whitish wood is brought that is entirely similar to Sandalwood, but not as hard, and which has several longitudinal veins almost like Fir wood. Three species of it are found.
The first and most polished wood is like white Sandalwood, but it is softer, and the interior parts are more yellowish. It has the scent of Sandalwood but more like Musk <note>Latin: Moschus</note>, and when rubbed or placed on coals, it spreads a most pleasant scent approaching that of Musk. However, the scent of the outer parts gradually disappears, so it must be kept wrapped or enclosed. This is the best and most expensive kind, and pieces larger than the palm of a hand are not found.
The second species has more notable longitudinal veins and is of a more intense color, almost liver-colored, with the veins tending toward brown. It likewise gives off a good scent, though weaker than the former. Pieces of this are found as long and thick as a leg, and they seem to be the heart or internal substance of the tree.
The third species is reddish, and sometimes slightly red like *Lingo-Batu* <note>a hard, stone-like wood</note>, having thin streaks almost like Beech wood. Externally it has such a brown color that it is sold as Red Sandalwood, but it is more solid and harder than the preceding. This is the cheapest...

<column-break/>

...which are found in short knots, and which appear much more yellow and withered to the eye.
**Name.** In Latin, *Agallochum spurium*, that is *Bastard Aloeswood*. In Malay, *Garo Tsjampacca*, because it comes close to the scent of that flower; in Banggai, *Angaro*.
**Location.** This wood occurs on Borneo, in the regions of Sambas and Sukadana, as well as in Palembang, located on the east coast of Sumatra. One also finds a few of these trees on the island of Banggai, located on the east coast of Celebes, but not on the whole island, only in the smallest part called Gape, near the villages of Bancalang and Labo. The trees are mostly unknown to the inhabitants because they only find the decayed pieces in the forest. The people of Kelang say that they also grow on their island, called *Bakewe* by them, and are considered a kind of wild *Champacca* growth. They have also been found on Sula Besi and in Ternate, but everywhere with leaves like those of the *Champacca*.
**Use.** It is a wood of very little value; for on Java one can buy a *Picul* for a *Real of Eight*, and it is used there for nothing else but the fumigation of their houses. Some also put it among common incense <note>Dutch: Dupa</note>, not for the good scent, but to increase the bulk, for it is of little use there because it adulterates the other scents.
Now we must also mention in passing another rare variety called *Calambac Puti*, or *White Aloeswood*, by which we do not mean the aforementioned light wood *Itthion* or *Simple Agallochum*, but another very rare variety, of which only one tree exists today in Coinam <note>Vietnam</note>. The wood from it is so expensive that it cannot be obtained even if one were willing to give a hundred *Tael* for one *Catty*. For the King will not allow the aforementioned tree to be cut because no more can be found. And it is said that if two or three of these leaves fall into the water and someone drinks from it, they will get a bit of a fever, which does not go away until the King goes to make an offering for this tree. Many, however, call the following *Muskwood* also *Calambac Puti*, but it is certain that this is a distinct tree.
The third variety of bastard *Aloeswood* occurs abundantly in these Eastern islands and comes from the tree *Arbor Excæcans*, which will be described in its place in the third Book, Chapter 37. It is also reckoned among the varieties of *Calambac*; indeed, it is held to be good *Calambac* which is found in the old trunks of the *Ligularia Lactea*, of which more will also be said in its place in the sixth Book, Chapter 46.

N. B. the figures of the *True and Bastard Aloeswood* were found in the *High-German Ephemerides*, decade 2, year 1, near page 55.

## XV. CHAPTER.
## Muskwood.

One also brings from Champa, Coinam, and Pegu a white wood, being entirely like Sandalwood, though not so hard, and which also has some veins in the length almost like Fir wood, and of which one also finds three kinds.
The first and finest is entirely like white Sandalwood, but much softer; the innermost parts are somewhat yellower, the scent also mostly corresponding with that of Sandalwood, but drawing somewhat toward *Musk*. When rubbed or laid on coals, it smells very lovely of *Musk*. But the scent in the outer parts fades over time, therefore it must be well wrapped and kept enclosed. This is the best and most expensive, and one has no pieces of it larger than just a hand's length.
The second type has more apparent veins in the length, is also higher in color, or liver-colored; the veins draw somewhat toward the reddish-brown, and it is also of good scent, though much weaker than the previous one. Of this one has pieces as long and thick as a leg, and they seem indeed to be the heart of a tree.
The third draws somewhat toward the reddish-brown, and is sometimes light-red, like *Lingo-Batu*, with fine streaks, almost like Beech wood, fading to such a brown on the outside that it is sold for red Sandalwood, being denser and harder than the preceding, and this is the poor...

### CHAPTER SIXTEEN.
->Sandalwood, Tsjendana.<-

Although this aromatic tree grows outside the territory of Amboina and the Moluccas, and it is not my intention to enlarge my work with such trees or plants, I nevertheless found it necessary to insert a description of Sandalwood here at the same time, though no fuller than I have been able to experience, and this chiefly for this reason: first, because I have not yet known the Sandalwood tree to have been fully described by any European until now; second, because certain trees grow in Amboina besides, which could boast of being from the family of the Sandalwood tree and related to it; and third, because I have something to advise readers and enthusiasts about, which has until now been erroneously believed concerning Sandalwood. And although it should not be considered a perfect description, it can at least be inserted as an accurate observation, and I shall commit the rest to the fair mind of the reader and the diligence of posterity, so that they may wish to supply what is lacking and correct the errors, if any should have arisen.

So that this description may be of greater authority, let the reader know that it was not indeed drawn from the sight of the trees themselves growing in Timor, but nonetheless from certain of their branches, pieces of wood, and roots, along with a short description of Sandalwood and Snakewood <note>Latin: Lignum Colubrinum; Dutch: Slangen-hout</note>, sent to me in the year 1680 through the care of *Antonius Hurt*, an ordinary Councilor of India and former Governor of Amboina, as well as by *Jacob Wyckerfoot*, the chief at Timor. To both of these men must be given the honor of further knowledge of these trees, which will shine forth in these writings. A figure has been depicted following those branches, and first I must remove a common error: namely, that white, yellow, and red Sandalwood are believed to come from the same trees. For I have inquired sufficiently into what might be the truth of this matter; and I have understood that white and yellow are indeed produced from related trees, but not from one single tree, although both grow on one and the same island. Red Sandalwood, however, comes from a completely different tree, too diverse from the others, and growing on far different islands, so that I cannot fathom why previous writers have included these so dissimilar trees under one name: wherefore I shall describe the red kind in a specific chapter.

White and yellow Sandalwood do not differ much, being found sometimes in one and the same tree, and sometimes in a different one. For all yellow is wrapped in white...

**Names:** In Latin *Lignum Moschatum*, after the Malay *Caju Casturi*, for the Malays call Musk *Casturi*; some call it (though wrongly) *Calambac Puti*, which belongs to the two other woods described in the previous chapters.

**Usage:** It is mostly used among fragrant ointments, which are ground fine on a stone, and with which one smears the body for the sake of the good scent, as well as among *Dupa* <note>incense</note>: It is also used by the Chinese among their medicines, and drunk with weak Arack, to moderately warm the body.

## BOOK II. Chapter XVI. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

<column-break/>

The yellow sandalwood <note>Latin: *citrinum*</note> occurs in greater or lesser quantities, so that the yellow is nothing other than the heart and internal substance of the tree; on the other hand, trees are also found that bear nothing but white wood, with no or very little yellow in the pith.

Outwardly, these trees have no difference, so that the inhabitants cannot distinguish them, even if they are uprooted or cut down; but it has been found that the place of growth makes the most difference. Sandalwood cannot be distinguished from other wild trees from a distance, except that its bark is ash-gray mixed with a little red, thin, and hard; in younger trees it is firmly attached to the wood, but in old ones it flakes off in layers, making most of the trunk appear bare. It reaches the height of a walnut tree, and the branches divide into many thin and smaller twigs, on which the leaves are positioned opposite one another in a cross shape.

The leaves are of common form, almost like those of the *Varinga* or *Microphyllos* <note>The *Varinga* is a type of Banyan or Fig tree; *Microphyllos* refers to a small-leafed variety</note>, but they are not as thick; they are four finger-widths long and three wide, with smooth edges and many fine parallel veins, as in the *Varinga*, protruding from both sides. On younger trees they are a deep green, but on old ones they are pale or yellowish. The twigs are richly adorned with these leaves and form a dense crown. I have not seen the flowers, nor has anything been recorded about them, and the native Timorese could tell me nothing certain about them, as they do not appear clearly on such tall and wild trees; however, according to the report of Garcia <note>Garcia de Orta, a 16th-century Portuguese physician and botanist</note>, they are said to be blackish-blue.

The fruits are like short olives, such as those that grow around Algiers and in Barbary, or like laurel berries. They vary in color according to their ripeness: first they are green, and finally they are blue-black. When dried and chewed in the mouth, these fruits stain it a dark red or purple color. Few of them reach full maturity, and they cannot be easily collected because they fall off easily and are greedily eaten by certain birds—a species of starling—which then scatter them with their droppings throughout the forest, from which new little trees sprout, just as the Nutmeg trees in Banda are propagated by the "nut-eaters" <note>likely referring to the Nutmeg Pigeon</note>.

Because these Sandalwood trees grow this way, if the fresh or dry wood yields no scent, they must be left alone until they are completely old. The sign of this, as mentioned, is when the leaves begin to turn yellow and fall off with most of the twigs, and the bark peels away from the trunk, making the wood appear whitish. Even then, these trees yield little scent, which no one can easily perceive except the natives, who have been accustomed to it from youth and have handled these trees. For this reason, they have persuaded foreign merchants that all Sandalwood would be of poor quality if it were cut by a foreigner. They are allowed to keep this opinion, as it would be difficult for foreigners to traverse those wild and vast mountains and drag back those heavy pieces. Therefore, when they enter into a contract with foreign merchants to deliver a shipload of this wood (which involves strange and stern ceremonies and duties), they send a troop of their people into the forest to fell the trees. The eldest among them stands quietly in the forest for an hour, looking up toward the heights; then he begins to cut a tree. If he perceives a good scent, all the others proceed with the cutting; but if he does not perceive a pleasant scent in the tree, he postpones the cutting for that day. This is usually done when the moon is not shining <note>during the dark of the moon</note>.

The inhabitants used to leave the roots with a part of the trunk two or three feet above the ground, but whether such a trunk sprouts anew, our people could not learn, as it was reported in different ways; this may perhaps be known to the Portuguese, as they are closer to the place where the most Sandalwood is found.

The trees themselves are often two fathoms <note>Latin: *ulnas*; Dutch: *vaademen*</note> thick in circumference, and in cleaning them, so much is often cut away that scarcely a fathom of thickness remains, which still yields quite large pieces. Today, however, at the request of our people, they uproot the entire tree along with the roots,

<meta>This page continues the botanical and commercial description of Sandalwood (Sandalum), focusing on the differences between yellow and white wood, grading practices by Timorese traders, and the history of its name.</meta>

### AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chapter XVI.

Since it has been found that a great quantity of yellow wood <note>Latin: *ligni citrini*</note> exists at the roots and around the knots, it is highly valued. Freshly cut wood has little or no scent; the fragrance is only perceived once it has become dry. At the center of the wood, or the yellow heart, some of the outer pale wood must always be left to retain and preserve the scent longer; for when the white wood is cut away entirely, the scent evaporates very easily. The yellow wood is sometimes of such an intense color that it approaches the color of a dandelion or egg yolk, often showing reddish veins along its length, which leads some to erroneously call it Red Sandalwood <note>Latin: *Sandalum rubrum*</note>; such yellow Sandalwood is considered the very best.

White sandalwood holds the second place, having only a small quantity of yellow wood in the middle. The cheapest, however, is that which is entirely white and possesses no yellow wood at its heart. It is important to know that all Sandalwood trees have no yellow wood at all in their youth. I was sent pieces of such wood that were about as thick as a thigh, entirely white and without any scent, possessing only a slight sweetness in the thin, dry, and hard bark. The people of Timor testify with one voice that the yellow heart only forms in adulthood and more advanced age in those trees whose nature it is to produce it. Once the Sandalwood has been cleaned and brought to the shore, it is piled into long, square heaps, usually formed to the length and width of the ship that is to transport it, which they have promised to fill. It is further divided into three types used by merchants: the first is "thick" (*grof*), the second "thin" (*corent*), and the third "mixed" (*carep*). The first contains the best and largest pieces; the second is thinner; and the third consists of branch pieces, which are the cheapest. For the first grade, the Timorese used to pack and deliver four *Pickols* <term>Pickol: a unit of weight used in Southeast Asia, here defined as 125 pounds</term> in one bundle; for the second grade, six *Pickols*; and for the third, eight *Pickols*, all for the price of forty Imperial Rix-dollars per bundle. They would sell at this price only to the Portuguese "Macau-navigators," because these men provided them with gold and other necessities on credit. To other merchants, they sell only four *Pickols* of wood for that price, and it is not sorted by grade but mixed together.

### Name.
In Latin it is called *Sandalum*; the yellow and best kind is *Sandalum pallidum* or *Citrinum*, while the pale or outer wood is *Sandalum album*. Garcia <note>referring to Garcia de Orta, a 16th-century Portuguese physician and naturalist</note> in his *Aromatics*, Book I, Chapter 17, calls the yellow part the "heart" (*cor*) and the white part the "wood" (*lignum*). In pharmacies and among modern Latinists, it is called *Santalum*, though the former name is better. The word is actually of Arabic origin, *Sandal*, and perhaps stems from the Malay and Macassarese *Tsjendana*, which the Portuguese write as *Chandana*. Both the yellow and white species are included under this name. This wood was unknown to the ancient Greek writers, and therefore it is not probable that it was known to the ancients, much less to the Israelites, even though modern translators wish to persuade us of this by interpreting the word *Ahalim* in Numbers 24:6 as Sandalwood. This seems even less likely because the Sandalwood is not a vast or spreading tree, nor does it grow by rivers or banks, but rather in sunny mountains exposed to the sun.

The first mention of it is found in the works of Avicenna and Mesue <note>famous medieval Islamic physicians</note>, where the best species is nicknamed *Makaffari*. This name has greatly troubled translators; Garcia wished to correct it to *Massafrani*, meaning "saffron-colored" or yellow. Others think, with better reason, that it is the name of a place, which is true. Macassar <note>Latin: *Macaffara*</note> has been a staple port for Eastern spices since ancient times, especially for Sandalwood, which they brought over from Timor, and where that nation still traded deeply in our own times. Thus, *Makaffari* signifies nothing other than Sandalwood brought from Macassar. The traders there used to convince merchants that it grew in their own country, just as we said above that the Javanese did with nutmegs and cloves. The people of Timor call it *Aycamenil*, those of Amboina call it *Ayafru*, and the Chinese call it *Bytboa*. In Canara it is called *Decan*, and in Gujarat *Sercanda*, as Garcia testifies.

### Place.
Both white and yellow Sandalwood grow only on the large island of Timor and certain adjacent islands, such as *Souw* to the west (called the Sandalwood Forest by our people) and *Nomba*, as well as on the southern side of *Ende*, though it is not highly valued there. It is also found...

<column-break/>

*because it has been found that there is much yellow wood at the root, as well as around the knots: Freshly cut wood has little or no smell, for it only gets it once it becomes dry: At the heart or the yellow wood one must always leave the outer or white part, so that it might retain its scent longer, otherwise when the white is chopped off all around, the scent flies away very easily: and the yellow Sandalwood sometimes becomes so high in color that it pulls toward yolk-yellow, also showing some reddish veins in the length, which some then also abusively call red Sandalwood, and this yellow Sandal is also held for the very best.*

*The second place is occupied by the white, having a little yellow around the heart: and the very worst is that which is white throughout, and has no yellow at all around the heart. One must also know that all Sandalwood trees in their youth have nothing yellow about them, as were the pieces sent to me, being nearly as thick as a thigh, white throughout, also without any scent and only having a small sweetness in the thin, dry, and hard bark: The Timorese declare unanimously that the yellow heart first comes in old age, namely to such trees whose nature it is to get it. The cleaned Sandalwood now being brought to the beach, is there piled into a long square heap, being commonly as long and wide as the Ship is over its whole stem, whose cargo they have promised to deliver: Furthermore, it is sorted into three parts, which the Merchants call 1. coarse, 2. Corent, 3. Carep; The first are the best and largest pieces, but Carep the thinnest, and from the branches, therefore the worst: Of the first sort the Timorese used to deliver four pickols (a pickol is 125 pounds) in a bale, of the second six, and of the third eight, for 40 Rix-dollars the bale: And that only to the Portuguese Macau-Fathers, because they were provided by them with gold-dust and other necessities, but to other Traders they will not give more for that price than four Pickols of wood, and that not sorted, but mixed through each other.*

### Name.
*Latin Sandalum, and from that the yellow or best Sandalum Pallidum, or Citrinum, the white or outer wood Sandalum Album. Garcia, Book 1, Aromatics, Chapter 17, calls the yellow Cor, that is heart, and the white Lignum, that is wood; In the Pharmacies and by the modern Latinists it was named Santalum, yet the former is better: For the Arabic word is Sandal, and perhaps descended from the Malay and Macassarese Tsjendana, which the Portuguese write Chandana, and both the yellow and white sorts were understood under that name: By the ancient Greek Writers this wood is unknown, and therefore by no means probable that it was known to the ancients, and much less to the Israelites: As nonetheless the new translators want to make us believe, translating the aforementioned Ahalim, Numbers 24: verse 6, as Santalos: such being the less believable because the Sandal is not a large and spreading tree, nor growing by water-streams, but in the mountains, in open and light places.*

The first mention thereof was then made by *Avicenna*, and *Mesue*, where the best sort was nicknamed *Makaffari*, which has greatly troubled the Translators, for *Garcia, Book 1, Chapter 17* wants it corrected to *Masafrani*, which would be called yellow: Others guess, and such with better reason, that it is the name of a place, which is true: For *Macassar* has already from old times been a staple of the Eastern spices, and especially of the Sandal, which they brought over from Timor, and on which Island that Nation has still negotiated deeply in our times: so that *Makaffari* is nothing else to say than Sandalwood that comes from Macassar: For they made the Merchants believe that it fell in their Lands, as we have said above that the Javanese have done with the Nutmegs and Cloves: The Timorese call it *Aycamenil*, on Amboina *Ayfaru*. Chinese *Bytboa*: In Canara, Decan, Gujarat *Sercanda*, as *Garcia* says.

### Place.
Both the yellow and white Sandalwood grow only on the large Island Timor, and some surrounding Islands, as, to the West on *Souw* (by ours named the Sandalwood-forest) and *Nomba*, likewise on the South side of *Ende*, but is not esteemed there: one also finds...
