### Book II. Chapter XVI. AMBOINESE HERBAL. 45

Rare trees also occur in Madura and the Eastern region of Java, but this wood quickly loses its scent and is not of great value. In Bali, in the region of Tata around Bassagium <note>Dutch: Ballagie</note>, which is a high mountain, Sandalwood is also found; however, this is only cut when they burn their kings, and it is not sent to other regions. Whoever cuts it must first perform a sacrifice to the tree with a white hen and a little incense, otherwise they say the wood will not be excellent in scent. In Timor itself, it does not grow in all places, nor is it equally good everywhere. In its western region, which the Dutch <note>Latin: *Belgae*</note> inhabit and possess around the Bay of Kupang <note>original: *sinum Coepan*</note>, it does not grow, but mostly in the southern <note>Latin: *Zephyream*</note> part of that island, not near the shore but in remote mountains. Even so, certain trees in the nearest mountains can be clearly distinguished from the sea by the whitish bark of the old trunks. It is also not equally good in all ports of that same region; for that of Amarassi is the whitest, which Garcia <note>The Portuguese physician Garcia da Orta</note> simply calls "wood." The best has been brought since ancient times from Batumeana, Tireisi, and Amanubana, situated in that same southern region.

In the northern part, the best grows at the ports of Mena, which is mostly yellow <note>Latin: *citrinum*</note>; this place is occupied today by the Portuguese. However, the people of Makassar and King Samboppa <note>The ruler of the Sultanate of Gowa-Tallo, whose seat was the fortress of Somba Opu</note> have claimed jurisdiction over the northern coast of Timor since ancient times. It is certain that shortly after the destruction of that place, which was accomplished by Dutch arms in the year 1667, they sent commanders to collect tribute through many places on the same coast, even where the Portuguese already lived. It would not have been necessary to recount all this in this Herbal, if it did not serve to confirm the explanation of that name *Macassari*.

The Sandalwood locations assigned by Garcia in the cited passage are as follows, though the names are mostly corrupted: Mena, Matonea, Camanafa, and Serviago, which should be called Mena, Batumeana, Amarassi, and Serviana. As for the capital city of Java called Verbali, I do not know which one it might be. In the Nassau voyages, one reads that on two islands, the *Ilha d’Fernandes* located in the Chilean sea <note>Latin: *Tsji-lefensi mari*</note> at thirty-three degrees Southern latitude, white Sandalwood also grows, but of a weaker scent; I believe, however, that this is another wood, for our Europeans easily confuse such things. On the Malabar coast in the Balaghat mountains, white Sandalwood is also found, and in the southern part of Masulipatnam the red kind grows. I believe, however, that the wood called *Sambarane* is taken for white Sandalwood, which is very similar to Sandalwood but harder.

**Use and Virtues.** Sandalwood, both white and yellow, has a very temperate quality, consisting of subtle and soft parts. Generally, however, the yellow is thought to possess a higher degree of heat, just as it has a more penetrating scent. This wood is in greater use throughout India than in our colder lands, which is why only a small part of it is transported to Europe. Since it has a temperate quality, it cools moderately and greatly restores lost spirits; hence it is more useful in these regions, where throughout India it is much used rasped or ground with water into a thin pulp. The Indians smear their bodies with this, both for cooling and for the pleasant scent, which they do not only on hot days but also in fevers, adding cooling flowers. It is not, or rarely, used internally.

The pleasant scent of the wood is noticed more in the raw state than if it is placed on coals, which is why it is added to no incense <note>Latin: *suffumigio*</note>. Although the Banians <note>Indian merchants; original: *Benjanenses*</note> and other pagans of India use this wood to burn their dead more out of luxury than for the sake of a grateful scent. Nor does it serve for cabinet-making on account of its pale and inelegant color, although some small boxes are formed from it, for which the yellow kind is used, though these lose their scent in a short time. Some merchants are so sharp-sighted that they can distinguish by the color where the Sandalwood grew. White Sandalwood ground and drunk with water for many days has cured virulent gonorrhea <note>original: *Gonorrhœam virulentam*</note> in both women and men. Sandalwood shavings sewn into linen pillows and placed with clothes impart a pleasant scent to them, which clings to them for a long time. The Macassarese and Malays, however, for what reason I know not, do not love the pure scent of Sandalwood in their garments.

<column-break/>

There are also a few trees on Madura and the Eastern part of Java, but that wood itself soon loses its smell and was likewise little esteemed. On Bali, in the district of Tata, near Ballagie (being a high mountain), Sandalwood is also found, but this is only felled when they burn their Kings, and not for export. And whoever wants to fell it must first make an offering at the tree with a white hen and a little incense, or they say that otherwise the wood would not smell well. On Timor itself it is also not found in all places, nor is it equally good everywhere: for on its West hook, which the Hollanders possess around the Bay of Kupang, it is not found, but mostly on the South side of that island, not close to the shore, but far in the mountains, yet so that one can clearly recognize some trees on the nearest mountains from the sea by the white bark of the old trunks. It is also not equally good in all harbors of the same side, for that of Amarassi is mostly white, which Garcia calls "wood." The best has been fetched since ancient times from Batumean, Tireis, and Amanuban, situated on the same South side.

On the North side, the best is found in the harbors of Mena, which is mostly yellow, that place being nowadays possessed by the Portuguese. However, the Macassarese, or the King of Samboppo, have claimed for themselves since ancient times the jurisdiction over Timor’s North coast, and it is certain that shortly after their destruction, which occurred by Dutch arms in the year 1667, they demanded tribute through their sent-out commanders in many places of the same coast, yes, even where the Portuguese live. And I would not have had to add all this to this Herbal, if it did not serve to confirm the explanation of the aforementioned name *Macassari*.

The Sandalwood places from Garcia in the cited passage are these, though mostly corrupted names: Mena, Matonea, Camanafa, and Serviago, and must be called Mena, Batumean, Amarassi, and Servian. The trading city of Verbali on Java I cannot guess what it might be. One reads in the Nassau voyage that on the two islands, *Ilha d’Fernandes*, located in the Chilean Sea at 33 degrees Southern latitude, white Sandalwood would also be found, but poorer of scent, and I believe it will be another wood, for our Europeans easily confuse such things. On the coast of Malabar in the mountains of Balaghat there is also white Sandalwood, and on the South side of Masulipatnam also the red; but I believe they take for this white the wood *Sambarane*, which very much resembles Sandalwood but is harder.

**Use and Virtues:** Sandalwood, both white and yellow, is of a truly temperate quality, airy and fine of parts, yet generally the yellow is attributed one degree more heat, as it is also stronger of scent. This wood is generally in much more use in the Indies than in our cold countries, which is why only the smallest part is transported to Europe. For because it has a temperate property, it cools moderately and remarkably refreshes the weary spirits, so it is much better suited in these countries, in a way that it is used throughout all the Indies ground or rubbed with water into a fine pulp, with which the Indians smear the body, both to cool and for the good scent. They do this not only on hot days but also in fevers, then adding some cooling flowers; internally it is not, or seldom, used.

The loveliness of the scent is greater in the raw wood than when placed on glowing coals, and why it is also used in no incense. Although the Banians and other Indian heathens use this wood for the burning of their dead more out of extravagance than for the sake of the good scent. It also does not serve for any cabinet-making because of its pale and unattractive color, although some small desks <note>Dutch: *Kantoirtjes*</note> are made of it, for which one then takes the yellow, but which nevertheless come to lose their scent in a short time. And some merchants are so clever that they can see by the color where the Sandalwood has grown. White Sandalwood rubbed and taken with water for many days together has cured, in both women and men, virulent gonorrhea. The sawdust of Sandalwood sewn into linen cushions and placed with clothes gives them a good scent.

# AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II, Chapter XVI.

...perhaps because they sprinkle corpses with it, which is why they call it the scent of the dead. Previously, as *Garcia* <note>Garcia da Orta, a Portuguese Renaissance physician</note> and his commentator *Clusius* <note>Charles de l'Écluse, a Flemish botanist</note> testify, yellow Sandalwood occurred so rarely that among fifty pieces, one could scarcely find a single true yellow one; for this reason, both men doubted whether this variety was even transported to *Portugal* and *Europe*, since almost everything sold as white in the Apothecaries was nearly devoid of scent, and the yellow variety itself cost more in *India* than it could be sold for in *Europe*. However, since the *Dutch* began to handle this trade, it has become better known and sought in greater quantities; and if, once brought to *Europe*, it should lose some of its scent, the cause must be attributed to the carelessness of merchants or sailors who placed it in the ship, as it should not be put or packed in dark places or near other foul-smelling things.

*Avicenna <note>The Persian polymath Ibn Sina</note>, in his book on the powers of the heart*, says that Sandalwood greatly strengthens and cheers the heart, which is why it is best mixed with those things prescribed against palpitations of the heart. Ground with Rose water and applied as a poultice to the stomach, it removes its heat and burning, especially in burning fevers. The thin bark of the trunk and the roots are also preserved for medicine, although they can only be acquired in short fragments. When chewed in the mouth, it offers a sweet taste, smelling of Sandalwood; and when ground and taken with some liquid, it promotes menstruation. The ground wood, smeared on the head and the entire face, removes a headache <note>original: "Cephalalgiam"</note> arising from heat, and protects the face from sunburn.

In *Celebes* <note>Modern Sulawesi</note>, near the bay of *Cajeeli*, another species of Sandalwood occurs, which is called *Tsjendana Ackar*, that is, Root Sandalwood, since the wood of that tree is not used, but only its roots, which are fragrant and smell of Sandalwood; the wood, however, agrees in color and scent with common Sandalwood, but its scent is stronger. It also grows in the Bay of Tomini near the village of *Parigi*, and is mostly used grated, with which they sprinkle corpses in *coffins* <note>original: "Sandapilis"</note>, for which purpose common white Sandalwood is also used. For the people of Makassar dedicate all Sandalwood to the dead in such a way that they will not place it with any other woods used for daily life; they so abhor and are averse to the scent of Sandalwood that they do not wish to perceive it except among the dead or at burials, just as our nation <note>Referring to Europeans</note> calls upon *Benzoin* <note>A balsamic resin</note> for those uses. Certain segments of this species of Sandalwood were sent to me from Makassar, which I took for true Sandalwood, since they breathed the same scent and had the color of pale Sandalwood; if they were cut, their chips flew apart into small pieces like glass, so that I could observe no difference between this and the root of true Sandalwood.

It should also be noted and observed that many scented woods are denoted by the name Sandalwood by writers, as among others *O. Dapper* <note>Olfert Dapper, a Dutch physician and writer</note> says in his description of Africa that in the kingdom of *Anfiko* (a region in central Africa), two species of Sandalwood are found in great abundance: namely a red one, called there *Tawille*, and a white one called *Zikongo*; the latter, being the best, is ground into powder and mixed with Palm oil by the inhabitants to anoint their bodies for the preservation of health.

To the preceding explanation I shall subjoin some things which Admiral *Cornelius Speelman* noted in his description of *Celebes* in the following manner:

An elegant and heavy Sandalwood occurs here furthermore in the region of *Keyely*. The small variety is devoid of scent, but the heavy variety breathes more strongly than that from *Timor*; it has not yet been transported from there, but it is certain to be found. The inhabitants have refused to cut it for fear that it would be harmful or disadvantageous to them regarding the King's favor; hence, whenever the king requested any Sandalwood, they gave him light and scentless Sandalwood, so that he would leave them undisturbed. It happened sometimes, however, that they sold some of good

<meta>catchword: quality,</meta>

<column-break/>

quality to private individuals, which stays with them for a long time; however, the people of Makassar and the Malays (I know not for what reason) do not want pure Sandalwood or its scent on their clothes, perhaps because they sprinkle dead bodies with it, and they therefore call it a scent of the dead. Before this (as *Garcia* and his commentator *Clusius* themselves testify), yellow Sandalwood was found so little that one could hardly obtain a genuine yellow piece among fifty sections. For this reason, both those gentlemen doubted whether it was actually brought to Portugal and Europe, since most everything sold in the Apothecaries was white and of little scent, and the yellow itself cost more in India than it could be sold for in Europe. But since the Netherlanders have also taken this trade in hand, it has come into better knowledge and can also be obtained in greater quantity; and if, having been brought to Europe, it might have lost some of its scent, then one must attribute the cause of this to the little care that the Merchants or Captains often take regarding the loading of the same, for it does not want to be packed in stifling holds, nor near other strongly smelling goods.

*Avicenna, in his book on the Powers of the Heart*, testifies that Sandalwood remarkably strengthens and gladdens the heart; therefore it is conveniently mixed among those things given for palpitations of the heart. From the ground wood, mixed with Rose water, a compress is made; and being laid on the stomach, it takes away the rankness and burning thereof, especially in hot fevers. The thin bark of the trunk and roots is also kept for Medicine, although one can only cut it off in short pieces. Chewed in the mouth, it tastes sweet and smells like Sandalwood. Ground and taken with some liquid, it promotes the menstrual period of women. The ground wood smeared on the head and over the whole face takes away the headache that comes from heat, and protects the face from sunburn.

On Celebes in the bays of *Cajeeli*, one has yet another sort of Sandalwood, which is called *Tsjendana Ackar*, that is, *Sandalwood of the Root*, because the wood of that tree is not used, but rather the roots, which are fragrant and lean toward Sandalwood; the wood being very similar in color and scent to common Sandalwood, but somewhat stronger in scent. It also grows in the bay of Tomini by the village of *Parigi*, and is mostly used, being grated, to sprinkle dead bodies in coffins therewith, for which purpose common white Sandalwood is also used. For the people of Makassar dedicate all Sandalwood to the dead in such a way that they will not lay it with any other woods that they use daily. They are also so averse and fearful of the Sandalwood scent that they will not suffer it, except with the dead or at burials, just as our nation does with *Benzoin*. From the aforementioned sort of Sandalwood, some pieces were sent to me from *Makassar*, which I have looked upon as genuine Sandalwood; for they were of the same scent and dye as pale Sandalwood; in the chopping it snapped as short as glass, so that I could find no difference between it and the root of the genuine Sandalwood tree.

One must also know, and be mindful, that many fragrant woods are known by writers by the name of Sandalwood, just as among others *O. Dapper*, in his description of *Africa*, says that in the Kingdom of *Anfiko* (a central province of *Africa*) one has a multitude of two kinds of Sandalwood, namely: red, called *Tawille* in that country, and white, named *Zikongo*; with the latter (as the best) beaten to dust and mixed with palm oil, the inhabitants smear their bodies for the preservation of their health.

To the explanation of the immediately preceding, I shall add here what the Honorable Admiral *Cornelis Speelman* has set down in his geography of *Celebes*, reading as follows:

Furthermore, there is beautiful heavy Sandalwood found here in that province, namely *Keyely*. The small is scentless; the heavy, on the other hand, is easily as powerful as that from *Timor*. It has not been drawn from there until now, but it is there, that stands certain. The inhabitants have declined to harvest it out of fear that it would serve as a burden to them in the favor of the King. Therefore, when now and then the Kings demanded some, they gave light and scentless material, so that they would remain unmolested

### OBSERVATION.

That white and yellow Sandalwood are collected and produced from one and the same tree is also testified by *Samuel Dale* in his *Pharmacology, p. 355*, where he says the cortical part <note>The outer bark or sapwood</note> of the tree is called *White Sandalwood*, but the medullary <note>The inner heartwood</note> part is called *Yellow. etc.* And *Valentyn* in his *Reformed History of Simples, p. 186*, writes: *White and Yellow Sandalwood* come from a single tree trunk, which in the East Indies is called *Sarcanda*, and on the island of Timor it fills entire forests. It is said to be similar to an Ash tree, and to bear fruit like cherries, first red, then black upon maturity, yet tasteless and useless; and that its outer part under the bark has white wood, while in the middle it has yellow wood, etc. See further *Pomet, History of Drugs, Book III, chapter 3, pages 107 and 108*, and *Valentyn, Literary India, letter 2, p. 386*, as well as *Ray, History of Plants, p. 1804; Parkinson, Theater of Plants, p. 1604; Chabraeus, 36; Jonston, Dendrography, p. 455; and J. Bauhin, volume 1, p. 486; C. Bauhin, Pinax, p. 392; and General History of Lyon, book XVIII, chapter XI, p. 1768, etc. By Breynius in Prodromus 2, page 99 of the new edition*, it is called TRUE SANDALWOOD with yellow and white wood and Laurel-like leaves, the figure of which you may see in *Table V, Figure 1 and page 19* of the description, and in *Ray volume 3, appendix page 68, and Hermann, Materia Medica, page 85, chapter 3, part 1, etc.*

### CHAPTER SEVENTEEN.
### Red Sandalwood. Tsjendana Djingi.

The similarity of the name with the preceding requires that we now also treat Red Sandalwood, and especially since from ancient times and even now, the greater part of Europe remains in the error that white, yellow, and red Sandalwood come from similar trees and grow in one and the same region. The contrary, however, has been discovered for about two hundred years now, since Europeans have traveled through the Indies on their voyages. It is, however, beyond my power to describe anything certain regarding Red Sandalwood, as this tree grows far outside the territory of my investigation; moreover, so many different red woods have come before me which are considered Red Sandalwood, and such different accounts of it have been related, that in this remote shore I can hardly conclude anything certain. I will therefore subsequently add here the most probable accounts of it, leaving their verification to those who shared them with me, and further inquiry to those who have obtained a better opportunity for this. In advance, therefore, I reject the opinion of those who maintain that all such red woods, especially those growing in the East Indies, are to be reduced to a single genus of Red Sandalwood, just as all such thickened red juices are held to be Dragon's Blood <note>original: "sanguine Draconis"; a bright red resin obtained from different species of several distinct plant genera</note>. Regarding these opinions, I have always thought that chaos arises and provides the occasion for great errors, as is read concerning a certain maidservant who had served Hemlock <note>original: "Cicutam"; a highly poisonous plant</note> in food to her Master instead of true Chervil <note>original: "Chærephyllo"; a mild culinary herb</note>. I therefore deem it necessary that its own name be given to each species, and that it be described; and lest species be needlessly multiplied, it can easily be noted in what part one agrees with another, and what characters of affinity are to be observed.

...found. It has happened, however, that they have now and then sold something good to private individuals, serving as proof that they are not disinclined to trade in it, which is further confirmed by the finding of the Chinese Doctor Entje Sabban, father-in-law of Intje Soulang, both residing in the quarter of the King of Ternate. Having performed a cure in the house of the King of Macassar some years ago, he was granted permission to make a trip there, at which time he brought some bars <note>original: "baaren" or Bahar, a traditional unit of weight in the East Indies</note> back from there and sold them here in Macassar for 60 Maas <note>A small gold coin or unit of currency</note> per Bahar. ### REMARK.

That white and yellow *Sandalwood* are gathered from one and the same tree is also testified by *Samuel Dale* in his *Pharmacology, p. 353*, where he says the part of the bark <note>meaning the outer wood</note> is called the *white*, but the pithy part the *yellow*. And *Valentyn* in his *Reformed History of Simples, p. 186, writes*: the white and yellow Sandalwood come from one and the same trunk of a tree, which in the East Indies is called *Sarcanda*, and on the Island of Timor covers whole forests, and is said to be like the Ash tree, and to bear fruits like Cherries, first white <note>Note: the Latin says red</note>, then black through ripeness, yet tasteless and of no use; which tree in its outward part under the bark gives the white, but in the middle the yellow Sandalwood, etc. Further see *Pomet, History of Drugs, book III, chap. 3, pages 107 and 108, and Valentyn, Literary India, second letter, page 386; as well as Ray, History of Plants, p. 1804; Parkinson, Theater, p. 1604; Chabraeus, 36; Jonston, Dendrography, p. 455; and J. Bauhin, volume 1, page 486; and C. Bauhin, Pinax, p. 392; and General History of Lyon, book XVIII, chap. XI, page 1768, etc. By Breynius in the 2nd Prodromus, page 99 of the new edition* it is called *True Sandalwood with yellow and white wood, Laurel leaves*, of which see the figure in *Table V, Fig. 1 and page 19 the description, as well as in Ray volume 3, appendix page 68, and Hermann, Materia Medica, page 85, chap. 3, part 1, etc.*

### XVII. CHAPTER.
### Red Sandalwood.

*The similarity of the name with the preceding would indeed require that we now also spoke of the red Sandalwood, the more so because from of old, and by most of Europe, people are still in the misunderstanding that yellow, white, and red are the same kind of trees and grow on one and the same land: though of which the contrary has been experienced, namely, since 200 years ago that the Europeans have navigated the Indies with their shipping. However, for me it falls impossible to describe anything certain of the red Sandalwood, because that tree grows far outside the district of my investigation, and moreover so many sorts of red woods have come before me, which are looked upon as red Sandalwood, and such various tales told of them, that at this remote place I can very poorly clear my way through them. I shall therefore hereafter set down, one after another, some of the most probable of the mentioned tales, leaving the responsibility for them to those who have given them to me, and the further investigation to such who have better opportunity for it. And beforehand I then reject the opinion of those who maintain that one should bring all such red woods, especially growing in the East Indies, under one genus of red-Sandalwood, just as those people also hold all red and dried-in juices for Dragon's-blood; of which propositions I have always been of the opinion that they create confusion and give cause for great abuses, as one reads of a Maid-servant who gave her master Fool's Parsley <note>Hemlock</note> to eat in his food instead of real Chervil. I therefore judge it necessary that one describes each sort with its particular name, and yet, in order not to multiply the species or genera unnecessarily, one can indeed indicate therein where the one corresponds with the other, and what signs of kinship are found there.*

### AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chapter XVII.
#### 48
<center>HERBARII AMBOINENSIS Liber II. cap. XVII.</center>

So that I may review in order all the red woods which have been thrust upon me as Sandalwood, I first exclude the red **Lingoo-wood**, which is very common here in the eastern regions, and which I believe has no commonality with Red Sandalwood except for the color alone; as well as the wood known everywhere as **Sapan**. The remaining woods held to be Red Sandalwood I divide into three species: first, the common Red Sandalwood used in medicine, which is exported to Europe for apothecaries and has been known since ancient times; the second is the **Malaccan** variety, held to be Sandalwood by the common inhabitants; the third is the **Portuguese** variety, which is the most expensive and rarest.

Regarding the first common or medicinal Red Sandalwood, I can offer nothing more certain than what the most skilled botanist, Mr. Herbert de Jager, shared with me. He was an eyewitness to those things he reported to me, having personally traveled through the regions where it grows. He affirms that all common Red Sandalwood known to our nation and continually brought to Europe comes from one and the same tree from which the wood called **Caliatour** <note>Also known as Red Sanders or *Pterocarpus santalinus*.</note> is obtained. This wood is very hard, solid, and dark red; today it can be acquired in great quantities in the northern parts of the Coromandel Coast. Various types of furniture, such as benches, seats, etc., are elegantly crafted from it. However, not all trees of this wood provide the true Sandalwood, but only the old ones; he demonstrates this most clearly in a letter sent to me in the year 1689, the text of which follows:

The common Red Sandalwood used in medicine, and available everywhere in the pharmacies of Persia, Arabia, Turkey, and Europe—of this I say it is one and the same as the wood called **Caliatour**, and does not differ from it. It is sought after as Sandalwood when it is old, as many Indian trees that produce fragrant wood have the most penetrating scent and most effective power in their final years, which is likewise observed in Yellow Sandalwood. That this is the true medicinal Red Sandalwood is declared by its name, as the Brahmins and other heathens of the Coromandel Coast, who are knowledgeable of the trees of that region, testify with one voice and agreement. They call this Caliatour wood in the Sanskrit <note>original: "lingua Santskrictenſi"</note> language ***Rakta-Tsjandanam***, <note>original: "h. e. Sandalum ſanguineum vel rubrum"</note> that is, blood-red or red Sandalwood; and in the Deccan language, which is the ordinary language of India, but with a Deccani inflection, they call it ***Reket-Tsjandan*** with the same meaning. These people deserve to be believed in the naming and knowledge of the <term>simples</term> <note>Medicinal plants used as individual ingredients.</note> which their own land supplies and which serve so many people. Furthermore, the name ***Tsjendan*** was converted by the Arabs into ***Tsjandal***, from whom it properly has its derivation. Together with the wood itself, through the trade of India, it was first transferred to Persia, Basra, and Arabia, and thus was first used in those regions, and then also in Europe for medicinal and other purposes. The ancients <note>Referring to Greek and Roman authorities like Dioscorides or Pliny.</note> left no trace of knowledge of this. The reason they count this wood among the Sandalwoods is that, especially if it is old and rubbed while dry until it grows warm, it gives off a scent of Sandalwood. This is stronger if at that time a thin shaving is cut off and smelled at that very moment. If this tree is freshly cut, it breathes a very sensible scent of Sandalwood, and the older the tree is, the more penetrating the scent, though it does not last long. Since the scent of this wood is so weak and quickly vanishing, it is not held in such high esteem among the heathens as Yellow Sandalwood; hence it can be acquired for a low price. For that reason, they never, or at least very rarely, use it for anointing the body (which they do primarily for the sake of a pleasant scent), and therefore they give this red wood, especially due to its weak scent, the name ***Koe Tsjandanam***, <note>Likely from the Sanskrit 'Ku-chandana,' meaning bad or inferior sandalwood.</note> which in the language of the learned Brahmins denotes "vile Sandalwood." This cause led **Matthiolus** <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century Italian physician and botanist.</note> to the opinion that Red Sandalwood is entirely devoid of scent, and if a scent were perceived in the wood, it had come to it by participation from being placed near White or Yellow Sandalwood.

<column-break/>

*To now treat in order all the red woods that have been pushed into my hands as Sandalwood, I first exclude from them the red **Lingoo-wood**, very common in these Eastern Quarters, and which I judge to have no fellowship with any Red Sandalwood, except only for the color; as well as the well-known **Sappan-wood**. The others, which are held to be Red Sandalwood, I divide into three sorts, namely: First, **Sandalum Rubrum Usuale**, or the common Red Sandalwood, which is transported to Europe for the pharmacies, and is the oldest in knowledge. Secondly, the **Malay** variety, which is held as such among the common natives there. And thirdly, the **Portuguese**, which is the most expensive and rarest.*

*Of the first common or medicinal Red Sandalwood, I know nothing more certain to bring forward than that which has been communicated to me by the experienced botanist, Mr. **Herbert de Jager**, being an eyewitness of what he claims, as having personally traveled through the lands where it grows. This gentleman maintains that all the common Red Sandalwood known by our nation, and brought to Europe from time to time, comes from one and the same tree from which one gets the so-called **Caliatour-wood**; being a very hard, massive, and dark-red wood, which can be obtained nowadays in great quantities in the northern parts of the Coromandel Coast; and from which also many kinds of beautiful furniture, chairs, and benches are made. Although not all the trees of that wood deliver the upright Sandalwood, but only the old trees; and this he proves in a letter written to me in the year 1689, in which the words sound thus:*

*The common Red Sandalwood that is used in medicine, and is found everywhere in the pharmacies of Persia, Arabia, Turkey, and Europe—of that I say once more, that the same is one with the **Caliatour-wood**, and does not differ from it. This is only sought as Sandalwood when it is old, just as most trees of India that have a fragrant wood are most powerful in scent and effect in their final years, as is also recognizable in the Yellow Sandalwood. And that it is indeed the right medicinal Red Sandalwood, the name points out, just as the **Brahmins** and other heathens of the Coromandel Coast (who are experienced in the plants of that land) agree in this; they call this Caliatour-wood in Sanskrit ***Rakta-Tsjandanam***, that is blood-Sandal or red-Sandal, and in Deccani (that is, in the ordinary Indian language of the Deccan) by the inflection of that head-speech, ***Reket-Tsjandan***, in the same meaning. They must surely deserve belief in the naming and knowledge of the drugs that their land itself provides, and which so many people use; the more so as the name of **Tsjendan**, changed by the Arabs into **Tsjandal**, flows properly from them, and together with that wood, through the commerce of India, was first brought from there into Persia, Basra, and Arabia, and thus came into use in those lands, and thereafter also in Europe for medicine and otherwise. Of this, the ancients have left us not the slightest sign of knowledge. The cause now why they count it among the Sandalwoods is because, especially when it is old and rubbed dry until it becomes warm, it then gives off a Sandal-scent, which is even stronger when one cuts off a fine thin shaving at that time and then smells that wood at that moment. But when they fell that tree, it gives off a very penetrating Sandal-scent at that time; the more years it has, the more powerful it is, though it does not keep it long. And because the scent of this wood is so weak and faint, it is also nowhere near as highly esteemed among the heathens as the Yellow Sandalwood, and thus also to be obtained for a low price, just as for that reason they never, or at least very rarely, use it for the anointing of the body for the sake of the lovely scent (as they almost always do with the other). Therefore, they have given to that red wood, because of its very weak power of scent, the name ***Koe Tsjandanam***, which in the learned Brahmin language means "bad Sandalwood." This cause also brought **Matthiolus** to the opinion that Red Sandalwood would have no scent in itself, and if one did find any there, it would have come to it by communication from the White or Yellow Sandalwood where it might have lain.*

# II Book. XVII Chapter. AMBOINESE HERBAL. 49

Furthermore, *Mr. de Jager* adds a little later that this wood is very well known by the general name *Chadja* among all the Choolias <note>Indian Muslim traders from the Coromandel Coast.</note> or the Ethiopians <note>A historical term used here broadly for dark-skinned inhabitants of the Indian coastal regions.</note> of the Coromandel Coast, and those born there where the Caliatour-wood itself grows, as well as among all their descendants and relatives, and here among the Malays and others.

So it is (he continues further) that all those whom I and others have questioned on this matter agree with me, testifying with one voice that the very same Caliatour wood comes from the Red Sandalwood tree, and they can point to no other besides this. Thus, credit should not be denied to these men, as they are shrewd and subtle merchants skilled in all kinds of natural goods, and witnesses to a thing so common in the markets of their own homeland, especially since they gain no advantage or profit from it. In a similar way, *Garcia de Orta* <note>A 16th-century Portuguese physician and pioneer of tropical medicine.</note> indicates in distinct terms in his *first book on aromatics, chapter 17*, that the Red Sandalwood tree grows on the Coromandel Coast; and since no other red wood besides Caliatour—which also breathes the scent of Sandalwood—is found there, and it appears there under the name of Red Sandalwood among the herbalists (a fact I have been assured of by those expert in the medicinal arts of that region), it is likewise evident that the heart of the Caliatour tree is one and the same as Red Sandalwood.

Furthermore, *Mr. de Jager* writes in the following manner:

Caliatour wood, which is solid, hard, and quite heavy, is mostly used in the dyer's art; from it are also crafted benches, seats, and other furniture, and a small part of it is used in medicine. That which is required for this last purpose does not represent a great quantity in proportion to the vastness and breadth of the regions from which it is distributed throughout the world. For this use, they mostly select that which is older and has an intense and dark red color, whence it also breathes a stronger scent of Sandalwood than the common Caliatour wood; this odor is only perceived by rubbing, as indicated above. The *Armenians* use this in *Shiraz* and *Isfahan* <note>Major cities in Safavid Persia (modern Iran).</note> for the distillation of spirit of wine <note>Brandy or high-proof alcohol.</note>, to which it gives a most elegant, intensely red color and tint, although its taste does not please me much.

This is the collection of things that *Mr. de Jager* communicated to me regarding Red Sandalwood, with which I gladly agree insofar as they regard the usual or common Red Sandalwood, especially that which is transported to Europe. However, I have always been of an opinion from which I would not easily depart: that the *Arabs*, from whom we in Europe first received knowledge of this red wood, brought it from regions situated on the East Coast of Africa, or the islands lying before them, such as *Zanzibar*, *Madagascar*, etc. Arab merchants have frequented these regions since ancient times, although it could have happened that in those same times it was also brought from India. I was moved to this opinion not only because I have read in various travelogues of different nations that those places enjoy entire forests of Red Sandalwood, but much more because I have heard all the inhabitants of these Eastern regions with whom I have dealt call Red Sandalwood *Tsjendana Djingi*, which denotes the Sandalwood of the Ethiopians. For it is known that *Zingi* and *Zangi*—or as our Malays pronounce it, *Djingi*—signifies in its origin among both the Hebrews and Arabs a curly-haired Moor or Ethiopian, and especially such a one who inhabits the East Coast of Africa, which region is called *Zanzibar* <note>original: "Sanguebaar"</note> to this day, and where *Ptolemy* <note>The Greco-Roman geographer.</note> also places the *Promontory of Zingis*. I do indeed grant to *Mr. de Jager* that in one of the languages of the people of Hindostan the same word also signifies "black," from which he says the black Myrobalans are called *Zengi Hararah*, but I have heard no one give Red Sandalwood the surname "black." Nor does it necessarily follow that the Malay, Javanese, or other Indian merchants must have visited the African islands in their vessels to bring back that wood and its name; they could have received this name either through trade or by some other...

<column-break/>

*A little further, Mr. de Jager testifies that among all the Choolias, or Coast-Moors, specifically in the Land of Coromandel where the Caliatour-wood itself grows—whether they were born there, descended from there, or have traveled there—as well as here among the Malays and others, it is best known by the general name of Chadja.*

*So it is that I have them on my side (says his Honor), all of whom, as many as I and others have asked about this, unanimously recognize the Caliatour-wood as that of the Sandalwood tree, and can point to no other besides it. To these men, as experienced negotiators and merchants well-versed in all types of goods, and as witnesses to a dry-good that is so common in their land, and in which they have not the slightest interest or stake, full credit must be given. Likewise,* Garcia de Orta, Book 1 on Aromatics, Chapter 17, *writes in very clear terms that the Red Sandalwood tree grows on the coast of Coromandel, and just as no other red wood except the Caliatour variety, which has a Sandalwood scent, is to be found there, it is known there among the herbalists under the name of Red Sandalwood, just as I have been fully assured by those experienced in the medicinal knowledge of that land; so it is also clear as day that the heart of the Caliatour tree is exactly the same as the Red Sandalwood.*

*And further still, Mr. de Jager writes thus:*

*The Caliatour-wood, which is quite firm, massive, and fairly heavy, is mostly used for dyeing, and also worked into benches, seats, and chairs; likewise a small portion of it is used in medicine. All that which is distributed throughout the whole world for this latter purpose makes up no great quantity in proportion to the vast extent of those lands. For this, they usually choose the wood that is older, higher, and darker red in color, and consequently also stronger in Sandalwood scent than the ordinary Caliatour-wood, which one only truly perceives upon rubbing, in the manner mentioned above. The Armenians in Shiraz and Isfahan use it most in their distillation of brandy, to which it gives a very beautiful high-red color, although the taste does not suit me much.*

*This is, in short, a summary of what the Honorable Mr. de Jager shared with me concerning Red Sandalwood, with which I gladly conform as far as the common and usual Sandalwood is concerned, and especially that which is carried to Europe. However, I have always been of the opinion, and am still hard-pressed to be moved from it, that the Arabs—from whom we in Europe gained our first knowledge of that red wood—originally fetched it from the lands situated on the East Coasts of Africa, or the islands situated before them, such as Zanzibar, Madagascar, etc. Arab merchants have visited these lands since olden times, though it may be that even in those olden times it was also brought from India. I was moved to this not only because I have read in various travel books of various nations that the aforementioned places have entire forests of Red Sandalwood, but much more because I have heard all the natives of these Eastern quarters with whom I have associated call the Red Sandalwood* Tsjendana Djingi, *which surely means the Moorish or Ethiopian's Sandalwood. For it is known that* Zingi *and* Zangi, *originally in Hebrew as well as Arabic, signifies a curly-haired Moor or Ethiopian, especially those who inhabit the East Coast of Africa, which region is called Zanzibar to this day, and where* Ptolemy *also places the* Promontorium Zingis. *I grant to Mr. de Jager that in one of the Hindustani languages the same word also signifies "black," from which His Honor says the black Myrobalans are named* Zengi Hararah, *but I have yet heard no one who gives Red Sandalwood the surname "black." It also does not strictly follow that our Malays, Javanese, or other Indian merchants must have been to the African islands with their vessels to bring back that wood and that name, whether by commerce or by some other chance...*

### AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II, Chapter XVII. ###

->HERBARII AMBOINENSIS Liber II. cap. XVII.<-

I wish to include what Mr. de Jager indicates in those letters concerning the great navigation of the Javanese from ancient times into the very regions of Africa. Thus Mr. de Jager also demonstrates that as long as a person lives, he must always be learning; for in those same letters he himself admits that on his last journey, undertaken with an honorable embassy to Persia in the year 1684, he was taught by his own experience. This corresponds to my own statement, the substance of which his subsequent words will provide to the reader.

Just as India and its islands produce for the most part the same plants as the East Coast of Africa, such as Madagascar etc., so it does not seem foreign to the truth to me (as my letters given to him will demonstrate) that the Red Sandalwood tree grows and is found in and around Africa. This has also been inferred for some time from those shores, as I learned during my last stay in Gamron <note>Modern Bandar Abbas, Iran; a major trading port for the Dutch East India Company</note> that in these times most Red Sandalwood is transported from the African coasts, and so onwards into Arabia, Persia, and perhaps even to Surat <note>A major port city in Gujarat, India</note> itself, due to the easy access of that navigation, which they complete quickly back and forth at certain times of the year, and moreover sell for a low price. Perhaps it might also happen that the soil and air contribute much to the quality or defect of a plant; thus this wood may be more effective and better there, though this has not yet appeared to me, since I have not yet been able to observe much difference between one and the other.

To these I add from the same letters that the place once called Caliatour is today no longer known by this name on the Coromandel Coast, but in time was changed to Krusjua-Patanam, or Kisjua-Patan, so that the memory of the first name is preserved only among Europeans.

Under Malay Red Sandalwood, which according to the aforementioned division is the second species, I understand various fragments that have been shown to me at intervals, which to the eye differ from the Caliatour wood. These are also blackish or dark red on the outside, but blood-red on the inside, consisting of thin fibers along their length, but yielding to Caliatour wood in weight. However, I can note nothing certain about these, as the fragments differ among themselves, and the natives speak of their origin in different ways, though they say with one voice that it is not from Caliatour wood. They have no notable odor, except that when placed on burning coals they give a little smell of roasted garlic, and pinch the eyes with sharp smoke; on the contrary, I have always found Caliatour wood to breathe a pleasant scent. Some natives affirm these are sought from Siam, others from Cambodia, and others again from Tenasserim <note>A region in modern-day Myanmar</note>, situated on the northern part of Malacca and subject to the rule of the King of Siam. However, Mr. de Jager says they are brought to the last-mentioned place from the Coromandel Coast, and then distributed throughout all of Siam, and used just like Caliatour wood for furniture and the other things mentioned above. But I leave these things to those who travel through the lands, nor do I mention anything further certain or demonstrated about them.

There occurs, moreover, a dark red wood which the Chinese call *Tsjidji*, *Tfidju*, and *Tsjudi*, growing nowhere but in Guangdong, Siam, and Cambodia, which many consider a species of Red Sandalwood. From this, the Chinese make their *Sompits*, that is, the sticks they use at the table for taking food <note>original: "fustes, quibus in mensa ad cibum capiendum utuntur" — chopsticks</note>, and the small cups from which they drink. They wish to ascribe to this wood the power to take away the strength of poison poured into such cups; however, by further investigation, a difference was found between *Tsjidji* and Red Sandalwood, for according to their report, the latter provides large logs, while *Tsjidji* is a small and crooked trunk, from which nothing but Arack-cups <note>Cups for drinking arrack, a distilled alcoholic spirit</note> or such sticks for eating can be made. In that Red Sandalwood which is brought from Champa and Cambodia, and has an intense and redder color than that which is brought from Coromandel, there is sometimes found a soft heart of a dark brown color, having many ridges, and shining like Dragon’s Blood <note>original: "Sanguis Draconis" — a bright red resin used in medicine and dyes</note>, which if chewed or scraped,

<column-break/>

...might have been obtained, which I cannot guess, and yet I am willing to believe, as the aforementioned de Jager states in the same letter concerning the great navigation of the Javanese, who in ancient times even traveled to the African lands. Thus Mr. de Jager also proves that a man must keep learning as long as he lives, for in the aforementioned letter he himself confesses that on his most recent journey in a significant commission in the year 1684 to Persia, he found through his own experience that which agrees with my saying, and of which I share with the reader his own following words.

But just as India with its islands produces very nearly, or at least in bulk, the same plants as the East Coast of Africa, Madagascar, etc., so it is not unlikely to me (as my letters to his Honor will show) that the Red Sandalwood tree might also be found in and around Africa, just as it has since been discovered there. Having also learned on my most recent stay in Gamron that in these times they now fetch the Red Sandalwood mostly from the African coast, and further transport it to Arabia, Persia, and perhaps even to Surat, because of the readiness of that voyage, which they complete back and forth in a very short time during the monsoon, besides the fact that they sell it for a reasonable price. It could also be that just as the soil and the air contribute much to the virtue or vice of a plant, this wood might come forth more powerfully and better there than in India and its islands, which however has not yet appeared to me; as of yet, I cannot make much distinction between the one and the other.

I also add here from the same letter that the place Kaliatours is today no longer known by that name on the Coromandel coast, but has in time changed to Krusjua-Patanam, or Kisjua-Patan, the memory of the first name now being kept only among the Europeans.

Under the Malay Red Sandalwood, being the second species according to my aforementioned division, I understand various small pieces which have been shown to me from time to time, and which by appearance differ from the Caliatour wood, being also blackish or dark red on the outside, and blood-red on the inside, fine-grained in length, but yielding in weight to the Caliatour wood. I cannot write anything certain about this, because the pieces differ even among themselves, and the natives speak variously of their origin, yet they stand together in agreement that it is not Caliatour wood. They have no remarkable smell, except that when placed on glowing coals, they smell a little like roasted onion skins, biting the eyes with a sharp smoke; on the contrary, I find the Caliatour wood always to be more pleasant of scent. Some natives want to fetch this from Siam, others from Cambodia; and again others from Tenasserim, located north of Malacca, and also under the King of Siam. But our Mr. de Jager says that it is brought to the last-named place from the Coromandel coast, and further transported through all of Siam, and used, just like the common Caliatour wood, for furniture and the things mentioned above. But I leave this to those who travel through the lands, without writing anything further positive or certain about it.

There is another dark-red wood, which the Chinese call *Tsjidji*, *Tfidju*, and *Tsjudi*, growing nowhere but in Guangdong, Siam, and Cambodia, which many look upon as a sort of Red Sandalwood, and from which the Chinese make their *Sompits*, that is, Eating-sticks <note>Chopsticks</note>, and Drinking-cups. They also want to ascribe to this the power of making poison, which one puts into such cups, powerless; but upon closer investigation, one finds a difference between *Tsjidji* and Red Sandalwood, which according to them falls in large blocks, whereas the *Tsjidji* remains a small crooked trunk, from which one can make nothing but Arrack-cups and eating-sticks. In that Red Sandalwood which comes from Champa and Cambodia, and is a higher red in color than that from Coromandel, one sometimes finds a soft heart, dark brown in color, with many ridges, and shining like Dragon’s Blood, being soft as wax when chewed and scraped, biting sharply on the tongue, and when placed on coals, smelling like the fattest Lingoo <note>Likely *Pterocarpus indicus*, known as Narra or Lingoum wood</note>, or even more pleasant, and entirely...

## II Book. XVII Chapter. AMBOINESE HERBAL. ##

G 3
Tom. II.
<meta>catchwords: Sandal-, The</meta>

...melted, it is soft like wax, biting the tongue sharply, and when placed on coals, it breathes forth the scent of the very fatty <term>Lingoo</term> wood <note>Pterocarpus indicus, or Narra wood; a prized cabinet timber in the East Indies</note>, but much more pleasant, and it melts entirely. This wood is so soft that in many parts it can be pushed in with a fingernail, though in some parts it is harder, in which it agrees with the true <term>Kilam</term> or primary <term>Agallochum</term> <note>Agarwood or Aloeswood, highly valued for its aromatic resin</note>. It is held in great price and esteem, and it very rarely occurs in old trunks, and never in the Coromandel variety; and if it is rubbed in the hands, whether dry or mixed with water, it stains the hands with a red color.

As for what concerns the Portuguese or red Timorese Sandalwood, which according to my division is the third species, I have never been able to acquire a certain account of it; even from various small pieces which I received from various friends in <term>Batavia</term> <note>Modern-day Jakarta</note>, I am not certain that there was one which came from Timor. The native Timorese living here deny with one voice that any red wood rivaling Red Sandalwood is found in their homeland, except for the red wood called <term>Lingoo</term>. Nevertheless, I have heard from trustworthy men that the Portuguese possess a rare and precious wood which they hold for Red Sandalwood, and it differs notably from the true <term>Caliatour</term> wood <note>Sandalwood from the Coromandel coast of India</note>, which is not unknown to them. According to their reports, this grows on the great island of Timor, but others think it can be sought among the Portuguese living in Timor, even if it does not originate in Timor itself, but is brought there from Siam, <term>Macoua</term> <note>Macao</note>, or other Portuguese territories. Finally, Raja Amassili-Saban, now named Salomon Speelman <note>A local ruler likely baptized or named in honor of the Dutch Governor-General Salomon Speelman</note>, and the King of Ademantutu gave me the following account: that he had seen a red wood which he took for Red Sandalwood growing in Samorro, which is a region of Timor located on a terrifyingly high and dismal mountain in the middle of the land, whose shore, Lacolo, verged toward the west; and from this wood the inhabitants made their flutes, which breathed something of the scent of Sandalwood. This wood can only be brought down in small pieces due to the difficulty of the paths. This so-called Timorese Red Sandalwood differs from the Coromandel type in its qualities as well as its color. For indeed it cools more effectively, and does not bite the eyes so much or excite a burning in the throat, but so small a supply of it can be acquired that an experiment can scarcely be conducted with it.

**Name.** In Latin, *Sandalum rubrum*; in Malay, *Tsjendana Djingi* <note>original: "Tsjendana Djingi"</note>, which is, as was said, Ethiopian Sandalwood, or more properly called Troglodytic <note>From the ancient term for inhabitants of the African coast</note>, since the Arabs call all inhabitants of the eastern part of Africa, both on the mainland and on the islands, <term>Zangi</term> or <term>Zingi</term>, from whose regions, as said above, this wood was originally brought. It is also called *Tsjendana mera* <note>original: "Tsjendana mera", meaning Red Sandalwood in Malay</note>.

**Usage.** Red Sandalwood is never used for incense, nor is it ever placed on coals for its scent, but only for medicinal use. It is of a cooling and drying nature without any astringency. The Indians mostly use it against fevers, ground up and drunk with water, and they also smear the body externally to extinguish the febrile heat and comfort the heart; for it cannot remove the fever itself unless it were an <term>Ephemera</term> <note>A fever lasting only a single day</note>. Shavings of Red Sandalwood taken with rice water cure dysentery <note>original: "Dysenteriam", referred to in the Dutch as "the red run"</note>. Furthermore, it is a common opinion that Red Sandalwood resists every kind of ingested poison, so that it is detected if it is placed in any vessel made of this wood; hence many of the elite of India use boxes for <term>Pinang</term> <note>Areca nut or Betel</note> and drinking cups manufactured from this wood so that in such a way they might detect poison, if by chance there were any; however, this has not yet been proven by experience, though it is certainly true that it is very effective against an ingested toxin to inhibit its power. Red Sandalwood is also held as a secret art and remedy against ingested poison by the nobles of the Malays and Ternatans: namely, red Sandalwood, white <term>Calbabaar</term> <note>Black or white coral used medicinally</note> or Indian white coral, with <term>Calappa Laut</term> <note>The "Sea Coconut" or Lodoicea maldivica, prized as an antidote</note> ground upon a porphyry stone, if they are drunk for several continuous days. If <term>Calappa Laut</term> is not at hand, two other things are equally good and of the highest use. This was tried in <term>Ternate</term> <note>An island in the Maluku Islands</note> in the year 1677 and found to have a good success in a Dutch merchant and his wife, into whose drink a maidservant had mixed a toxin made from spiders.

<column-break/>

...melting: It is so soft that in most places one can push into it with a fingernail, though in some places not, in which it corresponds with the upright <term>Kilam</term>, or primary <term>Agallochum</term>. It is held as expensive and precious, and very little of it is found in old trunks, and never in the Coromandel variety; and when one rubs it in the hand, whether dry or with water, it stains the hands red.

Concerning the Portuguese or red Timorese Sandalwood, being according to my division the third kind, I have likewise never been able to get a certain report of it, and even from the various pieces that I have received from Batavia and other friends, I am not assured that there is one among them which comes from Timor. The true Timorese people who are here unanimously deny that any red wood resembling the shown Red Sandalwood is found in their country, except for the red <term>Lingoo</term> wood. But notwithstanding this, I was informed by trustworthy persons that the Portuguese among them have a rare and precious wood which they hold for Red Sandalwood, and it would differ significantly from the <term>Kaliatours</term> wood, which is not unknown to them, and this would, according to their claim, occur on the large island of Timor. Others, however, believe that it is indeed obtainable from the Portuguese living on Timor, although they did not get it on Timor itself, but obtained it from Siam, Macao, or other Portuguese places. Finally, Raja Amassili-Saban, now named Salomon Speelman, King of Ademantutu, gave me the following report thereof: namely, that he had seen a red wood which he took for Red Sandalwood, occurring on Samorro, a landscape of Timor, situated on a terribly high and dismal mountain range in the middle of the land, whose shore, Lacolo, came out on the South side, and that the natives made their flutes from the same wood, also smelling somewhat of Sandalwood; and one can only break it off in small pieces because of the difficulty of the roads. This so-called Timorese Red Sandalwood differs (besides the color) from the Coromandel type also in properties; for indeed it cools more noticeably, does not bite so much in the eyes, and does not burn in the throat: but we can get so little of it that one cannot take a proper test of it.

**Name.** Latin *Sandalum Rubrum*, in Malay *Tsjendana Djingi*, that is, as said, *Sandalum Æthiopicum*, or more properly *Troglodyticum*, because the Arabs call all the inhabitants of the Eastern part of Africa, both on the mainland and the islands, <term>Zangi</term> or <term>Zingi</term>, from whose lands, as said above, this wood was originally brought: it is also called *Tsjendana Mera*.

**Usage.** Red Sandalwood was never used for incense, nor to smoke raw on coals, but only as medicine: It is cool and drying in nature, without any astringency. The Indians use it most against all kinds of fevers, rubbed and taken with water, and the body also smeared with it from the outside, only to somewhat quench the feverish burn and to strengthen the heart; for the fever itself it cannot take away, unless it were an <term>Ephemera</term>; the shavings of the mentioned Sandalwood enjoyed with rice water, cures the "Red Run" <note>Dysentery</note>. It is also a common opinion that Red Sandalwood resists all kinds of ingested poison, yes, such that it reveals itself if it is put into any vessel made of this wood; as such many Great Ones of India have their <term>Pinang</term> boxes and drinking cups made of this wood, to betray the poison put therein; however, this is not yet confirmed by experience, but it is confirmed that, being taken in, it is capable of much to break the raging of any given poison: it is also held among the great ones of the Malays and Ternatans for a secret art and remedy against ingested poison: namely that one takes Red Sandalwood, white <term>Calbabaar</term> or East-Indian white coral, with <term>Calappa Laut</term>, everything rubbed on a stone, for several days after one another. But when one does not exactly have the <term>Calappa Laut</term>, the other two are nevertheless good and useful: which was tested in the year 1677 in Ternate and found true on a Dutch Merchant and his wife, who had been poisoned by their maid with spiders.

### AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chapter XVII. ###

The Javanese also use this Red Sandalwood against <term>bloody urine</term> <note>original: "mictionem cruentam"</note>; they grind it with water upon a <term>porphyry stone</term> <note>A hard igneous rock used as a grinding surface</note>, expose it to the dew overnight, and drink it with rose water. It is likewise used against the vomiting of blood, not caused by lung disease, but by "raw" blood produced by a ruptured vein or some other accident. The Arabs say that Red Sandalwood is cold and dry—at least colder and drier than all other species of Sandalwood. They claim that when ground with rose water and smeared on the temples of the head, it removes and dries up <term>catarrhs</term> <note>Inflammatory discharges of mucus</note> that flow down to the eyes and teeth. When mixed with the juice of <term>Nightshade</term>, <term>Stonecrop</term>, and <term>Purslane</term> <note>original: "Solani, Sedi, & Portulacæ"</note> and applied, they say it mitigates the pain of arthritis, gout, and other inflammations. On the coast of Coromandel, they fashion gaming boards, discs, and other turned works from this wood; these are smooth on the outside and remain a polished brownish-black. Otherwise, it is not held in great price or medicinal use among them, except that they smear the body with this wood during fevers, and from the larger pieces they carve images of their idols, as well as the posts and beams of their temples. At least, this is what the Portuguese claim, and it must necessarily be understood as referring to the first species or <term>Caliatour wood</term> <note>A high-quality commercial grade of Red Sandalwood from India</note>, since according to the testimony of the esteemed Mr. de Jager, no other red wood is known on the Coromandel coast. The Arabs also wish to persuade us that Red Sandalwood is devoid of scent and lacks a sweet flavor, though this should be understood as referring to an "excellent" or overpowering scent and taste. For I do not believe any red wood can be found which, when ground, does not exhibit some scent or flavor, or which, when chewed in the mouth, does not imbue the saliva with some color. Indeed, <term>Brazilwood</term> itself, which according to the account of <term>Piso</term> <note>Willem Piso, a Dutch physician who wrote on the natural history of Brazil</note> is used in Brazil against fevers and inflammations of the eyes, provides a sweet taste. I have often wished I had it at hand to use in place of common Red Sandalwood; for among all those woods thrust upon us as Sandalwood, it seemed unlikely that one could easily be found which, according to the Arabic account, was of a cold and drying nature. From all the pieces sent to me as Sandalwood thus far, produced here and there in various places in the Indies, I have been able to find none that possessed these stated virtues; indeed, I have always observed the contrary in them. For in the year 1680, when I was vexed by great pain from an inflammation and swelling of the eyes, I ground the best of this wood into a very fine powder, with which I smeared my eyes and even dripped a little into them, drinking the rest. I found that instead of bringing coolness to the eyes where it was applied, it stung them; when swallowed, it scraped the throat and was of a sharp quality—though it did cool slightly afterward, as others who used it at the same time testified with me. There were some, however, who claimed they felt nothing but cooling when they drank it. When the Portuguese wish to take it internally for cooling and drying, they combine these three: namely Red Sandalwood, <term>Pedra Canapeor</term> <note>A medicinal stone or mineral</note>, and <term>Coquinho</term> (or the small <term>Sea Coconut</term>), which they grind together and serve with water. If the <term>Coquinho</term>, which is rarely to be found, is not at hand, the other two are nonetheless of good reputation. If they use it to provoke sweating and expel poison, they then grind and mix together Red Sandalwood, <term>Caliga-Kackaa</term> (that is, the <term>Bezoar Stone</term>, or common bezoar, which they consider a "Monkey stone"), and <term>Culiga Landa</term> (called by them <term>Pedra de Porco</term> or <term>Porcupine Stone</term>), and they drink these together.

The Kings of Makassar had platters and betel boxes which, according to their account, were fashioned from Red Sandalwood brought there from Timor in pieces three or four feet long and half a foot thick. These were blackish on the outside, and on the inside they were fine and long-grained, consisting of blood-red fibers of a uniform color. If it were scraped or cut, it yielded a somewhat pleasant scent, not unlike recently cut red <term>Lingoo</term> <note>Narra wood, *Pterocarpus indicus*</note>; however, it was different from Caliatour wood, because the latter has a deeper internal color, is more brownish, and is also harder, not allowing for lengthwise splitting. Furthermore, when placed on coals, Caliatour wood immediately spreads an acrid smoke, whereas Red Sandalwood spreads a somewhat pleasant scent.

<meta>catchword: Expe-</meta>

<column-break/>

*The Javanese also use Red Sandalwood against bloody urine, it being rubbed by them on a stone with water, set in the dew for a night, and then drunk with rose water. Likewise against the spitting of blood, not coming from lung disease, but from raw blood from a burst vein or some other accident. The Arabs hold Red Sandalwood to be cold and dry, indeed colder and drier than all Sandalwood sorts, and they also say that the same, rubbed with rose water and smeared on the temples of the head, dries up the catarrhs that fall upon the eyes and teeth; as also that it, being mixed with the juice of Nightshade, Stonecrop, and Purslane, and then spread on, softens the pain of the Gout, Podagra, and other inflammation. On the coast of Coromandel, they make beautiful backgammon boards, discs, and other turner's work from it, which are all smooth on the outside and turn a blackish-brown. Otherwise, it is of no particular value among those people, nor much in medicinal use, except that in fevers they smear the body therewith, and out of the largest pieces they make their images, idols, as well as the posts and beams in their temples. Indeed, as the Portuguese claim, it must also necessarily be understood as the first sort, or Caliatour wood, since according to the testimony of the mentioned Honorable Mr. de Jager, no other red wood is known on the Coromandel coast. The Arabs also want to say that Red Sandalwood would be of no smell nor sweet taste: which, however, one must understand as being of an "extraordinary" smell and taste: for I do not believe that one shall find any red wood which, being rubbed, does not give off some smell or taste, and being chewed in the mouth, comes to dye the saliva more or less. For even Brazilwood, according to Dr. Piso's writing, being used against fevers and soreness of the eyes in Brazil, is of a sweet taste; and I have often wished to have the same wood at hand to be able to use it in place of common Red Sandalwood; for to find such a one among all those woods that are served up to us as Sandalwood (which according to the claim of the Arabs would be cold and drying of nature), there seems little likelihood. For among all the pieces that have been sent to me for it until now (growing here and there in the East Indies), I have not been able to find one that has those aforementioned powers; indeed, I have found the contrary. For in the year 1680, when I had great pain from an inflammation and swelling of the eyes, I rubbed the best of it fine, smeared it on the eyes, and let a little come into them, as well as drinking the rest; whereupon I found that which was smeared on, instead of cooling, bit into the eyes, and that which was drunk itched somewhat in the throat and was sharp, although it cooled a little thereafter, which others alongside me also testified, who used it at that time as well. However, there were also some who maintained they felt nothing but cooling while drinking it. The Portuguese, when they want to use it for cooling and drying inside the body, take these three things together: Red Sandalwood, Pedra Cananeor, and Coquinho (or small Sea Coconut), which they rub together and so drink with water. However, if one cannot have the Coquinho, which is seldom found, the two first-named are nonetheless good. If they want to use it to sweat and against ingested venom, they rub and mix together Red Sandalwood, Caliga Kackaa (that is, the Bezoar Stone, or common Bezoar, which they hold for a Monkey-stone), and Culiga Landa (named by those people Pedra de Porco), and take that so together.*

The Kings of Makassar have had platters and betel boxes which, according to their own saying, were made of a Red Sandalwood that was brought there from Timor in pieces of 3 to 4 feet long and as many thick. On the outside, they were a weathered black; on the inside, fine and long-grained, deep and blood-red, uniform of color, and when one scraped it, it was not unlike red Lingoo; yet differing from Caliatour wood, because the same is a higher red and browner on the inside, as well as harder and not easily splitting lengthwise; also being laid on coals, it immediately gives off a sharp smoke, whereas Red Sandalwood is somewhat sweet-smelling.

## Book II. Chapter XVII. AMBOINESE HERBAL. ##

I will add here some tests that I conducted on all the fragments I possessed, concerning their natural color and appearance when smeared with <term>lime</term> <note>original: "calce"; Rumphius often used quicklime to test the chemical properties and color stability of wood resins</note>, as well as the <term>tinctures</term> <note>Infusions or extracts</note> that these pieces yielded when soaked in <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>Alcohol or brandy</note>, etc. The common and well-known <term>Caliatour wood</term> <note>original: "Lignum Caliatiorense"; a red timber often confused with sandalwood, likely Pterocarpus santalinus</note> is of a dark blood-red color, although I have also observed it to be a bright red in chairs and benches made from it; furthermore, it is heavy and solid, but does not have longitudinal fibers and is difficult to split lengthwise. The applied lime remains white for some time, but then becomes a bright purplish or flesh color. Among the pieces sent to me as Red Sandalwood, some were bright red or like <term>minium</term> <note>Red lead pigment</note> on the inside, but were blackish-brown on the outside, and all had longitudinal fibers. On most of these, the applied lime appeared slightly purplish as above, except for two pieces—one of which was bright red and the other blood-red inside—where the lime appeared yellow. Among these was also a small fragment which, when rubbed, distinctly gave off the smell of mustard; another breathed a faint scent of Sandalwood, but most gave off no scent at all.

->These things were added in Rumphius’s Supplement.<-

<term>Dapper</term> <note>Olfert Dapper (1636–1689), a Dutch physician and geographer famous for his descriptions of Africa and Asia</note> believes that both types of Sandalwood are found in Africa, for he relates in his description of *Ansiko, page 180:*
> „ There is an abundance of Sandalwood here, namely
> „ the *red*, which is called *Favville* by the inhabitants, and the *white*,
> „ which is called *Sikongo*; the latter, being considered the best,
> „ is crushed into powder and mixed with palm oil,
> „ and the inhabitants smear their bodies with it for the preservation of health.

A certain friend from Batavia in the year 1697 sent me a round fragment of red wood called *Caliatour*, along with another oblong piece; he reported that the first kind is sold there as Red Sandalwood and even smelled somewhat like Sandalwood, but the other, smaller and oblong part was devoid of scent. Both grow in Java, in the southern part, but occur rarely and are only obtainable from the <term>elites</term> <note>original: "Primores"; high-ranking officials or nobles</note>. That round segment had been given as a gift by the Captain of the Balinese to the <term>Pangeran of Bantam</term> <note>A prince or high-ranking noble from the Sultanate of Bantam in Western Java</note>, and at his estate sale it was purchased for fifteen <term>imperial thalers</term> <note>original: "imperialibus"; also known as Rijksdaalders, large silver coins</note>, weighing about ten pounds. According to the account of this friend, he intended to take a similar segment with him to his homeland, the Netherlands, to investigate whether that which is imported from the West Indies—and which is ground in great quantities at <term>Regensburg</term> <note>original: "Ratisbonæ"; a city in Bavaria</note> under the name of Red Sandalwood and sold in pharmacies—was of the same quality or matched this wood.

### O B S E R V A T I O N.

Regarding RED SANDALWOOD, see further *Valentinus, History of Simples Reformed, p. 186*, and the *second letter of Literary India, p. 387*, as well as *Samuel Dale, Pharmacopoeia, p. 376*, who collected various authors, such as *Ray, History, p. 1805; Parkinson, Theater of Plants, p. 1605; Johannes Bauhinus, vol. 1, p. 489; and Chabræus, p. 37; as well as Jonston, Dendrology, p. 456; and the appendix of Ray, vol. 3, p. 84; and Hermann, Materia Medica, p. 89*, who says it is a pod-bearing tree with <term>papilionaceous flowers</term> <note>Flowers shaped like butterflies, typical of the pea family (Leguminosae)</note>.

These three types of Sandalwood are also described in *Valentinus, Description of Amboina, pages 206 and 207*, who also provides short descriptions of the preceding <term>true and false Aloeswood</term> <note>original: "Agallochi veri & spurii"; also known as Gaharu or Agarwood</note>.

*I will add here a few more tests of all the small pieces I have had, concerning their natural color and appearance when smeared with lime, as well as the tinctures they give off in brandy, etc. Common and well-known Caliatour wood is dark blood-red, though I have also found it to be light red in chairs and benches; furthermore, it is heavy and massive, though not straight-grained and difficult to split lengthwise. The smeared lime remains white for a long time, but after that becomes light purple or the color of apple blossoms. Among the small pieces sent to me as Red Sandalwood, some were light or minium-red on the inside, but blackish-brown on the outside and all straight-grained. The smeared lime appeared mostly light purple on all of them, as mentioned above, except for two pieces—one of which was light red and the other blood-red on the inside—where the lime appeared yellow. There was also a small piece among them which, when rubbed, clearly smelled like mustard; another had a weak sandalwood scent, and most had none at all.*
