<header>AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. cap. XVIII.</header>

# CHAPTER EIGHTEEN.

## False Amboinese Sandalwood: Sasuru.

**T**his is not a tall but a thick tree found in the highest mountains of Ambon, though it is encountered very rarely. It possesses a straight trunk and takes on the form of a large <term>Jambosa</term> <note>Rose Apple tree</note>; its leaves, however, are large, similar to <term>Bancudu</term> <note>Morinda citrifolia, or Noni</note>, or like the <term>Manga foetida</term> <note>Horse Mango</note>, being a foot or fifteen inches long and over eight inches wide or more. They are smooth, a deep green, and patterned with yellow parallel and transverse ribs. The younger leaves are slightly <term>dentate</term> <note>toothed like a saw</note> at the edges with very short and sparse teeth, traces of which also appear on the old leaves. These leaves sit without order upon round, firm stalks <note>petioles</note> about a span long at the ends of the branches, emerging from a sort of round cup-like base which is attached to the branch itself and falls off with the leaf, bearing two sharp "ears" <note>stipules</note>. When crushed, the leaves give off a scent and a taste that is pleasant and slightly acidic.

The flowers appear in large <term>umbels</term> <note>flat-topped clusters where the stalks spread from a common center</note> extended in a circle like a large plate, formed from thick and long stalks joined at the center like the spokes of a wheel. Each spoke is about a foot long, or a little more, and is divided at the top into three smaller stalks, each of which is extended at the tip like a disk. Upon these sit many whitish granules, at first a little larger than millet grains, but later growing into berries like peas or small black cherries, remaining whitish and adorned with a little crown. If these flower-heads are separated, they somewhat resemble the form of Lemon flowers, as they also gradually grow to that size, but they are much juicier and not as white as Lemon flowers. What fruit might follow, I do not know, for these buds open slowly and do not grow into fruit, but fall off in vain. They do not grow all at once on those disks, but one flower opens after another. This umbel resembles a very well-decorated crown, such as those hung during wedding festivities, for which purpose it is indeed used in the weddings of certain Amboinese Princes.

Traces of the disks from which the leaf stalks grew are also visible on the branches; these have a spongy pith inside like Elderberry, but more watery. The bark of the trunk is smooth and ash-gray with brown spots and warts; inside it is spongy, soft, and patterned with yellow lines, having an acidic taste and an unpleasant smell. In old trees, the bark exudes a yellow and sticky gum, which dries into a blackish and dark brown resin, though not in great quantity. The fresh wood of the trees is white and soft, but when dry it turns towards a reddish color, almost like yellow <term>Lingoa wood</term> <note>Pterocarpus indicus, or Narra</note>; sometimes it is also a reddish-gray, consisting of many tangled veins, which makes it difficult to cut, as it cannot be easily split lengthwise. The resin, as was said, is found only in the very oldest trees, and only in certain places on the trunk that have cracked naturally or have been cut. Fresh wood breathes no scent, but the dry wood does—especially that collected from old trees that have fallen of their own accord—having the scent of Lingoa wood but much stronger; the scent also leans toward Rosemary or <term>Spike Oil</term> <note>Lavender oil</note>. The Amboinese use the fresh resin for incense, but the wood placed upon coals breathes an unpleasant odor. The flowers usually appear in the months of September and those following.

Name. In Latin, <note>original: "Pseudo-Sandalum Amboinense"</note> False Amboinese Sandalwood; by the Amboinese in Leytimor it is called Sasuru; in Hitoe it is called Tonokuko, which means "incense wood"; and our nation <note>the Dutch</note> has given it the name Rosemary-wood, or Amboinese Sandalwood.

Location. These trees occur only rarely in the Amboinese mountains on the Hitoe coast, from where the <term>Rajas</term> <note>local rulers</note> of Saja formerly brought some small trees and planted them in Leytimor, in a shady valley near the Onoway stream, which forms one of the headwaters from which the river called the Elephant flows near Castle Victoria.

The Amboinese regard this tree as their Sandalwood, by which name they enticed me to that place to see it there, where in the year 1665 I saw two... 
<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the catchword is "two trees".</meta>

<column-break/>

# XVIII. CHAPTER.

## False Amboinese Sandal-wood.

**T**his is no high, but a thick tree, which one finds in the high Amboinese mountains, and that yet very seldom, having a straight trunk and the appearance of a large Rose-apple tree. The leaves are large and resemble those of the <term>Bancudu</term> <note>Morinda</note>, or those of the <term>Manga Foetida</term> <note>Horse Mango</note>, a foot or 15 inches long, over 8 fingers and more wide, smooth, deep green, and patterned across with yellow parallel ribs. The young leaves are a little toothed at the edges with very short and thin points, of which one also sees some signs in the old ones. They stand without order on round, stiff stalks a span long around the front branches, each in a small round saucer which sits against the branch and falls off with the leaf, having two sharp ears; and being rubbed, they smell and taste lovely and somewhat acidic.

The blossom comes forth in wide clusters <note>umbels</note>, spread out in a circle like a wide dish, consisting of long thick stalks that all come together in the middle like the spokes of a wheel. Each of these rays is about a foot long, or indeed more, divided at the front into three other stalks, which are wide at their ends like a small table-plate; and upon these stand many white granules, at first a bit larger than Millet, but thereafter becoming berries like a Pea or small black Cherry, yet remaining white, with a little crown at the front. If one pulls these buds apart, they somewhat show the blossom of Lemons, as they also in time become such, though they are much juicier and less white than Lemon-blossom. What kind of fruits follow thereon is to me until now unknown, for these buds open slowly and then fall off without fruits. They also do not become large at the same time on the little plates, but one after the other. And this cluster resembles well a decorated crown that one hangs up in Weddings, for which it is also used—to wit, at the Weddings of certain Amboinese Princes.

On the branches one sees the marks of the little saucers where the leaves have stood, and on the inside they have a hollow pith like Elder, though more watery. The bark of the trunk is even, gray with brown spots and warts, hollow and soft inside and patterned with yellow lines, in scent acidic and to us unpleasant. On the old trees the bark sweats out a yellow and sticky gum, which dries up into a blackish and dark-red resin, yet very scarcely. The fresh wood of the trees is white and soft, but the dry wood pulls somewhat toward the red, almost like yellow Lingoa-wood, and sometimes a grayish-red with many veins that run very tangled through one another, for which reason it is difficult to cleave, as not wanting to split well in the length. The resin, as said, is seen only on the very old trees and that only in some places on the trunk that have burst of themselves or where one has chopped into it. The fresh wood has no scent, but the dry wood does, especially that which comes from old and naturally fallen trees, smelling like Lingoa-wood but much stronger, and the scent also pulls somewhat toward Rosemary or Lavender-oil. The Amboinese use the resin for incense—to wit, the fresh—but the wood laid on coals smells unpleasant. The blossom is usually seen in September and the following months.

Name. In Latin <note>original: "Pseudo-Sandalum Amboinicum"</note>, in Amboinese on Leytimor, Sasuru; on Hitoe it is called Tonokuko, that is "Incense wood"; and our Nation has given it the name of Rosemary-wood, or Amboinese Sandal-wood.

Place. One finds only some few trees in the Amboinese mountains, and that on the coast of Hitoe. From there the Rajas of Saja formerly fetched some small trees and planted the same on Leytimor, in a dark valley by the little river Onoway, being one of the heads that make the River Elephant, which runs by Castle Victoria.

The Amboinese hold it for their Sandal-tree, with which name they enticed me thither to view it, where I then in the year 1665 found two trees, both...

...these trees, both equaling the thickness of a man, yielded no resin because they were still too young. They also occur beyond Way near the <term>Dammar</term> <note>Resin-producing</note> trees, but they undoubtedly grow in greater numbers in neighboring regions, namely on Ceram and in the Uliasser islands. Since I have often found large pieces of these trees—indeed, almost half-trees—here and there on the shore, which the inhabitants well knew did not grow in that region, I could likewise observe in them that they had floated in the sea for some time and had been tossed about. In the land of Hitoë, in the district of the village of Senalo, such a cast-up tree lay for a long time in my day, from which the women cut chips for <term>suffumigation</term> <note>incense or scenting by smoke</note>, and in the same district and that of Keytetto we later found several such trees which were still growing, though they were unknown in other villages.

*Use.* Since this tree occurs so rarely, I can comment little on its use, and have only seen of the Hitoëse that they bring its chips down from the mountains to use for scenting their clothes. They cut these into very small pieces along with the root of *Tacari* (that is, the fragrant <term>Gladiolus</term> <note>likely *Eleutherine bulbosa*</note>), <term>Benjoin</term> <note>Benzoin resin</note>, and a little white sugar, placing them together on coals. However, they first immerse this wood two or three times in salt water and dry it in the burning sun, which makes its odor more penetrating, so that the Amboinese use this wood in place of <term>Agallochum</term> <note>Eaglewood or Agarwood, a highly prized aromatic heartwood</note>, from whose scent it nevertheless differs greatly. Nonetheless, they value this wood as much as its resin and consider it very pleasing to their nostrils; in this, in my judgment, they are to be mocked, for I found the odor of the crushed leaves and freshly cut bark so heavy that it triggered a headache in me. If elegant pieces of this wood occur that are not knotty, they can be cut into small boards, from which I manufactured small boxes that were elegant in appearance, since the wood consists of very fine fibers and veins; but it cannot be polished well. While being smoothed, this wood excited such a strong odor of <term>Camphor</term> that I could hardly tolerate it in my bedchamber, and the boards exuded a certain liquid for more than a year afterward, which resembled oil spots. With the coarser shavings of this wood, I packed some shells in another such box, which in a similar way fixed a certain tenacious gummy substance to the shells, adhering to them as firmly as pitch, although one would have believed this wood had been thoroughly dry before. Chewed in the mouth, it gives a strong and aromatic taste approaching Rosemary or Lavender. And this is perhaps the tree called *Bitau* in Macassar; but it occurs very rarely there, and only in the high mountains, bearing a very straight trunk and leaves like <term>Bancudu</term> <note>Morinda citrifolia, or Noni</note>, but a little larger. Its wood or trunk is only used for the masts of the King's vessel, since it does not easily develop cracks, wherefore no one else is permitted to use it. As was said, pieces of this wood are often found on the shore, not long tossed by the sea tide, nor often dried by the sun, which, when cleaned and placed in a room, preserve their Lavender-like odor for a long time and fill the space with it.

---

This tree seems to be related to three or four species of shrubs described later in Book 6 under the name *Scutellaria*, all of which also yield a similar gum, like other plants that produce <term>Opoponax</term> <note>a medicinal gum resin</note>, to which the gum of this tree is similar.

*Roweyl*, growing on Boero <note>Buru Island</note>, is a variety of the preceding tree and is of the same size and thickness. Its leaves are placed without order at the ends of the thick twigs, twelve and fourteen inches long, five inches wide, smooth on both sides, pointed, and resembling those of *Bancudu* or the narrow-leaved <term>Polot</term>, intense green, smooth, and shining on both sides, with a few lateral ribs that end in arcs at the edges, and ending at the top in a sharp, firm point like a needle. At the edges they seem smooth, but if carefully observed, distant and shallow serrations appear, with a short and blunt point, which is a clear sign of affinity with the preceding *Safuru* and the *Scutellaria*. Their stalks <note>petioles</note> are about the thickness of a straw, round and firm, four or five inches long, and standing with a broad base on the branches, whereas the previous ones formed a small plate; they fall off easily, leaving their footprints or a mark on the spot...

<column-break/>

...a man thick; they gave no resin, because they were still too young. They are also found behind Way, near the Dammar-trees, but they must also occur in greater numbers on the neighboring islands, such as on Ceram and in the Xula islands. For I have often found large pieces, and almost half-trees, here and there on the beach, which the inhabitants well knew did not grow there, and one could see that they had rolled in the sea for a long time. In the land of Hitoe, in the district of the village of Senalo, such a tree lay for a long time in my day, from which the women cut chips to make incense; and in the same district, as well as in that of Keytetto, we later found some similar trees that were still growing, but in other villages they were not known.

*Use.* Since this tree is so rarely found, I can yet write little of its use, having only seen of the Hitoe people that they brought the chips down from the mountains to use for the scenting of their clothes, chopping them small with the root of *Tacari* (that is, *Gladiolus odoratus*), *Benjoin*, and a little white sugar, then throwing it all together onto coals. However, they dip this wood two or three times in salt water beforehand and dry it again in the hot sun, whereby its scent becomes stronger, so that the Amboinese use this wood in place of *Agallochum*. From whose scent it nevertheless differs much. Nonetheless, they make much of both the wood and the resin and hold it very lovely for their noses, in which, in my judgment, they are to be laughed at; indeed, the scent of the crushed leaves and freshly cut bark I have found so strong that they cause headaches. When one finds beautiful pieces of this wood that are not knotty, one can saw small planks from them, from which I have made small boxes that presented themselves beautifully because the wood is finely veined and watered; but it will not allow itself to be worked smooth. In the planing, it gave off such a strong Camphor-scent that one could hardly endure it in the room; also the planks sweated out some moisture more than a year afterward, which was mistaken for oil stains. With the coarse shavings of this wood, I also had some seashells packed in another box, which likewise put a tough gumminess on the shells, and clung as firmly as pitch, although one would have regarded this wood as being entirely dry. Chewed in the mouth, it has a strong spicy taste, drawing very near to Rosemary or Lavender. And this is perhaps the tree that is named *Bitau* on Macassar; though it is very little found there, and then only in the high mountains, having a very straight trunk and leaves like *Bancudu*, but somewhat larger; the wood is used only to make masts in the King's Galley because it does not easily split, and therefore no one else may use it. One sometimes finds, as said, pieces of this wood on the beach that have not rolled long in the sea-water nor been often dried by the sun, and which, being cleaned and placed in a room, keep their Lavender-scent longer and fill the room with it.

---

It seems as if this tree wants to have some kinship with the 3 or 4 sorts of shrubs described hereafter in Book 6 under the name *Scutellaria*, which all want to do the same as the plants from which the *Opopanax* comes, which the gum of this tree also resembles.

*Roweyl*, growing on Boero, is a fellow-sort of the aforementioned tree, as well as of the same size and thickness. The leaves stand without order at the ends of the thick twigs upon one another, 12 and 14 inches long, 5 fingers broad, smooth front and back, pointed, and much resembling those of *Bancudu* or narrow-leaved *Polot*, deep green, smooth and shining on both sides, with few side-ribs that run very curved at the ends, and at the front with a short stiff point like a needle. At the edges they seem smooth, but looking closely, one sees wide and shallow notches with a short blunt point, which is a clear sign of agreement with the preceding *Safuru* and the *Scutellaria*. Their stalks are about a straw-stalk thick, round and stiff, 4 to 5 inches long, and standing with a broad little foot on the branches, where the former ones made a little dish, and they fall off easily, leaving their footprints or a sign on the place...

<header>HERBARIUM AMBOINENSE Book II. Chapter XVIII.</header>

indication in that place where they were situated: Their scent and flavor is not as unpleasant as that of the ***Safuru*** <note>original: *Safuru*; a resinous tree mentioned in previous chapters</note>, but conforms mostly to that of the ***Scutellaria*** <note>original: *Scutellaria*; Skullcaps, known for their bitter but sometimes aromatic properties</note>: The flowers and fruits have been entirely unknown to me until now, nor could I learn from the people of Buru that they had ever seen them; the small branches, from which the leaves grow, are a finger thick, light, and filled inside with a spongy pith: I have never seen its fresh wood, but only the dry, which turns yellowish, consisting of thin fibers with thick and fatty yellow veins, which are not as tangled as those in the ***Safuru***. The fresh wood in a green and vigorous tree is odorless, but the inner pieces of old and fallen trees have a sweet and fatty, though faint, odor, if raw and not placed upon coals; this scent is more pleasant and better when kept in closed tubes, though it would soon dissipate. From the opened bark, or that which has cracked of its own accord, there drips a yellowish, thin, and mucilaginous Oil of a pleasant odor, very much approaching that of <term>Amber</term> <note>original: *Ambrum*; here referring to the fragrance of ambergris or fossil amber</note>, which dries into a dark reddish Gum, and can be pulled from the bark in a few small pieces or granules. This Gum resembles <term>Opoponax</term> <note>original: *Opoponax*; a medicinal gum resin with a heavy, sweet scent</note> reasonably well in appearance, but it does not have a bitter taste, being instead fatty and bland, almost like some kind of roasted food: so that it is not as pleasant as the fresh Oil, unless it has become harder than pitch.

### *The Name.*
This tree can be called in Latin the *Pseudo-Sandalum Boeronense* <note>False Sandalwood of Buru</note>, but in Buru it is called ***Roweyl***; on Manipa they have a certain tree which they call ***Lowelle*** and ***Rawelle***, which is the same name, but according to the accounts of the inhabitants it must be a different tree, since it bears wrinkled and hairy leaves like those of the ***Canarium Trigonum***; otherwise called by them ***Habumalo-fey***, that is, "pig's food."

### *The Location.*
This tree has been found nowhere else so far except on the western side of Buru around ***Maferette***, far from the shore in the high mountains; from there the wood and Oil are mostly brought down by the <term>Alfurs</term> <note>original: *Alphorenses*; a term used for the indigenous mountain-dwelling peoples of the Moluccas</note> or wild inhabitants of the mountains, who have no other use for it than to anoint their hair and bodies with this fresh oil, which flows spontaneously from that tree.

### *The Use.*
Nothing else is known of its use, except that the women of Buru sometimes receive the fattest pieces, and the first liquid pitch or Oil, as a gift from the Alfurs; they then mix it into their own oils, to which they wish to impart a pleasant scent. Indeed, this would be a precious <term>Turpentine</term> <note>original: *Terebinthina*; a fluid resin</note> if those wild inhabitants of the mountains knew how to collect it in the proper manner and preserve it rightly before it hardens.

For if this turpentine or liquid pitch is allowed to dry on the trees into a hard resin, then no pleasant odor remains, and when placed on coals it gives off the smell of roasted tallow. From Buru in the year 1666, certain small pieces of this Resin were brought to me, which the deceitful inhabitants at that time called ***Ambergunong***, that is, <term>Mountain Amber</term>, pretending that it was very rarely found and of a precious scent, dripping in the highest mountains from certain trees. These pieces were fairly large, like turnips, so similar to <term>Gum Elemi</term> <note>original: *Gummi Elemi*; a fragrant resin used in lacquers and inks</note> in color and substance that they might be taken for it; some indeed had spots of a flesh-colored and opaque hue, while others were pale red and yellowish, but they gave off no scent, except that when placed on coals they smelled of roasted tallow. Thus, I could consider them as nothing else than the Resin of that ***Roweyl***, which without doubt exudes abundantly in the mountains of Buru; and since that region has bituminous soil, it also exudes a black <term>bitumen</term> <note>original: *bitumen*; a naturally occurring petroleum product like asphalt</note> toward the western part, which, sliding pure into the sea, hardens into very black and shining masses. These they sell and foist upon strangers as black Amber, but if this bitumen is soft and falls on the shore, it mixes with sand, pebbles, and shells, and so gradually hardens into tough, dark gray, brown, and blackish stones, which melt when exposed to fire and emit a heavy odor. From Manipa there was brought to me a certain earth, which contained decayed wood and small sticks, which breathed a most pleasant scent of Amber; and when kept enclosed or protected from the air, it retained this scent for a long time: the inhabitants wanted to persuade me that the scent was natural to this earth, which was found in no other place except in a narrow strip of land around ***Tuboe***, situated on the northern side of Manipa; however, through further investigation I discovered

<column-break/>

that they had stood there: Their scent and taste are not as strong or unpleasant as those of the **Safuru**, but markedly tend toward **Scutellaria**: The flowers and fruits are unknown to me until now, and I have not been able to learn from the Burunese whether they have ever seen them; the branches or twigs on which the leaves grow are a finger thick, light, and filled inside with a spongy pith. I have never seen the fresh wood, but I have seen the dry, which is yellowish, fine-grained, with fatty yellow veins that do not run as tangled as those on the **Safuru**. The fresh wood on the growing tree is without scent, but the innermost pieces of the old and fallen trees have a sweet, fatty, though faint scent, not on the coals, but raw, and even better when enclosed in small boxes, though it disappears in a short time: From the cut bark, or from the cracks that burst by themselves, flows a yellowish, thin, yet sticky Oil, pleasant of scent, and markedly tending toward Amber, which dries into a dark reddish Gum, and hangs on the bark in a few small chunks or crumbs: This Gum does not look unlike Opopanax, being however not bitter of taste, but fatty and bland, like some roasted food, just as it also smells that way on coals: therefore it is by far not as pleasant as the fresh Oil, when it has become no harder than tar.

### *The Name.*
This tree may be called in Latin *Pseudo-Sandalum Boeronense*, on Buru itself it is called **Roweyl**, on Manipa they also have a tree which they call **Lowelle** and **Rawelle**, which is intended to be the same name; yet according to the story of the islanders, it must nevertheless be a different tree: For it supposedly has rough and hairy leaves, like those of *Canarium Trigonum*: Otherwise named by their people **Habumalofey**, that is, **Pigs' food**.

### *The Place.*
Until now this tree has been found nowhere else than on the south side of Buru, around the village of **Maferette**, far from the shore in the high mountains, and therefore the wood and the Oil are mostly brought down by the **Alfurs** or wild mountain dwellers, who make no other use of it than to smear their hair and bodies with the same fresh Oil that drips out.

### *The Use.*
Nothing else is known of its use, except that when the women on Buru sometimes receive the fattest pieces and the first soft tar or Oil as a gift from the aforementioned Alfurs, they then mix it among their oils which they want to make fragrant; and indeed this would be a precious tar if those wild mountain dwellers knew how to gather it properly and take good care of it before it became hard.

For when this tar dries up or hardens on the trees into a hard resin, there is no scent or pleasantness left to it, and, being laid on coals, it smells like roasted fat. From the mentioned Buru, in the year 1666, some small pieces of Resin were brought to me, which the deceitful inhabitants at that time called **Ambergunong**, that is, mountain-Amber, claiming that it was rarely found and of a precious scent, dripping in the high mountains from a certain sort of trees: They were reasonably large pieces or nodules, so similar to Gum Elemi in color and substance that one would have taken them for it—namely some of them: having spots horn-colored and dark, also some light-red and yellowish: But they had no scent, except that when laid on coals they smelled like roasted fat; therefore I could take them for nothing else than a Resin of the aforementioned **Roweyl**, which without doubt yields its burst more richly on the Buru mountains, since that land has a bituminous soil, which on the south side also sweats out a black Bitumen, which, coming pure into the sea, hardens into pitch-black shining lumps, which they sell to strangers for black Amber; but when that soft Bitumen comes onto the shore, it mixes with sand, pebbles, and shells, and thus in time becomes hard, dark-gray, and blackish stones, which being held to the fire melt and give off a strong scent: also there was brought to me from Manipa a certain earth, through which ran crumbled wood and sticks, which smelled very lovely like Amber, and being kept well-enclosed or protected from the air, it kept the same scent for a long time: And the inhabitants wanted to make me believe that it was its natural scent, and that this earth was found nowhere else than only on a narrow strip of land around the village of Tuhoe, located on Manipa’s north side,

## CHAPTER NINETEEN.
### Papuan Wood. Caju Rassamala.

Although this tree is exotic and unknown in Amboina, it is nevertheless necessary to describe it here, since its wood is brought from neighboring places to the market for sale, at least as much as I have been able to learn of its form from reports. According to the testimony of the people of Ceram-Laut <note>original: Ceram-Lauwerensium</note>, it is a vast and lofty tree, growing equally on the shore as in the mountains and valleys. The leaves have the shape of Ironwood <note>original: Syderoxyli</note>, but are a little smaller. Its further form is unknown even to the people of Ceram-Laut themselves, since the inhabitants of Onin-Cubiaya <note>Onin and Kowiai in western New Guinea</note>, where it grows most abundantly, are very barbarous people who do not permit strangers to enter their forests. No part of this tree is put to use except its thick roots, which are dug out and cut from the earth with great labor, and left in the forests for so long that the outer wood, having a thickness of two fingers, rots away and perishes. The substance that remains is called the heart, which is brought for sale in large pieces; these usually have the thickness of a leg or more, and are one cubit or two feet long, very hard and heavy, tangled, and very difficult to split. Their color is two-fold: in the large pieces, it is of a honey color mixed with a little gray, consisting of many very thin veins which are whiter than the rest. The smaller pieces or roots are more whitish or yellowish with fewer veins, and consist of a thinner substance, similar to Yellow Sandalwood or dirty ivory, but they are harder than Sandalwood. The odor of both, however, is the same, tending toward the scent of flowers, or as the Malays say, approaching Liquid Styrax <note>original: Styracem liquidam</note>, called by them *Rassamalla*. But it is so faint that it is scarcely perceived in the raw wood, but more so if it is scraped, and most of all if it is placed upon coals. In the large pieces, it is also not so pleasant, and rivals the sour scent of Sagumanta <note>a type of fermented sago</note>; and if chewed, the flavor of Rassamalla is likewise perceived, which tends greatly toward the salty, or like stale water from a mineral spring, yet without any acrimony or heat.

Since these trees and roots bear such hard wood, and the inhabitants are almost destitute of axes, they leave these trees for a long time until they rot and fall from old age; they then separate the roots with the help of fire. The people of Ceram-Laut cut or chop these into orderly segments, as they are better provided with axes and can easily dig out the fresh roots, which nevertheless do not provide as good an odor as those which rot spontaneously. I have often pondered whether it might be a species of the Styrax tree, but since the people of Ceram-Laut assured me that no gum or resin exudes from it, nor is any peculiar odor observed in the wood of the trunk, I have retreated from that opinion.

Name. In Latin, *Lignum Papuanum* <note>Papuan Wood</note>: In Malay, *Caju Rassamala*, and *Caju Papua* according to the place in which it grows. The people of Ceram-Laut themselves call this wood *Caju Sammar-*

<column-break/>

side, but upon closer investigation I found this to be untrue, and that this good scent was imparted to the earth by some fragrant liquid or tear that happened to drip from the trees; see more of this in the following book, Chapter 4, in *Fragrant Canarium*, and Chapter 6, in *Smallest Nanarium*.

## XIX. CHAPTER.
### Papuan-Wood.

Although this tree is unknown here in Amboina, I must nonetheless describe it, because its wood is brought to market here from the nearest places, at least as far as I have been able to learn of its appearance, being according to the account of the Ceram-Lauters a large, tall tree, growing as well on the beach as in the mountains and the valleys. The leaves resemble those of Ironwood, though they are somewhat smaller. Its further appearance is unknown even to the Ceram-Lauters themselves, because the inhabitants of Onin-Cubiay, where it is most common, are very wild people who do not want to let strangers come into their forests. From these trees nothing is taken or used but the thick roots, which one chops out of the earth with great effort, and then lets lie in the forest until the outer wood (being about two fingers thick) rots off, and the inner core remains, which one brings for sale in large pieces; for those pieces are commonly as thick as a leg or somewhat more: an ell or two feet long, very hard and heavy, gnarled, and difficult to split. The color is of two kinds, namely that of the large pieces honey-colored mixed with some gray, and full of fine veins, which are whiter than the others. The smaller pieces or roots are whiter or pale yellow, with few veins and finer of substance, very much like yellow Sandalwood or dirty ivory, yet harder than Sandalwood, but the scent of both is of one kind, namely: drawing toward flowers, or as the Malays say, toward Liquid Styrax, called *Rassamalla* by those people, yet so weak that one hardly notices it in the raw wood, but more in the rasping, and even stronger on coals. In the large pieces it is also not so lovely, drawing somewhat toward stale Sagumanta, and in the chewing one also feels the taste of *Rassamalla*; but it draws significantly toward the brackish, or like flat water from a sour spring, without any sharpness or bitterness.

Because these trees and roots are so hard of wood, and the inhabitants are poorly provided with axes, they mostly let them stand until they rot from old age and fall over, whereupon they afterwards burn off the roots, and which the Ceram-Lauters then saw or chop into decent chunks, as they themselves (being better provided with axes) can easily chop out the fresh roots, which however are not as good of scent as those that rot of themselves. I have often thought whether it might not be a kind of Styrax tree, but since the Ceram-Lauters assured me that no gum or resin came out of it, and that also in the wood of the trunk there was no special scent, I had to abandon that thought.

Name. In Latin *Lignum Papuanum*: In Malay *Caju Rassamala*, and *Caju Papua*, after the place where it occurs: The Ceram-Lauters themselves call it *Caju Sammarra*, a

<header>AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chapter XIX.</header>

[Sama]marra, a name it shares in common with the *Casuarina* <note>The Ironwood tree</note>, from which it nonetheless differs greatly, as the true name is *Caju-Samada*, which is an abbreviation of *Caju Rafamala* <note>The Rasamala tree, known for its fragrant resin</note>.

*Location.* This wood is brought from that part of *New Guinea* called *Onin-Cubiay* and *Cobiay* <note>Regions in western New Guinea</note>, and is frequented by the *Ceram-Lauters* <note>Traders from the islands east of Ceram</note> who sell *Maffoy* <note>Massoy</note> bark there. It also grows in other places on the western side of *New Guinea* called *Sergile*, which is situated to the east of the island of *Weygeu* <note>Waigeo</note>. Likewise, it is found in many other *Papuan* islands, especially in the largest of them, *Meffoala* <note>Misool</note> and *Ruma-Soala*, but deep inland in the mountains, where the tree is said to bear leaves like those of the *Anona* <note>The Custard Apple</note>. The inhabitants allow the tree to fall and rot on its own, and afterward they take its heartwood and its roots, though these latter are not the best. The wood is called *Calambac* <note>A term usually reserved for high-quality Aloeswood</note> by the inhabitants of *Meffoala*, and the *Macassans* also call it by that name, although it differs much from the true *Calambac*.

*White Caju Rafamala*, which resembles ivory, must be distinguished from the grey variety, although both agree in scent. The white is brought from *Tsjampaa* <note>Champa, an ancient kingdom in modern-day Vietnam</note> and has a much finer substance; the grey comes from the *Papuan* islands, consisting of coarser fibers with a salty taste, and is brought in larger pieces.

*Use.* When rasped, this wood provides white shavings, which are then ground into a paste on a porphyry stone <note>A hard volcanic rock used as a grinding surface</note> with fragrant or floral distilled water. The women smear their bodies with this paste, not only for the sake of the pleasant scent, but also for cooling, just as is done with *Sandalwood*, which is also mixed with rice flour for this purpose. However, this wood is somewhat more cooling than *Sandalwood*. When placed on coals, it gives off a pleasant scent approaching that of *Styrax* <note>A fragrant resin used in incense</note>; yet it is rarely burned alone as incense, but is always mixed with other woods. It is not very expensive, for fifteen or twenty pounds are bought from the *Cerammers* for one Imperial <note>A Rijksdaalder, a silver coin used in trade</note>. That which is brought from the *Papuan* islands appears of a poorer color than the *Cubiay* variety, having longer fibers and a darker color, mixed of grey and honey-tones. The whiter and more solid this wood is, the better it is considered. If lit, it catches fire slowly, but burns more fiercely and crackles somewhat.

*This wood is also sold in Java*, having been brought there from *Ceylon* and the *Malabar* coast <note>The southwestern coast of India</note>, as I have been told. It is much finer, whiter, and more solid in substance; if rasped, it has a pale honey color and turns blackish at the ends or knots. In scent it entirely matches *Caju Papua* <note>Papuan Wood</note>, or is perhaps even more pleasant. Thus, it remains to be investigated whether *Caju Rafamala*, *Caju Papua*, and *Sembrane* from the *Malabar* coast, and the aforementioned white variety from *Champa*, are not one and the same wood, as I have believed until now. Upon further inquiry, I have found that the white, grey, and reddish varieties all grow in the *Papuan* islands, especially on *Meffoala*, from where it is brought for sale to the villages situated in the *Hatu* Gulf on the northern coast of *Ceram*. The white is found in the lower buttresses <note>original: vlerken</note> of the tree near the roots above the ground, while the grey-reddish variety, which is inferior, comes from the actual roots beneath the earth.

## OBSERVATION.

This tree appears to be the same as that called in the *Thesaurus Zeylanicus, page 28*, the fragrant *KÆKURIAGHAHA* tree, from which flows *Gummi Elemi* <note>Elemi resin</note>, as mentioned by *Herman* in his *Museum Zeylanicum, page 52*; concerning which see further in the *Thesaurus Zeylanicus* at the cited place.

[This wood shares a] name in common with the *Casuarina*, from which it nonetheless differs much, the true name being *Caju Samada*, which is a shortening of *Caju Rafamala* mentioned above.

*Place.* This wood is brought from that part of *New Guinea* which is called *Onin-Cubiy* and *Cobiay*: and which is navigated by the *Ceram-Lauters* (who trade the *Maffoy* bark there). it is also found in other places on the western side of *New Guinea*, called *Sergile*, and located directly to the east of the island *Weygeu*. Likewise on more other *Papuan* islands, and especially on the largest of them, *Meffoal* and *Ruma-Soal*, yet far inland and on the mountains, where this tree is said to have leaves like those of the *Anona*: The inhabitants let it fall by itself and rot, and after that they take the heart and the roots thereof, though these latter are not the best. It is called *Calambac* by the inhabitants of the aforementioned *Meffoal*, just as the *Macassans* name it so, although it differs much from the true *Calambac*.

*The white Caju Rafamala*, which truly resembles ivory, must be distinguished from the grey, although they both resemble each other in scent; for the white comes from *Tsjampaa*, and is much finer of substance, but the grey comes from the *Papuan* islands, being much coarser and brackish in taste, also in much larger pieces.

*Use.* This wood, being rasped, gives a white shaving, which one then rubs again on a stone with some fragrant or floral water into a paste, wherewith the women smear their bodies, not only for the sake of the good scent, but also for cooling, as one also does with *Sandalwood*, which one also mixes with rice flour therein; but this wood is somewhat cooler than the *Sandalwood*; being placed on coals, it also has a good scent, drawing somewhat toward *Styrax*, yet it is seldom smoked alone, but always mixed with some other woods. It is not very expensive, for one buys from the *Cerammers* 15 to 20 pounds for one Rijksdaalder. That which comes from the *Papuan* islands is much poorer in appearance of color than the *Cubiay* variety, also long-fibered and darker of color, mixed of grey and honey-colored; but the whiter and denser this wood is, the better it is esteemed. Being lit, it burns slowly, yet more fiercely, and crackles somewhat.

The same is much finer, whiter, and denser of substance; when it is rasped, it is light honey-colored, and blackish around the ends or knots. In scent it is entirely like the *Caju Papua*, or even somewhat more lovely. So that it remains to be investigated whether *Caju Rafamala*, *Caju Papua*, and *Sembrane* on the coast of *Malabar*, and the aforementioned white variety from *Champa*, are not the same woods, as I have thought until now. Having found by closer inquiry that both the aforementioned white and the greyish-red occur in the *Papuan* islands, especially on *Meffoal*, from where it is brought for sale to the villages located in the *Hatu* Gulf on *Ceram's* north coast; the white is found on the lower buttresses of the same tree, next to the root above the earth, but the greyish-red, which is poorer, comes from the actual roots under the earth.

# CHAPTER TWENTY.
## Caju Galedupa.

CAju Galedupa is an exotic tree <note>native to foreign lands, not local to Amboina</note>, yet it has its relatives in Amboina, and thus should be mentioned here as well. It is a reasonably tall tree, whose trunk can scarcely be embraced with one's arms, bearing many short and knotty branches. From these grow many leaf-stalks, which put forth five or six pairs of opposite leaves sitting on short stems, much like the female Ironwood <note>original: *Sideroxyli*</note>, though greater in number and similar in appearance, but somewhat narrower and sharper. Some are four inches long and two or two and a half wide, almost like the leaves of the *Gajang-Laut* <note>The Sea-Gajang or Tahitian Chestnut</note>; others are shorter with a blunt tip, smooth and firm, with few and thin ribs. The fruits are nearly round and flat pods, the size of a Rix-dollar <note>original: *nummi imperialis* / *ryksdaalder*, a large silver coin used in the 17th century</note>, or like those of the *Lingoo* <note>The Padauk tree</note>, formed from two dark brown or blackish skins. Their tip always leans to one side, and they bulge significantly in the middle, where one or two flat, oblong beans are located. These are larger than Lupins and so hard, black, and smooth that they look like black pebbles; on one side they bear a fleshy and wrinkled scar <note>term: *hilum* — the point where the seed was attached to the pod</note>, like a small pouch, by which they are joined to the pod.

The fresh wood of the tree is hard, solid, and difficult to split; its bark is even and smooth. Old and dry wood turns black on the outside and grey on the inside, with a scent that is not unpleasant, though weak, approaching that of Benzoin <note>a balsamic resin from trees of the genus *Styrax*</note>. Freshly opened fruits also exhale such a scent. From a wound in the bark of the trunk flows a blackish and sticky tear, like liquid pitch, which remains liquid for a long time, having the form of brown sugar, and finally dries into a black and hard gum. The Macassans call this *Gale-dupa* and sell it in small bamboo tubes. This gum is so sticky that it can hardly be washed from the hands; it is also shiny and possesses no particularly sweet scent on its own, but smells as if it were a mixture of Benzoin and *Canari* <note>The Java Almond tree</note>. However, when added to other incenses, it exalts their scent and makes them more lasting. This gum is much sought after by the Macassans because it is the basis of their *Dupa* <note>term: *Dupa* — a general term for incense or perfumes burnt over coals</note>, as it binds all the other woods and resins into a single mass and makes their fragrance durable. The hard *Gale-dupa*, which sometimes seemed to me to have the scent of the *Canari*, I suspected to contain the resin of the *Nanarium minimum* <note>A species of small incense-bearing tree described later in Book 3</note>, and I believe that this resin is often sold as Galedupa, especially that which is brought from the Kei Islands and sold to the Macassan merchants.

For the inhabitants affirmed to me that it was a tree that bore very small *Canaria* seeds, just like those of the Amboinese *Nanarium minimum* which I showed them. Nevertheless, a significant difference is found between the two: *Galedupa* is hard and black like pitch, and when placed on coals, it approaches the scent of Benzoin, whereas the resin of the *Nanarium minimum* is dingy and has no scent other than that of *Canari* resin.

*Name.* It is known to me by no other name than the Macassan *Caju Galedupa*, after the aforementioned resin which flows from this tree and is called *Galedupa*.

*Location.* It is found on the western side of Celebes around *Maros*, but it occurs much more frequently in the region of Borneo, as well as on the islands of *Salayer* and *Kalao*, everywhere not far from the shore.

*Usage.* The aforementioned tear flowing from the bark of this tree is used to make the famous incense called *Dupa*, which cannot be formed into a mass without this fresh and sticky resin, as most of its ingredients are dry woods, gums, and shavings. Although another sticky oil, called *Tinjo* (also described below in Book 3 in the chapter on *Nanarium minimum*), is also used for this composition, *Gale-dupa* is the basis of all incenses, just as Aloe is for pills; its description will likewise follow hereafter.

Such trees also grow in the Amboinese empire—

# CHAPTER XX.
## Galedupa-Tree.

CAju Galedupa is a foreign tree, yet it also has its kinship in Amboina, and must therefore be remembered here as well. It is a reasonably tall tree, whose trunk is barely to be embraced, with many short and knotty twigs, and upon them many short thin sprigs, on which stand 5 and 6 pairs of leaves, arranged against one another on short stalks, similar to the female of the *Ironwood*, yet more in number, and they also resemble it well, though they are somewhat narrower and more pointed. For some are 4 inches long, 2 or 2 1/2 wide, almost like *Gajang-Laut*; some are also shorter, with a round point, smooth, and stiff, with few and subtle small ribs. The fruits are nearly round and flat pods of the size of a Rix-dollar, or like those of the *Lingoo*, made from two brown-black skins, but the point always stands closer to one side. In the middle they are markedly raised, and inside lie one or two flat elongated beans, larger than Lupins, and so hard, black, and smooth that one would take them for black stones; they have moreover at one end a furry or rough growth, like a purse, wherewith they hang to the shell.

The fresh wood is dense, hard, and difficult to split, the bark even and smooth. The old and dry wood turns black on the outside, and grey on the inside, with a not unlovely scent, though weak, and drawing somewhat toward Benzoin. The fruits, freshly opened, also give off such a scent. From the wounded bark of the trunk flows a black sticky tear, like tar, which stays soft for a long time, in the form of brown sugar, and finally hardens into a black and hard gum, which the *Macassans* call *Galedupa*, and sell in small bamboos. It is so sticky that one can hardly get it off the hands, being also shiny, and of no singularly pleasant scent, but such as if it were mixed together from Benzoin and Canari. Yet when added to other perfumes, it makes their scent more powerful and durable, and this gum is much sought by the *Macassans*, because it is the basis or foundation of their *Dupa*, for it makes all the other woods and resins stick fast together, and maintains their scent. The hard *Galedupa*, which sometimes appeared to me with a scent like that of the *Canary*, I have accordingly held to be the tear of *Nanarium minimum* (described hereafter in Book 3) and I believe also that the same tear is often sold for Galedupa: especially that which comes from the islands of *Key*, and is sold to the *Macassan* traders.

For the locals assured me that it was a tree that bore entirely small Canaris, just as were those of the Amboinese *Nanarium minimum*, which I showed to those people; and yet there is still a marked distinction between the two: for the *Galedupa* is hard, and black as pitch, and placed on coals drawing toward Benzoin, but the resin of the *Nanarium minimum* is dirty, and smells of nothing else than resinous *Canaris*.

*Name.* It is known to me by no other name than the *Macassan*, *Caju Galedupa*, after the aforementioned resin which flows therefrom and is named *Galedupa*.

*Place.* One finds it on the west side of Celebes, around *Maros*, but much more over against it on *Borneo*, likewise in the islands of *Saleyer* and *Kalao*, everywhere not far from the beach.

*Use.* The aforementioned tear flowing from the bark is that which is used from this tree, as said above, to make that famous perfume named *DUPA*, which cannot be brought to a mass without this fresh and sticky tear, as most ingredients are dry woods, gums, and shavings, although another sticky oil, named *Tinjo* (and likewise described hereafter in Book 3 in the chapter on *Nanarium minimum*) is used for it: and therefore the *Galedupa* is the basis of all perfumes, like the *Aloe* among pills: whose description shall likewise follow hereafter.

Similar trees we also have here in the Amboinese [territory]—

...they grow in the western part of Ceram, in the district of Caybobbo, not far from the shore. The branches and fruits sent to me from Macassar clearly demonstrate they are the same trees, with only this difference: the leaves of the Caybobbo variety are rounder and firmer, more closely resembling the common *Ironwood* <note>original: *Sydaroxyli* / *Yzer-hout*</note>. The Amboinese fruits or pods are larger and wider, distinct, but with a shorter tip leaning to one side. Each pod from Ceram or Caybobbo usually carries one seed-stone, rarely two; these are as hard as stone and shine black, but are flatter and thinner than those from Macassar. They bear a scar <note>term: *hilum* — the attachment point of the seed</note> on the side, like a small pouch, by which the seed is joined to the pod. The greatest difference lies in this: the Caybobbo tree does not yield a black resin like the Macassar tree, even when cut, except for some fissures that occur naturally where a small amount can be seen. The wood is hard and consists of thick fibers, bearing fatty and black spots here and there. It gives off a pleasant but faint scent; if worked while fresh, or if its fruit is placed in a bed-chamber, it fills the whole space with its aroma.

*Name.* In Latin, *Galedupa Ceramenfis*. In Ceram itself, around Caybobbo, it is called *Caju Goa* and *Ay Goa*, perhaps because of its similarity to the Macassar tree, whose capital is called *Goa*. Others, however, call this tree *Aycoa*, which means "scented tree."

*Use.* The wood of this tree is not currently in use outside the regions where it grows. It has been sawn into planks, but it cannot be polished because it is too fibrous <note>original: *villoſum* / *hairig*</note>, nor does it have an elegant color. The scent is not perceived throughout the whole wood, but only in its fatty parts near the root, where it turns blackish and reddish. I also had the root dug up, but I perceived even less scent in it. The women of Caybobbo and Camarian grind the scented wood as a substitute for *Sandalwood*, mixing it into *Boborri* <note>a traditional medicinal or cosmetic ointment</note>, with which they anoint their bodies.

Since this book frequently mentions the Macassan incense called *Dupa*, famous throughout all of maritime India for perfuming clothes, and since the aforementioned resin is its base, we must subjoin a general description of it here, dividing it into two types.

*First: Dupa Radja*, or Royal Dupa, which the common people are not permitted to compose or use. *Second: Dupa Balandja*, which is the common or commercial Dupa.

*Dupa Radja.* It is prepared in the following manner: take the best Aloe-wood or *Calambac* <note>highly prized agarwood</note>, and the best *Garo* or *Agalloch* wood (of which there are three kinds). All of these are chopped into tiny pieces the size of *Cadjang* <note>original: *semimum Cadjang* — mung beans</note>. One tea-cup <note>original: *catillus* / *Teekopje*</note> of each is taken. Of *Caju Rafamala* (which in Macassar is erroneously called *white Calambac*) and *Caju Lacca* <note>Laka wood, a red scented heartwood</note>, half a cup each. Of three types of *Cominjan* or *Benzoin* <note>a balsamic resin</note>, one cup of each is taken. Also, two kinds of *Scented Nail* <note>term: *Unguis Odoratus* / *Unam* — the opercula or "trapdoors" of certain sea snails, which release a musky scent when burned</note>, namely the common *Ambelauw* and the *Ambelauw Key* (which is a long, thin *Onyx* <note>another term for the operculum</note>), likewise one cup. Of *Rafamala* or *liquid Styrax* <note>a fragrant resinous sap</note>, three cups; of *Pangkilang*, two cups; and half a cup of *Timbai* oil. The woods, having been finely chopped, and the resins finely crushed, are first mixed together while dry. All of these are weighed together, and half of that weight is divided into four equal parts. Three of these parts are for the *Galedupa* resin, and one part is for *Tinjo*, which is of two kinds. The thickest part distilling from this tree is a fatty and mucous gum that gradually hardens; the other part is a thin, yellow oil called *Pamassa*, which flows from the same tree like *Coconut oil* <note>original: *Calappi*</note>. When poured into small jars, it is yellow and thin, later becoming reddish and sticky, breathing a strong scent. The hard *Galedupa* and the dry *Tinjo* are worked by hand over glowing coals until they soften like pitch. Each servant girl works a particular lump, moistening her hands with the aforementioned *Pamassa* so that it does not stick to her hands. This material finally becomes as thin as turpentine, and this mass, along with the *Rassamala*, is placed in a large, sturdy, heated dish. The aforementioned woods and resins are continuously and vigorously mixed and worked into it by hand until everything is well blended and becomes a thick...

...Government, growing on the western side of Ceram, in the district of *Caybobbo*, also not far from the beach. *Name.* In Latin, *Galedupa Ceramenfis*. On Ceram itself, near *Caybobbo*, it is called *Caju Goa* and *Ay Goa*, perhaps because of the similarity to the *Macassan* tree, where the capital is named *Goa*. However, others call it *Aycoa*, which means "fragrant tree."

*Use.* The wood has had no use until now outside of those places where it grows. It has been sawn into planks, but it would not allow itself to be worked smooth because it is too hairy <note>fibrous</note>, and for that reason, it has no beautiful color. The scent is also not in the whole wood everywhere, but only in the fatty parts near the root, where it turns blackish and grey. I also had the root dug up, but found even less scent in it. The women of *Caybobbo* and *Camarian* rub the fragrant wood, in place of *Sandalwood*, into their *Bobori* salves to smear upon the body.

Because this book often mentions the *Macassan* incense named *Dupa*, very famous throughout all of maritime India for perfuming clothes, and since the aforementioned resin is the foundation of the same, we must give a general description of it here, dividing it into two main types.

1. *Dupa Radja*, or *Royal Dupa*, which the common man may neither make nor use. 2. *Dupa Balandja*, which is common or trade Dupa.

1. *Dupa Radja* is made thus: one takes of the best *Aloes-wood* or *Calambac*, of the best *Garo* or *Agel-wood* (of which one has three kinds), all finely chopped, like *Cadjangs*, a teacup full of each. *Caju Rafamala* (which is abusively called white *Calambac* in *Macassar*) and *Caju Lacca*, each half a cup. *Caju Tay* and *Putsjoc* (*Indian Costus* <note>a medicinal root</note>), each a little less than half a cup. Three kinds of *Cominjan* or *Benzoin*, a cup of each. *Unguis Odoratus* or *Unam*, two kinds, namely *Ambelauw* (the common) and *Ambelauw Key* (being a long and thin *Onyx*), a cup of each. *Rafamala* or *liquid Styrax*, three cups. *Pangkilang*, two cups. *Timbaus* (specifically the oil thereof), half a cup. The woods, being chopped small as said, and the resin crushed small, are first mixed very well and thoroughly while dry, and all weighed together to see how heavy it is. Half of that weight is divided again into four: three parts are for the *Galedupa*, and one part for *Tinjo*, which is of two kinds. For the thickest that runs out of this tree is a fatty and greasy gum which in time becomes hard, but the thin and yellow oil that runs out of the same tree like *Coconut oil* is called *Pamassa*. It is filled into little pots, being first yellow and thin, thereafter somewhat red, also sticky and strong-smelling. The hard *Galedupa* and the dry *Tinjo* are worked by hand over glowing coals until they become as soft as pitch, each servant girl holding or working a particular lump and moistening her hands with the prescribed *Pamassa*, which ensures it does not stick to the hands. And this material finally becomes as thin as tar, which is then put with the *Rassamala* into a large, strong dish, also made warm...

# Book II. Chapter XX. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

The mixture is prepared as a paste, which is exposed briefly to the sun so that it may dry and harden moderately. Then, small balls are formed from this mass and wrapped in the leaves of the *Licuala* <note>a genus of fan palms</note>. The aforementioned *Galedupa* incense is sold in small bamboo tubes a hand-span long and a finger thick, while *Tinjo* is sold in bamboo tubes half as long but slightly thicker. It should be further noted that Royal Incense (*Dupa Radja*) can be distinguished from the common variety by its scent, as a large amount of *Calambac* <note>high-quality Agarwood or Aloeswood</note> is added to it, which is not found in the common sort. The nobles of Macassar so strictly claim this incense for themselves that if they notice its scent on a private citizen, they hold him in suspicion of having had an affair with their wives, and for this scent alone they may plot against his life. This same incense can be further improved if the amount of *Calambac* is increased and the proportion of other woods is reduced, or some are omitted entirely. Nor is it necessary to mix in *Tinjo*. The primary ingredients of the Royal Incense (*Dupa Radja*) are the six following items: *Calambac, Garo, Cajulacca, Unan, Pangkilung,* and *Rafamala.*

Common Incense (*Dupa*) is further divided into "marketable" and "cheap" varieties; in both, however, *Calambac* is omitted, and it is mostly prepared in the following manner. Four parts each are taken of False Aloe (*Agallochum spurium*), *Caju Mattabuta*, and *Caju Rafamala*; two parts each of *Caju Lacca, Caju Garo* (or some common Aloe-wood), and *Putsjoc-Ana*; one part of *Caju Castorei* and, if available, common *Calambac*; and two parts of *Tacari* roots. Let a bowl be filled with these woods, all coarsely crushed in a mortar. Then, mix in four pieces of *Unam*, a small cup full of *Rafamala*, a piece of black *Gale-dupa* and *Benjowin* <note>Benzoin resin</note> the size of a whole *Pinanga* <note>Areca nut</note>. Furthermore, add the juice of both *Tinjo* and *Timbaus* in such quantity until everything can be gathered into a single mass. These are melted together in a pan into one lump, with a little *Pangkilung* and *Zibethum* <note>Civet musk</note> mixed in. To the common incense, one also adds *Dammar Selan* <note>a type of resin</note> and other fragrant resins, and it is formed into balls as indicated above. *Pangkilung* are rough pouches or, as they say, the testicles of some animal, black inside like ink, each costing two or three imperial guilders. *Timbaus* is a white fruit like the *Pinanga*, from which a fragrant liquid flows when opened, which is also used for the incense.

<column-break/>

The mixture is prepared by pouring the aforementioned woods and resins into a pan with the liquids, working them together vigorously without stopping until everything is well blended into a thick paste. This is then set in the sun for a while to dry moderately and harden. From this mass, small balls like marbles are formed and wrapped in *Licuala* leaves. The aforementioned *Galedupa* is sold in bamboo tubes a hand-span long and a finger thick, but the *Tinjo* in bamboo tubes half as long, though somewhat thicker. It is also worth knowing that the Royal Incense can be distinguished from the common by its scent, because it contains much *Calambac*, which is not used in the common kind. The Macassar nobles claim this incense for themselves so exclusively that if they perceive the scent on a common man, they would suspect him of having been with their wives, and for this scent alone they would seek his life. The same incense can be improved by increasing the amount of *Calambac* and decreasing the other woods, or by leaving some out entirely. For the principal ingredients of the *Dupa Radja*, these six items are held: *Calambac, Garo, Cajulacca, Unan, Pangkilung,* and *Rafamala.*

The common incense is again divided into "merchant-incense" and "poor-incense," both of which omit the *Calambac*, and are mostly made as follows. One takes False Aloe-wood (*Agallochum spurium*) of *Caju Mattabuta* and *Caju Rafamala*, four parts each; *Caju-Lacca, Caju Garo*, or any common Aloe-wood, and *Putsjoc Ana*, 2 parts; *Caju Castoeri*, and (if one has it) poor *Calambac*, one part; the roots of *Tacari*, 2 parts. One ensures there is a bowl full of these woods, all coarsely chopped and pounded in a mortar. Then one adds 4 pieces of *Unam*, a teacup full of *Rafamala*, and a piece each of black *Gale-dupa* and Benzoin, each as large as a whole Areca nut (*Pinanga*). Further, add the juice of both *Tinjo* and *Timbaus* until it all becomes one mass. This is melted together in a pan into a lump, mixing in a little *Pangkilung* and Civet. Into the common incense are also mixed *Dammar Selan* and other fragrant resins, and these are handled to make balls, as said above. *Pangkilung* are rough pouches or, as is said, the testicles of some animal, black inside like ink, worth 2 or 3 imperial guilders a piece. *Timbaus* is a white fruit like the Areca nut, from which, when cut open, a fragrant water flows that is also used for the incense.

In Macassar, if *Rafamala* is lacking, white cake-sugar is taken in its place. If one wishes to perfume clothes so that they retain the scent for a long time, one must first sprinkle them for one night with all kinds of flowers (which mixture is called *Bonga rampe* <note>a traditional floral potpourri</note>), then moisten them gently with a little rose-water in which some Musk and Civet have been rubbed, and then smoke them with the aforementioned incense (*Dupa*). You may flower them for another night and smoke them a second time, but for this work one should not use white linen, as it will turn yellow from it.

There is also a certain incense described by Dioscorides <note>ancient Greek physician</note> in Book 1, Chapter 24, and there called *Cyphi* <note>Kyphi</note>, which he says the Egyptian Priests used as incense for their idols. But since that chapter is held in suspicion by the learned, and the mixture itself is of little virtue for giving a good scent, it cannot be held in any consideration.

# BOOK II. CHAPTER XXI. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

# TWENTY-FIRST CHAPTER.

## Onin Bark, Massoy.

From the same Onin-Cubiay <note>a region in western New Guinea</note> an aromatic bark is also brought, with which much trade is conducted throughout all the parts of watery India <note>the Malay Archipelago</note>. I shall describe as much of it as I have been able to learn from the people of Ceram-Laut <note>islanders known for their extensive trade networks</note>, who also gave me a small branch laden with leaves and fruit, as seen in the drawing, where the leaf and fruit are depicted in their natural size.

The tree is tall and upright, and usually so thick that a man can hardly wrap his arms around it. Its bark is smooth and pale ash-colored, but at the lower part of the trunk, it is rough, cracked, and spotted with green mossiness to the thickness of a pinky finger; nonetheless, it dries easily and remains firm. The leaves have the shape of the *Lansium* tree <note>the Langsat, *Lansium domesticum*</note>, but they are a little smaller and thinner, and they agree more with the leaves of the Amboinese Wild Laurel (*Lauraster Amboinensis*). They are five, six, or seven inches long, and two or three inches wide, with a long and thin tip that usually bends to one side. They have a few oblique ribs protruding on the underside; however, the upper surface of the leaf is smooth, even, and not as wrinkled as the *Lansium* leaf. They are placed without order on the branches on short stalks <term>petioles</term>, and when crushed, they give off an aromatic scent and flavor. The fruits are round berries similar to grapes, hanging in short clusters like the *Lansium* fruit, crowned at the top with a small crown and a point, around which some rays appear. Fresh berries turn yellow like the *Lansium*, but the dried ones sent to me were of a dark or dusky color. These are covered with a brittle and woody shell that can be easily broken. Inside this is contained a roundish-oblong stone, consisting of various joined pieces like the flesh of the *Lansium* fruit, but which is much more transparent and softer, with an aromatic taste and smell that is much weaker than in the bark. The bark, however, is the best part of this tree, and when it is brought for sale, it is split into long pieces about two and a half feet long and tied into large bundles weighing twenty or twenty-five pounds. This bark is of two types, yet gathered from the same tree; for that of the lower trunk is a pinky-finger thick, reddish inside and spotted or variegated with short, whitish veins, as if it were sprinkled with dry lime. In the upper trunk and thicker branches, this bark is only the thickness of a knife or two <note>approximately 2 to 4 millimeters</note>, even, and sprinkled with dirty white or yellowish spots, without internal white veins, and it is a little sharper and hotter than the preceding; however, the scent of the thicker bark is more pleasant. Nevertheless, both have a very aromatic smell and taste, approaching that of Cubebs <note>a pungent spice from the pepper family</note>, being hot and dry in the third degree <note>a classification in Galenic medicine indicating a powerful warming effect on the body</note>. When chewed, it pricks the tongue, though not as much as Pepper, but fills the mouth with a pleasant warmth. If it is rubbed on the body, it excites such heat in the skin that it can hardly be endured, and it fills the whole place with its scent. The test of the best bark is to scrape the pieces strongly and crosswise with a fingernail; if a black line appears and some moisture is seen, it is of high quality. Pieces in which this sign does not appear are considered old, dried out, and devoid of strength, although this bark can preserve its oiliness or viscosity for many years, even if kept in dry and airy places; for I have kept such bark for twelve years, and most pieces were still equally good; however, the fruits cannot last so long.

**Name.** In Latin, it is called *Cortex Oninius* <note>original: "Cortex Oninius"</note>, after the place from which it is brought; furthermore, it is known throughout all of India by the name *Massoy*, while the tree itself is called *Aycora* by the inhabitants.

**Location.** This bark, as far as I know, grows nowhere except in the western part of *New Guinea* (which is commonly called *Onin*, and *Woni* by the people of Ternate), but not everywhere. For the front or most western part, which is called *Slaves' Onin* and is twenty-eight miles distant from Ceram and situated to the north, yields no *Massoy*, but rather to the more eastern part in the mainland region

<column-break/>

# XXI. CHAPTER.

## Massoy Tree.

*From the same Onin-Cubiay an aromatic bark is also brought, with which one conducts great trade throughout all of Watery India, which I shall describe as much as I have been able to learn from the Ceram-Laut people, who also shared with me a branch with the leaves and fruits, and which are depicted here nearby, with the leaf and fruit shown in their natural size.*

*It is a straight, tall tree, and usually so thick that a man can barely embrace it: the bark is smooth, light gray, yet on the lower trunk it is rough, cracked, and spotted with a gray mossiness, and there it is a small finger thick, as well as stiff, yet nevertheless drying easily. The leaves look much like those of the Lansium tree, yet are somewhat smaller and thinner, corresponding even more with those of the Amboinese Wild Laurel; they are five, six, and seven inches long, two, two-and-a-half, and three inches wide, with a long narrow point, which for the most part stands curved to one side, with few slanted ribs that stick out from below, for on top the leaf is smooth, even, and not as wrinkled as those of the Lansium. They stand without order around the twigs on short stalks, and being rubbed they give off an aromatic smell and taste of their own. The fruits are round berries, like wine grapes, hanging together in short clusters, like the Lansium, at the front with a small crown and point, and around the same some rays show themselves: the fresh ones are pale yellow, like the Lansium, but the dried ones that were brought to me were dark gray, or earth-colored: they are covered with a brittle woody shell, which one can easily crush into pieces: and therein lies the kernel, somewhat pointed from the round, made of various pieces standing against each other, like the flesh of the Lansium, yet lighter and softer, also aromatic in smell and taste, yet much weaker than the bark: for the bark is the best part of this tree, being split into long pieces when brought for sale, about two and a half feet long, and bound together in large bundles weighing 20 to 25 pounds: the bark is of two kinds, yet nevertheless from one tree: for that from the lower trunk is a small finger thick, reddish inside, and speckled or run through with short white veins as if it were dry lime: on the upper trunk and the thick branches the same bark is only one or two knives thick, even, covered with a dirty white or yellowish skin, without white veins inside, and somewhat better and sharper than the preceding, though the smell of the thick bark is just as lovely; nevertheless both are of a very aromatic smell and taste: mostly resembling Cubebs, hot and dry in the third degree, and being chewed in the mouth, biting somewhat on the tongue, yet not as much as Pepper, and filling the mouth with a pleasant warmth. Smeared on the body it also causes such heat on the skin as one can hardly bear: and fills the entire place with its smell: the test of the best Massoy is when one scrapes somewhat hard and crosswise on the pieces with a nail, that it then makes a black line, and some moisture shows itself, for the pieces that do not do that are considered old, dried out, and powerless, although this bark can keep its oiliness for many years, even if one stores it in dry and airy places, for I have kept them so bound until the 12th year, and found most pieces still just as good, but the fruits cannot remain good so long.*

**Name.** *In Latin Cortex Oninius, after the place where it comes from, being further known throughout all India by the name of Massoy, and the tree itself is called Aycora by the inhabitants.*

**Locations.** *This bark, as much as is known until now, occurs nowhere but on the Western part of New Guinea (which is commonly called Onin, and by the Ternatans Woni) yet not everywhere, for the foremost or Western part, which one calls Slaven-Onin, situated about 28 miles from Ceram to the North-east, has no Massoy, but somewhat further east on the mainland*
