# BOOK II. CHAPTER XXI. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

<meta>catchword: wor- (from the Dutch word "worden" or similar, indicating continuity)</meta>

In the region of the islands of *Caras*, where the village of *Fata* is situated, the harvesting of *Massoy* bark <note>Aromatic bark from *Cryptocarya massoy*, used in traditional medicine and perfumes</note> once began there; however, today it is neglected because a wicked and bloodthirsty nation lives there. Moving further toward the Eastern part, the land of *Onin* has two prominent headlands, located at four and a half degrees of southern latitude, and between these lie the villages called *Cattumin* and *Segala*. From there, the people of Ceram sought *Massoy* bark for a long time, but they later abandoned that business there, either because the inhabitants pursued them with hatred or because the bark began to fail.

However, three miles toward the east of the Southern region lies the island called *Ady*, known by our people as Weasel Island <note>original Latin: *Mustelarum insula*; Dutch: *Wesels Eiland*</note>. To its Northern part, many small islands are located in almost a single stretch, behind which a huge lake <note>likely a reference to a large bay or inlet</note> appears to the north. We do not know if it is closed and narrowed at the rear, or if it truly divides Western *Onin* from the actual *New Guinea*. At least twelve miles to the eastern part of Weasel Island, on the mainland coast of *New Guinea*, are situated the villages of the Ethiopians <note>A historical term used here to describe the dark-skinned Papuan peoples</note> known as *Namma-Totto*, *Cajumera*, and *Lackayba*, where trade in *Massoy* bark is conducted. These, together with the last two villages in the said Southern coast, are called *Onin-Cubiai* and *Cobiay* by the people of Ceram. Navigation to these regions has been established and frequented since ancient times by the *Ceram-Laut* people, who now inhabit the flat land of *Keffing* and are thus also called *Keffingers*. Among themselves, they maintain such a good standard of life and discipline that only two districts of that land, called *Kelilubu* and *Ruma-Tammeri*, sail to *Onin* to bring back the frequently mentioned *Massoy* bark. They then sell it to other foreign merchants or carry it to *Java* themselves. These people of Ceram, as has been said, must seek this bark from the said districts—sixty or seventy miles distant from their own region—with incredible labor and danger in their small, simple vessels. For that region of *Cabiay* has inhabitants who are wild and barbarian, of great stature, deformed, and grim-faced, having greatly distended nostrils which they dilate by inserting small sticks, so that one can almost see through them into the mouth. In ancient times, they had no conversation with foreign peoples, nor would they admit any into their region until now, were it not that necessity—arising from a lack of certain things—urged them to permit the arrival of some peoples, especially the *Ceram-Laut* and *Keffingers*, who exchange this bark for other things necessary to them. However, it is not permitted for these or any other foreigners to enter the forests themselves to seek this bark; instead, those wild men enter into a contract with the traders, who give them certain cheap swords or sickles. Then, the locals suddenly climb the remote mountains, where within the space of a month they strip and collect as much of this bark as one or two vessels can hold, which usually amounts to sixty to a hundred Pickols <term>Picul: a traditional unit of weight, roughly 125 pounds</term>, or a little more. Each Pickol contains one hundred and twenty-five pounds. When they have returned to the shore, they build certain heaps of this bark to the height of a Tambux sword <note>original: *Tambuxensis gladii*; likely a reference to a specific type of local machete or blade</note> and establish a fixed price with the merchants. The *Ceram-Laut* men, however, being fraudulent, give very little to these simple people, consisting mostly of cheap Tambux swords, coarse clothing, red sugar, and rice. But when this bark is brought to Amboina, they sell it for 15, 16, and 17 imperial coins <note>Rixdollars or Thalers</note> per Pickol, which we were later able to acquire for eight or ten imperial coins. In *Java*, however, during flourishing times, it was sold for 30 or 40 imperial coins.

This tree, as has been said, does not grow everywhere in the whole *Onin* region. For those who inhabit the outer *Onin* land, specifically the village of *Ruma-Batu*, declared in the year 1678 that only two trees were found in that district, nor do they occur near the shore except for a very few. The inhabitants of the three principal districts testified that the nearest village was so cut off that it was necessary for them to travel through the mountains for a space of three to five days before they could collect this bark.

In the year 1678, our people under the command of *Johannes Keyts* invaded the island of *Ady*, or Weasel Island, in various places, but they found no people there; however, they observed a penetrating odor of cloves there, which perhaps from *Maf-*

<column-break/>

On the mainland, opposite the Islands of *Caras*, where the village of *Fata* lies, people also used to fetch *Massoy* in former times, but nowadays this is neglected because a wicked and murderous people live there. Somewhat further east, the land of *Onin* has two protruding points located at 4 1/2 degrees southern latitude, and between these two are the villages of *Cattumin* and *Segala*, where the *Cerammers* also traded *Massoy* for a long time, but later abandoned that trade, either because they also fell into hatred among the locals, or because the *Massoy* began to decrease.

Then, three miles east of the South-east corner lies the island of *Ady*, called the *Weasel Island* <note>original: *Wesels Eiland*</note> by our people, and north of it many more small islands, mostly all on one reef, behind which one sees to the north a large bay. It is not known whether it is closed or if it separates western *Onin* from the actual *New Guinea*. Indeed, 12 miles east of *Weasel Island*, on the solid coast of *New Guinea*, lie the villages of *Namma-Totto*, *Cajumera*, and *Lackayba*, where *Massoy* is traded nowadays. Together with the two last-mentioned villages on the aforementioned South corner, they are called *Onin-Cubiai* and *Cobiay* by the *Cerammers*. The voyage to those villages has been frequented since olden times by those of *Ceram Laut*, who now live on the flat land of *Keffing* and are therefore collectively called *Keffingers*. They maintain such order among their people that only two authorized districts or camps, called *Kelilubu* and *Ruma-Tammeri*, may sail to *Onin* and fetch the aforementioned *Massoy*, which they then later sell again to other foreign traders or carry to *Java* themselves. These *Cerammers*, as said, must fetch the *Massoy* from the aforementioned villages—which lie some 60 to 70 miles from their land—with an incredible amount of effort and peril in their small, simple vessels. For the land of *Cubiay* itself has very wild, ugly, and barbarian people as inhabitants; they are large of stature, deformed and ugly of face, with distended nostrils into which they stick small pegs, making them gape so wide that one can almost see through them into their mouths. From of old, they have had no dealings with foreign nations and would still allow no one onto their land if the lack of many things did not force them to allow some foreigners on their beach, especially the *Ceram-Lauwers* and *Keffingers*, to exchange this bark for other necessities. However, they and all other foreigners may not go into the forests themselves to fetch this bark; instead, these wild people first contract with them, and having received some cheap swords or brush-knives, they run with speed into the distant mountains. There, within a month's time, they peel and gather as much of this bark as one or two vessels can load, which amounts to 60 to 100 Pickols, and sometimes a bit more. Each Pickol is 125 Dutch pounds. When they have returned to the beach, they make some heaps of that bark to the height of a *Tambux* sword, and then set the final price with the merchants. But the *Ceram-Lauwers*, being sly fellows, give these dull people very little for it, which then mostly consists of cheap *Tambux* swords, poor cloths, black sugar, and rice. But having brought this bark to *Amboina*, they want 15, 16, and 17 Rixdollars <note>original: *Ryksdaalders*</note> per Pickol, which one has nevertheless been able to get for 8 and 10 Rixdollars afterward. And on *Java* in good times, it used to be worth as much as 30 and 40 Rixdollars.

This tree, as said, does not grow everywhere throughout the entire land of *Onin*. For those of the foremost *Onin*, in the village of *Ruma-Batu*, declared in the year 1678 that only two trees stood in their district. They are also not found close to the beach, except for a few, and the inhabitants of the three aforementioned villages said furthermore that the nearest *Massoy* was so thinned out that they had to go 3 to 5 days' journey into the mountains to fetch it.

In the year 1678, our people under Commander *Johannes Keyts* visited the island of *Adi*, or *Weasel Island*, at various places, but found no people there, though they did notice a strong smell of cloves...

# AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chapter XXI.

<column-break/>

[This bark] comes from the **Massoy** trees: these wild people, seeing that this bark is so sought after throughout the entire world, are so envious that they not only prohibit foreigners from entering their region, but even from taking any small trees away from there, although I have often attempted to do so through the *Ceram-Lauwerenses* <note>People from the Seram Laut islands, known as intermediaries in the spice trade</note>, who are held in great estimation by those forest-dwelling peoples.

**Uses.** This bark is not sought after throughout all of **India** <note>Referring to the East Indies</note>, but only by the **Malays** in **Sumatra**, **Borneo**, **Java**, and **Bali**; for these regions, a cargo of two vessels called *Sampans* <note>A type of flat-bottomed wooden boat</note> is sufficient each year. Now, however, it is also sent to **China** and **Japan**, where it is sold for a good profit. It is mostly used for anointing the body, for both men and women, and especially on rainy and cold days; for it warms moderately and settles pains of the abdomen arising from cold. It also strengthens limbs weakened and loosened by cold, as its nature is dry, hot, and so penetrating that if this bark is rubbed on the skin of Europeans, it causes redness. The **Javanese** and **Balinese women** are very skilled at preparing a warming mash <note>original Latin: *pultem*; Dutch: *pap*</note> from this bark, with which they continually rub the body, not only for the sake of warming it, but also for its excellent scent. They then add **Culilawan** bark <note>Aromatic bark from *Cinnamomum culilawan*</note>, a small quantity of **Cloves**, and **Yellow Sandalwood**; this ointment is called the "hot" **Bobory**. The inhabitants of **Coebiay** <note>Kobiay, a region in New Guinea</note> are said to lead certain dogs with them when they enter the forests to search for **Massoy** trees, and they consider those to be good and fully mature whose trunks are gnawed by these dogs. The *Ceram-Lauwerenses* also bring some pieces of this wood and branches with them and sell them at a low price, as this wood also has its use in medicine, reflecting the scent of the **Massoy** bark, though it is one degree weaker in heat; for this reason, it is much used for the **Bobory** ointment prepared for infants, who cannot tolerate the heat of the bark. Some **Malays** also use this bark in food in place of other spices, and they mix it into medicinal drinks called **Djudjambo**.

Around the year 1654, there were two deceitful *Orangkayenses* <note>From the Malay *Orang Kaya*, meaning "rich man" or a local nobleman/leader</note> from Seram Laut, named **Sinoos** and **Backer**, who for several years had cheated the **Coebiayenses** in a clever way when setting the price of the **Massoy** bark. For this purpose, they used a large mirror, persuading the **Coebiayenses** that they would see their idol **Rewata** or **Lewata** in this mirror (for by this name all these surrounding pagan islanders call God). They placed the locals on one side, while meanwhile, they had placed another companion behind them but directly in front of the mirror, whose image represented the idol **Rewata**. **Sinoos** and **Backer** then asked this figure whether it was indeed fair that they should pay as high a price for the **Massoy** as the **Coebiayenses** were demanding. To this, the fake **Rewata** replied by shaking his head "no." They asked again and again, until the price was so diminished as had been determined between them; once they agreed on a price, the **Rewata** nodded in approval. The **Coebiayenses** did not dare to contradict him, since their own God had approved it. They carried out this trick for a long time, until this fraud was uncovered by others who were envious of the *Ceram-Lauwerenses* and revealed it to the **Coebiayenses**. In their anger, they seized one of those deceivers, whom they put to death and tore into pieces.

It is believed that **Chinese** and **Japanese** doctors will seek out and use this bark more and more for medical purposes, since it is a most excellent and suitable medicine for those nations, who are so accustomed to friction and anointment, and who, in their climate, must endure intense cold in addition to great heat. It is suitable for them to preserve the natural heat of the body and to settle pains arising from cold and suppressed winds <note>flatulence or internal "vapors"</note>. This bark is not transported to Europe, and if by chance it should be brought there, it is not much valued, doubtless because its virtues are not known there, or other spices are preferred.

I have seen the *Ceram-Lauwerenses* fill their pillows with the leaves of this tree, saying that this is good for warming the head...

<column-break/>

...which perhaps came from the **Massoy** trees. These wild people, seeing that this bark is thus sought after by the world, are so jealous over it that they not only forbid strangers from going deep into the land, but also will not let any young trees be transported, although I have several times had the *Ceram Lauwers* <note>Seram Laut traders</note> undertake it, who nonetheless have great credit with those wild people.

**Use.** This bark is not desired or sought throughout all of the **Indies**, but only by the **Malays** on **Sumatra**, **Borneo**, **Java**, and **Bali**, for which countries a cargo of two vessels (called *Sampans*) is enough annually; however, they are now also beginning to send it to **China** and **Japan**, and to sell it there with good profit. It is used most to smear the body, for both **Men** and **Women**, and especially in rainy, cold days: for it warms moderately and stills the stomach-ache that comes from the cold; it also strengthens all limbs that are paralyzed by cold, being dry, biting, and penetrating by nature—indeed, such that when smeared on the skin of **Europeans**, it makes it red. The **Javanese** and **Balinese women** are very skilled at making a warming mash from this bark, with which they also constantly rub the body, not only (as said) to warm it, but also for the sake of its good scent. But then they also add the following bark, **Culilawan**, a few cloves, and **Yellow Sandalwood**, which ointment is called the "biting" **Bobory**. It is said that the inhabitants of **Coebiay** lead some dogs with them when they go into the woods to seek out **Massoy** trees, and that they consider those to be good and fully ripe at whose trunks the dogs gnaw. The *Ceram-Lauwers* also sometimes bring some pieces of the wood and the branches, and sell them for a low price, for this wood also has its use in **Medicine**, smelling strongly of **Massoy**, but it is a degree weaker in bitterness, and is therefore much used for the **Bobory** ointment made for small children, who cannot endure the bitterness of the bark. Some **Malays** also put the **Massoy** in their food, in place of other spices, and they also mix it into the **Medicinal** drinks called **Djudjambo** by them.

About the year 1654, there were two crafty **Orangkayen** from Seram, **Sinoos** and **Backer**, who for many years had neatly deceived the **Coebiayers** in making the price for the **Massoy**, using a large mirror for that purpose, making the **Coebiayers** believe that they would see their God **Rewata** or **Lewata** (so all these surrounding islands, who are still heathens, call God) in it. Placing the people somewhat to the side, they had meanwhile dressed up one of their mates, who stood somewhat behind them but directly before the mirror, and whose image in the mirror would then be the God **Rewata**. **Sinoos** and **Backer** then began to ask this image whether it was indeed fair that they gave as much for the **Massoy** as the **Coebiayers** demanded: and when the counterfeited **Rewata** shook his head at this, they asked him once more, twice more, and so on, each time with a reduction of the price, until it came as low as they had determined upon; at which point **Rewata** then nodded. Those simple people could have nothing against it, as it was approved by their God. They did this as long as the fraud remained undiscovered, until it was revealed by some others who were envious of the *Ceram-Lauwers*. After this, the angered **Coebiayers**, catching one of the deceivers, also brought him to his death and tore him into pieces.

It is trusted that the **Chinese** and **Japanese Doctors** will seek, desire, and use this bark more and more as **Medicine**: for it is indeed a very necessary and capable means for that nation, who are so used to rubbing and smearing, and in their climates must endure many cold days along with the heat, to preserve the natural warmth of the body and to drive away all pain that comes from trapped, hidden, and cold winds. It is not transported to **Europe**, and if now and then it is brought there, it is not esteemed there, without doubt through ignorance of its powers, or because it can be replaced by other spices.

I have also seen that the *Ceram-Lauwers* make their sleeping-pillows from the leaves of this tree, claiming that this serves to warm the head...

# AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chapter XXII. 65

<column-break/>

[This bark] is used for warming [the head] on sea voyages, during which they suffer much from the cold, and which they endure for almost their whole lives; as has been said, they seek this bark with a thousand dangers from those barbarian regions, and they carry it further in small vessels called **Sampans** <note>A type of flat-bottomed wooden boat used in Southeast Asia</note> for forty miles <note>The Dutch text curiously notes 400 miles, suggesting a possible printer's error in the original volumes</note> across the sea to the capitals of **Java**.

It remains to be investigated whether this tree does not have a great affinity with that tree which bears aromatic bark and grows in the Strait of Magellan. This is described by Charles de l'Écluse <note>A famous 16th-century Flemish botanist, also known as Carolus Clusius</note> in Book 4, Chapter 1, under the name of **Winter's Bark** <note>original Latin: *corticis Winterani*; a spice bark used by early explorers to prevent scurvy</note>; the tree itself is called by him the Aromatic Magellanic Tree.

### OBSERVATION.

This bark, called **Oninius** or **Massoy** <note>original: *Maffoy*</note>, is shown depicted in the *German Ephemerides* <note>original: *Ephem. Germ.*; one of the earliest scientific journals</note>, 2nd decade, year 3, plate on page 53, and is described on page 55; as also in Valentinus' <note>François Valentijn, a Dutch minister and naturalist</note> *Indian Literary Epistles III*, page 397, and *Epistle IX*, page 422, and in Valentinus' *Description of Amboina*, page 208.

## CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO.

### Clove-like Bark. Culitlawan.

This bark is also aromatic and is gathered from a wild tree that bears a tall and straight trunk, which a man can hardly embrace with his arms; its crown is not very widely extended, but it bears dense foliage, resembling a **Laurel** in form. Its branches are few and mostly rise upwards; the leaf-stalks or green and firm branchlets are always in opposite pairs, forming a cross with the next pair, and each junction resembles a three-pronged fork. The leaves are likewise placed in a cross-shape, always two opposite each other, three or four pairs on one stalk, which has the shape of an iron spear-head. These leaves resemble **Cinnamon** leaves, or even more closely those of **Cassia lignea** <note>A spice bark similar to cinnamon, often called "Chinese cinnamon"</note>, with both of which trees this **Culit-Lawan** <note>Cinnamomum culilawan</note> has great affinity. Each leaf on old trees is a hand's length, three or four fingers wide; on younger trees, it is hardly a span long, four or five fingers wide near its base, where they gradually narrow and end in a point. They are furthermore firm, dry, and if broken, they crackle; on top they are a deep green and smooth, underneath they are a pale bluish-green or ash-colored, and they have three nerves running through the length of the leaf, like the broad-leaved **Plantain**, meeting about a finger's width from the base and protruding on the upper side, while the intermediate spaces are woven with fine veins. Their taste is mucilaginous and slightly aromatic, approaching that of **Cloves**.

The fruits are rarely observed, as the trees are very tall and they mostly fall off prematurely and imperfectly. Trees that are well-exposed to the sun and not much stripped of their bark show their fruit best, and produce them without a noticeable flowering; for soon they offer green and sharp little heads, from which oblong berries spring forth, very similar to **Acorns** but much smaller, smooth, and of a sea-green color. Under the outer thick and green husk, an oblong pit is hidden, very similar to the fruit of the **Laurel** <note>The Bay berry</note>, of a purplish-red color, divisible into two parts. The little cup <note>The calyx</note> in which the berries are held is much deeper than in Acorns, divided into six points, and closely joined to the fruit. This fruit, having reached the size of a half-grown **Olive**, in some begins to burst open on one side and sends forth an outgrowth of a fine, soft, spongy, and yellow substance, resembling the finest **Ochre** or a certain yellow fat, the size of a shelled **Walnut**. And this outgrowth or abortion eventually covers the entire green bark in such a way that only a certain part is seen in its center. The purplish-red pit is then entirely consumed, and the green husk or skin...

<column-break/>

...that this served to warm the head on the cold sea voyages, in which they spend most of their lives, fetching, as said, this bark with a thousand kinds of dangers from the mentioned barbarian lands, and they bring it from further away with their simple vessels, called **Sampans**, nearly 400 miles over the sea to the commercial cities of **Java**.

Furthermore, it remains to be investigated whether this tree might not have a great similarity with that tree that has a spice-like bark and grows in the Strait of Magellan: described by Charles de l'Écluse <note>Carol. Clus.</note> in Book 4, Chapter 1, under the name of **Winter's Bark** <note>Winteranus Cortex</note>, though the tree itself is named by him the Aromatic Magellanic Tree.

The **Massoy** tree <note>Maffoy-boom</note> is also described by Valentinus in the *Description of Amboina*, page 208, and by Valentinus in *Indian Letters, Epistle III*, page 397, and *Epistle IX*, page 422, and is illustrated in the *German Ephemerides* <note>Ephemer. ## TWENTY-SECOND CHAPTER.

### Culit-lawan Tree.

This is also a spice-like bark, and comes from a wild tree with a high and straight trunk, which a man can usually just embrace; its crown is not very broad, but dense with foliage, appearing like a **Laurel**. The branches are few and mostly stand upright; the twigs are green and stiff, standing two and two against each other, making a cross with the next pair, each joining showing a three-pronged arrangement. The leaves also stand in a cross, two and two against each other, three and four pairs on a twig, having the shape of the iron or the point of a pike, and they resemble **Cinnamon** leaves somewhat, or to say it even more closely, those of **Cassia Lignea**, with which two trees the **Culit-Lawan** also has great similarity. Each leaf on old trees is a hand long, 3 and 4 fingers wide, and on the young ones a span long, and four and five fingers wide near their origin, and from there gradually tapering or running to a point. Furthermore, they are stiff, dry, and crackling when broken; from above deep green and smooth, and from below tending toward grey or Spanish-green. They have three nerves running lengthwise, like the leaves of **Plantain**, meeting about a finger above the origin and also bulging on the upper side, the intermediate spaces being woven with fine veins. The taste is slimy and a little spice-like, pulling somewhat toward **Cloves**.

The fruits are seldom seen, because they are very tall trees, and the fruits mostly fall off untimely and imperfectly; the trees that stand well in the sun and are not much stripped of bark show their fruits best, and produce them without a noticeable blossom, showing immediately or at first green pointed buds, from which oblong berries come forth, very much like **Acorns**, but much smaller, smooth, and sea-green in color. Under the outermost thick green shell lies an oblong kernel, like **Bay berries** <note>Bakelaren</note>, purple-red, which can be divided in two; the little cup in which they stand is deeper than that of the **Oak**, divided into six points, and sitting or lying close against the fruit. The fruit now having come to the size of a half-grown **Olive**, some of them, or one kind of them, begin to burst open a bit on one side and get an outgrowth of a fine, soft, dry, and yellow substance, resembling the finest ochre or some yellow grease, to the size of a shelled **Walnut**. And this outgrowth finally covers the green shell in such a way that one only sees a piece of it remaining in the roundness. The purple-red kernel is then also entirely consumed, and the green shell...

<header>HERBARIUM OF AMBOINA Book II, Chapter XXII.</header>

...it nevertheless degenerates into a cartilaginous substance, recalling **Cloves** <note>Latin: *Caryophyllos*</note> in taste and smell, and it retains this aromatic scent for a long time if it is enclosed or well-preserved. Not all berries suffer this abortion <note>Referring to the irregular growth or "culling" of the fruit</note>, but most fall off; the most mature of these, upon touching the ground, sprout into small trees, while the few remaining ones adhering to the stems gape open and emit that aforementioned overgrowth. This gives those fruits an irregular shape, namely like a clod of earth, which is so soft to the touch that it might be taken for tallow. **Cinnamon** <note>Latin: *Cinnamomum*</note> also produces such a substance, which stains the hands with its yellow color when handled; this substance is harder on the inside and has the form of a kernel, though these do not sprout.

The fruits are seen in the month of April and fall in August. The bark of the trunk is smooth on the outside, ashen or whitish; internally it bears a paler color than **Massoy** <note>An aromatic bark from the *Cryptocarya* or *Cinnamomum* genus, often used in traditional medicine</note> bark, tending from reddish to yellow, like a half-baked brick. In old trunks it is a finger thick, but in the upper part it is only half a finger thick or a little thinner. The outer part is often beset with warts; two types of bark are collected from a single tree: for the lower and thicker bark is much drier and more brittle, yet much tougher than Massoy. In taste and smell it is so sharp and so close to **Cloves** <note>Latin: *Caryophyllum*</note> that it might be taken for the bark of that tree; however, **Culitlawan** <note>From the Indonesian *Kulit Lawang*, meaning "Clove Bark"</note> has something peculiar, as its scent is so heavy that it affects and burdens the head. The upper bark is much thinner and harder, and of a more pleasant taste and smell; if chewed, it exhibits a sliminess with a slight astringency, as in fresh **Cassia Lignea** <note>A spice similar to cinnamon, often called Chinese Cinnamon</note>. In the dried bark, however, less astringency appears but only a small bitterness; at first, it exhibits greater heat and sharpness than Massoy, but the heat of the latter lasts longer, since Culitlawan consists of more airy parts. Chewed in the mouth, this bark sharply nips the tongue, especially the lower thick bark; however, that which is only the thickness of a quill or half a finger has a much more pleasant taste and fills the mouth with a grateful flavor of Cloves. The fresh bark must be dried in the sun for several days before it is stored away, at which time it has a vinous and pleasant smell; otherwise, it easily contracts mold. It is not to be kept in closed chests, but in windy and open places, such as in the dining rooms under the roof of the house, where I have preserved it for twelve years.

**Culitlawan** brought from the **Papuan** and **Moluccan** islands is a little darker and sharper than the **Amboinese** variety, but it does not have such a pleasant taste, and it might be mistaken for **Massoy**, which is generally harder and heavier. The entire bark is stripped and peeled from the tree, and nothing is thrown away, as is done with Cinnamon bark, where only the outer part is cleaned. I have compared the leaves of Cinnamon, Culitlawan, and Cassia Lignea, and found that they all consist of three longitudinal nerves and are interwoven, and furthermore are smooth, firm, and of an aromatic smell and taste. The Cinnamon leaves were wider, shorter, and rounder; those of Cassia Lignea were oblong and pointed; while those of Culitlawan were the longest and firmest, and had a more peculiar taste.

Although these three trees are very closely related, they do not grow in the same place, but in very diverse regions. For **Cinnamon** grows in the western part of **Ceylon** <note>Modern-day Sri Lanka</note>; **Cassia Lignea** grows in the eastern region of the **Philippine Islands**, through **Celebes** <note>Sulawesi</note>, **Borneo**, as far as **Cambodia** and **Tonkin** <note>Northern Vietnam</note>, mostly toward the northern side of the equator; for some trees, though few, occur in the southern part of Celebes in the **Buginese** <note>Latin: *Boegenibus*; referring to the Bugis people of Sulawesi</note> mountains and near **Balante**. **Culitlawan** grows in these eastern islands on the southern side of the Equator. However, this also has an exception, for in **Mindanao**, the southernmost region of the Philippine Islands, Cassia Lignea and Culitlawan occur on one and the same island; and if one pays close attention, a twofold difference appears in the Amboinese variety, namely white and red. The white bark resembles a raw brick and is more moist, tougher, and thicker, and is peeled from the tree in long pieces, which pleases merchants more. The red is more reddish like a half-baked brick, is thinner, and more fragile, and cannot be peeled into long pieces; yet both are equally...

<column-break/>

*...the shell changes into a cartilaginous substance, well-resembling the taste and smell of **Cloves** <note>Dutch: *Nagelen*</note>, retaining its spicy scent for a long time if it is enclosed or well-preserved. However, not all berries acquire this overgrowth, but most fall off, of which the ripest, when they touch the earth, produce young trees; and the few that remain on the stems burst open and obtain the aforementioned overgrowth, which gives those fruits an irregular shape, namely like a small clod of earth, being so soft to the touch that one would take it for tallow. The **Cinnamon tree** <note>Dutch: *Kaneelboom*</note> also produces such a substance, and in handling it also stains the fingers yellow; inside it is somewhat harder and has the shape of a grain, though it does not reproduce.*

*The fruits come forth in April, and in August they fall off. The bark of the trunk is smooth on the outside, light gray or whitish, and inside much lighter in color than the **Massoy**, tending somewhat from reddish toward yellow, like a half-baked stone <note>A brick</note>; on the lower trunks it is a finger thick, and toward the top half a finger or even thinner, and on the outer side mostly beset with warts. One also has two kinds of bark or skin from one tree, for the lowermost and thickest is much drier and more brittle, yet still tougher than the Massoy. In taste and smell it is very sharp, and so closely approaching the scent of **Cloves** <note>Dutch: *Nagel-reuk*</note> that one would take it for the bark of that tree; yet the **Culitlawan** has something special, being so strong that it burdens the head. The uppermost bark is much thinner and harder, also more lovely in taste and smell, and in chewing one notices some sliminess with a small astringency, as in fresh **Cassia Lignea**; but in the dry bark one finds less astringency, and in contrast a small bitterness. At first it shows a greater bite and sharpness than the Massoy, but the bite of the Massoy is longer-lasting because the Culitlawan is made of more airy parts. Chewed in the mouth, it bites bravely on the tongue, and especially the lowermost thick bark; however, that which is only the thickness of a quill <note>Dutch: *schaft*</note> or half a finger is much lovelier in taste and fills the mouth with a pleasant clove-scent. The fresh bark must be left to dry in the sun for several days before it is put away, smelling then vinous and lovely; otherwise it easily becomes moldy. It must not be kept in closed chests or cases, but in airy places, such as in attics under the roof, where I have kept it good for twelve years.*

*The **Culitlawan** that comes from the **Papuan** and **Moluccan** Islands is somewhat browner and sharper than the **Amboinese**, yet not so lovely in taste, and one would take it for **Massoy**, which is generally harder and heavier. The entire bark is pulled off the tree and nothing of it is thrown away, as is done with the outside of the Cinnamon bark, but only the roughness is scraped off. I have had the leaves of Cinnamon, Culitlawan, and Cassia Lignea together and found that they were all threaded with three nerves lengthwise, smooth, stiff, and aromatic in smell and taste. Those of the Cinnamon were shorter, wider, and rounder; those of Cassia Lignea oblong and pointed. Those of the Culitlawan were next to those, yet smaller, and both tasting like cinnamon. Those of Culitlawan were the longest and stiffest and had more of their own taste.*

*And although these three trees have great fellowship with one another, they nonetheless do not grow in one place, but in very diverse lands: as the **Cinnamon** in the West on **Ceylon**, the **Cassia Lignea** in the East from the **Philippine Islands** onwards, through **Celebes**, **Borneo**, to **Cambodia** and **Tonkin**, mostly north of the line <note>The Equator</note>; for one also finds a few trees on the southern side of Celebes in the **Buginese** <note>Dutch: *Boegische*</note> mountains and near **Balante**. The Culitlawan possesses these Eastern islands south of the line. However, this also has its exception, for on **Mindanao**, the southernmost of the Philippines, one has Cassia Lignea and Culitlawan on one and the same island; and if one pays close attention, one can find two distinctions in the Amboinese Culitlawan, namely white and red. The white bark resembles a raw brick <note>Dutch: *moppe*</note>, is moister, tougher, also thicker, and therefore allows itself to be peeled from the tree in long pieces, which is more pleasant to the merchants. The red is more reddish in color, namely like a half-baked stone, also thinner and more brittle, from which one can get no long pieces; yet both are equally good and spicy.*

<meta>This page continues the botanical description of the Culitlawan tree (Clove-bark). # Book II. Chapter XXII. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...is good and aromatic. The white variety bears those fruits which, when they gape open, reveal that yellow tallow <note>Original Latin: *febum*; Dutch: *ongel*. This refers to a waxy or fatty substance found in the fruit.</note>. The fruits of the red variety, however, are like small olives, but more oblong and do not gape open—at least not as much as the white variety. Indeed, the fruit and leaves of both have almost no difference. Sometimes the fruits grow so large that three or four clusters together resemble a small bunch of grapes; when split, they exude a yellow, dry, and greasy tallow. Beneath this, a dry, sponge-like substance is located, which has an aromatic taste; in the center of these clusters, the seed-stones are hidden and found.

The wood of the tree is whitish and spongy <note>Original: *fungosum*</note>, unsuitable for use in buildings, but excellent for building a hearth fire. The bark of the roots differs greatly from the bark of the trunk in taste; for besides that aromatic flavor, it also shares much of the flavor of Fennel. This fennel-like quality agrees so well in taste, color, and substance with that of the *Western Sassafras* <note>Referring to the North American *Sassafras albidum*</note> that our doctors and surgeons in Batavia <note>The administrative center of the Dutch East Indies, modern-day Jakarta</note> have begun to use it as a medical substitute for true *Sassafras* since the year 1676. However, how much it differs from that Western tree—which grows in Florida and Virginia and provides the true Sassafras—can be seen in the works of *Nicolas Monardes, Chapter 24* <note>A famous Spanish physician and botanist (c. 1493–1588)</note>, where almost nothing in the form of the whole tree matches our *Culitlawan*, except for the fennel-like scent and taste of the bark. In my judgment, the Western Sassafras possesses that flavor in a much more penetrating and pleasant way, and it has a lower degree of heat <note>Refers to the "humoral" temperature or pungency of the spice</note> than the *Culitlawan*.

<margin>Name</margin> In Latin it is called *Cortex Caryophylloides* <note>Literally: Clove-like Bark</note>, in Malay *Culitlawan*, which is as if you said *Culitlawan*, by abbreviation from *Culit-Buguliwan*, that is, *Clove Bark*, because of the scent it bears. In Amboinese it is called *Salackal* and *Salackar*. Some Javanese also call it *Sindoc*, which I believe to be a different bark and will describe in the following chapter. Otherwise, it is called *Tedjo* by the people of Ceram-Laut, and *Eyck* in Aru-Haumo.

I do not know from where the affinity arose between the word *Salackal* and the Arabic *Salicha*, which the Arabs use for fragrant Cassia <note>A spice similar to cinnamon</note>, coming from a word meaning "to strip" or "to despoil." For the Arabic *Salaba* means "he pulled off the skin," because all *Cassia* is, as it were, stripped of its bark. It is not without reason that one may suspect the ancient inhabitants of Amboina once took some names of plants and animals from Arabic—which was formerly a universal language throughout the East—and named this *Salackal* from its similarity to the true *Salicha* (that is, *Cassia Lignea*). Just as *Alballa* descends from *Alhanna* (that is, *Cyprus and Moluccus*). *Senya* or *Sunya*, a very thorny shrub otherwise called *Sappan*, comes from the Arabic *Sent* (that is, *Dog-Brier* <note>Latin: *Rubus Caninus*</note>), which further comes from the Hebrew *Seneh* (that is, *Brier*). Likewise *Schid* means *Brier*, and also *Schid* means "trifles of the woods" <note>Latin: *Nugæ silvarum*</note>, from the Hebrew *Schayth*, meaning "thorns" <note>Latin: *vepres*</note>.

<margin>Place</margin> This tree is quite widely distributed through the eastern islands, but the best is found in Amboina—though not throughout the whole island, but only in Leytimora around the villages of Saya, Rutton, and Ema. There, its abundance is already decreasing, since in the year 1664 a large enough quantity of this bark had to be sent to Europe as a sample, whereby most of the old trees perished from being stripped of their bark. However, the loss will be easily repaired within a few years by newly sprouting saplings. On the southern part of Great Ceram, in the bay of Elipaputi as far as Keffing, these trees also occur, though their bark is not as excellent as that of the Amboinese. They also grow in the Moluccan island called Batsjan, as well as in the Papuan islands, where the bark exceeds the Amboinese in heat <note>Original Latin: *fervore*; meaning its pungent or medicinal strength</note>. A great abundance of these trees is found on the islands of Key and Aru, from which entire shiploads of this bark could be taken. Similar to the Papuan variety, it is found in reasonable quantities on the northern coast of Celebes <note>Sulawesi</note>, in the region of Caudipan. Likewise in Sumatra near Palembang, and in Borneo near Succadana. *Culitlawan* is also brought from Java, but I think that bark is actually *Sindoc*. This bark was also found on Solor, but likewise differing in taste from the Amboinese, as also in Mindanao, as was said above.

<column-break/>

*The white variety bears the aforementioned fruits, which, when bursting open, give off that yellow tallow. But the fruits of the red variety remain like small olives, though somewhat more oblong, and do not burst open: at least not as much as the white variety, for the fruits and leaves of both have almost no difference. Also, the fruits sometimes become so large that they show 3 and 4 clusters like a small bunch of grapes; the burst ones are butter-yellow in color, dry and greasy, and beneath them is a dry substance like a sponge, spicy in scent; in the largest of these clusters one finds the seed-grains.*

*The wood is whitish and spongy, not suitable for building, but provides good firewood. The bark of the roots differs significantly in taste from the bark of the trunk, for it has, besides the aforementioned spiciness, a Fennel-like taste, which comes so close to that of the West Indian Sassafras in taste, color, and substance, that it has begun to be used in medicine as genuine Sassafras by our Doctors and Surgeons in Batavia since the year 1676. However, how much it differs from that West Indian tree growing in Florida and Virginia, from which the original Sassafras comes, can be seen in Nic. Monardus, Chapter 24, where one will find almost nothing in the appearance of the whole tree that matches our Culitlawan, except for the Fennel-like scent and taste of the bark. In my opinion, the West Indian Sassafras has the aforementioned taste much more clearly and pleasantly; it is also a degree lower in heat than the Culitlawan.*

**Name.** *In Latin Cortex Caryophylloides, in Malay Culitlawan, as if one said Culitlawan, being shortened from Culit-Buguliwan, that is Clove-bark, after the scent it has. In Amboinese Salackal and Salackar: some on Java also call it Sindoc, which I view as a distinct bark, and will describe in the following Chapter; otherwise it is called Tedjo by the Ceram-Lauwers: and Eyck on Aru-Haumo.*

*I do not know where the agreement comes from between the word Salackal and the Arabic Salicha, with which the Arabs name the fragrant Cassia, derived from and meaning to rob or despoil, for the Arabic Salacha means: he has stripped off the skin, because all that Cassia is mostly despoiled of all its bark. For which reason one may guess, not without cause, that the old inhabitants of Ambon borrowed some names of plants and animals from the Arabic inflection then common throughout the whole East, and that this Salackal was named from the resemblance to the true Salicha, that is the Cassia lignea, just as Alhalla descends from Alhanna, that is the Cyprus and Moluccus: Senya or Sunya means a very thorny bush, which is otherwise named Sappan, from the Arabic Sent, that is Rubus Caninus, or dog-brier, which word furthermore is also derived from the Hebrew Seneh, that is Rubus or Brier, just as Schid also means Brier, and Schid the "trifles of the woods" from the Hebrew Schajith, that is Vepres, or thorns.*

**Place.** *This tree grows very widely through the Eastern Islands; the best is found in Amboina, though not over the entire Island, but only on Leitimor, around the villages of Saya, Rutton, and Ema, where it now also begins to decrease, because in the year 1664 a reasonable portion of that bark had to be sent to Europe as a trial, through which most of the old trees were peeled and died off: But that damage will be seen to be compensated again in a few years by the newly sprouting small trees: on the south side of Great Ceram, in the bay of Elipaputi, as far as Keffing, one also finds those trees, but their bark is not as good as the Amboinese: they also grow on the Moluccan Island of Batsjan, and the Papuan Islands, whose bark, as said, exceeds the Amboinese in heat: In greater numbers one finds them on the Islands of Key and Aru, where one could get an entire shipload of it, agreeing with the Papuan variety; it also occurs in reasonable quantity on the North coast of Celebes, near the village of Caudipan. As also on Sumatra, near Palembang, and on Borneo, around Succadana; from Java one also brings Culitlawan, but I believe it would be the bark Sindoc: it has also been found on Solor: But also differing in taste from the Amboinese, and likewise also on Mindanao, as was said above.*

### AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chapter XXII.

**Uses.** In terms of external sensation, this bark surpasses Massoy bark in heat, so much so that it is considered hot beyond the third degree <note>In Galenic medicine, "degrees" measured the intensity of a plant's qualities—heat, cold, moisture, or dryness—on a scale of one to four.</note>; it is also more penetrating, but its powers vanish more quickly, just as the heat of Pepper penetrates much faster than that of Ginger, but is not as long-lasting. It is not used as extensively as Massoy, and for the most part, it is used on the island of Baleya <note>Likely referring to the Banggai Islands or a specific locale in the Moluccas</note>, where it is worth only half the price of Massoy bark. Its most common use, however, is in the preparation of the famous **Bobori** ointment, which is usually of two kinds: The first is composed of various fragrant woods, barks, and flowers, all of which are ground into a fine paste; with this, the native women rub their bodies, both for a moderate warmth and for its excellent fragrance. The other, or second species, is prepared from Massoy, Culitlawan, Cloves, and similar "burning" barks and fruits, ground together as mentioned above, to bring greater warmth to the body on colder days. Furthermore, to remove all abdominal cramps, pains, and headaches arising from "cold" causes, they chew these two barks—not finely, but coarsely—either alone or with **Siri Pinanga** <note>Betel leaf and Areca nut</note> and a few Cloves; by this chewing, they spray <note>original: *conspergunt*; Dutch: *besproeyende*</note> the belly or the forehead of the sick person, who soon feels a burning or tingling of the skin, by which the trapped cold vapors are drawn out and vanish. This action is called **Sumbor** by the Malays, meaning "spraying"; though it may seem repulsive to fastidious people, it has been found that medicines chewed and sprayed in this manner are more penetrating and effective than if they had been ground upon a porphyry stone; their powers are undoubtedly enhanced by the grinding of the teeth and the heat of the mouth.

The Balinese and some Javanese also use Culitlawan in their food as a spice, as was said above regarding Massoy bark. Chewed in the mouth, either alone or with **Pinanga** <note>Areca nut</note>, it gives good breath and promotes the digestion of the stomach.

It has also been found that if pregnant women use this bark, whether in food or chewed with **Pinanga**, the fetus is greatly strengthened, and they do not suffer miscarriages as easily—a quality also attributed to Rosemary. It should further be noted that the thicker bark should be used externally because of its acrimony <note>harshness or stinging quality</note>, while the thin or medium bark is for internal use; however, that which is only the thickness of a knife produces too much sliminess when eaten. Therefore, the medium thickness should be chosen. By pharmaceutical art, an oil can also be extracted from this bark, though it is produced sparingly, indicating that little oil is hidden in this bark. This oil is thin, yellow, smells pleasant, and is strengthening; at the same time, one detects in it the scent and spice of Cloves and Nutmeg, but it flies away quickly, like Cinnamon oil.

From the leaves, a water is distilled that rivals fragrant Cinnamon water, though it is a little weaker. A few small pieces of this bark placed in small jars filled with **Bocassam** <note>A fermented condiment, often made of fish or shrimp, known as *Bokassan* in Ambon</note> preserve it and give it a pleasant taste and smell. In all the spice boxes sold in Java, some pieces of this bark are always found, and the Chinese are now beginning to carry it to China and use it in medical practice. To Holland, as was said, it was sent as a specimen in the year 1664, but it was not further sought after there, perhaps out of ignorance. It was also mentioned above that the roots of this tree are used today in place of Western Sassafras.

In the year 1691, several thin barks of this Culitlawan growing in Bacan <note>original: *Batsjam*</note> were sent to me; they did not differ much in color and substance from the Amboinese variety, but were greatly different in taste, which was sweet and perfectly anise-like, as in true Sassafras. This was especially true of the thin barks, which might be considered a different species, but according to reports, they were from one and the same tree. Otherwise, the ordinary Culitlawan scent was present, but weak; the leaves, however, were not included. The distilled oil by no means provided the aromatic scent observed in the Amboinese variety. Culitlawan also grows in the mountains of Java, but its bark is thin and slimy, and therefore not esteemed; the best, however, is brought from Borneo under the name **Sindock**, which nevertheless differs greatly from this Culitlawan, as it is drier and has a bitterish taste.

EXPLA-

<column-break/>

**Use.** This bark, according to outward sensation, surpasses the Massoy in heat, so that it exceeds the third degree; it is also somewhat more penetrating, though its powers also vanish more easily, just as the heat of Pepper comes on much sharper and better than that of Ginger, but does not last as long. It is not gathered as much as the Massoy, and is mostly used on the island of Baay <note>Referencing Baleya/Banggai</note>, and may fetch about half the price of Massoy. Generally, it is used to prepare the famous **Bobori** salve, which is mostly of two sorts: the first being made of all kinds of fragrant woods, barks, flowers, etc., and ground together into a fine paste, with which the native women smear their bodies, both to warm them moderately and for the good scent. The other or second sort is made from Massoy, Culitlawan, Cloves, and similar biting barks and fruits, also ground as before, to bring more warmth to the body on cold days. But furthermore, to drive away all kinds of stomach aches, cramps, and headaches coming from the cold, they chew the two aforementioned barks—not very finely, but somewhat coarsely in the mouth—either alone or with a **Siri Pinanga** and some Cloves, spraying the belly or the forehead of the patient from their mouth. The patient immediately feels a certain burn or tingling on the skin, through which the enclosed cold vapors are drawn out. This action is called **Sumbor** in Malay, that is, "to spray"; it is a repulsive sight to fastidious people, but it has nonetheless been found that those medicines, chewed and sprayed in such a manner, work more powerfully than if one grinds them on a stone, doubtlessly excited by the grinding of the teeth and the heat of the mouth.

The Balinese and some Javanese also use the Culitlawan, as was said above of the Massoy, in place of spices in their food. Chewed in the mouth, either alone or with **Pinanga**, it makes for good breath and promotes the cooking <note>original: *kooking*; referring to the metabolic "cooking" or digestion of food in the stomach</note> of the stomach.

It has also been experienced that when a pregnant woman eats this bark now and then, either in her food or with **Pinanga**, the fetus is thereby markedly strengthened and held fast, just as it is said that Rosemary does. Now it should still be noted that one should use the thick bark externally for its sharpness, but the thin or medium internally; however, that which is only a knife's thickness gives too much sliminess in chewing. One can also draw an oil from this bark through the apothecary’s art, although it comes out somewhat sparingly, being a sign that it is very meager. This same oil is thin, yellow, very fragrant, and strengthening, and one perceives at the same time the scent and spiciness of Cloves and Nutmegs, but it also flies away as easily as that of Cinnamon oil.

From the leaves comes a fragrant water, which looks somewhat like Cinnamon water, though it is a bit weaker. Some small pieces of this bark put into the jars filled with **Bocassan** keep it good and give it a pleasant scent. In all spice boxes sold on Java, one always finds some pieces of this bark, and the Chinese are now also beginning to carry it to China and to use it in their medicine. To Holland, as said, it was carried as a trial in the year 1664, but was not in demand there, perhaps through ignorance. And that the roots of this tree are nowadays also used in place of West Indian Sassafras was said here above.

In the year 1691, some thin barks of Culitlawan growing there were sent to me from Bacan; they did not differ much in color and substance from the Amboinese, but markedly in taste, which was clearly sweet and anise-like, as in the upright <note>meaning "true" or "genuine"</note> Sassafras, especially the thin bark, which one would have taken for a special sort; however, according to the correspondence, they were from the same kind of trees. Otherwise, the usual scent of Culitlawan was also present, but weak, and the leaves were not sent with them. The distilled oil also did not have nearly as aromatic a scent as that which was made from the Amboinese. On the mountains of Java there also falls a Culitlawan, but that is thin of bark and slimy, and is therefore not esteemed; but the best comes from Borneo under the name of **Sindock**, though differing markedly from our Culitlawan, for it is drier and somewhat bitter in taste.

### EXPLANATION
->Of the Fourteenth Plate.<-

Which shows the **LAUREL** with monstrous and spongy fruit, and an aromatic, clove-like bark; called **CULITLAWAN** by Rumphius.

**A.** *Indicates the spongy and swollen fruit.*

### OBSERVATION.

This tree most closely resembles **Cinnamon**, **Laurel**, and similar species, but it differs from them by its abortive and fungous fruit; otherwise, the flowers, foliage, and indeed its entire form are very similar to them. For this reason, I have called it the **LAUREL with abortive fruit and clove-like bark**.

This bark is further described in *Valentinus's* <note>François Valentijn (1666–1727), a Dutch naturalist and minister in the East Indies.</note> *Indiae Litteratae*, Letter 24, page 450 and following, as well as in the *Ephemerides of the German Academy of Natural Curiosities* <note>A prominent scientific journal of the era.</note>, decade 2, year 3, page 53, where its illustration is also found; it is described under the name **Coelit-Lawan-tree** in *Valentinus’s Description of Amboina*, page 210, No. 37.

In *Valentinus’s Reform of Simple Medicines*, page 172, it is asked whether this bark is the same, and collected from the same tree, as the **CLOVE CASSIA** <note>original: *CASSIA CARYOPHYLLATA*</note>. The author doubts this, as the former is much thicker than the bark of Clove Cassia—a point I leave undecided, since Rumphius makes no mention of this. Furthermore, the synonyms, description, and virtues of Clove Cassia appear in *Samuel Dale’s Pharmacologia* in quarto, page 323, and in the famous *Paul Hermann’s Materia Medica*, part 1, chapter 2, etc.

---

### CHAPTER TWENTY-THREE.

### Sindoc.

In **Borneo** and **Java**, another bark occurs called **Sindoc**, which the common people confuse with **Culitlawan**. But I consider it to be a distinct bark from a different tree, although no one has been able to describe the form of the tree to me. Certainly, this bark differs significantly from Culitlawan; for it is more solid, harder, and darker, smooth on the outside as if it had been planed. The taste initially approaches that of Culitlawan, but then a bitterness follows with an astringency <term>astringency: a sharp, drying sensation in the mouth</term> that is not found to such a degree in Culitlawan; nor is that mucilage <term>mucilage: a thick, gluey substance produced by plants</term> detected in Sindoc which is hidden in Culitlawan.

*Name.* It has been known by no other name so far than **Sindoc**.

*Location.* It grows in **Borneo**, near **Succadana**, and in **Sumatra**, near **Palimbang**.

*Use.* It is used against **intestinal worms**, as well as for the **stings and bites of venomous animals**. However, the wounds must first be irritated or pricked with the hard fibers of the **Tamarind** so that the black blood may flow out; then the crushed Sindoc is to be applied to them. Otherwise, it is used both internally and externally in the same manner as Culitlawan.

### OBSERVATION.

**SINDOC** is also mentioned and described by *Valentinus* in his *Description of Amboina*, page 217.

<column-break/>

### EXPLANATION
->Of the Fourteenth Plate,<-

Which shows a **LAUREL TREE** with a monstrous and spongy fruit with a spice-like and clove-like bark; called **CULITLAWAN** by Rumphius.

**A.** *Shows the swollen, spongy fruit.*

### OBSERVATION.

This tree comes closest to the **Cinnamon** and **Laurel tree**, and the like, yet differs from them by the deformity of the swelling fruit; otherwise the flowers, leaves, and also the entire appearance are very similar to the aforementioned, which is why I have also named it *Laurus* or **Laurel with a deformed and swelling fruit, and with a clove- and spice-like bark.**

This bark is further described in *Valentinus’s Ind. Litterat.*, 24th Letter, page 50 and following, as well as in the *Ephemer. Germ. Acad. natur. curios.*, decade 2, year 3, page 53, and under the name of **Coelit-lawan-tree** by *Valentinus in the description of Amboina*, page 210, No. 37.

In *Valentinus’s Hist. Simpl. Reform.*, page 172, it is asked whether this bark is the same, and gathered from one and the same tree, from which the **CLOVE CASSIA** <note>original: *CASSIA CARYOPHYLLATA*</note> comes; about which the writer doubts, because the *Culitlawan* is thicker than that of the *Clove Cassia*, which I leave undecided, as *Rumphius* mentions nothing of this. Furthermore, the names, writers, and the powers of *Clove Cassia* are to be found by *Samuel Dale in his Pharmacologia* in quarto, page 323, as well as in the *Materia Medica* of the famous *Paul Hermann*, first part, chapter 2, etc.

### XXIII. CHAPTER.

### Sindoc.

On **Borneo**, and **Java**, there occurs yet another bark, named **Sindoc**, which the common man confuses with **Culitlawan**: But I judge that it is a different bark from a particular tree, although no one has been able to explain the appearance of the tree to me as of yet: And certainly this bark also differs markedly from the *Culitlawan*; for it is denser, browner, and firmer, smooth on the outside, and as if planed. The taste at first clearly draws toward *Culitlawan*, but one soon becomes aware of a **bitterness**, with an **astringency**, the likes of which is not found in any *Culitlawan*, and in the *Sindoc* one also does not find the **sliminess** that is in the *Culitlawan*.

*Name.* It is known until now by no other name than **Sindoc**.

*Place.* It occurs on **Borneo**, near **Succadana**, and on **Sumatra**, near **Palimbang**.

*Use.* It is used against **worms of the belly**, as well as against the **stings** and **bites of venomous animals**, yet one must first **provoke** or **prick** the wounds with the hard threads of **Tamarind**, so that the black blood flows out, and then lay the rubbed **Sindoc** upon it: for the rest, it is mostly used both internally and externally, like the **Culitlawan**.

### OBSERVATION.

The **Sindoc** is mentioned and described by *Valentinus in the Description of Amboina*, page 217.

<header>HERBARIUM AMBOINENSE Book II. Chap. XXIV.</header>

## CHAPTER TWENTY-FOUR.

### Amboinese Lauraster: Leytun.

**T**his should be considered a false Laurel; it is a tall forest tree with a medium-sized trunk. Its leaves resemble those of the Laurel, and also that species of Nutmeg tree which bears oblong nuts, though these are narrower and firmer than either. They have a long tip and a few transverse ribs; furthermore, they are pale green and, if touched, feel rougher than the others. There are two species of this tree, differing in size.

The first or largest *Leytun* species bears leaves a hand-span long—indeed often longer—and two and a half fingers wide, placed without specific order and appearing singly.

The fruits hang from short stalks <term>peduncles; the stalks supporting a fruit or flower</term> sprouting from the leaf axils. At first, they are dark green, then blackish, about the size of pigeon eggs or like the Sorb-fruit <note>The fruit of the Service Tree (*Sorbus domesticus*), known for being edible when overripe.</note>, but pear-shaped. They are wrinkled on the outside and marked with small pits. The outer husk is as thick as two knife-blades, dry, brittle, and sandy, as if prepared lime had been mixed into it. The inner kernel is the size of a round plum stone and easily divides into two segments, one of which is usually smaller than the other. This kernel is sometimes oblong, the size of an acorn kernel, and of a dry substance. If opened while fresh, it is saffron-colored inside like Turmeric <note>original: *Curcumae*</note>, but when dried it becomes paler. It has a strong, aromatic scent very similar to Laurel berries—pleasant to those born in Amboina, though perhaps less so to a European. The taste is somewhat bitter, but without any notable sharpness.

The second or small *Leytun* species is similar to the former, but its leaves are smaller and about an inch shorter—three or four inches long and over two fingers wide. They are distinguished by a few very slanted ribs and are so smooth and even on the upper side that the middle vein or groove cannot be felt. On the underside, they are sea-green <term>glaucous; a pale greyish-blue or green color</term> and have a resinous scent. The fruits are half the size, some pear-shaped, others rounder and wrinkled, turning black when ripe. The internal kernel is sometimes like Laurel stones, sometimes wider and rounder, also divisible into two segments of the same color and substance. However, the scent and taste in this small species are stronger than in the first, and in both, it is more pleasant than the Laurel, though with a slight sharpness and no astringency. The aromatic scent somewhat disappears when dry but is heightened and returns again if the fruits are rubbed.

**Name.** In Latin, I call this tree *Lauraster Amboinensis* <note>original: "Amboinese False-Laurel"</note> because of the taste and smell of the fruit, which are like Laurel berries. In Hitoe it is called *Leytun*. In Leytimora, *Hiber* or *Hiyr*. In Oma, one of the Uliasser islands, *Ittir* and *Ayboo-Ittil*. In Hoea-Mohel, *Ley-itir*.

**Location.** It occurs rarely, and only in the high mountains of Amboina near the Dammar trees <note>Trees of the genus *Agathis*, prized for their resin.</note>, which always grow in the highest places of this region; it is also found in the mountains of Oma. Among other peoples, as far as I know, it has remained unknown until now.

**Use.** Only the aromatic fruits of this tree are in use, and even then, not commonly. The Amboinese women take the fresh kernels and grind them with a little Turmeric, rice flour, and *Culit-lawan* <note>Clove-bark, described in previous chapters.</note> upon a porphyry stone <note>A hard igneous rock used for grinding spices and medicines.</note>. After bathing, they anoint their bodies with this mixture to gain a scent pleasing to their nation, though others say this body-ointment also benefits certain skin ailments. It is certainly true that such aromatic fruits are of good use and virtue in medicine, and perhaps agree with Laurel berries in their properties. However, this has not been fully tested, as these trees are found so rarely. Wild pigeons also eat these fruits and pass the inner kernels whole; these, falling to the ground, sprout into small trees. I have occasionally planted these in gardens, but they do not grow easily there, just like other wild trees destined for solitudes and deserts.

<column-break/>

## CHAPTER XXIV.

### Wild Amboinese Laurel-tree.

**T**his may be considered a bastard-type of the Laurel tree. It is a tall wild tree with a medium trunk; the leaves also somewhat resemble Laurel leaves, as well as that kind of Nutmeg tree that bears long nuts, yet they are narrower and stiffer than both, with a long point at the front and few cross-ribs. Furthermore, they are pale green and feel rougher than the others when touched. In size, they follow the two types of this tree, which are also of two kinds.

The first or largest *Leytun* has leaves a hand-span long, and sometimes more, 2½ fingers wide, standing without order and sparsely on the twigs.

The fruits hang on short stalks, coming forth from the lap <term>axil; the angle between the upper side of a leaf and the stem</term> of the leaves. They are first dark green and finally blackish, the size of pigeon eggs or like a *Sorbum* <note>Sorb or Service-berry.</note>, though shaped like a pear. On the outside they are somewhat wrinkled and covered with small pits. The outer husk is two knives thick, dry, crumbly, and sandy, as if mixed with prepared lime. The inner kernel has the size of a round plum stone and allows itself to be split in two, with one half usually being smaller than the other. Sometimes this kernel is oblong and as large as an acorn kernel, and of a dry substance. When broken open fresh, it is deep yellow inside like Turmeric <note>original: *Curcuma*</note>, but the dried ones are somewhat paler, with a strong and spicy smell, very closely resembling Laurel berries <note>original: *Bakelaaren*</note>. This is pleasant to an Amboinese nose, but not much so to a European one. The taste is somewhat bitter, though without sharpness.

The second or small *Leytun* is like the former, but the leaves are somewhat smaller and an inch shorter, three and four inches long, over two fingers wide, with few very slanted ribs. On top they are so smooth that one does not even feel the middle groove; underneath they are blue-green and have a resinous smell. The fruits are at least half as small, some pear-shaped, some rounder, and also wrinkled and black when they are ripe. The inner kernel is sometimes like Laurel berries, sometimes a bit broader and rounder, also divided in two, of the same color and substance. But the smell and taste in this small kind are stronger than in the large one, and in both more pleasant than in Laurel berries, yet with a small sharpness and without any puckering of the mouth <term>astringency</term>. The spicy smell fades somewhat in the dry fruit, but becomes lively again if they are rubbed.

**Name.** In Latin I have named it *Lauraster Amboincus* after the taste and smell of the fruits, which most closely resemble Laurel berries. On Hitoe it is called *Leytun*. On Leytimor, *Hiber* or *Aiyr*. On Oma, one of the Uliasser Islands, *Ittir* and *Ayhoo-Ittil*. On Hoea-Mohel, *Ley-itir*.

**Place.** One finds it little, and then only in the Amboinese high mountains and near the Dammar trees, which always stand on the highest part of the land, as also in the Oma mountains. Among other nations, as far as I perceive, it is unknown.

**Use.** The spicy fruits of this tree are the only part in use, which is not yet very great. The Amboinese women take the fresh kernels, rub them with a little Turmeric, rice flour, and *Culit-lawan* on a stone, and smear their bodies with this after bathing to have a pleasant scent for their people, although some claim that such anointing also serves against some ailments. For it is certain that such spicy fruits have good powers in medicine and perhaps share some agreement in many things with Laurel berries. But it has not been investigated until now because one finds so few of those trees. The wild pigeons also eat this fruit and pass the inner kernels through their droppings, which then falling on the earth bring forth new little trees. I have sometimes planted these in gardens, but they do not wish to come up well there, just like other similar trees that are accustomed to and belong to the wildernesses.

# Plate XV.

**The Amboinese Lauraster**

The central figure shows a woody branch characterized by large, oval-shaped leaves that taper to a sharp point. These leaves feature distinct, rib-like veins branching from the center. At the tips of the stems and nestled where the leaves meet the branch <note>These areas are known as the leaf axils.</note> are clusters of small, round buds that will eventually develop into the tree's aromatic fruit.

# Second Book. Chapter XXIV. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

The wood of the larger species is white and not durable; however, the smaller species, if it is from older trunks, is reddish, hard, and durable, so that it can be used for the posts of houses. It also gives off a pleasant scent when it is worked. The bark of the trunk, and especially of the root, also provides an aromatic scent and a taste that burns the tongue. The people of Amboina use it for washing both their clothes and their bodies so that they might smell pleasant. The broad-leafed species occurs quite frequently around *Tiel*, as well as in *Hoeamohel*.

"Fire Bark," called *Culit Api* <note>Malay: *kulit* means bark, *api* means fire.</note> in Malay, is a thin and smooth bark, similar to *Cassia lignea* <note>A type of cinnamon bark used as a spice.</note> but paler and thicker. When chewed, it has a very fiery taste with a notable bitterness, surpassing *Massoy* and *Culit-lawan* <note>Other aromatic barks native to New Guinea and the Moluccas.</note> in its heat. I have not yet seen the tree itself, but it grows in *Key* and certain islands situated to the Southeast. Rare specimens of these trees were found in the region of *Hoeamohel*, in the *Wey-poeti* mountains. Based on its outward appearance and taste, I would judge it to belong to the *Lauraster* <note>Wild Laurel</note> genus. This bark is commonly held to be full of medicinal virtues; it is especially useful when ground and taken with weak Arack <note>A distilled spirit made from grain or palm sap.</note> to drive away stomach cramps and abdominal pains caused by cold. Likewise, when mixed with other milder woods and applied externally, it warms the limbs. However, since this bark can only be found rarely and in small quantities, its uses are scarcely half known.

The *Smaller Lauraster* <note>original: *Lauraster Minor*</note> has very stiff leaves like parchment, with an elongated and firm tip; they grow singly, as was mentioned earlier in the text.

The flowers sprout from short clusters, barely a finger-joint long, and on these appear many green heads like mustard seeds, each sitting on its own little stalk and cup. The flower is very small, formed of two pale-whitish petals, one of which hangs down like a Lily and curves back, while the other stands upright, giving off a good but faint scent. On each cluster, only one or two fruits develop; some are the size of Langsats <note>original: *Lansiorum*, a tropical fruit.</note>, while others are like the Service-berry <note>original: *Sorbi*</note> or a little smaller and pear-shaped. This small species grows deep in the mountains near the Dammar trees <note>Resin-producing trees.</note>. The larger species bears leaves five inches long and two wide, though not as stiff as those of the smaller species, and grows closer to the settlements <note>The Latin *Aethiopum tractui* refers here to the inland villages of the local inhabitants.</note> on the open mountains around *Caju-Poeti*. The small species flowers in September, and the fruits ripen with the West Canary nuts <note>original: *Canari Barat*.</note>.

*The wood of the large species is white and not durable, but the small one, if it is from old trunks, has a reddish wood, is hard and durable, and therefore useful for the pillars of houses. It also has a good smell when it is worked. The bark of the trunk, but especially of the root, is also spice-like in smell and taste, somewhat biting on the tongue, used by the Amboinese both to wash their clothes and their bodies, and thereby to obtain a good scent. The broad-leafed variety is found reasonably often around Tiel, as well as on Hoeamohel.*

*Fire Bark, called Culit Api in Malay, is a thin, smooth bark, very similar to Cassia lignea, though paler and thicker, and when chewed in the mouth, very biting of taste, with a noticeable bitterness, surpassing both the Massoy and Culit-lawan. The tree of this is still unknown to me, for it grows on Key, and some South-eastern Islands; a few have also been found on the Land of Hoeamohel, in the mountains of Wey-Poeti: and according to the outward appearance, as well as the taste, I would judge that it belongs among the genera of Lauraster. This bark is held to be very medicinal, and particularly useful when rubbed and taken with weak Arack, to dispel belly-ache and cramping that arises from cold. As also mixed with other temperate woods, and smeared on the outside, to warm the limbs; but because one can find only a little of this bark, its use is also only half known.*

*Lauraster Minor has very stiff leaves, like parchment, with a longish stiff tip; they stand singly, etc., as is further mentioned here above.*

*The blossom comes forth on short clusters, scarcely a joint of a finger long, and on them many green buds, like mustard-seed, each on a particular little foot. The little flower is very small, made of two pale-white leaves, of which one hangs down like a lily, the other stands upright, or somewhat bent over, good but somewhat faint of scent. On a cluster only one or two fruits come forth; some as large as Langsats, some like Service-berries, or the "Sucking-pears," or a bit smaller and pear-shaped. This small kind grows far in the mountains by the Dammar trees. The large kind has leaves 5 inches long and 2 wide, yet not as stiff as the preceding, and grows closer to the villages on airy mountains, around the Caju-Poeti. The small one blooms in September, and the fruits ripen with the West Canary nuts.*
