# AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chapter XXV.

## CHAPTER TWENTY-FIVE.

### White Tree. Caju Puti.

The following three trees are very closely related to the Myrtle, and could not improperly be called "Indian Myrtles." However, let it not offend the reader that certain shrubs and herbs known in Europe grow into the form of a tree in the East Indies, as will be indicated later, especially regarding Ferns.

*I have observed three species of this White Tree, the first and largest of which is described in this chapter: The **Greater White Tree** is a fully-formed tree with a single trunk—not particularly straight, but rather arched—which is usually as thick as a man, though some reach the thickness of two men or more. It bears sparse and curved branches, which form a thin and untidy crown. The leaves have a peculiar shape that distinguishes them from other trees; at first they have the shape of willow leaves, or, to use an Indian comparison, they are like the leaves of the **Dammar** <note>original: "Dammarae"; a resin-producing conifer</note>, but much larger and with smooth edges. They have nine or ten veins running along their length, four or five of which stand out more than the rest. Most of them are curved toward the end almost like a saber, measuring six, seven, or eight inches and more in length, and one inch wide. They are firm, smooth, and of a pale green, almost sea-green color. If they are crushed, they appear dry and brittle, with a strong, somewhat aromatic but also slightly acidic scent. Their taste is resinous with a slight astringency, approaching that of Myrtle leaves, or smelling like a certain drink in the Indies called **Kilang** <note>A fermented beverage made from sugar cane or palm sap</note>. They are almost equally pointed at both ends, where the four or five larger veins meet. They are placed without order on the branches and are almost stalkless.*

*At the ends of the twigs, and from the armpits of the nearest leaves, woody stalks sprout, half a foot long, which are covered everywhere with oblong green buds, whitening at the top. These open into small white flowers consisting of five narrow petals, filled with many long, limp, and whitening hairy stamens, bearing white anthers. In the middle or center, these stamens hide a green pistil which, after the flowers have fallen, remains in a small hollow like a little cup or chalice. This flowering stalk resembles a white ear of grain, which breathes out a strong but somewhat acidic and not very pleasant odor. After the flowers fall, the buds remain joined in twos or threes, attached so firmly and closely to the stalk as if they were glued, being about the size of a coriander seed. They are open at the top in the shape of a little cup, in which the aforementioned green crowned pistil remains until it eventually falls out. These buds best resemble the suckers <note>original: "acetabula"; literally 'vinegar cups', referring to the suction cups</note> seen on the tentacles of the **Cuttlefish** <note>original: "Sepiae"</note>. They are green at first, then grayish-black or earth-colored, remaining seated on the branch even when fully ripe. They follow an order such that if three are placed on one side of the stalk, the next three appear on the other side, so that their position is alternating. In these little cups, a fine seed is hidden, like chaff or having the shape of broken thorn tips, slightly curved and pale brown, which eventually falls out if the berries remain on the tree for a long time.*

*The trunk is covered with a soft bark about a finger thick, composed of innumerable very thin and delicate membranes, just as is seen on the **Birch** tree. These layers lie closely upon one another and are ash-colored; they can be easily separated, but are so delicate that if handled individually, they break immediately.*

*The lower part of this trunk always appears blackish, as if it were burnt, and all the signs of charring can be seen there. What is remarkable is that no one has ever seen this tree on fire. Those who do not look closely might think that fire was perhaps thrown against the trunk by passers-by, which would easily catch in this dry bark and creep along slowly. But this cannot be the cause, at least not in all of them, nor in those trees which are far from the path. For if this bark had caught fire and indeed burned—*

<column-break/>

## CHAPTER XXV.

### White-Tree.

These three following trees have a great affinity with the Myrtles, and might also not improperly be called Indian Myrtle-trees. Yet the reader must not be startled by the fact that some shrubs and herbs known in Europe grow up into trees in the Indies, as we shall say hereafter, and especially regarding the Ferns.

*Of the **White Tree** <note>original: "Arbor Alba"</note> I have observed three kinds, of which the first and largest is described in this Chapter: The **GREATER WHITE-TREE** is a full-grown tree, with a single, though not very straight, but crooked trunk, usually having the thickness of one man, some also of two men and more. The leaves also have a special shape, differing somewhat from other trees; they first resemble Willow-leaves, or (according to the Indian comparison) the **Dammar** leaves, yet they are much larger, having smooth edges, striped lengthwise with 9 and 10 veins, of which 4 to 5 stick out above the others, almost all of them slightly curved at the front, nearly all in the shape of a Saber. Six, seven, and eight inches, or somewhat longer, one inch wide, stiff, smooth, of a dead green, drawing somewhat toward Spanish-green <note>Verdigris or a bluish-green</note>, dry and crumbling when rubbed, and of a strong smell, which is somewhat spicy, yet also drawing toward the sour. The taste is likewise resinous, with a small contraction <note>astringency</note>, and inclining somewhat toward Myrtle-leaves, as well as toward a certain drink, which they call **Kilang** in the Indies. They are almost equally pointed at the back and front, where the four or five large veins strike together. They stand without order around the twigs, almost without stalks.*

*At the ends of the shoots, and from the lap of the nearest leaves, woody stalks come forth, half a foot long, beset all around with oblong, green buds, which are white on top, and open themselves into small white flowers, made of five narrow petals, and filled with many long limp and white threads or flakes, on which white knobs hang. These threads hide in their middle a small green borer <note>the pistil</note>, which after the falling of the blossom remains standing in a round little cup. This flowering stalk looks much like a white Ear of corn, and gives off a strong smell, though somewhat sour, and not very lovely. After the falling of this blossom, the buds remain sitting, two and three opposite each other, and so close against the stalk as if they were glued there, being about as large as a Coriander-seed, yet open in front, in the shape of a little cup, in which the aforementioned green borer still stands, and finally also falls out. These buds resemble best the round warts <note>suckers</note> which one sees on the beard <note>tentacles</note> of the **Cuttlefish**, first green, thereafter grayish black, or earth-colored, remaining sitting against the branch, even when they are entirely ripe; they also mostly keep that order, that if three stand on one side of the stalk, the next three stand on the other side. In these little cups lies enclosed a fine seed, as if it were chaff, or like broken-off tips of thorns, a little curved, and light-brown, which likewise falls out in time, if the berries remain hanging long on the tree.*

*The trunk is clothed with a soft bark, about a finger thick, made of countless very thin and tender little skins, just as one sees on our Birch-trees, lying close upon one another, dirty-white or fawn-colored; one can indeed separate them from one another, yet they are so tender that they break immediately if one handles the individual ones.*

*The bottom of this trunk always looks mostly black, as if it were burnt, in which one can also notice all the signs of fire, and what is to be wondered at, no one has ever seen this tree burning; those who pay the least attention to it think that sometimes some fire was thrown against this trunk by those passing by, which very easily catches in this dry bark, and continues to eat while smoldering. But this cannot be, at least not to all of them, and those that stand far from the road. For if the bark had caught the fire, and indeed had burned—*

<summary>This page introduces the White Tree (Cajuput), describing its physical characteristics, its unique saber-shaped leaves, and its layered bark similar to birch. Rumphius notes a mysterious charred appearance at the base of the trunks that occurs even in remote areas without known fires.</summary>

<keywords>Arbor alba, Caju Puti, Cajuput, Melaleuca, Myrtle, Dammar, Kilang, Birch bark, botanical description, Amboina, charred trunks, Sepia suckers</keywords>

[if a fire] had been sparked, then the surrounding brush would also have been burned; and this appears not in all, but only in certain trees, whereas the opposite is observed. Thus, I believe that on hot summer days this dry and delicate bark—which resembles nothing so much as tinder—is ignited by the burning heat of the sun; yet not so much that it catches fire, but rather is scorched so that it appears as if burnt. My opinion is supported by the fact that these trees are always found solitary, not mixed with other forest trees, and occupy a place for themselves alone on high and windy mountains, nor do they admit much wild brush around them, except for sedge and other creeping ferns. These trees also always grow scattered and remote from others, so that these forests are always open and easy for walking, but consequently very exposed to the sun's rays.

If we walk through these forests on hotter days, a resinous odor is perceived, and they do not easily provide shade for weary and panting walkers; but in the evening, or if the sun sends out no rays, these forests are quite pleasant, and indeed provide such a delightful prospect that some compare them with the forest at The Hague <note>original: "Hagana silva" / "Haagſe-boſch"; a famous ancient forest in the Netherlands</note>. These trees can be easily distinguished from a distance by their white or ashen color, and they mostly grow in red, rich, and clayey soil mixed with white earth and small stones, which is a hard ground that does not easily produce other plants.

The mature berries or fruits provide a resinous flavor, also approaching the Myrtle, with a notable astringency without any heat; but the old berries are quite dry, fragile, and almost flat and insipid.

The leaves are also so dry that hardly any juice can be drawn from them when crushed. The wood is quite hard and heavy, consisting of longitudinal fibers, nor does it have an elegant color, for it is whitish, shifting from ash-gray to a light reddish-brown; it splits easily along its length, indeed almost spontaneously if exposed to the sun; its pith is softer, more spongy, and very often develops cracks. It is of no use for house-building, since it cannot be worked smooth, splits easily, and worms quickly get into it. For this wood has false and malignant spots inside that appear decayed and easily admit worms or grubs, which, however, is mostly observed in trees that have fallen of their own accord. On the other hand, it is quite durable in seawater, but then one does not take fallen trees, but recently cut ones, which are then sawn into ribs for ships or planks. When being sawn, this wood gives off a pleasant but weak odor, almost like Sandalwood; and if good solid pieces can be obtained and smoothed, they appear finely grained, though they do not allow themselves to be polished.

The tree is easily cast down by stronger winds and rains, because it stands so solitary and has few roots, where it is then ruined in a short time by the rain and air.

**Season.** They bloom in January, and some in March; the ripe fruits are seen from August into November, and they reproduce so poorly that one very rarely finds young saplings from them, nor do they allow themselves to be transplanted by human hands.

**Name.** In Latin, *Arbor Alba major* <note>Greater White Tree</note>. In common Malay *Caju-puti*, as it is also called by our nation *Witte-boom* <note>White Tree</note>; some call them *Kilang-trees*, after the odor of the leaves <note>Kilang is a fermented sugar-cane drink</note>; others call them *Brant-boomen* <note>Burnt Trees</note> or scorched trees, since signs of fire appear on the trunk. But the true Malay name is *Caju-Gelam* and the fruit *Gelam*. In Javanese and Balinese, the fruits are called *Bollong* and *Bobolong*. They specifically collect the chaff-like seed from the little cups and call it *Sari-bollong*. In Ternate it is called *Hate-kelang* and *Badjule*. In the Amboinese language it has various names according to the places where it grows. Commonly they call it *Ay-puti*, but more properly *Kilam*, *Ilan*, and *Elan*. In Hitoe: *Camelan*, as if they said *Comal-Ilan* or *Dammar-Ilan*, because the leaves and scent of this tree have a great similarity to the **Dammar tree** <note>A resin-producing conifer</note>. On Ceram, by the people of Luhum it is called *Sakelan*; on Banda, *Kelan*; all of which names undoubtedly originate from the Malay *Gelâm*. In Makassar it is called *Baru-Gallam* and also simply *Gelam*.

**Location.** It is found in almost all the islands of this Moluccan Archipelago, from the eastern part of Celebes through the Moluccas, Ceram, and Amboina, but mostly through all

*had been sparked, the surrounding brush would also have burned, and thus would not be seen on all, but only on some trees, of which both the opposite is now seen: It is therefore my opinion that on hot summer days, this dry and delicate bark, which merely resembles tinder, is ignited by the burning sun-heat, though it does not actually catch fire, but is so scorched that it thereby dries as if burnt: To this, namely to this my opinion, it also helps that these trees always stand together, and are never mixed among other forest trees, but as if for themselves take a place on high airy mountains, and do not suffer much brush under them, except for Sedge-grass, and other kinds of creeping Ferns: Standing also empty and far from each other, so that in these forests it is always light and easy to walk, but consequently they also stand open to the sun's rays.*

*If one also walks through these forests on hot days, one perceives a resinous smell, and one can hardly find shade there to rest under a bit, or to catch one's breath, but when there is no sun, or in the evening hours, then they give such a pleasant view that some come to compare them to the Hague Forest: By their white color or hue, one can well recognize them from afar, and they commonly stand on a red rich clay-ground, mixed with white earth and stones, being a hard ground that cannot easily bring forth other plants.*

*The ripe berries or fruits have a resinous taste, also drawing toward the Myrtles, with a notable astringency, and yet without bitterness, though the old berries become very dry, crumbly, and almost without taste.*

*The leaves are also so dry that one can hardly get any juice out of the crushed ones. The wood is reasonably hard and heavy, long-grained, and of no beautiful color, to wit, drawing from white toward gray, where some light-red runs underneath, it splits gladly in length, and that of itself, when it lies in the sun, the pith is softer, spongier, and mostly cracked. For house-building it is no good, because it does not let itself be worked smooth, splits easily, and the worm soon gets into it, for this wood has false spots inside, which show themselves as decayed, and where the worm also enters, though which one mostly sees on trees that fall over by themselves: On the contrary it is reasonably durable in seawater, but then one takes no fallen ones, but freshly chopped trees, which one then saws into timbers or planks. In sawing, this wood gives off a pleasant, though weak smell, almost like Sandalwood, and if one can get good massive pieces of it, and they are planed, then they show themselves fine-grained, though they do not let themselves be polished.*

*The tree is easily overthrown by strong winds, because it stands so emptily, and has few roots, where it then spoils in a short time through rain and air.*

**Season.** *They bloom in January, and some in March; the ripe fruits are seen in August until November, and reproduce so poorly, that one very seldom finds young trees from them, and those do not let themselves be transplanted by human hands.*

**Name.** *In Latin Arbor Alba major. In common Malay Caju-Puti, and so also by our Nation White-tree, some call them Kilang-trees, after the smell of the leaves: Others Burnt-trees, because they always have some signs of fire on the trunk: The right Malay name is Caju-Gelam, and the fruits Gelam, in Javanese and Balinese, the fruits Bollong, and Bobolong. The chaff-like seed from the cups they gather particularly, and call it Sari-bollong. In Ternatese Hate-kelang, and Badjule. In Amboinese it has various names according to the places where it grows. Commonly they call it Ay-puti, but more properly Kilang, Ilan, and Elan: On Hitoe: Camelan, as if they said Camal-Ilan, or Dammar-Ilan, because this tree's leaves and smell have great similarity with the Dammar-tree. On Ceram by the Luhunese Sakelan, on Banda Kelan, all which names probably come from the Malay Gelâm: On Makassar Baru-Gallam, and also simply Gelam.*

<meta>This page continues the description of the Cajuput tree (Melaleuca leucadendra), specifically discussing its geographic distribution across the East Indies, the practical uses of its bark in shipbuilding, and its medicinal applications.</meta>

->## AMBOINESE HERBARIUM Book II, Chapter XXV<-

...through the islands situated to the East and perhaps as far as *New Guinea*, in Buru and Ceram it occupies entire mountains, and admits hardly any other tree in its district, except for the *Mountain Casuarina* <note>original: *Casuarina Montana*; a type of she-oak or ironwood</note> and other similar dry trees which it tolerates around itself, especially on the mountains of Leitimor behind Fort Victoria <note>The primary Dutch fortification on Amboina</note>. And as it is said, the village of Kilang took its name from this tree, since it was built on a hill that was previously entirely occupied by these trees, just as this region produces many such trees. It rarely occurs near the shore, but presents itself in the mountains at a cannon-shot's distance from the coast. In the highest and coldest mountains it does not sprout healthily, but rather in those neighboring places better exposed to the solar rays.

*Usage.* The bark of this tree is very much in use, at least by the people of Amboina and in all the Moluccas, for sealing their vessels; it is placed between the joints when one plank is fastened to another, for this dry and tender bark swells in seawater, whereby it solidifies the vessels very tightly, so that it serves the Indians in place of tow <term>stupa: hemp or flax fiber used for caulking</term>. It has, however, this defect: when placed in the joints it contracts and falls out, which is nonetheless sufficiently prevented by pitching. This bark is called by the general name *Baru*, which is a name common to all things used for solidifying vessels. And although this bark may be stripped off, this tree produces new bark again in the same place, and the wound heals again within a few years, just as happens in the Cork Oak <note>original: *Suber*</note>.

The fruits or berries are of no use to the people of Amboina, which I ascribe more to their ignorance than because they possess fewer virtues than the Javanese ones; for in the Amboinese ones a greater aromatic force is perceived, or at least the flavor is more penetrating than in those which are transported in the spice boxes of the Javanese, which are mostly insipid, since they do not grow in Java itself, but in Borneo.

In taste, however, there is some difference; for in the Amboinese berries it is more resinous and stronger, with greater astringency, while in the Javanese ones, if they are fresh, it is without doubt more aromatic; in both, however, it is without any heat, from which I conclude that the Javanese and Borneans did not pick these berries from the broad-leafed *Caju-Puti*, but from the following narrow-leafed variety, for which reason I defer their further virtues to the following chapter.

The tender bark, chewed with a little *Turmeric* <note>original: *Curcuma*</note> and *Tamarind* <note>original: *Tamaryn*</note> and applied to open abscesses, draws out the pus and cleanses them. If the leaves are boiled in water with those of *Lagondi* <term>Vitex trifolia: a medicinal shrub used for skin conditions</term>, and the body is washed with them, they remove difficult itching.

The wood has hitherto been rarely in use: the Amboinese, and especially the people of the Uliasser islands, used to form planks from this for smaller vessels, which they even now employ if other wood is lacking, since it is indeed durable, but too heavy and not so suitable for smaller vessels. On the contrary, our nation <note>The Dutch</note> after the year 1670 called it into great use, and uses it not only for the construction of houses—for which, as was said, it is not particularly durable or worthy—but also for the ribs and supports of larger ships, for which they have observed it to be good and durable; hence most of the forests of these trees around Fort Victoria have already been cut down.

The *Caju-Kelam*, growing in the Western islands such as Java, Borneo, and Malacca, has a more slender trunk, no thicker than a thigh, which rises straight like a Pitch Pine to a height of five or six fathoms. Its leaves are thicker and broader, and the wood is also hard and heavy. There it grows not in the mountains, but in flat plains and along river banks in red clay. Its wood serves there for posts and ribs which must sustain a heavy weight because of its solid strength; hence it also serves for bridges which are extended from one Coconut tree <note>original: *Calappo*</note> to another, which the *Tiffadores* <note>Tappers who collect palm sap</note> cross, connecting two such bridges together, as is otherwise done with Bamboos. This dry bark or *Baru* is used not only for the joints of ships, but also, when mixed with the thick oil *Minjac-Caju*, for forming torches and candles; this oil is drawn from the *Koring* tree, which has leaves like the white Mangium; if its trunk is cut or a hole is bored in it, and a slow fire is placed beneath it, then this oil drips—

<column-break/>

...from the *South-Eastern Islands*, and perhaps as far as *New Guinea*, on Buru and Ceram it covers entire long mountain ranges, hardly suffering another tree in its district, except for the *Mountain Casuarina* and other such dry trees, which it allows by its side, especially on the mountains of Leitimor, behind Fort Victoria: and as they say, the village of Kilang received its name from this, because it is built on a hill that was previously full of these trees, as the district of the village still is. Close to the shore one does not see it, or rarely, but in the mountains about a cannon-shot away from there, it begins to appear: On very high and cold mountains it will also not come forth, but indeed on places that lie just below them, where the sun's rays can better take hold.

*Usage.* The bark of this tree is most in use, certainly by the Amboinese, and in all the Moluccas, namely, for making their vessels tight, being laid between the joints when one wants to set one plank upon another; for this dry and tender bark swells up in seawater and makes the vessels very tight, so that it serves these Indians for oakum. But it has again that fault, that it shrinks in the joints and falls out, which is however sufficiently prevented by caulking. This bark is called by a general name *Baru*, a name common to everything used for stopping and caulking vessels: Although it does not strictly serve for caulking, and even if this bark is stripped off, the tree gets a new one again in the same place, and the wound grows shut again in a few years, just as happens to the Cork tree.

The fruits or berries have no use among the Amboinese, which I ascribe more to their ignorance than that they would be less powerful than the *Javanese* ones: for one finds in the Amboinese ones more spice-like quality, or at least a more notable taste than in those that come over in the Javanese spice-boxes, which are mostly without taste, because they do not grow on Java itself, but on Borneo.

There is however still a small difference in the taste, for in the Amboinese berries it is more resinous and stronger, with more contraction, but in the *Javanese* (if they are fresh) it is without doubt more spice-like, though in both without any heat, from which I guess that the Javanese and Bornean do not come from this large-leafed Caju-Puti, but from the following small-leafed one, for which reason I postpone the further virtues to that chapter.

The young bark chewed with a little *Turmeric* and *Tamarind*, and laid on open abscesses, draws out the pus and cleanses the same. The leaves boiled in water with those of Lagondi, and washed therewith, drive away troublesome itching.

The wood has until now also been in small use: The Amboinese, especially in the Uliassers, used to make planks of it for small vessels, and which they still do for lack of other wood, because this wood is indeed durable, but also heavy, and not very fit for small vessels; On the other hand, our Nation has brought it into greater use since the year 1670, taking the same not only for house building—for which, as said, it does not serve so well—but also for the frames and ribs of large vessels, for which they have found it good and more durable, and by which most of the forests around Castle Victoria are now already cut down.

The *Caju-Kelam* occurring in the *Western Islands*, such as on *Java, Borneo, and Malacca*, is somewhat more slender of trunk, not above a thigh thick, as straight as a fir, and five or six fathoms high. The leaves are somewhat fattier and broader, and the wood is also hard and heavy: It grows there not exactly on the mountains, but on the flat fields and along the river-sides, where it has red clay. The wood is useful there for posts and ribs that must carry some weight, because of its sturdiness, as also to make the bridges from one Coconut tree to the other, where the tappers run over, binding two of them next to each other, as one otherwise does with Bamboos. The dry bark or Baru is used not only to lay in the joints of the vessels, but also to be mixed with the thick oil *Minjac-Caju*, to make torches or candles thereof, the same oil being tapped from the tree Koring, which has leaves like those of the white Mangium, and if one cuts the trunk or bores a hole in it, and...

The leaves are shaped like a narrow spearhead <note>original: *lanceolata*</note> and are marked by five distinct longitudinal ribs. When crushed, they release a potent and refreshing aroma. # EXPLANATION
### *Of the Sixteenth Plate,*

Representing the **MYRTLE-WHITE-TREE** <note>original: *Myrto-Leuco-Dendron*</note> *with whole leaves, curved in a spear-like shape, with thread-like flowers and pitcher-shaped fruits, which is called* WHITE TREE *or* **CAJU PUTI** *by Rumphius.*

**A.** *Denotes the flower.* **B.** *Denotes the fruit.*

# OBSERVATION.

I received a branch of this tree several years ago from **Dr. Garcin** under the name of the Indian **MYRTLE-WHITE-TREE**, called **Caju-Puti** by the inhabitants; a description of which the same **Illustrious Dr. GARCIN** very recently shared with me, which I include here for the benefit of the **Kind Reader & Lovers of Botany**.

Of this Moluccan tree, which is sometimes 50 or even 60 feet high, branches occupy the top of the trunk; these are usually one or two cubits <note>original: *ulna*; an ancient unit of length based on the forearm</note> long, and their circumference is mostly two feet. Furthermore, this tree is twisted and enjoys a white bark, which you might not undeservedly compare to the bark of a Birch tree <note>original: *Betulae*</note>, although it is much thicker and therefore consists of more membranes. The outer layers of these peel away and, as they age over time, are divided into tiny particles and roll up into a spiral (as happens in the Birch) and fall off of their own accord. A certain kind of worm, whose numbers increase there daily, often infests the bark of our tree; in many places, it drives tunnels in the form of a labyrinth.

The higher branches are sparse, bare, twisted, thin, and fragile; they are covered with a thin bark, not unlike that on the trunk, and therefore white like the trunk (from which this tree obtained the Malay name *Caju-Puti* <note>meaning "White Wood"</note>). These small branches, divided two or three times, diverge only at their very ends. Born around the upper part of the branches are alternate *Twigs*, round, thin, and more brittle than flexible, covered with a double membrane: the outer is thin and gray, like that of the Birch; the inner is thick and greenish. Each of these emerges from the leaf axil <note>the angle between the leaf and the stem</note> and they all end in very long spikes, crowded along their entire length with flowers and fruits.

The leaves are whole, long, and thick, ending in a pointed tip—though somewhat blunt—and are a little dry and fragile, of a greenish color mixed with a bit of dark yellow. In shape and veins they somewhat approach the leaves of the *Broad-leaved Hare's Ear* <note>original: *Bupleuri latifolii*</note>; they are sometimes straight, sometimes sickle-shaped. They sit upon a flat stalk (as in the *White Dammar*) which continues into the leaf for a space of 4 lines <term>line: an old botanical measurement, about 1/12 of an inch</term>, and then branches into 4 veins reaching to the very end of the leaf (just as is seen in the narrow-leaved *Plantain*). These veins are thin and greenish-white; they are distinguished more easily by these characteristics than by touch (by which they can hardly be perceived on the back of the leaf).

The leaves that have just emerged are paler, tender, flexible, not unpleasant to the touch, and triple-veined; when rubbed, they pour forth a strong, aromatic scent. However, the oldest leaves are the largest, most persistent, and most fragile. They are four or five inches long, twelve or fourteen lines wide, and are placed alternately on the twigs.

The flowers are complete, five-petaled, regular, and hermaphrodite <term>hermaphrodite: containing both male and female reproductive parts</term>; they crown the ovary and enjoy many stamens <note>original: *staminibus*; the pollen-bearing threads</note> united in the form of a ring at the base, usually divided into 5 parts, some of which support 8 or 9 white stamens, others 10 or 11. Those stamens in the middle are longer than those surrounding them. Their anthers <note>the tips of the stamens</note> are tiny and yellowish; the petals are very small, white, and hollowed out in the shape of a spoon, at most one and a half lines long. The calyx <note>the outer protective cup</note> is divided into 5 segments which also crown the ovary. The tube <note>original: *tuba*; the style</term> rising from the middle of the ovary is simple, straight, whitish, and everywhere equally thick and round.

The ovary, upon which all these parts sit, is semi-spherical and thus wider than it is high; it lacks a stalk and is firmly attached to the twig of the spike at the center of its circumference. Its greatest diameter at the upper part equals one and a half lines. Its external shape approaches the cup of an acorn <note>original: *glandis calicem*</note>, but the internal part is filled with seed all the way to the edges.

The flowers and fruits are arranged alternately in the form of a spike, sitting upon a thin, very flexible twig, sometimes half a foot in length; it does not stop growing, especially where all its flowers have emerged.

**NB.** *Since I have not seen the fruit ripe, I do not describe it.*

# EXPLANATION
### *Of the sixteenth Plate,*

*Which depicts a* **MYRTLE-WHITE-TREE** *with hanging and whole leaves that are curved like a lancet, with fibrous flowers and pitcher-shaped fruits, called* **WHITE-TREE** *or* **CAJU-PUTI** *by* **Rumphius**.*

**A.** *Shows the Flower.* **B.** *The Fruit.*

# REMARK.

Several years ago, I received a twig of this tree from Mr. **Garcin** with the name **MYRTO-LEUCO-DENDRON** *Indicum*, called **CAJU-PUTI** by the natives, the description of which I also recently received from the same Mr. **Garcin**, and which I herewith share with the readers and lovers of this study.

On this Moluccan tree, which is 50 and sometimes 60 feet high, many branches are placed in the crown, which generally have a length of one or two fathoms <note>original: *vademen*</note> and a thickness of two feet in circumference; this tree being very gnarled and crooked, and bearing a white bark which is similar to the bark of the *Birch tree*, although it is much thicker and therefore consists of more skins, of which the outermost peel off and, growing old over time, are divided into very small pieces and curl up (as is seen in the Birch tree), and finally fall off by themselves. The bark of this tree is often damaged by a sort of little worm, which increases from time to time, and which in some places even forms whole hollows like a labyrinth.

The uppermost branches are few, bare, crooked, and easily broken, and are surrounded with a thin and white bark, just as on the trunk, from which also the Malay name of *Caju-Puti* was given to it; being divided two or three times, and these twigs gape apart from each other. The twigs that grow above the larger branches stand opposite each other; they are round, thin, more brittle, and not flexible, and are covered with a double membrane, of which the outermost is thin and gray, similar to that of the *Birch tree*, and the innermost is thick and green. Each twig comes forth from the lap of the leaves and ends in a very long point, everywhere set and laden with flowers and fruits.

The leaves are whole, long, narrow, and thick, ending in a pointed tip, though somewhat blunt, being somewhat dry and brittle, of a green color mixed with some dark yellow, in the shape and with veins like those of the *Broad-leaved Hare's Ear*, being sometimes straight, sometimes curved like a scythe, and they stand on a flat little stalk, like those of the *White Dammar*, which runs into the leaf for the space of four lines, ending in 4 veins (as is seen in the narrow-leaved plantain leaf), which are thin, of a greenish-white: and by which signs they are better discovered than by touch, through which they can hardly be distinguished at the bottom of the leaf.

The young leaves are pale, tender, flexible, and not unpleasant to the touch, interwoven with three veins; when rubbed, they give off a strong and spicy scent, but the broadest and oldest are brittle, yet long-lasting, four or five inches long, twelve or fourteen lines wide, standing opposite each other on the branches.

The flowers are perfect, five-petaled, regular, and hermaphrodites, which surround the ovary <note>original: *Eyersak*; literally "egg-sack"</note>, set with very many fibers <note>stamens</note> which are united at the base, as in a ring all around, which is generally divided into five parts, of which some are set with 8 or 9 fibers, others by 10 or 11, but the middle ones of these fibers are the longest, and their little nubs <note>anthers</note> are small and yellowish. The petals of the flowers are very small, white, and hollowed out like a spoon, at most one and a half lines long. The calyx is divided into five parts, also surrounding the ovary. The pipe <note>style</note> coming forth from the middle of the ovary is simple, straight, whitish, everywhere equal, thick, and round.

The ovary, upon which all the preceding parts are placed, is half-round, and therefore broader than it is high, without a stalk, and sits very firmly on the twig in its circumference, and its greatest extent is one and a half lines; its outward shape looks much like a calyx, or the cap of an Acorn, but from the inside it is filled with seed.

The flowers and fruits stand opposite each other like a head of grain <note>original: *koren-helm*</note> on a thin twig that is very flexible and has a length of a foot or half a foot, where primarily all the flowers come forth; for as long as the flowers sprout, so the twig also grows.

**NB.** *Since I have not seen the fruit ripe, I do not describe it.*

# CHAPTER TWENTY-SIX.
## XXVI. CHAPTER.

->The Lesser White Tree: *Caju puti*, *Small Leaf*, as well as *Kilan Wood*.<-
->Small White-Tree.<-

---

The smaller species of Cajuput <note>original: *Caju-puti*</note> is similar to the preceding species in all aspects of its external appearance, except that all its parts are smaller; it does not become a full-grown and perfect tree, and sometimes it grows with multiple stems, so that it resembles a shrub.

These stems are rarely thicker than a foot, and very rarely thicker than a leg <note>original: *crus*; referring to the thickness of a human calf or thigh</note>; they are covered with a thin, pale yellow, and multilayered bark, as in the previous species, but it is much thinner, more wrinkled, and more jagged, such that it is unsuitable for sealing cracks <note>This refers to the practice of using bark for caulking ships</note>. The leaves are similar to the former, but half as large, three or four inches long, and scarcely a little finger wide. They resemble the leaves of a small Willow, and are slightly curved back, with three longitudinal veins that bear certain small and curved transverse veinlets. Their color is similar to the preceding species, but not so pale, being more grassy-green; they are firm, dry, and brittle, with a pleasant aromatic scent approaching that of Cardamom, so that those who are uninformed might take these for Cardamom leaves.

The fruits or berries are also much more aromatic and of a hotter flavor than the previous kind, with a similarly slight astringency, whereby they rival the flavor of Myrtle berries. If the trunks are thicker, they also appear black and scorched at their lowest part, as in the previous species. The roots often run in an arching fashion half-exposed above the ground, and are fixed into the earth with few small fibers, for which reason it cannot be easily transplanted. The wood is harder than that of the previous species, tending more toward reddish, and is far more durable; but it is rarely used, as it does not grow thick.

*Name.* It shares the same name everywhere as the preceding species, except that it is nicknamed "small" or "small-leaved"; thus in Latin it is called *Arbor alba minor*, and in Malay *Caju-puti, Daun-Kitsjil*, and it is also called *Caju-Kilan*.

*Location.* It grows in Amboina, though not as frequently as the preceding kind, and it loves drier and rockier soil mixed with large and sharp stones, such as is found on Great Amboina behind the village of *Suly*, as well as on the promontory of *Nussanive*, and on the islands of *Manipa* and *Buru*. In all these places it is not far from the sea, for it loves the sea air more than the previous species. It also grows abundantly in the southern part of *Borneo*, and I believe that from this kind of tree are produced the aromatic *Bollong* fruits <note>These are likely the seeds of a related Melaleuca or similar aromatic plant</note> which are found in spice-boxes and are brought for sale to the market in *Banjarmasin*, and from there are carried further to all the capital cities of *Java*, although these trees also grow in *Karimata* and *Madura*. They do not sprout in *Bali* or *Java*, yet their fruits are sold everywhere.

*Usage.* This bark cannot be used to plug the seams of ships, since it is so woody and brittle. The fruits and leaves, which have a much stronger aromatic power and are by nature one degree hotter than the preceding kind, also offer much greater use in medicine. From these *Bollong* fruits (which I consider to be the same as those of the Javanese), many medicinal potions are prepared, called *Dju-Djambu* by the Javanese and Balinese, into which they mix so many spices and which they offer for such various and diverse diseases, that it can hardly be determined what power each ingredient exerts. However, that potion in which *Bollong* is the base has been found to be effective for correcting and comforting a weak stomach; it is also given to women recovering from childbirth to strengthen and contract the internal parts. Some also praise it against headaches <note>original: *Cephalalgiam*</note>, but no certain successes have yet been observed from this.

The Amboinese also use these leaves, which they macerate with flowers in fresh oil, which they then impregnate with the smoke of Benzoin <note>A fragrant resin from trees of the genus *Styrax*</note> and other incenses; from this they make their *Minjac Mony*, that is, scented oil...

<column-break/>

The small variety of *Caju-puti* is in all things equal to the preceding one in outward form, except that it is smaller in all its parts; it also does not become a full-grown tree, and sometimes shoots up with more stems, so that it indeed resembles a shrub.

The stems are also not more than a leg, or very rarely a thigh thick, covered with a fine, pale, and multilayered bark, just like the former, though much thinner, more wrinkled, also more torn, and unsuitable for filling joints. The leaves are likewise as on the former, but indeed half smaller, 3 and 4 inches long, barely a small finger wide, and like the small Willow leaves, also slightly bent forward, striped with three nerves along the length, which have some small and crooked cross-veins, of a color likewise as the preceding, though not so pale, but pulling toward yellow-green, stiff, dry, and crumbly, moreover with a pleasant spice-like smell, coming very close to *Cardamom*, so that the ignorant take them for *Cardamom* leaves.

The fruits or berries are also more spice-like, and better of taste than the preceding, still with a small contraction <note>meaning an astringent or "puckering" quality</note>, and therefore approaching the taste of Myrtle berries. The stems, if they are somewhat thick, are seen at the bottom to be black and burnt, like the former. The roots sometimes lie half-naked with bends upon the earth, and are fastened into the earth with few fibers, which is why one cannot easily transplant it. The wood is harder than that of the preceding, pulling more toward the reddish, and more durable; yet it is little used, because it is not thick.

*Names.* It has the same name everywhere as the preceding, except that one adds the surname of "small" or "small-leaved" to it, as in Latin *Arbor alba minor*, and in Malay *Caju-Puti, Daun-Kitsjil*, and so it is also named *Caju-Kilan*.

*Place.* It grows in *Amboina*, though not as much as the preceding, and requires a drier and rockier ground, where large and sharp stones run beneath, as one finds on Great *Amboina*, behind the village of *Suly*, as well as on the corner of *Nussanive*, on the Islands of *Manipa* and *Buru*, everywhere not far from the Sea, for it loves the Sea-air more than the preceding: one also has it abundantly on the South-side of *Borneo*, and I hold it to be so, that from this sort of tree comes the spice-like *Bollong*, being found in the spice-boxes, and which one brings to market at *Banjarmasin*, and from there carries further to all the merchant-cities of *Java*: although those trees also grow on *Karimata*, and *Madura*: But on *Bali* and *Java* one does not have them, and yet the fruits were sold everywhere.

*Use.* This bark one cannot use to lay in the joints of vessels, because it is so woody and crumbly: The fruits and leaves, being much more spice-like, and indeed a degree better of nature than the preceding, are in greater use for Medicine: For from these *Bollonghs*, (which I hold to be one and the same as the Javanese) many Medicinal drinks were made, named *Dju Djambu* by the *Javanese* and *Balinese*, though therein they mix so many spices among one another, and use them for so many different sicknesses, that one can hardly judge from that what power each has: Nevertheless, that drink in which the *Bollong* is most prominent has been found to be good to improve and strengthen an unwilling or bad stomach, being also given to women who rise from their childbed, to strengthen and close the internal members again: Some also use them against the headache, though one has seen no certain successes from that.

The *Amboinese* also use these leaves, and soak the same with other flowers in fresh Oil, which they then thereafter smoke with *Benzoin*, and other perfumes, and from that make their *Minjac Mony* (that is, sweet-smelling...

# Book II. Chapter XXVI. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...they prepare, with which they smear their head; some Javanese and Malays also fill their pillows with these leaves for the sake of the pleasant scent, though it would be too heavy for our nation. These same leaves, gathered on a clear day and slightly dried in the open air, then placed in chests or boxes, keep away various insects with their heavy odor; however, some leaves must sometimes be rubbed with the hands so that the piercing scent of Cardamom is more strongly excited. It is also said that pillows filled with these leaves drive bedbugs out of the bedrooms.

The *Sari* <note>original: "Sari seu paleosum semen"; refers to the floral remains or chaff-like seeds</note> falling from the fruits is collected separately and sold in apothecary chests, which also serves for medicinal drinks called *Dju-Djambu* <note>A traditional medicinal concoction</note>, but always mixed with other ingredients.

The younger saplings, if dug up carefully, can be transplanted into gardens, where they also grow, as we have experienced twice.

These leaves, gathered on a hot day and placed in a sack while quite dry, will spontaneously heat up and become as moist as if they had been soaked in water. If these are cut into pieces and steeped in water to ferment overnight, and then distilled, a thin, clear, and subtle oil is extracted from them, though only in a small quantity; from two sacks full of these leaves, barely three drachms <note>A unit of apothecary weight, approx. 3.9 grams</note> of that oil are obtained. It breathes a very strong scent of Cardamom, but gradually becomes more pleasant, yet it evaporates very easily. Two drops of this oil, taken with beer or wine, excite heavy sweating, for which purpose India offers very few suitable medicines.

## CHAPTER TWENTY-SEVEN.

->*Amboinese Myrtle. Hurong.*<-

**T**his is the smallest species of Caju-Puti <note>Cajuput</note>, resembling the narrow-leaved Myrtle in form and habit: nor does it grow into a mature tree, but remains a small trunk, indeed often lower than the preceding species. This trunk usually has the thickness of a leg, rarely of a thigh, and is also covered with a thin, wrinkled, dry, and fissured bark. The branches are mostly upright and divided into very thin and woody twigs, which form an elegant crown, so that from a distance it resembles a large Rosemary bush. The leaves are placed in an irregular order and surround the twigs so closely that they cover them; they are about a finger's breadth long and a straw-stalk or quill wide, more pointed at the back than at the front, where they are mostly round, though some bear a very small tip. They have a notable central nerve and two others running along the sides, much finer than the middle one. They are of a bright green color, with an aromatic-sour taste and a slight astringency; they are not as sharp as the preceding species, but more pleasant. When the lower leaves of the twigs fall off, which happens in September and October, the upper ones remain in clusters with some smaller leaves in between, thus together forming the appearance of a flower.

The blossoms are small flowers, like those of the *Alcanna* <note>Henna, *Lawsonia inermis*</note>, the size of a finger-

<column-break/>

the oil), with which they smear the head. Some Javanese and Malays also fill their pillows with these leaves for the sake of the good scent, though it would be too heavy for our nation. The same leaves, gathered on a clear day, dried somewhat in the air, and then laid in chests or cupboards, prevent cockroaches or other vermin from entering with their strong scent; however, one must sometimes rub some leaves to pieces with the hand, so that the Cardamom scent is thereby awakened. And it is also said that pillows filled with these leaves drive the bedbugs out of the bedsteads.

The *Sari*, or chaff-like seed falling from the fruits, is collected separately and sold in the spice boxes, also serving for medicinal drinks, or *Dju-Djambu*, though always mixed with other things.

The young trees, if dug out carefully, can be transplanted into the gardens, and they also come up there, as has happened to me twice.

These leaves, gathered quite dry on a hot day and put into a sack, will brew in such a way that they become hot, and the next day they are as wet as if they had lain in water. Chop these into pieces, pour water over them, and let them ferment for a night, and then distill them; thus you get a thin, clear, and subtle oil, though very little, and from two sacks full of leaves, barely three Drachms. It smells very strongly of Cardamom, but becomes more pleasant with time, and also easily smokes away or evaporates. A couple of drops of this oil, taken with beer or wine, causes violent sweating, for which one otherwise has few suitable medicines in the Indies.

### XXVII. CHAPTER.

->*Amboinese Myrtle Tree.*<-

**T**his is the smallest kind of Caju-Puti, coming closest in appearance and taste to the *Narrow-leaved Myrtle*: It also does not become a full-grown tree, but remains a small trunk, and sometimes even lower than the preceding. The trunk commonly has the thickness of a leg, rarely of a thigh, and also with a thin, rough, dry, and torn bark. The branches stand mostly upright and are divided into very thin and woody twigs, making a graceful crown, so that from afar it resembles a large Rosemary tree. The leaves stand without order, and so close around the twigs that they cover them; about a finger's length, and a straw or shaft wide, sharper from behind than from the front, where they are mostly round, some with a very small point, together with a notable middle-nerve, and two others that run along the sides, much subtler than the middle one, of a bright green color, of a sourish-spicy taste, with a small contraction, and not as sharp as the preceding, but somewhat more pleasant. When the hindmost leaves fall off from the twigs, which happens in September and October, the front ones remain in clusters, with some smaller leaves in between, and thus together make the appearance of a flower.

The blossoms are small flowers, like those of the Henna-

being about the size of a finger-joint, composed of five whitish, somewhat round and slightly wrinkled petals, in the center of which twenty to twenty-five stamens appear, and in their center a straight, pointed pistil rises.

*Fruits* are rare, sitting here and there on very short stalks, solitary, the size of a Pea or a Bilberry <note>original: "Myrtilli"; the European blueberry or bilberry</note>, with the tip of the pistil remaining in a small pressed-in pit; these fruits have a round shape, are wrinkled, and divided into five furrows; they are blackish in color, and are dry and resinous, divided inside into five cells. In each of these a small, brown, chaff-like seed is hidden, resembling cut thread. These berries have an aromatic taste, but a weak one, approaching that of Myrtle berries, but the seed itself is tasteless. Each berry is set upon a round and flat disk—the pericarp—which is persistent and does not easily fall off, but remains on the tree for a long time, eventually falling with the stalk; however, these seeds rarely or never sprout into new little trees. When these berries are ripe while still joined to the tree, they gape open into five parts, casting out their seeds.

The trunks of this *Tree* mostly rise straight up and provide a hard wood that is easily split lengthwise. The flowers appear in the month of April, and the fruits are seen in the rainy months, remaining until other flowers emerge again.

*Name.* In Latin *Myrtus Amboinensis*; in Amboinese *Hurong* and *Hulong*; in *Luhoe Lele* <note>A region in western Ceram</note>, some call this by the Malay word *Caju-Puti* <note>White wood</note>, or *Camelan-Daun Kitsjil* <note>Small-leaved Camelan</note>, which is a name held in common with the preceding species.

*Location.* It grows on low and barren mountains, as much on the coast as in the interior, which favor low-growing plants and are well-exposed to the Sun. It also loves black soil mixed here and there with larger stones. I found the best ones, filled with the strongest flavor, on the mountains situated on the northern part of *Luciela*, as much on the coast as on the lower hills near *Liela*, both of which are locations on Little *Ceram*. It also occurs in *Amboina*, but there it raises a taller trunk in the interior, usually in clear and open forests where Damar trees <note>Resin-producing trees of the genus Agathis or Shorea</note> grow, or sometimes Kilang trees are found, as in the mountains of *Enna* and at the promontory of *Nuffanive*. This tree is also found in *Keya* and the islands situated to the Southeast.

*Use.* Its medicinal virtues have not yet been explored by the Amboinese; only its straight trunks are used for roof supports, as its wood is hard and durable, as well as for the handles of axes and larger knives. The elegant form of this little tree is worthy of being transplanted and cultivated in gardens, which can be done if it is carefully dug up while still tender with the black earth clinging to it, and its roots are not harmed; for the few roots it enjoys are quite dry and often curved above the ground at the trunk. If it is transplanted in this manner during the rainy months, it forms a more elegant crown in gardens than in the wilds, and serves solely for the decoration of a garden. I have observed no small trees sprouting from the fallen seeds, nor do the branches easily take root, as they are very dry.

In the mountains of *Alangh*, these trees were found as thick as a man’s body, but it was discovered that they had grown together from various trunks, which could be separated with little effort, and each was covered with a thin bark; the wood, however, was so hard that it defied axes and would break them, so that this wood could only be split with great force, and even then with difficulty.

similar, and about as large as a fingernail, made of five white, round and somewhat wrinkled petals, and inside them twenty to twenty-five white threads <note>stamens</note>, as well as a green mound in the middle, with a straight point on top.

*The fruits* are few, hanging here and there individually on short stalks, the size of peas or bilberries <note>original: "Myrtille-kraack-bezien"</note>, with the aforementioned point on top, standing in a small pit; they have a round shape, yet are not smooth but wrinkled, and divided into five furrows or ribs. In color they are smoky-black or dark brown, dry and somewhat hard, also divided inside into five cells, and containing a small, brown, and chaffy seed, like thread that has been cut into pieces. The berries have a spice-like but not sharp taste, coming very close to the Myrtle, but the seed does not. Each berry stands on a round and flat disk that does not easily fall off, but stays on the tree for a long time, finally falling with the stalk and all; however, it seldom or never produces young trees. While still hanging on the tree, they split into five parts and thus cast out their seed.

*The stems* mostly grow straight up and have a hard wood that nevertheless splits easily lengthwise; the tree blooms in April, and the fruits are seen in the rainy Monsoons, which hang there until it blooms again.

*Name.* In Latin *Myrtus Amboinica*, in Amboinese *Hurong* and *Hulong*, on *Luhoe Lele*; some call it in Malay *Caju-Puti*, or *Camelan-Daun Kitsjil*, a name common with the previous one.

*Location.* It grows on high and bare mountains (both on the beach and inland) that have low scrub and stand well in the Sun. It also likes a black soil, mixed here and there with large stones; the best and strongest in taste I have found on the mountains lying north of *Luciela* on the beach, and also on the low hills near *Liela*, both places on Little *Ceram*. On *Amboina* one finds them as well, but with a taller trunk, also far inland, and commonly in light forests where Damar trees stand, or sometimes also Kilang trees, such as on the mountains of *Enna* and on the corner of *Nuffanive*. One also has this tree in *Key* and in the South-eastern Islands.

*Use.* Its medicinal powers have not yet been investigated by the Amboinese. Only the straight trunks are used for rafters on roofs, and also because the wood is hard and durable, for handles of axes and hafts of bush-knives. The beautiful appearance of this little tree well deserves to be transplanted into gardens, which can indeed be done if one digs them out carefully while small with their nearby black loose earth, and does not happen to injure the roots; for the few they have are dry, and sometimes make a small bend at the trunk above the earth. And being thus transplanted in the rainy months, it also shoots up with a more decorative crown than in the wilderness, serving only for the ornament of a garden. No little trees have yet been seen to come forth from the fallen seeds, and the branches also do not allow themselves to be transplanted <note>as cuttings</note> because they are very dry.

In the mountains of *Alangh*, these trees have been found as thick as a man, but it was found that they had grown together from several trunks, which after some effort could be separated from each other, and each piece was covered with a thin bark, the wood being so hard that the axes jumped into pieces from it, and it could hardly be sawn through even with great effort.

Book II. Chapter XXVIII. AMBOINESE HERBAL. 79

# CHAPTER TWENTY-EIGHT.

-> The Dye-Tree. Galuga. <-

This is a low tree, about the size of a Plum tree, consisting of a reasonably thick trunk, curved branches, and a thick, spreading crown. The bark of the trunk is smooth, a grayish-green or mossy color, thick, yellow on the inside with whitish veins, juicy, and stains the hands a reddish or fiery color; it is tough and firmly attached to the wood.

The wood is white, soft, and of little use. The leaves are like the narrow-leaved <term>Arum <note>A genus of flowering plants; the author likely refers to the shape of the Cuckoo-pint or similar plants</note></term> or the *Siri* <note>Betel leaf</note> leaves, but they are much longer, round and broad at the back, and tapering to a long point at the front. They have smooth edges, though they appear somewhat wavy like a flame of fire. They are a hand-span long or slightly less, four fingers wide at the base, and sit on long stalks, arranged without order around the branches.

At the base of the stalk, five nerves meet with some transverse ribs. The outermost twigs are green and covered with a soft, reddish down, though this is not seen on old trees. From their <term>axils <note>the angle between the upper side of a leaf or stem and the supporting stem</note></term>, green buds emerge in clusters, which open into wide flowers made of five whitish, oblong, and limp petals. In the center, they bear many long and thin <term>stamens <note>the pollen-producing parts of the flower</note></term>, yellowish below and adorned with gray <term>anthers <note>the part of a stamen that contains the pollen</note></term> above. In the middle appears a reddish <term>pistil <note>the seed-bearing part of the flower</note></term>, curved like a horn. These petals are sometimes spotted on their outer side with reddish dots or points, but they wither as soon as they are plucked. They are open in the morning, but only for a short time; for when the sun rises and touches them with its rays, they soon contract until the evening. The scent of the flower is of little consequence and almost unpleasant. After these come round fruits, much like <term>Chestnuts <note>original: "Castaneas"</note></term> still in their green husks, but smaller, being covered with a light green husk which is beset all over with soft points like small thorns, yet not at all stinging. Each fruit is mostly divided into two chambers inside, and in each chamber one sees two, three, or four red kernels enclosed in a thin membrane and hanging from the middle partition. Each kernel is the size of a grain of wheat, broad at one end and pointed at the other, where they hang by a short vein from the middle partition; they are not round but somewhat angular and pear-shaped; some are even hollowed out. On the inside they are hard and white, but on the outside they are covered with a thin, red, and slimy flesh, which easily comes off if they are soaked in water and stirred a little. This makes the water entirely red, and after a short time, a thick substance like a paint-pigment settles on the bottom. The husk of the dry and fallen fruits turns a dusky black, and in these, the kernels are so dried out that no dye can be obtained from them. They rarely sprout, even if the fruits fall to the ground. This dye has an unpleasant smell, as does almost the entire tree, especially the green bark, which smells so strongly of sulfur that it can hardly be tolerated. It blooms in the dry or hot <term>Monsoon <note>original: "Mousson"</note></term>, though the fruits are seen on it almost the whole year. It has many roots, which have many hanging fibers that are knotty.

Name. In Latin *Pigmentaria* <note>The Painter's Plant</note>, after the Malay *Galuga*, which generally signifies all kinds of painter's pigments, because one can dye red with the kernels of this fruit. In Javanese it is called *Cassomba Kling*, in Ternate *Rambuta*, and in Ambon *Talucca*. *Galuga* has its origin either from the Arabic *Gal*, that is, to make bright and clear, or to clothe, or from the Chaldean *Gelach* <note>original: "Gelab"</note>, which is to shine.

Location. It is not found very often in these islands, and grows nowhere spontaneously, but here and there a tree is planted in the <term>Negories <note>native villages or settlements</note></term>. It grows more abundantly in the West Indies <note>the Americas</note>, as will be mentioned hereafter. Since it has no true indigenous name in the East Indies, I guess that it was first brought to the nearby Moluccas from the Manila islands, and perhaps there by the <term>Castilians <note>the Spanish</note></term> from America. For *Galuga*, as was said, is a general

# CHAPTER XXVIII.

-> The Dye-Tree. <-

This is a low tree, the size of a Plum tree, with a reasonably thick trunk, curved branches, and a dense, spreading crown. The bark is smooth, of a grayish-green or mossy hue, thick, yellow inside with white veins, juicy, staining the hands a reddish or fiery red, very tough, and sticking firmly to the wood.

The wood is white, soft, and of poor quality. The leaves resemble the narrow *Arum*, or the *Siri* leaves, yet are much longer, round and broad at the back, and tapering to a long point in front, with smooth edges, though they appear somewhat wavy, like a flame of fire; they are a hand-span long, and sometimes less, four fingers wide at the back, standing on long stalks without order around the branches.

At the origin of the stalk, five nerves meet, along with some transverse ribs. The outermost twigs are green and covered with a soft and reddish down, though on old trees one does not see this. From their leaf-axils come green buds in clusters, and from those come wide-open flowers, made of five white, longish, and limp petals, with many long and thin threads in the middle, yellowish below, and with gray tips above. The middle part is a reddish curved thread like a horn. On the outer side, these petals are sometimes sprinkled with reddish drops or dots, and they wither immediately if one breaks them off. In the morning hours one sees them open, but only for a short time, for having been touched by the sun, they immediately close again until the evening. The scent is nothing special and almost unpleasant. After the flowers come round fruits, very much like Chestnuts that are still in their green husk, yet smaller, being covered with a light-green husk, which is set all around with soft points like thorns, yet not at all stinging. Each fruit is mostly divided into two chambers inside, and in each chamber one sees 2, 3, and 4 red kernels, enclosed in a thin membrane and hanging from the middle partition. Each kernel is the size of a wheat-corn, but somewhat broad at one end and pointed at the other, where they hang by a short vein to the middle partition, not round, but somewhat angular, pear-shaped, and some somewhat hollowed out. Inside they are hard and white, and surrounded by a thin, red, and slimy flesh, which easily comes off if one lays them in water and stirs them a bit, from which the water also turns entirely red, and after a short time a thickish substance settles on the bottom, like some painter's pigment. The husk of the dry and fallen fruits turns smoky black, and in these, the kernels are then so dried out that one can get no dye from them. They also rarely propagate, even if the fruits fall on the earth. This dye gives an unpleasant smell, as does almost the entire tree, and especially the green bark, which smells so strongly of sulfur that one can hardly or not at all endure it. It blooms in the dry or hot Monsoon, although one sees the fruits on it almost the whole year. The roots are many, and have many fibers hanging from them that are knotty.

Name. In Latin *Pigmentaria*, after the Malay *Galuga*, which in common signifies all kinds of painter's dyes, because one can dye red with the kernels of this fruit. In Javanese *Cassomba Kling*, in Ternate *Rambuta*, in Ambon *Talucca*. *Galuga* has its origin from the Arabic *Gal*, that is to make bright and clear, or from the Chaldean *Gelach*, that is to glisten.

Place. One finds it in these islands not very often, and nowhere growing by itself, but here and there a tree planted in the villages. It grows more abundantly in the West Indies, as shall be said hereafter, and because it has no proper indigenous name anywhere in the East Indies, I guess that it was first brought into the nearby Moluccas from the Manilas, and perhaps thither by the Castilians from America. name, and the people of Ternate called it *Rambuta* <note>original: *Rambuta Ternatenses*</note>, undoubtedly because of the shape of the true Rambutan, which is another fruit of the Javanese.

**Usage.** Among these inhabitants it has so far been in rare use, for the reddish seeds serve only for dyeing a red color, both on white linens and on paper. These fresh seeds are stirred in lukewarm water for a long time until they imbue it with a red color, and in this they dip *Badjus* <note>A traditional blouse or jacket</note>, which are small garments of the women made of white linen, which they mostly wear at the time of weddings. However, these seeds do not provide a true or elegant red, but a yellowish-red or purple, and this color is so fleeting that it pales within a few days; the people of Macassar dye with these the doorposts of that house where a bride lives, or in which a wedding is celebrated. For the color red is a sign of joy for the Chinese and almost all these peoples. The <term>Moors <note>The author uses 'Aethiopes' in Latin and 'Mooren' in Dutch to refer to local Muslims</note></term> also make ink from these, with which they write the name of God and the Prophets, or when they join a period to a speech. This, however, is for lack of <term>Minium <note>A bright red lead pigment</note></term> or another red color, for these seeds give the paper a pale and fleeting redness; otherwise, there is no other use for this tree among this people. But it is clear from authors that this tree is of greater value and use in the West Indies. For the Spaniard <term>Eusebius Nierenberg <note>Juan Eusebio Nieremberg (1595–1658), a Jesuit physicist and naturalist</note></term> in his *Natural History, book 15, chapter 48*, writes of the *Achiotl* tree growing in the Province of Mechuacan in such a way that I consider it to be one and the same as this *Galuga* tree, and all the more so since he describes not only its various medicinal virtues but also adds that very strong and hard threads are woven from its bark, which are more solid than those made of hemp.

In <term>Rochefort's <note>Charles de Rochefort, author of a 17th-century history of the Antilles</note></term> French history of the *Antilles*, this tree also occurs described by the name *Urucu*, growing in Brazil, of the shape and size of an Orange tree, enjoying heart-shaped leaves; and that the pigment attached to the seeds stains the fingers and sticks to them if handled; and that these seeds should be cast into and stirred in lukewarm water until they have released all their pigment. The superfluous water is then poured off, and the sediment is dried in a shady place, from which <term>troches <note>Small medicinal or pigment cakes</note></term> are formed for the use of painters and dyers.

Also that the wood is brittle and dry, most suitable for catching and maintaining fire, and two pieces of it rubbed strongly against each other catch fire so well that tinder can be ignited. Also that threads are drawn from its bark, and its root reconciles a good flavor to food, and has the smell and color of Saffron; furthermore, that the <term>Caribs <note>Indigenous people of the Caribbean</note></term> diligently cultivate these trees in their gardens and paint their bodies and furniture with their red color, etc. From which it must be concluded that this American tree is of a more pleasant taste than the Oriental one, or at least its roots and bark; for when the latter are boiled in water by these people, they imbue it with a dark reddish color like thick <term>Mum <note>original: "pinguis Cerevisiæ" / "mom"; a strong, dark Brunswick beer</note></term>, but impregnate it with an unpleasant smell and taste, almost as if old red beet roots had been boiled in it.

On the mainland coast of Guiana and in the Caribbean islands, especially in Dominica, and on the island of Maranhão, this tree and fruit also grow, and it is called there *Rocku* and *Rucku*. The Indians take the seeds of this and smear their bodies so thickly with them that it serves them in place of clothes, for all the Caribs go about dyed with a red color, and they do this against the cold of the air. In the <term>Berbice <note>A region in modern-day Guyana</note></term> islands, the Dutch some years ago traded in tablets formed from these seeds, which they sent to Holland, with which they dye a scarlet color.

This tree is also described quite obscurely by <term>Julius Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a famous scholar and polymath</note></term> in his *Exercise 181, section 3*, under the name of the "Tree for Marking Boundaries" <note>original: *Arbor finium regundorum*</note>, where he says—though from the report of others—that its seeds are used by the Mexicans to make red ink with which they delineate areas and fields. If linens soaked and impregnated with that juice, as soon as they are nearly dry, are dripped a second time in lemon juice, they acquire a bright purple color, quite fixed, which method of dyeing is frequently practiced in Macassar.

<term>Willem Piso <note>Willem Piso (1611–1678), a Dutch physician and pioneer of tropical medicine</note></term> in *book 4, chapter 14*, also testifies that the *Uruc-*

**Usage.** Among these inhabitants it still has very little use, for only the red grains serve to dye red with, both on white linen and on paper. The fresh grains are stirred in lukewarm water until they dye it red, and then they dip the *Badjus* into it—these are the small body-coats of the women, made of white linen, which they commonly wear at weddings. The grains, however, do not give a true, fine redness, but a yellow-red or fire-colored hue, and the color is so fleeting that it fades in a few days; the people of Macassar also dye the posts of the doors of a house where a wedding is held with it: for red color is a sign of joy among the Chinese and almost all these nations. The <term>Moors <note>referring to local Muslims</note></term> also make red ink from it, with which they write the name of God and the Prophets, or when they want to conclude a period in a speech. But this is only for lack of <term>minium <note>red lead</note></term> or other red color, for these grains give an ugly and unstable redness on paper; otherwise, there is no use for this tree among this nation. But from the writers, it appears that in the West Indies it must be of much greater value and use. For the Spaniard Eusebius Nierenberg, *Natural History, Book 15, Chapter 48*, writes of the *Achiotl* tree growing in the province of Mechuacan in such a way that I hold it to be one and the same tree as this *Galuga*, and all the more so because not only are many medicinal powers described of it, but it is also added that very firm ropes are braided from its bark, which are firmer than those made of hemp.

In the French History of Rochefort, regarding the Antilles, one also finds this tree described under the name *Urucu*, growing in Brazil, of the shape and size of an Orange-Apple tree, with heart-shaped leaves, and further, that the dye clinging to the grains easily stays on the fingers when handled; that the grains must be thrown and stirred in lukewarm water until they have yielded all their dye. Pouring off the thin water, the dregs are dried in a shady place, and from them little cakes are made for the use of painters and dyers.

As also that the wood is brittle and dry, very capable of holding fire for a long time; that two dry pieces rubbed strongly against each other catch fire in such a way that tinder can be lit from them. That ropes are also made from its bark, and the root gives a good taste to food, as well as the scent and color of Saffron; that the Caribbeans diligently plant these trees in their gardens and paint their bodies with the red dye, as well as their household furniture etc., from which one must conclude that this American tree is more pleasant in taste than the East Indian one, at least the root and bark, which when boiled in water from the latter makes it brown-red like <term>Mum <note>A dark, thick beer</note></term>, but gives it an unpleasant smell and taste, almost like that of old beet-roots.

On the mainland coast of Guiana and the Caribbean Islands, especially on Dominica and on the island of Maranhão, this tree and fruit also grow, and it is named there *Rocku* or *Rucku*. The Indians take the grains and smear their bodies so thickly with them that it serves them in place of clothing, for all the Caribs go about dyed red, and do so against the cold of the air. In Berbice, some years ago, the Dutch began to trade with the cakes made from these grains and to carry them to Holland to dye scarlet with them.

This tree is also very darkly or obscurely depicted by Julius Scaliger, *Exercise 181, Section 3*, under the name of the "Tree for Marking Boundaries," where he writes—though from the account of others—that the grains were used by the Mexicans for red ink to mark off their fields and plots. If the linen that is dyed with the aforementioned juice, as soon as it is wind-dry, is dipped for a second time in lemon juice, it gets a light-purple color that is somewhat permanent, and which manner of dyeing is much used in Macassar.

Willem Piso, *Book 4, Chapter 14*, also testifies that the tree *Uruc-*

The **Uruccumi** in **Brazil** <note>Achiote or Annatto</note> is diligently cultivated by the inhabitants, not only for use in food and **medicine**, but also to form red pellets from it, which they sell to the **Portuguese**, who dye with this the red color called **Orellana**: There it is undoubtedly more fertile, and provides a more pleasant flavor, as thirty or forty seeds are found in each of its fruits, whereas in the **East** only eight to twelve are observed. These are also taken internally against poison, **diarrhea**, and burning fevers, for which however the root is considered **more excellent**; they also use it in food to imbue them with a yellow color, as well as for several other things mentioned by other authors. In our **Eastern** tree, however, these things have not yet been observed or are still unknown.

# TWENTY-NINTH CHAPTER.

## *Alliaria.* Onion Tree. <note>original: "Caju Bawang"</note>

This often grows into a huge and vast tree, which is sometimes so thick that two men can scarcely embrace it: Its trunk is straight, and slightly furrowed at the roots; the small branches are long, green, slightly angular, and marked above with a dark stripe or groove, firm, and at their origin flat or knotted, but in old trees the leaf-stalks <note>raches</note> are shorter, and are placed more abundantly and irregularly on the branchlets, which support the leaves placed somewhat in oblique rows, but above sometimes opposite, sometimes alternating.

These leaves sit on short stems <note>petioles</note> of common form, somewhat similar to the leaves of the **Lanset** <note>Lansium parasiticum</note>, but smoother and wider, pointed at the top, and this apex in old leaves is curved and bent backward, while on the upper part they are smooth, shining with a dark green color, and below they show many parallel lateral ribs at a distance of about a finger, and as a peculiar mark they have one lower part of the leaf much narrower and shorter than the upper, so that the large nerve does not run directly through the middle of the leaf, and the other part of the leaf extends longer at the stem, as in the leaves of the **Nightshade**.

They are six to nine inches long, three or four quatu- <note>Latin: quatuor, meaning four</note>

These same are also taken internally against poison, diarrhea, and burning fevers, for which however they consider the root to be better, and which they also use in their food to dye it yellow, and also for other things: Of which can be read more in that Author, but on our **East Indian** tree such things are not found, or are yet unknown.
