# XXIX. CHAPTER.

## Garlic-Tree. <note>Dutch: Look-Boom. This is likely Dysoxylum alliaceum, named for the garlic-like odor of its wood and leaves.</note>

This becomes a large and high tree, sometimes so thick that two men can scarcely embrace it: The trunk is straight, at the roots it has some buttresses <note>Dutch: vleugels, literally "wings"</note>; the twigs are long, green, a little angled, and above with a dark furrow, stiff, at their origin somewhat flat or with a node, though on the old trees they are shorter, and stand on the small branches quite many, and without order one after another, on which the leaves stand, somewhat in rows across from each other, though on the old trees some (namely the foremost) stand opposite each other, and some alternating, or differing on short stems.

They are of a common shape, somewhat like the **Lanse** <note>Langsat</note> leaves, yet smoother and wider, and at the front with a noticeable point, which on the old leaves stands crooked and bent backwards, on the upper side they are smooth, shining out of blackish-green, from below they show many parallel side-ribs, standing about a finger apart, and having as a special mark that the back half is noticeably narrower and shorter than the front, so that the large nerve does not go straight through the middle of the leaf, and the front half at the stem is also longer, like the **nightshade**.

They are from 6 to 9 inches long, 3 and 4 across vin- <note>Dutch: vinden, meaning find</note>

## AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chapter XXIX.

four fingers broad, rigid, dark green, and turning black when dry and fallen. The younger leaves on the branchlets are brown and have a more piercing odor than the old ones; indeed, all the leaves, when handled or kept in a room, give off the smell of Garlic <note>Latin: Allium</note>. From the base of the branchlets, a cluster sprouts out, a palm's length, divided into one or two lateral parts, from which numerous fruits grow, like those of the **Lansium** <note>A tropical fruit (Lansium domesticum) native to Southeast Asia</note>, but more scattered, and few reach full perfection; at first, they are greyish little globules, angular rather than round, marked with a small pit at the top. These fruits, if perfect, take on the appearance of small **Jambos** <note>Rose-apples (Syzygium species)</note>; four or five hang together from the clusters, some single like a small Plum, but most are double, resembling the scrotum of a dog <note>original Latin: "instar feroti canis", though the parallel Dutch text "kloot-zak" confirms the anatomical reference</note>. Externally, they are whitish or pale green like apples or white Rose-apples; beneath the outer husk lies another covering a thumb’s breadth thick and blood-red in color, which surrounds the inner nut just as **Mace** surrounds the **Nutmeg**. This covering, however, is smoother and invests the entire kernel; beneath this is found the true kernel, covered by another thin and woody shell, which however often does not enclose the whole nut. The nut itself is grass-green on the outside and whitish on the inside, and can be divided into three, four, or five segments by various curved lines, like a **Canarium** nut.

The outer husk gradually turns black, splits open, and releases the red kernel with its covering, which easily takes root upon touching the earth and sprouts new little trees. The single fruits are usually somewhat curved and irregular, shaped like a Kidney. Three kernels are also found, though very rarely, in one husk; if these fall to the ground, the wrapping loses its redness and degenerates into a dirty grey or blackish color; the older the kernel is, the greener it becomes.

The fruit, and especially the kernel, breathes a strong odor so similar to Garlic that it might be taken for it. The same odor is also perceived in the bark of the tree, so penetrating that it fills the whole house and can hardly be endured. In the green wood it is weaker, and in the dry wood it vanishes. It is most faint in the old leaves, yet still approaching the scent of Garlic. The bark of the trunk is greyish-green on the outside and often turns black; the wood is whitish, light, and soft.

**The Season.** Because the trees are so tall, it can hardly be observed at what time the flowers appear; thus the season is reckoned from when the ripe fruits fall, which happens in the months of February and March; and if they are not collected then, or are eaten by wild boars, a whole forest of young trees is seen beneath the old mother tree in the subsequent rainy months.

**Name.** In Latin *Alliaria*, from the natural smell of Garlic; in Malay *Caju-Bawang* <note>literally "Onion Wood" or "Garlic Wood"</note>; in Amboinese *Tamaluffel* and *Tamalaffe*.

**Location.** This tree grows in the high forests of the Amboinese islands, but not in great numbers, appearing only here and there. It is found mostly on Great Amboina, or in the region of Hitoe, especially near that great road that runs obliquely through that region; likewise in Leytimora near Hoettomoery; and it should be noted that this wood is erroneously taken by the inexperienced for the true *Caju-Lassi* <note>another local timber tree</note>, because of the similarity of the names.

**Use.** This fruit formerly served the Amboinese in place of Garlic and Onions, as it is still used by those who are accustomed to it and live in the forests; for the internal kernel, placed briefly on coals and roasted, then ground with Ginger and Lemon juice, provides a good condiment suited for fish. The younger and tender leaves, which give a stronger and more piercing odor than the old ones, are likewise boiled with fish for the sake of that Garlic smell. All these seasonings, however, are out of use today, after Garlic and Onions began to be transported annually from Java and other regions.

The wood is little used, except that planks are sometimes fashioned from it to build small dugout canoes <note>term: monoxyla</note>; the Amboinese used to tie the fallen kernels onto strings and dry them in smoke until they turned black on the outside, carrying them on sea voyages to prepare condiments. For this purpose, they would roast them over the fire and mix them with Ginger and roasted fish—

*fingers broad, stiff, arched-green, and the fallen dried ones become black: The young leaves on the budding twigs are brown and stronger in scent than the old ones, yet all the leaves generally, when handled a little or standing in a house, give off a garlic-like smell from them: From the bosom of the twigs comes forth a cluster, a hand long, and divided into one or two side-branches, where the fruits appear many together, like the **Lansium**, yet more sparse and few come to perfection, being at first grey little balls, angular out of the round, and with a little pit in front. The mature ones have the shape of small Rose-apples, hanging 4 or 5 in clusters together, some single, like a small plum, but most double, like the scrotum of a dog; from the outside whitish or pale-green, like Apples or white Rose-apples; under the outermost husk lies another covering a knife-blade thick, blood-red, and surrounding the inner Nut, just as the **Mace** does the **Nutmeg**, yet this covering is more even, and clothes the entire kernel; under this lies the true kernel, still surrounded by another thin and woody shell, which however often does not cover the entire kernel; the kernel itself is grass-green on the outside, and white on the inside, letting itself be divided with various curved lines into three, four, and five pieces, like a **Canarium**.*

*The outer shell becomes blackish in time, splits open, and lets the red kernel with its covering fall out, which upon reaching the earth easily shoots roots and brings forth new little trees: The single fruits are commonly somewhat crooked, and shaped like a kidney. One also finds (though very rarely) indeed three kernels in one husk, and when they fall from it onto the earth, the wrapping also changes its redness, and becomes ugly-grey or black, and the older the kernel, the greener it becomes.*

*The fruit, especially the kernel, has a strong smell, so like garlic that one would take it for such: the same smell is also in the bark of the tree, and there so strong that it fills the entire house, and one can hardly bear it: It is somewhat weaker in the green wood, but in the dry it vanishes; it is weakest in the old leaves, yet still smelling of garlic. The bark of the trunk is greyish-green on the outside, and almost black; the wood white, light, and not hard.*

***Season.*** *Because they are such high trees, one can hardly notice when the blossom comes forth, so one reckons its season when the ripe fruits begin to fall, which happens in February and March, and if one does not pick them up then, or if the wild Pigs do not snap them up, one finds in the following rain-months a whole thicket of young trees under the old ones.*

***Name.*** *In Latin **Alliaria**, from the natural garlic smell; in Malay **Caju-Bawang**: in Amboinese **Tamaluffel** and **Tamalaffe**.*

***Place.*** *This tree grows in the high Amboinese forests, yet by no means in abundance, and only here and there one: one finds it most on Great Amboina, or the land of Hitoe, especially around the great road that goes across the Land: Likewise on Leytimora near Hoettomoery, and it is also to be noted that the wood is abusively held by the inexperienced for the true **Caju-Lassi**, because of the similarity of the names.*

***Use.*** *In former times this fruit served the Amboinese in place of Onions and Garlic, as it still does for those who are used to it and live in the forest, for the inner kernels roasted a little on coals, and rubbed with Ginger and sour Lemon-juice, give a good sauce to eat with fish. The young and tender leaves, which smell stronger than the old ones, were also boiled with fish for the sake of the aforementioned smell, yet all those things have today fallen into decline or disuse, since one has begun to bring in Onions and Garlic annually from Java and other Lands.*

## CHAPTER THIRTY.

### *Cassia Fistula.*
<note>Latin: *Cassia fistula*, commonly known as the Golden Shower Tree or the Drumstick Tree.</note>

In the subsequent chapters of this book, certain trees will be described which bear fruits used equally for medicinal and culinary purposes, the majority of which are already known to us Europeans. We shall explain them here again, however, as there were still several things to be added which have been omitted or not fully perceived in European books.

First, therefore, we encounter the *Cassia Fistula* tree, of which many species and varieties are found in the East; namely, one with small and narrow leaves, and another with larger leaves. We shall treat only of the latter, as it is well known in these Oriental islands and has not, to my knowledge, been fully described with its entire form in European books.

It is a tall and widely spreading tree, shaped like a Walnut tree, though its crown is somewhat broader, bearing a smooth bark of a pale ashen color. The leaves sit upon long, straight stalks in two opposing rows, shaped like those of a Walnut or Ash tree, although they differ from them significantly. There are five or seven pairs to a single stalk, and rarely an odd one at the end <note>The leaves are paripinnate, meaning they end in a pair rather than a single leaflet</note>. They are of a common shape, rounded at the bottom and slightly pointed at the top, generally five inches long and over two inches wide, woven with many thin and mostly parallel ribs that can scarcely be felt by touch. The lower leaves, however, are only three inches long, similar to *Lingoo* <note>original: *Lingoo*; referring to *Pterocarpus indicus* or the Angsana tree</note> leaves, smooth, at first a bright green, then turning blackish and tasteless. In most European books, they are compared to Peach leaves, but I have never found them so narrow, even on quite old trees. Furthermore, each leaf sits on a short and somewhat thick petiole, which resembles a small knob, and the stalks are placed closely together at the ends of the branches, bearing a thick "joint" at their origin.

The flowers come forth in large and extended clusters, which are immense and almost resemble the shape of Violets, but they are larger. Each sits upon a long green stalk; they are not crowded together but stand loosely, yet by their weight they pull the cluster downward. Each flower consists of five yellow petals, of which the three lower ones hang extended to the sides, while the two upper ones are hunched and curved inward. In the center appear various long, greenish filaments, slightly curved with ashen anthers, four of which extend beyond the flower. The middle one of these is longer, thicker, and greener than the others, curved like a sickle and simple (this is the pistil), which grows into the fruit. Thus, from one flower only a single fruit or pod germinates, and not two or three as some have falsely thought; however, most of the flowers turn into fruit, and few fall away in vain.

And these fruits are those long pods or "pipes" well known everywhere, about two feet long, some straight

<column-break/>

roasting it over the fire, and then rubbing it in water with ginger and a roasted fish head, adding some lemon juice if they have it, and straining it through a cloth, which is then the proper sauce to eat with their Papeda. What Papeda is has been said here above in the Chapter on Sago.

The wood is also used for beams in houses and for roof-work, because it is light and nonetheless durable. The young leaves are also cooked with fish to give them a scent and flavor.

## CHAPTER XXX.

### *The Drumstick Tree.*

In the following chapters of this book, several trees shall be described from which one obtains such fruits that, being used as much for medicine as for food, are for the most part known to us Europeans; yet we cite them again because here and there several things fell to be added which are not yet known in European books.

And first there appears before us the tree of *Cassia Fistula*, which is found in the East in many forms; namely, one with small or narrow leaves, and the other with larger ones, of which latter we shall only treat, as it is known in these Eastern Islands and (to my knowledge) has not yet been described in European books in its full form.

It is then a high and widely spreading tree, in appearance like a Walnut tree, but quite as broad of crown, with a smooth and pale-grey bark. The leaves stand on long, straight stalks in two rows across from one another, in the shape of Walnut or Ash leaves, although they differ somewhat from them, with 5 and 7 pairs to a stalk, and seldom with a single one at the front. They are of common shape, round at the back and tapering to a short point at the front, usually 5 inches long and a good two wide, shot through with many fine and mostly parallel ribs that one can hardly feel. The hindmost leaves are only 3 inches long and like the *Lingoo* leaves, smooth, cheerful green, but finally black-green and tasteless. In most all European books they are compared to the leaves of a Peach tree, but I have never found them so narrow, even on reasonably old trees. Each leaf stands on a short, thickish little stalk, which rather resembles a bud, and the stalks stand close together at the front of the branches, having a thick little joint at their origin.

The blossom comes forth on large and extended clusters; on them one sees large flowers in the shape of violets, but larger, each on a long green stalk, not crowded but standing loosely from one another, yet which nevertheless by their weight bend the cluster down somewhat. Each is made of 5 yellow petals, of which the three lowermost hang curved outwards, the uppermost are humped and curved inwards, and inside there stand several greenish and long threads, also a little curved with grey tips, of which four stick out beyond the flower. Of these, the middle one is yet longer, thicker, and greener than the others, curved like a sickle and without a tip, from which the fruit comes forth, so that from one flower only one fruit or pod grows, and not two or more as some have thought, although the most part of the flowers become fruits, and few come to fall off.

And these fruits now are the long pods or pipes, well known everywhere, about two feet long, some straight

...[pods], but most are slightly curved, oblong-round, like a staff <note>original: "instar baculi"</note>, barely an inch wide, and marked by a seam along the length on one side, as if they were sewn together there. At first, they are green and so soft that they can be bent, but when mature they grow hard and woody; some are a deep brown on the outside, while others turn black, smooth, and marked with thin transverse rings, such as one sees in intestines. Inside, they are divided into cells, which are filled nearly halfway with a soft and black pulp, and in each a small stone <note>the seed</note> is hidden, just as they are known in Europe, offering a sweet and nauseating taste. This pulp is the only thing sought from this tree, which is why these fruits or pods are transported to Europe for medical use. The scent of the flowers is faint, yet pleasant, and especially so in the morning.

The wood of this tree is solid, pale yellow, heavy, and hard; in older trees, it is reddish, and around the heart, it is grayish-black, eventually turning entirely black like Lignum Vitae <note>original: "Guajacum," a very hard, dark wood</note>, which is nonetheless rarely seen on these islands.

**Name.** In Latin, it is *Cassia Fistula*, *Cassia Solutiva* <note>Solutive Cassia</note>, *Cathartica* <note>Purgative</note>, *Siliqua Ægyptia* <note>Egyptian Pod</note>, and among pharmacists, *Canna Fistula* <note>Pipe-Reed</note>. In Dutch, *Trommel-stokken* <note>Drumsticks</note>. By the Arabs, *Cassaat Falus* and incorrectly *Gafat Falus*, which seems to be a corruption of *Cassia Fistula*. Avicenna calls it *Chajar Xambar*, or more properly *Chyar Schambar*, which denotes a "long cucumber" measured by spans. The first mention of it occurs in the Greek physician Actuarius, who calls this *Cassia* "Melæna" <note>original: "Melænam," from the Greek word for black</note>. In Egypt and Persia today, it is still called *Hiar Xambar*, but the *X* should be read as *Sh*. The Indian names in the Gujarati language are *Gramala*, and further along the Malabar coast to Cape Comorin, *Condoca*, *Hafangua*, *Bava Simgua*. In Canara, *Baboo*, etc. In the Malay and Macassarese languages, some call it *Caju Radja* <note>King’s Wood</note>, while others, mostly the Balinese, call it *Caju Dulang*. In the native Amboinese language, it is called *Uttamanu*; in Hitu, *Pappe pauna*, which signifies something with which one's back is struck. By the Javanese, it is called *Bongoe alas* and *Tangkuli*, or something wild. The Arabic and Persian names are taken from the oblong shape of the *Chyar* or cucumber, but the word *Cassia* is taken from the shape of the pipes <note>original: "fistularum," referring to the hollow, reed-like pods</note>. Just as the bark of aromatic *Cassia* or Cinnamon <note>Canella</note> is stripped from its tree, this name comes from the Hebrew *Ketzia* signifying the same, and that from *Kazar* meaning to scrape or skin, because the bark of Cinnamon is skinned from its tree.

In Figure 22 of the *Hortus Malabaricus*, it is called *Conna* in the Malabar tongue and *Bajo* by the Brahmins; its description agrees mostly with ours, though the illustration differs slightly. Piso in Book 4, Chapter 22, calls it *Tapiraco-Aynana* in the Brazilian language, but attributes smaller leaves and flesh-colored flowers to it; in Mexico, it is called *Guauhay Ohuatli*. In Ceylon, *Æhæla*.

**Place.** Since these pipes were unknown to the ancients <note>referring to Greek and Roman botanists</note>, I believe they are found frequently nowhere but in the regions of Ethiopia and around the sea coasts inhabited by the Troglodytes, whom the Arabs call by the common name *Zangi* or *Zingi* <note>Zanj, the historic name for the East African coast</note>, a trace of which is found in the Indian name mentioned above, *Bava Sanguia*, which perhaps denotes a tree from *Sangi* or Ethiopia. From there, these trees were undoubtedly transferred to Egypt and other regions, although today they occur frequently in the region of Cambay and other provinces of ancient India. They also grow spontaneously in the forests of Java and Bali, but rarely in Macassar. In these Eastern islands, only here and there has a tree or two sprouted from seeds brought in. They love hard and clayey soil, which is why they grow more happily in the Hitu region than in sandy Leitimor. Some of these trees are also found in Banda, but they are more frequent in Makian and the Moluccas. The modern Spaniards in the West Indian islands, especially in Dominica and San Juan de Puerto Rico, have these fruits so plentiful and fine that, in the opinion of Monardes (in *Simple Medicines*, Chapter 44), they are not inferior to the Oriental ones but are, on the contrary, preferred. Thus, they are mostly transported to Europe from there, since they can be shipped in the space of two months, while the Oriental ones are at least six months distant. Among the latter, the best are considered to be those brought from Cambay, which the Portuguese also bring to their own homeland; for the Dutch take none from the East...

...they bring it from India in this way, although, as has been said, it can be obtained more fresh and more quickly from the Caribbean Islands or from Alexandria.

*Usage.* This medicinal pulp is tempered in heat and humidity, but the heat prevails. I do not wish to recount everything here regarding its powers and use, as they can be found sufficiently in other books. It is truly surprising that this medicine—to which our European surgeons attribute such great and reasoned utility—is so little valued by the inhabitants of the Water-Indies <note>the Indonesian archipelago</note>, even though it occurs everywhere there, as has been mentioned. For the Malays, Javanese, Macassarese, and others hardly deem it worthy of being consumed; indeed, the common folk consider it harmful. As long as they can obtain any other purgative, they will not use these pods. This, however, is by no means to be attributed to a fault in the medicine, but rather to the ignorance of the inhabitants. Many of them, however, have been better taught by our Europeans and are now beginning to use it in our manner. Generally, this pulp is not liked when dissolved in water or any other liquid to be taken as a drink; instead, they used to suck out these pods and then take some drink or eat some food afterward, so as not to cause such nausea to the palate and throat. It seems, moreover, that the Javanese and other Indians have recoiled from the use of these pods because an old fable has long been spread among the common people—and believed by many—that cows eating the green pods under these trees not only fall into diarrhea, but also those who eat their meat. This, however, was long ago refuted by Garcia da Orta <note>A 16th-century Portuguese physician in India</note> in Book 1, Chapter 29, and by others.

*The green and soft pods are first boiled slightly in water by the Portuguese, then dried again and preserved with sugar. They transport these packed in vessels to Portugal for the use of women, children, and other delicate people, for they cause a bowel movement without distress. For the same purpose and in a similar manner, the flowers are prepared into a preserve, both whole and crushed. The pulp extracted from these pods with the help of warm water and reduced again into a thick electuary <note>a medicinal paste mixed with honey or syrup</note> can be eaten without a drink, adding a small amount of ginger and anise seed to prevent the griping of the abdomen and intestines to which delicate people are otherwise often prone. Those who suffer from a weak stomach and are troubled by mucous and flaccid intestines should not use this pulp much, as it harms the stomach, unless some rhubarb or myrobalan <note>a dried plum-like fruit used as a laxative</note> is added.*

*Children also play with these green pods, which they bend into bracelets, for they can easily be folded together without cracking and threaded with a string. The pulp should always be used half an hour before food to soften and loosen the belly; however, to cleanse the kidneys and bladder, it should be taken two hours before food, as this thick pulp is otherwise not sufficiently digested unless aided by food at the same time. One should not keep it long in the stomach, as it is quite contrary to it. Furthermore, it should be noted that Cassia not only purges the intestines but also penetrates to the remote parts, namely to the kidneys and bladder, serving both by cleansing those parts and soothing their pains.*

*The particular power of Cassia is first to discharge bilious humors and then also to dissolve phlegmatic ones that stick in narrow passages and cause obstructions there. If a small amount is taken after dinner when we go to bed, and swallowed slowly, it benefits those who suffer from catarrhs <note>excessive mucus</note> of the lungs and are prone to them, becoming short of breath and asthmatic. Furthermore, it is held as a secret remedy against all kidney diseases if this pulp is taken mixed with liquorice and sugar; indeed, it is said that if taken often prepared in such a way, it prevents kidney stones.*

*Bontius <note>Jacobus Bontius, a Dutch physician in Batavia</note> in Book 6, Chapter 10, mixes in Venice Turpentine and uses it to cleanse the kidneys and gonorrhea, where he also warns that Cassia should not be used in the East Indies for dysentery or bilious cholera...*

<column-break/>

...of those mentioned, the best are considered to be those coming from Cambay <note>a port in Gujarat, India</note>, which the Portuguese also bring to their country; for the Dutch do not export them from the East Indies because, as said, they can be obtained fresher and sooner from the Caribbean Islands or from Alexandria.

Usage. *This medicinal pulp is tempered in heat and moisture, though the heat is somewhat greater. I do not wish to list everything about its powers and use here because one finds it sufficiently in other books; and it is to be wondered that this medicine, to which our European masters (not without reason) attribute so much utility, is so little esteemed by the inhabitants of the Water-Indies, although, as said, it is found everywhere. For the Malays, Javanese, Macassarese, etc., hardly deem it worthy to be taken; indeed, the common folk hold it for a harmful thing, and as long as they can get any other purgatives, they will not use these sticks. Yet this must by no means be attributed to the defects of the medicine, but to the ignorance of the locals. For many have now been better instructed by our Europeans and are now beginning to use it in our fashion. Generally, people do not care for it when the pulp is made so thin in water or some moisture that it must be drunk, but they used to eat the sticks out of hand and then take a drink on it, or consume some food afterward, so that it would not cause so much loathing in the mouth and throat. It seems that the Javanese and other Indians have been frightened away from the use of these pipes because an old fable has reached the common man—and is also partly believed by most—that cows grazing on the green pipes under these trees not only get the belly-run themselves, but also those who eat of their meat, which has long before this been refuted by Garcia da Orta, Book 1, Chapter 29, and by others.*

*The green, soft pipes are first boiled a bit in water by the Portuguese, thereafter dried again and preserved with sugar, and so they carry them in whole small barrels to Portugal for the use of women, children, and other delicate people: for they provoke a bowel movement without trouble. To the same end and in a like manner, the flower is also made into a preserve, both whole and ground. The pulp drawn from these pipes with warm water and brought again to a thick electuary can also be eaten out of hand without adding any moisture, but with a little ginger and aniseed to prevent the cutting in the belly or intestines, to which delicate people are otherwise subject from this pulp. Also, those who are weak of stomach and slippery of bowel must not use it much, because it is hindering to the stomach, or they should add some rhubarb or myrobalans to it.*

*Children also play with the green pipes, making them into bracelets, for they allow themselves to be bent entirely together without tearing and pierced with a thread. They must always be used before eating—namely, to merely soften the belly, half an hour before; but to cleanse the kidneys and bladder, a couple of hours before, because this thick pulp will not otherwise descend unless it is pressed down by the food. It also should not remain long in the stomach because it is so contrary to it; whereby one must also know that Cassia not only cleanses the intestines but also penetrates to the distant parts, such as the kidney and bladder, for both of which it is good, cleansing them and soothing the pains.*

*The actual power of Cassia is indeed to carry off or set aside the bilious humors, but after that, it also attacks the phlegmatic ones, and especially those sticking in narrow passages and causing obstructions there. Taken a little after eating when one wants to go to sleep, swallowing it slowly, it helps those who are tormented with catarrhs on the chest and resulting shortness of breath. Against all ailments of the kidneys, it is held for a secret remedy when one mixes this pulp with liquorice and sugar and takes it so; indeed, they say that those who use it often would be freed from the kidney stone.*

...bilious, and brings on fevers, because if it remains in the stomach too long, it easily turns into bile itself. The **Egyptians** mix it with **Agaric** <note>a type of medicinal fungus used as a purgative</note> and use it against coughs and **asthma**, as well as against all pains of the joints arising from heat, such as "hot" **gout** <note>original: "podagram"</note>. They apply it to the affected area in the form of a plaster, and if used in this way, it cures all hot tumors, inflammations, and **St. Anthony’s Fire** <note>original: "Eryſipelas," a skin infection</note>. Those who suffer from **quinsy** <note>original: "κυνάνχῃ," a severe throat inflammation</note> or inflammatory angina, and gargle with this pulp dissolved in **plantain water** <note>original: "aqua Plantaginis"</note> or a similar liquid, find great relief therein. Furthermore, when smeared on the outside, it cures all mange and impurity of the skin, and ripens abscesses.

These "pipes" <note>the long, cylindrical seed pods</note> must be kept in dry and closed places; for if they are exposed to damp air or dew, they contract mold and are ruined within a year. In **India**, however, people do not care so much about this, since fresh ones can always be obtained.

The **Egyptians** teach us that these fresh pipes should not be taken internally unless they have been picked from the tree for four to six months, as they otherwise cause diarrhea. Once the **Cassia** pulp is extracted, it cannot be kept good for twenty-four hours unless preserved in closed boxes, and even then, it is not as good as if it were freshly extracted. This pulp cannot endure boiling, as it then loses its laxative power. The **Balinese** take the fresh bark of the trunk, cleaned of the outer gray layer, and having pounded and mixed it finely, they apply it as a plaster externally to all limbs, and especially to those who have been burned by gunpowder, as well as applying it to wounds torn by explosions, by which they successfully draw out the burning heat.

The seeds enclosed in the small cells, if they are fresh, smooth, and full, and are committed to the earth, grow within a year into small trees five or six feet high. In this way, I took care to propagate these trees on the coast of **Hitoe** <note>a region in Ambon</note>, where our soldiers fared much better (using their pulp as a daily purgative) than from the uncertain preparations of the **Chemists** <note>referring to alchemical or early pharmaceutical compounds</note> which are carelessly made, yet are sent to our Governors from the fatherland at great expense. From the **Caribbean Islands**, the **French** also carry them back to their own country, finding them better and fuller than those brought from the **East Indies**. In those islands, they grow abundantly in vast and level forests, where these dry pipes, hanging on the trees and striking one another when driven by the wind, excite such a clatter and sound that not only do animals and birds take flight, but even foreigners and newcomers think they hear the surging of the sea in their ears—though it is often very far away—or sometimes they think a troop of armed soldiers is approaching. At this same sound, the monkeys and long-tailed macaques, which inhabit these trees in great numbers, congregate in **Java** and **Bali**.

The **Caribs** use this pulp every month, an hour or so before a meal, to clear the body of all impurity, and they have found that by this means they keep their bodies healthy and unharmed. The **Cassia fistula** growing in the **American** islands and regions is said to be smaller, bearing yellowish leaves and small, bright red flowers, and in all things to agree very well with the following "wild" **Cassia fistula**, as was told to me by an eyewitness.

Likewise, the **Javanese Pipe-Reed** <note>original: "Canna Fiſtula Javanica"</note> growing around **Karawang** and in the district of **Cirebon** bears small leaves, similar in order and shape to the small **Bilimbi** <note>original: "Blimbingh Buloe," a sour tropical fruit</note>. The flowers are also much smaller than those described above, but larger than those of the Bilimbi, colored with a mixture of bright red and white. The pods, however, are like the preceding ones, and the wood is yellowish, knotty, and does not easily split lengthwise. In older trunks, the core is a dark brownish-black, heavy, and a durable wood, so that it is much used there for house posts. These trees are also durable in the ground in **Java**, **Bali**, and **Makassar**. Cows graze on the leaves if they can reach them, but not the pods, and the people use the bark of the trunk in the absence of **Areca nut** <note>original: "Pinangæ"</note>, chewing it with **Betel leaf** <note>original: "Siri"</note> and lime; this is only done by the common folk, however. This bark is quite brittle and dry when chewed, almost like old Areca nut, but there is some mucilage mixed with it, which is why the **Javanese** also mix it into their **Bobori** ointment so that it might stick better. Finally, it should be noted—

## Book II. Chapter XXX. AMBOINESE HERBAL. 87

it must be noted from the teaching of the Egyptians that not only should recent pipes <note>original: "fistulas"; the long, cylindrical seed pods</note> not be used for internal use, but neither should immature ones, which do not yet turn black on the outside, since they easily cause Dysentery <note>original: "Dysenteriam"; a severe inflammation of the intestines</note>.

The root, dug up on dry days, slightly roasted under hot ashes, cut into small pieces, and chewed with Siri-Pinanga <note>a quid of betel leaf and areca nut</note>, or ground with water and drunk, is beneficial to those who have swallowed poison; for this purpose, the dug-up root should be kept dry. In Java, this fruit is rarely or hardly ever used for medicinal purposes, but the old wood of the tree is used for the sheaths of *Parrangs* <note>original: "Parrangharum"; a type of large Javanese knife or machete</note>, as well as for small posts in house building.

In Java, there are three species of Cassia, all of which bear smaller leaves than ours, some of which are no larger than those of the *Blimbingh Boeloe* <note>the cucumber tree, Averrhoa bilimbi</note>, and they differ mostly in the color of the flowers. The first of these species bears white flowers; the second has flowers that are purple on the outside and white on the inside—both of these perhaps correspond with the following wild Cassia Fistula. The third enjoys yellow flowers, and the true medicinal pod is called *Tanguli Ginteng* by the Javanese. The Javanese use a decoction of the leaves or a mash made from them for mild purges, but the pulp of the pipes is used to adulterate opium, for which it serves better than the previously mentioned *Bilac* fruit <note>Bael fruit or wood apple</note>.

### OBSERVATION.

This tree is called in the *Clifford Garden page 158*: *Cassia with leaflets of five pairs, lance-shaped, the outermost smaller*, which is the *Alexandrian Cassia Fistula* of Caspar Bauhin in his *Pinax page 403*, and of Commelin in the first part of the *Amsterdam Garden page 215, Figure 110*. It is also the *Black or First Pipe Cassia*, or *Alexandrian Cassia Fistula* according to Sloane’s *Catalogue of Jamaican Plants page 145*, and the *Purgative Cassia* of Jean Bauhin, volume 1, page 416. It is the *Black Cassia* of Dodoens in his *Pemptades page 787*, and called *Cassia Fistula Chairaxambar* by Prosper Alpinus in his *Plants of Egypt, page 2, Plate 1*. For other synonyms, see our *Treasury of Ceylon page 56*, regarding the Ceylonese Cassia Fistula, as well as in Sloane’s *Catalogue*, and in the new quarto edition of Samuel Dale’s *Pharmacologia page 369*. See further Valentini’s *History of Simple Medicines Reformed page 234*, where he has a splendid illustration of this tree, which nevertheless differs greatly from those in the *Amsterdam Garden* and the *Garden of Malabar, part 1, Plate 22*. Furthermore, see other species of *Cassia Fistula* proposed in Pomet’s *History of Drugs, chapter 27, page 217*. An illustration of it is likewise shown in Blackwell’s *Herbal, Plate 381*.

However, all these illustrations differ so much from one another that this variety should be attributed not to different climates or soils, but to various species of this genus. Thus, I conclude that the trees which provide the pods of the Cassia Fistula are entirely different and distinct, which will be clear enough to those who study and compare the various figures of the praised authors with an attentive mind.

<column-break/>

to make the same more sticky: Finally, it remains to be added here that, according to the prescribed lesson of the Egyptians, one must not only avoid using freshly picked Drumsticks <note>original: "Trommelstokken"; a common name for the long Cassia pods</note>, but also unripe ones, which are not yet black-brown on the outside, for internal use, as they very easily provoke a bloody flux <note>original: "bloet-gang"; dysentery</note>.

The root, dug up on dry days, slightly roasted under hot ashes, cut into small pieces, and chewed with Siri-Pinang, or ground with water and drunk, helps those who are poisoned, and for that purpose, one can also keep the dug-up root dry. On Java, the fruit is little or not at all used as medicine, but indeed the old wood is used for the sheaths of *Parrangs* <note>machetes</note>, and small posts in house building.

On Java, one has three kinds of Cassia, all with smaller leaves than ours, some of which are no larger than those of the *Blimbin Boeloe*, and are mostly distinguished by the color of the flowers. The first bears white flowers, and the second is purple on the outside and white on the inside, both perhaps corresponding with the following wild Cassia Fistula. The third bears yellow flowers, and the actual medicinal variety is called *Tanguli Ginteng* in Javanese. The Javanese use a decoction of the leaves or a mash made from them for mild purges, but with the marrow of the pipes <note>the medicinal pulp</note>, opium is adulterated, for which it serves better than the fruits of the aforementioned *Bilac*.

# CHAPTER THIRTY-ONE.
## The Wild Pipe Cassia.

The wild Pipe Cassia <note>original: "Canna fistula silvestris"; likely referring to *Cassia javanica* or a similar species</note> is a tall tree, usually rising with a straight trunk, or sometimes slightly curved, bearing a narrow crown. Its bark is smooth, ash-gray or pale yellow. From the branches, long and straight stalks <note>original: "raches"</note> emerge alternately, and on these are small leaves similar to the small *Blimbing* <note>The Bilimbi or cucumber tree, *Averrhoa bilimbi*</note>, placed in long, opposing rows, with fourteen to seventeen pairs on a single stalk. They are two to two and a half inches long, barely an inch wide, rounded at the top, smooth, and sea-green or emerald green. At the base of each stalk near the branch are two small scales, resembling little ears or the Mesentery <note>the membrane attaching the intestines to the abdominal wall</note> when spread out, as they are mostly folded together. The lower or older stalks lack these, or bear only one. The bark of the branches is smooth, even, and brownish-black. The flowers hang together in clusters, matching the form of the true Pipe Cassia <note>the medicinal *Cassia fistula*</note>, but they are much smaller, like the flowers of the smallest beans. In one species, they are pale yellow; in the other, they are a bright red. These are followed by fruits or pods <note>original: "siliquæ"</note> hanging in clusters, which are long pipes, entirely similar to the Pipe Cassia or even longer, barely an inch thick. When they ripen, they turn ash-gray on the outside, but are not as smooth as the medicinal Cassia. They are curved and narrow near the stem, but rounded at the tip with a firm point. The shell of these pods is thicker than in the Pipe Cassia and shows protruding rings on the outside, like those seen on the bellies of snakes. Inside, these pods are also divided into cells, but in these, no black and juicy pulp is stored; instead, it is dry, whitish, tough, and spongy <note>original: "fungosa"</note>, filling the entire cell. This covers a round and flat seed <note>original: "officulum"</note>, shaped like a compressed pea, which is hard, shining, saffron-yellow or light brown, and divided by a groove through the middle. The wood is pale yellow and consists of thick fibers; it is sappy, tough, and heavy when green, but dries out pale without a noticeable heartwood and cannot be easily worked unless it is from very old trees.

**Name.** In Latin, *Cassia* or *Canna fistula silvestris*, meaning wild Pipe Cassia, according to common speech, because it is of less use than the true one; for otherwise, both these trees grow wild in the forests. The Malay name is unknown to me. In Amboina, the people of Luhu call it **Barus**; those of Hitu call it **Habay-muli** and **Hea-muli**, which signifies something with which one's back is struck, like the previously mentioned *Pappe-Pauma*; for the Hitu language varies according to the different villages. The white species is called **Habya Mulippal**, that is, the spongy one. To the Javanese, it is called **Caju Backat**.

**Location.** It occurs rarely in Amboina; formerly many were found in Hitu, but today most have perished. In the year 1668, I found a double tree that had grown with two tall trunks in the Luhu region near the district of Luciella, which was said to have been planted there long ago by foreigners. There, in the month of May, I found nearly ripe fruit but no flowers. I later learned that they grow abundantly everywhere on little Ceram, Bonoa, Manipa, as well as in Celebes <note>modern Sulawesi</note>.

**Use.** In the medical arts, this tree is of no use, at least among the Amboinese. It is mostly planted for the pleasure of old men, who like to gently beat their backs with these pipes <note>the long, sturdy seed pods</note> so that they do not become too stiff—a condition common to old age. For this reason, it might also be called *Solatium senum*, that is, "Old Men’s Comfort." However, the seeds have some use in medicine; when ground with water and drunk, they help those who have carelessly eaten harmful fish or crabs. Furthermore, the inner pulp has no use but dries out completely hard. The wood of the red species is more saffron-yellow, harder, and more solid, and thus more useful for certain posts; but the white species gives a whitish wood

# CHAPTER XXXI.
## The Wild Drumstick Tree.

The wild *Canna Fistula* becomes a tall tree, usually with a straight trunk, or also somewhat crooked and a narrow crown. The bark is smooth, light gray, or pale. On the branches stand long, straight twigs, arranged alternately, and on these are small leaves, like those of the small *Blimbings*, directly opposite one another in long rows—specifically from 14 to 17 pairs on one twig. They are two and a half inches long, scarcely one wide, rounded at the front, smooth, and sea-green or emerald green. At the branch are two green flaps in the shape of an ear, or Mesentery, if one spreads them out, for they mostly stand folded together; the rear or oldest twigs do not have them, or perhaps only one. The bark of the branches is even, smooth, and black-brown. The blossom hangs in clusters together, shaped like that of the true *Canna Fistula*, though much smaller, namely like that of the smallest beans. In one kind they are pale yellow, and in the other light red. Following these are the husks or fruits, also hanging in bunches together, and they are long pipes, entirely like the *Canna Fistula* or even as long, barely an inch thick. When they ripen, they are gray on the outside, crooked and narrow at the stem, but rounded at the front with a stiff thorn or point, and the shell is thicker than the *Canna Fistula*. This shell shows some protruding rings on the outside, like the belly of a snake. Inside they are also divided into chambers, but therein lies no black and juicy matter, but a dry, white, tough, and spongy pith, filling the entire chamber, and which hides a round, flat grain in the shape of a pressed pea—hard, shining, deep yellow or light brown, and divided across the middle with a groove. The wood is pale yellow, coarse-grained, sappy, tough, and heavy when it is green, but dries out easily without apparent heartwood, and does not allow itself to be worked, unless it be from very old trees.

**Name.** In Latin *Canna* or *Cassia Fistula Silvestris*, that is, wild *Canna Fistula*, after the common way of speaking, because it is used less than the true one; for otherwise both these trees grow in the wild. The Malay name is unknown to me. In Amboina the Luhu people call it **Barus**, the Hitu people **Hahay Muli** and **Hea Muli**, that is, something with which one strikes the back, like the previous *Pappe Pauma*, for the Hitu language is diverse or different according to its villages. The white variety they call **Hahya Mulippal**, that is, the spongy one. In Javanese, **Caju Backat**.

**Place.** One finds them little in Amboina; formerly many stood on Hitu, but nowadays they have mostly died out. In the year 1668, I still found a double tree that had shot up with two high trunks on the Luhu land, near the village of Luciella, which was said to have been planted there in former times by foreigners. On it, I found nearly ripe fruits in May, though no blossoms; later I learned that they grow much everywhere on little Ceram, Bonoa, Manipa, as well as on Celebes.

**Use.** In medicine this tree is in no use (at least among the Amboinese), and it is mostly planted for the convenience of old men, who take pleasure in gently tapping their backs with these pipes so that they do not become too stiff, a defect common to old age; therefore one might well call it *Solatium Senum*, that is, old men's comfort. The seeds, however, still have some powers in medicine; for being rubbed with water and drunk, they help those who have incautiously eaten some harmful fish or crabs. Furthermore, the inner pith has no use, but dries up entirely hard. The wood of the red variety is a deeper yellow, firmer, and therefore useful for some posts; but the white

...and is almost spongy, similar to *Gabba Gabba* <note>original: "Gabba Gabba"; the dried midribs of sago palm leaves, used as a light building material</note>, which is why it is not in common use. If, however, it should happen by chance that someone, by the striking of these pipes <note>the long, tube-like seed pods</note>, breaks them upon their own back, they consider it an ill omen; yet it is actually good fortune, for it is better for this pipe to be broken than one's own back.

I believe it will not be useless to add here certain trees that bear such leaves and similar pods, although I am unsure whether they are related to the preceding ones or not, as I describe them from the reports of others.

The *Andawas* or *Dawas* is a tree growing in Bali, and it is most closely related to the previous ones; for it bears leaves similar to the sour *Blimbing* <note>The Bilimbi or cucumber tree, *Averrhoa bilimbi*</note>, and yellowish-white flowers in the shape of the *Bonga-Manoor* <note>Arabian Jasmine, *Jasminum sambac*</note>. The fruit is like the Pipe Cassia, but they never turn so black. Its seeds are darker and more wrinkled than those of the previous trees, and the pulp degenerates into a white *Capock* <note>The silk-cotton fiber of the Kapok tree</note> and vanishes in the wind. If the bark of the tree is cut, it pours out a copious milk <note>sap</note> that is harmful to the eyes, which distinguishes it from the previous trees that lack this milk. Its wood is white and consists of fine fibers; once dried, it is used to make the sheaths of daggers called *Krissen* <note>traditional wavy-bladed daggers</note>, which the Balinese carve from a single piece and do not wrap in rattan as the people of Makassar do. It is said that pillars in royal palaces are also made from it, and therefore the common people are forbidden from cutting these trees, whose trunks are sometimes as thick as two men.

The Balinese claim that the souls of the damned are placed under this tree, and there they are continually tormented as if they were being pierced by *Kris* daggers.

The crushed leaves of this tree are applied to inflamed and burning eyes.

In Makassar, another similar tree is found, bearing such leaves and fruit, called *Bilalangh*. However, this tree has a hard and brown heartwood from which the Kings' tobacco boxes and betel-nut cases are made, as well as other small baskets, since it is very hard and takes a high polish. Our people take its wood for *Caliature* wood <note>original: "Ligno Caliaturensi"; Red Sanderswood, *Pterocarpus santalinus*, a prized dye-wood from India</note>, which is otherwise brought from the Coromandel Coast. The people of Makassar, however, say it differs from that, as the color of *Bilalangh* is paler than *Caliature*; another wood called *Catudju* has an even paler color. Both bear pod-like fruits and small leaves, and are found in Makassar planted near courtyards and in gardens. On the eastern coast of Celebes near Tambucco, the *Wild Pipe Cassia* <note>original: "Canna Fistula Silvestris"</note> frequently occurs and is called there *Ke-Ule* or *Caju-Ular*—that is, "Snake-tree"—from the shape of the fruits, which are longer there than in other places. It grows in the wild, and the fruits are not used, but its older trunks are sought after and collected for making pillars for the houses of the nobility. These are heavy and difficult to fetch from the forest, yet they are durable, even underground. They have an elegant, polished, solid, and yellow wood, which is reddish and brown around the heart. Its fruits, sent to me in the year 1680, showed a great difference from the true Pipe Cassia; they were much longer, about three feet long, over a finger thick, black in color, and externally divided into dark segments like the belly of a viper. Inside, they contained cells similar to those in the true variety, but in each place where the pulp should be, there was a thick disc, as if it were a small piece for a board game <note>original: "alvei lusorii"; likely referring to checkers or backgammon pieces</note>, consisting of a thick, dry, and tough substance. Within this was hidden a flat seed, thicker and rounder than in the Pipe Cassia. From this, I immediately recognized it was not the medicinal but the wild Pipe Cassia, which I later found to be true; for the seeds, when planted, sent forth small trees bearing such small leaves as described above. I compared the wood of both the domestic and wild Pipe Cassia from old trunks and found them to be almost the same—both solid, fine-grained, and yellow—though the wood of the domestic variety tended toward black around the heart, while the wild one tended toward dark red. In Celebes, both have the same Malay name, *Caju radja*, that is, "King’s wood," because kings and nobles mostly build the pillars of their houses from these woods. The leaves...

In my judgment, it will not be unhelpful to add several other trees here that also bear such or similar leaves and pods, although it is unknown to me whether they have any relationship with the previous ones or not, as they are described from the accounts of others.

The *Andawas* or *Dawas* is a tree growing on Bali, having the most in common with the preceding; for it would also have leaves like the sour *Blimbings* <note>Bilimbi fruit</note>, the flowers white-yellow, shaped like the *Bonga Manoor* <note>Jasmine</note>, the fruits like the *Pipe Cassia* <note>original: "Canna Fistula"</note>, though they would never turn so black. When one cuts into the bark, much milk <note>sap</note> would flow out, and the same is harmful to the eyes, in which it differs from the previous ones, which do not have this milk. The wood is white and fine-grained, from which, once dried, the *Kris sheaths* <note>daggers</note> are made, which the *Balinese* take from a single piece and do not bind with rattan, as the *Makassarese* do. It is also said that pillars are made from it in the palaces of the Kings, and therefore the common man is forbidden from cutting them; these trunks become as thick as two men.

The Balinese say that the *souls of the damned* are placed under this tree, and that they would constantly feel such pain as someone who is stabbed with *Krissen* <note>daggers</note>.

The crushed leaves are also laid upon burning and inflamed eyes.

On *Makassar*, they have another tree with similar leaves and fruits, called *Bilalangh*, but this has a hard and brown heart inside, from which the Kings make their tobacco and betel boxes, as well as other small trays, because it becomes very hard and smooth. Our people take it for *Caliatour-wood* <note>Red Sanderswood</note>, which otherwise comes from the Coromandel coast, but the *Makassarese* say it differs, for the *Bilalangh* is lighter in color than the *Caliatour-wood*, and even lighter is another wood called *Cajudju*. Both have fruits like drumsticks and small leaves, and they are found on Makassar near the villages <note>original: "Negoryen"</note> and planted in the gardens. On the *East Coast of Celebes*, near *Tambucco*, the wild *Pipe Cassia* is also common, and is called there *Ke-Ule* or *Caju-Ular*, that is, *Snake-tree*, after the shape of the fruits, which are longer there than in other places. It grows in the wild, and the fruits are of no use, but the old trunks are desired and sought after to make pillars for the houses of great lords, which are heavy and difficult to fetch from the forest. They are also durable, even in the earth, and have a beautiful, smooth, dense, and light-yellow wood that is somewhat reddish or brownish near the heart. Its fruits being brought to me in the year 1680 showed a significant difference from the true *Pipe Cassia*, for they were quite as long, namely nearly three feet, and a good finger thick, black in color, and divided on the outside into dark segments, like a snake's belly. Inside, it also had similar little cells as the true one, but in each layer, instead of the pulp, a thick disc, like that of a small checkerboard piece <note>original: "dam-bort"</note>, made of a thickish, dry, and tough substance. **B.** The very long pod.

This seems to be the same plant as that which is called by Breynius <note>Jacob Breynius (1637–1697), a Polish-German botanist known for his work on exotic plants</note> in his *Prodromus 2*, page 51, the Indian Pipe Cassia with flesh-colored flowers of Mr. Jager; the pod described there matches ours perfectly. The characteristics of the Cassia are provided on page 50.

### CHAPTER THIRTY-TWO.

->Tamarind. Assam Java.<-

The Tamarind is a vast and widely spreading tree, with a thick and tall trunk, whose bark is blackish, rough, and fissured. The branches are divided into many short and knotty twigs, which form a dense canopy with a pleasant shade. For this reason, they are often tied to laths and guided around like the canopy of a Lime tree <note>The Linden or Tilia tree, often pruned for shade in Europe</note>; for it becomes more elegant and provides a wider canopy when planted and tended near houses than when it grows in the wild, where it usually bears a sparse and thin crown. The twigs in turn sprout various stems which support the leaves, though in an irregular order; sometimes they are solitary, and at other times many are joined together. They are about four inches long, bearing thin, small, and narrow leaves on both sides, directly opposite one another, just as appears in the leaves of Vetch <note>A group of leguminous plants in the genus *Vicia*</note>, or what others attribute to the leaves of the Female Fern <note>The Lady Fern, *Athyrium filix-femina*</note>, although I have not observed that species of Fern in Europe, but I have found such a kind in India, described below by the name *Calamary Fern* <note>original: "Filix Calamaria"</note>. These leaflets are scarcely a finger's breadth long, forming a parallelogram shape, the width of a quill, broadest at the lower part, but protruding at an angle at the upper part. They are woven through with thin veins, bright green on top and ash-colored underneath. Their taste is acidic like Sorrel <note>original: "Acetosæ"</note> and without luster; they are tender when young, but rigid if old, with fourteen to seventeen pairs on one small stem. These are so sensitive that if the branchlets are broken off, they spring upward; indeed, if the Sun hastens toward its setting, or if the sky becomes rainy and windy, they first lift themselves obliquely toward the upper part of the branchlet, and then, if the Sun is below the horizon, they fold themselves downward under the stem, and remain thus folded and closed until an hour before the Sun rises, raising and opening themselves again in a similar manner—namely, upward and forward. This sun-following nature <note>original: "Solisequam naturam"; this describes nyctinasty, the "sleep" movements of plants in response to light and darkness</note> we shall later note in many other plants in various parts of this work, as it is almost the natural or general rule for all those that have similar tender leaflets positioned opposite one another on one stalk. Indeed, in some species, the leaf-bearing stems are pulled backward during the night and almost hide the fruit or pods against the branch itself until the Sun rises again, at which time they restore themselves to their original posture. Furthermore, every leaf-bearing stem has a small joint or "knee" at its origin, as does the stalk that supports the flowers. On older trees, the branches are so rough from the fallen stems that they appear thorny.

The flowers are few and scattered, hanging from small clusters, and they always sprout at the very end of the twigs

...make tubes from them; the leaves, rubbed with some grains of black and long Pepper, cure stomach pain.

### CHAPTER XXXII.

->Tamarind Tree.<-

The Tamarind tree is a large and widely extended tree, with a thick high trunk and a blackish, rough, and cracked bark. The branches are divided into abundant short and knotty twigs, making a dense crown with a pleasant shade; therefore, one often trains it on laths, like a broad lime tree, for it then becomes much more beautiful and spreads out better when planted and tended near human dwellings than when it stands in the wild, where it usually has an empty and thin crown. The twigs again have various little stalks that bear the leaves, though entirely without order, sometimes singly, sometimes standing in bunches together, and about 4 inches long, occupied on both sides with fine, small, and narrow leaflets, directly opposite each other, in the manner like Lentils, or as others write, like the Female Fern, although I have not seen that Fern in Europe, but indeed such a one here in the Indies, and described by us under the name *Filix Calamaria*. These leaflets are barely a finger's breadth long, and almost a parallelogram, a quill wide, but broadest at the back and sticking out somewhat with a corner at the front edges, permeated with fine veins, grass-green above, somewhat gray underneath. The taste is sour like Sorrel, without shine, and tender, though the old ones are somewhat stiff, and they stand in 14 to 17 pairs on a stalk. They are so tender that when one breaks off the twigs, they bounce upward or jump up; indeed, even when the Sun wants to set, or if the weather is rainy and windy, they first move upward or somewhat slanted toward the tip, and after that, when the Sun is far below the Horizon, they bend downward under the stalk and remain so closed until fully an hour before the Sun's rise, opening themselves again in the same way; namely, forward and upward, which sun-turning nature we must still note of many plants in the continuation of this work, being almost the nature or a general rule for all those that have such tender leaves opposite each other on one stalk. Indeed, even the leaf-bearing stalks are pulled backward at night and hide the pods or fruits almost against the branch until the Sun rises again, then restoring themselves again to their proper posture. Furthermore, every leaf-bearing stalk has a little knee or bud at its origin, as does the stalk that bears the flower or the blossom. On the old trees, the branches are so rough and prickly from the fallen stalks that they seem as if thorny.

The flowers stand few together in small clusters, and always at the front of the twigs, shaped—

# BOOK II. Chapter XXXII. AMBOIN HERBAL.

...shaped like Violets, consisting of seven narrow petals, of which the four outer ones are the smallest, pale white, somewhat thick, and bent backward in a cross shape. The three internal ones have the same form and are also bent backward, but they are flimsier and wider, and on their white part, they are variegated with very elegant small brown veins. In the center of the flower are placed three greenish and curved stamens with brown anthers; the fourth, however, is a longer and simple pistil, wider in the middle and curved like a horn, which grows into the fruit. This fruit is a short pod, about a finger or a little more in length and one finger wide; however, in other regions it is larger and usually curved, flattened and compressed like Broad Beans or Kidney Beans, but much thicker, uneven and wavy at the edges, and divided into various cells. At first, it is grayish-green, but when ripe it becomes a dull brown; its outer skin is fragile and, when pressed, easily breaks open like the crust of a pastry <note>original: "artocreatis" / "pasteitjes"; referring to a thin, brittle dough or pie crust</note>. Inside this pod are hidden three or four flat stones <note>seeds</note>, according to the number of lobes, which are nearly square with oblique angles, having the shape of Lupin seeds but thicker and larger, hard, smooth, and chestnut-colored. Each one is hidden in its own thin skin, as if in a little cell. These stones are furthermore covered with a brown, moist, and spongy pulp, around which are located certain thick threads, which all end together in three larger ones, and these terminate in the lower part of the pod.

This pulp very much resembles a certain <term>Electuary</term> <note>a medicinal paste made by mixing powder with honey or syrup</note>, and it has a taste so sour that such is rarely found in any other fruits, yet it is always mixed with a pleasant flavor, as if sugar had been added to it. This pulp cannot be easily separated from the filaments, and therefore it is left together in a sort of compact lump, with only the outer shell being thrown away. These lumps are then formed and pressed into square cakes, resembling bricks, such as those offered for sale in the market. Alternatively, they are preserved in small jars or vessels with plenty of powdered sugar; first, a layer of dry sugar is spread, then a layer of these lumps, and so on, ensuring above all that the sugar is plentiful until the vessel is filled. If this pulp is thus preserved with white sugar, it acquires the consistency of a brown electuary, such as that which is transported to Europe in large jars for the use of apothecaries, and which is prepared more purely since most of the stones are picked out of it. For the common people, however, it is only preserved with red "tree-sugar," such as is collected from the <term>Sagueero</term> tree <note>The Sugar Palm, *Arenga pinnata*</note>; this is of very little value, and this confection is as black as if it were pitch, though it is no less sweet than the preceding kind. For the pulp of the Tamarind does not like pure white sugar, but rather yellow or <term>Muscovado</term> sugar, as it becomes much sweeter from it. Those cakes which are for sale in the market are the most impure, for mixed within them are found pieces of the outer skin, stems, and leaves; they serve only for culinary and daily household use. If they are to be kept for a long time, they must be sprinkled with salt, otherwise worms will breed in them; and although some of the pleasant sour taste is lost through the salt, it does not matter much, as they can still be used for various purposes. These ripe pods must be pulled from the trees with hooks or cut down with long sticks fashioned like shears; otherwise, they fall off by themselves and burst open on the ground, which is why they are often handled messily and are impure.

The wood of this tree is pale white, solid, hard, and heavy; around the knots, it is spotted with blackish-brown marks like Ebony wood. Sometimes such veins and spots are seen in the wood itself, but very old trees have a black heart, though it is not very thick. The Tamarind blooms in these islands in the months of January and February, but the fruits ripen very slowly, and only in the subsequent rainy months <note>the monsoon</note>. For this reason, they rarely produce ripe fruit in these regions, and those they do produce are smaller and sourer than those from Java; in Java, however, they have a better opportunity for ripening and become ripe there in the dry months.

Name. In Latin, *Tamarindus*, and the fruits are called *Tamarindi* and *Palmulae Indicae* <note>Indian Dates</note>, from the Arabic *Tamarhindi*, or "Indian Dates." Not because this tree has any similarity with the Date-bearing tree <note>the Date Palm</note> which in India...

<column-break/>

...shaped like Violets, and made of seven narrow leaves, of which the four outermost are the smallest, pale white, thickish, and bent backwards in a cross. The three innermost or front ones have the same shape and are also bent backwards, but are flappier and somewhat wider, and very prettily marked with brown veins on the white part. In the middle stand three greenish and curved threads with brown knobs <note>anthers</note>, and a fourth one a bit longer and without a knob, wide in the middle and curved like a small borer <note>an auger or drill bit</note>, from which the fruits also emerge. These are short pods, about a finger or more long and one wide, though in other lands they are somewhat larger and usually somewhat curved, also somewhat flattened and as if pressed, like Roman beans <note>broad beans</note>, yet much thicker, somewhat wavy at the edges, and divided into various tubes or purses. At first they are gray mixed with green, but when ripe they are a dirty gray; the outer husk is brittle and, when pressed, bursts easily as if it were a thin crust of a pastry. Inside these pods hide 3 or 4 flat kernels, according to the number of joints in the pods; they are not round but almost square and slanted at the corners, in the shape of Lupins, but thicker and larger, hard, smooth, and yellowish-brown. Each is enclosed in a particular little cell as if in a tube. These seeds are further surrounded or encompassed by a brown, moist, and soft marrow <note>pulp</note>, around which hang some thick threads, all of which hang together on three main stems, and these hang at the back of the pods.

The marrow looks very much like an Electuary and is as sour in taste as few fruits are found to be, yet always mixed with some pleasantness, just as if there were some sugar in it. This marrow cannot be pulled off from the fine threads; therefore, it is left together in a lump, and only the outer shell is thrown away. But the lumps are afterwards packed together, and square cakes, like bricks, are made of them, just as they are brought to market. Or they are laid in jars and small vessels with some powdered sugar, taking first a layer of dry sugar and then a layer of these lumps, and so on. Above all, do not spare the sugar until the vessel is full. And when this is done with white or coarse powdered sugar, it gets the consistency of a brown Electuary, like that which is transported in large jars to Europe for the convenience of pharmacies, and which is prepared a bit more purely, with most of the stones or kernels picked out. But for the common man, it is laid in with brownish-black tree-sugar, such as comes from the Sagueer trees, because it can be had very cheaply. And this confection looks as black as tar, yet in sweetness it is in no way inferior to the previous one. For the Tamarind does not want pure white sugar, but yellow or Muscovado sugar, because it becomes much sweeter from it. The aforementioned cakes sold on the market are the filthiest of all, for pieces of the broken shells, stems, and leaves run through them; they are only made for use in the kitchen and daily household. If one wants to keep them long, they must be sprinkled with some salt, otherwise they get worms; and although they lose some of their pleasant sourness through the salt, it does not matter much, because they can still be used for various services. The ripe pods must be pulled from the trees with hooks or clipped off with long shear-sticks; otherwise, they fall off by themselves and burst open on the ground, which is why they are handled somewhat messily and are also impure.

The wood is pale white, dense, hard, and heavy; around the knots, it has black-brown spots like Ebony wood, sometimes also with similar veins or spots here and there in the wood. Very old trees get a black heart, though it is not very thick. The Tamarind tree blooms in these islands in January and February, but the fruits ripen very slowly and not until the rainy monsoon, which is why they produce few ripe fruits in these quarters, and those are even smaller and sourer than the Javanese ones; but on Java they have a different opportunity and become ripe there in the dry monsoon.

Name. In Latin, *Tamarindus*, and the fruits *Tamarindi*, and *Palmulae Indicae*, after the Arabic *Tamarhindi*, or Indian Dates; not because this tree has any resemblance to the Date tree, which in India...

# AMBOIN HERBAL Book II. Chapter XXXII.

[...not only] grow in India, but because the fruits resemble fingers, with which Date fruits are also compared. The Arabs also call these *Homar* <note>original: "Homar"</note> due to their dark reddish color, and for the same reason it is called by certain Greeks *Phœnico-Balanus* <note>original: "Phœnico-Balanus"; literally "Date-Acorn"</note>; and *Oxyphœnix* <note>original: "Oxyphœnix"</note>, that is, acid Dates. To the ancient Greeks, however, this tree and its fruit were unknown. Among the Turks and Persians it bears the same Arabic name, but to the Egyptians it is called *Derefilede* or better *Derelside*. The Indian names according to Garcia de Orta and Cristóvão da Costa are *Puli*, *Ambili*, and *Chineba*. In Malay it is *Assam* or *Assam-Java*, that is, "acid," or "something acidic from Java," all names derived from its excellent sour flavor. In Java itself it is called *Sunda Assa* in the Sundanese language, that is, "acid from Sunda" (which is today Batavia <note>modern-day Jakarta</note>). The fruits and trees are called by a specific name in Java, *Tjcbampabu*, but the extracted pulp, packed into jars, is called by them *Assam*, which is the true Tamarind. Those of Makassar name it *Tjcbamba*, the people of Banda call it *Tamalachi*, those of Madagascar call it *Quille*, and according to Ogilby Dapper, *Monte*. By the Portuguese it is called *Tamarinbo*, and by the Dutch *Tamaryn*. In the *Hortus Malabaricus* <note>A famous 17th-century botanical treatise on the plants of the Malabar Coast</note> volume 1, Figure 23, it is called in the Malabar language *Balam Puli* or *Madaram Puli*. Among the Brahmins, however, it is *Sinza*.

Among the Arabs, *Tamar* <note>original: "Tamar"</note> properly signifies a Palm or the fruit of a Palm, but not the tree itself, which is called *Nachali*; however, among the Hebrews *Tamar* signifies any Palm properly so-called.

**Location.** This tree was formerly found only in the region of India called Gujarat, where the best are considered to be those that grow in the mountains and in Northern places. From there, in time, it was translated to Persia, Arabia, and Egypt, and today it occurs frequently in Java, as well as in Bima, Timor, and Makassar; these trees are rare in Ambon and in the Moluccas, where they also yield rare fruit and have a narrow canopy, and grow so slowly that it becomes tedious. Without doubt, this is because Ambon is too rainy a region, which prevents these "cold" trees from growing tall and producing ripe fruit. In Banda, however, they are loftier and give larger fruit, since its soil is warmer, being filled with sulfurous minerals.

**Usage.** No part of this tree is in greater use than the pulp of the fruits, which the almighty Creator produced as most useful for these hot regions, just as He distributed hot spices for the greater use of the Northern regions rather than for the peoples in whose lands they grow. Thus, He granted these islands many other cooling things, among which the Tamarind is the best fruit, since its nature is cold in the third degree and moist in the second <note>The author refers to the Galenic system of humoral medicine, which classified substances by degrees of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness to balance bodily health</note>, whence its power is cooling and cleansing. Its fresh pulp, formed into cakes, has a daily use in the kitchen, being added to seasonings for fish, chickens, and similar foods, to which it imparts a pleasant acidity, healthful to the stomach; such seasonings in India are called *Carri* or *Carril* <note>Curry</note>. Our nation <note>the Dutch</note> uses much of this pulp to compose a sugared beer from it, which is a common Indian drink, extremely cooling, but causing too much looseness of the bowels in those not accustomed to it. With this Tamarind pulp, the head and body are also washed to cleanse away filth and spots. Any items made of silver, if boiled in Tamarind water, become clean and shining. As for its further and manifold use among the Javanese, Chinese, and Malays, I knowingly pass over it.

Sugared Tamarind pulp specifically serves the Apothecaries, and for this purpose, placed in jars and vessels, it is transported to Europe; it is particularly beneficial to those sailing across the sea, for whom it is most healthful if they use it occasionally, either in the form of a lick <term>electuary; a medicinal paste</term> or dissolved in water and taken in place of broth, for it gently moves the bowels, purifies, and thins the thick blood generated from the coarse and salted ship's food, and preserves against scurvy <note>original: "scorbuto"</note> if the predisposition is present.

Furthermore, the same sugared pulp is used in the Medical Art for gentle purges, but only in those diseases arising from bilious humors and where great heat is present, as in burning fevers, choleraic flux, etc. For the power of the Tamarind is to settle the raging bile, to purify the blood, and to cool...

...does not grow [only there], *but because the fruits resemble fingers, to which the Date-fruits are also compared.* The Arabs also call them *Homar*, *on account of their brown-red color, and for the same reason some Greeks also call it Phœnico-Balanus, Oxyphœnix, that is, sour Dates*: For to the ancient Greeks that tree and its fruit were unknown. Among the Turks and Persians it also has the aforementioned Arabic name, but in Egypt it is called *Derefilde*, or better *Derelside*. The Indian names, from Garcia and Cristóvão Acosta, are *Puli*, *Ambili*, and *Chineba*. In Malay *Assam*, or *Assam-Java*, that is, *acid*, *and something sour from Java, all so named for its excellent sourness*. On Java itself it is called *Sunda Assa*, *that is, sourness from Sunda, which is nowadays Batavia*. The fruits and trees are specifically named *Tjchampabu* on Java, *but the extracted and packed-together marrow they call Assam, which is the actual Tamarind*: On Makassar *Tjchamba*: On Banda *Tamalachi*: On Madagascar *Quille*, and, according to Ogilby Dapper, *Monte*.
