Among the Arabs, *Tamar* properly signifies *Palmam*, a Palm, or the fruit thereof, and not the tree itself, which is named *Nachali*, but among the Hebrews *Tamar* signifies a Palm tree.

**Place.** This tree was formerly only found in India in the Kingdom of *Gujarat*, where one also finds the best wood, those that grow on mountains and in places facing the North: From there they were brought in time to Persia, Arabia, and Egypt, and nowadays one finds them abundantly on Java, as well as on Bima, Timor, and Makassar, yet they are scarce in Ambon and the Moluccas, where they also bear little fruit and have narrow crowns, and also shoot up so slowly that it is vexing: Without doubt, because Ambon has too much rain, which prevents these "cold" trees from growing and ripening. But in Banda they become larger and bear better fruits, because the ground there is better from below, as it is pregnant with sulfur mines.

**Usage.** Of this tree, nothing is in such great use as the brown marrow <note>pulp</note> from the fruits, which the all-wise Creator lets come forth as very useful for and in these hot lands: And just as He created the hot spices more for the convenience of the cold Northern World than for the lands where they grow: So has He likewise provided these hot lands with many cooling things: *Among which the Tamarind is perhaps the most fit, being by properties cold in the third, and moist into the second degree: therefore cooling and cleansing.* The fresh marrow alone, made into cakes, has its daily use in the kitchen, to be put into the sauce for Fish, Chickens, and similar food, giving them a pleasant sourness, which is also healthy for the stomach, and such soups are called *Carri* or *Carril* in the Indies. Our Nation at Batavia and elsewhere sells or consumes much of this marrow in the making of sugar-beer, being a common drink in the Indies and very cooling, though it makes those who are not used to it loose-boweled. With this Tamarind one also washes the head and body to wipe away all grease and filth. All kinds of silver-work boiled in Tamarind-water also become very pure and clear from it: And as for its other and various uses in the daily household of the Javanese, Chinese, and Malays, those I pass by.

The sugared Tamarind properly serves the Pharmacies, and is for that purpose carried to Europe in whole pots and barrels full, being especially very precious and useful for Seafarers, when they occasionally consume it, whether they swallow it as a lick <term>electuary</term> or mix it with water to make a "cold bowl" <note>a refreshing drink</note>, for it makes a person open-boweled, purifies, and thins the thick blood that one gathers from the coarse and salty ship's food, and preserves him from scurvy, with which Seafarers are so greatly plagued.

The same sugared marrow is further used in Medicine for gentle purges, yet only in such diseases that arise from bilious humors, and where great burning is present, as in hot fevers, for the Tamarind’s own power is to still the raging bile, to purify the blood, and to cool, being the purging...

## II Book. XXXII. Chapter. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...and its purging power is so weak that it rarely takes effect by itself without other ingredients being added; indeed, in some people it does nothing at all, which is why some add *Cassia fistula* <note>The Golden Shower tree, known for its laxative pods</note>, though it then makes for a nauseating drink. This same pulp is also beneficial for those suffering from hot and dry mange <note>original: "scabie"; likely referring to various itchy skin irritations</note>; and in water in which Tamarind pulp has been dissolved, they wash the bodies of children who have suffered from smallpox, in order to cleanse their bodies. The Arabs, when they set out on journeys through vast and dry wildernesses, take Tamarind with them to quench their thirst; and if they wish to increase its cooling power, they mix in crushed Sandalwood or Cedar wood. The leaves also have an acidic and cooling quality, and are simultaneously drying; in the absence of other herbs, they are used like Lettuce, and when crushed in water, they wash the head with it for cleansing. Furthermore, when crushed into a poultice, they are applied in place of a plaster to Erysipelas <note>A bacterial skin infection, often called "St. Anthony's Fire"</note> to extinguish its heat. Those, however, who have a cold stomach <note>In the humoral theory of medicine, a "cold" stomach was thought to cause poor digestion</note> or are subject to obstructions of the Spleen should abstain from the use of Tamarind, unless some spice is added such as *Cassia lignea* <note>Chinese cinnamon</note>, Mace, Mastic, etc. The inhabitants of Madagascar also use Tamarind in daily cooking, as the trees are common among them and produce fruit twice a year.

*Eusebius Nieremberg, Natural History, Book 15, Chapter 17* writes that Tamarind trees also grow in the American regions, in the provinces of Mexico and Acapulco, but they were brought there from elsewhere. He compares Tamarind leaves (though somewhat improperly) with the leaves of Rue, and he does not concede that it should be considered the *Oxyphoenix* <note>original: "Oxyphoenicem"; Greek for "acid date"</note> of the Greeks. In this matter he is somewhat correct, since by *Oxyphoenix* one might also understand a certain species of thorny Palm, as well as the acidic Tamarind; for it is known to the Greeks that *oxys* <note>original: "ὀξύς"</note> refers equally to things that are acidic or sharp/thorny.

The oldest and blackest Tamarind pulp, mixed with crushed Cumin seed and reduced into a thick mass, is used by the Malays as a suppository to move the bowels quickly.

In Timor and Bima, this tree also grows abundantly and spontaneously in the forests, and its wood is used there for shipbuilding; from it, planks, ribs, supports, and similar parts are fashioned, as it is extremely hard and durable. Its color is a pale white, but in very old trunks, the heartwood is somewhat brown.

*Cristóvão da Costa* relates from the reports of the Indians that it is just as harmful and unhealthy to lie down and sleep under this tree and its shade as it is said of the Walnut tree in our own country.

The people of Makassar use the ripe fruits in place of Lemons when they wish to prepare the red pigment called *Cassomba* <note>Safflower dye</note>; for this purpose, the people of Turatte bring immature pods, or those not yet opened, in great quantities to the capital of Makassar to be sold.

*Jacobus Bontius, Book 6, Chapter 4* describes a second species of Tamarind, which he calls *Carandje* in the Javanese language (and some call *Carandjang*), and he believes—though mistakenly—it to be the *Carandas* described by *Garcia de Orta, Book 2, Chapter 6 on Aromatics*. He attributes to it leaves similar to the common Tamarind, but in those that were planted in my garden and sprouted from Javanese seed, I observed them to be different; I found them to be similar to *Lingoa* <note>The Narra tree, *Pterocarpus indicus*</note> leaves, but a little narrower, sharper, and arranged alternately. Its fruits are small pods containing only one small stone, not very large, surrounded by an acidic flesh or pulp which is drier than that of the common Tamarind, not as black, nor possessing any purging power. Thus, it is eaten like other fruits, either to quench thirst or for its flavor and for pleasure.

<column-break/>

...purging power therein is so weak, that it will hardly work of or by itself, indeed in some people not at all: And for this reason some also mix some *Cassia Fistula* <note>Pipe Cassia</note> into it, but that produces a loathsome drink: The same pulp is also good when consumed by those who are burdened with a hot and dry mange, and in the water in which Tamarind is soaked, one washes children who have had the smallpox, to cleanse the body. The Arabs, wishing to travel through or over great and dry Deserts, carry the Tamarind with them to quench their thirst, and if they wish to increase its cooling powers further, they add some grated yellow Sandalwood and Cedarwood. The leaves also have a sour and cooling power, and are also somewhat drying; for want of other greens, one can also use them as a Salad, as well as washing the head with them when rubbed in water, to cleanse the same. And further, being rubbed into a paste alone, they are also laid like a plaster upon the "rose" <note>Erysipelas</note> to cool its heat and burning: But those who have a cold stomach, or are prone to spleen-sickness, should not use the Tamarind without adding some hot spices, such as *Cassia lignea*, Mace, and Mastic. The inhabitants of Madagascar also have the Tamarind in daily use, specifically in their food, for the trees grow abundantly among them and bear fruit twice a year.

*Eusebius Nieremberg, Natural History, Book 15, Chapter 17* writes that Tamarinds also grow in the American Lands, in the Province of Mexico and Acapulco, though they were brought there from elsewhere. He compares (though somewhat improperly) the leaves of Tamarind with those of Rue, and also will not allow that they should be held for the *Oxyphoenix* of the Greeks, in which he is somewhat right, since by *Oxyphoenix* one can also understand a sort of the stinging Palm, as well as our sour Tamarind: For it is known that the Greeks use the word *Oxys* <note>original: "Oxys"</note> for sour as well as for stinging <note>sharp or thorny</note> things.

The oldest and blackest Tamarind, when it is brought to a thick substance with crushed Cumin, is used by the Malays as a suppository to immediately cause a bowel movement.

On Timor and Bima this tree grows abundantly in the wild, and its wood is used there for ship-carpentry, such as in timbers, planks, ribs, etc., because it is very hard and durable, of a pale-white color, though in old trunks one finds the heartwood a little brown.

*Cristóvão da Costa* writes, from the account of the Indians, that it is as heavy or harmful and unhealthy to sleep under the shadow of a Tamarind tree as they say in the Fatherland of the Walnut tree.

The people of Makassar use the unripe fruits also in place of Lemons when they wish to make the red dye *Cassomba*, and for which purpose the inhabitants of Turatte bring the unripe pods, or those not yet opened, in great numbers for sale to the capital city Makassar.

*Jacobus Bontius, Book 6, Chapter 4* describes a second kind of Tamarind, which he calls *Carandje* in Javanese (some also *Crandjang*) and maintains, though erroneously, that it is the *Carandas* described by *Garcia de Orta, Book 2, Chapter 6 on Aromatics*: He also makes its leaves equal to those of the Tamarind, but in those that were planted in my garden and came up from Javanese seed, I have found them quite otherwise, namely, similar to those of the *Lingoa*, though somewhat narrower and sharper, and arranged opposite one another. The fruits are small short pods, in which lies a bean-stone, which is not large and is surrounded with a sourish flesh, drier than that of the Tamarind, also not so brown, and having no purging power: So that it is indeed eaten out of hand, whether to quench the thirst, or also for the taste and out of pleasure.

# CHAPTER THIRTY-THREE.

### The Pomegranate. Delima.

Pomegranate trees in India only grow as shrubs; indeed, they are generally shorter than those in Europe, spreading themselves into various thin trunks, and they can hardly be trained to grow with only a single stem. Otherwise, in both form and fruit, it entirely agrees with the European variety, so I shall not describe it at great length here and will only make mention of it, noting that the flavor of the fruit is neither sweet nor sour, but as if mixed and wine-like. Its branches are so long and tender that they must be propped up, as they would otherwise easily break under the weight of the fruit. These trees bear the best fruit if they are planted in gardens or in flat areas near houses, and if a stone arch is placed around them and they are frequently pruned; for this tree perishes very easily if it is not supported by human cultivation. The color of the seeds is mostly rose-red or red as in the European ones; however, another species occurs here in India which bears entirely white seeds. At the beginning of the dry months—that is, in October—it sheds its dry leaves and puts forth shoots, which produce flowers in the following months.

*Name.* In Latin, *Malum Punicum* <note>original: "Malum Punicum," meaning "Phoenician Apple"</note> and *Granatum* <note>original: "Granatum," meaning "Seeded"</note>; in Dutch, *Granaat-Appel*. By the Arabs, it is called *Ruman* or *Roman*, which has its origin in the Hebrew *Rimmon*, and hence in the Spanish language *Romana* and the Portuguese *Romanca*. In Malay, *Delima*; by the Chinese, *Saliu* or *Tsjialiu*.

*Location.* It is found in all these oriental islands, but not in abundance; for only a few of its shrubs occur here and there in gardens. In China, it grows frequently, and there it takes the form of a small tree.

*Use.* I do not intend to comment much here on its nature and powers, as it is sufficiently described in European books, and we shall only demonstrate the uses for which the Indians employ it. Its rinds and the interior grains of the seeds are much used against Diarrhea and tenesmus <note>A painful and constant urge to pass stool, even when the bowels are empty</note> if they are crushed and taken with rice water. It is beneficial to boil the flowers in water and rinse the mouth with it for those who have flabby gums and cannot chew. And just as a wild species occurs in Europe which bears nothing but flowers and is called by the specific name *Balaustium*, so also a rare species occurs in India which produces nothing but flowers; it does not grow in the wild but is cultivated with the greatest care in gardens for the elegance of its flowers. Its shrub and leaves indeed agree with the common variety, but the flowers are larger, having the size of an imperial coin <note>original: "imperialis nummi"; likely referring to a large silver thaler or crown</note>, with many

# CHAPTER XXXIII.

### Pomegranate Tree.

Pomegranates in the Indies also remain like a shrub, indeed usually even shorter than in Europe, spreading out into several thin stems, and one can hardly bring them to shoot up with just one. Otherwise, in both appearance and fruit, this tree is entirely similar to the European one, so I shall not describe it more broadly here, and will only mention that the taste of the fruits is neither sweet nor sour, but as if mixed or wine-like. The twigs are so long and tender that they must often be propped up, or they would otherwise easily break from the weight of the fruit. They bear best when planted in the upper or flat yards near the houses, and also if a high stone base is laid around them, and if they are pruned somewhat often: For this tree fails very easily if one does not keep a hand to it. The color of the kernels is generally Rose-red, as in Europe, though one finds here in the Indies also a kind that remains entirely white. At the beginning of the dry Monsoon, that is in October, it begins to throw away its dry leaves and bring forth young shoots, upon which the flowers then follow in the subsequent months.

*Name.* In Latin, *Malum Punicum*, *Granatum*; in Dutch, *Granaat-Appel*; in Arabic, *Ruman* or *Roman*: Derived from the Hebrew *Rimmon*, and after that the Spanish *Romana*, and the Portuguese *Romanca*. In Malay, *Delima*; Chinese, *Saliu* or *Tsjialiu*.

*Place.* They are found throughout all these Eastern Provinces, though not in abundance, but only some shrubs here and there in the gardens. In China, they grow more abundantly and become a small tree there.

*Use.* Of its nature and powers we shall likewise not bring up much here, as it is sufficiently known in European books, but only point out for what our Indians use the same: The rind and the inner stones in the kernels are much used against diarrhea and straining <note>original: "persing"; referring to tenesmus</note>, when they are crushed and taken with boiled rice water. The flower boiled in water, and then held in the mouth, is good for those who have loose gums and therefore cannot eat. And just as in the Fatherland <note>referring to the Netherlands</note> one also has the wild Pomegranates, which bear nothing but flowers and are specifically called *Balaustium*: So one has here in the Indies also a rare sort, which indeed bears nothing but flowers, yet does not grow in the wild, but is properly and carefully brought up or cultivated in the gardens: And that because of the beauty of the flowers: The shrub being

# Book II. Chapter XXXIII. AMBOINESE HERBAL. 95

These consist of reflexed petals, so tightly joined that the center of the flower cannot be seen through them. The most common flowers are scarlet, like those that produce fruit, though some occur that are purest white, and others are flesh-colored. All of them, however, are entirely scentless and serve only to delight the eyes. Because they grow on such short stalks that they can hardly be held in the hand, and yet the Malay people love to adorn their hair with them, they add a false stem to them for that purpose. In Malay it is called *Delima Wangza*, which seems to be a Javanese name meaning "Great Flower" <note>original: "Magnum florem"</note>; by the people of Ternate it is called *Lima Susso*. I know of no other use for it except as an ornament for gardens; its propagation is done during the rainy months by placing cuttings into the earth.

In China, there are two species of Pomegranates, the first and most important of which is called *Butliu*, pronounced *Bulliu*, that is, the *Honey Pomegranate*, as its apples or fruits are of a very sweet flavor, and its seeds <note>original: "officula grana"</note> are sometimes larger, sometimes smaller. The other species is called *Tscholiu*, that is, the *Stony Pomegranate*, which has a wine-like flavor but bears small grains and larger seeds, thus agreeing most closely with the Indian variety. They use the first species on hotter days to refresh the stomach, while the second is called into medical use to stop all forms of diarrhea. However, because its rinds and grains boiled in water alone produce a harsh and unpleasant drink, two oak galls <note>original: "gallæ Quercus"</note> are added in the boiling along with the fruit of *Putsjoc* <note>original: "Putsjoc"; likely the medicinal root Saussurea lappa</term></note> and a little honey; this drink is then strained and administered. Over this is eaten the pulp of *Soccuncapas* <note>original: "Soccuncapas"; likely a variety of breadfruit or cotton-tree fruit</note> boiled and mashed into a paste, mixed with a little honey. This medicine is only suitable for dysentery and straining <note>original: "tenesmo"</note>, but not for cholera, where honey is harmful. In certain years, something peculiar is found on the Pomegranate leaves: on their upper part, a bump grows like a green *Catjang* <note>a type of bean</note>, closely resembling the shape of a skull or a monkey's head, first grey, then brown. When these little heads open, a grey butterfly emerges; it can be observed in these that other butterflies previously deposited their eggs on this leaf. Further mention of such skull-like heads will be made later regarding the *Vidara* <note>the Jujube tree</note>.

In some years, one also finds something special on the Pomegranate leaves, namely on their upper surface a bud somewhat larger than a green *Catjang*, very nearly representing the shape of a little death's-head or a monkey-head, first gray and thereafter brown, at which time these buds burst open and let out gray-white moths, which were much larger than the cases were; and one can see that they were brought or set there by other preceding moths. Of such and similar death's-heads, a broader account will be given hereafter regarding the *Vidara*.

# 96 BOOK II, CHAPTER XXXIV. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

### CHAPTER THIRTY-FOUR.

->*The Great Lemon, Pomelo, or Lomen Caffomba.*<-

We will now recount the rank and file of Lemons that occur in this Oriental part of the Indies, and at the same time we shall demonstrate whether and in what part they differ from those of Europe. First, therefore, there comes into our view the largest species of all, the *Assyrian Apple* <note>original: "Pomum Assyrium"</note>, called *Pom-Sires* by the French, which we have nicknamed the *Decuman* <note>The Latin "decumanus" refers to the tenth in a series, but was often used to describe anything exceptionally large, like a "tenth wave."</note> because of its great size, and of which we have observed four varieties.

1. The first variety does not have a tall trunk but spreads itself out wider than other Lemon trees; the lower its branches spread, the better the fruit it produces, so that it must often be propped up with wooden stakes. Its leaves bear the common character of all Lemon leaves: namely, that at their lower part they are heart-shaped <note>botanical term: cordate</note>, as if a second leaf were growing out from there <note>This describes the "winged" petiole or leaf-stem common in citrus plants.</note>. All of them have a spine at their origin, though these differ between older and younger trees. In the younger trees, the leaves are over seven inches long, and their lower heart-shaped part is two inches, while the upper part is about a hand-breadth wide, nearly entire at the edges, smooth, and not notched. If such small trees are placed in a shaded spot, the leaves grow a span long and six fingers wide, with their heart-shaped base being three transverse fingers long and wide, ending at the top in a rounded and bifurcated tip. Opposite each leaf stands a spine as long as a thumb joint; the older the trees become, the rarer these spines are. On adult trees, the leaves are five, six, or even seven inches long, but they are less and more thinly heart-shaped—scarcely half a finger wide and a thumb's length, though in some an entire finger wide. They are divided by parallel ribs which protrude on the underside in younger leaves and on the upper side in older ones. Old leaves likewise turn yellowish underneath and are somewhat woolly to the touch; if the tree is advanced in age, it bears almost no spines, or at least very small and short ones, and then only on the younger shoots or branches.

The flowers grow in clusters <note>original: "racemosi"</note>, sprouting from large, white buds contained in wide, concave calyxes. Upon opening, they consist of four, and rarely five, oblong, somewhat thick petals, reflexed outwards, which are very fragile and fall off if touched. They have a piercing scent, more pleasant even than that of white lilies. In their center is found a circle composed of white, upright stamens bearing yellow anthers like white lilies, and in the middle of these is placed a green embryo which grows into the fruit, bearing at its top a green, headed pistil sprinkled with a sticky moisture. The fruit has the form of an apple, the size of a human head, flattened or compressed from its roundness, though not quite as much as a common cheese <note>The Dutch column specifies "an Edam cheese."</note>. It has an even surface on the outside, except that it is bumpy here and there. Furthermore, its entire surface is spotted with little dots or small pits. The color is lemon-yellow, but not as smooth and vivid as in the true Citron, for it is paler and more dull. Its outer rind <note>original: "cortex"</note> is over an inch thick, spongy, whitish, dry, bitter, and smelling of sulfur. The interior flesh forms a globe divided by membranous skins into various segments, usually fifteen or sixteen, both large and small, joined in a circle as in Oranges. This flesh is reddish-purple like that of Pomegranates; it is juicy, with a flavor ranging from acidic to wine-like, though in the ripest fruits it becomes sweet like currants. In each of the larger segments are placed two or three seeds <note>original: "ossicula"</note>, over a joint of the little finger in length, flat, wrinkled, and whitish. However, in the entire fruit, those considered the best often do not contain a single such seed, or only very rare and small ones. Often three or four of these great fruits hang together from one branch, which then bends downward and often breaks, hence why they must be propped—

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER XXXIV.

->*The Pomelo Tree.*<-

Now we shall touch upon the company of the Lemon-kinds that one has in this eastern part of the Water-Indies, and show whether, and in what ways, they differ from the European ones. First, there appears to the largest sort, *Pomum Assyrium*, named *Pom-Sires* by the French, and which we have nicknamed *Decumanum* because of its size, having also noted four kinds of it.

1. The first gains or gets no high trunk, but spreads itself further out than other Lemon trees, and the lower its branches spread out, the better fruit it bears, having therefore often to be supported with laths. The leaves have their characteristic in common with all Lemon-kinds: namely, that at their rear they have a little board <note>A vernacular term for the winged petiole.</note> like a second leaf, and every leaf at its origin has a thorn, though both differ on the old and young trees; for on the young trees they are a good seven inches long, and of that, the "board" or rear leaf is almost two inches. The front part is about a hand broad, at the edges almost whole, smooth, and not toothed. But if such small trees stand in a shady place, then these leaves are indeed a span long, six fingers broad, and their "board" three cross-fingers long and broad, rounding toward the front and mostly cloven in two. By each leaf stands a long thorn, a good joint of a thumb long, and the older the trees become, the more these thorns diminish. On the grown trees the leaves are five, six, and seven inches long, but their "board" is much smaller and narrower: namely, an inch long and barely half a finger, though on some also a whole finger broad, and divided with parallel ribs, which on the young leaves bulge out below, and on the old ones, above. Also, the old leaves are yellow-green from below, and somewhat woolly in the touching, and the old trees have no thorns, or at least they are very small and short, and that only on their young shoots or branches.

The blossom comes forth cluster-wise together from large and white buds, which, standing in wide calyxes, open into white flowers of four, and seldom five, longish, thick petals, mostly bent outwards or towards the outside, easily breaking or falling off if one touches them, being furthermore of a strong pleasant smell, and lovelier than White Lilies. Inside there stands a ring made of white and straight threads, bearing yellow nubs, like the White Lilies, and they enclose in their middle a grass-green little hill from which the fruit comes forth, and on the same stands a little pillar, bearing a green knob with a sticky moisture upon it. The fruit gets the shape of an Apple, as large as a human head, somewhat flat from the round, though not so much as an Edam cheese, from the outside with an even surface, or showing a bump here and there: the whole surface being as if it were pricked with small holes or small pits. It is a true Lemon-color, yet not so smooth and lively as the Lemons, but somewhat dirtier and duller. The outermost shell is a good inch thick, spongy, white, dry, bitter, and of a sulfurous smell. The innermost flesh still makes a round ball, divided by many separating skins and various pieces, and commonly in fifteen and sixteen, both large and small, standing against each other in the round, like those of the Orange-Apples. This flesh is red, drawing toward purple, like that of Pomegranates, very juicy, from the sour drawing toward a wine-like taste, though in the entirely ripe ones drawing more toward the sweet, like our Red-currants. In each of the large pieces lie two or three seed-grains, a good joint of a pinky-finger long, flat, wrinkled, and white. Yet sometimes in the whole fruit there is not one grain, or some small ones (which are also held for the best), and of these large fruits, some three or four hang pressed together on one branch, which they also pull downwards so much that they often break—

must be propped up so that it can better support the weight of the fruits. If one or two of these younger fruits are picked, the remaining ones grow larger and more succulent. There is another variety of this first major species very similar to it, or perhaps a little smaller, which has an internal flesh that is whitish, somewhat sour, tasteless, and watery; this is considered of lower quality, but since this variety is very closely related to the following third species, we shall treat them as one and the same.

---

The wood of the tree is pale, solid, and knotty, not easily developing cracks; when dry, it is suitable for the handles of woodworking tools, especially the wood from the thicker roots, which is streaked and distinguished by veins.

**Season.** These trees flower in October and the following months, and the fruits ripen in April and May.

**Name.** In Latin *Limo Decumanus* <note>original: "Limo Decumanus"</note> or *Great Assyrian Apple* <note>original: "Malum Assyrium Decumanum"; the term "decumanus" refers to something of exceptional size, like a "tenth wave."</note>. In Malay *Lemon Cassonba*, which means *Red Lemon from its flesh-color*. Some in Malay call it *Jamboa* after the Portuguese *Samboa*, which properly denotes the *Pomp-Sires* or *Adam's Apples* <note>original: "Adami poma"</note> to the Spanish, though these Indian apples differ greatly from those. To the Javanese, it is called *Djurru* or *Djerru*, or *Djerru-Matsjang*, which means *Tiger Lemon*. To the people of Makassar, it is *Lemon Calucku*, meaning *Coconut Lemon* <note>original: "Limo Calapparius"</note>, because of its size and the shape of a coconut. In Dutch, it is called *Pompelmoes* <note>The origin of the modern word "Pomelo."</note>. To the Chinese, it is *Fu* or *Noay*.

**Location.** These trees are not native to these East Indian regions; they seem to have been brought here in the past from the upper regions. They are cultivated by enthusiasts only in gardens, both for the fruit and for the shade of their canopy. They build a wide stone base around the trees and tie the larger branches to wooden frames. Indeed, trees that have a narrow canopy, upright branches, and a tall, straight trunk are not considered as excellent as those that are lower to the ground and bear a wide, spreading canopy. The Amboinese do not value them highly, and the fruits growing in their colder mountains are small and sour; for this tree loves a warm, flat soil and location. For this reason, those from Banda are always considered better than those from Amboina, as the soil there is warmer.

**Use.** This fruit is only eaten raw and is frequently served with desserts. Its flesh, either alone or prepared with Spanish wine and sugar, provides a pleasant refreshment on hot days. The wine mixed with it ensures that stomach cramps <note>original: "tormina abdominis"</note> do not easily arise. If this fruit is being sliced, one must take care that the knife, having passed through the bitter rind, does not touch the flesh itself; or that it is not handled with the hands that stripped the rind, as it would acquire a bitter taste therefrom. Thus, to open the fruit properly, a slice should first be cut from both its upper and lower flat ends, like the lid of a pie <note>original: "instar integumenti crustuli"</note>, to the thickness of a thumb until the red flesh appears; then one can better observe how the rest of the rind may be skillfully removed or cut away with a knife so the flesh itself is not damaged. It is also a noble fruit for sea voyages, as it can be preserved for a long time and remains unspoiled if handled gently when picked from the tree, taking care that it does not fall to the ground but is instead hung from cords in the ships. If eaten during a sea voyage, it refreshes the stomach and quenches thirst.

**The second species** occurs in Banda. Its foliage agrees with the common variety, but it has a taller trunk and upright branches. Its leaves are rounder and more significantly serrated at the edges; the lower part of the leaf is heart-shaped <note>botanical term: a winged petiole</note> like the leaves of the *Itam* Lemon, or even a little larger. At their origin, a small, short spine emerges, though not on all of them, nor do they observe a fixed shape. Its leaves are seven inches long in total; their lower heart-shaped part is one and a half or two inches long, while the upper part of the leaf is about four fingers wide. It is thicker than the common variety, and the lateral ribs do not protrude as much; the leaf itself is more pointed and slightly cleft or bifid at the end. Others, moreover, are irregular, wavy, and with hollowed edges, as if they wished to form another

<column-break/>

break, which is why one must prop up these branches to better bear the weight of the fruits. And if one or two of the young fruits are broken off from the branches, the remaining ones become that much larger and juicier. There is also a second sort of this first Pomelo genus, mostly similar to the previous one, or perhaps a bit smaller, having a white pith inside, of a tart, bland, and watery flavor, which is also held to be of lesser quality; but because this sort has a great affinity with the following third one, we shall consider them as one and the same.

---

The wood is pale, dense, and gnarled, not easily splitting, and when dry is suitable for handles for all kinds of carpenter's tools, especially that of the thick roots, which are somewhat veined.

**Season.** They bloom in October and the following months, and the fruits become ripe in April and May.

**Name.** In Latin *Limo Decumanus*, or *Malum Assyrium Decumanum*: In Malay *Lemon Cassonba*, that is, red Lemon of the fleshy color; some call them in Malay *Jamboa*, after the Portuguese *Samboa*, which actually signifies the *Pomp-Sires* or Adam's Apples in Spain, but from which these Indians differ somewhat. In Javanese *Djurru* or *Djerru-Matsjang*, that is *Tiger Lemon* <note>original: "Limo Tigrinus"</note>. In Macassarese *Lemon Calucku*, that is, *Coconut Lemon*, from its size and shape like a Coconut <note>original: "Calappus"</note>. In Dutch *Pompelmoes*. In Chinese *Iu* or *Noay*.

**Place.** The Pomelo trees are not common among the Indians in these Eastern quarters, and it seems they were brought here formerly from some of the uplands; and enthusiasts cultivate them in their gardens, primarily to have the shade of their canopy, making a wide base around them and training the heavy branches on a trellis of laths. Trees that do not spread their canopy and have mostly straight branches and a high trunk are not considered as good as the low and spreading ones. The Amboinese do not make much of them, and also the fruits that grow in their cold mountains are small and sour; for this tree loves a flat and warm place. This is why the Bandanese are always held to be better than the Amboinese, because they have a warmer soil there.

**Usage.** This fruit serves only to be eaten raw, and is mostly set out with banquet-work, as much the flesh alone as prepared with Spanish wine and sugar, which gives a pleasant cooling in the hot days; and the wine ensures that one does not so easily get cramps in the belly from it. In slicing it up, one must take care that the knife, which goes through the bitter rind, does not cut too deep into the flesh, or that it is touched too much with the hands with which one has pulled off the rind, to prevent it from getting a bitter taste. And therefore, if one wants to open them properly, one must first cut a bit off the top and bottom flat sides, like a lid of a pasty, to the thickness of a thumb, until the red flesh is seen, and then one can best notice how to set the knife in cutting through the remaining rind. It is also a wonderful fruit on sea-voyages, for one can keep them a long time and keep them unspoiled, if one only handles them gently in taking them from the tree and does not let them thud onto the earth; and then hang them up with small cords, and being then eaten at sea, they refresh the stomach and also quench the thirst.

**2.** In Banda, one has a particular sort of Pomelo tree, with leaves much like the common one, though with a higher trunk and straight branches, the leaves being somewhat rounder at the front and more noticeably serrated on the edges than the common ones, and with a "board" <note>The Dutch "bertje" or "little board" refers to the winged petiole, the small leaf-like structure on the stem.</note> like that of the *Itam* Lemon, or somewhat larger. At the origin with a small short thorn, though not on all, and they also keep no fixed shape; the leaves in total are 7 inches long, and of that the "board" is one and a half or two inches; the upper leaf is in the middle barely four fingers wide, somewhat thicker than on the common ones, and the cross-ribs are not so noticeable or raised; somewhat pointed at the front, or tapering sharper, and a little cleft; others are moreover also with irregular bends and bulging edges, as if they wanted to form a "board"—

The fruit of this variety is smaller, not round but pear-shaped like the larger winter pears; when ripe, it thickens at the stem and becomes lumpy in various places. It is about half a foot long and five inches thick. When unripe, it is a grass-green color, but once it reaches maturity, it turns a Citrine yellow. The inner flesh is redder than in the common variety and forms a cavity at the center. It has few seeds—indeed, some are entirely devoid of them—and its flavor is vinous. This species rarely occurs in Amboina, but it is found frequently in Banda, for which reason some call them the *Bandense* <note>original: "Bandenses"; meaning from the Banda Islands.</note> variety.

The third species of these trees bears fruit the size of a bowling ball <note>original: "globi, qui conorum lusui inservit"; literally, the ball used for the game of "cones" or nine-pins.</note>. These are slightly lumpy near the stem, and their rind is not particularly thick nor bitter, but almost edible. The inner flesh or marrow is white, very juicy, and slightly acidic, though it becomes sweeter in the ripe fruit, similar to the *Martinjo Lemon* <note>original: "Limo Martinjo"; a specific cultivar of citrus known to the author.</note>.

It bears smaller leaves than the preceding kind, almost like those of the aforementioned *Martinjo Lemon*, but stiffer and smoother; their heart-shaped base is about the size of the *Itam Lemon* <note>original: "Limonis Itam"; likely the "Black Lemon" or a dark-fruited variety.</note>. Short and sparse thorns sprout here and there at the base of the leaves. The trunk grows taller than the common variety, sending out many upright branches like the *Martinjo Lemon*, but its canopy is broader. This species rarely occurs in Amboina, where it is called the *Japanese Pomelo* because it was first brought over from there. It is not highly esteemed, however, as its fruits are neither acidic nor sweet. They are mostly used to make the commoners' drink called *Pons* <note>original: "Pons"; the historical origin of the word "Punch," a mixture of water, arrack (a distilled spirit), lemon juice, sugar, and various spices.</note>.

The fourth species is the rarest of all. Its leaves are similar to the first species but smoother; they are not serrated at the edges and end in a rounded shape at the top, though some have a short point, and others are grooved or split. They are not downy on the underside like the common variety. Its fruit is the largest of all, slightly elongated, irregular, and bumpy; five or six often hang together from a single stem. They are marked with distinct little dots or pits, and their color is like the others. The fruit's rind is over an inch thick, bitter, and sulfurous, though in other respects its scent and flavor agree with the preceding kinds. Its marrow or flesh is white, juicier and sweeter than the common kind, and contains almost no seeds. In this species, it often happens that another smaller fruit is found inside, about the size of a peeled orange, separated from the rest of the larger fruit's flesh by a thin, downy membrane. Indeed, some of these smaller internal fruits even bear a layer of new rind on their upper part; otherwise, this internal little "apple" is of the same substance, color, and flavor as the rest of the flesh. However, this does not occur in all of them, but only in a few fruits on the tree. This is most often observed in the *Bandense* variety; when these fruits were brought to Amboina and their seeds planted, they grew quite well and produced huge, full fruits, but they very rarely contained that double fruit.

In Batavia, white-fleshed fruits of this tree also occur, though the red ones are preferred. However, they do not produce double fruits there unless they have been propagated from the seeds of Banda, where the most beautiful ones grow on *Plo-Ay* <note>original: "Plo-Ay"; Pulau Ay, one of the Banda Islands.</note>. They are very difficult to propagate, as one rarely finds seeds in them.

**Name.** This species is called the *Pregnant Lemon* <note>original: "Limo Praegnans"</note>, in Malay *Lemon Bonting*, and also *Lemon Banda*.

The *Atlas Sinensis* (page 131) states that the true homeland of these trees and fruits is the twelfth and southernmost Chinese province, *Quantong* <note>original: "Quantong"; modern Guangdong.</note>, where it is called *Yeucu*, and by the Portuguese *Jamboam*, which is the same as *Zamboa*. The size of these fruits exceeds a human head; inside, the flesh is red, juicy, and slightly acidic like semi-ripe grapes. If they are hung up inside a house, they can be preserved for a year. The leaves of a young tree, when crushed between the hands, give off a most pleasant scent, which is very similar to that of the *fragrant nail* <note>original: "Unguis odorati"; referring to the operculum of certain sea snails (Blatta Byzantina) used in traditional incense and perfumery.</note>.

The fruit is somewhat smaller, not round, but pear-shaped like the large winter pears, and the ripe ones become somewhat thicker at the stem and develop some bumps here and there. It is about half a foot high and five inches thick. The unripe fruit is grass-green, but the ripe is lemon-colored. The inner marrow is redder than the common kind, with a small cavity inside and few seeds; indeed, some are without seeds, and also vinous in taste. This variety is little seen in Amboina, but they have it in abundance in Banda, which is why some also call them *Bandanese Pomelos*.

3. There is also a variety of these trees that bears fruit as large as a ball used for bowling, being a little lumpy at the stem, having a rind that is not very thick and not bitter, but almost edible. The inner marrow is white and very juicy in taste, tart, and the ripe ones are a little sweeter, like the *Martinjo Lemon*.

The leaves are smaller than the preceding ones, and almost like those of the mentioned *Martinjo Lemon*, but stiffer and smoother, and the heart-shaped base is as large as that of the *Itam Lemon*, here and there with a few short thorns at the origin of the leaves. The trunk shoots up higher than the common kind, mostly with straight branches, also like those of the *Martinjo Lemon* aforementioned, but with a broader crown. They have few of these in Amboina, and they are called *Japanese Pomelos* there because they were supposedly first brought from there. They are also little esteemed because they are neither sour nor sweet, and are mostly used for *Farmer's Punch* <note>original: "Boere Pons"</note>, a drink made of water, Arrack, lemon juice, sugar, and some spices mixed together.

4. The fourth variety is certainly the rarest, having leaves like those of the first variety, yet quite smooth and not serrated at the edges; at the front, they run to a round shape, and there some have a short tip while others are split; they are not woolly underneath like the common kind. The fruit is as large as the largest pumpkins <note>original: "Pomponeen"; likely referring to large gourds or pumpkins.</note>, not round but somewhat tall, irregular, and lumpy, hanging four or five together on one stem, marked on the outside with notable pits, but of the same color as the others. The rind is a good inch thick, bitter, and sulfurous; otherwise of the same scent and taste as the previous ones. The flesh is white, juicier, and sweeter than the common kind, and almost without seeds. Regarding this variety, it often happens that inside the fruit another small Pomelo or "little apple" is found, the size of a peeled orange, separated from the surrounding flesh of the large fruit by a thin woolly membrane. Indeed, some even have a piece of a new rind at the upper end; otherwise, this internal fruit or little apple is of the same substance, color, and taste as the other flesh. However, as said, one does not find it in all those large fruits, but only in a few on the same tree, and mostly in Banda. Having been brought from there to Amboina as seeds, they also grow large and full there, but they very rarely come to show that double fruit.

In Batavia, they also have white Pomelos, the red ones being preferred or esteemed above them; but they likewise bear no double fruits there unless they have come from seeds from Banda, where the most beautiful ones occur on *Plo-Ay*. They are very difficult to propagate, since one rarely finds seeds in them.

**Name.** They are called *Limo Praegnans*; in Malay *Lemon Bonting*, and also *Lemon Banda*.

The *Chinese Atlas*, page 131, identifies the true homeland of these Pomelo trees and fruits as the 12th and southernmost Chinese province of *Quantong*, being called *Yeucu* there, but by the Portuguese *Jamboam*, which is the same as *Zamboa*. It is nearly as large as a human head, and red of flesh inside, also juicy and tart like half-ripe grapes, and can be kept good for a year if hung in the house. The leaves of a young Pomelo tree, when rubbed a bit between the hands, give off a very pleasant scent, almost corresponding with that of the *fragrant nail* <note>original: "Unguis Odoratus"</note>.

II Book. XXXV. Chapter. AMBOINESE HERBAL. 99

## OBSERVATION.

These trees, and their fruits mentioned here by *Rumphius*, are varieties rather than distinct species. Because they differ in their manner of growth, foliage, and cultivation, they should be considered a single species, called the *Indian Orange-apple* <note>original: "Malus aurantia Indica"</note>, with the largest fruit of all known as the *Pomelo* <note>original: "Pumpelmus"</note>. It has a pale or reddish flesh, as described by *Herman in the Garden of Leiden, page 405*. A branch of this tree with its fruit is elegantly drawn and engraved by *Merian in Insects of Surinam, page 9* <note>referring to Maria Sibylla Merian, a famous naturalist and illustrator</note>; see the *notes* there, as well as our *Ceylonese Treasury, page 39* <note>original: "Thesaur. nostrum Zeyl."</note>, where I have collected its various synonyms and authors.

Furthermore, this is the tree held by Botanists to be the "Tree of Knowledge," the fruit of which was forbidden to our first parents in the earthly Paradise; for this reason, it is also called *ADAM'S APPLE* <note>original: "POMUM ADAMI"</note> by *Caspar and Johannes Bauhin*, as is further evident from *Plukenet’s Mantissa and Amaltheum* and the aforementioned *Ceylonese Treasury*. This tree is also recorded by *Valentyn in the Description of Amboina, page 188*.

---

## CHAPTER THIRTY-FIVE.

->The Citron: Susu Lemon<-

Citrons in the Indies do not grow so much on trees as they do on a shrub, which rises with several stems and bears long, limp branches like whips <note>original: "flagella"</note>, so that they must lean upon the surrounding vegetation. The leaves also differ from all other lemon species, as they are not heart-shaped <note>a reference to the winged petiole common in citrus, which Rumphius calls a "second leaf" or "heart"</note> but rather resemble laurel leaves, being oblong, rounded at both ends, and having deeply serrated edges. They are a brighter green than other lemon leaves, four or five inches long and two wide, and mostly hang forward.
   At the base of the leaves, younger trees bear short thorns, while older ones have long and sharp ones. The flowers are white and larger than in any other species, consisting of five oblong, thickish petals that are bent backward; however, their scent is weak. In the center are many stamens with yellowish tips. The fruit has two forms, which for the sake of distinction I shall divide into the wild and the domestic. The wild is the most common, similar in shape to Spanish lemons but slightly larger and oblong, wide at the base and ending in a sort of nipple; its rind has small bumps here and there but is otherwise smooth and yellowish. The fruit itself is about five inches long and four wide or thick, and it is lumpy and uneven near the stem. Its outer rind is barely a finger thick and spongy, lacking the sulfurous scent of other lemons; it is tasteless and hardly edible. The inner flesh is very sparse, making up barely half the fruit's thickness; it is white, juicy, and acidic like others, but not as pleasant, which is why it is only used for sauces when better options are lacking.
   The domestic variety bears a fruit twice as large, namely like a melon, about a foot long and six inches thick; some are a bit smaller and more humped than the preceding kind, also ending in a nipple. The external color is not a true lemon-yellow but pale, leaning more toward green. Its rind is an inch thick, and the flesh or marrow is like the previous kind, but the flavor is more vinous. This rind is also juicier and firmer than in other lemons, making it very suitable for candying.
   Name. In Latin *Malum Citrium*. In Malay *Lemon Sussu*, which means *Nippled Lemon* <note>original: "Limo Mammosus"; from "Susu" meaning breast or milk in Malay</note> from the shape of the nipple. In Dutch *Citroenen*. In Portuguese *Cidra*. In Amboinese on Hitoë *Uffe Wale*, meaning the "rope-creeping lemon" because of its long, limp branches. In Banda it is called *Uffe Ala*, which is *Lemon Bras*, or *Rice Lemon*.
   I wish to note here a philological discourse on the origin of...

## OBSERVATION.

These trees and their fruits, mentioned here hereafter by *Rumphius*, are more variations than distinct species, differing through various methods of cultivation, soil, and air. For this reason, they are not held to be separate species, and this tree is named by *Herman in the Garden of Leiden, page 405* as the *Indian Orange-tree*, with the largest fruit called *Pomelo* <note>original: "Pumpelmoes"</note>, having pale flesh. A branch of this tree with the fruit is also beautifully depicted and shown by *Merian* on the Surinam Insects, page 19, where one may see further notes, and our *Ceylonese Treasury, page 39*, where I have cited various names and writers.
   This is furthermore that tree which is held by herbalists to be the "Tree of Knowledge," whose fruit in the earthly Paradise was forbidden to our first ancestors; therefore it is also named *Adam's Apple* <note>original: "Adams appel"</note> by *Casparus and Joannes Bauhinus*, as further appears from *Plukenet in his Mantissa and Amaltheum*, according to the cited passage in our *Ceylonese Treasury, etc.* The Pomelo tree is also described by *Valentyn* in the description of *Amboina, page 188*.

---

## THIRTY-FIFTH CHAPTER.

->Citron Tree<-

The Citrons in the Indies do not actually grow on a tree, but rather on a shrub that shoots up with several small trunks and produces long, limp branches as if they were vines; therefore, they must rest on the nearest thicket. The leaf also differs from all other lemon species because it does not have a "heart" or second leaf <note>the botanical term is a winged petiole</note>, and better resembles a laurel leaf, being elongated, almost smooth and round at the front and back, and the edges significantly saw-toothed. They are also a lighter green than those of other lemons, 4 and 5 inches long, 2 wide, and mostly facing forward.
   At the base, the young trees have short thorns, but the old ones and most branches have long and stiff thorns. The flowers or blossoms are white and also larger than those of any lemons, made of five elongated and fatty petals, which are somewhat bent backward and have a faint scent. Inside stand white threads with yellow tips. The fruit is also of two types of appearance, which I shall divide into the Wild and the Tame for distinction. The Wild is the most common, and in shape like Spanish Lemons, though somewhat larger, elongated, wide at the back, and ending in a nipple at the front. The outermost rind has small bumps here and there, otherwise it is smooth and pale yellow, and the fruit is about five inches long and four fingers thick, mostly somewhat crooked or lumpy near the stem. The outermost rind is barely a finger thick, pithy, and without the sulfurous quality of other lemons, but tasteless and almost inedible. The inner marrow is very little, making up barely half of the thickness; furthermore, it is white, juicy, and sour, like other lemons, though not so pleasant, which is why it is only used for sauces and dipping when better is lacking.
   The Tame variety has a fruit that is easily twice as large: namely like Melons, almost a foot long and six inches thick, though some are a bit smaller, more lumpy than the preceding, and also ending in a nipple. The color on the outside is not a true yellow, but somewhat pale, drawing more toward green. The rind is an inch thick, and the flesh is like the preceding, though of a more vinous taste, this rind being also juicier and more solid than those of other lemons, and very capable of being candied.
   Name. In Latin *Malum Citrium*. In Malay *Lemon Sussu*, that is *Nippled Lemon* <note>original: "Limo Mammosus"</note> or *Teat-lemon*. In German <note>meaning Dutch here</note> *Citroenen*. In Portuguese *Cidra*. In Amboinese on *Hitoë, Uffi Wale*, that is "creeping lemon" because of its long and limp vines. On Banda *Uffe Ala*, that is *Lemon Bras*, or *Rice-lemon*.

### AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chapter XXXV.
# XXXVI.
<meta>catchword: CHAPTER</meta>

...origin of the word *Citrus* from Bauhin, Book 1, Chapter 25, where he judges this fruit to be indicated in Holy Scripture by *Etzadar*, that is, a branch of a beautiful tree, which the Israelites were required to use in the Feast of Tabernacles <note>the Jewish holiday of Sukkot</note>. From this comes the Chaldean name of this fruit, *Extrogin*, in the singular *Etog* and *Etrog*, and from there the Arabic *Atrog*, from which names the Greeks perhaps derived <term>kitros</term> <note>original Greek: κίτρος; the citron fruit</note>.

Furthermore, the German Jews, around the eighth of September for the Feast of Tabernacles, are still compelled to seek them from Marseille, because they know of no more beautiful fruit than this Citron. It is therefore the *Median Apple* <note>original: "Malum Medicum"</note> of Dioscorides, the *Median and Persian Apple* of Theophrastus, the <term>kitros</term> <note>original Greek: κίτρος</note> or the *Golden Apple* of the Greeks, and the *Assyrian Apple* of Athenaeus. It is the *Hesperian Apple* of Pliny and the Ancients; however, it differs from the *Citrus* of the Ancients <note>Rumphius is distinguishing the Citron fruit from the 'Citrus' wood prized by Romans</note>. Concerning this matter, see Book 3 in the chapter on the *Lingoom*, and at the end of this chapter.

<margin>Location.</margin>
In these islands, it does not occur frequently, as its use is rare; hence, only one or two shrubs may grow here and there in the yards near houses. In Banda, however, it is observed in greater abundance, partly in the woods and partly in abandoned gardens, where these small trees had been planted in place of hedges. A larger species is cultivated there in gardens, from which it was also brought to Amboina, though it does not produce such large fruits there as it does in Banda. In Java, they are more frequent, and mostly in the woods, as they are also in Brazil; however, everywhere it is a shrub, not a true tree.

<margin>Usage.</margin>
The thicker peels of both species are used, though mostly the domestic ones, to be preserved in sugar. This is done by scraping off the outer green part, soaking them for several days in water, and then boiling the peels in sugar; some are coated with crystalline sugar to serve as confections. This is mostly done by the Chinese and Europeans, as the Indians are ignorant of this art, and they have no other use for it besides using the sour juice as a dipping sauce. In the Javanese language, it is called by some *Lemon Java*, that is, the Javanese Lemon, since it is considered a native fruit there. Another variety of the wild species occurs, which grows a little taller than the previous one, but its leaves are very similar, though slightly larger, sharper, and more finely serrated at the edges, and it is covered everywhere with long, sharp thorns, so that it can hardly be touched. The flowers are also smaller than in the preceding kind; the fruits are oblong-round, in the shape and size of Spanish Lemons, and also adorned with a nipple at the top and smooth on the outside. The peel of these is very thin, while the flesh is abundant, juicier, and more acidic than in the others. This species occurs rarely in Amboina, having been brought there from Banda, and it is used for nothing else but the acidic pulp, which is used for dipping sauces like other lemons. From the former species, a sweet fruit has been propagated through cultivation, which is so pleasant that both the inner pulp and the outer peel are edible; this fruit possesses an elegant yellow color when it becomes ripe.

All these trees (as other authors also warn) differ from the *Citrus of the Ancients*, which grows in Mauritania near the mountain called Atlas. That is a species of <term>Oxycedrus</term> <note>a type of prickly cedar or juniper</note>, which bears leaves, fruit, and a scent very similar to the Cypress, according to the testimony of Pliny, Book 3, Chapter 15. From its wood, in ancient times, precious tables were manufactured, called *Citrine and Citrus Tables* <note>original: "Mensae Citreae & Citrinae"</note>, which were categorized according to various patterns and spots into *Tiger-patterned*, *Panther-patterned*, and *Parsley-patterned* <note>referring to the mottled grain of the wood</note>.

---

## EXPLANATION

->Of the Twenty-Fifth Plate.<-

Which displays the Citron with linear petioles <note>the stalks of the leaves</note>, as it is named in the *Hortus Cliffortianus* <note>The "Garden of Clifford," a famous work by Linnaeus</note>, perhaps page 379, where you may see other authors, and especially in Sloane’s *Catalog of the Plants of Jamaica*, page 208, which contains a countless number of authors.

<column-break/>

...on the word *Citrum*, according to J. Bauhin’s first book, chapter 25, where he believes that this fruit is expressed in Holy Scripture by *Etzadar*, that is, a Branch of a beautiful tree, which the Israelites had to use in the Feast of Tabernacles. For this reason, the Chaldean name of this fruit is *Etrogin*, in the simple or singular *Etog* and *Etrog*, and from that the Arabic *Atrog*, from which names the Greeks possibly made *Kitros*.

The German Jews must, around the eighth of September for the Feast of Tabernacles, therefore also fetch this fruit from Marseille, because they know no more beautiful fruit than this Citron. Therefore, this is the *Malum Medicum* of Dioscorides, the *Medicum and Persicum* of Theophrastus, *Kitros* or the *Malum Aureum* <note>Golden Apple</note> of the Greeks, the *Assyricum* of Athenaeus, and the *Hespericum* of Pliny and the Ancients. Yet it differs from the *Citrum* of the Ancients. Concerning which, see the third book on the *Lingoom*.

<margin>Location.</margin>
In these islands, one does not find them much, because they are little in use, with only a bush here and there on the plots by the houses. But in Banda, I have found them in greater multitude, partly in the wild, and in some abandoned gardens where they had planted them in place of a hedge. They put the large variety in the gardens, from where they were also brought to Amboina, though they do not wish to bear such large fruits there as in Banda. On Java, one finds them more abundantly, and mostly in the wild, as also in Brazil, though everywhere it is a bush and not a tree.

<margin>Usage.</margin>
The thick peel of both sorts, but mostly of the domestic ones, is in use for candying, which happens when one scrapes off the outer greenness, soaks it for some days in water, and thereafter boils it up with sugar; some are also candied with sugar-candy to be served among banquet-work. And this is mostly done by the Chinese and Europeans, for the Indians do not know how to handle it, having no other use for it but the sour juice for dipping. Some also call it in Malay *Lemon Java*, that is, Javanese Lemon, because it is held there to be a native plant. One has yet a second sort of the wild Citron, shooting up a little higher than the former, but the leaves are mostly like the former, although somewhat larger, sharper, and more finely sawed on the edges, set all over with fierce and long thorns, so that one can hardly touch them. The flowers are also smaller than the former; the fruits are oblong-round in shape and size like the true Spanish Lemons, also with a nipple in front, and smooth on the outside, with a very thin peel, and in contrast, the inner flesh is very much, also juicier and sourer than in other Lemons. But of this sort, one finds little in Amboina, being brought there from Banda, and in no other use than that one uses the sour marrow for dipping, like that of other Lemons. But from the above-mentioned variety, one has obtained a sort that has become so sweet through cultivation that one can eat the inner marrow as well as the peel, which also becomes a pretty yellow when the fruit is entirely ripe.

All these trees (as other authors also warn) differ from the *Citrus Antiquorum*, which grows in Mauritania by Mount Atlas, and is a sort of the *Oxycedrus*, in leaves, fruits, and scent like the Cypresses, according to the testimony of Pliny, book 3, cap. 15, and from which in old times the costly tables were made, which were called *Mensas Citreas* and *Citrinas*, and according to the variety of paintings and spots, were divided into *Tigrine*, *Pantherine*, and *Apiate* <note>referring to wood grains resembling tigers, panthers, or parsley/celery</note>.

II Book. XXXVI. Chapter. AMBOINESE HERBAL. 101

# CHAPTER THIRTY-SIX.
## The Tuberous Lemon. Lemon Martin.

Among the species of sour Lemons, which occur throughout the whole of India in greater abundance than the sweet varieties, those which possess the most bumps <note>original Latin: "tuberculis", referring to the warty or uneven texture of the skin</note> excel in size; the largest of these are commonly called *Lemon Martin*. This tree, when it reaches its full height, is similar to a common Apple tree, though its branches are quite curved, as is the trunk itself. The leaves are very similar to Citron leaves, but they are shorter and not significantly heart-shaped <note>original Latin: "cordata", a botanical term for leaves shaped like a heart at the base</note>, appearing almost winged, though this heart-shaped figure appears more clearly in the younger leaves. At the edges, they are slightly serrated; if rubbed, they breathe out a strong scent, which is not unpleasant, nor do they give a bitter taste. They are three or four inches long. On the younger branches near the leaves, short and soft spines sprout, but on the lower parts where the leaves have fallen, the spines are longer and sharper, which so densely beset and surround the branch that it can hardly be touched. These, however, gradually fall off the older branches, so that fewer spines are seen on the small boughs. All Lemon flowers first form white buds, and from these, small flowers are formed, mostly consisting of five (rarely four) white, thick, and oblong petals. Inside, they bear certain upright, whitish stalks <term>stamina</term> with yellow tips <term>anthers</term>, and in their center sits the <term>embryo</term> <note>the developing fruit or ovary</note> supporting a small pillar <term>pistillum</term>, from which the fruit is formed and grows. Their scent is weak but pleasant, approaching that of white Lilies. The flowers in this species are larger than the common ones and composed of five petals, which are purplish on the outside.

The fruits are not uniform in shape; some are as large as two fists and somewhat pear-shaped, or like a Quince, and are covered with larger bumps only near the stem, while the rest of their part is covered with lower bumps like warts. Others are oblong, egg-shaped, or pointed at both ends, covered over their entire surface with low bumps or larger warts. When ripe, these Lemons turn from green to yellowish, and finally bear a more yellow or citron-like color, almost like Spanish Lemons. Their rind is quite thick, and if it is peeled, it emits sulfurous sprays <note>this refers to the volatile oils that spray out when the skin is squeezed or broken</note> which appear oily, but they have a thoroughly pleasant and citron-like scent and taste, though also somewhat bitter and stinging to the tongue. The inner pulp <note>original Latin: "medulla", literally 'marrow' or 'pith'</note> is like that of European Lemons, with a sour taste, but weaker than in any other species, which is why it is also eaten raw. However, if it is cooked with seasonings, it is too weak, and therefore other more acidic Lemons are to be chosen for this purpose.

*Season.* This tree produces its fruit almost the whole year round; for it gives flowers, half-grown, and fully mature Lemons all at once. It must be carefully pruned, however, as it otherwise sends out too many upright and thorny shoots which emaciate the tree—a fact which should also be observed regarding other species.

*Name.* In Latin, it is *Limo Tuberosus* or *Martinicus*. It should be noted that all Indian species of Lemons are called by the general Malay name *Lemoen* <note>the root of the English word "lemon"</note>, a name which in Europe is attributed to only one species. This tree is called *Lemon Martin* in Malay, but the reason this surname was given to it is entirely hidden from me; yet it seems likely that it first came to notice through a certain Portuguese man named *Martin*, and was named after him.

Since these fruits were not distinctly known to the ancients, they designated all these species by the general names of *Citron*, *Median*, or *Hesperian Apples*. In subsequent times, however, they investigated the species more accurately; they called one variety *Limonium* in the Latin tongue, and *Limon* in the pharmacopoeias. We shall retain this latter name, as *Limonium* is properly a type of herb <note>likely referring to sea-lavender or similar herbs historically called Limonium</note>.

<meta>catchword: De-</meta>

<column-break/>

# THIRTY-SIXTH CHAPTER.
## Bumpy-Lemon.

Among the types of sour Lemons, which are found in greater quantity throughout all of India than the sweet ones, those which are covered with many bumps stand out in size, and among those, the largest are commonly called *Lemon Martin*. This tree reaches its full height like a common Apple tree, and the branches stand quite crooked, as the trunk itself often does as well. The leaves come closest to Citron leaves, yet are somewhat shorter, and without a noticeable little heart-shape—its place can be seen, but the "heart" itself is so narrow that one can barely recognize it, though in the young leaves it is much more recognizable. At the edges, they are a little serrated, with a strong scent if rubbed, yet not unpleasant, nor bitter in taste; they are 3 to 4 inches long. On the young branches, short and soft thorns stand by the leaves, but further back, where the leaves have fallen off, there are long and fierce thorns, so thick and all around the branches that one can hardly handle them. However, these also gradually fall off the old branches, so that one then sees only a few thorns on the small twigs. All Lemon blossoms first have white buds, and from those, the flowers are formed or come forth, having a lovely scent. They are made of thickish petals, having some white and straight threads <term>stamens</term> inside with yellow caps <term>anthers</term>, and in the middle a green bump (on which a little pillar <term>style</term> stands) from which the fruit is formed. They have a mild but lovely scent, tending somewhat towards Lilies. Specifically, the blossom of the *Lemon Martin* is larger than the others and, as said, made of five petals, which are somewhat reddish or purple on their outer side.

The fruits are not of a single shape, for some are as large as two fists, somewhat pear-like, or like a quince, and only near the stem are they covered with some large bumps; the rest is mostly full of low warts and bumps. Others again are oblong, egg-shaped, or somewhat pointed at the back and front, and covered over the whole body with low bumps or large warts. When ripe, they turn from green to yellow, and finally also somewhat deeper in color, almost like the Spanish Lemons. The rind is reasonably thick, and if one breaks or bends it, it gives off sulfurous sprays which seem oily, yet are lovely and truly Citron-like in scent and taste, though also somewhat bitter and sharp on the tongue. The inner marrow is like that of our European Lemons, sour in taste, but weaker than any others, for which reason one can also eat them raw; but in cooking and in sauces, they turn out too weak, so that one must choose other sharp Lemons for that purpose.

*Season.* This tree bears mostly throughout the entire year, showing blossoms, half-grown, and mature fruit all at once. But one must prune it diligently, otherwise it gets too many young, straight, and thorny shoots that starve it, which one should also understand to apply to other Lemons.

*Name.* In Latin *Limo Tuberosus*, *Martinicus*, where it should also be known that in India all types of these trees are called by a common name in Malay, *Lemoen*, which in Europe is given only to one specific kind. In Malay, it is *Lemoen Martin*, but why they have given it this surname, I cannot yet guess, but I can venture a guess with a show of truth that it was first brought to knowledge by one or another Portuguese person whose name was *Martin*, and was named after him.

And because these fruits were not fully known to the ancients, they included all those types under the common names of *Malum Citrium* <note>Citron Apple</note>, *Medicum* <note>Median Apple</note>, and *Hespericum* <note>Hesperian Apple</note>; but the following centuries, distinguishing the types more narrowly, called one type *Limonium* in Latin, and *Limonem* in the pharmacies, and we shall use only this last name, because *Limonium* is actually a herb.
