->AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. chapter XXXVI.<-

One would search in vain for the derivation of this name in European languages, for the word is Arabic, *Leytun*, and Persian, *Limum*, which both indicate every type of small medicinal citrus <note>original Latin: "malum Medicum", literally 'Median apple', an ancient name for citrus fruits</note>. Just as *Torung* and *Toronga* is the same for the larger variety among the Arabs, which the Arabs also write as *Altrung* and *Ottrong*; however, *Torong* is properly Persian, from which comes the Spanish *Toronja*. By this is understood that larger Citron which has a sweeter rind and equals a Melon in size, such as was described in the preceding chapter, although it also applies somewhat to our Martinico variety. Among the people of Amboina and the surrounding islands, it bears no peculiar name, as it is largely unknown to them; generally, however, all Lemons are called by them *Aussi* and *Ussi*, just as they are called *Lemon* by the Malays, *Djodji* by the people of Ternate, *Lemo* by the Macassarese, *Jeroc* by the Javanese, *Djohoc* by the Balinese, *Usse* by the Bandanese, and *Cam* by the Chinese.

*Location.* Throughout these Oriental islands, the *Limo Martin* occurs everywhere, but nowhere does it grow wild or among the Amboinese; it is found only among the Europeans, from which I believe it was brought from elsewhere, and especially by the Portuguese, who perhaps brought it from the Western islands <note>the West Indies/Americas</note> into the East Indies.

*Usage.* Since its internal flesh is the most wine-like among all species of sour Lemons, it is eaten raw when cut into slices and sprinkled with sugar, providing an excellent refreshment and restoration on sea voyages. If eaten in such a manner, the white flesh of the outer rind should not be entirely cut away, but a part of it should be left, as its bland <note>original: "fatua", meaning tasteless or insipid</note> substance tempers the acidity of the other part. For this rind, if its outermost part has been scraped off, is edible, and the juice of this Lemon is especially suitable for a drink called *Boerepons* <note>a type of punch or "farmer's punch" often made with citrus, spirits, and sugar</note>, to be prepared from it; it is better than that of other Lemons because it is less acidic and does not cause abdominal cramps. The rind of this fruit also contains an aromatic spirit, but it is little used in these lands, except that it is often cooked with meat or fish, to which it imparts a pleasant flavor. It is also used for washing the head, but mostly in the absence of others. Its raw pulp, eaten with sugar, cuts through and clears away the stubborn and thick phlegm that clings to the chest and bronchial tubes of the lungs, which often causes troublesome asthma and convulsive coughing.

Furthermore, this tree does not grow very old unless it is diligently pruned and carefully tended; otherwise, it easily contracts rot <note>original: "cessos", likely referring to decay or canker</note>, from which it sends out many "tears" and exudes a copious amount of gum, by which it wastes away and perishes, so that often half of the trunk and canopy is dead while the other part yields meager fruit.

Related to the description of the *Lemon Martin* above are also certain other tuberous <note>warty or bumpy</note> species, which we shall describe in succession; the first of these to occur is the *Bellied Lemon* <term>Limo Ventricosus</term>, in Malay *Lemon Purrut*: This tree is of the same size as the preceding one, but it bears a denser and narrower canopy, and its branches are mostly upright. The leaves also differ much; for although these are about four inches long, the lower part <note>the petiole or leaf-stalk</note> is so large and wide that it constitutes almost half of the entire leaf, making it look as if two leaves were placed one upon the other; they are finely serrated at the edges, thicker, and a darker green than in the preceding variety. Its flower is the smallest of all, consisting of four white petals, and although it is open, it is scarcely as large as the nail of the little finger. Its fruit is half the size of the *Lemon Martin*, scarcely equaling a fist, and pear-shaped, but so covered with tubercles <note>bumps or warts</note> that it hardly maintains that shape; these tubercles, when observed individually, are smoother than those of the *Lemon Martin*. It is mostly green, and turns only slightly yellow when fully ripe. Its rind is more solid and juicier than the preceding one; its scent is more pleasant than in any other Indian Lemons, and better than or approaching the best Spanish Lemons. The interior flesh is greenish, grainy, and very acidic with a certain sharpness, almost corrosive, and is not very juicy, but contains many seeds. The branches are beset with rare, smaller spines, more frequent than in the *Lemon Martin*, but long spines occur much more rarely on that tree, providing a better climb than the preceding tree.

*Name.* In Latin *Limo Ventricosus*: in Malay *Lemon Purrut*, because of its many tubercles, which like warts—

<meta>catchword: carum</meta>

<column-break/>

*The derivation of its name will be sought in vain in the European languages; but the Arabic word is* Leytun, *and the Persian* Limum, *with which they signify all small sorts of Lemons: Just as* Torung *and* Toronga *among the Arabs denotes the large sort, which the Arabs also write as* Altrung *and* Ottrong, *but* Torong *is properly Persian, from which comes the Spanish* Toronja, *by which they understand that large sort of Citron, which has a sweeter skin and has the size of a Melon, which is described in the preceding Chapter, although it also applies in some sense to our* Martinique *variety. Among the Amboinese and surrounding Islands it has no special name, because it is mostly unknown, but in general all Lemons are called* Aussi *and* Ussi, *just as the Malays call them* Lemon, *Ternatans* Djodji, *Macassars* Lemo, *Javanese* Jeroc, *Balinese* Djohoc, *Bandanese* Usse, *and Chinese* Cam.

*Place. In these Eastern Islands one finds the* Lemon Martin *everywhere, yet growing nowhere by itself, or among the Amboinese, but only among the Europeans, and therefore I judge that they were brought in from elsewhere, and particularly by the Portuguese, who perhaps brought them from the Western Islands into the East Indies.*

*Usage. Because the inner flesh is the most wine-like among all sour Lemons, it can be eaten raw when cut into slices and sprinkled with some sugar, which is a good refreshment on Sea-voyages: But if one wishes to consume them so, then one must not cut the white flesh of the outer shell entirely away, but leave it partly on, because its flat dryness comes to restrain the sourness of the other: For the shell itself, when the outermost part is scraped off, can be eaten, and above all the juice of these Lemons is fit to make the drink* Boerepons <note>Punch</note> *from, for which they serve better than any other Lemons, because they are less sour and cause no cutting in the belly. The shells are full of a sharp spirit, but are little used here in this country, except that they are sometimes boiled with meat and fish to give them a pleasant scent. They are also used for washing the head, but mostly for lack of others. The raw marrow <note>pulp</note> eaten with sugar cuts through and wipes away the tough phlegm that sticks in the chest and lung-pipes, and causes a troublesome whooping cough.*

*Furthermore, this tree reaches no great age, unless one diligently prunes and tends it; otherwise the worm gets into it, from which it tears and sweats out much gum, whereupon it gradually expires, so that one often sees one half of the trunk and crown entirely dead, and the other half still bearing meager fruits.*

*With the above-mentioned* Lemon Martin, *some other knotty sorts also have affinity, which we shall discuss or list here one after another, as first* Limo Ventricosus, *in Malay* Lemon Purrut: *The tree is of a size like the preceding, but has a denser and narrower crown, and the branches stand mostly upright. The leaves also differ quite a lot from it: for although they are also scarcely four inches long, yet their back tail-leaf <note>the winged petiole</note> is so large and broad that it makes up nearly half of the whole leaf, just as if two leaves were set upon each other, being finely sawed <note>serrated</note> on the edges, thicker than the former, and also a darker green: The flower is the smallest of all, consisting of four white petals, and when entirely opened, being hardly the width of a nail on a little finger. The fruits are only half as large as the* Lemon Martin, *namely smaller than a fist, shaped like a pear, but occupied with so many bumps or boils that it can hardly keep that shape; but these bumps, viewed in particular, are smoother than those of the* Lemon Martin; *they remain mostly green: The entirely ripe ones become only a little yellow; the skin is denser and juicier than the former, in scent lovelier than all sorts of Indian Lemons, equal to or better than the best Spanish Citrons: The inner flesh is greenish, small-grained, and very sour, with some sharpness, although not very juicy, but having many seeds. The branches have only a few small thorns, yet somewhat more than* Lemon Martin, *but the long thorns are little seen on that tree, whereby it is also better to climb than the preceding.*

*Name. In Latin* Limo Ventricosus, *after the Malay* Lemon Purrut, *from the many bumps, which like boils—*

# Book II. Chapter XXVI. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...hang all around it; some also call it *Lemon Papua*, that is, the *Curled Lemon* <note>original: Limo Crispus</note>, named after the shape of the curly hair in which the Papuans delight; others, however, call it *Lemon tay Ayam*, that is, the *Chicken-dung Lemon* <note>original: fimum gallinaceum</note>, referring to the shape it mimics, as if it were a clotted lump of chicken dung; to the people of Ternate <note>An island in the Maluku Islands</note> it is known as *Djuru purrut*.

*Location.* It is found in Celebes <note>Modern-day Sulawesi</note>, and nearly all the Amboinese islands, as well as in Banda; however, it is not frequent anywhere, but rather rare.

*Use.* The rinds of these Lemons are most commonly used; they are rasped and mixed with a little water to serve as a scrub for the head after it has been washed and cleansed with something else. This serves to further remove grime and to impart a pleasant scent to the hair. Its acidic juice is rarely used in food, but is mostly employed for dyeing, for which purpose the sharpest Lemons are chosen. Some also wash their head and body with this juice, but it turns out poorly for them, as its sharpness erodes the skin, especially if the rays of the Sun touch it <note>This describes a phototoxic reaction, common with citrus oils</note>, causing the roots of the hair to weaken and be destroyed. Its fresh rind is also boiled in meat broth, and it can be preserved with sugar, much like the Martinique Lemon, though this is seldom done.

The third species of these lumpy Lemons is the *Limo Curamas*, which bears smaller leaves than the preceding one, though otherwise similar to its leaves, and constructed primarily of two parts <note>referring to the winged petiole characteristic of citrus</note>. These nearly agree with those of the lemon called *Maas*, but their heart-shaped part is larger. The fruits mimic the Martinique Lemon in both size and shape, but these are so irregularly round and deformed, beset with lumps and fissures, that no true form can be attributed to them; they are usually longer than they are wide, narrowed near the stem. They mostly bear a dull, dark green color, or a brownish-green, though eventually some yellowish spots appear on them. Furthermore, they are wrinkled and covered everywhere with small lumps, though these lumps do not protrude as much as in the *Lemon Purrut*. The internal flesh is white and dry, consisting of various small granules like lice <note>original: instar pediculorum</note>; it is not as juicy as the Martinique Lemon, for even when fully ripe, it remains mostly dry, giving little juice that is entirely sour. The scent of the rind is strong, and not as pleasant as that of the *Lemon Purrut*; indeed, it is almost goat-like <note>original: hircinus</note>, and the leaves breathe forth a similar odor.

The seeds are oblong, thin, slender, and wrinkled; on one side they bear a kind of tail made of many small veins, by which they cling to the internal membranes. The branches are beset everywhere with thorns, which on the larger branches become very short.

*Name.* In Latin it is called *Limo Unguentarius* <note>The Ointment Lemon</note>, following the Malay *Lemo Curamas*, named after the fragrant ointment with which the body is smeared, in which this rubbed rind is an ingredient.

*Location.* They grow in the wild gardens of Amboina and are planted in various villages, but these trees are little known.

*Use.* Nothing but the rind of this species is in use, which is rubbed and mixed into the aforementioned ointment; some, however, rub the head with it after washing, as was said of the preceding *Lemon Purrut*. However, this scent is less pleasing to our nation, as it is disagreeable, which is why it is not much esteemed even by the inhabitants. Others do better by using its dry flesh soaked a little in water to wash the head, as it removes grime and grease very well.

...hang all around it; some call them *Lemon Papua*, that is, *Curled Lemon*, after the shape of the curly hair of the Papuans. Others *Lemon tay ayam*, that is *Chicken-dung Lemons*, from the resemblance to a clump of chicken dung packed together. In Ternate, *Djuru Purrut*.

*Location.* They are found on Celebes, and almost in all the Amboinese islands, as well as in Banda; furthermore, not many elsewhere, but a few.

*Use.* The rinds of these Lemons are most in use, which one rasps and, mixed with a little water, rubs the head therewith, once it has been washed before with some other good thing, which then takes away the filth and subsequently gives the hair a good smell. The sour juice is not used much in food, but mostly for dyeing, for which one also seeks out the sharpest Lemons. Some also wash the head and body with this juice, but they usually fare poorly thereby, because by its sharpness it bites the skin (especially if the Sun shines on it) and makes the roots of the hair loose. The fresh rind is also boiled in meat broth, and one can preserve them with sugar, as well as those of *Lemon Martyn*, but this seldom happens.

3. The third sort of the lumpy Lemons is the *LEMON CURAMAS*, whose leaves are smaller than the preceding, otherwise the same, and made of two parts, almost agreeing with those of *Lemon Maas*, but the leaf-blade is larger. The fruits are like the *Lemon Martyn*, both in size and shape, yet these are so unevenly round and irregular, beset with lumps and clefts, that one can ascribe no right shape to them. They are generally longer than wide, narrowing or tapering somewhat at the stem. They mostly remain an ugly dark green or grey-green, but at last they become somewhat yellow in some spots or places; furthermore, they are entirely wrinkled and covered everywhere with small bumps, but those lumps do not bulge out as much as those of *Lemon Purrut*. The inner pith is white and dry, consisting of single small grains, like lice, not as juicy as the *Lemon Martyn*, for even if they become quite ripe, they nevertheless remain mostly dry, giving little juice, and that is also entirely sour. The smell of the rind is strong, and not as lovely as that of *Lemon Purrut*, indeed somewhat goat-like, as are also the leaves.

The seeds are elongated, thin, meager, and wrinkled, having at one end a small tail or little veins, with which they hang fast to the middle membranes. The branches are full of thorns, which on the old ones are very short.

*Name.* In Latin *Limo Unguentarius*, after the Malay *Lemo Curamas*, from a fragrant ointment with which one smears the body, in which this rubbed rind is also used.

*Location.* They grow on Amboina in the forest gardens and are planted in the villages, but are little known.

*Use.* Of this sort nothing is used but the rind, to rub into the aforementioned ointment; then some also use them to rub the head therewith after washing, like the aforementioned *Lemon Purrut*, but this smell is troublesome and unpleasant to our Nation, just as it is not even much esteemed by the Inhabitants themselves. Others do better when they soak the dry flesh of the Lemons a little in water and wash the head therewith, since it takes away the filth and the grease very well.

# OBSERVATION.

The species of Lemons described by our author in this chapter, like the others, are varieties produced by the luxuriant play of nature and clever cultivation, especially those that share similar leaf structures. Most of these are described or mentioned by other authors in *Sloane’s Catalogue of Jamaica Plants, page 209* and the *Hortus Cliffortianus, page 379*, where they are classified under the genus *Citrus*. These varieties of Lemons are also enumerated and briefly described by Valentijn in his description of *Amboina* from *page 188 to 191*.

# CHAPTER THIRTY-SEVEN.

## *Wild Lemon. Lemon Papeda.*

This tree is strictly a native of this island, and is much more common than all the preceding ones. It also grows taller than them, having a slanted and crooked trunk. The branches appear irregular and wild, and the smaller branches and leaf stalks are surrounded everywhere by sharp and firm thorns, so that this tree is more bristly and thorny than all other species of Lemons; for this reason, its crown does not allow for climbing. Its leaves appear to be constructed of two parts joined together <note>This refers to the "winged petiole," a leaf stalk that looks like a second, smaller leaf</note>, but the lower heart-shaped part is much smaller than the other or upper part, though it is quite wide; together they are about four or five inches long. No leaf is found without a thorn, and they are slightly serrated at the edges. Their pores are so large that the leaves appear perforated, and we can see the light through them.

Its fruit matches the Martinique Lemon in size, but it is not as pear-shaped; rather, it is rounder, smoother, and of a more solid substance. However, it is beset here and there with smooth bumps, so that it is never perfectly spherical, but irregular and slanted. The rind is of a very bright yellow color and smooth, not pitted with small hollows.

Its interior pulp is entirely white and juicy, extremely acidic and sharp, which is why its juice is not used alone in food, but mixed with other juices. The smell of the rind is like a citron, but not as pleasant as in the previous kinds. The tree produces solid and hard wood, yellowish, like Boxwood. The roots of old trunks are more yellow and are also streaked.

They love wild gardens and have a wilder nature than other Lemon trees. The Amboinese take no care to cultivate or prune it, although it is more esteemed by them than by our nation <note>Referring to the Dutch/Europeans</note>, and it occurs near almost all of their villages.

*Name.* In Latin, it is called *Limo Agrestis* <note>Wild Lemon</note>, since it loves the fields and has a wilder nature than all others; otherwise, it should be called *Limo Pultarius* <note>Porridge Lemon</note> from the Malay name *Lemon Papeda*. To the people of Macassar <note>In Sulawesi</note> it is called *Paralli*. To the Amboinese it is *Ussi Lapia*, and to the people of Ternate it is *Lemo Jabba*, which means Amboinese Lemons.

*Location.* It occurs in nearly all the Eastern islands from Celebes <note>Modern Sulawesi</note> as far as Amboina; in Saleyera the fruits are the best and largest, but in Java and Bali they are unknown.

*Use.* The rinds of these Lemons are of no use, but their pulp is, the juice of which the Amboinese use daily for condiments and dipping, specifically for the porridge they call *Papeda* <note>A staple starch made from sago pith</note>. Every morsel of this is dipped into this juice and eaten in that way, which is how these fruits earned their name. However, some broth of fish or meat must always be added, as otherwise it causes stomach cramps <note>original: tormina abdominis</note>; hence our nation does not use the juice much, preferring other milder Lemons. Furthermore, this juice is useful and serves in the preparation of the most precious pigment called *Cassombo*, which is made from the dried flowers of Safflower or *Cnicus* <note>Carthamus tinctorius</note>. For its preparation, the sharpest Lemons are always required, as is clear from its description. For this purpose, the inhabitants of Saleyera sell these fruits in great abundance—
<meta>Catchword: —ance</meta>

<column-break/>

# OBSERVATION.

The types of Lemons described by our author in this chapter are, like the rest, variations mostly brought forth by the luxuriant play of nature and clever cultivation, especially those that agree in their leaves: most of which are mentioned or described by authors in the *Catalogue of Sloane on Jamaica plants, p. 209 and in the Hortus Cliffortianus, p. 379*, where they are grouped with the *Citrons*. These various types of Lemons were also listed and briefly described by Valentijn in the description of *Ambon from page 188 to 191*.

# CHAPTER XXXVII.

## *Wild Pap-Lemon.*

This is properly an indigenous plant, and here much more common than the preceding ones. The tree also grows higher than them, with a slanted and gnarled trunk. The branches stand somewhat disorderly and wild; the twigs and its young branches are everywhere set with sharp and stiff thorns, so that this tree is thornier than any other Lemon species, and therefore the crown is unclimbable. The leaves also appear as if two are set upon one another, though the rear part is markedly smaller than the other half or the front part, but reasonably broad, and together four or barely five inches long; there is not a single leaf without thorns, and they are slightly saw-toothed on the edges. The sweat-pores are so large that one can see the sky through them.

The fruit is equal in size to the Martin Lemon, yet not pear-shaped, but rounder, smoother, and denser of substance, though also set with smooth bumps here and there, so that it never becomes spherical, but slanted and misshapen; otherwise the rind is smooth and without pits, very pale yellow.

The inner marrow is completely white and juicy, very sour and sharp, which is why this juice is not to be used alone in food, but mixed with other juice; the scent of the rind is also Citron-like, though not as lovely as the previous ones. The tree has a dense and hard wood, pale yellow, like Boxwood; the roots on the old trunks are somewhat yellower, and also veined.

They grow willingly in the forest-gardens, and are wilder of nature than other Lemons; the Amboinese also take no trouble to prune or tend them, although they are more esteemed by them than by our Nation, and are found near all their villages.

*Name.* In Latin *Limo Agrestis*, because it is wilder in nature and appearance than other Lemons, or one must call it *Limo Pultarius*, after the Malay *Lemon Papeda*. In Macassar *Paralli*, in Ambon *Ussi Lapia*, in Ternate *Lemo Jabba*, that is, *Amboinese Lemons*.

*Place.* One finds them mostly in all Eastern Islands from Celebes to Amboina; on Saleyer the largest and most beautiful of all are found, but on Java and Bali they are unknown.

*Use.* The rind of these Lemons is of no use, but the flesh is, whose juice the Amboinese use daily for sauces and dippings with their porridge called *Papeda*, of which every little lump must be dipped in this juice and then swallowed; from which these fruits have their name. However, one must always add some fish-broth or the like, otherwise it causes sharp pains in the belly, and for which reason our Nation does not use it much, preferring other milder Lemons. Furthermore, this juice is useful and necessary for preparing the costly purple dye called *Cassombo*, which is made from dry flowers of the *Carthamus* or *Cnicus*, for which one must always have the sharpest Lemons, as can be seen in its description. And to this end, the natives of Saleyers bring these fruits—

# CHAPTER THIRTY-SEVEN.

## *Wild Lemon. Lemon Papeda.*

This tree is strictly a native of this island <note>Amboina, in the Maluku Islands</note>, and is much more common than all the preceding ones. It also grows taller than them, having a slanted and crooked trunk. The branches appear irregular and wild, and the smaller branches and leaf stalks are surrounded everywhere by sharp and firm thorns, so that this tree is more bristly and thorny than all other species of Lemons; for this reason, its crown does not allow for climbing. Its leaves appear to be constructed of two parts joined together <note>This refers to the "winged petiole," a botanical feature where the leaf stalk is flattened and leaf-like, creating the appearance of a double leaf</note>, but the lower heart-shaped part is much smaller than the other or upper part, though it is quite wide; together they are about four or five inches long. No leaf is found without a thorn, and they are slightly serrated at the edges. Their pores are so large that the leaves appear perforated, and we can see the light through them <note>These are "pellucid dots," oil glands typical of the citrus family</note>.

# BOOK II. CHAPTER XXXVII. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...are brought in great quantities to Macassar <note>A major port city on the island of Sulawesi</note>, as much of the *Cassomba* <note>original: "Cassombae"; likely Safflower (*Carthamus tinctorius*), used as a red dye</note> is prepared and consumed there. The roots of old trunks are much sought after by the people of Macassar to manufacture handles for large knives and the grips of the daggers called *Krissen* <note>original: "Krissen"; the Keris, a traditional wavy-bladed Indonesian dagger</note>, as this wood is solid and beautifully grained. Some of the Amboinese take the squeezed juice of these fruits and boil it in a potsherd over a fire until half is consumed and the remainder turns black; with this, they coat the Amboinese pustules <note>original: "variolas"; likely referring to smallpox or similar skin eruptions</note> once they have reached suppuration, in order to dry them out more quickly. However, few can endure this treatment, as it stings excessively.

Another variety of this species is called *Lemon Carbou* <note>original: "Lemon Carbou" or Buffalo Lemon; *Kerbau* is the Malay word for water buffalo</note>, the fruit of which is the largest among the sour lemons. Its tree is taller than the others, bearing many branches and a wide crown. The leaves agree with those previously described but are generally larger, five inches long or more, and more serrated at the upper part. The lower or heart-shaped part of the leaf is smaller than the other half but quite broad, which makes these leaves likewise appear double. It bears fewer thorns than the preceding kind, and the flowers are the same. The fruits reach the size of an infant’s head, and some are even as large as a man’s head; they are not truly round or spherical, but pear-shaped and somewhat irregular, covered with large bumps like the *Lemon Papeda*. Otherwise, the fruit is smooth on the outside without pits, and when ripe, it turns yellow all over. Its rind is not thick but firm, with a heavy and unpleasant odor resembling "strong water" <note>original: "aquam fortem"; an old term for nitric acid</note>. The internal flesh is white, extremely sour, and corrosive; because of this sharpness, it is not fit for food, and its heavy scent is harmful to the head.

**Name.** In Latin, it is called *Limo Taurinus* <note>original: "Bull-like Lemon"</note>, matching the Malay *Limon Carbou*; for the Malays are accustomed to give the surname of "Bull" or "Elephant" to all larger things, just as the Greeks do with the prefix *Bu-* <note>original: "βου-"; a Greek prefix denoting greatness or intensity</note>, whence one might not ineptly call this fruit a *Bulimon*. By the people of Macassar, it is called *Lemon Cambar*, meaning the Swollen Lemon. In Amboinese, it is *Uffe Ela Bal* or *Djopoe Carboo*. In the Ternate language, it is *Lemo-Cabi*, that is, the "Goat Lemon," because of its heavy smell.

**Location.** It rarely occurs in Amboina but is more frequent in Macassar, where it is often planted in the streets around houses for the sake of its shade.

**Use.** The juice of these lemons is primarily used for cleaning weapons, as it eats away rust from both iron and copper; for this reason, some call this fruit *Lemon Padangh*, which means the "Sword Lemon." Once the Malays and Macassarese have cleaned their swords and daggers (*Krissen*)—whether with this juice or something else—they usually coat them with a blue color. This is likewise done with the juice of these lemons or the *Lemon Nipis* <note>original: "Limonis Nipis"; the Key Lime</note> if sublimated mercury is added, which they call *Warangau* <note>original: "Warangau" or *Warangan*; an arsenic-based wash used to preserve and pattern Keris blades</note>. This preserves the weapons from rust but simultaneously renders them poisonous. These lemons are also excellent for cleaning and polishing copper machinery, whether the juice is used alone or mixed with charcoal; the items are then rinsed with clean water and dried in the sun. It can also be used with the *Cassomba* pigment, although they prefer other lemons for that, as others give a better scent to the dyed clothes than these "bull-apples." Both of these mentioned fruits are covered in a soft and sticky gum. These and other sour lemons are used by the Macassarese to wash their clothes; for this purpose, they use more juice than water. This is done especially for the garments of Kings, as clothes washed this way better attract and retain the scent of musk, civet, and similar perfumes.

## OBSERVATION.
The *Lemon Papeda* and *Lemon Carbou*, or Buffalo Lemon, are also mentioned by Valentijn in his description of Amboina on page 189.

<column-break/>

...in great quantities for sale to *Macassar*, as they consume and use much *Cassomba* there. The roots of the old trunks are greatly sought by the *Macassarese* to make handles for bush-knives and grips for kris-daggers, because it is a firm wood and also somewhat figured. Some Amboinese take the pressed juice of the fruits and boil it in a potsherd over a coal fire until half is consumed and the rest turns black, with which they then smear the Amboinese pox when they have broken out properly, to dry them up more quickly; but not everyone can endure this cure because it bites too much.

Of the previous kind, there is yet another *Lemon*, which is the largest among the sour ones, named *Lemon Carbou*, and whose tree grows larger than the others, with many branches and a broad crown. The leaves are as on the preceding one, but usually somewhat larger, five inches long and even more, more serrated toward the front, and the back part is somewhat less than half and very broad. Therefore these leaves also appear double. It has fewer thorns than the preceding, and the blossom is like the rest. The fruit is of the size of a child's head, and some even of a grown man, not perfectly round, but pear-shaped, somewhat crooked, and set with some large bumps like the *Lemon Papeda*, otherwise smooth on the outside and without pits, and when ripe, pale yellow all over. The rind is not thick but firm and strong of smell, yet not pleasant, but rather pulling toward "strong water." The inner flesh is white, very sour and sharp, and as such, due to its sharpness, unfit to use in food, and with its heavy, unpleasant smell, it is also burdensome to the head.

**Name.** In Latin *Limo Taurinus*, after the Malay *Limo Carbou*, for the Malays are accustomed to give the surname of an Ox or Elephant to all the largest things in their kind, just as the Greeks are used to doing through the prefix *Bu*, which is why they might not poorly be named *Bulimo*. In *Macassar*, *Lemon Cambar*, that is, Swollen Lemon. In Amboinese, *Uffe Ela Bal*, *Djohoe Carboo*. In Ternatese, *Lemo Cabi*, that is, Goat Lemons, from their strong smell.

**Place.** It is found little on Amboina, but more on *Macassar*, and they are mostly planted near houses on the streets for the sake of shade.

**Use.** The juice of these lemons is mostly in use to clean weapons with, because it bites off the rust of iron as well as copper; therefore some call this fruit *Lemon Padangh*, that is, Sword Lemons. Item: when the Malays and Macassarese have cleaned their swords and krisses, be it with this juice or something else, they are then accustomed to "blue" the same, which likewise happens with the juice of these lemons or *Lemon Nipis*, where some sublimate has been rubbed in, which those people call *Warangau*, and that preserves the weapons from rusting but also makes them fierce <note>meaning poisonous or dangerously sharp</note>. And especially the lemons are useful to scour copper-work with, whether alone or mixed with charcoal, which one thereafter rinses again with pure water and dries in the sun. One can also use them in the dyeing of the *Cassomba*, although they prefer other lemons because those give a better scent to the dyed cloths than these "Ox-heads." Both the preceding fruits being hung with a soft and sticky gum, and these and other sour lemons are used by the *Macassarese* to wash their clothes with, taking more juice than water for that, though which is mostly done by the Kings because the clothes washed thus take up the perfume better.

# AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chapter XXXVIII.

# CHAPTER THIRTY-EIGHT.

->Wild Lemon, *Lemon Swangi*.<-

This species of Lemon is also indigenous or Indian, and of a wild nature. The tree is not particularly thick and is lower than the one described immediately before it, having a narrow crown and straight branches. Its leaves are similar to those of the *Lemon Papeda* <note>The Kaffir Lime or Makrut Lime, *Citrus hystrix*</note>, but a little longer and sharper—namely six inches long and more—slightly serrated toward the front. In the middle, between the heart-shaped base and the upper part of the leaf, there is a joint <note>original: "geniculum"; referring to the articulated wing on the leaf stalk characteristic of many citrus species</note>, and they are slightly curved. Its fruit is smaller than all the preceding Lemons, similar to the Spanish Lemon <note>The common Mediterranean lemon</note> but smaller, pointed at both ends; some are pear-shaped, others like a large plum or egg-shaped, covered everywhere as if with warts, dark green and slow to turn yellow. This yellow color is mostly observed in those that grow near houses and are cultivated there. Its internal flesh is scant and granular, but juicy and very sour, causing cramps <note>original: "tormina"; sharp, wringing pains in the abdomen</note>. The scent is not unpleasant, lemon-like, but weak and somewhat wild. The young shoots also bear long thorns, but the branches near the leaves have small ones.

*Name.* In Latin, *Limo Ferus* <note>Wild Lemon</note>; according to the Malay, *Limoen Swangi* <note>Sorcerer’s Lemon</note>, on account of its irregular and deformed shape. For the Malays attribute the nickname *Swangi* <note>original: "Swangi"; refers to a shapeshifting sorcerer or malevolent spirit in Indonesian folklore</note> to such things that are wild, fierce, and irregular in form, as are mostly the Sorcerers and Masters, whom they properly call *Swangi*. In Amboinese it is called *Uffe Malumeit* and *Aufsi Wolu*; by those of Ternate, however, *Limo Titigela*.

*Location.* In Amboina it is mostly found in the wild gardens of the Amboinese, as well as near their houses.

*Usage.* Its juice is rarely used, except that the Amboinese apply it to their *Papeda* porridge <note>The staple starch dish of Eastern Indonesia made from sago pith</note>, but mostly for the *Cassomba* pigment <note>original: "Cassomba"; Safflower dye</note>. Furthermore, this fruit—both its peel and its juice—is boiled with other medicines so that their power might be enhanced; it especially serves in bitter potions that are administered to purify the body and correct corrupted humors. The head is rubbed with its peel after washing, just as is done with the *Lemon Purrut*, but one must take care that its juice does not touch the skin or drip onto the body.

->The Twenty-Eighth Plate,<-

# XXXVIII. CHAPTER.

->Wild Lemon Tree.<-

This genus of Lemons is also truly native or Indian, and somewhat wild of nature. *The tree is not very thick, and also lower than the one directly preceding, with a narrow crown and straight branches; the leaves are like those of the Lemon Papeda, though somewhat longer and sharper, namely six inches long or a bit more, also somewhat serrated toward the front; in the middle between the base and the leaf they have a little joint, and stand somewhat bent. The fruit is smaller than all preceding ones, somewhat like the Spanish Lemons but much smaller, pointed at the front and back: some pear-wise, or like a large egg-plum, beset all around with warts, black-green on the outside, and slowly becoming yellow, which color one mostly sees on those that stand by the houses and are somewhat tended there. The inner marrow is small and grainy, yet juicy, very sour, and sharp; the scent of the peel is not unpleasant, lemon-like, yet somewhat faint and wild. The young shoots also have long thorns, but the branches by the leaves have small ones.*

*Name.* In Latin *Limo Ferus*, after the Malay *Limoen Swangi*, from its misshapen figure: For the Malays give the nickname of *Swangi* to such things which are wild, surly, and disturbed or unsightly of shape, as the Sorcerers and Witches <note>original: "Tovenaars en Hexen"</note> ordinarily show themselves, whom they properly call *Swangiers*. On Ambon, *Uffe Malumeit* and *Aufsi Wolu*; on Ternate, *Limo Titigela*.

*Place.* One finds them in Amboina mostly with the Amboinese in the forest-gardens, and also by their houses.

*Use.* One uses the juice little, except for the Amboinese for the eating of *Papeda*, though mostly for the dyeing of their *Cassomba* dye. Furthermore, this fruit is also used, both the peel and the juice, to boil with other medicines and thereby awaken their effect; and especially it serves with bitter medicines that are given to purify and to improve spoiled humors. With the peel one also rubs the head after washing, just as with the *Lemon Purrut*, though likewise taking care that the juice does not come upon the body.*

# AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chapter XXXVIII.

# CHAPTER THIRTY-EIGHT.

->Wild Lemon, *Lemon Swangi*.<-

This species of Lemon is also indigenous <note>original: "indigena"; native to the region</note> or Indian, and of a wild nature. The tree is not particularly thick and is lower than the one described immediately before it, having a narrow crown and straight branches. Its leaves are similar to those of the *Lemon Papeda* <note>The Kaffir Lime or Makrut Lime, *Citrus hystrix*</note>, but a little longer and sharper—namely six inches long and more—slightly serrated toward the front. In the middle, between the heart-shaped base and the upper part of the leaf, there is a joint <note>original: "geniculum"; referring to the <term>winged petiole</term>, an articulated wing on the leaf stalk characteristic of many citrus species</note>, and they are slightly curved. Its fruit is smaller than all the preceding Lemons, similar to the Spanish Lemon <note>The common Mediterranean lemon</note> but smaller, pointed at both ends; some are pear-shaped, others like a large plum or egg-shaped, covered everywhere as if with warts, dark green and slow to turn yellow. This yellow color is mostly observed in those that grow near houses and are cultivated there. Its internal flesh is scant and granular, but juicy and very sour, causing cramps <note>original: "tormina"; sharp, wringing pains in the abdomen</note>. The scent is not unpleasant, lemon-like, but weak and somewhat wild. The young shoots also bear long thorns, but the branches near the leaves have small ones.

*Name.* In Latin, *Limo Ferus* <note>Wild Lemon</note>; according to the Malay, *Limoen Swangi* <note>The Sorcerer's Lemon, from "suangi," a term for a malevolent spirit or witch in local folklore</note>.

->Book II. Chapter XXXIX. AMBOINESE HERBAL.<-

# CHAPTER THIRTY-NINE.

## *Limonellus. Limon Nipis.*

Among all the acid Lemons, this one is the most widespread and commonly used. Its trunk is lower than the preceding ones, barely thicker than a leg, mostly crooked and bent, possessing few branches which are curved and spreading. These branches bear many very short and thorny twigs, forming a crown that is wide but irregular. Its leaf is smaller than in any of the previous kinds, about three inches long, with a small but notable heart-shaped part <term>winged petiole: a leaf-like expansion on the stalk of the leaf</term>, lightly serrated at the edges, and a brighter green than other Lemon leaves. Each leaf is joined by a firm thorn, which is long and slender on the younger shoots. The flowers are similar to the earlier ones, constructed of five whitish, oblong petals reflected outward. In the morning hours, they offer and spread a pleasant scent, like those of the Martinique Lemon.

Its fruits are much smaller than those of the preceding types, about the size of an apricot, spherical, and without bumps. In place of bumps, however, some bear a protruding ridge, mostly near the stem or on its lower part, with a few small bumps like warts. They are green at first and then a Citrine-yellow color. Its rind is very thin, no thicker than a straw. The internal part is filled with a white or greenish pulp, extremely juicy and pleasantly acidic, which has a delightful smell and flavor. Its flesh and rind almost match the Spanish Lemons in taste. The seeds are whitish, round, and oblong, sprouting easily if they touch the earth or are committed to it. Some of these fruits even grow to such a size as the species of apples called in Europe *Malum Orthomasticum* <note>original: "Malum Orthomasticum"; literally "Breast Apple," a variety of lemon or citron shaped like a breast</note>, which breathes a pleasant scent if rubbed or held in the hands. But if those trees are not properly cultivated, they yield small and lumpy fruits that turn yellow slowly and are covered in a mucous-like gum. This tree does not love rich and fertile soil; rather, the harder it is, mixed with stones and rubble, the more vigorously and happily it grows—especially in places well-exposed to the sun.

*Name.* In Latin *Limonellus* or *Limo tenuis* <note>Thin Lemon</note>, according to the Malay *Limon Nipis* <note>original: "Limon Nipis"; from "nipis" meaning thin, referring to the rind</note> because of its thin rind; in Ternate *Lemo Fava*; in Amboinese *Aussi Pipis*; in Macassar *Lemo Capas*, as it is not much larger than the bolls of the Cotton plant; in Banda *Usse-Crawo*; in Bali *Djoboc*; in Chinese *Suyn Cam*, which is a general name for all acid Lemons.

*Location.* It occurs from Java through all the Eastern islands, not in the forests, but everywhere planted near houses and diligently cultivated. It bears fruit throughout the entire year, though more frequently at one time than another.

*Usage.* The juice of these Lemons is in daily use, by which every kind of food is made acidic, since all the peoples of India <note>The East Indies</note> much prefer Lemon juice in their food over vinegar—excepting lettuce—and among these, this juice is most savory and delightful. They were also accustomed to preserve its green rind in sugar and to pickle the whole fruit in brine so that it would be at hand at all times of the year, which is done in the following way. The fresh Lemons are rubbed a little until the outer green skin falls away, then they are pricked with a very sharp wooden point so that they are pierced with small holes everywhere. Then they are soaked for three or four days in pure water so that their bitterness disappears, then dried a little in the sun, and finally pickled in brine. This is done in seawater which is so impregnated with salt that an egg floats. If they are placed in well-sealed jars in this manner, they can be kept whole for years, though they must lie in the brine for a month before they can be used. These Lemons preserved in brine, mixed with crushed sulfur, cleanse and dry out every kind of Scabies <note>A skin infestation by mites</note> as well as spreading ulcers. If it is dry scabies, gunpowder is used instead of sulfur, and if it is too sharp, a little lime is mixed in.

<column-break/>

# THIRTY-NINTH CHAPTER.

## *Lime Tree.*

Among all the sour Lemons, this is the most common and most used. The trunk is lower than the preceding ones, not thicker than a thigh, mostly crooked and bent, with few crooked and spreading branches, and those are full of short and thorny twigs, making a wide but untidy crown. The leaf is smaller than all the preceding ones, about three inches long, with a small but recognizable heart-shape <note>Referring to the winged petiole</note>, darkly serrated on the edges, and lighter green than the other Lemon leaves. By every leaf stands a stiff thorn, though on the young shoots they are long and slender. The blossom is like all others, made of five oblong white petals, all bent outwards, and smelling somewhat lovely in the morning hours, just like those of the Martinique Lemon.

The fruits are also smaller than all the preceding ones, the size of apricots, perfectly spherical, and without bumps; but in place of these, some have a piece of a protruding seam, mostly either by the stem or at the bottom with some low bumps like warts. They are green at first, and thereafter a true Lemon-yellow. This rind is very thin, and of no more thickness than a straw. The interior is filled or stuffed with a white or greenish and very juicy pulp, pleasantly sour and of a good scent, the flesh and the rind coming very close in taste to the Spanish ones. The seeds inside are white, round, and longish, also sprouting easily if they touch the earth. Some of these fruits become as large as a type of round apples called in Europe *Malum Orthomasticum* <note>Breast Apple</note>, giving off a good smell if one rubs or turns them in the hand. But if the trees are not well cultivated, then they bear small, lumpy fruits that slowly turn yellow and are hung with a sticky gum. This tree asks for no good rich ground, but the harder it is, mixed with stone and rubble, the more luxuriantly it grows, and even better in places that stand well to the sun.

*Name.* In Latin *Limonellus*, or *Limo Tenuis*, after the Malay *Limon Nipis*, on account of its thin rind. In Ternate *Lemo Java*; in Amboinese *Aussi Pipis*; in Macassar *Lemo Capas*, because it is not much larger than the bolls of Cotton; in Banda *Usse-Crawo*; in Bali *Djohoe*; in Chinese *Suyn-cam*, being a general name for all sour Lemons.

*Place.* They are found from Java through all the Eastern Islands, not in the wild, but everywhere planted by houses and industriously cultivated. And one has the fruits mostly the whole year through, though more at one time and less at another.

*Use.* The juice of these Lemons is in daily use to make all sorts of food sour therewith, since all Indian nations much prefer Lemon juice over their food than any vinegar (except on salads), and among which this juice is the tastiest. The green rind they also used to preserve in sugar, so that they could have them in the house at all times, which happens thus. The fresh Lemons are first rubbed a little until just the outermost greenness comes off, thereafter one pricks them full of holes with a sharp wooden pin, and soaks them three or four days in fresh water so that the bitterness might be drawn out. Then one dries them again in the sun, and lays them finally in brine, taking seawater for that purpose, which one makes so thick with salt until an egg floats on it. And done thus in well-closed pots, one can keep them good for years and days, though they must have lain in brine for a month before one can use them. These pickled Lemons mixed with rubbed sulfur, cleanse and dry up all sorts of scabies and creeping sores, and if it is a dry scabies, one takes gunpowder instead of sulfur, and if such falls too sharp, then one puts some lime under it, for two sharp things dull one another...

quantity, for two sharp substances mitigate each other, as we experience in the chewing of lime and Siri <note>original: "calcis & Siri"; Siri is the betel leaf, which is chewed with lime and areca nut in Southeast Asia</note>.

For coating weapons with a blue color, such as the daggers called Krises and swords, no Lemons are better than these. They are superior to the Papeda Lemon and the Carbou Lemon, which are only used if these are lacking, for in their juice something mucous is observed, which Mercury sublimate or *Varinga* <note>original: "Varinga" or "Warangan," an arsenic trioxide used to etch and preserve kris blades</note> better retains and adheres to the blade. If these weapons have been cleaned and polished with other materials, they are then smeared (as indicated in chapter 37) with this prepared juice, which immediately turns them from blue to black; once dried, they are gently wiped with a cloth dipped in oil and put away.

They also smear cleaned weapons with the simple juice of acid Lemons, from which they take on a bluish tint, but they must be wiped more frequently with such an oily cloth. And although it is taught in Europe that Citrons there resist all poisons, the Indians teach us the contrary: namely, that many (though not all) poisons are activated by Lemon juice, as is evident from those weapons coated with the blue color. They strictly forbid the use of this juice to those who have ingested any poison, especially since it is brought into action by this juice.

If eight or ten of these Lemons are cut open, and their juice is squeezed into a clean pan and digested for a night or eight hours with half a part of water, we obtain an excellent eye-wash <term>Collyrium: a medicinal lotion for the eyes</term>, with which dimmed eyes should be washed if they are externally covered by a mucous cloudiness that hinders or plagues the sight. If these Lemons are picked by hand when ripe and hung by small cords, or stored in such a way that they do not touch each other, they can be kept whole for a very long time on sea voyages.

In the month of December of the year 1677, I was shown a young branch of the Limo Nipis, whose two lower thorns bore flower heads at their tips, such as these trees produce. One of these was already open, but when this cut branch had been placed in water overnight, both heads fell off, as if they had merely been stuck on.

The hands are rubbed with the leaves if any grease or fish have soiled them, so that their unpleasant odor may be removed; for these leaves, when crushed, spread a Citrine scent above all others, which in other Lemon leaves is more sulfurous.

The juice of these Lemons is also used for dyeing and preparing the pigment *Cassomba* <note>Cassomba usually refers to Safflower dye</note>, just like the Papeda Lemon. For this use, other species growing in Celebes and on the eastern coast of Ceram are also useful; these are called *Tsjamburaga* in Macassar, and are larger than the Limo Nipis, granular on the outside and dark green, flat on top where a circle appears, in the center of which the apex is raised. The internal flesh is like the common Limo Nipis, with an acid taste, but the scent does not match these, nor is it as pleasant. The mountain dwellers of the eastern coast of Ceram bring them for sale to the coastal villages, where they are used cooked with fish as an acid seasoning. These can be kept longer and carried better across the sea, as they do not rot as easily as the Limo Nipis.

*For the bluing of weapons, such as krises and swords, in the Macassar fashion, there are no more suitable Lemons than these, and they are even better than the Papeda Lemon and the Carbou Lemon; these others are not used except in the absence of this one, because one feels a small stickiness in this juice, which holds the rubbed-in sublimate or Warangan <note>Arsenic etch</note> better. And although one learns in Europe that the Citrons there fight against all poisons, the Indians teach us the opposite: namely, that many (but not all) poisons are sharpened by the juice of these Lemons, just as is evident in the previously described bluing of the weapons, and they most highly forbid the consumption of this juice to those who have taken any poison, especially since the same, as said, is made active by this juice.*

*If one cuts eight or ten of these Lemons straight through, squeezes them into a clean copper basin, adds half water to it, and then lets it stand for a night or eight hours, one obtains a good eye-water, with which one can wash dark eyes that are beset on the outside with some sliminess or cloudiness which hinders the sight. If one picks these Lemons (when ripe) with the hands, binds and hangs them with small strings, or lays them away so that they do not touch each other, one can keep them good for a very long time on sea voyages.*

*In December 1677, I was shown a stem or young branch of a Limo Nipis tree, whose two hindmost thorns each had a bud at the tip of such a flower as the same tree bears, and of which one had already opened; but when the cut branch had stood in water for a night, both buds fell off, just as if they had only been attached there.*

*One also rubs the hands with the leaves if one has handled any fat or fish, to take away their smell, for these leaves give off a Citron-scent above others when rubbed, which in other Lemon leaves is somewhat more sulfurous.*

*The juice of these Lemons is also used for dyeing, or the preparation of the Cassomba, as well as the Papeda Lemon; for which purpose another sort is also useful, which grows on Celebes and the eastern part of Ceram, and is called Tsjamburaga in Macassar, being somewhat larger than a Limo Nipis, grainy on the outside and dark green, somewhat flat in front, and there one sees a little hill surrounded by a circle. The flesh inside is like that of the mentioned Limo Nipis, sour in taste, but in scent one does not perceive that agreement, and therefore it is also not so pleasant. The mountain-dwellers on the eastern corner of Ceram bring them to the beach-villages for sale, where they are then used and cooked with fish to have a sour soup or sauce; one can also keep them longer and carry them better over the sea (for they do not rot so easily) as the Limo Nipis.*

For coating weapons with a blue color, such as the daggers called Krises and swords, no Lemons are better than these. They also smear cleaned weapons with the simple juice of acid Lemons, from which they take on a bluish tint, but they must be wiped more frequently with such an oily cloth. And although it is taught in Europe that Citrons there resist all poisons, the Indians teach us the contrary: namely, that many (though not all) poisons are activated by Lemon juice, as is evident from those weapons coated with the blue color. They strictly forbid the use of this juice to those who have ingested any poison, especially since it is brought into action by this juice.

### OBSERVATION.

Just as there are many varieties of *Lemons* <note>original: "Limonum"</note>, so too are there many varieties of *Limes* <note>original: "Limonelli"</note>, which should properly be considered a smaller species of the former. That many varieties occur is evident not only from the authors cited below, but is especially clear to the eye in the following fortieth chapter.

Various species or varieties of *Limes* are enumerated in *Sloane's Catalog of the Plants of Jamaica, page 211*, which may be compared with those mentioned in our *Thesaurus Zeylanicus, page 143*, where the *Indian* species are primarily found. See further *Ray's Dendrologia, page 80; Plukenet's Almagestum, page 239; Ferrari's Hesperides, page 209; J. Commelin's Dutch Hesperides, page 9; Valentyn's Description of Amboina, page 190, etc.*

---

## CHAPTER FORTY.

### The Gold Lime. <note>original: "Limonellus Aurarius" or "Lemon Maas"</note>

This is the smallest species among all the Lemons, yet its tree grows as tall as the *Limo Nipis* <note>the common small lime, Citrus aurantifolia</note>. Its leaves are smaller than those of the latter, or at least narrower, being two and a half or three inches long, of which the heart-shaped part <note>referring to the winged petiole, a leaf-like stalk</note> constitutes nearly a third part. They are not as vibrant a green as those of the Limo Nipis, but are a dark, dusky green and are covered with spots; nor do they give off as pleasant an odor as the preceding one. Its branches are thinner and mostly bare of leaves, and the thorns are the shortest of all and not as frequent. The fruits are the smallest of all, about the size of a large musket ball, spherical, and covered as if with small warts, usually divided by faint grooves. They have a small pit or navel at the top and remain green for a long time, though they eventually acquire a lemon-yellow color. They are covered with a thin rind, as if it were merely a skin, and provide little scent even if rubbed; this scent is not lemon-like, but rather spicy, almost like *Lagondi* <note>Vitex trifolia, a medicinal shrub with a pungent aromatic scent</note>. The internal flesh is juicy, yellowish, translucent, and extremely sour, containing many small seeds resembling grains of wheat.

<margin>Name.</margin> In Latin it is called *Limonellus Aurarius*, following the Malay *Lemon Maas*, not because of a resemblance to gold, but because of its use, as will be indicated below. It is called by similar names in other languages: in Ternate as *Lemo Tinagara*; in Makassar as *Lemo Buleyn*; and in Amboina as *Ussi-Helawan*.

<margin>Place.</margin> It is found in Celebes, Ternate, and Amboina, but it does not grow abundantly anywhere.

<margin>Use.</margin> These limes are not used in food, but mostly by goldsmiths, who wash and purify all gold-work with their juice when they wish to color it afterward. For this purpose, these limes are more effective and suitable than others, which is how they earned their name. They are also mixed into various medicines and juices used to cleanse the eyes, for which they serve better than others because they are less sharp or stinging. Where they are found in abundance, they are also used to wash the head and body, not so much for scrubbing, but to impart a good scent.

Among all species of Lemons, these branches bear the most thorns <note>Note: the author clarifies here that while short, they are numerous and firm</note>, which are short, thick, and stiff. The two parts of the leaves drop off very easily and separate from one another, with the back half remaining on the stalk so that one might mistake it for the leaf of another tree. When crushed, the leaves possess almost no smell or taste of lemons.

### EXPLANATION

## XL. CHAPTER.

### The Gold Lime-Tree.

This is the smallest genus among all the Lemons, and the tree nevertheless grows as tall as a *Limo Nipis*. The small leaves are smaller than those on the same, certainly narrower, two and a half and three inches long, of which the little board <note>the winged petiole</note> occupies a bit more than a third part. Not as living-green as those of the Limo Nipis, but black or dirty-green, and occupied with spots, also not as good of scent as the mentioned *Limo Nipis*. The thorns are also the shortest of all, and not as many as those of the aforementioned Lemon Nipis. These twigs also stand thin and mostly empty and bare of leaves. And, as said, the fruits are the smallest of all, about as large as a large musket ball, round, and occupied with small warts, commonly divided into some dark furrows. At the front with a small pit or navel, they stay green a long time, yet at last also become Lemon-yellow, clothed with a thin shell, as if it were only a skin, of little scent, even if one scrapes them, not Lemon-like, but spice-like, almost like *Lagondi*. Inside is a juicy flesh, translucent from the yellow, and also very sour, with many small seed-grains, like barley-grains.

**Name.** In Latin *Limonellus Aurarius*, after the Malay *Lemon Maas*, not after any resemblance to gold, but from their use, as shall be said hereafter, and so also in other languages, as in Ternate *Lemo Tinagara*; in Makassar *Lemo Buleyn*; in Amboina *Ussi Helawan*.

**Place.** One finds them on *Celebes, Ternate, and Amboina*, yet nowhere in abundance.

**Use.** These Lemons were not used in meals, but mostly by the goldsmiths, who wash and clean all kinds of made gold-work with the juice when they want to color it thereafter, and for which these Lemons are capable above others, moreover having their name from it. They were also mixed among all kinds of Medicines and juices that one uses to purify the eyes, for which they also serve better than others because they are less sharp. And where one has them in abundance, they are also used to wash the head and body therewith, not so much because they wipe clean, as because they come to give a good scent thereto.

Among all sorts of Lemons, these branches have the most thorns; they are short, thick, and stiff. The two parts of the leaves fall off easily and from each other, the back half remaining standing on the stalk, so that one would take it for another tree's leaf. The rubbed leaves smell and taste also the least like Lemons.

### The Madura Lime : Lemon Madura.

<margin>
Madura Lime
p. 467
</margin>

On the island of Madura, a certain species of sweet fruit or lime occurs, growing on small but elegant shrubs scarcely two feet high. The branches of these are nonetheless firm, angular, and slightly striped. The leaves are solitary and simple, about the length of a thumb joint and one finger wide; they are not heart-shaped at the base, are marked with thin parallel ribs, and have smooth but wavy edges. No thorns are observed on the branches. Their taste is bitter, and if held up to the light, small holes <note>These are oil glands, typical of the citrus family</note> appear in them, just as in other species of limes. Its fruits are spherical, slightly compressed at the top and marked with a small pit, about the size of a musket ball. They are always green, and only one or two grow from a short stalk. Beneath the thin peel, a soft and juicy flesh is hidden, divided into cells as in other limes. Its flavor is somewhat acidic but simultaneously aromatic; it is orange in color. A single seed <note>original Latin: "ossiculum feminale," literally 'feminine little bone'</note>, or rarely two, is found in this fruit, having the size and shape of a grain, pointed at both ends.

*Name.* In Latin, *Limonellus Madurensis*, and *Limonellus Pumilus* <note>Dwarf Lime</note>. In Malay, *Lemon Madura*: for it received its name from the island of Madura, located in the bay of Great Java, where it has its origin and from where it was brought; it is diligently cultivated in the gardens of Batavia <note>modern-day Jakarta</note>.

*Usage.* Its fruits are not eaten raw but are preserved in syrup with one or two leaves of the tree; they then acquire a pleasant and sweet flavor and are served at the table with other sweetmeats <note>original Latin: "tragematibus"</note>.

<margin>
angular
Spec. emend.
3: 1426
(9)
</margin>

To this, I shall also add another species of wild lime, which first became known to me in the year 1694; I call it the *Angular Lime* <note>original Latin: "Limonellus Angulosus"</note>. Its tree does not exceed the thickness of a leg, but is usually the thickness of an arm; it is sparse and winding, and its branches are curved and knotty. The leaves are positioned at the tips of the branches, closely joined together and alternating. The lower and larger leaves bear two thorns at their base, positioned at a sharp angle. These leaves have the size of the *Limonis-Nipis* <note>the common lime, Citrus aurantifolia</note> leaves, but they are not heart-shaped at the bottom like the others. They are two or three inches long and two fingers wide, somewhat rounded and notched <note>original Latin: "bifida"</note> at the top. The edges are even and not serrated, but slightly wavy. The leaves are smooth on the upper side, but the old leaves are wrinkled on the lower side; the veins are scarcely visible. When crushed, they smell of orange, though their scent is weak. The flowers are unknown to me thus far.

The fruits differ from all other limes; they are the smallest, along with the *Gold Lime* <note>original Latin: "Limone-Maas"</note>, and do not even match the size of the *Vidara* <note>the Indian Jujube, Ziziphus mauritiana</note>. They are all angular—the largest are four-sided, while the smaller ones are five-sided—and are compressed at the sides. They are mostly green, but when ripe, they turn somewhat yellowish. Beneath a thin rind, four or five flat seeds are hidden in cells filled with a viscous juice resembling birdlime <note>a sticky substance used to trap birds</note>, which is useless as food but has the scent of the common lime.

*Name.* In Latin, *Limonellus Angulosus*. In Malay, *Lemon Utan Bafagi* <note>Wild Divided Lime</note>.

*Location.* This tree was finally found, as stated above, in the year 1694 behind the village of *Hative* near the shore, amidst the swampy Mangrove <note>original: "Mangi Mangi"</note> forest. It is almost entirely unknown to the inhabitants.

*P.S.* Its leaves and thorns very much resemble those of the *Bilak* <note>the Bael fruit tree</note>. A leaf is located in the middle of a sharp angle; a little above that, a solitary leaf is placed without thorns, and so they alternate. The upper and younger leaves are solitary and lack thorns. These leaves are rough but smooth on both sides, with a lime-like flavor and scent, but they are very acrid in the mouth. These small trees grow among the Mangroves in seawater when the tide is high. The flowers are solitary and resemble those of the common lime, but are smaller, constructed of five whitish petals.

The following small varieties of Limes or little Lemons also belong to this fortieth Chapter, which have been taken over here from the 16th Chapter of the *Supplement* <note>original Dutch: "Auctuarium"</note> by Rumphius.

### Madura Lime Tree.

On the Island of Madura, one finds a kind of sweet apples or sweet Lemons on small and well-formed little trees with stiff twigs, not over two feet high; the twigs are also squared and somewhat striped. The leaves stand singly on the sprigs, about the length of a thumb joint and a thumb wide, without a heart-shape at the base, with fine parallel ribs and smooth, hemmed edges. One also sees no thorns on the sprigs. Their taste is clearly bitter, and when held against the light, one sees the same little holes as on other Lemons. The fruits are round, somewhat pressed on top with a little pit, the size of a musket ball; they always remain green and stand singly or in pairs on a short cluster. Under a thin peel lies a soft, juicy flesh, also divided as in other sweet Lemons. The taste is acidic, though with a spicy scent, and of an orange color. In it, one finds one or, rarely, two seeds, the size and shape of a barley corn, pointed at both ends.

*Name.* In Latin, *Limonellus Madurensis*, and *Limonellus Pumilus*. In Malay, *Lemon Madura*. it takes its name from the Island of *Madura*, situated in the lap of great *Java*, from where they originate; they are diligently maintained in the gardens at *Batavia*.

*Usage.* They are not eaten raw, but are laid in syrup with one or two leaves attached to a fruit; they then become pleasantly sweet and are served among other confectionery.

To this, I shall add another wild variety of small Lime, which first came to my knowledge in the year 1694, and is named by me *Limonellus Angulosus*. The tree does not grow thicker than a leg, but generally remains the thickness of an arm; it is low and winding, and the branches are crooked and knobby. The leaves stand close together at the ends, and the rear ones have two thorns at their origin standing in a sharp right angle <note>original Dutch: "winkelhaak"</note> or triangle. They have the size and length of the *Common Lime* <note>original: "Lemon-Nipis"</note> leaves, but lack the little heart-shape at the back like other Limes. They are 2 to 3 inches long, 2 fingers wide, mostly round at the front and somewhat cleft at the tip. The edges are smooth, not saw-toothed, but a little wavy. They are smooth on the top side, but the old leaves are somewhat rough on the bottom side with barely visible veins; when rubbed, they smell of Orange, though faintly. The blossom is as yet unknown.

The fruits differ from all other Lemons, for they are the smallest along with the *Gold Lime* <note>original: "Lemon-Maas"</note>, agreeing in size with the *Wild Vidara*. The largest of these are truly four-sided; the smallest are divided with five ridges, and the sides are somewhat sunken. They are mostly green, though in ripeness they also pull toward yellow. Under a thin peel, one finds four or five flat, elongated seeds lying in cells surrounded by a sticky sap like birdlime, unfit to eat, but with a scent like the *Common Lime*.

*Name.* In Latin, *Limonellus Angulosus*. In Malay, *Lemon Utan Bafagi*.

*Place.* It was first found, as said, in the year 1694 behind the village of *Hative*, near the shore, under the swampy Mangrove forest, and is still mostly unknown to the locals.

*P.S.* The leaves and thorns mostly resemble *Bilak*; for in the middle of the sharp right angle stands a leaf. Shortly above that stands a single leaf without thorns, and so they alternate; however, the front and young leaves mostly stand alone and without thorns. The leaves are stiff and smooth on both sides. In scent and taste, they are lime-like, though quite sharp in the mouth. The little trees grow among the Mangroves in seawater when the water is high. The blossom stands alone and resembles that of the *Common Lime*, but smaller, composed of 5 whitish petals.

### CHAPTER FORTY-ONE.

#### *The Sour Orange: Black Lemon.* <note>original Latin: "Aurantium Acidum: Lemon Itam"; original Dutch: "De zuure Oranje-Appel-boom"</note>

Having described all the species of acidic Indian limes, it remains for us to also treat the Oranges <note>original Latin: "Malis Aurantiis"</note>, which constitute a peculiar genus of their own. These can by no means be produced from the preceding types through skillful budding or grafting, as some European writers have falsely thought and written. For these fruits grow throughout the whole of India in their natural soil, and among such peoples who neither know nor understand the art of grafting. I am also certain that this practice was never established in the Western part of the world, where in North Africa <note>original Latin: "Mauritania"</note> and Guinea, as well as in the West Indies and its islands, whole forests of these Oranges are found growing wild, having undoubtedly sprouted there by their own nature. However, these East Indian fruits differ somewhat from the Western ones, as we shall demonstrate in the following sections, dividing them into the sour and the sweet.

1. First, the sour Oranges, commonly called *Lemon Itam* <note>meaning "Black Lemon," referring to its dark green color</note>, grow on tall trees whose trunk is quite thick, not round, but angular, and as if hollowed out with grooves or channels. Its branches mostly stand upright. The leaves are the largest after the Pomelo <note>term: <term>Pompelmoes</term>—The Shaddock or Pomelo (Citrus maxima), the largest citrus fruit</note>, but the heart-shaped base <note>original Latin: "pars cordata"; original Dutch: "bertje"—referring to the winged petiole common in citrus leaves</note> is very small in proportion to the rest. Indeed, the whole leaf is four or five inches long, of which the heart-shaped part is only a finger’s breadth and very narrow, almost unserrated at the edges, ending in a point, smoother and of a darker green than in the previous types, distinguished by notable transverse and winding ribs. If the leaf is rubbed, it breathes out a strong and sulfurous scent.

The thorns are longer than in any other kinds, equaling the length of a common needle, and are very firm and sharply stinging, especially on the younger and long shoots <note>original Latin: "flagellis"; original Dutch: "gerten of looten"</note>, where they are about a finger's length. On the older branches and stems, however, they mostly fall off, so that they may be handled without fear; and if the tree is diligently cleared of these shoots, it provides an easy climb. However, young trees, until they are as thick as an arm, are covered everywhere on both trunk and branches with horrendous and stiff thorns. The flowers are also white and constructed of five petals, like the preceding ones, but a little larger.

The fruits are almost spherical, slightly compressed on both ends without bumps, but marked all over with small pits. They bear a color ranging from green to blackish, even when they are fully ripe. If they hang too long from the trees, they often become saffron or orange in color on one side, and some even eventually acquire an orange color throughout, but these are then considered over-ripe and withered. The peel breathes a sulfurous odor, though less so than the sweet oranges, and is about as thick as the largest quill-pen. The internal flesh or marrow is divided into ten segments separated by membranes; however, they adhere as tightly and firmly to each other and to the outer peel as they do in the sweet oranges, such that they cannot be easily peeled away. This marrow is very juicy and somewhat slimy, also vinous and acidic, just like the Spanish sour Oranges, but it is not as pleasant and is mixed with a slight bitterness.

<column-break/>

...bitterness: In its center are located many oblong, wrinkled, and winding seed-stones, which bear a thick white husk, under which a thin purplish skin is hidden, surrounding the white internal substance.

The wood of the tree is a pale white and quite hard, but no many or large machines can be made from it, as it is so crooked and irregular. This tree is also more fertile than any other species of Lemon found in these regions, as it bears fruit throughout the entire year, even though they are picked daily for use. It grows in every soil, but most of all it loves places near buildings and human dwellings.

**Name.** In Latin, *Sour Orange* <note>original: "Aurantium Acidum"</note>; in Malay, *Lemon Itam*, that is, *Black Lemon*; by the people of Banda, *Uffe Mettin*; by the Amboinese, *Uffe Metten*.

**Location.** It does not occur in all the islands of the watery Indies; for in Java, Bali, and Celebes <note>Modern-day Sulawesi</note> this fruit is unknown; in Amboina they are more plentiful, but in Ternate and Banda they are found more rarely.

**Usage.** Although these Oranges are full of juice, they are nevertheless rarely or never used in food, especially raw, since their juice, though wine-like, is nevertheless unpleasant and mixed with a certain bitterness. However, they are used in a rustic drink called *Punch* <note>original: "Pons" (Latin) or "Boere-pons" (Dutch), literally "farmer's punch"</note>, for which the *Martin Lemon* <note>likely a variety of Citrus limetta</note> is the best choice, although this remains an unhealthy drink, as it is prepared from things very contrary to one another which are mixed raw—namely, boiling *Arack* <note>A strong distilled spirit</note> and cooling Lemon juice are its bases.

Furthermore, these blackish fruits are very effective for cleaning and polishing copperware, either alone or mixed with crushed charcoal. This makes the copper bright and shining, if it is immediately washed with water and dried in the sun. They are also excellent for washing the head <note>as a shampoo or scalp treatment</note>, as they cleanse thoroughly and wipe away sweat, and do not sting the skin as much as the preceding types; for this purpose, they are first roasted under hot ashes until they turn black and charred on the outside, and then they are cut open. They can also serve to dye the *Caffomba* color <note>original: "Caffombæ colorem"; likely referring to Safflower/Kasumba dye</note>, though not alone but mixed with other Lemons; they must be peeled before the juice is squeezed out, which is also observed if copper is being cleaned with them.

To this I shall add another species, which occurs mostly in Makassar and Bali, and is called there *Lemon Maritsja*, that is, *Curly Lemon* or *Pepper-Shine* <note>original: "Limon Crispus" and "Nitor Piperis"</note>, which has the size of the *Nipis Lemon* <note>a small lime</note> or is a little smaller, but flat or compressed on both sides like the Amboinese sweet oranges. It is wrinkled on the outside and covered everywhere with little warts like peppercorns, from which it also received its name. Its rind is thin and can be peeled so easily that the internal pulp remains whole, just as in the Amboinese sweet oranges. Its pulp is sour and is also used in food by the people of Makassar.

A huge species of this occurs in Amboina, whose fruits are the size of an infant's head, granulated on the outside, and containing few seeds within; the flesh of these, however, gives a weaker flavor than the common kind.

### OBSERVATION.

Just as with *Lemons*, there are many varieties of *Oranges*, which are enumerated by various authors. This one is the *Common Orange* with sharp pulp <note>original: "Aurantium vulgare medulla acri"</note>, described by Ferrari in *Hesperides* page 377, and Boerhaave in *Index of the Leiden Garden* page 239, where you may see the other varieties. One can also find many cited authors in Sloane's *Catalogue of Jamaican Plants* page 210, and an elegant illustration in Blackwell's *Herbal* Plate 349, etc.

Furthermore, this species is described under the name *Lemon Hitam* by Valentijn in his *Description of Amboina* page 190.
