...Oranges, though not so pleasant, but mixed with a little bitterness: Near the center they are full of large seeds, which are oblong, wrinkled, or somewhat curved, having a white thickish husk on the outside, under which lies a thin light purple membrane that surrounds the white interior.

The wood is pale white and reasonably hard, but one cannot make large works from it because it is so crooked, bent, and misshapen. This tree is also more fruitful than those of any other Lemons in these regions; as one has fruits on the trees all year round, even though they are plucked daily for domestic use. It grows on all kinds of soil, but prefers to be near the houses and dwellings of people.

**Name.** In Latin *Aurantium Acidum*, after the Malay *Lemon Itam*, that is black Lemon: on Banda, *Uffe Mettin*. In Amboinese *Uffe Metten*.

**Place.** One does not find them on all islands of the Watery Indies, for on *Java, Bali*, and *Celebes*, they are mostly unknown; in *Amboina* there are many, but in *Ternate*, and *Banda* quite a few less.

**Usage.** Although these Lemons are full of juice, they are nevertheless used in food either not at all or very little, especially raw, because the juice, though wine-like, has a foul taste with a little bitterness. However, one uses them for *Farmer’s Punch* <note>original: "Boere-pons"</note>, for which they are, next to the *Martin Lemon*, arguably the best, although it remains an unhealthy drink; because it is made from very conflicting things, mixed together raw: namely the hot *Arack* and the cooling Lemon juice.

But these black Lemons are most suitable for scouring all kinds of copperware, whether alone or mixed with ground charcoal: from which the copper becomes very bright, when one immediately rinses it with water and lets it dry in the sun. They are also most suitable for washing the head, for they cleanse greatly, wipe away sweat, and do not bite the skin so much as other Lemons; for which purpose one also lets them roast first under hot ashes until they become black and burnt on the outside, and then one cuts them through the middle. One can also use them for the dyeing of the *Caffomba* color; though not alone, but with other Lemons; however, one must peel them then before squeezing them out, which one also does when one wants to scour copperware with them.

To this I shall add another sort, which is found mostly on *Makassar* and *Bali*, and is called there *Lemon Maritsja*, that is *Curly Lemon* and *Pepper-Shine*, being of the size of a *Nipis Lemon*, or even a bit smaller, but flat at the bottom and top like the Amboinese sweet Oranges, wrinkled on the outside, and set thick with warts like peppercorns against each other, from which it also has that name, but the rind is thin, and lets itself be peeled so well that the inner pith remains whole, like the Amboinese sweet Oranges; the pith is sour, and is used by the Makassarese also in their food.

One has in Amboina a large variety of this, whose fruits are as large as a child's head, also granulated on the outside, within with few seeds, and the flesh is a bit flatter in taste than the common one.

### CHAPTER FORTY-TWO.
### Chinese Orange. Chinese Sweet Lemon.

THESE fruits are considered indigenous by some of the common people of Amboina, but it is better if they are called **Chinese Oranges** <note>original: "Aurantia Sinensia"</note> along with the others, primarily for the following reasons.

This tree is a little taller than the preceding one, with erect branches, while the crown is spread out in a round and fuller shape: The leaves are narrower and sharper than those of the previous tree, three or four inches long, smooth, provided with few ribs, and similar in scent to the former. The heart-shaped part <note>The "pars cordata" refers to the winged petiole, a leaf-like structure on the stalk common in citrus plants.</note> is also a transverse finger’s length, but so narrow that its heart-like shape can hardly be discerned, though it is still a little wider than that of the **Martinique Lemon**: The younger shoots bear long and narrow thorns, but in adult trees, none are seen.

The fruit has a double form, for on one tree the apples are larger than on the other: The larger ones are like those of the preceding tree or a little smaller, spherical, except that a bump appears near the stem, and they are compressed at the top with an indented pit. The rest of the rind is smooth but pierced with many small holes or pores; this rind is quite thick, spongy, and can easily be separated from the flesh; externally it turns blackish-green, even when the fruit is fully ripe; it is furthermore bitter, sulfurous, and of a very strong scent, and if it is broken, it emits such a vapor.

If these apples are picked and set aside for some time, they turn yellow on one side as if they were true oranges; however, if they turn entirely saffron-yellow on the tree, they are judged to be juiceless and useless, and usually, they have not reached their proper size but fall off in that state. The internal flesh is exactly the same as that of the **Spanish Oranges**, divided into many segments, all of which are joined together in a circle and form a small cavity in the center; if this internal globe or peeled apple is to be eaten, it must be carefully cleaned of its dry fuzz <note>The white, bitter pith or albedo.</note>, which is bitter: Then the individual segments can easily be separated and eaten: This internal pulp is tawny, semi-transparent, sweet in taste, with a little wine-like acidity: Its seed-stones are a little oblong, round, and solid.

The second variety of these apples is a little smaller and smoother, compressed on both sides, more closely resembling the **Spanish Oranges**, pierced externally with very small holes or pores, with a thin rind about the thickness of a straw, which is likewise easily separated; its flesh is like the preceding one, and this species turns more yellow on the tree; and if they are set aside for a little while, these apples become entirely saffron-colored like true Oranges: These trees are not fertile in Amboina, or at least they do not bear fruit every year, and the trees must already be adult before they produce fruit; they love a flat place well-exposed to the Sun, whereas those that grow in the cold mountains of Amboina ripen their fruit slowly, and they are mostly sour: The tree itself does not reach a great age, but often begins to "weep" a sour sap and exudes a copious amount of gum; then for one or two years, it bears more fruit than usual, many of which turn yellow on the tree, and then the tree perishes. This plague can hardly be prevented, but it can be delayed for some time if a hole is bored through the tree so that the superfluous sap may drain out; others drive a huge iron nail through the trunk.

*Name.* In Latin **Chinese Orange** <note>original: "Aurantium Sinense"</note>: In Dutch **Chinese Apples** <note>original: "Sineese Appels"</note>. In Malay **Chinese Sweet Lemon** <note>original: "Lemon Manis Tsjina"</note>, which name best suits the latter or smaller species, since it grows frequently in China and is sent everywhere by the Chinese preserved in sugar. Some, however, as was said, call these fruits **Amboinese Sweet Apples**, especially the first species, which the Amboinese cultivate mostly in their mountains; by the Portuguese it is called *Laranza*; by the Spaniards *Naranza*, but by the Indian Portuguese *Limondoce* <note>Literal translation: Sweet Lemon.</note>. Truly the Latin name for this kind is **Golden Apple** <note>original: "Malum Aureum"</note>, and **Hesperian Apple**, whence some think...

### CHAPTER XLII.
### Chinese Orange Tree.

THESE fruits are held by some of the common folk on Amboina to be locally grown, but one does better to call them **Chinese Apples** along with the majority, and that for the following reasons.

The tree is indeed as high as the previous one, with straight upright branches, the crown somewhat rounder and more expanded. The leaves are somewhat narrower and sharper than the former, three and four inches long, smooth, with few ribs, smelling like the former; the winged stalk <note>original: "bert"</note> is also a finger's breadth long, but so narrow that one can hardly recognize the shape of a wing, yet it is still somewhat broader than on the **Martinique Lemon**: The young shoots also have long and slender thorns, but on the grown trees one sees none of them.

The fruit is of two kinds of shape; for one tree bears larger apples than the other: The largest being almost like the preceding, or a little smaller, perfectly round, except that they have a bump near the stem, and are somewhat flat in front with a small pit; the rest of the shell <note>The rind or peel.</note> is indeed smooth, but set with many noticeable holes or pores, reasonably thick, pithy, and allows itself to be easily pulled from the meat; on the outside it remains blackish-green, like the former, even if it is completely ripe: furthermore bitter, sulfurous, and very strong of scent, giving off a vapor upon breaking.

These apples, when they are plucked and lie for a time, become as yellow as **Orange Apples** on one side, but those that become entirely yellow on the tree are considered dry and of no virtue, and these also commonly do not reach their full size but fall off so. The innermost meat is entirely like that of the **Spanish Orange Apples**, namely, divided into many slices, which all stand in a circle against one another, and make a small roundness in the middle, and one must clean this inner ball or peeled apple very thoroughly of its dry woolliness <note>The pith.</note>, because it is bitter: After that one can pull them apart, and eat each part individually; the inner marrow is reddish-yellow, half-transparent, sweet of taste, with a small wininess; the seed-grains are a little elongated, round, and dense.

The second sort of these apples is a little smaller, and smoother, flat on the bottom and top, and coming somewhat closer to the **Spanish Orange-Apples**, on the outside as if pricked with very small pores or holes, with a thin shell, barely a straw-breadth thick, which also allows itself to be easily pulled off; the meat is like that of the former; this sort becomes somewhat yellower on the tree, and if they lie for a bit, they become entirely yellow like right Orange-Apples. These trees do not bear much in Amboina, at least not every year, and they must be fully grown trees before they begin to get fruit; they want a flat ground, and to stand well in the Sun, therefore those that grow in the Amboinese cold mountains ripen their fruits slowly, and remain mostly sour; it also comes to no great age, but often begins to "tear out" a sour sap, and to sweat out much gum, bearing for a year or two an unusually large amount of fruit, which also mostly become yellow on the tree, and thereafter it dies out. This plague one can hardly prevent, but one can delay it for a time, namely if one bores a hole in the trunk, and thereby lets a quantity of superfluous sap run out: Some also drive a coarse iron nail into the trunk.

*Name.* In Latin *Aurantium Sinense*, after the Dutch *Sineese Appels*, in Malay *Lemon Manis Tsjina*, which name fits the last and smallest sort best or most closely, because it grows much in China, and having been preserved in sugar by the Chinese, is transported everywhere: Some, as said, call them **Amboinese Sweet Apples**, especially the first sort, which the Amboinese have or cultivate much in their mountains: In Portuguese *Laranza*: In Spanish *Naranza*, but in Indian Portuguese *Limondoce*. The right Latin name of this genus is *Malum Aureum*, and *Hespericum*, of which some th-

the Orange-Apple <note>original: "Pomum Aurantium"</note> and the Italian *Pomeransi* are derived from the same source. I, however, believe all these names take their origin from the Modern Greek word *nerantion* <note>original: "νεράντιον"</note>, and this from the Arabic *Nerang*, or the Persian *Naring* or *Naran*, by which they denote this fruit. These names were undoubtedly introduced into Spain long ago by the Western Moors <note>original: "Occidentales Aethiopes" / "Westersche Moren"</note>, which later degenerated into the word *Naranja*. The modern Latinists, being ignorant of the word's origin, call it *Aurantium*, which they feel better matches its golden color and the name "Golden Apple" <note>original: "Pomi Aurei"</note>. The Javanese call it *Djerroc Lecki*, the Macassarese call it *Lemo Songalea*, that is, *Chinese Lemons*, while the Amboinese call it *Massussu*. The Chinese call it *Tyng-Cam*.

The Romans attributed honor and glory to a certain Palladius for being the first to bring Asian Citrons and Lemons into Italy; while this may perhaps be true for those fruits, it is by no means true for Oranges. The name *Hesperian Apple* <note>Referring to the golden apples of the Hesperides in Greek mythology.</note> sufficiently declares that they originated from the Western parts of the world. Furthermore, since the Oriental and especially the Indian oranges differ so greatly from the Spanish and Western ones—both in their foliage and in the green color of the fruit—one can easily conclude that neither did the Western Oranges come from the Eastern ones, nor vice versa. Much less were both produced or propagated from Citrons through the art of grafting.

**Location.** It is found in almost all the Oriental islands, such as Java, Celebes, and the Moluccas, all the way to Amboina.

**Use.** These apples are mostly eaten raw on hotter days to refresh the stomach, but they are best suited for an empty stomach. In their own country, the Chinese have very elegant, spherical fruits of a second variety, which are smaller than the common ones. They preserve these whole in sugar, having cut certain slits into them and pressed them flat into the shape of a large disc. In these, little or no bitterness is perceived. They are transported in full jars from China to other regions. The Chinese living in Java preserve them in a similar manner, though they do not know how to coat them in sugar as elegantly as is done in China. The same Chinese also transport these apples to other lands entirely dried and preserved between papers, which are very pleasing to the sick.

### OBSERVATION.

This tree is called the *Chinese Orange Apple* by *Jonston* in *Dendrol. p. 26.* and in *Sloane’s Catalogue of Jamaican Plants p. 211.* and the *Chinese Orange* by *Ferrarius* in *Hesperid. p. 430.* It is the same as the *Low Orange Tree* named by *Caspar Bauhin* in his *Pinax p. 436.* and by *Plukenet* in *Almag. p. 238.* and the *Chinese Orange Apples* of *Valentijn* in the *Description of Amboina p. 189.* which further agrees with that which is called the *Royal Sweet Orange of Ceylon* in the *Treasury of Ceylon p. 39.* etc.

<column-break/>

the Orange-Apple, and the Italian *Pomeransi* are derived: but I judge that they are all descended from the Modern Greek *Nerantion*, and the same from the Arabic *Nerang*, or the Persian *Naring*, or *Naran*; with which they name these fruits, and which the Western Moors undoubtedly brought into Spain in former times, from which *Naranja* was then made. But the modern Latinists, not understanding the origin of the word, made *Aurantium* from it, so that it would better agree with the gold-colored hue and the name *Pomum Aureum*. In Javanese it is *Djerroc Lecki*, in Macassarese *Lemo Songalea*, which are *Chinese Lemons*; in Amboinese *Massussu*. In Chinese *Tyng-Cam*.

The Romans attributed the honor to a certain Palladius that he brought Asian Citrons and Lemons into Italy for the first time; and this may well be true of those fruits, but not at all of the Oranges, because the name *Pomum Hesperium* shows sufficiently that they are originally from the Western parts of the world. Also, because the Oriental, especially the Indian Oranges, differ too much from the Spanish and Western ones, both in leaves and in the greenness of the fruit. From this one can also easily conclude that neither the Western Oranges are from these Eastern ones, nor on the contrary the Eastern from the Western, and much less were both brought forth from Citrons by the art of Grafting.

**Place.** They are found almost throughout all the Eastern Islands, such as Java, Celebes, and the Moluccas, even unto Amboina.

**Use.** They are mostly eaten raw during hot days to refresh the stomach, yet they fit best in an empty stomach. The Chinese have in their country, of the second sort, very fine round Lemons, a size smaller than the common ones, which they know how to preserve whole, making only a few cuts therein, and then pressing them down flat in the shape of a large disc, in which one also perceives no, or certainly very little, bitterness. They are also transported in whole pots full from China to other places. The Chinese living on Java make the same likewise, but cannot candy <note>original: "candaliseeren"</note> them as well as is done in China. Of the same Lemons, the mentioned Chinese also bring some from their country that are entirely dried and kept between paper, falling very pleasantly for sick people.

### CHAPTER FORTY-THREE.
### The Warty Orange: Large Sweet Lemon.

Among all the kinds of Lemons, this tree bears the highest trunk and crown; but its branches are not as upright as in the preceding ones. The younger trees bear a few thorns, but in the old ones none appear, or at least their traces appear on the stems as unarmed and not stinging. The leaves are similar to the previous ones or a little larger, over five inches long and three fingers wide, pointed at the top, and there slightly notched. The heart-shaped part <note>The winged petiole typical of citrus leaves</note> is small and can hardly be distinguished, especially in adult trees, for in younger ones it is long and narrow, where it distinguishes itself more. The scent is weaker than in the preceding ones, and the flowers likewise consist of five oblong and whitish petals, turned back, larger than in the rest, except for the flowers of the **Pomelo** <note>original: *Pompelmoes*</note>, which they also closely approach in their pleasant scent.

The fruits of this kind are larger than the preceding Oranges, about as thick as two fists, perfectly spherical, but covered with various large and hard warts, as if they were boils; however, the rind does not turn as dark a green as the former, but is more pale; it is not as thick or sulfurous as the preceding ones and is very firmly attached to the internal flesh, so that it is not to be peeled by hand but must be cut away with a knife. The flesh likewise consists of and is separated by various but simple membranes, which however cannot be separated into segments at all as in other Oranges; nor is it as reddish-yellow as in the preceding, but yellowish, semi-transparent, and sweeter and juicier than in the former, for which reason it is preferred by many. For this sweetness is not so mixed with that vinous flavor, but is milder, approaching the taste of **Cherries**.

The seed-pips are numerous and larger than in the preceding ones, nor does a cavity appear in the center of the fruit. The Amboinese neglect and do not cultivate this fruit, since it cannot endure the colder mountains, but loves only a loose and black soil mixed with sand and well-exposed to the Sun, such as can be prepared in the villages near the houses. It is planted more by Europeans than the preceding one, since it grows more rapidly, bears fruit sooner, and is generally more fertile than the one immediately preceding.

**Name.** In Latin *Warty Orange* <note>original: *Aurantium Verrucosum*</note>, in Dutch *Sweet Apples* <note>original: *zoete Appelen*</note>; in Malay *Large Sweet Lemon* <note>original: *Lemon Manis Bezaar*</note>, though some Amboinese call it the *Chinese Lemon* <note>original: *Lemon Tsjina*</note>, since it is mostly cultivated by the Chinese living here; by those of Ternate it is called *Siricaya*. In China there are two kinds of these fruits: first the common one, which is called here *Royal Lemon* <note>original: *Bit-Cam*, likely from the Hokkien for "honey orange"</note>; second the *Seng-Cam*, and these are twice as large as the common ones, but not as sweet.

**Location.** This species is not as common as the preceding, since it was brought to these islands from elsewhere by the Chinese and other foreigners.

**Use.** They are eaten only raw and are placed on the tables with the desserts <note>original: *tragematibus*</note>; once the outer rind has been cut away with a knife, its flesh is to be sliced into fragments not crosswise, but obliquely, and the internal mass is kept whole as much as possible, since it consists mostly of various simple and larger juice-vesicles closely packed together. The Chinese allow these oranges to many sick people to refresh the stomach and excite the appetite, since they have none of the vinous sharpness of the preceding ones, and do not excite sweats as much. However, a warning must be given here: these fruits should not be devoured too greedily after dinner if the stomach has been filled with various kinds of food, and especially with milk-dishes; for when taken then, they have often caused a **choleric flux** <note>A sudden onset of vomiting and diarrhea</note>, as I have experienced in the entire family of a most noble house, which was accustomed to eat these fruits after the use of milk.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER XLIII.
### Sweet Orange Tree.

Among all lineages of Lemons, this tree is indeed the highest in trunk and crown, yet the branches do not stand as straight as on the preceding ones. The young trees have few thorns, and on the old ones one sees none or only some remnants on the twigs, which do not prick. The leaves are like the previous ones, or even somewhat larger, fully 5 inches long and three fingers wide, pointed at the front, and there slightly notched. The little heart <note>The leaf base</note> is also small, and barely recognizable, especially on the full-grown trees; for on the young ones it is indeed long and narrow, yet more recognizable. The scent is somewhat weaker than on the previous ones, and the bloom also consists of five oblong white petals, bent backwards, somewhat larger than the preceding, except those of the **Pomelo**, which they also come closest to in loveliness of scent.

The fruits are also larger than the preceding Oranges, making up nearly two fists, perfectly round, yet beset with various large and hard warts, like **boils** <note>original: *bloet-vinnen*</note>; not as dark-green as the previous ones, but somewhat lighter. The rind, which is also not as heavy or sulfurous as the previous, hangs or sits so fast to the inner flesh that one cannot pull it off, but must peel it with a knife. The flesh is also separated from one another with various, yet single membranes, but one can by no means pull it apart into slices or parts like the Oranges; furthermore, it is not as red-yellow as that of the previous, but light-yellow, half-transparent, also sweeter and juicier than the previous, and why it is preferred or deemed better by many. For this sweetness is mixed with no notable wine-like quality, but is somewhat milder, and drawing more toward the taste of **sweet cherries**.

The seed-grains are many and larger than the previous, making no hollowness in the interior of the fruit. The Amboinese do not tend or cultivate this fruit at all, because they cannot well endure the cold mountains, but want a loose and black soil mixed with some sand, and to stand well in the Sun, such as one can have in the **villages** <note>original: *Negoryen*</note> around the houses. It is planted more by the Europeans than the previous, because it shoots up more quickly and bears early, and is generally more fruitful than the preceding.

**Name.** In Latin *Warty Orange* <note>original: *Aurantium Verrucosum*</note>, in German <note>Rumphius often uses "Duits" to mean Dutch</note> *Sweet Apples*, after the Malay *Large Sweet Lemon* <note>original: *Lemoen Manis Besaar*</note>, yet some Amboinese call them *Chinese Lemon* <note>original: *Lemon Tsjina*</note> because they are mostly tended by the Chinese living here; in Ternate *Siricaya*. In China they are of two kinds: 1. The common and here-known-in-the-land called *Bit Cam*, that is, *Honey-Lemon*. 2. *Seng-Cam*, and these are twice as large as the common ones, but not as sweet.

**Place.** One finds this sort not as commonly as the preceding; for they were first brought to these islands from elsewhere by the Chinese and other foreigners.

**Use.** They are likewise only eaten raw, and served among the banquet-work, the outer rind having been peeled off with a knife; then one must not cut the flesh crosswise, but in slanted pieces, leaving the inner clump as whole as one can, because it consists mostly of single large grains packed tightly upon one another. The Chinese allow these Lemons in almost all illnesses to refresh the stomach and provoke appetite, because they have no wine-like sharpness about them like the previous, and cause less sweating. However, I must yet add a warning here, namely that one must not swallow these Apples too greedily after eating, when one has filled the body with many kinds of dainty food, especially with milk-dishes; for these Lemons coming upon that sometimes cause vomiting, as I have experienced in an entire family of a prominent house, who had it as a habit to eat these Apples after milk.

# AMBOINESE HERBARIUM Book II. Chapter XLIII.
### Page 116

In Banda <note>An archipelago in the Moluccas famous for nutmeg</note> another species is found, which bears sweeter fruits than the preceding one, and its citrus fruits <note>original: *mala*; literally "apples," but used here for any large round fruit</note> are covered everywhere with warts, and its internal flesh is white and completely sweet when it is ripe—indeed, sweeter than those of Batavia <note>Modern-day Jakarta</note>—and there it is called the *Pouleron Lemon* <note>original: *Limon Pouleron*; named after the island of Pulau Run</note>, although it also occurs on *Ai Island* <note>original: *Plo Ay*</note>.

In *Madura* <note>An island off the northeastern coast of Java</note> a species of sweet *Lemon* is also found which is the smallest of all, even smaller than the thin-rinded *Lime* <note>original: *Limonis cortice tenui*; likely referring to the *Jeruk Nipis*</note>; its rind is not bitter, and its internal flesh consists of many soft granules. It serves excellently for preserves, for which purpose it is used by the Chinese inhabitants of *Gresik* <note>original: *Grieffeckam*</note>, which is situated across from *Madura*.

Name. In Latin, the **Dwarf Madura Orange** <note>original: *Aurantium Pumilum Madurense*</note>. In Malay, **Lemon Suaffi** and **Lemon Colte**.

So that the branches of all Lemon species may be set and transplanted in such a way that they bear fruit within a few months, one should choose from the oldest trees such branches that are almost ready to put forth flowers or buds. These are to be struck with a stone for the width of a palm's distance from the trunk until the bark is gently bruised; then, they are to be covered with rich and fertile earth, which, so that it does not fall off, must be wrapped with a split Bamboo leaf or another weaving. Such a branch must then be left to itself for five or six weeks until you believe this bruised bark has sent out little roots into the earth. Then, let it be cut off below the split Bamboo leaf or covering and transplanted into a box filled with good, fertile earth. In that same month, it will yield full fruits, but not more than once or twice, for after that it perishes. However, if it is committed to fertile soil, it grows into a complete tree. This is a common but profitable custom of the Chinese living in Batavia, who rent certain gardens or a part of the land for a series of years, and by this art they ensure that they may gather fruit immediately. Furthermore, to make old trees fertile, many of their branches are lopped off, and a huge nail is driven through the trunk; this same thing can be done and is beneficial for the **Jackfruit** <note>original: *Nanca*</note> and **Spanish Cherry** <note>original: *Bonga Tanjong*; *Mimusops elengi*</note> trees.

In Banda they have yet another kind and sweeter **Oranges** <note>original: *Appels*</note> than the previous ones, covered everywhere with similar warts; the flesh inside is white and entirely sweet when it is ripe—yes, sweeter than those of Batavia. They call them there the *Pouleron Lemon*, although they are also found on *Ai Island*.

On Madura there is also a sort of sweet **Lemon**, being the very smallest of all—even smaller than a *Lime* <note>original: *Lemoen Nipis*</note>—with a thin rind that is not very bitter, and the inner flesh is full of small and soft granules. It is very commonly used for preserves, specifically by the Chinese living in Gresik, which lies opposite Madura.

Name. In Latin **Dwarf Madura Orange**, in Malay **Lemon Suaffi**, and **Lemon Colte**.

*Now, to set and transplant the branches of all kinds of Lemon trees in such a way that they bear fruit in a few months: choose some branches on the old trees that are nearly ready to bud or blossom; knock them with a stone about a hand's breadth from the trunk until the bark is gently bruised, and there cover or surround it with good, rich earth. Then secure the same with a split Bamboo or some fibrous material so that the earth does not fall off, and let this branch stand thus for 5 or 6 weeks, until you guess that the bruised bark has shot little roots into the earth. Then saw it off shortly behind the split Bamboo or the wrapping, and plant it in a box full of good earth; it will then bear full fruits in that same month, though not more than once or twice. For after that it expires; but if one plants them in good soil, they become complete trees. This is a common and profitable art for the Chinese living in Batavia, who rent some lands or gardens for only a few years, and by this art ensure they can have fruit from them immediately. Otherwise, to make old trees fruitful, one sometimes chops most of the branches out of them and drives a large iron nail into the trunk, which can also be done to the Jackfruit and Spanish Cherry trees.*

# BOOK II. CHAPTER XLIV. AMBOINESE HERBARIUM. 117

### CHAPTER FORTY-FOUR.

->Indian Apple. Vidara.<-

This little tree is exotic to Amboina <note>The modern island of Ambon in Indonesia</note>, having been brought there only a few years ago; it is now beginning to produce fruit quite well, though it does not grow as tall here as it does in Western regions. Here it is only a small tree with a crooked and slanted trunk, no thicker than a man’s leg, which divides into many branches and forms a dense crown.

The bark of the branches is smooth and a yellowish-red, but on the trunk, it is rough, fissured, and a finger-breadth thick. The wood is hard and knotty. The leaves resemble those of an apple tree, but are smaller and rounder, two or two-and-a-half inches long and slightly less wide. They are blunt at the front with a tip that looks almost broken off—as if it had been cut or worn away—and are patterned with three slanted veins that meet near the petiole <note>The stalk that joins a leaf to a stem</note>. They have several lateral ribs and are finely serrated at the edges. On the underside, they are soft and whitish like Sage, with a slimy taste and a slight bitterness, much like the Marshmallow plant <note>original: *Althaea*</note>, with which the scent also agrees. When chewed in the mouth or rubbed by hand in water, they produce a foam like Soap, though without any pungency. They are positioned singly on round, stiff branchlets, and at the base of each leaf, one or two short thorns are seen—sometimes straight, but mostly curved backward like those of a Dog Rose <note>original: *Rosa Canina*</note>. These thorns also appear on the lower branches where the leaves have already fallen. On younger trees, they reach the length of Lemon thorns, but on older ones, these thorns are shorter and mostly fall off.

The flowers sprout from the leaf axils <note>the angle between the upper side of a leaf and the stem</note>, several together on short stalks. They first appear as grey buds, which then open into star-shaped or rose-like flowers consisting of five whitish petals with some short stamens; they have no scent. The fruits hang two or three together in the shape of pigeon eggs or slightly larger. They are flat at the bottom with a small pit where the stalk is attached. When unripe, they closely resemble half-grown Olives; some are oblong while others are round like small plums. Externally, they are apple-green in color, eventually turning yellowish, covered with a thin skin like our European Apples. Beneath this is a somewhat hard but juicy flesh, which in Amboina is never fully sweet but rather astringent like sloes <note>small, bitter wild plums; original: *Prunellorum*</note>, and it has an oily smell. In its center is found a hard stone that is not striated but granulated or wrinkled, and which is usually free from the surrounding flesh. In other regions, these fruits are much more elegant and larger than in Amboina—even in the neighboring Celebes <note>Modern-day Sulawesi</note> and Bali <note>original: *Baleya*</note>, where the tree reaches the size of a Lemon tree and the fruit is as large and round as a small Key Lime <note>original: *Limo Nipis*</note>. When ripe, it turns yellowish and has a sweeter, juicier taste than the Amboinese variety, though still with a slight tartness. The best are considered to be those from Bengal, Arakan <note>A coastal region in modern Myanmar</note>, and those growing in the province of Patna situated on the upper part of the Ganges river. However, Portuguese writers give the prize to those of Balaghat <note>A region in central India</note> and those growing around Malacca, for there they are as large as a medium-sized apple, and are juicy, vinous, and sweet in taste. Here in Amboina, they produce their fruit slowly; I had two trees that were always flowering but never bore fruit until their eighth year, at which point they were cut down. Later, other trees were propagated by other people from new and exotic seeds, which bore abundant fruit by the fourth year, though much poorer and smaller than in the lands where they are native. They flower in the month of December and show ripe fruit in March and April.

Christophorus da Costa <note>A 16th-century Portuguese physician and botanist</note> writes in Chapter 51 that in those regions, during the hottest months, these trees are continually inhabited by a kind of flying ant which prepares "Lac" gum <note>original: *Gummi Laccam*; shellac resin produced by the lac insect</note> on the branches, so that the branches are entirely covered by this gum.

Name: In Latin, *Malum Indicum* <note>Indian Apple</note>, following the Portuguese—

### CHAPTER XLIV.

->Indian Apple-Tree.<-

This little tree is foreign to Amboina, and was first brought there only a few years ago; however, it is now beginning to bear well, but it is not nearly as large as in the Western Lands. It remains only a small tree with a crooked, slanted trunk, no thicker than a thigh, which nevertheless divides into many branches and thereby creates a dense crown.

The bark of the branches is smooth and yellowish-red, but on the trunk, it is very roughly fissured and at least a finger thick. The wood is hard and knotty. The leaves are like those of the Apple tree, though somewhat smaller and rounder, 2 to 2 1/2 inches long and a bit less wide. At the front, they have a blunt and broken tip, as if they were cut or eaten away, marked with three slanted veins that meet at the back by the stalk, and some additional small ribs. They are small and finely saw-toothed at the edges. Underneath, they are soft and whitish like Sage, with a greasy taste and a small bitterness, almost like Marshmallow <note>original: *Althaea*</note>, with which the smell also agrees. When chewed in the mouth or rubbed in water with the hands, they foam like Soap, yet without any sharpness. They stand singly on round and stiff twigs, and at each origin is one or two short and stiff little thorns; some are straight, but most are crooked and bent backward like the *Rosa Canina* <note>Dog Rose</note>. These can still be seen at the back of the branches where the leaves have already fallen. On young trees, they are as long as Lemon-thorns, but on the old ones, they become shorter and mostly fall off.

The blossom comes forth from the lap of the leaves, many together on short stalks, being at first grey buds that thereafter become small starry flowers consisting of five white petals with some short threads, without scent. The fruits hang two or three together in the shape of Pigeon eggs, or a little larger; somewhat flat from behind and with a small pit where the stalk stands or is attached. When unripe, they very much resemble half-grown Olives; some remain oblong and some become somewhat round like small plums, Apple-green on the outside, and finally light yellow, covered with a thin skin like our European Apples. Underneath lies a somewhat hard but juicy flesh, which here in Amboina is never perfectly sweet, but tart like sloes <note>original: *sleen*</note>, and additionally somewhat oily in smell. Inside lies a hard stone, like an olive stone, not striped but granulated or wrinkled, which is commonly loose from the surrounding flesh. These fruits are much more beautiful and larger in other Lands than in Amboina—yes, even on the neighboring Celebes and Bali, where the tree becomes as large as a Lemon tree, and the fruit almost as large and round as a small Key Lime <note>original: *Limo Nipis*</note>, light yellow in ripeness, and much sweeter and juicier in taste than the Amboinese ones, though still with a small contraction <note>astringency</note>. The very best are considered to grow in Bengal, Arakan, and in the Province of Patna, situated up on the River Ganges, although the Portuguese writers give the prize to those of Balaghat and those growing around Malacca; for there they become as large as a medium-sized small apple, and are also juicy and vinously sweet. Here in Amboina, they bear slowly, and we had 2 trees here, a bit smaller than the preceding, always blooming but bearing no fruit until the eighth year, when they were chopped down. Thereafter, others were cultivated by other people from foreign seeds, which bore abundant fruit in the third year, though much poorer and smaller than in the lands they came from, blooming in the month of December and ripening in March and April.

Christophorus da Costa, Chapter 51, writes that in the aforementioned lands, one sees this tree in the hot monsoon constantly laden with a kind of flying Ant, which prepares the Lac-gum <note>original: *Gummilacca*</note> on its branches, and that one sees it hanging all around there.

Name: In Latin, *Malum Indicum*: After the Portu-

# AMBOINESE HERBARIUM Book II. Chapter XLIV. 118

The *Mansana* or *Massana* of India according to Acosta <note>Cristóvão da Costa, a 16th-century Portuguese physician and botanist</note>, as it is also called in Ancient India <note>The Indian subcontinent</note>, where according to that same writer it is known as *Ber* or *Bor*. In Malay it is called *Vidara*, and in Macassar and the nearby islands it is known as *Balis Buckol*.

<margin>Location.</margin> This little tree occurs most frequently throughout Ancient India, as well as in Bengal, Arakan, and Malacca, extending as far as Java and Bali. From there it was brought to Celebes and the Moluccas, though it is rarely found here in Amboina or in Banda, and where it does grow, it is much degenerated from the original.

<margin>Use.</margin> These fruits are eaten raw with great appetite in the regions where they are native; in both scent and flavor, they most closely resemble European apples. However, in these parts they are little esteemed because of their bitterness. All botanical writers consider them a species of Jujube <note>term: Jujube (Latin: *Zizyphus*), a fruit-bearing tree known for its medicinal berries</note>, mostly due to their shape, but they differ greatly in their properties. For these bitter fruits do not benefit the chest by clearing it or making breathing easier, nor can they be dried or shipped to other regions like true Jujubes. Nevertheless, some Malays living in Amboina teach us that eating these fruits when half-ripe helps to clear the chest and treat asthma, as well as to strengthen the stomach and quench thirst—a matter that may be further investigated by those who so desire. I and others with me have found that they cause a heavy feeling in the chest and weigh down the stomach, though this is said without prejudice toward the Oriental *Vidara*. The leaves, when rubbed in water, create a foam used to wash the head and the body during burning fevers and headaches <note>original: *Cephalalgia*</note>.

The root of this tree, which is a yellowish-red on the outside, greatly resembles Snakewood <note>term: *Lignum Colubrino*, a bitter wood used in traditional medicine to treat snakebites and fevers</note>, leading some to think they are of the same genus. However, only a slight bitterness is observed in this root—mostly in the bark—along with a notable astringency that is not found in Snakewood. The roots of the sterile trees mentioned above were even more notably bitter, a quality not detected in the fruit-bearing trees we have today.

The bark of this root, crushed with a little *Putchuck* <note>term: *Putſjock*, a fragrant medicinal root (Costus)</note>, *Pulasari* <note>term: *Pulæſari*, the fragrant bark of *Alyxia stellata*, used in traditional Indonesian medicine</note>, and a roasted onion, and then drunk, cures painful and bloody urine. The Balinese use the hard wood to make handles for *Parangs* <note>term: *Parrangs*, large knives or machetes</note>, axes, and similar tools.

In the year 1673, *Vidara* seeds were sent from Batavia <note>Modern-day Jakarta</note> to Amboina. By the sixth year, they had grown into a tree the thickness and size of a Lemon tree, with deeply fissured bark, which the Balinese use in a decoction to treat all forms of diarrhea.

Its fruits were a little larger than the common ones of this region, less bitter, and of better flavor. The juice of the leaves, crushed with a little water and pressed out, is also given as a drink in fevers to extinguish heat and thirst.

In regions where these trees are abundant, people used to use the leaves crushed in water to wash corpses.

In Timor and other places, two species of this *Vidara* occur: one species provides larger and sweet fruits, while the other provides smaller and bitter ones, like those in Amboina. Both grow on medium-sized trees like Lemon trees, which have crooked trunks.

In Java, another species occurs called *Vidara Puti* <note>White Vidara</note>. It is mostly wild and grows near the shore, but rarely bears fruit. Its leaves are whiter underneath than the common variety. The best fruits of this tree are considered to be those that grow in Malacca. Its thick roots are much sought after for medical use; they have a notable bitterness, so much so that they might be mistaken for Snakewood, though they possess the astringency peculiar to the *Vidara*. They are often taken crushed to quench the heat of fevers, strengthen the stomach, and stop bilious vomiting.

On some leaves of the common *Vidara* in certain years—mostly in the month of February—one observes "skulls" <note>likely small insect galls or growths</note> such as those described above in Chapter 33 regarding the Pomegranate.

<meta>catchword: EXPLI-</meta>

<column-break/>

The yellowish *Mansana* or *Massana* of India, from the aforementioned Acosta, as it is also called in Ancient India, and according to the same writer, *Ber* and *Bor*. In Malay *Vidara*, also called in Macassar and throughout these surrounding islands *Balis Buckol*.

<margin>Place.</margin> It is found mostly throughout all of old India, and further through Bengal, Arakan, and Malacca, as far as Java and Bali, from where it was brought to Celebes and the Moluccas; but few are found here or in Banda, and as said, they are much degenerated from the original.

<margin>Use.</margin> These fruits are eaten raw, and with great appetite in the places where they are native, coming closest to European apples in smell and taste. But here in this country, they are little esteemed because of their tartness. By all writers, they are held to be a kind of Jujube (In Latin *Zizyphus*), mostly because of their shape, but they differ significantly in power. For in these tart fruits, one finds no benefit for the chest to cleanse it and make it free; likewise, they cannot be dried and shipped like those same Jujubes. Nonetheless, some Malays here in Amboina tell us that the half-ripe fruits, when eaten, are good to cleanse the chest and also for shortness of breath, as well as to strengthen the stomach and beat back thirst, which investigation may be left to those who desire it. I, and others with me, have found that they oppress the chest and press upon the stomach, though this is said without prejudice to the Eastern *Vidara*. The leaves rubbed in water make the same foam, and with it, one washes the head and body when one has fevers and heat.

The root of this tree, being a rusty-yellow on the outside, has a great resemblance to snakewood; and for which reason it has been maintained that they were of the same genus, although in this root one feels only a small bitterness, and that mostly in the bark with a notable contraction <note>astringency</note>, which is not in snakewood. The roots of the aforementioned barren trees had an even more notable bitterness, but in the fruit-bearing ones that we have now, one can hardly taste it.

The bark of this root, rubbed with a little *Putchuck*, *Pulasari*, and a roasted onion, and drunk, heals the most painful and bloody urination. The Balinese use the hard wood for the handles of their *Parangs*, or cleavers and chisels, and other carpentry tools.

In the year 1673, the seed of *Vidara* was brought from Batavia to Amboina, which in the 6th year was a tree as large and thick as a Lemon tree, with a large, split bark, which the Balinese use as a decoction against all kinds of diarrhea <note>original: *buikloop*</note>.

The fruits were a little larger than the common ones here in this country, less tart, and somewhat better in taste. The juice of the leaves, rubbed with a little water and pressed out, they also give to drink internally to reduce the heat of fevers.

In the lands where these small trees are numerous, people used to use these leaves rubbed in water to wash dead bodies.

On Timor and other places, one has two kinds of *Vidara*; the first and largest is sweet, the second is smaller and tart, like the Amboinese, both growing on medium trees, like Lemon trees, which are crooked of trunk.

Furthermore, one has on Java a sort that they call *Vidara Puti* there, mostly in the wild and growing near the beach, but bearing little fruit, and whose leaves are whiter underneath than the common ones. Those that grow on Malacca are held for the best. The thick roots are much sought after for medicine, for they have a notable bitterness, so that one would judge or regard them as snakewood, yet with a contraction proper to the *Vidara*. They are often rubbed and taken to reduce the heat of the fever, strengthen the stomach, and prevent bilious vomiting.

On the leaves of the common *Vidara*, in some years and mostly in February, such "death’s heads" <note>gall formations</note> are found as was said here above in Chapter 33 regarding the Pomegranates.

## OBSERVATION.
That these trees belong to the *Jujubes* or *Zizyphus* <note>original: *Zizyphos*</note> is easily established not only from the flowers and fruits, but from its entire thorny habit and its solitary and alternate leaf arrangement. It is the thorny, round-leaved Indian *Jujube*, with larger leaves that are downy and gray underneath, as described by *Breynius* in *Prodromus 2, page 60*, and in the new edition by his son, *page 74*. There, it is rightly noted that it is not the same plant that I showed in *Thesaurus Zeylanicus, Plate 61*, as I had also warned on *page 131*. The figure in the *Hortus Malabaricus* <note>Garden of Malabar; a famous 17th-century botanical work on Indian flora</note> by no means agrees with ours, though the description fits it better, and it should be considered a variety or another species. It is commonly confused with the silver Indian *Zizyphus* with flowers like the aromatic *Clove* described by *Hermann*, which I showed in the same *Thesaurus, Plate 39*, as I noted more extensively there on *page 92*, and in *Commelin’s Flora Malabarica*, as well as in the notes on the *Hortus Malabaricus*; these are wrongly joined together by others. Furthermore, this tree described here is called by *Dale* in his *Pharmacology, page 946*, the tree whose exuding sap is *Gummi Lacca* <note>term: Lac or Shellac; a resin secreted by the lac bug, often found on these trees</note>, which in the new quarto edition, *page 33*, is referred to the Indian *Jujube* of *Ray’s History, volume 2, page 153*, where it is also called the somewhat thorny *Malaccan Apple*. See there for the remaining synonyms and various opinions on the generation of this Lac resin. The *Perim Toddali* of the *Hortus Malabaricus, Volume 4, Plate 41*, agrees very well with ours, but the veins of the leaves are not as accurately marked as in *Rumphius's* figure, which we subjoin here. This genus is referred by *Linnaeus* to *Rhamnus* in *Genera Plantarum 165*, whose species are enumerated in *Hortus Cliffortianus, pages 69 and 70*.

# CHAPTER FORTY-FIVE.
## Shore Vidara. Sea Vidara. <note>original: *Vidara Laut*</note>
The Shore Vidara is a true shrub, raising itself with various thin and arched stems scarcely as thick as a leg. Many leaves come forth together from knotty branches, sitting on short petioles <note>leaf stalks</note>, near which certain small thorns also appear, but they are rarer and shorter than in the previous kind, so that some larger branches bear none at all.
The bark of the trunk is smoother than the preceding, thinner, and more brown. The leaves are much smaller and of two forms: for the upper ones are similar to the leaves of the *Lemoen Nipis* <note>term: Key Lime; *Citrus aurantiifolia*</note>, but the lower ones are blunt and almost bifurcated like a heart, with entire edges that are not serrated. They are not gray or soft underneath like the preceding, but smooth and even, distinguished by a few very oblique ribs. The younger branches are angular and striated, upon which solitary leaflets are placed, very similar to *Lemoen Nipis* leaves, and likewise a little serrated in the upper part, but smaller, smoother, and flappier, two inches long and scarcely one wide. At the side of each leaf a long small thorn arises, and upon that thorn such leaflets often appear here and there. Their taste is astringent, very similar to the pits of Plums or Cherries, and they are used for *Sayor* <note>term: Sayur; a Malay term for a vegetable dish or stew</note>. Near the leaf stalks, small clusters of flowers sprout forth, first in the form of green heads, like the first buds of *Cloves* <note>original: *Caryophyllorum*</note>, which open into little flowers slightly larger than the preceding, consisting of four white and oblong petals reflected outwards, covered inside with soft down

## OBSERVATION.
That these trees belong to the *Jujube* or *Zizyphi* is evident not only from the flowers and fruits, but also from their entirely thorny appearance, as well as the placement of their leaves, which is alternate; and this is the Indian thorny *Jujube* with round leaves, rough and gray underneath, as it is named by *Breynius* in his second *Prodromus, page 60*, and in the new edition *page 74*, where his son very rightly notes that it differs from that plant which I showed in my *Thesaurus Zeylanicus, page 61*, as I have cited on *page 131* there. Namely, that the figure from the *Hortus Malabaricus* did not agree with ours, but the description agreed better with it, and therefore it was to be held as a related sort or a variation thereof, and which is generally mixed up with the Indian *Zizyphus* with silver leaves and the flower like the clove described by *Hermann*, which I showed in the same *Thesaurus Zeylanicus* on *Plate 39*, as I also noted more broadly there on *page 92*, and in the *Flora Malabarica* of *Caspar Commelin*, and in the notes on the *Hortus Malabaricus*, they are wrongly joined together. Furthermore, this tree described above is called by *Samuel Dale*, in his *Pharmacology, page 446*, a tree whose dripping sap is the *Gummi Lacca*, or the *Gum-lac* <note>Shellac</note>, which in the new edition *page 335* is brought under the *Jujuba Indica* of *Ray* in his *History, page 153*, where it is called the *Malaccan* thorny Apple-tree. See there for the further names and the various opinions on the Gum-lac. The *Perim Toddali* of the *Hortus Malabaricus*, 4th part, *Plate 41*, agrees well with our tree, though the veins of the leaves are not as well indicated as in the figure of *Rumphius*, which we add here. This genus was brought by *Linnaeus* to the *Rhamnus* in his *Genera Plantarum, page 165*, whose species are listed in the *Hortus Cliffortianus, pages 69 and 70*.

# CHAPTER XLV.
## The Shore Jujube Tree.
*Vidara Littorea* is a formal shrub, shooting up with various thin and bowed stems, barely as thick as a leg. The small leaves stand on knotty twigs in bunches together on short stalks, by which one also finds some thorns, though fewer and shorter than on the previous one, so that some old branches have none at all.
The bark of the trunk is smoother than that of the previous one, as well as thinner and rougher. The leaves are much smaller and of two types of shape: for the front ones are like those of the *Lemoen Nipis* <note>Key Lime</note>, the back ones are broad in front and almost cleaved in two like a heart; both are unserrated on the edges, yet not whitish and soft underneath like the previous one, but smooth and even, with few and very slanted ribs. The young branches are angular and very striped, on which the leaflets stand singly, very much like those of the *Lemoen Nipis*, and also a little serrated near the tip, yet smaller, smoother, and flappier, two inches long, and barely as wide. Each leaf has a long small thorn out to the side, and on the same one sees here and there similar small leaves, though smaller. The taste is more astringent, closely resembling the pits of plums or cherries, and they are indeed used for *Sayor* <note>vegetable stew</note>. Near the stalks of the leaves also come small clusters, like the first creations of *Cloves*, which open into little flowers somewhat larger than the previous ones, and made of 4 white longish petals, somewhat curved outwards, and on their
<meta>catchword: inside.</meta>

the inner side with a soft silk-like down, bearing certain stamens in the center.

The fruits hang two or three together like Olives, being wider at the lower part as long as they are immature; but when ripe, they are oblong-round like Plums or *Lansiums* <note>A tropical fruit native to Southeast Asia, also known as Langsat</note>, always narrower near the stem, where a small pit is indented. They are larger than the true *Vidara* found here, and when ripe they show a yellow color, variegated on the outside with green spots. They contain little flesh and have the taste of acidic apples, enclosing a large egg-shaped kernel within a woody but brittle shell; this kernel is white, covered with a gray skin, and has the taste and substance of Hazelnuts. This kernel is pleasant in taste if eaten raw, but it is dangerous; for if more than three are eaten, they cause dizziness in the head and a commotion in the belly. Because of this, our sailors call them *Shit-plums* <note>original: *Schyt-pruimkens*</note> or *Little Nuts*, as they experience their effect through imprudent gluttony. The outer flesh can be eaten raw without harm to quench thirst, or, what is better, it may be preserved in brine and used like other pickles <note>original: *Salgamatum* or *Adstjar*</note>.

The immature fruits are not acidic but almost tasteless with a certain astringency. The wood of the tree is hard, solid, and durable, while the roots are thick and creep through the sand. This tree grows nowhere more happily than on the shore, at the edges and borders of forests, or in sandy ground that is flat, sandy, and mixed with small stones.

*Name.* In Latin *Shore Vidara* <note>original: *Vidara Littorea*</note>; in Malay *Vidara Laut*; by *Pyrard* in the Maldivian tongue, and in the Amboinese, Baleya, and Bucola languages it is called *Hitton Uffi Layn*, that is, *Little Shore Lemon*, since with its thorns and acidic taste it seems in some way to belong to the genus of *Lemons*.

*Location.* It occurs in all the Amboinese islands, but not on every shore; most grow on the coast of *Hitoe* and *Loehoe*, as well as in *Celebes* and *Baleya*, and perhaps in many other islands.

*Use.* In Amboina its fruits are rarely used, and only by the common people are they eaten raw among fish or other foods to excite the appetite, and on journeys to quench thirst; however, they must first be peeled and a little salt added. By some, they are also preserved in brine. The inner kernels are quite tasty if eaten raw, but as indicated above, they cause dizziness and stir the belly—more in one person than in another. For I have seen six or seven such kernels provide a good purge for a slave, while others among our people said they had eaten ten and wanted more, experiencing nothing other than a slight dizziness and a small commotion in the belly. These same kernels can also be eaten safely if boiled in water and then crushed, provided they are soaked for one or two nights in pure water; prepared in such a way, they are mixed with *Sagu-manta* <note>Raw sago flour</note>, and from them *Sago-bread* is baked, which is eaten by the inhabitants of *Affa Hudi*.

The roots, ground with water and drunk, cure the disease called by the Malays *Upas Purrut Banca*, which is *flatulent colic*. The wood, because of its hardness, is used like the wood called *Sappan* <note>term: Sappanwood; a species of flowering tree in the legume family used for dye and cabinetry</note>, namely for wooden nails in ships.

There is a ridiculous craft and opinion held by some who collect the fruits of this tree if they have fallen of their own accord so that their tip is fixed in the earth and the lower part near the stem is raised; they throw these mixed with other food to cats, believing that their appetite is thereby excited so that they may better catch mice.

These trees or shrubs can be divided into two species: the thorny and the mild. The first is properly the *Shore Vidara*, which bears many short thorns on the branches; its leaves also most closely resemble the leaves of the *Nipis Lemon*. The bark of the trunk and roots has a notable bitterness. The other species bears oblong and smoother leaves, and few or almost no thorns on the branches. The root of the first species is used for medical purposes; it is cut off, crushed, and drunk with water. To extinguish heat in burning fevers, and against stinging pains in the abdomen and limbs, the bark of the branches is to be bitten off and chewed with *Pinanga* <note>Areca nut or Betel nut</note>, and the branches themselves must be cut without iron <note>A common folk-medical belief that using iron tools would spoil the healing virtue of the plant</note>
<meta>ab-</meta>

<column-break/>

the inner side with a soft woolliness like plush, and inside with some threads.

The fruits also hang two and three together, like *Olives*, somewhat wider at the front or bottom end as long as they are unripe, but the ripe ones become oblong-round like *plums*, or *Lansats* here in this country, always narrowest by the stem and having a small pit there. They are somewhat larger than the true *Vidara* here in this country, and when ripe they are high-yellow, also speckled on the outside with some green spots. They have but little flesh and taste like sour *Apples*, having inside a large egg-shaped grain or little nut, which, hidden in a woody but brittle shell, contains a white kernel covered with a gray membrane. In taste and substance it is like *Hazelnuts*, being quite lovely to eat raw, yet not without danger; for if one consumes more than three of them, one gets some dizziness in the head and an upset in the belly. For this reason, our *Sailors* call them *Shit-plums* or *little nuts*, because they have felt their power through the careless swallowing of them. The outer flesh can be eaten raw without worry to quench thirst, or (which is even better) pickled in brine and used just like other *Atjar* <note>term: Atjar; Indonesian pickles, usually made from vegetables or fruits in vinegar and salt</note>.

The unripe fruits have no sourness but are almost tasteless with some astringency; the wood is hard, massive, and durable; the roots thick and creeping in the sand. It grows nowhere more gladly than on the beach, at the edges or borders of the Forest, or on dry land where it is also flat and sandy, mixed with some small stones.

Name. In Latin *Vidara Littorea*; after the Malay *Vidara Laut*. *Pyrard* calls them this in the *Maldivian* language; in *Amboinese, Baleya*, and *Bucola* it is *Hitton Uffi Layn*, that is *Little Shore Lemon*, because with their thorns and sour taste they wish to be somewhat of the *Lemon* family.

Place. They are found in all the *Amboinese* Islands, yet not on all beaches; but the most are found on the Land of *Hitoe* and *Loehoe*; they also grow on *Celebes* and *Baley*, and perhaps on more other Islands.

Usage. They are little used in *Amboina*, and only by common people are they eaten raw with fish and among their food to stir the appetite, and when traveling to quench thirst; but one must first peel them and add some salt; they are also sometimes pickled in brine by some. The inner kernels are quite tasty to eat raw, yet they cause, as was said above, a small dizziness in the head and upset the belly, though in some more than in others. For I have seen that 6 or 7 pieces were a good purgative for a slave, where others of our people declared that they had eaten as many as ten pieces and looked for more, without feeling anything but a small dizziness and rumbling in the body. These same grains can also be eaten suitably and without harm or disadvantage if one boils them in water and afterwards mashes them small, provided they are left to soak for a night or two in fresh water; and being thus prepared, they are mixed among *Raw Sago* and from this *Sago-bread* is baked, which is also used by those of *Affa Hudi*.

The root, rubbed with water and drunk, cures the disease called by the *Malays Upas Purrut Banca*, which is a windy colic; and the wood, because of its hardness, is also used like *Sappan-wood* for wooden nails in and on vessels.

It is a ridiculous art of some who seek out the fruits of this tree when they have fallen of themselves, such that the point is in the earth and the back part by the stem stands upwards. They give these among other food to the cats to eat, from which they believe that they become eager to catch mice.

One can divide these trees or shrubs into two kinds, namely, into thorny and smooth, the first being the true *Shore Vidara*, full of short thorns on the twigs; the leaves also resemble the *Nipis Lemon* more, and the bark of the trunk and root has a notable bitterness. The other kind has oblong and smoother leaves, and few or no thorns on the twigs. The root of the first kind is used for Medicine; one cuts it off with a *Parang* <note>term: Parang; a type of knife or machete used in the Malay Archipelago</note>, rubs it, and drinks it thus with water. But to drive away the burning in severe fevers, and against great stings in the body and in the limbs, one must bite off the bark of the branches and chew it with *Areca*, also one must

A superstitious art also prevails among the inhabitants, and it is held as a secret for detecting *Swangis* <note>original: *Swangis seu Magos*; local terms for sorcerers or witches</note>: they take the root of the best or "thorney" species, which they grind with water and lime. Both of these trees occur under the names *Bidara tree* and *Coastal Bidara* in Valentyn's *Description of Amboina*, page 191.

# CHAPTER FORTY-SIX.

## Snakewood: Caju-Ular.

**I**n the East Indies, various woods occur under this name; for instance, Garcia [ab Orta] in his first book on *Aromatics*, chapter 44, enumerates three species of it, all growing in Ceylon. Likewise, three species are commemorated by Cristóvão da Costa in chapter 33, along with certain others added by Carolus Clusius in his notes to those chapters, all of which differ from one another. However, I have been unable to find any of those species in these Eastern regions; therefore, in their place, I shall describe here the one which is used today as the unique and true *Snakewood* <note>original: *Ligno Colubrino*</note>, or is at least known by this name. It does not grow in Ceylon or in Amboina, but in Rote, Timor, and the neighboring islands, from whence branches laden with leaves and fruits, as well as the wood, were sent to me through the help and care of the noble Mr. Antoni Hurdt, Ordinary Councilor of the Indies, and Jacob van Wyckerloot, Chief of Timor (as was mentioned above in the chapter on Sandalwood); from these, the accompanying figure was drawn.

This tree generally has the height and thickness of the *Nipis Lime* <term>Nipis Lime: the Common Lime, Citrus aurantifolia</term>; however, in some places, it is like the *Itam Lime* <note>original: *Limonii Itam*; the Black Lime</note>, which bears a trunk as thick as a man. The common ones, however, are no thicker than a leg, and their trunk is not round but angular and furrowed with pits like the Lime trees. Their wood is also hard, solid, and yellowish, becoming more yellow in the lower part of the trunk and the roots. The bark is smooth, thin, and ash-colored, adhering so firmly to the wood that it cannot be stripped off. On the roots, however, it is thin and reddish, covered and variegated with many thin circles.

The branches are divided into smaller, firm side-twigs which support the leaves. These always stand in opposite pairs, and with the subsequent pair they form a cross <term>decussate: leaves arranged in pairs at right angles to the pair above or below</term>, as in the Nipis Lime. But they are shorter and lack the little "ear" <note>original: *cordata* / *oortje*; referring to the winged petiole common in citrus</note> at the base; they are two inches long and one wide, with a blunt tip and smooth or entire edges. At the leaf-stalk, three veins run together, just as in the true *Vidara*. On both sides, the leaves are green and firm, though the lower ones are smaller and mostly...

<meta>The catchword "con-" in Latin and "en" in Dutch both point to the continuation of the word "continually" or "and" on the following page.</meta>

<column-break/>

to break the branches without iron: The other sort, which does not have many thorns and bears fewer fruits, is not as good, nor as bitter.

There is also a superstitious little trick, held as a secret by the Inlander, to learn to recognize the *Swangis* or Sorcerers. They take the root of the best or thorny sort, rub it with water and a little lime, and give this to the suspected persons to drink or to eat in Pinang <note>betel nut</note>. If they feel poorly from it, they are held to be *Swangis*. On the contrary, the same root rubbed in water is a remedy when someone believes they are enchanted.

### The Thirty-Seventh Plate

Shows a branch of the Shore Jujube, which is called *Vidara Littorea* by Rumphius.

This corresponds with the Indian thorny Jujuba, with longer leaf and fruits, as it is named by Plukenet in his *Almagestum*, page 199, and by Ray in the third part of the *Dendrologia*, page 44. This is the *Prunus Zeylanica, spinosa, longiore folio* of Herman in his *Paradisus Batavus*, page 367, and the *Prunus Zeylanica, spinosa, longiore folio viridi, fructus officulo orbiculari scrobiculis referto* of Plukenet in his *Phytographia*, Plate 216, Figure 6, which differs from the preceding by its rough leaves and its irregular seed- <insert>-</insert> kernels <note>The Dutch text "Zaa-ern" is likely a typo for "Zaden" or "Zaa-kern" (seed-kernels)</note>. For other sorts and variations of this, see my *Thesaurus Zeylanicus*, pages 131 and 132.

These two trees were described under the names of *Bidara-tree* and *Shore-Bidara* by Valentyn, page 191.

# XLVI. CHAPTER.

## Snakewood.

**O**ne finds in the East Indies various woods of that name, as in Garcia, book 1, *Aromatics*, chapter 44, three sorts, all growing on Ceylon. Also three sorts in Cristóvão da Costa, chapter 33, with yet some others that Carolus Clusius adds in his notes on the same chapters: all differing from one another, and of which I have not yet been able to find any in these Eastern regions. I shall therefore in their place describe here only that which is used nowadays as the one and only true Snakewood, or is most well-known by that name, not occurring or growing on Ceylon, nor in Amboina: but on Rote, Timor, and the nearby islands. From there, the branches with their leaves, fruits, and blocks of wood have come to me through the help and favorable care of Mr. Antoni Hurdt, Ordinary Councilor of the Indies, and Jacob van Wyckerloot, Chief on Timor (as mentioned above in the Chapter on Sandalwood); and according to which the adjacent figure was prepared.

This tree is commonly as high and thick as a Nipis Lime tree, though in some places as an Itam Lime, namely with a trunk as thick as a man, where the common ones are no more than a leg thick; not round, but angular, and with pits like the Lime tree, having also a similar hard, firm, and pale-yellow wood, which on the lower trunk and the roots is pulling somewhat more towards yellow. The bark is smooth, thin, and gray, and lying so tightly to the wood that one cannot peel it off there; furthermore, on the roots it is thin and reddish, surrounded or encircled by many fine circles.

The branches divide themselves again into stiff side-twigs, where the leaves stand, two and two opposite one another, being in a slanted cross, like those of the Nipis Lime, or perhaps somewhat shorter, and without the little "ear," two inches long and one wide, with a blunt point and smooth edges. Near the stalk, three veins run together, like those of the true Vidara, green and stiff on both sides, but the hindmost are even smaller, and...

they match those of the *Coastal Jujube* <note>original: *Vidara Littorea*</note>; furthermore all the twigs are hard, covered everywhere with leaves without any thorns, just as the whole tree is mild.

The flowers, perhaps due to their similarity, sprout from the axils of the leaves and branches, and without doubt do not differ much from the flowers of the *Jujube* <note>original: *Vidara*</note>, since the fruits grow in the same manner, emerging two, three, and at most four together, sitting erect on very short stalks. They resemble the form of little apples, some perfectly spherical, others truly oblong like the *Jujube*, and of the same size. All are smooth, yet complete, but marked with small dots like a little Lemon <note>original: *Limonelli*</note>, and equipped at the top with a short and hard point. The color of the younger fruits is green, while the older ones are a dark yellow, and gradually become dusky and dark. Under the outer rind a moist pith is hidden, which in the ripe ones is mostly dried up; in this are one, two, or three seed-stones, of which the solitary ones are flat like a coin but thicker, while others are sinuous and set opposite one another. All are covered with a soft and ashy down like silk <note>original: *instar serici*</note>; their internal substance is white and tough like the seeds of Lemons, which can be divided into two segments. All parts of the tree give a bitter taste, approaching lemon seeds more than Wormwood <note>original: *Absynthio*</note>. The greatest bitterness appears in the fruits and roots, especially in their bark, then in the lower part of the trunk, and finally in the leaves.

The roots, which are no thicker than a child’s arm, are considered the best; on them appear warts like blunt thorns, which are properly the ends or traces of the fibers or smaller roots that have been cut off from the larger root.

Nature seemingly wished to demonstrate which was the best part of this tree, and above all else created the roots, which creep very widely under the earth, and from a small piece of them remaining in the ground, a tree similar to the first eventually grows. These roots are cut into pieces a foot or a cubit <note>original: *ulna*</note> in length, and such are sent to foreign shores; their bark must not be removed, as the greatest bitterness resides within it.

**Name.** In Latin *Lignum Colubrinum* <note>Snake wood</note>, and for distinction from others, *Timorense* <note>from Timor</note>; in Dutch *Slangen-hout*: in Malay *Caju Ular*, which name, I think, it received from the Ceylonese wood, with which this Timorese wood agrees in bitterness, color, and the circles seen in the thin roots, which in some way represent the belly of a snake. In Timor and Rote it is properly called *Caju Nassi*: the Portuguese call it *Pao de Cobra*, like the Ceylonese variety.

**Location.** This tree is wild and grows equally in flat fields and on the forward parts of mountains on the island of *Rotthe* <note>Rote Island</note>, which is considered the best wood, then the Timorese, then the Wetterese (which our people call Etter), then the Lethense, and it is further found in the neighboring islands.

**Usage.** By the people of Rote and Timor, this wood was previously held in no esteem, just as even today it is scarcely valued by them. They are mostly accustomed to use it to make their *Towack* <note>palm wine</note> bitter, in the same way that *Saguer* <note>palm wine</note> is prepared here in Ambon with another root. Its common use is against quartan fevers <note>original: *quartanas*; a form of malaria</note>, if after the shivering a cupful is drunk—that is, if such a quantity is ground upon a porphyry stone with water until it is cloudy, and then the person settles into bed to sweat. In the same way, but made into a thinner emulsion, it is taken to strengthen the stomach and to consume its mucus, which hinders digestion. Some also mix it with *Cajoe tay* <note>literally "foul wood" or Stinkwood</note> when they administer it against fevers. Both give an unpleasant taste and smell, which is easily overcome if a draft of pure water is drunk afterward or the mouth is rinsed. *Cajoe tay* is added because it easily provokes sweat and extinguishes the heat. From the thickest pieces, some turn drinking cups, which they keep curiously and religiously, thinking they have a ready remedy if they drink from these during a time of fever; however, I consider this a useless waste of this good wood, since they do not properly hold water, and it must infuse for half a day before it becomes bitter; moreover, if used three or four times for this purpose and—
