and they more closely resemble those of the *Coastal Jujube* <note>original: *Vidara Littorea*</note>, all the twigs being hard, densely set with leaves, and without any thorns, as is the whole tree.

The flowers will likely, because of their form, come forth from the lap of the leaves and side-branches, and apparently do not differ much from the *Jujube’s* <note>original: *Vidaras*</note> blossoms; for the fruits grow in that same manner, two, three, and at most four together, on stiff and very short stalks, mostly standing upright. These are like small Apples, some perfectly round like a ball, and others somewhat oblong like the *Jujube's*, some also as large, yet all complete, smooth, and on the outside with small pimples like Lemons, and on top with a short and hard little point. The color of the young fruits is green, and of the old ones dark yellow, also in time smoky-colored and somewhat brown. Under the outermost shell lies a moist pith (which in the ripe ones mostly dries up) and therein one, two, and three seeds, of which the single ones are flat like a penny, though somewhat thicker, and the others curved and standing against or across from each other. All are covered with a soft and gray down like Satin, and inside with a white and tough substance like Lemon seeds, which can also be split in two. Everything on the entire tree has a bitter taste, closer to Lemon seeds than to Wormwood <note>original: *Alsem*</note>, but the most bitterness is tasted in the fruits and roots, and especially in their bark, thereafter in the lower trunk, and finally in the leaves.

The roots, which are no thicker than a child's arm, are held to be the best, and one sees on them some warts like blunt thorns, being properly the ends of the hairy fibers or small roots that have been cut off from the large roots.

Nature has also wished to show which is the best part of this tree, having created the roots for this purpose above or before other parts, for they shoot very wide and broad under the earth, and from a small piece that is left in the earth or remains lying there, a tree grows again over time with its root, like the previous one. These roots are chopped into pieces of a foot or an ell <note>approximately 27 inches</note> and so sent to foreign places, and one must never take off the bark because the most bitterness sticks therein.

**Name.** In Latin *Lignum Colubrinum*, and to distinguish it from others *Timorense*: in Dutch *Slangen-hout*. In Malay *Caju-Ular*, having received this name, so I guess, after the Snake-woods of Ceylon, with which the Timorese agrees in bitterness, color, and the circles seen on the thin roots (which somewhat represent the belly of a snake). On Timor and Rote it is properly called *Caju Nassi*. The Portuguese call it *Pao de Cobra*, like the Ceylonese.

**Location.** This tree grows in the wild, both on flat fields and in the front of the mountains, on the Island of *Rotthe*, which is also held for the best, thereafter on Timor, Wetter (called *Etter* by our people), Lethi, and the Great Land, as well as the islands lying nearby.

**Usage.** By the Rotinese and Timorese this wood was previously held in no esteem, just as it still is not; for they are accustomed to use it mostly to make their *Towack* bitter, in such a manner as one in Ambon made the *Saguer* bitter with another root. Its ordinary use is against the tertian fever, when one takes a tea-cup full after the cleansing thereof—to wit, so much rubbed on a stone with water that the water becomes just cloudy from it, and upon that one goes to sweat. In the same way, but prepared a bit thinner, one also takes it in to strengthen the stomach and to consume the sliminess that sits therein. Some also mix it with *Cajoe Tay* when they want to give it against the fever; both making a vile smell and taste, which however is easily overcome if one drinks a sip or draft of pure water upon it and rinses out the mouth. The *Cajoe tay* is used with it because it causes sweating and diminishes the heat. From the thickest pieces some let little cups be turned, and hold these for a great rarity, as if they then have a ready remedy to drink from in fevers; but I hold that for a useless waste of the good wood, for it not only holds water poorly, but it must also stand therein for half a day before it becomes bitter,

# Book II. Chapter XLVI. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...of a pale yellowish color. In Batavia, some people mix it into weak Arrack <term>Arrack: a distilled spirit common in South and Southeast Asia</term>, distilling it again with the wood, and use it as a daily dram instead of Wormwood wine <note>original: *vini Absynthitii*</note> to strengthen the stomach. With a couple of spoonfuls of these shavings or sawdust, one can also make a jug of white wine bitter, though it is not as pleasant as that made with an extract of Wormwood. Our nation [the Dutch] also brought this wood to Japan for sale; at first, it was held in great esteem and sold for a very high price. But when greed led followers to bring it there in great quantities, it became despised and was regarded as mere firewood. This is the way of the Japanese: to value nothing highly unless it is brought rarely or only in small amounts.

This wood is also credited with the power to expel all kinds of abdominal worms and to powerfully resist the bites of venomous animals. Those who desire further instruction on the Snakewood of Ceylon <note>original: *Lignum Colubrinum*</note> we refer to Garcia de Orta, Book 1, Chapter 44; Cristobal Acosta, Chapter 33; and among the newer writers, the History of Ceylon by Philippus Baldaeus, Book 2, Chapter 49, where he calls it *Nay-Lelli* in the Sinhalese language <note>original: *Cinghalensium lingua*</note>. One may also look to the writings of Dr. Paul Hermann, who calls his specimen *Ebaweya* in Sinhalese and considers it an Indian Clematis <note>original: *Clematis Indica*</note> with leaves like a Peach tree and fruits like Honeysuckle <note>original: *Caprifolium*</note>. He considers it the first kind of Snakewood described by Garcia, though he believes Garcia wrongly named it *Cametul* (even though his copy mistakenly reads *Rametul*). Conversely, he says that *Cametul* is a root that is sweet at first taste but also sharp and biting on the tongue, and when placed on the skin, it draws blisters; the Sinhalese place it, crushed, upon the bites of vipers.

Now we must still investigate what *Accar Luffa Radja*—that is, the "Root of the King's Island"—might be. Regarding this, one should know that it has the thickness of a pinky finger, is also yellowish, and only slightly bitter. it comes from a small tree that grows on the island of *Luffa Radja*, or more properly *Nuffa Radja*, meaning "King's Island," so named because seven kings live upon it. It is situated on the north side of the Great Island <note>likely Flores or a neighboring large island</note> and is inhabited by a treacherous and wicked people, with whom the Portuguese of Larantuka nevertheless trade, and from whom these roots must be obtained. They are praised against all types of swallowed poison, which they expel through vomiting. Just as it is said that the powers of Snakewood on Ceylon were discovered by the little animal *Quir* or *Quilpele* <note>The mongoose, known for its immunity to snake venom</note>, they say the powers of these roots (which they name after the island of Luffa Radja) were discovered by chance by certain fishermen. They had strung their fish together using small cords made from the long, thin twigs of this tree and found that, contrary to the nature of other caught fish, they remained alive for a very long time. From this, they concluded that a life-giving or life-preserving power must reside in that wood. Two kinds of these roots were shown to me: one coming from the aforementioned island of Luffa Radja, which is thin and pale yellow; the second is thicker and a deeper yellow, found on Timor. Both are reasonably bitter, but in no way to be compared with Snakewood.

AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chapter XLVII.

<column-break/>

# OBSERVATION.

It is clear from various authors besides our own that several trees are found in India which bear what is commonly called **Snakewood** <note>original: *Lignum Colubrinum*</note>. The primary sources to be consulted on this matter are **Caspar Commelin** in his *Flora Malabarica*, page 63; **Jakob Breyne** in his *Prodromus 2*, pages 97 and 98; **Samuel Dale** in his *Pharmacology*, pages 357 and 358; **Paul Hermann** in his *Paradisus Batavus Prodromus*, page 357, and many others whom I have collected in the *Thesaurus Zeylanicus*, pages 141 and 171. These authors have proposed various species and trees of this wood, among which the most excellent are the **CANIRAM** (described in the *Hortus Malabaricus*, Volume 1, Plate 37), the **TSJERU KATU-VALLI-CANIRAM** (Volume 7, Plate 5), and the **MODIRA-CANIRAM** (Volume 8, Plate 24). However, it is not easy to determine which of these trees is the genuine species that bears that famous, yet at the same time highly suspect wood. **Samuel Dale** felt that the *Modira Caniram* was the true Snakewood; **Breyne**, in his second *Prodromus*, reckons the *Caniram* from Volume 1 and the figure in Volume 7 to be this type, which also most closely approaches the figure provided by **Rumphius**, as does the one shown in Plate 5, Figure 2 of the new edition of Breyne. The illustrious **Hermann**, in the first part of his *Materia Medica*, Chapter 3, testifies that it is the woody root of a Timorese tree whose fruits are the larger **Vomit-Nuts** <term>Vomit-Nuts: *Nuces Vomicæ*, the seeds of the *Strychnos nux-vomica* tree, which contain strychnine and were used historically in small doses as a stimulant or emetic</term> of the apothecaries. This is undoubtedly the same tree described by our author, as it occurs most frequently in Timor. In **Ray**, Volume 3 of his *Dendrology*, page 169, a Snakewood called **Marungai** is described, to which extraordinary medical virtues are attributed; in his *Appendix*, page 88, two other species of Snakewood are listed among the poisonous trees. Thus, it is no wonder that in former times many conjectures were brought forward and debated concerning these trees, as can be seen especially in **Caspar Bauhin’s** *Pinax*, Book 12, Section 6, and in **Johann Bauhin**, Volume 1, Book 3, page 179. Snakewood is also described in **Linschoten’s** *Itinerary*, page 95.

<column-break/>

# ANNOTATION.

That there are several trees found in the Indies that produce **Snakewood** <note>original: *Slangen-hout*</note> is evident from many other witnesses than those cited by our author. The most important to consult on this matter are the following: **Caspar Commelin** in his *Flora Malabarica*, p. 63; **Breyne** in his second *Prodromus*, p. 97 and 98; **Dale** in his *Pharmacology*, p. 357 and 358; **Hermann** in the *Paradisus Batavus Prodromus*, p. 357, and others whom I have cited in my *Thesaurus Zeylanicus*, p. 141 and 171. They have presented various sorts and trees of this, among which the **CANIRAM** of the *Hortus Malabaricus* in the first part, Plate 37; the **Tsjeru Katu-Valli Caniram** in the seventh part, Plate 5; and the **Modira-Caniram** in the eighth part, Plate 24, stand out above the rest. Yet which of these trees is the upright sort that gives the true, famous, yet also very suspect Snakewood is not easy to determine. **Samuel Dale** holds the *Modira Caniram* for it. **Breyne** includes the *Caniram* from the first part and that which is depicted in the seventh part on Plate 7, which also best corresponds with the figure of **Rumphius**, as well as that which is shown in the new edition of Breyne on the fifth plate, Figure 2. The famous **Hermann**, in the first part, chapter 3, of his *Materia Medica*, testifies that it is a woody root of a Timorese tree, whose fruits are the **Large Vomit-Nuts**, or the "Large Crane-Eyes" <note>original: *groote kraan-oogen*</note> of the druggists. This is also without doubt the same tree described by our author, since it is found most often on Timor. In the third part of **Ray’s** *Dendrology*, p. 169, a Snakewood named **Marungai** is described, to which many excellent medicinal powers are attributed, and in his *Appendix* on p. 88, two other sorts of Snakewood are counted among the poisonous trees. So it is not to be wondered at that in previous days many guesses about these trees and this wood have been brought forward and appeared, as can be seen primarily in **Caspar Bauhin** in his *Pinax*, book 12, sect. 6, and in **Johann Bauhin** in his first part, third book, page 179. Snakewood is also described in **Linschoten’s** *Voyages*, page 95.

# CHAPTER FORTY-SEVEN.

->Root of the Mother of God. *Rais Madre de Deos.*<-

This small tree is also to be numbered among the species of **Vidara** <note>original: *Vidara* usually refers to the Indian Jujube (*Ziziphus mauritiana*)</note>. It grows in many places in India, but as far as I know, it is not used in the medical arts except around Malacca, where it has been celebrated by the Portuguese since ancient times, and its root is sold throughout India as a precious medicine. Until now, I have found no mention of it in any writings, but around the year 1654, it began to become known to me from the oral account of the Noble Lord **Arnold de Vlaming van Outshoorn**, then our Commander and Admiral, who had previously been Governor of Malacca. From there, I finally received it twenty-four years later, and perceiving from its form that a false species <note>original: *spuriam* / *bastaart*</note> of it also grows on our neighboring Celebes, I decided to incorporate and set down its description here as well.

The tree has the height and thickness of a **Key Lime** <term>Key Lime: *Lemoen Nipis*</term> or a *Vidara* tree, and it is also held and named by the Portuguese as a wild species of *Vidara*. For the most part, it is so low and gnarled that it resembles a shrub more than a small tree. All its branches are beset on all sides with horrific, long, and firm thorns, appearing in opposite pairs, with four forming a cross, just like in the **Buckthorn** <note>original: *Rhamnus*</note>—to which genus this also belongs. These thorns painfully injure the unwary and cause the stung limb to swell up. From the crotches of the thorns, the leaves also sprout crosswise, opposite each other, though they are solitary on the lower part of the branches. On the upper part, one or two small leaves peek out from the larger shoots, very closely resembling the leaves of the **Shore Vidara** <note>original: *Vidara Littorea*</note>, though a bit smaller. The largest of these are two finger-widths long and one thumb-breadth wide, firm, not serrated at the edges, somewhat grayish and woolly underneath, and with a taste like fat or grease. On the thorns themselves, one also finds such small leaves,

II Book. XLVII. Chapter. AMBOINESE HERBAL. 125

...but much smaller, namely like a fingernail; the branches divide themselves into smaller, firm, and crossed twigs. The flowers are small, yellowish, and woolly, like those of the **Sea Vidara** <note>original: *Vidara Laut*, likely a species of *Ziziphus* or *Strychnos*</note>. The fruits are also like those of the same Vidara, but smaller, like half-grown olives, blunt at the top and narrow at the bottom, sitting in a small four-cleft, narrow cup; they are placed singly, or in twos or threes together, first green, then gray-yellow, and are useless for eating. They contain a hard stone, though not as wrinkled as that of the Vidara. The wood is pale, fairly hard, and filled inside with a small spongy heart or pith, though the lower part of the trunk and the roots are solid.

Its roots are very long, extending themselves horizontally but not deep under the earth, mostly having the thickness of a finger or thumb; they are dark gray on the outside and yellowish on the inside like **Liquorice** <note>original: *Liqueritia*</note>, but when cut they become more yellow at the edges, much like **Rhubarb** <note>original: *Rhabarbarum*</note>. The taste of the fresh roots is slightly bitter with a mild astringency that quickly vanishes, leaving behind a pleasant aromatic sweetness, especially in the bark, which is entirely like **Pulesari** <note>An aromatic bark from *Alyxia stellata*, often used in traditional Indonesian medicine and cooking</note> mixed with **Anise**. At least, such I observed in the roots sent to me by the Pastor **Theodorus Sas** and the Malaccan citizen **Reinier Bronken**; therefore, I cannot understand why they are considered bitter by others, unless they perhaps refer to the slight bitterness noted above, which might be more prevalent in the fresh roots.

The Portuguese, as the former possessors of **Malacca**, have passed down to us—and it is still accepted by our nation there—that there is a great distinction among the roots of this tree. Indeed, it is claimed that those which grow toward the North are a precious medicine and even an antidote; on the contrary, those which grow toward the South are harmful, even poisonous; while those pointing East and West are considered to have no power at all. This would indeed be an unfathomable masterpiece of nature, if the investigation and testing of it does not prove false. However, the aforementioned Dutch citizen and elder of that city assured me with great solemnity and conviction that this had been duly investigated and sufficiently proven there.

Yet this miracle of nature was observed in no other place except near the city of Malacca, and even there not everywhere, but only in those small trees growing on and around the little hill of **St. Francis**, or **Bukit China** <note>original: *Boukit 't Sina*; a historic hill in Malacca with significant Chinese heritage</note>, located a quarter-hour outside the city, where formerly the Chinese lived, or the descendants of their famous Admiral **Sampo** <note>The legendary Chinese Admiral Zheng He, also known as Sam Po Kong</note>.

I wish to advise lovers and seekers of nature to investigate this secret of nature more closely: specifically, whether (setting aside Chinese and Roman Catholic superstitions) this wonderful distinction is to be ascribed to the specific nature of that land, or if it might occur in all other places. For until now, it has not been investigated or confirmed by any other nations in their own lands where it nevertheless grows.

<margin>*</margin>
**Name.** In Latin *Vidara Agrestis*, according to the Portuguese *Macana de Mato*, which means "Wild Vidara." The medicinal root lying on the northern side is called by the Portuguese by the specific name *Rais Madre de Deos*, which is in Latin **Radix Deiparae** (Root of the Mother of God). This name was given to it because of its excellent virtues, or because these roots were annually dug up by the Portuguese on the feast day of **Mary’s Candlemas** <note>original: *Maria Ligt-mis*; February 2nd</note>. Today, however, they are dug throughout the year, though it is better and more suitable to do so in the dry monsoon. Furthermore, the entire plant is called *Bulangan* by the Malays; on Java and Bali it is called *Bangyan*, though upon closer inquiry I find *Bangyan* to be another thorny shrub; on Celebes it is called *Lowara*, and in Javanese *Warren*.

**Place.** The best root, as mentioned, grows around Malacca, specifically the one used for medicine. It grows as well on other islands, though its medicinal use is unknown there, such as on Sumatra, Java, Bali, and Celebes, and especially on its eastern side in the kingdom of **Tambucco**. The **Bugis** people say that this tree is also abundant in their homeland, likewise bearing the name *Lowara*, but I believe it differs from the former; for that of the Bugis grows into a large tree with larger leaves, hard wood, and somewhat edible fruits.

### AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II, Chapter 47. 126

*Uses.* Since these trees and roots do not grow in Amboina, nor are they in use here, I shall present here what was reported to me regarding their qualities and powers by Mr. Theodore Zas and Regnerus Bronken, as I shall insert here from the latter’s letters sent to me on October 15, 1678.

Those who desire to dig up these roots take with them iron bars and a magnetic needle <note>a compass</note>; the bars are used because the soil is so stony that it cannot be dug with a spade, and because these roots would be too greatly damaged; when they have reached the point where the roots appear, then the magnetic needle is called into use, and it is carefully observed so that those roots which face the Northern quarter are extracted, which are the true roots of the *Root of the Mother of God* <note>original: *Rais Madre de Deos*</note>. Those which are situated toward the South are left behind and not dug up, as they are a most wicked poison, directly opposite to the Northern ones, and they have no name. Those which grow to the East and West have no virtues; however, the closer they are to the Arctic pole, the more they participate in the powers of the northern quarter, and the same holds true for those near the Southern pole.

This *Root of the Mother of God* is held in great esteem by the Portuguese, and every year a great quantity is transported from here to Goa, and it is used in the following manner.

First. If anyone is infected with poison, this root, ground with water upon a porphyry stone <note>a hard volcanic rock used for grinding medicine</note>, is offered to drink, and it is an excellent antidote; but if it does not work sufficiently, this ground root should be placed in a bronze pan and mixed with the white of a duck egg, and then taken, it will provide a better effect.

Second. If someone is bitten or stung by a venomous serpent, centipede, scorpion, or similar venomous animal or fish, this root is to be ground with lemon juice; a portion of this should be drunk, and another portion smeared on the wound, which has been proven effective. It does not matter what the dose is, as it does not cause harm: the root is somewhat bitter; if the dose is a handful <note>original: *pugillum*</note>, it is enough, though a larger dose suits one person more than another, as the time and circumstances require.

Third. This root is also suitable in fevers, ground upon a porphyry stone and consumed.
Fourth. Against diarrhea, and indeed dysentery, likewise offered with water.
Fifth. Against a severe headache <note>original: *Cephalæam*</note>, ground with lemons and smeared on both temples of the head, as well as the forehead.

Sixth. Against a sore throat <note>original: *Anginam*</note>, swallowed with water, and the neck should also be smeared with it.
Seventh. Against wounds, ground with lemons and placed upon them.
Eighth. For a polyp of the nose or a recent cancer therein, or in whatever part it may be, ground with lemons and smeared on the evil, taken both externally and internally.

Ninth. If someone suffers from a skin-rash <note>original: *inpetigine*</note>, called *Hairy Worm* <note>original: *Bicho Cabeludin*</note> by the Portuguese, which creeps through the skin; if this root is ground with lemons upon a porphyry stone and smeared on the affected part, it removes it most effectively and inhibits its further spreading.

The fruits of this tree are excellent for washing the head for those troubled by dandruff <note>original: *porrigine*</note>, which then falls away; however, they should not be taken internally, as they are unhealthy. Thus far *Regnerus Bronken*.

In Java there is also a common shrub, but neither the root nor the fruit is of any use there, and it is called *Waren* <note>a Javanese name for various shrubs</note> there. I have also observed the flower of the true Malaccan tree to agree with other wild species, namely in the width of the calyx; the flower consists of one larger and three smaller petals, the largest of which projects like a lion’s mouth, intense yellow with three reflexed filaments on the inner part.

The leaves also do not differ much in form or size from the wild variety, for some are angular,

*Uses.* Because these roots do not grow in Amboina, and therefore are not in use here, I must make do with what has been written to me by the aforementioned gentlemen *Theodorus Zas* and *Reinier Bronken* regarding their properties and power, just as I shall incorporate it here from the latter's letter of October 15, 1678, in his own words.

Those who want to dig these roots take their iron *crowbars* <note>original: *Koevoeten*</note> and a *compass*; the crowbars are because it is a very stony ground that cannot be entered with shovels, and also because one would damage the mentioned root too much with shovels; having come so deep that one can see this root, it is carefully noted with the compass that one obtains the root that lies directly toward the North, which is then the true *Root of the Mother of God* <note>original: *Rais Madre de Deos*</note>. But that which lies directly in the South is never dug, because it is a very foul poison, directly contrary to those of the North, and it has no name; but those that grow in the East or West have no powers. However, the closer to the North, the more they share in the Northern powers, and so it is also with those growing closest to the South.

The mentioned *Root of the Mother of God* is in great esteem among the Portuguese, and is annually transported in large quantities from here to *Goa*, and used as follows.

*First*, when someone is poisoned with venom, this root rubbed on a stone with water and administered is a good antidote; but if that does not help, one must put this rubbed root in a copper basin and add the white of a duck egg, and beat that vigorously together in that copper-work or basin, and so taken it will be good.

*Second*, when someone is bitten or stung by a venomous snake, *centipede, scorpion*, or other venomous creatures or fish, one must rub this root with lemon juice on a stone and administer it, and smear it on the injury; this is very good. The quantity of how much one may give is not so precise, for it will do no harm: it is a bitter root, and a little, as much as may fit in 2 or 3 thimbles <note>original: *vinger-hoeden*</note>, is enough; though one person may need a bit more than the other, as the situation requires.

*Third*, for fevers this root is also good, rubbed with water on a stone and taken.
*Fourth*, for heavy bowel movements or the bloody flux <note>dysentery</note>, also taken with water.
*Fifth*, for a great headache, rubbed with lemons on a stone and smeared on both sides of the temples of the head, and also on the front.
*Sixth*, for a sore throat, rubbed with water, taken, and the neck smeared therewith.
*Seventh*, for any injuries, rubbed with lemons and placed on the wounds.
*Eight*, for a sore nose or cancer in the same, when it first begins, or in whatever places it might occur, rubbed with lemons and stroked on the sore, both outside and inside where one can reach, with a small feather.
*Ninth*, if a person is touched by the *hair-worm* <note>original: *Bicho Cabeludin*, likely referring to *Larva migrans* or a similar skin parasite</note>, which hairs remain stuck in a person's body, one must rub them with lemons on a stone and smear that on the place where it was touched, which can easily be seen against the light and pulled out.

The fruits are very good for washing the head for those who have scales <note>dandruff</note> on it, which go away because of it, but they must not enter the body, for it is an unhealthy fruit. Thus far *Reinier Bronken*.

## CHAPTER FORTY-EIGHT.

### *False Root of the Mother of God: Lowarra.*

Although a thorny shrub is found among the Javanese, Balinese, and those of Celebes <note>Sulawesi</note>, which has such a great affinity with the Malaccan shrub called the Root of the Mother of God that they give both the same name, I have nevertheless found such a difference in them that I have described each in a specific chapter, and reduced this second little tree to a species of the Root of the Mother of God. For although the resemblance between them is very great, only the Malaccan one possesses the aromatic root, which is precious and has a pleasant taste—a quality observed in no other root growing outside Malacca, nor is it used in medical practice by any other nation.

A certain citizen of Malacca, around the year 1680, brought this root and fruits from Tambucco <note>Located on the eastern side of Celebes/Sulawesi</note>, trying to persuade me that these were the Malaccan *Bulangan* <gloss>Local name for the shrub</gloss> or the true Root of the Mother of God, and did not differ from it. Therefore, I committed several of its seeds to the soil in my garden, of which only a single one sprouted. It produced a woody shrub that spread itself upward into long and switch-like branches; on these, the thorns and leaves were mostly opposite and crosswise, but the thorns were shorter and not placed so regularly, and the topmost twigs bore no thorns at all. The leaves also differed greatly from the Malaccan variety, and more closely resembled the leaves of *Oxyacantha* <note>Hawthorn</note> than the cultivated or wild *Vidara* <gloss>Jujube</gloss>. They are two inches wide and long, and on their edges they have a blunt incision on both sides, giving them a triangular shape. The older leaves, however, are not so incised, or at least not so deeply. On the upper side they are smooth and dark green, on the lower side pale, but not downy like the Malaccan *Vidara*. They grow in opposite pairs and have an unpleasant taste, whereas the Malaccan ones have a fatty taste very similar to the *Vidara*. In each leaf-axil a firm thorn is placed, upon which two or three smaller triangular leaflets appear, though they are not so regular. The aforementioned small twigs are likewise devoid of thorns.

The flowers have the shape of a little shoe or a thimble, about an inch long, and are formed from a concave petal divided into four lobes. The largest is at the top, like a concave little shoe covering the flower, and it is firm; below, three smaller lobes appear, of which two are at the sides and the third is below. All are yellow in color but without scent. In the center of the flower, five long, saffron-colored stamens appear. The flower itself narrows at the lower part and sits upon a small green head, which grows into the fruit, which is round or slightly
<meta>catchword: oval</meta>

<column-break/>

yet those from Malacca are somewhat softer, like wool, on the underside, and those of the wild ones are rougher and more veined.

On the Malaccan variety, the blossoms come in a large cluster, not all at once, but opening one after another, and all become fruits, so that as many hang together as a bunch of grapes. The wild one grows much around Batavia, named there *Massaan de Mato*, that is *Vidara Utan* <gloss>Wild Jujube</gloss>, and its use is unknown, for the fruits are not eaten as they are too foul in taste, though others hold its roots to be medicinal.

## XLVIII. CHAPTER.

### *False St. Mary's Root.*

Although one finds a thorny shrub among the Javanese, Balinese, and on Celebes, having such great resemblance to the Malaccan *Radix Deiparae* <gloss>Root of the Mother of God</gloss> that they give them both the same name, I have nonetheless found such a distinction therein that I have had to make a separate chapter for each, and consider this second sort a [type of] Root of the Mother of God. For as great as the resemblance between the two may be, one finds however that only the Malaccan has a precious, spice-like root, full of medicinal powers and of a pleasant taste, which is not to be found in any root growing outside of Malacca, nor is it used by any other nation for medicine.

A certain local citizen of Malacca brought me this root and fruits from Tambucco, situated on the east side of Celebes, around the year 1680, convincing me that they did not differ from the Malaccan *Bulangan* or Root of the Mother of God. I therefore planted several grains of it in my garden, but only one came up, producing a stalky shrub which expanded itself far and wide upwards with long and slender branches. And on these the thorns and leaves also stood somewhat opposite each other and crosswise, but the thorns were shorter and did not stand so orderly; also the foremost or first twigs had no thorns. The leaves also differed significantly from the Malaccan, resembling those of the Hawthorn better than the tame or wild *Vidara* <gloss>Jujube</gloss>, for they are two inches long and broad, having a blunt corner or flap on each side, and thereby a triangular shape. But the oldest do not have these corners, or they are less noticeable. From above they are smooth, dark green, and from below pale, but not white or woolly like those of the Malaccan *Vidara*. They are also two-by-two across from each other, unpleasant of taste, whereas the Malaccan are greasy, matching those of the *Vidara* most closely. In every leaf-axil stands a stiff thorn, and on it two or three smaller leaflets, with the following pair almost crosswise, or in place of the thorn a new side-twig. The small leaves also do not have the three corners so perfectly, and the aforementioned twigs are also almost without thorns.

The flowers that come forth are like a little shoe or thimble, about an inch long, and made of a rounded leaf, yet divided into four flaps: the largest stands on top, like a rounded little shoe covering the flower, and is stiff; underneath one sees three smaller flaps, of which two stand on the side and the third below, all yellow in color and without scent; in the middle bulb one sees five long yellow threads. The flower tapers narrowly at the back and stands on a green bud, from which the fruits come forth, being round or a little

# HERBARIUM AMBOINENSE Book II. Chap. XLVIII.

The fruit is oval, like small plums, but crowned at the top like apples. Its external color is a dark yellow, similar to ripe medlars <note>original: "Mespilorum"; the medlar is a fruit that looks like a small brown apple</note>, but the flesh inside is juicy and acidic, though unfit for eating and possessing an unpleasant odor. Hidden within is a hard, oblong stone like an olive, but possessing a long neck like a flask; it is somewhat angular, reddish, and a short point is visible on its thicker end, so that it differs greatly from the Malaccan fruit.

The wood of the trunk is hard, angular, and knotty. In older trunks, it is dark brown around the heartwood, and rarely thick or straight enough to be used for house posts. The roots are very long and straight, creeping horizontally but not deeply through the earth, generally the thickness of a finger or thumb, bearing few small fibers. They are grayish-yellow on the outside and pale like licorice <note>original: "Liqueritiæ"</note> on the inside with thin rings, but if cut, they turn reddish there; when dry, they are heavier, more solid, and harder than the Malaccan variety. I received pieces of this root from Tambucco <note>An area in eastern Sulawesi</note> eight or ten feet long and a finger thick, as straight as if they were a walking stick or a rattan <note>original: "Rottang"</note>. These had been dug up with the help of a magnetic compass <note>original: "Indicis magnetici"</note> toward the northern side, a foot deep in the red, solid earth found throughout that region. When they were unearthed, they were entirely dry, showing no moisture. The taste was initially somewhat bitter and astringent, mixed with a slight flavor of anise, and therefore not as pleasant as the Malaccan kind, but closely matching the roots of the *Vidara* <gloss>Ziziphus/Jujube</gloss>. A year later, similar long pieces of this root were brought to me, which had a foul and unpleasant taste, but the one who brought them testified that they had been splashed with seawater during the sea voyage. In these pieces, whether dug up toward the North or the South, I could observe no difference in odor or taste. Over time, however, the smell and taste became musty, and although these roots are considered similar to the Malaccan ones, they in no way approach them in strength or flavor; I judge them to be entirely devoid of potency and unfit for medical use.

**Name.** In Latin, *Radix Deiparæ Spuria* <gloss>False Root of the Mother of God</gloss>. In Javanese it is called *Warran*; in Celebes <note>Sulawesi</note> it is called *Lowarra*. These names belong specifically to these "spurious" species and are given to distinguish them from the Malaccan *Bulangan*, or the true *Root of the Mother of God*. It might also more rightly be called *Oxyacantha Indica* <gloss>Indian Hawthorn</gloss> rather than *Cudrang*, as is done in Batavia <note>Jakarta</note>; at least the leaves resemble it best, though certainly not the thorns, flowers, or fruit.

**Location.** This small tree or shrub grows in Java and Celebes, in the districts of Bugis and Luwu, as well as abundantly in Tambucco. It is unknown in Amboina. Whether it also grows in Baleya <note>Possibly the Banggai Islands</note> is not certain to me, although the people of Baleya say that such thorny trees also grow in their homeland, where they are called *Banghian*.

**Use.** This root, as far as I know, is nowhere in medical use except in Malacca; on the contrary, it is regarded as a harmful thorn, which the people greatly fear. For if anyone is wounded by these thorns, the injured part swells with great pain. For this reason, many peoples have the custom of planting live hedges of these thorny shrubs around their houses, not only for protection against wild animals but also against thieves; for even if the thieves were bold enough not to fear resisting armed men, they could not endure penetrating through these thorns.

In the Bugis region, many hedges are formed from them, either by placing young shoots in a row or, what is easier, by sowing the fruits in the earth. If these shrubs grow high, they entwine themselves very tightly at the top, but leave an opening below through which a person or a pig can crawl. These openings are then blocked with *Ligularia Lactea*, or *Daun Sudu-Sudu* <gloss>the Malayan Spurge Tree</gloss>, which is also thorny; or where that cannot be planted, they cut off thorny branches and stuff the remaining holes with them, as is otherwise done with the thorny branches of lemon trees.

The wood is reasonably durable and is used for house posts if straight pieces can be found, though in older trunks it is very hard and blackish inside. The fruits are not utilized, but in Java they are boiled and eaten; if roasted under ashes and their juice dripped into the ears, it cures deafness. From its...

<column-break/>

*...oval, like small plums, with a little crown on top, just like apples. The color is dark yellow on the outside, like that of ripe medlars, and on the inside is a juicy and greasy flesh, yet unfit to eat, and foul of smell; and therein lies an oblong hard stone, like an olive stone, but with a long neck, like a flask, a little angular, high reddish-pink, and with a short point at the thickest end, so that they differ much from the Malaccan fruits.*

*The wood of the trunk is hard, crooked, and tangled; on the old trunks near the heart it is dark brown, and seldom so thick or straight that one can have posts for houses from it. The roots are also very long and straight across, yet not creeping deep into the earth, uniform in thickness, about a thumb or finger, with few fibers on them, grayish-yellow on the outside, and pale yellow on the inside like licorice, with some thin circles, though turning reddish on the cut; also heavier, denser, and harder than the Malaccan. I have received pieces of this root from Tambucco that were 8 and 10 feet long, a finger thick, and as straight as a stretched rattan, being dug with a compass on the Northern point, about a foot deep out of a red and firm earth, such as one has in that whole region. It was dry upon digging, and gave off no moisture at all. The taste was at first somewhat bitter, astringent, with a small aftertaste of anise, and therefore not as lovely as the Malaccan, but more closely resembling the roots of Vidara. A year after that, similar long pieces of the same roots were brought to me, but which were very foul and dirty of taste. But the bearer declared that they had been splashed with seawater along the way; and I have been able to notice or perceive no difference, neither in smell nor in taste, among the pieces that were dug up either to the North or to the South. In time they all got a musty smell and taste. And they may be as similar to the Malaccan as they want, I judge them to differ much in virtue and taste, and unusable in medicine.*

**Name.** *In Latin, Radix Deiparæ Spuria. In Javanese, Warran. In Celebes, Lowarra, which names more properly belong to these bastard sorts, and may be given to them rather than the Malaccan Bulangan, or the upright Root of the Mother of God. One might also more fairly call it East Indian Hawthorn than Cudrang, as happens in Batavia; indeed the leaves look most like it, but not the thorns, flowers, nor fruits.*

**Place.** *This tree or shrub grows on Java, and also on Celebes, in the Bugis and Luwu territory, as well as much in the territory of Tambucco. In Amboina it is unknown; whether it also grows on Baley, I cannot well know, although the Baleyers say that they have similar thorns in their land and call the same Banghian.*

**Use.** *This root, for as much as is known to me, has no use in medicine among any nation outside of Malacca, but is on the contrary held for a harmful thorn, of which they are very afraid. For if someone hurts themselves on these thorns, it swells up with great pain, and therefore many nations have a custom to make living hedges or fences of these thorns around their houses and yards, not only for protection from beasts, but also for thieves, who, though they were so bold that they dared press through even armed men, yet before these thorns they must remain standing.*

*In the land of Bugis they also make many hedges of it, planting the young sprouts in a row, or what is even easier, sowing the fruits; and these shrubs shooting up somewhat high, tangle themselves together quite tightly at the top, but leave some opening below through which a human or pig can crawl, and which holes are then also planted shut with Ligularia Lactea, or Daun Sudu-Sudu, which is also thorny, or where one cannot plant it, they chop off the thorny branches and stick the other fences <note>original: "paggers"</note> with them, as one otherwise also does with lemon-thorns.*

*The wood is reasonably durable and is used for posts of houses, if one can get straight pieces of it, but on the old trunks it is very hard and blackish on the inside. The fruits are not usable, yet on Java they are still boiled and eaten; and being roasted under the ashes, and the juice thereof in the ears...*

## CHAPTER FORTY-NINE.
### King of Bitterness. Caju Soulamoe.

While we are engaged in the description of bitter plants that are effective against poisons, there follows in order the Amboinese King of Bitterness <note>original: "Rex Amaroris"</note>, which in our judgment is no less in virtue or strength than any of the preceding. It is sometimes a shrub and sometimes a tree, depending on where it is located; for if it grows by the shore in open places, it mostly remains a shrub, but growing further landward and sprouting under the shade of other trees, it becomes a tree with a curved and leaning trunk, whose bark is smooth or covered with small warts, of a gray or whitish color, yellowish on the inside, dry and brittle, though on the small branches it is whiter and smoother.

The branches are few and brittle, and upon them the leaves are placed in an irregular order, being huge and long, of common shape—namely twelve or thirteen inches <note>original: "pollices"</note> long and three and a half wide—broad at the top, ending in a blunt point, and so similar to the leaves of the *Goelong Tsjoetsjoe* <note>original: "Goelong Tsjoetsjoe"; likely a species of Plumeria or Tabernaemontana known for milky sap</note> that they can hardly be distinguished, except for the milky sap which is abundant in the latter but is not found in the Soulamoe. These leaves are also flimsier than others, soft to the touch, interwoven with many parallel ribs that protrude underneath, which end in arches near the edges. From the armpits <note>original: "alis"; the junction between leaf and stem</note> of these leaves, short stalks sprout, from which the clusters of flowers emerge; these are very small flowers, somewhat similar to grapevine flowers, consisting of small whitish and barely visible petals, bearing in their center a green scale <note>original: "germen" / "schubbetje"</note> from which the fruit comes. This grows to the size of a *stuiver* <note>a small Dutch coin about 2cm wide</note> or slightly more, being otherwise flat, thin at the edges, and raised in the center, reflecting the shape of a little heart; however, in place of the cleft, it shows a semi-round arch, with the apex connected to the stalk. It is a pale green color, and the fruit is entirely dry and divided by a seam into two segments, in which two white little stones <note>original: "officula" / "korrels"</note> are found, resembling cucumber seeds but smaller and slenderer, each hidden in a particular cell. Over time they indeed become wrinkled and decayed. These fruits hang from the tree for a long time and eventually turn smoky-colored, but those that fall to the ground turn tawny and often sprout new little trees here and there.

The roots are thick, few, and not long, almost without fibers. On the outside, they are covered with a yellow and dry bark, and inside they have a yellowish or pale-white wood, which becomes very light when dry. When fresh, it smells somewhat like the *Scented Nail* <note>original: "Unguis Odorati"; also known as Onycha, an aromatic operculum of a sea snail used in incense</note>; indeed, some dry pieces still do this if they are rubbed upon a stone. The entire plant is very dry in all its parts and, furthermore, exceedingly bitter, especially the fruit.

<column-break/>

[If oil is] dropped [into the ears], it heals deafness. From the wood, one makes yokes for the oxen in Java and other places, with which they plow.

This shrub is properly called *Baly Banghian* on Bali, being a nasty and poor-quality thorn-forest, because its thorns burn very fiercely if one is wounded by them. One also finds two kinds there, the large-leaved and the small-leaved, but both are of poor quality and grow wild.

## XLIX. CHAPTER.
### The Heart-fruit Tree.

Since we are now busy with the bitter plants that can serve against poison, we shall also introduce or bring forward our *Amboinese King of Bitterness*, which in our judgment needs to yield to none of the preceding in either virtue or power. It is sometimes a shrub and sometimes also a tree, according to where it stands; for when it grows out on the beach in an open place, it mostly remains a shrub, but coming forth a little landward and under the shadow of other trees, then it becomes a small tree with a bent and overhanging trunk, whose bark is smooth or set with small warts, of a light gray or whitish color, yellow towards the inside, dry and crumbly, though on the twigs it is somewhat whiter and smoother.

The branches are few and brittle, and around them stand the leaves without order, being large and long, of common appearance, namely 12 and 13 inches long, 3 1/2 wide, with a blunt point at the front, and so like the leaves of the flowers of the *Goelong Tsjoetsjoe* that one can hardly distinguish them, except in the milky sap, which is abundant in the latter, but is not in those of the Soulamoe. And these leaves are also weaker than the others, soft to the touch, threaded with many parallel ribs protruding from below or underneath, closed together with arches close to the edge; and from the lap of these leaves come forth short stalks, and there the blossoms grow in small clusters, being very small flowers, somewhat like the grapevine blossom, made of small white and barely visible petals, showing in the middle a green little scale, from which the fruit comes. This grows to the size of a *stuiver* or a bit more, being furthermore flat, thin at the edges, bulging a bit in the middle, and having the shape of a little heart, though in place of the cleft showing a half-round bend, with the point standing at or fixed to the stalk, and of a pale-green color. This fruit is entirely dry and mostly divided in two with a seam, in which one finds two white grains, quite resembling the seeds of cucumbers, yet somewhat smaller, leaner, and each in a special chamber; then in time they shrink and decay; the fruit stays long hanging on the tree and at last becomes smoky, but those that fall on the earth become tawny and bring forth new little trees here or there.

The roots are thick, few, and not long, almost without filaments or fibers. Covered from the outside with a yellow and dry bark, and from the inside they have whitish or pale-yellow wood, which becomes very light when dry, and when fresh it smells somewhat like the *Scented Nail*, yes, some pieces still do that being dry, to be well understood if one rubs them on a stone. The whole growth is very dry in all its parts, and besides that, bitter beyond measure.

# AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chapter XLIX.

The fruits are the most bitter part, followed by the roots, then the bark, leaves, and wood, such that every part of this tree or shrub may be employed in medicine. This bitterness is always present in the fruits, but it fades in the roots after about ten years; nonetheless, these older roots are still beneficial for children and those of a weak constitution. This small tree is rarely encountered and grows nowhere except on desolate and rocky shores where many large, smooth, and separated boulders are found. It is a wondrous sight, and scarcely understood, from whence this little tree draws its nourishment, since it grows so exposed among the rocks. Those that are found further from the shore and grow in the earth itself have a soil consisting of crushed pebbles mixed with a small amount of red earth. It does not grow upon high cliffs, but in sloping places that are inundated by the sea. It flowers in December and bears fruit in January, as well as in other months. The fruits must be plucked from the tree while still green, or just as they begin to turn blackish or saffron-colored; for those that fall and turn pale lose their potency, or are eaten by the <term>hermit crabs<note>original: "Cancellis Limacum", literally "crabs in snail-shells"</note></term> that inhabit snail shells, which is why they are so rarely found beneath the tree.

*Nomenclature.* In Latin it is called the *King of Bitterness* <note>original: "Rex Amaroris"</note> because of its predominant bitterness. In the Malay or Amboinese language, it has no name that I know of, but it is known by the Ternate name *Soulamoe*, which means *Great Medicine* <note>original: "Pharmacum magnum"</note>, as the people of Ternate regard it as the king of all remedies. However, since they have another plant of the wild *Siri* <note>betel vine family</note> genus which they call by the same name, they usually call our tree *Soulamoe Caju* or *Soulamoe Pohon* <note>Tree Soulamoe</note>, and that wild vine *Soulamoe Tali* <note>Rope/Vine Soulamoe</note>, which we shall describe in its proper place. Others call our tree *Panawar Pipis*, or more properly *Pittis*, meaning *Coin Medicine* <note>original: "Pharmacum Nummularium"</note>, from the shape of the fruits, some of which resemble coins, especially those Chinese copper coins called *Pittis*. The fruits themselves of this *Soulamoe Caju* they call *Boahati*, which means *heart-shaped fruit*. Our Amboinese scholars call it *Oepas Poeti* <note>White Poison/Antidote</note>, as it is used against the disease called <term>choleric passion<note>In this context, a severe gastrointestinal illness or "The Oppression" of the chest</note></term>; others call it *Oebat Pamali*, as it is effective against harmful fish, crabs, etc., which the Amboinese call *Pamali*, meaning *unlucky* or *forbidden*. I have also heard some Ternatans call it *Oepas Massou*, meaning *Remedy for the Oppression*.

The Ternatans have two primary medicines: this one, which they call *Panawa Massou* or the *female Panawa*, used against cholera (the other, the *anti-choleric* described in Book 6, is called *Panawa Mas* or the *male*). They seek these on small islands where there are no pigs, for they believe pigs running over the ground and urinating defile these health-giving roots.

*Habitat.* In Amboina, as was said, it occurs rarely, and only on the shores mentioned above, such as the rocky coast of *Mamöa*, *Capaha*, and *Tiela* in the region of Hitoe; the coast of *Nuffanive* in Leytimor; the rocky *Caybobo* coast; the southern coast of *Oma*; as well as the *Lissatetto* coast in Buru; and finally in Ternate and the adjacent Moluccas, where it grows in greater abundance, though still on similar shores.

*Uses.* With many pleas and gifts, I obtained knowledge of this tree from a <term>cleric<note>original: "Æthiopum flamine", likely a local Muslim religious leader or Imam</note></term>, who showed me this tree under a vow of silence, as at that time it grew in only one place on the Hitoe coast. He performed many cures with it. Later, I learned it was in common use among the Ternatans. This cleric had noted forty virtues of this tree on a piece of paper, which he promised to share with me, but he delayed so long and continually put me off until I was forced to depart. Its primary use was against *Oepas*, by which they mean the <term>choleric passion<note>A term for severe cramps or gastrointestinal distress</note></term>, and also against <term>pleurisy<note>Inflammation of the chest lining</note></term>, both of which are dangerous and common diseases in the Indies. To the sick, they give the fruit cut into small pieces to be chewed with *Pinang* <note>betel nut</note>, and they swallow the juice. It is used in a similar way for the following diseases, but it is a difficult task, as the horrific bitterness lingers in the mouth for so long, and often causes nau-

<column-break/>

...causes nausea, which is why others prefer to grind two such fruits on a porphyry stone <note>A hard, purple-flecked stone used as a mortar for grinding medicines.</note> with water, and to give it to the sick person to drink all at once.

In every kind of fever arising from corrupt humors <note>Historical medical theory suggested diseases were caused by an imbalance of bodily fluids called "humors."</note>, these heart-shaped fruits are also called into use; previously only two or three of them were applied, but later five or seven were taken with good success. Furthermore, this medicine—namely both the fruits and the roots ground with water—is given for Colic, coughs, and especially that convulsive cough <note>original: "tussim... convulsivam"; Dutch: "kinkhoeft" (whooping cough).</note>, asthma, and all pains of the abdomen. It strengthens a weak stomach and restores a lost appetite. By its penetrating power, it resolves and opens obstructions of the intestines, and it has been used with success against other diseases as well. The locals, however, practice such an irregular method of application and confuse diseases so much that almost nothing certain can be concluded from them. They also say this medicine is so effective that while using it, there is no need for one to abstain from this or that kind of food (which the people of Ternate call *Fosso* <note>A local term for dietary restrictions or taboos observed during medical treatment.</note>), as must usually be observed in the use of other medicines. That aforementioned priest also affirmed to me that if someone took one fruit every five or seven days, they would remain immune to many diseases, especially if an epidemic disease were spreading in such a region. The root is a proven antidote against harmful fish; if anyone has eaten them incautiously, and if this medicine does not work, the patient's health is "called out" <note>original: "conclamatum est"; a Latin expression meaning all hope is lost, referring to the Roman custom of calling the name of the deceased.</note>. It is also effective against every kind of poison taken with food, for it rejects it by vomiting if it is in the stomach; otherwise, it expels it through heavy sweating and urine if it is nestled in the intestines. Its ground leaves, placed upon the abdomen, draw out watery humors, for which purpose some use its fresh bark, which they give ground with water; taken in this way, it also rejects poison by vomiting and resists it with its own strength. This same bark, boiled in water and given with a little Nutmeg, is also administered for the disease *Oepas Ajam* <note>Malay: "Chicken poison," a term for epilepsy and spasms.</note>, that is, Epilepsy and Spasms, in which case the people of Ternate use two fruits.

The leaves, boiled in water with a little Cloves, Ginger, and *Massoy* bark <note>A fragrant bark from New Guinea used in traditional medicine.</note> in a pot sealed on all sides until a third part has been consumed, serve as a steam treatment <note>original: "suffitui"; a medicinal fumigation or steam bath.</note> for those who suffer from pains and stabbings in the back or loins and have a swollen body. Indeed, this water is also given to them to drink, and the remaining boiled portion is bound to the affected parts with *Bancudu* <note>Also known as Noni or *Morinda citrifolia*.</note> leaves.

In Nusalaut and the Uliassers <note>Groups of islands in the Maluku Islands.</note>, there is a certain species of venomous snakes that have broad heads and are called *Munalatu*; likewise, the *Chalcidica* lizard, called *Pananat* in Malay, by which people are sometimes bitten. The venom of the former soon seeks the heart and causes great anxiety and burning in men, so that many die from it; however, many of them were cured by the roots of this *Soulamee* if ground with water and given to them, but one must then beware of using lemon juice.

Another priest, a native of Asahudi, boasted that when he was in Java—where a great portion of men were dying suddenly from heart failure <note>original: "Cordis Syncope".</note>—he had fallen down as if dead, such that he was thrown into a pit dug on the shore and covered with a little earth; but on the following night, he woke up again and recovered as soon as, by chance, the root of this little tree growing there touched his mouth. Its penetrating virtues soon ran through his body and strengthened him so much that he rose again. Wondrous are the things that can happen, but it is necessary that many possibilities concur.

I carefully dug up these little trees, about a span high <note>About 9 inches.</note>, with the adjacent stones and earth, and transplanted them into my garden for medical use, but they grew slowly and finally perished, since they love their own soil, and the root fibers are so few and tender that they are easily broken during digging.

We must further inquire whether the *Accar Lampau* or *Lampan* growing in Sukadana <note>A region in Borneo.</note> is the same or a similar root, which is also yellowish and bitter, and...

<column-break/>

*...some others do better, who rub a couple of these "little hearts" <note>Referring to the heart-shaped fruits.</note> on a stone with water and give it to the sufferer to drink all at once.*

*In all kinds of fevers that come from corrupt humors, these little hearts are also used, of which previously only 2 to 3 pieces were taken, but thereafter it came to 5 and 7 pieces, and that with good success. Furthermore, this medicine is used—both the hearts and the roots—rubbed in water and drunk, against colic, coughs, and especially the whooping cough, shortness of breath, and all kinds of stabbings felt in the body. It strengthens the weak stomach and brings back the lost appetite. It opens with its penetrating power all obstructions of the intestines, and for many other defects it has been used with good success. But the locals have such an unsuitable way of applying it, and confuse the diseases so much, that one can get no right account of it. They also say that this medicine is so powerful that one does not need to abstain from one food or another (which the Ternatans call Fosso) while using it, as one must do with almost all other cures. The mentioned priest also assured me that if someone consumed one of these hearts every 5 or 7 days, they would remain free from many diseases, especially when some disease was spreading over the land. The root is a proven or tested antidote against the harmful fish called "blowers" <note>Pufferfish.</note>, if someone has eaten them incautiously; and when this will not help, they despair for the patient's preservation. Against all other kinds of poison that someone has taken in their food, they are also praised, for they throw or cast out the same through vomiting if it is still in the stomach, or through a violent sweating and passing of water if it has sunk into the intestines. The leaves, rubbed and bound on the belly, draw out the dropsical humors, for which some use the fresh bark; the same rubbed in water and drunk also throws out the ingested venom through vomiting, and resists the same through its own power. The same bark boiled in water and drunk with a little Nutmeg is also used in the disease Oepas Ajam—that is, the falling sickness—and the cramp; the Ternatans do the same by giving one or two hearts.*

*The leaves boiled in water with a few Cloves, small Ginger, and Massoy, being well closed or stopped up until a third has boiled away, with that one steams those who have great pains and stabbings in the back and loins and are swollen thereby, giving them the same water to drink, and the boiled material, well-rubbed, was bound on the limbs with the broad leaves of Bancudu.*

*On Nusalaut and the Uliassers, there is a kind of venomous adders and snakes with broad heads, called Munalatu, as well as the copper-colored and venomous lizard called Pananat in Malay, by which now and then some people are bitten. And most often by the first, the venom running straight to the heart, bringing the people great distress and burning, so that many come to die; but these were also finally cured with the roots of this Soulamee, if one rubs the same in water and gives it to them, though they must take good care not to consume any lemon juice therewith.*

*Another priest, born in Asahudi, boasted that while he was on Java during a great mortality—when the people fell away suddenly from a heart-seizure—he had also once fallen down for dead, whereupon they threw him into a poor pit made on the beach and barely covered him with some earth; and that he came to himself again the following night as soon as, by chance, the root of this plant that stood there touched his mouth, and whose strong powers immediately pierced into his body and so strengthened him that he rose up again. These are wondrous things that may well happen, but many coincidences must first strike together or agree.*

*I have also carefully dug up these little trees about a span high, with the surrounding stones, earth and all, and so planted them in my garden for the convenience of medicine, but they shot up slowly and finally died out, since it wants its own ground, and the fibers on the roots are so few and tender that one breaks them off very easily in digging.*

*Furthermore, it remains for us to investigate whether the Accar Lampau or Lampan, growing on Sukadana, is not also such or a similar root: as being likewise...*

->Of the Forty-First Plate,<-

Which shows a branch of the tree called *Radix Amara* <note>original Latin: "Bitter Root"</note> by *Rumphius*, which I consider to be a species of *Lignum Colubrinum* <note>original Latin: "Snakewood"</note>, as is explained more extensively below.

### OBSERVATION.

This tree is without doubt a species of the one we showed in Plate 64 of our *Thesaurus* <note>A reference to the *Thesaurus Zeylanicus*, Burman’s work on the plants of Sri Lanka.</note>, which is named there on page 141 as *Ligustrum* <note>Privet</note> with three leaves at each node, believed by the apothecaries to be *Lignum Colubrinum* <note>Snakewood</note>. Its flowers and heart-shaped fruits match the flowers and fruits of this tree exactly; however, in that work they are shown in clusters, while here they are represented in a spike, and the leaves on this tree stand without a specific order, whereas in the Ceylonese variety they always appear in threes. Furthermore, they agree in taste and potency, for the powers of both are very famous against poisons, all venomous or malignant diseases, and fevers, as is further evident in the cited passage of my *Thesaurus Zeylanicus*, where various authors and opinions concerning Snakewood are cited.

<margin>In Valentijn’s description of Ambon <note>François Valentijn was a 17th-century Dutch minister and author of a massive history of the East Indies.</note>, this tree occurs on page 193 under the name *Boha-Hati*, which means "Heart-fruit-tree," and is shown in Plate no. XXVIII.</margin>

## CHAPTER FIFTY.
->*Moluccan Anise: Camelan.*<-

This is a small tree about the size of a Pomegranate tree, but its trunk is thicker, usually the thickness of a leg and sometimes even a thigh. It bears a rough bark of a greenish-gray color, spreading out with few and crooked branches like the *Limonellus* <note>Small lemon tree</note>, thereby forming a divided crown. The branches are full of short twigs, which bear leaves almost like the shape of Pomegranate leaves, but smaller, stiffer, and of a dark black-green. They are arranged in opposite pairs of two, three, or four on a twig, with one leaf at the end that is the largest and most like the Pomegranate leaf; the others are subsequently shorter, slightly and shallowly serrated at the edges, and the two bottom-most are the smallest and more rounded. When crushed, these leaves give off a strong odor, almost like that of the *Limonellus*, but more unpleasant and approaching the scent of Coriander leaves. The branches are full of short and stiff thorns, making them difficult to handle, especially on young trees. At the ends of the twigs, sparse clusters emerge on few but long stalks, which open into small five-petaled, whitish flowers, slightly hollowed like the Lily of the Valley. In the center, they show a small green hillock from which the fruit grows. This fruit is a round berry, somewhat smaller than a peppercorn, standing in pairs opposite each other, black-green, and covered with small bumps like tiny lemons, separated by a yellow vein. When fully ripe, these fruits become dark yellow and then blackish. Under a thin skin, they contain a seed or black grain inside like Coriander, the smell of which corresponds entirely with European Anise, but the taste differs: for at first it is indeed sweet and anise-like, but it disappears quickly on the tongue and turns woody. The wood of this small tree is solid, hard, and heavy, ranging in color from white to a reddish tint.

## L. CHAPTER.
->*The Moluccan Anise-tree.*<-

This is a small tree about as large as a Pomegranate tree, yet with a thicker trunk, generally a leg, and sometimes even a thigh thick, with a rough, green-gray bark, spreading out with few and crooked branches, like the Limonellus, and therewith making a divided crown. The branches are full of short twigs, and on the same the leaves: Almost of the shape of Pomegranate leaves, yet smaller, stiffer, and black-green, directly opposite each other, with 2, 3 to 4 pairs on a twig, and one in front, which is the largest, and most like the Pomegranate leaf: the others being subsequently somewhat shorter, on the edges a little and widely serrated, and the two hindmost the smallest, moreover running somewhat round: Being crushed they give off a strong smell, almost like that of Limonellus, yet more unpleasant, and coming closer to the Coriander leaves: The branches are full of short and stiff thorns, which is why they are also difficult to handle, and especially on the young trees: At the outer end of the twigs small and sparse clusters come forth, made of few yet long stalks, and thereon small five-petaled whitish flowers, standing a little hollow, like the Lily of the Valley, in the middle showing a small green hillock, from which the fruits come forth: Being the same round berries, somewhat smaller than the pepper, standing two and two against each other, black-green, set with some points, like small Lemons, and distinguished with a yellow vein: The fully ripe ones become dark yellow, and thereafter blackish, under a thin shell they have inside a seed or black grain, like Coriander, whose smell entirely corresponds with the European Anise, but the taste differs: For the same is at first indeed sweet, and also Anise-like, yet disappears quickly on the tongue, and becomes woody: The wood is massive, hard, and heavy, pulling from the white and somewhat towards the reddish.

# Book II. Chapter I. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

**Name**. In Latin it is called *Anisum Moluccanum* <note>original: "Moluccan Anise"</note>, not at all because of its shape, but because of its anise-like scent and flavor. Although the common people of Ternate call it by the bastardized name *Anisum Castela* <note>original: "Castilian/Spanish Anise"</note> and *Anys Oetan*—that is, wild Anise—among our Amboinese it is called *Camela*. This is a name they also give to other strong-smelling leaves, and thus it is quite common. On Java, near Gresik, it is named *Carancang*, and by the Eastern Ceramese *Samirin*, while the Ternatans themselves call it *Catti Catti Garo*.

**Location**. In Amboina, and especially around Fort Victoria, this small tree is rarely found. The Rajas <note>local rulers</note> of Soya had planted one in their garden here, but the local women <note>Latin: "mulierculae"; Dutch: "vrouwtjes"</note> harassed it so much by plucking its leaves and fruits that it eventually died, and it is now unknown there. However, it grows spontaneously on bare, stony mountains or cliffs, both near the seashore of Leytimor and in its other regions, such as in the district of *Oerimessing* near the sea-cliffs of *Seri*, as well as on the stony mountain of *Ema*. Both locations are situated on the southern side of Leytimor, from where these small trees are dug up with their stony soil and transplanted. It is also found in Java near Gresik, but most abundantly in the Moluccas, and especially on Ternate near Gammalamma in rocky places not far from the shore. It is likewise found in Eastern Ceram on high, bare cliffs, both on the shore and in the mountains.

**Usage**. Although this plant breathes such a remarkable scent that its seed fills the entire place where it lies, its use is rare, at least among the Amboinese. Their womenfolk, however, sometimes take the berries and mix them into their *Bobori* <note>a traditional cosmetic or medicinal ointment applied to the skin</note> ointments, which they rub on their bodies after washing for the sake of the sweet scent. The Javanese were also accustomed to adding its leaves and fruits to their *Boccassam* <note>likely a reference to *bakasang*, a fermented condiment, here used for its fragrance</note> to give it a pleasant aroma. Among the Eastern Ceramese, it has no particular use except that the wood is used for axe handles, as it has the hardness of Lemon wood.

In Java, around Batavia, a tree grows to the size of a Lemon tree, which is called there *Boa Balangan*, by the Javanese *Cabestan*, and by the Portuguese *Folho d’Anis* <note>original: "Anise Leaf"</note>. Its leaves agree in shape, scent, and flavor with the aforementioned plant, but they taste more strongly of Anise and are sharp when chewed in the mouth. Their stalks are grooved and have a wide border on both sides, making them "winged" <note>term: "alati" or winged; this refers to a leaf stalk with leaf-like tissue running down its sides</note>. Its fruit differs greatly from the previous one, for it is the size of a *Bilac Tellor* <note>likely the Bael fruit or "Egg Bael"</note>, being broad at the bottom and having a narrow neck at the top like a small pot, from which it received its Malay name. Its outer shell is woody, like the Bael fruit, variegated with very fine greenish-white spots, and it also smells of Anise. Its inner flesh is sweet and more pleasant to eat than the Bael fruit, of which we provide a separate illustration here.

I intend to describe this small tree more elaborately in my *Supplement* <note>original: "Auctuario"</note> when it provides me with flowers and fruits to examine. A small tree with similar foliage is found in the *Hortus Malabaricus* <note>A famous 17th-century botanical work on the plants of the Malabar Coast</note>, Part 4, Figure 14, under the Malabar name *Tsjeria-Katoe-Naregam*, which the Portuguese call *Limoins da Folha Crusado* <note>original: "Cross-leaf Lemons"</note> and the Dutch call *Claver-appels* <note>original: "Clover-apples"</note>.

->### Plate Forty-Two<-

This plate shows a branch of the small tree called *Anisum Moluccanum* by Rumphius. It is easily recognized as belonging to the family of umbelliferous plants <note>term: "Umbelliferae"; plants like carrots or parsley that have umbrella-like flower clusters</note>, and as it appears to me, it belongs to the genus *Oreoselinum* <note>Mountain Parsley</note>. It seems to be a species of that plant called *African Oreoselinum with Anise leaves* by Tournefort, from which it is commonly thought that *Galbanum gum* is collected. Therefore, it is named *Galbanifera* <note>Galbanum-bearing</note> by many authors, as is further evident from the *Hortus Cliffortianus, page 69*, where it is referred to the genus called *Bubon* by Linnaeus.

NB. In Rumphius’s *Supplement* I have found no further description of the *Boa Balangan*. Therefore, I hope the Kind Reader will be content with this brief account, which they can easily supplement from the accurate and elegant figure provided.

<column-break/>

**Name**. In Latin *Anisum Moluccum*, not at all according to its form, but according to its anise-like scent and taste, although the common man in Ternate calls it by a bastard word *Anys Castela* and *Anys Oetan*, that is, wild Anise. By our Amboinese it is called *Camelan*, being a name they also give to other strong-smelling leaves, and consequently, it is common. On Java, around Gresik, it is called *Carancang*, and by the East Ceramese *Samirin*, and by the Ternatans themselves *Catti Catti Garo*.

**Location**. In Amboina, especially around Fort Victoria, this little tree is found but little. The Rajas of Soya had planted one here below in their dwellings, which, however, the womenfolk so tormented by tearing off and plucking the leaves and fruits, that it finally perished, so that it is now unknown there. But it grows of its own accord on bare and stony mountains or cliffs, both near the seashore of Leytimor, and a little away from it, such as in the district of Oerimessing, near the sea-cliffs of Seri, and on the stony promontory of Ema, both situated on Leytimor's south side, from where one can dig up and transplant the little trees with the stony earth. They are also found on Java, around Gresik, but most of all in the Moluccas, and especially on Ternate, around Gammalamma, in cliff-like places, not far from the beach, as also on East Ceram, on high bare cliffs, as well on the beach as in the mountains.

**Usage**. Although this plant has such a notable scent that the seed also fills the place where it lies, it has nevertheless a very small use, at least among the Amboinese. But the Amboinese women sometimes take the berries and mix them among their *Bobori* ointments, with which they smear their bodies after washing, (in their judgment) for the sweet scent. The Javanese also used to mix the leaves and fruits among their *Bocassam*, to give it a good fragrance. Among the East Ceramese it has no special use, except that the wood is used for handles of axes; for it is as hard as Lemon wood.

On Java, around Batavia, grows a tree the size of a Lemon tree, named there *Boa Balangan*, in Javanese *Cabestan*, by the Portuguese *Folho d’Anis*; The leaves in form, scent, and taste agree with the above, but the leaflets taste more strongly of Anise, are sharp in the mouth, and their little stalks are grooved, having on both sides a sharp edge like little wings. The fruit differs much from the preceding, for it is the size of a *Bilac Tellor*, broad at the back, and in front with a narrow neck like a little pot, from which it has its name in Malay. The outer shell is woody, similar to the Bael fruit, green with fine white speckles, and also smells of Anise. The inner flesh is sweet, and more pleasant to eat than the Bael fruit, of which a separate figure is to be seen here alongside.

This little tree I intend to describe more extensively in my *Supplement*, when it shall bloom and bear fruit here. A little tree agreeing in leaves with the preceding, see in *Hortus Malabaricus* part 4, Fig. 14, under the Malabar name *Tsjeria-Katoe-Naregam*, in Portuguese *Limoins da Folha Crusado*. In Dutch *Claver-appels*.

->### The Forty-Second Plate<-

Displays a branch of a little tree, which is named *Anisum Moluccanum*, or the Moluccan Anise by Rumphius, which one can easily see belongs to the *umbelliferous plants*, and as it appears to me, to the *Oreoselinum*, it seeming to me to be a sort of that plant which is named the *African Oreoselinum with Anise leaves* by Tournefort, and is a plant that gives the *Galbanum Gum*, why it is also commonly nicknamed *Galbanum-bearing* by the writers, as is to be seen more broadly in the *Hortus Cliffortianus* p. 69, where it is placed under the genus named *Bubon* by Linnaeus.

NB. In the *Supplement* of Rumphius I have found no further description of the *Boa Balangan*, wherefore the well-disposed Reader must be content with this short one, which he can further make out from the accurate and neat figure added.

A second species of *Indian Anise* is found in our pharmacies, which is commonly called *Star Anise* <note>original: "Anisum stellatum"</note>, and which appears to belong to the *Fraxinella* <note>Dittany</note> genus, or at least Samuel Dale categorized it there in his *Pharmacology*, page 194. However, I have observed other species of this genus in the Medical Garden, as they appeared to me, which were referred by the famous Caspar Commelin to the *African Spiraeas*; for the seed vessels of these small trees match those of the *Star Anise* entirely. If this holds true for the flowers as well, they belong entirely to the same genus, which was called *Diosma* <note>a genus of flowering plants in the rue family</note> by Linnaeus in the *Hortus Cliffortianus*, page 71.

*Moluccan Anise* is mentioned by Valentinus in his *Description of Amboina*, page 194, and is displayed on Plate number XXX.
