This shows a branch of the tree which is called *Anise leaf* or *Anise Leaf* <note>original: "Foelio d'Anis"</note> by Rumphius, and it appears to be a species of *Limonellus* <note>Little Lemon</note>. It was referred to that genus by Ray in his *History of Plants*, page 1658, as well as by Plukenet in the *Almagestum*, page 239. It is the same as that depicted in the *Hortus Malabaricus*, part 4, Plate 14, with this distinction: that one bears only solitary flowers, whereas Rumphius’s plant produces many flowers clustered together.

Furthermore, I have collected the synonyms and authors for this small tree in the *Thesaurus Zeylanicus*, page 143, where the *Mal-Naregam* from the *Hortus Malabaricus*, Plate 12, Volume IV, belongs among the wild Lemons.

# CHAPTER FIFTY-ONE.

## Saponaria. Rarak.

This is properly a Javanese tree, but since it has sprouted in Amboina from seeds sent there, it also earns a place in this book. The tree itself grows with a very straight, very tall, and slender trunk, which bears a smooth and even bark. It has few large branches, but many of these enjoy furrowed <term>rachises</term> <note>the main axis of a compound leaf</note> that bear leaves on both sides, creating a dense crown.

The leaves on some stalks are alternate, but on others opposite, similar in shape and growth habit to the *Caju Cuda* <note>literally "Horse Wood"</note>, but smaller, being about four inches long and one wide. They are narrowed at the top, even at the edges, bright green, and gifted with a red middle vein; they have an unpleasant taste. On younger trees, however, they are over six inches long, sitting on long stems, with twelve pairs or more on each, resembling *Peach* leaves. On older trees, eight or ten pairs are joined to each stalk, sometimes ending with an odd leaf at the tip, sometimes not. Small, pale florets sprout from the axils of the stalks on the branches, followed by the fruits. These hang down in many clusters, round like musket balls <note>original: "globulorum sclopeti"</note> but slightly larger and marked with a protruding seam. They are yellow at first, then turning red when ripe. Beneath a smooth skin, they contain a little saffron-colored, mucilaginous flesh, which is tasteless at first but then unpleasant and sharply stinging to the tongue. Inside this is hidden a round, hard, and entirely black <term>stone</term> <note>original: "officulum"</note>, like a boy's marble, smooth like the beads of a rosary, though slightly furrowed on the lower part. The wood of this tree is very dry and constructed of various rings, like a roll of paper, having a blackish heart or marrow in the center. Its bark is more succulent and clings so strongly to the wood that it can only be separated in small segments. The branches are so fragile that they are often broken by the wind, and no one can stand upon them.

**Name.** In Latin *Saponaria* <note>Soap-plant</note>, in Dutch *Soap-grains* <note>original: "Zeep-korrels"</note> from its use; it is likewise called *Boa-Sabon* <note>Soap-fruit</note> by the Malays and *Rarak* by the Javanese.

**Location.** It grows mostly in Java, spontaneously in the flat forests, where it rises into a very tall tree; its stones in

A second kind of *Indian Anise* is found in our pharmacies, which is generally called *Star Anise*, which would seem to belong to the genus of the *Fraxinella*, or at least Samuel Dale has placed it there in his *Pharmacology*, page 194. And I have discovered other species of this genus in our Medical Garden, which were described by the famous Caspar Commelin under the name of *African Spiraea*; these small trees bear seed-pods very much resembling the *Star Anise*, and if the flowers also match, they certainly belong to one genus, which was named *Diosma* by Linnaeus in the *Hortus Cliffortianus*, page 71.

The *Moluccan Anise tree* is also mentioned by Valentinus in the description of *Amboina*, page 194, and represented on Plate No. XXX.

# CHAPTER LI.

## The Rarak tree, or Soap-bead Tree.

This is a Javanese tree, but having come forth in Amboina through transferred seed, it has also found a place in this book. The tree shoots up with a very straight, high, and slender trunk, having a smooth and even bark. The main branches are few, but they are full of thin, somewhat striped twigs, and these are laden with leaves on both sides, so that they nevertheless make a dense crown.

The leaves stand on some stems alternately, and on others directly opposite each other, in shape and manner of growth similar to the *Caju Cuda*, though smaller, being more or less four inches long and one inch wide, narrowed to a point in front, even at the edges, bright green, smooth, and with a red vein in the middle, unpleasant of taste. On the young trees they are well over 6 inches long, standing on long twigs in 12 pairs and more on each, looking much like *Peach leaves*, but on the old trees there are only 8 and 10 pairs on a twig, sometimes with one alone at the tip, and sometimes not. The blossom comes from the armpit of the twigs on the branches, being small pale flowers, and upon them follow the fruits, which hang many together and are round of shape like *musket balls*, though somewhat larger, and with a protruding seam on the outside, yellow at first, and then red when ripe, covering under a smooth membrane a little orange-yellow and slimy flesh, tasteless at first, but thereafter unpleasant and sharp on the tongue. Inside there lies a round, hard, and pitch-black stone, like a small marble, smooth as the beads of a rosary, though on the bottom side somewhat striped. The wood of this tree is very dry and composed of various wrappings, like a rolled-up book of paper, with a blackish heart in the middle. The bark is somewhat juicier and clings so firmly to the wood that one cannot pull it off except in small pieces. The branches are very brittle and easily broken by the wind. Also, one cannot stand upon them.

**Name.** In Latin *Saponaria*, in German <note>meaning Dutch/Low German</note> *Soap-grains* from its use, and so also in Malay *Boa Sabon*, in Javanese *Rarak*.

## Saponaria. Rarak <note>original: "Ra..."; referring to the Soapberry tree, *Sapindus rarak*. The name "Saponaria" comes from the Latin *sapo* (soap), as the fruit of this tree contains natural surfactants used for washing throughout the East Indies.</note>

II Book. LI. Chapter. AMBOINESE HERBAL. 135

Those trees transported to Amboina have sprouted there into tall and slender trees <note>original: "instar Abietis"; like a fir or spruce tree</note>, which even into their twelfth year have not yet produced fruit, as is the case with many Javanese trees, since the seasons (as has been said more often) differ from the seasons of this region.

**Uses.** Commonly in Java, its fruits are used in place of soap for washing and purifying linens; for if these are rubbed by hand in warm water, the outer slimy pulp foams like soap, the infusion or water of which removes all filth from the cloths. However, it has been found that this pulp is too sharp and corrosive, so that it often as it were "burns" the cloths or linens, whereby they perish more quickly and are not as durable as those washed in another way. Chinese merchants bring these dried fruits for sale in full sacks to these Eastern regions to be used in place of soap, which indeed are not for sale there every year. Some have attempted to wash their heads with these fruits, but they found them to be too corrosive, and the hair fell out as a result.

The black seeds <term>stones|The hard inner seeds of the fruit</term> of these remain whole during washing and are thrown away, or are given to the Moorish clerics <note>original: "flaminibus Æthiopum" / "Moorse Papen"; likely referring to local Muslim religious leaders who used the seeds for prayer beads</note> for rosaries; for if they are polished or carried, they shine and become black like ebony wood, though they are much lighter. They are not easily broken, and are scarcely split even by a strong hammer blow. These fruits seem to agree with, or at least differ little from, those which grow in the West Indies, both in Hispaniola and on the mainland and Guiana, of which Oviedo <note>Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo y Valdés (1478–1557), a Spanish historian</note> in his *General and Natural History*, book 9, chapter 5; Nicolas Monardes in *On Simple Medicines*, chapter 65; and Charles Clusius in *Exotic Books*, book 2, chapter 16, have made mention. They are called by them "Soap Spheres" <note>original: "Spherulæ Saponariæ"</note>, and in English "Soap Berries," testifying with one voice that their external pulp is used in place of soap, and the internal black and hard seeds for rosaries. However, one should not be offended that the leaves of the tree are compared by them to the leaves of Ferns, as it is familiar to Spanish writers to compare all such leaves—whether they be long or short—which are arranged in opposite pairs on long stalks, with Ferns. In Java, the pulp of these fruits is also used to clean the surfaces of certain silver vessels or works, if they have become bluish in color or spotted.

Another such tree, whose bark provides a similar use and is called "Soap Bark," and in Malay *Langir*, will be described later in book 6, chapter 73.

A similar Soapberry tree also occurs described in the *Hortus Malabaricus* <note>A 17th-century botanical treatise on the medicinal properties of flora in the Malabar coast of India</note>, part 4, Figure 19, under the name *Poerinsji*. In Portuguese, *Sabaon dos Canarins* <note>Soap of the Canarese</note>. In Dutch, *Zeep-nooten* (Soap-nuts): which also grows in Bengal.

### OBSERVATION.

In other places in India, Soapberry trees also occur, as in Ceylon, which is called by Hermann in the *Paradisus Batavus Prodromus* and *Museum Zeylanicum*, page 69, "the three-leaved Ceylonese Soap-tree with lupin-like seeds," and is listed in my *Thesaurus Zeylanicus*, page 209. It seems to agree with that of the *Hortus Malabaricus*, where in the notes other authors are cited, including those praised by Rumphius above; see the rest in the *Thesaurus Zeylanicus* at the place cited, and Ray, volume 3, appendix page 65, number 11. However, the tree described by Rumphius seems to agree entirely with that which is called the "Racemose Plum-bearer, with a winged leaf and a midrib provided with membranes standing out on both sides, with Soap-fruit" by Sloane in the *Catalog of the Plants of Jamaica*, page 184, where many authors of this tree are seen collected, as well as in Samuel Dale's *Pharmacologia*, page 338, and the *History of Jamaica*, volume 2, page 131, where the figures in the *Hortus Amstelodamensis*, part 1, Plate 94, and Plukenet's *Phytographia*, Plate 217, Figure 7, are assigned to this tree above all others. This Soapberry tree occurs under the name of the *Rarak*-tree in Valentijn's description, page 194.

<column-break/>

*In Amboina, having been transplanted, they have indeed shot up into tall, slender trees, like firs, but in their 12th year they have not yet wanted to bear fruit, as many Javanese trees do, because (as has been said several times) the Monsoons—that is, the seasons—happen to differ from those of these countries.*

***Use.*** *The common man on Java uses the fruits in place of soap to wash all kinds of linen; for when one rubs them with the hands in warm water, the outer slimy flesh begins to foam like soap, and which water then takes away all filth from the linen; yet it has also been found that this flesh is somewhat too sharp and burns the linen somewhat, whereby it cannot last as long as it otherwise would. Chinese merchants bring these dried fruits by the sackful into these Eastern quarters to use in place of soap, which one cannot obtain there every year. Some have also undertaken to wash the head with these fruits, but found that they were also too sharp and made the hair fall out.*

*The black grains remain whole in the washing and are thrown away, or given to the Moorish priests <note>original: "Moorse Papen"</note> to make rosaries from them; for when one turns and polishes them, they become as beautifully black as ebony wood, though much lighter. They also do not break easily, needing to be hit with a good hammer blow before one gets them apart. It seems that these fruits correspond to, or at least do not differ much from, those that grow in the West Indies, both on Hispaniola and on the mainland and in Guiana, of which Oviedo in his General and Natural History, book 9, chapter 5; Nicolas Monardes in his book on Simple Medicines, chapter 65; and Carolus Clusius, book 2 of the Exotics, chapter 16, make mention under the name of* Sphærulæ Saponariæ, *and in English* Soap Berries, *unanimously testifying that one uses the outer flesh in place of soap and the inner black and hard grains for rosaries. Yet one must not take offense that they compare its leaves to those of Ferns, because Spanish writers have the habit of comparing all such leaves—be they long or short—that stand in two rows against each other on long stalks, to the Fern herb. On Java, the flesh of these fruits is also used to clean silver edges that have been roughly beaten out.*

*Yet another tree, from whose bark one also has a similar use, named* Cortex Saponarius <note>Soap Bark</note>, *and in Malay* Langir, *is found described hereafter in book 6, chapter 73.*

*A similar Soap-tree see described in the* Hortus Malabaricus, *part 4, Figure 19, under the name* Poerinsji. *In Portuguese* Sabaon dos Canarins, *in German* Soap-nuts, *which are also found in Bengal.*

### OBSERVATION.

*In the other places of the Indies, various Soap-ball trees were found, such as among others in Ceylon, which by Herman in the* Par. Bat. Pr. *and the* Museum Zeylanicum *was named* Saponaria Zeylanica, trifolia, femine Lupini, *which is listed in my* Thes. Zeyl. *p. 209, and seems to correspond with the* Poerinsji *of the* Hortus Malabaricus, *represented in the fourth part, Plate 19, where in the remarks the writers mentioned by our Rumphius are also cited. See the rest further in our* Thesaurus Zeylanicus *and in the Appendix of the third part of Ray p. 65, No. 11. But with the tree described by Rumphius, that one seems to correspond which is mentioned by Sloane in the Catalog of Jamaican plants page 184, where very many writers of these trees are cited and mentioned, as also in the* Pharmacologia *of Samuel Dale p. 338 and in the* History of Jamaica *second part page 131, where the figures in the first part of the Amsterdam Garden Plate 94 and those of Plukenet in his* Phytographia *Plate 217, Figure 7, are attributed to this tree. This Soap-ball tree is also mentioned by Valentijn in the description of Ambon page 194 under the name of the* Rarak-tree.

AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chapter LII. 136

# FIFTY-SECOND CHAPTER.
## The Medicine of Sagueer: Oebat Sagueer: Sefoot.

This tree is tall and wild, but it can also be counted among the aromatic trees due to the daily use of its roots, from which the common drink called <term>Sagueer|A traditional fermented drink or palm wine made from the sap of various palm trees</term> is prepared. It does not have a very wide canopy, but it is elegant and well-ordered, bearing dense leaves and branches like a larger Clove tree. Its trunk is usually so thick that one can scarcely wrap their arms around it. It is divided into two species: the female, also called the <note>original: "Pharmacum Legitimum"; the True Medicine</note>, and another called the Lemon-like Medicine. We shall first describe the True Medicine or "Female" type, called <note>original: "Oebat Sagueer"; Medicine of Sagueer</note>, which is the most commonly used.

It bears dense branchlets and <term>rachises|The main stems of a compound leaf or flower cluster</term> (as mentioned), but they are arranged in a regular order. On the branches, the leaf stems are upright and opposite each other, consisting of four or five pairs of leaves. They are not truly cross-shaped as in the Clove tree, but are arranged without a strict order, although some do form a cross. On these are placed other smaller stems, thin but firm, which divide again into even smaller ones, many of which are cross-shaped. On these stems, both large and small, the leaves are also arranged in a regular opposite order on short stalks. On the longer branchlets, they consist of six or seven pairs, but on the shorter ones, two or three pairs; and where the smaller stems meet, a smaller leaf is placed under each such stem.

The leaves somewhat resemble Clove leaves, yet with this difference: they are generally shorter and do not narrow as much at the bottom as Clove leaves do. At the top, they end in a long point. They are rough, smooth, and shining, four or five inches long and two fingers wide. They are often dark green and so smooth on the upper side that no protruding veins appear there; the middle nerve forms a kind of groove. On the underside, however, many thin and parallel veins are visible, running obliquely toward the front (which in Clove leaves are narrower and more transverse). The edges of these leaves are even. Their taste is subtle and bitter, but weak, unpleasant, and slightly acidic at the end.

The flowers have not yet appeared, and the tree bears fruit so rarely that they are almost unknown to most inhabitants—even those who dig up the roots of this tree daily. I believe the reason for this is partly the height of the trees and their green color, which makes them hard to distinguish among the dark green leaves, and partly because these trees are, as it were, <note>original: "castrentur"; castrated or sterilized</note> by the constant stripping of their roots, so they cannot produce fruit. For this reason, fruits are only found on those trees that stand far off, are a <term>fathom|The span of a man's outstretched arms</term> in thickness, and have been rarely or never disturbed by the diggers. Its fruit has the shape of a curved horn or a pouch ending in a point, which is about two inches long, a finger wide, and almost round or slightly compressed. It is flat and bulging, grooved along its length on one side; furthermore, it is green and soft, feeling like an inflated little bag when touched. Inside is hidden a flat stone like a peeled <term>Canarium|The Java almond, a common nut-bearing tree in the region</term>, covered first with a thin whitish skin and then a brown one, under which is hidden a yellowish and oily marrow or pulp, similar to that of the <term>Bintangor|A tree of the genus Calophyllum, known for its oily seeds</term>. It has no particular taste, except for being a little bitter. This stone or kernel is also bumpy and has a <term>hilum|A scar or mark on a seed showing where it was attached</term> on one side, almost like a pea or bean, where the rays of the skin meet as if at a single center, and where a short, hard point is visible. Between this kernel and the outer green skin is hidden a sticky, semi-transparent liquid like <term>Turpentine|A resinous fluid obtained from trees</term>. These fruits are mostly dark green, or finally become a little yellow on their lower part, where they eventually burst open when ripe and release the kernel, which, when brought to the ground...

# LII. CHAPTER.
## The Sefoot Tree.

*This is a tall and wild tree, yet it may also find a place among the spice-like plants because of the daily use of its roots, with which the common drink is prepared. It does not have a completely broad crown, but one that is well-arranged and elegant, thick with foliage and branches, much like a large Clove tree. The trunk is generally as thick as a man can embrace. It is divided into two sorts, which differ little from one another in appearance, namely: 1. the female, or True Medicine, and 2. the Lemon-like Medicine. We shall first describe the True Medicine, or the female of the Sagueer Medicine, as it is the most useful.*

*It has, as said, its crown full of small branches or twigs, standing mostly in a regular order. On the branches one first sees the twigs pointing upward and standing directly opposite each other, with four and five pairs, not exactly in a cross like the Clove trees, but without order, although some also stand in a cross. On these stand again other smaller, thin, and stiff twigs, which divide again into other shorter ones, and most all stand in a cross. On the aforementioned twigs, both large and small, the leaves are also arranged opposite each other in rows, and on short stalks; on the longer twigs with 6 and 7 pairs, and on the shorter ones with 2 and 3 pairs; and where the twigs meet, another smaller leaf stands under each twig.*

*The leaves somewhat resemble Clove leaves, but with this difference: they are generally shorter and do not taper as narrowly at the back as Clove leaves do, and they have a long point at the front. They are stiff, smooth, and gleaming, 4 and 5 inches long, 2 fingers broad, blackish-green, and so even on the upper side that one sees no veins bulging out there; also the middle nerve there makes only a groove. However, on the underside one sees many fine and parallel veins, running somewhat diagonally forward (being somewhat denser and more transverse on Clove leaves), furthermore with smooth edges. The taste is subtly bitter, yet weak, unpleasant, and in the end somewhat tart.*

*The bloom has not yet been seen, and it also seldom bears fruit, so that they are almost unknown to most inhabitants, even to those who daily dig up its roots. I guess the cause of this is partly because, due to the height of the trees and the green color, they are difficult to recognize among that black-green foliage, and secondly because the trees, being somewhat as if gelded by the constant digging up of the roots, can bring forth no fruit. Therefore, one finds none except on trees that stand quite far from the shore and are a fathom in circumference, and have been visited not at all or rarely by the diggers. This fruit then resembles a curved horn, or a pointed little bag, being about 2 inches long, a finger broad, and almost round, or as if a little flattened, with a belly on one side and a seam along it. Furthermore, it is grass-green, and feels like an inflated little bag when touched. Inside lies a flat grain, like a peeled Canarium nut, covered with a thin skin that is first white and then brown, and under that a yellowish and oily meat, like that of the Bintangor, of no singular taste, except only a small bitterness. This grain is also somewhat bumpy, and has a navel on one side like a bean, where the rays of the skin meet as if in a center point, and one also sees a short and hard little point on it. Between this grain and the outermost green shell lies a gristly and half-transparent moisture like Turpentine. They remain mostly dark green, or also become somewhat yellow on the belly, where they then finally burst open and let their aforementioned inner grain fall out, which then touching the earth, a...*

II Book. LII. Chapter. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

trailing down, they sprout a new little tree. The bark of the trunk is wrinkled and blackish-green, but on the branches, it is smooth and reddish.

The roots of this tree are almost the only part sought after, which is why the wise Creator of nature did not hide them deep under the earth; instead, they mostly run winding just beneath the rough surface of the soil, here and there even protruding, indeed extending beyond the reach of the tree’s canopy, so that they are very easily dug up. Where they protrude in this way, they form a knotty substance. The bark of these roots is quite thick and reddish-yellow where it is covered by earth; it is also brittle, and if cut, a dry substance presents itself like sulfur <note>original: "instar Sulphuris"; likely referring to the bright yellow color and crumbly texture rather than the scent</note>. The taste is bitter with a notable <term>astriction|A dry, puckering sensation in the mouth caused by tannins</term>. However, where it rises out of the ground, this bark is thin, whereas under the earth it is thick. The wood of the trunk is pale but turns yellow when dry; if it has been cut, it shows a more yellow color toward the roots. It is not hard and is easily crushed; its bitterness is greater than that of the bark.

**The Lemon-like Medicine**, or the other species called the *Male*, differs so little from the preceding one that it can hardly be recognized or distinguished by sight. The small branches and leaves are placed in the same order, but they are not always so strictly opposite as in the former. The leaves also have the same shape, except they are narrower, longer, thinner, and more pointed. The bark of the branches is not reddish but ash-gray; on the trunk, it is also ash-gray but smoother and thinner, both on the trunk and in the roots, being no thicker than a straw-stalk <note>original: "culmum"; a common historical measurement referring to the thickness of a stalk of grain</note>. That yellow and sulfur-like substance is not as plentiful as in the previous one. The taste also differs greatly, being more bitter in the male and approaching the taste of lemon peel, so that the best identifying characteristic for distinguishing these trees lies in the thickness of the bark and the taste. Hence, the diggers look not at the tree, but at the roots, which in the male also do not seek the deep earth but rise above it here and there with knots, and are generally not as thick or reddish, neither in the wood nor in the bark. The wood of the tree is whiter, harder, and more solid, making it more useful for mechanical tasks. Its fruit is shorter and rounder, almost like a small plum, also green, and its liquid is not so viscous, bearing the scent of *Cananga* flowers <note>The Cananga or Ylang-Ylang tree, famous for its sweet fragrance</note>. Its small stone is paler, brown, shorter, and thicker, but at the same time winding and navelled, or marked with a <term>hilum|the scar on a seed marking the point of attachment to its seed vessel</term> as in a bean, not unlike the cocoon of a silkworm. The fruits of both species appear in the month of April, more frequently on the male than on the female, as its roots are less often dug up. The fallen stones sprout in great numbers under the trees, growing into little saplings.

*Name.* The first species is called the *True Medicine of Sagueer* <note>original: "Pharmacum Sagueri Legitimum"</note> in Latin; in the Amboinese and Malay languages, it is called *Ubat Thuni*; on Hitoe, it is called *Sefoot* and *Sefoat*, which generally denotes anything by which Sagueer and similar drinks are made bitter and potable. In Leytimora and other places, it is called *Alat*, *Ay-Alat*, *Malul*, *Malun*, and *Malu*; however, this species is specifically called *Ay-Alat Wabba* by the Amboinese.

The second species is called the *Lemon-like Medicine*, in Malay *Ubat Lemon*, in Amboinese *Ay-alat Auffi*, because the taste of those roots, as well as the Sagueer in which they are infused, approaches that of lemon peels. Regarding the naming of male and female, there is a great controversy between me and the inhabitants. I have called the first species the female because it bears a softer bark and wood, but they consider it the male, and on the contrary, they think the other species is the female; however, it is not worth the effort to dispute the matter.

*Location.* This tree grows mostly in Amboina, but not in all its districts, only in the mountains of Hitoe, far from the shore, in high and wooded places. From there, the <term>Tiffadores|Local collectors or tappers who harvest the sap and roots for making palm wine</term> bring down its roots with great labor; for those that were closer have long since been exhausted by frequent use, so they must be sought far in the mountains. This tree offers this advantage: it spreads its roots widely and abundantly, and the best and most numerous of these trees grow around the village of *Xuli*.

Vol. II. <meta>catchword: Ubat</meta>

<column-break/>

*...produces a new little tree. The bark of the trunk is wrinkled and black-green, but on the branches smooth and reddish.*

*The roots are almost the only thing one seeks from or on this tree, and therefore wise nature did not want to hide them deep under the earth, for they run mostly along under the brushwood, or with bends under it, and here and there bulging out, even beyond the reach of the tree's crown, so that one can easily dig them out. And where they bulge out in such a way, they also make knots of a tangled substance. The bark of these roots is reasonably thick, and reddish-yellow where the earth covers it, furthermore brittle, and when one cuts into it, a yellow dry substance like sulfur comes out, being bitterish of taste, and with a notable contraction. But where it protrudes above the earth, it is thin, but under the earth thick. The wood of the trunk is pale, then soon turns yellow when one chops into it; at the roots it is somewhat yellower, not hard, but lets itself be easily beaten into pieces, and the bitterness is more notable or greater therein than in the bark.*

*The* Pharmacum Limonicum, *or otherwise the* Male *of this genus, differs, as said, so little from this preceding one, that one can hardly distinguish them by sight, for the twigs and leaves stand in the same order, though not so precisely opposite each other as on the previous; the leaves also have the same fashion, except that they are somewhat narrower, longer, and thinner, and also have a longer point. The bark of the branches is not reddish, but gray. On the trunk it is also grayer, and smoother, also generally thinner, as well on the trunk as on the roots, namely not above a straw-stalk thick, and there does not come out as much yellow sulfur-like matter as from the previous. The taste also differs notably, being more bitter in this Male, and tending toward lemon peels, so that the best tokens by which one can distinguish these trees consist in the thickness of the barks, and in the taste. Wherefore the diggers do not look to the tree, but to the roots, which also of the Male do not run deep under the earth, also here and there bulging out with knots, but are generally not so thick or reddish-yellow, neither in wood nor in bark. The wood is also whiter, harder, and more massive, and therefore more fit for house-building. The fruit is somewhat shorter and rounder, almost like a plum, also grass-green, and the inner moisture is less glue-like, smelling distinctly like the flowers of the* Cananga. *The inner kernel is paler, brown, shorter, and thicker, as well as winding, and with a navel like a bean, resembling not poorly a little barrel <note>original: "tonnetje"; referring to the shape of the cocoon</note> of a silkworm. The fruits of both these sorts are seen in April, and then the male more than on the preceding, or the female, because its roots are less dug out; the fallen kernels one sees sprouted in multitude under the trees, and become young saplings.*

*Name. The first sort is called* Pharmacum Sagueri Legitimum *in Latin, in Amboinese and Malay* Ubat Thuni, *on Hitoe* Sefooten, and Sefoat, *which in general signifies all things with which one makes Sagueer and such drink bitter and drinkable. On Leytimore and other places it is called* Alat, and Ay-Alat, Malul, Malun, *and* Malu, *but in particular this sort is named in Amboinese* Ay-Lat Wabba.

*The second sort is called* Pharmacum Limonicum, *in Malay* Ubat Lemon, *in Amboinese* Ay-alat Auffi, *because the taste of those roots, and of the Sagueer in which they are put, draws toward lemon peels. Regarding the name of male and female, there is quite some difference between me and the natives: the first sort I have named the female, because it is softer of bark and wood, but they hold it for the male, and on the contrary the second sort for the female, which however is worth no disputing.*

*Location. This tree grows mostly only on Amboina, and that still not in all its places, but only in the Hitoe mountains, far from the shore, in high wild forests, where the Tiffadores must fetch its roots from there not without great trouble, for those that stand close or nearby are already long dug out by much use, and one must now therefore go very far into the mountains. But this advantage is there, that the tree spreads its roots very far, and one can have many from one tree, with the most and most beautiful standing near the village of Xuli.*

### AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. Chapter LII.

The Lemon-Medicine <note>original: "Ubat Lemon"</note> also grows on Leitimor near the Cajeput <note>original: "Caju Puti"</note> forests, and mostly on the highest mountains.

**Usage.** Only the roots of this tree are in use, and primarily those of the first species, or the female, although the other species grows in greater abundance and in closer locations. The <term>Tiffadores|Local laborers who specialize in tapping palms or gathering forest products</term> dig up the largest roots, as thick as an arm or a leg, in such a way that they do not entirely strip the tree. Instead, they cut only one or two here and there so that the tree itself does not perish; they then cover that spot with the red and fatty earth found there so that it might sprout new roots. However, in recent years, due to the envy and greed of the Tiffadores, these trees have been so emaciated and diminished that they are rarely encountered, and must be sought from the more distant and higher mountains of Capaba and Waye.

We previously warned in the first book concerning the drink <term>Saguer|A fermented wine made from the sap of various palms</term> that when recently distilled from the tree, it is a pleasant and sweet liquor, but at the same time unhealthy if consumed daily. Thus, nature seems to have produced these roots and taught men to apply them to this drink, through which it is imbued with a pleasant bitterness, <term>astringency|A dry, puckering sensation</term>, and heat, making it much healthier for the stomach and more beneficial. Furthermore, regarding their use and method of preparation: the roots of this tree are chosen and cut into pieces half a foot or slightly longer, which are then split into smaller parts about the thickness of a finger or a little thinner. These are pounded slightly upon a stone, causing most of the bark to separate, and are then gathered into bundles a foot thick. One or two of these are infused into a vessel called a *Tampajang* <note>A large earthen storage jar</note> filled with sweet Saguer. This liquor soon begins to effervesce slightly, becoming thicker and whiter in color; within six or eight hours, it absorbs all the bitterness, harshness, and moderate heat. Then this drink is considered fit for use, so that this Saguer drink, as was said in its proper place, conceives all its strength and virtue from this root. The roots of the Lemon-Medicine are not chosen except in the absence of the "True Medicine" <note>original: "Ubat Tuni"</note>, because they are not only harder and more difficult to prepare, but they also impart a lemon-like bitterness to the Saguer, making it more flat and less pleasant, and it cannot be kept for three days without turning sour. The True Medicine roots can also be kept whole and good for a long time if stored in dry and shaded soil; indeed, they can even be transported across the sea to other regions to make tree-drinks bitter and preserve them, provided their ends are coated with clay. Some have even infused these into common sweetened beer in place of *Indian Bitters* or *Margosa* <note>The Neem tree, known for its extreme bitterness</note>, and found it to be warmer and better for the stomach.

The <term>Cuscus|A tree-dwelling marsupial (Phalanger) common in the Moluccas</term> <note>original: "Coescoefenses"</note>, being lovers of this tree's fruit, eat them, which also makes this tree rarer. However, Saguer prepared with Lemon-Medicine turns more easily into vinegar than that in which True Medicine has been infused.

Old and fallen trees, but mostly the Lemon-Medicine, yield a pale wood consisting of thin fibers; it is hard and similar to the best <term>Cofassu|A highly durable Indonesian hardwood (Vitex cofassus)</term>, which is extremely durable and therefore greatly sought after for the posts of large houses.

<column-break/>

The Lemon-Medicine is also found on Leitimor near the forests of Cajeput, and usually on or in the steepest parts of the mountains.

*Usage. Of this tree, only the roots are in use, and mostly those of the first sort, or the Female, although the second sort is found in greater quantity and closer at hand. The Tiffadores dig out the largest roots, as thick as an arm or a leg, in such a way that they do not entirely rob the tree, but cut only one or two closer at hand, so that it does not die out: then covering the place again with red and fatty earth (such as is found there), to let it sprout new roots. However, in these latter years, through the envy and greed of the Tiffadores, these trees have been so diminished and emaciated that one can find few anymore, and they must now walk quite far into the high mountains of Capaba and Way to encounter them.*

*Now, we have said here above in the first book of the Saguer, that this drink, as it comes from the trees, is indeed lovely and pleasantly sweet, but also at the same time unwholesome to drink daily: and therefore it seems that nature brought forth these roots and taught men to use them in that drink, whereby it also receives a pleasant bitterness, contraction, and warmth, and consequently becomes much healthier and more useful for the stomach. As for the further use, or actually the manner of preparation, one takes the roots, which are cut into pieces of 1/2 foot or a bit longer, and splits them again into small pieces, the thickness of a finger or even a bit thinner. These are then bruised a little on a stone, by which most of the bark springs off, and then one ties them in bundles as thick as a leg, of which one or two are put in a pot (called a Tampajang) full of sweet Saguer. From this, the drink immediately begins to boil a little, further becoming thicker and whiter in color, and within 6 or 8 hours drawing all the bitterness, tartness, and moderate warmth out of the mentioned root. Only then is the drink considered fit for use, so that the Saguer, as has also been said in its place, must obtain or receive all its strength and virtue from this root. The roots of Lemon-Medicine are not taken except for lack of True Medicine, because they are not only harder and more difficult to pound, but also impart a lemon-like bitterness to the Saguer, and make it flat and less pleasant, being unable to be kept for three days without sourness. The roots of True Medicine can also be kept good for a long time if they are buried in dry ground and a shady place; indeed, they can even be transported across the sea to other provinces to make tree-drinks bitter, if the ends are smeared with some clay. Some have also put them in common sugar-beer, in place of Indian Bitters or Margosa, and found that it was warmer and healthier for the stomach.*

The Cuscus also eat the fruits very gladly, which makes the scarcity of these trees even greater: and the Saguer prepared with Lemon-Medicine is more easily turned to vinegar than that infused with True Medicine.

The old and fallen trees, but most of all those of the Lemon-Medicine, have a pale, fine, and hard wood, being like the best *Cofassu*, very durable, and consequently much sought after for the pillars of large houses.

### CHAPTER FIFTY-THREE.
->**Capraria. Goat Tree.**<-
<note>original: "Capraria. Caju Cambing."</note>

**This tree** grows to the thickness of a man and bears a few large main branches that mostly stand upright. At their tips, many long, green, and straight twigs sprout without order; these are somewhat striped and rounded, with joints at the branch base where they break easily. Upon these twigs, leaves sit in eight or ten pairs, so similar to the *Wild Boarau* <note>original: "Boarau Oetang"</note> that they can hardly be distinguished from them. They are likewise five or six inches long, two to two and a half inches wide, rounded at the base and tapering into a long point at the top. They are textured with many parallel ribs and are hairy like the *Boarau*, yet much more limp, thinner, and softer to the touch—especially the leaves, stems, and twigs of young trees, which seem as if they were made of cloth. These leaves lack the acidity found in the *Boarau*, possessing instead a flat and dry taste with a slight astringency. The edges are very finely serrated, though this is scarcely visible on older leaves. Sometimes they are placed in pairs, and sometimes a single leaf ends the twig. The midrib does not run directly through the middle but sits closer to the forward edge, making the rear half wider; its connection to the stalk is rounder and more protruding, similar to the leaves of the **Nightshade** <note>original: "Solani"</note>. The upper leaves usually bear another smaller leaf, like a little flap or ear, at their base, and the young leaves are reddish-brown.

Neither I nor anyone else has ever observed flowers or fruit on this tree, although the people of Hoehoen claim that where it grows wild in their country, it sometimes produces fruit like the **Gnomon** <note>original: "Gnomon"; likely referring to Gnetum gnemon</note>. Its branches are brittle and filled with a dry, spongy pith. The bark of the trunk is quite thick, rough and shaggy on the outside, dark green in color, very sappy, and filled with a gluey liquid that sticks like **Papeda** <term>Papeda|A traditional glue-like preparation or a type of citrus sap</term>, which eventually dries into a gum without any notable smell, though it hints slightly of the resin of the **Nanari** tree. The taste of this bark is sweetish, like the soft shell of a young **Coconut** <term>Calappus|An older botanical term for the Coconut palm, Cocos nucifera</term>. The wood is white, soft, and of poor quality, rotting quickly if left in the rain. This tree is propagated by its branches, though many of them wither and die; for this reason, some believe it is better not to plant freshly cut branches immediately, but to leave them in a shady place on the ground for a few days until they begin to bud on their own, and only then commit them to the earth.

**Name.** In Latin, *Capraria*; in Malay, *Caju Cambing*; in Amboinese, *Aybibi*. Some believe these three names were given to it because goats <note>Latin: "capra"; Malay: "cambing"</note> seek out and eat its leaves so greedily.

**Location.** In Amboina, it is not very common or well-known; it is only found planted in some gardens near houses. It was brought there as cuttings from **Plo-Tiga**, which are three small, rocky islands situated off the coast of **Hitoe**, where these trees grow wild, as they also do in the region of the Hoehoenese.

**Use.** It is mostly cultivated in gardens because its bark is a proven and tested remedy for **Dysentery** <note>original: "Dysenteria"</note> when the intestines are already ulcerated. It is prepared in the following manner: a piece of bark is peeled from the tree trunk, about a hand's length and width, and taken with a fourth part of a young **Coconut**. This is lightly crushed and boiled in water with a handful of **Pangaga** <note>Indian Pennywort</note> and some leaves of **Daun Cucuran**, until half the water has boiled away. It is then strained through a cloth, and a small draught is taken twice a day; however, one must strictly avoid eating pork or lard during this time. Some add sugar to this potion if it is too bitter, but I do not recommend this, as it makes the drink nauseating; it is better if the **Cucuran** is omitted entirely. This same bark, boiled alone in water and drunk, loosens and draws out the stubborn phlegm sitting on the chest. Furthermore, this tree is useful and beneficial for various other abdominal ailments. The young leaves are used for food and added to **Sayor** <term>Sayor|A traditional vegetable soup or stew</term>. The wood of the lower trunk is quite hard and striped—

### CHAPTER LIII.
->**Goat Tree.**<-

***This** tree is as thick as a man, with few main branches, which mostly stand upright. At the tips of these, all around and without order, grow many long, green, and straight twigs, somewhat striped from their rounded shape, and standing on the branches with small joints where they are easily broken off. Upon these, the leaves stand directly opposite each other in 8 to 10 pairs, so similar to those of the* Wild Boarau *that they are hard to distinguish, for they are also 5 to 6 inches long, 2 and 2 ½ inches wide, rounded at the back, and ending in a long point, textured with many parallel ribs, and hairy like those of the* Boarau, *but much flimsier, woollier, and softer to the touch, as are the leaves, stems, and twigs, especially those of the young trees, so that they seem to be made of cloth. Also, there is no sourness in these leaves, as in the* Boarau, *but rather a flat and dry taste, with a small astringency. At the edges they are very finely serrated, though one can hardly recognize this on the old ones; they stand sometimes in pairs, and sometimes one alone at the tip. The large vein does not go straight through the middle, but always lies somewhat closer to the front edge, whereby the back half is always wider, and its base runs somewhat rounder and further out by the stem, as those of the* Nightshade *do. The forward leaves also commonly have at their origin another smaller leaf, like a scrap of cloth, and the young leaves are round and light brown.*

*No blossoms or fruits have I, nor others with me, ever been able to see on this tree, although the* Hoehoenese *claim that where it grows wild in their land, it sometimes produces fruits like* Gnomon. *The branches are also brittle, and have a dry, spongy pith inside. The bark of the trunk is reasonably thick, rough on the outside, and black-green, very sappy and full of a glue-like moisture, sticking fast like* Papeda, *but eventually drying into a* Gum, *without a noticeable smell, and drawing only a little after the resin of* Nanari. *The taste of this bark is sweetish, like the soft shell of a young* Coconut. *The wood is white, soft, and poor, and rots in a short time if it lies in the rain. It is replanted by its branches, but those mostly fail, for which reason some judge it better that one does not replant the freshly cut ones so immediately, but lets them lie for some days in a shady place on the earth until they come to bud of themselves, and only then sets them in the ground.*

**Name.** *In Latin* Capraria, *in Malay* Caju Cambing: *In Amboinese* Aybibi, *and some wish to say that these three names are given to it because the Goats eat its leaves so gladly.*

**Place.** *In Amboina it is little known, and it is only planted in some gardens around the houses, being brought there as sticks or branches from* Plo-Tiga, *3 small and rocky islands situated before the coast of* Hitoe, *where those trees come forth of themselves, as also in the* Hoehoenese *land.*

**Use.** *It is mostly planted in the gardens because its bark is a proven or tested remedy in long-lasting bloody flux <note>Dysentery</note>, and where the intestines are already ulcerated. It is used and prepared in the following manner: one takes from this bark of the trunk a piece a hand long and wide, with the 4th part of a young* Coconut, *crushes it somewhat and boils it in water with a handful of* Pangaga, *and some leaves of* Daun Cucuran, *until about half of the water be boiled away. One then strains it through a cloth, and drinks a small draught of it twice a day, guarding oneself well against eating bacon. Some also add some sugar there, if this drink falls too bitter for them, but which I cannot praise much, because it makes the drink loathsome, and one also does better to leave the* Cucuran *entirely out of it. The same bark boiled and drunk alone, loosens and draws out the tough phlegm that sits on the chest, and moreover this tree is also very useful and serviceable for more other ailments of the belly. The young leaves—*

Against *Gomutu Mengate* <note>original: "Gomutu Mengate," likely referring to shingles or erysipelas, often called "wildfire."</note>, that is, Shingles or "wildfire," its dried leaves may be used if the affected parts are first washed with water in which these leaves have been boiled, and then sprinkled with a fine powder made from them and further wrapped. These same leaves, when green, are placed over a jar of *Bocassan* or *Atsjar* <note>Indonesian condiments; *Bocassan* is a fermented fish paste (terasi) and *Atsjar* refers to pickles.</note> so that they cover it well; if the jar is then sealed with these, it preserves the condiment from rot and prevents worms from entering—indeed, if worms were already present, they would die if the leaves were placed over them. The younger leaves can also serve for *Bocassan* in place of *Oelang* <note>original: "Oelang," referring to raw vegetable side dishes or salads.</note>. # CHAPTER FIFTY-FOUR.
## *Songium. Ay Macuninu.*

Because of the similarity this tree bears to the **Lemon tree** <note>original: "Limonio"</note>, I have placed it in this book as well. I shall say that it reaches roughly the height of a **Durian** <note>original: "Durionis"</note>, its trunk being nearly a fathom thick and bearing a smooth bark. The leaves are positioned at the very tips of the branches, closely joined to one another without a specific order, as in the *Sayor Catappan* <note>The Tropical Almond, *Terminalia catappa*.</note>, with which they most closely agree. However, they sit upon short, thick stalks, over two inches long. These leaves are the longest of those found in the forests, having a length of twenty to twenty-four inches, and are seven or eight inches wide in younger trees. In older trees, they are no more than sixteen inches long and six wide; they gradually narrow at the lower part and are widest at the upper part, ending in a slight point. The midrib is very thick, protruding from both sides; the transverse ribs are also thick, opposite, and parallel, and the leaf edges are deeply serrated.

At the tip of the branches, or from the axil of the highest leaf, a round and green pouch appears, the size of an Imperial Thaler <note>original: "bursa imperialis," a reference to the large silver Reichsthaler coin.</note>, which opens itself into two flaps. Within these, a tender new leaf is hidden, which also bears a similar pouch at its origin. In this manner, the leaves multiply and grow out, which is a peculiar characteristic of this tree. Its flowers and fruit also have something particular that differs from other trees. Its flower is properly composed of a thick head, which encloses the fruit with thick scales that initially lie close to it. These scales, upon opening, present the form of a round cup <note>original: "cupellæ," the Dutch version uses "kammetje" or little comb/cup.</note>, which is whitish and soon falls off; for this reason, the inhabitants say and believe that this fruit is produced without a preceding flower.

This fruit, when fresh after the flower has fallen, is roughly the size of a plum, but it then grows to the size of an **Orange** <note>original: "Mali Aurantii"</note>. It is compressed from a round shape, with a pit or depression at the bottom where it was attached to the branch by a short stalk; two or three grow out together. If the fruit is viewed from the outside, it resembles a closed **Peony** flower, consisting of seven or eight thick, round, and concave overlapping scales. Two of these are extreme and opposite to each other, and so on for the rest. It is a dull green color, or a mixture of gray and green, and is downy to the touch.

When this fruit is fully ripe, these scales open and exhibit the form of a second flower. The internal flesh is then visible, which has the size of a peeled orange and is divided in the same way into many—usually twenty—cells or segments, separated by thin incisions. It is saffron-colored, juicy, and slimy. Each individual segment has hidden within its flesh eight small, flat, and brown seeds or little stones, very similar to the seeds of the **Eggplant** <note>original: "Solani esculenti" or "Trong."</note> or
<meta>catchword: or</meta>

<column-break/>

are also eaten and used as *Sayor* <note>A general term for cooked vegetable dishes.</note>. The wood of the lower trunk is quite hard, somewhat veined, and useful for some carpentry work. Against *Gomutu Mengate*, which is "flying fire" <note>Erysipelas or shingles.</note>, its dried leaves are also used: first wash the sores with the water in which they were boiled, then sprinkle the fine powder on top, and finally cover or bind it. These same leaves, when green and placed on a jar of *Bocassan* or *Atsjar* so that they cover it well, and then tied shut, keep it fresh, protect it from rotting, and never let worms get in; indeed, even if worms were inside, they will die if the leaves are placed upon them. The young foliage is also suitable to eat as *Bocassan* in place of *Oelang*. One can also dry the bark a little in the smoke and preserve it that way for use in times of need, since these trees are so rarely found, and consequently, fresh bark cannot always be obtained.

# CHAPTER 54.
## *Rose Apple Tree.*

*Because of the resemblance this wild tree has to the Lemon trees, I have also given it a place in this second book. I shall say of it that it is about as high as a Durian tree, and about a fathom thick in circumference, having also a smooth bark. The leaves stand at the front of the branches close behind one another, and resemble those of the Sayor Catappan, with which they have great similarity, being without order on short thick stalks, over 2 inches long. These leaves are among the longest found in the woods, namely from 20 to 24 inches, and 7 to 8 inches wide—that is to say, on young trees, for on old trees they are not more than 16 long and 6 wide. They taper gradually toward the back, being widest at the front half, with a short point. The midrib is also very thick and bulging on both sides; the cross-ribs are also thick, parallel, and mostly stand directly opposite one another, being also coarsely serrated at the edges.*

*At the front of the branches, or at the base of the outermost leaf, one sees a round and green pouch, about as large as a Ryksdaalder <note>A large silver coin.</note>, which opens into 2 flaps, and therein one finds a young leaf, which also has a similar pouch at its origin. Thus the leaves continue to put themselves forth, being a hallmark or natural character of this tree. The flowers and fruits also have something special, which differs from other trees: for the flower is actually a round bud, which covers the enclosed fruit with thick scales or lies close to it. These scales, upon opening, take the shape of a round cup, which is whitish in color and falls off immediately; therefore the locals also say that the fruit comes forth without a blossom.*

*The young fruit, after the falling of the flower, is about as large as a plum, but it grows thereafter to the size of an Orange, rounded and somewhat flattened, with a pit in the back where they sit close against the stem with a short thick foot, hanging 2 and 3 together. The fruit, viewed from the outside, looks not unlike a closed Peony Rose, with 7 and 8 thick, round, and convex scales lying upon one another, of which 2 are the outermost, and so the others also lie upon one another. The color is a dirty green, or a mixture of gray and green, and woolly to the touch.*

*Now when the fruit is perfectly ripe, these scales open and remain standing like a second flower, showing the inner flesh, which is still the size of a peeled Orange, and also divided in the same way into many—commonly 20—pieces, distinguished by thin notches. It is deep yellow, juicy, and slimy, each piece having in its flesh about 8 small flat and brownish seeds, very much like the seeds of Solanum Esculentum or **Trong** <note>The Malay word for eggplant.</note>. The taste is twofold,*

...or very similar to the *Trongi* <note>A type of eggplant or citrus, depending on the context, but here likely referring to the shape of a Citron</note>. The flavor of these fruits is twofold, following the two different species. The first has a flavor that is initially slightly acidic, but as it matures, it becomes wine-like and sweetens. In the second variety, however, the flavor is always sour, and one cannot tell from the smell alone that the fruit is so acidic. Nevertheless, both are eaten and used either raw or pickled in brine, and the inhabitants of Celebes <note>Modern-day Sulawesi</note> seek these fruits out eagerly. When such a "pomme" or apple is open, it hangs from the tree for a long time with its flesh exposed and surrounded by its scales, but eventually, everything falls off together; these fruits are picked as soon as these scales begin to open.

If the bark of the trunk is cut, a copious amount of juice flows out, just as from a Mango tree, but it does not dry into a Gum. Its wood consists of coarse fibers; it is soft and of little use.

Another species of this tree occurs in Celebes, called the "male" variety, similar in form and growth to the first, but this tree produces no edible fruit. From the buds, which are about the size of boys' playing marbles, nothing grows but scaly flowers, which produce no true fruit and are of no use.

*Name.* In Latin, *Songium*. In the part of Amboina called *Hoeamohel* <note>The Hoamoal Peninsula</note>, it is called *Aylassalinu* and *Ay Macuninu*. The first name denotes a fruit having a form mixed between a *Lansium* and a *Blimbing* <note>Starfruit</note>; the second indicates a sour fruit. In Celebes, around *Tambocco*, it is called *Songi* and *Menampa*. By the Buginese, it is *Songin*; by the Macassarese and people of Malabar, *Songo*; and by the Javanese, *Sambu*.

*Location.* In Amboina proper, the tree is unknown, but it grows wild in the forests of northern *Hoeamohel*, near the *Nassau* strait near *Nanat*, and behind *Lada* in the mountains. It occurs more abundantly on the eastern coast of Celebes around *Tambocco*, where three species are found: namely the sweet, the sour, and the sterile or "Male" kind. Furthermore, it is found in the Bugis and Macassar districts, both in the wild and planted around houses.

*Use.* Among those peoples where this fruit grows abundantly, it is used in place of sour Lemons; it is also eaten raw when fully ripe, either alone or with a little salt. However, it is most often cooked with fish as a sour seasoning. The opened fruits are preserved in brine like *Atsjar* <note>Atchar, a type of South Asian/Indonesian pickle</note> and eaten with meals. In Celebes, they are much sought after by those suffering from fever to extinguish their thirst, as well as by pregnant women who crave them. These fruits, once opened, cannot be kept for long because they rot easily and acquire a flat taste like weak vinegar. The fallen fruits are eaten by land tortoises, which are often found under these trees. The wood of the tree, if dried, becomes hard, making it suitable for forming *Pangayen* <note>Poles or rowing oars</note>.

### Plate Forty-Five

Displays the *Dillenia*, which is called *Songium* by Rumphius.

### OBSERVATION.

Although the truly wonderful and almost inimitable flowers and fruits of this tree were perhaps not fully expressed by our author due to their peculiar shape, it is clear to me from the author's description that this is, if not the same, at least a species of the admirable tree called *Syalita*. Under that name, it is described in the **Hortus Malabaricus** <note>original: "H. Malab." — The Garden of Malabar, a massive 12-volume botanical work on Indian flora</note> *Volume 3, Plates 38 and 39*, where it is elegantly displayed and should certainly be examined. This tree is called DILLENIA by *Linnaeus* in the **Hortus Cliffortianus** <note>A work by Carl Linnaeus describing the gardens of George Clifford</note> *page 221*, and in *Plukenet's Mantissa, page 124*, it is called the *Malabar Rose-Apple called Syalita* <note>original: "Malus rosea Malabarica Syalita dicta"</note>. It is also mentioned by *John Ray* in his *History of Plants, page 1707*, as the *Indian tree with a very large flower, upon which many pods grow* <note>original: "Arbor Indica flore maximo, cui multae innascuntur siliquae"</note>.

<column-break/>

...of the two kinds found there: in one, it is initially a dull sour, but in ripeness, it becomes vinous and sweetish. However, in the other, it is and remains sour, and one could not tell from the scent that this fruit is sour. Nevertheless, both are used and eaten, both raw and pickled: and the inhabitants of Celebes make much use of them. The opened Apple remains with its naked flesh and the surrounding scales for a long time hanging on the tree, but they finally fall off together; however, they are plucked as soon as one sees them open.

If one hacks or cuts into the bark of the trunk, a rich or fairly large amount of sap runs out, just like from the Mango tree, but it congeals into no Gum. The wood is coarse-threaded, also soft, and entirely worthless <note>Referring to its quality for construction when fresh</note>.

There is another kind of this tree on Celebes, which is also called the male, being similar in growth and appearance to the previous one, but no edible fruits come to it, for from the buds, which are the size of a marble, nothing else comes forth than scaly flowers, which give no real fruits, and are therefore useless.

*Name.* In Latin *Songium*, in Amboinese on *Hoeamohel Aylaffalinu*, and *Ay Macuninu*. The first name is intended to mean a fruit that has a mixed shape of *Lansium* and *Blimbing*, and the other is to say sour fruit. On Celebes, near *Tambocco*, it is called *Songi* and *Menampa*; by the *Buginese Songin*; at *Macassar* and in *Malay Songo*; in *Javanese Sambu*.

*Place.* On Amboina, it is unknown, but grows wild on the north side of *Hoeamohel*, near the *Nassau* gap, at *Nanat*, and behind *Laala* in the mountains. One finds it more abundantly on the East coast of Celebes, near *Tambocco*, where one has three kinds of it, such as sweet, sour, and barren, or the Male. Furthermore, it is also to be found in the Buginese and Macassarese district, both in the wild and planted by the houses.

*Use.* By that nation where it falls abundantly, the fruit is used in place of sour Lemons: and they are also eaten raw, when they are entirely ripe, both with and without salt. But the most is cooked with Fish, to make the broth sour. The opened ones are pickled, like Atchar, and eaten with food. On Celebes, they are much sought for feverish people, to beat the thirst, and for pregnant Women, who have a craving. The opened fruits one cannot keep for long, because they rot easily, and get a flat taste, just like stale Vinegar. The fallen fruits are eaten up by the Land Tortoises, which one then finds under these trees; its wood dries hard, and is suitable for making *Pangayen* <note>Poles or paddles</note> from it.

### REMARK.

Although the wonderful flowers and fruits of this tree, possibly because of their particular appearance with their parts, were not extensively depicted by our Writer, it appears to me from the description, that if this is not the same, it is at least a kind of the *Syalita*, as it is named in the third part *Plate 38 and 39* of the **Hortus Malabaricus**, which is the DILLENIA of *Linnaeus* in the **Hortus Cliffortianus** *p. 221*, which by *Plukenet* in his *Mantissa p. 124* is named *Malabar Rose-Apple called Syalita*, and by *Ray* in his *History of Plants page 1707*, *Indian Tree, with the largest flower, on which many pods grow*.

# AMBOINESE HERBAL Book II. chap. LIV.

Related to the *Songium* is the *Sangius*, which we subjoin here from the twenty-ninth chapter of the *Supplement*.

**S**angius is a vast and widely spreading forest tree, scattering its branches very broadly like a *Mango*, which is divided into male and female varieties that share similar foliage.

First; the *Male Sangius* or *Sangi* bears a taller trunk, covered in a rough bark that is whitish or ash-colored on the outside; the branches are curved, upon which the leaves sit solitary but closely joined. These leaves extend from 9 to 14 inches in length and are five inches wide on older trees, while on younger trees they are 18 inches long and 9 wide. They are supported by short, thick petioles <note>The stalk that joins a leaf to a stem</note>, and are sharply toothed at the edges as if they were prickly, though not deeply so. On the underside, many oblique and swollen ribs protrude; furthermore, the leaves are resonant <note>original: "sonora"; they make a rattling sound when dry or shaken</note> and have a slightly acidic taste. The tip of the small branches ends in a flat pouch shaped like a coin but more oblong, and from its side a small leaf grows out, which, when it opens, emits another new leaf, to which a similar small pouch is joined.

From the axils <note>The upper angle between a leaf stalk and the stem</note> of the upper leaves, a round peduncle <note>flower stalk</note> grows out, about the length of a pinky finger, which divides into two others, each bearing a specific head. From the origin of these, a third peduncle sprouts, producing a similar head. These small heads are round, slightly compressed, the size of a *Nipis* Lime <note>original: "Limonis Nipis"; the Key Lime, Citrus aurantiifolia</note>, and are covered on the outside by five concave, thick, wrinkled, and hairy scales, which will be described more broadly in the female section. When these open, they display a mass of thick yellow threads <note>stamens</note> arranged around the head, and together these present the form of a rose. However, this central tubercle does not grow into a fruit, and the entire flower falls away uselessly, leaving the stalk bare.

Second; the *Female Sangius* agrees with the former in its trunk and leaves, and the flower heads sprout in a similar manner, but they are larger; indeed, when they are open, they have a diameter of six inches. On the outside, they are likewise adorned with five somewhat round and very thick petals hollowed out like spoons, which are yellow on the outside like apples, but thinner at the edges. Two of these outer petals are smaller than the rest and surround the entire fruit. The other three middle ones are the largest and placed in a triangle, together representing the form of a rose or flower. In their center is placed a round "apple," which takes the appearance of a peeled Chinese Orange <note>A mandarin or similar citrus</note> composed of many scales; in each scale or fold, a soft thread or stamen is hidden, all of which meet and join at the top. These "apples" fall off when ripe, offering a flavor between sweet and acidic; however, as long as they cling to the tree, they are mostly acidic and have an odor like Oranges.

In Amboina, two species of this are found, but in *Celebes* <note>Modern-day Sulawesi</note> four are found, the first of which is the Male described above. Of the Female, three varieties are observed: the first is yellowish on the outside, or apple-colored, which is the most common; the second is whitish on the outside, which is considered the sweetest; the third is red on the outside, like the color of *Cafomba* <note>Likely referring to safflower or a similar reddish dye</note>. This last one is rarely eaten raw due to its acidity and hangs so abundantly from the tree that its entire canopy often appears red.

*Name.* In Latin, the *Sangius* tree, and *Sangium* its fruit; in Celebes around Tambacco, *Sangi* and *Songi*; in Macassar, which is also the same as in Malay, *Boeboeken*, that is, "wood of the Borers," for *Boeboe* denotes a wood-borer <note>original: "Cossis"; referring to wood-eating larvae or beetles</note>, as its wood is prone to decay and is much eaten by borers. In the more northern parts and in the mountains around Toleta, it is called *Dengen*; in Java, *Copaal*; in the Loehoe region, *Ay Macianinu* and *Ay Massaninu*, which denotes an acidic fruit like the *Bilimbing* <note>The Starfruit, Averrhoa carambola</note>.

*Location.* In Amboina, it is exotic <note>Not native</note>, but it occurs in the Loehoe region though not abundantly; it is more frequent in Celebes, both in its eastern region around Tambacco and in the West around Macassar, and in the mountains of Toleta. It is also found in Java, but its fruit is not eaten there, although it reaches the width of two palms; there it is left for the wild boars.

<meta>Usage.</meta>

<column-break/>

*To the Songium belongs also the Sangius, which we add here from the 29th Chapter of the Supplement.*

**S**angius is a large and widely-extended forest tree, its branches spreading out wide like a Mango tree, divided into Male and Female, which are similar to one another in their leaves.

1. *Sangius Mas* or *Sangi*, the Male, becomes somewhat higher in the trunk, clothed with a rough bark, white on the outside or pulling towards gray, and the branches are crooked. On them stand the leaves singly, yet shortly after one another; they are from 9 to 14 inches long, and 5 wide on the old trees, but on the young trees they are 18 long and 9 wide, standing on short thick stalks, sharply toothed on the edges as if prickly, yet not deep, and occupied underneath with many slanted and sharply bulging ribs; furthermore stiff, rattling, and sourish of taste. The extremity of the twigs ends in a flat little pouch like a small coin <note>original: "dubbeltje"; a small Dutch coin</note>, but oblong, and has at the side a young leaf, which, opening itself, brings forth another young leaf whereon another pouch sits.

From the leaf-axil of the foremost leaves comes a round stalk, a small finger long, which divides itself into two others, of which each bears a particular ball; from this origin comes a third stalk, which bears a single ball. These balls are round or flat, the size of a Nipis Lemon, clothed outside with 5 convex and thick scales, rough and hairy, as follows more broadly hereafter in the Female. These opening up show from the inside a clump of thick yellow threads, which stand around a middle-globule, together representing the form of a rose; yet the middle globule becomes no fruit, and the whole flower falls off for nothing at all, leaving behind the bare stalk.

2. *Sangius Foemina* or the *Female* is like the previous one in trunk and leaves, and the flower-balls come forth in a similar manner, but they become larger, namely, the opened ones are 6 fingers wide, having on the outside five roundish and very thick leaves <note>petals</note>, convex like spoons, apple-yellow on the outside, and thin at the edges. Of these, the two outermost are smaller than the others, which have kept the entire fruit enclosed. The three innermost are the largest, and stand in a triangle, together making up the form of a flower or rose. Inside stands a round Apple, in the form of a peeled Chinese sweet Apple, made of many folds, and in each fold lies a soft thread, which together close at the top. The ripe ones fall off entirely, of a taste mixed from sweet and tart, but on the tree mostly sour, of a smell like Orange-Apples.

Here in Amboina we have but two kinds, but on *Celebes* one finds four kinds, of which the first is the Male, described above. Of the Female one has 3 variations: The first is yellowish on the outside or Apple-colored, which is the most common. The second are whitish on the outside, which one considers the sweetest. The third are reddish on the outside or *Cafomba*-colored, and are eaten raw by few because of their sourness, and hang so much on the tree that it appears red.

*Name.* In Latin *Sangius* the tree, and *Sangium* the fruit. On Celebes around Tambacco *Sangi* and *Songi*, at Macassar, which one can also take for Malay, *Boeboeken*, that is worm-wood, for *Boeboe* is a wood-worm, because its wood easily becomes worm-eaten. Somewhat further north, and in the mountains around Toleta, he is named *Dengen*, on Java *Copaal*, in the Loehoe Land *Ay Macianinu* and *Ay Massaninu*, which is to say a fruit that is as sour as *Bilimbing*.

*Place.* Here in Amboina it is exotic, but one finds it on the Land of Loehoe, and that but little; it occurs more on Celebes, as well in the East around Tambacco, as in the West around Macassar, and the mountains of Toleta. On Java one finds it also, yet it is not eaten there. Although its fruits are two hands wide, it is left there for the wild hogs.

II Book. LIV. Chapter. AMBOINESE HERBAL. 143

Uses. The fruits of the "female" tree <note>Rumphius often categorized plants as male or female based on fruitfulness or robustness, rather than modern botanical sex</note>, as has been said, are eaten raw, but it is necessary that they ripen on the tree itself and fall of their own accord. They are not much different from sweet Oranges and provide a pleasant refreshment in the fields for the rice harvesters. For this purpose, gardens are even established there so that thirst may be quenched. Its wood is also used for the hearth, as it is not suitable for building houses nor is it durable. In Tambocco, the fruits are eaten raw and are also cooked with fish; they are also sought after in the forests to quench thirst. The bark of the trunk, crushed with water, is used as a gargle against <term>aphthas<note>original: "aphthas"; refers to thrush or small mouth ulcers</note></term> in infants. The leaves serve as plates for tables as well as napkins; however, it is harmful for those suffering from <term>rhagades<note>original: "rhagadibus"; painful cracks or fissures in the skin, often on the hands or feet</note></term> to place their food on these leaves.

In the *Hortus Malabaricus, part 3, Figure 38*, it is called *Syalita* in the Malabar language. In the Brahman language <note>referring to Konkani or Sanskrit terms used by scholars in Goa</note> *Karinbalapala*, and in Portuguese *Fruita Estrelada* <note>Star Fruit, though here referring to the Dillenia's appearance</note>. By the Dutch it is called *Roos Appel* <note>Rose Apple</note>, and the Latin name given in the annotations is *Malus Rosea* <note>original: "Malus Rosea"; literally "Rose Apple"</note>, which pleases me greatly. The Malabar name signifies sincerity or purity. The parts of the flower and the fruit, or apple, are described there at length, though not all of those details are observed in the Amboinese variety.

Use. *The fruits of the Female, as stated, are eaten raw, but must ripen on the tree and fall off by themselves, at which time they do not differ much from sweet Apples. On Tambocco they are eaten raw, and also cooked with fish, as well as in the forest to quench thirst. The bark of the trunk, rubbed in water and used to rinse the mouth, serves against the <term>thrush<note>original: "sprauw"; a fungal infection of the mouth common in children</note></term> of children. The leaves serve as table-plates and napkins, but those who have cracked feet and <term>chapped heels<note>original: "kakbielen"; painful fissures in the skin of the heels</note></term> must not lay their food upon these leaves.*

### CHAPTER ONE.
#### *Common Canarium. Black Canari.*

This tree also belongs to those from which the inhabitants of these Eastern regions take their daily food, as was indicated above regarding the *Calappa* <note>Coconut</note>, *Pinanga* <note>Areca or Betel nut</note>, *Sagu* <note>Sago</note>, and similar plants; however, it has been reserved for this third book so that it might serve as the leader of the resin-bearing trees. Various species of it occur, of which the first two are specifically used for food; these also provide the smallest amount of resin and are divided into domestic and wild varieties, although properly speaking, both are propagated without human assistance.

The first species is the domestic or common *Canarium*, which is a tall and noble tree, bearing a whitish bark and branches extended like an Oak. On these, many curved and knotted twigs are found, and on these are numerous irregular leaf-stalks <note>original: "raches"; the main stem of a compound leaf</note>. These are jointed at their base where they break easily, and the stalks themselves are likewise jointed once or twice. The younger and uppermost stalks emerge from their joint between two scaly leaflets of a peculiar structure and form, usually triangular or shaped like a tongue; their lower part is tightly bound to the branch and surrounds the stalk like a sheath. They are deeply serrated at the edges, wrinkled, and pale green—this is always found as a certain identifying characteristic in the *Canarium* species. As the leaf-stalks mature and grow older, these small leaflets fall off. These are observed more abundantly in the wild species than in the domestic one. On the stalks, three, four, or five pairs of opposing leaves are placed. These are usually a span long <note>about 9 inches</note>, or eight, nine, or ten inches in length, and more than a palm or five fingers wide, tapering to a point at the top. On older trees, they are smaller, with even edges, and are woven through with many parallel yellowish ribs that are also opposite each other. The larger middle vein does not pass directly through the middle of the leaf to the stem; the lower part of the leaf is very wide, smooth, firm, making a rattling sound, and blackish. If the leaf is broken, it wrinkles or contracts and dries to a hard state. If these leaves are rubbed, they breathe out a strong, resinous scent by which they are quickly recognized. This tree forms a high, dense canopy that appears blackish from a distance.

At the tips of the branches, other thick and woody stems grow out, dividing into a few others, from which the flowers sprout. These are at first pale green heads contained between two green leaflets which open on both sides like valves. These heads have the shape of a small jug <note>original: "crateris"</note>, the belly of which is a round calyx. In its center are placed three thick and narrow petals which end in three thick points and open up, forming the mouth or orifice of the jug. Gradually these dilate more, and in their center they reveal a green, headed pistil, which is the germ or the beginning of the fruit. Such are the flowers of the common fruit-bearing *Canarium*, which is called the female; besides this, however, a male occurs, whose trunk and leaves do not differ much from the common one, but its flowering cluster is larger.
