### CHAPTER I.
#### The Common Canary-Tree.

This tree also belongs among those from which the inhabitants of these Eastern quarters have their daily food, as was said above of the *Calappus*, *Pinang*, *Sagu*, etc., but it has been saved for this third book so that it might be a precursor of the resin-bearing <note>Dutch: "hars-dragende"</note> trees. One has several sorts of them, of which the first two are properly used for food, just as they also give the least resin; they are divided into domestic and wild, although properly speaking both mostly come forth without the help of men.

Firstly: The first kind is the domestic or common *Canary*, a tall and full-grown tree with a smooth, whitish bark and wide-spreading branches like an Oak. <note>The Dutch text here omits the "Oak-tongue" description found in the Latin but mentions the scaly leaflets as "sheaths"</note>. These sheaths surround the aforementioned shoots; they are bearded or deeply saw-toothed at the edges, ribbed, and pale green in color, and all the *Canary* kinds have this as a special characteristic. When the shoots become old, these little leaves fall off, and one sees them more on the wild sort than on the domestic. On the shoots stand 3, 4, and 5 pairs of leaves directly opposite one another. They are commonly a span long, or 8, 9, or 10 inches, and a good hand or five fingers wide, running into a narrow point or tip at the front. On the old trees they fall somewhat smaller, with smooth edges, and threaded with many parallel yellow ribs standing alternately against each other. Also, the large vein does not run straight through the middle by the stem, and the rear half of the leaf is wider there, smooth, stiff, rattling, blackish-green, and when broken, it shrinks together and dries hard. When one rubs them, they give off a strong resinous scent from themselves, by which one can recognize them immediately. The tree makes a high and dense crown, appearing black from afar.

At the front of the branches, other thick woody stems come forth, dividing into a few others, and on these the bloom, which is first pale green buds, which stand closed between two green leaflets that open to both sides like caps <note>original: "klapmutzen"</note>. These buds have the shape of a small jar <note>original: "kroesje"</note>, whose belly is a round cup; in there stand three thick narrow leaflets which open themselves into three thick points, making up the mouth of the jar. With time they open a bit wider and show in the middle a green bud with a little knob on top, from which the creation of the fruit comes. Such is the bloom of the common fruit-bearing *Canary*, which is held to be the Female; besides which there is also the Male, not differing much from the common one in trunk and leaves, though the flowering cluster is larger and more spread out; the bloom...

<columns>
...is larger and more extended, so that the flowers—which consist of three notable, thick, waxy, and dull-white petals contained in a wider calyx—also have a pistil or germ surrounded by five stamens boasting brown anthers. This flower, moreover, gives off a faint scent approaching that of the *Champaca* <note>original: "Sjampaccae"; the fragrant Magnolia champaca</note> flower, which is likewise observed in the flower of the common *Canarium* if it is kept in the house for several days; after the male flowers, no fruits follow, wherefore it is not highly valued and also rarely occurs except near the shores.

The fruits hang from long clusters, two or three on a specific stalk, and they resemble Walnuts <note>original: "Juglandes"</note> not poorly, except that they are smaller and more oblong, covered on the outside by a grey-green, smooth, and even husk, which gradually turns black or bluish, like the larger Plums. These fruits are oblong rather than truly round, but somewhat triangular and compressed in the upper part, with a small and short tip, joined at their lower part to a certain small cup-like disk from which they are easily separated and fall when they ripen. Under this husk, which is about the thickness of a straw, a hard and bony nut is hidden, also triangular, but its angles are somewhat rounded; since the differences between the species or varieties are best distinguished by this nut, we divide it into four species: namely, two larger and two smaller, and of these, the larger are either oblong or round, as are the smaller.

The first, the large oblong species, bears fruit about three fingers long and a thumb thick, which is also the size of the interior nut, for the substance of the husk is barely a knife's thickness. It has three sides, each a thumb wide, which meet below in three sharp angles, but above these nuts are flatter and form a blunt cone. Its shell is about the thickness of a quill, but brittle, and shatters like glass if struck; if it is crushed, the central cavity contains an oblong and compressed kernel, protruding more from one side as if it were also triangular. It is round on one side and pointed on the other, very similar to Almonds <note>original: "Amygdalis"</note> but twice as large, and covered on the outside with a similar reddish skin, under which a white substance is hidden, composed of six oblong and sinuous segments; a seventh and smallest part is found in the cone. All of these can be easily separated in a fresh nut and, if done carefully, joined together again; but in dry nuts, this cannot be done. If such peeled kernels are viewed from the lower or flat part, they present the form and appearance of a certain Chinese person walking dressed in long and wide sleeves. The flavor of the kernel is sweet like Hazelnuts, but its substance is flatter and softer. Among all *Canarium* species, this largest one is the most tasteless, and hence not so pleasing if eaten raw, but it is mostly used to form the oblong sticks called *Bagea* <note>A traditional snack or biscuit made from sago and nuts</note>, which will be discussed later.

This tree is not wild, but grows around villages and in the "forest-gardens" of the Amboinese; its leaves are very large, ten or eleven inches long and five fingers wide. Its trunk is rounder and straighter than in others, not as tall, but thicker, and slightly buttressed near the roots.

The second *Canarium* species is the one that bears large round fruits, whose leaves are very similar to the first, but their tip is shorter, and the trunk itself is taller; the fruits are about a finger's breadth shorter than the preceding ones, but rounder and thicker. The nut itself is two fingers long, and each side or angle is a thumb wide and triangular, but its angles are mostly rounded or flat; its substance is harder than in the preceding one and is opened with difficulty. Inside it has only a single cavity, and in that is contained a similar kernel, shorter and thicker, but of a harder substance, which is better than the first.

The third species is the small oblong, which has a taller trunk but smaller leaves than the preceding: the nut is over two fingers long, and each of its angles is a small finger wide; its internal kernel is very similar to the first species, but thinner, of a fattier substance, and better flavor.

The fourth species is the small round, entirely similar to the second species except that it bears smaller kernels.

<column-break/>

...the structure is also larger, made of three remarkably thick, fatty, and dull-white petals standing in a wider cup; also the inner bud or creation of the fruit is surrounded by five threads with brown tips. It has a weak scent, approaching the flower of the *Champaca*, which one also notices in the blossom of the common *Canary* if it is kept in the house for a few days; after the blossom of the male, no fruits follow, therefore they are not esteemed and seldom found, and that mostly near the beach.

The fruits also hang in large clusters together, two or three together on a specific stalk, and do not poorly resemble our Walnuts, except that they are smaller and more oblong, covered on the outside with a blue-green husk, smooth and even, which in time becomes black or slightly bluish, like the large Plums. These fruits are not truly round in their length, but somewhat three-sided, and somewhat flat at the front, with a small short tip, and are fixed at the back to the disk, like a saucer, from which they easily fall when they become ripe. Under this husk, about a straw-stalk thick, lies a hard stony nut, also mostly three-sided, though the edges are somewhat round; and because one can best know the difference of the varieties by this nut, we shall divide them into four, namely into two large and two small, the large consisting of an oblong and a round one, and likewise the small.

First, the large oblong possesses fruits about three fingers long and one thumb thick, as large as the inner nut is, for the flesh of the husk is barely a knife thick. It has three sides, each a thumb wide, and at the back they run together with three sharp edges, but at the front they fall somewhat broad and make there a blunt tip. This shell is quite a quill thick, yet crumbly, and snaps like glass if one knocks on it; inside they have but one cavity, and therein an oblong flat kernel, except that one side bulges out a bit as if it were also three-sided. At one end round, and at the other somewhat pointed, very like the Almonds, yet twice as large, also covered on the outside with a similar red skin, under which a white set of six oblong and curved pieces is put together, with the seventh and smallest at the tip, which one can easily separate from each other in the fresh nuts, and also if one pays close attention, put together again, but not in the dry ones; also if one sees these peeled kernels from the back or from the flat side, they show the appearance of a Chinese person walking with his long sleeves. The taste is sweet, like the Hazelnuts, or else so bland, also softer of substance. Among all *Canary* sorts, this large one is indeed the blandest, and therefore not so pleasant to eat raw, but is mostly used to make the oblong sticks thereof, which one calls *Bagea*, of which more hereafter.

These trees are not found in the wild, but around the villages, and in their Amboinese forest-gardens, and they have indeed the largest leaves, ten and eleven inches long, and five fingers wide. The trunk is rounder and straighter than the others, not so high, but thicker, and with small wings <note>buttress roots</note> at the roots.

The second sort, being large round *Canaries* with leaves mostly like the previous, though the front tip on them is a bit shorter, and the trunk a bit higher; the fruits are about a cross-finger shorter than the previous, thicker, and rounder; the nut is two cross-fingers long, having each side a thumb wide, three-sided, though the edges are mostly round or flat; they are harder of substance than the previous and more difficult to knock open. Inside they also have but one cavity, and therein a similar kernel, though somewhat shorter and thicker, of harder substance, and better of taste than the previous.

The third, the small oblong, have a yet higher trunk, but somewhat smaller leaves than the previous: the nut is fully two fingers long, and each side a small finger wide, from within with a kernel like the first kind, but narrower, fattier of substance, and better of taste.

The fourth, small round, are in everything like the second sort, except that they bear smaller kernels.

# III Book. I. Chapter. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

<columns>
All these four species have only a single cavity, which distinguishes them from the wild species; however, by a quirk of nature, some are occasionally found that bear two and rarely even three cells, with a separate kernel in each, which is most often observed in those two round species. On the contrary, two kernels often appear joined and grown together in one cell, or separated only by a thin brown skin. The third species also has this peculiarity: when struck with a stone, it breaks into three oblong parts, as if it were composed of three segments. The two smaller species are also of a more solid and oily substance, which is why they are most often used for pressing oil.

Furthermore, all Canarium species have this peculiarity: they bear wing-like growths near the roots above the ground around the trunk, as if thin pillars were built against the tree. The Malays call these wings by the general names *Tambi, Tabir,* or *Panir,* which we call a "seat" <note>original Latin: "sedem"; Dutch: "stoel"</note>; the Amboinese call them *Lakin*. The two larger species bear the smallest wings, but in the smaller and wild species, these wings are very large and wide, rising to the height of two men against the trunk—sometimes straight, sometimes curved—and are generally as thick as a hand's breadth, so that it appears as if several small chambers were fixed to the trunk. There are some other forest trees that bear similar growths, but none so large and singular as the *Canarium*.

The wood of this tree is whitish, solid, and hard, but not very durable because of its oiliness, which easily breeds woodworms <note>original: "cossos"</note>; and when it is dry, it is brittle. When the Canary fruits turn black, most of the tree's leaves fall off, so that it stands almost bare and naked, and the fruits hang exposed. Then the locals must climb the tree, tying long poles with rungs to the tree to make the ascent easier, and they strike the ripe fruit with long sticks; otherwise, the ripe Canary fruits fall easily of their own accord and serve as food for the pigs, like acorns. The pigs greedily devour these nuts, and they are often caught by this habit, as one can hear them from afar or at night cracking the nuts with their teeth. Immediately after the fruit has fallen, the tree puts forth new leaves, and one often sees on one and the same tree one part flourishing with fresh and green leaves, while the other has cast off most of its older leaves; however, fruits are never seen on such a green branch as they are on the others.

*Season.* All Canary species that are considered domestic bloom at the beginning of the rainy months—that is, in May or June—and the fruits ripen and are gathered in the first dry months, which is October and November. But those which open their flowers in the month of September give ripe fruit in March and April, and are called *Canari Barat* <note>meaning "West-monsoon Canary"</note>; these constitute almost a distinct kind, about which more in the following chapter.

*Name.* In Latin, *Canarium Vulgare*. In Malay, *Canari*, and of these, the first two species are *Canari Besar* <note>Great Canary</note> and *Canari Baggea* <note>named for their use in making Baggea cakes</note>. The two other species, *Canari Kitsjil* <note>Small Canary</note>, are subdivided into *Pand-jang*, which means long, and *Pende*, which means short and round. By those of Ternate, the Canary is called *Nya* and *Niba*. By the Amboinese, *Yar* and *Yal*. By those of Banda, *Nanari*.

*Place.* This tree occurs in all the islands of the Moluccan and Amboinese territories, especially on the two islands of Manipa and Kelang; furthermore, throughout all of Ceram as far as the South-Eastern islands; indeed, some confirm that it is found in New Guinea itself and the adjacent southern region. It also occurs in Banda, but only the smaller species; however, every year a sufficient supply of another species is brought there from the islands of Key and Aru. In the western islands, such as Celebes, Bali, and Java, it is unknown, except that a certain small species of Canary occurs in Java near Semarang, the fruit of which is brought to Batavia <note>modern-day Jakarta</note> for sale. In Makassar there are also some trees, but propagated from fruit brought from elsewhere. Although they now grow in these islands without human help, they are mostly sown by wild pigeons and bats, which swallow the whole fruits; when the husk is nearly digested, they void the whole nuts again through their excrement. These, touching the earth, sprout into small trees, in which manner many other fruit-bearing trees are propagated; nevertheless, all these trees have their owners.

<column-break/>

*All four species usually have only one cavity inside, by which they can be distinguished from the wild ones; yet there are some among them that have two, and rarely three little chambers inside, and a particular kernel in each, which is mostly seen in the two round species. On the contrary, one often finds two kernels grown together in one chamber, or separated only by the brown skin. The third species also has the characteristic that, when knocked open with a stone, it falls apart into three oblong pieces, as if it were composed of three parts. Likewise, the two small species are much firmer in substance and more oily, which is why they are mostly used to press oil from them.*

*Furthermore, all Canary lineages have this mark: that near the roots above the earth, around the trunk, they have certain outgrowths in the shape of wings, as if some thin pillars were masonry-built against the tree; the Malays call these wings by the general name* Tambi, Tabir, *or* Panir. *We call it a* seat <note>original Dutch: "stoel"</note>, *the Amboinese* Lakin, *and the two large species mentioned above have the smallest wings; but in the small and wild species, they are very large and wide, rising two men high against the trunk, some straight, some curved, and generally a hand-breadth thick, so that it seems as if several little chambers were built onto the trunk; there are a few more forest trees that have such wings, yet none so rare and large as the Canary tree.*

*The wood of this tree is indeed white, dense, and hard, yet not so durable because of its oiliness, which easily produces worms, and because it breaks easily when dry. Now when the Canaries begin to turn black, most of the leaves fall from the tree, so that it stands almost bare and the fruits hang exposed. Then the locals must climb the trees, tying some long poles with rungs against the tree to come up more easily, and likewise strike off the ripe fruits with long sticks; for otherwise the ripe Canaries fall very easily of their own accord and become prey for the pigs, like acorns, which are very greedy for these nuts, by which they are also often caught when one hears them cracking them with their teeth at night or from afar. As soon as the fruits have fallen, the tree begins to get new foliage again, and one often sees that on one and the same tree sometimes one half stands youthful and full of leaves while the other has cast off most of the old ones, but on the green branch one will see no fruit, as on the other.*

*Season.* <note>original: "Sayfoen," a corruption of the Arabic-Malay "musim" or season</note> *All Canary lineages that are reckoned as domestic bloom at the start of the rainy monsoon, that is in May or June, and bear harvest in the first dry monsoon months, that is in October and November: But those which begin to bloom in September become ripe in March and April, and these they call* Canari Barat, *making almost a particular lineage, of which more in the following chapter.*

*Name. In Latin* Canarium Vulgare, *in Malay* Canari, *and from that the first two species* Canari Besar, *and* Canari Baggea, *from the following use. The two other species* Canari Kitsjil, *being both subdivided into* Pand-jang, *that is long, and* Pende, *that is short round. In Ternate* Nya *and* Niha, *in Amboinese* Yar *and* Yal, *on Banda* Nanari.

*Place. This tree is found in all islands of the Moluccan and Amboinese territory, especially on both islands Manipa and Kelang: Furthermore through all of Ceram to the South-Eastern Islands, yes, some assure us that they are even found on New Guinea and on the adjacent South-land: In Banda one has them too, but only the small lineage, but they are yearly sufficiently provided from the islands Key and Aru: In the more westerly islands, such as Celebes, Bali, and Java they are unknown, except that one finds a species of small Canary on Java around Semarang, which they sometimes bring to Batavia for sale. # AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. Chapter I.

<columns>
and owners, nor is it permitted for anyone to cut them down as they wish, since they serve the inhabitants for their daily and necessary food.

<margin>Usage.</margin>
The inhabitants of these islands derive a great deal of their nourishment and food from the fruits of this tree; for these are not only eaten raw to fill the stomach, as is most common among the locals, but also as a delicacy, as is done by our people <note>The "our people" refers to the Dutch colonists and traders of the 17th century</note>, by whom they are sought after for dessert courses and to accompany the drinking of tea. They are used in the same way as <term>Almonds<note>original Latin: "Amygdalæ"</note></term> are in Europe, from which a newcomer or traveler can hardly distinguish them; hence it is read in some journals that these islands also produce almonds. These fruits are, however, somewhat unhealthy and harmful if eaten when too fresh, which is known if their outer skin is not yet reddish but a pale white, marked here and there with purple streaks. At that stage, these fruits very easily cause diarrhea and dysentery due to their excessive sliminess, though this can be corrected to some extent if a little salt is added to them. However, the greater part of them, still enclosed in their shells, are dried in smoke so that they may serve for daily use. These "Canary" fruits, once hardened by smoke, are not good if eaten raw, as the outer skin cannot be separated and they are too oily; instead, they are used for pressing oil or for preparing other foods. In the Molucca Islands, as well as in Banda and other islands situated to the Southeast where <term>Calappus<note>The Coconut palm (*Cocos nucifera*)</note></term> nuts are not frequent, a large quantity of oil is pressed from these dried kernels. This oil is thin and has a reddish color, like rapeseed oil, or is perhaps a little thicker. This oil is considered more pleasant and suitable for food—specifically for frying fish in a pan—than coconut oil, provided it is fresh; for old Canary oil serves only for lamps, and it is of a hotter nature than coconut oil. In Amboina, this oil is rarely made, since it can be more readily prepared from coconut nuts.

Secondly, a delicate Amboinese bread is cooked from these kernels, called *Baggéa* and *Mangéa*, which are rods about an <term>ell<note>A historical unit of length, roughly the length of an arm</note></term> long and a thumb thick, which are eaten in place of bread. These are composed of coarsely chopped Canary nuts mixed with a little <term>Sagumanta<note>Sago flour or meal</note></term>; this paste is then pressed into tubes made of bamboo of that length, or wrapped in certain thick leaves collected from a species of <term>Pandangha<note>The Pandanus or Screw Pine</note></term>, and for this reason they are also called *Daun Baggéa* <note>The "Baggéa Leaf"</note>. These are roasted over a fire until the outer leaves are burnt, which are then removed, or they are preserved with the half-burnt leaves. These rods formed from this paste resemble sticks made of chopped almonds and black sugar mixed together. They are quite hard and difficult to bite, and they quickly fill and satisfy the stomach, but they often constipate the bowels so vehemently that pains follow. Their flavor is somewhat rancid and oily, which is why our nation does not seek them out much, but they are used by the locals as sweets and are sent to others as gifts; otherwise, they provide excellent provisions and food for those sailing across the sea, as they can be kept for a long time without spoiling.

There is, moreover, another species of these rods also serving as bread, which is composed of chopped Canary kernels mixed with a little black sugar and rice, which is baked in bamboo tubes. A third, better species is prepared called *Uba*, but Canary nuts are not mixed into this, as it is cooked from sago meal. The best *Baggéa*, however, is brought from Manipa, where a wider species of these Canary cakes is prepared, about a foot long and a span wide, which is much more delicate than those aforementioned rods.

Fresh Canary fruits, crushed and pressed in water, provide a white milk like the liquid of the coconut, which is used in the same way to enrich vegetables and porridges, but only by the mountain dwellers and common people, in whose lands the coconut tree does not grow.

There is a peculiar knowledge and art to opening these nuts by striking them so that the kernels are not broken or crushed. For this purpose, the inhabitants choose stones hollowed out on one side into the shape of a pit; they place the nut in the lower of these and strike it quite forcefully with the other until the shell is broken, and in this way the kernel remains unharmed. However, no more are struck than those to be eaten immediately, since they are better preserved in the shell.

Thirdly, these kernels are used by the Amboinese for other sweets...

<column-break/>

all the trees have their owners, and one may by no means freely chop them down, because they serve the inhabitants for their livelihood.

<margin>Usage.</margin>
The inhabitants of these islands have a large part of their support from this tree, namely from the fruits, for they are not only suitable to be eaten raw, both to satisfy the belly (as mostly happens among the inhabitants) and for pleasure, as our nation does, being served at dessert tables and with tea, just as one does in Europe with almonds, from which a newcomer will hardly distinguish them. Therefore, one finds written in some journals or daily registers that these islands produce almonds. These fruits, however, are somewhat unhealthy and quite harmful if one eats them too young, the sign of which is when the outermost skin is not yet reddish, but pale white, here and there with purple streaks; for then they very easily provoke stomach-ache and bloody flux <note>An old term for dysentery</note> through their great sliminess, which one improves somewhat if one eats some salt with them. The most part are left in the shells and dried in the smoke, so that one can have a daily supply of them. These smoked Canary nuts are not very suitable for eating raw, because one cannot then get the outer skin off, and they are also too oily, but they serve to strike oil, or to make other food from them. For in the Molucca Islands, as also in Banda and other South-eastern islands, especially where one does not have coconut nuts in abundance, a multitude of oil is pressed from these dried kernels, thin and reddish of color, like rapeseed oil, or somewhat thicker. This oil is held to be more lovely and suitable to use in food, and to fry fish in, than coconut oil, namely when it is fresh, for the old Canary oil serves only for the lamps, and it is warmer of nature than the coconut oil. In Amboina, this oil is little made, because one can have it more readily from the coconut tree.

Secondly, from these kernels is made the tasty Amboinese bread called *Baggéa* and *Mangéa*, which are sticks about an ell long and a thumb thick, which one uses in place of bread. These are made of coarsely cut Canary nuts, kneaded together with a little sago meal, which dough one then stuffs into bamboo pipes of that length, or rolls in certain thick leaves, being a kind of Pandanus, for that reason called *Daun Baggéa*, which are then roasted in the fire until the outer leaves are burnt, which one then takes off, or keeps with the half-burnt leaves; they resemble the sticks of cut almonds and black sugar mixed. They turn out quite hard and difficult in the biting, satisfy quickly, and stop the belly sometimes so violently that one gets pain from it. The taste is somewhat burnt and oily, therefore our nation makes little of them, but by the inhabitants they are used for banquet-work, and sometimes sent as a present; otherwise they are a suitable provision for those who travel by sea, because one can keep them for a long time unspoiled.

There is nevertheless a better kind of these bread-sticks, which one makes of cut Canary nuts, mixed with a little black sugar and rice, and baked in bamboo pipes; and still a better third sort called *Uba*, yet no Canary nut goes into that, but it consists of baked sago meal. The best *Baggéa* comes from Manipa, where one makes yet a broad kind of these Canary cakes, about a foot long and a hand-breadth wide, which are much tastier than the above-mentioned sticks.

The fresh Canary nuts, rubbed and pressed out in water, give a white milk like the coconut milk, being used in the same ways to fatten porridge and potherbs, yet only by the mountain-dwellers and poor people, where no coconuts fall.

It is also a particular science to strike the nuts open without crushing the kernel <note>original Dutch: "beest"</note>; the inhabitants look for two stones for this, each being somewhat hollowed on one side like a little pit; on the bottom one lies the nut, and one gives a reasonable blow upon it with the other, so the shell breaks and the kernel remains whole; yet one strikes no more than one wants to eat at once, for in the shell one can keep them better.

Thirdly, one uses these kernels for yet another...
</columns>

<columns>
dainties are used, called *Halua* or *Alua*, which are prepared from coarsely chopped *Canarium* kernels, mixed with <term>Calappa<note>Coconut</note></term> and black or tree-sugar and reduced into a thick paste, from which square cakes are formed, which they toast slightly over the fire in a frying pan. Their banquets on festive days are filled with these "Marmalades," in which they take great delight and indulge, although they provide an oily flavor, unpleasant to our nation <note>The author refers to the Dutch</note>. But it is with these cakes as it was with Aesop's donkey, who ate thistles instead of lettuce, and said: <note>original Latin: "ut sunt labia, ita et olus est"</note>
> As the lips are, so is the herb.

The word *Halua*, in my judgment, can be derived from the Arabic *Halwan* and *Halwa*, that is, a foodstuff made from honey and sugar, or any kind of confectionery, for the Amboinese delight in this *Aluwa*, and present it in the same form as some <term>Quince Jelly<note>original Latin: "Cyduniatum"</note></term> or Marmalade among us.

If fresh *Canarium* fruits are consumed in large quantities, they cause oppression of the chest, thus harming those who suffer from a dry cough. If eaten in abundance while drinking <term>Saguer<note>Palm wine or fermented sap</note></term>, they weigh down the head and quickly cause intoxication. From dried *Canarium* nuts, ground with sugar and rice flour, little cakes are formed, which the Portuguese call *Boruwa* and *Lado*; they are also used in pastries in place of almonds; they are also covered in sugar, but they give an oily taste, since this can only be done with old and very dry *Canarium* nuts.

If these trees grow old, they tend to exude a white and tenacious resin, but it is very rare if the lower part of the trunk or near the roots of the tree is cut. The older the trees are, the more abundantly they pour forth this resin, which is not found in younger ones, or at least very rarely; on the contrary, they spread a strong and resinous odor if their trunk is wounded. The more wild these trees are, and the less they are cultivated or their fruits picked, the more abundantly they pour forth resin; for as long as they are fertile and bear many fruits, this resin is not found. This gum or resin, if it is dry, is white, and adheres to itself in small granules, like white <term>Camphor<note>original Latin: "Caphura"</note></term>, but it is softer and more tenacious like tallow, and gradually turns yellow. If it is fresh, it breathes such a heavy odor that it infects the head and fills the entire room in which it is placed. In Amboina this resin is rare, but it occurs more frequently in Ceram and the remote mountains, and is used for no other purpose than being wrapped in dry leaves and burned like a torch, though it spreads a heavy odor. When these trees pour forth this gum abundantly, they no longer yield any fruit; hence the inhabitants would be foolish if they preserved these trees just so such gum might trickle out, since these trees are so beneficial to them for food, and other similar trees provide them with enough in addition, and they would also lose the fruits, which are so necessary to them.

Ob eandem quoque rationem hujus arboris lignum non expetitur ad ædificia vel mechanica, excepto quod ex amplis ejus fruſtis ac ſegmentis vetuſtiſſimorum truncorum ingentia formentur dolia ac crateres *Doelangs* vocata, ut & breves remi, vel cochlearia *Pangajos* dicta: Vetuſtarum arborum lignum foco optime inſervit, unde & adhibetur ad furnos calcarios exſtruendos.

For the same reason, the wood of this tree is not sought after for buildings or mechanical works, except that from its large pieces and segments of the oldest trunks, huge vessels and bowls called *Doelangs* are formed, as well as short oars or spoons called *Pangajos*. The wood of old trees serves best for the hearth, hence it is used for constructing lime kilns.

This tree, although it bears a smooth and clean bark, nevertheless nourishes and sustains many plants on its branches, which, being spurious and parasitic, so exhaust and emaciate it that it eventually becomes sterile; this happens because during the night many birds rest in this tree, indeed more than in other trees, and especially wood-pigeons, which through their droppings drop the seeds of other trees onto the branches of this tree, which take their nourishment from its bark. Among the other small birds is one called *Cacopit*, very similar in form to our <term>Goldcrest<note>original Latin: "Regulo"</note></term>, from whose droppings a strange plant grows on various trees like Mistletoe on the Oak, which is described in its place under the name of Mistletoe *Cacopit*. This is seen particularly abundantly and frequently on the *Canarium* trees, and it is a sight to see such green "forests" as it were, growing on the tree, especially at that time when it has shed almost all its own leaves. Many species of *Angrea* <note>Orchids</note> also grow upon it, which bear a marvelous flower and never grow on the ground, likewise *Phyllitis Indica* and other species of *Ferns* and *Driopteris*; but no plant harms it more than the *Varinga* <note>The Banyan or Ficus tree</note>, and especially that small-leaved variety, which without doubt...

the Amboinese banquet-work called *Halua* or *Alua*, which is made of coarsely cut kernels, mixed with <term>Calappa<note>Coconut</note></term> and brown or tree-sugar, into a thick dough, from which they make square cakes, and roast them a little over the fire in a pan. One sees all the festive meals on holidays stuffed with this marmalade, and it is held in great esteem by those people, although it is very oily in taste and unpleasant for our Nation. However, it goes with these "brown cakes" as with that Donkey in Aesop, who ate the thistles instead of Salad, and said:
> As the lips are, so is the herb.

The word *Halua* can, in my opinion, be derived from the Arabic *Halwan* and *Halwa*, which is an edible food prepared from honey and sugar, or all sweet food, for the Amboinese love such sweetness very much, and use it in the same way as we use *Marmalades*, or the <term>Jelly of Quinces<note>original Dutch: "Cheley van Quéen"</note></term> and such like.

If one eats many fresh *Canaries*, one often feels an oppression on the chest, therefore they are not good for those who are troubled with a dry cough. Eaten much between the drinking of *Saguer*, they weigh down the head and make one drunk early. From the dry *Canaries*, rubbed with sugar and rice-meal, one also makes gingerbread-cakes and morsels, which the Portuguese call *Boruwa* and *Lado*; they are also used in Tarts instead of Almonds, as well as coated with sugar, though those taste quite oily, because one can only make them from old and very dry *Canaries*.

When these trees grow old, they tend to give a white and tough resin, but very sparingly; when one cuts into the lower trunk or bare roots, the older the trees are, the more resin they give, but on the young ones one sees none, or very little; on the other hand, they give a strong and resinous smell when one wounds them in the trunk. The wilder these trees are, and the less they are tended and picked, the more resin they give, for as long as they bear fruit richly, one does not find the resin. The Gum or resin dries white with small crumbs clinging together, like white *Camphor*, but softer and tougher than <term>tallow<note>original Dutch: "ongel"</note></term>, and also turns somewhat yellow over time. When fresh it is so strong of smell that it weighs down the head and fills a whole room where it lies. On Amboina one finds this resin little, but certainly on Ceram and in the remote mountains, and it is used for nothing else than that one wraps it with the grit and all in some dry leaves, and burns it in place of torches or candles, like other <term>Dammers<note>Resins used for light</note></term>, although they also have a heavy smell. Now when the trees give out this Gum richly, they will bear no more fruit, therefore the Inhabitants would do unwisely to accustom these trees—from which they have such necessary maintenance—to the dripping of this *Dammar*, which they can have in abundance from other trees, and would then cause the fruits above to spoil, which is of more concern to them.

For the same reason this wood is also used for no carpentry, except that one makes large wooden basins called *Doelangs* from the wide buttresses, and even then from the old trunks, as well as the short oars or scoops called *Pangajos*. The wood of old trees gives good firewood, therefore it is customary to make lime-kilns from it.

This tree, although it has a smooth and clean bark, must nevertheless feed many strange plants on its branches, which parasitic plants <note>literally "farmer's children"</note> so emaciate it that it finally becomes infertile; this comes about because many kinds of birds rest on these branches at night, more than on other trees, especially wild pigeons, which then through their droppings let seeds of other trees fall on the branches of this tree, which then remain and draw their nourishment from the bark. Among others is a small bird called *Cacopit*, resembling our <term>Goldcrest<note>original Dutch: "Koninxken"</note></term> in appearance, from whose droppings a strange plant sprouts on various trees, like the Mistletoe on our oak trees, described in its place under the name of *Viscum Cacopit*; which one sees particularly much and often on the Canari-trees, being a sight to see such green bushes on a tree at the time when it has cast off most of its leaves. One also finds many kinds of *Angree* <note>Orchids</note> on it, a rare flower that never grows on the earth, as well as the *Phyllitis Indica* or Hart's-tongue fern, and other sorts of *Driopteris*. But no growth is more harmful to it than the *Varinga*, especially...

...injury is brought to it by pigeons: For this ungrateful offspring <note>Referring to a parasitic Banyan-type tree</note> first grows quite luxuriously from its branches and bark, and then sends out its tendrils down along the trunk even into the ground itself; these later become larger and more swollen, and being increased by many other tendrils, they so surround and compress the mother trunk that it perishes as if suffocated. Then this parasitic and bastard offspring raises itself in the form of a great tree, leaning upon the body of the suffocated mother. From this, the Amboinese have made a proverb about the <term>Varinga<note>A species of Ficus or Banyan tree that often begins life as an epiphyte</note>,</term> which they compare to sycophants who, by their flatteries, insinuate themselves into the favor of the powerful, whom they then exhaust and pluck.

The hard shells of the *Canarium* provide the best charcoal, which holds and fosters fire for a long time; these are used by goldsmiths and for heating water. The *Canarium* fruits of Banda, since they are small, are not eaten raw very much, but oil is mostly expressed from them, as they are fattier than the larger ones which they receive from elsewhere, and which they call by the specific name *Amboinese Canaria*.

Since the seasons of the year vary in the Amboinese islands—such as in Manipa and Kelang, where the West and East winds constitute the dry times of the months, which in Amboina are rainy—hence the time of year when the larger and domestic *Canaria* ripen is in the month of October in Amboina, and in those other islands in the months of June and July. Conversely, the smaller or wild *Canarium* species, called *Yal balat* by them, ripen in the middle of the northern <note>monsoon</note> months, when heavy rains fall among them.

It should be further noted that the four above-mentioned species, called domestic, sometimes diminish and degenerate, so that they can hardly be distinguished from the wild species.

Book III. Chap. II. AMBOINESE HERBAL. 151

### CHAPTER TWO.

->**The Western Canarium, or the first wild species. *Canari Barat*.**<-

This species does not differ much from the preceding one, especially its last two varieties; the distinction lies mostly in the season of the year and the fact that these trees fruit later. Its trunk is taller, usually straight, though sometimes slightly curved, covered in a white or ash-colored bark, which on older trunks appears reddish, like a decayed cheese <note>original: "instar casei cariosi"</note>. Its canopy is not as elegantly arranged as in the domestic variety, but is unkempt, and its branches are much more curved. It is numbered among the tallest species of forest trees, making it nearly impossible to climb; instead, its fruits are left to fall on their own. Its "wings" <note>These are buttress roots, large wooden flanges at the base of the trunk common in tropical rainforest trees</note> near the roots are quite extensive and huge, forming various small chambers; indeed, they are the largest among all the *Canarium* species, especially if it grows in the high mountains, though if it is placed near human dwellings, these wings remain small.

The leaves are positioned in the same manner as the previous kind, with four or five pairs on a single rachis <note>The main stem of a compound leaf</note>, but they are much smaller than the preceding. Specifically, the lower leaves are five or six inches long, while the upper ones are seven or eight inches; on younger trees, they reach ten or eleven inches in length. They are two-and-a-half to three inches wide. Their scent is not as resinous as the previous kind. They end in a sharp, narrow point about an inch long, woven with parallel, yellowish veins. They are thick, rough, and dark green. Every leaf has a small bump <note>tuberculum</note> at its base, just as every rachis is jointed <note>geniculata</note> where it meets the branch. The rachis itself is round, slightly striated, and often bent with one or two "knees" in the middle; the entire rachis consists of six pairs of leaves with an odd one at the end, which is rarely missing. These stalks also bear two ear-like, scaly, and triangular leaflets at their base, within which they are held as if in a sheath; these scales are more abundant and larger in the wild species than in the domestic one. At the ends of the branches, large clusters also grow, consisting of thick, woody stalks that support the flowers. These are similar to the domestic flowers but generally smaller. These flowers first consist of two or three green buds joined together, which open into two or three segments, shining like white silk on the inside and shaped like a cup. In their center, little flowers appear, made of three small, white, oblong petals, also cup-shaped, which contain short, thick stamens with saffron-yellow anthers in their center, surrounding a green head or pistil that grows into the fruit. These two or three green heads, before they open, are enclosed in a little purse formed of two leaves, which hang down from both sides like valves <note>original: "instar Valvularum"</note> after the buds open. The scent is similar to <term>Champaca<note>A fragrant flowering tree, *Magnolia champaca*</note></term> flowers, but weaker than in the domestic variety. These little flowers are not located everywhere on the cluster, but only at the ends of the small stalks, where the fruits also sprout.

These fruits are entirely similar to the domestic ones, especially the second and fourth varieties, though they taper more sharply from a flat base to a slight point. They are somewhat triangular in their roundness. When ripe, they are not as elegant, polished, or black as the domestic ones, but are more brownish-gray. No more than six or eight hang from a single cluster, whereas the domestic tree bears more.

The nut itself is very similar in shape and size to the aforementioned second variety, but a little smaller. Besides being triangular, each side also bears a protruding rib. Its shell is thick and these nuts are very difficult to open by cracking. Their point is always sharper than in the domestic kind, and sometimes the third segment is divided in two.

In the opened nut, a more significant difference from the first kind is observed: it is divided into three chambers, each of which carries its own kernel similar to the domestic one, but a little smaller, and of the same flavor, but the substance
<meta>catchword: is</meta>

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER II.

->**The first wild Canari-Tree.**<-

This genus does not differ much from the preceding, particularly the last two sorts, and the distinction consists mostly in the <term>Season<note>original Dutch: "Saysoen"</note></term> and the wildness of the trees. The trunk shoots up higher, mostly straight, and sometimes somewhat bowed, also covered with a white or light-gray bark, which on old trunks appears reddish, like moldy cheese. The crown is not as well-ordered as on the tame tree, but broken, and the branches much more crooked. Furthermore, it is reckoned among the highest forest trees, therefore it is difficult to climb, and one lets the fruits fall off by themselves. The "wings" <note>buttress roots</note> at the roots are very large and broad, representing several small rooms; indeed, they are the largest among all the <term>Canari-kinds</term>, especially if it stands in the high mountains, but standing near the dwellings of men, it has them small.

The leaves stand in the same manner as on the preceding, four and five pairs on a stalk, but are much smaller than on the preceding—namely, the rear ones five and six, the forward ones seven and eight inches, but on the young trees ten and eleven inches long, and two and a half to three inches wide. They do not have as resinous a smell as the tame ones. They have a narrow point at the front, about an inch long, also shot through with parallel yellow ribs; they are thick, stiff, and dark green. Each leaf has a small knob at its origin on the stem, just as the stalks have a "knee" at the branches. Furthermore, they are round, somewhat striped, sometimes bent in the middle with one or two "knees," and the whole stalk has six pairs, with one alone in front, and seldom without that. The stalks at their origin also have two bearded, scaly, and three-cornered leaflets, in which they stand as if in a sheath, and these scales are seen more and larger on the wild kind than on the tame. At the front of the branches, large clusters also come forth, made of thick woody stalks. On these one sees the blossom, which mostly resembles the tame but is generally smaller. In particular, this blossom consists first of two or three green buds joined together, which open themselves into two or three pieces, shining from within like white silk. Between them one sees the little flowers also made of three small, white, and longish petals, resembling a little cup. In the middle of the same stand several short thick threads, with saffron-yellow tips, surrounding a green knob from which the fruit comes. These two or three green buds, before they open, stand closed in a little purse made of two green leaves, which after opening hang down on both sides like "flap-caps" <note>original: "klapmutzen"; referring to the valves or sepals</note>. The smell is also like the <term>Champaca</term> flowers, though fainter than on the tame ones. These little flowers do not stand everywhere on the cluster, but only at the ends of the small branches, just as the fruits grow.

The fruits are mostly like the preceding tame ones, especially the second and fourth sorts, yet these run to a sharper point from a broad beginning, with a short tip in front, also somewhat three-sided from the roundness. Being ripe, they do not become as beautiful, smooth, and black as the tame ones, but remain grayer, and do not hang more than six to eight on a cluster, where the tame have more.

The nut is in form and size most like the above-mentioned second sort, or a little smaller, and not only three-sided, but each side has in the middle an additional protruding rib. Furthermore, it has a thick shell; they are difficult to strike open, and their forward point is always sharper than on the tame, and sometimes the third side is divided in two.

In the broken-open nut, one finds a more remarkable difference, for it is divided into three chambers, in each of which is a separate kernel, like the tame, though a little smaller, and of the same taste, but fattier and harder of substance...

is of a fattier and harder substance. These three chambers are always found in the wild species, but in the domestic kind they are observed only by chance or a whim of nature; most often only two appear, and the third is not always filled with a kernel, but is more often empty or contains only a tiny seed.

A second species of this tree is also found, much smaller than the preceding one; its nut is scarcely a finger long and truly triangular, divided into three sharp angles, each side or segment being about a finger's width. The nut is likewise divided into three chambers, containing one or two small, narrow kernels with a sweeter but drier flavor than the former, and not nearly as fatty.

If the trunk of this tree is cut, it pours out a strong and resinous odor, and its white resin is more abundant than in the domestic variety. It closely resembles unrefined camphor or tallow <note>original: "Camphurae... vel Sebo"</note>, and is collected in large lumps to be used for torches. However, it mostly drips onto the ground and mixes with other dirt; furthermore, it gives off such a heavy scent that it is almost intolerable. In the trees of Ceram, and especially in Hatuwe, this resin is found more abundantly than elsewhere; it turns from white to yellowish like yellow wax, but is more brittle and softer. The trunk above the "wings" <note>buttress roots</note> is so thick that two men can scarcely embrace it, and its wood is much more solid and durable than the domestic kind, making it useful even for construction.

*Season.* They bloom at the start of the Western months—that is, in September—from which they take their name, and they ripen in April. They are considered wilder in nature than the preceding kind because the trees are too tall to climb; thus, they are left undisturbed, and their fruits mostly serve as food for birds and wild boars. They have no owners or masters, and anyone is free to cut them down, just as with other forest trees.

*Name.* *Western Canarium* <note>original: "Canarium Zephyrinum"</note> or *First Wild Species*. In Malay it is called *Canari Barat*, meaning "Western Canarium," because it blooms and matures during the time of the Western monsoon. Also *Canari Utan*, meaning "Wild Canarium," and the "First," as there is another true wild variety. In Amboinese it is called *Yar* or *Yal-Halat*; some also call it *Kitsjil* Canarium <note>Malay: "kecil," meaning small</note>, since its leaves and fruits are smaller than the domestic species.

*Location.* It grows in the same places as the domestic kind but in the forests, further removed from human dwellings. Indeed, it is found on certain islands where no domestic trees occur, such as in Banda on the high lands of Lonthor.

*Use.* These fruits, as mentioned, are rarely gathered in Amboina since the domestic species is so abundant, even though these are of a more delicate flavor and harder substance than the larger ones. However, they require too much labor to open if one wishes to keep the kernels whole.

The trunks of these trees, which are very straight and tall, are excellently suited for ship masts, though they are not very durable and break easily if forced. Nevertheless, our nation <note>The Dutch</note> has often had to make do with them, and has sent for these masts from Amboina for the naval shipyard in Batavia <note>Modern-day Jakarta</note>. The wood from the "wings" is used for the same works mentioned above, for which it is even better suited.

In the year 1669, a white, soft, and fresh resin was brought to me from Xulabessi <note>The Sula Islands</note>, very much resembling white Dammar <note>A generic term for various tree resins in the East Indies</note>, which is collected from old, wild Canarium trees, but it was fattier. Its nut was scarcely the length of a finger joint. It was also triangular, but the third side was much narrower than the other two; because of its thick shell and tiny kernel, it is not eaten. The leaves were very similar to the preceding Canarium but a little smaller, and the trunk was also "winged" at the lower part. These trees grew in the high mountains of that island. Little resin is collected there, and it is used for torches like other Dammar, though it has a much stronger smell. To distinguish it from the former, it may be called *Canarium Resin of Xulabessi*.

Canarium wood is not only useful for masts but also for joinery, from which they make chests, for it can be easily polished and resembles our beechwood.

substance. These three chambers are ordinarily found in the wild variety, but in the tamed ones they occur only by chance, and usually only two; the third chamber is also not always full, but often empty and occupied by a tiny grain.

Secondly, there is a second sort of this, much smaller than the previous one, for the nut is barely an inch long, truly triangular, divided with three sharp sides, each side remaining a small finger's width. Inside they are also divided into three chambers, and therein only one or two small and narrow kernels, sweeter but drier in taste than the previous ones, with little oiliness.

If one cuts into the trunk, it gives off a heavy, resinous smell, and more white resin than the tamed kind, like dirty camphor or tallow, which is gathered together in large clumps and used for torches, but it mostly falls to the earth and mixes with other filth; otherwise it is also so strong of smell that it is hard to endure. On the Ceram trees, especially at Hatuwe, one finds this resin or Dammar more abundantly than in other places, pulling from white toward yellow, like yellow wax, yet more brittle and softer. The trunk above the wings can barely be spanned by two men, and its wood is firmer and more durable than the tamed kind, therefore useful for some carpentry work.

*Season.* They bloom in the beginning of the West Monsoon, in the month of September, from which they have their surname, and become ripe in April of the same Monsoon. They are held to be wilder of nature than the previous ones because the trees cannot be climbed due to their height, and they are therefore left unmolested, so their fruits mostly become prey for birds and wild pigs. They also have no owners, and one may freely chop them down, like other forest trees.

*Name.* *Western Canarium* or *First Wild Species*. In Malay *Canari Barat*, that is Western Canarium, because it blooms and becomes ripe in the West Monsoon. As also *Canari Utan*, that is wild Canarium, the first, because there is yet another right wild one. In Amboinese *Yar* or *Yal Halat*, some also call it *Canary Kitsjil*, because its leaves and fruits are smaller than the tamed varieties.

*Place.* They grow in the same places as the tamed, but more in the mountains and separated from the dwellings of men, yes, even on some islands where there are no large tamed ones, like in Banda on the high land of Lonthor.

*Use.* These fruits, as said, are little gathered in Amboina, where one has the tamed sort in multitude, although they are tastier and harder of substance than the large ones, but they cost too much effort to crack open so that the inner kernels remain whole.

The wood of the trunks, which one can find very straight and tall, is fit to make masts therefrom, although they are not very durable, and if they suffer force, they break off short. Nonetheless, our nations have often had to make do with them, and therefore ordered these masts from Amboina for Batavia's shipyard. The wood of the wide wings at the base is used for the same works as said above, for which it is more fit.

In the year 1669, there was brought to me from Xulabessi a white, soft, and fresh resin, very like the white Dammar obtained from the old wild Canarium trees, but fattier; the nut thereof was scarcely a joint of a finger long. It was three-sided, but the third side was much narrower than the two others, and because of its thick shell and small kernel it is not eaten. The leaves were said to be like those of the previous Canarium, though somewhat smaller; the trunk also has some wings at the bottom. They grow in the high mountains of that island. They gather little of the resin there, and use it for torches like other Dammar, although it turns out quite a bit stronger in smell. To distinguish it from the above, one may call it *Sula Canarium Dammar*, in Latin *Resina Canarina de Xulabessi*.

The Canarium wood is not only useful for masts, but also for joinery, to make chests from, for it lets itself be worked smooth, and very much resembles our beechwood.

# Book III, Chapter II. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

Called **Cana**, it is very similar in form and habit to the small-leaved Canarium, but its leaves are even smaller; its fruits are oblong and sharp, and the nuts are triangular, pointed at both ends, and divided into three cells containing three narrow kernels.

However, this **Chinese Cana**, when planted in my garden, showed by the shape of its leaves that it is not a species of Canarium, but rather belongs to the genus of the **Wax Plum** <note>original: "Pruni Cerei"; likely referring to a type of yellow plum or Mirabelle</note>, which is well known in Europe; see more on this in the *fifth chapter of the Appendix*.

These Canarium trees growing on **Ceram** and other larger islands produce such abundant resin that it hangs from the trunks in large lumps and cones—even from the thickest branches. However, this only occurs when the trees are very old and have not been disturbed by humans. This resin is initially white, liquid, and viscous; later it turns yellowish and hardens like wax. It does not have as harsh or unpleasant an odor as the resin from younger trees or the domestic Canarium. In substance, color, and scent, it is so similar to **Gummi Elemi** <note>original: "Gummi Elemi"; a fragrant resin used historically in ointments and plasters</note> that it might be mistaken for it; and who knows if they are not the same trees? This could be determined if the Ethiopian species of that tree, from which *Gummi Elemi* flows, were known to us.

It is said that *Gummi Elemi* is the resin of the **Ethiopian Olive**, but others believe it flows from a species of **Cedar**, while others say the tree is still unknown. One might not be far wrong to guess that the small, oblong fruits of that tree are Canariums, which foreigners mistook for Olives—since semi-ripe Canariums look very much like them. Thus, our aforementioned **Canarium Dammar** <term>Dammar: a generic Malay term for resin used for torches or caulking</term> would rightly and reasonably be an East Indian or Amboinese Elemi. Indeed, I know that some surgeons have used this Canarium Dammar in the absence of Elemi for **temporal plasters** <note>original: "Emplastra temporalia"; medicinal patches applied to the temples of the head</note>, which are applied to the temples to draw out **catarrhs** <note>original: "Catharros"; in 17th-century medicine, these were "runny" humors or fluids thought to drop from the brain</note>. I have melted this Canarium Dammar to purify it of filth and formed it into cakes; these were semi-transparent, ranging from yellow to a brownish or pale red color, and had a more pleasant scent than the raw resin. However, they broke very easily into tiny pieces and shone like glass. They must be kept separately in a jar or pot; otherwise, this resin imparts its very strong and penetrating scent to other nearby things, and the scent never leaves them.

From this, the absurd opinion of some is revealed, who believe that **white Amber** or **Sperma Ceti** <note>original: "Sperma Ceti"; Rumphius refers to Ambergris found on beaches, which was often confused with the waxy substance from whales</note> found in masses floating in the sea around these Eastern islands is nothing other than this Canarium Dammar. They think that if it is accidentally carried into the sea and mixed with sand, pebbles, and shells, it degenerates into this *Sperma Ceti*. But if one simply pays attention to the fatty, fishy smell of *Sperma Ceti* and compares it to the resinous scent of Canarium Dammar—which never perishes, even when rolled in seawater for a long time—one will easily recognize that these things have different origins.

### Plate Forty-Eight

This displays a branch of the **Zephyrine Canarium** <note>original: "Canarii Zephyrini"</note>, which is called the first wild Canarium, or **Canary Barat**; in its upper part, the flower-bearing and fruit-bearing clusters appear.

### O B S E R V A T I O N.

The tree that yields *Gummi Elemi* is properly the one called by **Ray** in his *History of Plants, page 1546*, the "Brazilian tree yielding Gummi Elemi," with pinnate leaves, whorled flowers, and fruit the shape and size of an Olive. This is called **Icicariba** by **Piso** and its resin **Icica** on *page 122 of the 1658 edition*. However, the arrangement of its flowers differs from our figure, though the foliage matches better. This also applies to the **Curaçao Elemi-tree** shown by **Herman** in *Paradisus Batavus, page 332*, whose figure appears in **Plukenet's** *Phytographia, Plate 173, Fig. 5*. There is also a tree common in **Ceylon** called the "fragrant Kakuriaghaha," from which *Gummi Elemi* flows, mentioned by **Herman** in *Museum Zeylanicum, page 52*, and cited in *Thesaurus Zeylanicus, page 28*. It perhaps corresponds with the **Paenou** in the *Hortus Malabaricus, part 4, Plate 15*, where other trees yielding *Gummi Elemi* are mentioned in the notes. **Plukenet** also shows another of this kind in *Phytographia, Plate 217, Fig. 4*. Thus, there are various trees that yield this gum, others of which have been collected by **Samuel Dale** in *Pharmacologia, page 337*, **Valentini** in *History of Simples Reformed, page 258*, and **Herman** in *Materia Medica, page 207*, who says it is collected from an East Indian plum-bearing tree.

<column-break/>

growing **Cana**, very similar in appearance and growth to the small-leaved Canarium, though the leaves are still smaller, the fruits are oblong-slender, and the nuts are also triangular, sharp at the back and front, divided inside into three cells, and containing three narrow kernels.

However, this **Chinese Cana**, planted in my garden, showed by the form of its leaves that they are not Canariums, but from the genus of *Prunum Cereum* or **yellow plums**, well known in Europe; concerning which see more in my *Appendix, chapter 5*.

*This kind of Canarium tree growing on Ceram and other large islands gives such abundant resin that it hangs in large lumps and cones from the trunk, and even from the thick branches; but the trees must then be very old and remain undisturbed by people. This resin is at first white, flowing, and sticky; thereafter it becomes yellowish and hard, like wax, not as harsh and unpleasant in smell as that of the young tree or the domestic Canarium, but comes so close in substance, color, and smell to Gummi Elemi that one would take it for it; and who knows if they are not the same kind of trees, if only the appearance of that Ethiopian tree were known to us, from which the Gummi Elemi comes.*

*It is indeed said that Gummi Elemi is a resin from the Ethiopian Olive tree, although others take it for a kind of Cedar tree, and others for an unknown tree from those lands. One could not guess wrongly that the fruits of that tree are small oblong Canariums, which foreigners have mistaken for Olives, which the half-ripe Canariums quite resemble; and so one might with reason take our aforementioned Canary Dammar for an East Indian or Amboinese Elemi. I also know that some surgeons have used this Canary Dammar, for lack of Elemi, for black head-plasters, which are worn on the head to draw out the catarrhs. I have also had the prescribed Dammar-Canary melted to purify it from filth, and then cast into cakes, which became semi-transparent, turning from yellow to brownish or light red, lovelier in smell than the raw resin, but breaking very short and shining like glass. One must keep them separately in a box or pot, for otherwise it imparts its strong smell to all things it lies near, which it also never loses.*

*From this appears the absurd feeling of some who think that the white Amber or Sperma Ceti in mass, which one sees drifting out of the sea in these Eastern Islands, is nothing else than such a Canary Dammar, which by chance being carried into the sea and mixed with sand, stones, and shells, is changed into that Sperma Ceti. But if anyone will only pay attention to the train-oil or fatty smell of the Sperma Ceti, and to the resinous smell of Dammar-Canary, which never perishes, however long it rolls in seawater, he will easily be able to perceive that they are things of different origin.*

### N O T E S.

The tree that gives the **Gum Elemi** is specifically that one which was named by **Ray in his History of Plants, p. 1546**, *Arbor Brasiliensis Gummi Elemi fundens* <note>original: "Brazilian tree yielding Gummi Elemi"</note>, with pinnate leaves, whorled flowers, and fruit of the shape and size of an Olive, which is the **Icicariba** of **Piso** in his edition of the year 1658, *page 122*, whose blossoms however differ from our figure in their origin, though the leaves correspond more; as also from that which was named the **Elemifera Curassavica arbor** <note>original: "Elemi-bearing tree of Curaçao"</note> by **Herman in his Paradisi Batavi Prodromus, p. 332**, whose figure is found in **Plukenet in his Phytographia, Plate 193, Fig. 5**. There is also a tree growing in Ceylon named the fragrant **Kakuriaghaha**, from which Gummi Elemi flows according to **Herman in his Museum Zeylanicum, page 28**, which is cited in my *Thesaurus Zeylanicus, p. 52*, and possibly corresponds with the **Poenou** of the *Hortus Malabaricus in the 4th part, Plate 15*, described and depicted, where in the note on *p. 35* more other trees that give this gum are mentioned, of which sort **Plukenet in his Phytographia, Plate 217, Fig. 4** also shows one. So there are several trees that give the Gummi Elemi, of which yet more others have been gathered by **S. Dale in his Pharmacologia, page 337**, **Valentini in his History of Simples Reformed, p. 258**, and **Herman in his Materia Medica, page 207** says that they are collected from an East Indian plum-bearing tree.

In the fifth chapter of the Appendix, the following description is found:

### Chinese Canarium or Cana.

This Chinese tree seems to have a mixed form of the Canarium and the Wax Plum <note>original Latin: "Pruni Cerei"; a type of yellow plum or Mirabelle</note>, which is why I briefly described it in Book 3, Chapter 2 of the Herbal under the Zephyrine Canarium. Here, however, I will provide a more extensive history, as I observed it growing vigorously in my own garden, produced from a seed-stone brought from China. Within a year, it grew taller than a man with an upright trunk, the upper part of which was downy, as were its side branches. On these branches are placed three or four pairs of opposite leaves, with a single leaf at the end, just like the leaves of the true Canarium. The upper leaves were six or seven inches <note>original: "pollices"</note> long, and the lower ones four inches long and two wide. However, I have heard that on older and more mature trees, they are much smaller. The edges of these leaves are smooth and entire, but on the tender and younger leaves, they were very finely serrated <note>toothed like a saw</note>, traces of which could still be seen on the upper parts of the subsequent leaves. These leaves are broadest at the base and end in a sharp point, sitting upon short stalks. The midrib protrudes from both sides and, in the larger leaves, is divided into twelve sinuous ribs; in the smaller ones, into seven or eight. When crushed, these leaves have a resinous scent, very similar to that of the Canarium. The flowers have remained unknown to me thus far. The fruits, however, are oblong and pointed at both ends like Wax Plums. The inner nut closely resembles the oblong wild Canarium, which is called **Nanary** <note>a local name for a wild Canarium species</note>; it is pointed at both ends and triangular, also divided into three cells in which three narrow kernels are located.

Three species of this tree are counted. The first is called **Tsjacana**, as its fruit is woody and very large, having large stones similar to the common Canarium, the description of which has been given. The second is called simply **Cana**, whose fruits resemble the fragrant, triangular Canarium, but are pointed at both ends like the stones of the Wax Plum. The third and smallest species is named **Tengio-Cana**, that is, the Clove-like Cana <note>original Latin: "Cana Caryophyllacea"</note>, because its stones have the shape of cloves and possess the best flavor. All three species grow into tall and upright trees. From the bark of the trunks, a black gum <term>Gummi nigrum</term> occasionally oozes out, though it is rare; it is hard and congeals, and when placed upon coals, it gives off a not unpleasant odor.

**Name.** In Latin, *Canarium Sinense*; commonly called "Chinese Cana."
**Location.** It grows in China, Tonkin, and Cochin-China <note>Modern-day northern and southern Vietnam</note>.
**Use.** In China, the fruits are used raw as confections <note>original: "tragemata"</note> and in other foods, just as the Canarium fruits are used here, or they are preserved in brine and often transported to these regions. Surprisingly, the Chinese use these to quench their thirst when undertaking journeys, even though they are extremely salty with a slight bitterness. All three species are used both in prepared dishes and eaten on their own, for the Chinese consider these fruits a nutritious and very sustaining food. They are, however, unsuitable for expressing oil.

On the kernels of the first species, sculptors practice their art. He who carves the most human heads upon them receives the prize; I possess such a kernel in which eighteen distinct faces are visible and marked.

<column-break/>

In the 5th Chapter of the Appendix, one finds described in the following manner:

### The Chinese Canary Tree.

This Chinese tree seems to be of a mixed fashion between the Canarium and the Wax Plum <note>original Dutch: "Prunum Cereum"; yellow plum</note>, for which reason I also partly described it in my Herbal, Book 3, Chapter 2, under the Zephyrine Canarium. However, here I shall set down its history more fully, as it appeared in my garden, grown from a dried seed brought from China. Within a year, it shot up higher than a man with a straight little trunk, whose upper part was woolly, as were the side branches. On these stand 3 or 4 pairs of leaves directly opposite each other, with one alone at the front, like the Canary leaves. The front leaves on the twigs of this tree are 6 and 7 inches <note>original: "duimen"</note> long, the rear ones 4 long and 2 wide, though on the old trees I understand they are much smaller. Their edges are smooth, yet on the first emerging leaves they were finely toothed, so that one could still recognize the traces on the front part of the following ones. At the back they are broadest and end in a long point, standing on short little feet. The mid-vein bulges out above and below, dividing itself in the large leaves into 12, and in the small ones into seven or eight riblets that run curved. The scent of the crushed leaves is resinous and draws noticeably toward the Canary scent. The blossom is still unknown to me. The fruits are oblong, pointed at the back and front like the yellow plums; the inner nut resembles best an oblong wild Canary, which is called **Nanary**, being pointed at the front and back and three-sided, inside also divided into 3 little cells, and therein 3 narrow kernels.

There are three sorts of it: The first is named **Tsjacana**, because it is coarse like wood, being the size of fruits and stones like our common Canary, according to which the description is made. The second is called simply **Cana**, whose fruits resemble our Fragrant Triangular Canarium, but pointed at both ends like the seeds of the aforementioned yellow plums. The third and smallest is called **Tengio Cana**, that is, Clove-Cana, because it has small kernels inside like cloves <note>original Dutch: "Kruit-nagelen"</note>, and the best flavor. All three become high and straight trees; from the bark of the trunk sweats here and there, though sparingly, a black gum, which dries hard; laid on coals it has a not unpleasant smell.

**Name.** In Latin *Canarium Sinense*, commonly "Chinese Cana."
**Place.** They grow in China, Tonkin, and Cochin China.
**Use.** In China the fruits are used raw for banquet-work <note>sweets and desserts</note> and various cakes, just as one does here with the Canaries, and also pickled, which are sometimes transported to these lands. And what is a wonder: the Chinese use them to beat back thirst when they travel, although they are exceedingly salty with a small tartness. All three are used both as a side dish and to be eaten alone, for the Chinese hold them for a nutritious food. To make oil from them, they are useless.

On the kernels of the first sort, the sculptors wish to show their art, for he who can carve the most heads upon them wins the prize. I have such a kernel upon which 18 complete faces can be recognized.
