# CHAPTER THREE.

## *The Second Wild Canarium, or the Nanary Nanarium.*

<column-break/>

# CHAPTER III.

## *The Second Wild Canarium Tree.*

This is properly the wild species of the Canarium, yielding to the previous two in the size of its trunk, which is no thicker than a man can embrace with his arms. Its lower part consists of a few small "wings" <note>These are buttress roots, common in tropical trees</note>, and this trunk is not ash-gray like the preceding ones, but its bark is dark green or blackish. The crown is also narrower and sharper, the branches fewer, and equipped with many fragile and knotty twigs. From these, the rachises <note>The main stem of a compound leaf</note> grow shorter than in those previously mentioned, bearing two eared scales <note>original Latin: "squamas auriculatas"; small leaf-like appendages at the base of the stalk</note> at their origin. On these rachises, there are only two, three, or four pairs of opposite leaves with a single odd leaf at the end. The leaves are smaller than in the Barat Canarium, from four to seven inches <note>original: "pollices"</note> long, and two to two and a half inches wide; they are more pointed at both ends than in the previous species, ending in a long tip. They are also rough and dark green with a yellowish midrib and parallel side veins, some of which are opposite each other and some alternating.

The flowers are similar to the previous ones, but generally smaller and not as brilliant.

The fruits hang sparsely and almost solitarily from long woody stalks, not only at the ends of the branches but also emerging from the thicker branches at their origin. The fruits themselves have the shape of large Myrobalans <note>original: "Myrobalanorum"; a dried plum-like fruit used in historical medicine</note>, broader at the top and narrower at the bottom near the stalk. They are oblong-round rather than three-sided, contained in a flat pericarp <note>the Dutch text calls this a "schooteltje" or little saucer</note> to which they remain attached longer than other Canarium fruits. At first they are green, then lead-colored, and finally black, but they are not as smooth and polished as the previous ones, being rougher and marked with ash-colored spots. The nut is oblong, two finger-widths long and about as wide as a pinky finger, pointed at both ends, mostly round or slightly three-sided, and narrowest near the stalk. It is darker than the common variety. It also has a second form like other Canariums, namely a short and round one, barely an inch long and a bit thicker than the previous one, somewhat angular despite its roundness, often protruding with three, four, or six corners.

These three nuts always contain three cells, rarely four, and are rounder than in the common Canarium. Each of these is filled with a narrow, oblong kernel covered in a very thin brown skin. Its internal substance is white and sweet in taste, like other Canarium fruits or approaching the Catappa <note>The Tropical Almond, Terminalia catappa</note>, being both dry and oily.

These nuts are not opened by striking them with stones like the others, because they are so tightly and fully filled that all the kernels would be crushed by the blow. Instead, they are sliced crosswise with a cleaver <note>Dutch: "Houw-mes"</note>, and the two segments of the kernels are pulled out from each side with a needle or a small hook, though this is done more for pleasure than out of necessity.

Two kinds of resin are collected from these trunks. From the upper part of the trunk, a dry, white, and brittle resin drips out, similar to impure lime or Camphor, with a weak scent and produced in small amounts, so it is rarely gathered. The lower part of the trunk yields a larger quantity, though still not a great abundance; it is blackish and liquid, yet not sticky but brittle, and never hardens as much as other Dammar <term>Dammar: a generic term for natural resins in Southeast Asia, used for incense, torches, and caulking ships</term>. It is mostly mixed with bits of bark or dirt from the ground.

This resin is almost identical—and perhaps a related species—to the West Indian Caranna <note>A fragrant resin from Central and South America</note> in terms of substance and scent. However, when placed on coals, the Caranna gives off a more pleasant odor, while the Amboinese variety smells more strongly of Canarium.

**Season.** This fruit ripens in Amboina at the beginning of the rainy months, namely in May. However, they are also gathered in September when they have fallen beneath the tree, so they do not seem to observe a fixed season.

**Name.** In Latin: *Canarium Silvestre alterum* (The second wild Canarium), *Canarium Montanum* (Mountain Canarium), and *Nanarium*. In Malay: *Canari Utan* (Wild Canarium). In Amboinese: *Nanari*. In Hoeamohela and other neighboring regions...

<column-break/>

This is properly the wild Canary, yielding in trunk size to both the previous Canaries, as it is no thicker than a man can just embrace. At the bottom, it has few and small "wings," and is not whitish like the previous ones but dirty-green or blackish of bark. The crown is also narrower and more pointed, the branches fewer, set with many brittle and knotty twigs. On these, the sprigs are shorter than on the previous ones, having two bearded scales at their origin and only 2, 3, or 4 pairs of leaves directly opposite each other, with one leaf alone in front. The leaves are even smaller than those of the previous Barat Canary, from four to seven inches long, and two to two and a half wide, more pointed at the back and front than the preceding ones, with a long sharp point in front. They are likewise stiff and dark green, with a yellow midrib and parallel cross-ribs, some standing straight and some slanted against each other.

The blossom is as in the preceding, though generally smaller and does not shine so.

The fruits hang sparsely and few together on long woody stalks, appearing not only at the outer tips of the twigs but also from their origin at the thicker branches. The fruits themselves have the appearance of large Myrobalans, namely broadest in front and narrower behind by the stalk, oblong-round and not three-sided, standing in a flat little saucer to which they stay attached longer than other Canaries. They are first green, then lead-colored, and finally black, yet not as smooth and even as the previous ones, but rougher, being marked with gray spots. The little nut is oblong, two finger-widths long, barely a pinky-finger thick, pointed at the front and back, mostly round or a little three-sided, and sharpest at the stalk, browner than the common ones. They also have their second variety, like other Canaries, namely the short round one, being barely an inch long and somewhat thicker than the previous, somewhat angular from the roundness, with 3, 4, and 6 protruding ridges.

The little nuts always have three chambers inside, and rarely four, which are rounder than in the common Canaries. Each is tightly filled with a narrow, long kernel, covered on the outside with a very thin and brown skin, and inside with a white marrow, sweet of taste like other Canaries, or somewhat approaching the Catappan, being dry and also oily.

These nuts are not knocked open with stones like others, because they are too tightly filled and all the kernels would be crushed in the striking, but one chops them crosswise with a cleaver, and the pieces of the kernels are pulled out from both sides with a curved needle or hook; though more for pleasure than for utility.

From these trunks one has two kinds of resin, for from the upper trunk drips a dry, white, and brittle resin, like dirty lime or Camphor, faint of scent and very little, therefore it is not gathered. The lower part drips a bit more, yet also in no great quantity; the same is blackish, soft, yet not sticky, but crumbly, and never becomes as hard as other Dammar, being for the most part mixed with the filth of the bark or the ground.

This resin is almost like, and perhaps a related species of, the West Indian Caranna in substance and scent, though the Caranna is somewhat more pleasant on the coals, whereas the Amboinese smells more strongly of Canary.

**Season.** They become ripe in Amboina with the start of the rainy Monsoon in May, though one also finds them lying under the trees in September, so that they seem to keep no steady season.

**Name.** In Latin *Canarium Silvestre alterum*, and *Canarium Montanum* & *Nanarium*; in Malay *Canari Utan*; in Amboinese *Nanari*. In Hoeamohel, and the...

## CHAPTER FOUR.

### The Fragrant Canarium. Camacoan.

**A**lthough all species of *Canarium* exude a fragrant resin or "tears," I have chosen to give the name "Fragrant" specifically to this one, because its resin, and especially its tears, possess the most delightful scent among all *Canarium* species. It is an entirely wild and rare species of *Canarium* that is seldom encountered, with only one or two trees found here and there in the forested mountains.
This species has many varieties, which I shall reduce to these two types: the smooth and the wrinkled.
First, therefore, the **Smooth Fragrant Canarium**, in Dutch called *gladde* <note>smooth</note> or *witte* <note>white</note> *Canacoan*, bears a much taller and larger trunk than the one immediately preceding. It is so thick that two men can hardly embrace it with their arms. Its bark is pale yellow or a dull whitish color, smooth, but marked with certain dots that make it appear somewhat rough. Its branches are knotty and fragile, ending abruptly at their upper part. On these are located the leafy rachises <term>Rachis: the main axis or stem of a compound leaf</term>, mostly toward their ends, joined closely and irregularly to one another. Each rachis bears a small joint <note>original: "geniculum"</note> at its origin, making them more flexible than the branches of other *Canarium* trees. However, those eared scales <note>leaf-like appendages at the base of the leaf-stalk</note> observed in other species of *Canarium* are not present here.
The leaves have the shape of the *Barat Canarium*, but are shorter and wider, broadest at the lower part and gradually tapering to a point. They are also interwoven with yellow veins, smooth, firm, deep green, and marked with many spots. The lower leaves are always the shortest, being six, seven, or nine fingers wide, and three or four wide. Six, seven, and often eight pairs are found opposite each other on one rachis, with an odd leaf at the end.
There is a variety of this species which bears no more than three or four pairs of leaves on one rachis, which are a little more oblong than the preceding, from five to nine inches long and three wide. Both, however, bear the common characteristic of the *Canarium*, namely, that the rachises are jointed at the first and second pair of leaves

<column-break/>

on the neighboring islands *Yanele*, that is, *Other Canarium* <note>original: "Canari Lain"</note>, as if they said *bastard Canarium*.
**Location.** They do not grow near the dwellings of men or in their gardens, but in the distant mountains and high forests, and are known on all the Amboinese islands.
**Use.** *These fruits are not esteemed by men, because they cost too much effort to crack open and extract the kernel, which is then so small. They are only eaten sometimes for pleasure when one is in the forest and happens to come under these trees. The rest is left for the wild pigs, which are very fond of them for the sweetness of the kernels. Some collect them and fatten the swine at home with them.*
*The black Dammar dripping from the lower trunk is called Dammar Itam Cring, that is, brittle black Dammar. Where it can be had in quantity, it is used for torches, either alone or mixed with other black Dammar, at which time it also burns better, though it is much lovelier in scent than the common black variety.*
The trunks were also used for masts, like the preceding *Canarium*, though not as much, because they are found less often and are more difficult to fetch out of the mountains.

## CHAPTER IV.

### The Fragrant Canarium Tree.

**A**lthough all *Canarium* sorts give off a fragrant resin or tear, *yet I have wanted to give this one specifically the name of "sweet-smelling," because its resin, and especially the tear, is the loveliest of scent among all Canariums. It is also an entirely wild and rare sort of Canarium, seldom to be found, and no more than a tree here and there in the wild mountains.*
*This genus has various variations, which I bring under these two sorts: the first the smooth, the second the rough.*
First, **Smooth Fragrant Canarium**, in Dutch *gladde* or *witte Canacoan*, produces a much higher and larger trunk than the last-mentioned, so thick that often two men must embrace it, with a dirty-white or pale bark, smooth, yet set with some points that make it somewhat rough. The branches are knotty, break off short, and also taper quickly at their front end. On these stand the twigs or leaf-bearing stems, near their ends, close behind one another and without order, each having a small knee at its origin, through which they are more flexible than other *Canarium* twigs; however, they have by no means the ears or scales which one sees on other *Canarium* sorts.
*The leaves resemble those of the Barat Canarium, but are shorter and broader, broadest at the back and gradually pointed, also shot through with yellow ribs, smooth, stiff, and deep green, mostly set with freckles or spots, 6, 7, and 9 cross-fingers long, 3 and 4 wide, the hindmost being always the shortest; they stand with 6, 7, and 8 pairs on a stem against one another, with one alone at the front.*
*One finds a variation of this sort where no more than three or four pairs of leaves stand on a stem, and they are somewhat more oblong than the preceding, namely, from five to nine inches long and three wide; also they both have the common mark of all Canariums, namely, that the stems at the first and second pair of leaves*

In the islands it is called *Yanele*, which means *Other Canarium* <note>original: "Canari Lain"</note>, as if they were calling it a "bastard Canarium."

**Location.** These trees are not found near human dwellings or in cultivated gardens; instead, they grow in remote mountains and deep forests. They are well-known trees found across all the Amboinese islands.

**Uses.** These fruits are not highly valued by people, as they require too much effort to crack open just to reach the kernel, which is remarkably small. They are eaten only for occasional pleasure if someone happens upon them in the woods. The remainder of the crop serves the wild boars, which seek these fruits out eagerly because of the sweetness of the kernels. Some locals collect these fruits specifically to fatten their domestic pigs at home.

*Black Dammar* <term>Dammar: a natural resin or pitch harvested from trees of the Burseraceae family, used for waterproofing and light</term> or resin that drips from the lower part of the trunk is known locally as *Dammar Itam Cring* <note>original: "Dammara nigra friabilis", meaning brittle black dammar</note>. In places where it can be gathered in great quantities, it is used to make torches—either on its own or mixed with other black resins. It is preferred because it catches fire more easily and gives off a more pleasant fragrance than the standard black dammar.

The trunks are also used as masts for ships, similar to other species of *Canarium*, though they are used less frequently because they are rarer and difficult to transport from the steep, distant mountains.

...are curved. Between these stems, other short stalks sprout from the branches, bearing green heads in simple clusters that open into flowers. These flowers are irregular in shape, constructed from three short, thick petals. These flowering clusters grow not only at the tips of the branches—as is the case with the common Canarium—but also among and beneath the leaves.

The fruit is similar to the round wild Canarium, or perhaps slightly rounder, tapering likewise to a point and being three-sided. Externally, it is a blackish-green, wrinkled, and spotted with a dusky color. Beneath a thick husk, a nut is hidden, about the size of a small wild Canarium nut; it is round, three-sided, and flat at the top with a blunt tip. Its sides or segments are not smooth but rough, marked with certain little warts or characters, much like a peeled walnut. Its shell is hard, thick, and divided into three cells, in which one or two kernels are located, tasting like other Canarium nuts.

Some fruits, however, are oblong and are not marked with those "characters," but are instead striated or wrinkled, such as those observed in the Leytimor region.

Two types of "tears" or resin are collected from the trunk. That which oozes from the upper part and the branches is whitish, dry, and brittle, somewhat resembling *Dammar Selan* <term>Dammar Selan: a high-quality, clear resin often used for incense or varnish</term>. Some unskilled Amboinese people mistake it for that, but the greatest difference lies in the fact that *Dammar Selan* grinds between the teeth and crumbles into powder, while all species of *Camacoan* soften during chewing like frankincense. From the lower part of the trunk, a tear drips out that is a mixture of reddish-brown, yellow, and black, like common turpentine. If it is squeezed, it exudes a thin, fragrant oil that is pleasant but not strong; it is more piercing in one tree than in another. The best resin is yielded by trees situated on windy hills and well-exposed to the sun. In older trees, lumps and clods are found similar to our turpentine or pale colophony <note>original: "Colophoniæ", a translucent resin obtained from pines</note>, but they are almost devoid of scent.

The second type, the **Hairy Scented Canarium** or **Rough Camacoan**, bears thick, knotty branches that end bluntly. These consist of a few firm stems, thicker than a quill, unequal, and angular—rounded below and sharpened above—bearing a wide and flexible "knee" or joint at their origin. On these, eight or ten pairs of leaves are positioned, sometimes with an odd one at the end. At the fifth or sixth pair, a similar joint occurs; the two lowest pairs usually fall off. These leaves are six to nine inches long and four or five fingers wide, sitting on short, thick stalks. They are thick, firm, and wavy; the upper part is rough like the skin of a shark <note>original: "Lamii piscis" / "baye-vel"</note>, while the lower part is woolly and yellowish.

In the *Manipense* variety, these leaves are hairier and more stinging. Just as leaves on various trees vary in shape and size, these do not constitute a distinct species. From the armpits of the leaves, the flowering cluster sprouts, a palm or a span long, bearing small flowers consisting of heads similar to the previous ones.

The fruits hang in extended clusters like Canariums, about as long as a finger joint and as thick as a thumb, sharpened at the tip. When young, they are very rough and covered with many stinging hairs that cause the skin to itch; they are roundly three-sided. The internal nuts are larger than those of the Amboinese fruits, elegantly "engraved" and three-sided. The shell beneath the outer husk seems composed of three segments, each side formed by one segment, which bears points or "characters" on the outer surface and protruding angle. The interior of the fruit is the same as in the former species.

The fruit-bearing clusters sprout at the ends of the twigs, composed of many stalks, and the fruits themselves are blunt at both ends. From its trunk, a liquid and mucous gum drips if it is notched; it is reddish-brown and yellowish. If squeezed, an oil exudes, which the inhabitants use to grease their hair, as it is not sticky. This gum gradually dries into a dark reddish or blackish resin. When fresh, it breathes a pleasant odor approaching that of Amber, 

<column-break/>

*...possess a little "knee" or bend. From these stems among the branches come forth other short stalks, which show green buds in empty clusters, from which the blossom develops. These are unformed flowers made of three short and thick leaves; these flowering clusters appear not only at the front of the twigs, after the manner of the common Canarium, but also between and behind the leaves.*

*The fruit is like that of the round wild Canarium, or indeed quite round, and tapering quickly, also somewhat three-sided, blackish-green on the outside, rough, and mottled with gray. Beneath a thick husk lies the nut, the size of a small wild Canarium, perfectly round, three-sided, and broad at the front, with a blunt point. The sides are not smooth, but somewhat rough, as if engraved with some small warts or characters, like a peeled walnut. The shell is hard, thick, and divided inside into three chambers, in which two or three longish kernels lie, tasting like other Canarium.*

*Some fruits are more oblong and do not have many raised "characters," but are much more striped or wrinkled, as are mostly those from Leitimor.*

*From the trunk, one gets two kinds of tears and resin; for that which comes from the upper trunk and branches is whitish, dry, and crumbly, somewhat resembling Dammar Selan, for which some inexperienced Amboinese take it. However, the difference consists mostly in this: that Dammar Selan grates between the teeth and crumbles to dust, but all the sorts of Camacoan become supple when chewed, like incense. From the lower trunk, one has a mixed tear of reddish-yellow and black, like common pitch, and if one presses upon it, a thin oil sweats out, pleasant and fragrant, though not strong. It is more powerful in one tree than in another, and those trees that stand on airy hills and well in the sun give the best tears. On the old trees, one finds clumps like our pitch or pale Colophony, but those have little smell left.*

*The second Scented Hairy Canarium, or the Rough Camacoan, has thick knotty branches, tapering bluntly at the front, with a few stiff stems around them, thicker than a shaft, and uneven, angular, or round below and with a sharp ridge above. At their origin is a broad and flexible "knee," on which are 8 to 10 pairs of leaves, some with one protruding alone, and at the fifth or sixth pair is also a "knee," and the two hindmost pairs usually fall off. They are six to nine inches long, four and five fingers broad, on short thick feet, thick, stiff, and somewhat bowed; the upper side is rough, like a shark-skin, the underside is woolly and there yellow-green.*

*In the Manipense variety they are hairier and pricklier, just as the leaves on various trees differ somewhat from each other in size and appearance, from which, however, no special sort is to be made. From the lap of the leaves, the flowering cluster comes forth, a hand or span long, and on it the small bud of the blossom, like the previous one.*

*The fruits hang on extended clusters, like Canariums, scarcely a joint long and a thumb thick, with a short point in front. When they are young, they are very rough and occupied with many prickly hairs, which cause an itching on the skin; they are three-sided from a round base. The nuts inside are larger than those of the Amboinese, prettily engraved, and perfectly three-sided. The shell under the outermost husk seems to be put together from three pieces, each piece making up one side, which has points or characters on the outer surface and the protruding rib. The inside is arranged as above.*

*The fruit-bearing clusters come forth at the end of the twigs, made of many stalks, and the fruits are blunt at the back and front. From this trunk drips a soft, slimy gum when it is notched, dark reddish and yellow, from which oil sweats when one presses on it. With this oil, the natives smear their head-hair, for it is not sticky. The gum dries up in time to a dark red and blackish resin; the fresh is lovely of scent, drawing toward Amber, but it comes so...*

# 158 HERBARIUM AMBOINENSE Book III. Chapter IV.

...but it exudes so rarely and in such small amounts from the tree that it is hardly considered Dammar <term>Dammar: a natural resin from dipterocarp trees, used in incense and varnish</term>, nor is it collected; by contrast, fairly large clumps drip from the former smooth species.

The wrinkled species possesses its best quality in that oil which drips spontaneously from this tree, which is mixed with that impure and rare Dammar. This oil emits a very pleasant scent, closely approaching the Western Balsam called *Decopal* <note>original: "Decopal"; likely referring to Copal resin from the Americas</note>. This same oil, dripping from the trunk into the ground, forms a dirty mass mixed with leaves, chaff, and earth, which nonetheless provides a pleasing fragrance, such that it might be considered an "earth made of Amber," about which more will be said below.

**Name.** I call the first species in Latin *Canarium Odoriferum Leve* (Smooth Fragrant Canarium); the Malay name is unknown. The Amboinese name in Leytimor is *Camacoan*, which generally denotes a fragrant Dammar. The people of Hitu, as mentioned, erroneously call it *Caman Silan* or *Dammar Selan*, unless we wish to believe that this Dammar was properly called *Cama Silan* by them after the western part of Ceram, located near the Bay of Haya, which is called *Silan*, where these trees grow.

The other species is called *Canarium Odoriferum hirsutum* (Hairy Fragrant Canarium); in Leytimor it is called by the same name as the preceding, namely *Camacoan*. In Waya it is called *Soë-Weyer*; in Manipa it is known by the name *Hahumalofsey*, that is, "the cracking of pigs," because wild boars greedily crack these fruits with a snapping sound.

**Location.** This tree grows in the mountains of Great and Little Amboina, but is quite rare. They do not wish to stand near other forest trees, but love a sunny place exposed to the open air. The best and most abundant occur in Manipa and Kelang; they would be found more frequently if the inhabitants gained some return from them to fill their bellies or make a profit.

**Use.** This resin would be excellent for making torches, which are used for daily and domestic purposes, but *Dammar Batu* <note>original: "Dammara Batu"; literally 'stone resin,' a common, harder variety</note> can be acquired in sufficient quantity; conversely, they neglect this resin because these trees supply it so sparingly, and do not drip it until they are a fathom thick <note>original: "ulnam crassae"; 'ulna' or 'vadem' refers to a measurement roughly equal to the span of its circumference</note>.

Those Ceramers from Silan, however, use it for torches and sometimes sell it to the people of Banda. Goldsmiths also use this Dammar, just as *Dammar Selan* or *Gummi lacca* (called *Ambalo* by the Malays) is used in other places. For they take one part of these Dammars ground into powder, and two parts of crushed Javanese vessels called *Gogeletten* <note>original: "Gogeletten"; small earthenware jars or goglets</note>, which are composed of a certain species of earth similar to *Terra Sigillata* <term>Terra Sigillata: 'sealed earth,' a refined medicinal clay used as a base in various crafts</term>, and they mix these with coconut water <note>original: "Calappae lympha"</note> into a thick paste. Over this they stretch very thin gold leaf, into which they then press various figures with iron stamps, continually heating the mass if it becomes too hard. The heads of daggers <note>original: "pugionum," likely referring to the Malay kris</note>, bracelets, and the heads of golden necklaces—which are fashioned in the shape of serpents or dragons—are filled with this or a similar mass; without this filler, all the figures would quickly perish due to the extreme thinness of the leaf from which they are composed. In medicine, it has had no use thus far.

The second or wrinkled species would provide more utility if better and more experiments were conducted with it. However, its fruits (the Canarium nuts) are not collected because their kernels are so small, but are left to the wild boars, from which it received the aforementioned name. It is to be hoped that its oil could be separated from the impure and brittle Dammar with which it is mixed and fouled, or that it would drip more copiously from the tree; then we would have a fragrant oil that could be compared with a certain Indian Balsam, and especially with that called *Copal*. The bark, too, if boiled down, might perhaps yield a thicker substance similar to *Liquidambar* <term>Liquidambar: a fragrant resin or 'sweetgum' used in perfumes and medicine</term>, an experiment I have not yet been able to perform since the trees occur so rarely. The inhabitants, however, collect neither this oil nor the resin for any use, since it drips in such small amounts; the oil drips in vain and falls into the ground below, where it is mixed with filth, dross, and earth, to which it imparts a pleasant Amber-like scent. If the earth impregnated with this oil is dug up and exposed to the burning sun, a small quantity of this fragrant oil floats to the top, with which the Amboinese women anoint their heads, when

<column-break/>

it oozes so sparingly from the tree that it is not counted as Dammar, nor is it gathered; on the other hand, from the previously mentioned smooth species, reasonably large clumps are obtained.

The greatest virtue of this rough species is the oil, which flows from the tree of its own accord and is mixed with the aforementioned dirty and scarce Dammar. This oil has a uniquely pleasant scent, coming very close to the West Indian balsam, named Decopal. The same oil, dripping from the trunk into the ground beneath, creates an unsightly mud of leaves, stubble, and earth, yet it is very pleasant of smell, so that one would take it for an Amber-earth, of which more will be said hereafter.

**Name.** The first species we call in Latin *Canarium Odoriferum Leve*; the Malay name is unknown. The Amboinese name on Leytimor is *Camacoan*, which generally signifies fragrant Dammar. The people of Hitu, as said, call it abusively *Caman Silan*, or Dammar *Selan*. Unless one wished to guess that they have properly named the Dammar *Cama Silan* after Ceram’s southernmost side, near the bay of Haya; which is named Silan, where these trees grow.

The second species is *Canarium Odoriferum hirsutum*; on Leytimor it has the same name as the preceding, namely *Camacoan*. On Waya it is *Soë-Weyer*; on Manipa it is known by the name *Hahumalofsey*, which is "Pig's crunching," because the wild swine like to crunch these fruits.

**Place.** One finds this tree, though very sparingly, in the mountains of Great and Little Amboina. They do not wish to stand among other forest trees, but here and there alone, where it is airy. The best and most are found on Manipa and Kelang, and one would discover more of them if the locals had something from them with which they could fill their bellies or make a profit.

**Use.** This resin would be more suitable for making torches, which one uses daily in the house, than the Dammar Batu which can be obtained in sufficient quantity; on the other hand, they are mostly abandoned because the trees give so little, and that no sooner than when they are a fathom thick in circumference.

The aforementioned Ceramers of Silan use them nonetheless for burning, and sometimes sell them to the inhabitants of Banda. Likewise, the goldsmiths use this Dammar, just as they do in other places with the Dammar Selan, or with Gummi lacca (named *Ambalo* by the Malays), for they take one of these Dammars rubbed to powder, and therein two parts of crushed Javanese Gogeletten, which are made of a certain earth (like Terra Sigillata), and mix such with coconut milk into a thick dough, over which they then beat thin gold plate, and thereafter with iron stamps drive all kinds of figures into it, each time making the mass a little warm if it becomes too hard. With this or a similar mass one sees filled the heads of their daggers or krisses, arm-rings, and the heads of their golden necklaces, which they make in the shape of snakes or dragons, and without this filling all figures would shortly be ruined, due to the thinness of the plate of which they are made. In medicine it is as yet unknown.

From the second or rough species one would have greater utility if it were better investigated. People do not gather the fruits of these Canaries because there is too little kernel in them, but leave the same for the wild swine, from which it has the above-mentioned name. But it was to be wished that one could separate the oil from the dirty and brittle Dammar with which it is mixed, or that it would weep more richly from the tree, so one would have fragrant oil, which could be compared with one or another West Indian balsam, especially with that of Copal. Also one could perhaps, by boiling the bark, have a thicker substance to compare with Liquidambar, which I have not yet been able to investigate due to the scarcity of the trees. Now neither oil nor resin is gathered by the locals for any use, because it comes out so sparingly, and the oil drips for nothing into the ground below, where it mixes with stubble, filth, and earth, and gives the same a pleasant Amber-smell, if one digs out the same muddy earth and places it in the hot sun, so a small portion of that fragrant oil comes...

### Book III. Chapter IV. AMBOINESE HERBARIUM. 159

it does not become viscous, and it dries quickly. However, that which is mixed with pure and dry earth can be preserved for a long time in closed small jars, so that it retains its pleasant scent. Such "Amber-earth" <note>original: "Ambræ terra"; referring to soil saturated with fragrant tree resin</note> impregnated with this scent was sent to me from Manipa, with the report that the odor was natural to that soil, which was otherwise entirely pure. Upon further investigation, however, it was discovered that two species of *Canarium* have this nature: they exude a subtle oil from the lower part of the trunk which, dripping onto the ground below, impregnates it with this scent.

The first and best oil drips from the **Hairy Canarium** <note>original: "Canario hirsuto"</note>, which endows the soil beneath it with such an Amber-like <note>original: "Ambarato"</note> scent that one might conclude for certain that true Amber was mixed into it, or that Amber had its origin there, although something of that Western Balsam scent always seems to be present. I add this not only for further investigation, but also to highlight the probability of a certain account which our countrymen living on the island of Mauritius sent to Governor **Joan Maetsuycker** <note>Joan Maetsuycker (1606–1678) was the Governor-General of the Dutch East Indies</note>: namely, that huge and vast trees grow on that island, whose trunks and roots exude a certain gum so closely resembling and smelling of Gray Amber <note>original: "Ambram griseam"; Ambergris</note> that they concluded all Gray Amber comes from such trees, as will be discussed further below regarding the *Small Nanarium*. Indeed, from that tree a fertile Amber-earth is collected, which I first thought was the best because it smells the strongest; but by further investigation, I found that the earth collected under the Hairy Canarium was much more pleasant, and thus it rightly deserves the first place. Whether one may conclude from this that Amber has no other origin than from such trees will be discussed further in the following chapter.

It is probable that this oily resin possesses a balsamic or healing <note>original: "consolidantem"</note> virtue, as I would conclude from this account: the inhabitants say that wild boars like to stay under these trees, not only to crack the nuts, but it has also been observed that they rub themselves with great force against these trees to squeeze that oil out of the bark and anoint themselves with it, especially when they are wounded. From this, it is gathered that the boars use this oil and its resin as a wound balsam.

The people of Buton, who are a greedy and deceitful folk, sell to strangers a certain resin that has a great similarity to *Camacoan*, but it is purer and condensed into larger lumps. It is semi-transparent; in some spots it turns blackish-green like bottle-glass, while in others it turns yellowish or white like impure birdlime <note>original: "visci bovini"</note> or **Gum Elemi**, which it resembles in substance and hardness. It easily shatters into splinters and is crushed if struck or bitten, whereas Elemi is softer. Its scent is also weaker—indeed, this resin is almost odorless; placed on coals, it breathes only a sweet scent which soon degenerates into a fatty smell <note>original: "nidorosum"</note>. When chewed, it is tasteless. The Butonese call it and sell it as **Mountain Amber** <note>original: "Ambra Montana"</note>, persuading people that they find it underground. However, from the adhering debris, it is clear that it dripped from a tree and was mixed with its bark and other filth from the ground. Upon further investigation, I found this Butonese *Dammar* <term>Dammar: a general term for various resins used for incense, torches, or varnish</term> to be from another tree called *Rowayl* in Buru, the description of which can be seen above in the chapter on the **Amboinese False Sandalwood** <note>original: "Pseudo-Sandali Amboinensis"</note>, Book 2, Chapter 20.

Furthermore, another resin under the name of *Dammar Selan* was brought to me from the bay of *Elipa Puti*, also located on the western part of Ceram. It was a lump a hand-span long and wide, composed of many whitish and transparent grains joined together like scales, similar to white *Dammar* but more viscous and mixed with bits of bark. Placed on coals, it crackles like *Dammar Selan*, but it smells like *Dammar Camacoan*. I believe it is the same as *Dammar Selan*, but collected from a younger tree.

In the Uliasser islands, a fragrant *Canarium* is found which is called *Canary* or **Yalanaffoy**, that is, the "Orphan Canarium," because these trees are encountered so rarely, and like abandoned orphans, they grow and are found here and there solitary in the mountains. This name, however, is given to two...

...a fragrant oil floats on top, which the Amboinese women use to smear their hair; for it is not sticky and dries quickly. That which is mixed with pure and dry earth can be kept for a long time in closed jars so that the good scent remains. And such "Amber-earth" was sent to me from Manipa, with the claim that it was the natural scent of that soil, especially since it was a pure earth. However, after much investigation, it was found that two *Canary* species had that nature: they let a subtle oil drip from the lower trunk, which gives the underlying ground such a scent.

The first and best comes from this **Hairy Canarium** <note>original: "Canarium Hirsutum"</note>, which imparts such an Amber-scent to its underlying ground that one could firmly believe that Amber was mixed in there, or that Amber must have its origin there, although something of the West Indian balsam scent still runs through it. I include this here not only for further research, but also to show the probability of a certain story sent by our nation residing on the island of Mauritius to the Lord General **Joan Maetsuycker**: that on the same island certain large trees grow, whose trunk and roots sweat out a certain gum, smelling and looking so much like Ambergris <note>original: "Ambergrys"</note> that they maintained all Ambergris came from such trees, as will be said more broadly hereafter regarding the *Small Nanarium*. For from the same comes the second Amber-earth, which I at first held for the best because it has the strongest scent; but by closer investigation, I found that the one under the Hairy Canarium was much more pleasant, and therefore ought to have the first place. Whether one may now conclude from this that Amber has no other origin than from such trees will be spoken of more broadly in the following chapter.

That it is now probable that this oily "tear" <note>original: "traan"; referring to a drop of resin</note> has a balsam or healing power in it, I would conclude from this: because according to the story of the natives, the wild pigs like to stay under these trees, not only to crack the nuts, but it has also been seen that they rub themselves strongly against that tree to press that oil out of the bark and smear themselves with it, especially when they are wounded, from which one guesses that the pigs use this tear as a true wound-balsam.

The **Butonese**, being a greedy and deceitful people, sell to strangers a certain resin having great similarity with the *Camacoan*, though purer and in larger pieces. It is semi-transparent, in some spots blackish-green like bottle-glass, in some yellow or whitish, like dirty ox-glue <note>original: "Ofschen-lym"</note> or **Gum Elemi**, not unlike it in substance and hardness; for it is brittle and snaps off short if one strikes or bites it, whereas Elemi is more flexible. It is also weaker, indeed almost without a noticeable scent; only on the coals does it first smell somewhat sweet, but it immediately turns to the smell of roasted fat; when chewed, it is without taste. The Butonese call and sell it as **Ambra Montana**, or Mountain Amber, making people believe that they find it under the earth, though it is evident from the adhering bits of straw that it has dripped from a tree and mixed itself with the bark or other filth from the ground. However, upon closer investigation, I consider this Butonese *Dammar* to be a resin from another tree, called *Rowayl* on Buru, for which see the description above in the chapter on **Amboinese False Sandalwood**, Book 2, Chapter 20.

Another resin was brought to me under the name **Dammar Selan**, from the bay of *Elipa Puti*, also located on the south side of Ceram, which was a lump a hand long and wide, made of many white, mostly transparent pieces sticking together like scales, like the white *Dammar*, though stickier and mixed with bits of the bark. On coals, it crackles like *Dammar Selan*, with a scent like the *Dammar Camacoan*, and I thought that it was the same *Dammar Selan* and taken from a young tree.

In the Uliassers, they have a fragrant *Canary* which they call *Canary* or **Yalanaffoy**, that is, "Orphan-child's Canary," because the trees are found so seldom, and stand alone like abandoned orphans here or there in the mountains; however, I find this name given to two types...

I have found that different names were given to various trees; for in Oma <note>An area on the island of Haruku</note> this is called *Nanarium*, and in Honunoa this is also called the **Scented Canarium** <note>original: "Canarium Odoriferum"</note>. Indeed, they showed me a small, triangular, and spotted nut, such as was described above, and a dull-white, brittle, and fragrant Dammar resin collected from that same tree.

**Camalanan** or **Camalane** is sought from a tree growing on the western coast of Borneo, which is similar in form and leaves to the wild *Canarium*.

The nuts, however, are smaller than those of the *Camacoan*, also triangular, but more wrinkled and more striated. Its resin is collected in larger lumps than the *Camacoan*, but is otherwise of nearly the same substance and color, except that it is more reddish. At first it is liquid and viscous, but in time it hardens just like **Selan Dammar** <note>original: "Dammara Selan"; a high-quality resin typically from trees of the Shorea genus</note>, with which it also mostly agrees in scent, or perhaps slightly more resembles the western **Tacamahaca** <note>A medicinal resin from Tropical American trees, known for its fatty, balsamic odor</note>, which has a fatty smell, whereas Selan Dammar has a herbaceous or floral scent. In Borneo it is also used for incense, but it is not found in great abundance.

From there, a similar resin was also brought under the name **Cotoarus**, similar to true Selan Dammar, but it was softer and stickier when chewed. It was said to be collected from a tree that bears small and triangular Canarium nuts, for which reason I consider it the same resin as the previously mentioned *Camalanan*. When thrown into the fire, it also gives a great crackling sound, although it is quite impure. Trees of this kind are rare, occurring only in remote mountains.

# CHAPTER FIVE.

## Black Dammar. *Dammar Itam*.

This tree is also of the *Canarium* genus, but it does not produce such a thick trunk or so wide a canopy. The leaves have two forms: on younger trees they are hairy and limp, while on adult trees they are smaller, rougher, and smoother. They are arranged in two or three pairs on a stalk, with a single odd leaf at the end. They are of the common shape, with the lower ones being five inches long and the upper ones nine or ten inches long, and four inches wide. They are smooth and dark green on the upper side, and wrinkled on the lower side, but not hairy, ending in a sharp point. Their ribs are yellowish and run more obliquely than in the true *Canarium*, interwoven with many intermediate veins which make the leaves wrinkled on the underside. At their base, both on the main stalk and on the leaf-stalks, joints <note>original: "genicula"; node-like swellings at the base of the petioles</note> are observed as in the *Canariums*. When crushed, they do not give off such a strong and penetrating resinous scent, but rather lean toward something slightly acidic. The main stalks of the leaves do not have those thick scales at their base where they emerge from the branches, which the true *Canariums* possess, but instead have only two small, cell-like structures in their place.

The flowers do not emerge at the very tip of the branches, but between the leafy stalks on many clustered woody stems. At first, they are small sharp buds that open into little flowers formed of three short, thick petals, which do not open very wide and are scarcely the size of a grain of wheat.

Many fruits hang together from these same stalks in the form of small *Canariums*, about the length of a fingernail, not truly round but slightly compressed along their length with a short point at the top. They remain green for a long time but finally turn black.

The nut has the same shape, being somewhat compressed and flat

<column-break/>

I have found that these were [the same], for on Oma they call it **Nanari** in this way, and on Honunoa this is called the **Scented Canarium** <note>original: "Canarium Odoriferum"</note>, for they showed a small triangular and spotted nut, like the one described above, and a dirty-white, crumbly, and fragrant **Dammar** <note>Resin</note> taken from its tree.

**Camalanan**, or **Camalane**, comes from a tree growing on the southern side of Buru <note>The Latin text says "Borneo," but the Dutch "Boeroos" refers to the island of Buru</note>, similar in appearance and leaves to the wild *Canarium*.

The nuts are somewhat smaller than those of the *Camacoan*, also triangular, but rougher and more wrinkled on the outside. Its resin is found in larger clusters than the *Camacoan*, otherwise mostly of the same color and substance, except that it is a bit ruddier; at first soft and tough, but over time it dries and becomes as hard as **Selan Dammar**, which it also mostly resembles in smell, or leaning somewhat toward the West-Indian **Tacamahaca**, which smells fatty, whereas the true Selan Dammar should smell somewhat flower-like. On Buru it is also used for burning <note>as incense or fuel</note>, but it is not to be found in abundance.

Additionally, a similar resin was brought to me from there under the name of **Cotoarus**, like the true Selan Dammar, but softer and tougher when chewed. It was also said to come from the tree that bears small and triangular *Canariums*, therefore I regard it as one and the same as the aforementioned *Camalanan*. In the fire it also crackles greatly, although it is reasonably dirty. Few trees of it are found, and those are far off in the mountains.

# V. CHAPTER.

## Black Dammar or Canarium Tree.

This tree is also from the lineages of the *Canariums*, but it does not grow as large in the trunk nor as wide in the crown. The leaves have two types of appearance, for on the young trees they are hairy and limp; on the grown ones they are smaller, stiffer, and smoother. They stand in two or three pairs on a small stalk, with one alone at the front, of common shape; the hindmost five inches, the foremost 9 and 10 long, four inches wide, smooth and black-green on top, rough from beneath, yet not hairy, with a stiff point at the front. The ribs are yellow and run much more obliquely than on the *Canarium*, with many small veins in between which make the leaf rough from below. At their origin, both on the stalk and by the small branches, they also have joints like the *Canariums*; being rubbed, they do not have such a strong resinous smell, but lean somewhat toward the sour. The small stalks do not have the green scales at the branches like the true *Canariums*, but instead have two small cells near their origin.

The blossom does not come exactly at the front of the branches, but emerges between the small stalks on woody stems, in clusters together, being small pointed buds that open into very small flowers made of three short and thick petals, which are not opened wide and are barely as large as a barleycorn.

The fruits hang together on the same clusters, in the shape of small *Canarium*, about the length of a fingernail, not exactly round but somewhat pressed in the length, with a short little point at the front, staying green for a long time, finally becoming black.

I have found that different names were given to various trees; for in Oma <note>An area on the island of Haruku, part of the Lease Islands in Maluku</note> this is called *Nanarium*, and in Honunoa this is also called the **Scented Canarium** <note>original: "Canarium Odoriferum"</note>. Indeed, they showed me a small, triangular, and spotted nut, such as was described above, and a dull-white, brittle, and fragrant **Dammar** <note>term: Dammar; a natural resin harvested from trees in the East Indies, used for incense, varnish, and caulking ships</note> resin collected from that same tree.

**Camalanan** or **Camalane** is sought from a tree growing on the western coast of Borneo, which is similar in form and leaves to the wild *Canarium*.

The nuts, however, are smaller than those of the *Camacoan*, also triangular, but more wrinkled and more striated <note>marked with thin lines or ridges</note>. Its resin is collected in larger lumps than the *Camacoan*, but is otherwise of nearly the same substance and color, except that it is more reddish. At first it is liquid and viscous <note>sticky or thick</note>, but in time it hardens just like **Selan Dammar** <note>original: "Dammara Selan"; a high-quality resin typically from trees of the Shorea genus, often called "cat's eye" dammar</note>, with which it also mostly agrees in scent, or perhaps slightly more resembles the western **Tacamahaca** <note>A medicinal resin from Tropical American trees, known for its fatty, balsamic odor</note>, which has a fatty smell, whereas Selan Dammar has a herbaceous or floral scent. flat without notable angles, but wrinkled and striated <note>marked with thin lines or ridges</note> all over, with a short tip that remains and does not fall off, which is not observed in other *Canarium* species. These fruits have a thick shell and cannot easily be opened by crushing; inside they bear a single cell containing a single kernel, as in other *Canariums*. The bark of the trunk is blacker than in the other *Canariums*. Its wood is white, soft, and not durable unless it comes from very old trees. If the lower part of the trunk is cut, it exudes a reddish, soft, and viscous <note>sticky</note> tear, which dries black within a few days and adheres to the trunk in small lumps. These never harden but stain the hands like birdlime <note>original: "Visci"; a sticky substance used to trap birds</note> if handled. On old trunks, however, they harden enough to be separated and collected, yet they remain soft and viscous inside. This resin, when kept at home for a long time, usually hardens like wax. While it is still liquid and flowing down the tree, it mixes with the filth of the bark, and falling to the ground, it becomes so defiled with leaves, stalks, and other fallen rubbish that it is the foulest and most difficult to handle among the Amboinese resins. It has a heavy odor that harms the head <note>causes headaches</note>, though not as much as the resin of the white *Canarium*. That which flows from the upper part of the trunk is always whiter and more translucent; the older the trees, the harder it is and the blacker it dries. It is collected in large lumps the size of a head, impure with filth, and is sold in that state.

This is the most well-known common *Dammar Itam* <note>Black Dammar</note>, but another species occurs, which is called the female, whose trunk bears a whitish or yellowish bark. Its leaves are like the preceding one but larger and mostly hairy. From its wounded trunk, an oily and reddish tear drips out, but more sparingly, and it slowly dries black, hence it is not collected. The wood of this trunk is softer and of less value than the preceding, almost like willow wood.

*Season.* <note>original: "Anni tempus"</note> The first species flowers in the months of November and December; it gives fruit in February and March.

*Name.* <note>original: "Nomen"</note> In Latin *Dammara Nigra* <note>Black Dammar</note> and *Canarium Nigrum* <note>Black Canarium</note>. In Malay *Canari* or *Dammar Itam*, and *Dammar Galla Galla*, which is to say, *resinous Dammar* <note>original: "Dammara resinosa"; pitch-like dammar</note>. In Ternate *Salo Coclu*. In Amboinese *Yar Yal Mette*, or by some *Iffe Seloe*. In Hitoe *Cama Mette*. All these names denote one and the same thing, derived from the black color of the resin.

*Location.* <note>original: "Locus"</note> This tree is known in all the Amboinese islands, especially on Great and Little Ceram, and the northern part thereof around old Liffa Batta, in Kelang and Manipa, in the Moluccas, and the Sula Islands. In Amboina, it occurs mostly in the Hitoe region, in high mountains among <term>Sideroxyla</term> <note>Ironwood trees</note> and other tall wild trees. Those that grow in rocky and sloping places provide good **Dammar** <note>term: Dammar; a natural resin</note>, but they give no or rare fruit, just as these are also rarely found on trees that are cut to elicit or collect the sap or resin.

*Use.* <note>original: "Usus"</note> Its fresh tear, especially from younger trees, is liquid like pitch but much more viscous, and it is used by the Amboinese in its place to coat their larger vessels, as is done with pitch among us. For this purpose, this liquid resin is placed in large earthen pots and mixed with **Coconut oil** <note>original: "Oleo Calappi"</note> or its milk, which are boiled together until they acquire the consistency of pitch, with which mass they coat the vessels. If a harder consistency is desired, a small quantity of common pitch is mixed in. The inhabitants of the Amboinese and Moluccan islands use this resin for their medium-sized vessels, which they call **Sampans** <note>original: "Tsjampans"</note> and skiffs. For larger ships, it is not used as much since it is not found in great quantities, and it obtained its name from this pitch-like coating. For this purpose, old and dry resin can also be used if the quantity of oil is increased and it is boiled longer, and the filth is skimmed off. That which is very dry and mixed with bark and ground-filth serves for torches; for all such lumps and clods are packed together and wrapped in leaves in the form of torches. These resins burn better and more slowly than *Dammar Batu* <note>Stone Dammar</note> and give less smoke. In Amboina, however, such torches are rarely used due to the small quantity of the former and the abundance of the latter. On the contrary, on the northern coast of Ceram, this black Damma-

Those that stand on stony and sharp grounds give indeed good *Dammar*, but bear then no or few fruits, just as one also generally finds them seldom on trees that one cuts to draw or tap any sap or resin therefrom.

If one wants it a bit harder, one puts a little of our country's pitch <note>European pitch</note> under it. To this also one may use that which is somewhat dried up from age, but one must add some oil, cook it longer, and skim off the filth. All that which is now a bit drier, and mixed with the bark and filth of the ground, is used for burning, all the little clusters packed together and wound in dry leaves in the shape of a torch. # CHAPTER SIX.

## The Smallest or Oily Nanarium. Nanari Minyak.

This tree is upright and tall, consisting of a trunk standing straight like a mast <note>original: "instar Mali"</note>, and a dense but not very wide crown. Its bark is smooth, ash-colored, spotted with dark and yellow points, barely as thick as a pinky finger and brittle; at the root it is hardly winged <note>referring to buttress roots</note>, but is knotty there.

Many leaf stalks are joined together at the ends of the small branches as in the *Canarium* trees, but they have no scales at their origin like those observed in the *Canariums*; on these stalks, four or five pairs of leaves occur, sometimes opposite a single terminal leaf, and sometimes with no terminal leaf at all.

The leaves and fruit are the smallest of all *Canarium* species, indeed they are smaller than the preceding Nanarium; specifically, its leaves are five, six, or seven inches long, two inches wide, and form almost a parallelogram, though they are a little wider at the lower part, rough, blackish-green, shining, and usually somewhat folded and wavy. The middle vein is whitish, protruding from both sides, as are the transverse ribs, which turn purplish on the underside of the leaf.

The branches are brittle, and from them, near the leaf stalks, other long stems arise like clusters of grapes; on these are flowers of almost the same form as the preceding *Black Dammar*. The fruits are the smallest of all *Canariums*, scarcely reaching the size of the *Black Dammar*, but more round than oblong; like young olives, they have the length of a fingernail, growing and hanging few together in clusters—first green, then a blue-black like Indigo. Beneath a thin husk, a nut is hidden of almost the same size, pointed at both ends and triangular with smooth edges, ash-colored. Beneath this hard shell, a small kernel is hidden, soft and white like tallow or grease <note>original: "Sebi vel exungiae"</note>, which is not edible and rots easily: in the center of this kernel, another small cavity is observed.

From the wounded bark of the trunk, a yellowish and clear oil exudes, though it is scarce at least in these regions; this is followed by another slime like egg white or mucus, which turns black within a few days like *Dammar Itam*, never drying completely but remaining like a sticky gum, adhering to the tree in small lumps. That aforementioned oil likewise exudes even if these lumps are removed; if they are squeezed slightly, the oil flows out, and in greater quantity if such impure lumps, as they are collected from the tree, are exposed to the heat of the sun.

This

<column-break/>

[This resin is] burned; on the other hand, on the north coast of Ceram, they mostly burn this black Dammar. In medicine, it is as yet unknown. That which comes from Sula Besi is much purer than the Amboinese, half-transparent like horn, also very sticky, and drying slowly.

From this resin, one can obtain a water through Chinese art, called *Preserving water*, clear, yet yellowish, with which one can coat many kinds of animals, from small birds, small crabs, and small fish, and afterwards let them dry, which one wishes to preserve for a long time.

Additionally, from the same Dammar, one has a thin Balsam, the color of *Balsam of Sulfur*, which is a good wound-balsam and is used in the same manner and against the same defects as *Spirit of Turpentine*.

# CHAPTER VI.

## The Oily Canarium Tree.

This is a straight, tall tree with a smooth trunk, erected like a mast, with a dense but not wide crown; the bark is smooth, gray, set with dark yellow spots, barely a pinky-finger thick, and brittle without notable "wings" <note>buttress roots</note> around the root, though somewhat knotty there.

The leaf-stalks stand many together at the ends of the twigs, similar to the *Canariums*, without the aforementioned scales at their origin, and on them are four to five pairs of leaves right against each other, some with one alone at the front, some not.

The leaves and fruits are the smallest of all *Canarium* kinds, and even smaller than the preceding Nanari, namely: the leaves five, six, and seven inches long, two inches wide, and almost parallel-sided, though just as wide at the back, stiff, black-green, shining, usually a little bent together or wavy. The mid-rib is whitish, and somewhat protruding on both sides, as are the cross-ribs, which are somewhat purple on the underside.

The branches are brittle, from which, near the leaf-stalks, other long stems come forth like grape-clusters, and on them the blossom, mostly of the same form as that of the preceding *Black Dammar*. The fruits are also the smallest of all *Canariums*, hardly as large as those of the *Black Dammar*, though somewhat rounder in their elongation, like young olives, the length of a fingernail, hanging a few together on their clusters, first green, then blue-black like Indigo. Beneath the thin husk lies the small nut, of almost the same size, pointed at the front and back, and three-sided with smooth sides, light gray in color. Beneath the hard shell lies a small, soft, and white kernel <note>original: "beest"</note>, like fat or tallow, which one cannot eat and rots very easily; in the middle of the kernel one sees another small cavity.

From the injured bark of the trunk, a yellowish clear oil comes sweating out, but very sparingly, at least in these lands, and upon this follows another sliminess like the white of an egg or snot, which in a few days turns black, like the *Dammar Itam*, never drying up, but remaining like a sticky gum hanging in small lumps on the tree, still sweating out all the prescribed oil; also when one takes these lumps off and presses them a little, the oil flows out, and even more abundantly if one puts the dirty lumps, just as they come from the tree, in

<meta>This page continues the botanical account of the Oily Nanari tree (Nanarium Oleosum) from page 162, detailing the properties of its oil and resin, its local names, and its geographical distribution across the Moluccas.</meta>

# BOOK III. CHAPTER VI. AMBOINESE HERBARIUM.

This oil first turns yellow, resembling olive oil in its clarity and hue, but over time it turns reddish, like Spanish wine <note>original: "Vini Hispanici," likely referring to Sherry or Sack</note>, and becomes thicker. The resin, when pressed out, turns blackish and dries into brittle clumps that hardly stick together. Both have a very strong scent, though it is more pleasant than the resin of other *Canarium* trees. Nevertheless, this scent can cause a heavy head as long as the oil and resin are fresh. They catch fire very easily if brought near a flame, even though they appear liquid. I once boiled a quantity of it in a pan over a fire to dissolve the oil, but it gave off such a powerful and strong smoke that everyone standing nearby suffered from a headache <note>original: "Cephalalgia"</note>; thus, I concluded it is much better to let the oil seep out naturally under the gentle rays of the sun.

I later learned that it is much better if the resin and oil remain joined together and are preserved that way, for their mixed scent resembles liquid storax <note>a fragrant balsamic resin</note>, lemon peels, and *Canarium* resin. This oil, when fresh, is so subtle that it penetrates the skin and warms it like a distilled oil. The best quality is collected from very old trees growing in rocky places well-exposed to the sun. Two such trees were observed on the small islands of *Nusa Telu* <note>original: "Nussatello"</note>, whose oily resin breathed a most pleasant scent approaching that of lemon peels, but it seeped out so sparingly that in an entire dry monsoon season <note>original: "menses siccos"</note>, barely two small cups <note>original: "cyathi"</note> could be obtained. The gum should not be separated from the oil, even though the mass then resembles a dirty and impure substance. That which is collected during rainy weather is useless, as it acquires a sour smell.

**The Season.** The fruits ripen during the west monsoon and are found fallen under the tree, mostly stripped of their husks. They are left there for the wild pigs, for since they are so small, they are not sought after by humans.

**Names.** In Latin, *Nanarium Oleosum* and *Nanarium Minimum*. In Malay, *Nanari Minyak* <note>original: "Nanari Minjac," meaning Oily Nanari</note>. Among the Amboinese, it has no specific name yet, except that the people of Hitu call it *Aybau Madelle*, which means "Sweet-smelling Tree." In Manipa it is called *Yaniri*, and in Bonoa, *Yasefel*.

**Location and Use.** These trees are rare and little known; in Ambon, only two or three are found on the Hitu coast near the Mamoa promontory, not far from the shore on the mountain slopes. They are hardly thicker than a man and yield little oil, which clings to the bark of the trunk with its gum and is very impure.

**In the year 1668**, it first came to our notice there, and since that time, the Moorish wives <note>original: "Æthiopum uxores" / "Moorse Vrouwen," referring to the local Muslim women</note> have collected that oil to make scented oils. For this purpose, they made incisions in the lower part of the trunk, from which this aforementioned gummy oil seeped out after several months. The oil from Nusa Telu was only discovered in 1676 and had, as mentioned, a much finer scent than that from Hitu. At the Cape of Nusaniwi <note>original: "Nussanive"</note>, a similar tree was also found, which bore larger and rounder nuts, but its oil is not yet known due to the ignorance of the inhabitants.

**Those** which grow in Manipa, Kelang, and Bonoa are of the same form as those mentioned above. Their leaves are four to six inches long and two inches wide; their ribs are a brownish-yellow, and they are otherwise smooth and a deep green on both young and old trees. The fruits have the same form, appearing in small clusters on short stalks. The liquid Dammar <note>a type of resin</note> dripping from the trunk is similar to the Amboinese variety, but it is blacker, has a more pleasant scent, and can be collected in greater quantities.

**The oil** from these tears <note>resin drops</note> dripping onto the ground from the trunk during the dry months gives the earth itself a lovely scent, which remains in the excavated soil for a long time if it is kept sealed. Such earth, under the name "Amber-earth" <note>original: "Ambar-aarde"</note>, was first discovered in 1681 on Manipa near the village of Luhu. For a long time, it was held to be true amber, and the inhabitants believed the scent was natural to that earth, since no tree grew exactly there and the scented earth occupied only a small space where it was dug up. Consequently, the owner of that place imagined that an "Amber-spring" must surely be hidden there. However, when they dug deeper, the scent vanished, from which I immediately concluded that this scent was accidental, namely originating from a certain tree which was around

<meta>illam / boom (that tree)</meta>
<meta>Tom. II. (Volume 2)</meta>

<column-break/>

*...the hot sun. This oil at first looks entirely like olive oil, namely yellowish and transparent, but over time it turns reddish, like Spanish Sack, and becomes thickish. The pressed-out resin then becomes blackish and dries into brittle clumps that hardly stick together. Both have a very strong smell, yet lovelier than other Canarium resins, though still weighing on the head as long as they are fresh. They also burn very easily if they touch fire, even though they seem moist. I once put a quantity in a small pan over a charcoal fire to melt the oil out, but it gave off such a strong smell and vapor that all the bystanders got a headache from it, so I found it much better to let it sweat out on its own by weak sunbeams.*

*Later I learned that it is even better if one leaves the resin and oil together and preserves them thus, for that smell was a mixture of liquid storax, lemon peels, and Canarium resin. Also, this oil being fresh is so subtle that it warms the skin and penetrates like any distilled oil. The best is obtained from very old trees that stand on stony mountains and well in the sun, like two such trees found on the small islands of Nusa Telu, whose oily resin had a very pleasant smell, tending toward lemon peels, but it came out so sparingly that in an entire dry monsoon one could hardly get two small measures, and one must not separate the gum from the oil, although the mass then looks like a dirty matter. That which is gathered in rainy weather is no good, for it gains a rancid smell.*

***Sayfoen.*** <note>This appears to be a local name or a specific term for the fruit/season</note> *The fruits are seen ripe in the West Monsoon, lying fallen under the trees, mostly stripped of their husks, lying there for the wild pigs, because due to their smallness they are not valued by people.*

***Name.*** *In Latin Nanarium Oleosum, and Nanarium Minimum. In Malay Nanari Minjac, among the Amboinese it has as yet no special name, except that the Hitu people provisionally call it Ayhau Madelle, that is, a sweet-smelling tree: On Manipa Yaniri, on Bonoa Yafefel.*

***Place, and Use.*** *These trees are rare and as yet little known; in Ambon one finds only two or three, on the coast of Hitu, near the corner of Mamoa, not far from the beach, in the ascent of the mountains, which are not much thicker than a man and give little oil, which hangs with its gum on the bark and is very dirty.*

***In the year 1668.*** *it first came to knowledge there, and since then the Moorish women have had its oil fetched to make sweet-smelling oil from it; to that end, notches were cut into the lower trunk, out of which after some months the aforementioned gummy oil came. But that from Nusa Telu first came to knowledge in the year 1676 and was, as said, much better of smell than the Hitu variety. On the corner of Nusaniwi a similar tree was also found, whose nuts are somewhat larger and rounder, but the oil from them is still unknown through the ignorance of the inhabitants.*

***Those which*** *grow on Manipa, Kelang, and Bonoa are mostly of the above form, having leaves four and six inches long, two wide, their ribs are brown-yellow, further smooth and arch-green <note>likely "high-green" or deep green</note>, on young as well as old trees. The fruits are of the same form, a few together in short clusters. The soft Dammar dripping from the trunk also resembles the Amboinese, yet is blacker and lovelier of smell; it can also be gathered in greater quantity.*

***The oil*** *of these tears dripping from the trunk onto the earth in the dry months gives it a lovely smell, which remains in the excavated earth for a long time if one keeps it stopped up. Similar earth under the name Amber-earth was first found in the year 1681 on Manipa, near the place Luhu, and was long held to be such, that it was a natural smell of that earth, for no tree stood exactly around there, and it occupied only a small place where it was dug out. Therefore the owner imagined that an Amber-fountain must surely be hidden in that place, but digging deeper that smell disappeared, from which I immediately concluded that it must be accidental, namely from a...*

On that island, therefore, many locations were explored, and it was found that the soil near the *Fragrant Canarium* <note>original: "Canarium Odoriferum," likely the Java Almond or Kenari tree</note> breathed out a most excellent odor. This was also observed around this *smallest Nanarium* <note>original: "Nanarium minimum"</note>, many trees of which are found on this island. Their liquid resin and the oil distilling from the trunk far surpassed the variety from *Hitu* <note>a peninsula on the island of Ambon</note> in the excellence of its scent. All the soil upon which this oil had fallen exhaled the same pleasant odor, resembling *Ambergris* <note>original: "Ambra," a highly prized fragrance found in the sea</note> mixed with a certain oil. I have kept this "Amber-earth" enclosed in small boxes and jars and found that it retains its scent for a long time.

Since in the preceding book, in the chapter on the *Amboinese Pseudo-Sandalwood*, the tree of the people of Buru called *Roweyl* is described, and it is simultaneously indicated that a blackish and viscous tear flows from it which somewhat smells of *Ambergris*, I conclude from this that on the island of *Mauritius* certain trees also occur (as mentioned above) which exude a gum or resin that smells like natural *Ambergris*. Our resident official living there wrote to Governor *Joan Maetsuycker* <note>Governor-General of the Dutch East Indies from 1653 to 1678</note> that those trees are vast, growing not far from the shore, and their roots always extend toward the sea. They exude that fragrant gum which, falling into the sea, becomes natural *Ambergris* through the motion of the waves, mixed with pebbles, sand, and shells. Thus, those people thought they had finally discovered the true origin of *Ambergris*.

It can easily be granted that trees grow on that island which exude a similar resin or "tears," as is evident from the examples of the *Fragrant Canarium*, the *Smallest Nanarium*, and the *Roweyl*. However, it seems far from the truth to claim that all *Ambergris*—found in such diverse parts of the world, separated by many thousands of miles, such as in the *West Indies*, the *East Coast of Africa*, *Madagascar*, the island of *Mauritius*, the *Maldives*, and all the islands situated to the *Southeast*—comes only from such trees. At the very least, this cannot be said of the trees growing on the island of *Mauritius*. If such trees also grow on the *East Coast of Africa* and *Madagascar*, it is most surprising that these trees were not observed or detected earlier by the sagacious *Arabs*, who already traveled through those regions a thousand years ago and diligently investigated their plants and herbs, yet never found them. Even if it were true that the *Ambergris* in *Mauritius* and *Africa* draws its origin from such trees, how does it happen that this same substance is carried so many hundreds of miles to the *East*, against the wind and current, to the *Maldive* islands? And furthermore, how does it travel so many hundreds of miles to the islands situated to the *Southeast*? It is well known that in the *Torrid Zone* <note>the tropics</note> in the open *Ocean*, the wind and current blow and flow from the *East* for almost the entire year. There is no example of any fruits or other things from these Eastern islands drifting *Northward* toward *Africa* and *Madagascar*, much less from those islands toward the *East*. For what could more easily happen than that the famous *Sea Coconut* <note>original: "Nucem Cocum," referring to the Coco de Mer</note>, which is cast up by the sea only in the *Maldive* islands, might sometimes be thrown *Northward* into those islands? Yet this has never been found. If, therefore, such "Amber-bearing" trees occur on the island of *Mauritius*, as we willingly concede, the origin of *Amber* <note>referring here to fossil amber, "Succinum"</note> is like its origin in the *Eastern Sea* <note>the Baltic Sea</note>, which according to modern experiments is produced from a clear liquid *Bitumen* or *Naphtha* generated under the earth in the regions of *Prussia* and *Pomerania*. This *Bitumen*, if it discharges its springs or flows into the sea, is hardened and congealed into *Amber* by the cold and saltiness of the sea water, and is then cast onto the shores.

Truly, the same *Bitumen*, when drawn up through the roots of certain trees that agree with its nature—such as the *Pine*, the *Pitch-pine*, the *Fir*, and similar trees which grow in great abundance in those regions, and especially along the *Vistula* river—is changed into the *Resin* of such trees. Yet no one would say that all *Amber* is generated from the *Resin* of such trees, even though it has the same origin and a similar affinity. Experience provides us with a demonstration of this, teaching us that natural *Amber* is not only found in the sea and on the shore, but in

If they also occur on the East Coast of Africa and Madagascar, then it is a great wonder that those trees were not known sooner to the curious *Arabs*, who visited those lands a thousand years ago and closely investigated their plants and herbs, yet never found these trees. For it is known that under the *Torrid Zone* in an open ocean, the wind and current fall out of the Eastern side nearly the whole year through. One has almost no example of any fruits or things from these Eastern islands drifting Westward to Africa and Madagascar, much less from there Eastward. Indeed, what else could more easily happen than that the famous *Coconut* <note>referring to the Coco de Mer</note>, which is only cast up by the sea in the *Maldive* islands, might also sometimes be thrown Westward onto the aforementioned lands? Of this, however, one has no experience. If then such Amber-trees are found on *Mauritius*, as we grant, it happens there just as it does with *Amber* <note>original: "bernsteen," fossilized resin</note> in the *Baltic Sea*, which according to modern research has its origin from a clear *liquid Bitumen* or *Naphtha* generated under the earth in the lands of *Prussia* and *Pomerania*.
