### The Smallest Nanarium
### *Nanarium minimum*

This tree is a smaller variety of the species previously described. On the island where it is found, the locals value it highly for the aromatic liquid it produces. 

**Description.** The trunk of this tree is quite slender and rarely grows taller than a man’s height. Its wood is tough but flexible, supporting numerous branches that extend outward. The leaves are **lanceolate** <note>shaped like a spearhead, tapering at both ends</note>, smooth to the touch, and marked with fine, feather-like veins. In the illustration, these leaves are shown growing in an alternating pattern along the woody stems.

**Flowers and Fruit.** At the tips of the upper branches, the tree produces clusters of tiny, star-shaped flowers. These develop into small, oval berries.
*   **A** <note>referring to the separate branch at the bottom of the plate</note> This segment shows the fruit in its more mature state, where it becomes larger and more distinct.

**Resin.** The most remarkable feature of this *smallest Nanarium* is its "tear" or resin. Unlike the thick, hard resins of other trees, this tree exudes a thin, clear oil or liquid resin when the bark is pierced. This substance is far superior in fragrance to those found on the peninsula of *Hitu*. When the oil drips onto the ground, it saturates the soil, creating what is known as "Amber-earth," which retains its pleasant, musky scent for many months, even when stored in jars.

<margin>The fragrance of this oil is said to mimic the finest perfumes of the East.</margin>

As noted previously, the roots of these trees often reach toward the shore, leading many to believe that the fragrant resin flows directly into the sea, where it hardens into the substance we call Ambergris. While this theory is debated by scholars, the similarity in scent between this tree's oil and true Ambergris is undeniable.

...it is also often dug up in the middle of inland regions, just as much in Prussia as in the Chinese provinces of Szechuan and Yunnan, situated several hundred miles from the sea at Edo <note>original: "Edo fitis"; likely referring to the Eastern regions or a specific mapping coordinate used by the author</note>, where many Pine trees <note>Latin: *Pini*</note> also grow. This can be seen in the *Chinese Atlas* <note>The *Novus Atlas Sinensis* (1655) by Martino Martini</note> on page 65, where Father Martinus testifies that he saw not only red and white Amber <note>Latin: *Succinum*; fossilized tree resin</note> (though yellow amber is not found there) dug out of the earth. He notes that the Chinese believe with one voice that it has its origin from the fatty and translucent segments of Pine trees, which over a long series of years have changed or degenerated into red amber. He further says that the Chinese can skillfully imitate or compose red amber from pure Pine resin, which they know how to prepare by boiling so that it not only carries the color and substance of amber, but also attracts light chaff <note>a reference to the static electrical properties of true amber</note>. However, a great difference is found between true amber and Pine resin, even if the latter is prepared by art. This same reasoning should be understood regarding Ambergris <note>Latin: *Ambra*; a rare substance produced by sperm whales, though historically debated</note>: while it is a natural cast-off of the sea, it is possible that this same juice, if drawn into certain trees, could generate an amber-like scent within them.

For a long time, I considered the dried resin of the <term>Smallest Nanarium</term> <note>Nanarium minimum</note> to be a certain dry and black resin called <term>Galedupa</term> by the people of Macassar. Later, however, I discovered that this comes from a different tree, described above in Book 2, Chapter 20. When I showed its oil to the Macassarese, they called it <term>Tin-fo</term>. This substance is necessary for them to create <term>Dupa</term> <note>a type of traditional incense or aromatic preparation</note>. It is of two kinds, though both flow from the same tree. The first is a yellow oil similar to Coconut oil <note>Latin: *Olei Calappi*</note>, which flows spontaneously from the tree, but gradually turns reddish and becomes viscous; they call this <term>Tinjo Calau</term>. The other kind turns black and is somewhat harder; it is collected in <term>Bamboo</term> <note>Latin: *Bambu*</note> tubes and offered for sale, much like *Galedupa*. Both are used for *Dupa* so that their stickiness can bind the other dry ingredients together. They are collected from unknown trees that grow on the islands of Salayera and Calaua, located to the south of Macassar, which they call <term>Silayer</term> and <term>Calautoa</term>—meaning "Great Calau" to distinguish it from another smaller island.

# SEVENTH CHAPTER.

## The Giant Canarium. Canari Besar.

We shall now describe the largest species of Canarium, both in terms of the tree and its fruit. Indeed, this tree is the tallest and most massive of all those found in these islands, and it is so thick that four or five men can scarcely embrace it. At the lower part of the trunk, it is greatly extended and augmented by wide "wings" <note>These are buttress roots, common in tropical rainforest trees to provide stability in thin soil</note>; further up, it stands erect like a very high mast, without side branches until the very top, where it spreads them out as widely as possible, making it impossible to climb. Its bark is smooth, whitish or ash-colored. Its branches are brittle and filled inside with a large and spongy pith <note>The soft, central tissue in a stem</note>. At the ends of these branches, many long leaf-stalks are situated together, as in other Canarium species, covered in a soft, reddish down, as are the tips of the branches. These stalks are long and firm, and upon them about six pairs of leaves are arranged opposite one another, resting on very short or almost no stems—nearly sessile <note>Attached directly by the base without a stalk</note>. They are slightly larger than the common Canarium but not as rough, and entirely woolly on the underside. They are nine or ten inches long, four or four and a half wide, tapering at the top into a short point, woven with many transverse and parallel ribs, and covered on the underside with reddish hairs. They are a brighter green than the common Canarium, and the two lowest leaves are always the shortest; however, on younger trees, they reach fourteen or fifteen inches in length and five or five and a half in width, and the entire branches and leaves are very woolly.

The flowers are unknown to me because of the tree's height, but without doubt, they do not differ much from the common large Canarium. The fruit has the size and shape of a goose egg, slightly wrinkled on the outside and marked with reddish spots like the *Atun* fruit <note>original: "Atun"; likely referring to the fruit of the *Atuna racemosa*, used in the Indies for oil and caulking</note>. Under a thick and viscous outer hull, a huge nut is hidden, about three inches long and two thick. It appears in three forms: the most common are triangular with protruding edges as if hemmed, but between these edges, the sides are wrinkled on the outside, carved with many streaks or hollowed areas, and pointed at both ends, though not sharply. Others on the same tree are square like a small box, but these are rarely found. Those of the third form are round, without notable edges, also wrinkled and slightly pointed at both ends; these seem to constitute a peculiar species or variety, for the leaves of this tree are also rounder and shorter. Most of the first species are not "hemmed" along their entire length, but only at the lower and sharp angle, while the rest of the part is wrinkled all over. The shell is very thick, solid, and apparently difficult to break; however, it is found to be otherwise, for if these nuts are soaked in water and then exposed to the sun, they develop many cracks which contract and close again when the nut is dry. It is even more marvelous that if this nut, which appears as hard as bone, is placed on a table and struck in the center with an ordinary knife, the blade penetrates at the first blow, and the shell shatters like glass.

The triangular and round nuts contain three cells inside, while the square ones have four, but only one kernel <note>original: "nucleus"</note> is found in these, rarely two, and the other intermediate parts are empty. This kernel is like the common Canarium but larger and wider, covered with a thicker skin that adheres slightly to the shell by a "wart" on its side. It has a more oily taste than the common Canarium, like dried walnuts, and is edible to the wild mountain dwellers; however, it is not valued by the coastal inhabitants, who have better Canariums, because its reddish skin can hardly be separated from the kernel. If these fruits are kept for some time without removing their hulls and they begin to rot, they emit a juice so viscous and clinging to everything that they can hardly be handled.

From the tree's trunk, a slow and viscous resin also flows, which is unmanageable when fresh, but dries into a clear and transparent resin almost like Gum Arabic <note>original: "Gummi Arabici"; a natural gum made of hardened sap</note>. In some places, this gum is more yellow than Amber <note>original: "Succinum"</note>, and is everywhere full of small...

<column-break/>

# CHAPTER VII.

## The Largest Canari-Tree.

*We shall now describe the very largest kind of the Canaris, both in tree and in fruit. The tree is among the very largest and tallest in these islands, so thick that four or five men can hardly span it with their arms. At the bottom, it has a large base or broad "wings," and is otherwise upright like a tall mast, without branches until the crown, where it spreads out very widely, and is therefore not to be climbed. The bark is smooth, whitish, or light gray. The branches are brittle, and have a large and spongy pith inside. At their front, the long twigs stand close together, as with the other Canaris, with a soft and reddish-yellow down, just as the ends of the branches are covered. The twigs are long and stiff, and on them the leaves usually stand in six pairs against one another, on very short and almost no stalks. They are quite as large as on the common Canari, though not as stiff, and on the underside entirely woolly, 9 and 10 inches long, four and four and a half wide, quickly pointed at the front, with many parallel cross-ribs, covered underneath with rough hairs, lighter green than the common Canari. The two hindmost are always the shortest, but on young trees they are a good fourteen and fifteen inches long, five and a half wide, and the entire branches with leaves are very woolly.*

*The bloom is unknown due to the height of the trees, but it will without doubt not differ much from the common large Canari. The fruit is in size and shape like a Goose-Egg, somewhat rough on the outside, and set with reddish spots, like the Atun fruit. Under the thick and slimy hull lies a large nut, about three inches long and two thick, of three kinds of shape; for the most common are three-sided, with protruding edges, as if hemmed, but between the edges the sides are wrinkled on the outside, carved with many stripes or furrows, pointed at the back and front, though not sharp. Others on the same tree are square, like a little box, but these one finds little of. Those of the third shape are round, without noticeable edges, also wrinkled, and at both ends a little pointed; these seem to make a special sort on their own, for the leaves of their tree are also somewhat rounder and shorter. Of the first sort, most are also not hemmed throughout the length, but only at the hindmost or sharpest corner. The rest is full of wrinkles all around. The shell is very thick, massive, and to all appearances hard to break, which one finds however to be otherwise; for if one makes the nuts wet and lays them in the Sun, they become full of cracks, which however close again when one dries them again. Even more wonderful it is, if one lays this seemingly stone-hard nut on a table and strikes it right in the middle with a common knife, one chops it through the middle with the first blow, the shell springing apart like glass.*

*Inside, the three-cornered and round ones have three little cells, the four-cornered four, but one finds only one kernel <note>original: "beest"; an old Dutch term for the edible part of a nut</note> in it, seldom two, and the rest stands empty. The kernel is like the common Canari, but larger, broader, covered with a thicker skin, which clings a little to the shell at the side with a wart. In taste, it is somewhat more oily than the common one, and like old Walnuts, and is edible by the wild Mountain-dwellers, but by the beach-dwellers, who have better Canaris, they are not esteemed, because one can hardly peel the brown skin from the kernel. If one keeps the fruits for a long time without taking off the hull, and it begins to rot, such a slimy sap comes out of it, sticking to everything, that one can hardly handle them.*

*From the trunk flows likewise a tough and slimy resin, which, being fresh, is not to be handled, but hardens into a clear and mostly transparent resin, almost like Gum Arabic. In some places yellower than Amber <note>original: "Bern-steen"</note>, full of little shoots all around, by which one can tell this Gum from others...*

...is collected, by which it is easily distinguished from others; however, the majority of it is impure, approaching a green or blackish color, as it drips down the tree and mixes with the bark and other filth from the ground; nevertheless, this serves best for torches. Its transparent pieces resemble the Amboinese *Dammar Batu* <note>Stone resin</note>, but they are not as clear, nor as elegantly yellow, but rather greener like glass, yet tougher and not as prone to shattering into shards as *Dammar Batu*. Pieces of this resin, even when dry, stick to one another if they are placed upon each other for some time, which is not observed in other resins. When placed on coals, it gives off an unpleasant, even foul smell; nonetheless, it is used by the inhabitants for torches. It crackles more when thrown into the fire than *Dammar Selan*, and it softens or becomes liquid in warm water—an argument that this substance is of a more gummy and watery nature than other resins.

***The wood of the trunk*** is white, soft, light, and not durable, filled with a spongy pith; it reaches a significant age, but due to its brittleness, it is easily broken off near the roots by strong winds and scattered.

***Season. The fruits*** ripen in the western months <note>The Western Monsoon, typically the rainy season</note>, which are the rainy months in the islands situated to the West, and at that time no resin is found on the trees; but in the Eastern months, when the dry season occurs there and the trees begin to produce flowers. Men do not cultivate these trees, nor do they grow around human dwellings, but only in the high mountains on the large islands.

***Name. In Latin*** *Canarium Decumanum*. ***In Malay*** *Canari Besaar* and *Canari Xula*. ***In Ternate*** *Nia*, *Haffu Haffu Xula*, and simply *Haffu*; of these, the longer fruits are called *Haffu Gogira*, and the round ones *Haffu Boppolulo*. ***In Amboinese*** on Buru *Yar* or *Yal Amin*, and around Tomahou *Cami*. Its resin is called *Dammara Amin* and *Camal Amin*.

***Location.*** In Amboina this resin is unknown, but most is found in the Sula Islands, and in the Moluccas on Halmahera, Buru, and Great Ceram, though not frequently; also in smaller quantities on Buton and the eastern coast of Celebes. In places situated furthest to the West it is unknown, as it is on all the small islands here. However, this tree is easily propagated, for I have often thrown its nuts here in Amboina into my garden, most of which, upon touching the ground, took root and sprouted, just as some trees are found here and there that were propagated in such a manner.

Its kernels are found on the seashore, cast up by the sea, elegantly cleaned and grey, but these do not sprout; they are undoubtedly washed away by large rivers on the major islands and carried into the sea, where after floating for a long time they are finally cast onto the shore.

***Use.*** The tree itself offers almost no use, except for its resin or *Dammar*. First, among the people of Sula and Buru, it is used for torches; they take this resin in its impure, natural state and mix it with the dust of crushed earth or ash, which are wrapped together in *Gomuto* <note>Fiber from the sugar palm, Arenga pinnata</note> leaves in the shape of a torch. The ash and earth are mixed in so that it burns steadily and crackles less. Secondly, it is used by the Ternateans for caulking vessels; it is boiled mixed with Coconut Oil and *Santang* <note>Thick coconut milk</note>, as was said above regarding Black Dammar. However, this resin is more difficult to boil because it swells up violently during the process and often rises above the vessel so that it can hardly be contained; therefore, it must be boiled over a slow fire, and the oil must be poured in gradually.

Certain mountain dwellers of Sula eat its kernels like other *Canariums*, although, as was said, they can hardly be peeled and cause headaches for those who are not accustomed to them. The Alfurs <note>Indigenous inland peoples</note> of Ceram make *Baguea* bread <note>A traditional dry sago biscuit</note> from them, mostly around the Bay of Cauwa. Some coastal inhabitants of these islands rub the shell of the Great Canarium upon a porphyry stone with water and smear this paste on their eyes against pain and burning caused by the heat of the sun. Every kind of weapon that has a handle is secured with this *Dammar*; it is first crushed, and the powder is filled into the hollows of the handles,

***The wood of the trunk*** is white, soft, light, and not durable, with a spongy heart; it reaches some age, but because of its brittleness, it is often broken off at the roots by strong winds.

The fruits*** become ripe in the West Monsoon, which are the rainy months in the Western Islands, and thus one finds no *Dammar* on the trees; but rather in the East Monsoon, when it is dry weather there and the trees begin to bloom. People do not tend these trees, just as they do not grow near human dwellings, but in the high mountains and on large islands.

***Name. The resin from it is named *Dammar Amin* and *Camal Amin*.

***Location.*** In Amboina this *Dammar* is unknown, but one finds it mostly in the Sula Islands, in the Moluccas on Halmahera, on Buru, and Great Ceram, though not abundantly, and furthermore somewhat on Buton and the East coast of Celebes; in the more westerly places it is unknown, as also on all small islands around here. It is, however, easy to propagate, for I have often thrown the nuts here in Amboina away in the garden, of which most that touched the ground sprouted, just as one still finds some trees here and there propagated in that manner.

The kernels are found here and there along the beach, cast out by the sea, beautifully cleaned and quite grey, but those do not grow; being without doubt washed away by the rivers on large islands and carried into the sea, where they have then floated a long time until they come against this coast.

***Usage.*** From this tree almost nothing is in use but the resin or *Dammar*. Firstly, by the people of Sula and Buru for burning, taking this *Dammar* as dirty as it is and mixing even more dust of finely rubbed earth or ash into it; and they wind it together in leaves of *Gomuto* into the shape of a torch. The dust or ash is added so that it burns more steadily and crackles less. Secondly, it is mostly used by the Ternateans for the pitching of vessels, mixed with Coconut Oil and *Santang* and boiled up, as was said above of the Black *Dammar*; but this *Dammar* is quite a bit more difficult to boil, because when it comes to the boil it swells so powerfully and overflows that one can hardly keep it in the vessels; therefore one must boil it with a slow fire and pour the oil in gradually.

Some mountain-dwellers of Sula also eat the kernels, like other Canariums, although, as said, they are difficult to peel and cause headaches for those who are not used to them. The Alfurs of Ceram make their *Bagéa* bread from them, but mostly around the Bay of Cauwa. Some local sailors rub the shell of the large Canarium with water on a stone and smear their eyes with it against the pain and burning they get from the heat of the sun. ## CHAPTER EIGHT.

### *Dammara Selanica: Dammar Selan.*

This provides the most common and widely used resin throughout all of the Indies, and by our nation is held to be and named Indian Colophony <note>original: *Colophonia*; a type of rosin traditionally made from pine</note>, but its tree is almost unknown to our people, since it grows on the large islands far from the sea and shore. It is divided into male and female, not differing much in the shape of the trunk and leaves, but we shall describe each specifically.

*Dammara* therefore called *Selan* or the male, is a thick and tall tree, usually straight, but sometimes curved; it bears a thick, reddish bark, usually wrinkled and split, but smooth on younger trees. Its branches are large and extended, forming a light and irregular crown, for these branches bear few shoots, and on them the leaves are sparse and mostly perforated or torn, so that this tree presents an unpleasant and deformed appearance.

This male tree bears leaves like those of the *Cananga*, or a little larger, thin, dry, and rustling <note>original: *tremula*; Dutch: *rammelende* — suggests a dry, rattling sound in the wind</note>, dull green, smooth on top, wrinkled underneath, five to eight inches long, two to two-and-a-half wide, ending bluntly but with a slight tip, woven with many parallel and transverse ribs. These are placed alternately on long shoots, which are slightly downy, and six or seven leaves are found on one side of them. The bark of the branches is blackish-brown, marked with many small dots; they are much heavier and sturdier than in the *Cananga*, and these branches are divided as if into joints.

The flowers sprout from the armpits <note>axils</note> of the upper leaves as well as at the ends of the branches in clusters a span long, divided into short lateral branchlets, which are not uniform or of equal length. On these first appear sharp and yellowish little heads, which open into small flowers formed of five narrow and yellowish petals, resembling tips, and these sit upon a calyx, which in its upper part forms a sort of box, in which five stamens like narrow petals are fixed; these enclose a certain roundish head. After the fall of this first flower, another flower entirely emerges from that same box, and from this comes the true fruit. This flower is composed of three narrow petals, about as long and wide as a little finger, narrow at the bottom and wide at the top, like a surgeon’s spatula <term>spathæ Chirurgorum | a flat, leaf-shaped tool used for spreading ointments</term>; it is at first purplish and downy, but then withers to a brown color, striated along its length, and wrinkled with many lateral veins. Between these petals, two or rarely three others are found, shaped like little tongues, which contain in their center a small nut, like half a hazelnut, wide at the lower part, but quickly tapering to a point with an oblong tip at the top.

Under a fragile shell is hidden a green and fatty kernel, bitter in taste and astringent, but many of the nuts are spoiled and useless for food.

## VIII. CHAPTER.

### *The Dammar Selan Tree.*

*This is the most common and useful resin through all the Water-Indies, and is held and named by our Nation as Indian Rosin, though the trees are mostly unknown to our people, because they grow on large islands somewhat far from the beach. They are divided into Male and Female, not differing much from each other in the fashion of the trunk and leaves, but we shall describe each in particular.*

*Firstly, Dammar Selan the Male; its tree is thick and high, mostly straight, and sometimes somewhat bowed, the bark thick, reddish, generally rough and torn, though smooth on the young trees. The branches wide, with a hollow, unsightly crown; for one sees few twigs on the branches, and there the leaves are each or mostly eaten through, so that it is an ugly tree to look upon.*

*The Male has leaves like those of the Cananga, or quite as large, thin, dry, and rattling, dead-green, smooth above, and rough below, from five to eight inches long, two and two and a half wide, blunt in front, with a short point, and many parallel cross-ribs. They stand arranged against each other on long twigs, which are somewhat woolly, with six or seven leaves on one side. The bark on the branches is black-brown, set with many dots, and are much heavier and stiffer than those of the Cananga, as if divided into joints.*

*The bloom comes out of the lap of the front leaves, and the ends of the branches themselves, a span long, and divided into short side-twigs, which are not uniform in position and length. On these one first sees pointed and yellowish buds, which change into small flowers of five narrow and pale-yellow leaves, or rather points, which make a little foot, bearing on top a little cup or pot, in which one sees five other threads or narrow leaves, hiding a small bud, like a pin-head. After the falling of this first bloom, an entirely different flower comes out of the aforementioned pot, and the true fruit. This flower is made of three narrow leaves, about a pinky-finger long and wide, narrow behind, and wide in front, like a surgeon's spatula, first brown-red and woolly, but fading to a sallow color, ribbed lengthwise, and wrinkled with many cross-veins; between these stand yet two, and seldom three other leaves, also formed like little tongues, and they enclose in the middle a small nut, like a half Hazel-nut, wide below, and suddenly pointed, with a longish little point on top.*

*Under a breakable shell lies a greenish and fatty kernel, somewhat bitter, and drawing together in taste, though most nuts are harsh, and unfit to eat.*

younger ones, for at the very top of the leaf stalk <note>original: *rachis*</note> such clusters arise, bearing many small scaly petals or leaflets, which appear like little flowers, but then degenerate into stalks and leaves. I cultivated such a tree until its sixteenth year, and I held such clusters to be true flowers, but nothing else ever followed from these except leaves, until at last the described and true flowers came forth.

The wood of the trunk is reddish when green, but when dry it is brown like Ironwood <note>original: *Sideroxyli*</note>, which it also resembles in its hardness and weight; however, it consists of coarser fibers and is less durable, nor can it be polished so brightly, for its substance is so coarse that here and there in this wood thick veins appear filled with white resin, which falls out during the working of the timber, making the planks uneven and hollowed out with small pits. Otherwise, no resin or very little drips from these trunks, and only in their great old age; this resin is white and brittle, and is not collected.

The Female <note>Rumphius frequently categorized plants as 'male' or 'female' based on their robustness or fruit-bearing habits, a common practice in pre-Linnaean botany</note> bears a rougher trunk and a denser crown; the leaves are of the same shape but larger, also arranged alternately, six or eight on one side, of which the lowest and uppermost are the shortest, six and eight inches long, while the middle ones are nine and ten, and a palm's width broad. They sit on short, thick stems <note>original: *petiolis*</note> and are interwoven with many transverse and parallel ribs; they are rough underneath, but not as much as the male, and are more limp, as well as being much eaten away [by insects]. They have a pale green color and, if handled or moved, they rustle.

In younger trees, nine or ten leaves are located on one part of the stalk, and they are more downy than in the old ones. At the ends of the twigs, as seen first in younger trees, certain leaflets appear crowded together in clusters and scaly, which are mistakenly taken for flowers; such things also sprout from the leaf axils. However, true flowers follow these, of the same shape as the male but a little larger, and after these again another flower of the same shape as described, but larger and more closely resembling the *Cananga* <note>The Ylang-ylang tree (*Cananga odorata*)</note> flower. It is formed of three large, spatula-shaped petals, positioned in a true triangle and more extended than in the *Cananga*; they are more rough and bear a paler color, namely a mixture of yellow and green. Furthermore, they are veined and wrinkled, and as noted above, provided with two or three narrower, tongue-shaped intermediate petals. These flowers are clustered as in the *Cananga*, whose scent they also faintly imitate. In their center, a fruit is formed resembling a Hazelnut, slightly pointed, whose shell is thinner and contains a soft, ash-gray kernel of a more unpleasant taste than the *Canarium* <note>The Java Almond</note>, and which is mostly bored through by a thick and fat worm. The flower hangs withered around this nut for a long time, and mostly falls off with it while immature; otherwise, if these nuts are ripe, they fall alone and serve as food for wild boars.

The wood of the female is not as brown or hard as that of the male, and is much lighter, more spongy, and useless for buildings. However, from these trunks, when they reach great old age, even if they are not wounded, a copious yellowish resin flows spontaneously, exuding everywhere from the cracks and fissures of the bark. It is also found in great quantity between the bark itself and the wood—indeed, even in the wood itself, contained in thick veins—so that no other tree is known to me that yields resin in such abundance. Indeed, branches are often observed on this tree consisting almost of pure resin to a length of three or four feet, and having the thickness of a man's thigh; for it is common for cones of resin hanging from the branches to have the thickness of an arm. I have received pieces of this resin from Xula <note>The Sula Islands in Indonesia</note> that resembled an artificial reef. This resin (which is called by the common name <term>Dammara</term> <note>Dammar: a resin obtained from trees of the family Dipterocarpaceae</note>) soon hardens as soon as it exudes from the tree. In some trees it is yellow, in others dark green or blackish, and in other parts semi-transparent, and so similar to raw and unrefined Amber <note>original: *Succino*</note> that it can hardly be distinguished, especially certain segments of it which are transparent and of such an elegant and intense yellow color as the best Amber. This *Dammara*, however, is generally more brittle, and that which comes from younger trees is crumbly. On the other hand, pieces from old trees are found which have the color of Colophony <note>Rosin</note>, which, falling into the rivers and being carried by them into the sea, become rough on the outside through continuous and long-lasting currents,

for at the ends of the twigs similar clusters come forth, with many small and scaly leaflets, which one would take for blossoms, yet they change into twigs and leaves. I have raised such a tree for about sixteen years, and always took the same for the true blossom, upon which nothing followed each time but leaves, until finally the aforementioned true blossom came forth.

The wood of the trunk, when green, is light reddish, but it seasons to brown, like ironwood, which it also resembles in hardness and weight, though it is much coarser-grained, less durable, and does not allow itself to be worked so smoothly; for it is so coarse in substance that one sees here and there in the wood thick veins of white resin, which falling out during the work, makes the planks uneven and full of little pits. Otherwise, little or no resin drips from these trunks, and only in their high old age, which is white and crumbly, and is not gathered.

The Female has a rougher bark and a denser crown; the leaves are of the same shape, but larger, also standing alternately opposite each other, six and eight on one side, of which the backmost and foremost are the shortest, six and eight inches long, the middle ones nine and ten, and a hand's breadth, standing on short and thick stalks, also threaded with many parallel transverse ribs, also rough underneath, though less than on the Male, and flimsier, also very much eaten through, of a pale green color, and rattling when handled.

On the young trees, nine or ten leaves stand on one side, and are more woolly than the old ones. At the ends of the twigs one likewise sees, and first on the young trees, some small leaflets in a cluster, joined together like scales, which are mistakenly taken for the blossom; similar ones also stand here and there at the origin of the leaves. Upon this follows the true blossom of the same shape as on the Male, though somewhat larger, and upon that the second flower, also mostly of the same shape, though larger, and better resembling the Cananga flower, made of three large spatula-shaped leaflets, standing right in a triangle, and more opened than on the Cananga, also stiffer and paler in color, namely, mixed from sallow and green, furthermore veined and wrinkled, as above, with two or three narrow little tongues in between; they hang in bunches together, like the Cananga, whose scent they also weakly imitate. In the middle the fruit is formed, which resembles a Hazelnut, with a short point, whose shell is somewhat thinner, and inside has a soft grayish kernel, more unpleasant in taste than Canaries, and mostly eaten through by a thick fat worm. The flower remains hanging fast around this nut for a long time, and mostly falls off unripe with the same; otherwise, the ripe nuts also fall off alone, and are eaten by the wild Pigs.

The wood of the Female is not as brown and hard as that of the Male, much lighter, more pithy, and unfit for building. Now from these trunks, when they have also become heavy trees, even if one does not wound them; an abundant yellowish resin flows, sweating out everywhere from the cracks and grooves of the bark, which one also finds richly between the bark and the wood, yes, even with thick veins in the wood, so that no other tree in the world is known to me that gives off resin in such quantity, for one finds branches hanging on this tree of pure resin, three and four feet long, and as thick as a thigh, but cones as thick as an arm are common, and I have obtained pieces from Xula that one would take for an artificial rock. This resin (which is called by a common name <term>Dammar</term>) becomes hard immediately as soon as it sweats out of the tree, is pale yellow, in some parts half transparent, so like foul Amber that one can hardly distinguish it, especially some fragments that are beautiful and clear, and as high-yellow in color as the best Amber, yet this Dammar is generally brittler, and those that come from young trees are crumbly. On the contrary, one finds pieces from old trees, of a color like Colophony, which falling into the Rivers, and being carried by the same into the Sea, become rough and white on the outside by the long rolling, while remaining clear inside, and generally becoming so hard that I have picked them up on the beach for Amber. ...and white, but internally transparent, and they usually harden to such an extent that I have collected them on the shore as Amber <note>original Latin: *Succino*</note>. Indeed, the pieces that drip from the trunk onto the ground and are dug up from the earth in large clods are much more impure, and are more blackish, darker, and stained with more filth. This Dammar also, when handled with the hands, breathes a notable but unpleasant odor, coming very close to Rosin <note>original Latin: *Colophoniam*; a solid form of resin obtained from pines</note>, which odor also remains for a long time on the hands, which become sticky from this resin. When placed upon coals, it breathes a more pleasant odor, as if Frankincense <note>original Latin: *thus*</note>, Rosin, and Cananga flowers were mixed together; however, the odor is not so pleasant that this alone would suffice for incense, but it is mixed with other perfumes. Furthermore, it is not as fatty as our Rosin, whence it does not catch fire as easily, but rather it crackles and leaps apart as if salt were mixed in, if it is placed on coals—especially if it has been recently collected from the trees or wrapped in water for some time. However, that which has been preserved for a long time or crushed gives a smaller noise when cast into the fire; if chewed with the teeth, it also crackles and is crushed into powder, so that it is the most suitable of all resins to be ground into powder. Exposed to the burning sun or poured into hot water, it by no means softens but hardens more; however, if the flame of a fire is brought near, it liquefies, burns gently, and raises bubbles, but its fire quickly perishes, from which it can easily be concluded that a large part of Volatile Salt <term>Salis Volatilis</term> <note>In early modern science, this referred to the "spirituous" or reactive chemical components that evaporated easily</note> is contained in this resin, which is also the reason that its resinous fatness easily catches fire, but due to the continuous crackling and jumping, it can neither contain nor nourish it.

*Name.* The resin of this tree is more well-known and is called *Dammara Selanica*; in Malay, *Dammar Selan* and *Dammar Sila*, and by some also *Dammar Malejo*. By those of Ternate, *Salo Garo*, that is, scented Dammar, after the fashion of *Garo* or Eaglewood <note>original Latin: *Agallochi*</note>; our people call it Indian or Malay Rosin; in Amboinese it is called *Cama Lilan*. The tree which exudes this is named in Boero by the Ternate word *Caju Bappa*, but by the inhabitants themselves *Hiny*, and its resin *Salo-Hiny*. In the southern part of Boero, *Babut* and *Biabut*. From where the name *Dammar Selan* takes its origin is not yet certain to me: see, however, the speculation proposed above in the chapter on the *Fragrant Canarium* <note>original Latin: *Canarii Odoriferi*</note>, which nevertheless does not correspond to this Dammar, since it rarely or never occurs in those regions of Ceram.

*N. B.* *Dammar* is a Malay-Indian name and denotes every resin and tear that flows spontaneously from a certain tree and burns when brought to a fire, just as *Gatta* or *Gitta* denotes such watery tears that drip like sap or milk from trees, which we call Gums or condensed juices, which liquefy in water and do not easily catch fire.

The word *Dammara* is derived from the Arabic *Damma* or *Dammea*, which signifies any kind of hardened tear dripping from a tree; this furthermore has its origin from the Hebrew *dema*, likewise signifying a tear; in the middle of the Arabic word *Dammar*, an apostrophe is inserted to indicate the letter *Ain* or *Ugain*, which cannot be expressed in Latin letters, and merely teaches that it is to be pronounced through the nose after the following vowel.

*Location.* This Dammar occurs in almost all the large islands of watery India <note>The East Indies/Maritime Southeast Asia</note>, such as in Sumatra around Jambi and Palembang, in Borneo around Sukadana, as well as in the two smaller islands of Belitung and Karimata. In Java and other eastern islands further on, as well as in Celebes, where however it is not much known or encountered; it is found copiously in Great Sula, and especially in the bay of Lickatobi, in Boero around old Luciela and Kelanga. Ceram also provides it, but in small quantity, for the *Dammar Selanica* which is brought from there is thought by me to be the above-mentioned Fragrant Canarium or *Camacoan*. It is found equally on the shore as on high mountains, but nowhere in the flat forests, but always at the sloping feet of mountains which are situated next to the shores of rivers and the sea. Hence in Boero this Dammar is found floating equally at the shore as in the larger rivers which run out into the Bay of Kayeli. In the eastern part of this bay, certain trees on the mountain slopes rise so high that they lean their crowns over the sea.

*Usage.* This resin is used throughout all of watery India in place of Rosin for strengthening <note>caulking or pitching</note> ships, but by far...

<column-break/>

*...being dug out, they are much purer, blackish, dark, and mixed with filth. This Dammar also, merely handled with the hands, gives a notable and unpleasant smell of its own, coming very close to our Rosin <note>original Dutch: *Harpuis*</note>, which smell also remains long on the hands, which also become stiff through the handling of this resin. On coals it smells even more lovely, as if incense, Rosin, and Cananga flowers were mixed together, yet by no means so lovely that one could make perfume from it alone, though it is mixed among others; it is not nearly so fatty as our Rosin, therefore it does not catch the fire so easily; it crackles and jumps on the coals as if it were mixed with salt, especially that which comes fresh from the trees or has rolled in water for a long time; but that which has been kept for a long time, or is rubbed, crackles little on the fire, so that it also crackles between the teeth when one bites into it, and it crushes entirely to dust, allowing itself to be brought to powder most easily of all resins. Placed in the hot sun or hot water, it will by no means become soft, but even harder; held to the flaming fire, it nevertheless melts, burns gently, and throws up bubbles, but the fire goes out immediately, from which one may conclude that much Volatile Salt <term>Sal volatile</term> dwells in this resin, which is the cause that the resinous fatness indeed catches the fire easily, but because of the constant crackling and jumping, cannot keep it long.*

*Name. The resin of this tree is best known and is properly named <term>Dammara Selanica</term>. In Malay, <term>Dammar Selan</term>, and <term>Dammar Sila</term>, by some also <term>Dammar Malejo</term>. In Ternatean, <term>Salo Garo</term>, that is, fragrant Dammar, like <term>Garo</term> or Eaglewood; our people call it in Malay or Indian Rosin. In Amboinese, <term>Cama Lilan</term>. The tree from which it comes is named on Boero with a Ternatean word <term>Caju Bappa</term>, and by the islanders themselves <term>Hiny</term>, and the resin <term>Salo Hiny</term>. On the south side of Boero, <term>Bahut</term> and <term>Biahut</term>. From where the name <term>Dammar Selan</term> comes is not yet properly known to me, except for the guess that I have placed above in the chapter of the <term>Fragrant Canarium</term>, which however does not fit this Dammar, because it falls little or not at all in the same region of <term>Ceram</term>.*

*NB. <term>Dammar</term> is a Malay-Indian word, and signifies all sorts of Resins and Tears that flow of their own accord out of some trees, and burn when held to the fire, just as <term>Gatta</term> or <term>Gitta</term> signifies all sorts of watery tears that drip like a sap or milk from the trees, which we call Gums or dried saps, which melt in the water but do not easily burn.*

*The word <term>Dammara</term> is derived from the Arabic <term>Damma</term> or <term>Damea</term>, which means every sort of resin or Gum run together and dripping from the trees: and this has again its origin from the Hebrew <term>Dema</term>, also meaning a resin; in the middle of the Arabic word <term>Dammar</term>, an apostrophe is inserted to signify the letter <term>Ain</term> or <term>Ugain</term>, which can be expressed in no Latin letter, and is only pronounced after a following vowel as if through the nose.*

*Place. This Dammar is found in almost all large islands of Watery India, such as on Sumatra, around Jambi and Palembang, on Borneo around Sukadana, as well as on the two smaller islands, Belitung and Karimata. On Java and further eastern islands, as well as Celebes, it is not much known, but again abundant on Great Sula, especially in the bay of Lickatobi, on Boero around old Luciela and Kelang. Ceram has it also, though little, for the Dammar Selan coming from there I hold to be the aforementioned <term>Fragrant Canarium</term> or <term>Camacoan</term>. It grows as well along the shore as the high mountains, yet nowhere in flat forests, but always on the slopes of the mountains that stand along the banks, both of the Sea and great Rivers. Therefore one finds on Boero this Dammar not only on the shore but also floating in great Rivers that come out in the bay of Kayeli. On the east side of the same bay, some trees stand so steeply on the mountains that they hang with their crowns over the Sea.*

*Usage. This resin is used throughout all of Watery India in place of Rosin, to pitch <note>original Dutch: *pikken*</note> the vessels...*

### BOOK III. Chapter VIII. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...far differently than is done among us, for this **Dammar** cannot be liquefied over a fire alone, like **Rosin** <note>original: Colophonia</note> or pitch; therefore, it is melted with **Coconut oil** <note>original: oleo Calappi</note>, though not without effort. In contrast, the **Malays** <note>original: Maleyenſes</note> use another method: they crush this **Dammar** into a fine powder, either alone or mixed with water, which they then gently pour off. They then mix this paste with **coconut water** <note>original: Calappi lympha</note>, or gradually with its oil, in small doses, which they rub with great force in large basins and work together with sticks until it becomes a paste as supple and soft as pastry dough. For this powder mixes itself with the coconut water and oil, and separates the rest of the mass from the superfluous water, if any was mixed in. This mass is then drawn into long and narrow strips, which are applied to the seams of vessels with the help of glass or porcelain tools—to which the paste does not stick—where it joins and adheres as firmly as any other **Rosin**, and even hardens further in seawater. To coat the remaining wood of the ships, the **Malays** use another pulp in place of pitch, which is composed of **Lime** and **Castor oil** <note>original: Oleo Ricini</note>, which in these Eastern islands is prepared with the aforementioned **Black Dammar** <note>original: Dammara-Itam; 'Itam' is the Malay word for black</note>. If they desire this paste to be black, they mix in charcoal powder burned from old **Rattan** <note>original: Rottangae</note> cords. However, no greater quantity of this paste should be prepared than is necessary for immediate use, as it hardens so much that it cannot be handled afterward.

Furthermore, this simple resin serves for torches which are in common use and are prepared in an ingenious way; great quantities are sent for sale to **Batavia** <note>modern-day Jakarta</note> from **Bantam**, **Siam**, and other Malay regions. They are made in the following way: **Ceylon Dammar** <note>original: Dammara Selanica</note> is crushed into a fine powder, which is mixed with a third part of black earth or ash, and dry **Betel-nut** <note>original: Pinangae</note> husks or rice chaff, which are mixed together with water into a paste. This is wrapped in dried shoots of **Coconut** or **Betel-nut** trees, or dry leaves of the **Lontar** or **Gomuto** <note>Sugar Palm</note> palms, in the form of a torch about a foot long, which is coated on the outside with lime. These torches are lit at the upper end and carried by hand through the streets; they catch fire easily but do not resist strong winds well. They give off a pleasant scent, though it is heavy for newcomers and those unaccustomed to it. The people of **Buru** <note>original: Boeronenſes</note> do not value this resin as much; they only crush it with black earth and wrap it in leaves of the **Gomuto** or similar trees. As long as they can find other **Dammar**, they will not use this kind because of its crackling and the throwing of sparks, which burn fiercely when they touch the skin—though this crackling is hindered by mixing in earth and other debris, as is seen in the **Batavia** torches. The people of **Sula** <note>original: Xulanenſes</note> do not use it for this reason, as they can find other kinds in sufficient quantity. Those of **Masassar** choose the finest fragments, closely resembling **Amber** <note>original: Succino</note>, which they mix into the **Incense** <note>original: Dupae; likely from the Malay 'Dupa'</note> made for the common people to increase its scent, but it does not enter into the **Royal Incense**.

Since our nation <note>the Dutch</note> is often not well supplied with its native **Rosin**, they often use this **Dammar** in its place, or at least mix it with the same, taking thirty pounds of **Dammar** to ten pounds of **Rosin**, and more than a pint of **Coconut oil**, which they melt together and use to caulk their ships.

The **Male trees**, since they are very straight and solid, provide the best wood for sawing planks, just as is otherwise done with **Tsjicki** wood. These are very heavy, so that they are regarded by the common folk as **Ironwood** <note>original: Syderoxylo</note>. These planks are cut thick and used in shipbuilding, but it has been found that they easily attract **shipworms** <note>original: teredines</note>, which the locals attribute to the ignorance of our carpenters, who use the wood while it is still fresh and full of potent sap. The fruits are greedily sought after and eaten by wild boars and animals called **Cuscus** <note>original: Coescoeſen; a type of Australasian marsupial</note>. Our hunters have especially observed that a wondrous boar called the **Babirusa** <note>original: Babi-Ruſſa; literally 'Pig-Deer'</note>, which occurs on the islands of **Buru** and **Sula**, likes to linger under these trees, not only chewing the fruits but also raising itself against the tree with its front feet, rubbing itself against it as if it were delighted by the scent of the **Dammar**; hence, many are captured under these trees.

<column-break/>

...yet much in another way than we do with our **rosin** <note>original Dutch: harpuis</note>, for this **Dammar** does not let itself be melted over the fire alone like Rosin or pitch. Therefore, it must be melted with **Coconut oil**, and that not without difficulty. In contrast, the **Malays** use another method, for they crush this **Dammar** small, either alone or with water, which they afterwards gently pour off; they mix the dough with **coconut milk** or oil gradually and in small portions, rubbing strongly in large basins and working it together with sticks until it becomes as supple as a pastry-cook's dough. For this powder mixes with the coconut milk or oil and separates the mass from the remaining water that might still be in it. This mass is thereafter beaten or drawn into long narrow straps, which one lays on the seams of the vessels and pastes against them with a piece of porcelain or something smooth that the dough cannot stick to, as wide as one wishes, where it sticks as firmly as any **Rosin**, becoming harder and harder in seawater. To smear the remaining wood of the vessels, the **Malays** use in place of tar another slurry which they make of lime and **Castor oil**, which they perform in these Eastern Islands with the aforementioned **Black Dammar** <note>original: Dammar-Itam</note>. If they want this dough to be black, they put under it the powder of charcoal burned from old plaited **Rattan** ropes; one must not make more of this dough than one intends to use at once, because it becomes so hard that one cannot handle it thereafter.

Furthermore, the simple resin is used for burning, and all the common torches are made from it, which, being skillfully prepared, come for sale in great numbers to **Batavia** from **Bantam**, **Siam**, and other Malay places. They are made thus: one crushes the **Ceylon Dammar** <note>original: Dammar Selan</note> to powder and mixes it with a third part of black dust-earth or ash and dry **Pinang-chew** <note>betel nut</note> or rice-chaff together with water into a dough, which one winds in dried shoots of **Coconut** or **Pinang** trees, or dry leaves of **Lontar** or **Gomuto**, into the shape of a torch about a foot long, being smeared on the outside with lime. These torches one lights at the top and carries in the hand across the street; they burn easily but cannot withstand a hard wind. They smell lovely, yet for newcomers and those unaccustomed they are still burdensome. Those of **Buru** do not make much of it but crush it with black earth and bind it in leaves of **Gomuto** or suchlike. As long as they can get other **Dammar**, however, they will not use this because of the crackling and jumping of sparks, which burn fiercely when hitting the skin—though this crackling is broken with the earth and other brush that goes into it, as one sees in the **Batavian** torches. Those of **Sula** do not use it at all for that reason, because they are sufficiently provided with others. The **Macassars** <note>original: Maſſaren</note> choose the most beautiful pieces, which best resemble **Amber** <note>original: Bern-fteen</note>, which they mix among the **Incense** <note>original: Dupa</note> that they make for the common man to strengthen the scent, but in the **Royal Incense** it has no place.

Since our Nation is sometimes not so well provided with **Rosin** from the Fatherland, they must use this **Dammar** in its place, or at least extend it therewith, taking for thirty pounds of **Dammar**, ten pounds of **Rosin**, and a good measure of **Coconut oil**, which they let melt together and therewith caulk the ships.

The **Male trees**, because they become very dense and straight, are fit to saw planks from, as one otherwise does with **Tsjicki** wood, yet they are very heavy, so that they are regarded by the inexperienced folk as **Ironwood** <note>original: Yſer-bout</note>. They are sawn thick and used for shipbuilding, yet it has been experienced that the worm easily enters it, which the locals attribute to the inexperience of our carpenters, who use this wood while it is still fresh and full of rank sap. The fruits are greedily sought and eaten by the wild pigs and **Cuscus**, especially our hunters have experienced that the wondrous swine falling in **Buru** and the **Sulas** <note>the Babirusa</note> gladly stayed under these trees, not only snapping up the fruits but also standing upright with the front legs against the tree and rubbing themselves against it as if they had pleasure in the scent of that **Dammar**, whereby they are also mostly caught under them.

### AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. Chapter VIII.
<meta>catchword: Fruit; catchword: Concerning</meta>

It is peculiar that this wood provides such a copious supply of resin and yet is useless for the hearth; for in the year 1666, our sailors brought a ship laden with this wood to the fort for fuel, having felled it on the shores of **Boero** <note>Buru Island</note> and **Kelanga**, thinking they were **Mangrove** <note>original: "Mangi Mangi"</note> trees. The cooks, however, detested this wood, as it would neither catch nor sustain a fire, but only made a great crackling noise in the flames. This is because the wood, as stated above, contains many veins filled with transparent **Dammar** <note>a type of resin</note>, which we later extract from the decayed logs like icy veins.

The **Alfur people** <note>original: "Alphorenfes"; indigenous people of the Moluccas</note> on **Boero** crush its thick bark, which they first dry and then preserve to feed the fires with which they forge iron, though only for forming knives and small wedges. This same dried bark, chopped small, is also mixed into the **Dammar** used for making torches. This resin is brought to **Batavia** <note>modern-day Jakarta</note> in such great quantities that a **Picul** <note>a traditional unit of weight</note>, which contains one hundred and twenty-five Dutch pounds, is bought for one or two imperial dollars, or three if it is expensive.

I saw to it that young saplings of this tree were brought from **Boero** and planted in **Amboina**; one of these grew into a tall tree, but by its sixteenth year, it had produced no flowers or fruit, nor had its trunk, which was as thick as a man, exuded any **Dammar**, from which I recognized it to be a male. However, in that same year, it began to produce flowers and fruit. On the eastern coast of **Sumatra** near **Jambi** and **Palembang**, various pieces of **Dammar** wash up on the shores, called **Dammar Kretje**, which are crushed and used for torches.

The terms **Malay Dammar** <note>original: "Dammara Maleyo"</note> and **Stone Dammar** <note>original: "Dammara Batu"</note>—the first of which we have applied to the described **Selan Dammar**, and the second to our common **Amboinese Dammar**—are used with a different meaning by the **Malays** around **Malacca** and **Patani**. By **Malay Dammar**, they mean prepared torches, which in those regions they compose from a certain oil called **Dammar Oil** <note>original: "Minjac Dammar"</note> or **Wood Oil** <note>original: "Minjac Caju"</note>. For behind **Patani** in the mountains live the wild peoples called **Bata** or **Alfurs**; these bring down the **Dammar Oil**, collecting it from the **Collulut** tree. It remains always thin, white, clear, and sweet-smelling, and they keep it in small jars and vessels, concerning which see further in our *Supplement*. From this, **Malay Dammar** is composed: a certain portion is taken and mixed with the crushed and shredded bark of the **Gelam Wood** <note>original: "Caju Gelama"</note> or **White Wood** <note>original: "Caju Puti"; likely Melaleuca</note>, then the bark or shoots of the **Nibung** palm <note>original: "Nibun"</note> are taken and packed tightly into this prepared oil with the help of a stick; it then hardens like a stone, and from this mass, torches are formed. By **Stone Dammar**, however, they mean that **Selan Dammar** which is also found in those mountains; large pieces of it are found in the forests, but it is rarely collected, as it is hardly used for incense because of its crackling, except by the common people, who crush it and mix it with **Rice** <note>original: "Padi"</note> chaff and the aforementioned **Palepa** <note>the midrib of a palm frond</note> or the bark of **Nibung** branches, which they melt with a glowing coal.

**Cawan Oil** <note>original: "Minjac Cawan"</note> is another oil expressed from the fruits of an unknown tree, having the thickness and substance of white tallow, which is brought for sale in **Bamboo** tubes, into which it is poured while still thin and fluid.

This tree is also called **Cawan Wood** <note>original: "Caju Cawan"</note> and grows abundantly in **Java** as well as in the **Malay** regions, so that it is of low price.

The common people use this oil in place of **Canarium Oil** <note>original: "Olei Canarini"</note> to fry fish; they also use it against the **thrush** <note>mouth sores</note> of infants, melted with a small amount of garlic and prepared into a thin ointment.

Concerning this tree, see further in my *Supplement*; it is described there in Chapter 26 under the name **White-and-Black Dammar** <note>original: "Dammara Leucomelæna"</note>, as it appears to me, in the following manner.

This tree has a tall, erect trunk covered in smooth, ash-colored bark. Its branches consist of many curved and knotty stems which bear opposite leaves, at the base of which joints also appear. These leaves very much resemble **Canarium** leaves but are a little smaller; however, the stems at their origin do not bear those scaly leaflets observed in the **Canarium** genus.

<column-break/>

*It is strange regarding this wood, that it yields such abundant resin and yet is of so little use for burning; for in the year 1666, our sailors brought a cargo of firewood made from this wood to the Castle, which they had cut on Buru and Kelang near the beaches, thinking they were Mangrove trees. But the cooks cursed this wood because it would not burn and lay crackling in the fire; for this wood, as said, has many veins full of clear Dammar, which we afterwards extracted from the rotted logs like branches of ice.*

*The Alfur people on Buru beat this thick bark a bit first, dry it, and keep it to stoke fires by which they forge their iron, though only for knives and small axes. This same dried and finely chopped bark is also mixed into the Dammar when one wants to make torches from it. This resin is brought in such quantity to Batavia that one Picul of 125 Dutch pounds is bought for one or two Imperial Dollars, and when it is expensive, for three Imperial Dollars.*

*I also had the young trees brought from Buru and planted on Amboina, of which one indeed shot up into a high tree, but in its 16th year had no flowers or fruits yet, nor did the trunk (being the thickness of a man) yield the least Dammar, by which I noticed it was a male. But in that same year, it first began to give its blossoms and fruits. On the beaches of Sumatra’s East Coast, near Jambi and Palembang, various lumps of some Dammar are washed up, which they call Dammar Cretje, all of which they crush and use for burning.*

*The words Malay Dammar and Stone Dammar—the first of which we applied to the aforementioned Selan Dammar, and the second we shall give to our common Amboinese Dammar—the Malays around Malacca and Patani use somewhat differently. For by Malay Dammar, they understand the prepared torches which they make in those lands from a certain oil called Dammar Oil or Wood Oil; for behind Patani in the mountains live the wild peoples, Bata or Alfurs, who bring down the Dammar Oil from the Collulut tree, which remains always thin, white, clear, and fragrant, prepared in small casks and pots: of which see more extensively in the Supplement. From this, the Malay Dammar is made: one takes the oil, mixes it with the chopped bark of Gelam Wood or White Wood, then takes the bark or sheaths of Nibung, stamps it in there tightly with sticks, and so it becomes as hard as a stone; and they make torches from this. On the other hand, by Stone Dammar, they understand the aforementioned Selan, which also occurs in the said mountains and lies in the forest in large pieces, because it is little used for burning on account of its crackling, except by common folk, who crush it and mix it with the chaff of Rice and the aforementioned Palepa or bark of the branches of Nibung, melting it with a coal of fire.*

*Cawan Oil is another oil pressed from the fruits of an unknown tree, in the thickness and substance of white tallow, which is brought for sale in Bamboos, into which it is poured while still thin.*

*The tree is also called Cawan Wood and grows abundantly both on Java and in the Malay lands, so that it is cheap.*

*The commonest people use it instead of Canary oil to fry fish in, as well as against the thrush of children, melted with a little Alum and made into a thin salve.*

*Of this tree, see more broadly in my Supplement: which is described there in the 26th Chapter under White-and-Black Dammar, as it appears to me, in the following way.*

*This gains a straight high trunk, clothed with a smooth and whitish bark. The branches have many curved and knotty twigs, on which the leaves stand directly opposite each other, also with some joints on their twigs. The leaves look very much like the Canary leaves or somewhat smaller, but the twigs at their origin do not have the bearded leaflets like other Canaries.*

### AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. Chapter VIII.
<meta>catchword: Fruit; catchword: Concerning</meta>

It is remarkable that although this wood yields such an abundance of resin, it is quite useless for the hearth. In the year 1666, our sailors brought a ship laden with this wood to the fort to be used as fuel, having felled the trees on the shores of **Buru** <note>original: "Boero"; an island in the Maluku archipelago</note> and **Kelang** <note>original: "Kelanga"</note> under the mistaken impression that they were **Mangrove** <note>original: "Mangi Mangi"; a local term for various coastal mangrove species</note> trees. The cooks, however, grew to detest this wood, for it would neither catch nor maintain a fire, but instead produced a loud crackling noise in the flames. This occurs because the wood, as noted previously, contains many veins filled with transparent **Dammar** <term>Dammar: a natural resin exuded from trees in the Dipterocarpaceae family, used for incense, torches, and caulking ships</term>, which we later extract from the decayed logs like veins of ice.

The **Alfur people** <note>original: "Alphorenfes"; a historical term for the indigenous non-Muslim inhabitants of the Moluccas</note> on **Buru** crush the thick bark of this tree, which they first dry and then preserve to feed the fires used for forging iron—though this is only done for shaping knives and small wedges. This same dried bark, finely chopped, is also mixed into the **Dammar** used for making torches. This resin is transported to **Batavia** <note>modern-day Jakarta, then the administrative center of the Dutch East Indies</note> in such vast quantities that a **Picul** <term>Picul: a traditional unit of weight across East Asia, defined here as 125 Dutch pounds (roughly 60kg), or what one man can carry on a shoulder pole</term> is purchased for one or two imperial dollars, or three if the price is high.

I arranged for young saplings of this tree to be brought from **Buru** and planted in **Amboina** <note>modern-day Ambon</note>. One of these grew into a tall tree, but by its sixteenth year, it had produced neither flowers nor fruit. Nor had its trunk, which was as thick as a man, exuded any **Dammar**, leading me to recognize it as a...

III Book. IX. Chapter. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

The fruits are produced in short, tightly packed clusters, arising from the branches and even from the leaf stalks. These resemble small **Canarium nuts** <note>original: "Canarios"; the fruit of the Canarium indicum, common in the Moluccas</note>, but they do not consist of a hard shell; rather, beneath a soft skin, a hard, dry pith is hidden. This pith is generally divisible into two segments, though some fruits can be divided into four oblong parts; they are bitter, astringent, and unpleasant in flavor.

A yellowish and soft gum oozes from the trunk, which never dries completely hard. It is rarely encountered but is found most often in **Oma** <note>An island in the Haruku island group of the Maluku Islands</note>, and it is called by the inhabitants *Kamal Metten Poeti*, that is, "black-and-white **Dammar**" <term>Dammar: a natural resin from trees of the Dipterocarpaceae family</term>, and for this reason, I have named it *Dammara Leucomelæna* <note>original: "Leucomelæna"; Greek for white-black</note>. Its wood is used for the construction of houses.

# CHAPTER NINE.

## Flesh-Colored Resin: Ramack Daging, & Mor.

This resin is so similar to the *Selanic Dammar* that for a long time I considered it to be the finest pieces of that sort, or at least something prepared from it by human art; for from the external structure of the pieces, one might judge that they had been poured into some vessel. For the most part, they are flat segments, slightly curved, a finger thick and two inches long, and of uniform thickness. Externally they are whitish, as if they were moldy, and marked with many streaks and wrinkles. Inside they are clear, pure, and almost translucent, like yellow **amber** or the **Carnelian** stone <note>original: "Carneol"</note>, which the common folk call red **Agate** <note>original: "Gagatam" / "Agaat"</note>.

The scent which it breathes out when placed upon coals is similar to *Selanic Dammar*, but weaker and more pleasant, possessing something unique about it. Upon further investigation, however, I discovered it to be nothing other than old and naturally purified *Selanic Dammar*. It is not produced directly from the tree itself but flows out from the fissures of rocks like a **Mineral Colophony** <term>Colophony: Rosin; here "mineral colophony" refers to a fossilized or weathered state of the resin found in the earth</term>, from which they say it acquired its flat shape, having been formed in such a manner between the stones. It is rarely found, which is why it is very expensive, and most Malay merchants are ignorant of its origin; indeed, I have spoken with many who thought, as I did, that it was an artificial *Selanic Dammar*, prepared from its fattest fruits through melting and refining, just as **Rosin** <note>original: "Colophonia"</note> is prepared among us.

*Name.* In Latin, *Resina Carneola*. In Malay, *Ramak Daging* and *Dermack*, or *Dormack Daging*, so called from its flesh-like color; by some, it is also called *Lemmack Daging*.

*Location.* I do not know of it occurring in any other place except on the island of **Crimata** <note>modern-day Karimata Island, off the west coast of Borneo</note>, which is very rocky, where the stones are piled upon one another like large chests. Many *Selanic Dammar* trees also grow there, and many iron-stones are found in the low hills along the shore. The Malays claim it is found everywhere in their lands where *Selanic Dammar* trees occur, among the rocks at their roots.

*Usage.* This resin is not used for flames or as common incense, but only for the medical arts by the local women. Along with other simple ingredients, it enters into their famous drink, **Djudjambu**, which is given to young girls and to women recovering from childbirth. The Portuguese use it as incense in their churches, and as a fumigant for children's linens and cradles to purify them against "foul air."

The fruits come forth in short clusters close behind one another, from the branches themselves between the stalks of the leaves. They resemble small *Canarium nuts*, yet have no hard shell, but beneath a soft scale lies a hard dry pith, mostly divisible into two, though some are also divided into four oblong pieces, somewhat bitter, astringent, and unpleasant.

From the trunk runs a yellowish soft gum, never drying hard: it is seldom found, and mostly on **Oma**, and is named by the inhabitants *Kamal Metten Poeti*, that is, white-black **Dammar**, and therefore by me *Dammara Leucomelæna*. The wood is used for house building.

# CHAPTER IX.

## Flesh-Colored Resin.

This resin resembles the *Dammar Selan* so well that I held it for a long time to be the best pieces thereof, or at least made from it by human hands; for from the outward appearance of the pieces one would judge that they were cast in some vessel. They are mostly flat pieces or somewhat curved, a finger thick, and a couple of inches long, mostly of uniform thickness, whitish on the outside, as if moldy, and full of streaks or folds; inside clear, pure, and nearly transparent like reddish amber, or the **Carnelian** stone, which the common man calls red **Agate**.

The smell on coals is like that of *Dammar Selan*, but weaker and more pleasant, also having something special. Now upon closer investigation, I have understood that it is nothing other than an old and naturally refined *Dammar Selan*, though not coming forth on or out of its trees, but found in the fissures of stone rocks, as a **Mineral Colophony**, and from that, they say, it shall have its flat figures, being formed between the stones. It is found very little, therefore it is also expensive, and most Malay merchants do not know its origin, so that I have found many who thought with me that it was an artificial *Dammar Selan*, made from its fattest pieces by melting and refining, just as one prepares **Rosin** among us.

*Name.* In Latin *Resina Carneola*. In Malay *Ramak Daging* and *Dermack* or *Dormack Daging*, all from the flesh-colored hues, by some also *Lemmack Daging*.

*Place.* It is not known to me that it falls elsewhere than on the island of **Crimata**, which is very cliff-like, and where the stones lie upon one another like large chests, where also many *Dammar Selan* trees grow, as well as many iron-stones in the low hills along the beach; the Malays say that it falls everywhere in their lands where *Dammar Selan* trees stand, by their roots in the cliffs.

*Use.* This resin was not used for burning or incensing, but only for medicine by the women, who mix it with other drugs into their famous drink **Djudjambu**, which they give to the young daughters and women who rise again from the child-bed. The Portuguese use it for incense in the churches, for perfume, and to smoke the diapers of children against the "bad air."

From this, dark brown little cakes are prepared, about the size of a small coin <note>original: "denarii minoris"; a denarius was a small Roman silver coin, here used as a size reference</note>. I will not treat its origin further, but some note this distinction, saying that *Mor* or *Umor Daging* was so named because, when ingested, it assimilates itself with our flesh and veins and keeps them in a healthy state; whereas *Dormac Daging* penetrates further, namely into the very marrow of our bones. They commonly mix both together and give them to infants, as they say, to build healthy and solid flesh for them.

### CHAPTER TEN.
#### **White Dammar. Dammar Puti; or Stone Dammar.**

This is the second most used and most common resin in these regions. Its tree is nearly the tallest and largest of all; with an erect and round trunk, it resembles a tall Fir or Cedar. It is never crooked, nor does it have any branches except at the very top, where, in proportion to the trunk, only a small crown is seen.

Its bark is smooth, colored with a mix of red and grey; by its shape, this tree is easily distinguished from other forest trees. Its common thickness is eight or ten feet in diameter, and the lower part of the trunk consists of large knots like heads, from which its **Dammar** flows forth as if from breasts <note>Rumphius uses the term "mammis" to describe the bulging knots where resin beads up</note>.

Both male and female versions of it occur, differing little in trunk and foliage; therefore, we shall describe these trees together and note their difference in the fruits.

The leaf-stalks are straight, flexible, and green, and are placed almost in a cross-shape on the branches; they are round and striated on the front part. Upon these, the leaves sit mostly opposite each other, except on the younger shoots, where they are often placed alternately.

They are narrow and pointed at both ends, but on the younger trees they are longer and more pointed, namely four or five inches long and over a finger wide, very similar to Willow leaves but not serrated. On the older trees, however, they are three or three and a half inches long, scarcely a finger wide, and bluntly pointed, whereby they also emulate Olive leaves.

They bear no middle vein, but are slightly hollowed out there like a channel; furthermore, they are rough, smooth, and interwoven throughout their length with very thin and barely noticeable veins. They are sea-green, though the first sprouting and tender leaflets are pale green; the old leaves, however, turn back at the edges as if they would form a little boat from the underside. They sit on such short petioles <note>leaf stalks</note> that they are almost sessile <note>attached directly by the base without a stalk</note>, but they are slightly twisted there, so these leaves are not placed in a straight order but form an oblique cross. On the shoots, the leaf-stalks grow out sometimes opposite and sometimes alternating, and on them, three to six pairs of leaves grow.

in the form of Myrrh, but dirtier, and always staying soft, and not becoming hard, from which people make dark-brown cakes the size of a small shilling. They also resemble dirty honey that has been thickened with something, yet they are not at all sticky; the taste is bland, and almost tasteless, and sometimes a bit salty. In chewing, one also notices some sandiness, because it is taken from the cliffs. It is also found very little, and is even more expensive than the *Ramack Daging*. The Malays call it *Mor* or *Umor Daging*, which means either something that makes the flesh long-lasting, or something that always stays in the form of flesh.

*Use.* It is used by the women as the previous substance, in the *Djudjambu*, but more internally than the *Ramack Daging*. I had to place it here, although it seems to be a mineral which does not belong among plants, and that is because they both have great commonality with the *Selanic Dammar*, are sold together, and are used for the same purpose.

Indeed, its origin is deferred; so others also make this distinction, that the *Mor* or *Umor Daging* is so named because, being taken in, it mixes with our flesh and veins, and keeps them in a healthy disposition, but *Dormac Daging* penetrates deeper, even into the marrow of the bones of our body. They commonly mix them together and give them to the children, as they say, to make a healthy and hard flesh.

Drunk with *Padma*, a black scaly fruit, and *Djudjambu*, it makes the women *Rapat*, that is, closed after giving birth, drying up the nature, although they also give it to the young daughters.
