### CHAPTER X.
#### **The Stone-Dammar Tree.**

This is the second most useful and the commonest resin in these quarters. The tree is one of the tallest and largest, with a straight round trunk, representing a high mast or Cedar tree, never bent, and without branches until the top, where it has a small crown in proportion to the trunk.

The bark is smooth, mixed from light red and grey, and by its form is easily known from afar among other forest trees. Its ordinary thickness is eight to ten feet in circumference, and the lower trunk is set with large knots like heads, where the Dammar runs out as if from breasts.

It is Male and Female, differing little from each other in trunk and leaves, therefore we shall describe them together, and show the difference only in the fruits.

The small branches are straight, tough, and green, and stand almost in a cross around the branches, perfectly round, and somewhat striped towards the front. On these the leaves stand mostly right against each other, except on the young sprouts, where on some they stand alternating.

They are narrow, pointed at the back and front, on the young trees more pointed and longer in front, namely, four and five inches long, more than a finger wide, like the willow-leaves, but without notches; on the old trees three and three and a half inches long, scarcely a finger wide, and with a blunt point, therefore like the Olive-leaves.

They have no middle-vein, but are somewhat bulging there, like a gutter, furthermore stiff, smooth, laced throughout the length with subtle and barely recognizable small veins, arc- or sea-green, but the first coming out which are small leaves are pale-green; also the edges of the old leaves curve somewhat downwards, as if they wanted to make a little boat from underneath. They have such short feet <note>petioles</note> that they seem to have almost none, but are somewhat twisted there, for which reason the leaves do not stand in rows, but make a slanted cross. On the sprouts the small branches also stand across and right against each other, and on each from three to six pairs of leaves; when rubbed they give off a resinous smell, and

When crushed, these leaves breathe a resinous odor and have a similar taste; once plucked, they remain green for a long time. Because of the height of the trees, which makes them impossible to climb, the flowers are unknown; nor are they ever found fallen beneath the trees. From this, I conclude that the buds of the fruits soon spring forth without conspicuous flowers. Since the best distinction between the male and female trees is found in the fruits, I shall describe each fruit separately.

First, therefore, are the fruits of the female, which are the most common and best known. They have the shape and size of a Sweet Lemon <note>original: "Limonis Manis"; 'Manis' is the Malay word for sweet</note> or a Chinese Orange. They are somewhat round, slightly compressed at the top, of a glaucous <note>a dull grayish-green or blue color</note> color, and divided into simple scales like those of Pine cones. These scales, however, cling and are as if glued to one another as long as they are green. If the fruits are ripe or plucked, they gape open within a few days and these scales are separated. These are not thick, but many lie upon one another; they are whitish inside, soft, and narrowed at the lower part where they split and are attached to a common stalk. They are filled with large, flat seeds, like Cucumber seeds but wider and thinner, which also resemble scales. At first they are white, then brown, and they protrude slightly in the middle, where a white, soft, and dry flour is stored, in which the seminal power <note>the germinating essence or life-force of the seed</note> lies hidden. These fruits grow solitary or in pairs at the top of the branchlets, sitting upon many short, thick, and woody stalks, surrounded by many smaller branchlets, resembling a young Pineapple fruit as long as they have not yet grown into scales.

Second; the fruit of the male differs much from the preceding and is much smaller, being two inches long or a little more, and a finger thick. The tip resembles the end of a small sausage <note>original: "apexabonis," which the parallel Dutch text translates as "Soucys," an old term for a small sausage</note>. It is formed from many small and narrow scales which lie closely upon one another in a regular order. These young fruits are sprinkled with a yellow flour <note>pollen</note>, but then they are a mixture of green and purple; if they ripen, they are an intense yellow or brown. If their scales cling together, they are smooth and almost shining, but when they open, they do not prick like those of the Pine, but easily fall from the common stalk. There they are also split in two, and in this fissure something chaff-like is found, which mimics a seed; however, these fruits mostly fall off while immature, which is why these trees do not propagate much.

From both of these domestic trees, but especially from the female, a transparent resin <term>Dammar: a natural resin used for incense, torches, and varnish</term> flows. At first it is soft and viscous, but within a few days it hardens like a stone, becoming white and transparent like Crystal—especially that which adheres dried to the trees, where it hangs down like icicles. However, that which drips from the trees onto the ground turns blackish and is stained with dirt. These "ice cones" are sometimes a palm-breadth wide and a foot long, striated, and as if composed of many thongs, which offers an elegant sight.

During the first half-year, as has been said, this resin is white and transparent, but afterward it acquires an elegant golden color like Amber <note>original: "Succini"</note>. It is brittle, shining inside like broken glass. It is much harder than the aforementioned Selanic Dammar <note>resin from the Sula or Celebes islands</note>, and while cold it can be bent or drawn out to some extent, but when struck it is fragile. That which is collected from the male tree is more transparent and whitish, but it dries more slowly and drips out in small quantities; hence, little or none is collected from this tree. So that these trees might provide this resin in greater abundance, the lower part of the trunk is cut with large knives. From these wounds, this Dammar flows more copiously, whereby the tree generates large knots there, consisting of hard wood with many intricate veins like Maple <note>original: "Aceris"</note>. These protrude like heads and are continually covered on their surface with Dammar and are full of branches. The inhabitants also clear the ground everywhere around the roots of this tree and dig small pits in which they collect the dripping Dammar, so that it is not so stained with filth. Where the roots rise above the earth and are bare, they are knotty from the cutting and likewise sweat out this resin, which hangs upon them like a white crust.

The odor of fresh and soft Dammar is very resinous, but when dry it breathes no scent. Placed upon coals, it gives a mixed odor of Pine resin and Mastic <note>a resin from the Pistacia lentiscus tree</note>, which is also its taste, though it approaches that of the Canary resin <note>resin from the Canarium tree</note>. It catches fire easily and maintains it longer than

And because the best distinction between Male and Female is to be known by the fruits, I shall describe each in particular.*

*First, the fruits of the Female, being the most common and best known, are in the size and shape of a Sweet Lemon <note>original: "Lemon Manis"</note> or Chinese sweet-orange, namely, roundish, and pressed in a little at the front, light Spanish-green, and divided into single scales like the pine-apples <note>pine cones</note>, which however stick to one another as long as they are green, but when ripe and plucked they open themselves in a few days and fall apart. The fruits stand at the front of the small branches, one or two together, surrounded by many small branchlets, and on short, thick, and woody little feet, resembling a young Pineapple as long as they do not scale off.*

*Second; the fruit of the Male differs much from the preceding, and is much smaller, two inches long or somewhat more, a finger thick, resembling an end of a sausage <note>original: "Soucys"</note>, made of many small and narrow scales, which lie orderly and tightly upon one another. The young fruits are strewn with a yellow meal, thereafter green and purple mixed; when they are ripe, they are dark yellow and brownish. When the scales still stick to each other, they are smooth and almost shining, and once opened they prick not at all like the pine-apples, but also fall easily off from the middle stalk, where they are also cleft, and therebetween lies also something chaff-like, which would be the seed, yet these fruits mostly fall off unripe, and therefore these trees do not multiply themselves much.*

*From both these trunks, but primarily from the Female, flows a clear resin, at first soft and sticky, but in a few days becoming stone-hard, white and transparent as crystal, especially that which dries up on the trees, where one sees it hanging like icicles, but that which drips from the trees onto the ground is blackish and mixed with filth. The aforementioned ice-branches are sometimes a hand-breadth and a foot long, striped, and as if put together from many strands, beautiful to behold.*

*In the first half year they are, as said, white and transparent, but they acquire thereafter a beautiful gold-yellow color, like Amber <note>original: "Bern-steen"</note>, breaking off short, and shining from within like broken glass. It is much harder than the preceding Selanic Dammar, letting itself be bent and drawn out somewhat when cold, but it shatters when tapped or struck. That of the Male is clearer and whiter, dries up more slowly, and drips out very scantily, therefore none or little is gathered from the same. So that these trees should give out this resin more richly, they are chopped round about the trunk below with clearing-knives, from which wounds then this Dammar runs out more richly, through which the tree gains great knots there, of a hard wood tangled with veins, like Bow-wood <note>likely Maple or another curly-grained wood</note>, which stick out like heads, and are outside continually clothed with Dammar and full of branches. Also, the Inlanders make the ground clean around the roots of this tree, and some small pits, therein they gather the dripping Dammar, to be mixed with less filth; where the roots lie bare above the earth, they are knotty through the chopping, and likewise sweat out this resin, which hangs there with a white crust.*

*The smell in the fresh and soft Dammar is very resin-like, but in the dry one has none. Placed or burnt on coals, it has a mixed smell of pine-resin and Mastic, as also the taste is, though drawing somewhat toward the Canary resin. It catches the fire easily, and holds*

# AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. Chap. X.

...than Selanese Dammar. It makes little to no crackling sound when burned, but emits a great deal of slightly acidic smoke, which is unusually heavy. Just as the common Dammar sold in the marketplace is white and semi-transparent (the kind collected from the knots of the lower trunk), so too is this variety found in various colors: sometimes reddish, sometimes horn-colored, or even blackish. Nevertheless, it remains hard and semi-transparent, as seen in the large lumps and "heads" that hang from the thicker branches of very old trees. Because these trees are not climbed due to their extreme height, these lumps hang there for a long time, losing their original whiteness and becoming horn-colored. This is mostly observed on the Dammar trees near Way, from which I conclude that the difference in color arises from the passage of time—depending on whether the lumps have hung from the tree for a long while or have fallen and lain upon the ground.

In the year 1688, I sent such a piece to the University of Leiden which was shaped like an infant's head; it had been slightly modified by human hands into that form, though its nose was misshapen, near which ran a red streak as if it were blood. I also kept a white, semi-transparent piece shaped like a huge ox's gall bladder. I also sent those crystalline branches back to the Fatherland, but I am certain that none arrived there with their white color, but rather reached there yellow like amber <note>original: "Succini"</note>.

The wood of the tree is whitish, consisting of longitudinal fibers like a Wild Pine; one might think it was Cedar wood. It can be sawn into planks and polished quite well, and in a dry place it is durable enough. However, it is not at all durable in seawater, which is why it is not used for shipbuilding, especially since this timber is difficult to retrieve from the remote mountains. I have also observed that fallen trunks completely rot away within a few years, turning into red earth, just like the soil surrounding them. In that red earth, one could clearly see the veins of the former wood, and among them many transparent little branches of hard Dammar. In these rotted trunks, one also finds beautiful pieces of "fat wood" <note>resinous wood saturated with sap</note> here and there, honey-colored, semi-transparent in places and elegantly veined, which had been located near the knots of the trunk and branches. These fat pieces of wood do not rot, even if they lie on the ground for a very long time, but they are only large enough to be formed into knife handles or small beads for pin-makers' work.

**Name.** In Latin, *Dammara Alba*; in Malay, *Dammar Puti* <note>White Dammar</note> and *Dammar Batu* <note>Stone Dammar</note>, that is, stone-like resin, since it is the hardest of all Dammars, and thus comes closest to *Gummi Animæ* <note>a hard, transparent resin often used in varnishes</note>. The people of Ternate call it simply *Salo*, and *Salo Bobuda*. In the Amboinese language, it is *Camal*, *Camar*, and *Cama*, and around Lariqua, *Isse*. The Javanese near Gresik call it *Dama*, which agrees with the Arabic word explained in the previous chapter.

**Location.** These trees are found nowhere except on the highest mountains and in wildernesses far removed from human conversation; hence they are mostly unknown to our nation. They love the red, clay-like soil of which nearly all Amboinese mountains are composed, and they favor high places. Traveling through the Hitu region, one sees them as if planted halfway up the mountains, precisely where the land is highest and slopes down on both sides. However, they do not grow on the very highest, cold peaks. The male tree is found somewhat solitary among other forest trees; along the great road that runs through the Hitu region, four vast and huge trees are located near the path, all of which seem to have their roots joined and entangled with one another. At least two of these trees are joined above the ground in such a way that one can sit between them as if in a chair.

The female trees are always abundant and grow many together, forming a specific forest—not dense, but sparsely scattered—also near the ridges of the land. Such forests are found in the wild mountains of Amboina between Mamalo on the Hitu coast and Way, where the most Dammar used in Amboina is found. Furthermore, it occurs in Hoeamohela in the mountains behind Loke and Anin. Also on Batjan, on the great island of Halmahera <note>original: "Gelolo"</note>, and perhaps in most of the Molucca islands, as well as on Buru; however, not much resin is brought from there because its...

<column-break/>

This resin is better than the *Selanese Dammar*. It grinds little or not at all, but gives off much smoke from fire, which tends toward the sour, and the unusual smell is heavy. Just as the common *Dammar*, which is sold on the market, is white and semi-transparent (the kind one fetches from the knots of the lower trunk), so on the other hand one has it in other colors, namely reddish, horn-colored, and blackish; nevertheless, it is hard and semi-transparent, just as there are large lumps and "heads" which hang from the thick branches and very old trees. Because these trees are not climbed due to their height, the lumps remain hanging there for a long time, losing their first white color and becoming horn-colored; however, one finds this mostly on the *Dammar* trees near Way, from which I notice that the difference in colors comes from whether the lumps have hung long on the tree or, having fallen off, have lain on the ground.

In the year 1688, I sent such a piece to the University of Leiden, shaped like an oblong infant's head, being only a little helped by human hand, and the nose somewhat misshapen, where one saw a red stripe as if it were blood. I also have a piece of white and semi-transparent resin shaped like a large gall bladder of an Ox. The aforementioned crystalline branches I also sent in their original color to the Fatherland, but I trust that none of them arrived in their white color, but rather became amber-yellow.

The wood is white, long-fibered like fir wood, and one would think one was dealing with Cedar wood. It also allows itself to be sawn into planks and worked reasonably smooth, and in a dry place it can last for some time, but in seawater not at all; therefore it is no longer used for timber work, the more so because this wood is difficult to fetch from the far mountains. I have also found that the fallen trunks decay entirely in a few years and were changed back into red earth, just like the ground they stood on; one could still clearly perceive in the same red earth the veins of the wood, and between them many clear little branches of hard *Dammar*. In these decayed trunks one also finds here and there beautiful pieces of fat wood, honey-colored, and in some places semi-transparent and beautifully veined, which had stood at the knots of the trunk and branches. The fat pieces do not decay, even if they lie ever so long in the earth, but they do not fall larger than that one can make small handles and hafts or blocks for pin-making work from them.

**Name.** In Latin *Dammara Alba*, in Malay *Dammar Puti* and *Dammar Batu*, that is, hardest resin, because it is the hardest among all *Dammar*, and in that it corresponds very well with *Gummi Animæ*. In Ternate simply *Salo*, and *Salo Baboda*; in Amboinese *Camal*, *Camar*, and *Cama*. And around Larique *Isse*. In Javanese around Gresik *Dama*, which corresponds with the Arabic stated in the previous chapter.

**Place.** These trees are found nowhere but in the high mountains and wildernesses, entirely separated from human company, and therefore they are mostly unknown to our Nation. They love a red clay ground, as are most all the Amboinese mountains, and always the high places, such that passing over the Land of Hitu one finds them as if planted, halfway up exactly where the land is highest and one goes down on both sides. However, on the very highest and cold mountains they will not grow. The male stands mostly solitary, mixed among other forest trees, and of these one sees on the large country road that goes over the aforementioned Land of Hitu four powerfully large trees standing close to the road, all four (as far as one can perceive) with their roots fixed to one another; indeed, two of them are fixed to each other above the ground, so that one can sit between them as if in a chair.

The female always grows in abundance and in large troops together, making a particular forest, not dense, but idly scattered, also around the highest of the land, as in Amboina are the wild mountains between Mamalo on Hitu’s coast and Way, where one finds the most *Dammar* that is used in Amboina. Furthermore, one finds them on Hoeamohel, in the mountains behind Loke and Anin: on Batjan, on the large island of Halmahera, and perhaps in most of the Molucca Islands, as well as on Buru; however, not much is brought away, because its wild mountains are not well...

...the wild mountains can hardly be traversed. I have understood from certain Malays that this resin also occurs in Borneo, but with a slight difference, as it is not as white and transparent as the Amboinese variety.

**Use**. Just as Selanese Dammar <note>original: "Dammara Selanica"</note> is very commonly used for torches in the western parts of maritime India, so too is this *Stone Dammar* <note>original: "Dammara Batu"</note> used in Amboina and its adjacent islands. It burns better, and its preparation does not require as much labor as the Selanese kind, for its hard lumps—as they are found naturally, whether pure or impure—are taken indiscriminately. These are wrapped in the leaves of the *Sugar Palm* <note>original: "Gomuto" or "Sagueri"</note> to the length of a foot and the thickness of three fingers in the form of a torch, which is also commonly called *Dammar*. These torches, when lit at the top, burn steadily with little and often no crackling, but they emit a heavy smoke like pitch-hoops, which is heavy and uncomfortable to those unaccustomed to it, and it covers all furniture with a dark color where many of these torches are lit, especially in a closed room. They must often be poked, as they are frequently packed too tightly and will not catch the flame.

The Amboinese fashion peculiar small stools out of *Sago leaf-stalks* <note>original: "Gabba Gabba"</note>, upon which they place this Dammar; these stools often burn up entirely while the people are sleeping.

The burning drops that fall like little stars from this Dammar when it is carried through the streets are extinguished immediately, otherwise they would often cause damage; however, if they touch anyone's skin—which often happens to the slaves who carry them—they burn fiercely and produce a malignant ulceration, which often degenerates into Amboinese blisters <note>original: "phlyctænas"</note> if not quickly cured.

In medicine, its use is not yet fully explored, though some Amboinese—something which I and many with me would not care to try—whenever they contract foot wounds from caltrops or sharp wood splinters, as soon as they have extracted them, they drip one or two drops of this burning Dammar into the wound. This prevents the wound from festering, though the Indians, with their horny and calloused soles, hardly feel it.

This Dammar melts with difficulty on its own, but better with coconut oil <note>original: "Calappi oleo"</note> or our own pitch, with which some have coated vessels. However, it was found that it does not adhere strongly and falls off very easily, making it useless for that work; at least, it was not tested further, although the lack of pitch makes navigation dangerous in these regions, which is somewhat supplied by the aforementioned resins. For those who practice writing, or are clerks and secretaries, this Dammar is also of use: if they have expressed certain words or letters incorrectly and have erased them, they sprinkle this pulverized Dammar on the spot and rub the paper smooth, where they can then form and write other letters; however, these fall off again over time.

In fallen and rotted trunks, as has been said, those elegant fatty pieces are seen, the most elegantly striated and veined of which are those that resided in the knots from which the Dammar flowed. The Malays and people of Makassar choose these pieces to fashion handles for spears and knives <note>original: "telorum & cultrorum"</note>, which they know how to carve elegantly.

From the other thicker pieces, small spheres are manufactured for needlework, as well as rungs for chairs; however, the wood is brittle and cannot bear force. These pieces catch fire easily and breathe an elegant scent of mastic, especially if this wood is rasped and placed upon coals. This Dammar, when lit and held under a dish, coats it with a dark and light-red color, from which mass the Moorish scribes <note>original: "Æthiopes"</note> make their ink, just as printers among us prepare their book-ink from soot. That ink is very black, dries quickly, and can be easily scraped away if necessity requires it.

That Moorish ink <note>original: "atramentum"</note> is prepared with great difficulty from that soot of Dammar, which is acquired if a large quantity of Dammar is placed in a pit and lit, and an earthen dish, slightly moistened with a certain liquid, is placed over it. This soot must be ground two or three times with water, and must dry or evaporate twice with vinegar, and finally once more with water in which the bark of the *Tropical Almond* <note>original: "Catappan"</note> and *Wild Mango* <note>original: "Mangæ Utan"</note> has been boiled, moving it every day...

<column-break/>

*...can be easily walked. I have understood from some Malays that it also occurs on Borneo, though with a small difference in the resin, which is not as white and transparent as the Amboinese kind.*

*Use. Just as the Selanese Dammar, as said, is the most common for burning in the western parts of maritime India, so is this Stone Dammar in Amboina and these surrounding islands. It burns better, and one does not have as much trouble preparing it as with the Selanese Dammar, for one takes the hard lumps as they fall, clear and impure mixed together, and simply wraps them in the leaves of Sugar Palm or Sago trees, to the length of a foot and thickness of three fingers, into the shape of a torch, which is commonly also called Dammar. These Dammars, when lit at the top, burn steadily with little crackling, and sometimes none, but they give off a violent smoke, like pitch-wreaths, which seems troublesome to the unaccustomed and covers all furniture with black-red soot when much is burned in a closed place. One must frequently stir these torches because they are sometimes packed too tightly and do not want to burn.*

*The Amboinese make special little stools of Sago leaf-stalks <term>Gabba Gabba <gloss>The dried midribs of sago palm leaves, used as a light building material</gloss></term>, in which they set this Dammar, which sometimes burns away along with the stools and everything else while the house-folk are sleeping nearby.*

*The burning drops that fall from this Dammar like little stars when it is carried through the streets go out immediately, otherwise more accidents would come of it; but if they fall on someone’s skin, which often happens to the slaves who carry them, they burn very fiercely and cause a bad ulceration, from which the Amboinese pox often develops if one does not heal it quickly.*

*In medicine it has no known use yet, except for one which I and many with me would not care to imitate the Amboinese in: namely, when they wound their feet by stepping on caltrops or sharp wood, as soon as they have pulled it out, they drip one or two drops of this burning Dammar onto it, which prevents the wound from festering, which the Indians do not feel much on their bare, leathery soles.*

*This Dammar also melts with difficulty on its own, but well with Coconut oil, or mixed with a little of our country’s tar, with which some have smeared vessels; but it has been found that it does not hold fast and easily falls off again, therefore it is unfit for that work; at least, it has not been further investigated, although the lack of pitch and tar makes seafaring in these lands worrisome, which one can offset somewhat with the previously mentioned resins. For the writers in the secretariats, this Dammar also has its use, for having scratched out some erroneous words on the paper, they strew this finely scraped Dammar upon it and rub it smooth; thus they can write other letters upon it, though these letters fall off again over time.*

*On the fallen and rotted trunks, as said, one finds the beautiful fatty pieces, of which those are most beautifully veined that have stood in the knots from which the Dammar flowed; these pieces are sought by the Malays and Macassarese to make kris-handles <note>original: "kris-hegten"</note> from them, which they know how to carve artistically.*

*From the other pieces, which are more long-fibered, one makes pincushion-frames and rungs for chairs, but it is brittle wood and cannot stand force. These pieces catch fire easily when held to the flame and give a pleasant scent of mastic when the wood is scraped and laid on coals. This Dammar, when lit and held under a dish, deposits much black and fine-red soot, from which the Moorish scribes <note>original: "Moorsche Scbryvers"</note> make their ink, just as our printers make blacking; this ink is very black and dries immediately, and also lets itself be easily scraped out again if it is necessary.*

*The Moorish ink is made with great difficulty from the aforementioned soot of this Dammar, which one obtains when a quantity of this Dammar is placed in a pit, lit, and a moist dish is overturned over it. This soot one must rub two or three times with water, and twice with vinegar, letting it dry each time, and finally with water in which the bark of Catappan and Wild Mango have been boiled, moving it every...*

# HERBARIUM OF AMBOINA Book III. chap. X.

...stirring it for an entire month, until at last it becomes a mass or ink suitable for writing.

**Royal Dammar** <note>original: "Dammara Radja"</note>, called *Salo Colano* by the people of Ternate, is this same Dammar, but consists only of the largest and most beautifully transparent pieces which hang from the upper part of the trunk, unstained by any filth. That which occurs in Bacan <note>original: "Batsjana"</note> and Halmahera <note>original: "Hallemahera"</note> never turns as yellow as the Amboinese kind, but is mostly white or gradually turns only slightly yellow; otherwise, it is similar in taste and smell to the Amboinese kind and is found and collected from similar trees. This variety alone is used by the kings of the Moluccas for incense, which is why it is called Royal Dammar, and the common people are not permitted to burn it.

Novices provide a pleasant spectacle and a funny story if they frequent the market, for those who have this fresh Dammar mistake it for rock candy <note>original: "saccharo cantho"</note>, which it resembles perfectly. They buy it at a low price and happily seek out a corner to taste it, but they soon find themselves deceived.

As indicated above, it is recorded in certain nautical annals that a great abundance of Mastic <note>original: "Mastiches"</note> is found in these islands; by this, one must understand it to be this **Stone Dammar** <note>original: "Dammara Batu"</note>, which when lit gives off the scent of Mastic perfectly.

Young Dammar trees are most elegant and represent a smaller Cedar, for they bear a straight trunk which, not far above the root, puts forth small leaves and lateral branches. In these, a peculiar thing is observed: these transverse branches are placed in a circle of two, three, or four at the lower part of the trunk, and in the space between these branches, leaves grow in pairs directly from the trunk itself. If any of these are plucked or torn away, a viscous, resinous juice flows out, breathing a strong scent.

---

In the year 1691, white Royal Dammar, there called *Salo Colano*, was sent to me from Ternate, both small pieces of the resin itself and young dried saplings. From these it was clearly evident that the species of tree and resin was the same as the Amboinese White Dammar, but it was more pellucid and purer; indeed, some pieces of it were entirely transparent and white like crystal. Some, however, were impure and almost like horn, but all were brittle and could not be chewed into a mass under the teeth as happens with chewed Mastic, though they closely matched it in smell. The leaves were similar to those of the Amboinese tree, but a little longer, thinner, and more flaccid, turning yellow when dry, five and a half inches long and over an inch wide, whereas those of the Amboinese tree remain green. Otherwise, they were arranged in the same way, opposite each other on the stems. In Batavia, as I have heard, this resin is called *Dammar Kesi*.

**Royal Dammar** <note>original: "Dammar Radja"</note>, called *Salo Colano* by the people of Ternate, is the very same Dammar, but only the largest and clearest pieces that hang high on the trunk, mixed with no dirt. This kind falls in Bacan and Halmahera, which never sets as yellow as the Amboinese, but usually stays white or becomes a little yellow over time; otherwise, it is like the Amboinese in taste and smell, and also falls from similar trees. This is used only by the Moluccan Kings for burning, which is why it is called King's Dammar, and the common man may not burn it.

A delightful prank is seen with the newcomers who come to the Amboinese market and take this fresh Dammar for rock candy <note>original: "Candy-zuiker"</note>, which it resembles well; they then buy it for a small amount of money and run happily around a corner with it to gobble it up, but they immediately find themselves deceived.

As said above, one finds recorded in some ship journals that much Mastic would fall in these islands, by which one must understand this **Stone Dammar** <note>original: "Dammar Batu"</note>, which in burning floats very near to the scent of Mastic.

A young Dammar tree stands very decoratively and represents to us a small Cedar tree, for it sets a straight trunk, beginning to give out leaves and side-branches not far above the root. In this one sees a particularity: that the cross-branches from the bottom up stand in a ring of two, three, and four, and each time between these gatherings of branches one sees the leaves standing in pairs on the trunk itself; if one breaks anything off, a sticky sap runs out, smelling strongly and resinous.

In the year 1691, the white Royal Dammar, there called *Salo Colano*, was sent to me from Ternate, both the pieces of resin and young but dry trees, by which it appeared sufficiently that it is the same sort of tree and resin as the Amboinese white Dammar, but indeed as clear and pure, for some pieces were clearly transparent, white as crystal, some dirty and tending toward a horn-color, all entirely brittle under the teeth and not to be brought into a mass, as one can do with chewed Mastic, whose scent they came very near. Book III. Chapter XI. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

# CHAPTER ELEVEN.
## Celebes Dammar. Dammar Celebes.

*There is another species similar to the preceding Stone Dammar <note>original: "Dammaræ Batu"</note>, which we call Celebes Dammar, since it occurs most frequently in that region. Although the tree itself is unknown to me so far, I wished to place it here because such a great quantity of it is brought in.*

*It consists of large lumps or cakes <note>original: "placentis," literally "cakes"</note>, over a foot wide, grey and dusty on the outside, so that it might be mistaken for a type of earth. On the inside, however, it is pure, solid, semi-transparent, and horn-like; in some places blackish, in others white like Amber or Gum Anime <note>a hard, clear resin</note>. It is never as clear as the Amboinese Stone Dammar, but it is equally hard and brittle if struck or chewed. Although this Celebes variety may be very old, it never turns as reddish as the Amboinese, from which it also differs in smell and taste. This Celebes variety has almost no flavor, but when placed on coals, it gives off a richer <note>original: "pinguiorem," literally "fatter"</note> smell than the Amboinese, almost like Western Tacamahaca <note>a fragrant resin from the Americas</note>, with a certain sourness like Oxycroceum Plaster <note>a historical medical plaster containing saffron, vinegar, and resins</note>, though its substance does not match Tacamahaca at all. It catches fire quickly but burns with a slow flame, and it makes less noise <note>crackling</note> than the Amboinese, and its smell is not as heavy. That which occurs in the Province of Manado is very white in its clear segments, but in others it is black and horn-colored; indeed, both colors are often observed in the same pieces. However, that which is brought from Tambucko, Banaya, and Luboe has its most transparent parts leaning more toward yellow or reddish, while the rest is likewise horn-colored.*

*According to reports from eye-witnesses, the tree of this resin most closely resembles the Amboinese variety in form and appearance, being likewise very tall and straight, with large, protruding knots or heads at the lower part of the trunk. Its leaves, however, are shorter, wider, thicker, and more rounded than the Amboinese, but otherwise of the same shape and veined in a similar way. Its fruits also have the size and shape of lemons, falling apart in large scales. Its resin melts over fire and softens when cast into hot water, showing it to be oilier and more pliable than the Amboinese. It hangs in large lumps from the thick branches as well as from the trunk, and pieces are found that weigh a Pickol <note>a traditional unit of weight</note>—that is, one hundred and twenty-five pounds.*

**Name.** *In Latin, Dammara Celebica. In Malay, Dammar Celebes and Dammar Bangay, as it is found most abundantly in these islands. The Malays also call it Dammar Batu <note>Stone Dammar</note>, like the preceding one, as it should be considered a species of that genus. In Celebes, it is called Damma, and in Manado, Dammar. Around Tambuco Hulo. Some of our people take this for a species of Tacamahaca, just as it was sent to me from Manado under the name of Oriental Tacamahaca. However, it has little outward resemblance to that, except somewhat in smell, which is richer in true Tacamahaca. Furthermore, Tacamahaca is never found in such large lumps, is more reddish and darker in color, and is more brittle than the Dammar; for more on this, see Nicolas Monardes' book on simples, chapter 2 <note>Monardes was a famous 16th-century Spanish physician and botanist</note>.*

**Location.** *This species of Stone Dammar does not grow in the Amboinese islands, as far as I know, but in great abundance on the island of Celebes, especially on its eastern side, from the Tambucco region to Manado, as well as in the Province of Lubock, which is situated on the inner part of the great Bay of Boni <note>original: "Boegenfis"</note>; hence it is called Dammar Lubo by some. It is also found in Bangay and its district of Balante. In Manado, it occurs most frequently around the huge lake, near the village of Dandano, in the district of Tambuao, Bangay; and further, it grows along the eastern coast of Celebes, so that the trees often lean over the water, and elegant, transparent pieces of this resin are found and collected everywhere on the shore.*

**Use.** *The people of Bangay, Celebes, and Boni <note>the Bugis people</note> use this Dammar for candles. They first soften it in hot water and then shape it with their hands into*

# XI. CHAPTER.
## Celebes Dammar or Resin.

*The preceding Stone Dammar has a related variety, which we call Celebes, because it mostly occurs in that land. Its tree is unknown to me until now, yet I wished to place it here, because much of it is brought in.*

*It consists of large lumps or cakes, a foot wide and more, mostly grey and dusty on the outside, so that one would take it for a clod of earth. But on the inside it is pure, massive, half-transparent, horn-colored, in some spots blackish, in some white, like Amber or Gum Anime. It is never as clear as the Amboinese Stone Dammar, but just as hard and brittle when one knocks it or bites into it. No matter how old the Celebes variety is, it never becomes as deep yellow as the Amboinese. They also differ in smell and taste, for the Amboinese leans somewhat toward the scent of Canary resin when chewed or burned. The Celebes variety has almost no taste, but on coals it smells oilier <note>original: "vetter"</note> than the Amboinese, almost like the West Indian Tacamahaca, with some rancidity like the Oxycroceum plaster, although in substance it does not resemble Tacamahaca at all. It also burns easily and steadily, crackles less than the Amboinese, and the smell is not so troublesome. That which occurs in the Province of Manado is quite white in its clearest pieces, and black and horn-colored in others, both of which colors are often seen on one piece. But that which is brought from Tambucko, Banaya, and Luboe, leans more toward yellow and reddish in the clear pieces; the rest is also horn-colored.*

*According to the reports of some eye-witnesses, that tree would most closely match the Amboinese in appearance, being also very high and straight as an arrow <note>original: "pyl-regt"</note>, with large knots or heads at the lower trunk. The leaves are somewhat shorter, wider, thicker, and rounder at the front than the Amboinese, otherwise of the same fashion, and likewise striped <note>veined</note>. The fruits are similarly equal to lemons in size and shape, falling apart in large scales. The resin coming from it can be melted over fire and made soft in hot water, as a proof that it is oilier and more pliable than the Amboinese. It hangs in large lumps, as well from the thick branches as from the trunk, and one finds pieces there that weigh a Picol—that is, one hundred and twenty-five pounds.*

**Name.** *In Latin Dammara Celebica. In Malay Dammar Celebes and Dammar Bangay, because it occurs most on those same islands. The Malays also call it Dammar Batu, like the preceding, as it is also to be kept in that genus. In Celebes one calls it Damma, and in Manado Dammar. Around Tambocko Hulo. Some of our nation wish to take it for a kind of Tacamahaca, just as it was sent to me from Manado under the name of Tacamahaca Orientalis, with which it however has little agreement in outward appearance, but indeed somewhat in the smell, which in the true Tacamahaca is even oilier. It never falls in such large lumps, and is rougher and darker of color, and more brittle than the Dammar; regarding which see more broadly in Nicol. Monardus's Book of Simples, chapter 2.*

**Place.** *This kind of Stone Dammar does not grow in the Amboinese islands, so far as is known to me, but more abundantly on the large island of Celebes, and that mostly on its East side from the Tambucco district unto Manado, as well as in the Province of Lubock, situated at the inner part of the great Bugis Bay <note>The Gulf of Boni</note>, from whence it is called Dammar Lubo by some. It also occurs on Bangay, and its district of Balante, on the large land. In Manado one has it mostly around the large Lake, by the village <note>original: "Negory"</note> of Dandano, in the district of Tambuao, Bangay, and further on the East coast of Celebes it grows around the shores, so that the trees sometimes hang over the water, and the beautiful clear pieces are found scattered everywhere on the beach.*

**Use.** *Those of Bangay, Celebes, and the Bugis use this Dammar for burning <note>as light</note>, first making it soft in hot water, and then rolling it with their hands into*

They give a steady and even flame, truly with no crackling <note>original: "strepitum"</note>, and they maintain a fire better than the Amboinese varieties. ## CHAPTER TWELVE.
### The Camiri Tree. Camiri.

The Camiri is a thick tree, but not tall, since its trunk soon divides into branches. It bears a smooth, ash-gray bark, marked here and there with many dots; it is brittle and juicy. The leaves have two forms: on the younger branches they are much larger, triangular, and divided into three sharp points, almost like Ivy <note>original: "Hederæ"</note>, but much larger—usually six inches <note>term: "pollices," literally "thumbs" or inches</note> long and wide, and sometimes even ten or eleven inches. They bear three, and some five, large veins <note>original: "nervos"</note> that meet at the stalk <note>term: "pedunclum," the petiole</note>, which is seven or eight inches long, round, and rough, as if sprinkled with sand or even woolly, as are the uppermost branches and the underside of the leaves. Near the base of the leaves, on their stalks, two small warts are located; the leaves are joined closely together around the branches without any particular order.

The other and most common leaves on adult trees are very broad at the lower part and gradually taper to a point, but they have no angles, except that some of these are wavy at the edges. They are eight or nine inches long and five or six wide, with three huge veins meeting at the stalk, but consisting of few ribs; they are dark green on top and a yellowish-green <note>original: "ex viridi gilva"</note> underneath.

Flowers come forth among the leaves, sitting in short but extended clusters, with three or four joined together and supported by short, green stalks. These flowers resemble those of the Gayang <note>the Polynesian Chestnut</note>, but are smaller, consisting of five delicate and narrow petals. In their center, some short filaments <note>original: "stamina"</note> appear, equipped with yellow anthers, and they give off a pleasant scent. The fruits do not grow from the flowers themselves, but at the point where the flower-bearing stalks meet. They usually grow singly, though sometimes they are found in pairs joined on one short, thick, and woody stalk. Each fruit is again of two types, either single or double; the single one has nearly the shape and size of a Walnut <note>original: "Nucis Juglandis"</note>, but is irregular and equipped with a blunt point at the top. The double one has the shape of a scrotum, furrowed in the middle and bluntly pointed at the top; it is a grayish-green color and looks as if sprinkled with flour and sand. The outer husk is similar to a Walnut's, but it does not stain the hands with its color in the same way. Under this is hidden a nut—one in the single fruit and two in the double fruit—each wrapped in a thin membrane or cell which has a large hole on one side through which the nut can be seen. The double ones are the most common.

The nut itself has the shape of a round Canary nut, but is a little more flat and wide, and slightly compressed; it is blackish and wrinkled on the outside. The shell is truly thicker and harder than that of the Canary nut, and it cannot be opened except by a strong blow:

<column-break/>

into the shape of a thick candle, about a span long, which they then wrap with leaves of the Nipa so that they resemble the Batavian Dammar, except that they are smaller. They burn steadily without crackling and hold the fire better than the Amboinese ones. The Manaders melt this Dammar over the fire and pour it into thin bamboos, which they then burn like candles. Furthermore, it is used throughout all of Celebes to fix all kinds of weapons into their handles, as was said above in Chapter 7 regarding the Great Canary Tree.

In Manado, they also glaze earthen pots, dishes, and basins with this crushed and smeared Dammar, just as the Amboinese do with theirs. They also coat the wooden sheaths of their Krises with it to make them smooth and gleaming, and the wood from the knots serves for Kris-handles; but that of the trunk is not durable and serves for no carpentry.

Upon closer investigation, one will perhaps find that the Stone Dammar found on Borneo will correspond much more with this Celebes Dammar than with the preceding Amboinese one. It loses its horn-colored appearance when boiled for a long time and becomes white.

## CHAPTER XII.
### The Camiri Tree.

The Camiri tree is indeed thick, but not high in the trunk, which soon divides into branches, with a smooth light-gray bark, speckled here and there with some dots; it is brittle and juicy. The leaves are of two kinds of shapes, for on the young branches they are much larger, triangular, or divided into three points, almost like those of Ivy, but much larger—commonly six inches long and wide, sometimes also ten and eleven inches. They have three, and some also five, large veins that meet at the stalk. The stalk is seven to eight inches long, round, rough as if strewn with sand, or woolly, as are also the foremost branches and the underside of the leaves. On the stalks near the leaves, one sees two reddish little warts, and the leaves stand without order close behind one another around the branches.

The other and most common leaves on the full-grown trees are also broad at the back and gradually run to a point, but they have no corners, except that some fall a little wavy at the edges; they are eight and nine inches long, five and six wide, with three large veins meeting at the back, and otherwise few ribs; dark green above, and a faded green below.

Between the leaves, the blossom comes forth in short but extended clusters, three and four little flowers together on short grass-like stalks. The little flowers resemble the blossom of the Gayang, though they are smaller and consist of five tender and narrow petals, in the middle of which one sees some short threads with yellow nubs, which have a somewhat lovely scent. The fruits do not come forth from the flower itself, but at that place where the flower-bearing stalks meet; they also commonly come forth singly, sometimes two joined together on a short, thick, woody stalk. Each fruit is again of two kinds, either single or double; the single is nearly the shape and size of a Walnut, though somewhat lopsided and with a blunt point at the front. The double has the shape of a scrotum, in the middle from back to front with a cleft, and a blunt point; it is a grayish-green and as if strewn with flour and sand. The outermost husk is like the Walnuts, though it does not stain so: beneath it lies a nut—in the single one, and in the double two—each enclosed in a thin membrane or tube which has a large hole on one side through which one can see the nut; and the double ones are the most numerous.

The nut itself has the shape of a round Canary nut, though somewhat wider and flatter, at the end somewhat compressed, blackish and wrinkled on the outside. The shell is thicker and harder than on the Canary nut, which one cannot [open] except

...can be opened with a good strike. The internal part is filled throughout with a white and fatty kernel, similar in substance and taste to a Walnut <note>Latin: *Nuci Juglandi*</note>, but this is oilier and more nauseating. In the ripe fruit, the shell turns somewhat yellow and eventually blackish. The wood of the trunk is white and useless; in the branches, it is fragile and filled with a watery pith <note>The soft, spongy tissue in the center of the stem</note>, which makes it dangerous to stand upon its branches, as they break easily.

*The Season.* It blooms in September, and provides fruit in October and November; often its branches also sprout from the lower part of the trunk. The main branches do not grow upright but curved, and they extend broadly.

*The Name.* In Latin, it is called *Camirium*. In Malay, *Camirin*, *Camiri*, and *Boa Cras*. By those of Ternate, *Saketa*. In Amboina, *Yaro Mahu*; that is, the *Javanese Canarium*, either because it grows most abundantly in Java, or because they first received its use and kernels from the Javanese. Conversely, the Amboinese call the *Ricinus* <note>The Castor oil plant</note> by the name *Camirium*, because a fatty oil is also pressed from its seeds. In Buru, it is called *Sibu* and *Sibut*. By the Macassarese, *Sapiri*. By the Buginese, *Ampiri*. By those of Bima, *Callelli*.

*The Location.* It grows mostly in Java and in the Moluccas, especially in Batjan and Makian; likewise in Bonoa and Buru, as well as in the western part of Celebes <note>Modern Sulawesi</note> subject to the Macassarese. In Amboina and Banda, some of these trees are also found, but they are rare and not as large as in other places.

*The Use.* The most common use among the Javanese and Macassarese is to form candles from its kernels. Once cleaned, the kernels are pounded and mixed with a little cotton or coconut <note>Latin: *Calappi*</note> shell fibers, which are kneaded together until they have the consistency of thick tallow <note>Animal fat used for soap or candles</note>. Then, small sticks of split Bamboo or *Leleba* reed are taken, around which this paste is rolled like a wick, worked by hand until it resembles the thickness and appearance of a candle, which is then lit at the reed. These candles burn steadily, but they are consumed faster than tallow candles and emit an unpleasant odor of burnt hair; for this reason, they are not used by the nobility, but only by the common people. The people of Bonoa take less trouble, merely stringing the inner kernels onto a small skewer made of Bamboo. The Amboinese, out of innate laziness, do not bother with this, though some eat them raw mixed with a little pepper; however, many should not be eaten at once, as they cause intoxication.

It is safest if the whole nuts are thrown into the fire and roasted until the outer shell catches fire, which is immediately extinguished. The roasted kernel is then removed and eaten as is, or cooked in *Sayor* <note>A traditional vegetable stew or broth</note> in place of coconut meat, the lack of which is supplied by this kernel. Women also wash their heads with this instead of coconut. An oil can also be boiled out in the same way as from grated coconut, which poor people use for frying fish; however, if it is old, it is useful for nothing but lighting lamps, as it is thick and burns slowly. The shells can be used to make charcoal, like *Canarium* shells, as they are fatty, thick, and hold fire for a long time. These same shells are also mixed among *Calsomba* <note>Safflower</note> flowers to keep them fatty and good, so they do not dry out too much to the loss of the seller, even if the buyers object to this.

### OBSERVATION.
The *Camiri* is also described by Valentijn <note>François Valentijn (1666–1727), a Dutch minister and naturalist</note> on page 213; however, his figure presented under No. XL is entirely different from that of Rumphius, which otherwise corresponds in all parts and species with Rumphius's descriptions. ...can be opened with a good strike. The interior is tightly filled with a white and fatty meat, similar in substance and taste to Walnuts, though somewhat oilier and more nauseating. On the ripe fruit, the husk becomes somewhat yellow, and finally smoky. The wood of the trunk is white and poor, brittle on the branches, and with a watery heart <note>pith</note>; therefore, it is precarious to stand on these branches, as they break off short.

*Season.* It blooms in September; the fruit is available in October and November. One sometimes also sees the branches sprouting from the lower trunk, and the main branches do not go straight up, but crooked, and spread far out.

*Name.* In Latin *Camirium*. In Malay *Camirin*, *Camiri*, and *Boa Cras*. On Ternate *Saketa*. On Amboina *Yaro Mahu*, that is *Javanese Canarium*, either because it grows most on Java, or because they first received the use and seeds from the Javanese. On the other hand, the Amboinese call the *Ricinus* <note>Castor oil plant</note> *Camirium*, because supposedly a fatty oil is also pressed from its seeds. On Buru *Sibu* and *Sibut*. On Macassar *Sapiri*, on Bugis *Ampiri*, on Bima *Callelli*.

*Place.* It grows mostly on Java, and in the Moluccas, especially on Batjan and Makian. As well as on Bonoa, and Buru, and on the Western part of Celebes, standing under the Macassarese. In Amboina and Banda there are also some, though not many, and they do not grow as large as in other places.

*Use.* The most common use by the Javanese and Macassarese is to make candles from them, for one pounds the cleaned kernels, mixes the same with a little cotton, or coconut husk, kneading them thoroughly together to the consistency of thick tallow. After that, one takes the sticks of split Bamboos, or *Leleba*, and rolls this dough around them, as if around a wick, with the hands to the thickness and form of a candle, which one lights by that reed. These candles burn quite steadily, but consume faster than tallow candles; they also give off an unpleasant smell of hair, therefore they are not used by great Lords, but only by common folk. The Bonoese take less trouble with it, merely stringing the inner kernels on a skewer made of Bamboos, and lighting them so. The Amboinese, from innate laziness, make no work of it, except that they eat some raw, mixed with a little pepper; however, one must not eat many of them, for they make one drunk.

The surest way is that one first throws the nuts into the fire, and roasts them so long until the outer shell catches fire, which one immediately extinguishes again, and takes the roasted meat out again, which one then eats out of hand, or cooks with other *Sayor* <note>stew</note>, in place of coconut-pith, the lack of which one fulfills with these kernels, just as the women wash the head with the same, in place of coconut-pith. One can also boil an oil from it in the same way as from grated coconut-pith, which the common people use to fry fish in; but being somewhat old, it is fit for nothing but burning in the lamp, for it is thick and burns slowly. The shells can be used to make coals from them, like the *Canarium* shells, for they are fatty, thick, and hold the fire long. The same shells are also mixed among the *Calsomba* <note>Safflower</note> flowers to keep them fatty and good, and so that they do not dry out and shrivel too much, to the loss of the seller, although the buyers look askance at that.

# CHAPTER THIRTEEN.

## Pangium. The Pangi.

The Pangi tree bears a trunk that is taller and more upright than the previous species <note>The Camiri tree described on the previous page</note>. Its leaves are of two types, differing greatly from one another, as was noted regarding the *Canarium* genus. On younger trees, the leaves are very large and divided into three angles or lobes, about a foot long and ten inches wide or more; most, however, are ten inches long and nine wide. Some are angular only on one side because the angle on the other side has already grown out, while others lack these angles entirely. The very young leaves are heart-shaped, so that three or four different leaf shapes may be seen on a single young tree. Near the leaf stalk <note>Latin: *petiolum*</note>, five or sometimes seven large veins converge, and the leaf edges near the stalk are smooth and not lobed. The stalks themselves are long. The leaves of mature trees have lost all those angles and have an oblong-heart shape, nine inches long and seven or eight wide, ending in a blunt point; they are an intense green, smooth, and shiny, with an unpleasant and pungent taste.

I have not seen the flowers. The fruit, however, hangs here and there from the branches, simple in form and the size of an Ostrich egg, or more commonly like a Cassowary egg. Most are navel-like at the tip and bulging at the sides. The exterior is a dull reddish color, eventually becoming a brownish-gray like an old Coconut <note>Latin: *Calappi*</note>. They are wrinkled and marked with small dots like the *Atun* fruit <note>The fruit of Atuna racemosa</note>, hanging from a thick stalk that widens near the fruit. The outer husk is thick, like that of a Pomegranate, beneath which a small amount of whitish flesh is hidden, in which the nuts or "chestnuts" are packed together. These nuts are flat and vary in shape, though most resemble a compressed little purse. They are larger than Walnuts, lying against each other on their flat sides; their narrow part faces inward while the widest part faces outward. Some are thicker and triangular, while others have different shapes, usually one and a half to two inches long, and some three, for two varieties occur: one larger and one smaller. The smaller or most common variety is shaped like a Walnut, generally triangular, but others are so different and irregular that among ten nuts, hardly two can be found alike. The outer skin of the nut is rough, woody, blackish-gray, and wrinkled, interwoven with protruding and intricate veins like an old, shriveled leather pouch. The larger variety is shaped like a purse—flat, straight, black, and much more wrinkled, for the protruding veins run so intricately that they resemble little trees or branches and shrubs fashioned by a craftsman's hand. All these veins are raised, and in some places their edges are so sharp they are difficult to handle, resembling thorns. The lower part of the nuts is smoother and less wrinkled. The widest part, which lies against the husk, has an opening formed by an oblong fissure, covered by a lid of the same substance as the shell; this lid is so firmly attached that it can only be removed by force. The shell has the thickness of a knife blade, etc., matching the *Tampurong* <note>term: *Tampurong*; the Malay word for a coconut shell</note> of a Coconut. Inside is hidden a flat, large, white kernel shaped like the shell, which can be divided into two segments. It tastes like a Hazelnut but has a softer and tougher substance. If not fully ripe, it is somewhat bitter—at least it appears so in Amboina—but in other places, it is larger, fattier, and sweeter. These fruits are left on the tree until they fall of their own accord and the outer husk rots away; then the kernels turn black and are fully ripe, at which point the surrounding flesh can be easily separated. They are rarely or hardly ever eaten raw, for they have an intoxicating power that makes men dizzy, and some even fall into a faint, even though the taste is reasonably pleasant and sweet. However, they must be prepared as will soon be described. The wood of this tree is hard, solid, and heavy. The bark is brittle and adheres firmly to the wood.

<column-break/>

# XIII. CHAPTER.

## *The Pangi Tree.*

*The Pangi tree has a higher and straighter trunk than the one before. The leaves are of two kinds, differing much from one another, as was said of the Canarium, for on the young trees they are very large and divided into three corners or lobes, about a foot long and ten inches broad, some more; most are ten inches long and nine broad. Some have a corner on one side only, the curve of the other corner being almost grown out; others again are not angular. The very young ones are perfectly heart-shaped, so that one sees three or four kinds of leaves on a young tree. At the stalk, five and on some seven large nerves meet together, and the edges near the stalk are flat and without a curve. The stalks are long. The leaves of the grown trees have lost all the protruding corners and are formed like an oblong heart, nine inches long, seven and eight ditto broad, with a blunt point, forest-green, smooth, and gleaming, unpleasant of taste and somewhat biting.*

*The bloom is not known. The fruit hangs singly here or there on the branches, in size and shape like an Ostrich egg, commonly like a Cassowary egg, most with a nipple at the front and somewhat lumpy at the sides; on the outside dark-red or tawny, finally gray like the old Coconut, rough on the outside and set with small dots like the fruit of the Atun, hanging on a thick stalk which has a small wreath near the fruit. The outermost bark is as thick as on the Pomegranate, underneath which is a little white flesh; and therein certain nuts or chestnuts are packed. These nuts are flat and of many kinds of shapes, yet mostly like a pressed purse, somewhat larger than our walnuts, lying with the flat side upon one another, with the narrow end turned inward and the broadest outward. Some are somewhat thicker, entirely three-sided, and of other shapes, generally one and a half and two inches long, and some three, for there are two sorts of them, large and small. The small or commonest sort is in the shape of a Walnut, usually three-cornered, but some so different and round-bulging in shape that among ten one will find no two that are like each other. The outermost shell is rough, woody, of a blackish-gray, wrinkly, and with protruding veins running through one another, tangled like a leather bag that has been made wet and shrinks. The large kind is mostly formed like a purse, and flat, straight, black, and much rougher, for the protruding veins run so prettily through one another that they represent some little trees, or dry branches and shrubs carved into some ebony wood by a master's hand, and all of that is raised work, of which the edges in some places are so sharp that they are difficult to handle, and look much more like thorns; yet the underside is always smoother and less rough. The broadest corner, which faces the husk, has a little door, being an oblong crack which is closed with a lid of the same substance as the shell, which fits so tightly therein that it cannot be pulled off except with force. The shell has the thickness of a knife of substance etc., resembling the Tampurong of a Coconut. Inside lies a broad, white, and flat kernel, formed after the shape of the shell, which lets itself be divided into two leaves, in taste like Hazelnuts, of a softer and tougher substance, and if it is not thoroughly ripe, somewhat bitter; at least in Amboina it is so, but in other places it is larger, fattier, and sweeter. These fruits are left to hang on the trees until they fall off by themselves and the outer bark rots, for only then are the grains black and thoroughly ripe, from which the surrounding flesh can be easily shaken off. The innermost kernel is eaten little or not at all raw, for it has a dizzying or drunken-making power, from which some also fall into a swoon, although it is reasonably pleasant of taste, but one must prepare it as shall be said presently. The wood of this tree is hard, dense, and heavy. The bark is brittle and sticks fast to the wood.*

It warns that the kernels are intoxicating and can cause fainting if eaten raw due to their chemical properties.</summary>

III Book. XIII. Chapter. AMBOINESE HERBAL. 183

**Name.** In Latin *Pangium*: In Malay *Pangi*, *Capaya*, and *Copaya*. Among the Javanese it is called *Poutsjong*, but its prepared food is called *Caluac* and *Colowac*: Among the people of Makassar and Bali it is called *Pangy*, in Buton *Pany*, in Ternate *Bobbi* and *Sawan*. In Buru *Hami*. In Ambon *Any*, and by everyone *Salea*.

**Location.** The best and most numerous fruits of this tree are found in the region of Celebes <note>Modern-day Sulawesi</note>, under the rule of Makassar and Bugis, as well as in Java, Bali, Buton, Buru, and Ceram. They are rare in Ambon, found only here and there in the flat forests; and because they are not as pleasant in flavor as in other places, they are not much sought after or used by the Ambonese, and the common people are anxious about eating them, as these fruits are considered harmful.

**Usage.** Among the Malays, Makassarese, Buginese, and Butonese, this fruit is in great use for food, but never raw; rather, it is prepared in the following way: The mature nuts are boiled whole in water, then the shells are pounded into pieces and the kernels are removed and sliced into narrow strips like lettuce <note>Latin: *Brassicæ lactucariæ*</note>. These are placed in a small pit or basket lined with straw, then soaked for twenty-four hours in river or rain water, which extracts the malignancy <note>This "malignancy" refers to the high concentration of hydrogen cyanide in the raw seeds, which is lethal unless processed.</note>. Then they may be eaten without harm, either alone or with grated Coconut <note>Latin: *Calappa*</note>. Fish are also boiled with these to make the broth richer, as is otherwise done with Coconut milk. These strips are also dried and preserved so that food can be made richer during the rainy months. The Javanese know how to express an oil from the dried and reheated kernels by pressing them between two boards; this oil is used for lamps, though they deceitfully sell it in full jars as *Minjac Widjing* or Sesame oil <note>original: "Minjac Widjing seu Oleo Sesamino"</note>, which is much more precious.

The Buginese prepare that oil in another way; they pound and knead the cleaned and sun-dried kernels into a paste with their hands, gradually pouring on warm water until the oil floats to the top, which is then skimmed off. This oil, if fresh, tastes sweet and is suitable for frying cakes and fish, and it does not turn rancid as quickly as Coconut oil.

The bark of the tree, when crushed and thrown into water, kills the fish swimming there. The juice of the leaves, if dripped into ulcerations or putrid wounds, kills the maggots <note>original: "vermes"</note> and small creatures that cause itching and gnaw at the surrounding flesh. This was discovered by chance when a piece of putrefied and worm-eaten meat was wrapped in these leaves; the maggots died immediately and fell from the meat onto the leaf, and the meat itself turned red again, acquiring a healthy color.

These leaves have such an antipathy and power to kill all sorts of worms nesting in putrefaction, making them die and fall away. The fresh kernels perform the same task; if they are chewed or ground with water and smeared on the head, they kill lice. However, one must be careful not to swallow the juice while chewing. Chickens also die if they eat these kernels, whether raw or cooked. If the fallen fruits have not yet split open, they should be buried in straw or other dry matter until they rot, so that the kernels can be removed. These are also roasted under hot ashes, then the small pits are removed and prepared for food as described above. Some Chinese merchants have brought these kernels from Java for sale here in recent years, selling ten for a *stuiver* <note>A small Dutch coin</note> to be eaten roasted with fish, though they were not as wrinkled as the Ambonese variety.

When the Ambonese do prepare this fruit for food, they do so secretly and not in the sight of many people. They believe that if a malevolent person—such as those they call *Wangis* and *Matta Panas*, that is, a Sorcerer <note>original: "Magum"</note> and an "Evil-Eye" <note>original: "Ferventoculum"</note>—should happen to pass by and look at these kernels, the food would contract a harmful quality. They observe the same practice in the preparation of wild *Oebis* <note>Wild yams</note>. The hollowed-out shells of these kernels are used as tinderboxes, for which they fit a wooden lid. They often float in the sea and are cast up on the shore, which makes them black and polished.

The fruits grow from thick branches, hanging from a long and curved stalk, which is larger and thicker than the stalks of the leaves. The people of Bali will not eat these, unless they...

**Name.** In Latin *Pangium*, in Malay *Pangi*, *Capaya*, and *Copaya*, in Javanese *Poutsjong*, but the prepared food is called *Caluac* and *Colowac*. In Makassar and Bali *Pangy*, in Buton *Pany*, in Ternate *Bobbi* and *Sawan*: In Buru *Hami*, in Ambon *Any*, in Oma *Salea*.

**Location.** The best and most of these fruits are found in the land of Celebes, under the Makassar and Bugis territory, as well as on Java, Bali, Buton, Buru, and Ceram. Few are found in Ambon; here and there in the flat forests, and because they are worse in taste than in other places, they are not much used by the natives, the common folk being mostly afraid to consume them because they consider it a harmful fruit.

**Usage.** Among the Malays, Makassarese, Buginese, and Butonese, this fruit is in great use for food, not raw, but first prepared thus. The ripe nuts are thoroughly boiled whole in water, after which the shell is knocked into pieces, the kernels are taken out and cut into narrow strips like cole-slaw <note>original: "kool-salaat"</note>. These are placed in a basket lined with straw and soaked for a full day or a night in a river or other fresh water, which draws out the poisonous quality <note>original: "quaadaardigheid"</note>. After that, they can be eaten without harm alone or with grated Coconut <note>original: "Calappus"</note>. They also cook fish and *Sayor* <note>A vegetable stew or soup</note> with it to make them fatty, just as one otherwise does with Coconut meat. These strips are also dried and saved to enrich the food in the rainy months. The Javanese know how to press an oil from the dried and reheated kernels between two planks, used for lamps, which they deceitfully sell in pots as *Minjac Widjing*, which is much more expensive.

The Buginese make that oil in another way; they stamp and knead the cleaned and sun-dried kernels, gradually pouring on warm water until the oil floats on top, which they then scoop off. This oil, being fresh, is sweet and suitable for frying cakes and fish, not becoming rancid as easily as Coconut oil.

The bark of the tree, when rubbed and strewn on water, kills the fish therein. The juice of the leaves, dripped into rotting wounds or ulcers, kills the worms and little creatures therein that cause itching and eat into the flesh. This was discovered by chance when a piece of rotting and wormy meat was wrapped in one of these leaves; the little worms died immediately and fell from the meat onto the leaf, and the meat became red again and of a healthy color.

And such an antipathy and power do these leaves have to kill all kinds of worms in putrefaction and make them fall off. The fresh kernels do the same when one chews them or rubs them with water and smears them on the head to kill lice; taking great care that one does not swallow any juice while chewing. The chickens also die if they eat these pits, whether raw or cooked. If the fallen fruits have not yet burst, one must bury them in straw or other debris until they rot and the kernels can be removed; these are also roasted under hot ashes, then the seeds are taken out and made fit for eating as before. Some Chinese have brought these kernels from Java here to sell for some years now, giving ten for a *stuiver*, to be eaten roasted with fish, but they were not as rough as the Ambonese ones.

Even so, when the Ambonese want to prepare this fruit for food, they do it out of the sight of many people, for they believe if a malevolent person—such as they call *Wangis* and *Matta Panas*, that is Sorcerers and "Hot-eyes"—should happen to pass by and look at these kernels, the food would receive a harmful quality, which they also observe in the preparation of wild yams <note>original: "Oebis"</note>. The hollowed-out shells of these kernels are also used to keep tinder in, with a wooden lid made for them. They often float in the sea and are cast onto the beach, from where they are gathered black and beautifully polished.

The fruits also come forth on thick branches, on a long curved stem, larger than the others on the tree. The Balinese will not eat of them, or they must...

## CHAPTER FOURTEEN.
### The Mussel-shaped Fruit: Boa Assuesseng.

This fruit seems to be of the same genus as the preceding *Pangi*: It has the shape and size of a blue mussel shell <note>original: "coerulei conchylii"</note> standing open, and perhaps it is a hairy mountain *Pangi*, shaped with protruding ridges and points like the *Pangi*. From the back part, which resembles a spine, it is attached to some part just like a shellfish; and from that part both toward the top and everywhere toward the sharp tip there is a fissure, as if it were opening itself. On its uppermost part, a small lid <note>original: "operculum"</note> seems to have been attached, which falls off upon ripening, as happens with the *Pangi*. In its internal part, two somewhat thick and dry little leaves appear like lips, which are thickest at their lower part and consist of many dry, tangled filaments. On the external part of the fruit, a prismatic, spongy substance is sometimes found, like cork, which can easily be removed from between the dry wrinkles, as some of the filaments are still soft. The dry shell turns blackish mixed with gray, similar to the *Pangi* fruits.

The tree itself is entirely unknown. These dry and empty shells are found on the shore of *Ceram* near *Camaria* and *Hatifoa*, as well as in *Oma* in the rivers near *Aboro*; nor do the inhabitants know from which tree they fall, saying only that they are swept down from the high mountains by the rivers.

**Name.** In Latin it has been called by me so far *Fructus Musculiformis* <note>Mussel-shaped fruit</note>, and in Malay *Boa Assuesseng*, that is, the "Shellfish fruit" from its shape. The people of *Oma* call this *Ayhua Ettè* or *Ay Hoeamette*, that is, the "black fruit." Many do not have the perfect shape of a blue mussel—namely, flat at the top—but are compressed from both sides, so that they are thicker than they are wide. Some also end sharply at the top, and one side is shorter than the other.

**Usage.** Its use is not yet known, but since these fruits are rare, they are preserved as a curiosity; the inhabitants of *Oma* gather them to extract the internal marrow, which they apply to sores on the feet or to ulcers of the legs, which it cures.

<column-break/>

...they first soak them for several weeks in water, and then they first throw some to the chickens to test whether they can eat it without harm. The fresh leaves taken early in the morning, when they are wet with dew, rubbed with a little salt and juice of the *Lemon-Maas* <note>A local variety of citrus.</note>, and smeared on the dry scurvy, called *Cadel*, which creeps forward with great itching—first rubbed bravely, it cures the same. In the *Uliassers* they add another leaf to it, being yet unknown to me. On *Baley* <note>Baleya</note> it sometimes happens that the cattle incautiously eat these leaves, and then die from it. In the fruits that lie rotting on the ground for a long time, little worms are generated.

The Male *Pangi* is like the Female in its leaves, but it bears no fruit at all; it is found mostly on *Baley*, and is even more harmful in its leaves and bark than the Female, therefore it is used for killing fish.

The leaves of any *Pangi* rubbed and thrown into the water kill the shrimp, which one can however eat without harm.
