## XIV. CHAPTER.
### The Mussel-shaped fruit.

*This fruit seems to be a genus of the previously mentioned Pangi: It has the size and shape of a blue mussel that gapes, and is perhaps a mountain Pangi, figured on the outside with protruding wrinkles and edges like the Pangi. From behind (which would be the back) it also hangs attached for only a short distance, like the mussels, and from there up to the top, and all around again to the pointed end, is an opening as if they gaped; yet on top of that there seems to have been a small lid, which fell off through ripeness, as happens to the Pangi. Inside one sees two thickish dried little leaves like lips, which are thickest below, and consist of many dried threads tangled into one another. On the outside one sometimes still sees hanging a purplish, spongy substance, like cork, which one can easily pull out from between the dried wrinkles, when one also finds that some threads are still soft. The dried shell is blackish, with some gray, like the Pangi fruit.*

*The tree is still unknown. One finds the dry and empty shells on the beach of Ceram, around Camarien and Hatifoa, as well as on Oma in the rivers near Aboro, without the islanders being able to tell from what trees they come, saying only that they were carried down by the rivers from the high mountains.*

**Name.** *Provisionally it may be called in Latin Fructus Musculiformis, or in Malay Boa Assuesseng, that is Mussel-fruit, after its shape. Those of Oma call it Ayhua Ette or Ay Hoea Mette, that is black fruit; many do not have the perfect fashion of a blue mussel, namely flat towards the top, but are pressed from the front and back, so that they are thicker than they are wide. Some also run to a point at the top, and one side is somewhat shorter than the other.*

**The Use** *is not yet known, except that they are kept as a rarity because of their strange fashion, and that the islanders of Oma know to say that they seek these fruits to get the inner marrow out of them, and to lay it on sores of the feet, or old sores of the legs, and to heal them.*

### Book III. Chapter XIV. AMBONESE HERBAL.

In the Appendix of *Rumphius*, this chapter is found corrected and expanded in the following manner.

For thirty years, I was occupied with discovering from which tree this fruit originated, so that I might be certain, yet until now I was not able to know it correctly. For a long time, I thought its tree was a mountain species of the preceding *Pangi* <note>Pangium edule, described on the previous page.</note>, since the inhabitants were never able to show me its perfect flowers or leaves; they always found only the fruits, cleaned and rolled about by the water, on the southern coast of *Ceram* near the mouths of the rivers. This continued until finally, in the year 1693, during the great visitation of the *Kora-kora* <note>original: "Correnorum visitatione". These were official inspection voyages made in traditional "kora-kora" vessels by the Dutch East India Company to oversee the spice monopoly.</note>, perfect leaves and fruits were brought to me from the coast of *Ceram*. From these, I recognized that it has no affinity with the *Pangi*, but is rather a mountain species of the subsequent tree, the *Milk-wood* <note>original: "Lactariæ"</note>, or *Wild Mango* <note>original: "Mangæ Bravæ"</note>. Indeed, on a certain small branch shown to me, its leaves appeared situated in almost the same way, solitary around the twigs, of which three or four come forth together from one origin, from the center of which the flowering cluster rises. However, the leaves of this tree are smaller than those of the *Wild Mango*, narrowed at the lower part and more dilated or ending roundly at the upper part, like those of the *Cajeput* <note>original: "Caju-Puti"; Melaleuca leucadendra, known for its medicinal oil.</note>, six or eight inches long, three fingers wide, and their ribs are transversal.

The flowers sprout from a simple and short cluster, which are similar to those of the *Wild Mango*, but much smaller. In that cluster, only one or two fruits reach perfection, emulating those of the wild *Catappa* <note>The Tropical Almond.</note>; namely, three inches long, scarcely one wide, compressed from a round shape, and bearing a flat groove along the length on both sides. Externally it is grass-colored, while internally this muscle-shaped fruit is filled with a rather hard flesh. This flesh teems with milk, as do all the leaves and their stalks; however, in old fruits, this dries into a tough and tenacious substance which is attached to the protruding edges of the fruits. The dry fruit, as it is usually found, bears a wide fissure on the front side, to which, however, no lid was joined; but at the back and from the lower part up to the top, it is connected, whence it presents the appearance of a gaping mussel. This fruit is rugged on the outside, covered with protruding points and lines as if it were ornamental carving <note>original: "opus topiarium"</note>, in which matter it agrees with the *Pangi*. All its angles and pits are filled with a tenacious and dry substance, as if it were made of cork, which is covered by a thin external skin.

Inside are placed two triangular and dry lipped leaflets, widest and thickest at their lower part, consisting of many dry filaments joined and entangled together. If the substance of the kernel is scraped out, or worn away by the rotation of the water, then the fruit acquires a strange shape, as if it were carved by some art with certain protrusions, and some figures were impressed upon it; however, some of the edges of these forms are soft and fibrous.

Various forms of this fruit are also found, which perhaps are as many species; the most common, however, are oblong like a common shell or mussel, some are shorter and rounder, but the protrusions of these are larger and more circular, while some are smaller than acorns. The color of the shell is blackish-grey, like those of the *Pangi*.

*Name.* In Latin, *Muscle-shaped Fruit* <note>original: "Fructus Musculiformis"</note>. In Malay, *Boa-Affusseng*. In Dutch, *Mussel-fruit* <note>original: "Mossel-vrucht"</note>. The people of *Oma* call it *Ay-hua-ette* or *Ay-hua-mette*, that is, the "black fruit." Those of *Camarian*, however, name it the mountain *Wabo* or the terrestrial *Ohupaë*, that is, the "mountain Wild Mango."

*Location.* These fruits are mostly found on the shores of *Camarian*, and on the southern side of *Oma* around the mouths of the larger rivers. Their trees are almost unknown to the inhabitants, who believe they are located in remote mountains; however, during the mentioned visitation of the *Kora-kora*, it was found that these trees grow not so very far from the shore.

*Usage.* The inhabitants have nothing to communicate to us regarding its use, except that the people of *Oma* claim they seek these fruits to extract the internal marrow, which they apply to corns on the feet and to old ulcerations of the legs, which it cures. Otherwise, these dry and cleaned fruits are kept among curiosities.

<column-break/>

In the Appendix of *Rumphius*, this Chapter was found expanded and improved in the following manner.

I spent 30 years researching this fruit, to find out from what tree it comes, and until now I had gained no perfect knowledge of it. For a long time, I held it to be a mountain-variety of the preceding *Pangi*, because the inlanders could never show me leaves or perfect fruits of it, finding only cleaned fruits rolled by the water on *Ceram’s* south coast, at the outlets of the rivers. Finally, in the year 1693, during the great visit of the *Kora-kora*, leaves and perfect fruits from *Ceram’s* coast were brought to me, by which I noticed that it has no relation to *Pangi*, but is much more a mountain-variety of the following *Milk-tree* <note>Arbor Lactaria</note> or *Wild Mango*. For on a small branch brought with them, I found that the leaves stand in the same way, singly around the branches, of which 3 and 4 meet together at one origin, giving out from their middle the flowering cluster. Yet these leaves are smaller than those of the *Wild Mango*, narrow at the back, and broad or rounded at the front, like those of the *Cajeput*, 6 and 8 inches long, 3 fingers wide, with their small ribs running crosswise.

The blossom comes on a single short cluster, resembling that of the *Wild Mango*, yet much smaller. On the same cluster, only one or two fruits come to perfection, and they resemble those of the wild *Catappa*, namely, 3 inches long, and barely one wide, somewhat flat out of the round, having a flat gutter along the length on both sides, grass-green on the outside, and with a heart-like flesh hiding the innermost Mussel-fruit. This flesh is full of milk, as are all the leaves and stalks; however, on the old ones it dries up to a tough substance, which hangs fast to the protruding edges of the fruit. The dry fruit, as one commonly finds it, has on the front side, as said, a wide crack all around, on which however no lid has sat, and at the back and from below all around to the front half it hangs together, by which it represents the shape of a gaping Mussel. Outside it is rough with protruding points and lines, as if set with engraving, in which it agrees with the *Pangi*, all the nooks and pits being filled with a dry tough substance like cork, and covered on the outside with a thin skin.

Inside one sees two thickish and dried leaflets like lips, which are thickest at the bottom, and consist of many dried threads tangled together. When one picks out the cork-like substance, or it is worn away by rolling in the water, the fruit gets a rare shape, as if it were engraved by art with raised figures, though some edges of this engraving are soft and fibrous.

So one also has various shapes of this fruit, which are perhaps just as many species, for the most common are elongated like an ordinary Mussel, some are shorter and rounder, but the engraving is as small as acorns. The color of the shell is blackish, with some grey, like that of *Pangi*.

*Name.* In Latin *Fructus Musculiformis*. In Malay *Boa Affusseng*, in Dutch *Mussel-fruit*. Those of *Oma* call it *Ay-hua-ette*, or *Ay-hua-mette*, that is black fruit; those of *Camarian* call it *Mountain-Wabo*, or *Land-Ohupaë*, that is *Mountain Wild Mango*.

*Place.* The fruits are found much on the beaches of *Camarian*, and on the south side of *Oma*, around the outlets of large rivers, but the trees are mostly unknown to the inhabitants, believing that they stand deep in the mountains; but by the aforementioned *Kora-kora* expedition it was found that the trees do not stand so very far from the beach.

*Usage.* The inhabitants know to tell us nothing of its use, except that those of *Oma* pretend that they seek these fruits to get the inner marrow out of them, and to lay it on corns of the feet, and old sores of the legs, to heal them; otherwise, the dry and cleaned fruits are worthy of being kept among rarities.

AMBONESE HERBAL Book III. Chapter XV.

## CHAPTER FIFTEEN.
### *Broad-leaved Ampac. Ampac.*

**T**he *Ampac* is of two kinds: namely the larger and broad-leaved, and the other smaller and narrow-leaved; the larger *Ampac* will be specifically described in this chapter.

It is for the most part a huge shrub, rarely a tree, as thick as a man where it grows in wilderness places, and its trunk is not straight but curved and winding, and often even leaning over. Its bark is reddish-gray, brittle, juicy, and can be easily separated from the tree. The leaves are large, always three joined on a common long stalk, of which the middle one is longer than the two side ones; they are oblong, narrowed at both ends, and at the top rounded-pointed, usually eight inches <note>original: "pollices"; a thumb's breadth</note> long and four wide, though on younger plants they are twelve inches long and seven or eight inches wide, drooping, soft and woolly underneath like the leaves of the *Quince* <note>original: "Cydoniae"</note>, as are the stalks, which are placed crosswise on the thin and long branches; the transverse ribs lie close together and run obliquely. From the leaf axils, long clusters sprout forth, as in the *Alpina* <note>a genus of ginger-like plants</note> or the *Grapevine*.

The little flowers are numerous and crowded together, and consist of four small and rounded petals, which bear many rather short stamens in the center with yellowish anthers, in the middle of which a yellow style grows out; they are scentless, and beneath these clusters two small, drooping leaves are usually placed, smaller than the rest. After the flowers, small berries grow, joined two by two, similar to *Coriander* seed or a little smaller, green, which upon opening reveal a small stone like a *Mustard* seed, of a bluish-black color, smooth and shining like a pearl. If these berries gape open into four segments, they resemble a four-petaled flower, which remains on the cluster for a long time even after the seeds have fallen out; they have no notable taste.

The wood of the tree is soft, white, dry, and useless; from the trunk flows a very scant and rare yellow resin, mostly transparent, sometimes lemon-colored, sometimes saffron-colored like *Amber* <note>original: "Succini"</note>, which is very hard like *Stone Dammar* <note>original: "Dammarae Batu"; a hard, fossilized or semi-fossilized dipterocarp resin</note>, and if it be fresh, it breathes out no particular odor—indeed, it is almost unpleasant—but when old and saffron-colored, if placed on coals, it breathes an odor of *Styrax Calamita* <note>a fragrant resin used in incense</note> or properly of *Caju Lacca* <note>Lacquer-wood</note>; this resin is found only around the cracked bark near the knots that are exposed to the sun, in small granules.

The bark of the tree breathes a heavy, goat-like <note>original: "hircinum"</note> odor, yet pleasing to the inhabitants, though more pleasant in one region than another. In *Hitoe* at least and the *Uliaffers* islands it is not so unpleasant as in *Leytimor*: It bears flowers in June, and shortly after the ripe fruits are seen, which hang for a long time from the clusters split into four segments, having cast out their seeds.

<meta>catchword: Name.</meta>

<column-break/>

In my opinion, this tree has some kinship with another, which I also first came to know in the year 1693, and was discovered on the aforementioned journey, named *Healthy Milk-wood* <note>original: "Lactaria Salubris"</note>, or *Upas Lacki Lacki*, being also a relative of *Wild Mango* <note>original: "Manga Brava"</note>, which you may see in the following 42nd Chapter.

## XV. CHAPTER.
### *The Broad-leaved Ampac-Tree.*

**T**he *Ampac-tree* is of two sorts: the first large and broad-leaved, the second small and narrow-leaved. The large one, being the actual *Ampac*, we shall describe in this Chapter.

The same remains mostly a large shrub, seldom becoming a tree of a man's thickness, to wit, in lonely, wild places, whose trunk stands not straight, but bowing and leaning forward. The bark is light-reddish, mixed with gray, brittle, juicy, and lets itself be easily separated from the tree. The leaves are large, standing always three together on a long stalk, of which the middle one is longer than the two on the sides, longish, and narrowing at the back, round in front with a short point, commonly eight inches <note>original: "duimen"; thumb-breadths</note> long, four ditto wide, on the young trees twelve long, and seven to eight ditto wide, limp, soft and woolly underneath, like quince leaves, as also the stalks, which stand in a cross on the thin long branches, and the ribs are dense and run slanted. From the lap <note>axil</note> of the leaves come long clusters, like the *Alpina* or *Vine*.

The little flowers stand thick, and are made of four small and roundish leaves, with many short threads in the middle, and pale-yellow nubs, thereon in the middle a yellow little hill, and without scent: on these clusters one also commonly sees two weak leaves standing, smaller than the others. After the flowers follow small berries two and two together, like *Coriander*, or even as small and greenish, which opening up show each a small grain, inside like a mustard-seed, of a bluish black, smooth, and shining like a Pearl. When the aforementioned berries open up into four scales, they represent a four-leaved little flower, remaining a long time on the cluster even if the seeds have fallen out, which have no marked taste.

The wood is soft, white, dry, and useful for nothing; out of the trunk flows, though very scantily, a little pale-yellow resin, mostly transparent, some lemon-colored, some high-yellow like Amber, as hard as the *Stone Dammar* <note>original: "Dammar Batu"</note>; being fresh it has no particular scent, yes almost unlovely, but having become old and thoroughly yellow, it smells on coals like *Styrax Calamita* or properly like *Lacquer-wood* <note>original: "Caju Lacca"</note>. One finds this resin only around the burst bark by the knots that stand well to the Sun, and that still in small clumps.

The bark of the tree also has a strong goat-like, yet to the Islanders a pleasant scent, but in one Land more lovely than the other: Truly on *Hitoe*, and in the *Uliaffers* it is not so unlovely as on *Leytimor*: It blooms in June, and shortly thereafter one also sees the ripe fruits on the clusters, which hang there a long time, to wit, split in four, which have mostly cast out the seed.

# Book III. Chapter XV. AMBOINESE HERBAL. 187

*Name.* In Latin, *Ampacus*. In Malay and Balinese, *Ampac*. In Amboinese on Hitoe, *Sico Hajate*. In Leytimor, *Siu Huna* and *Suibumate*, which means "foul navel-dirt" <note>original: "foetentes umbilici sordes"</note>, due to the unpleasant odor of the bark, especially in Leytimor. In the islands of Oma and the Uliaffers, it is called *Ayassa*, *Assa*, and *Mattalan*. In Manipa, *Saffea*.

*Location.* It does not occur frequently in Amboina, but mostly in the region of Hitoe and in the three Uliaffer islands, not far from the shore in light forests exposed to the sun that do not have vast trees; for it emits no gum <note>Rumphius uses "gum" and "resin" interchangeably here, referring to the tree's sap</note> if it is not well scorched by the sun. It occurs in greater quantity on Great Bali, where it also exudes more resin, which hardens slowly and bears a honey-like color.

*Use.* Among the Amboinese, this tree and its resin are of no use; however, the Balinese use its resin to fix the handles of their weapons <note>Specifically referring to the *kris*, a traditional asymmetrical dagger</note>, for which purpose they judge this resin more suitable than any other. For although it hardens slowly on the tree, once it has become dry, it is very hard and firmly retains those parts joined to it.
They pour this resin into the handles after melting it again, and then insert the weapon.
In some places, they wash their heads and bodies with the leaves, as they best wipe away sweat and grime. Deer love to gnaw on this tree and eat its foul-smelling bark.
The *Saffea* growing in Manipa bears a fragrant bark like the Amboinese variety, which the women prepare into an ointment with which they anoint their faces to give the skin a clear and shining color.
The *Haulawan* tree—that is, the "Clove-scented" tree—growing in Manipa, seems to be of the *Ampacus* genus, although it does not bear <term>ternate</term> leaves <note>leaves arranged in groups of three</note>; for its leaves are oblong and wrinkled like the *Ampelaas* <note>The Sandpaper Tree, *Ficus ampelas*</note>, but longer and finely <term>serrated</term> <note>having a saw-toothed edge</note>. Behind the leaves on the small branches grow many grains sitting on long stalks, the size of <term>Cubebs</term> <note>a type of peppercorn</note>, green, and without a notable taste. The people of Manipa crush the bark of this tree in water and smear it on the body when they wash for the sake of purification.

### Plate Sixty-One

Displays a branch of the broad-leaved *Ampacus*, as it is named by *Rumphius*.

## OBSERVATION.

These trees are a true species of *Rhus* <note>the Sumac genus</note>, and this one is named by me **Sumac with three oblong petioled leaves, flowering from the stalks.** <note>original: "Rhus foliis ternatis petiolatis oblongis, ex petiolis florifera"</note>

<column-break/>

*Name.* In Latin, *Ampacus*. According to the Malay and Balinese, *Ampac*. On *Amboina*, on Hitoe, *Sico Hajate*. On *Leittimor*, *Siu Hunaë* and *Suihumate*, that is "stinking filth of the navel" <note>original: "stinkende vuiligheid des navels"</note>, because of the unlovely smell of the bark, especially on *Leittimor*. On *Oma* and the *Uliaffers*, *Ayassa*, *Assa*, and *Mattalan*. On *Manipa*, *Saffea*.

*Place.* One does not find it much in *Amboina*, and mostly on the land of *Hitoe*, and in the three *Uliaffers*, not far from the beach, in light groves that stand well in the sun and have no large trees around them; for otherwise it gives no gum if it is not thoroughly burned by the sun. On *Bali* one finds them in greater quantity, where they also give more resin, which dries slowly and is honey-colored.

*Use.* Among the *Amboinese*, this tree and its resin are in no use, but the *Balinese* use the resin to fix their <term>Krises</term> <note>traditional Malay/Indonesian daggers</note> into the hilts, for which they find this more suitable than any other resin; for although it dries slowly on the tree, once dry, it becomes very hard and holds fast everything to which it is attached. They must first melt it again, pour it into the hilts, and thereafter stick the weapon in.
With the leaves, they wash the body and head in some places, because they take away the sweat and filth. The deer also like to chew on this tree and eat the strong-smelling bark thereof.
The *Saffea* growing on *Manipa* has a bark as fragrant as the *Amboinese* sort, which the women also use for pastes to smear on the face to make the same clean and glowing.
The tree *Haulawan*, that is "clove-smelling," growing on *Manipa*, seems also to be from the family of the *Ampac*, although it does not have three leaves together; for the leaves are rough and oblong, like *Ampelaas*, but longer and finely saw-toothed. Behind the leaves on the twigs stand many round grains on longish stalks, the size of Cubebs, greenish, without a notable taste. The people of *Manipa* pound the bark of this tree in water and smear the body therewith when they wish to wash it, in order to cleanse the same.

These trees are a true variety of the *Rhus*, and this one is named by me **Sumac, with three oblong stalked leaves, bearing flowers from the stalks.**

# CHAPTER SIXTEEN.

## Narrow-leaved Ampacus. Large Gendarussa.

**T**he smaller or narrow-leaved *Ampacus* corresponds closely with the preceding one in form and manner of growth, but the leaves are generally smaller, namely five and sometimes six inches long, two and two-and-a-half inches wide, also growing in threes <note>original: "ternata"</note>, and placed cross-wise on long shoots; however, in this species they are not woolly, but smooth, and the leaves shine with a blackish tint. They sit upon longer, rounder, and narrower stalks <note>original: "petiolis"</note>, and three always sprout from a single origin, where these leaves are wider and joined to one another as if united. When crushed, they breathe out a somewhat acidic and aromatic scent, such as the bark also yields in certain places; one might think they were *Lagondi* leaves <note>The Lagondi (*Vitex trifolia*) is a common medicinal shrub in Southeast Asia</note>, were they not too large.

The wood of the trunk is quite heavy if it is freshly cut, and so dry that no moisture is observed in it; sometimes dry pieces of it are used for the hearth, which breathe out an aromatic scent if they are still covered with bark. The trunk is likewise mostly shrub-like, except if it is preserved for eight or ten years in forest gardens, where the shrub grows with two or three trunks to the height of a Fir tree and the thickness of a thigh; otherwise, in public ways and other uncultivated woods, it is a low and bent shrub. The bark is smoother and thinner than that of the preceding, blackish-brown, brittle, and easily separated from the wood, but it breathes a stronger odor, very closely approaching the *Cutana* fish <note>A type of leather-jacket or triggerfish</note>, which is a species of leathery fish smelling of a goat-like stench. Among the *Uliaffers* <note>Inhabitants of the Uliaser Islands</note> it does not have such a heavy odor; indeed, if it is dried and toasted, it diffuses a pleasant enough scent, so that it is also preserved there and mixed with other incenses; on the other hand, the variety from *Leytimor*, and that which grows around *Larique*, is the most penetrating and pure.

No notable gum exudes from this bark, but here and there in the cracks some resinous matter clings; indeed, sometimes small granules are collected from them, yellow like sulfur and brittle. The flowers, clusters, and seeds are as in the preceding, except that they are observed in greater abundance on the leaf-stalks, occurring in short and numerous clusters in those places from which the leaves have fallen. It blooms in February, and the seeds, darkly blackening and shining like pearls, remain placed upon and clinging to the seed-vessels for a long time.

**Name.** In Latin *Ampacus angustifolia*. In Malay and Balinese *Genda Russa Besar*, for they consider this a species of *Genda russa* <note>Known today as *Justicia gendarussa*</note>, since it agrees with it in its heavy odor; the Amboinese give it the same name as the preceding both in Hitoe and in the Uliaffer islands. In the Ternate language, it is called *Giba*.

**Location.** It is found in the same places in which the preceding occurs, but the best is found on the island of Oma.

**Use.** Since the wood of this tree is more solid, heavier, and lasts longer, it is used for rafters, although it is rarely found so straight, and only in remote mountains where it has stood undisturbed for many years, as in Leytimor in the *Oorimeffen* mountains, where it provides very elegant and straight timber. If, however, it touches the ground, it easily rots, but for roofs it is excellent and quite durable, especially in Amboinese houses which are often filled with thick smoke.

Those who inhabit the island of Oma set aside the lower part of the bark stripped from near the root, and they use it dried for incenses, which are commonly called *Tonobuho* by them. This bark, crushed in water with that of the *Pule* <note>The *Pule* tree is *Alstonia scholaris*</note> and sprinkled on vegetables, drives away worms and caterpillars. Deer gladly rub themselves against the bark of this tree.

A species of this seems to grow on the shore, which similarly bears leaves in threes, sitting on a common stalk, almost like the *Cacara* <note>Likely referring to a species of *Pachyrhizus* or similar legume</note>, but narrower and smoother. The fruits hang from long clusters like Pepper joined together by art, spherical like a coat button <note>original: "instar nodi Thoracis"</note>, of a red coral color, covered on the outside with soft flesh, and bearing a hard stone inside like a cherry stone. This tree grows on sterile and rocky shores; it bears fruit in the month of July.

<column-break/>

# XVI. CHAPTER.

## The Narrow-leaved Ampac Tree.

**T**he small or narrow-leaved *Ampac* is, in appearance and manner of growing, most like the preceding, except that the leaves are generally smaller, namely five and seldom six inches long, two and two-and-a-half wide, also three together on long stalks, likewise cross-wise around the long branches, which in this species are not woolly like the leaves, but smooth and black-brown; these twigs are longer, rounder, and more slender than on the preceding, and always stand three together, and as if set against one another. The crushed leaves have a sourish and almost spicy scent, as does the bark in some places. One would take them for *Lagondi*, if they were not too large.

The wood of the trunk is reasonably heavy when it is freshly cut, and so dry that one sees the least moisture therein; sometimes one finds dry pieces, which are used for firewood, that give off a spicy scent if the bark is still on them. The trunk also mostly remains a shrub, unless it were kept for eight to ten years in the Forest-gardens, when the shrub shoots up with two or three trunks to the height of a fir and the thickness of a thigh; otherwise it remains only low and crooked. The bark is smoother and thinner than the former, black-brown, very brittle, and falling easily from the wood, yet stronger in scent than the former, coming very close to the *Cutana* Fish, a kind of Leather-fish, which smells very goat-like. Among the *Uliaffers* it does not smell so strong; indeed, being dried and burned, it becomes reasonably pleasant, so that they also preserve it there to mix among other perfumes; on the other hand, that on *Leitimor* and around *Larique* smells the strongest and purest.

No notable Gum sweats out of this bark, but here and there in the cracks hangs some resinous matter, and sometimes also small crumbs, yellow as sulfur and crumbly. The blossom, clusters, and seed are as on the preceding, except that they stand in greater multitude on the twigs, in many short clusters together in places where the leaves have fallen off; and one sees them in February, and the gleaming black-brown little Pearls remain longer hanging in the little hulls.

**Name.** In Latin *Ampacus angustifolia*. In Malay and Balinese *Genda Russa Besaar*, for they hold it for a kind of the *Genda russa*, only because it somewhat agrees with the same in the strong scent of the bark. The Amboinese call it by the same name as the preceding, as well on *Hitoe* as in the *Uliaffers*; on Ternate, *Giba*.

**Place.** It is found in the same places as the former, yet the best is found on the Island of *Oma*.

**Use.** Because this wood is somewhat denser, heavier, and more durable, it is used for rafters, although one can seldom find it so straight, and then only in the remote mountains where it has had many years of rest, as on *Leitimor* in the mountains of *Oorimeffen*, where it grows very beautiful and straight. If it touches the earth, it decays very easily, but in the roofing it is durable, especially in the Amboinese houses where there is much smoke.

Those on the Island of *Oma* preserve the lower pieces of the bark, which are peeled off next to the root, and use them dried among their perfumes, which they commonly call *Tonobuho*. This bark, crushed in water with that of *Pule* and strewn on the garden herbs, drives away all vermin and caterpillars. The Deer-beasts gladly rub themselves against its bark.

Of this, a kind seems to grow on the shore, on which the leaves likewise stand three and three on a stalk, almost like the *Cacara*, yet narrower and smoother. The fruits hang on long clusters like pepper, crowded close together, perfectly round, like a coat-button <note>original: "Wambas-knoop"</note>, coral-red, outside with a soft flesh, inside with a hard stone, like a cherry-stone: It grows on lean and stony shores; the fruits are seen in July.

<header>Book III. Chapter XVII. AMBOINESE HERBARIUM.</header>

Meanwhile, the first may be called the **First Shore Ampacus** <note>original: "Ampacus Litorea prima"</note>; it is not known by any name or use among the Amboinese.

On the island of Leitimor, another smaller species of it occurs, which also bears three leaves joined together on long stalks <note>original: "petiolis"</note>, sitting upon their own short stems. These leaves are five inches long and two and a half inches wide, though the middle one is six, seven, or eight inches long. They very closely resemble the leaves of the Lansium <note>the Langsat tree, *Lansium parasiticum*</note>, being dry and thin, with the transverse ribs placed alternately.

The flowers sit in large clusters <note>original: "racemis"</note> consisting of four small, whitish petals, slightly bent backward. They give off a somewhat acidic but not unpleasant scent. In their center are located five whitish filaments <note>original: "stamina"</note>.

Some Amboinese women grind the bark of the aforementioned narrow-leaved species into a fine paste, which they smear on their faces so that they might acquire an elegant complexion <note>Rumphius often notes local cosmetic practices aimed at lightening or smoothing the skin</note>.

## CHAPTER SEVENTEEN.

### The Pointed Flower. Bonga Tanjong, Fula Kauki.

Intending now to describe those trees which are cultivated for their pleasant flowers, the first to come to mind is the **Bonga Tanjong** <note>The Spanish Cherry or Bullet Wood tree, *Mimusops elengi*</note>, which is held by the Malays (who have the best knowledge and judgment of flowers) to be the princess of flowering trees.

The tree is most closely related to the Clove tree <note>original: "Caryophyllum"</note> and is quite elegant, with a crown arranged in a regular and dense fashion. Its stalks and foliage also present a pleasing sight. It has the size and height of a common Lemon tree. Its trunk is single and erect, but not very tall or thick; it is rarely round, but mostly angular, as if constructed from various trunks joined together—at least when it is old, for middle-aged ones are mostly round. Its bark is thick, hard, rough, and fissured, and if it is cut, a small amount of thick milk <note>latex or sap</note> drips out. The leaves are solitary and irregular but abundant, somewhat resembling Lemon leaves or perhaps a little wider, with smooth edges. They are four inches long and two wide, equipped with a blunt tip; they are smooth, firm, and shining, woven through with many fine transverse veins that do not protrude and are not as parallel as those in Clove leaves. The edges of these leaves are somewhat hemmed on the underside and are slightly curved due to their stiffness.

From the axils <note>the "armpit" where the leaf meets the stem</note> of the leaves, three, four, but usually two buds sprout. They are pointed from a round base like linseed buds and are saffron-yellow. When these open, they reveal small flowers the size of a fingernail, constructed of simple pointed petals. First, they bear three, four, or five small petals that serve as an outer covering; joined to these is another row of ten or twelve other small, white, and narrow petals, more pointed and resembling the tip of an ear of corn <note>original: "spicae"</note>, and these are always joined in pairs. Near the center, a third row of petals occurs, which are bent outward when the flower is open. Finally, in the very center, a smaller fourth row of petals occurs, which incline inward and form a small cavity, beneath which is located the small head or germ <note>the ovary</note> which grows into the fruit.

All these pointed petals are joined together at the base and are placed around the aforementioned germ like a small crown; thus, they also fall off all together, leaving a round hole, which—

<column-break/>

Provisionally, this may be called the **First Shore Ampacus**; it has no name or use among the Amboinese.

On Leitimor, one finds a smaller variety, which also carries three leaves together on long stalks, attached to short stems. They are five inches long and two and a half wide, of which the middle one is six, seven, and eight inches long, very similar to the Lansium leaves, dry and thin; the cross-ribs are placed alternately against one another.

The flowers stand in wide clusters, made of four small and white petals, bent a little backward, smelling somewhat sour, yet not unlovely; inside they hide five white threads.

Some Amboinese women rub the bark of the above-mentioned **Narrow-leaved Ampacus** into a fine paste and smear their faces with it, to become fair in their manner.

## XVII. CHAPTER.

### The Tanjong-Tree, or Tree of the Pointed Flowers.

In now describing those trees that are cultivated for their lovely flowers, first appears the **Bonga Tanjong**, held by the Malays (who have the best knowledge and judgment of flowers) as the Princess of the tree-flowers.

The tree is next to the Clove-tree <note>original: "Nagel-boom"</note>, one of the most decorative with a well-ordered and thick crown, beautiful to look at in both its branches and foliage, in the size and height of a common Lemon-tree. The trunk is single, round, not high, but thick, seldom round, but angular, and as if put together from several trunks—namely, when it becomes old, for the middle-aged ones are mostly round. The bark is thick, hard, rough, and cracked, and when one chops into it, a little thick milk runs out. The leaves stand singly and without order, though many are on the twigs, somewhat resembling Lemon leaves, or else just as wide, and with smooth edges; four inches long and two wide, with a blunt point, smooth, stiff, and glowing, threaded through with many fine ribs crosswise, protruding nowhere, and not quite as parallel as on the Clove-leaves. The edges of these leaves are slightly hemmed from below, and stand somewhat bowed due to their stiffness.

From the lap <note>axil</note> of the leaves come three, four, but mostly two buds, pointed from the round, like Linseed-buds, orange-yellow. These opening themselves, show small flowers, the size of a nail <note>a fingernail</note>, mostly made of single points; for first they have three, four, and five small leaves, which serve them as a cover from the outside. Next to those stands another row of ten to twelve other small, white, and narrow petals, more resembling the tip of an ear of grain, and always two together. Somewhat inward one sees yet another such ring, whose petals are bent outward when the flower stands open. Finally, in the middle stands yet a smaller ring, made of even smaller petals, which strike inward and make a small hollowness, under which stands a small bud, from which the fruit is formed.

The points are all fixed to each other on the bottom, and stand around the aforementioned bud like a little wreath, wherefore they also fall off entirely like that, with a round hole in the middle, where—

where the bud was located. The color of the flowers is not truly white, but somewhat yellowish, and in dried specimens, it becomes a dark yellow. The scent is the most pleasant and penetrating of almost all the flowers in the Indies, yet it does not spread very far; some people cannot bear it because it is too heavy for them. Remarkably, the scent remains and persists even when the flowers are dry. The tree bears flowers throughout the entire year. Its flowering buds have a peculiar quality: during the day, few open flowers are seen on the tree; most are more "gaping" than fully open. However, as soon as the sun sets—or, as the Moors <note>A common historical term for Muslims in the region</note> say, at the time of *Mengarib* <note>original: "Mengarib", referring to Maghrib, the sunset prayer time</note>, which is the beginning of the night—they all open themselves and extend their little spikes. They remain open on the tree in this manner throughout the entire night until the early morning—at the final cock-crow—when they suddenly fall in such great numbers that they cover the entire ground. The remaining buds open gradually during that same day and meet the same fate the following night.

In this behavior, it closely matches the "Sorrowful Tree" <note>original: "Arbore Tristi", likely *Nyctanthes arbor-tristis*</note> mentioned by **Garcia de Orta** <note>original: "Garzia", a 16th-century Portuguese physician and pioneer of tropical medicine</note> in Book 2, Chapter 1 of *Aromatics*, and by other Portuguese writers. For a long time, I considered this *Tanjong* to be that same tree, but upon further inquiry, I found that the true Sorrowful Tree differs from this one, and our *Tanjong* should be considered a species of it. From that round bud or germ, which remains on the stalk after the flower has fallen, a fruit grows that is egg-shaped or like an olive, but thicker and widest at the bottom. It sits upon a pericarp <note>the fruit wall or casing</note> crowned with seven points, which grows along with it. This fruit is round, ending in a small point; its color is first orange, then a glowing, fiery red.

Beneath a thin and fragile golden skin, a dryish, golden-yellow flesh is hidden, which is sweet with a certain astringency; it is edible in a way <note>meaning it is palatable but perhaps not a primary food source</note>. Inside is located a stone-hard pit like a Lupin or Tamarind seed, but thicker and more oblong, brownish-black and somewhat wrinkled, with a navel at the narrower end.

The wood of the trunk is whitish or pale yellow on the outside, but the interior is brown or almost purple; it is solid, fine-grained, hard, and heavy. This brown "heart" is found only in old trees, while medium-sized ones lack it almost entirely.

*The Season.* This tree does not observe a fixed season of the year but is almost always flowering and fruiting. However, it sometimes rests for half a year, and the fruits mostly ripen during the months of the West Monsoon <note>the rainy season in the Malay Archipelago</note>. In clear weather, the flowers can be seen open on the tree throughout the day, though not as fully as in the evening; they fall in great heaps the following day. In rainy and windy weather, few open, and they hang longer from the tree, nor do they give off as strong a scent as they do in warm weather. The tree grows very slowly, as do all hard woods; it must stand for eight or ten years before it brings forth fruit or flowers. In contrast, the Ebony tree, planted in the same ground, gives its flowers by its sixth or seventh year; the *Tanjong* seems to have a great affinity with Ebony.

In these islands, it does not grow wild but must be diligently cultivated around houses, where it is desired for its elegant crown, dense shade, and fragrant flowers. One should by no means believe the claims of some Amboinese that this domestic tree was propagated from the wild or shore *Tanjong* (which will be discussed in the following chapter) through careful cultivation in gardens.

It reaches a great age. In the year 1667, a certain tree located near **Fort Victoria** <note>the Dutch East India Company's main fortress in Amboina</note> died of pure old age; its trunk was very angular and more than a fathom in circumference. It had already been in its prime during the time of the Portuguese, so it must have stood for about ninety years.

*Name.* In Latin, it is called *Flos Cuspidum* <note>Flower of Points</note> and *Tanjonus*. In Malay, *Bonga Tanjong*, which name it received not from stony mountains or promontories <note>a play on the Malay word 'Tanjung', meaning cape or headland</note> where the wild variety grows, but from the many points from which the flower is composed. The people of Makassar also call it *Tanjong*. In Batavia <note>modern-day Jakarta</note>, it is called *Kaucki* or *Foëla Kauki*.

*Location.* In Amboina, these trees occur rarely. At my arrival in the year 1654, I observed only two near Fort Victoria, which had been brought from other places—

<column-break/>

*where the bud stood; the color is not purely white, but draws toward yellow, and in the dried state becomes dark yellow. The scent is one of the loveliest and strongest among all the flowers of the Indies, yet it does not spread far, although some cannot tolerate it because it seems too strong to them; and what is wonderful is that it also remains in the dried flowers. The tree bears through the whole year. Its flower-bearing buds have special qualities in showing their gifts; for during the day one sees few flowers properly opened on that tree, but most more gaping than open; but as soon as the Sun is down, or as the Moors say, in the time of Mengarib, that is the beginning of the night, these little flowers open themselves properly, and spread their points wide, thus remaining on the tree the whole night through, until toward the morning, that is the last cock-crow, they fall suddenly and in whole troops from the tree, so that they cover the ground: The buds that remain there open gradually that same day, and can expect the same fate the following night: in which it very much agrees with the Tree Tristis, so famous by Garzias book 2. Aromat. chap. 1. and other Portuguese writers, for which I also long held this Tanjong, but upon closer instruction found that the true Arbor Tristis differs from it, and that our Tanjong is only to be held as a sort of it: From that round bud, which remains standing on the stalk after the falling of the whole flower, grows the fruit in the shape of a Bird-Egg, or short Olive, though thicker, broad at the back, and standing on a little star of seven points, which lies against it, and at the front with a small stiff point, round in front, of color first Orange, thereafter fire-red.*

*Under a thin and brittle skin lies a gold-yellow, dryish flesh, sweet with some contraction, which one can also eat in case of need. Inside lies a stone-hard kernel, like a Lupin or Tamarind-stone, but thicker, and more oblong, black-brown, and somewhat wrinkled, with a navel at the back or narrowest corner.*

*The wood of the trunk is white outside, or pale yellow, inside brown, or almost purple-colored, dense, fine-grained, hard, and heavy, yet this brown heart is found only on the old trees, for the middle-aged have it not or little.*

*Season. This tree has no proper Season, but bears its flowers and fruits mostly the whole year through, though at times it rests for half a year, and the fruits ripen mostly in the West-Monsoon; in fair weather one sees the flowers well opened on the tree throughout the whole day, also now and then some falling, but never so many opened as in the evening-time, which then toward daybreak, as said, fall down in heaps; in rainy and windy weather few open themselves, and remain longer hanging on the tree, nor do they smell as much as in warm weather; the tree shoots up very slowly, like all other hard woods, having to stand well eight to ten years before it bears flowers, whereas the Ebony-wood tree planted from seed in one and the same garden has borne in the sixth and seventh year, with which the Tanjong seems to have great fellowship.*

*It grows on these Islands not in the wild, but must be industriously maintained near the houses, where one likes to have it for its fine crown, thick shade, and sweet-smelling flowers; it being in no way to be believed the claim of some Amboinese, that these tame ones have come forth from the wild or strand-Tanjong, of which in the following chapter, through industrious practice in the gardens.*

*It comes to a great age, for in the Year 1667 one standing at the Castle Victoria died out through pure age, whose trunk was very angular, and more than a fathom thick in circumference, having already been in bloom for a long time in the Portuguese times, so that it must have stood for about 90 years.*

*Name. In Latin Flos Cuspidum and Tanjonus. In Malay Bonga Tanjong, having the name not from stony promontories, or Capes, where otherwise the wild one likes to grow, but from many points, from which the flower is made. In Macassar also Tanjong: In Batavia one calls them Kaucki, or Foela Kauki.*

*Place. In Amboina one finds few of these trees; indeed at my arrival in the year 1654 I found only two at the Castle Victoria, being from other places—*

brought from other places, but were later multiplied from seeds, of which scarcely one in twenty sprouts a kernel, just as young saplings are never seen growing beneath the parent tree. In Macassar and Greater Java they occur in abundance, but everywhere only in gardens.

*Usage.* The flowers of this tree are most frequently used; for the fallen ones are tied to a cord a cubit or a <term>fathom</term> <note>original: "orgyzam," a measurement of the span of outstretched arms</note> long, which is easily done since the flowers, as mentioned, are naturally perforated. These garlands are sold for a low price in the market. Women mostly wear these around their necks or braided into their hair; from a distance, they resemble a golden chain. Once worn out, they are kept for eight or ten days in bedrooms or among clothes, which they fill with their scent, even after they have withered.

The Javanese, and especially the Chinese living in Java, know how to express an oil from these kernels, which painters use for their pigments instead of Linseed Oil, and with which they also coat and repair paintings and <term>parasols</term> <note>original: "umbellas" / "quitasols"</note>. The green leaves of this tree, when thrown into a fire, make a loud crackling noise, though not as strong as the leaves of the Ebony tree; for this reason, they are often burned in gardens to drive away rats, snakes, and other nesting animals.

The fresh leaves of this tree, when crushed and smeared on the head, are beneficial for <term>cephalalgia</term> <note>headache</note> arising from cold and "winds" <note>in historical medicine, "winds" or "flatus" were thought to cause various internal pains</note>, for they draw out the pain.

The heart of the trunk, as was said, is quite solid, hard, and an elegant brown, which one might think suitable for lathe-work, but it easily develops cracks, even if taken from old trees, so that it has not been used for any work until now.

In the first volume of the *Malabar Garden* <note>original: "Horti Malab." / "Hortus Malabaricus," a famous 12th-century botanical work on the flora of the Malabar coast</note>, Figure 20, this tree is called by the Malabar name *Elengi*, and by the Brahmin name *Vavalli*, but it must be distinguished from the *Vavaveli* or *Pavate* described by Christóvão da Costa in chapter 14. In that aforementioned garden, its rarest quality was omitted: namely, that its flowers are mostly open during the night and fall off toward dawn. We shall add here those things further contained in that garden and discovered in those regions.

The wood of the trunk is very durable in water, but outside of it, it easily contracts and generates worms. Its medicinal use is as follows: its root, crushed with vinegar, removes swelling of the face if the affected part is smeared; the same crushed with water is conducive against <term>aphthae</term> <note>thrush or mouth ulcers</note> and other sores of the mouth, as well as against <term>angina</term> <note>sore throat or quinsy</note> if used as a gargle. A decoction of the bark cures sore throats and takes away toothache if the mouth is rinsed with it. A fragrant water is distilled from the flowers, which is given to drink and benefits those suffering from melancholy and fevers. Its ripe fruit, crushed with water, is given to pregnant women and those in difficult labor.

The *Tanjong Flower* <note>original: "Bonja Tanjong"</note> can be divided into male and female, not easily distinguished by the shape of the leaves and flowers, but the male produces nothing but flowers, while the female produces both flowers and fruit.

# AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. Chapter XVII.

### CHAPTER XVIII.

The characteristics of the Elengi were very recently and kindly shared with me by the renowned Mr. GARCIN in the following manner.

The flower of this genus is single-petaled <note>original: "monopetalus"</note> and lacks a tube; it is divided right down to the base <note>original: "ad unguem," literally "to the nail"</note> into many pointed, equal segments arranged in two rows (the inner and the outer). These are sixteen in number, standing in pairs but so slightly separated that this distinction cannot be noticed unless they are brought very close to the eyes. Spread out in the shape of a sun, or like radiant flowers, they are much like the flowers of the *small Daisy* <note>Latin: "Bellidis minoris"; Dutch: "Maagdelieven"</note> and have a diameter of 8 or 9 lines <note>A "line" is a historical unit of measurement, approximately 1/12th of an inch</note>.

The inner row is always closed, arranged in the shape of a pointed, conical pod <note>original: "folliculi"</note>; these cover and protect the reproductive organs <note>original: "genitalia floris organa"</note> of the flower, which are easily damaged by the air. They number 8, being equal in size and shape to the outer segments, and are of the same color (whitish, though a bit dull). The base, which is somewhat thick, is a little darker and more greenish in color.

Eight stamens are found, each arising from the inner part of the base of the segments; they possess <term>anthers</term> <note>the pollen-bearing part of the stamen</note> that are wide at the bottom and end in a sharp point at the top, straw-colored and wrinkled. These are observed to be twice as long as their stalks <note>original: "caudis," referring to the filaments</note>, which are likewise thick at the base and slender at the upper part. But, because the segments of the single-petaled flower are narrower toward their base than in the middle, they leave gaps between them through which the air could reach the interior of the flower. Nature has provided against this with a small valve or tongue <note>original: "lingula"</note> placed at the inner part of each gap, which closes it tightly from the inside. This tongue is nearly the same color as the flower segments and is shaggy with slender, transparent hairs, which more precisely block the entry of foreign bodies that might harm the reproductive organs. Therefore, the stamens always lie safely hidden.

The <term>ovary</term> <note>original Latin: "Ovario"; Dutch: "Eyerzak"</note> (whose shape and size are almost like a grain of Millet) is placed in the center of the <term>calyx</term> <note>the outer green cup of a flower</note>, surrounded on all sides by the single-petaled flower. It is simple, whitish, uniform throughout, and three lines high (though the diameter of the ovary is only one line). A tube or <term>style</term> <note>original: "Tuba, vel stylus"</note> sits upon it.

The calyx is also complete, divided into 8 segments, which are also arranged in two rows: four on the inside and four on the outside. The inner ones, arranged in the form of a cross, are slightly smaller than the outer ones; they are equipped with narrow bases, from each of which a small vein arises, extending like a rib through the entire length of the segment.

Because of their whiteness and similarity to the segments of the single-petaled flower, these segments of the calyx could easily be mistaken for petals by the unwary. But the outer ones, similarly arranged in a cross, are larger than the inner ones, arise from a broad base, and are of a dull, dark color—greenish, as seen on their stalk, and shiny on the inside. All these segments are pointed and more or less spread out, depending on how the flower expands and in proportion to the size of the <term>embryo</term> <note>original: "τῷ ἐμβρυῷ," referring here to the developing fruit</note>. When this has turned into a fruit, they dry up and spread out in the shape of an 8-rayed star.

The stalk <note>original: "pedunculus"</note> is the same color as the outer part of the calyx; it is as long as the flower's diameter and one line thick, though more slender at the bottom than at the top. The mass of this part of the stalk increases gradually with the fruit until it becomes twice as thick. Two, three, and sometimes even more stalks emerge together from the leaf axils.

I have not been able to observe the fruit.

<meta>The catchword "CAPUT" (Chapter) indicates the start of a new section, though the text below the image marks Chapter XVIII.</meta>

<column-break/>

The characteristics of the Elengi have recently been kindly communicated to me by the famous Mr. GARCIN in the following manner.

This genus bears a single-petaled flower without a tube, made of very many equal, pointed leaves divided into two rows (namely, the outer and inner) and split down to the base. These are sixteen in number; two stand together at a time, yet are so lightly divided that this separation is hardly noticeable unless held against the light. These stand like a Sun shooting out its rays, or like a radiant flower, similar to the flowers of the *small Daisies* <note>original: "Maagdelieven"</note>, which have a circumference of eight or nine lines.

The inner row of leaves is always closed and has the shape of a pointed and conical blunt pod, which covers and protects the reproductive parts of the flower that are easily damaged by the air. They are twelve <note>Note: The Dutch text says 12, whereas the Latin says 8; the Latin "8" is likely the correct botanical count for this species</note> in number, and in size and shape equal to the outer ones, and also of the same color, namely whitish; though the lower part of them, which is thicker, is somewhat darker and greener in color.

There are eight fibers <note>stamens</note> having their origin from the inner part of the base of the flower, which have "knobs" <note>anthers</note> that are wide at the bottom and end in a point at the top, straw-colored and rough. These, with their lower part being wider and the upper part narrower, are twice as large as the leaves <note>segments</note>, which are narrower at their beginning than in their middle, because they are parts of a single-petaled flower. Because of this, they leave middle-spaces open through which there is too much passage for the inner part of the flower. Therefore, a "valve-membrane" like a small tongue <note>original: "klapvlies als een tongetje"</note> is placed between each opening at its innermost part, which shuts it closed evenly, as Nature provides. This little tongue is almost the same color as the parts of the flower and is rough with thin and clear hairs, by which it so much more prevents the entry of external bodies that would be harmful to the reproductive parts of the flower, which is why the fibers lie safely hidden there.

The <term>Ovary</term> <note>original: "Eyerzak," literally "egg-sac"</note> (whose size and figure is like a grain of Millet) lying in the middle of the calyx and embraced on all sides by the single-petaled flower, is simple, whitish, uniform in everything, three lines high, and whose circumference is only of one line; it has a trumpet or style <note>original: "trompet of stilet"</note> on top.

The calyx is also entirely divided into eight parts, which also stand in two ranks, namely four outwards and four inwards. Of which the innermost, standing in a cross, are a little smaller than the outermost, and have a narrow base, from each of which a small nerve appears, spreading through the whole length of the flower-part like a little rib.

These parts of the calyx could easily be viewed by the unskillful as the very leaves of the flower because of their white color and the similarity to the parts of the single-petaled flower. However, the outer parts, standing like a cross and larger than the inner ones, emerge with a broad beginning and are of a dark-rusty color, as is noticed on the stalk—namely greenish and clear from within. All these parts are pointed and more or less gaping, according to how the flower spreads itself out, in proportion to the size of the fruit. When the fruit begins to grow and expand, those parts become dull and spread out in the shape of a star, showing themselves with eight rays.

The little stalk is of the same color as the outer part of the calyx and as long as the flower, one line thick, and in its lower part more slender and thin than in the upper. But the parts of this stalk become larger from time to time with the fruit, until it has become half as thick again. From the origin of the leaves, two, three, and sometimes more stalks emerge.

I have not been able to examine the fruit.

# CHAPTER EIGHTEEN.

## *Wild Shore-Tanjong. Bonga Tanjong Laut.*

The Wild or Shore-Tanjong <note>Latin: *Tanionus Litorea*; Malay: *Bonga Tanjong Laut*</note> possesses a taller, straighter, and rounder trunk, measuring a fathom <note>A fathom, or *orgyia*, is roughly the span of a man's outstretched arms, about 6 feet</note> in circumference, and sometimes a bit less. Its bark is rough, cracked, and a dirty-gray or blackish color; when wounded, it also yields a thick, fatty milk-like sap, though sparingly. Its crown is thick with branches and twigs. Its leaves are smaller and narrower than those of the domestic variety; specifically, those growing on the shore bear leaves four or five inches long and one and a half inches wide. On older trees, they are only four inches long and barely one wide. They are more pointed at the tip than the domestic kind, a sea-green or grayish-green color, stiff, and smooth, shot through with very fine veins—even more intricate than those of the Clove-leaf—which do not protrude on either side, though the midrib stands out on both sides.

The leaves are situated on the branches without a specific order, and from their leaf-axils <note>the inner angle between the leaf and the stem</note> various shoots emerge here and there with two or three leaves, making it a lush plant. Conversely, the blossoms do not emerge as copiously as on the domestic tree; one sees only two or three saffron-yellow <note>original: "crocea" / "boog-geele"</note> buds here and there standing on similar small stems. From these come the small flowers, very similar to the domestic Tanjong, though they never open quite as wide. They consist first of four reddish or saffron petals, spreading outward in the shape of a star or cross; within these are placed many other smaller white pointed petals, and in the center a small wreath of similar but smaller points, all of which are joined together and fall off at the same time. On the inside, they are whiter than the domestic variety and likewise smell pleasant, though more weakly. The fruit is generally similar to the domestic Tanjong or slightly smaller, like an average Olive; it remains mostly yellow and sits upon a small star of four points. Beneath the outer brittle skin lies a dry flesh and a hard, brown nut as in the domestic kind, but smoother and sharper. When this nut is opened, it reveals a shell like a Hazelnut, but much smaller, containing a white, thick, and sticky kernel of a bitter taste, which can be divided into two segments.

Inside are found two white leaflets in which all the veins and nerves can be clearly recognized; these open toward the back and are joined at the front with a small node <note>original: "capitulum"</note>, which protrudes through a small opening outside the shell, and from which the root of the young tree is formed.

Of the two or three flowers, only one grows into a fruit, while the others fall away, so that each fruit hangs alone.

The wood of the tree is pale and whitish on the outside, gradually becoming redder toward the interior; the innermost part is a beautiful light brown, leaning toward purple like the wood of our cherry trees. It is hard, fine, and solid like Ebony. In older trees, this brown heartwood is so large that it occupies almost the entire thickness of the trunk, leaving only two or three fingers of white wood <term>sapwood</term> <note>the outer, living layer of wood</note> surrounding it, which is considered useless. This brown heart is also found in the roots.

*Season.* The flowers are rarely seen on this tree; it blooms in May, at the start of the rainy monsoons, at which time the domestic Tanjong also has its most abundant blossoms. The fruits are seen ripening in October and during the West Monsoons.

*Name.* In Latin *Tanionus Litorea*, in Malay *Bonga Tanjong Laut* and *Tanjong Laut*. Others call it *Cumbang Jatu* and *Cumbang Jati*, perhaps so named because the flowers frequently fall off. Among the Amboinese it has many names according to the diversity of places: on Hitoe it is called *Lolan Key*, and near Oerien Patiatta, on Hoeamohel and Bonoa it is called *Leytin*, *Leytir*, and *Leytil*. On Nuffalaut it is *Ruffukey* or *Luffukey*; on Boero it is *Balan Tronga*.

*Location.* This tree grows wild on a few shores of Amboina and is not often found, and then nowhere but on barren, rocky shores which are difficult to traverse because of the cliffs, such as especially the entire district of the Capaha mountains and the promontory of Assaloelo, opposite

# CHAPTER XVIII.

## *The Wild or Shore-Tanjong Tree.*

The wild or shore-Tanjong has a taller, straighter, and rounder trunk, of a fathom in circumference, or a bit less, and a very rough, cracked, dirty-gray or blackish bark; which being wounded, also yields a thick and fatty milk, though also sparingly. Its crown is dense with branches and twigs: The leaves are smaller and narrower than on the domestic kind; namely those that grow on the shore are four and five inches long, one and a half wide; on the old trees they are but four inches long, and a good inch wide, more pointed toward the front than the domestic, bow- and sea-green, stiff, and smooth, shot through with very fine veins, even more tangled than on the Clove-leaves, and protruding on neither side, though the mid-nerve bulges out on both sides.

They stand without order on the twigs, and from their armpits come here and there other shoots with two or three leaves, so that it is a luxuriant growth. In contrast, the blossom does not come out as much as on the domestic kind, for one sees here and there only two and three bow-yellow buds standing on similar small stems, from which the small flowers develop, very much like the domestic Tanjong, though never opening so wide. They consist first of four bow-yellow or reddish leaflets, opened star-wise from the outside, in which many other white leaflets or points stand, and in the middle a wreath made of similar but smaller points, which all hang together, and fall off together; from the inside they are whiter than the domestic, also fragrant, but weakly. The fruit is commonly like the domestic Tanjong, or somewhat smaller, like a medium Olive, remains mostly yellow, and stands on a little star of four points: Beneath the outermost brittle skin also lies a dry flesh, and a hard brown nut, as in the domestic, though smoother and sharper; this nut being opened, has a shell like a Hazelnut, but much smaller, and inside a white, thick, sticky kernel, bitter of taste, which allows itself to be divided in two.

Inside one finds two white leaflets, on which one can recognize all veins and nerves, opening themselves toward the back, and hanging together at the front, with a node, which sticks out through a small opening outside the shell, and from which the root of the young tree is formed.

From the two or three flowers only one becomes a fruit, and the others fall off, so that each fruit hangs singly.

The wood is pale from the outside, whitish, and gradually toward the inside it becomes redder, the innermost being a beautiful light-brown, pulling toward purple, like our cherry-tree wood, hard, fine, and massive, like a liver- or Ebony-wood; on the old trees this brown heart is so large, that it occupies almost the entire thickness of the trunk, up to two or three fingers of white wood, with which it is surrounded, and which is held for sapwood, which brown heart is also to be found in the roots.

*Season.* The flowers are seldom seen on this tree, and it blooms in May, being the start of the rainy Monsoons, at which time the domestic Tanjong also has its most blossoms; the fruits are seen ripe in October, and the West Monsoons.

*Name.* In Latin *Tanjonus Litorea*, in Malay *Bonga Tanjong Laut* and *Tanjong Laut*, by others *Cumbang Jatu* and *Cumbang Jati*, being perhaps so named because the flowers like to fall off: Among the Amboinese it has many names, according to the variety of places, for on Hitoe it is called *Lolan Key*, and around Oerien Patiatta, on Hoe-Amobel and Bonoa, *Leytir*, and *Leytil*, on Nuffalaut *Rufflukey*, or *Luffukey*. On Boero *Balan Tronga*.

*Place.* This tree grows of its own accord on few shores of Amboina, and is not much to be found, and that nowhere but on barren rocky shores, which because of cliffs are difficult to walk upon, as especially is the entire promontory of Capaha, and the corner of Assaloelo, against

# THE AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. chap. XVIII.

...region of the three small islands of Nussatello, Nussanive, and Oma on Leytimora etc., where these trees sometimes grow upon bare rocks, which they embrace with their roots, or rather, they pierce through them; nevertheless, they still grow straight and tall. This tree occurs in greater abundance in the islands situated to the Southeast, especially in Key, from which it takes its surname.

*Use.* This wood is in great use among the inhabitants of Key, who fashion wooden nails and pins from it, with which they join together *Kora-kora* <note>original: *Corre-Corren*; a traditional large rowing vessel used in the Maluku Islands</note>, Sampans <note>original: *Champans*</note>, and other vessels, just as is done in other places with Sappan-wood <note>lignum *Sappan*; a wood used both for construction and as a red dye</note> or *Lolan*. The people of Key say, however, that this wood lasts three times longer than Sappan or *Lolan*. The inhabitants of Nussalaut and Oma, who are the primary shipbuilders among the Amboinese, use no other wood for such works except *Russa Key*, which nevertheless seems to differ somewhat from the previously described variety. There, it does not grow on the shore, but in the earth itself, namely in the mountains; its leaves are also a brighter green and larger, and the bark of the tree yields a certain milky sap. The wood is likewise heavy and solid, tending from purple into brown, and easily split along its length.

Because of this use, they call this wood in Malay *Lolan Corra Corra*, just as they call Sappan-wood *Lolan Tsjello*, that is, the *Lolan* of the dyers. The people of Leytimore, and especially those of Nussanive, as was said in the preceding chapter, consider this Shore-Tanjong to be one and the same as the previously described domestic variety; they say that the domestic tree was merely altered by human cultivation, a claim which we refuted above. This wood, especially when dry, has a great similarity to that *Ackoles* or *Eckores* wood, though the latter is more reddish, or has a liver-color, and shines more when polished.

*Lolan Key*, when cast into a fire, makes a crackling noise like salt or *Naniu* wood, and gives off an unpleasant odor, which is not observed in *Tackole*. In the Papuan islands, they also fashion the nails of their vessels from this wood. Furthermore, it is elegant and can be polished very well for cabinet-makers and turners, being suitable for making small chests, as well as handles, hatchets, and railings; but it must be entirely dry and have been kept for a long time, otherwise it develops cracks and becomes moldy due to the saltiness, a flaw from which most woods produced on the shore suffer if they are not completely dry and well-aged. The inhabitants also make the handles of *torans* <note>original: *toranorum*; a type of spear or javelin</note> and short spears from it, as well as house posts where it occurs in frequent abundance, though they spare themselves the labor of cutting this wood due to its hardness and the inaccessible places where it grows. On those cliffs, one often finds such trees fallen, whose outer wood has rotted away, but the inner heartwood—nearly as thick as a man—is elegant, hard, brown, and polished like marble.

The *Bala* of Buru <note>original: *Bala Boeronensis*</note> grows plentifully on its northern coast, where it is called *Balatetto*, both on the shore and further inland on rocky mountains mixed with Ebony wood; there they also use it for the handles of *Torans*, and they burn it for blacksmiths' charcoal, which those smiths consider the best.

It should be investigated whether this wood might be the red or brown Ebony growing on the island of St. Mauritius; at the very least, these trees have a great similarity to each other in their foliage, bark, and the weight of the wood.

...opposite the three small islands of *Nussatello*, the corner of *Nussanive*, and *Oma* on *Leytimor* etc. where these trees sometimes stand on the bare cliffs, gripping them with bare roots and penetrating them. Nevertheless, they are very beautiful and straight. They are found in greater numbers in the South-Eastern Islands, especially on *Key*, from which it takes its surname.

*Usage.* This wood is most in use by the inhabitants of *Key*, who make from it all their wooden nails or pins, with which they join their *Kora-kora*, *Sampans*, and other vessels together, as is done in other places with *Sappan*-wood or *Lolan*, and the *Keyers* say that this wood lasts three times as long as the *Sappan* or *Lolan*. Those of *Nussalaut* and *Oma*, being the principal shipbuilders among the *Amboinese*, also use no other wood for such works but the *Russa Key*, which however seems to differ somewhat from the aforementioned, for it does not grow there on the beach, but somewhat inland, and even in the mountains; the leaves are a more youthful green and larger, the bark of the tree also gives some milk, the wood is also heavy and dense, drawing from purple mostly towards brown, and splitting easily lengthwise.

Because of this use, they call this wood in Malay *Lolan Corra Corra*, just as the *Sappan*-wood is called *Lolan Tsjello*, that is, the dyer's *Lolan*. Those of *Leytimor*, especially of *Nussanive*, as said in the previous chapter, hold this shore-*Tanjong* and the previous domestic one for one and the same tree, and say that the domestic ones have become so through the cultivation of men, which we have refuted above. Furthermore, this wood, especially when dried, has great similarity to that of *Ackole* or *Eckore*, but this latter draws more toward the reddish or liver-colored, and when polished, shines better.

The *Lolan Key*, being burned, also crackles in the fire like salt or *Nani*-wood, and gives thereby an unpleasant smell, which one does not perceive in the *Tackole*. In the *Papuan Islands* they likewise make the nails for their vessels from it: Furthermore, this wood is very beautiful to be worked by cabinet-makers and turners for all kinds of small-work, such as handles, planes, boxes, and railings, but it must be thoroughly dry and have lain for a long time, otherwise it tears and stands out because of the saltiness settling therein, to which faults almost all woods are subject that grow on the beach if they are not thoroughly old and seasoned. The natives also make the handles of their *Torans* and short spears from it, as well as posts for houses where it is to be had in abundance, although they greatly dread the effort of felling it because of its hardness and the difficulty of the places where it stands; one sometimes finds trees fallen on such cliffs, of which the outer wood has perished, and the inner heart is almost a man's thickness, beautiful, hard, brown, and smooth as marble.

The *Buru-Bala* grows much on its North-West corner, from there called *Balatetto*, as well on the beach as inland on the cliffy mountains, and mixed among the Ebony-wood: They use it there for handles of *Torans*, and to burn blacksmith's coals from it, which their smiths judge to be the best.

It remains to be investigated whether this is not the red or brown Ebony-wood which our nation claims grows on the Island of *Mauritius*: Indeed, these trees have great similarity to each other in leaves, bark, and weight of the wood.
