# CHAPTER NINETEEN.
## Cananga. Bonga Cananga.
<note>Malay: *Bunga* means flower; this is the Ylang-ylang tree, *Cananga odorata*.</note>

The Cananga is a reasonably tall tree, consisting of a straight and round trunk about one fathom <note>original: *orgyiam*; a measurement of roughly six feet</note> in diameter, which bears an ash-gray and smooth bark, with few branches that are mostly set crosswise, with a light crown that is transparent from all sides. The leaves sit on long stalks <note>original: *rachidibus*</note> placed alternately in rows, as in the Peach tree <note>original: *Malo Persico*</note>, but they are much wider and longer; they do not stand erect but are joined obliquely to one another. Otherwise, they closely resemble the leaves of the *Monoa* and the Ceylon Dammar <note>original: *Dammarae Selanicae*</note>, being about a palm long and often longer, and three or four fingers wide. The younger leaves, however, are more than a span <note>original: *spithamam*</note> long, somewhat rounded at the lower part, of uniform width further on, decorated with a long tip, bright green, thin, and woven through with many oblique ribs, smooth on top, and slightly wrinkled on the underside due to the protruding ribs. Eleven or thirteen of these cling to a single stalk, except for those that have fallen off from the lower part, in addition to the leaflets clinging together at the top.

Older trunks are mostly winding, shrunken, and hollowed out.

The flowers come forth in clusters between and behind the leaves, hanging from limp stalks; at first sight, they would not be taken for flowers, but look like tassels made of linen, for they are never open, but hang down as if limp and withered. They consist of six long, narrow, and limp petals, a finger long and as thick as the little finger, which are joined together at a triangular calyx <note>the green outer part of a flower</note>. In the center of these, a flat mound appears made of many yellowish stamens, as in Buttercups <note>original: *Ranunculis*</note>, in the middle of which rises a small round head or pistil like a peppercorn, which grows into the fruit. The color of these flowers is threefold: in the tender ones, the petals are bluish-green and curved inward like a little crown; when they open more, the color is that of an unripe apple, namely a mixture of green and yellow; and the mature and old flowers have a yellow color, but always mixed with green.

Their scent is very strong, spreading far and wide, a mixture of the scent of Narcissus and Clove <note>original: *Caryophylli*</note>, which in the opinion of the inhabitants is the most pleasant of all, but to our nation it is too heavy. For the Indians always judge a very strong scent, even if it is not so sweet, to be the best. This scent is more pleasant from a distance than if one approaches closely, and it is much more penetrating in the evening, in dark and still air, and especially when mixed with a thin rain, when it is immediately observed and felt, so to speak, as soon as we walk around this tree.

Most of the flowers fall off, leaving no seed, except for a certain few that grow into fruits, which are oblong cones, almost like the upper parts of acorns, but not so hard, filled with certain soft little stones <note>seeds</note> that rarely sprout even if committed to the earth. But having been eaten by starlings <note>original: *sturnis*</note> or other animals and rejected through their droppings, they sprout into new little trees; hence these trees are propagated and transplanted in such a manner, being found in the forests and often even in gardens, sown as it were by these birds.

The bark of the trunk is smooth and ash-gray. The wood, however, is pale and becomes more yellowish toward the inside; it is neither hard nor durable, and brittle in the branches. When freshly cut, if it is stood upright, it emits much water and is useful for no work.

*The Season.* Every year around the end of the rainy months, or September, this tree sheds most of its leaves, so that with its few branches it is almost entirely bare and withered; then also few flowers are noted on it, but at that time the fruits ripen, which are rarely collected since starlings and other birds occupying this tree in great numbers eat them. At the same time also, from the trunk or the filth of its bark, deformed caterpillars <note>original: *Erucae*</note> are generated, marked with black spots and hairy, which crawl through the whole tree and devour the leaves and fruits. These, however, are devoured by the birds, so that within the space of one month they are generated and perish. Subsequently, in the following November, the tree sprouts again, puts forth new leaves, and produces flowers.

# XIX. CHAPTER.
## The Cananga Tree.

The Cananga is a reasonably tall tree, with a straight and round trunk, about one fathom <note>original: *vadem*</note> in circumference, which has a light-gray smooth bark, few branches, which mostly stand crosswise, and a hollow crown, through which one can see everywhere. The leaves stand on long twigs, arranged in rows alternating against one another, like the Peach tree, yet much broader and longer, not straight, but slanted against one another, otherwise corresponding much with those of the *Monoa* and *Dammar-Selan*, about a hand long or more, three and four fingers wide. But the young leaves are fully a span long, round at the back, mostly of uniform width, with a long point at the front, bright green, thin, and lined with many slanted ribs, smooth on top, but somewhat wrinkled underneath because of the protruding ribs. Of these, eleven to thirteen stand on a small branch, besides those which have fallen off at the back, and also a cluster of young leaves at the front.

The old trunk is mostly somewhat bowed, shrunken, and eaten away.

The flowers come forth between and behind the leaves in clusters, hanging on limp stalks, which one would not at first take for flowers, but for some tassels or bunches of ribbon, for they never stand open, but hang downwards as if withered. They consist of six long, narrow, and limp petals, a finger long, and a pinky-finger wide, which stand together on a triangular little plate; inside one sees a flat little hill made of very short bristles, pushed close together, as in the *Ranunculus* <note>Buttercup</note>, pale yellow, with a small grain on top, like a peppercorn, out of which the fruit grows. The color of these flowers is of three kinds: for while yet young, the petals are blue-green, and stand curved inwards like a little crown; having opened fully, they have the color of an unripe apple, namely green and yellow mixed; the old ones are truly yellow, yet in such a way that some green is always mixed in.

Their scent is very strong, and spreads itself far, mixed of Narcissi and Cloves <note>original: *Carioffel-nagelen*</note>, according to the judgment of the Indians one of the most lovely, yet for our Nation somewhat heavy, for the Indians always judge the strong scent, even if it is not so sweet, to be the best. From afar this scent is much more pleasant than close by, also much stronger in the evening, when it is dark and still weather, primarily during a thin drizzle, when one feels it sufficiently as one goes walking around these trees.

The flowers mostly fall off without seed, except for some few that bring forth fruits, which are some cone-shaped knots, almost like the front ends of acorns, yet not so hard, and filled inside with some soft grains, which rarely come up, even if they reach the earth; but being eaten by Starlings or other Birds, and being cast out again through the dung, they bring forth new little trees; therefore these trees are only propagated with such plants, which one finds sown by the aforementioned Birds in the wild, and sometimes also in the gardens.

The bark of the trunk is even, and straight-gray. The wood of the trunk is pale, and more yellow towards the inside, not hard, nor durable, and brittle at the branches. The freshly-cut wood, if one sets it upright, gives out much water, and is useful for nothing.

*Season.* Yearly around the end of the rainy Monsoon <note>original: *Mouyson*</note> or September, this tree sheds its most leaves, and stands then with its few branches very bare, and as if dried out; then one also sees few flowers thereon, but its fruits then become ripe, yet few come to any use, for in that time the starlings and other birds reside there in multitude, who eat them up. Likewise, in that time, from the trunk or the filth of the bark, certain ugly black-speckled and hairy caterpillars <note>original: *rupzen*</note> come forth, which crawl along the entire tree, eating up leaves and fruits, which are then destroyed again by the birds, so that in about a month they arise and perish; thereafter in November the tree begins to gain new foliage again, and to bear flowers.

<summary>This page describes the Cananga tree (Ylang-ylang), focusing on its distinctive "linen tassel" flowers, its powerful scent favored by locals but found heavy by Europeans, and its propagation via birds.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the botanical description of the Cananga tree (Ylang-ylang), moving from its physical appearance to its cultivation, its many regional names, and its significant role in the daily life and medicine of the Indonesian archipelago.</meta>

Since the tree is tender, its uppermost branches must often be pruned so that it does not grow too tall, but rather acquires a dense crown; this does not succeed well in old trees, for when these are cut back, they often perish due to rain penetrating the trunk.

It grows not only in and around villages where it is planted, but also in the forests, where it is sown by birds; there it rises higher, and the flowers gradually degenerate, except for another truly wild species, which we shall describe in the following chapter.

**Name.** In Latin, *Cananga*. In Malay, *Bonga Cananga* and *Canangan*. In Java, it is called *Tsjampe*, a name that generally denotes a fragrant flower. In Batavia <note>Modern-day Jakarta</note>, *Fula Cananga*, and by the Hindustani name *Fula Betele*, since its flower is often chewed with *Siri Pinanga* <note>A mixture of betel leaf and areca nut</note>. By the people of Ternate, it is called *Saja Cananga*. By the Macassarese, likewise *Cananga*. By the Balinese, *Sondat*. In Banda, *Cumbang Cayrano*. In Amboina, *Copabbar* and *Coppanabbal*, that is, "wild flower," since the Amboinese do not plant this tree but seek it out here and there in the forests. In Leytimor, it is called *Copawaarita*, that is, "thread-like flower," from the shape of a tassel or a bundle of linen filaments.

**Location.** It grows mostly in the islands of watery India <note>The East Indies</note>, such as Java, Malacca, Bali, Bima, Celebes, Amboina, and further in all the Moluccas.

**Use.** This tree is chiefly cultivated around houses and in the streets for the pleasant scent of the flowers, which the Malays and all Indians weave into their hair, place in their clothes and beds; these flowers retain their scent until the third day. When dried, they are also mixed with tobacco and the smoke is inhaled; others add a petal of these to *Siri Pinanga*, which they chew together for the pleasant aroma. Furthermore, festive arches at weddings and banquets are decorated with these; moreover, all scented oils are prepared with these and the flowers of the following *Tsjampacca*, if fresh flowers are infused in oil and this is frequently repeated. From this oil, an ointment is then composed, either with other spices or with the root of <term>Curcuma</term> <note>Turmeric</note>; both of these ointments are called *Borri-Borri* or *Boborri*, as will be indicated in that chapter. Some have thought this oil and ointment to be cooling, because the inhabitants use it in fevers to smear their bodies, but this is an error; for both these flowers are warmer than temperate by one degree, especially the *Cananga*, and the inhabitants smear their bodies in such fevers that come with great cold, so that this may be diminished. Furthermore, all *Boborri* ointment into which these flowers and Turmeric enter is used by the inhabitants to warm the body on cold and rainy days.

The bark of the tree is also used for similar ointments prepared against <term>Leucophlegmatia</term> <note>A pale swelling of the body, often related to dropsy or edema</note> to consume and dry it out.

The wood offers almost no use, as it is soft and brittle; however, the *Cananga* growing in the forests of Hitu provides a reasonably durable wood from old trunks, which the inhabitants there use for house posts, though it easily rots and breeds worms if it attracts moisture. It has been observed by our nation that these flowers make men dizzy if too great a quantity is chewed with the Betel nut.

->In Rumphius's Appendix these things are added.<-

*The fruits of the Cananga, further described and examined, are roughly as follows: In the month of December, they sprout from the same clusters from which the flowers bloom, hanging in the shape of half-formed acorns, but lacking caps, and somewhat dimpled, dark brown, covered with a soft shell; in these are located nine flat and wrinkled seeds, pale brown, shining, and somewhat resembling bedbugs; these sit in a viscous flesh which breathes a sweet and pleasant scent.*

<meta>catchword: EXPLI-</meta>

<column-break/>

*When this tree is still young, one must sometimes break off or cut off the top tips, which prevents it from shooting up so terribly high, but keeps it low and with a thick crown. This will not work on old trees, for if one chops off the tops of such, they often die out because of the rain watering into them.*

*It grows not only in and around the Villages <note>original: Negoryen</note>, where it is planted, but also in the wild forest, being sown there by the birds, where it also grows much higher, and the flowers turn somewhat wild over time, except for a truly wild species, of which in the next chapter.*

***Name.*** *In Latin Cananga. In Malay Bonga Cananga and Canangan. In Java Tsjampe, which however generally signifies a fragrant flower. In Batavia Fula Cananga, and with a Hindustani word Fula Betele, because the flower is often eaten with the Siri-Pinang. In Ternate Saja Cananga: In Macassar also Cananga. In Bali Sondat. In Banda Cumbang Cayrano. In Amboina Copabbar and Coppanabbal, that is, flower of the woods, because the Amboinese do not plant them, but find them here and there in the wood: In Leytimor Capawaarita, that is, little string flower, after the resemblance of a bunch of ribbons or little strings.*

***Place.*** *It grows mostly in the islands of the Water-Indies, such as Java, Malacca, Bali, Bima, Celebes, Amboina, and further all the Moluccas.*

***Use.*** *One builds <note original="bouwt">In this context, meaning to grow or cultivate</note> these trees mostly around the houses, and on the streets of the villages, for the lovely scent of the flowers, which the Malays and all the Indians very gladly wear, both in the hair, as in the clothes and bedsteads, keeping their scent until the third day. They are also dried, shredded into tobacco, and smoked together; others add a petal of the flower to the Siri-Pinang, and chew everything together to make a good scent. Besides that, the festive arches at weddings and feasts are also decorated with them; also all kinds of fragrant oil are made with these and the following Tsjampacca-flowers, if one soaks them fresh in oil, and repeats it often, which oil is afterwards made into a salve, either with other spices, or with the root Curcuma, both of which one calls Borri-Borri or Boborri, as shall be said in the same chapter. Some have thought that this oil and salve are cooling, because the inhabitants use them in fevers to smear the body; which is an error, for both these flowers are at least one degree better than temperate <note>meaning they are "warm" in the humoral sense</note>, especially the Cananga, and the inhabitants smear the body with this oil in such fevers that begin with great cold, to diminish the same somewhat. Also all Boborry-salves, in which many of these flowers and Curcuma enter, one uses to warm the body during cold rainy days.*

*The bark of the tree is also used in such salves that one makes against the cold dropsy <note original="koude zugt">Likely referring to edema or Leucophlegmatia</note>, to consume and dry it up.*

*The wood for the most part has no use, because it is soft and brittle, yet the Cananga growing in the Hitu forests has in the old trunks a reasonably durable wood, which the inhabitants there use for the posts of houses, which also easily perishes and becomes worm-eaten if it touches the least moisture. By our Nation it is experienced that in the flowers there sits a dizzy-making power for the head, if one chews too much of them with Pinang.*

->*In the Appendix of Rumphius this was added.*<-

*The fruits of Cananga more closely described are thus: In the month of December one sees them coming forth in little clusters together, on the same little clusters where the flowers hang, in the size of half-grown acorns, but without caps, and somewhat with little pits, dark-brown, and soft of shell; therein one finds 9 flat and somewhat wrinkled seeds, light-brown, shining, and somewhat resembling bedbugs; these lie in a sticky flesh, which is sweet and lovely of scent.*

## CHAPTER TWENTY.

### *Wild Canangas. Cananga Oetan.* <note>original Malay: *hutan*, meaning forest or wild</note>

**T**he wild Cananga is similar to the domestic one, except that its leaves are larger & wider, and its trunk is not as thick or tall as the domestic one. The flowers do not hang in clusters, but hang solitary, and are composed of three large & wavy petals, which would be mistaken for small leaves of the tree itself if they had ribs; they are pale, lemon-colored, and in the middle a short & triangular pistil <note>the central part of the flower</note> appears, larger than that of the *Ceylon Dammar* <note>original: *Dammaræ Selanicæ*; a resin-producing tree</note>, which when opened reveals yellow filaments or stamens inside. The fresh flowers of this tree breathe out a weak scent, but when dry, they are as penetrating as the domestic ones: It grows spontaneously in the forests near the shore and in the mountains, and especially in the *Hitu* region <note>A peninsula on the island of Ambon</note>.

*Name.* In Latin, *Cananga silvestris*. In Malay, *Cananga Oetan*. In Amboinese, *Coppanabbat*.
*Usage.* This tree offers little use, except that its thinner and straight trunks are used for rafters of roofs and the upper parts of houses; however, they do not last long, as they not only dry out quickly but also suddenly perish.

**In Rumphius’s Appendix, this Chapter has been expanded in the following manner.**

Under the name of the wild *Cananga*, three trees have come to my attention, all of which I shall describe in this chapter, as they are of little use or importance.

First, the *primary wild Cananga, or three-leaved* <note>original: *trifolia*</note> has a form mixed between the *Champak* <note>original: *Champaccæ*</note> and the *Cananga*; for this tree most closely resembles the *Champak*, bearing a medium-sized trunk, from which rare and short round branches sprout, covered with a smooth bark, which are divided into a few small branchlets. At the end of these sit large leaves supported by very short stalks without order, somewhat similar to the leaves of the *Canarium* <note>The Java almond tree</note>, but narrower, nine inches long, barely three wide; their upper part is smooth, but appears somewhat rough & almost granular, while from the lower part the midrib protrudes with a sharp ridge; the lateral ribs are few and thin, and the leaf itself in that place is soft and downy to the touch.

Between and under the leaves the flowers emerge sitting on a long stalk, the size of *Champak* flowers, composed of three large & wavy green petals, which sit upon a three-petaled, sharp calyx <note>the protective outer layer of a flower bud</note>, like the *Cananga* flower. From its center a triangular head is raised, which grows into the fruit: These three petals are striated and breathe somewhat pleasantly; otherwise, they would be taken for the younger leaves of the tree itself. This triangular and sharp head, opening itself into three hard scales, reveals many short stamens surrounding another little head, which is the very beginning of the fruit. Long after the leaves, these fruits grow to perfection, three and four, and often nine grow together in a cluster on one tree from a single stalk on the branches, which are great—

## XX. CHAPTER.

### *The Wild Cananga Trees.*

**T**he wild Cananga is most like the domesticated one, except that the leaves are larger and broader, the trunk also does not become as thick and high as the domesticated; the flowers do not hang in bunches together, but singly, and are made of three broad and wavy leaves <note>referring here to petals</note>, which one would take for small leaves of the tree if they were ribbed; they are pale, lemon-yellow, and in the middle one sees a short and somewhat triangular little cone, somewhat larger than in the *Dammar Selan*, which when opened, reveals some yellow threads inside. The fresh flowers have a faint smell, but when dried, they are just as strong as the domesticated ones. It grows of its own accord in the *forests*, both along the beach and on the mountains, and mostly in the *Hitu Country*.

Name. In Latin *Cananga Silvestris*, in Malay *Cananga Oetan*. In Amboinese *Coppanabbat*.
Use. One has little use for this tree, except that one sometimes takes the thin and straight trunks for rafters of roofs and upper-work of houses, which cannot last long, because it not only dries out easily, but also soon rots.

**In the Appendix of Rumphius, this Chapter is improved in the following way.**

Under the name of wild Cananga, three kinds of trees have appeared to me, which I shall describe all three in this Chapter, since they are after all of little use.

1. *Cananga Silvestris prima sive trifolia* <note>the first wild Cananga or three-leaf</note>, has a mixed shape of *Champak* and *Cananga*, for the tree looks most like a *Champak tree*, with a medium trunk, upon which stand few and short branches, round, and covered with a smooth bark, and divided into a few straight twigs; at the end of these stand large leaves, on very short stalks without order, which are somewhat like those of *Canary* <note>Canarium</note>, though narrower, 9 inches long, barely 3 wide; on the upper side nothing at all sticks out, except that they seem somewhat rough and grainy; on the lower side the midrib bulges far out with a sharp ridge, but the side-ribs are few and subtle; also the leaf is soft there, and like wool to the touch.

Between and behind the leaves the flower comes forth singly, on a longish stalk, the size of a *Champak flower*, made of 3 broad and wavy leaves <note>petals</note>, green in color, resting on a 3-pointed foot <note>calyx</note> like the Cananga flower; in the middle with a raised three-sided bud, from which the fruit becomes. These three leaves are somewhat striped, and somewhat sweet-smelling; otherwise one would take them for young leaves of the tree; the aforementioned three-sided and sharp bud, opening itself into 3 hard shells, shows many short threads, surrounding another sharp little bud, which is the true beginning of the fruit. Far behind the leaves these fruits come to perfection 3 and 4 and 9 together from one tree on a stalk on the branches; these are in—

they have the size of Plums, and are oblong-round, crowned with a short and blunt tip, and marked with a furrow along the side; on the outside, however, they are slightly wrinkled and granular. The outer shell is harder than a typical green plant substance, yet not at all woody. Inside are contained three flat little stones <note>botanically, these are the seeds or pits</note>, covered in a slimy flesh, positioned transversally, and separated in one part by a small membrane that is attached to the outer shell.

Each little stone or kernel is covered by a hard and chestnut-colored husk, wrinkled at the edges, and distinguished by a darker brown color. Beneath this husk is hidden a flat substance, resembling the color and form of a dried banana <note>original Latin: *Musæ emaradi*</note>, breathing out a somewhat pleasant and aromatic odor.

The bark of the trunk is ash-gray like the *Champac* <note>original: *Champacca*; a fragrant flowering tree in the magnolia family</note>, quite thick, and if it is cut, a viscous juice drips out, which dries and thickens into a white gum, which is fragrant like the kernel. The wood of the trunk is light and soft, and somewhat fragrant. The branches are short and easily broken.

**Name.** In Latin *Cananga silvestris trifolia* <note>Three-leaved wild Cananga</note>. In Malay *Cananga Oetan* <note>Wild Cananga</note>. Various names have been given to it by the Amboinese, but it is commonly called *Coeban Abbal*, which is to say, "wild flower." Specifically, however, this first species is called *Matta Auwe*, that is, "eye of the garden," though for what reason is unknown to me; others, however, take it for *Leyitir Poeti*, that is, "white Lustrafter" <note>likely referring to a bird or a glossy-leaved plant</note>, from which it nevertheless differs too much. The people of *Caybobbo* <note>A village on the island of Seram</note> call it *Matta Ayn* or *Ay-Hoa-Maroea*, and in Malay *Boa Djoedjaroe*, that is, "maiden’s fruit," because of its subsequent use.

**Location.** It occurs here and there in Amboina, but rarely; never in the high mountains, but in deserted wild gardens, both in the plains and in higher places, from which it obtained the aforementioned names.

**Use.** Few parts of this tree are in use, except for its kernels or little stones, which the womenfolk grind into a fragrant ointment or *Boborri* <note>A traditional cosmetic paste used for skin care and fragrance</note>, with which they rub their bodies while washing to provide themselves with a good scent; it has been discovered, however, that if the body is smeared with these fruits alone, it causes pain to the skin.

Its wood is light, yet it is used for building houses; for its thin and straight trunks serve as poles, as well as for the roofs of houses, though it is by no means durable, as it not only dries out quickly but also rots quickly.

**Second,** the *Second wild Cananga, or narrow-leaved*, matches the domestic one in form and manner of growth, for its leaves are also of irregular size, from six to nine inches long, and two and a half to three wide. The flowers sprout in clusters behind the leaves, both on their stalks and on the small branches, constructed of six petals, much shorter than in the domestic variety, not more than half a finger long; each is contained in a triangular and flat little cup <note>the calyx</note>, which is attached to a long pedicel. These petals are placed around a pistil, which is composed of blunt tubes, in the center of which is contained a granular little head like a piece of *Siriboa* <note>The fruit of the Betel pepper</note>. After the flower falls, this pistil thickens and becomes more woody, and the aforementioned thickish little head divides itself into 13 or 14 smaller heads, which grow into as many fruits; an example of this is seen in Europe in red cherries, of which four or seven often grow on one stalk; each fruit, however, has the size of a young hazelnut, which hides many flat and thin scaly seeds under a soft and thin shell, breathing out a penetrating odor.

**Third,** the *Third wild Cananga, or broad-leaved*, bears leaves more closely approaching those of the *Champac*, namely woolly underneath, yet much larger and rounded at the top, eight inches long, four wide.
The flowers hang in many clusters, not on the leaf-stalks, but on the branches; they are constructed of six petals shorter than in the preceding variety, of which the three outer ones are placed in a triangle, while the three inner ones sit at the top, containing a little head in the center as in the previous one. This top or germ is much larger, from which twenty or twenty-five fruits grow, sitting on short pedicels closely joined together, but not all of them reach maturity. These have the size of a full-grown Hazelnut, first whitening, then reddening, and finally

<column-break/>

*in the size of Plums, oblong-round, with a short blunt tip on top, and on the side along its length with a seam, somewhat rough and granular on the outside. The outer shell is harder than a green plant substance, and yet not woody. Inside one finds 3 flat kernels, surrounded by a slimy flesh, lying crosswise, and separated a bit from one another by dividing membranes, which are attached to the outer shell.*

*Each kernel is surrounded by a hard and chestnut-brown shell, wrinkled at the edges, and light brown. Under this shell one finds a flat meat, of the substance and color of old Betel nut <note>original Dutch: *oude Pinang*</note>, somewhat fragrant and spicy.*

*The bark of the trunk is light gray, similar to the Champak tree, reasonably thick, and when one hacks into it, a slimy sap runs out, which congeals into a whitish gum, and is also fragrant like the meat of the fruit. The wood of the trunk is light and soft, also of some scent. The branches are short, and break off easily.*

**Name.** *In Latin Cananga silvestris trifolia: In Malay Cananga Oetan; among the Amboinese it has various names, for commonly one calls it Coeban Abbal, that is, wild flower. In particular this first sort is called Matta Auwe, that is, Oculus Horti, eye or ornament of the Garden, for what reason I know not; others want to hold it for a Leyitir Poeti, that is, white Lustrafter, from which it nevertheless differs too much. Those of Caybobbo call it Matta Ayn, or Ay-hoa-maroea, and in Malay Boa Djoedjaroe, that is, maiden’s fruit, for its following use.*

**Place.** *One finds it here and there on Amboina, though not much, not at all in the high forest, but always in abandoned gardens, both in the plains and in the higher mountains, from which it has the above names.*

**Use.** *Little is used of this tree, except for the meats from the three above-mentioned flat kernels, which the local women grind into a fragrant salve, or Boborri, wherewith they smear the body during washing to get a good scent; though it has been found, if one smears these fruits alone on the body, that they hurt the skin.*

*The wood is light, yet is used for house-building, namely, one takes the thin and straight trunks for rafters of roofs and upper-work of houses, which however cannot last long, because it not only dries out easily, but also soon spoils.*

**2.** *Cananga silvestris secunda sive angustifolia, is in growth and fashion the closest to the tame one, for the leaves are also of unequal size, from six to nine inches long, two and a half, and 3 ditto wide. The flowers come forth behind the leaves, in bunches together, as well on the small stems as on the twigs, made of 6 leaves <note>petals</note>, much shorter than the tame one, namely, not over half a finger long, and each stands on a triangular flat little foot, and the same on a long stalk. They stand around a little hill, made of blunt little styles, and in the middle of the same one sees a granular bud, like a piece of a Siriboa. After the falling of the flower a long stalk becomes thicker and more woody, and the aforementioned thick middle bud divides itself into 13 and 14 other buds, from which so many fruits grow, of which one sees an example in Europe in the red cherries, on which sometimes four and seven sit together on one stalk; each fruit is the size of a young Hazelnut, hiding many thin flat seeds like scales under a soft shell, and strong of scent.*

**3.** *Cananga silvestris tertia sive latifolia, has leaves more closely resembling those of the Champak, namely, woolly from below, yet much larger, and rounder in front, 8 inches long, 4 wide.*

*The flowers hang in clusters together, not on the leaf-stalks, but on the branches, made of 6 little leaves somewhat shorter than the former, of which the three outermost stand in a triangle, and the 3 innermost on a little hill hiding a bud like the former. This little hill becomes much larger, from which 20 and 25 fruits grow on short thick feet crowded together, though they do not all come to perfection. These are in the size of a full hazelnut, first white, then red, at last shiny-black. Under a soft slimy shell hid-*

## CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE.
### *Sampacca. Bonga Sjampacca.*

**T**his flowering tree is also of two kinds, domestic and wild; the domestic is a medium-sized tree like an apple tree, with a long trunk and consisting of a few extended branches <note>original: *arboribus* — The Latin text uses "trees," but the Dutch column correctly identifies these as "branches" (*takken*).</note>. The leaves are mostly opposite in two rows, but they observe no strict order, nor are they as numerous on the branchlets as in the Cananga; they are usually a span <note>about 9 inches</note> or a palm long, two inches wide, ending in a long point, having few oblique ribs, and are rough, smooth, and a bright green <note>original: *laete viridia*</note>, but the older leaves often send out young branchlets. From the armpits of the leaves the flowers sprout, mostly in pairs on one stalk <term>petiole<gloss>the supporting stalk of a flower or leaf</gloss></term>, which at first are long and pointed buds like cones, from which are formed flowers similar to Narcissus, showing clusters of petals as in the Cananga, but much shorter and more open.
Each flower consists of fifteen or sixteen thickish and limp petals, of which the five outermost are barely half a finger long and bent outwards; five others more internal are upright and longer; the remaining five placed in the center are smallest and connected like a pyramid. Beneath these is hidden a <term>pistil<gloss>the central, seed-bearing part of the flower</gloss></term> surrounded on all sides by many rather short and thick <term>stamens<gloss>the pollen-producing parts</gloss></term>, which bear roundish, yellowish-green <term>anthers<gloss>the tips of the stamens</gloss></term>. The color of the flower is an intense yellow or saffron, like the yolk of an egg. The scent is pleasant and sweet, but strong <note>original: *fortis*</note>, approaching that of the Narcissus; indeed, from a distance it is more pleasant than the Cananga and less heavy on the head. By all the Indians these flowers are held among the most beautiful and sweetest, though to our nation they seem somewhat nauseating if one smells them for a long time. This pleasantness does not last for a long time, at least no longer than one night, for it gradually acquires a smell of hay, which is unpleasant when dried. These are so similar to Mace <note>the lacy reddish covering of the Nutmeg seed</note> or Nutmeg flowers that they might be taken for them by the unskilled, but the scent easily distinguishes them.
After the flowers fall, that middle stalk or germ grows out to a length of three or four inches, and from each little head a fruit comes forth in the shape and size of a Muscadine or <term>Apian grape<gloss>a variety of sweet grape particularly attractive to bees</gloss></term>, sometimes rounder, sometimes more curved like beans or kidneys, which together resemble a cluster of grapes. These berries are pale green on the outside, rough, and covered as if with small dots, each of which is star-shaped. The outer skin of these is as thick as a knife-blade, and when the fruit becomes ripe, it bursts open at its bulging or convex part, where it reveals inside six or eight reddish and angular stones, similar to the stones of a Pomegranate, but shorter. Within these is contained a hard, blackish, and almost triangular grain, which is the true seed of this tree. The bark of the trunk is very smooth and ash-gray. The wood is soft, sappy, and useless. Usually beneath each flower is placed a small green leaf, similar to the rest but barely half a finger long, which elegantly adorns this flower if they are picked together. I know of no tree having this peculiarity, namely, that from one flower many separate fruits grow.

## XXI. CHAPTER.
### *Grape-tree, or Orange-flower, and Champaka-tree.*

**T**his flower-tree is also of two kinds, domestic and wild. The domestic becomes a medium-sized tree, like our apple trees, with a low trunk and few thick extended branches. The leaves stand mostly in two rows diagonally opposite each other, yet keep no precise order, and do not stand as thickly on the twigs as on the Cananga, generally barely a span or a hand-breadth long, two inches wide, running to a long point, with few diagonal ribs, stiff, smooth, and a joyful green, yet the old leaves nearby occasionally push out young shoots. From the lap <note>the axil</note> of the leaves the flowers come forth, mostly two together on one stalk, being at first long and pointed buds, like cones, from which the flower is formed, most like the Narcissus, or also showing a bunch of leaves like the Cananga, but much shorter and more expanded.
Each flower consists of 15 to 16 thickish and soft petals, of which the five outermost are barely half a finger long and curved outwards, five others on the inside stand mostly upright and are somewhat longer, and the five innermost are the smallest and close against each other like a little pyramid; beneath that one sees a little pillar, set all around with pale green buds and with many short thick threads. The color of the flower is deep yellow, like the yolk of an egg. The scent is lovely and sweet, but pungent <note>original: *geil* — in this historical context meaning rank or heavily scented</note>, and drawing towards the Narcissus; indeed from afar more pleasant than the Cananga, and less burdensome to the head. They are counted by all the Indians among the sweetest and most pleasant, yet to our Nation they appear somewhat nauseating, especially if one smells them for a long time. Its loveliness does not stay with it long, indeed no longer than one night, for gradually it begins to become hay-like, and in the dried state unpleasant. The dried ones are so similar in color to Mace or Nutmeg flowers that one would take them for such, but the scent distinguishes them immediately.
After the falling of the flowers, the middle little pillar grows out to the length of three or four inches, and from each little bud standing on the same a fruit is formed, in the size and shape of a Muscadine grape, sometimes somewhat rounder, sometimes somewhat curved like beans or kidneys, and together resembling a cluster of grapes. The berries are pale green on the outside, rough, and as if set with small dots, of which each has the shape of a little star. The outer shell has the thickness of a knife, and being ripe, it bursts open on the bulging side, showing within six and eight red and angular grains, resembling those of a pomegranate, but shorter; in the same sticks a hard, black, almost triangular stone, which is the true seed of this tree. The bark of the trunk is very even and light gray. The wood soft, sappy, and of poor quality. Commonly by each flower stands a small green leaf, like the others of the tree, yet not over half a finger long, which adorns this flower not a little when one breaks them off together. I know of no other tree of that wonderful property as this, namely, that from one flower many and separate fruits come.

### Season of the Year.
The time of its flowering is uncertain, for it produces flowers and fruit throughout the entire year, though it sometimes rests for several months. Its flower gives off a much more pleasant scent in clear and bright air than in rainy weather, when its odor is much stronger but also heavier. This tree is cultivated around houses and fields, but not in gardens near vegetables. It is propagated through saplings that spring up from seeds which birds have eaten and excreted. It grows luxuriantly but does not reach a great age, and eventually develops a thin and irregular crown. In its younger years, this crown must be pruned so that the tree remains low and spreads out; it must also be treated somewhat roughly at times, and its branches should be broken off so that the foliage grows back thicker.

In Ternate, another variety of this domestic kind occurs, which is similar in form to this one, but its flowers are smaller, likewise saffron-yellow, and fragrant.

In Java, a *Sampacca* is also found that varies greatly in color, for the tree and its flowers are similar to the common type, but the color of the flower is a pale or weak blue; it is called there *Tsjampacca Biru* <note>original: "Biru" — Blue</note>. It is rarely found and is shown as a rarity.

Furthermore, a third and foreign species is found in Java and Bali, which is called the "white" variety. It is similar in foliage and flowers to the common type, but the flower is smaller, white in color, and has a more pleasant scent than the common one. It occurs nowhere except in the gardens of Nobles due to its singular form and pleasing scent; it must, however, be distinguished from the following "Amboinese white" variety, which is considered wild. The roots of the common type are reddish on the outside and bitter in taste, as is the bark of the trunk; it forms no fruit until it has reached old age.

**Name.** In Latin, *Sampacca*. In Malay, *Tsjampacca*, which the Portuguese writers call *Champacca*. In Javanese, *Tjampe* and *Cambang*, though this generally denotes any fragrant flower. Thus the Portuguese in India call this flower by the Hindustani name *Fula Champacca*. The Dutch in Batavia call them *Orange-flowers* from their color, or *Whore-flowers* <note>original: "meretricum" / "Hoere-bloemen"</note> from their use. By those of Ternate, it is also called *Tsjampacca*. By the Macassarese, *Tsjampagga* and *Bonga Eydja*. By the Balinese, *Tsjampacca*. By the Amboinese, *Copattum* and *Coppa Puckuri*, which means "saffron flowers." By the people of Loehu, *Cubane*.

**Location.** These flowers are common throughout all of India, but mostly in the Malay regions, "Watery India" <note>likely referring to the maritime regions or archipelago</note>, and throughout all these islands. These trees never occur spontaneously in the wild but are grown where they are cultivated by men.

**Use.** They have the same use as the preceding species, being used mostly by young people, both male and female. The Malay, Javanese, and Macassarese women especially seek out these flowers to weave into their hair, where these elegant saffron flowers, mixed among black and shining hair, provide an elegant sight and ornament. However, because this fashion is mostly practiced by lighthearted women to please men, some of our people—though with a hasty judgment—have named these "whore-flowers," not considering that this is a general Malay custom. They also strew these in bedrooms, chests, and small boxes in which they keep clothes and linens, but they do not remain there longer than a night, as they soon contract a musty odor. These flowers are the primary ornaments used for festive arches and wedding beds, as well as banquets; they provide an elegant appearance if tied to a string so that one *Bonga Manoor* <note>Arabian Jasmine</note> is knotted at a span’s distance <note>about 9 inches</note> between each *Sampacca* flower.

They are also in great use for the preparation of the fragrant *Minjac Boubou* or *Minjac Mani* <note>scented oils</note>, of which these flowers are the basis. It is composed in the following manner: Take flowers of *Sampacca*, *Tanioni*, *Cananga*, *Manoor*, or similar fragrant flowers and leaves as many as you wish; soak these in *Calappa-Oly* <term>Coconut oil<gloss>from the Malay "Kelapa" for coconut</gloss></term> or any other oil that has almost no scent. Digest them for three days in the Sun, adding new flowers every day and throwing away the old ones. Then pour the purified oil into a flat dish; place it in a pan over coals and sprinkle in *Benzoin* <note>a balsamic resin</note>, *Scented Nail* <note>original: "Unguem Odoratum" — likely Operculum or Onycha, a seashell used in incense</note>, or *Macassarese Dupa* <note>incense</note>. Over this, place another more hollowed-out dish or bowl so that the smoke, passing through the oil, can adhere to it. Then the oil becomes thicker and retains the scent; it is then stored in well-sealed jars or...

<column-break/>

...pots.

# Book III. Chapter XXI. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...is preserved: This oil serves for daily use among Indian women, which they apply after washing the body or head, and they also anoint the body with it to obtain a scent pleasing to themselves.

The Balinese women grind these flowers with *Cananga* flowers in *Calappa* <note>coconut</note> oil, to which they add a small piece of *Curcuma* <note>turmeric</note>, with which they smear the body more out of habit than utility. However, they say it serves to draw various diseases out of the body, cure the itch <note>scabies</note>, and make the skin smooth, though they then appear like saffroned or turmeric-dyed devils.

I have observed that spiders particularly seek out these flowers; for when I placed them on a table at a certain time and turned away, a huge spider soon joined them, undoubtedly extracting some power from them, from which time I have been anxious about placing these flowers on my bed or its coverlets.

Against *Nephritis* <note>kidney stones or kidney inflammation</note> take seven petals of this *Sampacca* and a knot of knotty *Curcuma* <note>turmeric</note>; let them be ground upon a porphyry stone with a little water, then pass it through a cloth or filter it. In this, extinguish a glowing potsherd <note>a piece of broken ceramic</note>, and drink it while warm. These same flowers are also beneficial for the heat of urine and *Gonorrhea*, in both men and women, if seven heads of these flowers are taken before they open, which you should boil in a young *Calappa* <note>coconut</note> nut, then drink its water, which expels the sharp pus.

The bark of *Djudjambo* <note>likely a species of Syzygium</note> is boiled, which they give to women after childbirth to drive out the *lochia* <note>postpartum discharge</note>. The wood of old trunks near the heart is quite hard, striated lengthwise, light, and does not crack, wherefore it is fit for forming the stocks of guns from it.

In the *Hortus Malabaricus* <note>The Garden of Malabar, a famous 17th-century botanical work</note> Figure 19, Part 1, page 31, it is called by the Malabar name *Champaccan*, and by the Brahmans *Champo*, but its leaves are described there as broader than those observed in the Amboinese variety, unless the description was made from a younger tree. Its medicinal powers in that garden are as follows: the roots dried with the bark, ground, and mixed with thick milk, mature and open abscesses if applied to them in the form of a plaster. The dry bark of the roots ground in water and drunk provokes the menses of women and expels the afterbirth if drunk in a large quantity. Its ground flowers boiled in *Calappa* <note>coconut</note> oil settle headaches and eye inflammation arising from heat, as well as the pain of gout, if the affected part is anointed. The same is also provided by oil in which the flowers have been infused and macerated for forty days. The oil expressed from its kernels expels flatulence of the abdomen when smeared on externally. These flowers, when distilled, yield a fragrant water which is drunk against *Lypothymia* <note>fainting or swooning</note> and to strengthen the heart.

## OBSERVATION.

I have given various synonyms for this tree in the *Thesaurus Zeylanicus* page 31, regarding the tall tree called *Hapughaha* in Ceylon, with oblong, yellow, fragrant flowers, called *Champacca* by the Malabarians, and *Pau Fule* by the Portuguese (*Hermann, Museum Zeylanicum* page 64). It is the *Tsjampacca* of the Indians, or the Indian Grape-bearing tree with leaves of the American Laurel (*Breynius, Prodromus* 2, page 101) and the Oriental Grape-bearing tree with an oblong leaf (*Hermann, Paradisus Batavus Prodromus* page 385). For the rest, see the *Thesaurus Zeylanicus* in the place cited, and in *Ray's History of Plants* page 1641, as well as in his third volume, *Dendrologia* page 77, and *Appendix* 83. Under the name of the *Tsjampacca* tree, it is described by *Valentijn* page 214.

This genus is called *MICHELIA* by *Linnaeus* in *Characters of Plant Genera No. 337*, where one may see its known characteristics.

...must be preserved in jars or small pots. *This oil is for daily use by Indian women, both natives and those of mixed descent, after washing the hair of the head, and sometimes they also smear the body with it to have a good scent.*

*The Balinese women rub these with the aforementioned Cananga flowers, entirely in coconut oil, adding a piece of turmeric, with which they smear the body, more out of habit than any utility, saying that it serves to draw many kinds of diseases out of the body, to cure all kinds of scabs, and to make the skin smooth, although they then look like saffroned devils.*

*I have experienced that spiders are great lovers of these flowers, for once when I laid them on a table and turned around, there immediately came a large spider that sat upon them, without doubt sucking some powers out of them, after which time I have been concerned about allowing these flowers on my bedding.*

*Against the gravel <note>kidney stones</note> take seven leaves of this Sampacca and a knob of the knotty turmeric, rub it with a little water on a stone, and strain it through a cloth. Extinguish in it some pieces of a pot, previously made glowing hot, and drink it while warm. The same flowers also serve against the "burning-piss" <note>painful urination</note> and the drip <note>gonorrhea</note>, for both men and women, if one takes seven buds of these flowers before they have opened, and boils them in a young coconut, and afterwards drinks that same water, which settles the sharp matter.*

*The bark is mixed among other things with Djudjambo to give to women in labor after the birth, to drive out the afterbirth. The wood of the old trunks near the core is reasonably hard, striped lengthwise, light, and does not crack, therefore suitable to make stocks for rifles and muskets.*

In the *Hortus Malabaricus* figure 19, Part 1, page 31, it is named in Malabar *Champaccan*, in Brahman *Champó*. However, its leaves are described as broader than those seen on the Amboinese one, or they must have had them from a young tree. The medicinal powers in the mentioned *Hortus* are these: The roots with their bark dried, rubbed, and mixed with thick milk makes abscesses break open when laid upon them like a plaster. The dried bark of the roots rubbed in water and drunk provokes the monthly periods in women and drives out the births <note>the placenta</note> if one drinks somewhat richly of it. The rubbed flower, boiled in coconut oil, stills the headache and pain of the eyes from heat; they also soften the pain of gout if one smears with it. The same is done by the oil in which these flowers have been soaked for forty days. The oil pressed out of the kernels expels the bloatedness of the body from winds <note>flatulence</note> when smeared on from the outside. The flowers distilled give a fragrant water which one drinks against fainting and to strengthen the heart.

AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. Chapter XXII.

# CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO.

->*Wild Sampacca. Forest Tsjampacca.*<-

This wild *Sampacca* <note>original Latin: *Sampacca silvestris*</note> bears a trunk more upright and taller than the domestic variety; otherwise, in its foliage and manner of growth, it agrees with it. Its branches, however, are more erect, and the leaves are larger and broader—eight or nine inches long and four finger-widths wide. They are a deeper green with fewer ribs than the common variety, softer to the touch, and the younger leaves are almost downy on the underside, as are the small branches and leaf-stalks. When crushed, they breathe out the scent of the flowers; they have a bitterish taste and dye the water reddish when infused after being crushed. When dried, these leaves retain their green color, whereas the common ones turn brown.

The flowers agree entirely with those of the preceding variety, except that the petals are broader, whitish, and straw-colored, with a weak scent. However, if the tree is cultivated, its flowers pour forth a more penetrating and, as it were, luxurious scent, though still less than the domestic kind. The pistil of these is shorter and broader, but the fruit-bearing cluster with its berries is similar to the common one. The seeds enclosed within are uncertain in number, ranging from two up to seven, and are not as red as in the former variety, though they are a bright red when ripe.

Another species of this wild tree occurs which bears yellowish-green flowers, otherwise agreeing in form with the previous one; the scent of these, however, is faint. Its trunk yields a soft and flexible wood of a dark lemon-yellow color when fresh or when soaked; it breathes out the scent of an ointment, not at all unpleasant, almost like Laurel Oil <note>Latin: *Olei Laurini*</note> or the ointment of *Diapompholigos* <note>a traditional cooling salve made from zinc oxide</note>.

**Name.** In Latin, *Sampacca silvestris* <note>Wild Sampacca</note> and *Alba* <note>White</note>. In Malay, *Tsjampacca Utan* <note>Forest Champaca</note> and *Puti* <note>White</note>; it must, however, be distinguished from the domestic White *Sampacca* described in the preceding chapter.

**Location.** It occurs rarely in the Amboinese forests and shady places, mostly in the Hitoe region <note>a peninsula on Ambon Island</note> and around Larique. It can also be cultivated in gardens, where it does not reach a greater height than the domestic *Sampacca*, but the scent of the flowers is heightened there.

**Usage.** The wood of this tree is indeed soft and can be easily worked, yet it is durable and does not easily suffer cracking; however, it cannot be well polished. Gun-stocks <note>the wooden frames of muskets</note> are fashioned from it, as well as other smaller items pertaining to joinery. It preserves the scent of ointment for a very long time, especially if it is kept enclosed.

Its younger leaves, crushed and soaked in water until it acquires a red color, are dripped into the eyes by the Amboinese to make the vision clear.

---

In *Rumphius's* Appendix, these notes are added:

Two trees are considered wild *Sampacca*: the first is the common white one found in the forests. The other is the Mountain *Sampacca* <note>Latin: *Sampacca montana*</note> described in the following chapter.

1. *White Sampacca* or *Tsjampacca Poeti*: this bears a taller and straighter trunk than the domestic one; the rest is as in the text.

This flower offers no peculiar use, since it is of a weak scent. The younger leaves, slightly crushed and soaked in water until it turns reddish, are dripped into the eyes by the Amboinese to increase the sharpness of the eyes and make them clear.

# XXII. CHAPTER.

->*The Wild Tsjampacca Tree.*<-

The wild *Tsjampacca* has a straighter and taller trunk than the tame <note>domestic</note> one, otherwise very similar in leaves and growth, though the branches grow more straight upright. The leaves are somewhat larger and broader, eight and nine inches long, four fingers wide, a darker green, with fewer ribs than the common kind, softer to the touch, and the young ones almost woolly on the underside, as are the young twigs. When rubbed, they smell more like the flowers, are bitter in taste, and dye the water reddish where they are laid after being bruised. The dried ones keep their greenness, whereas the common ones turn brown and die off.

The flower is altogether like the common one, except that the petals are somewhat broader, whitish in color like straw, with a faint smell; but when cultivated, it becomes stronger and more lush, though still yielding to the tame one. The middle small pillar <note>pistil</note> is somewhat shorter and broader, but the fruit-bearing cluster with its berries is most like the common one; the inner kernels are unequal in number, from two up to seven, not so red as the former, but light red when they are ripe.

One has yet a second wild sort, whose flowers tend from yellow toward green, otherwise similar in shape to the former; it becomes faint in scent. The trunk has a soft and tough wood inside, dark lemon-colored when it is fresh or soaked when dry; it has an ointment-like, yet not unpleasant smell, almost like the *Laurel Oil*, or the salve *Diapompholigos*.

**Name.** In Latin *Sampacca silvestris* and *Alba*. In Malay *Tsjampacca Utan* and *Puti*. Yet to be distinguished from the tame *Sampacca Puti* in the preceding Chapter.

**Place.** It is found little in the Amboinese forests and in shady places, mostly on the Land of Hitoe and around Larique; one can also plant it in gardens, where it becomes no taller than the common *Tsjampacca*, but the scent of the flower is improved.

**Usage.** The wood of this tree is indeed soft and lets itself be easily worked, yet durable, and does not crack easily, though one cannot polish it well. One makes stocks for muskets from it, as well as other small joinery. It retains its ointment-like smell very long, especially when it stands locked up.

The young leaves, somewhat bruised and soaked in water until it becomes reddish—this the Amboinese put into the eyes to clear the sight.

---

In the Appendix of *Rumphius* this was added:

For wild *Tsjampacca* two trees were held; the first is the common white one which one finds in the wild. The second is *Mountain Tsjampacca* described in the following Chapter.

1. *Sampacca Alba* or *Tsjampacca Poeti*. This has a taller and straighter trunk than the tame one. The rest is in the text.

One has no special use for this flower, because there is little scent to it. The young leaves, somewhat bruised and soaked in water until it becomes reddish, the Amboinese put into the eyes to clear the sight.

# CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO.

->*Wild Sampacca. Forest Tsjampacca.*<-

This wild *Sampacca* <note>original Latin: *Sampacca silvestris*</note> bears a trunk more upright and taller than the domestic variety; otherwise, in its foliage and manner of growth, it agrees with it. Its branches, however, are more erect, and the leaves are larger and broader—eight or nine inches long and four finger-widths <note>A "finger-width" or *digitus* was an informal unit of measurement approximately equal to 0.75 inches or 1.9 cm.</note> wide. They are a deeper green with fewer ribs than the common variety, softer to the touch, and the younger leaves are almost downy on the underside, as are the small branches and leaf-stalks. When crushed, they breathe out the scent of the flowers; they have a bitterish taste and dye the water reddish when infused <term>infused|The process of soaking plant material in water to extract its properties, similar to making tea</term> after being crushed. When dried, these leaves retain their green color, whereas the common ones turn brown.

The flowers agree entirely with those of the preceding variety, except that the petals are broader, whitish, and straw-colored, with a weak scent. However, if the tree is cultivated, its flowers pour forth a more penetrating and, as it were, luxurious scent, though still less than the domestic kind. The pistil <term>pistil|The central seed-bearing organ of a flower</term> of these is shorter and broader, but the fruit-bearing cluster with its berries <term>syncarp|A collective fruit, like a pinecone or a magnolia fruit, where many small fruits are fused together</term> is similar to the common one. The seeds enclosed within are uncertain in number, ranging from two up to seven, and are not as red as in the former variety, though they are a bright red when ripe.

Another species of this wild tree occurs which bears yellowish-green flowers, otherwise agreeing in form with the previous one; the scent of these, however, is faint. Its trunk yields a soft and flexible wood of a dark lemon-yellow color when fresh or when soaked; it breathes out the scent of an ointment, not at all unpleasant, alm<unclear>ost</unclear>...

# BOOK III. CHAPTER XXIII. AMBOINESE HERBAL. 203

# CHAPTER TWENTY-THREE.

### The Violet-Tree. *Caju Mera Banda*.

The elegant form of this tree and the delight of its flowers have earned it a place here, although it is an exotic tree and only a single specimen was observed by me in the year 1657 on the high island of Banda, near the small town of Lontor <note>original Latin: *Lonthoiram*</note>. It was a very tall tree, like a Tamarind tree or even taller, with a very thick trunk and rough, cracked bark, possessing a dense and wide-spreading crown.

Upon the branches, without any particular order, rose thin and straight leaf-stalks <note>original Latin: *rachides*</note> joined closely together, as in the *Blimbing Bulu* <note>The Bilimbi or cucumber tree, *Averrhoa bilimbi*</note>. Upon these were two rows of leaves opposite one another, with twelve or more pairs on each stalk. The leaves also had the shape of the aforementioned *Blimbing*, but they were narrower and more pointed at the top, like those of the *Cassia Fistula* <note>The Golden Shower tree</note>, though they are much smaller; they are pale green or yellowish on the upper side, and downy and pale yellow <note>original Latin: *gilva*</note> beneath.

Many of its flowers sprout together, sitting upon a long stalk at the ends of the branches, as if standing upon a single umbel <term>umbel|A flower cluster where the individual flower stalks grow from a common center, like the ribs of an umbrella</term>. Between the stalks of these flowers, scaly leaves grow out. The flower buds, before they open, are oblong like rosebuds, but smoother and of the same color.

The flower itself is composed of five petals, pale and rose-colored on the inside, bearing the shape of a large Violet or the flowers of the *Canna fistula*. In its center is located a curved little horn or a swollen and pointed pistil, brownish in color, from which pods or husks grow on other trees. Around it are located three other curved and twisted threads <note>original Latin: *stamina*</note>, which are also swollen and yellow in the middle. At the base of the flower, five other shorter threads appear. The scent of the flower is most pleasant, approaching that of a Violet. However, as far as I know, no fruits follow these flowers, at least on the tree in Banda. When it blooms—which was in the month of March in Banda—it is adorned with such copious flowers that from a distance it looks entirely like a rose bush, which offers an elegant spectacle to the eyes, but is even more pleasing to the nose, as it spreads a most delightful fragrance. Regarding its other properties and internal substance, I cannot add more, as its owner esteemed this tree too dearly to allow it to be cut.

<margin>Name.</margin>
To the Bandanese, its true name was unknown; they meanwhile called it *Caju Mero*, which is to say, "Red Tree." I give it the Latin name *Arbor Violaria*, or the Coromandel Violet-Tree. It remains to be investigated whether it is the same tree that is called *Senting* on Java.

<margin>Place.</margin>
As was said above, I found only a single tree in Lontor, located there on the mountain next to a certain citizen's house. As it was said, it had been previously planted there and brought by Javanese or Malay merchants, who always brought certain exotic trees to the older governors of this region so that they might sell their Mace or Nutmeg at a cheaper price. From this, this province abounds in various fruit-bearing trees more than the other neighboring islands. Others, however, told me that such trees are also found in great abundance on the Coromandel Coast <note>The southeastern coast of India</note>, and perhaps in other Malay and neighboring regions.

<margin>Use.</margin>
This tree was held in great esteem in Banda, since only a single one occurred in that whole region, and especially on account of its pleasant flowers, which the neighbors so greatly desired that they continually picked them for banquets, weddings, and other festive days. This often displeased the owner, who was a cranky fellow <note>original Dutch: *korzelig boost*</note>, so much so that he often wished to chop down the whole tree. However, he was prevented from doing so by constant discouragement and pleas, until at last he uprooted the whole thing, so that Banda was deprived of this dear and most rare gift. Whether this man's envy or the negligence of the Bandanese citizens (who could have easily propagated it by its branches) is more to be blamed, I leave for others to judge. Neither would be excused, if the custom of this age itself did not excuse them—an age that values no things unless they serve to increase the purse.

In that year, I brought three branches of this tree to Amboina and planted them there, two of which perished when...

# XXIII. CHAPTER.

### Violet or Red-Tree.

The beautiful form of this tree and the loveliness of the flowers has earned it a place here, although it is a foreign tree and only a single one was seen by me in the year 1657 in Banda, on the high island in the small town of Lontor. It was a very tall tree, like a Tamarind tree or quite as high, with a very thick trunk, rough and burst bark, and a dense and well-extended crown.

On the branches stood, without order and close behind one another, thin and straight twigs, like the *Blimbing Bulu*, and upon them small leaves in two rows directly opposite each other, in twelve and more pairs on each twig. The leaves were also like those of the aforementioned *Blimbing*, yet narrower and more pointed at the front, like those of the *Cassia Fistula*, although much smaller; light or yellow-green on top, and woolly and pale <note>original Dutch: *vaal*</note> underneath.

These flowers stand many together on long stalks, almost in a tuft <note>original Dutch: *dolle* (umbel)</note>, between which stalks at the ends of the branches, where they meet, stand various green and small leaves like scales. The buds of the flowers, before they open, are elongated like rosebuds, yet smoother and of the same color.

The flower itself consists of five petals, pale and rose-colored inside, fashioned like a large Violet or the flower of the *Canna fistula*. In the middle stands a curved little horn with a broad belly and a brown tip, from which the fruits or pods <note>original Dutch: *bouwen*</note> grow on other trees. Around it stand three other curved and twisted threads, also bellied and yellow in the middle; on the bottom of the flower one sees yet five other short threads. The scent of the flowers is very lovely, drawing toward Violets, but as far as I know, no fruits follow these flowers, at least on the Bandanese tree. When it blooms (which was the month of March in Banda), it stands so full of flowers that from afar it seems full of roses—a pleasant spectacle for the sight, but even more so for the smell, which it then spreads far from itself. Of its further qualities and internal substance I can write nothing more, because the owner held it all too dear to chop into it.

<margin>Name.</margin>
Among the Bandanese its right name was unknown; they called it provisionally *Caju Mero* (that is, "red tree"). I give it in Latin the name *Arbor Violaria*, or *Violaria Cormandelicæ*. It remains to be investigated whether it is the same as that which is called *Senting* on Java.

<margin>Place.</margin>
As said above, I found only one tree on Lontor, standing there on the mountain next to a citizen's house. As they said, it was brought there in former times by the Javanese or Malay merchants, who each time brought some strange trees to the old Regents of the land to find a better bargain for the Nutmegs or Mace, by which that province is better provided with all sorts of fruit trees than its neighbors until now. Others told me that similar trees were to be found abundantly on the Coromandel coast, and perhaps more in other Malay and nearer lands.

<margin>Use.</margin>
That tree was held in great esteem in Banda, because there was but a single one in the whole land, and because of its lovely flowers, for which the neighbors were so greedy that they continually took them for weddings and other feast days. This often vexed the owner (who was a cranky fellow) so much that he wanted to chop down the whole trunk, but was repeatedly talked out of it. Finally, he chopped it down anyway, and so Banda was robbed of one of its best rarities. Whether this man's envy or the Bandanese citizens' slovenliness (who could easily have propagated it with branches) is more to be blamed, I let others judge. They would both not be excusable, if the fashion of the present century did not itself excuse them—which regards no things that do not serve the purse.

I brought three branches of this tree with me to Amboina in the aforementioned year and planted them there...

...two had been ruined by sea-water, but the third grew elegantly. However, it met the same fate as its mother tree; for while it stood in a leased garden, the owner looked upon its flowers as greedily as a thief eyes the gallows <note>original Latin: *ac latro patibulum*</note>, and it was soon cut down.

Later, I understood that another such young tree could be found in a certain field near the same small town of Lontor, called Lackoy; whether it sprouted there spontaneously, or was recently propagated there by branches, is unknown to me.

->*In the Appendix, Rumphius wishes to substitute the* MOUNTAIN CHAMPACA *or* TSJAMPACCA GOENONG *for the* VIOLET TREE, *which is described there in the following manner.*<-

The true wild or mountain *Sampacca* <note>Champaca, a type of Magnolia</note> bears an upright trunk, taller than all those previously mentioned, and produces leaves similar to other *Sampacca* leaves, but rougher and not downy beneath; these are simple and solitary, sitting upon curved and knotty twigs. The flower grows solitary and is formed of nine petals, which are placed inward in three triangles, of which the three outermost serve as a lid. As long as the flower remains on the tree, it is yellow, but once plucked, the flowers soon turn brown, and their lower part becomes white; they have a scent approaching that of Medlars <note>original Latin: *Mespilos*, a small fruit related to hawthorns, eaten when overripe</note>.

From the middle tube grows a single fruit the size of a Plum <note>original Latin: *Pruni*</note>, but its upper part is slanted; externally it is rough and as if scaly or chaffy, but not bursting open, as in the fruits of the *Manoe* or *Chinese Pears*. When ripe, however, it opens itself, divided into about twenty cells, each of which contains a flat, red seed <note>original Latin: *officulum*</note> very similar to the fruits of the Small-leaved Coral-tree <note>original Latin: *Corallariæ Parvifoliæ*</note>, but thinner. Plucked fruits can hardly be kept whole for the space of 24 hours without cracking into many parts or segments according to the number of scales they show externally; each part represents a chamber inside, hollowed out like a small boat, in which the aforementioned reddish seeds are located, which are attached at their narrowest part by a small filament to a common central stalk.

The bark of the trunk is ash-colored, rough, fissured, and slimy, becoming yellowish on the inside. The wood is white and consists of longitudinal fibers, but it is not hard. If these trees are cut while fresh, they pour out a pleasant but faint scent, which disappears entirely in wood that has been cut down; thus, that sweet and pleasant odor is only observed in old and fallen trees, such as we found various examples of in the year 1693 around Alang and Hatoe in the remote mountains. These breathed forth a pleasant odor, but none of the inhabitants wished to show us a living tree, saying that they only gather the fragments and pieces of fallen trees from the forests for their wives, who prepare fragrant ointments from them. All those trees located behind the village of Soeli are younger trees, but the inhabitants said that the same wood from fallen trees was also used by their wives.

*Name.* In Latin I call it *Sampacca montana*. In Malay *Tsjampacca Utan*, or *Tsjampacca Goenong*, since the preceding white *Sampacca* is also considered a wild species. The people of Way and Soely call it *Pokor Coepan Waffi*; those of Alang, however, provided us with no other name than *Bour Hanit*, which is undoubtedly an error, since *Hanit* or *Hanet* is an entirely different tree described by us in the fourth book.

*Place.* It grows in high and windy mountains near the *Dammar* trees <note>Resin-producing trees of the genus *Agathis*</note> behind the villages of Way and Soely in the Elacka-Siaman mountains.

*Use.* Since this tree occurs so rarely and has not been well known until now, only its dry wood is used, which is sometimes collected from fallen trees in the high mountains. Some have acquired such wide planks from it that they have fashioned chests from them; however, since that wood was not of an elegant color, they used it for coffins <note>original Latin: *Sandapilas*</note>.

Our people <note>The Dutch colonists</note> valued it more highly and attempted to distill an oil from its small segments, which breathed a scent as strong as the leaves of the Kaffir Lime <note>original Latin: *Limonis Poerrut*</note>, but it yielded such a small quantity that it was hardly worth the effort. Another and better way is, if this...

->*In the Supplement, Rumphius desires that one substitute for the* VIOLET TREE *the* MOUNTAIN CHAMPACA, *or the* TSJAMPACCA GOENONG, *which is described there in the following manner.*<-

The true wild or mountain *Tsjampacca* grows a larger, straighter, and higher trunk than all the preceding ones; it has leaves like other *Tsjampacca*, yet stiffer and not woolly underneath, standing singly on curved and knotty twigs. The flower stands solitary, made of 9 petals standing within one another in 3 triangles, of which the three outermost are the cover; on the tree they are pale yellow, but the plucked ones soon become brown, and the bottom half remains white, with a scent like Medlars.

From the middle pillar grows a single fruit the size of a plum, yet the front corner stands somewhat crooked; from the outside somewhat rough and as if scaly. Yet not opening up, almost like the fruits of *Manoa* or *Chinese Pears*. The ripe one falls apart into about 20 little tubes, each hiding a flat and red grain, like the fruits of the *Corallaria Parvifolia*, but thinner. One can hardly keep the plucked fruits whole for a natural day <note>24 hours</note> before they burst into many pieces according to the number of scales they represent on the outside, and each shows a little chamber inside like a little boat, in which the mentioned light-red seeds hide, attached by the narrowest corner to a small thread to the middle pillar.

The bark is gray, rough, burst, and mossy, pale yellow on the inside. The wood is white and straight-grained, yet not hard. When one cuts fresh into these trees, one perceives a pleasant but weak scent, but in the cut-off wood, nothing at all. Therefore, that sweet and pleasant scent is sought only in the old and fallen trees. We found several such of a pleasant scent in the year 1693 near *Alang* and *Hatoe* far in the mountains, but none of the inhabitants knew or wanted to show us the growing tree, saying that they only fetched the fallen wood with chips and pieces out of the forest for their wives, to make fragrant salves from them. And all those that stand behind the village of *Soeli* are still young trees, but the inhabitants said that the same wood of fallen trees was also used by their wives.

*Name.* I call it in Latin *Sampacca montana*. In Malay *Tsjampacca Utan*, or *Tsjampacca Goenong*, because the preceding white *Tsjampacca* is also held to be a wild sort. Those of *Way* and *Soely* call it *Pokor Coepan Waffi*. Those of *Alangh* have given us no other name as yet than *Bour Hanit*, which is without doubt an error, since *Hanit* or *Hanet* is an entirely different tree, and described by us in the 4th book.

*Place.* It grows in the high mountains, where it is airy, and near the *Dammar* trees, behind the villages <note>original Dutch: *Negoryen*</note> of *Way* and *Soely* in the mountains of *Elacka-Siaman*.

*Use.* Because this tree is so rarely found, and until now is not thoroughly known, one has made do with the dry wood, of which one now and then finds a fallen tree in the high mountains. Some have obtained such wide planks from it that they have made chests from them, but because the wood was of no great appearance, they used this for coffins.

Our people have made a bit more work of it, and first sought to distill an oil from small-chopped wood, which was indeed powerful of scent, drawing toward the leaves of the *Kaffir Lime*, but so little came from it that it was not worth the trouble. Another...
