## CHAPTER TWENTY-FOUR.

### Lingoum: Anxana. Lingoa Tree.

Although this tree properly belongs among the timber woods used for building or beams, I have nevertheless chosen to place it here among the flowering trees on account of the remarkable flowers it bears, which are quite famous for their pleasing scent. Furthermore, its wood is worthy of being numbered among the fragrant trees because of its delightful odor. Three principal species of this tree are observed, varying among themselves, of which the first is called the *red*, the second the *white* (or "shaggy"), and the third the *stony* Lingoum <note>original: *saxatile*. This likely refers to a harder, denser variety growing in rocky soil</note>. In this chapter, we shall deal with the first two species.

The Red Lingoum, then, is a very tall forest tree, rarely consisting of a straight trunk, but most often a winding and thick one. At its lower part, it forms a large base consisting of "broad wings" <note>These are buttress roots, common in tropical trees for stability</note>, and above it often divides into two or three trunks. The bark is cracked and appears almost ragged, often overgrown with other parasitic herbs. The branches have a smooth, sappy, and supple bark like that of Willows. On these are situated straight sprigs arranged alternately in two rows, and upon them the leaves are placed in a similar manner, with one single leaf at the end.

These leaves are somewhat heart-shaped but without a notch at the base; they are round and wide at the back, but at the front they quickly taper to a point. They are very similar to the leaves of the *Canna fistula* <note>The Golden Shower tree or Purging Cassia</note>, but smaller—namely three or four inches long and two wide. They are woven with fine, parallel cross-ribs, are a youthful bright green, smooth, and present an elegant appearance.

On older trees, however, they are rounder at the front, shorter, and firmer. From the junction of the leafy sprigs, long clusters emerge, and on these many small flowers grow together, having the shape of a *Violet*. They are composed of three small petals, of which the widest and uppermost is bent outward, while the two lower ones stand opposite each other like two wings (or cheeks), covering ten stamens decorated with yellow anthers. These are closely joined together and are of a beautiful saffron-yellow color. They are tender and thus somewhat wrinkled, wilting quickly, but breathing forth a pleasant odor, exactly like the Yellow Wallflower <note>original: *Leucojum luteum*</note>, though this scent is not as lasting.

These flowers sit in a small green calyx, and their stalks have small "knees" (joints) at their origin, as do the sprigs on the branches. The taste of the leaves is grassy, and when chewed, they are somewhat slimy. After the flowers, the fruits grow on the same clusters in the form of thin discs, resembling a dried leaf more than a fruit. They are a bit smaller than an Imperial Taler <note>A large silver coin of the era</note>, but on one side they have a protruding angle or short point, and near the stalk, one edge forms a curve; they are somewhat hollowed like a spoon. Around the edges, these fruits are thin like a skin, but near the middle they are double, bulging, and wrinkled with certain raised veins; they are dry and hard. In this belly or fold, one finds two or three cells in which are placed as many oblong seeds, which are yellowish-gray, smooth, and hard, resembling the seeds of Cucumbers. However, at one corner they are wide and have a "navel" (hilum) like a bean, wherein...

# AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. Chapter XXIV.

...on one side they are wide and indented, like beans; within these is hidden a green substance divisible into two segments.

The wood of this tree exhibits various textures and colors; for beneath the sappy bark one finds a white wood, two or three fingers thick, though it is not this thick everywhere nor does it always appear so. In certain places, especially in the "wings" <note>botanical: buttress roots</note> and the roots, red wood appears immediately beneath the bark, hidden under a thin layer of white substance. Further inward, the substance is of a blood-red color, so similar to Red Sandalwood <note>original: *Sandalo rubro*</note> that it can hardly be distinguished, except that *Lingoum* consists of coarser fibers. This wood is difficult to split through the middle because it is quite tangled, twisted with various fibers and knots; for this reason, it must primarily be worked with a saw and planed diagonally. If it comes from old trees, it can eventually be smoothed and polished, but the worst quality is that this wood does not yield large pieces of a single uniform color; if one goes deeper toward the center, it acquires a white color again and is soft and decayed, or entirely hollow.

The scent of the freshly worked wood is aromatic and pleasing, very closely resembling Yellow Sandalwood <note>original: *Sandalo Citrinum*</note>, or even more so the wood called *Caju Lacca* <note>Lakawood, *Dalbergia parviflora*</note>, which, although it is a climbing plant, has a great affinity with this *Lingoum*. The best pieces of this wood are gathered from the buttress roots cut near the base, and from a medium-sized tree, quite sturdy posts and beams can be formed, since its heartwood possesses a solid substance.

In very old trees, pieces of this wood are found with a bright reddish color, elegantly striped and solid, and so oily that when placed near a fire they "sweat" oil, just as Eaglewood <note>original: *Agallochum*</note> does. Its scent is much more pleasing than that of the rest of the tree's wood; if the latter is burned, it yields little or no oil and scent, but gives off a copious and sharply stinging smoke.

These pieces are often so elegantly variegated that they represent, as it were, a flame with its smoke; such pieces are greatly sought after by the Malays and Macassareans, who fashion them into weapon sheaths <note>referring to the *kris*, a traditional wavy-bladed dagger</note>. These can be polished quite well, but they do not keep their reddish and coral-like color for long, as when dry they tend toward a brown and dark reddish color. Such segments are also observed around the bark where the trunk has split and is continually struck by the sun's rays, which draw the oiliness to these parts and make them blackish and seemingly scorched on the outside. Beneath this, the brown and then the bright red wood is hidden, everywhere so oily that the aforementioned oil sweats out of it at the fire. I have often found such trees on stony and steep shores, whose front roots were splashed by sea water and in turn scorched by the sun’s rays, but the rear roots—or those situated toward the land—were not so at all, as they were covered by other plants. In these I observed that those former roots were elegantly red, oily, and fragrant, from which I concluded that the heat of the Sun draws the oiliness of this tree into those parts and concentrates it there. For in other trees also possessing hollowed roots on the shore, likewise copiously splashed by sea water but little disturbed by the solar rays, almost no red or oily wood, or very little, was to be found.

The second type, the white or soft *Lingoum*, which is the most common, is similar to the former in its manner of growth and form, but its leaves are more oblong and larger, more closely resembling the leaves of the Purging Cassia <note>original: *Canna Fistula*; likely *Cassia fistula*, the Golden Shower Tree</note>, being over four and five inches long, and two or two and a half wide. Its flowers, fruit, and seeds are very similar to the former, except that the fruits are larger than an Imperial coin <note>Latin: *inperiali*; Dutch: *Ryxdaalder* — a large silver coin roughly the size of a modern silver dollar</note>, yellowish-grey, and their protruding edge is wider and larger; the seeds have a green marrow inside. In outward appearance, this tree can hardly be distinguished from the former; the greatest difference lies in the wood, which in this species is of two kinds. The first is citrine or yellow, and at its outer edges and around the knots it bears certain red spots, which are often so large that it might be mistaken for the first species. However, this wood is much more spongy and consists of coarser fibers, hardly ever to be split lengthwise because its veins run diagonally and are tangled together; it is difficult to work with saws and other instruments, and it can never be polished. The other kind is of a yellowish-grey mixed with a little redness,

similar to the former,

<column-break/>

inside sits a greenish little creature <note>referring to the germ or embryo of the seed</note> that one can divide into two parts.

The wood is very uneven in substance and color, for first, under the sappy bark, one has a white wood, two and three fingers thick, and even that not everywhere; for in some spots one finds immediately under the bark, especially on the wings <note>buttress roots</note> and roots, a red wood. Under this white sapwood, somewhat further inward, one finds a blood-red wood, so like the red Sandalwood that one can hardly distinguish them, except that the *Lingoo* is somewhat coarse-grained. This wood splits very difficultly in length, for it is tangled, fibrous or windy, and knotty; therefore one must work it mostly with the saw and plane it crosswise. Nevertheless, if it is from old trees, it can finally be worked smooth and polished; but the worst thing about this wood is that one cannot get large pieces of one color from it, for immediately toward the inside it becomes paler again, like a baked brick, the heart being furthermore whitish, soft, and decayed, or entirely hollow.

The smell of the freshly worked wood is spicy and lovely, very nearly like white Sandalwood, or even closer, like the wood called *Caju Lacca*, which, although being a rope-like plant <note>a climber or liana</note>, has great fellowship with the *Lingoo*. The best pieces are hewn from the wings next to the root, and from medium-sized trees one can also have solid posts and beams, for in these the heart is still firm of substance.

On the very old trees one also finds pieces of this wood, light red in color, beautifully veined, solid, so fat <note>oily</note> that when held to the fire, they sweat out oil, just as the Eagle-wood does, the scent being moreover much more pleasant than in the other wood of the tree, which in burning gives off no or little oil and scent, but a sharp biting smoke.

These pieces are sometimes so beautifully veined that one can speculate a great fire with a swirling smoke therein; such pieces the Malays and Macassareans greatly seek to make kris-sheaths from. They allow themselves to be polished reasonably well, but do not keep their coral-red dye long, and fade to a brown-red. Such pieces are also found around the bark where the trunk is split and constantly touched by the Sun, which pulls the oiliness to these spots, making them black and burnt on the outside, under which the brown, and thereafter the light-red wood lies; yet everywhere so fat that the aforementioned oil sweats out at the fire. I have found such trees on stony and steep beaches, whose front roots were splashed by the salt water and by turns burnt by the hot Sun, but the rear or more landward ones not at all, as they were covered with some brush; from which I noticed that the first roots were beautiful red, fat, and sweet-smelling, and from that concluded that the Sun's heat gathered the fatness in this tree together. For on other trees, which also stood with hollow roots on the beach, richly splashed by the Sea-water but little struck by the Sun, no or little red or fat wood was to be found.

The second. The white or soft *Lingoo*, being the most common, is most like the former in growth and shape; the leaves are somewhat more oblong and larger, coming closer to those of *Canna Fistula*, fully four and five inches long, two, and two and a half wide. Flowers, fruits, and seeds are as on the former, except that the fruits are larger than a Rixdollar <note>a large silver coin</note>, light-fallow, and the protruding corner is somewhat broader and larger, and the seeds have a green marrow inside; yet in outward appearance one can hardly distinguish these trees, the most notable difference being situated in the wood, which in this sort is of two kinds. The first is pale yellow and has on the sides and by the knots some red spots, sometimes so large that one takes it for the first kind; yet this wood is much more porous and coarse-grained, hardly or never splitting straight, because the veins run diagonally through each other, difficult for saws and planes, and never lets itself be worked smooth. The second is of a yellowish-grey, mixed with little or no red, otherwise like the former, both of a reasonable and solid heart, surrounded on the outside with a white sapwood,

# III Book. Chapter XXIV. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...otherwise similar to the former, and both bear a sufficiently solid heart, which is covered on the outside with a white texture, from which it serves better for coarser mechanical works than the red.

Furthermore, all species of *Lingoo* <note>The Narra tree</note> have this property: that from the wounded bark, especially of the branches and where it is smooth, they exude a thin and bright red sap, which soon thickens into a dark red and soft gum, like thick blood or an opaque Ruby or Garnet <note>original: *Pyropi*</note>. This tree is also so luxuriant and vigorous that not only do its branches take root if they touch the ground, but even large segments of the trunk, if cast away in the forests, send out so many branches on all sides that they form a thicket within a year; for this reason, these branches are suitable for garden hedges. However, they have this drawback: if they are committed to the earth, they usually produce white ants <note>termites</note>.

The flowering time is mostly in the months of August and September, when the red species in particular is so laden with flowers that the whole tree from a distance resembles a single yellow flower, and it spreads a pleasant odor everywhere. The fruits ripen from February until April.

**Name.** The first species is called in Latin *Lingoum Rubrum* <note>Red Lingoo</note>; however, the general Malay name is *Anxana*, which the Chinese pronounce *Angsela*. The most common and best-known name is *Lingoo* and *Lingoa*, and specifically for the first species, *Lingoa Mera* <note>Red Lingoa</note> and *Lingoa Bonga* <note>Flower Lingoa</note>, because this red species produces many flowers; others, however, call the first soft species *Lingoa Bonga*, which is red at the edges. By the people of Ternate it is called *Lingo*. By those of Makassar, *Pattene*. By the Amboinese, *Nala kiri*, from the red color similar to the *Kiry* bird <note>the Red Lory</note>; by the Malays, *Noeri* or *Loeri*. The Bugis people call it *Tsjendana*, confusing it with Sandalwood out of ignorance, perhaps due to the common scent of these woods; just as some Makassarese call every *Lingoo* *Tsjampagga* <note>Champaca-scented</note> because of its pleasant and rose-like scent. In Bima it is called *Narra*; in Timor, *Sana* and *Na*.

The second species is called *Lingoum molle* <note>Soft Lingoo</note>. In Malay, *Lingo Puti* <note>White Lingoo</note>, and *Gabba Gabba* <note>named for its resemblance to sago palm stalks</note>, and *Lingo-Parampuan* <note>Female Lingoo</note>: in Amboinese, *Nala Uppar* and *Nala Uppal*, meaning the same thing—not because the wood is so soft, but because it is rough like the spongy *Gabba Gabba* and cannot be easily polished.

**Place.** All the Amboinese islands produce this wood quite abundantly; it is found in all lighter forests. It also grows better in lower areas or on slopes than in the high and cold mountains, where it is rarely found. Furthermore, it is known throughout all of maritime India <note>South and Southeast Asia</note>, from Malacca through Sumatra, Java, and Makassar to the Moluccas; according to the account of the Chinese, it also occurs in the southern part of China, where it is called *Tjobet Zutt*.

**Use.** Both these woods are in great use for timber and cabinetry <term>original: *scriniaria opera*; the construction of chests and fine furniture</term>, so that they are numbered among the principal building woods of these islands, from which posts, beams, and planks are formed—though with a certain distinction. For the red wood is quite solid, but it does not yield large pieces because its heart is spongy and hollow; thus it is mostly sought after for chests, door frames, and other cabinetry.

From the white and pale species, sufficiently wide planks can be formed, but as said, they cannot be well polished, and if handled, they often emit splinters; thus they are difficult to plane and always retain rough spots. If the red wood is smoothed, it must be polished with its own shavings and rubbed vigorously with scraps, and then with a woolen cloth after being lightly coated with wax; thus it preserves its red and coral color for a long time. If over time it becomes blackish or dark red, it must be rubbed again with the rough *Ampelii* leaves <note>the leaves of the Sandpaper Tree, *Ficus ampelas*</note> and polished in the aforementioned manner.

If these woods are worked, they breathe a pleasant scent, especially the second kind, which is yellowish and mixed with red. Chests, boxes, and similar items retain this scent for a very long time if kept closed, so that this wood might be taken for Yellow Sandalwood. Furthermore, all *Lingoo* woods have this property: namely, if water—and especially seawater—is poured over it, the water immediately takes on a blue-green color <note>The wood contains a fluorescent chemical that reacts with water</note>. I believe the water acquires the color from this, not the wood; and all linens, if they are damp when they touch this wood, [are likewise dyed].

<column-break/>

and therefore more suitable for coarse woodwork than the red.

Furthermore, all *Lingoo* species have these further properties: that from the wounded bark, especially on the branches, or where it is smooth, a thin and light-red sap flows out, which soon sets into a dark, red, and soft gum, like clotted blood or dark Rubies. Likewise, such a luxuriant and growing nature resides in this tree that not only do all the branches grow out if they touch the earth, but even entire sections of the trunk, if they remain lying in the forest, sprout on all sides with so many branches that they make a thicket within a year; and therefore they are very suitable for garden stakes. However, these posts also have this fault: when they stand in the ground, they commonly generate white ants.

The flowering time usually falls in August and September, when the red species in particular hangs so full of flowers that the entire tree from afar appears as one yellow flower, and its pleasant scent is widely spread. The fruits are seen ripe from February until April.

**Name.** The first sort is called in Latin *Lingoum Rubrum*. The general name in Malay is *Anxana*, which the Chinese pronounce *Angsela*, but the most common and best-known name is *Lingoo* and *Lingoa*, and specifically the first sort *Lingoa Mera*, and *Lingoa Bonga*, because this red sort bears the most flowers; however, others call *Lingoa Bonga* the first sort of the soft species, which is red at the edge. In Ternate, *Lingo*. In Makassar, *Pattene*. In Amboinese, *Nala kiri*, from the red color of the bird *Kiry*. By the Malays, called *Noeri* or *Loeri*. The Bugis people call it *Tsjendana*, through ignorance confusing it with Sandalwood, perhaps because of the common scent, just as some Makassarese call all *Lingoo* *Tsjampagga*, because of its good or flower-like scent. On Bima, *Narra*; on Timor, *Sana* and *Na*.

The second sort is called *Lingoum molle*. In Malay, *Lingo Puti*, and *Gabba Gabba*, and *Lingo-Parampuan*; in Amboinese, *Nala Uppar*, and *Nala Uppal*, all of one meaning: not so much because the wood is soft, but because it is rough like spongy *Gabba Gabba*, and does not allow itself to be worked smooth.

**Place.** In all the Amboinese islands it is reasonably common in all kinds of forests, especially those that are somewhat light; it also prefers to grow in the lowlands or on the slopes of mountains rather than on high and cold mountains, where it is seldom found. Furthermore, it is mostly known through all of maritime India, from Malacca onwards, through Sumatra, Java, Makassar, to the Moluccas. According to the Chinese, it would also be found in the southern parts of China and named there *Tschet Zutt*.

**Use.** Both these woods are in great use for carpentry and cabinetry, so that they are to be counted among the principal building woods of these islands, from which posts, beams, and planks are made—though with some distinction: for the red has indeed firm wood, but one cannot get thick pieces from it because of the soft and bulging heart; therefore it is mostly worked into chests, moldings, and other cabinetry.

From the pale and white species one can indeed get broad planks, but these (as said) are not easy to work smooth, being very splintery when handled and difficult to plane, always retaining some rough spots. The red, being planed smooth, must be polished by rubbing strongly with its own sawdust and shavings, and finally with a woolen cloth, having first rubbed a little wax gently over the wood, by which it retains its coral-red color for a long time. If it has now become dark-brown or blackish over time, one must rub it over again with the rough leaves of *Ampelaas* and polish it as before.

In working, these woods give off a lovely scent, especially the second, which is yellowish and mixed with red. The chests, cabinets, and drawers retain this scent very long if they are kept well closed, so that one would take them for yellow Sandalwood. All the *Lingoo* sorts also have this property: that some water, especially salt water, being poured thereon, immediately becomes Spanish-green <note>A vibrant blue-green color</note> in hue. I say the water, and not the wood; and all the linen-work which, being damp, touches it, is also so dyed, which...

they take on a similar color, which especially occurs in the following *Lingoo Batu* <note>Stone Lingoo wood</note>, but less so in *Lingoo Mera* <note>Red Lingoo wood</note>.

Among the three types of *Lingoo* wood, the red is the most elegant for cabinetry; *Lingoo Gabba-Gabba* <note>The most common variety, named after the pithy stalks of the sago palm</note> is the most common, most fragrant, and largest; while *Lingoo Batu* is the most durable. For garden hedges, stakes, and similar posts where growth is desired, they are used everywhere; for what is planted in such a way grows quickly and lushly enough, but it rarely produces flowers until it has grown into a massive tree. This planted tree almost never bears fruit, yet I have seen branches planted in August and September—which are the flowering months for this tree—laden with flowers before they had even produced leaves; however, this happens only once, and thereafter it yields no flowers until it is a large tree.

Among the Malays and Macassarese, the flowers of this tree are held in great esteem, and they weave them into their hair; for this reason, the tree is planted near houses, and its flowers are sold in the marketplace. The bark of the tree, boiled in water, is much used for the porridge called *Papeda* <note>A staple starch dish made from sago</note>, which is thickened by it and acquires a solid substance. If lime water is sprinkled on boards of this wood, it turns yellow, just as seawater acquires a blue-green color <note>original: *glaucum*; Dutch: *Spaansch-groen* (Spanish green)</note>; from this, it is evident that certain pigments could undoubtedly be prepared from this wood if experiments were conducted. Beneath these trees, many pits often appear, dug by wild boars who greedily seek out the roots and young shoots.

The Malays, as mentioned, choose the reddest pieces of this wood which are most elegantly veined, from which they fashion the sheaths of their *kris* <note>traditional daggers</note>; they buy these at a high price if the veins run according to their liking, for they seek nothing but the most elegantly veined wood for this work. The common folk of Ambon and Hoëamohel use the most resinous <note>original: *pinguissima*, literally "fattest" or "most oily"</note> pieces of this wood for incense, in place of Eaglewood or *Caju Lacca* <note>scented woods used for fumigation</note>, with which it very much agrees. They know how to select such resinous pieces in both the white and red *Lingoo*, provided the trees were properly exposed to the Sun; these pieces must be well-cleaned of the adjacent leaner wood which yields no oil, even if it is of the same color, for that gives off a sharp and irritating smoke. Nor should this wood be used alone, but mixed with other incense.

In the outer segments that lie next to the charred bark, transparent veins often appear, as in true *Calambac* <note>High-quality Aloeswood</note>. These yield a brittle wood, but they are very resinous and have a most penetrating odor, which they gradually lose if kept for a long time. If a decoction of that bark is used as a gargle, it cures mouth sores <note>aphthas</note> and cleanses the mouth. The red sap or gum flowing from the trunk performs the same function; taken internally, it cures diarrhea. The best wood used for posts and other building purposes is found in the forests where it lies fallen, where the outer bark and other spongy substances have rotted away—especially of the red species—from which posts are fashioned that last ten years in the ground.

Fresh leaves of this tree crushed with a little salt, and their juice strained through a cloth, cure *Lappar Garam* <note>literally "Salt Hunger," a skin condition</note>, which is a serious skin malady where the skin becomes red and rough, variegated with small pustules and infested with itching, which is nevertheless less than in Herpes or *Koecurap* <note>Ringworm</note>.

Its tender leaves, handled a little with the hands until they become limp, are applied to ulcers and boils <note>original: *furunculis*</note> to make them ripen. These same leaves, crushed together with a piece of glowing charcoal and smeared on the forehead, cure headaches arising from heat.

On the shore of Combello, I found a trunk of red *Lingoo* so close to the sea that it was continuously sprayed by the tide, about five feet high; its roots were somewhat fixed in the ground, but it was entirely stripped of its bark, gray on the outside but red throughout the interior. I acquired various pieces of this and elegant small boards, some of which were entirely red, others of a bright red or glowing color, but all elegantly veined and solid, and so resinous as if they were pieces of hardened wax. Other segments of it, however, which were situated closer to the land and not splashed by seawater, were eaten away by white ants <note>termites</note>. From the white parts of white *Lingoo*, if they are not yet mature, nothing can be fashioned...

<column-break/>

...especially the following *Lingoo Batu* does, but *Lingoo Mera* the least.

Thus, among the three types of *Lingoo*, the red species is indeed the most beautiful for work, *Lingoo Gabba-Gabba* the most common, most fragrant, and largest, and *Lingoo Batu* the most durable. For garden stakes, or *paggars*-wood <note>fence wood</note>, and similar posts that one wishes to sprout, it is used everywhere; however, that which is planted this way shoots up quickly, but one rarely sees it bear flowers until it has become a large tree. The planted tree almost never bears fruit; nevertheless, I have seen stakes planted in August and September—being the flowering months of this tree—that were full of flowers before they had leaves, but that happens only once, for after that they bloom no more until they have grown large.

Among the Malays and Macassarese, the flowers are in great esteem for wearing in the hair, which is why the trees are also cultivated near houses, and the flowers are sold at the *passer* <note>market</note>. The bark of the tree is very commonly boiled in water, with which *Papeda* is prepared, which becomes stiff and gluey thereby. If lime water comes upon these planks, it turns yellow, just as salt water turns blue-green <note>original: *Spaansch-groen* (Spanish green/Verdigris)</note>, from which it appears that one could undoubtedly extract some dye from this wood, if it were ever investigated. One often sees many holes and pits made under these trees, which the wild pigs do, who are greedy for the roots of this tree, as well as for the young shoots.

The Malays, as said, seek the reddest pieces that are beautifully veined to make their *kris*-sheaths from, paying reasonably dearly for them if the veins only run to their liking, for they want no other than beautifully veined wood for such work. The common people of Ambon and Hoëamohel use the most resinous <note>literally "fattest"</note> pieces for incense, in place of *Agal-wood* or *Caju Lacca*, with which it most corresponds, and they know how to find such pieces in both the white and the red *Lingoo*, provided the trees stand well to the Sun. These pieces must be carefully cleaned of all the lean wood from which no oil comes, even if it is of the same color, for that gives off a sharp-biting smoke, and one must then not use it alone, but mix it with other incense.

In the outermost pieces, which lie next to the burnt shell, one sometimes finds shining veins, as in the upright *Calambac*. These are brittle of wood, but the most resinous and strongest in scent; however, being long kept, they lose much of their loveliness. A decoction made of the bark, used to rinse the mouth, cures the thrush and cleanses the mouth. The same is also done by the red juice or gum flowing from the trunk, which also, taken internally, cures the belly-run <note>diarrhea</note>. The best wood that one wants to use for posts and timber-work is that which one finds in the forests fallen of itself, and of which the outer sapwood or white wood has rotted away, especially of the red species, from which posts made stay good in the earth for ten years.

Various leaves rubbed with a little common salt and strained through a cloth cure *Lappar Garam*, a troublesome accident when the skin becomes red and rough, with small pimples and itching, though less than with *Herpes* or *Koecurap*.

The young leaves, handled a little with the hands until they become limp, are laid upon sores and boils to make them ripen. These same leaves, rubbed together with a piece of a glowing coal and smeared on the forehead, cure the headache that comes from heat.

On the beach of Combello, I found a stump of a red *Lingoo*, so close on a stony beach that it was continually washed by the sea at high water, about five feet high, with its roots still somewhat standing in the ground, entirely robbed of its bark, and turned gray on the outside, but red throughout the inside. From this, I obtained several pieces and beautiful small planks, some entirely red, some light-red and fire-colored, yet all beautifully veined, massive, and as resinous as if they were pieces of some hardened wax; however, many pieces that stood somewhat landwards and were not washed by the seawater were eaten through by the white ants. unless they are quite old, nothing can be made from them, as their wood is too soft, which even surrounds the entire trunk like a skin <note>original: *instar pelliculæ*; Dutch: *als een spint* (like sapwood)</note> three fingers thick, while the inner wood always has a dark color. Portions of the red wood, when chewed in the mouth, release a pleasant and aromatic scent and flavor, rivaling *Caju Lacca* <note>A resinous wood, likely *Croton laccifer*</note>, which again reveals the great affinity between these trees, although the first is a tree and the other a climbing shrub. The red *Lingoum* growing around Malacca and Pera is not hollow, but mostly solid, and so broad there that planks of three or four feet can be formed from it. It is not commonly permitted for the common people to cut it, except for the tax farmers <note>licensed contractors</note>, who sell it to the Company's merchants <note>The Dutch East India Company (VOC)</note>; they identify the solid trees by striking them with an axe and listening for a sound that is not hollow. The people of Ternate use red *Lingoo* in place of red Sandalwood, especially to stop dysentery, as it produces a good effect in this disease.

The sap of this tree, dripping into flat dishes, is dried in the sun or over a fire, and takes on the form and appearance of dried blood; its smallest fragments are as transparent as Rubies <note>original: *Robini*; Dutch: *robyntjes*</note>, as is mostly done in Java, where these trees are not as frequent as in Amboina. This gum has a powerful astringency, and at the same time it cleanses; for a small piece of it taken into the mouth contracts it like Alum, and cleanses as purely as *Acacia* or *Catechu* <note>An extract from acacia trees used for tanning and medicine</note>.

In the eastern part of Timor, in the Province of Ademantutu, a certain red *Lingoum* grows, which does not differ from the Amboinese variety, except that its wood at the buttresses <note>original: *alas*; Dutch: *vlerken* (wings)</note> and in the knots is a bright red, consisting of many intricate veins; when placed on coals, it releases a greasiness of the same color as the Amboinese kind. In Timor it is called *Naa* or *Sanda*. The Macassarese seek this wood greatly and call it *Tsjampaga Babyan*, from which they form elegant scabbards for their weapons <note>Specifically the *kris* or Malay dagger</note>, which preserve a pleasant scent for a long time; this, however, is gathered from the roots, not from the buttresses. Often it is red on the outside, while the inside is pale or yellowish. It would be no wonder if this red *Lingoum* were mistaken for red Sandalwood, since it is also brought from Timor, and until now it was unknown what kind of tree it was, until I compared it with our Amboinese tree, and found that the old *Lingoo* trees of Ceram and Amboina yield pieces just as elegant and oily as those from Timor. This elegantly red wood also occurs in Bima and is called *Narra* <note>The source of the name for 'Narra' wood, still a prized timber today</note>, which for a long time was considered a distinct wood by our people, but I find it to be nothing other than red *Lingoum*. The people of Bima make elegant chests and small boxes from it, consisting of many little drawers, and they sell the elegantly veined pieces to the Macassarese, who form elegant scabbards from them. The best pieces with the most beautiful flaming grain are found around the thick roots, of which I have seen planks over six feet long and three and a half feet wide, usually decorated with most elegant swirls and flames, which are kept as rarities.

That the ancient Romans likewise greatly sought after "Tiger," "Panther," and "Parsley" tables <note>original: *mensas Tigrinas, Pantherinas, & Apiatas*</note> is clear from Pliny, Book 13, Chapter 15, where he says that such precious tabletops were constructed from the roots of the *Oxycedrus* <note>Prickly cedar, also called *Thuja*</note> growing on Mount Atlas. They called them Tiger, Panther, or Parsley according to the varying run of the veins, flames, and spots; these were scarcely a foot in diameter and about four inches thick, and were sold for ten to fifteen sesterces—ten sesterces being equivalent to nineteen and a half weights of silver, or three hundred and twelve and a half Imperial Rix-dollars—such a table being part of the furniture of *Marcus Tullius Cicero*.

On younger *Lingoi* saplings, I have often found curled leaves beset with pale green nodules and warts, herb-like in substance on the outside, but woody on the inside, and within them lurked a small borer <note>original: *teredo*; Dutch: *wormtje*</note>, such as occurs in oak galls. Some warts were adorned with a tiny leaf on top and could be very easily separated from the stems and leaves to which they clung.

Since, as was said above, the sap of *Lingoo* can be dried into blood-red pieces, many of our nation in Batavia were moved to believe that this is the true *Sanguis Draconis* <note>Dragon's Blood resin</note>, and they called this tree the "Dragon Tree"—an error I do not consider worth many words to refute.

<column-break/>

unless they are quite old, nothing can be made from them, because they have wood that is too soft, which, like sapwood, surrounds the entire trunk to a thickness of three fingers, the inner wood always being dark in color. The pieces of the red variety, when chewed in the mouth, give a lovely and spicy scent and taste, coming very close to *Caju Lacca*, from which one perceives once more that there is a kinship between these two trees, although one is a tree and the other a forest-rope <note>a liana or climbing vine</note>. The red *Lingoo* occurring around Malacca and Pera is not hollow, but mostly solid, and so broad there that planks of three to four feet wide can be obtained from it. The common man may not fell it, but only the tax farmers, who sell it to the Merchants of the Honorable Company. They recognize the solid trees when they strike them with an axe and they do not sound hollow. The Ternatans use the red *Lingoo* in place of red Sandalwood, especially to staunch the bloody flux <note>dysentery</note>, and find great benefit in it.

The sap running from these trees, placed in flat dishes, can be dried in the Sun or over a fire, becoming like dried blood; however, the smallest pieces remain clear, like little rubies, as is mostly done on Java, where these trees are not as abundant as on Amboina. This Gum has a powerful astringency, with a cleansing effect; for a small piece taken into the mouth draws it together as much as any Alum, and wipes as clean as any *Acacia* or *Catechu*.

On the Eastern part of Timor, in the Province of Ademantutu, there grows a kind of red *Lingoo* in no way different from the Amboinese, except that the wood at the buttresses and the knots is light red, with many tangled veins, giving off some oiliness on the coals of the same scent as the Amboinese; on Timor it is called *Naa* or *Sanda*. The Macassarese seek this wood much and call it *Tsjampaga Babyan*, to make beautiful kris-scabbards from it, which retain their good scent inside for a long time; however, they take it from the roots and not from the buttresses. It is also often red on the outside and pale or yellowish on the inside. It would be no wonder if this red *Lingoo* were taken for red Sandal, since it comes precisely from Timor and has been unknown until now what kind of tree it was, until I, comparing it with our Amboinese, found that I have found just as beautiful and oily pieces on old *Lingoo* trees on Ceram and Amboina as the Timorese wood was. Likewise, this wood is found beautifully red on Bima and called *Narra*, having long been considered a special wood by our Nation, but I find it to be nothing else than red *Lingoo*. The Bimanese make fine boxes and chests of it with many internal drawers, and such pieces as are beautifully veined they sell to the Macassarese to make kris-scabbards. The best pieces, which are most beautifully figured, are found around the thick roots, of which I have seen planks over six feet long and three and a half feet wide, generally decorated with beautiful whorls and flames, which are held as great rarities.

That the ancient Romans were also very fond of tables of marbled or figured wood appears from Pliny, book 13, chapter 15, where he says that from the roots of the Cedar tree (otherwise called *Oxycedrus* and *Thyia*) growing on Mount Atlas, such costly tabletops were made, which they named according to the variety of the veins, flames, and spots: *Tigrinas*, *Pantherinas*, and *Apiatas*. These, having scarcely a foot in diameter and being about four inches thick, were sold for ten to fifteen sesterces—the ten sesterces making about nineteen and a half pounds of silver, or three hundred twelve and a half Rix-dollars—this having been a piece of *Marcus Tullius Cicero's* household furniture.

I have sometimes found small curled leaves on young *Lingoo* saplings, beset with pale green knobs and warts, herb-like in substance on the outside, woody on the inside, and therein a small hard worm, such as one finds in Gall-apples. Some warts had a small leaf on top, and they were easily pulled off from the stems and leaves where they hung.

Because, as said above, the sap of *Lingoo* can be dried into blood-red pieces, many of our Nation in Batavia have been moved to believe that this is the genuine *Sanguis Draconis*, and have also called this tree the Dragon Tree, which error I do not deem worthy of refuting with many words.

# OBSERVATION.

This tree is called in the *Amsterdam Garden, part 1, page 213*, the Pod-bearing Indian Dragon Tree with Poplar leaves <note>original: "Draco Arbor Indica siliquosa Populi folio"</note>, where its illustration differs from this one by having fewer leaves on the rachis <note>The central stalk of a compound leaf</note>; it is the Javanese Angsana, a pod-bearing tree with fragrant yellow flowers, whose trunk and branches pour out a fluid like dragon's blood, according to *Cleyer*. *Grimm* also made mention of this in the *German Ephemerides, year 13, Observation 37*, as did *Ray* in his *History of Plants* <note>original: "Dendrol."</note>, *page 113*.

There are, however, various trees that pour out a red sap like blood, which were collected by *Valentijn* in the *History of Simple Medicines Reformed, page 265*, *Dale* in his *Pharmacology, page 297*, and *Pomet* on *page 259*. It is described under the name *Lingoa* by *Valentijn* on *page 215*.

## CHAPTER TWENTY-FIVE.

### Stone Lingoo. Lingo Batu.

The third species of Lingoo is the "stone" variety <note>Malay: *batu* means stone</note>, whose trunk is indeed tall, but curved and winding, bearing a pale yellow and fissured bark that hangs from the trunk in rags. The branches, leaves, and flowers mostly agree with the preceding species, except that the branches are knottier and harder; if one pays close attention, a difference also appears in the leaves, which in this species are smaller and rounder, though otherwise arranged in the same order on the stalks.

The fruits are twice as large as in the two prior species, four or five finger-widths broad, but otherwise of the same shape; they do not turn as black as those of the red species when they fall. The wood is whitish and spongy on the outside, but internally it is pale yellow or liver-colored when fresh; when dry, however, its substance becomes entirely pale yellow, consisting of fine fibers, hard and heavy, with a solid heart.

It can be cut and planed better than the previous types and takes a reasonably good polish, though it does not split straight along its length because its veins run obliquely and in a tangled manner. Around the edges and knots, it sometimes bears elegant red spots which, although not as resinous as in the red variety, nonetheless breathe a pleasant scent of Sandalwood when fresh. The wood also releases this scent when worked, though much more faintly than the previous kinds. The trunk of this species is not "winged" <note>lacking the wide buttress roots common in tropical trees</note> near the root, and the roots seek the earth more deeply. If any moisture or seawater touches this wood, or if pieces of it are soaked in water, it acquires an elegant blue-green <note>original: "glaucum"; Dutch: "Spaansch-groen" (Spanish green)</note> color; the previous species do this as well, but much more faintly, and sometimes not at all. Lime water sprinkled upon it turns yellow.

This wood is also hardy and vigorous by nature, but not as active as in the preceding types, and for this reason, it is not used as well for fences <note>Dutch: "paggers"</note>, posts, and similar things. Nevertheless, segments of it are often observed in the forests surrounded by sprouting branches on all sides, having grown into a shrub.

It blooms in October and November, at which time most of its old leaves fall; the fruits, however, remain on the tree for a long time, sometimes beyond a year, which is why few are found beneath the tree. This species is not as common as the previous ones and is of a wilder nature. It occurs nowhere except in stony places, both in the mountains and on the plains.

## XXV. CHAPTER.

### The Stone-Lingoa-Tree.

The third kind is the Stone-Lingoa, whose trunk is indeed high, yet not straight, but stands somewhat bowed and crooked, with a pale and torn bark, which hangs in rags around the trunk; the branches, leaves, and flowers mostly agree with the previous ones, except that the branches are somewhat harder and knottier, and if one looks closely at them, one can also see the difference in the leaves, which in this kind are somewhat smaller and rounder, otherwise standing in the same order on the twigs.

*The fruits are indeed twice as large as on both the previous ones, four and five fingers broad, otherwise of the same fashion, and do not become as black as those of the red one when they fall off. The wood is white and sappy on the outside, pale or liver-colored inside when fresh, but when dry, it dies off entirely pale, of a fine-threaded substance, hard, and heavy, with a massive heart.*

*It takes the plane and saw better than the previous ones, and allows itself to be worked reasonably smooth, yet in the length it also does not split straight, because its veins also run slanted and somewhat tangled. At the edges near the knots, it sometimes has some red spots, which are not as fatty as on the red one, nevertheless they also have a good Sandal-scent when they are fresh, as does also the wood when one works it, though much weaker than the previous ones; the trunk has no wings at the root, and the roots stand more in the earth. If any moisture or Seawater comes upon this wood, or if one lays the pieces in water, then it becomes a beautiful Spanish-green, which the previous kinds also do, yet much weaker, and sometimes not at all. The lime-water poured upon it becomes yellow.*

*It is also living and growing of nature, yet not so much as the previous ones, therefore it is also not used as well for fences or posts: Nevertheless one finds the pieces of the chopped-down trunks lying in the Forest, entirely covered with the shot-up branches, and become into a shrub.*

*It blooms in October and November, in which time most old leaves fall off, the fruits remain hanging long on the tree, and sometimes over a year, therefore one finds few of them under the trees. This kind is not as common as the previous ones, and wilder of nature. One finds it nowhere but on stony places, both on the mountains and in the flats.*

# CHAPTER TWENTY-SIX.

## Sea Bintangor. Bintangor Laut.

As beautiful as this tree is regarding its foliage and flowers, so disordered and squalid is its trunk, bark, and external appearance, since it has a peculiar way of growing, such that, if the ancient Poets had frequented these islands, it would have supplied them with material for a singular Metamorphosis <note>A transformation story like those in Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*</note>; for it seems like a farmer who seeks something, or strives to seek from the sea that which he loves, for its roots always run out only to the edges of the forests, nor do they ever extend themselves sideways a step beyond them, but with its trunk it leans out so much as if it were continually falling into the sea, which however never happens, since it is firm enough.

If the shores are steep and sloping, this tree is located obliquely and more upright; but if they are flat, it inclines so much that one can hardly run beneath it, and only the upper part of the trunk raises itself a little, so that its green crown extends just above the water and provides a pleasant sight, if we observe with what zeal this tree attempts, with either a fully or semi-inclined trunk, to look upon the sea water as if it wished to smell it, yet it preserves its crown so that it is not defiled by the water itself.

The tree itself is very vast, consisting of a trunk so thick that almost no other tree bears one similar in thickness, and this, as was said, is never upright, but always leans, and its bark is very thick, wrinkled, rough, and irregular, which is as filthy as the back of any shark <note>original: "Lamii" in Latin, "Haymans" in Dutch. Both refer to the rough, sandpaper-like skin of a shark</note>; for it is squalid, black, thick, and in its fissures something yellow appears like a gum, though rarely. It bears few major branches, but so large that each of these almost resembles a trunk; these however divide themselves into many other wrinkled and knotty branches, all of which bear a dense crown.

On the contrary, the leaves are the most elegant of all that can be found, usually a palm's length or eight inches long, four or five fingers wide, in younger trees longer and wider, a joyful green, or yellowish-green, more yellow underneath, very smooth, thick, and firm like parchment; rounded at the top and slightly split or bifid, more narrowed at the bottom: The midrib protrudes from the lower part, where it is triangular and sharp, but not on the upper part of the leaf; furthermore, the leaves consist of parallel and thin, oblique veins woven through them so softly that they are hardly perceived by touch, which are positioned crosswise, four at a time, if they are counted.

The flower-bearing clusters sprout at the ends of the branches from the armpits of the leaves, huge and extended; on these sit the flowers, which are at first whitish little heads supported by long whitish stalks, resembling the flowers of European Apple trees, but larger, whose stalks are also positioned crosswise: These flowers are composed of nine or

with coarse veins, quite difficult to work, and not splitting along the length, but it gives nevertheless beautiful and wide planks for tables and chests, which being polished, show beautiful windings of veins, and are of uniform color, therefore they are with reason esteemed better than the red ones, if they did not have the fault that, touching moisture, they so easily turn green.

*Name.* In Latin *Lingoum Saxatile*, in Malay *Lingoo Batu*, not only because it grows on stony places, but because the wood is much harder and more massive than the previous ones; in Amboinese *Nala Pate*, *Nala Pata*, and *Nala Hatu*.

*Place.* It grows in all the Amboinese Islands, and the Moluccas, not so familiar by the dwellings of men, like the two previous ones, but in the Forests and mountains.

*Usage.* This kind gives the best timber for coarse work, beams, posts, and planks; this *Lingoo* sinks in the water because of its weight, which the others do not do.

# XXVI. CHAPTER.

## The Sea-Bintangor-Tree.

As beautiful as this tree is in leaf and flowers, so ugly is it in trunk, bark, and outward appearance, having therewith a rare manner of growing, such that, if the ancient Poets had been in these Lands, they would have found in it material for a rare Metamorphosis, for it seems to be a Countryman looking for something, or looking into the Sea for that which he loves, because it always stands with its root at the edge of the Forest, not daring to come a step beyond that onto the bare beach, and furthermore with its body hangs so far over the same into the Sea, as if it would fall at any moment, though there is no danger of it.

If the shores go down steeply, it stands slanted and more upright, but on flat shores it goes to lie in such a way that one can hardly crawl under it, and only the front part of the trunk does it right somewhat upwards, so that it keeps its youthful foliage just above the water; in short, it is pleasant to see with what zeal this tree endeavors, either with a whole or a half-bent and as if kneeling trunk, to look at the Sea water, as if it would smell it, and yet preserves its crown so that it is not splashed by the same.

It is a large wild tree, with a trunk as thick as one sees any others, as said, never standing straight up, but always leaning forward, with a very coarse, rough, and misshapen bark, as ugly as any shark's back <note>original: "Haymans rugge"</note> may be; filthy, black, thick, and hard, and in the cracks one sees something yellow, like a gum, though very rarely. It has few main branches, of which each can represent an entire trunk, but these divide themselves into many other rough knotty branches, all covered with a dense foliage.

The leaves on the other hand are of the most beautiful that one may find, generally a hand's length or eight inches long, four to five fingers wide, on the young trees they are longer and wider, youthful or yellow-green, yet yellower from below, very smooth, thick, and stiff, like Parchment: Rounded in front, or a little cleft, narrowing somewhat behind, the middle vein sticks out far below, where it is three-cornered and sharp, but not above; furthermore they are threaded crosswise with very fine and parallel small veins, which one can hardly feel, they stand against each other in fours in a cross.

The flower-bearing clusters come at the front of the branches, as if from the lap of the leaves; large and widely spread out, on them come the flowers, being first white buds on long stalks, very similar to the apple-blossom in Europe, but somewhat larger, with their stalks also in a cross, made of nine or ten snowy white, round, half-spherical, and

...or ten white, somewhat round, semi-hollowed and whole petals, representing the form of a smaller Rose; the two outermost of these are the largest, opposite which are two other crossed petals, and in their middle are five or six other smaller petals bent outward, whose hollow then rises again. The center of the flower is filled with very short stamens bearing saffron-colored anthers <note>the pollen-bearing parts of a flower</note>, such as are called "Anthers" in Roses, which are so tightly packed and full that the petals seem to bend outward; these small stamens hide in their midst a somewhat round and reddish little head <note>the ovary</note>, upon which is placed a whitish pistil, which grows into the fruit. The odor of the flowers is most pleasant, approaching that of white Lilies, which they preserve for 24 hours.

The fruits are perfectly spherical, in the shape and size of a small round Plum, or a musket ball, very smooth and even, slightly pointed at the top, and bluish-green as long as they hang from the tree; but when ripe and fallen, they are yellow or the color of wood. The outer skin of these gradually becomes wrinkled, splits, and falls off; beneath this one finds a perfectly spherical head of a pale color, which consists of a dry and spongy shell like cork. In the center of this is hidden the true kernel, pointed from a round base, with the substance of Chestnuts; it is whitish on the outside, and thick and yellow on the inside, exuding a viscous oil, which can be expressed even from old kernels, and is as thick as Turpentine mixed with animal fat.

In the whole tree is contained a viscous but sparse liquor, which appears thick like condensed milk in broken leaves, represents a yellowish gum in the bark, and a yellow oil in the fruits. If the leaves are handled, they breathe out the odor of toasted shrimp <note>original: "squillarum tostarum"</note>, an odor that is more penetrating in the bark, especially of old trees, which is mostly gummy. At first glance, the wood seems similar to Oak, but it is of a peculiar form that differs from other books <note>likely a typo for 'woods' or referring to the layers/grain</note>; for it is heavy, solid, consisting of thick fibers and many rare and twisted fibers and veins, so that it can hardly be split, and never lengthwise, but it always develops cracks into small segments along the course of the veins.

This wood is of two colors: the first is ash-gray like Oak wood, sometimes distinguished by pale or yellow spots as well as thicker fibers. The other is reddish, like a half-baked brick, having thinner fibers whose course is mostly longitudinal, and they form wide streaks; otherwise, both have the same substance and nature. The red is the most common, and if it is polished, it shines and emits rays or a reflection like Silk; however, these woods can only be polished with difficulty, as will be indicated further below.

This tree, as has been said, always grows on the shore, with its roots fixed in the edge of the forests, while the rest of its canopy leans toward the shore and the sea. Often it occurs in flat forests at the distance of a bow-shot; but if these places are accurately examined, it will appear that the tract was increased and added to by the sea, and that the kernels were cast there by men or birds. For in the middle of the land these trees can be planted well enough, where they grow quite upright at the beginning, but gradually as the years increase, their natural instinct betrays itself as they lean toward the sea again, though not so much as if they were situated on the shore.

On the isthmus where the old mountain called Soya is joined to another mountain on the northern side—a place situated a mile into the region itself—there stood from ancient times a very vast and entirely wild Bintangor tree. It was known to no one by what means it grew there; it occupied that whole isthmus with its roots, so that someone could hardly pass there, and most people thought those roots were rocks.

In the year 1664, however, a sudden fire infested this tree, for no known cause; and since it was overgrown with moss and other herbs, the flame so ignited the whole tree that it was entirely consumed and burned up, to the great sorrow of the inhabitants, who regarded this as an ill-omened sign. Its wood was likewise red, but not so elegantly streaked as that which grows on the shore.

Every year in the month of December it produces copious flowers, when it spreads a pleasant odor over a long distance. In the following months the fruits ripen, which mostly fall into the water; but the proud sea, scorning the gifts of its lover, casts them back onto the shore...

<column-break/>

*...and many petals, in the form of a small rose, of which the two outermost are the largest; by the flower stand two other petals in a cross with the previous ones, and within these five or six smaller petals bent outwards, and then with the roundness upwards again. The middle is filled with short threads, which carry saffron-yellow tufts, such as one calls Anthers in roses, so closely pressed together that they seem to push the petals outwards. These threads hide in their center a round and reddish bud, upon which stands a white thread, from which the fruit becomes. The scent of the flowers is very lovely, drawing toward white Lilies, and they retain it for over a natural day.*

*The fruits are perfectly spherical, the size of a round Plum, or a small musket ball, very smooth and even, with a small point on the front, Spanish-green <note>a bluish-green pigment</note> as long as they hang on the tree, but the ripe and fallen ones are yellowish or wood-colored. The outermost shell becomes wrinkled over time, tears and falls off; beneath it one then finds a perfectly round ball, pale of color, consisting of a dry and spongy husk like cork. In the middle lies the true kernel, somewhat pointed from the round, of substance like a Chestnut, whitish on the outside, thick, yellow, and sticky on the inside, sweating out Oil, which one can still squeeze out of the old ones, and it becomes as thick as Turpentine mixed with tallow.*

*In the whole tree sits a sticky but scarce sap, which shows itself thick in the broken leaves like white milk, in the bark as a yellowish Gum, in the fruits as a yellow Oil. The leaves, when handled a bit, smell like roasted shrimp, which scent one feels more strongly in the bark, especially of the old trees, which is mostly gummy. The wood is at first sight like Oak wood, yet of a special appearance and differing from other woods, for it is heavy, massive, coarse-grained, and so tangled with many rare twists of veins that it will hardly split, almost never splitting in the length, but only following the loop of the twists, and even then in short pieces.*

*It is of two kinds of color: the first is grayish, like Oak wood, and sometimes with pale or yellowish spots and coarse-grained. The other is pale-red like a half-baked brick, finer of veins, and whose twists mostly run in the length and make some broad stripes; otherwise both are of the same substance and nature. The red is the most common, and when it is polished, it glitters and gives a reflection like silk; yet these woods let themselves be polished very poorly, as shall be said here below.*

*It grows, as said, always on the beach, with the remaining body overhanging toward the Sea. One finds them indeed a bow-shot away from there in flat forests, but if one looks at the places properly, one will perceive that the fore-land there has grown on. Or that the kernels were brought there by people or birds. For one can indeed plant them landward, where at first they shoot up beautifully straight and look as if they would become a sturdy tree, but with the years the natural urge shows itself, beginning to smell the Sea <note>a poetic way of saying it turns toward it</note> and to bend forward, though not so much as those on the beach.*

*On the narrow neck with which the mountain of Old Soya in the North is attached to the other mountain, being a full mile inland, there has stood from olden times a very large and wild beach-Bintangor-tree, without anyone knowing how it came there. It occupied with its protruding roots that whole neck, so that one could barely pass by, and most people took them for rocks.*

*However, in the year 1664, a sudden fire came into this tree, one knows not how, and since this tree was very much hung with moss and other brush, the fire increased so much that it was entirely burned, to no small sadness of the inhabitants, who held that for a bad omen. Its wood was also of the red kind, yet not so beautifully veined as that which grows on the beach.*

*Yearly in December it stands full of flowers, when it spreads its lovely scent far. In the following months the fruits ripen, which mostly fall into the water, but the spiteful Sea, despising her lover's gifts, throws them again on the beach in heaps, and that...*

### III Book. XXVI Chapter. AMBOINESE HERBAL.
Dd 3

it casts forth in great abundance, and as far as it can, where those kernels lying hidden under the weeds grow into small trees; hence these trees are always located at the edges of forests.

*Name.* In Latin *Bintangor Maritima*. In Malay *Bintangor Laut* <note>original: "Bintangor Laut", meaning Sea Bintangor</note>. Some also call this *Bonga Tanjong*, a name shared with the tree described above in Chapter 17, because it usually grows on those mountains situated by the sea, which the Malays call *Tanjong* <note>meaning a cape or headland</note>. Our Dutchmen living in the Moluccas have given it the name *Caju Marea* <note>Tide Wood</note>, which they perhaps took from the Portuguese, who call the sea's tide *Marea*, or such shores that are alternately flooded by the ebb and flow of the sea, where these trees especially grow. By the Javanese it is called *Jampelong* and *Tsjankoc*; by the Balinese *Tsjampoelong* and *Tsjampelong*, by which name it is known to most Malays. By the people of Ternate *Fidacca*, and specifically its flower *Copratsja* and *Carpuratsja*, but the fruit *Tsjopelon*. By the Macassans *Punanga Boeg*: *Betau* and *Bitau*. By the Amboinese *Hataur*, *Hataulo*, and *Hutaulo*, as well as *Hattou-Ui*.

*Place.* This tree is well known throughout the watery regions of the Indies, and especially in the Molucca and Amboinese islands, both on flat and steep shores that are rarely frequented by men or animals. In Amboina it occurs most on the stony shores of Larique and Suli; on Ceram the entire stretch of flat shore from the Nassau isthmus as far as Assa Hoedi, for several miles, is planted with the massive *Caju Marea* trees, mostly lying down as it were, and leaning their crowns into the water, so that one can walk under them as if under an arbor; they grow so vigorously that their leaves are over a foot long. It has been observed that birds sometimes carry the kernels into the mountains, as well as to islands on whose shores they are not found nor known, where they often germinate. Hence some such trees occur in the higher region of Banda, and perhaps the aforementioned tree of Soya was propagated in such a manner.

In the western regions of the Indies this is also known, such as in Malabar and Ceylon <note>modern Sri Lanka</note>, and there it lies on the shore with a long and crooked trunk, raising the upper part of the trunk and crown so that it is not splashed by the seawater; there it produces many fragrant flowers, but its leaves there are smaller than in the Amboinese variety.

Since this tree, uprooted in Ceylon and neighboring islands, can by chance be carried across the sea to Coromandel, if we wish to accept as truth what the Portuguese writers—among others Jarricus <note>Pierre du Jarric, a Jesuit historian</note> in Volume I, Book 2, Chapter 17 of *Indian Matters*—relate from an old tradition of the inhabitants: that the Apostle St. Thomas, near the city of Meliapour or St. Thomé (which at that time was twelve miles from the sea), dragged a vast tree from the shore to the city with his girdle, from which he constructed his entire chapel. This wood King Sagamus had previously greatly desired for his own use, but could not move it with all the strength of his people. Therefore, one might not incorrectly conclude that it must have been such a tree; for no other massive trees grow on the shore that could serve this mechanical use.

*Usage.* As long as this tree stands, its flowers and fruits are of use. The flowers are desired by women, who gladly weave them into their hair or place them in chests with their clothes to provide them with a pleasant scent. The yellow anthers <note>original: "antherae", the pollen-bearing part of the flower</note> are preserved for medicinal use, to be used in drinks for women rising from the childbed <note>postpartum recovery</note>.

The wanton kings of Bali fill their pillows with these flowers because they breathe a pleasant scent, though they must be aired frequently, otherwise they breed thick and fatty worms. This seed (which is generally called <term>Sari</term>) is of a warmer nature than that of the <term>Naggasari</term> <note>likely Mesua ferrea</note>, which is used for similar ailments. For the sake of the flowers, this tree is also sometimes planted by the Malays and Macassans near their houses and used in place of the *Nagga-sari*.

From its ripe fruits an oil is extracted in various ways: first their outer husks are peeled off, and the inner kernels are dried in the hot sun until the yellow oil exudes; these are then pounded or rubbed, and placed in hairy sieves made of Calap-

<column-break/>

so that it goes as high up on the land as it can, where those kernels, which are thrown into the brush, sprout into new small trees; and from that it comes that these trees always stand at the edge of the forest.

*Name.* In Latin *Bintangor Maritima*. In Malay *Bintangor Laut*. Some also call it *Bonga Tanjong*, a name common with the tree described above in Chapter 17, because they commonly stand at the heads or promontories that project into the sea, which the Malays call *Tanjong*. Our Dutchmen, who live in the Moluccas, have given it the name *Caju Marea*, which they perhaps borrowed from the Castilians <note>the Spanish/Portuguese</note>, who call the tide of the sea *Marea*, or such strands that are alternately washed by the ebb and flow, where these trees mostly grow. In Javanese *Jampelong* and *Tsjankoc*; in Balinese *Tsjampoelong* and *Tsjampelong*, by which name it is also known by most Malays. In Ternaten *Fidacca*, and the flower in particular *Copratsja* and *Carpuratsja*, the fruits *Tsjopelon*. In Macassan *Punanga Boeg*: *Betau*, and *Bitau*. In Amboinese *Hataur*, *Hataulo*, and *Hutaulo*, also *Hattou-Ui*.

*Place.* It is known throughout all of watery India, especially much in the Molucca and Amboinese islands, as well on flat as steep shores, where there is little presence of people and cattle. In Amboina one has it most on the stony shore of Larique and Suli; on Ceram the entire flat shore from the Nassau opening onwards to Assa Hoedi, some miles long, is occupied with very heavy *Caju Maria* trees, mostly lying down, and reaching with their crowns to the water, so that one can walk through there as if under arbors, so luxurious in growth that the leaves are over a foot long. It has been found that birds sometimes bring some kernels into the mountains, also onto islands on whose shores they are unknown, and they sometimes come up there. Because of this one finds some such trees on the high land in Banda, and perhaps the aforementioned Soya tree was also propagated in this way.

In the western parts of India it is also known, such as in Malabar and on Ceylon, lying with a long and bowed trunk on the shore, and lifting its front crowns so that they stay out of the water, bearing there also many and fragrant flowers, though the leaves will be somewhat smaller than on the Amboinese ones.

Since this tree on Ceylon and the neighboring places was uprooted, it could by chance be brought by the sea to Coromandel, if one wanted to hold for truth what the Portuguese writers (and among others Jarricus Vol. I. Book 2. Chapter 17. *Indian Matters*) relate from an ancient tradition of the natives: that the Apostle St. Thomas, near the city of Meliapour or St. Thomé, which at that time lay twelve miles from the sea, supposedly dragged a large tree with his girdle from the strand to the city, from which his entire chapel was made; which wood King Sagamus had previously very much desired for his own building, but with all his power could not pull up. So one might not poorly guess that it must have been such a tree, because no large trees grow on the shore that are useful for that construction.

*Usage.* As long as this tree stands, one has the use of the flowers and fruits. The flowers are desired by womenfolk, who gladly wear them in their hair or lay them in their chests with their clothes to get a good scent from them. The yellow seed from within is kept for use in medicine, to use in drinks for women who rise from the childbed.

The wanton kings of Bali fill their pillows with them because it is of good scent, but one must air them sometimes, otherwise it breeds thick and white worms; and this seed (which one generally calls *Sari*) is better in nature than that of *Naggasari*, which one uses for similar ailments. For the sake of the flowers, this tree is also sometimes planted by the Malays and Macassans by their houses and used in place of *Nagga-Sari*.

oil is prepared from the sea-burr tree <term>Runut</term>, which is squeezed between two pieces of wood until a thick oil drips out; or these dry kernels are preserved until such oil is required, at which time they are pounded and roasted in a pan. It is expressed in the former manner, as is done with Nutmegs; these toasted and pounded kernels can also be boiled in water, and the floating oil removed with a spoon, just as <term>Calappa</term> <note>Coconut</note> oil is collected. However, the pressing method succeeds better, though a large quantity of these kernels is required. This oil is moderately warm, and is useful for removing and curing skin filth and scabies. In Macassar, Baleya, and Bima, candles are formed from these kernels; for they are used dried in the sun, and are tied to a sharp stick in the shape and length of a candle, or they are pounded and mixed with a certain amount of cotton, and wrapped in narrow segments of Bamboo reed, or made from <term>Gabba Gabba</term> <note>the dried midribs of Sago palm leaves</note> into the shape of a candle. Some collect the half-ripe fruits, which they preserve in brine; the outer husk of these is eaten just like Olives.

Its wood contains a material that is quite durable, but it is very difficult for hewers to work, as it is for the axe; a saw can only pass through it when it is fresh, and from it only short beams and wide boards can be formed. Whatever is desired from it, therefore, must first be formed from the fresh wood, then hewn and polished with frequent scrubbing.

It is best for axles, wheels, and the larger machines of huge war engines <note>gun carriages</note>, since it does not split or develop cracks, even if large nails are driven into it, owing to its curled and swirling substance. For this reason, the inhabitants of the island of Key use it for the curved ribs of ships, since it is exceptionally durable in seawater. It is also formed by the saw into reasonably wide boards, from which tables and chests are manufactured, but they require difficult labor before they are smooth and polished; for the wood can hardly be made smooth with a broadaxe, and is always rough and "hairy" in one part or another. Afterwards, however, it is rubbed with water and sand, and finally made dry and polished by means of scrubbers made of split <term>Rottang</term> <note>Rattan</note> reed, applied with great human force. By this friction, those rare swirls, streaks, and veined waves finally come into view; the wood itself shines, and the first species dries to a dark ash-gray, while the second is a pale reddish mixed with yellow, which shines even more than the gray and exhibits a luster.

The Portuguese chests constructed in Ceylon and Malabar from this wood have much coarser fibers and are rougher than those from Amboina, but they shine elegantly and have a dark brown color, like older Ironwood <note>original: "Sideroxyli"</note>, for which this wood is often mistaken by our countrymen. This wood, however, should not be used for any works made of boards unless it has been properly dried and kept for a year; these boards made from it should also be no thinner than a thumb's width. For this wood never cracks, neither from moisture nor heat, but boards cut thin and used too freshly will warp, especially in rainy weather, and contract. Fresh boards also have this defect: chests made from them very easily breathe a musty odor if they are kept closed for a long time. The inhabitants of Java, as well as the Moluccas and Amboina, rarely use this wood, since they are unable to work the huge masses of this wood with their small axes and other tiny instruments.

This wood also has another defect: there are often dry and rough spots in it which can never be polished but always remain rough. For this reason, it was later sold to our Indian Company <note>the VOC</note> by the people of Boero and Manipa around the year 1666 for forming the ribs, keels, and boards of a galley and a skiff. In the galley, it lasted over twelve years; in the skiff, no more than two. The reason was that the wood used for the skiff was too fresh, which caused it to contract too much and produce cracks.

The bark of this tree, cleaned of its outer roughness and peeling off naturally, when boiled in water with the bark of <term>Ironwood</term>, <term>Samama</term>, and <term>Sea Gayang</term> <note>original: "Gayang Laut"</note> and drunk, cleanses women after childbirth; it expels the white flux <note>leucorrhea</note> and other impurities, if a cup of it is taken in the morning for eight days, after which strengthening medicines are used.
