taken from the <term>Calappus-tree</term> (called <term>Runut</term>) and pressed between two planks until the thick oil comes out; or one saves these dried kernels until the oil is needed. At that time, they are pounded and roasted in a pan, and pressed as before, just as is done with Nutmegs. One can also boil the largest pounded kernels in water and take off the floating oil with a spoon, just as <term>Calappus</term> oil is made, though the pressing proceeds more quickly; however, one must have a good quantity of kernels. This oil is moderately warm, good for curing all filth and scabies of the skin. On Macassar, Baley, and Bima, they also make small candles from these kernels; for they take those dried in the sun, and thread the whole kernels onto a sharp stick to the shape and length of a candle, or they pound them, mix them with some cotton, and bind them with narrow shavings made of Bamboo or <term>Gabba Gabba</term> into the shape of a candle. Some take the half-ripe fruits and pickle them, of which only the outer husk can be eaten, like Olives.

This wood does indeed have a durable substance, yet it is very difficult to work for the plane and axe; only the saw can get through it when it is fresh, and from it one gains no more than short beams and wide planks. Whatever one therefore wants to have from it, one must first chop it roughly from the fresh wood, work it with a coarse plane, and make it smooth with much scrubbing.

It is most useful for wheels, axles, and the carriages of heavy cannon, for it does not split, even if one drives large nails through it, because of its marrowy substance. Therefore, the natives of Key use it for all kinds of curved timbers for their vessels, because it is particularly durable in seawater. With the saw, it is also brought into reasonably wide planks, from which table tops and chests are made, but they require constant labor before one gets them smooth; for with the plane one can do no more than make them even, as they remain rough and shaggy. Thereafter, one scrubs them with water and sand, and finally polishes them dry with brushes made of split <term>Rattan</term> and with the strength of men's arms. Through this rubbing, the rare swirls, stripes, and waves of veins first come to light, and the wood begins to shine properly, that of the first sort turning dark gray, and of the second light-red mixed with yellow, which also shines more than the gray and gives off a luster.

The Portuguese chests made on Ceylon and Malabar from this wood are much coarser-grained and rougher on the outside than the Amboinese ones, yet they shine beautifully and are dark brown in color, like old iron-wood, for which they are also mistakenly seen by our people. One must use this wood for no work made of planks unless it is thoroughly dry and has lain for about a year; also the planks should not be much thinner than a thumb, for this wood never splits, neither from moisture nor from heat. However, the thin-sawn ones used too fresh warp somewhat, especially in rainy weather, and shrink greatly. Likewise, these planks used fresh have this fault: that the chests made from them very easily smell musty if they stand closed for a long time. The natives on Java, as well as in the Moluccas and Amboina, otherwise use this wood little, because with their small axes and simple tools, they do not know how to work those unmanageable blocks.

This wood also has other defects, namely some dry and shaggy spots that take no polish but remain rough. This is why this wood, used for planks by the Boero-nese and Manipa-nese around the year 1666, stayed good for over twelve years on the yacht, but no more than two years on the boat. The cause may be that what was used for the boat was taken too green, whereby it shrank too much and caused great openings.

The bark of this tree, cleaned of the outer roughness and then peeling off by itself, boiled in water with the bark of Iron-wood, <term>Samama</term>, and <term>Sea Gayang</term> and drunk, cleanses women who are rising from childbed; it drives off the white flux and other impurities, if for eight days in the morning a small cup full of it...

### Book III. Chapter XXVI. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

->**[Column 1]**<-

...a decoction of the bark also cures the bloody flux <note>original Latin: *mixtum cruentum*; Dutch: *bloedpissen*</note> and Gonorrhea.

The leaves, soaked overnight in pure water, tint it with a blue color, similar to Tobacco, and make it very cool. With this, inflamed eyes are washed, or the face itself is submerged in a dish filled with this water, whereby the heat is extinguished or drawn out, and the sight is refreshed. For this reason, some surgeons in Banda have distilled these leaves, and that water has produced good effects in cases of ophthalmia <note>eye inflammation</note>.

In Java and Bali, the high-ranking lords <note>original Latin: *primores*</note> plant this tree around their houses, as well as in gardens, where it grows quite elegantly with an upright trunk, but it is shaped by art and labor by pruning the branches on the side to which it attempts to lean.

It is planted for its elegant shade and for its fragrant flowers, which resemble the <term>Nagassari</term> <note>The Ceylon Ironwood, *Mesua ferrea*</note>, as well as for its fruits, from which they fashion candles.

When the tree is young, it bears a smooth bark; but as the years increase, it becomes wrinkled and fissured, as on Ambon, and then the wood is suitable for making planks for chests and tables.

Another magical and superstitious use thrives among the inhabitants of <term>Boero</term> <note>Buru Island</note>, which they hide from us as a great secret. For they plant the fruits of this tree in a human skull—which for this purpose is usually freshly decapitated—digging out the eyes and placing these kernels in the sockets, covering them with a little earth. From these a tree grows, the use of which they leave to their children.

From the fruits of this tree they prepare an oil, which they carry in a small vial hung on the body, and they also smear themselves with it; by its power they believe they can strike everything, whether with throwing weapons or by projectiles from a musket and the like. In this art, Ginadi—brother of the <term>Radja Roemaite</term> on Buru—excelled among others; he could strike everything with the greatest certainty and was at the same time impenetrable to our musket balls fired at him when he challenged our men in <term>Cajeli</term> <note>Kayeli, a port on Buru</note> in the year 1680. However, he was not free from the executioner's axe and iron bar, which reached him the following year on the Amboinese scaffold.

This account may serve as a warning to our people: if they see anyone adorned with such a vial on their neck, it is a sign that they are usually such a champion <note>a warrior or vanguard fighter</note>.

If this wood is smooth and planed, it must be scrubbed with water and a type of pumice that has floated in the sea for some time, which is much harder than that collected from the land near the burning mountains <note>volcanoes</note>, which erupt with great force and are then found floating in the sea.

### In Rumphius’s Appendix the following are added.

In the year 1692, a wondrous piece of wood was brought to me from Caybobbo, which the inhabitants claimed to be the root of the Bintangor, having grown under water in the sea; but it had been broken off and had floated for a long time in the sea before being cast onto the shore. It was elegantly carved as if it had been fashioned by the art of sculpture. The following year it was sent to Batavia and placed on the small island called Edam, at the Japanese-style summer house of the Most Noble Lord, the former Governor-General Johannes Camphuis, where it serves as a handle for the stairs.

In the <term>Hortus Malabaricus</term> <note>A famous 17th-century botanical treatise on the plants of the Malabar Coast</note>, part 4, Figure 38, it is called *Punna* and *Punnaca* in the Malabar tongue, and "Yellow Gum-Apples" in Dutch, where its description matches ours reasonably well, except that it is not indicated to be a maritime or coastal tree. Nor should anyone think that the true yellow gum comes from this tree, which our nation collects from an entirely different tree called <term>Carcapæli</term> <note>The Gamboge tree, *Garcinia gummi-gutta*</note>, which is called <term>Cureas</term> in Ceylon, concerning which see the following forty-first chapter.

->EXPLA-<-

<column-break/>

->**[Column 2]**<-

...drunk from it, after which one applies the binding medicines; the decoction of the bark also cures the bloody urine <note>original: *bloedpissen*</note> and Gonorrhea.

The leaves, laid for a night in fresh water, give the same a bluish color, like Tobacco, and make it very cool. With this one washes the inflamed eyes <note>original: *verbitte oogen*</note>, or one dips the face into a bowl full of this water; this draws out the inflammation and refreshes the sight. For this reason, some surgeons in Banda have distilled these leaves and, with the water, likewise achieved good effects on inflamed eyes.

On Java and Bali, the great Lords plant this tree near their houses, and also further inland, where it grows beautifully straight, though it is turned to that purpose with effort, keeping the trunk straight and shortening the branches on that side to which it wishes to lean.

They plant it for its beautiful shade, for the sweet-smelling flower—which comes closest to the <term>Nagas Sari</term>—and for the fruits, from which they make candles.

Being young it has a smooth bark, but in old age it becomes rough and burst, similar to that on Ambon; then the wood is suitable for planks for chests and tables.

Yet another magical or superstitious use is practiced by the natives, mostly of Buru, which they keep very secret and hidden from us. For they plant the fruits of this tree in the skull of a human, which they usually chop off fresh for that purpose, digging out the eyes, sticking the aforementioned kernels in their place, and covering them with only a little earth, letting a tree grow from it, the use of which they leave to their children.

From the fruits of this tree, they make an oil that they carry in a small vial on the body, also smearing themselves with it, by whose power they can hit anything, whether by throwing-weapons or shooting from muskets <note>original: *roers*</note>. Through which art, among others, Ginadi was famous—brother of the <term>Radja Roemaite</term> on Buru—who truly had a certain shot at everything, and was free from our bullets that were thrown at him when he challenged ours in Kayeli in the year 1680; but not from the executioner’s axe and crowbar, which reached him the following year on the Amboinese scaffold.

This story can serve as a warning for our people, when they see someone carrying such vials of oil on the neck, who usually wish to be champions <note>original: *voorvegters*</note>.

When the wood is smooth and evenly planed, then one must scrub it with water and that sort of floating stones <note>pumice</note> which have been floating in the sea for a time, and have thereby become much harder than those taken from the land and near the burning mountains <note>volcanoes</note>, which erupt such things sufficiently, which then float in the sea.

### In the Appendix of Rumphius this was added.

In the year 1692, a wondrous piece of wood from Caybobbo was brought to me, which the natives claimed to be the root of the Bintangor, grown in the sea under water, yet broken off, rolled for a long time by the sea, and cast upon the beach. It was very prettily carved, as if it were made by a sculptor’s art. It was sent the following year to Batavia and placed on the little island of Edam, at the Japanese pleasure-house <note>original: *Speelhuis*</note> of the Noble Lord, the former Governor-General Johannes Camphuis, where it serves as a knob on the stairs.

In the *Hortus Malabaricus*, part 4, Figure 31, it is called in Malabar *Punna* and *Punnaca*, and in Dutch "Yellow Gum-apples," agreeing reasonably well with our description, except that one cannot notice whether it be a beach tree; also one must not think that the true yellow gum comes from this tree, which our nation fetches from another tree, <term>Carca Poeli</term>, and on Ceylon <term>Cureas</term>, about which see the following forty-first chapter.

# CHAPTER TWENTY-SEVEN.

## The Wild Bintangor. Bintangor Utan.

Just as the preceding Sea Bintangor bears an irregular and unsightly trunk, this Mountain or Wild Bintangor is so elegant and well-ordered that if they are compared to one another, they differ as much as a coarse and unkempt rustic from a delicate and polished young girl. The trunk of the Mountain Bintangor is very straight and slender like the <term>Pinanga</term> <note>A genus of palm trees</note>, rarely reaching the thickness of a <term>Calappus</term> <note>A Coconut tree, *Cocos nucifera*</note>.

Its leaves are eight or nine inches long and two wide; the old ones bear a sharp midrib on the underside and end in a long and sharp point, firmer than the preceding kind. They sit on the stalks without a fixed order and are otherwise similar to the Sea Bintangor. However, as the wood of this tree is of two types—namely, white and reddish—a small difference is also observed among the leaves: in one species they are pointed, while in the other they are blunt.

These are also placed without order, though sometimes they are opposite and form an oblique cross. Those that grow in <term>Boero</term> <note>Buru Island</note> bear longer and thinner leaves than those in Ambon. The bark of the trunk is of uniform thickness, ash-gray or yellowish and very smooth on the outside, and yellow on the inside; it can be stripped off in large segments so that channels or gutters can be formed from them.

The flowers are very similar to those of the Sea Bintangor, or perhaps a little larger, consisting of five somewhat round, thick, and whitish petals, which are filled inside with yellow anthers sitting on longer stamens than in the preceding kind. They give off a pleasant but weaker scent. Each flower also sits on a long whitish stalk and is arranged in a cross-shape, as in Cloves, clustered in large bunches, of which usually two come out opposite each other from the leaf axils.

The fruits are likewise round pills, twice as small as the preceding kind and slightly pointed. On the tree they are sea-green, sitting on a bare stalk without any trace of the flower. They bear two rinds or shells, the outermost of which is a knife's-width thick, at first woody and almost crumbly, as if composed of sand; beneath this is placed another thicker and harder shell, but fi...

# CHAPTER XXVII.

## The Wild Bintangor Tree.

As ugly as the previous Bintangor is in its trunk, so beautiful and well-proportioned is the Mountain Bintangor; when the two are compared with each other, they appear as a coarse, square-built peasant <note>original Dutch: *Boer*</note> next to a small young lady <note>original Dutch: *Juffertje*</note>. The trunk of the Mountain Bintangor is very straight and slender, like a Pinang tree, rarely reaching the thickness of a Coconut tree <note>original Dutch: *Calappus-boom*</note>.

The leaves are eight or nine inches long, two inches wide, and more, having a sharp midrib underneath and a long narrow point at the front. They are stiffer than the previous kind, stand without order on the stalks, and are otherwise similar to the Sea Bintangor. However, because this wood is of two kinds, namely white and reddish, a small distinction is also made in the leaves: on one variety they are straight-pointed at the front, and on the other they end bluntly.

Sometimes they also stand without order, sometimes opposite each other, making an oblique cross. Those from Buru <note>original Dutch: *Boero*</note> are also longer and narrower than the Amboinese ones. The bark of the trunk is of uniform thickness, light gray or pale yellow on the outside and very smooth; yellow on the inside. One can peel it off in large pieces, so that gutters <note>original Dutch: *gooten*</note> can be made from it.

The flower is most like the Sea Bintangor, or even just as large, made of five round, white, and thick petals, and filled inside with much yellow seed <note>anthers</note> on longer threads <note>filaments</note> than the previous one. It is also good of scent, though weaker. Each flower likewise stands on a long white stalk and in a cross, like Cloves <note>original Dutch: *nagelen*</note>, in large clusters, of which usually two come out opposite each other from the leaf axils.

The fruits are also round pills, twice as small as the previous ones, with a small point at the front, sea-green on the tree, standing on the bare stalk without any remnant of the flower. at last it likewise becomes crumbly, composed of something like a coarse sand; in the middle is a hollow cavity lacking a kernel. When falling from the tree, and if the fruit has lain upon the ground for some time, it becomes crumbly, whereas it was originally woody; it is dry and without any oil or resin. Perhaps not all are empty and lacking a kernel, but some may be filled with one, which propagate the tree.

Those trees which bear long, pointed, and dark green leaves—which dry to a green color rather than a reddish-brown—consist of a white wood. When fresh, this wood is very heavy, but it dries quickly at the edges. It has straight, short fibers that are thick and seemingly blunt, sometimes running obliquely; however, the internal fibers are thinner and more intricate. If this wood is polished, it shines like silk. It is extremely tough due to the longitudinal fibers and flexible, neither cracking nor breaking easily. Most of its strength lies in the longitudinal fibers of the outer edges, as the internal wood breaks more easily.

The second species is similar to the former in its fibers, but it is more reddish than white and consists of many parts filled with coarser veins. It cannot be easily polished, for these coarse veins, resisting the woodworking tools <note>original Latin: *dolabris*</note>, fall away and form grooves. The leaves of this species are bluntly pointed at the top and sometimes split <note>original Latin: *bifida*</note>, and are wavy along the edges toward the bottom. Furthermore, in both species, no resin is observed, neither in the leaves nor in the bark. They usually bloom at the same time as the *Coastal Bintangor* <note>original Latin: *Bintangor litorali*, likely *Calophyllum inophyllum*</note>, or the maritime variety; however, they are never found on the shore, but in dense forests both in the mountains and in the valleys. The drier and more rocky the places where they grow, the better their wood is considered to be.

**Name.** In Latin, *Mountain Bintangor* <note>original: *Bintangor Montana*</note>. In Malay, *Forest Bintangor* <note>original: *Bintangor Utan*</note>, and simply *Bintangor*, for the Malays consider this the true *Bintangor*, and the preceding tree to be the *Champelong*. In Amboinese, it is called *Hataul Lau-muri*.

**Location.** It occurs in all the islands of the Amboinese, but most frequently on *Buru* <note>original: *Boero*</note>, and in the region of *Hitoe*, or Great *Amboina*.

**Use.** Nothing of this tree is put to use except the straight trunk. If it is fresh and no thicker than a leg, it is used for roof supports; if they are larger, they serve as masts for smaller vessels. However, great care must be taken that not too much of this wood is shaved away, but that it is only trimmed into a round shape, for most of its strength, as has been said, lies in the outer part.

If it is used in ships, the uppermost part should be covered with a lead plate to protect it from the force of rainwater and rot. If it is properly preserved in this way, it can remain in use for a long time and withstand the great force of the winds.

Those pieces that will serve as roof supports should likewise merely be debarked, and nothing of the wood itself should be removed. The debarked trunks should be exposed to the sun so they may dry and harden; for if they are placed in roofs while too fresh and green, they warp. This should also be observed regarding the preceding wood. Many of our people, neglecting these things, have undeservedly given this wood a bad reputation for not being as durable as claimed, which must however be attributed to their own ignorance. This wood should always be used for the upper parts of houses, and never for the posts that touch the earth, as it rots easily and quickly there.

The *Mountain Bintangor* has another or third species, differing greatly in size from the former ones; for it is a slender little tree, scarcely more than a foot thick, yet likewise consisting of a straight trunk with a yellowish and smooth bark.

Its branches divide themselves into long and flexible switches; on these, the leaves sit sparsely, two by two opposite each other. They resemble the leaves of the Pomegranate, or the point of a small spear, three inches long and a small finger wide, gradually tapering to a point, firm, smooth, and interwoven with fine parallel veins, like all *Bintangors*.

The flowers and fruit have remained unknown to me until now, as they rarely come into view, as does the little tree itself. Its wood is tough, solid, and a reddish-white.

the latter also crumbly, and consisting of coarser sand; in the middle is an empty hollowness without a kernel. Falling from the tree and lying on the ground for a time, they first become crumbly; previously they were woody, though dry, and without any oil or gum. Perhaps they are not all empty, but some full, which propagate the tree.

The trees that have an oblong point and dark green leaf, which also dries up greenish rather than sallow or reddish, have a white wood. When fresh it is very heavy, but it dries out easily. At the edges it has straight but short veins, coarse and as if broken off, also running somewhat slantwise; toward the inside they are finer and run more curled. When polished, it shines like Satin; it is very tough because of the long threads, and very flexible without splitting or breaking, but its greatest strength consists in the long-fibered edges, for the inner wood breaks more easily.

The other sort is similar to the former in its threads, but it leans from the whitish a little toward the light-reddish, full of pieces of coarse veins, and does not allow itself to be worked smooth; for the coarse veins, standing up against the plane <note>original Dutch: *schaaf*</note>, fray out and make grooves. The leaves of this sort have a blunt point at the front, sometimes split in two, and at the edges they are somewhat hemmed downwards. Furthermore, in both sorts one sees no gumminess, neither in leaves nor in bark, and they bloom mostly at the same time as the shore-Bintangor. They are by no means found on the shore, but in dense forests, both in the mountains and in the valleys; and the drier and stonier the place is where they grow, the better they are held to be.

**Name.** In Latin *Bintangor Montana*, in Malay *Bintangor Utan*, and simply *Bintangor*, for the Malays hold this to be the right, proper Bintangor, and the former tree for *Champelong*; in Amboinese *Hataul Lau-muri*.

**Place.** One finds it in all the Amboinese Islands, but mostly on *Buru*, and the *Hitoe Country*, or great *Amboina*.

**Use.** From these trees nothing else is used but the straight trunks when they are still young and not more than a leg thick, for rafters of roof-work; but being larger, for masts and yards <note>original Dutch: *rheen*</note> of small ships and junks. However, one must take good care that one does not take much off the outside of this wood, but only trims it a little so that it becomes round; for its greatest strength, as said, consists in the edges.

When placed in ships, one must also cover the top with a piece of lead or tarpaulin <note>original Dutch: *presening*</note>, so that it remains protected from the soaking of the rain, which easily causes it to perish from the inside. Being thus preserved, it can last a long time at sea and, because of its stiffness, withstand great violence from winds.

That which shall serve for rafters must likewise merely be peeled, and nothing taken from the wood. The peeled trunks should be placed in the sun so that they dry out thoroughly and become stiff; for otherwise, used too fresh in the roof-work, they become crooked. This must also be noted with the former kind. However, many of our people, not noting these things, have without guilt brought this wood into a bad name as not being as durable as is claimed, which is yet to be blamed on sheer ignorance. One must always use this wood for the upper parts of a house, and by no means for the pillars that stand in the earth, for where they touch the same, they perish in a short time.

The Mountain-Bintangor has yet another or third sort, differing much in size from all the former; for it remains a thin, slender little tree, not becoming more than a leg thick, yet with a straight trunk and a pale yellow, smooth bark.

The branches divide themselves into long and tough switches: upon them the leaves stand very sparsely, also two and two against each other. The leaves somewhat resemble those of Pomegranates, or the point of a small pike, three inches long, a small finger wide, gradually pointed, stiff, smooth, and streaked through with fine parallel veins, like all Bintangor.

The flowers and fruits are yet unknown to me, because they are seldom seen, as is the little tree itself. The wood is tough, stiff, and whitish-red.

Name. In Latin, *Bintagor Tenuifolia* <note>Thin-leaved Bintangor</note>. In Malay, *Bintangor Daun Kitsjil* <note>Small-leaved Bintangor</note>. In Amboinese, *Hataul Laun Maun*.

# CHAPTER TWENTY-EIGHT.
## Novella: *Daun Baru*.

We shall now describe certain trees which likewise bear beautiful flowers and are related to the *Althaea* <note>the Marshmallow plant</note>; while these are small shrubs in our European lands, in these regions they grow into the form of a tree. We have distinguished these into four species, the first and most common of which, along with its varieties, we shall describe in this chapter.

The Novella or *Daun Baru* <note>Malay: "New Leaf"</note> is a tree found everywhere, mostly growing with one, but often with several trunks like a shrub, especially those growing on the shore. It is not tall but of medium thickness, like a common Apple tree; the bark of the trunk is ashy and almost whitish, though on the shore it is a pale reddish color, while further inland it is mixed with green. On the branches, it is variegated with brown and green, and on the upper parts a bluish-green. Everywhere it is very tough, juicy, and easily separated from the wood, much like with Willows.

The leaves are solitary and large, roundish, heart-shaped, and wider than they are long. The lower part is provided with two large roundish lobes <note>original Latin: *auriculis*, literally "little ears"</note>. Some are five or six inches long and seven or eight wide; some are four long and five wide. On younger branches, however, they sometimes occur about a foot wide and a palm long. At the edges, they are very finely serrated, but in older leaves the edges are smooth, and only small traces of the teeth remain at the tips or angles. Furthermore, these leaves quickly narrow at the top into a sharp but short point. They are smooth and bright green on top, ashy underneath, and woolly or wrinkled to the touch. They are often provided with five, seven, or nine protruding ribs which are dispersed across the leaf surface but meet at the leaf-stalk, besides many other transverse ribs.

The very tender and younger leaves are a brownish-green and folded together like a book; if they open themselves, they remain green on both sides for a long time. The older they are, the firmer and more ashy they become on the lower side. The smell and taste are insipid, herbaceous, and slimy, such as is detected in all types of the Mallow family <note>term: *Malvaceae*, the plant family including hibiscus and okra</note>.

They sit upon long, round leaf-stalks <note>term: *petioles*</note> which are bent back near the leaf like the handle of a spoon. When young, these bear two peculiar small leaflets near their origin on the branch, between which they are placed as if between two cheeks; these are also observed on the stalks of the flowers, but they gradually fall off. Old leaves are usually perforated by worms or ants and are torn, wrinkled, and often consist only of the remaining ribs, for this tree is vexed by black ants more than any other.

<meta>Catchword: Flower</meta>

<column-break/>

Name. In Latin, *Bintangor Tenuifolia*. In Malay, *Bintangor Daun kitsjil*, and in Amboinese, *Hataul Laun Maun*.

Place. One finds it little, and it always grows on stony ground on the slopes of the mountains, such as on Hoamoal near Liela, and on Great Amboina, in the mountains of Kapaha, everywhere not far from the beach, and in light forests of small timber.

Usage. The wood is indeed firmer and harder than that of the common Bintangor, therefore it is also used for roofing, but one cannot obtain it in abundance.

# XXVIII. CHAPTER.
## New-leaf-Tree.

Now we shall describe some trees which also bear a significant flower, and are of the kinship of *Althaea* or Marshmallow, which in our lands is mostly a weak shrub, but here in this land shows itself in the form of a formal tree. We have divided these into four main species, of which we shall describe the first or most common with its variations in this Chapter.

Novella or *Daun Baru* is a tree common everywhere, mostly with one, and sometimes also with more trunks, shooting up like a shrub, especially that which grows on the beach. It is not high, but moderately thick, like a common Apple tree. The bark on the trunk is light gray and almost whitish; on the beach it is light rosy, but landward mixed with a dirty green. On the branches it is mixed with brown and green, but at the front it is blue-green. It is everywhere very tough, juicy, and easily separated from the wood, similar to the willows.

The leaves stand singly and are large, roundish, shaped like a heart, wider than they are long. At the back, they have two large round ears that overlap each other. Some are five and six inches long, seven and eight wide; some are four long and five wide. However, on the branches one also finds them almost a foot wide and a hand long. At the edges they are very finely sawed, yet on the old leaves they are smooth, or retain some small remnants of teeth at the tips. At the front they end in a short or sudden point; they are smooth and youthful-green above, but gray or ashy underneath, and woolly or rough to the touch. They have five, seven, and nine protruding ribs, divided in a circle, all meeting together at the stalk, besides many other cross-ribs.

The entirely young leaves are brownish and folded together like a book, and when they open, they remain green on both sides for a long time; the older they get, the stiffer and grayer they become from underneath. The smell and taste is flat, grass-like, and slimy, like all Mallow-species.

They stand on long round stalks, bent near the leaf like the handle of a spoon, which when young have two small special leaves at their origin on the branch, between which they stand like two cheeks. These are also seen on the stalks of the flowers, but they fall off in time. The old leaves are mostly full of holes and eaten through by worms or ants, rough, torn, and often consisting of bare ribs, because this tree is plagued more than others by the black ants.

### AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. Chapter XXVIII.

->**[Column 1]**<-

Name. In English, the Thin-leaved Bintangor <note>original: *Bintagor Tenuifolia*</note>. In Malay, it is called the Small-leaved Bintangor <note>original: *Bintangor Daun Kitsjil*</note>. In Amboinese, its name is *Hataul Laun Maun*.

Location. It occurs rarely and always grows in rocky places at the feet of mountains, such as in the Hoamoal peninsula near Liela and in Great Amboina on Mount Kapaha; it is found everywhere not far from the shore in thinner forests consisting of smaller trees.

Use. The wood is harder and more solid than the common Bintangor, for which reason it is also used for roof supports <term>rafters</term>, though it cannot be obtained in great abundance.

# CHAPTER TWENTY-EIGHT.
## The New-Leaf Tree: *Daun Baru*.

We shall now describe certain trees which likewise bear beautiful flowers and are related to the Marshmallow <note>original: *Althaea*</note>; while these are small shrubs in our European lands, in these regions they grow into the form of a tree. We have distinguished these into four species, the first and most common of which, along with its varieties, we shall describe in this chapter.

The New-Leaf Tree <note>original: *Novella*</note> or *Daun Baru* <note>Malay: "New Leaf"</note> is a tree found everywhere, mostly growing with one, but often with several trunks like a shrub, especially those growing on the shore. It is not tall but of medium thickness, like a common Apple tree; the bark of the trunk is ashy and almost whitish, though on the sh...

--- Page 292 ---
<meta>This page continues the description of the New-Leaf Tree (Hibiscus tiliaceus), focusing on the intricate details of its flowers, fruit, and wood quality. It concludes with the tree’s nomenclature in various regional languages and its widespread habitat across the East Indies.</meta>

### Book III. Chapter XXVIII. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

->**[Column 1]**<-

The flower has a form like that of the Mallow <note>original: *Malva*</note> and Marshmallow <note>original: *Althæa*</note>, specifically basket-like <term>calathoides</term>, consisting of five large petals, firm at the bottom but limp and wrinkled at the top, and streaked along their length. Each petal overlaps its neighbor by half its width, so that the entire flower appears to be constructed from a single petal; however, this flower is not as widely spread or open as in the *Mallow*, but is more deeply cut and hollowed at the base. The color is yellowish, while the inner center is dark brown and almost blood-red. In the middle, a pistil is located in the manner of the Mallow family, over half a finger long, the top of which is surrounded by many flour-like stamens; at its peak appears a small brown head, which is entirely odorless. The flower sits upon a double bearded calyx <term>the protective outer layer of a flower</term>, of which the lower part is composed of ten, and the upper part of five long, green, pointed petals, lying closely against the flower. As long as the flower remains on the tree, it is opened no further than a bell shape, but toward evening it extends itself more like a dish, and usually falls off entirely, acquiring a more intense color and contracting into bright red streaks; on the outside, if touched, it appears wrinkled. This falling of flowers is mostly observed in mature trees, for on the younger ones many remain, which contract toward evening and close into a head that never opens again, in the manner of the Mallows; however, the flowers that have fallen to the earth remain open and rot there.

After the flowers fall, those five petals of the calyx contract and close, forming the fruit, which consists of an oblong cone, in the shape and size of a Nutmeg, but wrinkled on the outside and of a dark brown color. These fruit-heads very easily open upon maturity into five segments, each of which resembles a hollowed-out piece of cheese. Indeed, any segment removed divides itself again into two cells, and in each are located five seeds the size of grape pits, shaped like hunched kidneys and tasteless. Most of these seeds are not fully formed but rot, which is why new trees rarely grow from them.

The wood of this tree is white, spongy <note>original: *fungosum*</note>, and very light when dry, nor is it durable. The branches have a spongy and watery pith, but in older trunks, which are thicker than a man, they produce a grey pith, which is often as grey as *Salimoeri* <note>a reference to a greyish stone or wood texture common in the region</note>, and is covered by the outer white wood just as meat is by its fat, which is also seen in *Ebony* wood. This pith is durable and does not easily rot in the ground, even though it is spongy and light; and although the entire tree has a dull and watery taste, a subtle bitterness is nonetheless observed in this grey pith, which is detected by chewing, or if it is rubbed with water upon a porphyry stone. Since I have found that this grey pith is not found in all trees, especially those that grow in villages propagated from branches, I thought for a long time—as did many inhabitants with me—that this tree ought to be divided into two species. However, since most say there is only one species, because no notable variety is seen in the flowers and leaves, I shall defer that to further inquiry, although I am persuaded that I can show some difference in both the flowers and the leaves. The roots bear white wood and a slimy bark, like the entire tree.

This tree also has a vegetative nature, so that all its branches, however small, will sprout when committed to the earth; but they cannot be kept alive long outside the earth, as the whole wood is spongy, and thus the living sap very easily leaks out and dries up. Therefore, such branches must be planted as soon as they are cut, and not kept beyond a night. It produces flowers throughout the entire year, but most abundantly in the months of December, January, and February, which are the dry months.

Name. In Latin *Novella*. In Malay *Daun Baru* and *Caju-Baru*, that is, "new leaf," since new leaves are always observed on this tree, and it is so lush; by which meaning of the name it also occurs in other languages, such as the Ternate and Macassar *Baru*. In Javanese *Condong Waru*, in the Banda language *Varu Ranu* and *Varook*. In Amboinese *Haru*. In Luhoe *Pappatale*. In Baleya *Waru*, and in Portuguese *Volo Condan*.

Location. This tree is known everywhere throughout all of "Watery India" <note>original: *India aquosa*, referring to the maritime East Indies</note>, growing everywhere both on the shore and in the interior region, which is why it is considered the commonest among all trees.

<column-break/>

->**[Column 2]**<-

*The flower is formed like those of the* Mallow *and* Marshmallow *in general, namely bell-shaped, made of five large leaves, stiff at the bottom, limp and wrinkled at the top, striped lengthwise, and each almost embracing the other with its half, so that the entire flower seems to be made of one leaf, not opened as wide as in the* Mallow, *but deeper and more hollow. Its color is light yellow, dark brown on the inside base, and almost blood-red. In the middle stands a small pillar, after the custom of the* Mallow, *fully half a finger long, set at the top with many mealy nubs, with a brown little head on top, without any scent. It stands in a double bearded calyx, of which the lower part consists of ten, and the upper part of five long green points, which lie close against the flower. As long as the flower stands on the tree, it is no more than bell-shaped, but towards the evening they open wider, namely, like a saucer, and for the most part fall off, just as it is, becoming higher in color, gaining some light red stripes, and is somewhat rough to the touch on the outside. This falling happens mostly to the mature trees, for on the young ones many remain hanging, and close themselves in the evening into a bud, which never opens again, after the manner of all* Mallows; *the fallen flowers remain thus opened on the earth, and decay.*

*After the falling of the flowers, the five aforementioned beards close again, and form the fruit, which is an oblong bud, in shape and size of a* Nutmeg, *though rough on the outside, and dark grey in color. These buds open easily into five parts, of which each resembles a piece of cut cheese. Each part being taken off, divides again into two chambers or cells, and in each cell lie five seeds, the size of grape pits, in the shape of lumpy kidneys, without taste; the greatest part of these seeds does not come to perfection, but rots, for which reason also other trees seldom come forth from them.*

*The wood is white, spongy, and when dried very light, and not at all durable. The branches have a spongy watery heart, but in the old trunks, which are thicker than a man, it gains a grey heart inside, which sometimes becomes as grey as* Salimoeri, *with the outermost white wood, like meat covered with its fat, as one sees in* Ebony wood. *This heart is durable, and does not easily decay in the earth, although it is spongy and light. Also, although the entire tree is dull and bland in taste, one nonetheless finds in this grey heart a subtle bitterness, which one notices in chewing, or in rubbing with water on a stone; since I have now found that this grey heart is not in all trees, especially those that are planted with sticks in the* Villages <note>original: *Negoryen*</note>, *I have long been in consideration, as also many Inlanders with me, that this tree ought to be divided into two sorts, but because the greatest part maintains that it is but one sort, as one can see or show no remarkable difference in the flowers and leaves, I must conform myself therewith until further investigation, although I still imagine I can show a distinction, both in the leaves and flowers. The roots have white wood, and a slimy bark, like the whole plant.*

*This tree also has a very growing nature, so that all sticks (however small they may be) stuck into the earth shoot out again, yet they do not want to lie long above the earth, for because the whole wood is spongy, the growing sap runs out very quickly, and dries up; therefore one must replant the sticks as soon as they are cut, or at least not let them lie more than one night; it has flowers throughout the whole year, but mostly in* December, January, *and* February, *the dry months.*

*Name. In Latin* Novella, *in Malay* Daun Baru *and* Caju Baru, *that is New-leaf, because one always finds young leaves on this tree, and it is so lush in growing, and so it is called mostly in all other languages, as in Ternate and Macassar* Baru. *In Javanese* Condong Waru, *in Banda* Varu Ranu *and* Varook. *In Amboinese* Haru. *in Luhoe* Pappatale, *on Bali* Waru, *in Portuguese* Volo Condan.

*Place. This tree is everyone's friend; for it is known through all of* Watery India, *both on the beach and inland, growing everywhere, and therefore also the most* <note>text cuts off at "the most common"</note>

Rumphius notes its ease of propagation via cuttings and its ubiquitous presence across the Indonesian archipelago.</summary>

### AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. chap. XXVIII.
#### page 220

->**[Column 1]**<-

It is a common tree and does not care whether the location is wet or dry, shaded or open, or similar; for it grows in every soil and climate. However, the most elegant and luxurious specimens are found in coastal areas, where the trees grow thicker than two men can encircle, as appears among other places in Sumatra, in Lampong Bay, and in little Ceram, as well as in all the islands situated to the East. Furthermore, it is well known on the mainland of India as far as the Southern province of China.

**Usage.** Although this tree is considered very humble, it nevertheless provides many conveniences, not only in daily domestic use but also in medicine. First, it is of great use for garden hedges <term>known locally as *paggers*</term>, since branches of this tree sprout very easily when committed to the earth. However, they do not all grow out if they are joined too closely together, as the earth cannot nourish them all. But if posts or supports are placed here and there to hold something up, they sprout very quickly, provided they are exposed to the open air, as in walkways or similar structures.

*The tough bark is also useful, from which every kind of binding is formed; for the inhabitants of the Southern Islands use it in place of ropes for their ships. A slow-match for fire <note>original: *funis igniarius*</note> can also be made from it, but it is not of such good quality as that made from the Lontar tree <note>The Palmyra palm</note>. Its large leaves are excellent for covering food that is carried through the streets in dishes.*

*The tender and younger leaves, crushed in water, provide an excellent head-wash during heat and inflammation, for they cool moderately and nourish the hair.*

*Midwives use its mucilage to lubricate the birth canal during delivery. Our nation <note>referring to Europeans/Dutch</note>, however, if they wash their head with the juice of the New-Leaf <note>original: *Daun Baru*</note>, feel an itchiness that the natives do not notice.*

*The root of the New-Leaf, recently dug up, crushed with water and drunk, excellently cools those suffering from a burning fever. It is entirely tasteless, which is why others add the root of white Gendarussa <note>a medicinal shrub, *Justicia gendarussa*</note>; however, the roots of the Red New-Leaf <note>original: *Novellae rubrae*</note>, described below, serve this purpose better. Its younger leaves, squeezed between the hands until they become limp and warm, and applied to boils—with another leaf placed on top—resolve them if they are small, or cause them to mature if they are larger. These leaves, boiled and drunk, or infused in a bath, cure difficulty in urinating <term>dysuria</term>. The inner grey pith of the wood in very old trunks is as dark as in the great Salimuri tree. If it is worked, it breathes a sweet and ointment-like scent, but that odor quickly disappears. When placed in a fire, the wood catches flame quickly and exudes a small amount of oil, but much more rarely than the Salimuri.*

*This grey wood, although soft and light, is nevertheless more durable than the outer white wood, which should be cast aside as useless, much like the white sapwood of Ebony.*

*Small chests and boxes can be formed from it, as well as posts for common houses, if pieces of sufficient size can be found, for it also becomes durable in the earth. However, among our Amboinese, it has been in little use until now, especially since this heartwood or pith is often found hollow and eaten away.*

*The largest segments of this pith are to be gathered from trees located in the mountains or deserted places, which humans rarely frequent, since there the tree produces a reasonably straight trunk, which elsewhere is prevented by the continuous pruning of branches for daily domestic use.*

*Ropes constructed from the bark serve not only for ships but also for fishing nets. Thin cords are also manufactured from it by fishermen, which they carry on their belts, as is done elsewhere with the bark of the wild Gnetum <note>original: *Gne-monis silvestris*</note>.*

*This pith is also used by some in medicine, which they administer crushed with water against abdominal cramps <term>tormina</term>. Against Cholera, the root of the New-Leaf is also administered crushed with water, if its warmed leaves are simultaneously applied to the stomach. It should be noted for medicinal use that the roots of such trees growing spontaneously in the woods should be used, as these have been observed to be more effective than those propagated from planted branches.*

In China, this tree is also common, but is despised there. In Lampong Bay in Sumatra, from its bark...

<column-break/>

->**[Column 2]**<-

...the most despised among all trees, it also does not concern itself with moist, dry, shady, or airy places, for it grows on all sorts of ground. Nevertheless, the most beautiful and luxuriant grow by the seaside, where the trees become thicker than two men, as can be seen among others on Sumatra, in the bay of Lampong, and on little Ceram, as well as in all the South-Eastern Islands. It is furthermore known on the mainland of India, as far as the Southern Province of China.

**Usage.** Although this tree is so despised, it nonetheless has several great uses, not only in daily housekeeping but also in medicine. Firstly, one has a great convenience from it in the making of *Paggers*—that is, the hedges of the gardens—because one can easily get the stakes from it, and in the place of those cut down, others immediately grow. However, not all stakes grow when they are set close against each other in the hedges, for the ground cannot nourish them all; but if one sets posts here and there to carry something, those sprout very easily—namely, if they stand under the open sky, such as the posts of *Paggers* and open galleries.

The tough bark also has its use for making all kinds of binding-work, and the inhabitants of the South-Eastern Islands also use it for ropes for their vessels; one can also make slow-match from it, though that is not as good as from the upright Lontar tree. The broad leaves are very useful for covering all kinds of food that are carried through the street in small dishes.

With the young leaves rubbed in water, one washes the head when it is heated, for they cool moderately and cause the hair to grow.

The midwives use the same mucilage to make the passage smoother in time of childbirth. Our nation feels some itching from the juice of the New-Leaf <note>original: *Daun Baru*</note> when washing the head, which the natives do not feel.

The roots of the New-Leaf, freshly dug, rubbed with water and drunk, cool very powerfully in burning fevers; they are entirely without taste, and some add the root of white Gendarussa to it, though more suitable for this are the roots of the Red New-Leaf <note>original: *Novella Rubra*</note>, described below. The young leaves, somewhat pressed between the hands so that they become limp and warm, and laid upon boils with another leaf over them, resolve the same if they are still small, or ripen them if they have become large. The leaves boiled and drunk, or used in a bath, cure the pressing of water <note>difficulty urinating</note>. The internal grey wood in the very old trunks becomes as brown and mouse-colored as in the large Salimuri: in the working, it smells sweet and ointment-like, but that smell soon passes; in the fire, it burns easily and sweats out some oil, though much scarcer than Salimuri.

This grey wood, although soft and light, is nonetheless more durable than the outermost white wood, which one must count as sapwood, like the white on Ebony wood.

One can make small chests and boxes from it, as well as posts for common houses, if one can get it so large, for it is also durable in the earth; yet it is still in little use among our Amboinese, the more so as one often finds this heartwood hollow and eaten out.

The largest pieces of this heartwood must be sought from the trees that stand in the mountains or lonely places where few people come, for there the tree gains a reasonably straight trunk, which is otherwise hindered by the lopping off of its branches, which are needed daily in the household.

The ropes made from the bark are used not only for vessels but also on fishing nets. Thus, thin lines are also twisted from it, like fishing lines, which the natives carry in their trousers <note>or waistbands</note>, as one otherwise does with the bark of wild Gnomon <note>Gnetum</note>.

The aforementioned heartwood is also used by some in medicine, giving the same rubbed in water to drink against the "krimzel" or belly-pain <note>abdominal cramps</note>. Against cholera <note>original: *bort of Choleram*</note>, drink the root of the New-Leaf rubbed with water, and lay some warmed leaves of the same on the stomach. But here it should be known that for all medicinal use, one must take the roots of such trees that grow by themselves in the wild, since those have been found more powerful than those coming from planted stakes.

In China, this tree is indeed also common, but is despised there. In the bay of Lampong on Sumatra, knowing...

III Book. XXVIII. Chapter. AMBOINESE HERBAL.
Ee 3
<meta>catchwords: CHAPTER, XXIX.</meta>

By soaking the bark in water, beating it vigorously, and stretching it out, the country folk form certain small garments of a rustic color, similar to those constructed from the bark of the *Sacca* <note>original: "Sacca"; likely refers to another fibrous tree described in Book 5, Chapter 9</note> in the Eastern Islands. From this bark they manufacture small tunics which they wear when fishing in the sea; they later wash them out again, though they must not be wrung out forcefully, as they render the water quite slimy <note>original: "mucilaginosam"</note>, and then they are dried once more.

Today they are planted extensively in Batavia in front of houses and along the roads for the sake of their shade. The inhabitants of Celebes soak the bark of this tree in water and beat it to form thick threads used for common fishing nets.

This first *Novella* <note>The local name Rumphius uses for the Sea Hibiscus</note> is called *Bu-Pariti* in Malabar <note>A region in southwestern India</note> according to the *Hortus Malabaricus* <term>Hortus Malabaricus<gloss>A monumental 17th-century treatise on the flora of the Malabar Coast</gloss></term> (volume 1, page 51, figure 29), and by the Brahmins it is called *Val-li-Cari Capoesi*. However, I myself have heard it named *Pu-areti* by the Malabars. Its description does not differ from the Amboinese variety, except that the Malabar kind is said to have the peculiar quality of not being gnawed by any ants, flies, or other insects; for this reason, it bears a much greener foliage than the Amboinese one, which is never free from ants. Furthermore, I am surprised that those learned Brahmins commented so little on its medicinal virtues, which I nevertheless know are familiar to the Malabars, for it is a very common practice to apply its leaves to ulcerations, which are merely bound up with them. Likewise, it is not an *Alcea* <note>Hollyhock family</note>, as the annotator <term>Dr. van Syen<gloss>Arnold Syen, a Dutch botanist who provided commentary for the Hortus Malabaricus</gloss></term> notes in that chapter, but rather an *Althæa arborescens* <note>original: "tree-like mallow"</note>, differing also from the true *Abutilon* described in our Book 6.

Our nation [the Dutch] in those regions often calls them *Indian Lindens* <note>original: "Tilias Indicas"</note>, and sometimes "bell-flowers." The Malabars also apply the old and yellowing leaves, crushed with lime, against toothaches.

### Plate Seventy-Three

This plate displays a branch of the *Novella*, as it is called by Rumphius, where the letter **A.** *denotes a young leaf that is pointed and notched, whereby it differs greatly from the older leaves of the branches.*

## O B S E R V A T I O N.

Since this tree occurs in various regions, it has been named and described by various authors, whom I have collected in the *Thesaurus Zeylanicus* <note>A botanical work on the plants of Sri Lanka</note> (page 136), where it is called the "Ceylonese Ketmia, evergreen and flowering, with a Linden leaf and a yellow flower." In Hartog's seed catalogue, it is listed as the "Greater Indian tree with Linden leaves, or the Greater Indian tree-like Alcea with Linden leaves, with ephemeral Ketmia flowers and orbicular grooved fruits, yielding a juice similar to Gamboge" <note>original: "Guttæ Gambæ"; a mustard-yellow tree resin used as a pigment</note>. (Hermann, *Museum Zeylanicum*, page 45). It is also called the "Indian Ketmia with a Linden leaf" (Plumier, *Catalogue of American Plants*, page 2), as well as the "Indian Ketmia with a Poplar leaf and compressed orbicular fruit" (Tournefort, *Institutiones*, page 100). Other names include the "Tree-like Indian Althæa with a Poplar leaf and ephemeral flower" (Hermann, *Hortus Lugduno-Batavus*, page 22), the "Greatest tree-like Indian Alcea with a Poplar leaf and a larger yellowish flower" (Breynius, *Prodromus 2*, page 10), and the "Tree-like Indian Alcea with a Poplar or heart-shaped leaf and a white-yellowish ephemeral flower" (Amman, *Hortus Bosnianus*, page 6, etc.).

This genus has now been called *Hibiscus* by more recent authors, and another variety of it is called by <term>Van Royen<gloss>Adriaan van Royen, a professor of botany at Leiden</gloss></term> in his *Flora Leydenensis Prodromus* (page 532) the "Hibiscus with a tree-like stem, and roundish heart-shaped leaves that are pointed and notched," which designation likewise fits this species very well.

<column-break/>

the essence of this bark, by soaking it in water, beating it hard, and stretching it out, is used to form certain small cloths, reddish in color, just as is done with the bark of the *Sacca* described in Book 5, Chapter 9, in the Eastern Islands. From this they make little jackets for when they want to go fishing at sea; these can be washed again, though without wringing them hard, as they make the water very slimy, and then they are dried again.

Nowadays they are planted much in Batavia in front of houses and along the roads to provide shade. The people on the east coast of Celebes soak the bark in water, beat it, and make coarse yarn from it, serving for poor-quality nets.

The first *Novella* was named *Bu-pariti* in Malabar in the *Hortus Malabaricus* (volume 1, page 51, figure 29), and in the Brahmin language *Valli-Cari-Capoesi*. However, I myself have heard the Malabars call it *Pu-areti*. Its description does not differ from the Amboinese, except that the Malabar one must have a special quality in that it is not plagued by ants, flies, or other vermin, and therefore bears much fresher foliage, whereas the Amboinese one, as said, is almost never without ants. Thus I am also surprised that those learned Brahmins have given so little of its medicinal powers, which I nevertheless know are known to the Malabars, for it is a very common use to lay the leaves on ulcerations, which are merely bound up with them. It is also not an *Alcea*, as the annotator Dr. van Syen states in the same chapter, but a tree-like *Althæa*, differing also from the upright *Abutilon* described by us in Book 6.

Our Nation in those lands sometimes calls them East-Indian Linden trees, sometimes Bell-flowers. The Malabars lay the old yellowish leaves, rubbed with lime, upon a toothache.

### The Seventy-Third Plate

Shows a branch of the *New-Herb-Tree* <note>A translation of "Nieuwe-kruid-boom," Rumphius's name for the Novella</note>, as it was named by Rumphius, where the Letter **A.** indicates a young leaf that is notched and angled, and thereby differs much from the older leaves.

## O B S E R V A T I O N.

Because this tree occurs in various regions, it has also received various names, which I have collected in my *Thesaurus Zeylanicus* (page 136), where it was named the Ceylonese *Ketmia*, being always green and flowering with the leaf of a Linden tree and a yellow flower, as it was named by Hartog in his Catalogue; it is the East Indian Sun-tree or great tree-like *Althæa* with the leaf of the Linden tree, and flowers lasting but a day, with round furrowed fruits that give a sap like the *Gutta Gamba* of Hermann in his *Museum Zeylanicum* (page 45); and the East Indian *Ketmia* with the leaf of the Linden tree, from Plumier in his *Catalogue* (page 2); as well as the Indian *Ketmia* with Poplar leaf, with round pressed fruits from Tournefort (page 100) in his *Institutiones*; and the tree-like *Althæa* with a Poplar leaf and a flower that lasts only one day from Hermann, in the *Catalogue of the Leiden Garden* (page 22); and tree-like *Alcea* with a Poplar leaf and a yellow flower from Breynius in his second *Prodromus* (page 10), and from Amman in the *Hortus Bosnianus* (page 6).

*Hibiscus* is the name given to this genus by the new herbalists, and a similar sort of this kind was named by Professor van Royen in his *Flora Leydenensis Prodromus* (page 532) as the *Hibiscus* with a tree-like stem, with round heart-shaped leaves, being pointed and notched, which name also belongs to this plant.

AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. Chapter XXIX.

# CHAPTER TWENTY-NINE. CHAPTER XXIX.

### The Creeping New-leaf. Rope Baru.

The Creeping New-leaf <note>original: "Novella repens"</note>, also known as the *Baru*, is a "lazy" tree <note>This refers to its habit of lying along the ground rather than growing upright</note>, possessing a trunk scarcely as thick as a man. It never raises itself upright but lies flat upon the earth; it rarely grows straight, but is mostly curved and bent into an arch, so that it often occupies as much space as would suffice for a house. Its bark is tough and slimy, just like the previous species, and it is the thickest and slimiest of all the *Baru* varieties. The wood is white, spongy, and light, though in very old trunks the heart or pith is dark or ash-colored, marked with red and yellow spots.

This prostrate trunk sends out thick roots and fibers into the earth from all sides, and many upright branches grow upward from it. The leaves are of the common shape but much larger, specifically nine or ten inches <note>original: "pollices"</note> wide and eight long. At the base, they are "eared" <note>original: "auriculata"; refers to lobe-like extensions at the base of the leaf</note>, with the ears resting upon one another and covering the stalk. The stalk itself is round, thin, and likewise ten inches long. Older leaves, however, are only seven inches wide and six long, provided with nine nerves across the surface which meet near the stalk, whereas the common *Baru* leaf has only seven nerves; they are also whiter on the underside than the common variety.

The flower is similar to the previous kind, or perhaps a little more oblong and flabbier at the edges. It does not extend or open as wide as the common one, but remains closed like a bowl <note>original: "instar crateris"</note>; it is yellow in color, but dark red at the base, which is not as visible from the outside as it is in the common variety.

It always grows in flat places, in somewhat cool hills, or on the banks of waters where it forms an elegant arch; however, in steep and uneven places, it does not grow long.

**Name.** In Latin, *Novella Repens*. In Malay, *Baru Tali* <note>original: "Baru Tali"</note>, because it lies on the ground like a thick cable or rope. In Amboinese, *Haru Paracca*, that is, *New-leaf of Secrets*, because with its arch and upright branches it creates a secluded or secret place; others call it *Haru Palacca*, that is, *Excellent New-leaf*, because it bears the largest leaves.

**Use.** From the bark, threads can be drawn just as from the previous species. The younger leaves, when crushed and smeared on the head, soothe the heat in burning fevers and headaches. The wood is used for light posts if it can be found straight, and also—due to its lightness—for buoyancy logs which are tied to boats so they float better in the water.

->**O B S E R V A T I O N.**<-

I have found no illustration of this tree, nor of the one following, which can be understood and conceived both from the illustrations in the *Hortus Malabaricus* <term>Hortus Malabaricus<gloss>A 17th-century botanical treatise on the plants of the Malabar Coast of India</gloss></term> and from our author's description. Furthermore, species of these trees are mentioned in passing by Valentijn <note>François Valentijn (1666–1727), a Dutch minister and author who wrote extensively about the East Indies</note> on page 217 of his description of Amboina.

<column-break/>

### The Creeping New-leaf Tree.

The *Novella Repens* or creeping *Baru* is a lazy tree, gaining a trunk scarcely a man thick, which never stands upright but lays itself flat down upon the earth, seldom shooting out straight, but mostly crooked and bent in a circle, often enclosing a place so large that a house could stand within it. The bark is tough and slimy, like the former, being the thickest and slimiest bark of all the *Baru* lineages; the wood is white, spongy, and light, though in the old trunks it also gets a brown or gray heart, with yellow or reddish spots.

This lying trunk shoots many thick roots or fibers into the earth everywhere, and many straight branches upright. The leaves are of the same shape as the common ones, yet much larger, namely, nine and ten inches wide, eight long, with two round ears at the back that overlap each other and cover the stalk, which is round, thin, and also ten inches long. The old leaves are only seven inches wide and six long, marked with nine veins in a circle, meeting at the back by the stalk, where the common *Baru* has only seven; they are whiter underneath than the common ones.

The flower is also like the common one, or rather as long, and flimsier at the edges; it does not open as much as the common one but remains closed like a little cup, light-yellow in color, and a little brownish-red at the base, which one does not see from the outside as much as with the common one.

It always grows on flats that are in the cool valleys or on the edges of the waters, where it then makes a beautiful circle, but on steep or uneven places, it does not grow long.

**Name.** In Latin *Novella Repens*. In Malay *Baru Tali*: because it lies like a thick cable-rope on the ground. In Amboinese *Haru Paracca*, that is, *New-leaf of Secrets*, because with its circle and upright branches it represents a secret place; yet others call it *Haru Palacca*, that is, *Excellent New-leaf*, because it has the largest leaves.

**Use.** From the bark, one can first spin ropes, like those from the previous one. The young leaves, rubbed and smeared on the head, cool the burning in hot fevers and headaches. The wood is used for light posts if one can get it straight, as well as for float-woods <note>original: "vlotbouten"</note> because of its lightness, which are bound to the prows <note>original: "praauwen"; traditional Indonesian boats</note> to make them float better on the water.

->**O B S E R V A T I O N.**<-

Neither of this nor of the following tree have I found an illustration in this work, which can either be easily supplemented from the *Hortus Malabaricus* or easily understood from the description of our Author. Furthermore, the sorts of *Daun-Baroe* or "New-leaf" are mentioned in passing by Valentijn on page 217.

BOOK III. CHAPTER XXX. AMBOINESE HERBAL. 223

## CHAPTER THIRTY.
### Red New-leaf. <note>original: "Novella Rubra"</note> Daun Baru Mera. <note>Malay: "Daun Baru" (New-leaf), "Mera" (Red)</note>

The third species of the New-leaf <note>original: "Daun Baru"</note> agrees in form with the common variety, but its trunk is not so white on the outside, being more reddish and marked with green and black spots. Its leaves are smaller than those of the common kind, lightly saw-toothed at the edges, and also provided with seven nerves, which are red on the lower part; the stalks and small branches are also red on top, but green on the bottom and rougher than the common kind. The redness of the veins gradually disappears in the older leaves.

The flower is smaller than the common one: it opens in the morning, at which time it resembles a bell, and is yellowish in color with a blood-red center inside; toward evening it closes itself again, and the whole flower becomes reddish or purplish, though with yellow stripes interspersed. The fruits are like those of the common variety.

The wood is white, harder, and more solid than the common kind; its heart or pith also gradually turns reddish. The bark is slimier than in the common kind and drips a viscous juice if it is cut into.

The roots are long, uniform, and about two fingers thick; they send out few fibers and likewise have a reddish heart or pith inside.

Name. In Latin, *Novella Rubra*. In Malay, *Daun Baru Mera*. In Amboinese, *Haru Cou*.

Location. This species occurs very rarely, both on the shore and in somewhat cool valleys, such as those Waytombo valleys in Laha and Hitu, near the Wayalla stream in the district of Kaytetto.

Use. The wood and leaves can generally be used like other species of *Baru*, but the roots and wood of this tree in particular possess a cooling power beyond other *Baru*. Therefore, they are ground in water and given to drink when the heat of fevers comes on; this drink is followed by a mild sweat, which brings great relief. For the same purpose, these leaves are also crushed and applied to the chest and forehead.

When in the year 1678 burning fevers raged violently in Banda, a certain wood called *Caju Dingin*—that is, "cooling wood" <note>original: "lignum refrigerans"</note>—was in great demand and held in high esteem there, as it was used daily with success for cooling in those fevers. Since a great abundance of it was not found there, they sought it from Amboina, sending us small pieces as a sample, which were white, solid, and light. After an accurate investigation, we could judge it to be nothing other than this Red New-leaf, of which we also sent some pieces there. However, since the leaves and flowers of the Bandanese *Caju Dingin* were never sent to me, the matter and conclusion remains uncertain and is left undecided.

In the *Hortus Malabaricus* <note>A famous 17th-century botanical treatise on the plants of the Malabar Coast</note> volume 1, Figure 30, page 53, this New-leaf seems to be named *Pariti* in Malabar, and *Cari Capusi* by the Brahmins; for the leaves there are said to be smaller than the common kind, finely saw-toothed at the edges, provided with many ribs on the underside, and woolly.

Regarding its virtues, the Brahmins noted nothing except that the flowers are ground with woman's milk and dripped into the ears to quiet a headache <note>original: "Cephalalgiam"</note>.

## OBSERVATION.

This variety seems to be only a variation of the first species of *Baru*, which is why no figure was added by Rumphius; the same synonyms seem to apply to this as are further listed in Commelin's *Flora Malabarica* page 2; see also the *Hortus Malabaricus* at the place cited, as well as Breynius and Plukenet's *Almagestum* page 17.

<column-break/>

## CHAPTER XXX.
### The Red New-leaf Tree.

The third sort of *Daun Baru* <note>Malay: New-leaf</note> corresponds in appearance to the common one, though the trunk is not so white on the outside, but sometimes light-reddish, spotted with black and green. The leaves are somewhat smaller than on the common one, finely saw-toothed at the edges, and also spread with seven nerves in a circle, which are red underneath: just as the stalk and twigs are on top, but on the bottom they are truly green and rougher than the common ones, and the redness of the veins also fades somewhat in the old leaves.

The flower is a bit smaller than the common one: rising in the morning it truly resembles a little bell, light-yellow in color, blood-red on the inside at the base; towards evening it draws together again, and the entire flower becomes light-red or somewhat purple, yet with yellow stripes in between. The fruits are like the common ones.

The wood is white, denser, and somewhat harder than the common kind; the heart also becomes gray in time. The bark is somewhat slimier than the common one, with a sticky slime when one cuts into it.

The roots are long, uniform, about two fingers thick, from which few filaments hang, with a reddish heart inside.

Name. In Latin *Novella Rubra*. In Malay *Daun Baru Mera*. In Amboinese *Haru Cou*.

Place. This sort is found very seldom and in small amounts, both on the beach and in cool valleys, such as in the valleys of the Waytombo, in Laha, and on Hitu, near the little river Wayalla in the district of Kaytetto.

Use. The wood and leaves can be used in general like other *Baru*, but especially the roots and the wood of this tree are gifted with a cooling power above other *Baru*; therefore they are rubbed in water and drunk at the onset of the heat in fevers, upon which one begins to sweat gently and feels great relief. For the same purpose one also rubs the leaves and smears them on the chest and the forehead.

When in the year 1678 the hot fevers reigned violently in Banda, a certain wood named *Caju Dingin*—that is, "cool-wood"—was in great report and esteem there, because it was used daily for cooling in those fevers; and because it was not to be found there in abundance, they also requested it from Amboina, sending us some small pieces as a specimen, being a white, dense, and light wood. After diligent investigation, we could judge it to be nothing else but this *Novella Rubra*, of which we also sent them some pieces; however, because they never showed us the leaves and flowers of the Bandanese *Caju Dingin*, the final decision on this remains somewhat suspended.

In the *Hortus Malabaricus* volume I, Figure 30, page 53, this *Novella* seems to be called *Pariti* in Malabar, and *Cari Capusi* in Brahmin, for the leaves are stated there to be smaller than the common ones, finely saw-toothed at the edges, very ribbed underneath, and woolly.

Of its powers, the Brahmins have stated nothing else than that the flowers, rubbed with woman's milk and dripped into the ears, will still the headache.

## REMARK.

This seems to be only a variation of the first sort of the *Baru*, which is why no illustration was provided by Rumphius for this Chapter; it is found in the *Hortus Malabaricus* at the cited place, and to this belong those names found in Commelin's *Flora Malabarica* page 2, by Breynius, and by Plukenet in his *Almagestum* page 17.
