<meta>catchwords: In, Aan</meta>

# CHAPTER THIRTY-ONE.

### *Shore New-leaf. Sea Baru.* <note>original Latin: "Novella Litorea"; Malay: "Baru Laut". This is the Sea Hibiscus, *Hibiscus tiliaceus*.</note>

The fourth species is a coastal type, sometimes growing with a single trunk and sometimes with several, like a shrub. The single-trunk variety grows as thick as a man, not very tall, but crooked, soon dividing itself into branches. The bark is soft, and although it is drawn into thin fibers, it is nonetheless slimy and tough. The leaves differ greatly from the previous three species and have two different forms: on the younger branches and trees, they are provided with three angles and points, of which the middle one is the longest. Near the stalk, they are notched and eared <note>shaped like earlobes at the base</note>, at most ten or eleven inches long and eight wide, though usually they are eight long and five inches wide. These side angles gradually decrease in the older leaves, so that they often disappear entirely; sometimes, however, only one appears on one side. They are shorter than the earlier ones, consisting of a blunt tip; furthermore, these leaves are heart-shaped, but oblong and smooth-edged, bearing five white and protruding nerves that meet at the stalk. They are thick, smooth, and sea-green <note>original: "glauca"</note>, having an aromatic and slightly salty taste. They sit upon long, firm stalks, joined closely together without a specific order, and are mostly covered with galls, which are the nests of insects hiding within them; at the edges, they are often nibbled and deformed.

The flower is very similar to the common *Baru* <note>the common Hibiscus</note> but larger, likewise constructed of five overlapping petals, which are wrinkled and rough to the touch at the base and on the outer part, while the upper and internal part is limp, thin, and streaked. It is yellowish, blood-red at the base—at least not as dark red as in the common variety—and this flower is more closed, never opening as widely as the common one. Throughout the whole morning and before noon, it is open like a bowl or a tulip; after three o'clock in the afternoon, it gradually contracts and closes, acquiring a flesh-colored hue, and toward evening, when it falls off, it turns a dark red. In its center is placed a pistil as long as a finger joint, covered with yellow anthers, which is implanted so deeply in the cup <note>calyx</note> that, being erect and slanted, it can hardly be seen from the outside.

After the flower, the fruit or seed vessel grows out, shaped like a small loaf of bread or a cheese <note>original: "instar panis vel casei"</note>, five-angled out of a round shape, so that those five angles meet in the middle and end in a point. It is two fingers wide and one inch thick. The rind or shell of this fruit is smooth on the outside, woody, and blackish, not opening by itself; however, it can be easily split and opened along those five sutures. Its interior part is white and shining like silk, divided into many cells by thin, white membranes, in which are hidden fifteen or sixteen large seeds, shaped like segments of a cheese, hard, yellowish-gray on the outside, white inside, dry, tasteless, and marked throughout their substance with very fine black spots.

The branches are fragile, covered with a smooth, ash-colored, and tough bark. The wood is of two kinds: the outer part is white, soft, and useless sapwood, gradually becoming redder toward the internal part. In trunks that are no thicker than a thigh, it forms no distinct heartwood, but in old trees, a brown heart is found, in some places interwoven with blackish streaks, distinctly separated from the outer part. It is not exceptionally hard and shows splinters along its length; it also has an aromatic scent approaching that of wine, as is the taste when it is rubbed or worked, stinging the tongue. It is the most pleasant of all medicinal woods to take internally, lacking the bitterness found in the common *Baru*. Conversely, the outer white wood is tasteless, even unpleasant. If this wood grows on the shore in such a way that it is repeatedly splashed by seawater, its taste is also somewhat salty, which is better for medicinal use, but not for cabinet makers. Often this heartwood is exposed at the lower part of the trunk near the thick roots, where it is so scorched by the sun that it becomes black like the following <term>Salimoeri</term> <note>a local name for a hardwood tree</note> and <term>Caju Matta Batu</term> <note>Malay: "Stone-Eye Wood"</note>, yet no such resinous fatness exudes when this wood is burned in a fire.

<column-break/>

# CHAPTER XXXI.

### *The Shore New-leaf Tree.*

*The fourth variety is a coastal genus, sometimes with a single, sometimes with several trunks, shooting up like a shrub; the single one is about as thick as a man, not tall, but crooked, and immediately dividing itself into branches. The bark is soft, nevertheless torn into thin scales, mossy, and tough. The leaves differ remarkably from the previous three kinds, and are moreover of two types of shape, for on the young branches or trees they have three corners or points, of which the middle one runs out much longer, being split at the stalk and divided into two ears; at most ten and eleven inches long, eight ditto wide, but on average eight long and five wide. These side corners disappear on the old leaves, or sometimes one sees only one on one side, and they are somewhat shorter than the former ones, with a blunt point, and furthermore truly heart-shaped, yet elongated, and unserrated at the edges, having five white and protruding veins, flowing together at the stalk; they are thick, smooth, and deep sea-green, with a spice-like taste that pulls somewhat toward the salty. They stand on long, stiff stalks, without order, and close upon one another; they are also mostly covered with some knobs, which are the little tubes of some insects that hide therein, nibbled and disturbed at the edges.*

*The flower is most like that of the common Baru, yet somewhat larger, also made of five leaves embracing one another, stiff and rough to the touch at the bottom and outside, but its upper part is limp, thin, and wrinkled, light yellow, truly yellow somewhat lower down, and blood-red at the base, at least not as brown as on the common one; it also stays more closed, and never opens itself as wide as that of the common kind. The entire forenoon it stays open like a cup or tulip; after midday at three o'clock it closes itself gradually, and becomes light red. In the middle stands a small pillar about a joint of a finger long, hung with yellow nubs, so deep in the cup that one can hardly see it from the outside and standing somewhat askew.*

*After the flower comes the fruit, or the seed-tube, formed like a small loaf of bread or a little cheese, somewhat five-angled out of the round, so that the five corners close together in a little mound toward the middle, two fingers wide and an inch thick. The shell of this fruit is smooth on the outside, woody, and dark gray or blackish, not splitting of its own accord; however, one can easily open it along the five seams. On the inside they are white and gleaming like satin, with thin and white skins, divided into as many chambers, wherein hide fifteen or sixteen large seed-grains, formed like slices of a cheese, hard, mouse-gray on the outside, white within, dry, tasteless, and speckled through the whole substance with fine black dots.*

*The branches are brittle, clothed with a smooth, gray, and tough bark. The wood is of two kinds: the outermost is the white, soft, and worthless sapwood, gradually becoming redder toward the inside; in the trunks that are not more than a thigh thick, it makes no special heartwood, but in the old ones this heart becomes brown, and in some places streaked with blackish lines, remarkably separated from the surrounding sapwood, not unusually hard, and splintery in length, also having a spice-like smell pulling toward the wine-like, as is also the taste when one rubs or works it, somewhat sharp on the tongue, and among all medicinal woods the most lovely to take in, without any bitterness such as is in the common Baru. In contrast, the outer white wood is tasteless, yes, altogether unpleasant; when this wood grows on the shore such that it is splashed by turns by the seawater, the taste is also somewhat salty, which is the better in medicine, but not for the cabinet makers. Sometimes this heartwood lies bare at the lower trunk or thick roots, where it is so scorched by the sun that it becomes as black as the following Salimoeri and Caju Matta Buta, though one finds no such fattiness when burning this wood.*

<meta>This page continues the detailed description of the "Shore New-leaf" tree (Hibiscus tiliaceus). The previous page described its physical appearance and leaves; this page focuses on the quality of its heartwood, its preferred habitats, its local names across the Indonesian archipelago, and its significant medicinal uses, particularly for respiratory and digestive ailments.</meta>

### III Book. XXXI. Chapter. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

In very old trunks, this internal heartwood is mostly hollowed out, decayed, or eaten away, so that it is best to harvest those in which the hollowing is just beginning; for if the wood is still entirely solid, it is considered too "green" and not mature enough.

It can also be propagated through branches planted in the earth, as well as by seeds, but then it usually grows into a shrub, for it does not grow vigorously unless it is near the sea.

<margin>*Name.*</margin> In Latin, it is called Shore New-leaf <note>original: *Novella Litorea*</note>. In Malay, it is Sea Baru <note>original: *Baru Laut*</note> and Beach Baru <note>original: *Baru Partey*</note>. In the Amboinese language, it is *Haru Layn*. The people of Ternate call it Javanese Baru <note>original: *Bayn Java*</note>, and some Amboinese erroneously call it *Holla Holla* and Fish Eyes <note>original: *Yan Matta*</note>, confusing this tree with another of that name.

<margin>*Location.*</margin> It grows spontaneously nowhere except on the shores, and especially those that are rocky and steep, where its broken roots are often seen exposed, revealing a dark brown-to-black heart. This wood is of little value in medicine when it is too old, dry, and tasteless. It also loves solitary shores rarely visited by humans, such as the promontory of Hoeamohel, which they call *Ciel* or the Dry Rice Promontory, where these trees are observed in their most elegant form.

In the Bay of Ambon, it occurs rarely and there only grows as a shrub, because its straight branches are continually cut and lopped off. Those that grow in stagnant inlets and marshy places do not produce wood suitable for craftsmanship or medicinal use.

<margin>*Use.*</margin> No part of this tree is used except its internal brown heart or pith. First, if the pieces are long and fine, it serves the cabinet-maker’s trade, used to form chests and small boxes, as well as the stocks for firearms <note>original Latin: *sclopetorumque fistulae*</note>, because it is light, of an elegant color, and does not easily crack; for in those long pieces, black streaks sometimes appear which decorate the wood.

Boxes constructed from this and kept closed retain a wine-like scent for a long time; thus, the wood also breathes a pleasant odor while being worked.

Its leaves are cooked by the Amboinese (though rarely) like a vegetable dish <note>original: *Sayor*</note> and eaten as greens, which are not unpleasant with their moderate saltiness.

In medicine, I have been taught by experience that this wood is most wholesome because of the immediate relief it brings in certain diseases. Its brown heart, ground upon a porphyry stone with water and given as a drink, is wonderfully beneficial to those suffering from the Red Affliction <note>original: *Oepas Mera*; referring to Pleurisy</note>. This is a sudden and dangerous ailment among the Malays, which causes the patient to have a red face, stabbing pains in the chest, pain in the side and back, and painful breathing. It performs no less, if not greater, effect in every kind of cholera-like passion, called Yellow Affliction <note>original: *Oepas Couening*</note> by the Malays, when people belch and vomit a great quantity of yellow bile.

In "windy colic," this wood is mixed with Dung Wood <note>original: *Caju Tay*; a Javanese wood known for its foul smell when worked</note> and given as a drink to dissipate gas. The powers of this wood are well known to the Amboinese, though the tree itself is despised by them; from this, one recognizes the truth of the wise proverb: that God and His workings through nature are nowhere so present as in things despised by men. I barely learned its powers through money and pleas from an Amboinese midwife, whose mother refused to reveal the wood's secrets to anyone until her death, except to her daughter. I later found the same knowledge among certain people of Ternate. The use and knowledge of it were thereafter restored and called into use by me in Ambon, and I use it daily in my own family. It is also given in burning fevers to strengthen the heart and extinguish the heat. I have often experienced the patient immediately vomiting the drink, even though (as said) it is very pleasant to take; but this is a sign of a stomach overwhelmed by foul matter <note>term: *saburra*; a historical medical term for a collection of undigested humors or "grime" in the stomach</note>, and that this medicine is not enough to overcome the enemy, wherefore such a drink must be administered again.

To find heartwood fit for medicine, one must choose and cut such trees whose heart is not yet decayed, and use that part contained in the roots or the lower trunk, which has drawn its nourishment from the seawater, for that wood is salty when chewed.

<column-break/>

On the very old trunks, this heart is generally hollow, decayed, and eaten away from the inside, so that it is best found in those where it is just beginning to become hollow; for the completely solid wood is still considered too young.

One can also transplant it inland with cuttings, as well as by seeds, but it mostly remains a shrub there, for it will not thrive unless it "smells the sea" <note>idiom meaning "is within range of the sea air"</note>.

<margin>*Name.*</margin> In Latin, *Novella Litorea*; in Malay, Sea Baru and Beach Baru <note>original: *Baru Laut and Baru Partey*</note>. In Amboinese, *Haru Layn*. On Ternate, Javanese Baru <note>original: *Bayn Java*</note>. Some Amboinese erroneously call it *Holla Holla* and Fish-eye <note>original: *Yan Matta*</note>, confusing it with another tree of that name.

<margin>*Location.*</margin> It will grow of its own accord nowhere but on beaches, especially those that are somewhat stony and slope steeply, where its thick roots sometimes lie exposed and reveal the brown-black heart, which is of little value in medicine because it is too old, dry, and tasteless. It also prefers to grow on lonely beaches where there is no feeling of humans, as among others on the projecting corner of Hoeamohel, called *Ciel* or Dry Rice Cape, where these trees stand very beautifully.

In the Bay of Ambon, one finds it rarely, and only as a shrub, because its straight branches are continually chopped off. That which grows in still bays and marshy places does not have good wood for working, nor is it fit for medicine.

<margin>*Use.*</margin> Nothing else from this tree is used except the inner brown heart; first, if they are fine long pieces, for the Cabinet-makers and Gunstock-makers, to make small boxes from it or stocks for muskets, because it is light, beautiful of color, and does not easily crack; for in the long pieces, black stripes and spots sometimes appear that decorate the wood.

The boxes made from it, if kept closed, retain a wine-like smell for a long time, so that this wood is pleasant to work with.

The leaves are cooked and eaten by the Amboinese (though very rarely) like other vegetable pottage <note>original: *Sayor*</note>, which in the mash, with their moderate saltiness, are not unpleasant.

In medicine, I have learned and experienced that this is a blessed wood, because of its present help which it shows in some diseases; for the brown heart, rubbed on a stone with water and drunk, wonderfully helps those who are attacked with the Red Poison <note>original: *Oopas Mera*; that is, pleurisy</note>. A sudden and dangerous accident called *Oepas Mera* by the Malays, because the patient becomes red in the face, feels great stabs in the chest, sides, and back, and breathes painfully. It performs no less, if not more, of an operation in all sorts of "the bile" <note>term: *bort*; likely referring to a biliary disorder or cholera</note> called by the Malays Yellow Poison <note>original: *Oepas Couening*</note>, because it makes people vomit much yellow matter.

In "windy colic," one mixes this wood with Dung Wood <note>original: *Caju Tay*</note> and gives it to drink to break the winds. The powers of this wood are mostly unknown to the Amboinese, and the tree itself is despised by those people; from which one notices the saying of the wise to be true: that God and His workings through nature are nowhere so present as in despised things. I barely learned it through money and the pleading of an Amboinese midwife, whose mother until death would not make the powers of this wood known to anyone but this, her daughter; although I later found the same knowledge among some Ternatans. Furthermore, the knowledge of this wood was made fresh again by me in Ambon, just as I still use it daily in my household. In hot fevers, it is also administered to strengthen the heart and reduce the burning. However, I have often experienced that the patient immediately vomits it back up, although, as said, it is pleasant to take; which is then a sign of a very fouled stomach, and that this rescue is too weak for that enemy: one must not be offended by this, however, but give it again.

To seek and cut this heart for medicine, one must look for such a tree whose heart is not yet decayed, and take that which sits in the roots or the lowest trunk, and has its nourishment from the seawater, which is a little brackish when chewed.

<header>AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. Chapter XXXI.</header>

This brown heartwood must be carefully cleaned of the remaining white sapwood and any decayed internal parts. It should be submerged once or twice in salt water, dried in the sun, and then stored; in this way, it preserves its medicinal powers for up to ten years, provided it is occasionally dipped in salt water again. For the saltiness of this wood is particularly effective at calming burning bile, as I have observed in many other salty woods. Since such a heart is never found to be thick in very old trees, as it is usually hollow, almost no large objects can be crafted from it, except for long prayer beads <note>original: "longae coronae"</note> and the barrels and stocks of muskets <note>original: "sclopetorum fistulae"; Dutch: "laden tot roers"</note>. For these works, parts of the upper trunk are taken, which are further away and free from the salt water, and in which little or no saltiness appears.
The fresh leaves are not unpleasant if chewed with Betel <note>original: "Siri Pinang"</note>, filling the whole mouth with their pleasant scent and slightly acidic flavor.

->The following is added in Rumphius's Appendix.<-

Some fishermen fashion the handles of their large knives, called *Parangs* <note>original: "Parranghs"; broad-bladed knives or machetes</note>, from the brown and medicinal heart of this tree, primarily for this purpose: if they should unfortunately eat some harmful fish <note>Dutch: "opblazer," referring to a pufferfish or blowfish</note> and feel ill because of it, they then rub these handles upon a porphyry stone with water and drink the mixture as an antidote.

# CHAPTER THIRTY-TWO.

## Black New-leaf: Salimoeri.

This tree is also classified under the *Baru Tree* <note>original: "Caju Baru"</note> species, although it differs greatly from them; nevertheless, we have followed the common opinion. It grows sometimes with a single trunk, sometimes with several together, not upright but curved and leaning to one side. It bears few branches and leaf-stalks, which spring from them without order, sitting upon yellow petioles <note>leaf stalks</note>. These are not heart-shaped like those of the *New-leaf* <note>original: "Daun Baru"</note>, but lance-shaped like the broad head of a spear, ending in a more obtuse point, six or seven inches long, and four or five wide; they are a bright green, whole and not saw-toothed, woven with a few oblique veins. When they fall, they turn black, and when crushed, they give off a more unpleasant odor and taste than the *New-leaf*.
The flowers hang in many clusters, but they do not all open at the same time; the flowers resemble the Thorn-apple <note>original: "Stramonia"; the Datura flower</note>, but are much smaller, the size of the *Marvel of Peru* <note>original: "Mirabilis Mexicana"</note>, consisting of a thin and long funnel that opens at the top into five or six wrinkled petals, joined so closely together that they seem to be made of a single petal. They are orange in color, or like a Marigold <note>original: "Calendula"</note>, and are scentless. As many as there are petals, so many yellow stamens are located inside, mixed with other shorter and whitish ones. Indeed, many flower heads hang from one broad cluster, but only one or two open at a time. These are followed by fruits or rare berries hanging together from a small cluster; they are rounded and pointed like a blunt cone, crowned with a short, hard tip, barely the length of a finger joint. On the outside, they are smooth and mostly green, but they gradually turn black and open near the tip. Inside, they contain a pyramidal stone, pointed at the top and broad at the bottom, where it is hollowed out like a small pit; at the sides, it is extremely angular and covered with sharp warts as if 

<column-break/>

carved by a master's hand. It is pale and wood-like in color, and all the little pits are hollowed out...

# Book III. Chapter XXXII. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...grooves and small pits, as if it had been fashioned by the hand of a craftsman; it is, however, pale and woody. All these small pits are filled with a dry and cork-like substance, which adheres so firmly to the stone and its outer skin that it must be separated and stripped away with an iron tool. The cleaned kernel resembles a Turkish gallnut <note>original: "gallam"; a growth on oak trees used for making ink</note> or an Emblic Myrobalan <note>original: "Mirobalanum Emblicum"; the fruit of *Phyllanthus emblica*, known for medicinal properties</note>, though that lower pit makes it nearly hollow.

The fully ripe fruit is divisible into four or five segments, and in each is contained a small kernel, matching the *Canarium* <note>the Java Almond</note> in substance and flavor.

The branches are fragile, and if they are broken, they give off a somewhat bitter scent.

The bark is whitish, smooth, and thin, also breathing out an unpleasant odor.

The outer wood <note>sapwood</note> is very white, the useless part of which is about two fingers thick. The inner heartwood <note>original: "cor"; literally "heart"</note> is a grayish-black or earth-colored or dusky hue, dry, tough, and wrinkled when cut. If it is cut or hewn crosswise, it appears to be composed of many thin rolls laid upon one another, blacker at the edges—or as the common folk say, browner and harder—where black longitudinal stripes run through the gray wood; and if it is polished, it exhibits a dark green reflection in certain places. For this reason, many compare it with European Walnut wood or the West Indian *Palo Santo* <term>Palo Santo; "Holy Wood," referring to Lignum Vitae, prized for its extreme hardness and medicinal resin</term>. Indeed, pieces of it are found so black that they vie with Ebony wood, though its lightness and the flow of its stripes reveal the difference. The internal pith is gradually browner and more spongy, but never split or hollow except at the knots.

This wood is of two kinds: the first and best is the black described above, which is called the "male," and its bare heart is no thicker than a thigh. The other is grayish, consisting of blackish veins running lengthwise almost like Fir; this is called the "female" and is much lighter, and large pieces can be formed from it so that planks can be sawn from it, though it is considered of less value than the former.

If these woods are worked or cut while fresh, they give off a musk-like <note>original: "Moschi"</note> scent, though a weak one, which becomes more piercing if they are placed upon coals; the blackest pieces, when exposed to fire, catch flame very easily and exude oil, though only a little.

It also grows near the shores, or not further than a stone's throw from them inland; however, the best wood is provided by that which grows on the small shores of islands, where the roots mostly raise themselves bare above the ground and the trunk is so curved that it almost leans toward and rests upon the earth. For this reason, these trees are very easily uprooted or cast down by the sea or winds; their outer and useless wood rots away in a short time, but the inner heart is found scattered in large pieces along the shores, appearing gray on the outside but elegantly black on the inside. These pieces are considered better and are preferred over those cut fresh from the tree, though only small items can be fashioned from them.

Other trees, which are often as thick as two men, carry an elegant and wide heartwood, but as long as they are growing, it is never as black as those that are dead and cast upon the shore, although elegant and black parts of this heart may stand out even in vigorous and growing trees, especially if they have been well-exposed to the sun. Even in one and the same tree, the trunk or certain branches are often bare on one side, with their black heart standing out, while the other part is covered with vigorous and green wood.

**Name.** In Latin, *Novella Nigra* <note>Black New-leaf</note> and *Ebeniformis* <note>Ebony-like</note>. Our nation calls it *Baſtaart Ebben-hout* <note>Bastard Ebony</note>. To the people of Ternate it is called *Salimoeri, Tsjalimoeri*, and *Salungeri*. Some call it in the Malay language *Baru Laut*, confusing it with the preceding species. To the Amboinese, *Kanawa, Kanawan*, and *Kanewan*; in Banda and the islands situated to the Southeast, *Cenau* and *Caju Waro*; in Buro, *Fana* and *Fala*. At Makassar, *Ama*. The other or grayish species is called in Banda and Key *Waranderck*.

**Location.** This wood is known in all the Moluccas, Amboina, and the remaining islands situated to the Southeast. This tree also grows abundantly and most elegantly on the stony mountains of Ciela, or the dry promontory of the Hoeamohel region, where these and the preceding trees—

<column-break/>

—filled with a dry and corky substance, so attached to the stone and the outer skin that one must pick it out with an iron tool. The cleaned kernel then resembles a Turkish gallnut, or *Mirobalanus Emblicum*, though the bottom pit makes it nearly spherical.

The entire ripe fruit can be divided into four or five parts, and in each sits a small kernel, in substance and taste like *Canary* <note>The Java almond, *Canarium indicum*</note>.

The branches are brittle; when broken off, they give off a somewhat bitter scent.

The bark is whitish, smooth, and thin, also of an unpleasant scent.

The outer wood is very white, and making up the sapwood, it is about two fingers thick. The inner heart is from grayish-black or earth-colored, dry, tough, and shaggy when chopped. When one saws or chops it crosswise, it appears to be put together from many thin rolls lying upon one another, blacker at the edges, or as the common man says, browner and harder, where one sees the black stripes or flames running through the gray wood lengthwise; and when one polishes it, it gives a dark green reflection in some places, therefore many compare it with European Walnut wood, also with the West Indian *Palo Santo*; indeed, one finds pieces so black that they can defy Ebony wood, but the lightness and the flow of the flames betrays them immediately. Toward the inside it becomes gradually grayish again and more porous, yet never cracked or hollow, except at the knots.

One finds this wood in two sorts: The first and the best is the black one, described here above, which one calls the male, and is not more than a thigh thick—I mean the bare heartwood. The second is light gray, with blackish veins in the length, almost like Fir wood. This is held for the female; it is much lighter, and one can get large pieces of it, so that one can also saw planks from it, but it is held to be of lesser quality than the first.

When one works these woods or chops them fresh, they give off a musk-like, though weak scent, which one notices more strongly when burned on coals; the black pieces held to the fire burn very easily and sweat out an oil, though sparingly.

It also grows near the beaches, or no more than a stone's throw from there inland, but the best is that which grows on the bare beaches of small islands, where one sees the roots mostly bare above the ground, and the trunk so bent that it almost lies upon the earth; therefore these trees are also very easily uprooted and broken by the sea or winds, from which the outer sapwood rots off in a short time, and the inner heartwood lies scattered in large pieces along the beach, looking gray on the outside but beautiful black within; these pieces are held to be better than those one chops from the fresh tree, but one can only have small work from them.

Other trees, which become as thick as two men, indeed have a beautiful broad heart, but as long as they grow, it is never as black as the others that are dead and lie on the beach, although one also sees beautiful black pieces of this heart sticking out bare on the still-growing trees, especially those that stand well in the sun. One also sometimes finds on this tree the trunk or some branches bare on one side, with the black heart sticking out, and the other half covered with the growing wood.

**Name.** In Latin *Novella Nigra* and *Ebeniformis*. Our nation calls it *Baſtaart Ebben-hout*. In Ternate *Salimoeri, Tsjalimoeri*, and *Salungeri*; some call it in Malay *Baru Laut*, mixing it with the previous one. In Amboina *Kanawa, Kanawan*, and *Kanewan*; In Banda and the South-Eastern Islands *Cenau* and *Caju Waro*; on Buro *Fana* and *Fala*. On Makassar *Ama*. The second or gray species is called in Banda and Key *Waranderck*.

**Location.** It is known in all the Moluccas, Amboina, and South-Eastern Islands, but the best is found, as said, on small and uninhabited islands. It also stands very much and beautifully on the stony promontory of Ciel, or the dry rice-corner of the Hoeamohel territory, where the—

### AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. Chapter XXXII.

The trees are so lush and grow so tightly packed together that the steep shore can hardly be traversed, nor can the different types of wood be distinguished as long as they have not been stripped of their bark. All the northern part of Boëro <note>modern Buru Island</note> is also filled with this wood, but mostly the ash-colored variety, which is harvested in the interior of the region, although the black variety is also found on the rocky coast of Liffatetto. In Great Amboina, near the promontory of Liena and on the nearby island of Puloana, many elegant and long pieces of this wood are found washed up along the shore.

*Uses.* From the straight trunks of this tree—first cleared of the outer, useless sapwood—or from the black pieces found already cleaned on the shore, the inhabitants fashion the posts for their houses and huts. This wood, although it appears light and spongy, is nevertheless extremely durable; it resists rain, wind, and the earth, and does not crack much even when exposed to the open sky. Thus, these posts are found undecayed and bare, fixed into the ground here and there in the mountains of Ceram, where houses were destroyed many years ago.

A certain native inhabitant told me a ridiculous story, claiming he had seen such posts in Keya <note>the Kei Islands</note> that had stood there since the beginning of the world. He likely thought this because it was the time when that place was first inhabited, for the Malays sometimes call the beginning of a settlement the "beginning of the world."

Certainly in Ceram, such posts can be shown in places where no houses have been built for a hundred years, such as in Tanuru, which is on the coast of Great Ceram situated toward the Northwest <note>original Latin: "Argestem"; referring to the Northwest wind</note>. Those black and streaked pieces are also greatly used and sought after today by joiners, turners, and cabinetmakers. Elegant railings, feet, and posts for chairs, bedsteads, and benches can be fashioned from them, and from the widest pieces, small tables, splints, boxes, and similar works can be made. Nowadays, such wide planks of this wood are found—three feet wide, in fact—that large chests and tables can be manufactured from them. From the common and inferior wood, various gunstocks and barrels are prepared; for this purpose, the East India Company seeks a large quantity of this wood from Boëro, because since it is a light and extremely durable wood, it is judged and found to be the best and most suitable for these works.

If this wood is hewn, it shows no splendor at first; but if it is dry and is polished and rubbed, it acquires an elegant chestnut color, and then those streaks or "flames" come into view. Furthermore, the closer the wood is to the edges or the exterior, the blacker and more elegantly streaked it is.

In Europe, it would undoubtedly be greatly desired by cabinetmakers if it were known there and imported. I have seen the sheaths of the weapons called *Krissen* <note>the Kris, a traditional Malay dagger with a wavy blade</note> fashioned from the best pieces of it, not covered in any silver, so that those streaks and flames might better show themselves and refresh the nose with their pleasant scent.

NB. It should be noted in passing that we call it *flamed* <note>original Dutch: "vlamd"</note> in wood, roots, stones, and the like, which the Latins call *Wavy* <note>original: "Undulatum"</note> and *Crisped-wavy* <note>original: "Undatum crispum"</note>, while the twists of the veins they call *Whirls* <note>original: "Vortices"</note> and *Swirls* <note>original: "Gyri"</note>.

Although the scent of this heartwood—especially when placed on coals—is sweet and like Musk, but heavy at the same time, the Amboinese nevertheless shun it as destructive and harmful to those standing nearby, as it makes them weak and listless, just as the wood itself is held to be. This slander was brought upon it by a Moorish priest <note>original: "flamen"; likely an Imam or religious leader</note> of Hitoe, who by chance cooked his food on a fire made of this wood and shortly after felt a pain in his belly along with his companions, which he ascribed to the smoke of this wood. Since he was very skilled and knew all kinds of woods and planks best, they gave him great credit. Furthermore, I saw this same priest and other native root-diggers <note>original Greek: "Rhizotomos"; herb-gatherers</note> cutting the blackest and richest pieces of this wood, which protruded at the root or the lower part of the trunk on trees that were still growing. Before doing so, however, they would mutter certain words and lay down a small gift of a copper coin or silk threads, which is their custom if they dig up medicinal roots, as if to prove themselves grateful to nature for her gifts. They use these pieces for almost the same purpose as the preceding, namely for a certain kind of *Oepas* <note>Upas; a potent plant extract used as medicine or poison</note>, which they call the black variety, and
ple-

<column-break/>

these and the previous trees grow so luxuriantly and close to one another that one can hardly walk along that steep beach, nor distinguish the timbers, as long as they are not peeled. The entire North side of Boëro is also full of this wood, though mostly of the gray variety, which is cut somewhat further inland, although the black is also to be found on the stony point of Liffatetto. On Great Amboina, near the point of Lien and the nearby small island of Puloanan, one finds many beautiful and long pieces washed up along the beach.

*Usage.* From the straight trunks, first entirely cleaned of the outermost sapwood, or from the black pieces found already cleaned on the beach, the inhabitants make posts for their houses and huts; for this wood, although it appears light and pithy, is nonetheless uncommonly durable against rain and wind as well as the earth, also cracking little or not at all, even if it stands under the open sky. Thus one finds these posts uncorrupted and bare, standing in the earth here and there on the mountains of Ceram, where the villages <note>original: "Negoryen"</note> were cleared out many years ago.

A certain native said to me ridiculously, and held it to be true, that he had seen such posts on Key that had stood there since the beginning of the world: He perhaps wanted to say from the time that the place had been inhabited, for the Malays sometimes call the beginning of the habitation of a land the "beginning of the world."

Indeed, they can show posts on Ceram in such places where no villages or houses have stood in the last hundred years: as among others at Tanuru, the Northwest point of Great Ceram. Also, the black and "flamed" pieces are used very much nowadays and are sought daily more and more by the cabinetmakers, turners, and gunstock makers, for one can have especially beautiful railings, feet, and small posts from them for chairs, bedsteads, and benches. From the widest pieces, whole tops for small tables, chests, small boxes, and similar works are made. And now such wide planks are found, three feet wide, that one can make large chests and tables from them: from the poorest sort, all kinds of stocks for muskets and firearms are made, for which the Honorable Company <note>The Dutch East India Company (VOC)</note> sends for a large quantity from Boëro every year; because it is a light and nonetheless durable wood, it is found to be especially fit for that purpose.

When first planed, this wood shows no luster or form, but when rubbed dry and polished, it first becomes a beautiful brown, and the "flames" appear; and the more it has stood at the edges, the blacker and more beautifully veined it is.

In Europe, it would without doubt be well-received if it were known to the cabinetmakers and exported there. From the best pieces, I have also seen Kris-sheaths made, not covered with silver or gold plates, so that they would show the "flames" better and be pleasant from within with their sweet smell.

NB. To note in passing, that we in Dutch call it *flamed* <note>original: "gevlamd"</note> on timbers, roots, stones etc., that which the Latins call *Undulatum* and *undatum crispum*, but the turnings of veins, that which they call *Vortices* and *Gyros*.

Although the smell of this heartwood, especially on coals, is sweet and musk-like, yet heavy, it is nonetheless shunned by the Amboinese, who hold it to be harmful to bystanders, as making them weak and powerless, just as the wood itself is. A Moorish Priest of Hitoe brought it into this bad reputation, who by chance cooked his food with this wood and shortly thereafter felt some belly-pain with his companions, which he attributed to the smoke of this wood; and because he was a particular connoisseur of plants, he was given the more belief. Furthermore, I have seen that same Priest and other native root-diggers cut off the blackest and fattest pieces of this wood, which stuck out bare at the roots or the lowest trunk of still-growing trees, but first muttering some words and laying a small gift of a copper penny or some silk threads by the root, which is a common custom among those people when they dig out some medicinal roots, to be, as it were, grateful to nature for her gifts. These pieces they use for almost the same purpose as the previous ones, namely for a kind of *Oepas*, which they call the black, and thereby

...mostly they mean a "windy" colic <note>Latin: *Colica ventosa*; a digestive ailment characterized by gas and cramping</note>, though I do not have as much experience with this as with the former, nor is it so well known in common medicine.

If one rubs their hands with the tender and younger leaves of this tree until they are impregnated with their scent, they will be safe from the stings of venomous fish, such as the *Ican Swangi* <note>Malay: "Ghost Fish," likely a scorpionfish</note> and *Ican Sambilang* <note>Malay: "Striped Eel Catfish"</note>; if someone has already been stung by them, and the affected part is rubbed with these leaves, they will feel no pain.

The ribs <term>ribs|the curved timbers forming the hull of a ship</term> of smaller vessels are also fashioned from this wood, though our shipwrights have found that iron nails do not stay fixed for long in this wood when it becomes dry, as it is too spongy and tends to shrink. To prevent this, the locals say that this wood should be used while green <note>freshly cut</note>, so that the nails hold more firmly as they rust.

The people of the *Kei* Islands use it in this same manner for the ribs of their vessels, taking it freshly from the trees, and by no means using the black wood or that which floats upon the shore. If this wood is sliced into thin sticks and bundled together, they provide excellent torches on the beaches, which are not easily extinguished by the wind.

I have understood that this wood is also found on the *Coromandel* Coast, where it is known by the name of *False Ebony* <note>Latin: *Ebeni spurii*</note>, from which chairs, bedposts, and tables are fashioned; these are then stained with ink, polished, and sold as true *Ebony*, even though it is much lighter. The same can be done with our Amboinese *Salimoeri*. Whether the Coromandel variety is the same as this remains to be investigated; for my part, I doubt it.

When the people of Ternate row toward a place where they intend to bring peace, they sing in their *Corre Corre* <note>A traditional swift rowing vessel</note> that the flagpole is made of *Bali-Njawa* or *Bayn Java*—that is, the previously mentioned *Baru Pantey*—and the socket in which it stands is made of *Salimoeri*. This is because these two woods are great medicines and are always joined together like male and female, whether rubbed and made into a poultice to be applied externally to draw out various diseases, or taken internally. By this song, they wish to signify that wherever these two woods arrive, two powerful remedies have arrived.

The people of *Makassar*, on whose shores this wood is found quite black, use the wood for *Balira*—that is, the shuttle <term>shuttle|a tool used in weaving to carry the thread across the loom</term>, called *Parang* by the Malays—as well as for spinning wheels.

If one rubs the hands vigorously with the young leaves so that they smell of them, one shall be secured against the stinging of venomous fish, such as the *Ican Swangi* and *Ican Sambilang*; but if one has been stung by them beforehand, and rubs the same leaves upon it, one shall feel no pain.

The internal timbers and ribs in small vessels are also made of this wood, though our carpenters have experienced that iron nails do not hold well in this wood when it becomes dry, because it is too porous and shrinks somewhat. To prevent which, the locals say that one should use the green wood, in which the nails rust more firmly.

In the same manner, the people of *Kei* use it mostly for the internal timbers of their vessels, taking for that purpose those which are half-old and from fresh trees, and by no means that which is black and drifts on the strand. This wood, cut into thin sticks and bound together again, makes good torches to provide light on the beach, which do not easily go out from the wind.

I understand that this wood also occurs on the *Coromandel* coast under the name of *bastard Ebony-wood*, from which they make chairs, feet for bedsteads, and tables, which they then coat with ink, polish, and sell for genuine Ebony, although it is much lighter; which could also be done with our Amboinese *Salimoeri*. Whether the Coromandel variety accords with this remains to be investigated; I for my part doubt it.

When the Ternatans row <note>Dutch: *pangayen*; to paddle or row</note> toward somewhere where they wish to bring peace, they sing on their *Corre Corren* that the flagpole is made of *Bali Njawa* or *Bayn Java*—that is, the aforementioned *Baru Pantey*—and the little tube in which it stands is of *Salimoeri*, because these woods are two great medicines, and are always joined together as male and female, whether rubbed and made into a pulp and smeared on the outside to draw out various illnesses, or taken internally. Wishing thus to make known that wherever they come, two great remedies have come.

The Macassarese, on whose shores it occurs quite black, use the wood for *Balira*, that is, shuttles, called *Parang* by the Malays, as well as for spinning wheels.

# CHAPTER THIRTY-THREE.

## The Shore Gelala, the Beach Gelala, and the Black Gelala.

The three following trees hold a primary place among the flowering trees, as they are conspicuous for their most elegant flowers at a certain time of year and are visible from a great distance, making them easily distinguishable from others—especially the first species, which I shall treat in this chapter. Indeed, I have observed three species: 1st, the *Shore* or *Black Gelala*; 2nd, the *white*; and 3rd, the *aquatic*.

The *Shore* or *Black Gelala* <note>Latin: *Gelala litorea*; today known as the Indian Coral Tree or *Erythrina variegata*</note> is the most common, very similar to an **Oak** in the size and thickness of its trunk. This trunk is very thick but not tall, soon dividing itself into thick branches covered in a smooth, ash-colored bark. However, it is everywhere beset with short, firm, and broad thorns like those of wild roses, except for the lower part of the old trunk where they are not seen; all other parts up to the tips of the branches, and even the leaf-stalks <term>rachides|the main stems of a compound leaf</term>, are so covered with them that they defy climbing or touching.

The leaves bear a great resemblance to those of the **Garden Bean**, but they are much larger and smoother, four or five inches long and slightly less wide. They have large lobes <note>Latin: *sinus*; meaning indentations or "cheeks" in the leaf shape</note> at the edges and always grow in threes. The middle leaf sits on a longer stalk, and at the base of this leaf are two wart-like bumps; the two rear leaves likewise have two small warts and very short stalks. Otherwise, these three leaves are very similar to one another, except that in the two side leaves—in the manner of **Beans**—the large vein does not run straight through the middle. Their outer lobe is much wider than the inner one; they are smooth and dark green on the upper side, and slightly wrinkled underneath.

Many flowers sprout together in a long cluster and are constructed of a single petal, which is placed on one side and slightly curved like a little boat. It is the color of Kermes <note>Latin: *Kermesinus*; a brilliant crimson or scarlet dye derived from insects</note>. On the other side are ten long, firm red stamens with dark brown anthers; five of these are shorter and five are longer, and the middle or eleventh one (which is the *pistil*) is the longest. The entire flower is about the length of a small finger. The stamens are joined near their base, where two other small, round, concave leaves appear like little shells, resting upon two other similar leaves. The two outermost of these have a more intense color than the flower petal itself, while the two inner ones are blood-red, together forming a sort of small hood located between that petal and those stamens; they never open.

The flowers are followed by the fruits, which are round pods about a hand-breadth long or slightly less, and a small finger thick. They are divided into various round segments <term>isthmos|narrowed sections between the seeds in a pod</term>, which are usually joined by a narrow neck. In each such segment is hidden an oblong, thick bean, compressed on both sides as if many had been cut from a single roll, marked with a seam along the back. Some of these are red and marked with a "navel" <note>Latin: *hilo*; the scar on a seed indicating where it was attached to the pod</note> in the manner of beans, similar in size and shape to horse beans. Many such pods hang together from a common stalk, remaining on the trees until they are cast down by the winds, for neither humans nor animals eat these beans raw. The wood of the tree is white, soft, and useless, easily succumbing to rot; if it is cut, it gives off a smoky odor.

Among all Indian trees, there is none that observes its time of flowering and fruiting as precisely as this *Gelala*. It produces its flowers once a year at the end of July, when the Sun enters Leo. At this time, the tree casts off most of its leaves and produces these elegant red flowers everywhere on its large branches, so that from a distance the tree looks as if it were covered with a red cloth, with only one or two leaves remaining here and there on the branches.

It remains in this state until the middle of August, when the flowers fall in great abundance, covering the ground like a crimson cloth. Then, in the month of Septem-

# XXXIII. CHAPTER.

## The Shore or Black Gelala Tree.

The three following trees also have a place among the flower-bearing ones, *because at a certain time of year they are made conspicuous by their flowers and recognizable from afar, especially the first kind, which we deal with in this chapter; for I have noted three of them: 1. The Shore or Black Gelala. 2. The White or Striped. 3. The Water Gelala.*

*Firstly, the Shore or Black Gelala is the most common, most like the Oak tree in the size and thickness of its trunk; for this trunk is very thick, though not high, and immediately divides into thick branches, covered with a light-gray smooth bark, yet everywhere set with short, stiff, and broad thorns, like those of wild roses, except at the bottom of the old trunk, where they are not noticed. The rest, up to the tips of the twigs, is so full that one can nowhere climb or touch it.*

*The leaves have a great likeness to those of the Turkish beans <note>likely Kidney beans or Runner beans</note>, but much larger and smoother, four and five inches long, and somewhat less wide, with large "cheeks" on the sides, always standing three together; the middle one on a longish stalk, with warts at the beginning of the leaf, and the two rear ones together have two little warts and very short stalks. Otherwise they are all three very much alike, except that the two at the sides, after the manner of beans, do not have the large veins right in the middle, and thereby the outer "cheek" is much larger than the inner; smooth on top and high- or dark-green, and somewhat rough underneath.*

*The flowers come forth many together on a long cluster, and consist of only one leaf <note>petal</note>, which stands on one side, slightly bent together like a little boat, a true scarlet-red. On the other side stand ten long and stiff red threads <note>stamens</note> with brown tips, among which five are shorter and five longer, and the middle or eleventh is the longest. The whole flower is a small finger long. These threads are fixed to each other at their origin, and behind them one sees two other small leaves, round and bold like little shells, lying on two other similar leaves, of which the two outermost are higher in color than the petal, and the two innermost are blood-red, together making a little hood, standing between the large petal and the aforementioned threads, yet never opening.*

*After the flowers follow the fruits, which are round pods, about a hand long or less, and a small finger thick, divided into various round bumps, which mostly hang together by a narrow neck. In each bump hides an elongated and thick bean, somewhat pressed at both ends as if many were cut from a roll, with a seam on the back; some are reddish, and marked with a navel after the nature of beans, in the size and shape of horse-beans. Many of these pods hang together on a cluster, remaining on the trees so long until they are beaten off by the wind, for neither humans nor cattle use these beans raw. The wood is white, weak, and unworthy for any carpentry, rotting easily, and of a smoky smell when one chops into it.*

*Among all Indian trees, there is none that keeps its season so precisely in bearing flowers and fruits as this Gelala; for it brings forth its flowers only once a year, and that in the latter part of July, when the Sun begins to enter Leo, when the tree sheds most of its leaves and brings forth these red flowers on all sides in large clusters, so that from afar the tree seems as if covered with a red cloth, with a leaf hanging here and there on the branches.*

*In this state it remains until past the middle of August, when the flowers fall in multitude and cover the ground as if with a scarlet cloth, whereupon in Sep-*

...tember, the fruits and new leaves follow. However, when around July (as is usually the case) there are great storms and frequent rains, the flowering time is delayed for more than half a month; otherwise, in lands where the summer is dry at that time, as is generally the case in all the islands located to the West of Amboina, it follows a fixed and stated order. It grows mostly on flat shores, but is also found further inland, usually planted by people using thick branches driven into the ground, although its beans also sprout very well.

**Name.** In Latin, *Gelala litorea* <note>The Shore Gelala</note>. In Malay, *Gelala Laut* <note>Sea Gelala</note> and *Gelala Itam* <note>Black Gelala</note>, because it grows spontaneously along the shores and bears dark green leaves compared to the following species. Some maintain that *Dadap* is the Malay name and *Kelala* the Ternate name, while in Macassar it is called *Rara* and *Caju Madjannang*, that is, the "quiet leaf," the reason for which will be indicated below. In Amboina, on the Leytimor peninsula, it is called *Ucken*; in Hitoe and Ceram, *Nackil* and *Lackin*. By the Balinese it is called *Dalundung*. By the Bandanese, *Dadap*. The word *Gelala* can be derived from the Arabic *Gal* or *Galal*, meaning to make clear or bright, because when it blooms, it spreads a brilliant red color.

**Place.** It is found in all the islands of Watery India <note>The East Indies</note>, growing everywhere on shores where small stones are found and mixed in; however, it is not found, or only rarely, on plain sandy shores, such as on the western side of Bali, though it appears further inland in that region.

**Use.** In the Western islands, this tree provides greater use than in Amboina, where through its copious flowers it often causes fish to be very rare in the months of August and September; at least, the common people attribute this cause to it, since its glowing red flowers, hanging from the trees as well as fallen on the ground, cast their glare far into the sea, by which the fish are terrified and leave the shore. However, this scarcity is also observed in those months in such places and shores where no *Gelala* trees are found; hence the Bandanese attribute it not so much to the flowers of this tree as to the "milky water" <note>likely bioluminescent plankton blooms</note> which infects the sea at that same time, making the sea appear fiery and milky-white at night, from which the fish flee toward waters of ordinary color.

Conversely, there is a great sympathy between the flowers of this tree and the Amboinese bird called the *Loeris* <note>The Lory, a type of parrot</note>, which is entirely blood-red in color over its whole body except the head; there is also another smaller species called *Perroquitten* <note>Parakeet</note>, which is variegated with red, yellow, and green. These birds have a natural instinct and passion for the red color of this tree, frequenting it in great numbers and sitting upon it when it brings forth its flowers, so that they can hardly be distinguished from the flowers as long as they sit quietly. With their beaks, they open that red little head or nectary placed in the center of the flower and drink the juice collected there from the dew.

Furthermore, this tree has a use in medicine, for the juice of the fresh leaves dripped into ulcers, with the leaf itself placed over them, cleanses them and preserves them from rot, and prepares the "raw flesh" <note>granulation tissue</note> for consolidation, to be procured by other plasters. However, this cure does not have a happy success in people who are "full of humors" <note>unhealthy body fluids</note> or too addicted to drink, who consequently have an excessively abundant flow of humor to those parts.

In the Amboinese smallpox, these leaves are especially celebrated for cleansing impure and foul ulcers, which also proceeds slowly, since the Gelala cannot complete its operation as long as new pus is generated by the continuous flow of humors; hence a dry and sober diet is prescribed for such people. Others treat ulcers with the help of the leaves in the following way: take tender leaves of the common *Gelala* with a fourth part of *Pangaga* <note>Indian Pennywort, *Centella asiatica*</note> roots, stems, and leaves; expose these together to the dew overnight, then squeeze out the juice without adding any water. Dip a lint-plug into this and place it in the ulcer, then cover it in the proper manner. This juice can be kept for several days in a bamboo reed. It consumes all corrupt flesh and will make the base of the wound clean within the space of three or four days, whereby the healing is quickly promoted. Others chew the leaves in their mouth with a little Cumin, which they place on the ulcer, putting another leaf of the same tree...

...covered with a leaf. This paste works for about half an hour and then the treatment is finished. If this is performed in the morning and the ulceration does not swell or hurt by evening, it is a sign that healing will follow; if the opposite is felt, this cure will achieve nothing. If it succeeds, a month’s time is needed to cure a large ulceration. The *bark of the tree*, chewed with *Pinanga* <note>Betel nut</note> and a little *Massoy* <note>an aromatic medicinal bark from New Guinea</note>, is beneficial for those suffering from Dysentery. Some also attempt to cure fresh wounds with these leaves, but I have rarely seen success, since they do not possess a consolidating or scarring power, but rather a purifying one. Its tender leaves, cooked into a pottage with those of *Gumira* and the milk of *Calappus* <note>Coconut</note> and eaten, or the leaves applied to the chest, generate and increase milk for nursing mothers and those recently delivered. The same leaves, taken with the flowers in any manner, provoke obstructed menstruation in women. However, a contrary effect is observed in the bark, which, as stated, when chewed with *Pinanga* and the juice swallowed, is useful against Dysentery.

Those birds called *Loeris* <note>Lories, a type of parrot</note> are caught in great numbers if poles are placed among the flowering branches and smeared with birdlime made from the milk of the *Soccus* <note>Breadfruit or Jackfruit tree</note>, upon which they land more easily since the natural branches of the tree are beset with thorns everywhere.

When the flowering time ends, these birds seek the mountains again and are no longer seen for the rest of the year, after we have heard their talkative screeching with great patience for over a month. It is especially marvelous that such birds, which are of a very wild nature and not easily tamed, so greatly desire the sap of these flowers that they come from the distant mountains to the houses of men where these trees stand, from which they can hardly be driven away by human noise and shouting.

The leaves are used with other herbs as a vegetable and eaten, especially for a certain kind of food called *Boboto* by the people of Ternate, in which certain fish are wrapped in the leaves and cooked.

Its wood also has a vegetative power, as it is easily propagated by branches; hence it is used for poles and hedges where living enclosures are desired. When these branches are planted, they grow into thick trees within a short space of time, from which the leaves can also be collected for use. This wood, however old the tree may be, is always spongy and light; when dry, it maintains a fire for a long time by smoldering, emitting smoke until the whole piece collapses into ashes, yet it never catches flame, even if fanned by wind or breath.

*Carolus Clusius* <note>A famous 16th-century Flemish botanist</note> seems to have depicted this tree in the first appendix of his book on rare plants, page 253; he received its leaves from a certain Portuguese physician, who called the tree *Coral*, perhaps from the red color of the flowers, and said that he had received it from America.

A certain species of this *Gelala* occurs in *Java* and *Bali* and is called by the peculiar name *Dap Dap*. Its trunk is taller than the preceding one but is not covered in thorns; its leaves are smaller, rounder, and thinner, but the flowers and fruits are similar to the preceding, though its beans are rounder. It is also used for poles and hedges like the former, but its leaves are not eaten. Its wood is of the same substance and use, namely for maintaining a slow fire.

A similar or not very different tree is the Chinese *Goudong*, growing in the coastal province of *Fujian* or *Hockien*. According to the report of the Chinese, it matches the common *Gelala* in its manner of growth and form, but its leaves are said to be larger and the branches thorny, though not the trunk. The flowers are likewise red, and the fruits are like the beans of the preceding.

Its wood is also soft and useless, except that it is used for certain musical instruments because it gives a good sound. It is said to be stripped of leaves for one half of the year and laden with leaves for the other half, shedding its leaves every year in the month of August; in contrast, the Amboinese tree is destitute of leaves for only one and a half months and does not observe such a precise time for shedding. The Chinese claim such a wondrous tree is located in the royal palace at *Beijing* near a famous well, as indicated to me by a certain Chinese man who is more learned and skilled than the rest of his countrymen; for this nation, being more addicted than others to Chaldean superstitions, [relates] wonderful thin...

<meta>catchword: things</meta>

<column-break/>

...half an hour, and after that it is done. If one does this in the morning and the ulceration does not swell or hurt in the evening, it is a sign that it will accept the healing, but feeling otherwise, nothing will be accomplished with this. And if it is to succeed, one still needs a month’s time for a large ulceration. The bark chewed with *Pinang* <note>Betel nut</note> and a little *Massoy* is good for those who have the "red flux" <note>Dysentery</note>. Some also want to heal fresh wounds with these leaves and their sap, from which I have seen little success, since there is no healing or scarring power in them, but rather a purifying one. The young leaves, cooked into a mash with those of *Gumira* and *Coconut* milk and eaten, and the leaves placed on the breast, increase the milk of nursing women. These same leaves, consumed with the flowers in any manner, provoke the stopped monthly courses of women. A contrary power is found in the bark, which, as said, chewed with *Pinang* and the juice swallowed, helps against the "red flux."

The aforementioned *Loeris* <note>Lories</note> are also mostly caught then, when one binds some sticks between the flowering branches smeared with birdlime made from *Soccus* <note>Breadfruit/Jackfruit</note> milk, upon which they sit more easily because the real branches are full of thorns.

When the flowers are over, the aforementioned birds fly back into the mountains, and one does not see them for the whole year thereafter, after one has had to endure their cackling and noise on those trees with patience for more than a month. It is surprising that such birds, which are very wild by nature and difficult to tame, are so greedy for the sap of these flowers that they come from the far mountains close to the houses where these trees stand and can hardly be chased away by the shouting of people.

The leaves are also used among other *Sayor* <note>vegetables/pot-herbs</note> as pottage and eaten, especially for a sort of food that the people of Ternate call *Boboto*, when some fish are bound with certain leaves and so cooked.

It is also a fast-growing wood, which is easy to propagate with sticks; therefore it is used for *Paggar* <note>fence</note> posts and large enclosures where one wants living *Palisades*. These sticks, when set, sprout in a short time and become thick trees, from which one can simultaneously have the use of the leaves. This wood, however old the tree becomes, always remains porous and light; when dry, it keeps the fire for a long time by smoldering, until the whole stick turns to ash, without ever giving off a flame, no matter how much one blows into it.

*Carolus Clusius* seems to have sketched this tree in his books on rare plants in Appendix 1, page 253, having received its leaves from a *Sevillian Physician*, who called them *Coral* (perhaps from the red color of the flowers) and claimed to have received them from *America*.

A kind of this *Gelala* is found on *Java* and *Bali*, specifically called *Dap Dap*, with a trunk as high as the preceding but without any thorns; the leaves are smaller, rounder, and thinner; otherwise, the flowers and fruits are like the preceding, but the beans are rounder. It is also used for the posts of *Paggars* like the former, but its leaves are not eaten. The wood is of the same substance and use, namely to maintain a slow fire.

A similar or not much different tree is the Chinese *Goudong*, growing in the coastal province of *Fujian* or *Hockien*, most similar in manner of growth and appearance to the common *Gelala* according to the word of the Chinese, though the leaves are said to be somewhat larger, the branches somewhat thorny, but the trunk not; the flowers likewise red, and the fruits like beans.

The wood is soft, white, and useless, except for some musical instruments because it gives a good sound. It is said to stand without leaves for one half of the year and laden with leaves for the other half, beginning to shed its leaves annually in *August*, whereas the *Amboinese* stands without leaves for only one and a half months and does not keep such a precise time for the falling of the leaves. The Chinese say such a wondrous tree stands in the Emperor’s Court at *Beijing* near a famous water well, as a certain Chinese man told me, who must be clever and learned above his countrymen; for this nation, being taken with *Chaldean* superstition above others, [relates] wondrous thin...

# Book III, Chapter XXXIII. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...about this Beijing *Goudonga* <note>Likely referring to a species of *Erythrina* or *Firmiana*</note> they tell stories and boast: namely that every year at the point of the *Lipsiu* <note>original: "Lipsiu"; likely a reference to the Chinese solar term *Liqiu*, marking the beginning of autumn</note>, which in my judgment is during the Sun's entry into the fourteenth degree of Leo, on the fourth day of August, it drops its first leaf. At that minute, previously announced and proclaimed by the Astronomer, the Emperor with his family and Nobles must fall on their knees and pray, at which time within a quarter of an hour either the leaf will fall, or the Astronomer is punished as a liar, or as one unskilled in his art. However, the other Chinese *Goudonga* trees would not observe that minute so precisely, just as I think the Beijing one could not perform so, unless the deceitful devil came onto the stage, who is simultaneously invoked.

If further investigation shows that these three last species differ too much from the common *Gelala*, a special chapter should be assigned to them in a revision of this work.

The Macassarese names *Rara* and *Madjanang* (that is, "peaceful leaf") are derived from the fact that they plant its green branches around the place where a woman in childbirth lies; by this they try to indicate that people ought to keep themselves quiet around that place. They also place its leaves under children's beds and pillows to prevent sudden cries and their terrors in sleep. Some of the common people roast the beans of the *Gelala* slightly in a pan over the fire, which they eat or cook with fish.

*In the Balinese Dalundung tree, a thick, fat, and white wood-worm is produced, which is edible like the Sago-worms, called Sibata by them, which they extract with sharp little sticks from the holes in which it sits, poking until it takes hold of them; otherwise such a hole is opened, and that worm is eaten by the bird Blatock, described by us under the name of the Javanese Woodpecker <note>original: "Pici Javani"</note>.*

Bontius <note>Jacobus Bontius, a Dutch physician and pioneer of tropical medicine</note>, in Book 6, Chapter 43, calls the first species of this *Boatsjin Kring*, which name properly belongs to the following third species, the aquatic *Gelala*, but it is not erroneous if in that chapter its beans are numbered among the edible fruits that grow on trees, which he describes in the same chapter. Concerning the use of *Tsjin Krings*, however, he indicated nothing.

In *Rumphius's* Appendix, the following is added.

In the *Garden of Malabar* <note>original: "Hort. Malab."; referring to the *Hortus Malabaricus*, a massive 17th-century survey of the flora of the Malabar coast</note>, part 6, Figure 7, it is called *Muricu*, in Portuguese *Folhas de Trinitade* <note>Trinity leaves</note>, in Dutch *Slackhout* <note>Hit-wood</note>, *Washout* <note>Wax-wood</note>, and *Elephants-Tree*, where its illustration and description agree sufficiently with ours. However, from the text there, it is not understood that three leaves are always joined together, nor that it drops its branches every year at a certain time of year, and is then entirely loaded with flowers, which perhaps does not happen in the Malabar regions as it does here.

*The Macassarese name Rara and Madjanang (that is, "quiet leaf") comes from the fact that they stick the green branches around the place where a woman in childbirth lies, wishing thereby to warn that one ought to be quiet thereabout; they also lay the leaves under the children's sleeping places to prevent sudden screaming and frightening in dreams. Some common people roast the beans of Gelala a little in a pan over the fire, and eat them or cook them with fish.*

For of the use of *Tsjin Krings* he has said nothing at all.

In the Appendix of Rumphius this was added.

# CHAPTER THIRTY-FOUR.

## White Gelala: White Gelala <note>original: "Gelala Puti"</note>.

**A**nother variety noted here is the *white Gelala* <note>original: "Gelala alba"</note> or variegated variety, similar in form to the preceding one, which grows quickly with a sufficiently thick and vigorous trunk, though it bears a thin crown of leaves.

The shape of the leaves matches the common variety; they are always joined in threes and sit upon a long stalk <note>original: "petiolo"</note>. The middle leaf is always the largest and, as a peculiar sign or mark, they are always marked along the central vein with a white or yellowish line running out to both sides in the manner of a flame. This marking is widest near the stalk and pointed at the top, usually irregular; for some leaves bear this "flame" to the width of a finger, others much narrower, some have it widest near the stalk, and others in the middle.

The color of the leaves is green, but much more cheerful and pale than the preceding variety, and they are marked with similar small bumps near their origin. This tree presents an elegant sight because of these variegated leaves.

The flowers and fruit mostly agree with the previous kind, appearing many together in long clusters <note>original: "racemis"</note> skillfully joined, though they are sparser and do not make the tree look so red. Not all of them open at the same time, and their petals are shorter, but wider and thicker than the common variety; the color is likewise scarlet <note>original: "Kermesinus"</note>. The pods <note>original: "Siliquæ"</note> are rarer and shorter than the first, but the seeds are of the same shape. Furthermore, all the branches and the trunk are beset everywhere with many short little thorns, though the leaf stalks are smoother. The wood has the same spongy substance, but its odor is much more penetrating than the common variety, being unpleasant and goat-like <note>original: "hircinus"</note>. This is not so noticeably perceived in the leaves, but especially toward evening and in rainy weather, when this tree diffuses that scent far and wide. It comes very close to the scent of hay observed in fresh rice, which the Malays call *Wangi* <note>original: "Wangi"; meaning fragrant</note>, and which they consider pleasant.

It does not observe the time of year for flowering and shedding leaves as strictly as the common variety, being about a month later; for at the end of August or the beginning of September the flowers only just begin to come forth, while the tree is still clothed in leaves. In the month of October it begins to form fruit, of which few grow to perfection, and then it gradually casts off its old leaves, though it is never as bare as the common kind. During the flowering time, birds called Lories and Parakeets <note>original: "Peroquieten"</note> frequent this tree as well, destroying the flowers so that they rarely produce fruit. It is propagated by branches, which sprout very easily; however, the little trees produced from fallen seeds <note>original: "officulis"</note> bear leaves similar to the common kind—intense green and not variegated—from which I conclude that this white variety is merely a degeneration or variation of the common one.

On Java, around Batavia, another species of this variegated Gelala occurs, which is likewise thorny but bears smaller leaves than the preceding. These have a bright red line in the middle instead of white, or at least are red around the central vein and whitish at the edges of those lines; otherwise, it is similar to the previous one.

*Name.* In Latin *Gelala alba & picta* [White and Painted Gelala]. In Malay *Gelala Puti* [White Gelala] and *Kelala Tulis* [Painted Kelala], by some *Kelala Lacki* <note>original: "Lacki"; meaning male</note>. In Amboinese *Ucke Puti* and *Ucke Moni*, that is, *fragrant Gelala*.

*Location.* This species rarely occurs in Amboina, with only one or two trees planted here and there near houses. It is best known in the Moluccas and the eastern part of Celebes, but to the west it is found very rarely or not at all.

*Usage.* The inhabitants of these islands used to employ these leaves to cover cooked rice so as to impregnate it with their hay-like odor, which is pleasing to them. These same leaves are also cooked and eaten like a vegetable with coconut milk <note>original: "Calappi lympha"</note>. In those places where it grows abundantly, its branches are used for garden poles and fences, because they very quickly—
