# CHAPTER XXXIV.

## The White or Flame-Variegated Gelala Tree.

* **T**he second kind of Gelala known here in this land is the white or painted one, mostly resembling the previous one in shape, also with a reasonably thick trunk that shoots up quickly, but with a narrow crown.*

*The shape of the leaves is like the common one, and they always stand three together on a long stalk, the third or middle one always being the largest. As a special mark, they have a white or yellowish stripe, flame-like around the middle vein, with some hooks running out to the sides, widest at the stalk and pointed at the front, generally very irregular; for some have these flames a finger wide, some much narrower, others have it widest at the stalk, and others in the middle.*

*The green of the leaf is also more cheerful and lighter than the previous one, and they are provided with similar warts at their origin, so that this tree has a beautiful appearance from the painted leaves.*

*The flowers and fruits mostly correspond with the previous one, coming forth close together in long clusters, though somewhat more sparsely, and they do not make the tree so red. They do not open all at once, and their leaf [petal] is somewhat shorter, but wider and thicker than the common one, also of a scarlet-red color. The pods are fewer and shorter than the common ones, the seeds of the same fashion. Furthermore, all branches and the trunk are likewise set with many short thorns, but the twigs are smoother. The wood is of the same spongy substance, with a much stronger scent than the common one, also unlovely and goat-like, which scent is not felt so strongly in the leaves, but especially in the evening and in rainy weather, when this tree spreads that scent far: it comes closest to the hay-like scent of fresh rice, which the Malays call *Wangi* <note>original: "Wangi"</note> and consider pleasant.*

*In flowering and changing leaves they keep no such precise time as the common ones, coming a good month later; for in the latter part of August or the beginning of September it first begins to show its flowers, while it still stands full of leaves. In October it begins to form the fruits, of which few come to perfection, and then it begins gradually to cast off the old leaves, never becoming so bare as the common one. In its flowering time it is also visited by Lories and Parakeets, which spoil the flowers so much that they rarely bear fruit. It is propagated with branches, which shoot up very easily, but the young trees coming from the fallen seeds gain leaves like the common ones—namely, entirely deep green and without flames—from which I guess that this white kind is merely a change [variation] of the common one.*

*On Java around Batavia one has yet another kind of this painted Gelala, whose tree is also thorny, the leaves somewhat smaller than the previous one, which have a light-red stripe in the middle instead of the white, or indeed red around the middle vein, and whitish at the edges of the flames, the rest like the previous one.*

Name. *In Latin* Gelala alba and picta. *In Malay* Gelala Puti *and* Kelala Lacki, Lacki *that is male. In Amboinese* Ucke Puti *and* Ucke Moni, *that is fragrant* Gelala.

Place. *This kind is found little in Amboina, here and there a tree planted by the houses. In the Moluccas and the eastern part of Celebes it is best known; further to the West one has it not at all or very little.*

Usage. *The inhabitants of these islands are accustomed to use the leaves to cover the cooked rice, to impart to it their hay-like scent, which is pleasant to those people; these same leaves were also cooked with coconut milk as a mash and eaten. In places where one has it in abundance, the branches were used for garden stakes, because they—*

**T**his plant is very similar to, and appears to be the same as, the plant called **ERYTHRIA** *with three leaves and a very simple, smooth stem* by Van Royen in his *Flora of Leiden* <note>original: "Fl. ## CHAPTER THIRTY-FIVE.

### *The Water Gelala: Tsjamghing.*

The third species known to us is the *Water Gelala*, which grows along the banks of rivers. It is much shorter than the two previous types, sometimes growing as a shrub and sometimes as a low, curved tree. The entire plant is far more thorny than the preceding ones—indeed, it is covered in thorns even up to the ribs of the leaves—and it is not easy to handle. Its branches are brittle, watery, and mostly hollow inside. The leaves also sit upon long stalks, arranged without a fixed order in groups of three <term>ternate: arranged in threes</term>. They are smaller and narrower than the common variety, being oblong in shape. On older trees, they are five or six inches long and three fingers wide; they are sea-green on the upper side and ash-gray underneath.

The flower is of two kinds, both emerging from short clusters at the ends of the branches, smaller than those of the common species but otherwise of the same form. In the male flowers—found on the more thorny trees—the buds are initially oblong and slightly curved at the tips, of a purplish-brown color, sitting in green cups <term>calyx: the green outer part of a flower that protects the bud</term>. When open, the upper petal of the flower is bent backward like a bean blossom and is blood-red in color. In the center of these, a whitish head or germ appears, flanked by two small violet leaves, from which ten long, white, and firm stamens emerge. I have remained unfamiliar with the pods and seeds until now, as they are rarely found. However, those planted in my garden finally produced fruit: specifically, bumpy pods like the previous ones, but shorter and thinner. Inside are oblong beans, half the size of the previous ones, resembling pieces of a cross-cut cylinder or a small roll; they are slightly lumpy, hard, smooth, and dark brown. Occasionally, the upper petal of this flower is deep purple or violet, and its firm stamens lie so closely together that they resemble a small horn.

The female flowers—found on what is mostly a shrub with fewer thorns—are usually pale green but have a hint of violet on the upper petal. Otherwise, they are similar to the former. The flowers of both types are always joined in threes on short stalks, opposite another three, forming many diagonal crosses along the cluster;
<meta>The text breaks here; the Latin "cruces" matches the Dutch "kruissen".</meta>

<column-break/>

They grow quickly, and with their thorns, they block the way in.
*These leaves are also used for ulcers and, cooked in a vegetable dish <note>original: "Sajor"</note>, to increase the milk of nursing women, just like the previous one. For this use, those trees are selected that stand some distance from the beach, because otherwise the saltiness of the sea infects the leaves somewhat.*

## XXXV. CHAPTER.

### *The Water Gelala Tree.*

The third species known to us is the *Water Gelala*, because it grows along the banks of rivers, remaining much lower than both the preceding types—sometimes a shrub, sometimes a low and crooked tree. The whole growth is much thornier than the previous ones, even covered with thorns up to the ribs of the leaves, and is not at all easy to handle. The branches are brittle, watery, and mostly hollow inside. The leaves also stand on long stalks without order, also three and three together, but smaller and narrower than the common ones; they are longish, five and six inches on old trees, four inches long on young trees, and three fingers wide, blue-green or sea-green on top, and pale or gray underneath.

*The flower is of two kinds, both coming forth on short clusters at the tip of the branches, smaller than on the common one, but otherwise of the same shape. Those of the male (whose tree is thornier) are first oblong buds, somewhat curved at the tip, purple-brown, and standing in small green cups. The leaf of the open flower is somewhat bent backwards at the front, in the manner of bean blossoms, arch-red or blood-red. At the back of the flowers one sees a whitish mound, flanked on the sides by two small violet leaves, from between which peek ten long, white, and stiff threads <note>stamens</note>. The pods and beans are still unknown to me, as they are seldom found. But finally, those planted in my garden have given their fruit: namely, knotty pods like the previous ones, but smaller and thinner. In them lie oblong beans half as large as the previous ones, resembling pieces of a sliced cylinder or roll, a little bubbly, hard, smooth, and dark brown. Sometimes the uppermost leaf of this flower is high-purple or violet, and the stiff threads lie so close against each other that they resemble a little horn.*

*Those of the female (which mostly remains a shrub and has fewer thorns) are mostly pale green, with some violet on the uppermost leaf, otherwise like the previous one. The flowers of both always stand three together on short stalks, opposite three others, and make many diagonal crosses on the cluster,* unpleasant in taste, the wood is

branches; the taste is unpleasant. The wood is whitish, soft, and dries out very easily. It blooms in August, at the same time as the other Gelalas, but in Amboina I have never seen fruit produced from this species.

### Name.
In Latin **Water Gelala** <note>original: "Gelala Aquatica"</note>. In Malay and Javanese *Tsjankring* and *Tsjankre*, as well as *Gelala Ayer* <note>Malay: "Ayer" means water</note>. In Balinese *Tsjangbing* and *Fangbing*, which names are also in use among the Malays; in Macassarese, it is called *Canne*.

### Habitat.
It occurs rarely in Amboina. It grows as a tree in Lariqua and Hitoe, but as a long shrub along the banks of the Elephant River, always not far from the sea. It is found in great abundance in Java, Bali, Borneo, and Sumatra, as well as a small amount on the eastern coast of Ceram.

### Uses.
The Balinese and Javanese eat the younger leaves, both raw with fish <note>the Dutch text specifies eating them with "Bocassan," a fermented fish/shrimp paste</note>, and cooked in a vegetable stew with coconut water <note>original: "Calappi lympha"</note>. The flowers are also eaten after being soaked in water overnight and then cooked with coconut milk. The leaves are likewise crushed with the fragrant *Boborri* ointment <note>a traditional cosmetic and medicinal paste</note>, as are the old thorns of the trunk, so that the ointment acquires the proper consistency. Its root, when boiled and drunk or applied as a liniment, cures Beriberi. Others use the bark of the trunk in the same manner and for the same purpose as the *Seru* tree. Two pieces of the driest wood, when rubbed against each other, produce fire. This wood is also superior to others for preserving a fire and creates an excellent coal, much like a match-cord <note>original: "funis igniarius," used for firing cannons or muskets</note>.

The inhabitants use the lower-growing variety for garden hedges and enclosures, as they plant many of its branches closely in the earth; these grow into one another, becoming entangled and spreading widely. The tips of the branches must be broken off frequently to make the hedges denser and to produce smaller leaves without flowers or fruit.

The inner part of the bark from the branches, when scraped or crushed and applied to fresh wounds, heals them. The wood itself, crushed and drunk, is beneficial for those who urinate blood or pus.

white, soft, and very easily dried. It blooms in August with the other Gelalas, but I have never seen it bear fruit in Amboina.

### Name.
In Latin Gelala Aquatica, in Malay and Javanese *Tsjankring* and *Tsjankre*, also *Gelala Ayer*. In Balinese *Tsjangbing* and *Fangbing*, which name is also used by the Malays; in Macassarese *Canne*.

### Habitat.
In Amboina it is seldom found. The tree-like form in Lariqua and Hitoe, the long or shrubby form along the banks of the Elephant River, everywhere not far from the sea; but one finds it in greater abundance on Java, Bali, Borneo, and Sumatra, as well as a little on the East coast of Ceram.

### Use.
The Balinese and Javanese like to eat the young leaves both raw, with Bocassan <note>fermented shrimp paste</note> and fish, and cooked with coconut milk into a mash. They also rub the leaves into fragrant Boborri ointment, as well as the old thorns of the trunk, to give that ointment its proper consistency. Its root boiled, drunk, and smeared on, heals Beriberi. Others use the bark of the trunk with that of the Seru in the same manner. Two small pieces of the driest wood or twigs rubbed against each other produce fire; just as this wood is better than others for keeping a smoldering fire, leaving a firm coal, like a match-cord.

The inhabitants use the low variety much for fences or hedges, both around their fortifications and gardens, planting many stakes next to one another, which then grow tightly together and spread out wide; however, one must often break off the tops so that they grow denser and obtain smaller leaves, without fruit or flowers.

The inside of the bark of the branches, scraped or rubbed and placed on fresh wounds, heals the same. The wood is also rubbed and given against the urinating of blood and pus.

Book III. Chapter XXXVI. AMBOINA HERBARIUM.

# CHAPTER THIRTY-SIX.

## The Blinding Tree, Caju Matta Buta.
<note>original: "Arbor Excæcans, Caju Matta Buta." The name is derived from the Malay *Kayu* (wood/tree), *Mata* (eye), and *Buta* (blind), referring to the sap's ability to cause temporary or permanent blindness.</note>

Now follow those trees that pour out a harmful or purging milk, among which stands out that noxious tree commonly called *Blind-wood* <note>original: "Blindhout"</note> or the blinding and milky tree. It is considered a species of the tree-like *Lathyris* <note>original: "Lathyris arboreſcentis"; a type of spurge</note> and is the terror of all sailors who are sent out to cut wood for fuel, for they are so often deceived when they handle this tree recklessly and roughly.

The tree is unlovely, leaning with a curved trunk, knotty, split, and full of pits and cavities. It grows either with a single trunk or with several; those with a single trunk lean out over the shore and cling so low to it that one can only pass under them by crawling. Furthermore, its roots usually run exposed across the ground of the shore. The more exposed, curved, and hollowed out it is, the more potent its powers are. With its branches and leaves, it all the more entices those passing by, as they are elegant, smooth, and shining. The smaller branches often form elegant arcs and circles arranged in a ring, which send out various small shoots from the sides. It is divided into male and female forms, not differing much in appearance, except that the former bears only flowers, while the latter bears both flowers and fruit.

First, the male bears smooth branches and shoots covered in a brown and even bark. The leaves agree with those of the Pear tree, being four inches long and over two fingers wide, ending in a blunt tip. They are smooth, thick, shining, brittle, and woven with thin transverse veins that can scarcely be felt with the fingers; near the edges, they meet in a border. These edges are serrated or sparsely and shallowly toothed, which appears more at one time than another; for in the rainy months, they are thicker, more shining, and more sparsely serrated. The male's leaves are usually more toothed than the female's. They sit without order on short stalks around the branches. The older leaves turn red like fire and gradually fall off, so that the entire tree is often stripped of them.

From the leaf axils, small flower-bearing catkins <term>catkin: a slim, cylindrical flower cluster without petals</term> grow, as in the *Hazel* <note>original: "Corylo"</note>, as long as a little finger and as thick as a straw, of a greenish-yellow color. These are covered with mossy florets, mostly constructed of short and pale stamens with yellow anthers, joined three together. They present no distinct flower shape, and after they have adorned the tree for a month, they wither and fall off without fruit, so that this species is entirely sterile, like the *Labor-Lost Willow* <note>original: "Trugi Perda Salix"; likely referring to a sterile or non-fruiting variety</note>.

Second, the female has an ash-colored and rougher bark on its branches, and the tree itself is generally covered with more knots and bumps. The leaves can hardly be distinguished from those of the male, but anyone who observes them closely will see the female's leaves are somewhat longer and softer, more sparsely toothed, and not as smooth or brightly green as the male's, and more narrowed at both ends, with a more curved tip. From their axils likewise grow small, bright green catkins, but much shorter than the preceding ones, opening into no notable flowers, consisting of small green heads that grow into fruit. These hang in small clusters together on short and thin stalks, and are three-cornered, three-furrowed berries. Each bump is divided by an intermediate groove. On the outside they are smooth and a bluish-green, having the size of *Capers* <note>original: "Capparidum"</note>. They are marked at the top with a sharp three-pointed tip, like the fruit of the *Castor Oil Plant* <note>original: "Ricini"</note>, whose form—as well as that of the *Caper Spurge* <note>original: "Lathyris" or "Cataputia Minoris"</note>—they so exactly resemble that at first sight they would be taken for them; it undoubtedly seems to be a tree-like species thereof. Inside, three cells appear, and in each is contained a small stone or bean, the size of a *Catjang* <note>original: "Catjang"; a small tropical bean</note>, that is, the *Smallest Indian Bean* <note>original: "Phāſeoli Indici minimi"</note>. They are very similar to the seeds of the *Castor Oil Plant*, being smooth and marked with black stripes, but much smaller, and filled inside with white marrow.

<meta>catchword: Fruit</meta>

<column-break/>

# THIRTY-SIXTH CHAPTER.

## The Kape-Mata-Buta Tree, or the Tree of Blinding Eyes.
<note>This column is the Dutch translation of the same botanical description provided in the Latin column.</note>

Now follow some trees that give a harmful or purging milk, among which that fatal guest stands out, which is commonly called *Blind-wood* <note>original: "blind-hout"</note> or *Milk-tree* <note>original: "melk-boom"</note>, and which one would take for a *Tree-like Lathyris* <note>original: "Lathyris arboreſcens"</note>. It is the terror of all sailors who, being sent out to chop firewood, are as often deceived by this tree as they handle it incautiously.

It is an ugly tree, with a crooked trunk, overhanging, knotty, scarred, full of hollows and bumps, shooting up with either single or several trunks. However, the single ones mostly hang forward on the shore, and so low that one must crawl under them. Moreover, the roots stand mostly exposed above the shore; yet the more exposed, crooked, and bumpy it stands, the more virtues one finds in it. With its branches and leaves, it all the more attracts the passer-by, as they are beautiful, smooth, and even. The small branches also sometimes make strange bends and curls in a perfect circle, with various shoots on the sides. It is divided into Male and Female, not differing much in appearance, except that the first bears only flowers, and the other bears flowers and fruits.

First, the Male has smooth branches and twigs, covered with a brown and even bark. The leaves resemble those of the Pear tree, four inches long, fully two fingers wide, with a blunt point, smooth, thick, glistening, brittle, marbled with fine veins across that one can barely feel, and meeting in borders close to the edges. The edges are toothed or notched, but not deep or far apart, which notches one sees more at one time than another; for in the rainy months they are fuller, shinier, and with few notches. Thus, those of the male are generally more toothed than those of the female. They stand on short stalks without order around the branches; in old age they become fire-red and fall off gradually, often making the tree entirely bare.

From the axils of the leaves come small catkins <note>original: "kattekens"</note>, like those of the *Hazels*, a pinky-finger long and a straw-thick, green-yellow in color, and covered with a small mossy bloom, mostly consisting of short and pale threads with yellow nubs, standing three by three together, without the shape of little flowers. After they have graced the tree for about a month, they dry up and fall off without fruit, so that this sort is sterile, like the *Labor-Lost Willow* <note>original: "Trugi Perda Salix"</note>.

Secondly, the Female has a gray and rougher bark on its branches, just as the tree is generally set with more bumps. The leaves are hardly to be distinguished from the male, but he who pays close attention will find those of the female somewhat longer and softer, also more widely saw-toothed, and not as smooth or bright green as the male, narrower at the back and front, and the tip somewhat bent. From her axils also come small light-green catkins, but much shorter than the previous ones, opening into no noticeable bloom, set with small green buds from which the fruits come. These hang in short clusters together on short thin stalks, and are three-sided berries, divided with three furrows and as many bumps, of which each bump still has a furrow in the middle. On the outside they are smooth and blue-green, the size of capers, on top with a three-tongued point, just as the fruits of the *Castor Oil Plant* <note>original: "Ricinus"</note> have. These fruits resemble those of the *Lathyris* or *Caper Spurge* <note>original: "Cataputia Minor"</note> so well that one takes them for such at first, and it is undoubtedly a tree-like genus thereof. Inside one sees three little chambers, and in each a grain or little bean, the size of a *Catjang*, that is, the *Smallest Indian Bean* <note>original: "Phaſeolus Indicus minimus"</note>. They are also very like the seeds of the *Castor Oil Plant*, namely smooth and marked with black lines, but much smaller, filled inside with a white marrow.

<meta>This page continues the description of the Blinding Tree (Excoecaria agallocha), focusing on its fruit, the extreme danger of its milky sap to sailors, the various animals that inhabit its hollows, and the resinous "fat wood" known as Teda.</meta>

AMBOINA HERBARIUM Book III. Chapter XXXVI.

These fruits or berries remain green on the tree for a long time and finally turn brownish or red; if they are then heated by the sun's rays, or placed in a warm spot, they open with a crack and the small seeds leap out, a trait also found in the fruits of both types of *Cataputia*. <note>original: "Cataputia"; likely referring to the Caper Spurge or Castor oil plant, known for its explosive seed pods.</note> If chewed in the mouth, they initially show no notable flavor, but eventually they burn the throat slightly.

Both of these species pour out a copious white milk—thick, unpleasant, and nauseating—if they are wounded, and especially from the branches and broken leaves. This sap is even forcibly ejected if the tree is struck or cut with force, and it is as harmful as any *Tithymalus* <note>original: "Tithymali"; a general name for plants in the Spurge family (Euphorbia), which contain irritating latex.</note> milk or juice, especially to the eyes if it touches them; it inflames them so much and renders them so swollen with pain that one might lose their use, unless help is quickly provided.

Our own sailors in their first established voyages experienced this quite often to their own detriment. Being sent out to cut wood for the hearth, and seeing these trees conveniently located on the shore, they struck them forcefully with their axes. But soon, with the milk leaping out, their eyes were so afflicted that they ran along the shore as if driven mad, and some among them lost their sight entirely.

However, it is not enough for these splendid trees to be filled with such harmful sap; they are moreover inhabited by other harmful residents. In various pits or cavities of the trees, short tree-vipers make their nests, as do species of large ants that run across them with a swift gait, as well as various species of bees and wasps. In particular, certain small bees described in our *History of Animals* under the name *Apiculæ* or *Tobii* <note>original: "Apiculæ seu Tobii"; small stingless bees often found in the East Indies.</note> live there; they do not sting, but fly in great numbers into the ears and hair. I have often found these in the hollows of these trees with a large amount of edible honey; however, the mouths of such cavities were obstructed by a certain black and resinous gum that would melt by the fire and was somewhat fragrant, which is the *Melicera* <note>original: "Melicera"; a term for honeycomb or a mixture of honey and wax, here referring to propolis.</note> constructed and prepared by these little bees.

Now we must also describe the part of this tree endowed with powers, which is an old and "fat" <note>oily or resin-saturated</note> substance of the wood, located neither in its heart nor near the bark, but in such places of the lower trunk or thick roots that are raised above the ground and are split and bare, where they form pits and cavities as if eaten away. This fatty wood, called *Teda*, is a "spurious" <note>false or imitation</note> *Agallochum*. <note>original: "Agallochum"; also known as Aloeswood or Eaglewood, a highly prized fragrant resinous wood.</note> On the roots or where it protrudes, it is ash-gray and smooth on the outside, but in the hollows it is covered with a wrinkled, blackish bark, like a hairy skin, which is not however a true bark, but rather a thin film easily separated. Internally, it mostly bears a rusty color, sometimes darker, sometimes paler; however, near the edges, especially where it is scorched by the sun's rays, it turns perfectly black in the hollows. This wood is two or three fingers thick, though on the bare roots it is scarcely thicker than a knife, for it lies tightly against the white and living wood. Furthermore, it is hard, brittle like glass, and so fatty that it exudes abundant oil if moved near a fire, whence it easily catches flame and burns like a candle. If cut fresh, it pours out a sweet but weak scent of *Benzoin*, <note>original: "Benzoïnum"; a balsamic resin from trees of the genus Styrax, used in perfumes and incense.</note> which it retains for a long time if kept enclosed. Moreover, when shaved down and placed on coals, it pours out a strong scent of *Benzoin* mixed with toasted bread; indeed, the unskilled would take it for the scent of *Benzoin* itself, especially from the fresh wood, for that which has been kept for several years loses much of its pleasant odor. Its shavings soon curl up and stick to one another as if they were worms because of the fattiness; they likewise easily catch flame, and when placed on coals, they stir up a thick and blackish smoke, harmful to the eyes if it gets too close to them. This wood serves not only for fumigation, but is always mixed with *Unguis Odoratus* <note>original: "Ungui Odorato"; literally "Scented Nail," referring to Onycha, an incense ingredient made from the operculum of certain sea snails.</note> or any other fragrant wood, whose scent is thereby exalted and lasts for a long time. Held in the mouth, it offers a bitter taste like *Aloes*, but at the same time emulating the taste of cakes.

This wood has such a great similarity to *Agallochum*, especially if its knots are rare and only slightly veined, that they can scarcely be distinguished from one another by external appearance. Indeed, many pharmacists who have come to these shores have affirmed to me for certain that they have seen such wood in—

<column-break/>

*They remain hanging green on the tree for a long time; finally they become pale or reddish, and if the sun then touches them, or if they are placed in a warm spot, they burst open with a crack, and the grains spring out, just as the fruits of both Cataputias do. Chewed in the mouth, they show no special taste at first, but finally they burn somewhat in the throat.*

*Both these sorts yield an abundant white, thickish, and at first tasteless or somewhat brackish milk when they are wounded anywhere, especially the branches and broken leaves, which also splashes out bravely when one chops into it with force, being as harmful as any Tithymalus or Wolf’s Milk <note>Dutch: "Wolfs melk"; common name for Euphorbia.</note> might be; especially for the eyes, if it enters them, which it inflames and causes to swell with great pain, so that one would lose their sight from it, unless help is immediately applied against it.*

*Our sailors often experienced this to their detriment during the first voyages, when they were sent out to chop firewood, and finding these trees so ready at hand on the strand, chopped into them with their axes; they were immediately so struck in the eyes by the splashing milk that they ran along the strand like senseless men, of whom some also lost their sight.*

*Now it is not enough that these trees are naturally so remarkable, being endowed with a harmful milk, but they must moreover have various harmful inhabitants in the pits or where they are hollow, such as short tree-snakes, a kind of very large and fast-running ant, various sorts of wasps, and bees, especially a kind of very small bee described in our Natural History of Animals under the name of Apicula or Tohil, which do not sting, but fly in great numbers into the ears and hair. These I have often found in the hollows of this tree, with a quantity of edible honey, and the walls of the hollow lined with a black and resinous gum, melting over the fire and somewhat fragrant, which is a Melicera made by these little bees.*

*Now we must also describe the useful part of these trees, which is an old and fatty substance of the wood, not in the heart, nor nearest the bark, but at such places of the lower trunk, or thick roots that lie above the earth, where they are burst or stand bare, and there make some pits or hollows as if they were eaten out. This fatty wood, Teda, which is a bastard Eagle-wood <note>Dutch: "Agel-hout"; Aloeswood.</note>, is gray and smooth on the outside at the roots or where it bulges out, but in the pits it is covered with a rough blackish bark, as with a hairy skin, which is however no true bark, but much more a film that one can easily scrape off. On the inside it generally has the color of iron-rust, sometimes a bit browner, sometimes a bit lighter, but near the edges, especially where it is touched by the sun, it is truly black in the pits, and two or three fingers thick, but at the bare roots not much thicker than a knife, for it lies close against the white and growing wood. It is furthermore hard, breaking off short like glass, and so fat that it richly sweats out oil when held to the fire, by which it also easily burns, and holds the flame like a candle. When it is freshly chopped, it has a sweet but weak scent of Benzoin, which stays with it for a long time if it is kept closed. Otherwise, when scraped and laid on coals, it has a much stronger scent of Benzoin and burnt bread mixed together; indeed, the inexperienced would take it for the scent of Benzoin, especially from the fresh wood, for that which has been kept for some years loses much of its loveliness. Its scrapings immediately roll up and stick together like worms because of its fattiness; it also easily catches the flame on coals, and gives off a heavy thick smoke, which is somewhat bothersome to the eyes if one makes too much of it. It is not easily smoked alone, but always with Fragrant Onycha or other sweet-smelling woods, whose scent it strengthens and makes longer-lasting. In taste it is bitter in the mouth, like Aloes, yet at the same time tasting like cakes.*

*This wood has such a great resemblance to the Agallochum, especially if one finds rare knots in it that are somewhat veined, that one can hardly distinguish them by looking at the outside. Indeed, many apothecaries coming here to this land assured me that they had seen such wood in—*

### Book III. Chapter XXXVI. AMBOINA HERBARIUM.

...bought and sold in Europe as good *Agallochum* <note>original: "Agallochum"; also known as agarwood or aloeswood, a fragrant resinous wood</note>, and even in these lands it is so prepared by the Chinese that it passes for *Calambac* <note>original: "Calambaco/Calambacq"; the highest quality of agarwood</note>, which is the finest *Agallochum*. Hence I have often thought that the *compiler Matthæus Sylvaticus* <note>Matthaeus Silvaticus was a 14th-century physician and botanist known for his medical encyclopedia, the Pandectae</note>, when he writes that *Agallochum* is adulterated with *Chamelea* <note>original: "Chamelea"; likely a reference to a plant in the Daphne or Spurge family</note> wood, must have meant this wood; although he is rebuked by *Garcia* <note>Garcia de Orta, a 16th-century Portuguese physician and pioneer of tropical medicine</note> in Book 1, *Aromatics*, Chapter 16, on the grounds that no *Chamelea* grows in all of India. This may be true, but the *compiler*, hearing that this false *Agallochum* comes from a milky tree, no doubt judged it to be a *Chamelea*; on the other hand, *Garcia* never knew this milky tree well enough to know that a fragrant wood could be gathered from it, even though it grows throughout most of the East Indies. If, then, one does not wish to accept *Chamelea* as the *Pseudo-Agallochum* of the *compiler*, another milky wood can take its place, which bears leaves similar to the *Olive* tree and was described by us among the shrubs in Book 6 under the name *Ligularia lactea* <note>original: "Ligularia lactea"; likely Euphorbia nerifolia</note>.

It should further be noted that this false *Agallochum* is not found in all *Caju Matta Buta* <note>Malay for "Blind-eye tree"</note> trees; indeed, it is found in scarcely one in twenty. For those that enjoy this wood grow on stony shores, leaning over, and have been split here and there for a long time, alternately splashed by seawater and dried again by the sun. If certain hollows are observed in such trees, those *Tadae* <note>original: "Tadae"; resinous torches or fat-wood pieces</note> or fatty pieces will be discovered within, which can be identified by tapping on them if they give a hard sound. Then, most cautiously, the surrounding bark must be peeled away so that the person is not defiled or harmed by the milk; then those blackish-brown pieces must be cut out and immediately separated from the adhering white wood. For all the remaining wood of this tree is white, soft, tough, and useless, and when placed on coals, it gives off a sharp and unpleasant odor. In all other trees that stand upright and are too exposed to the sun, or located on sloping ground, or too entangled and as if suffocated among other shrubs, these fatty lumps will not be found, or will be found spoiled. They also perish and dry out if those aforementioned little bees nest in them too long, which, it seems, suck out and consume most of the fatness. Likewise, all such wood is useless that is inhabited by those large ants or covered with spiders' webs.

This fatty wood does not always have the same substance or color; for that from the "male" trees is much darker and fattier, indeed some pieces are as black as *Ebony* wood, breaking off short like glass and not tolerating a knife. That of the "female" is more reddish and gives larger splinters, though this is rarely found.

Moreover, another species is found variegated with red and yellow, and often as yellow as if it were the finest *Sandalwood*, consisting of longitudinal stripes; and this wood is gathered in large pieces.

The *Garo* <note>A term for Eaglewood or Agarwood</note> from Ternate is mixed with reddish and grey, sometimes entirely reddish, consisting of fine and tangled veins, resembling the best *Agallochum*. The scent of all of them is generally the same, but the Amboinese is usually the fattest and rivals *Benzoin* <note>original: "Benzoin/Benjoin"; a balsamic resin from Styrax trees</note>, while that from Ternate refers more to the scent of flowers. The yellow species breathes a pleasant scent when raw, but when placed on coals, in my judgment, it is inferior to the others.

Furthermore, so that the good pieces may be distinguished from the bad, once they are all cleaned, throw them together into seawater; discard those that float, and keep those that sink to the bottom, for they are the best. They can be dipped once or twice more in salt water and always dried in the sun, by which they are improved. After four or five years, this wood loses much of its pleasant scent, which is why the inhabitants do not keep it for long, but if they wish to use it, they always seek it fresh from the tree. However, old pieces can be somewhat refreshed if they are immersed in seawater.

*The Season.* This tree blooms several times a year: its ordinary time is in January and February, when the "female" also brings forth its fruits, which hang on the tree until May, at which time the tree simultaneously casts off most of its old leaves, regenerates new ones, and sends out new catkins, which in the male do not last more than a month. Its roots spread very widely...

<column-break/>

...had been bought and sold *in Europe as good* Agallochum*, just as it is still prepared here in this country by the* Chinese *in such a way that it passes for* Calambac *(being the best* Agallochum*). For this reason, I have often thought that the* compiler Matthæus Sylvaticus*, writing that* Agallochum *is adulterated with the wood of* Chamelea*, must have meant this wood, although he is rebuked for it by* Garcia *in Book 1, Aromatics, Chapter 16, for the reason that no* Chamelea *grows in all of* India*. This may be true, but the* compiler*, hearing that the false* Eagle-wood <note>original: "Agel-hout"; Dutch term for Agarwood</note> *comes from a milk-tree, no doubt judged that it must be a* Chamelea*. On the other hand,* Garcia *did not properly know this milk-tree, nor that one could get a fragrant wood from it, although it grows throughout most of the* East Indies*. If one then does not wish to accept the* Chamelea *for the* Pseudo-Agallochum *of the* compiler*, one can put in its place another milk-wood which has leaves somewhat resembling the* Olive tree*, and was described by us among the shrubs in Book 6 under the name of* Ligularia Lactea*.*

*Now it should further be known that one does not find this bastard* Eagle-wood *in all trees of* Caju Matta Buta*, indeed, in scarcely one in twenty; for those that have it must stand on stony shores, leaning over, cracked here and there, splashed by turns with seawater and then dried again by the sun. When one then sees some hollows in them, there one shall find the aforementioned* Taedas <note>original: "Tædas"; resinous pieces of wood used as torches</note> *or fatty pieces, which can be recognized by the sound when knocking on them, if they sound hard. One must then very cautiously peel off the surrounding bark so that one is not touched by the milk, cut out the black-brown pieces, and further clean them properly from the adhering white wood; for all the remaining wood of this tree is white, soft, tough, and worthless, and gives off a very sharp and unpleasant smell on the coals. In all other trees that are upright and stand too flat to the sun, or on a muddy ground, and are too smothered among other brushwood, one will not find these fatty lumps, or they will be worthless. They also spoil and are dried out if the aforementioned little bees stay in them too long, which, so it seems, suck the most fatness out of them. Likewise, all that is inhabited in the hollows by large ants or covered with spiders' webs is no good.*

*This fatty wood is also not of one kind of substance or color, for that from the male trees is much browner and fattier, some pieces as black as* Ebony wood*, breaking off short like glass and not suffering a knife. That of the female is redder and more splintery, which is also seldom found.*

*Still another sort is found which is mixed of red and yellow, sometimes as yellow as the best* Sandalwood*, with stripes along the length, which is found in large pieces.*

*The* Ternatean Garo *is mixed of reddish and grey, sometimes entirely reddish, with fine and tangled veins, imitating the best* Eagle-wood*. The scent of all is mostly the same; in the* Amboinese *it is indeed the fattest and drawing toward* Benzoin*, the* Ternatean *more toward flowers. The yellow sort smells lovely when it is raw, but on coals, in my judgment, it yields to the others.*

*To distinguish the good pieces from the bad, once they have been cleaned, throw them all together into seawater; those that float, let go, and those that sink, keep, for those are the best. These can be dipped once or twice more in salt water and dried each time in the sun, by which they are improved. After four or five years, this wood loses much of its loveliness, therefore the* Inhabitants *do not keep it long, but wanting to use it, they fetch it fresh from the tree each time; yet one can refresh the old pieces somewhat if one plunges them into seawater.*

Season. *This tree blooms several times a year: its ordinary time is in January and February, when the* Female *also brings forth its fruits, which hang on the tree until May, when it simultaneously sheds the most part of the old leaves, gains young ones, and brings forth new catkins, which in the male do not last more than a month. The roots spread themselves very widely...*

# AMBOINA HERBARIUM Book III. Chapter XXXVI.

[The roots] protrude, quite curved and knotty, and indeed are more often exposed on the rocky shore; in such places, where the bark has been stripped away, that black, fragrant wood is revealed. I have not only shown the leaves, flowers, and fruits of both the male and female trees in the illustrations, but also on a special sheet, I have shown how the entire tree, with its curved trunk, occurs on the rocky shore of Keytetto on the Hitoe coast, overgrown with many species of *Polypodium* <note>a genus of ferns</note>, *Filicum* <note>ferns</note>, etc.

**Name.** In Latin, *Arbor excæcans* <note>The Blindness-causing Tree</note>. In Dutch, *Melk-hout* <note>Milk-wood</note> and *Blint-hout* <note>Blind-wood</note>, which is derived from many Indian names, such as the Malay *Caju Matta Buta* <note>original: "Caju Matta Buta"; literally "Wood Eye Blind"</note>. In Baleya <note>a regional dialect</note>, *Caju Coëda* and *Capal*. In Ternate, *Garo-Matta Buta*, which is properly the "fat" or resinous wood gathered from this tree. In Macassar, *Sambuta*. In Amboina, *Matta Huri* and *Matta Huli*. In Buru, *Maccaſuta*. On the northern coast of Ceram, *Maccabita* and *Babuta*.

The resinous torches or those "fat" pieces chosen from this wood, which are considered a type of false *Agallochum* <note>agarwood</note>, are called *Garo-Laut* <note>Sea Fragrant-wood</note> and *Garo-Matta Buta*; by some they are called *Garo-Boaya*, that is, *Crocodile-wood* <note>original: "Caaymans-bout"</note>, because of the wrinkled skin or bark that usually covers it. In Banda, they are called *Garo tay aros*, as they are often found on the shore, mixed with other debris cast up by the tide. Perhaps it is the same as what is called *Meningan* or *Menongan* in Baleya, which we mentioned above in Book 2, Chapter 12, under the secondary *Agallochum*, and which we considered to be one and the same as *Madjagabu*; however, I later learned that *Menongan* is a "fat" wood from which a thick oil can be extracted and poured out. Hence, I think it is more closely related to *Caju Matta Buta*, all the more so because when this wood is fresh and rubbed against itself, it gives off a notable scent of Benzoin, called *Minjaan* in Malay.

**Location.** This tree is very well known in all the islands of the "Watery Indies" <note>the Indonesian archipelago</note>, though not on all shores, but only, as was said, on dry and rocky ones, or those mixed with pebbles or sand, and always on the shore not far from the mouths of major rivers. It is also found further inland, but there it is planted by human hands, as they sometimes build fences from its wood because it grows easily; however, one should not look for *Garo* <note>resinous fragrant wood</note> in those trees.

Since the shores of the larger islands, such as parts of Sumatra, Java, and Borneo, are muddy, the tree is not found there, or only rarely, and mostly among the *Mangi Mangi* <note>Mangroves</note> on the mainland and along the firmer banks of large rivers. It occurs in greater abundance in the eastern islands, which mostly enjoy rocky shores, such as in Amboina, the Hitoe coast, in Ceram, and the entire Hoeamohel region, and further on the northern coast around old Lissa-Batta. In Ternate, it occurs most frequently on the island of Mothir and on its large island of Gelolo, along the entire tract of Halmahera; it is further known in the Papuan islands, as well as those situated to the Southeast. However, that which grows in calm bays or marshy places does not participate much in, or provide, this kind of "fat" wood, and is unsuitable for incense.

### OBSERVATION.

These trees are likewise mentioned in *Valentyn's Description of Amboina, page 217*, and are shown in the *Plate under numbers XLVII and XLVIII*. For more on this wood, see *Miscellanea Academica Naturae Curiosorum, dec. III, year 3, obs. 22*, and *Valentyn's Mantissa Exotica, page 592*.

<column-break/>

[The roots] of the tree run very crooked and knotty, and are exposed on the stony shore, where one then also finds the black fragrant wood in those spots where there is no bark. I have not only shown in the figures the leaves, blossoms, and fruits of both the male and female, but also on a separate sheet an entire tree, as it can be seen with its crooked trunk and grown over with many kinds of *Filix* <note>ferns</note>, *Polypodium*, etc., on a stony shore of Keytetto, on the coast of Hitoe.

**Name.** In Latin *Arbor Excæcans*. In Dutch *Milk-wood* and *Blind-wood*, being formed mostly after all the Indian names, such as in Malay *Caju Matta Buta*. In Malay *Caju Coeda* and *Capal*. In Ternate *Garo-Matta Buta*, which is actually the fatty wood that comes from it. In Macassar *Sambuta*. In Amboina *Matta Huri* and *Matta Huli*. On Buru *Maccafuta*. On the north coast of Ceram *Maccahita* and *Babuta*.

The resinous torches or fatty pieces that come from this wood, and serve as a bastard Agarwood <note>original: "baſtaart Agel-bout"</note>, were named *Garo-Laut* and *Garo-Matta-Buta*, by some *Garo-Boaya*, that is, *Crocodile wood*, from the rough exterior with which it is commonly covered; in Banda *Garo tay aros*, because one often finds it on the shore, cast up among other debris. Perhaps it is the same which we called *Meningan* or *Menongan* on Bali, which we touched upon above in Book 2, Chapter 12, under the *Secondary Agallochum*, and held to be one and the same as *Madjagahu*; but later understanding that *Menongan* is a fatty wood from which one can melt a thick oil, I guess that it corresponds more closely with this *Caju Matta Buta*, the more so because when fresh and rubbed against each other, it has the marked scent of Benzoin, called *Minjaan* in Malay.

**Place.** This tree is well known in all the islands of the *Watery Indies*, yet not on all kinds of shores, but only, as said, on dry and stony ones, or those mixed with pebbles and sand, and that always on the shore, not far from there, at the outlets of large rivers. One also finds it deeper in the land, but mostly planted there by people, who sometimes make garden stakes from them, which sprout easily; but one need not look for the *Garo* <note>fragrant resin</note> on those.

Now because the shores of the large islands, like *Sumatra, Java*, and *Borneo* have one side that is marshy and silty, one does not find this tree there, or very little, and then among the *Mangroves* <note>original: "Mangi Mangis"</note> on the mainland, and on the hard edges of the large rivers. In greater quantity one finds it in these Eastern islands, which mostly have stony shores, like in *Amboina*, the coast of *Hitoe*, on *Ceram*, and the entire landscape of *Hoeamohel*, and further on the North coast around old *Lissa-Batta*; in *Ternate* one has it mostly on the island of *Mothir*, and on the large island of *Gelolo*, along the entire coast of *Halmahera*, and further through the *Papuan* and *Southeastern Islands* everywhere known. That which stands in still bays or marshy places does not have much of that fatty wood, and is unfit for incense.

### CHAPTER THIRTY-SEVEN.

#### *Uses of the Blindness-causing Tree.*

**T**he harmful qualities of this tree are known to everyone, which is why the inhabitants pursue it with such hatred and avoid it so much that they warn our nation to flee from it if they see anyone standing too close. Undoubtedly, they have experienced its harm more than our people, who do not fear it as much, perhaps knowing that this tree is often blamed unfairly. Indeed, if one takes care that its milky sap does not drip into the eyes, there is no danger to be feared from the tree itself. The sap is a very powerful purgative, yet it is not "hot" beyond the third degree <note>A reference to the "humoral" theory of medicine, where plants were classified by degrees of heat, cold, moisture, or dryness</note>. When tested on the tongue, it is tasteless; it causes a slight burning in the throat but does not harm the skin. Our sailors, as previously mentioned, used to cut this wood for fuel, often to their own detriment. Today, however, it is not used for that purpose unless there is a lack of other wood, as often happens in *Batavia* <note>modern-day Jakarta</note>, where that great city suffers from a shortage and wood must be sought from small islands. This remains a bad practice, as the wood hardly dries out, and when burned, it emits a sharp smoke that is harmful to the eyes. Otherwise, it is used for garden stakes and small posts, as it sends out long shoots if the thick trunks are frequently pruned, much like a *Willow*. Our gunpowder makers also burned charcoal from this wood, finding that its coals were fine, light, and soft; however, due to their acridity, the gunpowder gradually becomes moldy. For this reason, the wood of the following *Milky Tree* <note>original: "Arboris lactariæ"</note> is now chosen for that purpose, as it provides better charcoal.

Among the inhabitants of these islands, it has greater *medical* use than among Western peoples, who use the bark and its sap as a strong purgative, but only for those who have robust bodies, are strong in vigor, and are full of "malignant humors."

Indeed, it harms lean and bilious people, but it benefits those dominated by "foul humors," which result in skin eruptions, scabies, paralysis, and similar diseases. For an ordinary purge, they take a piece of bark two joints long and two fingers wide; they chew this with *Pinanga* <note>Areca nut</note> and swallow the juice. However, since this causes a burning in the throat, it has been found better to drop a few drops of this sap into *coconut water* <note>original: "Calappi lymphæ"</note>, *tea*, or some other juice. Any drink into which drops of this sap are instilled takes on the consistency and appearance of milk. These purges work quite strongly both "upwards and downwards" <note>causing both vomiting and diarrhea</note>; therefore, they should not be given to sick or weak people, though the inhabitants often do so at great risk to the patient. It is therefore to be wished that our East Indian doctors and surgeons knew better the art of preparing this sap so it could be ingested more safely, like *Gamboge* <note>a pigmented tree resin used as a drastic purgative</note>. Otherwise, its effects are tempered if a half-ripe *Banana* <note>original: "Musæ"</note> toasted under ashes is eaten afterward, or if some pieces of cold porridge, called *Papeda* <note>a traditional Moluccan starch porridge made from sago</note>, are consumed. This same sap is effective against the bites and stings of poisonous fish if it is smeared on the wound and a piece of red copper is bound over it. If it gets into someone's eyes, they should be washed with *coconut water* and gently squeezed, as this attracts and draws out the harmful sap.

Knowledge of this "false Aloeswood" <note>original: "Agallochi"</note>, which is gathered from these trees, did not reach our nation before the year 1665; indeed, it was not yet known to most *Amboinese*. But when at that time I had held the office of sub-governor on the coast of *Hitoe* for ten years—and during the first five years I fled from this tree just as much as the others—in that year, this wood was first revealed and demonstrated to me by *Patti Cuhu*, the chief of the *Hitoe* village called *Ely*. He had an exact knowledge of herbs and helped me greatly in describing this work; therefore, I thought it right to honor his memory here.

<column-break/>

### XXXVII. CHAPTER.

#### *Use of the Tree of the Blind Eyes.*

**T**he vices of this tree are known to every man, which is why the *Inlanders* hate and flee from it so much that they warn *our Nation* to stay away from it when they see it standing there. They have undoubtedly experienced its harmfulness more than our people, who do not have so much fear of it, perhaps knowing that this tree must suffer much innocent blame. For if one guards oneself so that the milk does not get into the eyes, one has no danger to expect from the tree. The milk is indeed strongly purging, but yet not hot above the third degree. For tasted on the tongue, it is bland; in the throat, it creates a small burn, and on the skin, it does no harm. *Our Sailors*, as said, formerly cut this wood often for firewood, and frequently to their harm, but nowadays it is not used for that, except for lack of other wood, as among other things still happens in *Batavia*, where it is very scarce for that large city and must be fetched from the small islands. It is nonetheless a bad custom, for the wood dries poorly, and when burned, it gives off a sharp, biting smoke that is harmful to the eyes. Otherwise, it is used for *garden stakes* and small posts, because one finds long poles on it when the thick trunks are often robbed of their crown, as one does with *Willows*. *Our gunpowder makers* have also burned coals from this wood for *gunpowder*, but it was found that although it gives beautiful, light, and soft coals, yet because of their saltiness, they cause the powder to bloom <note>to degrade or become damp</note> over time. Now one takes the wood of the following *Milky Tree* for that purpose, which gives more suitable coals.

Among the *Inhabitants* of these islands, it has more use in *medicine* than in the West; they use the bark and milk for strong purges, but in persons who still have reasonable strength and bodies full of bad humors.

In thin and bilious people it does no good, but it does in those who are stuffed with such humors from which smallpox, scabies, and lameness come. For a common purge, they take a piece of the bark, two joints long and two fingers broad, chew the same with *Areca nut* <note>original: "Pinang"</note>, and swallow the juice. But because this causes some burn in the throat, it has been found better if one mixes a few drops of the clear milk of this tree in *coconut milk*, *tea water*, or *Torwak* <note>likely a local palm wine or sap</note> and takes it. All the drink in which one puts a few drops of this milk immediately becomes like whey. These purges work from below and above quite strongly, and therefore one shall not give them to sick and decrepit people, which the *Inlanders* often do with the extreme peril of the patient. Therefore it was to be wished that our *Doctors* and *Surgeons* in the *Indies* learned to prepare this milk a bit better, whereby it would be taken more easily and harmlessly, like *Gamboge* <note>original: "Gutta Cambodjë"</note>. Otherwise, its working is stopped if one takes a half-ripe *Banana* <note>original: "Pissang"</note>, roasts it under the ashes, and eats it, or swallows some lumps of cold *Papeda* <note>sago porridge</note>. The same milk is good for the stings of venomous *fish* if one smears it on the injury and binds a piece of red copper over it. But if it comes into someone's eyes, one shall continually wash them with *coconut milk* and squeeze it out gently each time, for this takes the other harmful milk unto itself and carries it out at the same time.

The knowledge of the *bastard Aloeswood* <note>original: "Agel-hout"</note>, which one finds on these trees, was unknown to our Nation before the year 1665, yes, even until now to the most part of the *Amboinese*. But when I, around that time, held the office of *Subalternate head* over the coast of *Hitoe* for about ten years, and was as shy of this tree for the first five years as the rest, this wood was first shown to me in that same year by *Patti Cuhu*, a *Regent* or *Orangkay* <note>term: a person of wealth or status; a village leader</note> of the *Hitoean Village Ely*, an experienced man in the knowledge of plants, who has helped me much in this work, for which I also properly deem it right to place his memory here.

### AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. Chapter XXXVII.

At first, I endured much frustration in seeking out and identifying this wood because of the aforementioned dangers and difficulties encountered around this tree. However, fortune favored me, as I came across many trees both on the coast of *Hitoe* and in the opposite region of *Hoeamohel* <note>districts on the island of Ambon</note>, which supply this wood in quite large quantities. As soon as this became commonly known, the supply quickly dwindled, since the local people <note>original: "Æthiopes", here referring to the local Muslim populations</note> frequently use it for fumigations and scented oils. They used this wood in place of true *Garo* or *Agallochum* <term>Agarwood; a precious fragrant heartwood</term>, which is brought to these regions only in very small amounts. In the beginning, I also valued this wood highly, but later, finding that it gradually loses much of its pleasantness over time, I held it in lower esteem, seeing as it is not durable and becomes useless if kept for a long time.

A thick and viscous oil, similar to *Turpentine* but blacker, can be extracted from both old and fresh wood through a process of distillation "by descent" <note>a method where the substance is heated from above so the oil drips downward</note> prepared in the following manner: Chop and split this wood into small pieces, sprinkle them with seawater, and fill an ordinary earthen pot with them. Place an earthen dish over this, slightly wider than the opening of the pot, so that the back of the dish is joined to the surface or opening of the pot and covers the edges loosely. Carefully turn these over together and place them into another dish, slightly larger than the previous one. Cover the joints with green *Banana* leaves <note>original: "Musæ"</note>, which you should seal with clay, but everywhere so lightly that the oil can pass through. Then commit the lower dish to the earth so that the pot filled with the chopped wood stands out above. Build a fire over this, from which the resinous wood gradually melts and emits its oil, which drips through the joints into the lower dish. After about half an hour, carefully remove everything together so that no sand or earth falls into the dish below, in which you will find a thick, blackish, and viscous oil, slow and tenacious like turpentine, smelling of smoke—a scent it never loses. In the pot placed above, you will see black coals and half-burned wood, which should be discarded. When I repeated this process, I intended to sprinkle the wood with no water, judging that the smoky smell arose from it; however, my teacher, who showed me this art of distilling—named *Iman Reti*, who was a priest of the people of *Buru*—advised that the water was required, because otherwise the wood would catch fire and yield no oil. In this same way, oils can be extracted from all resinous woods, especially from the previously mentioned *Lingoo* and *Salimuri*, which remains to be investigated.

This oil is used to clear away all types of scabies and skin impurities when smeared on externally; however, since it is very viscous, it must be mixed with a little *Coconut* oil <note>original: "Calappi oleo"</note> and warmed. Over time it becomes resinous like turpentine, but it never loses its stickiness.

From the younger branches and thin roots stripped of their bark, toothpicks are formed, with which aching teeth are prodded when filled with *catarrhs* <note>in this context, inflammatory fluids or "runny" humors</note>, so that the rheum may flow out; however, it causes a great burning in the mouth.

Its ripe fruits, falling into the sea, are eaten by *Sardines*, *Cabelini*, and similar small fish; their intestines must be thrown away, in which the kernels of these fruits are found, because they impart a bitter taste. If the oil described above is lacking, shavings of this resinous wood mixed with coconut oil are used in its place to rub on scabies.

The Amboinese dig up these roots at sunrise, taking care that the shadow of the digger does not cover the roots. They cut these into seven small pieces, which they carry on their bodies as a protection against enchantments and sorcery. This same root, crushed with *Ginger* and applied, cures all inflammatory swellings of the hands or feet. Those of *Ternate* grind the resinous wood upon a porphyry stone and, mixed with water or a weak *Arrack* drink, administer it against *Cholera* and intestinal griping. I have also seen the Chinese provide this against *Asthma*, for which they use their own *Garo*, called *Timbion*.

When the Chinese and Malays wish to deceive foreign merchants and sell them this *Sea-Garo* <note>original: "Garo-Laut"</note> for true *Calambac* <term>the highest quality of Agarwood</term>, they select such knots and pieces that rival true Calambac in color and shape. These they sprinkle with rose water, or any other scented water in which shavings of true Calambac have been placed and...

<column-break/>

In the beginning, I took great pains to search for and recognize this wood, because of the aforementioned difficulties and perils to be endured regarding this tree. I had the good fortune to find many trees at that time, both on the coast of *Hitoe* and the opposite land of *Hoeamohel*, which yielded this wood in reasonable quantities. But no sooner did it become known among the common people than it quickly ran out, because the *Moors* <note>Muslim inhabitants of the region</note> are constantly dealing with perfumes and fragrant oils, and use this wood instead of genuine *Garo* or *Eaglewood*, which is brought to these islands very sparingly. We initially made something of it as well, but later finding that it loses much of its pleasantness over the years, it also lost much of its esteem, for it is not good for keeping a long time.

From the old as well as the fresh wood, one can melt a thick, sticky oil, in the form of *Turpentine*, though blackish, which is done "by descent" in this way: Chop and cut the wood into small pieces, moisten it with seawater, and fill an ordinary earthen pot with it. Put an earthen saucer on top, which should be a hair broader than the mouth of the pot, and in such a way that the back of the saucer fits into the mouth of the pot and closes loosely at the edges. Turn this over together into another saucer, which is again somewhat larger than the first, and wrap the joint with green leaves of *Pisang* <term>Banana</term>. Smear some clay over it, but everywhere loosely, so that the oil can run through between them. Bury the bottom saucer in the earth so that the pot with the chopped wood sticks out, upon which you shall then build a fire. Thus the fatty wood will begin to melt and give off its oil, which runs between the joints into the lower saucer. After about half an hour, pick everything up gently so that no sand or earth falls into the lower saucer; there you will find a thick, blackish, and sticky oil, as clinging as turpentine, but very smoky in smell, which it also never loses. In the top pot, you will find a quantity of black coals and half-burnt wood, which you should throw away. I did not want to moisten the wood with water when doing it again, because I judged the smoky smell to come from that, but my Master, who taught me this distilling, *Iman Reti*, a Moorish Priest of *Buru*, warned me that such was necessary, because otherwise the wood would catch fire and give no oil. In this way, one could get an oil from all kinds of fatty woods, especially from the above-mentioned *Lingoo* and *Salimuri*, which is still to be investigated.

This oil is used to drive away all kinds of scurviness and impurity of the skin, smeared on from the outside; but because it is very sticky, one must warm it and mix it with a little *Calappus* <note>Coconut</note> oil. In time it becomes resinous like turpentine, but it never loses its stickiness.

From the young twigs and thin roots stripped of the bark, toothpicks are made, with which one picks sore teeth that are burdened with *sinkings* <note>an old term for catarrhs or neuralgic pains</note>, so that the moisture then runs out: however, it bites the mouth quite a bit.

All the ripe fruits falling into the sea are eaten by the *Sardines*, *Cabelines*, and other small fish, whose intestines one must then throw away, as these grains are found in them, making the same bitter. If one does not have the prescribed oil, one can take the scrapings of the fatty wood, mix it with coconut oil, and smear the scurviness therewith.

The Amboinese dig up the roots with the rising sun, in such a way that the digger's shadow does not fall over the root. These they cut into seven small pieces and carry them around the body against all kinds of sorcery and conjuration. The same root rubbed with small *Ginger* and smeared on, heals all bitten swellings on hands and feet. The people of *Ternate* rub the fatty wood on a stone and give it with water or weak *Arrack* to drink against the chest <note>asthma/congestion</note> or griping of the bowels. I have also seen the Chinese give it for shortness of breath, just as they do with their *Timhion* or genuine *Garo*.

The Chinese and Malays, wishing to deceive foreign merchants and sell this *Sea-Garo* for genuine *Calambac*, choose such knots and pieces that come closest to genuine Calambac in color and shape; these they smear with rose or other fragrant water, in which scrapings of good Calambac have been soaked...

The fraud is, however, soon discovered if this wood is burned or chewed in the mouth, as the scent and taste of both these woods vary greatly.

It is true that both are bitter when chewed, but the bitterness of Calambac approaches the flavor of Citron peels and is pleasant, whereas *Garo Laut* <note>The "Sea Garo" wood previously described</note> rivals Wormwood <note>original: "Absynthium"</note> or Aloes.

The people of Buru <note>original: "Boeronenses"</note> burn entire branches of this tree around their rice fields, wishing to drive away mice with the smoke, as they cause great damage to the crops. The people of Bali <note>original: "Baleyenses"</note> fashion white clogs <note>original: "Cothurnos"</note> from the white wood of this tree, as it is supple and light; these are worn by the elite on their feet.

If anyone finds their vision darkened by the smoke of this wood, or of other fragrant woods, they should wash their eyes with the liquid squeezed from the cups of the *Globa* <note>A type of wild ginger plant</note> in which the fruits sit.

### CHAPTER THIRTY-EIGHT.
### The Milky Tree. Wild Mango. <note>original: "Arbor Lactaria. Manga Brava."</note>

Another milk-bearing tree is considered by the common folk to be a type of wild Mango, though we prefer to assign it its own genus. It has the size of a Mango tree, bearing a thinner trunk, usually the thickness of a man, with smooth bark. It otherwise has an extended crown; its branches are "fat," heavy, and brittle, bending downwards. They are covered in a blackish bark and are knotty, as if divided into segments; they defy climbing because of their fragility, except for the very thickest branches.

The leaves are placed in an irregular order, closely joined to one another, and are very similar to Mango leaves, but much larger—usually eight to ten inches <note>original: "digitos"</note> long and two to two-and-a-half inches wide. On younger trees, they are twelve to thirteen inches long and three wide. These leaves are flabbier and more succulent than Mango leaves, broadest at the upper part, ending in a blunt tip, and gradually narrowing further down. Their ribs and veins are whitish and run obliquely; they are not as parallel as in Mango leaves. They appear scabby and beset with warts, which is caused by fly eggs hiding within them; when they fall, they turn red like cooked crabs.

The flower emerges from a sheath <note>original: "vagina"</note> composed of two thin leaflets. The lower part of the flower consists of a star-like shape made of five narrow and bright green petals, which might be mistaken for a distinct flower. From the center of this, however, the true flower rises, consisting of a long tube and opening into five large white petals, resembling the form of a Narcissus. These petals are flabby, rounded and broad at the top, ending in a short, turned-back tip, just as the leaves themselves are somewhat wavy. In their center, a five-angled and hollow tube appears with red and toothed edges, fringed as it were, without any stamens and lacking any scent.

After the upper flower falls, the fruit grows out of the center of the lower star. It is an "apple," sometimes round, sometimes oblong-oval, the size of a half-grown Mango or the *Condondong* fruit <note>The Great Hog Plum or Ambarella</note>—at least here in Amboina. In Makassar and other western islands, these fruits are nearly twice as large, namely like a Pomegranate. They are smooth on the outside, pale green, and covered with a thin skin, under which is hidden a hairy substance made of thick and woody fibers. These contain a kernel in their center the size of a plum and with the substance of a chestnut, but oilier and unfit for food, un-

<column-break/>

macerated, then they wrap them with dry Banana leaves, and keep them for a month in a closed place or pot; thus these pieces acquire the smell and appearance of genuine Calambac.

The deceit is however immediately discovered when one burns it or chews it in the mouth, because the smell and taste of these two differ greatly.

It is indeed true that they are both bitter in the mouth, but the bitterness of the Calambac draws near to Citron-peels and is more pleasant, but this one draws near to Wormwood or Aloes.

The people of Buru burn the entire branches of this tree around their rice fields, wishing to drive away all mice with that smoke, which do great damage to the sown crops. Some throw the leaves of the tree *Lolowaral* or *Lolowaran* into the fire along with it (called *Fatahu Befaar* by the Buru people), which drive them away with their crackling and creaking. The Balinese make white clogs out of the white wood of this tree, because it is tough and light, which the most prominent persons wear on their feet.

If someone notices that his sight is darkened, as well by the smoke of this as other fragrant woods, he shall wash the eyes with the moisture that one presses out of the cups of the *Globa*, where the fruits grow.

### XXXVIII. CHAPTER.
### The Wild Mango Tree, or the Milk-wood.

The second Milk-tree was held by the common man for a sort of wild Mango, but we would rather let it keep its own genus: it is the size of a Mango tree, though with a thinner trunk, commonly a man thick, and a smooth bark; otherwise also with an extended crown. The branches are fat, heavy, brittle, bent downwards, covered with a blackish bark, and somewhat knotty, as if divided into limbs. One cannot climb them because they break so easily, unless one stands on the thick branches.

The leaves stand without order close to one another and are very similar to Mango leaves, yet much larger; namely, commonly eight and ten inches long, two and two-and-a-half wide; on the young trees twelve and thirteen long, three wide; floppier and juicier than the Mango leaves, broadest at the front with a blunt point, and gradually narrowing towards the back. The ribs and veins are whitish, slanted, and not so parallel as on the Mango leaves. They are mostly scabby in appearance and beset with warts, in which fly eggs hide; when they fall, they become fire-red, like cooked crabs.

The flower comes out of a casing or sheath made of two thin leaflets, and the lower part of the flower consists of a star, also made of five narrow and light-green leaflets, which one would take for a special flower, but out of the middle of the same the true flower first comes forth, with a long neck, and opened into five broad white leaves, in the shape of a Narcissus. These leaflets are somewhat floppy, round at the front and broad, with a short twisted point, just as the leaves themselves stand somewhat curved; in the middle one sees a five-cornered bulbous pipe with red edges that are somewhat notched, like fringes, without any threads in the middle and without smell.

After the falling of the upper flower, the fruit grows out of the middle of the lower star, being an Apple, sometimes round, sometimes long-oval, the size of a half-grown Mango, or the fruit *Condondong*; namely here in Amboina: for in Makassar and other Western Islands it becomes twice as large, namely as a Pomegranate; smooth on the outside, light green or pale, covered with a thin skin: under that lies a hairy substance made of coarse and woody threads, which hide in their middle a white kernel, the size of a Plum and substance like Chestnuts,
