<meta>This page continues the description of the "Milky Tree" (Arbor Lactaria), likely the Cerbera manghas, focusing on its physical properties, names in various local languages, and its medicinal use as a potent purgative.</meta>

<header>AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. chap. XXXVIII.</header>

...no longer considered harmful; at least by the Malays and Portuguese it is deemed fatal, but in these regions nothing else has been found, except that this fruit or its immature kernel, if eaten imprudently, brings about great anxiety <note>In 17th-century medicine, "anxiety" often referred to a physical sensation of oppression or tightness in the chest and heart area.</note>.

**The wood** is white, soft, and easy to dry; in older trees, it is ash-gray toward the center. All parts of this tree, when injured, pour out a copious milk <note original: "lac">latex</note>, certainly in greater quantity and thinner than in the preceding tree. For this reason, it could well be considered a tree-like species of Spurge <term>Spurge: plants of the genus Euphorbia, known for their milky, often irritating sap</term>. However, this milk does not burn or sting the tongue, but is bland, mixed with a nauseating bitterness.

**It grows mostly** on the seashores or not far from them, as well as on the banks of rivers in flat and muddy places. In swampy areas, it luxuriates and grows as thick as the thickest Mango tree, producing much larger fruits and leaves than described above. Often, two fruits are joined together like testicles in a scrotum, consisting of two distinct kernels.

**Its ripe fruits** are found cast up on the shore in great numbers, stripped of their outer skin so that nothing remains but the fibrous husk.

**The Name.** In Latin, *Arbor Lactaria* (Milky Tree) to distinguish it from the *Herba Lactaria*, which is the Spurge <note original: "Tithymalus"></note>. In Dutch, *Melk-hout*. In Portuguese and Malay, *Manga Brava* <note>meaning "Wild" or "Fierce Mango"</note>, and by the general name *Caju Sussu* <note>Malay: "Milk Wood"</note>. In Amboinese, *Wabba* and *Wabbo*; in Hoamohel, *Yabbal* and *Obopae*. In Ternate, *Goro* and *Gorogoro*. In Macassar, *Lambuto*. In Bali, *Bintaro* and *Saffuru Utan*. Some in Malay also call it *Caju Gretje*, which some pronounce *Caju Gorita*. It is wrongly called by some *Caju Matta Buta* or "Blind-wood" <note>This name usually refers to Excoecaria agallocha, which truly causes blindness</note>.

**The Location.** This tree is well known throughout most parts of India, especially on the large islands of "Watery India" <note>The Indonesian Archipelago</note>, which consist of estuaries and through which great rivers flow; the largest trees of this species are thought to grow in Macassar.

**The Use.** Although a harmful power is attributed to this tree, it is not so dangerous that some cannot be taken into the body. Those who place it among the blinding trees do it an injustice, for it has not been found to cause harm to the eyes, since its milk is by no means as caustic and sharp as the preceding one. Hence, some Amboinese cook the fresh and younger leaves of this tree as a vegetable and eat them like other herbs; this dish gently moves the bowels. The milk, however, has a strong purging power, though it does not work strongly on "bilious" people, but only evacuates "phlegmatic" and "watery" humors <term>Humors: according to ancient medicine, the four fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that governed health</term>.

Pieces of the bark of the trunk are taken from those trees that stand away from the sea, about the length of a palm, or a piece of the root a span long. The rough outer part should be scraped off and discarded; the remaining part, down to the wood itself, is grated into a very fine sawdust. This is then kneaded in the water of a young Coconut <note original: "Calappi"></note>, strained through a cloth, and a cupful of the liquid is drunk. Immediately afterward, chew some Pinang <note>Betel nut</note> to counter the nausea. After two hours, it will stir and move the bowels without much distress, yet in such a way that one can still walk and go about their business. However, since a fairly large amount of this potion must be taken, some prepare these scrapings with equal parts vinegar and water, or with weak vinegar alone, taking two of the small cups used for drinking tea; this works better and is not so nauseating. This is a common and daily purgative of the Amboinese, which has now also been adopted and put into use by European families. I have found, however, that it works little in certain temperaments, even if a large draft is taken, while conversely, it worked very strongly in others who had taken a smaller dose. The reason for this is that in some, the humors are not so prepared, nor in such quantity, as in others. If some wish only to have two or three bowel movements, they take a piece of the cleaned root, which they chew with Pinang and swallow the juice. The bark of younger trees does not exercise its power as strongly as that of older ones. There are also some who observe no certain dose, taking as much of the cleaned bark as they please, which they knead in water in which rice has been boiled. The inner kernels of the fruits, as said above, are harmful to humans and animals, and it is believed that if many are eaten—

<column-break/>

...yet fat, and entirely unfit for eating, indeed even harmful; for among the Malays and Portuguese it is held to be deadly, yet in these lands nothing else has been found, except that the unripe fruit or kernel, eaten incautiously, brings about a great distress.

The wood is white, soft, and dries easily; in old trees, near the core, it is ash-gray. On all sides where this tree is wounded, especially on the branches, the milk flows out abundantly; indeed more richly and thinner than the previous one, so that one would not judge wrongly that it is a tree-like genus of *Spurge*, yet this milk is not biting or sharp on the tongue, but rather bland, and mixed with a loathsome bitterness.

It grows mostly at the seaside, or not far from there, on the banks of rivers where it is flat and muddy. In marshy places, it becomes as thick and wild as the largest Mango tree, with much larger leaves and fruits than stated above. One also frequently finds two fruits grown against each other, like a Scrotum, also with two separate kernels.

The ripe fruits are seen in abundance cast up along the strand, cleared of the outer skin, so that one sees nothing on them but the fibrous husk.

**Name.** In Latin *Arbor Lactaria*, to distinguish it from the *Lactaria Herba*, which is the *Spurge*. In Dutch *Melk-hout*. In Portuguese and Malay *Manga Brava*, and in general *Caju Sussu*. In Amboinese *Wabba* and *Wabbo*, on Hoamohel *Yabbal* and *Ohopae*. In Ternate *Goro* and *Gorogoro*. In Macassar *Lambuto*. In Bali *Bintaro*, and *Saffuru Utan*, some also call it in Malay *Caju Gretje*, which some pronounce *Caju Gorita*, it is wrongly named by some *Caju Matta Buta*, or "Blind-wood."

**Place.** It is known mostly through all of the East Indies, especially on the large islands of "Watery India," which have large rivers and marshy forelands. The largest occur on Macassar, so it is believed.

**Usage.** Although a harmful power is attributed to this tree, it is nevertheless not so worrisome that one cannot take some of it into the body. They also do it an injustice who reckon it among the sorts of "Blind-wood," for there is no experience of it having done damage to the eyes, it being by no means as biting and sharp of nature as the previous one, therefore some Amboinese cook and eat the young leaves of this tree as other potherbs, which makes only a gentle bowel movement; the milk however still has a strong purging power, yet does not particularly attack the bilious humors, but only the phlegmatic and watery ones.

One takes the pieces of the bark of the trunk, which stands somewhat away from the sea, a hand-breadth wide, or a piece of the root a span long, scrapes off the outer rough part, and throws that away; the rest down to the wood is also scraped small, and kneaded in the water of the young Coconut, wrung through a cloth, and a good water-glass full of it is drunk, immediately thereafter chewing a Pinang for the nausea; so shall it after a couple of hours without great distress stir the belly, and set it off briskly, yet so that one can walk and stand. Because one must now take this stuff in a large quantity, some knead it with half vinegar and water, or even entirely with weak vinegar, and take a couple of tea-cups full of it, which works better, and causes less nausea. This is the common and daily purgative of the Amboinese, which is now also accepted among the European families. However, I have experienced that it works little in some temperaments, even if a large drink of it were taken, and on the contrary in a lesser quantity quite strongly in others, the cause of which is that it does not find the humors in one so prepared, nor in such abundance, as in the other. Some wishing to make only two or three stool movements, take a piece of the cleaned root, and chew the same with Pinang, and swallow the last juice thereof. The bark of the young trees also does not work as strongly as that of the old. There are also those who prescribe no certain measure, taking only as much purified bark as seems good to them, kneading the same in water in which rice has been boiled. The inner kernels, as said above, are harmful for humans and livestock, and it is believed that if eaten too much, they can kill. Indeed, the Portuguese writers mention such of their *Manga Brava*, just as—

### Book III. Chapter XXXVIII. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...are reported by many to bring death in great quantities; at least the Portuguese writers tell this of their *Manga Brava* <note original: "Manga Brava">Literally "Wild Mango," a common name for the poisonous *Cerbera manghas*.</note>, as several others have also indicated to me, saying it is much more harmful in the Western parts of the Indies than in the Eastern islands. Nevertheless, an oil is expressed from these kernels after they have been dried in the sun with little labor; this oil is suitable for lamps and is much used for that purpose in Makassar. The paste from which the oil was pressed, when mixed with cotton, is formed into common candles, though these give off a heavy <note>or foul</note> odor.

The people of Ternate fear this tree as much as the inhabitants of these regions fear the preceding "blinding tree" <note original: "excæcantem arborem">Referring to *Excoecaria agallocha*, known for its sap that causes blindness.</note>; they will not sit or rest peacefully under it, nor will they use its wood for the hearth to cook food, saying that the food contracts a malignancy from it that disturbs the body. However, they smear its sap on the stings of the *Sabandar* fish <note>A type of venomous fish, possibly a stonefish or lionfish.</note>, which it cures.

In the year 1678 in Amboina, they began to burn thin and light charcoal from this wood, which is suitable for making gunpowder; it can be prepared better than the charcoal from the previously mentioned "blinding tree" wood, since the cutting of this tree is not as dangerous as the former.

This *Manga Brava* has another terrestrial species growing on open and windy mountains, very similar to this one, but these are always lowly trees, and the leaves are much smaller and narrower, as are the flowers and fruit. The sap also flows in smaller quantities. The use of this variety is not yet known, as it occurs rarely. I found it most often on the bare mountains of the Hitu region, growing on plains of red clay mixed with sharp coral stones.

In the year 1686, the sap of the coastal species was found to be excellent against the stings of the *Ikan Swangi* <note original: "Ican Swangi">Literally "Sorcerer Fish" or "Ghost Fish" in Malay; usually refers to venomous scorpionfish or stonefish.</note>, which lives in fresh rivers. A certain man from Larique had been stung by one on his thumb, such that not only did his entire arm swell, but he also felt dizziness in his head and anxiety in his heart; all of which vanished with the treatment of the wound as soon as this sap was smeared upon it.

This tree seems to be the one described in the *Hortus Malabaricus*, volume 1, Figure 39, under the Malabar name *Odallam*. The Brahmins call it *Uro*. There is only a small difference in the flowers and fruit, which is to be attributed to the different climate and soil of the regions.

->In *Rumphius's Appendix* these things are found:<-

The *Bintaro* fruits in Java are larger and rounder, both those on the coast and those growing inland. From the kernels, a yellow and fragrant oil is extracted in the following manner: take mature kernels, dry them in the sun, then crush them and boil them over a fire in a small amount of water, just as is done with *Minyak Jarak* <note original: "Minjac Djarac">Castor oil.</note>. Then you obtain the mentioned oil, which is considered "hot"; mixed with other hot oils and certain pungent spices, it is smeared over chilled limbs. Otherwise, no harm is known from this tree there.

In Makassar it is called *Lamboetoe*, where the fruits are also larger than the Amboinese ones, and the kernels are used for making oil, though the leaves are narrower. There, the fallen fruits are collected after the outer husk has mostly rotted away, leaving only a thin woody skin surrounding the kernel, from which the oil is prepared.

The leaves are also much smaller and narrower, as are the flowers and fruits. The milk runs out of it somewhat sparingly: its further use is still unknown, for it is seldom found. I have seen it most on the bare mountains of Hitu's land, made of red clay and sharp coral-stones, where they are flat.*

AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. Chapter XXXIX.

## OBSERVATION.

This tree seems to vary wonderfully in its fruits, which is evident not only from *Rumphius’s* description but also from a comparison of the figures found in the *Hortus Malabaricus*, in *Rumphius*, in my *Thesaurus Zeylanicus*, and also in the works of *Petiver* and *Freyer*, which may be compared with one another.

Furthermore, I have collected the synonyms and authors of this tree that I could find in my *Thesaurus Zeylanicus* on pages 151 and 152, which I consider superfluous to repeat here; I have provided its illustration in **Plate 70**. To me, it is called the *Milky Manghas* <note original: "Manghas lactescens">Cerbera manghas, often confused with other milky-sapped trees</note>, with thick, veiny leaves like the *Nerium* <note>Oleander</note>, a flower like the *Jasmine*, and a poisonous fruit similar to a *Peach*; see there the description and observations, which, I freely admit, are somewhat confused in that work. Indeed, I encountered such difficulties <note original: "tricas">literally "trifles" or "perplexities"</note> in this plant that I could hardly extricate myself, especially being misled by the synonyms of others and by *Rumphius’s* own figure and description, which do not agree with each other at all. His description agrees with the *Odalla* in the *Hortus Malabaricus*, but the figure corresponds to that shown in the *Hortus Malabaricus* part 1, **Plate 46**, and is there called *Curutu Pala*, as is immediately clear from a comparison. The *Odalla*, however, agrees with the figures of *Petiver*, *Freyer*, and the *Thesaurus Zeylanicus*, and is called *Cerbera* by *Linnaeus* in his *Characteres Plantarum Generum* No. 178, where its characteristics can be examined more extensively. The *Curutu Pala* is joined by *Plukenet* in his *Almagestum* page 43 with the Javanese tree with peach leaves in *Herman’s* manuscript catalog, and with the Indian tree with the leaf of a peach tree in the *Hortus Beaumontianus* page 10.

## CHAPTER THIRTY-NINE.

### Scholar's Wood. Pule.

This third milk-bearing tree constitutes a peculiar genus of its own, different from the preceding ones. It also bears a reasonably thick trunk, but it is not tall, except when it grows in the forests where it shoots up undisturbed; there it has a taller and rounder trunk. However, when located near human dwellings, where it is frequently cut, peeled, and broken, its trunk remains thick and low, covered with a rough, thick, and cracked bark, beset here and there with various knots. In the wild, it also gains "buttresses" <note original: "vlerken" (Dutch) / "elatus" (Latin)> near the root. It immediately divides into two or three major branches which stand upright, and its crown has something peculiar about it by which the tree can be recognized from afar; for it is double, and sometimes even triple, resembling the upper part of a Parasol <note original: "Umbellae" / "Cuperzol">, with a particular erect branch rising above the lower and otherwise broad crown.

The bark of the branches is smooth and whitish. On the younger branches, the leaves sit in turns above one another, four, five, or six placed together in a circle <term>whorl</term>; indeed, six together form a perfect circle, from which three or four new small branchlets sprout together, bearing five or six leaves at their summit. In their center is placed a short tip like a bud; those which bear fewer "rays" <note>leaf points</note> are either not yet fully grown or have partly fallen off, which is why one always sees an "open book" <note original: "boek open ziet">A Dutch metaphorical description for the flat, spreading whorl of leaves.</note>.

These leaves most closely resemble those of the *Mango*, and they are of unequal size even in one and the same circle, a palm's breadth wide, some only four inches long and two wide, with a blunt tip, firm, smooth on the upper side, and woven through on the lower side with many parallel ribs or protruding streaks. The tips are bent somewhat downward, and they sit on short petioles. On the young shoots, several of these circles sit one above the other, which in adult trees, as has been said, divide themselves into three or four longer stalks.

The flowers sprout in a loose and wide-extending cluster <term>cyme</term>, which resemble *Papaya* flowers, but are much smaller; each flower is composed of five or six somewhat thick, whitish petals that are bent outward and tubular, forming a concave tube in their center, with a white crown...

## OBSERVATION.

This tree seems to vary wonderfully in its fruits, as appears not only from the description by *Rumphius*, but also from the figures found in the *Hortus Malabaricus*, by *Rumphius*, *Petiver*, *Freyer*, and in my *Thesaurus Zeylanicus*, which can be compared with one another.

Furthermore, I have collected the names and writers of this tree that I could find in my *Thesaurus Zeylanicus* on pages 151 and 152, which is redundant to cite again here; I have given the figure of it on **Plate 70**, which I have named the *Milk-bearing Manghas*, with thick leaves of the *Nerium*, the flower of the *Jasmine*, and the fruit like a *Peach*, yet poisonous; where further see the description and remarks, which are somewhat confused there; for I encountered some difficulty in this plant, from which I could hardly rescue myself, being primarily misled by the names of others, and if I shall tell the truth, by the figure and description of *Rumphius* himself, which do not very well agree with each other. For his description agrees with that of the *Odalla* of the *Hortus Malabaricus*, and his figure with the *Curutu-Pala* represented there in the first part, **Plate 46**, as is easily seen from the comparison of the figures. The *Odalla* therefore corresponds with the figures of *Petiver*, *Freyer*, and those of the *Thesaurus Zeylanicus*, which is called *Cerbera* by *Linnaeus* in his *Characteres Plantarum Generum* No. 178, where its characteristics can be further investigated. The *Curutu Pala* is added by *Plukenet* in *Almagestum* page 43 to the *Javanese* tree with *Peach* leaves of *Herman* in his written list, and with the East-Indian tree with a *Peach* leaf from the *Hortus Beaumontianus* page 10.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.

### Scholar's Wood.

The third Milk-tree also makes a genus of its own, differing from both the preceding ones. It is also reasonably thick of trunk, yet not high, except in the wild: when it shoots up undisturbed, it has a higher and rounder trunk, but standing near human dwellings, where it is often chopped, peeled, and broken, it remains thick and low of trunk, with a rough, thick, and burst bark, set here and there with knots. In the wild it also gains buttresses <note original: "vlerken">literally "wings"</note> at the root. It divides itself immediately into two or three main branches, which stand straight up, and its crown has something special, by which one can recognize it from afar, for it is double, and sometimes triple, resembling the top of a Parasol or Sun-shade <note original: "Cuperzol, of Zonne-scherm">, sticking out on a particularly raised branch above the lower, broader crown.

The bark of the branches is smooth and whitish. Now on the thin branches the leaves stand, also in turns above each other, four, five, and six in a ring; namely six in a complete ring, out of which three and four new twigs sprout, bearing on their crown five or six leaves with a short point in the middle; and those which have fewer ribs are either not yet grown out, or have partly fallen off, for which reason one always sees an "open book."

They most resemble the Mangas leaves, and are of unequal size, even in one and the same ring, a hand-breadth wide, some only four inches long, and two wide, with a blunt point, stiff, smooth on the upper side, and on the bottom interlaced with many parallel ribs or protruding stripes, with the point bent a little downwards, and they stand on short stalks: On the young shoots one sees these rings, some standing above each other, but on the mature trees they divide themselves, as has been said, into three and four other stalks.

The bloom comes forth in a hollow and wide-spread crown or cluster, and resembles the bloom of the *Papaya*, though it is smaller, each being made of five or six thick little leaves <term>petals</term>, whitish, and bent outwards, standing on a little stalk; in the middle they show a hollow little tube, with...

surrounded by a white crown; of a not unpleasant but faint scent, yet this tree spreads its odor in the evening hours to the distance of a javelin-throw, so that it is not certain where the tree should be sought: indeed the Balinese believe this scent penetrates even into heaven itself, though they do not know it is so high.

The fruits are long, narrow pods; the thickness of a straw, mostly round, always joined in pairs on one stem, spread apart from each other like the extended legs of a man, or a rustic pitchfork: two or three of these pairs sit together on a larger common stem, and five such pairs above those three, and at the very top two are placed together, all of which constitute the whole cluster, which thus appears somewhat tangled. These pods are slightly curved like a scimitar, pale green and smooth on the outside, so that they might be mistaken for long stems; they are eight or ten inches long, but inside they are filled with a white and milky pith, which hardens into thin, flat seeds, having the shape of a dill seed but more oblong and almost square, and they are crowned with a very fine, very white, silky, and upright down <term>pappus</term>. These seeds lie upon one another in a regular, oblique order like roof tiles; if the pods open upon maturity, these seeds are scattered by the wind, which also occurs in the *Milky Money-wort* <note original: "Nummularia Lactea">Possibly a species of Hoya or Dischidia</note>.

This whole tree is also filled with a whitening milk <note>latex</note>, which flows out in great abundance if its younger branches are wounded or the leaves are broken off.

The bark of the trunk is likewise filled with it, but in lesser and thicker quantity. The milk itself has a bitter and unpleasant taste, but in no way stings the tongue.

It produces flowers in the dry or Western seasons of the year, but pods in the month of April. Its wood is white, easy to dry, fine, the softest and whitest of all Amboinese woods, and it can easily be worked into light cabinetry, like the wood of our *Linden* <note original: "Tiliae">Lime or Basswood</note>: but it does not last long, and quickly becomes decayed and eaten by worms. The best wood is gathered from the spurs of the roots, which should be cut in dry times and during a waning moon.

This wood has a vegetative nature and can very easily be planted from stakes and branches driven into the ground, from which fence posts are formed, growing very quickly into huge trees; indeed, even if pieces of this wood lie upon the ground, they still put forth many branches. These trees love windy places, such as fields and light forests. White ants, called *Solot*, inhabit this tree, where they form huge nests like a water-jar. Its thin roots are very bitter and are used with the bark in medicine; this bark is often stripped off, yet it quickly grows back, which is why its trunk is so knotty.

Name. In Latin *Lignum Scholare*, in Dutch *School-hout* <note>School-wood</note>, because of its subsequent use. In Malay *Pule*, in Ternate *Hangi*, in Makassar *Rita*. In Amboinese on *Leytimor Rite*. In *Hitoe* and *Hoamohel Lite* and *Lyitohu*. By the people of Banda *Tewer*. In the *Hortus Malabaricus* volume 1, Figure 45, in Malabar it is called *Pala*. In Brahmanic *Santenu*.

Place. This tree is known in all the islands of watery India, and as far as I could discern from the reports of others, also in ancient India.

Usage. Where it occurs in great abundance and forms thick trunks, its wood is sawn into boards, as well as into beams and ribs from which houses are built; this is elegant and white, and it makes a resonant sound in the rooms, but it is not long-durable unless the aforementioned cutting time is observed, and such houses must be kept very dry. The most common things formed from this, however, are small boards a foot long or a little more, a finger thick, decorated on one side with scrollwork, where a hole is also carved for hanging; on these, boys write their lessons and receive them in turn in writing from the masters, which they must learn in both Christian and Moorish <note>Muslim</note> schools. What is written on these can be erased with *Ampelate* leaves <note original: "Ampelaceis">Leaves of *Ficus ampelas*, used like sandpaper</note> until the board recovers its original elegance and whiteness, when it can be written upon anew, just as is done among us with palimpsests and prepared donkey skins.

The Javanese and Malays form their spice boxes and other smaller cabinet works from this wood. From the wide

surrounded by a white wreath; not unpleasant, but a faint scent; however, in the evening hours after sunset, this tree spreads its scent a bow-shot around it, so that one does not know where the tree is to be found; indeed, the *Balinese* believe that it penetrates into Heaven, though they do not know that it is so high.

The fruits are long, narrow pods, the thickness of a straw, mostly round, of which two and two always stand together on a little stem, bent away from each other like opened legs or a farmer's fork: of these pairs, two or three stand on another large stem, and five similar ones above those other three, and at the very top two together in a circle, which make up the whole cluster, so that they hang like a tangled bundle. They are somewhat curved, like a sabre, light green and smooth on the outside, so that one would take them for long stems, eight or ten inches long; inside they are filled with a white milky pith, which changes into thin flat seeds, like Dill, but more oblong and almost square, whose ends are covered with very thin and snowy-white little beards, like the finest floss-silk, but straight. These seeds lie orderly and diagonally upon one another, like stacked slates, but when the pod bursts from ripeness, they fly out and scatter with the wind, as is also seen with the *Milky Money-wort* <note original: "Nummularia Lactea"></note>.

This entire tree is also full of white milk, which runs out richly if one wounds the young branches or breaks off the leaves.

The bark of the trunk also has it, but less, and thicker. This milk is bitter and unpleasant of taste, yet not at all biting or sharp on the tongue.

It blooms in the dry or West monsoon, and the pods are seen in April. The wood is white, drying easily, fine, the softest and whitest of all Amboinese tree-woods, and allows itself to be easily worked into all kinds of light cabinetry, like Linden wood among us: but it is a pity that it is not durable and so easily becomes worm-eaten. The best is obtained from the burls near the root, and then one must still cut it in dry weather and a waning moon.

It is also a fast-growing wood, and can easily be transplanted with stakes and branches, which is why fence-posts are made from it, which shoot up very easily and in a short time become large trees; indeed, even if the logs lie on the ground, they nevertheless shoot up with many branches. They like to grow in airy places, such as in fields and empty forests. The white ants (called *Solot*) also like to live on this tree, where they make large nests, as big as a water pot. The thin roots are very bitter and are used with the bark in medicine; the bark is often pulled off, which grows back again in a short time, and that makes it so knotty.

Name. In Latin *Lignum Scholare*: In Dutch *School-hout* <note>School-wood</note>, after the following use: In Malay *Pule*. In Ternate *Hangi*. In Makassar *Rita*. In Amboinese on *Leitimor Rite*. In *Hitoe* and *Hoamohel Lite* and *Lyitohu*: In Banda *Tewer*, in the *Hortus Malabaricus* volume 1, figure 45, it is called in Malabar *Pala*, in Brahmanic *Santenu*.

Place. It is known in all the islands of Water-India, and as I can perceive from the accounts of others, also in old India.

Usage. Where it is found in abundance and in thick trunks, it is sawn into planks and ribs, and houses are made from it, which are indeed very neat and white, and also make a resonant sound in the rooms, but they are not durable unless one observes the precise time in cutting mentioned before, and keeps those houses nice and dry. The most common thing made from it are certain small boards a foot long or more, and a finger thick, carved at one end with scrollwork and an eye made there so that they can be hung up; on these the schoolboys learn to write, or receive their lessons in writing from the master, which they must learn, in the Christian as well as the Moorish <note>Muslim</note> schools. This writing can be rubbed out again with the leaves of the *Ampelaas* <note>Ficus ampelas</note> until the board becomes white and clean again and can receive other writing, just as we do with slates and donkey skins.

The Javanese and Malays make their spice boxes and other small cabinetry from it. From the wide wings

# AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. Chapter XXXIX.

From the wide buttresses <note original: "alis">literally 'wings'</note> of the trunk, small tables and flat bowls called *Dulang* are manufactured. Segments of the trunk are used for the supports of fence posts, called *Mabangi* by the people of Ternate, because they send roots into the earth and remain green for a long time.

The bark possesses many proven virtues in the medical art; for when crushed with the juice of sour lemons and a little salt, then strained and drunk, it cleanses the stomach of phlegmatic viscidity by its detergent and bitter power, and restores a lost appetite, though it provides an unpleasant draught. For this reason, shavings of this bark, along with the underlying wood, are offered for sale in Chinese medicinal chests among other aromatics brought from Java. This same bark, crushed with vinegar, cures swollen bellies (though not the obstructions commonly called *Tekatu* <note>A term for a hardened mass or tumor in the abdomen</note>) from which putrid fevers arise.

This same bark, crushed with that of the *Ampaci* described above and the juice of sour lemons, and sprinkled upon potherbs, puts to flight all worms and caterpillars. Others crush this bark with the leaves of *Klitsij* and *Sombong* in a little water, and administer it against slow and almost continuous fevers. The thin roots of this tree, chewed with *Pinanga* <note>Betel nut</note> and swallowed, remove false pleurisy and all sharp pains of the chest and back. The inner bark, crushed in water and drunk, strengthens the stomach and intestines. To this end, many of the nobles of Makassar sometimes mix this crushed bark—both fresh and dry—into cooked rice or other foods which they eat together, saying that it strengthens the stomach and makes men stout; however, some Malays and Javanese use the wood itself for this purpose. The people of Ternate crush this bark with vinegar and drink it against fevers.

This tree is a great enemy and opposite to the Macassan poison tree <note original: "toxicariæ arbori">Referring to the Upas tree, *Antiaris toxicaria*</note>, so much so that if a small branch or leaf of it is brought into a room where the poison of that tree is hanging, and such a branch is moved near it, the poison will be entirely deprived of its strength. How the poison is to be extracted from wounds inflicted by weapons infected with this venom using the petioles of these leaves will be seen below under the "Poison Tree."

The milk <note>latex</note> of this tree is dripped into the wounds of animals infested with maggots, from which they die and fall out. They also use the roots, mixed with other medicines, to cure a nasal ulcer called *Roston*.

In certain small islands I found a species of this tree which I thought differed from the common one, for its leaves were much larger, like those borne by the *King of Lovers* <note original: "Rex Amatoris">A name for the *Graptophyllum pictum* or Caricature Plant</note>, and it was very full of milk; perhaps it is the coastal *Pule* tree, which I found on the tiny pigeon island called *Hulo-Anan*. The Javanese also form the sheaths of their weapons <note>kris sheaths</note> from this wood.

If anyone has fallen from a height or been struck, and thereafter feels great pains and burning in his internal parts, he should take the bark of this trunk, the root with one or two *Pule* leaves, and a piece of toasted coconut kernel; let these be crushed together with a little water, and then express the juice and drink it. Cleaned *Pule* bark, boiled in a well-sealed pot with half water and half vinegar, with a small piece of Turmeric, half a Nutmeg, and a piece of crushed Ginger added, is given to women after childbirth who have not been well cleansed. This same bark, crushed and taken with equal parts vinegar and water, softens and reduces a swollen spleen, and cleanses the intestines of watery humors. Its younger leaves, boiled in a bamboo tube with water and drunk in the morning, cure *Beriberi* or paralysis so quickly and safely that it is not necessary to repeat the dose more than twice.

NB. It should be investigated whether the tree called *Bindaus* by the people of Ternate (called *Mintäoffa* in Hoeamohel) differs from the preceding one. For its leaf is said to be like that of the *Pule*, and its wood is white and soft, suitable for weapon sheaths.

There is also another tree called *Poelo Batu*, regarding which see Book 4, chapter 11, under the *Yellow Cafaffu*.

<meta>Catchword: OBSER-</meta>

<column-break/>

From the wide buttress-wings of the trunk, one makes small tables and flat bowls (called *Duiang*). The sections of the trunk are used as supports for fences, called *Mahangi* by the Ternatans, because they shoot roots into the earth and stay green for a long time.

The bark has many proven uses in medicine; for rubbed with the juice of some sour lemons and a little salt, crushed small and drunk, it cleanses the stomach of phlegmatic sliminess with its wiping bitterness and brings back the lost appetite, although it is somewhat difficult to take. For this reason, one sees the grated bark with the nearby wood for sale in Chinese herbal boxes among other spices brought from Java. The same bark rubbed with vinegar and drunk heals swollen bellies (not commonly called the *Tekatu* cake) and the putrid fevers arising therefrom.

The same bark, rubbed with that of the above-mentioned *Ampac* and the juice of sour lemons, and strewn on potherbs, lets no worms or caterpillars grow thereon. Others rub the bark with the leaves of *Klitsij* and *Sombong* in a little water, and give that to drink against persistent internal fevers. The thin roots chewed with *Pinang* and swallowed drive away false pleurisy and various stabs in the chest and back. The innermost bark rubbed in water and drunk strengthens the stomach and the intestines. To the same end, many great people on Makassar have a custom of mixing the rubbed bark—both green and dry—now and then into cooked rice or other food and eating it together, saying that it makes a healthy stomach and a full-bodied person. Some Malays and Javanese even use the wood for this purpose. The Ternatans rub the bark and drink it with some vinegar against the fever.

This tree is a powerful enemy of the Macassan dart-poison, such that if one brings a small twig or leaf into a room where the prescribed poison hangs, and holds it underneath, the poison shall become entirely powerless. And how one can pull the poison out of wounds (made by darts) with the stems of the leaves can be seen hereafter in *Arbor Toxicaria*.

The milk is put into the wounds of beasts that are full of worms, from which they die and fall out. The roots they also use to heal the ulcer in the nose (called *Roston*), mixed with more other things.

I have found on some small islands a sort of this tree which appeared to me to differ from the common one, for the leaves were much larger, like those of the *Rex Amatoris*, and very full of milk; perhaps it is a strand *Pule*. I found it on the Pigeon Island *Hulo-Anan*. The Javanese make their kris-sheaths also from this wood.

If someone has fallen or been struck, and thereby feels great stabs and burning inside, they take the bark of the trunk, the root with one or two leaves of *Pule*, and a piece of roasted coconut kernel; rub it together with a little water, press out the juice, and drink it. The cleaned bark of *Pule*, boiled in a well-stopped pot with half water and half vinegar, adding a piece of Turmeric, half a Nutmeg, and a piece of small Ginger, is given to drink to women in childbed who are not well cleansed after bearing. The same bark, rubbed with half vinegar and as much water and taken in, makes the swollen spleen shrink and cleanses the intestines of dropsical humors. Likewise, the young leaves boiled in a bamboo with water and drunk in the morning heals the *Beriberi* so quickly that one does not need more than two bamboo-fuls of drink.

NB. To investigate whether the tree named *Bindaus* by the Ternatans, called *Mintäoffa* on Hoeamohel, differs from the preceding: for it shall have a leaf like *Pule*, a white and soft wood, suitable for kris-sheaths.

There is yet another tree called *Poelo Batu*, of which see Book 4, Chapter 11, in *Cafaffus Citrina*.

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of "milk-bearing" trees, transitioning from the Scholar's Wood (Lignum Scholare) to the "Fat Tree" (Arbor Pinguis). It maintains the scholarly dialogue with contemporary European botanists like Plumier and Breyne.</meta>

Book III. Chapter XL. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

### OBSERVATION.

Anyone can easily see that this tree belongs to the class of milk-bearing, pod-producing, and many-seeded trees with bowl-shaped flowers. I was long uncertain whether it should be classified under *Nerium* <note>Oleander</note>, *Apocynum* <note>Dogbane</note>, or similar genera, until I found in Charles Plumier’s <note>A French botanist (1646–1704) who explored the West Indies</note> new plant genera a genus he called *Tabernaemontana*. This tree corresponds perfectly to his description, specifically the one he calls "Milk-bearing *Tabernaemontana* with wavy Citron-leaves" <note>original Latin: *Tabernaemontana lactescens Citri foliis undulatis*</note>, and in the *Hortus Cliffortianus* <note>A work by Linnaeus describing George Clifford’s garden</note> page 76, it is listed as the *Tabernaemontana* with lance-shaped and shining oblong leaves.

Previously, this tree was referred to the *Nerium* genus by Jakob Breyne <note>A prominent 17th-century merchant and botanist from Danzig</note> in his second *Prodromus*, page 77. He called it the "Greatest Malabar milk-bearing *Nerium* with five leaves, many flowers, and very small, clustered, fragrant greenish-white flowers and very long hanging pods." It is also described under the name *Pala* in the first volume of the *Hortus Malabaricus* <note>A monumental 12-volume work on the flora of the Malabar Coast</note>, where a most elegant illustration of it is shown in Plate 46.

---

## CHAPTER FORTY.

#### The Fat-Tree. Mamina.

After the preceding and more well-known milk-bearing trees, there follow certain others which do not pour out an actual milk, but rather a viscous juice that is put to a specific use.

The *Arbor Pinguis* <note>The "Fat Tree," likely a species of *Rejoua* or *Tabernaemontana*</note> is a medium-sized, wild tree consisting of sparse, curved, and extended branches, the thinner of which are "fat" <note>oily or resinous</note>, flexible, and yet brittle. The leaves are placed without any particular order and are of a common shape, a palm-length or more in size, and three or four fingers wide. They are coarsely toothed along the edges like a large wooden saw, though these teeth are widely spaced and not deep. Furthermore, the leaves are smooth, firm, and oily, woven through with sparse transverse ribs. The younger leaves are slightly larger and floppier, of a color mixed from brown and dark blackish-green; they are so smooth and shining that they appear as if coated in oil. Each leaf does not rise directly from its stalk, but forms a curve near its origin, from which it bends backward.

> *The taste of the young leaves is at first slightly acidic, then bitter, but always with a notable astringency. From this, it is discovered that they are composed of contrary parts: they first loosen <note>act as a laxative</note>, then cleanse, and finally bind <note>act as an astringent</note>.*

The flowers hang from small, sparse clusters and are mostly mossy in appearance, composed of small yellow stamens and surrounded by three short yellow petals which form the bloom. The fruits likewise hang in sparse, small numbers, so that sometimes only one or two grow to their full size and perfection. These are oblong, olive-shaped berries, or similar to the fruits of the larger *Varinga* <note>a species of *Ficus* or Banyan</note> found in these lands, but shorter and rounder. They are navelled <note>dimpled</note> at the top, first green, then yellow, and finally turning red. On the outside, these berries are covered in a viscous flesh, barely the thickness of a knife, which, if cut, has a rosy-red color and exudes a thick yellow milk. Beneath this lies a woody shell, forming a round nut in fully ripe fruits; this shell is black and wrinkled on the outside. Inside, a kernel is hidden, much like in the fruits of the *Gnemon* <note>the Gnetum tree</note>, which is viscous and ash-colored, resembling the substance and color of a cooked kidney.

From a wound in the bark of this tree, a thick, whitish, but sparse milk drips out, which soon dries into a yellow color. It is extremely sticky, like a pigment or varnish, tasteless and unpleasant, and astringent on the tongue. If collected into a lump, it hardens into a dark yellow gum. The wood is soft, whitish, and useless. It grows at the edges of forests and in valleys, as well as in light scrubland. It is rarely found in the high mountains, and those found there always grow taller and straighter. It can be transplanted via cuttings from the branches, but it sprouts slowly.

<meta>catchword: Its</meta>
<meta>Vol. II.</meta>

<column-break/>

### REMARK.

That this tree belongs to the milk-bearing trees with long pods, many seeds, and bowl-shaped flowers can be easily seen by any expert. However, I remained uncertain for a long time as to which genus it should be assigned—whether to the *Nerium*, *Apocynum*, or similar—until I finally found a genus in the new works of Plumier called *Tabernaemontana*. This tree corresponds entirely with that genus, which he called the "Milk-bearing *Tabernaemontana* with leaves like the Citron tree but folded," and it is the *Tabernaemontana* with oblong leaves in the *Hortus Cliffortianus*, page 76, etc.

Before this, the tree was assigned to the *Nerium* genus by Breyne in his second *Prodromus*, page 77, and was named by him the "Malabar milk-bearing *Nerium* with five leaves and many small, cluster-like, fragrant greenish-white flowers with very long hanging pods." Under the name *Pala*, it appears in the *Hortus Malabaricus*, first part, Plate 46, where a beautiful figure of it may also be found.

---

## CHAPTER XL.

#### The Fat-Tree.

After the preceding and most famous milk-trees, there now follow some that *do not exactly give milk, but a sticky sap, which is used for something.*

The *Arbor Pinguis* is a medium-sized and wild tree, with few crooked and extended branches, of which the thinner ones are fat, flexible, and snap off easily. The leaves stand without order and are of a common shape, a hand-length or more, three and four fingers wide, coarsely toothed on the edges like a large wood-saw; however, the teeth stand far apart and do not go deep. They are smooth, stiff, and fat, with few transverse ribs. The young leaves are somewhat larger and flappier, of a brown color mixed with some dark green, as smooth and shiny as if they were smeared with oil. The leaf does not stand straight on its stalk, but always has a bend at its origin, and is therefore curved backwards.

> *The taste of the young ones is at first somewhat sour, thereafter bitter, yet throughout with a remarkable contraction <note>astringency</note>, from which one notes that they are made of contrary parts: at first laxative, thereafter cleansing, and at last astringent. The old leaves are mildly sweet, with a small contraction.*

The blossom hangs in small, empty clusters, mostly moss-like, and made of yellow threads, surrounded by three yellow and short leaves <note>petals</note> that make the little flower. The fruits also hang in small numbers together, sometimes on the whole cluster no more than one or two coming to perfection. These are oblong berries, like Olives, or like the fruits of the large *Varinga* in this country, yet shorter and rounder, with a small navel on top; first green, thereafter yellow, and finally red. On the outside they are covered with a sticky flesh, barely a knife-thickness, rose-red when one cuts into it, sweating out a thick yellow milk. Underneath lies a woody shell, making a round nutlet; when fully ripe, it is black and wrinkled on the outside. In it lies the kernel, as in the fruits of the *Gnemon*, slimy, grayish in substance and color, like a cooked kidney.

From the wounded bark of this tree drips a thickish, white, though sparse milk, which shortly thereafter becomes yellow and very sticky, like varnish; it is insipid and unpleasant, also contracting on the tongue. When much is gathered into a lump, it dries into a dark yellow gum. The wood is soft, whitish, and useless. It grows at the edges of the forests in the valleys, and among the light undergrowth. In the high forest one seldom finds it, and that which grows there becomes much taller and straighter of trunk. One can also transplant it with stakes <note>cuttings</note>, though it comes up slowly.

<header>AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. Chapter XL.</header>

A second species of this also occurs, which may be called the *Narrow-leaved Mamina* <note>original Latin: *Mamina Angustifolia*</note>, as it bears smaller leaves—specifically five or six inches long and two wide. These are thick, firm, and more rarely saw-toothed, possessing a sweet but nauseating astringency.

The flowers also sit upon short and tiny clusters; they are mostly yellow heads made up of many yellow stamens and three short petals. The clusters themselves turn yellow and are no longer than a finger joint. From every wounded part, a thick, white milk drips out, which turns yellow when dry and does not become as reddish as the milk of the previous tree.

It flowers in January, and the fruits ripen during the rainy months until August, hanging from the tree for a very long time before they reach maturity.

*Name.* In Latin, it is called the *Fat Tree* <note>original: *Arbor Pinguis*</note>. The Malay name is currently unknown, but in the Amboinese language, it is called *Mamina*, which means "fat wood" or "fat tree," named for the plump appearance of the leaves. Among the people of Luhon, it is called *Talabe*.

*Location.* It is found in all the Amboinese islands; whether it is known to other peoples, I have not yet learned.

*Usage.* The younger, dark leaves of this tree are in great use by midwives <note>puerperis</note> for purging newborn infants. They take these leaves along with those of the *Boa Rau-Utan*, wrap them in another leaf, and toast them under hot ashes. They then pour the juice of sour lemons over them and squeeze out the juice together, which they pour lukewarm into the infants' mouths. From this, the children are gently purged of their first excrement or meconium, and at the same time, all phlegm <note>pituita</note> is cleared from the tongue, stomach, and intestines. This medicine can also be given to infants at other times when they are restless or suffering from constipation, using either the juice alone or a decoction of the leaves, from which they soon have a bowel movement and sleep peacefully. Old leaves are unsuitable for this purpose. However, if these leaves do not work, one must assist the infants with a suppository prepared from Turmeric <note>Curcuma</note>. This custom is common among women throughout all of Amboina and has even now been adopted by European families. In adults, these leaves have no purging power; on the contrary, these younger leaves can be eaten with other foods, such as with *Bocassan* <note>a fermented fish or shrimp paste</note> like another *Ulang Ulang* <note>a traditional salad of raw or blanched vegetables</note>.

The Amboinese coat their paintings with the juice of this tree—mostly those on wood—just as we do with white varnish. These are made smooth and shining by that milk, though they appear somewhat yellowish due to the color of the sap.

Some grind the bark of the trunk with water and offer the expressed juice as a mild purgative for adults and the elderly. Other Amboinese mix this milk with that of the previously mentioned *Rite* tree and use them in place of varnish or wood pigments.

The inner kernel can be eaten for pleasure, as it tastes sweet like hazelnuts.

<column-break/>

A second kind of this is also found, which one may call the *Narrow-leaved Mamina* <note>original Dutch: *Mamina Angustifolia*</note>, for it has smaller leaves, namely five and six inches long and two wide; thick, stiff, and also widely saw-toothed, with a sweet and nauseous astringency.

The blossom also grows in short, small clusters, and are mostly yellow buds consisting of many yellow threads and three short petals. The little clusters are yellow and not longer than a finger joint; a thick white milk also runs out from everywhere, which dries yellow, though not as reddish as on the former tree.

It blooms in January; the fruits become ripe in the rainy monsoon until August, remaining a very long time hanging on the tree before they become ripe.

*Name.* In Latin, *Fat Tree* <note>original: *Arbor Pinguis*</note>; the Malay name is still unknown. On Amboina, *Mamina*, that is, fat-wood or fat-tree, after the fat appearance of the leaves. In the Luhonese language, *Talabe*.

*Place.* They are found in all the Amboinese Islands; whether they are known further afield, I have not yet heard.

*Usage.* The young brown leaves of this tree are in great use among midwives to cleanse newborn children from the inside; for they take the same leaves with those of *Boa-Rau-Utan*, wrap them in another leaf, and roast them in the hot ashes. Then they pour some juice of sour lemons over them, squeeze it out together, and having made it a little lukewarm, they pour it into the children's mouths, which cleanses the children through a gentle bowel movement of the first and maternal excrements, at the same time wiping away all sliminess from the tongue, stomach, and intestines. One may also give it to all small children at other times when they are restless and constipated—the juice alone as well as the decoction of the leaves—from which they immediately get a bowel movement and come to rest. The old leaves are unfit for this work; however, if these leaves do not work, one must come to their aid with suppositories of Turmeric <note>Curcuma</note>. This method is common among the women throughout all of Amboina, and is now also used in German <note>likely referring to Dutch/European</note> families. In old people, these leaves have no purging power, but on the contrary, one can eat the young leaves with *Bocassan* like other *Ulang Ulang*.

The Amboinese smear their paintings with the milk of this tree, though mostly those that stand on wood, just as we do with varnish; they become quite smooth and shining through it, but appear somewhat yellowish due to the color of the milk.

Some rub the bark of the trunk with water and drink the squeezed-out juice as a gentle purgative for old people. Other Amboinese mix this milk with that of the preceding *Rite*, and use it for varnish or all kinds of wood-dyes.

The inner kernel can also be eaten for pleasure, for it tastes sweet, like hazelnuts.

# CHAPTER FORTY-ONE.
## Note on Cambodia Gamboge.

**From** the reports of certain Malays, I have learned that a certain tree is found on Java which has a great similarity to the preceding *Mamina* <note>the "Fat Tree" described in the previous chapter</note>, from which a yellow sap is extracted. They consider this to be one and the same as *Gutta Cambodja* <term>Gamboge: a bright yellow resin produced from several species of evergreen trees, traditionally used as a pigment and a potent purgative</term>. However, when certain skilled Chinese men were asked from which tree the true Cambodia Gamboge is collected, they gave the following response, which I wished to set down here as a note to serve others in further investigation.

This *Gutta Cambodja*—which in pharmacies is called *Gitta Jemu*, *Gummi Gutta Gutta*, Yellow Gum, and by many other corrupt names—is called *Tin Uyn* by the Chinese and *Sari Luning* by the Malays. It is collected from a large milky tree growing in Cambodia, and not at all from a climbing shrub <note>original: "convolvulaceo frutice"</note> as some have wrongly noted. It is first received in certain leaves and packed into small baskets in large lumps, pressed one upon the other, and thus transported throughout all the Indies. Hence it was called by the first Malays *Gitta* or *Gutta Cambodja*, that is, the gum of Cambodia, from which the names *Gutta Cambodja* and other corrupted terms were derived.

Formerly, it was in great medicinal use among the Chinese, from whom other nations undoubtedly learned its use. Today, however, it is mostly out of use among them because it moves the bowels too violently during purging. Nevertheless, they sometimes employ it for people who are becoming excessively fat and wish to become leaner, in the following manner: take a half-drachm weight of this with an equal part of the whole root of *Henhussek* <note>original: "Henhuſſek," likely a reference to a Chinese medicinal root</note>, a rice-bowl full of water, and a cup full of vinegar. Boil these together and drink it like tea once every month.

The Malays prescribe it in the size of an *Amboinese Catjang* <note>a small bean</note> or a small pea with some liquid, and they eat a small amount of *Catsje* or *Gitta Gambir* <term>Gambir: an astringent extract used to counteract the nausea and sudden vomiting caused by the powerful gamboge resin</term> with it to suppress the nausea and sudden vomiting. Among our own nation living in the East Indies today, the best formula for it is found: namely, its Magisterium <term>Magisterium: a refined chemical precipitate or extract</term>, which is prepared from it with the aid of spirit of wine <note>brandy or distilled alcohol</note>; this works easily through the lower bowels and excites no vomiting.

*Bontius* <note>Jacob Bontius (1592–1631), a Dutch physician in the service of the Dutch East India Company</note> writes in book 6, chapter 57, that the so-called *Gutta Gemu* (in Malay *Lowan Cambodja*, that is, Incense of Cambodia) comes from a tree which in appearance, form, and manner of growth differs in no way from the thorny and milky plant that grows everywhere in Java. He calls it in the cited place *Efula* or *Lathyrus Indica* <note>Indian Spurge</note>, but we call it *Ligularia lactea*. Perhaps he, like us, had this from the reports of others; certainly, the Ceylonese doctors themselves would contradict him, as they collect their *Gutta Gemu* from a fully grown tree and not from a climbing shrub.

Furthermore, *Bontius* praises his extract, or rather the preparation of this gum, which he composes in the following manner: Take one pound of *Gutta Gemu*, crush it coarsely, and put it into a glass bottle. Pour strong distilled vinegar over it so that it rises to the height of three fingers above the gum. Having closed the bottle well, expose it to the sun for eight days, then filter it through a linen cloth, and according to the art, let it evaporate into a dry mass. The dose of this is from twelve to twenty grains, either dry or dissolved and ground in wine; it evacuates all malignant humors without vomiting through an easy bowel movement.

# CHAPTER 41.
## Note on the Cambodia Gum.

***F**rom the account of certain Malays I have noticed that a certain tree is to be found on Java, which has a great resemblance to the preceding Mamina, and from which a yellow sap is obtained, which they regard as one and the same with Gutta Cambodja. Thereupon, having questioned some experienced Chinese as to what kind of tree the real Gutta Cambodja comes from, I have received this little information, which I have only wanted to set down as a note to serve others for further investigation.*

*The Gutta Cambodiæ then, which in the pharmacies is called Gitta Jemu, Gummi Gutta Gumba, yellow gum, etc., and by several other corrupted names, is called Tin Uyn by the Chinese, and Sari Luning by the Malays. It comes from a large milky tree growing in Cambodia, and by no means from a climbing plant or twining vine, as some have claimed. It is first received in certain leaves, packed with large lumps in baskets upon one another, and further transported throughout all the Indies. From this it was named by the first Malays Gitta or Gutta Cambodiæ, that is, Gum of Cambodia, from which further Gutta Cambodiæ and the other monstrous names have come.*

*It used to be in great use among the Chinese in medicine, from whom other nations undoubtedly also learned it, but nowadays it has mostly fallen into disuse among them, because in purging it causes too great a violence in the body. However, they still use it sometimes, and mostly on such persons who are excessively fat and would gladly become somewhat thin, and that in this manner: take half a drachm's weight of it, with the whole root Henhussek an equal amount, a rice-bowl full of water, a teacup full of vinegar, boil it together, and drink it like tea, and that once every month.*

*The Malays give the same, in the size of an Amboinese Catjang or little bean, with some moisture, and eat upon it a little Catsjo or Gitta Gambir, to prevent the loathing or early vomiting. By our nation in the East Indies, the easiest recipe for this gum is found nowadays. The Magisterium, which is made from it with brandy; for the same works easily from below and causes no vomiting.*

*Bontius lib. 6. cap. 57. writes that the so-called Gutta Gemu, in Malay Lowan Cambodja, that is, incense of Cambodia, comes from a tree, in nature, shape, and manner of growth differing nothing from the prickly and milky plant growing everywhere in Java, called by him in the place cited Efula or Lathyrus Indica, and by us Ligularia lactea, which he perhaps, as well as we, has from hearsay. At least the Ceylonese doctors will contradict him, who fetch their Gutta Gemu from a full-grown tree, and from no climbing vine.*

*Furthermore, Bontius praises his Extractum, or much more the preparation of this gum, which he prepares in the following way: Take one pound of Gutta Gemu, pound it coarsely, put it in a glass bottle, pour strong distilled vinegar over it so that it covers the same three fingers high, which, being well-stoppered, place in the sun for eight days, then strain it through a cloth, and according to the art bring it back to a dry substance. His dose is from twelve to twenty grains, either dry or dissolved and rubbed in wine, purging all evil humors without vomiting, easily through the bowel movement.*

The fruits of this tree, preserved in brine and sugar, are carried throughout all of India to be used in place of Tamarind, and for this reason, they are also called *Tamarinjo Ceylon* <note>original: "Tamarinjo Ceylon" — Tamarind of Ceylon (Sri Lanka)</note>. In the works of Christophorus Acosta <note>a 16th-century Portuguese physician and pioneer in the study of plants from the Orient</note>, there is no mention made of its dye or gum. I do not wish to deny that it might possess the same purging power as Cambodia Gamboge, but I could then enumerate perhaps ten such milky saps growing here in Amboina which also have a purging power; if they were all to be called Cambodia Gamboge for that reason, what a confusion that would create in the field of Botany!

### OBSERVATION.

This gum is called *Cambogium* in pharmacies, as noted by Samuel Dale in his *Pharmacologia* <note>original: "Pharmacol. in 4to. pag. 357."</note>, who recounts various opinions on the production of this gum. He also cites authors who have named and described the trees from which this gum is thought to be collected in various ways. It is brought from various places and is likewise found in the region of Ceylon, where it was observed by Hermann <note>Paul Hermann, a physician and botanist who worked in Ceylon</note> on a tree he called the *Indian Tree yielding Gutta Gum, with sweet round fruit the size of a cherry* <note>original: "Arbore Indica Gummi Guttam fundens, fructu dulci rotundo, Cerasi magnitudine"</note>. This is found in Acosta’s *Museum Zeylanicum* page 26 and our own *Thesaurus Zeylanicus* page 37, where I have collected various synonyms for this tree along with a description and its medicinal powers, etc. See also Commelin’s *Flora Malabarica* page 6.

## CHAPTER FORTY-TWO.

### Note on Dragon's Blood.

In India, I have encountered three substances held to be *Sanguis Draconis* <term>Dragon's Blood: a bright red resin obtained from different species of several distinct plant genera</term>. All of them resemble dried blood compacted into a hard mass, and in my opinion, they differ entirely from one another, and perhaps also from that which is sold under that name in European pharmacies. They are as follows: The first species of Dragon's Blood consists of pieces formed into large and small cakes. The second consists of small heads or balls wrapped in dry leaves. The third is a mixed substance in the shape of a hat, a sugar loaf, or blunt cones. These three forms are prepared in the East Indies and are known by the Malay name *Dierennang* or *Diernang*, regarding which I shall note what I have learned from the reports of trustworthy witnesses.

The first, therefore, is the common Dragon's Blood consisting of two different types of cakes. One type is formed into large round cakes, one or two fingers thick and from half a foot to a full foot wide. They are uneven, blackish or dark brown on the outside, and purplish-red on the inside mixed with black. They are shiny and contain certain bits of straw or wood shavings. When placed on hot coals, this mass gives off a pleasant odor, almost like *Benzoin* <note>a balsamic resin from trees in the genus Styrax</note>, but it more closely resembles *Styrax* <term>Styrax: a fragrant resin used in perfumes and incense</term>. Because of this, it is called *Cominjan Mera* (that is, Red Benzoin) by some Malays, though erroneously; for the true *Cominjan Mera* appears to be a species of Benzoin, pure and semi-transparent like red amber but redder, and when placed on coals, it smells like *Dammara Selanica* <note>original: "Dammaræ Selanica" — Ceylon Resin</note> and does not stain paper red.

The other type consists of small, square cakes, five or six fingers long and one finger thick. These are irregular and wavy, also dark brown on the outside and a deep purple inside. They are pure and not mixed with any
<meta>translator's note: the word "mixtæ" (mixed) is split by the column break.</meta>

<column-break/>

from which I noticed that they were from the tree named by the Portuguese *Carcapoeli*, *Curcas*, and *Cannacorea*, of which the pickled fruits are transported throughout all the *Indies* to be used in place of Tamarind, and therefore also called *Tamarinjo Ceilon*. But the piece of gum brought along was found to be nothing less than yellow gum, or *Gutta Cambodja*, or I must not have received the genuine kind, for it would neither melt nor yield dye in water, and was tough under the teeth, like *Gummi Ammoniacum*. Likewise, the use of it for dyeing is not known by the *Balinese*, where this tree is called *Badong*, and whose fruits are used there in preference to Tamarind. It becomes a very tall and well-branched tree, maintained in yards and near houses.

In *Christoph. a Costa*, there is no mention of the dyeing or the use of the gum. I do not wish to deny that it has the same purging power as *Gutta Cambodja*, but then I could show 10 milky-saps here in *Amboina* which are also purging; if one were to call them all *Gutta Cambodja*, what a confusion that would give in Botany <note>original: "Kruydkunde"</note>!

### NOTE.

This gum is called the *Cambogium* of the pharmacies by *S. Dale in his Pharmacol. in 4to. pag. 357*, who gives several opinions on the origin of this gum and cites several writers who have described and named the trees from which they believe this gum is gathered in various ways. It comes from various places and also occurs in *Zeylon*, where it was discovered by *Herman* in a tree which he calls *East Indian tree, which gives the Gutta Gum, with round sweet fruits the size of a cherry, in his Mus. Zeyl. pag. 26*. It appears in our *Thes. Zeyl. pag. 37*, where I have cited various names and writers of this tree with its powers and properties. See also the *Fl. Malabaar* of Caspar Commelin on page 6.

## CHAPTER XLII.

### Note on Dragon's Blood.

Three things have come to my attention in the *Indies* which are held for *Sanguis Draconis*, or *Dragon's Blood*. All three are in the form of dried blood and packed into a hard mass; also by my estimation all differing among themselves, and perhaps also from that which is sold in the *European* pharmacies with that name, and they are these: The first are pieces in large and small cakes. The second are small balls wrapped in dry leaves. The third is a mixed substance in the shape of a sugar-loaf or blunt cones. All three are made and known in the *East Indies* with the *Malay* name *Dierennang* or *Diernang*, of which I shall note as much as I have learned from the account of credible witnesses.

1. The first then is the common *Sanguis Draconis*, consisting of two kinds of cakes: namely, one in large round cakes, a thumb or two fingers thick, from half to a whole foot wide, though not smooth; black or dark brown on the outside, red-purple mixed with black on the inside, and shining, under which one sees some stubble or chips of wood. On coals it is fragrant, somewhat like *Benzoin*, but mostly like *Styrax*; therefore it is also called by some *Malays Cominjan Mera*, that is, Red Benzoin, although named abusively <note>meaning incorrectly or loosely</note>, for the right *Cominjan Mera* seems to be of the genus of Benzoin, pure and semi-transparent like dark amber, but redder; on coals it smells like *Dammar Selan*, and in no way dyes the paper.

The other kind consists of small and square cakes, five and six fingers long, one finger thick, crooked and bowed; outside also black-brown, inside high-purple, pure, and without admixture of any stubble, on coals also well-

### Book III. Chapter XLII. | AMBOINA HERBAL.

...chaff; when placed on hot coals, they also give off a pleasant scent, though it is different from the previously mentioned kind.

The second species of **Dragon's Blood**, which I consider to be the genuine and true kind, consists of small nodules the size of hazelnuts, wrapped in dry leaves and joined three or four together. Externally, they are a dark black or blackish color; internally, they are a reddish-purple, resembling smoked meat that has been recently cut. It is fine in substance, and when placed on coals, it emits a unique scent—a mixture of red Sandalwood and Cloves—which is entirely different from the previous types. From this, I conclude that both of those juices come from and are collected from different trees. I shall note here what I have learned from others regarding them, leaving the credibility of the report to those informants.

This first species—though I do not know if it is the large or small kind—is collected from a tree about which various reports are given. Some say the tree has the form of the *Pandang Boubou* or *Kekermoni* <note>original: "Pandang Boubou" and "Kekermoni" — local names for Pandanus-like plants</note>, but its leaves are shorter, smoother, and neither thorny nor equipped with a sharp spine, being smooth and even like the *Toxicaria* <note>Antiaris toxicaria, the Upas tree</note> tree. This tree produces no fruit, and its trunk is much thicker than that of the *Pinang* <note>Areca catechu, the Betel nut palm</note> tree, bearing a smooth bark. When wounded, it pours out a red juice or **Dragon's Blood**, which is collected in leaves and called *Djerenne* in Macassar. Others say it is collected from a large tree growing abundantly in Borneo, which they described to me as having leaves much larger than those of the Mango. It is a tall and wide-spreading tree; from its wounds, a liquid juice first drips, which then dries. When chewed, it is tough and tenacious like *Mastic* <term>Mastic: a resin obtained from the mastic tree, used as a chewing gum and medicine</term>, and it tints the saliva a red color.

The third species comes from a certain large reed called *Rottang* <note>original: "Rottang" — Rattan (climbing palms of the tribe Calameae)</note>, which I believe to be the genuine source, as was reported to me by eyewitnesses who have processed it. On the eastern coast of Sumatra, there is a species of large Rattan, similar to the one we have in Amboina, though here it either lacks such juice or it is not extracted due to ignorance. It is described later in *Book 7* and called *Palmyuncus Calapparius* or *Rottang Calappa*. This Rattan sends out long shoots as thick as an arm and bears fruit slightly larger than our *Rottang Calappa*. In its old age, it develops a soft pith or heart that is pulled out and preserved with the fruit; it is left for ten days and then boiled. From the upper part, the thinnest "cakes" are prepared, and from the lower part, the thickest ones are formed, such as those sold in shops. It grows from Aceh <note>original: "Atekina" / "Atchin"</note> all the way to Palembang.

Another species, called *Tsjukiet*, is collected from a smaller species of Rattan reed, which consists of short and numerous joints. It is as thick as a pinky finger and four or five fathoms <note>original: "ulnas" / "vades" — units of length approximately 6 feet</note> long, growing in Banjarmasin. It is prepared like the preceding kinds and sold in small nodules.

The fruits sent to me from Bantam <note>a historic trading port in Java</note> corresponded entirely with those of the large Rattan mentioned above in *Book 7*, except they were a tiny bit smaller.

->*Name.*<-

The general Latin name for these red and condensed juices is **Sanguis Draconis**, in Dutch *Drakenbloedt* <note>Dragon's Blood</note>. In Malay, they are called *Djerennang* and *Djernang*, though the correct spelling is *Gerennang*. In Macassarese, they are called *Djerenne* and *Djerne*.

The first genus with its two different species is called **Dragon's Blood in Cakes** <note>original: "in Placentis" / "in koeken"</note>. Among the Malays, it retains the same names. To the Chinese, it is specifically called *Hoy-Gjeck* or *Hoyg-jet*, which means **Blood Drop**.

The second species is called **Dragon's Blood in Drops** <note>original: "in Guttis"</note>, although something similar is sold under this name in our pharmacies that comes from the West Indies. I call it **Dragon's Blood** in large and small globules; in Macassar, these globules are sold the size of a *Nipis* Lemon <note>a small Indonesian lime</note>, while among the Malays, it is as stated above. To the Chinese, this species is known by the specific name *Tsjug-jeck*, that is, **Dragon's Blood**, as precious as gemstones.

->*Usage.*<-

**Dragon's Blood** in cakes is rarely used internally by these inhabitants, as we do in Europe against the spitting of blood <note>original: "Hæmoptoen"</note> and dysentery <note>original: "Dysenteriam" / "roodeloop"</note>. However, the inhabitants mix the large variety with *Dupa* <note>incense</note> or other fumigants like *Benzoin* <term>Benzoin: a balsamic resin from trees in the genus Styrax, used in perfumes and incense</term>. The Chinese use the finer species, both in cakes and drops, to polish wood.

2. The second sort of **Sanguis Draconis**, which I hold for pure and upright, are small balls the size of hazelnuts, bound between some dry leaves, hanging three or four together. Outside they are dark red or blackish, inside purple-red, or like freshly cut smoked meat, fine of substance. On coals, they have a special smell—namely, of red Sandalwood and cloves mixed together—markedly different from the preceding. Therefore, I judge that both these juices come from various trees, of which I shall set down here what has been given to me by others, leaving the responsibility for the report to the providers.

The first sort—but I know not whether it be the small or large—comes from a tree that is also variously described. Some say it is a tree of the same shape as the *Pandang Boubou* or *Kekermoni*, but the leaves are said to be shorter, smoother, not thorny, nor with a sharp ridge, but even, like those of the *Spatwortel* <note>likely referring to the Upas or a similar toxic tree</note>. It is without fruit, the trunk much thicker than a *Pinang* tree, with a smooth bark which, when injured, gives out the red juice or **Dragon's Blood**, which is gathered in leaves and called *Djerenne* on Macassar. Others say it comes from a large tree growing much on Borneo, which they described to me with larger leaves than those of the Mango, tall and wide-spreading, dripping from its wounds first as a soft juice, thereafter drying up, tough in chewing like *Mastic*, and staining the saliva red.

The other sort comes from a kind of large Rattan, which I hold for the most probable, which was also reported to me by eyewitnesses who have worked on it themselves. Namely, on Sumatra’s East Coast there is a kind of large Rattan, such as we also have in Amboina, though such juice either is not there or is not extracted through ignorance. It is described hereafter in *Book 7* under the name of *Palmyuncus Calapparius* or *Rottang Calappa*. This aforementioned Rattan is very long in its vine and an arm thick, bearing fruit somewhat larger than our *Rottang Calappa*. in its old age, it gains a soft pith that one can pull out, which is crushed with the fruit and left to stand for ten days, then it is boiled. From the top part, the finest cakes are made; from the bottom, the coarsest are made, as they are for sale in the shops. It grows from Aceh down to Palembang.

The second sort, *Tsjukiet*, comes from a kind of small Rattan, full of short joints, a pinky finger thick, four to five fathoms long, growing on Banjarmasin. It is made like the preceding and is sold in small balls.

The fruits from Bantam sent to me agreed entirely with those of the aforementioned large Rattan, which can be seen hereafter in *Book 7*, except that they were a tiny bit smaller.

->*Name.*<-

The general name for these red and clotted juices is in Latin **Sanguis Draconis**, in Dutch **Draken-bloet**. In Malay *Djerennang* and *Djernang*, though the correct writing is *Gerennang*; on Macassar *Djerenne* and *Djerne*.

The first genus with its two sub-species is called **Sanguis Draconis in Placentis**, that is, **Dragon’s Blood in cakes**, with the Malays retaining the aforementioned names. By the Chinese, it is called in particular *Hoy-Gjeck* or *Hoy-Gjet*, that is, **blood's drop**.

The second genus is called **Sanguis Draconis in Guttis**, although something is also sold by that name in our pharmacies which comes from the West. I call it **Dragon’s Blood** in large and small balls, for on Macassar one has balls of it the size of a *Nipis* Lime, and among the Malays as above. By the Chinese, this is called in particular *Tsjug-Jek*, that is, **Dragon’s Blood**, as precious as gemstones.
