-> ### THE AMBOINA HERBAL Book III. Chapter XLII. <-

...wood should be rubbed with it until it grows warm and takes on a red color, as if coated in varnish, resulting in an intense red or nearly black hue.

The Chinese also know how to rub paper with these granules until it acquires a crimson or elegant red color, which is in daily use among them.

If crushed in oil or water, it yields an elegant red pigment, and thus it is much used in scented oils to give them a beautiful red color. The people of Macassar smear the dry and smooth leaves of the **Licuala** <note>A genus of fan palms; the leaves were used as wrappers</note> with this juice, then dry them over an inverted and heated pot so the pigment adheres better to the leaves; these are then used for tobacco rollers <note>likely cheroots or early cigar wrappers</note>, as they display an elegant and intense purple color on the outside. They tint paper in the same manner. It is not much used, however, for wood pigment, as it is too expensive and is counted among the precious wares in Japan. This Dragon's Blood, crushed into a powder with a knife, is sprinkled on fresh wounds like the preceding kind to stop bleeding and heal the wound.

From this, one should doubtless understand that fable occurring in the new *Notes on the East and West Indies* by *Simon de Vries* <note>A 17th-century Dutch author known for compiling travel accounts</note>, who writes in the first part of that book that a precious oil is pressed from the fruits of the Rattan <note>original: "Rottangae" — climbing palms of the genus Calamus</note> (not distinguishing from which species) in the East Indies, which cures all wounds, and especially those inflicted by a blow from a rattan stick. He says that this is a daily exercise in all households in India where slaves are kept.

A third species of Dragon's Blood occurs formed into large pieces like sugar-loaves, though smaller; these consist of a mixed substance composed of ordinary Dragon's Blood and rhinoceros blood, with many dry leaves and chaff mixed in. It is rarely found and is of a brighter red color than ordinary Dragon's Blood, as well as being more brittle. It is identified by placing it on coals: it first gives off a pleasant odor and then a stench of burnt blood; it is also called **Hoygjeck** by the Chinese. I believe this species is prepared in Java, and each such piece weighs two pounds or more, costing one real there, but ten such coins in China. It is pounded into powder and mixed with water or oil to dye them red. This same powder, sprinkled on fresh wounds, heals them. Chinese physicians also use it internally, mixed with other simples <note>natural medicinal ingredients</note>, against asthma and a long-standing cough from which consumption <term>phthisis: a historical term for a wasting disease, usually pulmonary tuberculosis</term> arises, called **Lui-Seang** by them. In cases of desperate and advanced dysentery, take equal parts of this last species of dragon's blood, **Madjacaan** <note>Gall-nuts, used for their high tannin content</note>, and old **Pinanga** <note>Areca or Betel nut</note>; let the latter two be toasted over a fire until they can be reduced to powder like the first ingredient; take a spoonful of this compound powder daily, mixed with rice water.

Other Chinese also divide Dragon's Blood into three species, the first and best of which is called **Tsjuckiet**. This is the second species mentioned above, collected in small globules, which they say is a gum exuding from a species of Rattan, growing mostly in Banjarmasin <note>original: "Banjar Maſſingh" — a major trading port in South Kalimantan, Borneo</note>.

The second species is *Common Dragon's Blood*, formed into cakes like a small dish, called by the specific name **Hoygjeck** or **Hoygjet**.

The third and cheapest is **Tsjaukiet**, which is foul or impure, blackish, and mixed with wood and chaff. They say both of these last species come from a large tree growing in Sumatra, which are brought for sale mostly in Palembang. However, they do not count that third species among the others, as it is a manufactured item, which they call **Hoygjec**.

There are some who, besides the species already mentioned, also refer many other condensed juices to Dragon's Blood, as we hinted above in the chapter on *Lingoum*. Thus *Herbert de Jager* <note>A Dutch Orientalist and botanist in the service of the VOC</note> writes to me in certain letters that from the tree of Caliatour wood, from which he says red Sandalwood is collected (as seen in Book 2), Dragon's Blood is likewise gathered. However, since these and other red juices differ too much from the common Dragon's Blood used here in the Indies, I deem it useless to describe them further, especially since

<column-break/>

*The Chinese use it to rub smooth-shaved woodwork until it becomes warm, giving it a red color as if it were lacquered, a deep red and blackish.*

*The Chinese also know how to rub paper with the little balls so that it becomes crimson or a beautiful deep red, which is in daily use among them.*

*Rubbed in oil or water, it gives off a beautiful red dye; therefore it is also much used with scented oils to give them a pleasant redness. The Macassarese use it to smear dried and smooth leaves of **Licuala**, which they then hold over an inverted and heated pot until the dye clings properly to the leaves; they afterwards use these for cheroots—that is, tobacco rolls—because they are a beautiful deep purple on the outside. In the same way, they can dye paper. It is, however, not much used for dyeing wood because it is too expensive and is a major trade item in Japan. Rubbed to a powder with a knife, it is sprinkled into fresh wounds, like the former kind, to staunch the blood and heal.*

*From this, one must undoubtedly understand that droll story found in the so-called new medley of "East and West Indian Notes" by Simon de Vries, who states in his first part that in the East Indies a precious oil is pressed from Rattan fruits (without saying of what sort), with which one heals all kinds of wounds, especially those made by being beaten with a Rattan, which he says is a daily practice in the Indies in all households where one has slaves.*

*The third sort of Dragon's Blood comes formed in large pieces like sugar-loaves, though smaller, and it is a mixed substance of the juice of common Dragon's Blood mixed with rhinoceros blood, among which many dry leaves and stalks run; it is rarely found, lighter-red in color than the common Dragon's Blood, also more crumbly, and its test is that when laid on coals, it first smells somewhat pleasant, then stinks like burnt blood; it is also called **Hoygjeck** by the Chinese. I thought it was made on Java, an entire piece weighing two pounds or more, and costing a real there, but in China as much as ten; it is pounded to powder and mixed in water or oil, which also dyes red. The same sprinkled on fresh wounds heals them. The Chinese physicians also have it in use to give internally, among other medicinal ingredients, against panting and an old cough from which consumption comes, called **Lui Séang** by them. In an old and desperate bloody flux <note>dysentery</note>, take of this last Dragon's Blood, **Madjacaan** or Gall-nuts, and old **Pinang**, of each an equal amount. Roast the last two over the fire until they can be brought to powder, like the first; take of this daily a spoonful with congee or rice water.*

*Other Chinese divide the Dragon's Blood also into three sorts; the first and best is **Tsjuckiet**, being the aforementioned second sort consisting of globules, which they also say is a gum sweating out of a kind of Rattan, and occurs mostly at Banjarmasin.*

*The second sort is the common Dragon's Blood formed into cakes like a saucer or small dish, properly called **Hoygjeck** or **Hoygjet**.*

*The third and poorest is **Tsjaukiet**, dirty, black, with wood and stalks; both these last sorts they say come from a large tree growing on Sumatra, and are mostly brought to Palembang for sale. But the aforementioned third sort they reckon less there, because it is a manufactured thing, and they also call it **Hoygjec**.*

-> ### Book III. Chapter XLII. THE AMBOINA HERBAL. <-

...since I am averse to that custom by which they bring together entirely different things that somewhat agree in color and flavor under the same genus and impose the same name—which is the quickest way to confuse everything, and which is contrary to the philosophers' rule and the proverb: *he who distinguishes well, indeed teaches well.* <note>Original Latin: "qui bene nempe distinguit, bene docet"</note>

These are the things I wished to comment on for the readers regarding *Dragon's Blood* <note>A bright red resin obtained from different species of several distinct plant genera: Croton, Dracaena, Daemonorops, Calamus, and Pterocarpus</note>, for which the opportunity was provided by those things I mentioned above: namely, that certain plants or trees are found here in Amboina which have a certain similarity with the *Dragon Tree*, such as those occurring and described below in Book 6, Chapter 40 under the name *Terminalis*, and in Book 7, Chapter 50 under the title *Palmyunci*.

## OBSERVATION.

It is clear from *Rumphius's* notes that *Dragon's Blood* is collected from various plants and trees. However, the kind prepared from a species of reed is that which is called *Indian Stuffed Reed* <note>Original Latin: "Arundo farcta Indica"</note> in the pharmacies by *Samuel Dale, Pharmacologist*, in 4to, page 29; it is also the *Stuffed Reed of the East Indies yielding Dragon’s Blood* in *Morison's Oxford History, volume 3, page 220, and Ray’s History, volume 3, page 615*. Concerning this, I found notes stating that the method of collecting this red material is to soak the fruits in hot water until that red matter settles at the bottom of the vessel. Then, after the water is either evaporated or poured off, the thickened juice is collected from the bottom of the vessel, from which a varnish is composed that the Chinese use to coat chests and boxes.

Next, there is a Palm with leaves and a trunk armed everywhere with long, very sharp black spines, called *Djerenang* <note>Likely Daemonorops draco</note> by *Dr. Sherard*, which means *Dragon’s Blood* obtained from the fruits of the spiny cone-bearing Palm, as described in *Kaempfer’s Exotic Pleasures, page 552*. This is the second type of Palm yielding Dragon’s Blood in *S. Dale’s Pharmacology, 4to, page 297*, where he writes that the juice is collected primarily from three species of this Palm, which are also listed by *Pomet in his History of Simples*.

There is also another Palm yielding *Dragon’s Blood* proposed and described by *J. Commelin in the Amsterdam Garden*, part 1, page 261, which is called the *Dragon Tree* by *Sam. Dale, page 297*, and is further presented there with cited authors and its medical use, where the rest may be seen.

The *Reed* itself, from which this *Dragon's Blood* is collected according to *Rumphius*, occurs in *Valentyn’s Description of Amboina, page 218*, and is shown in the Table under **No. XLIX**. Regarding Dragon's Blood and its types, as well as the artificial kind, see further *Valentyn’s History of Simples, reformed, from page 265 to 269*, and the second Letter, page 385; and in the same place, page 609 and following, the dissertation of *Joh. Ochsu* on Dragon's Blood, and *Ray’s Appendix, volume 3, page 65*.

## WHOLESOME MILK-TREE: or UPAS LAKI-LAKI is described in *Rumphius's* following Appendix in this manner, which *Rumphius* wishes to substitute in place of the preceding one; therefore, we add it here.

This tree has such a great similarity with the *Milk-Tree* <note>Original: "Arbore Lactaria"</note> described above that many inhabitants of these regions consider this one and that one to be one and the same, and all the more so since this one is rarely encountered. I wished to deviate from the common path and called it the *Wholesome Milk-Tree* <note>Original: "Lactaria salubris"</note>, which first became known to me through the *Corre Corre* expedition <note>A "Kora-kora" was a traditional large rowing vessel used in the Maluku Islands for trade and warfare</note> in the year 1693. It has the form of the *Milk-Tree* or *Wild Mango* <note>Original: "Mangae Bravae"</note>, since it bears a short and thick trunk, covered with smooth bark, variegated with green and grey.

The leaves are placed in pairs opposite each other, but at the very end of the branches, four are placed together. They are similar to those of the *Bintangor* <note>A tree of the genus Calophyllum</note>, but a little wider, thicker, and more wrinkled—seven, eight, and ten inches long, and two transverse fingers wide. At the top, they are rounded and slightly split; underneath, they bear many fine ribs, but not as closely joined as in the *Bintangor* leaves, of which the lower ones are parallel, while the upper ones run in a wavy pattern, and all end in wavy borders. The leaf itself is slightly bent downwards like a small dish or boat, and is bulging and smooth on top.

to describe more broadly, the more so because I have an aversion to that manner of bringing various things, which somewhat resemble each other in color and taste, under one genus and name, which is contrary to the rule of the Philosophers: namely, "he who distinguishes well, teaches well."

> *This is that which the reader will please take kindly, which I can report concerning Dragon's Blood, the occasion having been given to me to mention something of it because, as said above, I have found some plants here in Amboina that have some agreement with the Dragon-tree, and which will be described hereafter in book 6, chapter 40, under the Title of* Terminalis, *and in book 7, chapter 50, under* Palmyuncus.

## REMARK.

That *Dragon's Blood* is gathered from various plants and trees is evident from the notes of *Rumphius*. However, that which is gathered from a kind of reed is that species which is named *Indian Stuffed Reed* by *Sam. Dale in his Pharmacology in 4to, page 29*, and is the *East Indian Stuffed Reed yielding Dragon’s Blood* from *Morison in his History of Oxford, volume 3, page 220, and from Ray in his History, volume 3, page 615*. Concerning this, I find noted that the manner of gathering this red substance is that they let the fruit soak in warm water until the red matter falls from it to the bottom of the vessel, from which the water being poured off or evaporated, the same is gathered at the bottom of the vessel. From its thickened juice, a varnish is made with which boxes and chests are varnished by the Chinese.

Secondly, the *Palm tree* with leaves and its trunk everywhere pricking, named *Djerenang* by *Sherard*—that is, *Dragon’s Blood*—also comes from the fruits of a thorny *Palm tree* described by *Kaempfer in his Exotic Pleasures, page 552*. This is the *second Palm tree that gives Dragon’s Blood* from *Dale in his Pharmacology, page 297*, where he says that from three kinds of Palm tree such a fruit is gathered, which are also mentioned by *Pomet in his History of Drugs*.

There is yet another Palm tree giving Dragon’s Blood described by *Joh. Commelin in the first part of the Amsterdam Garden, page 261*, which is named *Dragon Tree* by *Sam. Dale* on page 297, and is further presented with the cited writers and its use, where the remainder can be looked up.

The *reed* from which, according to *Rumphius*, the Dragon's Blood is gathered, also appears in *Valentyn under the name of Dragon’s Blood Rattan on page 218*, and is represented in the plate **No. XLIX.** Concerning Dragon’s Blood and its kinds, as well as the imitation, see further *Valentyn in his Reformed History of Simples from page 265 to page 269, and the second letter, page 385*; and there, the dissertation on Dragon’s Blood by *Joh. Ochsu on page 609 and the following. See also the Appendix of Ray in the third volume on page 65.*

*With the above-mentioned* Milk-Tree, *this tree has such similarity that many Inlanders regard it as one and the same, the more so as it is rarely to be found. I have wanted to follow the common custom and named it* Wholesome Milk-tree, *it having first come to my knowledge through the* Kora-kora *expedition in the year 1693. It is of the same form as the* Milk-Tree, *or* Wild Mango, *namely short and thick of trunk, with smooth bark, also somewhat spotted with white and green.*

*The leaves stand two and two against each other, though at the end of the twigs four are together, and they resemble those of the* Bintangor, *though somewhat broader, thicker, and stiffer—7, 8, and 10 inches long, 5 transverse fingers wide, round at the front or a little split; from underneath they have many subtle ribs, not as dense as on the* Bintangor *leaf, of which the rear ones run parallel, but the front ones run somewhat curved, and all end in a hem along the edges. The leaf is somewhat bent downwards like a saucer or little boat, bulging and smooth on top.*

### THE AMBOINA HERBAL Book III. Chapter XLII.

The flowers come forth in a branched cluster, much like those of the **Wild Mango** <note>original: *Manga Brava*</note>, though these flowers more closely resemble **Jasmine** <note>original: *Jasminum*</note>. Five white, extended petals, bent backwards, are positioned on a long stalk; they are concave in the middle, limp, and have an unpleasant smell. These petals sit upon a small three-petaled calyx. In each cluster, only four or five fruits reach maturity, having the shape of the **Ambarella** <note>original: *Condondong*</note>, or like those of the **Wild Mango**. They usually lie closely in pairs, sitting on short and barely distinguishable stalks that do not pierce the fruit in the center but rather obliquely; the upper part consists of a hard and blunt tip. Externally they are green in color, turning yellow when ripe like a **Mango**, and finally becoming wrinkled and a reddish-black. Beneath the thick and wrinkled outer skin lies a husk that can be pulled apart lengthwise into thick fibers, much like the fruit of the **Wild Mango**. Each fruit is furrowed through the middle, yet it cannot be pulled apart by force, but must be split with a knife called a **parrang** <note>original: *Parrangh*; a large Indonesian cleaver or machete</note>. Inside, two flat kernels lie against each other, almost like two tongues, which are hollowed out below where they were joined to the stalk. These kernels consist of a hard, brown, and thin skin-like shell, in which a flat nut is hidden, almost horn-like and tough like leather, which has the flavor of hazelnuts. In the two rounded chambers that lie against these "tongues" on either side, nothing is found but those aforementioned thick fibers. From every part of the trunk and branches where they are cut, or where a leaf is broken off—even from the midrib of the leaf itself—there drips a certain whitish milk, tenacious and sticky, which dries up immediately.

It is said that in other places trunks have been observed that two men could scarcely embrace <note>meaning the circumference was two arm-spans wide</note>, and in certain fruits, often only one kernel is found and only a single "tongue" is described.

The root is the medicine sought from this tree. Externally it is a dark yellow and consists of many small fibers; internally the wood is a pale yellow color and woody, such that it resembles the **Anti-cholera wood** <note>original: *Anticholerica*</note> or **Upas Bidji** <note>likely *Strychnos colubrina*</note>. If it is fresh, it is so hard that axes and larger knives or **parrangs** grow dull if it is struck; however, it shatters easily into splinters like glass. Its flavor agrees entirely with the **Anti-cholera wood**, having a bean-like bitterness, but it is not nearly as bitter as the **King of Bitterness** <note>original: *Rex Amaroris*</note>.

**Name.** In Latin it is called *Lactaria Salubris* <note>Wholesome Milk-tree</note>, since I see that almost all the inhabitants consider this a species of the **Milk-tree** or **Wild Mango**; I have named it "wholesome" to defend and free it from the noxious qualities that the true **Milk-tree** <note>Lactaria</note> possesses. Otherwise, in Malay it is called *Upas Lacki Lacki* <note>Male Poison</note>, as it is considered the male of the one called **King of Bitterness**; it is distinguished from another species of *Upas Lacki Lacki* which will be described later under the name **Lani**. In Leytimor it is called *Wabbo Meyt* <note>Shore-manga</note>, because it grows nowhere but on the shore, whereas the *Wabbo* or **Wild Mango** also grows in the inland regions. The people of Alang call it *Lou Lite*, that is, a leaf mimicking the **Lite** or **Poete** tree. Those of Hoeamohel name it *Nantahule*.

**Location.** This tree was first found, as was said, in the year 1693 <note>The Dutch column lists 1623, likely an OCR or printing error for 1693</note> on the western side of Ceram near the village of **Tamilau**, and then upon further investigation, it was also found on the western shore of Leytimor at **Alang**, and at **Toelehoe**, **Boero**, and **Manipa**. But it is rare everywhere, with only a single tree found here and there in purely sandy shore soil, and sometimes near cliffs. It remained unknown for so long because it could hardly be distinguished from the **Wild Mango** in its leaves and fruit.

**Use.** It is used primarily against the same ailments for which the **Anti-cholera wood** is employed, namely against stomach cramps and pains, as well as against poisonous fish and crabs if they have been eaten; for this reason, they carry its roots with them on sea voyages.

The people of Hoeamohel, who are thought to have the most expert knowledge of this tree's virtues, use it first against convulsions and epilepsy; they call the inner leaflets of the fruit into use with a small amount of crushed root, pouring it drop by drop into the mouth and smearing the thick part on the nape of the neck. Second, against *Rofton*, or cancer of the nose: take the kernel of the fruit for this purpose, grind it with water, pour the thinnest part into the nose, and smear the thicker part on the outside. Third, against *Upas* <note>here referring to pleurisy or localized poison</note> or pleurisy: grind the kernel or the roo-

<column-break/>

The blossoms come forth on a branched cluster, also similar to the **Wild Mango** <note>original: *Manga Brava*</note>, yet these flowers look more like **Jasmines**, for on a long-stalked little stem stand 5 white extended petals bent backwards, bulbous in the middle, limp, and unpleasant of smell, made on a base of 3 points. On each cluster come only 4 to 5 fruits, which reach the perfect shape of an **Ambarella** <note>original: *Condondong*</note>, or like those of the **Wild Mango**. They usually sit two tightly against each other on short and barely recognizable stalks, which are let in not straight behind but somewhat to the side, ending in front with a hard, blunt point. They are green on the outside, and yellow when ripe, like a **Mango**; the ripe ones become full of wrinkles, colored with a mixture of russet and black. Under the outermost skin lies a coarse-threaded and thick husk, which allows itself to be split lengthwise into coarse threads, just like the fruit of the **Wild Mango**. Each fruit has a cleft in the middle, yet does not allow itself to be pulled apart with force, but must be chopped apart with a **parrang**. Inside one finds two flat grains lying against each other like two tongues, with a notched corner at the back where they were attached to a knob of the stalk; these tongues are made of a hard, brown, yet thin skin, and inside one finds a flat kernel, horn-colored, tough as leather, with the taste of hazelnuts. In the two bulges that lie on either side against the tongue, one finds nothing but the aforementioned coarse threads. Everywhere that one cuts into the trunk or branches, or breaks off a leaf—even from the wounded mid-vein—a white milk runs out, very sticky and stiff, and it dries up immediately.

It is said that in other places the trunk has been seen to be two fathoms in circumference, and in some fruits one also finds only one kernel and one tongue.

The root is the medicinal part that is taken from this tree, dark yellow on the outside and hung with many small fibers, with a pale yellow wood inside, so that they do not look unlike those of the **Anti-cholera wood** <note>original: *Anticholerica*</note> or **Upas Bidji**. The wood is so hard in the chopping that it makes axes and **parrangs** blunt; however, it breaks off as short as glass. The taste corresponds exactly with the **Anti-cholera wood**, namely, with a bean-like bitterness, though by no means as bitter as the **King of Bitterness** <note>original: *Rex Amaroris*</note>.

**Name.** In Latin *Lactaria Salubris*, because I see that almost all the natives hold it to be a species of Milk-tree or **Wild Mango**, I have named it "healthy" or "medicinal" to free it from the evil qualities which the true Milk-tree has. Otherwise, it is called in Malay *Upas Lacki Lacki*, because it is held to be the male of the **King of Bitterness**; but it is distinguished from another species of *Upas Lacki Lacki* to be described hereafter under the name **Lani**. On Leytimor they call it *Wabbo Meyt*, because it occurs nowhere but on the shore, whereas the *Wabbo* or **Wild Mango** also grows landward. But those of Alang call it *Lou Lite*, that is, a leaf that resembles the **Lite** or **Poete**. Those of Hoeamohel call it *Nantahule*.

**Place.** It was, as said, first found in the year 1623 <note>Likely error for 1693</note> on the south side of Ceram, around the village of **Tamilau**, and upon closer investigation it was also found on Leytimor’s southern shore, **Alang**, and **Toëlehoe**, **Boero**, and **Manipa**, though everywhere in small numbers, and here and there a single tree on a pure sandy beach, and sometimes also by cliffs. It remained unknown for so long because it can hardly be distinguished from the **Wild Mango** in its leaves and fruits.

**Use.** It is mostly used against the same ailments as the **Anti-cholera wood**, namely, stomach pain, cramps, and if someone feels ill from harmful fish and crabs; therefore they carry these roots with them on sea voyages.

Those of Hoeamohel, who are thought to have the best knowledge of this tree, use it: 1. against convulsions and epilepsy, taking the innermost leaflets of the fruit with a little rubbed root, pouring such with drops into the mouth, and smearing the thick part on the back of the neck. 2. Against *Rofton* or cancer of the nose: take the kernel of the fruit, rub it with water, put the thinnest part in the nose, and smear the thickest part on top. 3. Against the *Upas* <note>poison/pleurisy</note>: rub the kernel or the root, smear it on the chest, and also give it to drink with a

# CHAPTER FORTY-THREE.
## The King’s Tree. *Caju Radja.*

Although this is not a milk-bearing tree, I wished to place it here because, in place of a heart or <term>pith<gloss>the soft, spongy tissue in the center of a stem</gloss></term>, it carries a living creature that, if it touches a person's skin, brings a sharper pain than the sap of all the preceding trees.
It does not possess a very thick trunk, but it is quite tall, straight, and smooth, ending in a few thicker branches. The leaves approach those of the **Sea Hibiscus** <note>original: *Daun Baroe*; *Hibiscus tiliaceus*</note>; they are heart-shaped but much larger, not furrowed, tapering from a rounded base to a point, and have smooth edges. They are over a foot long and slightly less in width, pale, not showing an elegant green color, and are a little woolly to the touch.
Each leaf sits upon a long, firm <term>petiole<gloss>the stalk that joins a leaf to a stem</gloss></term>, which is attached to the underside of the leaf—making it a <term>peltate<gloss>shield-shaped</gloss></term> leaf. From this point of attachment, ten nerves run throughout the leaf in all directions, and near the origin of the leaf on that stalk, two green warts grow out.
The flowers appear in large, extended, and irregular clusters; they are white, mossy, and crowded closely together, similar to the flowers of the **Stinging Leaf** <note>original: *Folium ardens*</note>. Most of them fall off without leaving any fruit, as the flowers of this tree are rarely observed.
The fruits hang from a long and mostly bare stalk, which at the top is divided into other short and very small curved stems. Upon these sit berries similar to black cherries but smaller; they are <term>umbilicate<gloss>having a small depression or navel at the tip</gloss></term>, soft, whitish, and somewhat wrinkled, containing two or three small pits resembling hemp seed, which are mostly hollow inside.
The trunk and all the thick branches consist of no heartwood, but are hollowed out, and in its place are filled with many large and blackish ants. These ants pierce the trunk in one place or another, forming "windows" as it were, and they travel through it to the very tips of the branches like a hollow wall. Thus, this tree draws its nourishment solely from its bark. The thinner branches, however, do contain a pith, like that of the **Elder tree** <note>original: *Sambucus*</note>.
If any branch is cut off, these ants rush out with great force and speed, immediately attacking and biting the bystanders with such intensity that it is very dangerous to approach this tree; indeed, the whole ground around it is filled with these fierce creatures, which even infest the feet of those coming near.
I have observed, however, that the Indians do not feel these bites as much through their tough skin as we do, and therefore they approach that tree without fear.
The bark of the tree is ash-gray on the outside, smooth, and juicy; if it is cut, it turns a reddish color when dry. The wood consists of longitudinal fibers and is as light as any **Sago-stalk** <note>original: *Gabba Gabba*; the dried midribs of sago palm fronds used for light construction</note>, yet it is flexible and does not break easily as long as it is kept from moisture.
In the forests, one can quickly discover where this tree is located, as its surroundings are always more open to the air; for it allows no other trees to stand within several fathoms of itself, nor even certain plants beneath it. From this it earned its name, since with a sort of monarchal authority it claims the place for itself alone, though otherwise the tree shows no beauty or royal majesty. Wherefore the wisdom of the Supreme Being, which excels in all the handiwork of nature, is again to be praised...

<column-break/>

a little **Rice-Ginger** <note>original: *Allea Pady*</note>. 4. Against **lumbago** <note>original: *Loeffoe*</note> or pain in the loins, against colic, and side-stiches, use the root and kernel with **Rice-Ginger**, as above, and smear it on the painful limbs. 5. Against burning fevers, rub it without the ginger, give it first for two days to drink, and then smear it on the body from the outside.

# XLIII. CHAPTER:
## King’s Tree.

This is indeed no milk-tree, yet I have wished to place it here because in place of the heartwood it has a living creature, which, coming upon the skin, plagues a person more wickedly than all the preceding milk-trees.
It is not very thick of trunk, yet reasonably high, straight, and smooth, divided into few thick branches. The leaves resemble somewhat those of the **Sea Hibiscus** <note>original: *Daun Baroe*</note>, or a heart, yet much larger, without notches, tapering from the round, unserrated at the edges, a foot long or more, and a bit less wide, pale or an ugly green, and somewhat woolly to the touch. Each leaf stands on a long stiff stalk, which is attached underneath, and from where ten veins spread themselves around through the leaf; and by the origin of the leaf on the stalk one sees two green warts.
The blossom comes forth in extended and irregular clusters, white, mossy, and crowded close together, resembling the blossom of the **Stinging Leaf** <note>original: *Folium ardens*</note>, and falls off mostly without fruit, as one also seldom sees the tree bloom.
The fruits hang on a long, mostly bare stalk, which divides at the top into a few other small and curved stalks; on these stand berries like cherries, but smaller, with a navel on top, soft, whitish, and somewhat wrinkled, containing inside three to four grains, like **Hemp-seed**, mostly hollow inside.
The trunk and all the thick branches have no heartwood, but are hollow, and in place of that, swarming with large and black ants, which pierce the trunk here or there and make little windows, wandering through the same to the outermost branches, like a hollow wall, so that this tree lives only through the bark; but the thin branches have a pith, like elder.
When one now chops off any branches, these ants run out with great violence and quickness, immediately attacking and biting the bystanders with such power that it is very worrisome to go near this tree, the ground also being occupied by these grim little animals, which immediately come at the feet of those approaching.
Although I have noticed that the Indians with their bare skin do not feel these bites as much as we do, and therefore go more fearlessly near it.
The bark is light gray on the outside, smooth, juicy; if one cuts into it, it turns reddish. The wood is long-fibered and as light as any **Sago-stalk** <note>original: *Gabba Gabba*</note> may be, yet flexible, and not easily breaking, so long as it is kept from moisture.
One can clearly notice in the woods where this tree stands, as the place thereabout is always lighter, for it suffers neither next to nor under itself any other large trees for several fathoms around, yes, hardly any small brushwood, which dare not touch its body; and from this it has received the name, because with a monarchal authority it wants to keep a place for itself alone, being otherwise nothing beautiful nor kingly in the whole tree: Wherefrom once again...

...comes, and which usually suggests a certain character <note>original: "characterem quendam"</note> to all harmful trees, by which they can be recognized from a distance, whether by their separate and remote location, or by an irregular shape, smell, or similar traits.

**Season.** It brings forth flowers near the end of the dry months, and fruit indeed in the month of May. It occurs on the shore among light and low forests as well as in the mountains and higher forests, where among the dense trees a certain empty space suddenly offers itself, as can be most elegantly observed, among other places, on the great public road that runs through the forested Hitoe mountains.

**Name.** In Latin, *Arbor Regis* <note>The King's Tree</note>. In Malay, *Caju Radja* and *Caju Sommot*, which means "ant wood." In Amboinese, *Aylatu*. In Buru, *Aymiri* and *Amiri*. In Ternate, *Affo* and *Bisi-Mafalla*.

**Location.** It grows in the Amboinese and Moluccan islands, but not in great abundance. Whether it is found in other places I do not yet know, for *Caju Radja* is to certain Malays and Macassarese the *Cassia Fistula* <note>The Golden Shower tree, often used as a laxative</note>.

**Usage.** The wood of the younger trunks, which are no more than a foot thick, is much used in place of cork for floating devices <note>original: "machinis supernatantibus"</note> tied to fishing nets, which the Malays call *Plompen*, since these woods are naturally perforated and light. Some also fashion small masts from these trunks for the smaller vessels called *Orangbaeyen* and the like, as they are light and sturdy; however, the upper part of these masts must be covered so they do not rot or decay from falling rain. If the Amboinese wish to approach this tree, they clear away all the surrounding weeds, then place certain dry leaves <note>likely *Atap* or palm thatch</note> near the tree and set them on fire to drive away the ants. Once the tree is swiftly felled, the flame must be pressed until almost all the ants have been put to flight and driven out of this hollow tree. The Indians <note>The native inhabitants of the archipelago</note>, however, as was mentioned, often omit this, as their skin is not so sensitive.

**Dangerous & Harmful** as this tree is, it nonetheless has much use in medicine; for its bark, ground in a small dose and drunk with water, or taken as a decoction, purges the intestines from below of many watery and corrupt humors. Its leaves, heated and bound to the abdomen, soften a hardened spleen, called *Tebatu*, and resolve its swelling, provided that its decoction is simultaneously used internally.

**In the year 1667,** when we were waging a heavy war against the Macassarese, a certain Macassarese woman who had been captured revealed the powers of this tree as a great secret to her master, the Governor of Manipa <note>This refers to Captain Jonker, a famous native commander in the Dutch service</note>. She praised it against the horrible Macassarese poison which they extract from the *Toxicaria* tree <note>The Upas tree, used for poison arrows</note> and with which they soak their weapons. This leader of the Indians, a strenuous and brave soldier, explored its virtues and communicated the proven results to me. Namely, the thin roots of this tree are chosen, a piece of which the wounded person chews; half of this must be swallowed, and the other part placed upon the wound to draw out the poison. Truly, from where that Macassarese woman learned this, I do not know, since this tree is unknown to most Macassarese; yet it may be true that this tree is found in one or another place in that region, though it is certain it grows sparingly there. The same woman also added that Macassarese soldiers going to war carry this root in their belts, and that it is also effective against every kind of poison offered to someone in *Pinanga* <note>Betel nut</note>. Shavings of the bark, slightly warmed in its own leaf or a banana leaf and rubbed on the back, drive away painful stabbings perhaps arising from a "false pleurisy."

**Its younger leaves,** cooked as a vegetable and eaten with their juice, cause two or three bowel movements.

**Its wood,** which is light like *Gabba Gabba* <note>The dried midribs of Sago palm leaves</note>, is boiled in water with an equal quantity of the Chinese medicinal wood *Coyoe Tsjina* <note>original: *Cajoe Tsjina*; China root</note> and drunk to cure all malignant ulcerations. This decoction expels all malignant and corrupt humors from the body and softens swollen and hardened bellies, but it does not purge.

**Its green bark,** scraped upward and boiled in water with the bark of the female *Sideroxylum* <note>Ironwood</note> and a handful of *Cadjang* <note>likely Mung beans or similar legumes</note>, serves as a fomentation for edematous <note>swollen</note> feet, which it cures,

*the Creator’s wisdom showing itself in nature is to be praised, which usually has set a mark upon all harmful trees so that one can know them from afar, whether by their isolated place, strange shape, smell, or the like.*

**Season.** *It blooms in the latter part of the dry monsoon, and the fruits are found in May. One finds it on the beach among the low and airy brushwood, as well as in the mountains and high forests, where one will suddenly find a light spot among the thick trees, as one can see very exceptionally, among other places, along the great overland road that goes over the forested mountains of Hitoe.*

**Name.** *In Latin,* Arbor Regis. *In Malay,* Caju Radja *and* Caju Sommot, *that is, ant-wood. On Amboina,* Aylatu. *On Buru,* Aymiri *and* Amiri. *On Ternate,* Affo *and* Bisi-mafalla.

**Location.** *It occurs in the Amboinese and Moluccan Islands, and that in no great number; whether it occurs in other places as well, I have not yet experienced, for* Caju Radja *is, among the Macassarese and some Malays, the* Cassia Fistula.

**Usage.** *The wood of the young trunks, which are not thicker than a leg, is much used to make floats or corks, which are tied to the tops of nets. They are called* Plompen *by the Malays because these woods are naturally hollowed out and light. Some also make small masts from these trunks for* Orangbayen <note>A type of plank-built vessel or war canoe</note> *and similar small craft, because they are light and stiff; but one must cover them at the top with something to protect them from soaking in rainwater. When the Amboinese want to go to this tree, they first briefly chop away all the surrounding weeds, then they lay dry* Atap <note>Thatch made from palm leaves</note> *around the tree and set it on fire to drive the ants away somewhat. The tree having been chopped down with speed, one must still keep a fire burning until most of the ants have departed from the hollow tree. However, the Indians, as said, being not so sensitive in their skin, mostly leave this undone.*

**This wicked growth** *nonetheless has much use again in medicine, for the bark, rubbed in small quantities and drunk with water, or the decoction thereof used, cleanses the intestines from below of many watery and spoiled humors. The leaves, made warm and tied upon the belly, make the swollen spleen shrink and the swelling disappear, to be sure, if one also uses the aforementioned decoction internally.*

**Anno 1667.** *When we were conducting the heavy war against the Macassarese, a certain Macassarese captive woman revealed to her master, Captain Jonker of Manipa, as a great secret, the powers of this tree against the terrible Macassarese dart-poison <note>original: "spatten-gift"</note>. This Indian Captain, being a bold warrior and declaring that he had tested such things, communicated the same to me. Namely, one takes the thin roots of this tree and lets the poisoned person chew a piece thereof in the mouth, of which he must swallow half and lay the rest on the wound to pull out the venom. From where the aforementioned Macassarese woman has this, I cannot know, since this tree is unknown to most Macassarese, although it may nonetheless be that it is found here or there in their land, though found but little. Indeed, the same woman added to this that the Macassarese soldiers going to war carry this root with them in their belts, and that the same roots also served against all poisonings that one might do to someone in the Pinang <note>Betel nut</note>. The scraped bark, warmed a little in its own or a banana leaf and the back rubbed therewith, disperses the painful stabs, perhaps coming from the bastard pleurisy.*

*The young leaves cooked as a pottage and eaten with their own juice make two or three soft bowel movements.*

*The wood, which is as light as* Gabba Gabba <note>Sago palm leaf ribs</note>, *is boiled in water with an equal weight of* Cajoe Tsjina <note>China Root</note> *and drunk to heal all sorts of evil and pock-like ulcerations. It drives all malignant and spoiled moisture out of the body and heals the hard swollen bellies, yet does not purge.*

*The green bark scraped upward, with the bark of the female Iron-wood and a handful of green* Cadjang <note>Mung beans</note> *boiled in water, and steamed therewith, heals—*

# BOOK III. CHAPTER XLIII. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...as well as for swollen bellies and dropsy <note>Latin: *Hydrope*; a condition of excess watery fluid in the body</note>, if this decoction is drunk at the same time.

From its wood, rafters are also shaped for the roofs of houses, as well as posts for smaller dwellings, which are quite durable in the Amboinese habitations that are usually filled with smoke; however, they do not easily tolerate moisture. The Amboinese use this wood more for its supposed power against incantations <note>original: *incantamenta*; referring to local charms or sorcery</note> than for its durability. Although the younger leaves, as was said, can be eaten without harm, the old and mature ones possess a purging power; for two or three of them boiled in water within a bamboo tube, and this water being drunk, strongly purges all corrupt and malignant humors <note>In 18th-century medicine, "humors" were the bodily fluids believed to control health</note> that reside in the intestines.

Against swollen abdomens and against *Tebatu* <note>a local term for a hard swelling or tumor in the abdomen</note> others take the bark along with that of the "Forest Fire" <note>Latin: *Ignis Silvarum*; likely referring to a plant such as *Commersonia bartramia*</note>, which they grind together into a paste and smear upon the swelling, as well as upon swollen <note>original: *oedematosis*</note> feet.

The sap of the leaves or of their stalks, wherever it touches the skin, causes the hair to fall out without any trouble or pain. A certain sailor from Ternate, wishing to make a trial of this, smeared half of his beard and mustache with this sap, which all fell out completely, while the other half remained intact, so that he was half-bearded and half-beardless. However, this experiment did not succeed when using the sap from the trees in Amboina. They also say that if drops of rain fall upon someone's head while they are standing under the cover of this tree, their hair will fall out; for which reason the locals take care not to rest under this tree during rainy weather.

The Alfurs <note>the indigenous inland people of the Moluccas</note>, according to their popular custom, strip all the hair from their bodies with this sap.

# CHAPTER FORTY-FOUR.

## The Varnish Tree. *Caju Sanga*.

Although the tree from which the celebrated Chinese varnish is gathered—called *Cil* by authors and commonly *Tsjad* by the Chinese—is unknown in Amboina, it is nevertheless found growing wild in nearby Celebes <note>modern-day Sulawesi</note>. Having been raised here in Amboina from seed sent to me from there, I wished to include it in this Amboinese Herbal, all the more because its form, as far as I know, has not been depicted by anyone in any European book.

The tree itself agrees in size and form with a mature Mango tree, bearing spreading branches that have a dull grey, smooth bark, like washed leather. The thinner branches divide into many twigs, four or five of which are positioned together, firm, thick, and short.

The leaves sit upon the twigs without order, though most are clustered toward the ends; however, shortly below the origin of the twigs, five, six, or seven expand together in a circle, like star-shaped herbs. The leaves most closely approach the form of the leaves of the **Wild Mango** <note>original: *Manga Brava*</note>, being of unequal size; for some entirely resemble Mango leaves, except that their ribs are thinner and more curved, while others—indeed the majority—emulate the leaves of the *Wild Mango*, being nine, ten, or eleven inches long, and three or four fingers wide, ending in a sharp point, firm, 

<meta>catchword: ma,</meta>

<column-break/>

likewise for swollen or dropsical legs, bellies, and dropsy, if one also drinks the same decoction.

*From the wood, rafters are also made for roofing, and posts for light houses, reasonably durable in the smoke-filled Amboinese dwellings, but they cannot endure any moisture at all; and the Amboinese take them more out of an imagined power against all sorts of sorcery and incantations than for their durability. Although the young leaves, as said, can be eaten without concern, the old ones nonetheless have a purging power; for two or three of these boiled in a bamboo with water, and the water drunk, strongly purges all evil and corrupt humors that sit in the intestines.*

*Against swollen bellies and the Tebatu, others take the bark with that of the "Forest Fire" (the male kind), rub it together into a paste, and smear it on the swollen bellies and dropsical legs.*

*The sap of the stalks or leaves, wherever it touches the body, makes all the hair fall out, and that without effort or pain. A certain sailor in Ternate, wishing to try this, smeared half of his beard and mustache with this sap, which also fell out clean and bald, the other half remaining undamaged. But this being tried on the Amboinese trees, would not succeed. It is also said that a drop of rain falling on someone's head who stands under this tree makes all the hair fall out, and therefore the locals beware of sheltering under it in rainy weather.*

*The Alfurs, according to the custom of their land, make all the hair of the body fall out with it.*

# XLIV. CHAPTER.

## Varnish Tree.

Although the tree from which the famous Chinese varnish—called *Cil* by authors and *Tsjad* by common Chinese—is obtained is unknown in Amboina, it is nevertheless found growing wild on neighboring Celebes; also, having grown here in Amboina from seed sent to me from there, I have wanted to incorporate it into the Amboinese Herbal, the more so since its form, as far as I know, has been expressed by no European writers.

The tree is in size and form like a mature Mango tree, with extended branches, with a dirty grey smooth bark, like waxed leather. The thin branches divide into many twigs, whereon four and five stand together, stiff, thick, and short.

The leaves stand without order on the twigs, and behind them on thin branches, though mostly together toward the front; but shortly behind the gathering of the twigs they stand with five, six, and seven in a circle, like the *Poele* <note>likely *Alstonia scholaris*</note>. They most resemble Mango leaves, or more properly the *Wild Mango* <note>original: *Manga Brava*</note>, of unequal size; for some entirely resemble the Mango leaves, except that their ribs are thinner and more curved. Others, and indeed most, resemble those of the *Wild Mango*, nine, ten, and eleven inches long, three and four fingers wide, with a long point, stiff, deep green, smooth on top, and

# AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. Chapter XLIV.

...leaves, intense green, smooth and even on the upper side, while on the underside the ribs project sharply, and they sit upon short stalks.

The flowers hang from clusters and are similar to those of the Foetid Mango <note>Latin: *Manga foetida*; known locally as the Bachang</note>—namely, yellow or whitish flowers filled with many red stamens.

The fruits hang from the same clusters, three or four together, resembling small *Gajangos* <note>original: *Gajangos*; likely refers to the Kidney Bean tree, *Inocarpus edulis*</note>, two inches wide, somewhat oblique or irregular in their roundness, compressed on both sides like flat chestnuts, thick at the edges, and in many places appearing as if polished. Externally they bear protruding veins, ash-colored from the furrow and hard. Beneath the outer skin, a thin and spongy substance is hidden, which is juicy in fresh specimens like the Foetid Mango, but becomes hairy and easily hardens into a dry substance. Beneath this, a small nut soon appears of the same shape as the fruit, and under its thin and woody shell is a somewhat hard kernel like a chestnut, yellowish-white, exuding a copious resin that soon dries into a brown mass.

The trunk attains the thickness of a common Mango tree before it yields resin.

The wood is quite solid but spongy inside and difficult to cut; it is brown around the heart and white with intermixed black at the edges. Between the wood and the inner skin of the bark, a thick milk is hidden, which rarely exudes except through cracks or inflicted wounds. When it first drips out, it is thick, a dirty white, and viscous like the milk of the Breadfruit tree <note>Latin: *Socci*; refers to the *Artocarpus* species</note>, but it soon hardens to a yellowish-brown, and finally becomes as black as pitch, shining and hard, and brittle like Mastic or Sandarac gum. It is never found in large pieces or lumps, but in thin granules on both the trunk and the thinner branches. While this resin is liquid, and especially that first milk exuding from the trunk, it is so caustic that if it touches someone's skin, it burns and ulcerates that part much more vehemently than the milk of the wild *Cassoe*, or *Lenat*, or the Foetid Mango. However, once it has hardened, it no longer shows any harmful quality, even if one drinks from cups or bowls that are coated with this varnish. This resin, therefore, is that famous varnish mentioned above, with which every kind of joiner’s work—not only tables, chairs, and all types of furniture, but also plates, chests, and the like—and even the walls of houses in China are coated, which is called by the common term *Verlakken* <note>Dutch: lacquering or varnishing</note>. Foreigners mistakenly think that such coatings are prepared with *Gummi Lacca* <note>Shellac</note>, as is actually done in Bengal, Surat, and other places in India where that gum occurs and grows. The method by which this resin is boiled and prepared to be spread over woodwork will be indicated below.

As harmful as the milk or soft resin may be, I have nevertheless observed with great wonder that cockroaches <note>Latin: *Bruchos*; Dutch: *Kackerlakken*</note> not only gnaw this varnish off the wooden furniture where it was fixed, but also almost entirely ate the fresh fruits—which yield copious milk—that I had placed on my table. From this, I conclude that the harmful quality does not remain in that milk for long; the remaining flesh of the fruit is no longer harmful once the milk or resin has been exuded.

For the people of Celebes, inhabiting the regions of Bugis and Lubu, have assured me for a certainty that they eat these fruits harmlessly in their homeland if they have been roasted over coals, whereby all the resin in them has been consumed and burned away. The tree must have already reached ten years of age and have the thickness of a common Mango tree before it yields resin; also, the first three harvests produce larger fruits than the subsequent ones—namely, as large as a fist and shaped like a *Gajang*—after which it gradually bears smaller fruits.

A harmful exhalation is also attributed to the entire tree; the Macassans and other Celebes peoples fear it so much that they do not dare to stand under it for long, much less rest under its shadow, fleeing from this tree just as they do from the following poisonous one. They say the body swells up and is afflicted with malignant pustules if someone settles under its shadow for a long time or catches its drips. Since it yields such a famous varnish, other intrepid nations have visited this tree, especially the Chinese and Tonquinese, who use great prudence in collecting its resin:
<meta>Catchword: For:</meta>

<column-break/>

eat, while below the ribs project somewhat sharply, on very short stalks.

The bloom hangs in clusters and resembles that of the foetid mangos—namely, a yellowish and dirty white flower, filled with many red threads.

The fruits hang on the same clusters, three and four one after another, resembling small *Gajang*, two inches wide, somewhat lopsided from the round, and pressed on both sides like flat chestnuts, thick at the edges, and on many, as if polished. On the outside, they have some bulging veins, brownish-gray and hard. Under the outermost skin lies a thin, spongy substance, juicy in the fresh fruit like the foetid mangos, but drying up hairy. Immediately below that lies a small nut of the same figure as the outer fruit, and under its thin woody shell is a hardish kernel, like chestnuts, white-yellow, richly exuding a white resin that soon dies off into brown.

The trunk becomes as thick as a common Mango tree before it gives its resin.

The wood is indeed dense, yet spongy, and difficult to chop; brown near the heart, mixed with white and black at the edges. Between the wood and the inner skin of the bark sits a thickish milk, which exudes sparingly, both by itself through cracks and through made wounds. When it first comes out, it is thick, dirty-white, and sticky, like the milk of the Breadfruit tree, but soon dies off to a brown-yellow, and finally pitch-black, shining and hard, breaking off short like Mastic or Sandarac gum. It is by no means found in large pieces or clumps, but in thin droplets, both on the trunk and thin branches. While this resin is still soft, but especially the milk first exuding from the trunk, it is so burning in its property that if it touches someone on the body, it causes that part to burn and fester, more fiercely than the milk of wild *Cassoe*, or *Lenat* and Foetid Mango. However, once it has become hard, it shows no more harmfulness, even if one drinks from cups and bowls that are lacquered with it. This resin is now that famous Chinese varnish, named above, with which all kinds of joinery—not only tables, chairs, and desks, all sorts of small household goods, bowls, and saucers, but also entire walls inside the houses in China—are varnished, which is commonly called *Verlakken* <note>Lacquering</note>. This is because foreigners erroneously believe that such works are prepared with *Gummi Lacca*, as is truly done in Bengal, Surat, and other places in India where that gum grows. How this resin shall be boiled and prepared to lacquer the woodwork, see below.

The milk or soft resin may be as harmful as it likes, yet I have nonetheless experienced with wonder that the cockroaches not only gnaw the lacquer-work off the desks where it is cracked, but also almost entirely ate the fresh fruits, which gave rich milk, laid away on my table. From this I believe that the harmful property must not stay long with that milk, the remaining flesh of the fruit being no longer harmful once the milk or resin has exuded.

For the Celebes peoples of the lands of Bugis and Lubu assure me that they eat the fruits in their land without fear, when they have first been roasted on coals and all the resin is burned thereby. The tree must be at least ten years old, and as thick as a full-grown Mango tree, before it gives its resin; also the first two and three crops give much larger fruits than the common ones—namely, a fist-size, in shape like *Gajang*—after which it gradually bears smaller ones.

A harmful exhalation is also attributed to the whole tree; indeed the Macassans and other Celebes peoples are so afraid of it, as to stand long under it, much less to rest under its shadow, just as for the following poisonous tree, saying that it causes the body to swell up and break out with fiery pustules if one rests long under it, or the drip falls on us. Because it yields such a famous varnish, however, other nations have emboldened themselves to go to it unafraid, especially the Chinese and Tonquinese, who must yet use great caution,

# III Book. XLIV. Chapter. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...namely: It is done in the following manner. Many of the Chinese go out together toward evening to that place in which these trees grow—which are found nowhere that men or animals pass—and each chooses for himself certain trees. In their trunks, he fixes two bamboo reeds sharpened at the top, so that they pierce the bark and slant slightly; these they leave in the trees overnight and extract them the next day before sunrise, for during the day the tree emits no juice. One of these collectors receives a greater and another a lesser quantity of this resin, depending on whether the trees are located in a rich or lean spot. They also pour forth this resin only at certain times of the year, namely when they begin to produce flowers. These companions mix the collected resin together so that each obtains an equal portion; and this is the reason why this resin is sold at a high price, since a single *Picul* <note>A traditional Asian unit of weight, roughly 60 kilograms or 132 pounds</note>—containing one hundred Chinese pounds—costs two hundred and three hundred imperial dollars in those Chinese provinces where this tree does not grow, whereas in Tonkin and Cambodia it can be obtained for thirty, fifty, and sixty imperial dollars. It is also a custom among the Chinese that if they approach this tree, they first gently bite its trunk before they fix the bamboo reeds into it, as if wishing to indicate that they do not fear it; for they say that the fearful feel its harm sooner than the intrepid.

**Name.** In Latin, *Varnish Tree* <note>original: *Arbor Vernicis*</note>. The Chinese *Atlas* and Petrus Kircher call it *Chinese Sandarac* <note>original: *Sandaracham Sinicam*</note> and *Chinese Glue* <note>original: *Gluten Sinicum*</note>. In Malay and Macassar, it is called *Caju Sanga*. In Java, *Ingas* and *Rangas*. In Bali, *Safuru*, just as they named the preceding *Milk Tree* <note>original: *Arborem Lactariam*</note> "Wild Safuru" <note>original: *Safuru Utan*</note>. The Chinese call the tree *Tsjiu Tsjat*. The Buginese and Lubu people call it *Belawa*. Its resin is called by me *Chinese Varnish* <note>original: *Vernix Sinica*</note>; the Chinese call it *Ciè*, but those who live among us call it *Tsebat*. In Malay and Siamese, *Amrac*.

**Location.** The Chinese *Atlas* of Father Martini seems to indicate that this resin occurs only in the tenth province of China, called *Chekiang*; however, I have understood from Chinese merchants that it also occurs in other provinces—indeed even outside of China, such as in *Quantung*, *Tonkin* (which they call *Tamkia*), *Cambodia*, and *Siam*, as far as the region of *Malacca*. And furthermore in *Java, Bali,* and *Celebes*, also around the flat plains of Maros and in the bay of *Tellico*. For the Indian species grows mostly on flat plains near great rivers, whereas in China it mostly occurs in the mountains with which the province of *Chekiang* is filled. The Chinese who have seen both trees have assured me as a fact that the Celebes trees do not differ much from the Chinese ones, except that the Chinese tree bears larger leaves and fruits. They also yield a twofold varnish: the first and best is saffron-colored, shining like gold. The other is pitch black, which is the only kind our Indian trees provide.

The fruits sent to me from Macassar and kept in my chamber nearly all sprouted; and those which I committed to the earth nearly all shot up and grew into trees, from which it is clear that these trees are easily propagated. The younger saplings bore many leaves arranged in a circle at the point where the branches divide, which is rarely observed in adult trees.

**Use.** This harmful tree provides nothing except that varnish with which the Chinese, Tonkinese, and Japanese prepare and coat so many elegant works; hence they endure the danger of approaching this tree. However, it is best, according to their report, that those who are accustomed to it do not easily feel its harm; and a certain antidote against its malignancy is known to them, in which they trust most surely, but they are unwilling to reveal it to foreigners. Thus their tree is just as harmful as that of the Macassarese, from which men indeed swell up with a difficult itching and burning; and if they neglect to use a remedy for this, they eventually fall into a *consumption* <note>original: *Phthyſin*; a wasting disease of the lungs</note>, from which they gradually waste away and perish.

The resin, however, is prepared into varnish in the following way: For a pound of resin, take only the same weight of *Tang-Yhu* oil, which comes from a Chinese tree related to the *Bonga Tanjong* <note>likely *Mimusops elengi*, the Spanish Cherry</note>, from whose fruits they prepare a transparent saffron-colored oil, not unlike our linseed oil. Others take one part weight of oil to three parts resin, which they cook gently together, and it yields a pitch-black varnish. If, however, one takes two parts of oil to one part of resin...

<column-break/>

...to gather the resin, **and it happens thus.** The Chinese go out in whole troops toward evening to the place where these trees stand, which are found nowhere near where humans and livestock frequent. Each chooses some trees for himself, in whose trunks he sticks two small bamboo pieces, sharpened at the tip so they enter the bark; hanging down slightly, they let them stay there overnight, and pull them out the next day before sunrise, for during the day they will not drip. Thus one gets much and the other little, depending on whether the trees stand on rich or lean soil. They also give this resin only at certain times of the year, namely: when they begin to bloom. Those who are of one company then throw the gathered resin together, because each individual has so little, and from this it comes that it is a costly ware, being worth a *Picul* of a hundred Chinese pounds in the Chinese provinces where it is not found, two and three hundred imperial dollars; but in Tonkin and Cambodia one can have it for thirty, fifty, and sixty imperial dollars. The Chinese also have a custom that when going to these trees, they first bite gently into the trunk before sticking the bamboos in, wishing to show that they are not afraid of it; for they say that the hesitant feel the injury from it sooner and more easily than the bold.

**Name.** In Latin, *Arbor Vernicis*; in the Chinese *Atlas* and by Petrus Kircher, the resin coming from it is called *Chinese Sandarac* and *Chinese Glue*. In Malay and Macassarese, it is called *Caju Sanga*. On Java, *Ingas* and *Rangas*. On Bali, *Safuru*, as they call the previous *Milk Tree*, *Wild Safuru*. The Chinese call the tree *Tsjiu Tsjat*. By the Buginese and Lubu people, *Belawa*. Its resin I call in Latin *Chinese Varnish*; in Chinese, *Ciè*; but the common Chinese who live among us call it *Tschat*. In Malay and Siamese, *Amrac*.

**Place.** From the Chinese *Atlas* of Father Martinus, it would appear as if this resin fell only in the tenth province of China (named *Chekiang*), but from the Chinese merchants I understand that it is also found in other provinces, even outside China, such as in *Quantung*, *Tonkin* (which they call *Tamkia*), *Cambodia*, and *Siam*, as far as the district of *Malacca*. Furthermore on *Java, Bali,* and *Celebes*, around the flat fields of Maros, in the bay of *Tellico*, for this Indian variety grows mostly on flat fields near large rivers, but in China it falls mostly on the mountains, of which the province of *Chekiang* is full. That the Celebes trees do not differ much from the Chinese ones, I have been assured by such Chinese as have seen both trees, except that the Chinese trees are somewhat larger in leaves and fruits. They also give two kinds of varnish: the first and best is deep yellow, shining like gold. The second and next best is the pitch-black one, like our Indian trees alone produce.

The fruits from Macassar sent to me and placed in a room nearly all sprouted, and as many as I put into the earth became small trees, from which it appears that they are easy to propagate. The young saplings had many rings of leaves at the place where the branches divide, which one does not see much on the old trees.

**Usage.** From this harmful tree, one has nothing but the aforementioned varnish, with which the Chinese, Tonkinese, and Japanese make so many beautiful and lacquered works, just as they dare to approach that perilous tree; but the best is, according to their saying, that those who are used to it do not easily feel any harm, there being a certain antidote known among their people against its harmfulness, on which they rely firmly and will not reveal to foreigners; so that their trees are just as harmful as the Macassarese ones, causing people to swell up with a troublesome burning or itching, and finally, if they do not use that remedy, they fall into a consumption, from which they die while pining away.

The resin was thus prepared so that it becomes a varnish: to one pound of resin take one pound of oil of *Tang-Yhu*, which is a Chinese tree from the family of the *Bonga Tanjong*, from whose fruits they make a clear gold-yellow oil, not unlike our linseed oil; others take to three pounds of resin one pound of oil, and cook that gently together, so you have a pitch-black varnish. But if one takes to one pound of resin two pounds of oil, then...

...processed, it provides a brownish-yellow varnish, sometimes also a pale yellow, with which the wood is lightly coated so that its grain remains visible; furthermore, if red lead, powdered gall nuts, or other dry pigments are mixed in during the boiling process, the objects coated with this varnish acquire whatever color the added pigment carries. The liquid decoction, called *Tsjat* <note>original: *Tsjat*; likely a variant of the word "lacquer" or "chat" used in Southeast Asia</note>, must always be kept covered with water so that it does not harden. Objects coated with the varnish must always be placed in a damp and cool location to dry, which proceeds slowly; however, once they have dried, they never soften again, unless warm water is poured over them, which often causes the varnish to dissolve.

The Chinese bring this soft, boiled resin in pots from Siam and Cambodia to Japan with great profit, for today the art of the Japanese is the best for preparing and coating woodwork with this varnish; hence, they consume a great quantity of this varnish annually, and their elegant black lacquered wares are distributed throughout the whole world.

It was indicated above that the Bugis and Lubu peoples can harmlessly eat the fruits of this tree after they have been roasted over a fire. The Chinese, however, refuse to ingest anything from this tree.

If the dry fruits of this tree are handled, their outer skin is crushed and causes an itching of the skin; it is also forbidden to build a fire from the wood of this tree, as it exhales and pours forth a harmful smoke. In the aforementioned *Maro* <note>A region or river mentioned in previous sections</note>, it often stands so close to the river that its fruits and leaves fall into the water, wherefore one should take care not to swim in that vicinity. When the Macassarese wish to fell this tree, they cover and wrap their heads, hands, and feet in linens, lest they be defiled or touched by its breath, which is nonetheless imperceptible.

*Sangites*—in Malay called *Mestica Sanga* <note>A "Mestica" or Bezoar stone believed to have magical properties</note>—is a hard, smooth, and cold stone, growing like flint, but very rarely found within the *Sanga* fruits; it retains nearly the shape of the fruit itself, but smaller. It is the size of a Dutch Shilling <note>original: *Denarii Batavi*; a small silver coin</note>, about the thickness of a thumb in the middle, but protruding from both sides and surrounded everywhere by a wide rim, so that it is nearly lentil-shaped; on its surface, some parts of the veins or small protruding dots appear, such as are seen on the fruit itself. It is so hard that it cannot be scraped away, but can be used as a touchstone; furthermore, it is heavy and cold, of a rusty or chestnut-brown color, and smooth. A Macassarese man, from whom I received this, affirmed to me as true that his countrymen had seen the fruit hanging from the tree, the upper part of which had turned into stone <note>original: *dendritem*; a stone with tree-like markings, or here, a petrified object</note>, while the lower part was still growing; they therefore tied a cord to the tree to observe and wait for the time when the entire fruit would be changed into stone. After several weeks had passed, they indeed saw the mark on that branch, but the fruit was entirely stony, had fallen off, and was lying beneath the tree.

It is seen depicted here with a small branch of the tree, and his friends kept a similar stone of the same shape and size as described.

Such stones are held in high esteem by the Macassarese, who tie them to their bodies, either alone or joined with other stones, believing through superstition that they will thereby be lucky and immune to wounds in wars. All metals can be tested against it, as if on a touchstone <note>original: *Lapidem Lydium*; Lydian stone or basanite used to test the purity of gold</note>, but silver shows better than gold because of the stone's dark brown color. In Java, this tree occurs more frequently in the mountains than in the plains, but the inhabitants there are ignorant of the art of preparing and collecting varnish from it, except for the Chinese living there, who sometimes collect a small quantity, which they do not draw from the trunk, but from the uprooted roots.

Its hard and durable wood is indeed suitable for house posts, but no one presumes to cut it down, except for a class of Javanese called the *Vunnam*, who handle it intrepidly and, as they say, without harm; the common folk, however, do not dare to approach it.

In the district of Cirebon <note>original: *Tsjeriboni*</note>, it is found near the mouths of large and muddy rivers, in which many sharks <note>The Dutch column uses "Caymans," referring to crocodiles or alligators</note> are found; for this reason, the tree is avoided, as well as for the troublesome itching and scabies which the hairs and raindrops

one obtains a brownish-yellow varnish, sometimes also light brown, with which one lightly lacquers the wood so that its grain can be seen through it. Furthermore, if one mixes vermilion, fine ochre, or other dry pigments into it while boiling, the lacquerware becomes red-yellow, or of such a color as you mix into it. The soft-boiled *Tsjat* must always be kept covered with water so that it does not become hard. The lacquered works must be placed in a damp, cool place and left there to dry, which proceeds rather slowly; but once dried, it never becomes soft again, except with warm water, which causes the lacquerwork to come loose.

The Chinese transport it soft-boiled in large pots from Siam and Cambodia to Japan, and that with great profit; for nowadays the Japanese hold the prize for making the most beautiful lacquerware, and therefore they ship a great multitude of this varnish annually, their beautiful black lacquered works being drawn through the whole world.

That the Bugis and Lubu peoples can eat the fruits roasted on coals without harm was said above: But the Chinese know nothing of this, wishing to consume nothing of it.

When one handles the dry fruits, the outermost skin crushes and causes a simplified itching on the skin; it is also forbidden to burn the wood of the tree, as it gives off a harmful smoke. At the aforementioned *Maro*, it sometimes stands so close to the riverbank that the fruits and leaves fall into the water, near which no one will then bathe. When the Macassarese want to fell the tree, they wrap their heads, hands, and feet with cloths so that they are not touched by its sharp breath, which is nonetheless imperceptible.

*Sangites*. In Malay *Mestica Sanga*, is a stone hard, smooth, and cold, growing like a common flint, yet very rarely from the fruit of the *Sanga*, also almost retaining the shape of the fruit, though smaller. It is the size of a Dutch Shilling and in the middle barely a thumb thick, for on both sides it bulges out with a round belly, and all around it has a wide rim, so that it is almost lentil-shaped. On its surface run some pieces of veins or pimples that bulge out somewhat, such as one also sees on the fruit. It is so hard that one cannot scrape anything off it, but can indeed use it as a touchstone; it is cold and heavy, of a color like iron-rust or chestnut-brown, yet smooth. The Macassarese from whom I have it assured me that his countrymen have seen the fruit hanging on the tree, being already half changed into stone at the front, and the back still growing; therefore they tied a small rope to the tree to watch when it would be entirely changed into stone: But after the lapse of some weeks, they found the mark indeed on the branch, but the fruit was entirely changed into stone, fallen off, and lying under the tree.

You see it depicted by the small branch of the tree, and there was another such stone with his friends, of the same size and shape as mine.

They are held in great esteem by the Macassarese to wear on the body according to their superstition, both alone and mixed with other *mesticas*, to be lucky and invulnerable in war. All metals can be tested on it, as on any other touchstone, but the silver stands out better than the gold, because of its dark brown color. On Java one finds this tree more on the mountains than in the plains, but the natives do not know how to draw the varnish from it, except for the Chinese living there, who sometimes draw a little from it, which they do not tap from the trunk, but from the chopped-off roots.

Its hard and durable wood is well-suited for posts in houses, but no one dares to undertake felling this tree, except for the Javanese lineage called *Vunnam*, who handle it fearlessly and, as they say, unharmed, but the common man is too afraid to approach it.

## O B S E R V A T I O N.

There are various opinions regarding the generation of *Varnish* and *Lac Gum* <note>original: *Gummi Lacca*; a resinous secretion from insects, though here being debated as a tree sap</note>; for some believe it is prepared by winged ants, as wax is prepared by Bees; others, however, state that it flows spontaneously from trees, which seems to agree more with the truth. These trees are again of various kinds, entirely different from one another, as collected by *Valentijn in his History of Simples, page 276 and following; Dale in his Pharmacopoeia, page 335; Pomet in the History of Drugs, page 273.* Among Botanists, mention is made by *Hernandez, Ray, Bauhin, Cleyer, Hermann*, and others who have commented on these, as can be gathered from the previously praised writers. All those trees, however, are entirely different from this one of Rumphius, as has become clear to me upon examination.
