# CHAPTER FORTY-FIVE.
## The Poison Tree. Ipo.

I have not found until now a more horrible or detestable poison produced by any vegetable than that which is collected from this milk-bearing tree. I call this a milk-bearing tree because it yields a dark red sap, whereas the previous ones give a white milk. This sap is its poisonous juice, in which the Indians throughout all of watery India <note>referring to the Malay Archipelago</note> especially glory, and with which they elude the Dutch weapons. Our soldiers formerly feared this more than war-engines and muskets; however, its nature and antidotes being better known and discovered today than before, they do not fear this poison so much, nor is it so highly esteemed.

The true form of this tree is unknown to most, since prudent Nature has separated this harmful plant far from human habitations and placed it in unknown mountains and solitudes, where the coastal inhabitants can hardly reach. Instead, they receive that poison from the wild mountain dwellers, who cannot or will not describe the true form of the tree. For it is believable that they hide this tree as much as possible from coastal people and foreigners. Indeed, *Mr. Cornelis Speelman* <note>a prominent Governor-General of the Dutch East Indies</note>, who waged war for four years in the region of Celebes <note>modern-day Sulawesi</note> around the year 1670 and finally brought that proud nation of the Macassarese under his command, could not discover the true figure of this tree nor knowledge of it himself. But he commanded *Maximilian de Jong*, who was prefect over the newly conquered territories, to use every effort to acquire knowledge of this tree for him.

From him, I understood nothing other than the method of collecting that poison from this tree, and of preparing and using it, but nothing of the tree's form, which I shall describe hereafter. Finally, in the year 1681, *Mr. Cops*, Extraordinary Councilor of the Indies and then Governor of Macassar, upon my continuous requests, sent me not only a deeper knowledge of this tree, but even its branches and the poison collected from this tree. This tree is found to be of two kinds, namely male and female; and first, he fetched branches and poison of the female through a delegated ensign from a single tree found in the Maros region near the village of Sudyan.

<meta>catchword: To the other</meta>

<column-break/>

which the particles and rain-drops falling from this tree cause on the skin, and because of the presence of the Crocodile <note>original: *Cayman*</note> which basks beneath it. I also understand that *Rangaas* in Javanese means the bump or knob that the Crocodile has on the front of its nose, to which they compare the wrinkled fruits of this tree, and have named it accordingly.

### The Eighty-Sixth Plate

Shows a branch of the Varnish Tree. Where Letter **A.** represents its fruit in its size. **B.** and **C.** are two stones that grow in the fruit, and from that are called *Sangites*.

## O B S E R V A T I O N.

Various are the feelings regarding the generation of the Varnish and the Lac-Gum; which some mean that the winged Ants prepare, just as the wax is prepared by the Bees; others state, which also seems the most probable, that it flows of itself out of the trees, and these are again very different, which have been gathered together by *Valentijn in his History of Simples, page 276 and the following; Dale in his Pharmacopoeia, page 335; Pomet in the History of Drugs, page 273.* Among the Botanists are *Hernandez, Ray, Bauhin, Cleyer, Hermann*, and others, who make mention of it, which are easy to find from the first writers; yet all those trees differ from this one, which appears in *Rumphius*, as has appeared to me upon investigation.

# XLV. CHAPTER.
## Macassar Poison-Tree.

I have until now not heard of a more terrifying and foul poison, which comes from any plants, than that which this sort of *Milk-tree* gives out. I call it a *Milk-tree* because it gives out a brown-red sap, just as the preceding ones yield white milk, this sap being the greatest pride of the Indians throughout all Water-India, wherewith they dare to provoke the Dutch weapons, and for which the Soldiers formerly were more afraid than for the Cannon and Musket; though its nature and antidotes being better known nowadays than before, it is now no longer so much respected or feared.

The right appearance of the same tree is mostly unknown, because prudent nature has separated this foul plant far from the dwellings of men, and placed it in the unknown mountains and wildernesses, where the Beach-dwellers cannot well come, but receive the same from the wild Mountain-dwellers, who cannot, nor will, clearly describe the actual appearance. For it is unbelievable how much they keep that tree hidden from the Beach-dwellers and foreigners as they can. Even the *Honorable Mr. Cornelis Speelman*, who around the year 1670 waged war for four years on the land of Celebes, and finally completely brought down that bold Nation of the *Macassarese*, could nonetheless not arrive at the right knowledge of that tree, yet left orders to *Maximiliaan de Jong*, being appointed as President over the new Conquests, to employ all possible diligence to get knowledge of that tree.

From the same I have obtained nothing else than the manner to collect the poison from that tree, to prepare it, and its further use, but nothing of the appearance of the tree, which I shall set down hereafter. Finally in 1681, Mr. *Cops*, Extraordinary Councilor of the Indies, then President of *Macassar*, at my insistent request sent me not only further report of that tree, but also its branches, and gathered poison. It consisted of two sorts: Namely, the first were twigs and poison of a Female-tree, which His Honor had fetched by an expressly commanded Ensign from a single tree, which stands in the land of *Maros* near the Village of *Sudijan*.

The other small branches and reeds filled with this poison were sought by the people of the Radja of Tanette <note>Tanette was a small kingdom in South Sulawesi</note> from the midst of the mountains inhabited by the people called Toradjas. They affirmed with certainty that these were branches of the "male" tree, which is the true tree from which this genuine toxin is collected. I have seen to it that a branch of the male tree was illustrated, and I have composed the following descriptions of both; first, I shall describe the female, which is the most well-known.

Firstly, therefore, the female Poison Tree <term>Toxicaria arbor femina</term> <note>original Latin: *Toxicaria arbor femina*; Dutch: *Gift-boom het Wyfken*; refers to the *Antiaris toxicaria*</note> bears a thick trunk and is very widely spread, much like a Mango tree. Its bark is wrinkled, cracked, and a dark ash-gray.

The trunk and thick branches are divided somewhat into joints <note>original: *geniculos* / *leeden*</note>, though these are not complete and are widely spaced. The wood is pale yellow, solid, and variegated with black spots. The leaf stalks are thin, short, and crowded with many leaves without order, appearing almost sessile <note>attached directly by the base without a stalk</note>. These leaves have the shape of *Lanzium* leaves or more properly those of the *Ampelas* <note>original: *Ampelas*; likely *Ficus ampelas*, the Sandpaper Tree</note>, but they are thinner and more flaccid than both. They are six or seven inches long, three or four finger-widths broad, wrinkled on the upper side and woolly underneath, with even or entire edges, woven through with oblique veins, and ending in a notable point; when dry, they turn a pale yellow. It undoubtedly produces fruit, but these have not yet been observed by me, nor could those who brought the branches describe them to me.

One can approach this tree without harm, provided care is taken that the head and shoulders are covered with cloths, lest any of its dripping sap touch the person, which would cause the body to swell. They also say that no plants or grasses grow beneath it, just as with the male tree.

To collect its juice, a thin bamboo reed called *Bambu* is used, sharpened at the top like a throwing spear. This is thrust into the trunk, into which a bloody sap <note>original: *sanguineus succus* / *bloedige zap*</note> trickles, which soon congeals into a dark reddish color. This is the poison of the female tree, much less effective than that of the male and not lethal by itself, which is why it is used for capturing wild beasts. If, however, it is used for war, it is infected with the poison of the male tree so that the strength of both is exalted.

The other, the male Poison Tree <term>Toxicaria arbor mas</term>, bears a taller trunk and a narrower crown, and its thick branches are also divided into joints. Its stalks are numerous and short, beset on all sides with leaves sitting on very short petioles, so that some seem to have none. These are not unlike those of the female, but smaller and firmer, more similar to the *Ampelas*; they are five or six inches long and two or three fingers wide, also woolly or soft like cloth underneath, and they remain green for a long time even when dried, whereas those of the female turn pale.

Whether it bears fruit or not, no one could tell me, not even those who collected its poison. Under this tree, no plants, shrubs, or grasses grow in its entire periphery, indeed not even within a stone’s throw; the earth beneath it is sterile, brownish, and as if scorched. These most pernicious species of tree bear a sign of their malignancy: bird feathers and down are found beneath them, for the air around this tree is so infected and poisonous that birds wishing to perch on its branches become dizzy and fall down dead. Its branches, sent to me in a large bamboo reed and well sealed, were still so effective and caustic that if one’s hands were placed on this reed, they soon felt a tingling, much like frozen limbs do when they are warmed. All things perish that are touched by its breath, so that all animals avoid passing this tree, and birds even fly away to avoid passing over it.

No man dares to approach it unless his arms, feet, and head are wrapped in cloths; otherwise, he soon feels a heavy tingling in his limbs, from which they grow stiff and lose sensation. Its dripping, falling on someone’s body, makes it swell; nor should anyone stand under this tree with an uncovered head, lest his hair fall out. Indeed, Death seems to have pitched her tent near this tree.

Under this tree alone lives a horned snake that cackles like a hen or crows like a cock, whose eyes shine like fire through the night; in Macassar it is called *Ular Balu*. It sometimes goes near human habitations or villages, where its cackling is often heard. Other inhabitants of the Celebes describe the form and appearance of this serpent to me, which...

The other small branches and reeds with poison had been fetched by the people of the Radja of Tanette, from far in the mountains where the wild Toradja peoples live, with full assurance to His Honor that these were from the Male, being the actual Poison Tree from which the true "spat-poison" <note>original Dutch: *spatte-gift*; refers to a poison that acts quickly or is used on projectile weapons</note> was made. I have had a small branch of the Male illustrated, but of both, I have made the following description, placing first the Female, as she is best known.

The first Poison Tree, the Female, sets a thick trunk and spreads itself out like a Mango tree; the bark is wrinkled, torn, and dark gray.

The trunk and thick branches are somewhat divided into segments, which do not go all the way through and stand far from one another. The wood is white-yellow, dense, and speckled with small black dots; the twigs are thin, short, and full of leaves, at the ends almost without stalks or order. They have the shape of Lanze-leaves, or more properly of *Ampelas*, but thinner and floppier than both, six and seven inches long, three and four cross-fingers wide, rough on the upper side, woolly on the bottom, with smooth edges, very slanted ribs, and a notable point; the dry ones turn a pale color. It will bear some fruits, but they are as yet unknown to me, and the bringers did not know how to describe them.

One can approach it without fear, as long as the head and shoulders are covered with cloths so that its drip does not touch us, from which the body would swell up. It is also said that neither foliage nor grass grows under it, just as under the Male.

To get the sap out, one takes a thin bamboo, sharpened at the front end like a javelin, and sticks it into the trunk; thus a bloody sap runs into it, which quickly turns dark reddish. This is the Female's poison, much weaker in power than the Male, and by itself not deadly; therefore it is used for hunting game. But when one wants to use it for wars, it is mixed with the Male's poison to make both equally powerful.

The second Poison Tree, the Male, is higher of trunk and narrower of crown, likewise divided into wide segments at the branches. The twigs are many and short, densely beset with leaves, one after another without order, on very short stalks, so that some seem to have none. These are not unlike the Female, but smaller and stiffer, more like those of the *Ampelas*, five and six inches long, two and three fingers wide, also woolly or soft like cloth from below, keeping their greenness long even after they are dried, whereas those of the Female turn pale.

Whether it bears fruit or not, no one could tell me, even those who have been under it and gathered the poison. Under this tree, and even a stone’s throw around it, neither foliage nor grass nor any trees grow, the earth remaining barren, reddish, and as if singed. Among the most powerful sort, one will also find bird feathers as a sign, for the air around these trees is so poisoned that any birds wanting to rest on its branches soon become dizzy and fall down dead. The branches stuck into a large bamboo and well-stoppered, sent to me from Macassar, were still so powerful that if one put their hand in there, a tingling was felt, just as one does in frozen limbs when coming back into the warmth. Everything expires that it touches with its wind, so that all animals avoid passing this tree, and birds avoid flying over it.

No man dares approach it without having head, arms, and legs wound with cloths, or he perceives a heavy tingling in the limbs, such that they become stiff and without feeling. The drip from the leaves hitting someone's body makes it swell; one must also not stand under the tree with an uncovered head, or the hair falls out; so that Death seems to have pitched its tent by this tree.

Only a horned snake lives under it, cackling like a hen, or as others will have it, crowing like a cock, and at night with fiery eyes; in Macassar called *Ular Balu*, which sometimes comes near the villages <note>original: *Negoryen*; local settlements</note>, where one becomes aware of it by its cackling. # Book III. Chapter XLV. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...which lives under the Poison Tree, like a **Basilisk** <note>original Latin: *Baſiliſci*; a legendary reptile reputed to be a serpent king who can cause death with a single glance or breath</note>. It is said to be a small animal, standing on two short feet on the front part of its body, by which it walks with its head held high. It has a crest or horn on its head and infects men and birds with its breath as if with poison; for this reason, it is killed from a distance with arrows. King Lubo or Tolubo (which is a region located on the northern coast of the great southern bay of Celebes <note>modern-day Sulawesi</note>) possessed a stone or **Mestica** <term>Mestica</term> <note>A magical bezoar or stone found inside animals, highly prized in Southeast Asia for medicinal and mystical properties</note> of the first-described "clucking snake," which was red and almost fiery. Of the second animal, the **Basilisk**, I have one the size of a double *libella* <note>a small Dutch coin</note>, semi-spherical on top and flat below like a dissected globule. It is of an opaque crystalline color, with a white spot on one side; I have described it elsewhere under the name **Dracontias** <note>literally "Dragon Stone"</note>.

*Name.* In Latin, we call this tree **Arbor Toxicaria**. In Dutch, **Makassar Poison-tree** <note>original: *Macaſſerſe Gift-boom*</note> or **Blowpipe-tree** <note>original: *Spatten-boom*</note>. In Malay, **Caju Upas**. Its poisonous sap is called **Makassar Toxin**; in Dutch, **Blowpipe-poison** <note>original: *Spatte-gift*</note>; in Malay, **Upas**. In the Macassarese language and throughout Celebes, it is called **Ipo**, which is also the name they give to the tree itself. The first, reddish kind of poison, collected from the female tree, is named by the Macassarese **Pacanre Sama Jang**, and in Malay **Maccan Cawul**, which means "eat or keep your faith" <note>original: *ede vel ſerva fidem*</note>, as it is weaker in strength and one can be cured of its toxin if they keep their faith—which usually consists of the cured person providing a feast. The other, most deadly kind from the male tree, is called in Malay **Upas Radja** <note>King's Poison</note>, and in Macassarese **Lupo Matta Joe**, or in Malay **Djato Matti**, because one infected and wounded by this poison immediately falls down and dies. This second toxin is always harder and blacker than the first, almost like pitch, but it liquefies through the heat of fire. Both can be handled harmlessly and cause no damage as long as they do not touch living blood; indeed, the inhabitants of Celebes dare to ingest it as an internal remedy, as will be indicated later.

*Darts.* The darts which are infected with this poison are called **Sompit** in Malay. They are thin sticks over a foot long, and often a foot and a half, made from thin wood or reed about the thickness of a straw, straight and firm. At the end of these, a broad and jagged tip made from the tooth of the **Lamia** fish <note>likely a shark or a ray</note> is fitted, which is coated with the poison in the form of a blackish gum. On the lower part of the dart appears an oblong cork, shaped to fit the channel of the blowpipe. This blowpipe, or **Sompittan**, is as long as a man is tall, manufactured from hard and blackish wood, hollowed out inside with a straight and even channel about the thickness of a pinky finger. These darts are placed into it and blown out with such force that they are ejected to the distance of a small pistol shot. As soon as such a dart touches something, its hook remains fixed, and the small dart is either pulled out or falls off of its own accord.

*Poison.* Its poison, being hot, soon spreads through the whole body upon penetrating the blood, so that it can be felt in the veins; for it causes a great burning heat and simultaneously a heavy dizziness in the head, followed by fainting and death.

*For war.* When preparing for war, these poison-infected darts are placed into a case made of Bamboo reed, which is firmly closed with a lid. However, if these darts are kept for a year, they are of less efficacy.

*Location.* Nature has separated this harmful tree, as has been said, far from the habitations of men. Its proper homeland is Celebes <note>Sulawesi</note>, the mother of all venom, where it has its seat among the **Toradjas** <note>original: *Toradias*</note>, who are wild mountain-dwellers living between **Mandar** to the north, **Tomontano** to the east, and to the north of the province of **Lubo**, which borders the Toradjas. Those from Lubo first go to the village of **Tamboge**, which is half a day's journey from the shore and situated near the **Moyke** river, a day's journey from the village of **Massamba**, from whence they seek this **Ipo** or poison, as well as from the villages subject to Lubo. They also take another route near the villages of **Paloppo** and **Walendra**, from whence after a day's journey they come to **Bolonga**, then **Awang**, and further to **Sadania**, where these trees are shown to them. To ensure the collection of this poison is conducted properly, they employ some king or prince of the Macassarese or Buginese, so that the Toradjas do not deceive them. From there, the Buginese and those of Mandar buy it.

The *Tree* itself grows there on desert and bare mountains, and is easily recognized from a distance, since no...

...snake that lives under the Poison-tree, like a **Basilisk**, said to be a small animal with two short legs at the front, by which it walks with its head upright, having a crest or horn on the same, poisoning men and birds with its breath; for which reason it is shot dead from afar with arrows. The King of Lubo or Tolubo (being a region located at the northern end of Celebes' great South-bay) is said to have had a stone or **Mestica** of the first-mentioned clucking-snake, red and fiery; of the second, I have one about the size of a *dubbeltje* <note>a small Dutch coin</note>, rounded on top, flat below like a cut bullet, in color like dark crystal, with a white spot on one side; described by me in another place under the name **Dracontias**.

*Name.* We call the tree in Latin **Arbor Toxicaria**, in Dutch **Makassar Poison-tree** or **Blowpipe-tree**. In Malay **Caju Upas**. The poisonous sap gathered from it is called **Makassar Toxin**; in Dutch **Blowpipe-poison**. In Malay **Upas**; among the Macassarese and generally on Celebes **Ipo**, as they also call the tree. The first reddish sort (coming from the female tree) is nicknamed in Macassarese **Pacanre Sama Jang**, in Malay **Maccan Cawul**, that is, *eat or keep your promise*, because it is weaker in power and one can be cured of it if one keeps their promise, usually consisting of giving a feast. The other or most evil sort from the male tree is called in Malay **Upas Radja** <note>King's Poison</note>, in Macassarese **Lupo Matta Joe**, or in Malay **Djato Matti**, because the wounded person immediately falls down and dies. This second poison is always harder and blacker than the first, almost like pitch, yet melts by the warmth of the sun. Both are harmless to handle and do us no harm as long as they do not touch the living blood; indeed, the inhabitants of Celebes dare to take it internally as some medicine, as will be said hereafter.

The darts or arrows that are smeared with this poison, called **Sompit** in Malay, are thin sticks a good foot long, and some a foot and a half, made of a thin wood or reed, the thickness of a straw, yet straight and stiff. At the front end is fixed a small bone or shark-tooth <note>original: *baayen-tantje*</note>, where the venom is smeared on in the form of a black gum; at the back is fixed an oblong cork, fashioned according to the pipe of the blowgun. This blowgun or **Sompittan** is as long as a man, made of hard and blackish wood, with a hollow pipe running through the inside into which a pinky finger might just fit, bored very straight and evenly. In this they place the aforementioned blow-darts and blow them out with a sudden force, which hits at about the distance of a pistol-shot. As soon as this dart enters anywhere, the barb stays stuck, and the loose dart is pulled out or falls off by itself.

The venom, touching the warm blood, spreads immediately over the whole body, so that one can feel it in the veins, causing a great burning, and thereafter a heavy spinning in the head, followed by fainting and death.

When going to war, these darts are placed in a quiver of Bamboo, on which the lid closes tightly; nevertheless, after a year, these darts decrease significantly in their power.

*Place.* Nature has separated this harmful tree, as said, far from the dwellings of men, and its own homeland is **Celebes**, the mother of all venom, where it has its seat among the **Toradjas**, being wild mountain-dwellers between **Mandar** in the West, **Tomontano** in the East, and north of the province of **Lubo**, which borders closest to the Toradjas. Those of Lubo first go to the village <note>original: *Negorye*</note> of **Tamboge**, half a day from the shore by the river **Moyke**, from there another day's journey to the village of **Massamba**, where they fetch the **Ipo**, both villages falling under Lubo. They use another way by the villages of **Paloppo** and **Walendra**; from there a day's journey inland one comes first to **Bolong**, from there to **Awang**, and further to **Sadanii**, who point out the trees. For this commission they use one or another Macassarese or Buginese **Creyn** <note>a local petty king or prince</note>, so that the Toradjas do not mix any deceit therein. From here the Buginese and those of Mandar buy it.

It grows there on bare mountains and is well known from afar, because no trees stand around it, and the land...

# AMBOINESE HERBAL Book III. Chapter XLV.

...no trees stand near it, and the earth beneath it is sterile and as if scorched. The **female tree** <note>Dutch: *Wyfkens-boom*</note> grows in sloping places behind **Maros** near the village of **Sudian**. It undoubtedly also occurs in Sumatra and Borneo; namely in Borneo in the provinces of **Landak** <note>Latin: *Landas*</note> and **Kutei** <note>Latin: *Cute*</note>, on its eastern side facing **Makassar**, everywhere in the desert mountains; for this reason, the form of the tree is unknown to the coastal peoples, while the **Orang-Dayas** <note>the Dayak people of Borneo</note> or wild mountain men bring its sap. The sap from Kutei is considered the most piercing, not because the Celebes variety is not considered equally good, but because it is believed that those mountain peoples, or **Toradjas** <note>the Torajan people of Sulawesi</note>, reserve the best for themselves and grant the cheaper sort to the Macassarese. For since the people of **Mandar** and **Luwu** <note>Latin: *Lubenses*</note>, along with their Torajans, are subjects of Makassar, they must ensure through their mountaineers that every person brings a small reed or bamboo tube filled with this poison as a tribute to the King of Makassar whenever he intends to wage war.

In **Baleya**, in the region of **Batur** on the eastern side, such a poison tree is also found, the sap of which the mountaineers bring as tribute to the King of Baleya, collected in pots made of bamboo. This poison is of three kinds: black, red, and saffron-yellow, which is the most effective and the best. With this poison they smear their arrows and blowpipe darts, which they keep under the bed chambers where they live, as if unwilling to have these harmful and deadly instruments hanging over their heads. The antidote for this poison is the white root of the **Djerudju** <note>the Sea Holly, *Acanthus ilicifolius*</note>, chewed and smeared on the wound; they also forbid the wounded person from seeking shelter under a roof.

This poison is gathered in the following manner: no one dares to approach this tree closely enough to catch its sap with their hands. For they would soon feel all their limbs as if freezing and affected by spasms. Therefore, they first veil their heads, hands, and feet with cloths; then they take the long, sharpened bamboo reeds described above, which they drive with great force and at an angle into the bark of the lower trunk. For the closer it is to the root, the more effective the poison is. Four or five such bamboo reeds are fixed into one tree and left for three or four days; through that channel the bloody sap drips out, which shortly afterward thickens and hardens, turning reddish in one species and blackish in another. Only the uppermost joint of these bamboos is filled with this sap; the rest is cut away. To make this poison even more malicious, they soon fell the tree itself with long axes once they have extracted its sap, saying that if the tree itself dies, then all those must also die who are infected and wounded by this final sap. But if the tree survives, the poison gradually loses its strength. However, I believe this is done with very few trees, otherwise they would have been diminished long ago; they preserve this species only for the **Radjos** <note>Kings or Rajahs</note> and nobles.

While the extracted sap is still somewhat soft, it is packed into large and small lumps, or formed by hand into long rolls which they insert into the bamboo reeds.

All these rolls and lumps are transported to Makassar to one of the nobles called **Creyns** <term>Creyns</term> <note>From the title *Karaeng*, a high-ranking Macassarese or Bugis lord</note>, who is usually **Creyn Sumana**, whose duty it is to keep them sacredly in a separate house in the **Castle of Boerenbong** <note>likely Fort Panakkukang or a similar fortification</note>, so that they might be preserved in a moderate degree of heat. For too much cold harms them, and too much heat is much more harmful; therefore, they are wrapped in a tenfold covering of linens, and every week they are unwrapped, wiped, and the cloths and rags are cleaned of the lumps, in which they are then re-wrapped.

The rolls are also removed from the bamboo reeds every week and rubbed with cloths until they shine, as are the bamboo reeds themselves, into which they are then re-inserted and wrapped so that air cannot penetrate.

This work is performed mostly by women, for they fear that if men approached, they might subtract or steal some of it. Other **Creyns** or nobles also keep a certain portion. This is also the cause of a little story, once spread among our people by a pseudo-learned Moroccan, that **menstrual blood** <note>original Latin: *menstruum muliebre*</note> was mixed into this poison, and for that purpose the women of Makassar wore metal plates in which they collected it and delivered it to the chief guardian of this poison; however, this was never heard from any Macassarese man or wo-
<meta>catchword: wo-</meta>

<column-break/>

the land beneath it is parched and scorched. The **female tree** grows in the lowlands behind **Maros**, by the village of **Sudian**. On Sumatra and Borneo it will also be found, namely on Borneo in the **Province of Landak**, and **Kutei** on its eastern side opposite Makassar, everywhere far in the mountains; therefore the appearance of the tree is likewise unknown to the beach-dwellers, because the **Orang-Dayas**, or wild men, bring the sap down. That from Kutei is held to be the most powerful, not as if that on Celebes would not be as good, but because it was thought that the mountain people or **Toradjas** keep the first for themselves, and give the poor quality to the Macassarese. For since **Mandar** and **Luwu** with their Torajans stand under Makassar, they must arrange through their mountain people that every person, head for head, must bring a reed or bamboo filled with this gift as tribute to the King of Makassar when he wishes to go to war.

On **Bali** <note>Dutch: *Baley*</note> in the district of **Batur**, located on the eastern side, such a Poison Tree is also found, whose sap the mountain people bring to the King of Bali as a tribute, gathered in pots and bamboos, of three kinds of color: black, red, and yellow, which last is the best. They smear their arrows and blowpipes therewith, which they then keep beneath their living quarters, wishing, as it were, not to have this death above their heads. Their antidote there is the white roots of **Djerudju**, chewed and smeared on, commanding therewith that the wounded person may come under no roof.

*This poison is gathered in the following manner: no one dares to embolden himself to approach this tree in such a way that he would want to take the sap out with his hands. For he would feel as if all his limbs wanted to shrivel and stiffen. Therefore they first wrap the head, hands, and legs with cloths; thereafter they take the aforementioned long and sharpened bamboos, which they thrust with strength and somewhat slantwise into the bark of the lower trunk, for the nearer to the root, the more powerful the poison is. They leave four or five bamboos sticking in one tree for three or four days, so then a bloody sap runs out along that gutter, where the soft substance shortly thereafter becomes hard, and dies off reddish in the one sort and black in the other. The front joint of these bamboos is just filled; the rest is chopped off. To make this poison even more malicious, they immediately chop the tree down with long axes when they have drawn out the sap, saying that if the tree dies, all those must also die who are wounded with the last sap drawn therefrom; but if the tree remains in life, so the poison also becomes less sharp in time. But I believe that they do this with the fewest trees, otherwise those would have been diminished long ago, and they keep this sort only for their Rajahs and Great Ones.*

While the extracted sap is still somewhat soft, it is packed in large and small lumps, or formed with the hands into short rolls, which fit exactly into a bamboo.

*All the balls and rolls now being brought to Makassar, they were kept by one of the great Creyns, whose work it is, being commonly Creyn Sumana, in his Castle Borrenbong, in a separate house to be very carefully preserved, and maintained in a moderate warmth, for too great a cold is harmful to it, but too great a heat even more harmful; therefore it is wrapped at least tenfold, and precisely once every seven days made loose, wiped, the cloths and rags shaken out and cleaned, then packed up again.*

The rolls are likewise taken every week out of the bamboos, rubbed with old cloths until they become gleaming, as also the bamboos, and then stuck back therein and wrapped so that no air comes to them.

*This work they generally let be done by women, fearing that if the men came near, they might steal something thereof; however, the other Creyns also have something in their keeping. This is the cause of a foolish talk, formerly spread among ours by the meddling Moroccan, that the menstrual blood was mixed among this poison, and that to that end the women in Makassar had to wear breeches to gather the same and deliver it to the general master of ordnance, which we have never heard from any Macassarese man or woman cou-*
<meta>catchword: cou-</meta>

# BOOK III. CHAPTER XLV. AMBOINESE HERBAL.

...we have heard. In those houses where this poison is kept, no shrimp or shells are to be roasted or burned.

When they are about to go to war and wish to prepare this poison to smear upon their arrows or blowpipe darts <note>Dutch: *flitzen* or *spatten*</note>, all the clumps and rolls of resin are brought together. These consist of various colors and strengths; those of the same color are gathered into one pile. However, which are the most effective cannot well be discerned by sight alone, but is discovered by this experiment: Take the root of the **Lampoejang** <note>Scientific name: *Zingiber zerumbet*, a type of bitter ginger</note>—called *Lampoem* by the Macassarese and *Allia Paya*, that is, **bitter ginger**—pound it and soak it in water until it becomes mucilaginous. Squeeze and strain it through a cloth, and pour a small portion of this water into a bowl, into which a small piece or scraping of the poison is placed. Experts can immediately judge its strength by the suddenness and the greater or lesser degree of boiling and bubbling. Clumps of the same strength are then pounded together and placed into that mucilaginous water. One then observes with great wonder how this poison begins to exercise its power and rage, boiling and turning with such force that a hollow is often seen in the middle, through which the bottom of the bowl or basin appears. That which shows only a slight stirring or commotion is judged to be weak.

The tips of the weapons are soaked in this viscous juice. These tips, as has been said, are fashioned from the teeth of the **shark** <note>Latin: *Lamii piscis*</note>; but if they lack these, they use a sharpened reed in their place, which they keep in well-sealed quivers. The best kinds of these weapons retain their potency for two years, though there are some that lose their strength within a month or two and become, as it were, dead. Indeed, the entire mass of this poison, if not properly cared for and preserved as required, quickly spoils. It is commonly believed of the ordinary sort that after a year has passed, it is no longer lethal; the sign of this is if the poison no longer boils when infused with the juice of the **Lampoejang**, by which it is otherwise sharpened and exalted. Handling this does no harm to anyone, except that one may feel an internal heat, mostly from the best kind.

This poison is held to be harmless as long as it has not been mixed with the juice of the **Lampoejang**; indeed, they say that without it, the poison never hardens sufficiently and is easily wiped off by clothing if it passes through them. But when mixed with this juice and smeared on, it becomes so hard that they can shoot through a shield with it. The most effective variety of this poison is the **Upas Radja** <term>Royal Poison</term>, which is reserved only for the King and his nobles; according to common opinion, it inflicts an incurable wound. The cheaper sort is distributed to the common men when they go to war.

It sometimes happens that by good fortune someone is delivered from sudden death by an antidote, and yet dies from it after two or three years have passed (even though they believed themselves cured). For such people, intercourse with women is extremely harmful and dangerous. And just as the **Lampoejang** is edible among herbs and used as a vegetable <note>Dutch: *Sayor*</note>, so this herb brings certain death to anyone who thinks himself cured of a wound from these darts, if it be eaten.

In the last **Majene War** <note>Latin: *Madjerasensium*</note>, when the Macassarese intended to overrun all of Ambon, we gradually learned to frustrate their pride and the confidence they placed in their wicked darts, not only by various antidotes (which we shall present in the following chapter) but also by a certain manner of clothing. For officers and those of means had wide garments made of **Spanish leather** <note>high-quality, thick goatskin leather</note>, so spacious that they could easily wear them over other clothes, such as tunics, breeches, and boots. On their heads, they wore a high miter or a rugged Spanish cap. The sailors and grenadiers <note>Dutch: *branders*</note> who had to lead the assault made such clothes from **canvas** <note>sailcloth</note>; because these hung loose and free from the body, the tips of the blowpipe darts would get stuck in the fabric. In front of the soldiers, a blind or screen of tarred canvas was erected, which had a horizontal slit through which they could fire their muskets; nevertheless, a dart would sometimes fly through it if the screen was stretched too tightly. We also had to guard against the blowpipes themselves, on the ends of which the front-line fighters had iron points like pikes, smeared with poison, and as they charged into our ranks, the pikes were effective for...

<column-break/>

...in those houses where it is kept, one must not roast or burn shrimp or shells.

When they now wish to go to war and prepare this gift to smear on the arrows or darts, all the clumps and rolls are brought together, which are then of various colors and strengths, with those of one color placed together. But to distinguish the strongest from each other cannot well be done by sight, but they are tested thus: Take the root of **Lampoejang**, in Macassarese **Lampoein**, and **Allia Paya**, that is, named bitter ginger; crush it and soak it in water until it becomes somewhat sticky, then squeeze and strain it through a cloth. Pour a little of it into a small bowl and cut a small clump or scraping of the poison into it. The most experienced can then immediately judge the strength by the hasty boiling and the low or high bubbling. All the clumps of one strength are then joined together and placed in that sticky water, where one sees with wonder how this poison begins to rage and show its strength, boiling and turning so that sometimes one can see a hole in the middle, and in it the bottom of the dish or tray; but that which shows only a small stirring is considered weak.

This sticky sap is then smeared on the point of the arrow, being made, as said, of shark teeth, or if they do not have them, of a sharpened reed, which they then keep in well-closed quivers. The best kind can remain good for as long as two years, and there are also those that within a month or two become quite dead and powerless; for the whole mass, if one does not look after it and watch and keep it as required, can spoil in a hurry. Ordinarily it is believed of the common kind that after the passing of a year it is no longer deadly, and a sign of this is if it will no longer boil in the sap of **Lampoejang**, with which one otherwise revives it. This handling harms no one, except that one feels an internal heat from it, mostly from the best.

This poison is then held for harmless as long as it is not mixed with the sap of **Lampoejang**; indeed it is said that without the same it does not harden properly, and is easily wiped off by the clothes when shooting through them; but mixed with that sap and smeared on, it becomes so hard that they can shoot through a shield with it. The strongest sort of this poison or **Upas Radja**, which is kept only for the King and his greats, is according to common opinion incurable, but the lesser sort is distributed among the common men when they go to war.

It happens sometimes that one is by luck delivered from a hasty death by some antidote, and after the passing of one, two, or three years (though one thinks to be cured) one still dies of it anyway; and for such people the mixing with women is very bad and dangerous; and just as among the earth-growths the **Lampoejang** is edible and also used as **Sayor** <note>a vegetable dish or soup</note>, so is that substance for someone who thinks to be cured of a dart-wound a certain death, if one partakes of it.

We have in the last **Majene War**, when the Macassarese intended to overrun all of Ambon, gradually learned to frustrate their pride, which they had placed on their evil darts, not only by various counter-remedies which we shall propose in the following chapter, but also by a certain manner of clothing. For officers and those who had the means made wide clothes of **Spanish leather**, so roomy that they could easily pull this on over other clothes, such as coats, breeches, and boots, and on the head a high miter or rough **Spanish cap**; sailors and those who threw fire-balls <note>grenadiers</note>, who had to make the attack, made such clothes of sailcloth; for because everything hung loose and roomy around the body, the points of the blow-arrows remained stuck therein. Before the front of the soldiers a blind of tarred sailcloth was set, with a slit across it through which they could give fire; however, sometimes an arrow flew through this because they stood stretched too stiffly. We also had to watch ourselves for the blow-tubes themselves, on which the vanguard had iron points like pikes, smeared with poison, and running in upon ours, for which the pikes were good...

In the year 1694, a fruit was sent to me, which they claimed was from the Macassarese Poison Tree. I shall describe it here as accurately as I can, and I have added it to the illustration. It was the size of a musket ball, very hard, dried out, and wrinkled, for it had already been kept for four years. On the outside, it was a dark dusky brown, like certain **oak galls** <note>growths on trees used for making ink</note>. The outer shell is attached so firmly to the internal substance that it cannot be separated. This internal substance is as hard as horn and can only be split with force. The color is likewise horn-like, similar to the pith of the small **Sea Coconut** <note>original: "Calappi-Laut" or "Calappa-laut"; likely the Sea Heart or Xylocarpus</note>.

III Book. XLVI. Chapter. AMBOINESE HERBARIUM.

# CHAPTER FORTY-SIX.

## *On the powers and qualities of the preceding poison, and its antidotes.*

In the preceding chapter, we stated that the most effective kind of this poison brings about immediate and inevitable death within the span of half an hour—indeed, often in less than fifteen minutes—and that against this, no antidote has yet been discovered, as the kings of the Macassarese have often tested on those condemned to death. To further explore the destructive power of this venom, they inflicted a wound with a weapon infected with this poison only on the thumb of the hand or the big toe of a condemned man, and immediately amputated the wounded joint, applying bandages in the proper manner to see if such a person could survive. Yet this horrendous and cruel poison had already spread through the veins so quickly that the entire contaminated body soon perished, and thus the man died. However, while this venom has many degrees of its malignancy, and though the most effective kind may lose much of its power in a short time if neglected or not properly and tightly stored, kind and gentle Nature has revealed many antidotes to man, which we shall soon recount.

First, however, it must be known that this ***Ipo*** <note>The local name for the Upas tree poison, *Antiaris toxicaria*</note> cannot exert its powers as long as it does not touch living blood; and secondly, that it can be used harmlessly for various things, but is first exalted and brought into action by the juice of ***Lampoejang*** <note>A type of wild ginger, *Zingiber zerumbet*</note>; this is truly a secret of nature: that such an enemy of the human race can be taken into the body harmlessly, and that it receives its malignant quality from such a root, which is related to **Ginger** and **Zedoary**, which are otherwise antidotes to poison.

Raw and unmixed *Ipo* is therefore itself an antidote against the stings of poisonous fish and the bites of Centipedes <note>original Latin: "Millepedarum"</note>, if a plaster of it is applied to the wound, which settles the pain more quickly and extracts the poison better than any other remedy. Furthermore, if someone's body is swarming with ulcers and scabies, they may take a pill of this *Ipo* mixed with the flesh of a **Banana** <note>original Latin: "Musae fructus"</note>, which will attract and expel all impurity from the intestines. This *Ipo* can also be prepared in such a way that wild animals, and especially Deer, can be killed by it, and their meat eaten harmlessly. For this purpose, one must by no means choose the strongest kind, lest the deer die too quickly and quietly and therefore cannot be tracked, but rather the weakest kind, which is mixed with the juice of the plant ***Rami*** <note>Likely referring to a species of *Urticaceae* or stinging nettle family</note>, which causes the wounded beasts to cry out vehemently so that they may be pursued; and what is wonderful, their meat is eaten without harm. If this poison is so prepared, it also brings great pain to a wounded man, so that it violently agitates and rolls the body about, contorts the eyes, and causes foam to come from the mouth. Those, however, who are wounded by the cheaper and weaker kind feel the same burning and dizziness of the head, but no danger of death threatens them, provided suitable remedies are soon supplied to them.

In the first Amboinese wars, no other remedy was known except a nauseating and abhorrent one: human excrement, which the wounded man was forced to swallow with good courage. From this, violent vomiting followed, by the force of which, it seems, the <term>force</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐνέργεια" (energeia)</note> of the poison was weakened and expelled from the body, or eliminated outward. This was done among the soldiers with such readiness that if someone who required this remedy could not supply it for himself, he was forced to ask another comrade to discharge and provide a dose for him. The valiant Captain of **Bonoa**, called ***Tabalille***, neutralized the wounds of four or five of these darts by this remedy, which he had received in his body and even his face. When we later captured some Macassarese, we were taught better remedies by them and their women, sometimes through flattery, and sometimes through threats and force; some of these, however, were...

<meta>catchword: effica- (effective)</meta>

<column-break/>

# XLVI. CHAPTER.

## *Of the powers and properties of the preceding dart-poison, and the remedies against it.*

In the previous Chapter we have said, that the most powerful kind of this poison brings an unavoidable death, and that within the time of half an hour, yes, sometimes less than a quarter of an hour, and that against it until now no remedies have been found, which the Macassarese Kings have often tested on criminals. And to discover even more the wickedness of this venom, they have let some criminals be pricked only in a toe or thumb with a dart, chopped off the wounded limb immediately, and bound it properly to see if the man might be saved: But the ghastly poison had already flown through the veins and the whole body, and killed the man. But because the aforementioned gift has many degrees of its evil, even the very strongest in a short time—and by neglect of close storage—markedly decreases in its powers, so good Nature has again pointed out various counter-remedies to men, which we shall relate here shortly.

But first it should be known, that the ***Ipo*** cannot exercise its power as long as it touches no living blood; secondly, that it can be used harmlessly for many things, and is first made active and ignited by the juice of ***Lampoe-jang*** <note>Wild ginger</note>, which is indeed a mystery of nature: that such an enemy of man's life can be taken into the body without damage, and that it is ignited by such a root, which is of the family of **Ginger** and **Zedoary**, which one otherwise uses against venom.

The raw and unmixed *Ipo* is then itself a counter-poison, if one is stung by poisonous fish, or bitten by centipedes; when a plaster is laid on the wound, it draws the pain and the venom out immediately, more readily than any other thing. Again, if someone has a body full of ulcerations and scurvy, they shall take a small pill of this *Ipo* with the flesh of a **Banana** <note>Dutch: "Pisang"</note>, which shall draw all impurity in the intestines to itself, and carry it out. So one can also prepare this *Ipo* such that one can shoot wild animals, especially deer, therewith, and may eat their meat without fear. For this one must by no means take the strongest kind, so that the beast does not die suddenly and quietly and one cannot subsequently find it, but the weakest, which one then mixes with the juice of the herb ***Rami***, which makes the beasts scream violently, so that one can pursue them, and what is a wonder, this meat was eaten without damage. Thus prepared, it also causes a wounded man great pain, throwing the body about violently, turning the eyes, and foaming at the mouth. Those now, who are wounded by the lesser or weaker kind, also feel the same burning and turning in the head, but have however no peril of life, if one only comes to their aid immediately with suitable means.

In the first Amboinese Wars, one knew no other than that repulsive and hideous cure, namely **human excrement** <note>Latin: "Excrementum humanum"</note>, which the wounded man had to swallow with good courage, upon which a strong vomiting followed, by whose force (so it seems) the powers of the poison were broken and driven out of the body. This happened so readily among the Soldiers, that one who was at a loss for it and could not do it himself, had to request another comrade to press out a lump for him. The Valiant Captain of Bonoa, named ***Tabalille***, has through this means made four or five darts powerless, which he had received in his body, and some also in the face. Afterwards, when we got some captured Macassarese, we learned some better means from them, as well as their women, through coaxing and compulsion, of which however some were more powerful than others, and some not at all...

### AMBOINESE HERBARIUM Book III. Chap. XLVI.

...were more effective than others, while some provided no effect at all, as we shall recount here in their proper order.

First, therefore, we encounter the ***Toxic Root*** <note>original: *Radix Toxicaria*</note>, called ***Spit-root*** <note>original: *Spat-wortel*; likely referring to its emetic properties</note> by our people, which is certainly a species of Sea Onion or ***Indian Moly*** <note>original: *Moly Indicum*; a type of wild garlic or Allium</note> described below in Book 11. Its white roots are chewed and the juice swallowed, while the remaining pulp is applied to the wound. This induces and excites violent vomiting, by which the poison is expelled; however, if vomiting does not follow immediately, as often happens, a larger dose must be taken, for this poison is not overcome except by violent vomiting.

Second, to extinguish the immense burning heat <note>the inflammatory "fire" caused by the toxin</note>, the juice that flows naturally from a ***Watermelon*** <note>original: *Melopepone*</note> should be dripped into the wound, and a small portion of it should be eaten; for this fruit possesses a peculiar power to restrain the raging spread of this terrible poison.

Third, the chewed or crushed bark of the ***Broad-leaved Banyan*** <note>original: *Varinga latifolia*</note> should be applied to the wound.

Fourth, the bark of the ***White Amaranth*** <note>original: *Sayor Bayang* or *Blitum*</note>, scraped from the stem, should be placed upon the wound.

Fifth, the thin reddish fibers or smaller roots of the ***Narrow-leaved Banyan*** <note>original: *Varinga angustifolia*</note>, crushed, are to be partly drunk in a potion and partly applied externally.

Sixth, the crushed stalks and roots of the ***Indian Amaria*** or ***Parari***.

Seventh, the roots of the ***King's Wood*** <note>original: *Cajoe Radja*</note>, which were discussed in the preceding chapter.

Eighth, the most certain antidote, which the Macassarese have hitherto hidden from us, is the milk-bearing ***Poele Tree*** <note>*Alstonia scholaris*, known for its milky sap and medicinal bark</note>, called ***Rite*** by them. They select the leaf stalks, sharpen them slightly, and tie a thread around them. These sharpened tips are placed into a wound inflicted by these poisoned darts; the stalk penetrates the wound of its own accord and sucks out all the poison. The thread is tied to them so that they can be pulled out again.

Ninth. In a similar manner, small pieces of Macassarese sea-darts called ***Pana-Docki*** are applied; like the previous remedy, they are tied with a thread, enter the wound, and draw out the venom.

The ***Poele Tree*** maintains such hatred and antipathy toward this poison that if a small branch or leaf is placed beneath it, or hung in a room where this poison is kept, it weakens the venom so much that it is entirely deprived of its strength.

The sick or wounded person must, above all, beware of ***Wild Ginger*** <note>original: *Lampoejang*; *Zingiber zerumbet*</note>, taking none of it in food or drink, especially every year at the same time when they were wounded. For it has often been found that this poison "revives" at that time and exerts its power again. Thus it has often happened that certain men died from this poison only in the second or third year, as we observed in a certain German sub-prefect. In the year 1654, before Laala on the island of Ceram, he was wounded in the chest by such a dart; he was indeed cured of it, but in the third year afterward, he felt a burning in that same spot on his chest, followed by a burning fever, from which he died. Furthermore, the wounded should take the greatest care to avoid intercourse with women for two or three months, and if investigated further, perhaps also from all drinks that significantly heat or inflame the blood.

->End of the Third Book, and the Second Volume.<-

<column-break/>

...helped, as we shall set forth here one after another.

First, is the ***Toxic Root***, called by our people ***Spit-root***, being a kind of ***Sea Onion*** or ***Indian Moly***, described here below in Book 11. One chews its white roots, swallows the juice, and lays the rest on the injury: this also provokes a violent vomiting, and thereby drives out the poison. But if one does not vomit immediately, as sometimes happens, one must take more, for without strong vomiting one cannot overcome this poison.

Secondly, to quench the great burning, one shall drip into the injury the juice running naturally out of a ***Water-Lemon*** <note>Watermelon</note>, and also eat some of it; which fruit has a singular power to stop the raging of this poison.

Thirdly, the bark of the ***Broad-leaved Banyan*** <note>original: *Varinga*</note> chewed, or rubbed, and laid on the injury.

Fourthly, the bark of ***White Sayor Bayang***, or ***Amaranth*** <note>original: *Blitum*</note> scraped off the stem, and applied.

Fifthly, the thin reddish threads or small roots of the ***Small-leaved Banyan*** rubbed, partly drunk, and partly applied from the outside.

Sixthly, the stalks and roots of ***Indian Amaria***, or ***Parari*** rubbed, and applied.

Seventhly, the roots of ***King's Wood*** <note>original: *Cajoe Radja*</note>, for which see the preceding Chapter.

Eighthly, the surest antidote, which the Macassarese have kept hidden from us until now, is the milk-giving tree ***Poele***, called by their people ***Rite***. They take the stalks of the leaves, make them a little sharp, and tie a thread around them. The points are held on the wound made by the darts <note>original: *spatten*</note>, so it draws into it of its own accord, and sucks all the poison out from there. The thread must be tied around it so that one can pull it out again.

Ninthly, in the same way, one also acts with the small pieces of Sea-arrows of Macassar called ***Pana-Docki***, which, like the preceding, are tied with a thread, creep into the wound, and suck out the poison.

The tree ***Poele*** has such an enmity with this poison, that if one holds a small branch or leaf under it, or hangs it in a room where this poison is, it becomes entirely powerless.

The patient must, above all, guard himself from consuming the least bit of ***Wild Ginger*** <note>original: *Lampoejang*</note>, whether in food or drink, especially every year around the time that he was wounded. For it has often been noticed that this poison stirs itself anew around that time, and through that, it happens that some persons only pass away from this poison in the second or third year. As we have seen in a German Lieutenant, who in the year 1654 before Laala on Ceram was struck in the chest, from which he indeed recovered, but three years later in the same place felt a burning again, such that a burning fever set in, of which he died. So also the wounded are most highly advised that they refrain for two or three months from conversation with women, and if one examined it more closely, perhaps from all such drinks that remarkably heat the blood.

->End of the Third Book, and the Second Volume.<-

<summary>This page concludes the study of the Macassarese "Ipo" poison by listing nine botanical antidotes, including the Poele tree and various emetics. It highlights the persistence of the toxin, noting that it can "awaken" years later and cause death, as illustrated by the case of a German officer.</summary>
